title: Holiday E-Commerce Shopping on the Rise
author: Carla Anderson
content: According to a new comScore forecast, 2012 will see an increase in the amount of eCommerce sales this holiday season. The research company is predicting eCommerce sales in the United States will increase 17% this holiday season to $43 billion over last year’s mark, which saw a 15% gain during November and December. The 2012 online shopping season is already off to a good start as the first week and a half of November saw eCommerce shopping increase 16% to $10 billion. Two reasons why 2012’s eCommerce shopping is on the upswing is higher consumer confidence and early retailer promotions. In fact, consumer confidence is at a five-year high as shoppers start preparing for their holiday shopping needs. According to Thomson Reuters and the University of Michigan, the index of consumer confidence as increased to 84.9% from 82.6%. Another contributing factor to the increased revenue projections for eCommerce shopping this holiday season is the fact that Black Friday, the biggest shopping day of the year, was two days earlier than in 2011, providing an extended holiday shopping season. With two additional shopping days on the calendar this year, it only makes sense that eCommerce shopping figures would increase. While other eCommerce shopping forecasters agree with comScore’s forecast that eCommerce spending will increase in 2012, these forecasters do not agree that eCommerce shopping will increase as much as comScore suggests. Shop.org is only projecting a 12% increase in eCommerce shopping based on data collected from the U.S. Department of Commerce while Gartner is also only projecting a 12% increase in online sales. In their forecast, Gartner also projects 51% of consumers will shop online during the holiday season. With the increased number of people shopping online and taking advantage of the deals being provided by online retailers, JPMorgan is predicting eCommerce sales to increase 19% in the fourth quarter across both desktop and mobile devices. In addition to these increased eCommerce sales figures, JPMorgan expects “showrooming” – the process of going to the store to look at different products and then returning home to buy them online – to increase to its highest levels ever as 37% of consumers will browse products in the store. This perfect storm of higher consumer confidence, more shopping days in the holiday season and increased number of consumers who will make a purchase online during the holiday season will see eCommerce shopping figures continue their upward trend in 2012. title: UCLA Ranked “Most Dangerous” College in U.S. but Where is USC?
author: Brandon Jones
content: A report by BusinessInsider.com named UCLA the most dangerous college in America based on FBI crime data. UCLA has taken issue with this report in saying that the study is a “reckless mischaracterization of data”. Living in Los Angeles like I do, I also take extreme caution to this data in knowing that UCLA is not nearly as dangerous as many other colleges. The area UCLA is located in is called Westwood which happens to be a very nice, upscale part of the city. I have never felt frightened or in danger walking through the area and the UCLA campus feels extremely clean, friendly and safe. Across town is USC which has had several high profile shootings recently yet was not named in the report as a dangerous school. This is because USC is a private institution and this study only addressed public colleges. Evidently other readers of the study were outraged with comments like “The FBI List that you used is a joke. It’s lacking so much”, and “I have never felt my safety threatened when i was at ucla. title: More leaks draw new fire on mill
author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: The Port Townsend Paper Corportation mill sits clouded in fog and steam on the shore of Port Townsend Bay. The mill has come under scrutiny after a former employee turned whistleblower spoke to the Seattle Times about a Nov. 20 wastewater spill. The mill claims the spill was 150 gallons, while the whistleblower claims it was much more. Leader photo by Lloyd Mullen In a recent interview with The Leader, Port Townsend Paper Corporation CEO Rob Kreizenbeck stood by his assertions that the Nov. 20, 2025, spill reported in the Seattle Times is not as serious as whistleblower and former mill employee, John Tippins claims. The Washington Department of Ecology is investigating the spill, and in their notice of violation referenced not only the Nov. 20 incident, but a spill event on Nov. 7 that sent 600 gallons of untreated waste-water into Port Townsend Bay. According to the mill’s own spill report filed with Ecology, 150 gallons of wastewater discharged into Port Townsend Bay via a saltwater overflow pipe that utilizes seawater to cool systems within the mill. The wastewater entered the saltwater system through the damaged wall of a holding tank within a separate wastewater system. Although the hole was patched after workers discovered wastewater pouring from the saltwater pipe, Tippins, according to the Seattle Times, was on site at the time and participated in the initial response. Tippins told reporters that he disagrees with the mill’s assessment of the environmental damage and says that hundreds, if not thousands, of gallons of wastewater spilled into the bay. Tippins explained that because there is no way to know when the damage occurred, wastewater potentially spilled into the bay for days, weeks or even months, instead of just minutes as the mill’s report asserts. While Tippins provided background information on the saltwater overflow pipe, he would not go on record with The Leader for this story. “We have investigated this incident multiple times with all parties involved and we still stand behind our report,” said Michael Clea, the mill’s environmental manager. “The numbers the party involved are claiming are not mechanically, physically possible considering the low flow to the actual equipment. Our report has those details in it.” A view of Port Townsend Paper Company from the Boat Haven at the Port of Port Townsend. Leader photo by Lloyd Mullen AN ADDITIONAL SPILL On Oct. 14, 2026, Ecology filed an official notice of violation that highlights the Nov. 20, 2025, incident and an additional spill on Nov. 7 that sent an estimated 600 gallons of untreated process wastewater directly into Port Townsend Bay during a planned power outage. The 600-gallon estimate is also based on the mill’s own findings as part of the current self-reporting process that governs industrial sites across the state. “Ecology is now evaluating potential enforcement options in response to the violation which could include monetary penalties, a compliance order directing the facility to take corrective actions, or both,” wrote Andrew Wineke, Ecology deputy communications director. The mill is also facing a $734,000 fine from Ecology for improperly operating its treatment system since the fall of 2025. This led to six discharge limit violations in April. A September Ecology press release regarding the fine stated that five water-quality penalties had been issued to the mill since 2021 for releasing “tens of thousands of gallons of improper or inadequately treated wastewater into Port Townsend Bay.” “We have filed the appeal; it’s in process.” Kreizenbeck said of the $734,000 fine. In an op-ed piece in The Leader, Kreizenbeck wrote that “We disagree with significant aspects of Ecology’s findings.” When asked what specific findings the mill disagreed with, Kreizenbeck stated he did not wish to litigate such details in the newspaper, and would instead trust the process with Ecology. Kreizenbeck also described water quality exceedances as “minor” in the same opinion piece and said the mill operates within its daily effluent parameter limits 99.8% of the time, not in volume discharged into the bay. “It’s just a simple average of those eight parameters that we monitor in our pond every day,” Kreizenbeck said when asked to explain the 99.8 percent figure. “And that is specific to our pond performance, right? And that’s what the penalty was levied on.” Kreizenbeck also wrote that mill employees and their families were “not abstractions in a political debate.” When asked what was political about the situation, Kreizenbeck said, “We weren’t going to focus on political motives, just, you know, ‘Hey, we’re focusing on our process of responding to Ecology, but to the information we have. And I think that might have been in respect to the fines and the penalties that we’ve received recently. But I think we always said that we weren’t going to speculate on anything other than the fine we received in our appeal process regarding that fine.” MISSING IMAGES, CONFLICTING NARRATIVES After being fired from his position as a millwright, Tippins brought his claims, along with a collection of photographs and videos, to the Seattle Times. Tippins believes he was fired for his efforts to address the spill within the company, while the mill insists he was let go for performance and conduct-related issues. “He had already been suspended and on administrative leave when he made his whistleblower report,” said Randy Coté, Senior VP of Fearey, a Seattle-based public relations firm hired by Crown Paper Group, which owns the mill. “When it comes to Mr. Tippins, we have from HR documented what was happening as far as his unrelated performance and conduct within the mill before any of that happened, and we stand by all of that and that timeline.” In early July of 2026, Tippins approached The Leader while still employed at the mill, but did not agree to go on record out of fear of losing his job. As a result, The Leader did not run the story. Certain images in the Times’ story, such as the one showing a substantial amount of liquid flowing from the pipe, were not seen by The Leader, though Tippins insists that he did share them with Ecology, The Leader and higher-ups at the mill. Port Townsend Paper Corporation also claims to have not seen Tippins’ images prior to their publication in the Seattle Times piece, and told The Leader on Oct. 15 that they had to file a public records request from the Department of Ecology to view them. “Mill managers gave Ecology all the relevant photos that they had at the time,” explained Coté, “And so I think that’s part of the, you know, frustration is the fact that there were photos and videos being withheld.” When asked for more information on the Nov. 7 spill incident mentioned in the most recent notice of violation from Ecology, neither Coté nor Kreizenbeck could offer many details. “We received [the notice] yesterday and are going through the process of responding,” Coté said. “So we can just ensure that if there’s any sort of additional statement, that we can get that back to you here in short order.” CAUSE OF THE BREACH According to the mill’s initial one-page report to Ecology, the flow of water was discovered at 8:41 p.m., and operational staff shut down the pump leading to the flow three minutes later. By 9:06, the report says, “the discharge had slowed to a trickle.” Afterward, the hole was discovered and patched with epoxy. This hole allowed a percentage of the wastewater material to escape the normal pathway and infiltrate the saltwater overflow line,” the report read. “The estimated flow rate of the discharge from 8:41 to 9:06 was six gallons per minute.” The report estimates 150 gallons were discharged in total. The cause of the hole remains officially unexplained. Kreizenbeck did not provide a specific method as to how the 6 gallon-per-minute figure was calculated. “In my role, I’m not the one that does the calculation,” Kreizenbeck explained. “I’m just the one that asks that when we fill reports out, we do them correctly and accurately. And then in this case where we had more information come to light through an employee and then later through our request to ecology, we looked at it again and made sure we’re confident in how we assessed it.” “The maximum flow of the process before the discharge point is measured at 300 gallons per minute and it has a flow meter on it,” said Coté. “And only a small percentage of that possible flow was discharged.” Coté provided The Leader with a ribbon-sized screenshot from the software allegedly used to monitor the system upstream from the breach. The readout describes the system as the “Reitz press sludge flow,” and the maximum flow is listed as 300 gpm. This however measures speed of flow, not total volume. Kreizenbeck added that the mill had technically trained, well-informed personnel on site during the incident that were able to make an accurate estimation based on a combination of process automation and on-the-ground observations. Tippins was among those personnel that night, and as stated in the Seattle Times, documented what he says is much more than 6 gpm of discharge. Coté said the location of the discharge would have been “very apparent,” meaning that it was unlikely the leak was occurring unnoticed for an extended period of time. “[The discharge] was audible to folks in the area that the event happened,” Coté said. “They found it, they fixed it and they voluntarily reported the estimated discharge.” Coté continued, “As there’s been more speculation or whistleblower activity, like questioning that timeline part of what the mill stands by, is that, it’s a lot based on, like Rob said, that familiarity with the process and what comes before [the discharge location] and the size and all that, but also the fact that the response time was so quick. And I think that’s just a key piece.” Coté also showed interest in sharing documentation surrounding the origin of the break, but within proper cadence with Ecology’s investigatory process. “The spill remains under investigation, so I can’t say everything that is going to happen, because it is actively being investigated,” explained Wineke. “We are continuing to evaluate reports submitted by the paper mill. We will take appropriate actions.” While the mill is required by law to submit accurate reports on such incidents, enforcement can be a challenge. Wineke said there are approximately 20 engineers and support staff tasked with monitoring 43 designated industrial facilities throughout the entire state. “These are complicated facilities. That’s why we have engineers working on compliance,” Wineke said. “There is a tremendous amount of data. You’ve seen some of this from Port Townsend Paper. But at the same time, they have been around a while; the process is understood.” The post More leaks draw new fire on mill first appeared on Port Townsend & Jefferson County Leader .

title: False alarm clears theater
author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: Engine L1 from East Je­erson Fire Rescue responds to a false alarm at the Rose Theater Oct. 15. Moviegoers waited outside while fire crews cleared the building. Leader photo by Jon Decker Moviegoers at the Rose Theater found their films interrupted by a false fire alarm Oct. 15 just after 8 p.m. “There was like 20 minutes left in our movie,” said Luke Silliman, who was watching the climax of “Primetime,” a dramatic biopic about “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hanson, played by Robert Pattinson, whose infamous role as a moody vampire heartthrob living in nearby Forks launched him into stardom. Meanwhile at the Rose’s second theater room, viewers were into the last half hour of Tom Cruise’s latest film, Digger, when it was interrupted by an alarm. “It was a scene where everything was falling apart and then the fire alarm started going off in the other room,” Silliman said. “And then they have to actually leave and everything is falling apart for a moment. So it’s like the movie kind of came to life for a little bit.” Both theaters were evacuated out onto the sidewalk while one engine from East Jefferson Fire Rescue responded to the scene. After the building was emptied, a team of firefighters cleared the premises and deemed it safe. Firefighter Andrew Hayden confirmed the false alarm with The Leader before departing. Silliman had the choice to return to the film or get a refund for another ticket. “We’re gonna go see another movie next week,” Silliman declared. Most other moviegoers elected for option one and quickly funneled back into the theater to finish their feature. The post False alarm clears theater first appeared on Port Townsend & Jefferson County Leader .

title: Concerned citizens share their thoughts on mill controversy
author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: ALO MENTADO, PORT TOWNSEND RESIDENT Former millwright John Tippins went to the Seattle Times with photo and video evidence of a Nov. 20, 2025, spill incident. On Oct. 11, the story was published and has stirred up perennial concerns surrounding the mill’s impact on the environment. The mill says 150 gallons of wastewater spilled into Port Townsend Bay during the incident, while Tippins claims the damage is worse by magnitudes. Reaction to the article and the situation was mixed among the public, with many showing skepticism at the mill’s claims, while others highlighted the mill’s fixture in the community as a primary employer and questioned the integrity of the whistleblower. Local man Louis Salisbury called the Seattle Times’ article “yellow journalism” and described it as “prejudicial and slanderous.” “The citations in that article about the employee having problems unrelated to his work as a whistleblower, those issues, those negative interactions with coworkers, those problems with performance with his job were numerous,” Salisbury said. The mill claims that Tippins was fired for poor performance and workplace behavior, while Tippins says it was related to his whistleblowing efforts inside the company. Tippins went to the Seattle Times after he was fired, but stands by his assertions that the spill is much larger than the company claims. Salisbury criticized the Seattle Times piece for failing to mention positive traits of the mill, including its massive cardboard recycling program. “[The article] made no mention of any of the well-established positive accomplishments over the decades and the vast number of millions of dollars in improvements made since ownership went from the prior entity to Atlas Holdings,” Salisbury said. Aurora Childe, a Seattle-based musician and artist, spent the past 15 years visiting Port Townsend to visit friends and play music. At the time of her interview, she was set up on Water Street, picking a sea shanty on her black mandolin and selling bracelets. “I’m not surprised that they [the mill] would lie about it,” Childe, a former Navy sailor, said. “I think it’s probably true that the guy is telling the truth.” AURORA CHILDE, PORT TOWNSEND VISITOR Childe also noted the self-regulating practices by the mill and called for more regulation and monitoring. “I feel like when they’re dumping, somebody from a different agency should have to come out and watch,” Childe said. As a former sailor, Childe is no stranger to pollution. “I saw a lot of stuff like that in the Navy with contractors and people working for the government that did things that were not supposed to happen, as far as greasy things going in the water. It’s like if you can get away with it, you can get away with it,” Childe said. “But it’s unfortunate because I think we’re at a point where we’re seeing environmental impact everywhere.” Resident Elleyna Thompson had a different approach and wished to see more efforts to strengthen and clean up local manufacturing instead of “pushing it out of our backyard and into someone else’s backyard,” referring to the great outsourcing of American industry and manufacturing to the Global South. “People have jobs here, where there is at least oversight, instead of outsourcing abroad,” Thompson said. “It’s very convenient to not want a factory here because it’s ugly and smells bad, it still has to go somewhere.” “I think it’s really good that people are speaking out about it, but it’s also complicated because the mill is one of the biggest employment sources in town,” first-year Port Townsend resident Alo Mentado said. “It brings a lot of employment and stability to town, but at the same time I don’t know what it is affecting the population that live here.” Mentado continued. “I wish that they can be more honest with the town and people, because this town is such a nice community and we take care of everybody, and I think they should do the same for us.” Mentado said. “We deserve clean water and nice air to breathe.” Mayor Amy Howard told the Leader that she wants a “full investigation” of the incident. On Oct. 14, the Washington Department of Ecology sent a notice of violation to the mill for the Nov. 20 incident, and another event on Nov. 7 in which 600 gallons were flushed into Port Townsend Bay. The post Concerned citizens share their thoughts on mill controversy first appeared on Port Townsend & Jefferson County Leader .

title: County takes a hard look at what’s left to cut
author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: Less than a year after cutting staff and tapping reserves to address a projected $5.2 million budget gap, Jefferson County officials are again staring at difficult financial decisions, with a projected 2027 deficit that could approach $2.5 million. “I’m still wrestling with this feeling of disappointment a little bit, in the sense that I was hoping that the difficult work that we all did together last year would be in the past and that this year things would be different,” County Administrator Josh Peters said. Peters and other department heads addressed elected officials during the county’s first Budget Day Oct. 13, a special daylong meeting to examine the deficit and identify potential savings. Last December, commissioners adopted a 2026 budget that eliminated 10.18 full-time-equivalent positions and relied on approximately $1.1 million in reserves to balance expenditures against available resources. By April 2026, the projected deficit had grown to approximately $1.3 million, threatening parks and recreation services. Voters approved a dedicated parks levy in August. “If that hadn’t have happened, the numbers that we’ve shared so far with the board would be a lot worse,” Peters said. Despite last year’s cuts, the county continues to face rising personnel costs, declining sales tax revenue and higher insurance expenses. The county’s 2027 budget requests include an anticipated 25% increase in its liability insurance rate, along with higher costs for public defense and central services. And with much of last year’s budget already cut, officials have fewer options this time around. “Since we’ve already gone through a process to cut a lot of things out of our budget, you could make the case that there may not be a whole lot extra to do,” Peters said. Finance Director Judy Shepherd presented three possible budget scenarios, ranging from a preliminary $669,859 deficit to nearly $2.5 million if additional departmental requests are included. A third scenario, eliminating expenses classified as discretionary, would still leave a projected $1.7 million deficit. “Repeated deficits year after year have a huge impact,” Shepherd said. “Because eventually, we will run out of money.” Treasurer Stacie Prada warned that the county’s declining cash reserves are already threatening its ability to meet financial obligations. The county began 2026 with approximately $5.2 million in cash but had to delay an insurance payment until March. Updated projections indicate the county could begin 2027 with less than $3.7 million. “We can’t pay bills the first three months of the year until property taxes start coming in,” Prada said. “And right now, we are structurally setting ourselves up to fail.” Other department heads warned that any more staff reductions could affect essential services. Sheriff Andy Pernsteiner said approximately seven deputies could retire within the next year, potentially leaving the department severely understaffed. “If I lost seven officers, I don’t know,” Pernsteiner said. “We move down to very minimal staffing. There’d be one officer going to calls by themselves, which is obviously not good.” “If I cut staffing, well, the calls still keep coming in,” Pernsteiner added. “So, I’m still gonna have to have someone answer the call.” Prosecuting Attorney James Kennedy said his office could be down to just two attorneys this winter because of departures and upcoming parental leaves, potentially forcing prosecutors to prioritize cases. “We’re going to have to triage our cases, which has a deleterious impact on public safety,” he said. As officials discussed possible savings through shared services, purchasing changes and other operational efficiencies, commissioners questioned whether those measures could close the gap. Commissioner Greg Brotherton criticized the county’s previous approach of requiring departments to make across-the-board reductions. “Last year we had basically a 12% off-the-top cut, which I don’t see as a strategy,” Brotherton said. No cuts or staffing changes were approved during Budget Day. Commissioners will continue reviewing departmental requests and potential savings as they work toward adopting the 2027 budget. The post County takes a hard look at what’s left to cut first appeared on Port Townsend & Jefferson County Leader .

author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: The Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office responded to a total of 274 calls for service Oct. 7-13. OCT. 8: A vehicle hit a deer on Center Road in Chimacum. The driver declined aid for possible injuries. The deer was stunned but seen in the wood line, seemingly fine. They also found a modified firework, which resembled a bomb. The firework was collected and disposed of by the Washington State Patrol bomb squad. title: Port to remove boat ramp floats; rebuild possible
author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: Port of Port Townsend staff expects to remove the floating docks from the Port Hadlock public boat ramp on Oct. 23. Port staff has recommended replacing the entire facility with a new boat launch ramp and adjacent handling float. Leader photo At least for the upcoming winter season, the Port Hadlock public boat ramp is about to have its floating docks removed by Port of Port Townsend staff. At the same time, the future shape of the Port-owned boat ramp, pier, pilings and floating docks remains under debate within the Port Commission. One option, recommended by the staff, is to remove the entire facility – ramp, pier, pilings and floating dock – to replace it with a new boat launch ramp with an adjacent floating dock for handling launched boats, according to Port Executive Director Eron Berg. “Our next steps are part of an active discussion within the Port Commission,” Berg said. He advised residents interested in the Port Hadlock launch to contact Port Commission members with their guidance. “The commission would like to hear from people,” he said. The current pier extends 90 feet from the Lower Hadlock beach to the floating docks. The two sections of floating dock are about 40 feet long each and often serve as a dinghy dock. The creosote log pilings are significantly deteriorated, Berg said. The same kind of pilings hold the pier. The current boat launch ramp can get piled with tidal sand. The three-member commission has authorized Berg to seek a Recreation and Conservation Office grant to fund a rebuild, but funds are not yet in hand. title: Aid opens for college, job training
author: ops@our-hometown.com
content: High school seniors and others can now apply for financial aid for the 2027-28 academic year. “Washington provides more free money for students to attend college or job training than virtually any other state in the nation — but to access it, you have to fill out the form,” Governor Bob Ferguson said. “I want every eligible student to take advantage of this money for college, apprenticeships and other education or training. Apply today — you will never know how much financial aid you qualify for unless you do.” In Washington, there are two ways to apply for financial aid. U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens can apply for both federal and state aid with the FAFSA (Free Application for Federal Student Aid). People who are ineligible to file the FAFSA, or who choose not to, can apply for state aid only with the WASFA (Washington Application for State Financial Aid). As of Oct. 1, 2026, the 2027-28 FAFSA and WASFA are both available. Washingtonians have an extra incentive to consider education beyond high school. The Washington College Grant is one of the most generous and flexible programs in the country. Through WA Grant, about half of families in Washington can get free money from the state to help pay for career training or college. For 2026-27, a family of four making up to $139,500 can qualify for state financial aid in Washington; in 2027-28, that income cutoff is expected to be even higher. Students and families can use the newly redesigned Washington grant calculator to estimate their award. WA Grant supports low-and middle-income people of all ages pursuing certificates and degrees, as well as apprentices participating in approved registered apprenticeship programs. The grant is available to eligible Washington residents, including undocumented students. Grant amounts vary based on income, family size and the school or program attended. The grant is available year-round and is guaranteed to anyone who meets the requirements. There’s no deadline or separate application — people who complete a FAFSA or WASFA are automatically considered for WA Grant. title: Aggies advocate in style: Party at the Polls
author: Antonio Mattox Jr., Senior Editor
content: The ambitions of student advocacy and celebrity appearances from Marsai Martin and Trinity Tatum led countless Aggies to march from the Dudley Memorial Building to Union Square Campus in Greensboro on Oct. 22. Students came together to vote and get registered at what students dubbed “Party at the Polls.” After not receiving an on-campus early polling site for midterms, students fought to get it back, even after being denied by the Guilford County Board of Elections. The rejection didn’t stop students from trying though. In fact, they turned it up a notch, using the former polling location they lost as a launching pad to march in an effort to get a polling site back on campus. When We All Vote , a nonprofit voting organization, brought Martin, an organization ambassador, renowned actress and producer, alongside Tatum, Love Island’s season eight winner, to get students together and excited to take civic action. Martin already knew the history of A&T’s polling site and encouraged students to keep going. Marsai Martin encourages students during a speech before their march to the polls. (Kevin Pernell) “You have been denied, you have been delayed, but one thing is clear: you will not be silenced,” she said. “When the path to the polls got harder, you guys all found a way forward and that’s why I’m here to party at the polls with y’all.” The passionate students crowded Tatum and Martin with every step they took on campus, but they also made sure to crowd the streets of Greensboro on their march to the nearest polling site downtown. However, there was one persistent question left in the minds of students during their march. ‘Why is it this far?’ That was one of the many phrases students chanted on their way to the polls. The walk from the Dudley Memorial to Union Square Campus took over 45 minutes and over 2,000 steps, a distance and unfair reality many students didn’t want to deal with anymore. A&T is home to at least 15,275 students who don’t all have accessible means to reach a polling site as far as where students marched. Olu Rouse, a senior and co-founder of Protect Ours NC, knows he deserves a say in what goes on in the community where he lives. “We as students are residents of Guilford County and are their constituents,” said Rouse. “I’ve lived here for the past four years at this point. I believe we deserve to be heard above anything else.” And heard they were. Inside the polling site, the halls were filled with people standing shoulder to shoulder, eager to vote. Registration forms and voter guides were passed out and Aggies spent hours at the site. The event was more than just a “hype fest” and fanfare; students like senior Kelly Jones came educated for this year’s election. Jones is a political science student and serves as Miss Black Girls Vote for A&T. Naturally, she also has deep convictions about her civic duty as a student. “Everybody needs to be civically educated and civically knowledgeable about everything that’s going on in their community … it all matters,” said Jones. “And we don’t like what’s happening right now, so what does that mean? You change it.” Early voting runs through Saturday, Oct. 31. On Election Day, which is Tuesday, Nov. 3, voters must cast their ballot in their assigned precinct. Find more details about voting at the Guilford County Board of Elections website. The post Aggies advocate in style: Party at the Polls first appeared on The A&T Register .

title: Is it NCAT, A&T or just the ‘T?’ What is the right nickname for our HBCU?
author: Kaleb Moore, TheYard Reporter
content: If you ask anyone how they refer to our illustrious HBCU, the answer really might just depend on the person. Some will say A&T, others would say NCAT and someone might even call it by its full government name and say North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University. But with so many names, how can we know which one is the university’s official nickname? North Carolina A&T State University’s name carries more than a century of history. Founded in 1891, the university has undergone a few official name changes, but the “A&T” abbreviation has remained a recognizable part of its identity since 1915. The university was originally named the Agricultural and Mechanical College for the Colored Race when it first opened. In 1915, the North Carolina General Assembly renamed it the Negro Agricultural and Technical College of North Carolina. The name change helped establish the “A&T” abbreviation that students and alumni continue to use today. While the term “A&T” has remained a recognizable part of the university’s identity for more than a century, the way people refer to the school continues to evolve. Some popular variations included “Ayantee”, “The T”, or even just “T”. In recent years, the use of “NCAT” has become increasingly apparent especially through social media. Particularly through the hashtag #NCAT, students, alumni and fans use the acronym to talk about campus experiences, athletic events and university pride. However, its widespread use has also sparked conversations among members of the Aggie community about how the university should be identified. Some students and alumni have begun taking to social media to express their concerns about the school being referred to as “NCAT,” arguing that shortening its established identity diminishes its history and tradition that extends way beyond a social media hashtag. Some Aggies say that people from their home state only refer to the university as NCAT and have difficulty recognizing it by its other titles. During an interview with Jonathan Brown, a junior from Dallas, Texas, he stated that back home no one calls it A&T. “I always have to say NCAT when talking about it. Every time I say A&T they act like they don’t know what I’m talking about,” Brown said. Brown’s experience highlights how the university’s name can vary depending on where someone is from. Students from or more familiar with North Carolina may be more likely to call the school A&T, while those from out of state might still know it as NCAT. And of course there’s still the occasional slip up of someone unfamiliar calling the school “AT&T”, after which they are always quickly corrected. For Alyssa Cofield, a junior from Fayetteville, North Carolina, the university has always been known as A&T. Cofield said both of her parents and several other family members are Aggie alumni who have consistently referred to the university by that name. “I’ve always known it as A&T because that’s what my parents have always called it,” she said. The names used to refer to North Carolina A&T, whether they are A&T, NCAT, the T or just “T,” represent the various relationships and experiences that people have with the university. In the end, these discussions highlight what it means to be an Aggie. While the nicknames for the school we call home differ, the bond of our community goes far beyond a name. The post Is it NCAT, A&T or just the ‘T?’ What is the right nickname for our HBCU? first appeared on The A&T Register .

title: Fly Navy: A&T’s flyest new organization
author: Khali Roberson, Contributor
content: For students at North Carolina A&T State University, fashion and creativity goes way beyond what someone wears. They can be a reflection of identity, personality and how someone chooses to show up in the world. FlyNavy, one of campus’s newer organizations, is here to help Aggie students do just that. Dedicated to creativity, personality and community, FlyNavy caters to young people interested in fashion, modeling, photography, business, branding and even self expression. Instead of trying to build on a one-dimensional definition of style, students are encouraged to find out what that expression looks like individually. “Fly Navy is less about what you wear, but how you choose to represent yourself and present yourself to society,” said, Kyndall Ussery, the secretary of Fly Navy. According to Ussery, one of Fly Navy’s goals is to create an environment where students feel comfortable showcasing their creativity without feeling pressured to fit a certain image. Whether someone owns a clothing brand, enjoys photography, wants to model or simply wants to meet other creative students, the organization aims to give them a place to connect. That feeling of “fitting in” is also an area where the group feels it might set itself aside from other organizations that exist on campus. Ussery explained that student organizations can sometimes begin with one purpose, but gradually stray away from what originally brought people together. Fly Navy remains grounded in its mission by making sure that the organization is welcoming and authentic. Fly Navy hopes students will walk in feeling comfortable like they can just be themselves and meet new people in an environment that is inviting and creative, rather than having to perform to make an impression. The vision to achieve this would be through hosting events that were beyond the scope of regular meetings. Some previously hosted events included a hiking trip to Hanging Rock and sunset yoga followed by a creative showcase, which would allow students the opportunity to model, promote, sell their brands and show off their work to other students on campus. These events reflect Fly Navy’s broader vision of creativity as something that can happen anywhere, not only on a runway or through an outfit. They also hosted celebrity stylist and style educator Darris Rushing, better known as D. Rushing, for his third stop on The Rush Way: HBCU Tour on A&T’s campus. At this event, designers, brand owners and those interested in what the workshop had to offer, were invited to sit in and learn all there is about style and the basics of the modeling space. Attendees who chose to model were able to practice runway walks and the confidence that it takes to make an outfit feel dynamic or unique. There were also photographers available to take photos of the models as they walked and of the event as it went on, which opened a new avenue of teaching moments for those interested in the visual media aspects. For students interested in joining, Ussery emphasized that getting involved does not have to be complicated. Students can start by following @flynavy.ncat on Instagram, joining the organization’s GroupMe and attending upcoming events. Most importantly, she emphasized that students do not need to rock a certain style, belong to a certain organization or subgenre of creators. “Come as you are,” Ussery said. That simple invitation represents much of what Fly Navy hopes to contribute to N.C. A&T’s campus life. As the organization begins building its presence, its focus is not only on what students create, but also on creating an environment where students feel safe enough to share it. At a university filled with different personalities, interests and talents, FlyNavy has the right trajectory to develop into another major outlet for Aggies interested in fashion or differing styles to find their people. For FlyNavy, the message is simple: express yourself earnestly, bring good energy and come get fly. The post Fly Navy: A&T’s flyest new organization first appeared on The A&T Register .

title: The Internet Is Warping Our Sense of Reality
author: Kyla Mahasa, Contributor
content: Social media has made it possible to create an entirely different identity and present it to thousands, sometimes millions, of people. With enough evidence, almost anyone can make their life look entirely different from their reality. A carefully created profile, a few convincing pictures and consistent enough posts can make an online identity seem completely real. This can make it hard for people to know who or what to trust, especially when they only know someone through social media. Recent stories involving a woman who allegedly attended physician assistant (PA) school, and a man accused of pretending to be a San Francisco 49ers player, show the seriousness and depth of this issue. Angel Murdock, a social media influencer, documented what she claimed was her nearly two-year journey through PA school at Duke University. Duke stated she never attended or applied to the university. In a somewhat similar case, two men, Daejon Love and Taylor Jamie Chan, were federally charged in connection with a fraud scheme involving women they met online. Prosecutors found that Love posed as a San Francisco 49ers player using a fake online identity to gain women’s trust. Investigations showed that 26 women were targeted and that the scheme resulted in approximately $1.3 million in losses. These cases show how false identities can move beyond social media posts and can have serious consequences for real people. Although both situations are different, they point to a larger issue: people cannot always determine what is real and what is fake online. Sometimes, the problem also lies in how most convincing lies are not completely false. When a few real details are mixed with exaggerations or false information, the story can become much more believable. Social media especially brings this concern to the forefront because a lie can become a lifestyle. A person can appear to be a doctor by posting pictures in scrubs, just as someone can appear wealthy or famous by posting expensive cars or luxury homes. If these images are repeated enough, people may begin to believe in this version of someone’s life without ever questioning whether it is accurate. Social media allows people to shape how they want to present themselves. Karin Thomas, a freshman marketing student, understands how social media can make people believe they know someone. “I think social media makes it easy for people to create a version of themselves that they want other people to believe. Sometimes you see someone online and assume you know their whole life, but you really only know what they choose to post,” she said. Naomi Anisso, a junior accounting student, added her perspective with a warning to others about the trustworthiness of online profiles. “People should be more careful about trusting everything they see online. A profile can look professional and still not tell the whole story,” she said. “I think checking information before believing someone can prevent people from being easily misled.” Dating and social media platforms have made it easier to build relationships with strangers, but having such profiles makes information hard to verify. When someone creates a false identity, they can use photos, job titles, locations and other details to make themselves appear trustworthy before ever meeting in person. At the same time, social media itself is not the problem. Social media has helped people stay connected, spread information, build communities and find easier ways to draw attention to largely ignored issues. The problem arises when we stop questioning the information we consume and assume that everything online is automatically true. We are entering a world where fake pictures, artificial intelligence and carefully constructed online personas are becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish from reality. All that means for most people is enforcing the idea that social media does not always show the complete picture within their minds. Before believing an online identity, we should ask: What do we actually know about this person, and what have we been shown? Questioning such things is not being negative; it protects us. Not everything we see online deserves our trust. Checking information, seeking reliable sources and thinking critically about what we consume can help protect us from deception that could derail entire lives if not careful. title: For A&T’s 100th GHOE, gospel royalty and student choir share the stage
author: Joslyn Lindsay, Contributor
content: Gospel great Kirk Franklin will headline the annual Gospel Concert for this year’s 100th GHOE. N.C. A&T’s Fellowship Gospel Choir will open the Nov. 1 concert and perform alongside Franklin and special guest Kierra Sheard Kelly. This year’s Gospel Concert will have two scheduled showtimes, one at 1 p.m. and another at 6:30 p.m. Franklin is a Grammy Award-winning gospel artist who has spent more than three decades in music. He is known for blending gospel with R&B and hip-hop. His 1993 debut album, “Kirk Franklin & The Family,” reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Gospel Albums chart. Franklin has earned 20 Grammy Awards, including a 2024 Grammy for Best Gospel Performance/Song for “All Things.” Kelly, who is also a songwriter, has received four Grammy nominations, including Best Gospel Album for “Kierra” in 2021. She has also collaborated with other gospel artists, including her mother, Karen Clark-Sheard. The N.C. A&T GHOE Gospel Concert will be at the Steven Tanger Center for the Performing Arts at 300 N. Elm St. in downtown Greensboro. Resale ticket prices start at around $114, while tickets for the general public are available through Ticketmaster. For more information about the event, visit the Steven Tanger Center for the Performing Arts website or contact the venue at 800-513-7540. Antonio Mattox, a senior multimedia journalism student from Stone Mountain, Georgia, has been a member of the Fellowship Gospel Choir for four years and serves as the choir’s president. Mattox, who is also senior editor for The A&T Register, said attendees should come to the concert with an open mind and expect the choir to “take you to church.” “If you aren’t familiar with the church culture, we will educate you on what that’s like,” he said. “Our choir is different than your average choir,” Mattox added. “We do a lot of moves with our songs that aren’t considered traditional.” Attendees can expect an energetic performance from the Fellowship Gospel Choir, but Mattox said the group also hopes to create meaningful moments that connect with the audience. “We just want our moves to be able to lift somebody’s spirits,” he said. Antonio Mattox, president of N.C. A&T’s Fellowship Gospel Choir performs a solo. Photo courtesy of Fellowship Gospel Choir Mattox said the choir’s goal goes beyond simply performing. Some of the choir’s songs are slower and more reflective, with the goal of touching the audience’s hearts and encouraging them to grow closer to God. “We don’t do it just to do it,” he said. “ We want to make an impact in people’s lives.” Mattox also highlighted the significance of sharing the stage with the featured artists, describing Franklin as “the top of the gospel genre” and Kelly as “one of the top female vocalists.” He also said the Fellowship Gospel Choir is “one of the top HBCU choirs.” The Fellowship Gospel Choir is more than a performing group. It also hosts Bible studies and participates in outreach events, using its platform to encourage and connect with others. While the choir prepares to bring its own energy and message to the stage, dancers will also play a role in bringing the performances to life. Cassie Heard, a junior journalism and mass communications student and dancer with the choir from Houston, Texas, said audiences can expect to see a wide variety of technique, talent and energy from the dancers. “The choreography adds a certain kind of visual element to the gospel choir singers behind us. It really puts into perspective what we are doing to glorify God,” she said. Heard also said that being able to meet Franklin and perform alongside him is especially meaningful because he has always been a role model in the gospel community. “I would encourage everyone to come, even if you have a small relationship with God or if you’re super righteous,” she said. “It’s something for everybody.” Joslyn Lindsay is a junior multimedia journalism student from Oak Ridge, North Carolina. title: When sexualization overshadows women in sports
author: Amirah Stallworth, TheScene Editor
content: Sydney Sweeney’s recent advertisement was supposed to be about sports. Instead, the conversation surrounding it has become less about athletic competition and more about a familiar image: A conventionally attractive woman’s body being used to sell something. “Sydney Sweeney has nothing to do with women in sports…celebrities are kind of taking over their spaces,” said Keith Boston, a senior journalism and mass communication student. The actress starred in a new campaign for Novig, a sports prediction platform, appearing to have little to no clothing on, while posing with sports equipment and pretending to play sports including tennis, golf, baseball, and hockey. The ad ends with Sweeney topless on a pool table, telling viewers that Novig is about “just sports.” The campaign quickly went viral, receiving more than 33 million views, but the attention has come with significant criticism from female athletes who argue that the advertisement sexualized women in sports rather than celebrating them. And that criticism deserves more attention than the question of whether Sweeney was simply “too naked.” American gymnast Gracie Kramer responded to the ad by sharing a video of herself competing with the message, “This is what a woman in sports looks like.” Other athletes followed, posting images and videos of themselves training. Australian Olympians, including four-time Olympic gold medalist Arianne Titmus, criticized the campaign for reducing women’s participation in sports to their appearance. Titmus argued that the advertisement was a disservice to women who dedicate their lives to teamwork, excellent and athletic performance. That distinction matters to a lot of athletes. This is especially true with the most recent media boom surrounding the topic and the newly expanded platform. USC Annenberg reported that advertising spending on women’s sports more than doubled, while campaigns placed alongside women’s sports content were 40% more effective than the average prime-time advertisement. There is clearly an audience for women’s sports. That makes representation even more important. The racial part of the conversation also deserves some consideration. Sweeney represents a specific version of American beauty: white, blonde, conventionally feminine and traditionally considered attractive within mainstream American culture. Advertising her repeatedly tells audiences which type of people are considered desirable, marketable, and worthy of being placed at the center of attention. “They’re just sexualizing women off of sports…I don’t think it has a great light on it because a lot of women really work hard in sports,” said Destiny Brewer, a junior journalism and mass communication student. The advertisement did not even have to completely ignore the athletic ability aspect to contribute to a larger problem. Sometimes the problem is what receives the most attention. That raises an uncomfortable question: if women’s sports were finally gaining the attention they have demanded for years, why is a woman’s body once again being used as the shortcut to capture that attention? The answer may have something to do with the audience that advertisers assume they are trying to reach. One former Olympian and Australian politician, Zali Steggall, criticized the ad as overt sexualization intended to attract young men to sports gambling. This is where the male gaze enters the conversation. The male gaze describes a cultural pattern in which women are presented primarily from a presumed heterosexual male viewer’s perspective. The sports industry itself recognizes the problem. In 2026, the European Broadcasting Union and European Athletics introduced guidelines discouraging broadcasters from using lingering shots, revealing angles and excessive slow motion that sexualize female athletes rather than highlighting athletic performance. Sweeney is not the problem. A woman choosing to take part in a pro-active ad is not the problem either. The problem is an advertising culture that continues to treat the sexualization of women as an easy way to make people look and then confers that attention a marketing success. Novig may have gotten millions of people to watch, but the campaign has started a much bigger conversation about what women are expected to look like in the space. Despite all the discourse, there is still a push for the bigger message that many are siding with: Women’s sports deserve attention, women athletes deserve attention and women should not have to look a certain way to earn either one. title: 8k miles by motorcycle: One man’s journey to raise awareness
author: Akilah Abdulraheem, TheYard Editor
content: Robert Horne is a counselor and counseling consultant who recently embarked on an 8,000-mile motorcycle ride, starting out on the campus of N.C. A&T on Sept. 26. The ride is referred to as the 8-for-8 challenge because it features 8,000 miles of road with a goal of $8,000 raised. This challenge is meant to bring awareness to mental health and addiction counseling. With this in mind, the money raised will fund a scholarship that would be awarded to a current counseling student who will commit to working in a rural or military community. The creation of this challenge was inspired by Horne’s personal experiences with counseling services and his background. “I got a scholarship during my doctoral program…the Minority Fellowship Scholarship through the National Board for Certified Counselor Foundation,” said Horne. “It made a difference for me, and I wanted to give something back to the organization and to another student as well.” The ride itself was inspired by Horne’s passion for riding. Being an avid motorcyclist for 55 years, he wanted to give back by doing something that he enjoyed doing. Starting his journey on the campus of A&T was especially important to Horne. “I chose A&T because they have a strong counseling program,” Horne said. “When you look at the impact of the A&T counseling program, it has been local and global and I think that should be highlighted,” Horne continued. In addition to Horne being fond of the counseling program here at A&T, Greensboro is also home to him. The 8-for-8 challenge specifically brings awareness to the importance of mental health counseling and addiction counseling for those who have served in the military and those residing in rural communities. “There’s not enough counselors in these communities,” said Horne. “I was in a town about 40 miles west of Kalamazoo, Michigan and one of the challenges is that the closest counselor was an hour away…for them to go to counseling, they’d have to take off half a day’s work.” Horne continued to discuss how having to take off work for a day every week for individuals living in these kinds of communities is seen as more of an inconvenience than help. In addition to a lack of access to qualified professionals in these communities, the stigma surrounding mental health issues is a major barrier. “Usually when you tell someone ‘I think you should see someone’, their response is ‘I’m not crazy’,“ Horne explained. The consequences that result in individuals not being able to receive mental health services are reflected in the country’s suicide and crime rates every year. “A lot of individuals have mental health issues that aren’t being addressed,” said Horne. “But we can make a difference; mental health isn’t an individual problem but a community one.” For those looking to stay up to date on the challenge or get involved, more information can be found on the 8-for-8 website . title: How can Crosby Kids breathe with no air?
author: Kennedi L. Goode-Bey and Rheegan Wright
content: Crosby Hall is a bustling hub of life for journalism, media production, public relations and marketing students of all kinds. It is a place full of love, warmth and support from professors who are passionate about uplifting their students and making sure they have all the tools they need to go out and conquer the world. Through the ups and downs, Crosby Kids persevere, but recently the building became unbearable to set foot in. This school year, Crosby has experienced temperature problems since as early as Sep. 8, forcing teachers to move classes online or cancel course meetings entirely. This proved to be unsustainable for daily operations, while robbing students and their professors of valuable instruction time. Although the heating and air conditioning issues seem more severe this year, the building experienced similar problems in Spring 2026. “This issue has been going on for some time. For the last 3-4 years, I was told that they have been doing the fixes temporarily,” Dr. Masudul Biswas, Professor and Journalism & Mass Communication Department Chair, told the Register. He recently spoke with the facilities’ Director of Operations and Director of Environment and Safety about this issue. Building officials have told staff that technicians are actively working on the air conditioning system to try and rectify the problem, but this caused Aggies to wonder: is this just a temporary solution to a more permanent problem? Biswas continued to say, “They are working on it, getting a quote to replace some of the alarm systems in the building, so that our HVAC system doesn’t shut down as frequently as it has been happening. They’re getting a quote for that.” Older buildings on campus are known to have more problems than newer buildings due to their aged infrastructure and utilities. Solving maintenance issues has been known to be a prolonged process for these buildings. “The facilities, they want to help us– but they’re also working with limited resources. They don’t have enough people to take care of building issues in multiple buildings. I’m sure Crosby Hall is not the only building that has [had] any issues,” Biswas said. Due to the slow pace of resolution, buildings like Marteena Hall have gained a reputation for being one of the worst buildings to reside in because of its AC problems, similar to Crosby. However, Marteena did not gain this reputation over the summer as Crosby has. Marteena has had AC complications in the past, but unlike Crosby, classes were only continued or let out early. Students who frequent Marteena have become accustomed to the dread of taking classes in unbearably hot conditions. Aggies don’t want Crosby Hall to adopt this reputation. On top of the stressors college students already face on a daily basis, dealing with constant maintenance issues every other semester or weather cycle should not be as common as it is. Commuter students who live off campus may be coming to school expecting to hear lectures in person, without getting proper notice that their classes were cancelled. This can prove to be inconvenient or derailing for someone’s day who would typically be notified a few minutes before the start time after they’ve gotten to campus. This happened to Younisa Lee, a concerned junior journalism student who says, “I came [to school] for my 11 a.m. class and I was in the classroom… when I saw the email that we were doing Zoom.” Lee felt she had wasted gas, time and rest to make her way to school. She expressed her frustrations with the disruption of her homework schedule and being inconvenienced by it. Lee also shared her lingering hesitancy to get up and get ready for school due to the unknown possibility of the classes being cancelled. “[I] hope the AC can be fixed and remain that way for the remainder of the school year, so classes can continue [and] students won’t have to work in unbearable heat,” she said. As of Sep. 23, the heating and cooling units in Crosby are functioning again as usual. Only time will tell whether these Aggies can truly “beat the heat” once and for all. title: Destin Conrad finds freedom in identity on ‘ROADRUNNER’
author: Naima Adams, TheCulture Editor
content: “IN THE AIR”, in dancehall studios and in the hearts of many. “ ROADRUNNER ” is Destin Conrad’s newest album that was released on Aug. 21, 2026. There are three features on the project: Amanda Reifer, Stalk Ashley and kwn. The album is rooted in Conrad’s own personal identity as a queer Jamaican man as well as the good, bad and ugly parts that come with it. Conrad originally rose to fame through the app Vine, where he shared humorous videos of himself singing musical samples. When he started his professional music career, his “COLORWAY” album put him on the radar. “IN THE AIR” and “EXCITED!” were some of the most notable songs from the piece. Since then, Conrad has grown into a decorated artist and “ROADRUNNER” is evidence of that. “ ROADRUNNER ” started building anticipation prior to its release with “NERVOUS” and “I LOVE YOUR BODY” released as lead singles. However, those tracks only scratched the surface of the reggae journey Conrad would later embrace. Following the full release of “ROADRUNNER”, the identity of the album became abundantly clear. This piece went beyond music to dance and whine too. It was oozing with identity, style and culture. Torri Harvey is a senior elementary education major and self-proclaimed music connoisseur. “I love the album because, like many of Destin Conrad’s projects, it feels like movement/dance is encouraged with the music. Destin Conrad truly understands how to showcase a genre, make it his own sound, and add his own perspective,” Harvey said. Conrad is just as confident in his Jamaican identity as he is in being queer.   However, with that comes a hard reality about Jamaica’s homophobic history towards queer people. Since 1864, Jamaica has upheld homophobic laws and traditions, especially with its “Offences Against the Person Act”. With the progress of society, queer people should have the freedom to live in their skin without ridicule. Conrad addressed this problematic history the best way he knew how: through music. He sampled “Chi-Chi Man” by T.O.K., which notoriously sings about killing a gay man and makes it a reclamation of freedom and confidence. What was then recognized as a national anthem could now be sung in higher spirits with Conrad’s new spin on it. Alayna Jjanae is a junior majoring in mass media production and a minor in history. She has been listening to Destin Conrad since 2022. “As someone of Caribbean descent, I just love how balanced Destin is as an artist. There’s this really healthy balance of who he is and where he wants to take you musically. It’s like a fresh reintroduction to what the islands can be for Caribbean American girls like myself,” she said. Overall, Conrad did a superb job of making fans proud of themselves and their respective identities, whether they are Caribbean or not.   Alongside the tropical sounds of his ancestry, Destin provided stunning visuals to immerse fans in his world. Music videos were released for two tracks on the album: “FAVORITE LOVER” and “NERVOUS”. Both music videos transport fans into an oasis, meant to feel homey and comforting. Even down to the color grading of the videos, viewers get an atmospheric feel of Jamaica. The styling was strategic and the details were thoughtful. Dancers were wearing vibrant colors and gave off that dancehall vibe. One of the dancers even had the Jamaican flag painted on her nails, a thoughtful attention to detail. Zhamia Greer is a senior Sociology and Psychology Major. Her favorite songs from the album are “FAVORITE LOVER” and “DADAMAN”. “He creates a sound that feels natural, effortlessly blending reggae and dancehall with R&B. Although the album feels a little short in my opinion, it is still an enjoyable project,” says Greer. Needless to say, Conrad has shown what it means to be unapologetic, brave and confident in your own skin with this album. To follow this latest work, you can find more about it on his Instagram @destinconrad . The post Destin Conrad finds freedom in identity on ‘ROADRUNNER’ first appeared on The A&T Register .

title: A New NSP Event: Sunsets, Sips, and Masterpieces Recap
author: Caitlyn King, Contributor
content: N.C. A&T’s New Student Programs is no stranger to hosting vibrant student events. They did just that with their inaugural hosting of the Sunsets, Sips, and Masterpieces event. The event was held on Thursday, Sept. 17 at 6 p.m. on Dudley Lawn. Upon entering, students received a blanket, brush, mini easel, palette, canvas and paint. Additionally, students were free to pick from an assortment of sodas and energy drinks, such as Poppi and Ryse Fuel Energy, to go with the light snacks available. As a way to add to the ambiance of the event, organizers included a live saxophonist, A&T student, Najm Khalik Muhammad. Students gathered on the lawn to paint, dance, and enjoy mingling with other new students. This event was a marked change in pace for NSP, with some students noting the difference in atmosphere. “It’s so relaxing. I feel like it brings everyone together without bonding over, you know, partying and sweating,” says freshman Lyric Johnson.   Many of this school year’s NSP programs have been high-energy, celebration-style events, which can occasionally leave introverted students feeling more isolated. Sunsets, Sips, and Masterpieces bridges that gap, attracting a different crowd of students. This has been a topic of discussion in the larger scene of college social events and parties in general. Less diversity in the type of “fun” people have, or spaces for bonding, has led to several mixed opinions from students. “I wanted more quality events that weren’t so loud and chaotic,” Johnson shared. As the event got more crowded, students began to gather to socialize and line dance to the sounds of the live saxophone. While painting and dancing, Aggies could be seen socializing with new people, really allowing the laid-back energy to set in for everyone. Attendees noted that it was easier to socialize with one another in a calmer setting. “If I wanted to, I could definitely walk into a group or two of people and introduce myself,” said Makhii Brooks, a sophomore journalism student. As many students voiced their opinions on the new event, organizers and Aggie Success Leaders (ASL) spoke on their hopes in creating this program. “This time, especially for the class of 2030, we wanted to make sure y’all have actual student engagement where you can actually connect with one another,” shared ASL, Brandon Moore Jr. This event was one in a continuing series of New Student Programs events, focused on uniting the class of 2030 and creating a way for new students to bond with each other. “For future events, I want to see y’all actually engaged with each other, [coming] out and for the participation of your class [2030] to be more,” Moore continued to say. After the sun set, attendees took home refreshments and newly painted canvases, bringing Sunsets, Sips, and Masterpieces to a close. NSP hosts events all year long, with their next one being the 5v5 basketball tournament tomorrow, Oct. 2, at the campus blacktop courts. More information can be found @ncatnsp on Instagram. title: How a Johnson Mentor Shapes the Next Generation of NASA Talent
author: Sumer Loggins
content: 3 Min Read How a Johnson Mentor Shapes the Next Generation of NASA Talent Daniel Cohen, Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, leads an outdoor orbital mechanics lesson for interns on Oct. 9, 2026. From left are Cohen, Lucas Anton Alonso-Munoyerro, Nathan Samuell, Marcos Pena, and Malvika Bhardwaj. Credits: NASA When Rice University student Malvika Bhardwaj asked her mentor Daniel Cohen, a Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, whether he had time to keep teaching interns with his busy workload, he answered, “You decide what’s important.”  In honor of National Mentoring Day on Oct. 27, Bhardwaj reflects on how Cohen’s advice and support has shaped her internship experience at Johnson.  Through NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement , interns like Bhardwaj contribute to agency projects while learning from NASA mentors and gaining technical skills and hand-on experience to build a future career in space exploration.  Bhardwaj studies computational and applied mathematics at Rice University and interns with the GN&C team, which focuses on how spacecraft determine their position and maneuver in orbit. She is developing tools to analyze thruster firings on the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle that will help NASA safely deorbit the International Space Station at the end of its operational life. Bhardwaj also uses computer simulations to test the vehicle’s control system and identify conditions under which it could fail.  “I’ve learned about the culture of community and support at Johnson and NASA as a whole. Daniel made an effort to introduce me to the team and include me in conversations and meetings. I saw how team members step up to help one another and keep the whole unit moving forward,” Bhardwaj said.  Cohen, a Rice University alumnus with a master’s in mechanical engineering, began his NASA career as a flight operations intern in 2020. He later held internships in docking dynamics, propulsion systems, and GN&C analysis before joining Johnson as a full-time engineer in August 2024.  His current work includes developing simulations and models for studies of the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle, analyzing its control algorithms and GN&C performance, and evaluating SpaceX’s design at multiple life-cycle reviews. He also analyzes settings for the Orion spacecraft’s docking camera, which provides positioning measurements that can help inform navigation during future Artemis rendezvous activities.  Cohen supports Bhardwaj beyond her internship, giving her a closer look at how colleagues collaborate on projects and share ideas. He sets aside a couple of hours each week to teach interns topics such as orbital mechanics and control systems.  Bhardwaj took Cohen’s advice to heart: How she spends her time and energy reflects what she values. She believes that her internship has shown her that problem-solving is rarely an individual effort. Team members bring different perspectives and need to understand how their work connects to a larger project.  Working alongside interns in outreach, social media, and digital design has also broadened Bhardwaj’s view of STEM careers. “No matter what interests you, there’s likely a role for you here,” she said.   She was proud to complete her first project, a set of analysis tools she built from scratch. Working through the debugging process and seeing a finished, functioning product was especially rewarding.  Bhardwaj’s advice to students interested in NASA internships is to apply even if they do not feel fully prepared.  “You’re probably never going to feel 100% ready, but so much of the learning happens on the job,” she said. “Trust in your ability to navigate new environments.”  About the Author Sumer Loggins Share Details Last Updated Oct 27, 2026 Related Terms General Explore More 6 min read NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust Article 11 hours ago 1 min read NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland Article 6 days ago 2 min read NASA’s SR-1 Freedom Advances with Progress on Nuclear Power Module Article 7 days ago Keep Exploring Discover More Topics From NASA Missions Humans in Space Climate Change Solar System

title: APOD: 2026 October 27 – Noctilucent Clouds over Sweden
author: nasa.gov
content: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 27 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Noctilucent Clouds over Sweden Explanation: Sometimes it’s night on the ground but day in the air. As the Earth rotates to eclipse the Sun, sunset rises up from the ground. Therefore, at sunset on the ground, sunlight still shines on clouds above. Under usual circumstances , a pretty sunset might be visible, but unusual noctilucent clouds float so high up they can be seen well after dark. Normally too dim to be seen, they may become visible just after sunset during the summer when illuminated by sunlight from below the horizon. Noctilucent cloud s are the highest clouds and are known more technically as polar mesospheric clouds . Featured here as they appeared in early August, a network of blue noctilucent clouds was captured in the distant sky above a field of green grass near Linköping , Sweden , with trees in stark silhouette across the horizon. Much about noctilucent clouds has been discovered only in the past two decades, while how they form and evolve remains a topic of active research . title: A-81 Reaches South Georgia
author: nasa.gov
content: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory A-81 Reaches South Georgia Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Iceberg A-81 slows its drift near the edge of South Georgia’s shallow underwater shelf in this image, acquired on October 20, 2026, by the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite. NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison Some Antarctic icebergs linger close to home for decades, running aground near the ice shelves that spawned them or circling partway around the continent on coastal currents. Others, like Iceberg A-81, make a faster exit, heading north out of the Weddell Sea along a route well-traveled by the region’s bergs. Fast is relative, though. After breaking from the Brunt Ice Shelf in January 2023, the roughly 1,550-square-kilometer (600-square-mile) berg spent more than three years in the Weddell Sea, carried along the coast by the clockwise-flowing Weddell Gyre. By May 2026, it reached the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula. It then moved north into the Scotia Sea, and by late October 2026, it approached the remote island of South Georgia in the South Atlantic Ocean, 2,300 kilometers (1,400 miles) north-northwest of the Brunt Ice Shelf. This image, acquired by the MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite, shows the berg on October 20. In the days before, its progress slowed noticeably, and it appeared to be bumping along the edge of the island’s underwater shelf, according to Jan Lieser of Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology and Christopher Shuman of the University of Maryland (retired). South Georgia has slowed and even stopped icebergs before. In 2025, for instance, Iceberg A-23A ran aground on the shelf and later broke apart . Though Iceberg A-81 was a steadfast traveler once it broke free, it took its time in becoming an iceberg in the first place. For about 35 years, one of the Brunt Ice Shelf’s rifts known as Chasm 1 was relatively stable. Then, around 2012, it began growing again, and by 2019, it was advancing quickly enough that a break seemed imminent . But the floating glacial ice held on for several more years until finally, in January 2023, the berg let go . Calving is a normal part of the life cycle of ice shelves, but scientists keep a close eye on Brunt, which has recently shed several large icebergs in quick succession and is home to the British Antarctic Survey’s Halley Research Station , a major base for Earth, atmospheric, and space science research since the 1950s. Besides A-81, the ice shelf calved Iceberg A-74 from the North Rift in 2021 and Iceberg A-83 from the Halloween Crack in 2024. A-74 has since broken up, while A-83 remains intact and is trailing A-81 northward, along with a handful of other icebergs that appear to be clearing out of the Weddell Sea.
