title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
author: Amanda Barnett
content: 6 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) This 360-degree panorama from NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover shows Neretva Vallis, the dusty, long-dried river channel that cuts through the western rim of Mars’ Jezero Crater. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including some that are small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings will be published Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars. “NASA has a long history of turning challenges into workable solutions and of finding creative ways to use the data that we have to answer questions beyond what it was originally collected for,” said Lindsay Hays, acting director, Planetary Science Division, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Dust has been a surface-exploration challenge since the Apollo program. Perseverance is giving our engineers and flight surgeons measurements they can use to improve our existing designs well before the first American astronauts arrive on Mars.” Lunar dust scratched visors, degraded outer spacesuit layers, and damaged their seals during NASA’s Apollo missions, and some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever. Rounded by wind-driven collisions with other particles, dust grains on Mars are less abrasive than those on the Moon. They also are enriched in sulfur, chlorine, and iron and contain more silica than lunar dust. Regional and global dust storms on Mars can keep the grains recirculating throughout the atmosphere as well.   The rover carries a set of five samples of spacesuit material. The swatches , each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are part of a calibration target used to test the settings of SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals), an instrument on Perseverance’s robotic arm. The calibration target for another instrument that provided the dust measurements, called PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry), carries a sample of Teflon and of basaltic glass. Because Teflon contains no elements that PIXL can directly detect, whatever elemental signals the X-ray spectrometer picks up from that sample comes from dust resting on it. The team also analyzed swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits, on SHERLOC’s calibration target. NASA sent the swatches to Mars to study how spacesuit materials hold up on the planet’s surface. “Perseverance’s main job is to search for signs of ancient microbial life, but the mission was also designed to help prepare for human explorers. That effort includes technology demonstrations like MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) and Ingenuity , as well as the spacesuit samples,” said Katie Stack Morgan, Perseverance’s project scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. Fine, ultrafine While earlier measurements on Mars resolved dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across, PIXL detected two categories of even smaller particles: fine particles measuring less than 2.5 micrometers (a human hair is about 70 micrometers wide) and ultrafine particles around 100 nanometers (about 700 times thinner than a human hair). Particles on PIXL’s Teflon target and SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers. On PIXL’s basaltic glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, dust particle sizes ranged down to about 100 to 300 nanometers. This annotated composite image shows the location on NASA’s Perseverance of the calibration target for rover’s SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals) instrument. At right is a close-up of the calibration target. NASA/JPL-Caltech Static electricity appears to determine which size dust particles stick to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the calibration target attract grains of different sizes. The finest particles stayed attached through years of driving and drilling. Organic polymers like SHERLOC’s Teflon spacesuit sample are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust. The study also found that some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future choices of materials and protective coatings for spacesuits and habitats. Designs such as suitports , which let astronauts enter a suit attached to the outside of a habitat, and dual-chamber airlocks could reduce how much dust gets inside astronauts’ living quarters. “The existence of Mars dust at these ultrafine sizes has been predicted for a long time, and PIXL gave us the chance to measure it directly on Mars,” said Scott VanBommel, a Perseverance scientist at Washington University in St. Louis and the paper’s lead author. “The larger clumps, the Martian dust bunnies, get shaken off over time. But the smallest particles stay behind, and those are the ones that pose the greatest challenge for human support systems.” Chemically, the dust matches the iron- and sulfur-rich composition that earlier missions measured. The PIXL instrument also found the dust to be enriched in phosphorus and detected signs of calcium sulfate. Protecting crews On Earth, airborne particles, or particulate matter, below 2.5 micrometers (that is, fine particles) are tied to a range of negative health effects because they can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Studies have shown that ultrafine particles (those no larger than 100 nanometers) can travel from the nasal cavity to the brain along the olfactory nerve. Martian dust is composed predominantly of silicate minerals and carries chemically reactive compounds, including perchlorates that can disrupt thyroid function and reactive iron that induces cellular damage. Scientists believe that the health risks of Mars dust depend on the quantity of dust and length of exposure. The PIXL results are the first on-site measurements of fine and ultrafine particles on Mars, and this research can inform broader efforts to refine indoor dust-exposure limits for astronauts, develop safe habits, and establish ways to remove dust while exploring Mars. NASA is already working on solutions to extraterrestrial dust hazards, using ground test facilities and lunar missions as proving grounds for future Mars explorers. In March 2025, the agency tested an Electrodynamic Dust Shield , which used electric fields to clear lunar regolith from glass and thermal radiator surfaces on the Moon. Developed at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, it landed on the Moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1. At NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, engineers at the Lunar Development and Test Facility use vacuum chambers and lunar regolith simulant to test spacesuit components, mechanisms, and a Handheld Lunar Electrostatic Dust Mitigation tool ahead of Artemis missions to the lunar surface. NASA JPL also built PIXL and SHERLOC. title: NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected
author: nasa.gov
content: 2 Min Read NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected PIA26780 Credits: BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems Photojournal Navigation Science Photojournal NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets… Photojournal Home Photojournal Search Latest Content Galleries Feedback RSS About Downloads NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected JPEG (1.17 MB) Description The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor is mounted on an assembly ring during inspections in a clean room at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in July 2026. The sunshade structure stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide at its base. Its two flat panels, joined at a 23.5-degree angle, were covered with 864 interconnected solar cells and then tested before arriving in Colorado. This specialized solar array can produce up to 2 kilowatts of power and will generate all the required electricity to charge the onboard batteries that power the spacecraft’s systems. Built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, the sunshade structure was outfitted with its solar cells by SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in January. Environmental testing of the sunshade and solar array was completed at a commercial thermal vacuum testing facility in El Segundo, California, in March and it was delivered to BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems ahead of schedule in May. When in space, NEO Surveyor will seek out some of the hardest-to-find asteroids and comets, some of which may be located in the direction of the Sun — a region of sky where ground-based optical telescopes have a harder time searching. title: NASA SEES Interns Tackle Real-World Challenges in Lunar Exploration
author: nasa.gov
content: Explore This Section Science Science Activation NASA SEES Interns Tackle… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation 4 min read NASA SEES Interns Tackle Real-World Challenges in Lunar Exploration The Matrix Team developed a sophisticated interactive dashboard for the IM-3 mission that allows users to vary engine, spacecraft, and orbital parameters to investigate the effect on propellant margins and landing zone availability. The NASA STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) Enhancement in Earth Science (SEES) Internship Program at the University of Texas Center for Space Research places high school students on small, mission-focused research teams mentored by NASA, academic, and industry experts. During summer 2026, the SEES Mission Architecture Tool for Research, Integration, and eXploration (MATRIX) team focused on applying a method for measuring propellant mass in microgravity, where liquid fuel clings to tank walls instead of settling – a challenge central to NASA’s Artemis missions. The MATRIX team was mentored by Dr. Kevin Crosby, who, along with colleagues at NASA, developed the Modal Propellant Gauging (MPG) approach to microgravity propellant mass gauging at Carthage College in Kenosha, WI. MPG uses the acoustic response of propellant tanks to estimate the mass of fuel inside a tank. The method has been used successfully in several spaceflight experiments and is scheduled for demonstration on the Intuitive Machines IM-3 mission. The IM-3 lander, Trinity, is scheduled to touch down on the Moon in the Reiner Gamma region in 2027. The team developed models for predicting when MPG can take reliable readings during the mission, giving the interns direct experience with a technology preparing for spaceflight and lunar surface operations. Reconstructing a Lunar Mission from Public Data The MATRIX team relied entirely on publicly available sources, including Intuitive Machines’ published mission data. The NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory’s Navigation and Ancillary Information Facility (NAIF) provided detailed trajectory records for the IM-1 and IM-2 missions. By comparing the IM-2 spacecraft’s reconstructed flight path with a model of its motion without engine thrust, the team identified engine burns and estimated the change in velocity associated with each burn. Because a complete IM-3 trajectory is not public, the team wrote a reconstruction algorithm using published IM-1 and IM-2 flight data. To model fluid behavior, the team ran computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations to estimate slosh dynamics within the tanks and conducted Monte Carlo simulations to predict the range of possible propellant states. Identifying Windows for Measurement The team’s analysis showed that MPG can take reliable readings during the two primary burns, Lunar Orbit Insertion (LOI) and Powered Descent, and in some cases during Descent Orbit Insertion. The spacecraft’s starting mass had the greatest effect on how long each gauging window lasts. The MATRIX team also identified candidate IM-3 launch opportunities for 2027 and produced a landing analysis for the Reiner Gamma site that showed the distribution of possible landing sites near the target. Presenting to the Scientific Community The team briefed the Intuitive Machines propulsion group, walking the engineers through their methods and results and demonstrating that a rigorous analysis of an active lunar mission could be built from public data. The students presented their research, “Computational Models to Estimate Modal Propellant Gauging (MPG) Windows on the Intuitive Machines IM-3 Mission,” at the SEES Annual Symposium and the Wisconsin Space Grant Consortium Annual Conference. The team will present again at the American Geophysical Union (AGU) Annual Meeting in San Francisco in December 2026. “This high school team, in a period of less than a month, developed a depth of understanding and facility with advanced methods that rivals advanced graduate students in the field,” said Crosby. “Their work product is exceptional, and their presentation to Intuitive Machines engineers impressed everyone with the sophistication and creativity of their work. The SEES program has consistently provided a unique environment for students to demonstrate they can achieve far more than what is asked of them, even in the most advanced classes.” The SEES program gives 11th and 12th grade students direct experience with the data, tools, and analytical methods used across the aerospace industry. By applying NASA and commercial mission data to an active lunar mission, the MATRIX team contributed analysis relevant to propellant management, a capability needed for in-space refueling, fuel depots, and sustained exploration of the Moon and beyond. Thank you to all the mentors, project assistants, and volunteers who have made SEES possible for over a decade. Crosby, Carthage College and Wisconsin Space Grant Consortium Project Assistant: Mauro Esquivel, mathematics teacher, McAllen, TX For more information, visit: https://www.csr.utexas.edu/sees-internship/ The SEES project is supported by NASA cooperative agreement award number NNH15ZDA004C and is part of the NASA Science Activation Program portfolio, which connects learners with authentic NASA science experiences through partnerships with educators and community organizations. title: NASA Invites Media to Moon Landing Simulation Experience in California
author: Jeanne Neal
content: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Members of the media are invited to tour a new lunar landing simulation at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley on Thursday, Oct. 29, and Friday, Oct. 30. Using a combination of in-house and partner motion-based simulators, NASA is giving astronauts and engineering support teams simulated experiences before crew members pilot commercial human landing systems to the surface of the Moon. Through the Artemis program, NASA is targeting the next lunar landing in 2028. During the tour, media will have an opportunity to participate in a Vertical Motion Simulator ride-along and interview subject matter experts. Media interested in participating should RSVP by Tuesday, Oct. 27 at 5:00 pm PT to the NASA Ames newsroom at: arc-dl-newsroom@mail.nasa.gov . Space is limited, and media must register in advance for consideration. NASA’s media accreditation policy is online. In your RSVP, please note your preference for Oct. 29 or Oct. 30. The landing simulation at Ames was developed by NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston and integrated into the recently upgraded simulator flight deck . As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars. For more information about NASA’s Artemis program, visit: https://www.nasa.gov/artemis -end- Jeanne Neal Ames Research Center, Calif. 650-604-4789 jeanne.c.neal@nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Oct 26, 2026 Related Terms Ames Research Center Artemis Explore More 7 min read NASA, Partners Accelerate Lander Development for 2028 Moon Missions Article 3 days ago 8 min read NASA’s Artemis III Mission to Test Future Moon Lander Operations Article 3 days ago 1 min read NASA to Conduct Low-Altitude Flights Over Texas Farmland Article 6 days ago Keep Exploring Discover Related Topics Ames Research Center Vertical Motion Simulator (VMS) Artemis Human Landing System

title: The best portable chargers
author: Brittany Vincent
content: The best portable charger is the Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) ($229.99 at Anker as of October 2026), because it can fast-charge two laptops and a phone at once, gets back to 80 percent in 40 minutes by Anker’s rating, and stays just under the 100Wh airline limit. If you carry an iPhone, the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro ($109.99 at Anker) snaps on magnetically and charges at up to 25W with no cable, and if you want a laptop-capable bank for less, the UGREEN Nexode 20,000mAh 130W costs $59.99. Plenty has changed since our last update: our previous budget pick appears to be a model INIU recalled in December 2025, Anker recalled several of its own banks in 2025, Qi2.2 magnetic banks raised wireless charging speeds from 15W to 25W, and airlines tightened power bank rules this spring. This guide is for anyone who wants to keep a phone, tablet, or laptop running away from an outlet; if you need to power appliances or camp for a week, our guide to the best portable power stations fits better. Best overall: Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) Best for travel: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 20,000mAh 130W Best MagSafe: Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro Best multipurpose: Anker Power Bank (10K, Fusion, Built-In Cable) Best for laptops: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 25,000mAh 145W Best with AC outlet: Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC Best for hiking: Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 Best budget: Anker Zolo Power Bank (10K, 30W) How we chose the best portable chargers We’ve used power banks for years to keep phones, cameras, and laptops alive while covering events, traveling, and working away from a desk, and our own testing covered the UGREEN 145W bank here and the predecessor of our travel pick. For this update, we also read the 2026 power bank reviews and roundups from outlets including Macworld, Digital Camera World, Expert Reviews, Engadget, Tom’s Guide, and CleverHiker, logged which products independent testers kept landing on, and noted where testers disagreed with each other or with the maker’s numbers. Then we checked every finalist against its maker’s current product page and a live retail listing on October 21, 2026. We also checked each brand’s recall history with the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which changed two of our picks. The other seven picks are researched rather than tested by us, and each section says which is which. We have a MagGo 2 Pro on the way for review and will update this guide as our own results come in. The best portable chargers: Recommendations The picks below run from a $30 pocket battery to a $250 bank with a wall outlet built in. Before you buy, know the two numbers that matter most: how much your devices draw when they charge, and whether you plan to fly with the battery. Output figures in the table are the makers’ ratings. Prices were checked on October 21, 2026 at the retailer named in each pick’s section, and power banks go on sale often, so check before you buy. Pick Capacity Max output Price Anker Prime 26K 26,250mAh 300W $229.99 UGREEN Nexode 20K 20,000mAh 130W $59.99 Anker MagGo 2 Pro 10,000mAh 45W (25W wireless) $109.99 Anker 10K Fusion 10,000mAh 30W $52.99 UGREEN Nexode 25K 25,000mAh 145W $79.99 Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC 25,600mAh 100W AC $249.95 Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 10,000mAh 22.5W $83.95 Anker Zolo 10K 10,000mAh 30W $29.99 Best overall: Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) Anker See It Pros 300W total output, with up to 140W from each of two USB-C ports, per Anker 26,250mAh, just under the 100Wh carry-on limit Anker rates it at 80 percent recharged in 40 minutes Display shows battery level and what each port is doing Cons $229.99 is a lot for a power bank 1.32 pounds, per Anker, so it lives in a bag, not a pocket Don’t confuse it with the older Prime 27,650mAh 250W model Specs Model: A110A Capacity: 26,250mAh (99.75Wh) Ports: Two USB-C, one USB-A Max output: 300W total; 140W per USB-C port, 22.5W USB-A (Anker’s rating) Weight: 1.32 pounds (600 grams, Anker’s spec) Price: $229.99 at Anker as of October 26, 2026 (on sale) Anker’s Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W), model A110A, is the one power bank we’d buy if we could only own one. It’s expensive, at $229.99 at Anker as of October 26, 2026 (a sale price; Anker shows $30.01 off), and Macworld found it for $199.98 at Amazon in July. What you get for that is a battery with no real ceiling for everyday gear. Anker rates each of its two USB-C ports at 140W and the bank at 300W total, so it can fast-charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro and a second laptop at the same time and still run a phone off the 22.5W USB-A port. Most banks make you wait as long to refill them as they took to drain. Anker rates the Prime at 50 percent in 13 minutes and 80 percent in 40 minutes, Anker’s page doesn’t say which setup those figures assume, but its fastest refill uses both USB-C ports at once with two 140W chargers, so expect slower results from a single charger. A built-in display shows the remaining charge and what each port is drawing, and the capacity is tuned for flying. At 26,250mAh, it comes in at 99.75Wh, just under the 100Wh line airlines use for carry-on batteries that don’t need approval. Expert Reviews, Engadget, and Macworld all ranked it at or near the top of their 2026 power bank roundups. The trade is size. At 1.32 pounds, per Anker, it’s a bag battery, and if you only ever charge a phone, the UGREEN 20,000mAh bank below does that job for a quarter of the price. Check the model number before you buy, too. Anker also sold an older Prime 27,650mAh 250W bank (model A1340), which shows as sold out on Anker’s site, and the A110A is also sold in a bundle with a charging base. This recommendation covers the A110A power bank on its own. Best for travel: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 20,000mAh 130W UGREEN Pros 130W total output, per UGREEN, enough to fast-charge most laptops Color display shows remaining charge, voltage, and current 20,000mAh works out to roughly 74Wh by our arithmetic, well under the 100Wh carry-on line Its predecessor held up well in our own testing Cons About 480 grams (16.9 ounces), per UGREEN, so it’s a bag battery, not a pocket one No built-in cable $59.99 is a sale price; UGREEN lists it at $89.99 Specs Model: PB721 Capacity: 20,000mAh Ports: Two USB-C (UGREEN’s US page) Max output: 130W total (UGREEN’s rating) Weight: 480 grams (UGREEN’s spec) Price: $59.99 at UGREEN as of October 21, 2026 (regular $89.99) A 20,000mAh battery is the size that covers the most situations without becoming a burden. It’s enough to recharge most phones more than once, top off a tablet, or buy a laptop a couple more hours, and it still slides into a backpack’s laptop sleeve. UGREEN’s Nexode Power Bank 20,000mAh 130W (model PB721) is the one we’d buy at that size. It costs $59.99 at UGREEN as of October 21, 2026, a sale price against a $89.99 list price, and UGREEN rates it for 130W of total output across two USB-C ports. This is the successor to the 20,000mAh, 100W UGREEN bank that earned our travel award last time, and the predecessor’s results are why it’s back in that slot. In our testing, that model took an iPhone 16 Pro Max from empty to 55 percent in 30 minutes and to full in about an hour and a half, with 66 percent of the bank’s own charge left afterward. It also fully recharged a 2024 iPad Pro in two hours with 36 percent to spare. We haven’t run the same tests on the 130W version yet, so treat those as results from the previous model, not this one. The feature we’d miss most on any other bank is the screen. It shows the remaining charge plus the voltage and current going to each device, so you can tell at a glance whether your laptop is actually fast charging or trickling along on a bad cable. The bank weighs about 480 grams, per UGREEN, and there’s no built-in cable, so pack a USB-C cable rated for 100W if you plan to charge a laptop with it. UGREEN’s US page names two USB-C ports; some international listings add a USB-A port, so check the listing if you still need one. Best MagSafe: Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro Anker See It Pros Up to 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging on iPhone 16 and newer Built-in fan with Cool and Silent modes, per Anker 45W USB-C in and out; Anker rates it at 80 percent recharged in 52 minutes Adjustable kickstand and a status display Cons Older iPhones are limited to 15W wirelessly Reviewers found the fan audible on a quiet desk No built-in cable, and pricey for 10,000mAh Specs Model: A110R Capacity: 10,000mAh Wireless output: Up to 25W Qi2.2 (Anker’s rating) Wired output: 45W USB-C (Anker’s rating) Weight: 7.7 ounces (Anker’s spec) Price: $109.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026 A magnetic battery snaps onto the back of an iPhone and charges it with no cable at all, which is why it’s the kind of power bank people actually carry every day. Anker’s MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro (model A110R) is the one to get right now. It costs $109.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026, and it was $87.99 at Amazon during October’s Prime Big Deal Days. It’s built on Qi2.2, a newer version of the magnetic wireless standard that grew out of Apple’s MagSafe, and Anker rates it at up to 25W wirelessly and 45W through its USB-C port. That 25W figure only applies to the iPhone 16 lineup and newer. Per Macworld, the iPhone 15 and older, plus the iPhone 17e, charge at 15W and the iPhone Air at 20W, and Anker excludes the iPhone 16e, which lacks MagSafe magnets. Macworld’s reviewer charged an iPhone 16 Pro to 50 percent in 30 minutes with the fan running. Faster wireless charging means more heat, and Anker’s answer is a small built-in fan with Cool and Silent modes. Reviewers at Macworld and Digital Camera World both found it audible up close, and Digital Camera World’s tester noticed the phone still got warm. If it bothers you on a nightstand, Silent mode turns the fan off. The rest of the package earns the price. A fold-out kickstand props the phone up for video calls or watching something on a flight, the display shows battery level, temperature, and battery health, and 45W input means the bank itself refills quickly. Anker says it’s designed for Apple devices, so Android owners should look elsewhere, even though one reviewer did get a Pixel to charge on it. If you’d rather have a built-in cable than a kickstand, Ugreen’s MagFlow Pro is the rival Macworld compared it against. We have a MagGo 2 Pro on the way for a full review and will update this section with our own results. Best multipurpose: Anker Power Bank (10K, Fusion, Built-In Cable) Anker Pros Folding wall prongs make it a wall charger too Built-in USB-C cable plus a second USB-C port Up to 30W output, per Anker Replaces two things in a travel bag Cons Heavier than a standard wall charger, so it can sag out of loose outlets 30W is fine for phones and tablets but slow for laptops The built-in cable is short Specs Model: A1637 Capacity: 10,000mAh Ports: Built-in USB-C cable (0.82 feet, per Anker), one USB-C port, folding AC plug Max output: 30W (Anker’s rating) Price: $52.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026 (on sale) Our previous multipurpose pick was the Anker PowerCore Fusion 10000. Anker’s current US lineup leads with a newer version, and the idea is unchanged. The Anker Power Bank (10K, Fusion, Built-In Cable), model A1637, is a 10,000mAh battery with folding wall prongs, so it works as a wall charger when you’re near an outlet and a power bank when you aren’t. The new version adds a built-in USB-C cable, which fixes a familiar power bank problem: having the battery but not the cord. There’s also a second USB-C port for charging two devices at once, and Anker rates the output at up to 30W. That’s plenty for a phone, earbuds, or a tablet, but slow for a laptop. It costs $52.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026, on sale, and B&H listed it for $44.99 the same day. Like the model it replaces, it’s heavier than a normal wall charger, and in a loose hotel outlet, the weight can pull it partway out. If that happens, plug it into a power strip instead. For anyone who travels light, losing a separate charger from the bag is worth the trade. Best for laptops: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 25,000mAh 145W UGREEN See It Pros About 90Wh, per UGREEN, while staying under the 100Wh carry-on line Charges a laptop and a phone at the same time Side display shows remaining charge Held up through months of our testing Cons Runs warm with a laptop plugged in for long stretches UGREEN’s own listing is inconsistent about the total output No AC outlet for laptops that need their own power brick Specs Capacity: 25,000mAh (about 90Wh, per UGREEN) Ports: Three Max output: 145W total in the product name; UGREEN’s images list 140W, 65W, and 22.5W by port Price: $79.99 at UGREEN as of October 21, 2026 If you work from coffee shops, libraries, or airport gates, the power bank that matters is the one that keeps your laptop alive until an outlet frees up. UGREEN’s Nexode 25,000mAh 145W Power Bank has been our pick for that since we tested it, and it’s still on sale at $79.99 at UGREEN as of October 21, 2026. UGREEN rates the battery at about 90Wh, which leaves it comfortably under the 100Wh limit for carry-on bags. After using it regularly for months, it never let us down. It extended a 16-inch MacBook Pro by a few hours and fully recharged an iPhone 15 Pro Max and a Nintendo Switch OLED . It did run warm when a laptop drew power from it for long stretches, though never hot enough to worry us. A side display shows the remaining charge, so you know whether to plug it in before you leave. One thing to know about the numbers: UGREEN’s product name says 145W, while its own product images list 140W, 65W, and 22.5W for the three ports. Either way, the main USB-C port has enough power to fast-charge most laptops, and the other two cover a phone and earbuds at the same time. The one thing it can’t do is run a laptop that only charges from its own AC adapter. For that, see the Goal Zero below. Best with AC outlet: Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC Goal Zero See It Pros 100W AC outlet for gear that only runs off its own wall adapter Two USB-C ports at 60W and 100W, plus 15W wireless charging 94.7Wh, under the 100Wh carry-on line Cons Expensive at $249.95 The AC outlet is modified sine wave, which some electronics dislike Some owners report port and display failures Specs Model: 22200 (4th generation) Capacity: 25,600mAh (94.7Wh) Ports: AC outlet, two USB-C, two USB-A, Qi wireless pad Max output: 100W AC; 100W USB-C (Goal Zero’s rating) Weight: 2.1 pounds Price: $249.95 at Goal Zero and B&H as of October 21, 2026 Some gear still only charges from its own power brick: older laptops, camera battery chargers, a drone charger. The Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC gives you a real AC outlet, rated at 100W, in a bank that stays under the 100Wh carry-on limit. It costs $249.95 at Goal Zero and B&H as of October 21, 2026. Goal Zero shows that as a discount from $274.85. The current model is the fourth-generation Sherpa 100AC, part number 22200. Beyond the outlet, it has two USB-C ports rated at 60W and 100W, two USB-A ports, and a 15W wireless pad on top. Goal Zero has sold several Sherpa generations under nearly the same name, and the previous one, model 22050, had a much weaker 5W wireless pad. Make sure the listing says 4th generation or 22200. Know a couple of things before you buy. The AC outlet is modified sine wave rather than pure sine, which is fine for most chargers but can make some motors and audio gear hum or run poorly. Owner ratings are also mixed: REI showed a 3.9-star average across 63 reviews in October 2026, with some owners describing port and display failures. Goal Zero is now owned by BioLite, which bought the brand in April 2025 and has kept its products on sale. If you need more than about 100W of AC power, a portable power station is the better tool. Best for hiking: Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 Nitecore Pros About 5 ounces (143 grams), per Nitecore’s retailers IPX7 waterproof rating Two USB-C ports with pass-through charging Carbon fiber composite shell Cons 22.5W maximum, slow for anything bigger than a phone No built-in flashlight Expensive for 10,000mAh Specs Capacity: 10,000mAh (39Wh) Ports: Two USB-C Max output: 22.5W (Nitecore’s rating) Water resistance: IPX7 Weight: 143 grams (5 ounces) Price: $83.95 at Garage Grown Gear as of October 21, 2026 Our previous outdoor pick, Goal Zero’s Venture 75, was sold out at Goal Zero and Backcountry when we checked in October 2026, with no successor announced. For hiking and backpacking, we’d now carry the Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4. It’s a 10,000mAh battery that weighs about 5 ounces and carries an IPX7 rating, meaning it’s built to survive brief submersion, so rain, a creek crossing, or a soggy tent won’t kill it. It costs $83.95 at Garage Grown Gear as of October 21, 2026. Weight is the whole point here. Most of the other 10,000mAh banks in CleverHiker’s 2026 testing weighed between 6.6 and 8.5 ounces, and on a multi-day trip, those extra ounces add up. Nitecore gets the weight down with a carbon fiber composite shell and silicon-carbon cells, and the bank has two USB-C ports with pass-through charging, so you can recharge it and your phone from one wall plug at a trailhead motel. It was the top backpacking pick in CleverHiker’s power bank testing this year. It’s not a fast charger. Nitecore rates it at 22.5W, which is fine for a phone, a headlamp, or a GPS messenger but slow for a tablet. Like every power bank, it also delivers less than its label suggests, because energy is lost converting the cells’ voltage up to USB levels. If you’d rather recharge from the sun on longer trips, see our guide to the best solar power banks . Best budget: Anker Zolo Power Bank (10K, 30W) Anker See It Pros $29.99 list, and often less on sale Built-in 5.4-inch USB-C cable plus a second USB-C port 30W output, per Anker, quick enough for most phones Not one of the Anker models in the 2025 recalls Cons The built-in cable is short Anker’s FAQ caps pass-through charging at 5V/3A Fewer ports than our larger picks Specs Model: A1688 Capacity: 10,000mAh Ports: Built-in USB-C cable, one USB-C port Max output: 30W (Anker’s rating) Price: $29.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026 Sometimes you just want a cheap battery that won’t let you down. The Anker Zolo Power Bank (10K, 30W), model A1688, costs $29.99 at Anker as of October 21, 2026, and Amazon has sold it for about $22 in sales this summer. It has a 5.4-inch USB-C cable built in, a second USB-C port for another device, and enough capacity to get most people through a long day of heavy phone use. We replaced our previous budget pick, a 10,000mAh INIU bank with a paw-print light, because it appears to match the INIU BI-B41 that the Consumer Product Safety Commission recalled in December 2025 after reports of overheating and fires. Only certain serial numbers were affected, but we’d rather not recommend a model with a recall on its record. If you already own one, check the serial number printed on the bank against INIU’s recall page. Anker had recalls of its own in 2025, and the model number matters with this brand. The 10K Zolo we recommend here, the A1688, isn’t on either recall list. The Zolo 20K with built-in cables (models A1681 and A1689) was recalled in September 2025, so don’t assume the bigger Zolo is the same product. Check the model number printed on the back of any Anker bank you already own. Picks we retired, and why Every pick from our previous version of this guide either changed or left. Here’s what happened to each. OtterBox Performance Fast Charge 20,000mAh (former best overall): In October 2026, we only found it at business and overseas resellers, and its 18W output is slow next to current banks. Anker PowerCore Fusion 10000 (former best multipurpose): Anker’s US store now leads with the 10K Fusion with a built-in cable, our new multipurpose pick. UGREEN Nexode 20,000mAh 100W (former best for travel): UGREEN’s US store now lists the 130W version in its place, and it keeps the travel award. Goal Zero Venture 75 (former best with flashlight): Sold out at Goal Zero and Backcountry in October 2026, with no successor announced. Mophie Charge Stream (former best with wireless charging): No longer in Mophie’s lineup, and its 10W wireless pad is slow next to today’s Qi2.2 magnetic banks. INIU 10,000mAh (former best budget): Appears to match the INIU BI-B41 recalled in December 2025. More in the budget section above. What to consider when buying a portable charger A power bank is a battery plus the electronics that turn its power into something your devices can use. These are the specs that separate a good one from a disappointing one. Capacity: mAh, watt-hours, and why you get less than the label Capacity is listed in milliamp-hours (mAh), measured at the cells’ own voltage, about 3.7 volts for most lithium-ion banks. Your phone charges at 5 volts or more, and converting between the two loses energy as heat. That’s why a 10,000mAh bank won’t charge a phone with a 5,000mAh battery twice. In Macworld’s 2026 capacity tests, 10,000mAh banks averaged 174 percent of a phone battery, not 200 percent. Watt-hours (Wh) are the more useful number, because they don’t depend on voltage and they’re what airlines use. Multiply mAh by the cell voltage and divide by 1,000: a 20,000mAh bank at 3.7 volts is about 74Wh. As a rough guide, 10,000mAh covers a day of phone use, 20,000mAh covers a weekend or a tablet, and 25,000mAh or more is for laptops. Output: match the watts to your devices Output, in watts, decides how fast a bank charges your devices. Most current phones fast charge at 20W to 45W, tablets want 30W or so, and laptops need 45W to 140W depending on the model. Look for USB Power Delivery (USB PD) on the USB-C ports, since that’s the standard laptops and iPhones use, and check whether the advertised maximum comes from one port or is split across several. A bank rated for 100W total might only give 60W to each of two laptops. Wireless and magnetic charging Wireless power banks use the Qi standard. Qi2 added MagSafe-style magnets that line the phone up with the charging coil, and Qi2.2 raised the speed to 25W. Every iPhone since the iPhone 12 (except the 16e) has the magnets; Android support is spotty, and some phones need a magnetic case. Wireless charging is convenient but less efficient than a cable, so it gets more heat and fewer total charges out of the same battery. Our explainer on wired vs. wireless charging goes deeper, and our MagSafe accessories guide covers the cases, mounts, and wallets that use the same magnets. Flying with a power bank in 2026 Power banks have to go in your carry-on, never checked luggage. The FAA allows any number of batteries up to 100Wh, and up to two between 101Wh and 160Wh with airline approval. Airlines added rules of their own this year. Southwest allows one power bank per passenger as of April 2026, American and Delta cap passengers at two banks of 100Wh or less as of May 2026, and several airlines now bar power banks from overhead bins. International aviation rules adopted in March 2026 also limit passengers to two and ban recharging a power bank in flight. Rules are still changing, so check your airline’s page before you fly. Every pick in this guide is under 100Wh. Recalls and safety Power bank recalls have become common enough that checking is worth a minute. In 2025, Anker recalled more than 1.1 million PowerCore 10000 banks (model A1263) in June and about 481,000 more banks across five models in September. INIU recalled about 210,000 BI-B41 banks in December 2025. Recalls usually cover specific model and serial numbers, which are printed on the bank itself. Search the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s recall site for your brand. Whatever you own, stop using a bank that’s swollen, cracked, or too hot to hold, and don’t charge one on a bed or couch where heat can’t escape. Buy from brands that sell under their own name and have a working support page, since they’re the ones that issue recalls and replacements when something goes wrong. FAQs Q: What’s the best portable charger in 2026? The Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W). It costs $229.99 at Anker as of October 2026, can fast-charge two laptops at once, and stays just under the 100Wh carry-on limit. For less money, the UGREEN Nexode 20,000mAh 130W ($59.99) still charges a laptop, and iPhone owners who want a magnetic battery should get the Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro. Q: How much does a portable charger cost? As of October 2026, a good 10,000mAh bank from a known brand costs $25 to $60. Magnetic wireless banks cost $60 to $150. High-output laptop banks run $80 to $230, and banks with a built-in AC outlet cost $200 or more. Q: Can I bring a power bank on a plane? Yes, in your carry-on only. The FAA allows batteries up to 100Wh without approval, and some airlines, including Southwest, American, and Delta, now limit how many you can bring and where you can stow them. Check your airline’s rules before you fly. Q: How do I know if my power bank was recalled? Find the model number and serial number printed on the bank, then search the Consumer Product Safety Commission’s recall site and the maker’s support page. Recent recalls include Anker models A1263, A1257, A1647, A1652, A1681, and A1689 and the INIU BI-B41, though some recalls cover only certain serial numbers. Q: What’s the difference between MagSafe and Qi2.2? MagSafe is Apple’s magnetic charging system for iPhones. Qi2 is the open standard built on it, and Qi2.2 raised its top speed to 25W. A Qi2.2 power bank like the Anker MagGo 2 Pro charges an iPhone 16 or newer at up to 25W and most older iPhones at 15W. Q: Will a portable charger damage my phone? No. Your phone controls how much power it accepts, and a power bank from a reputable brand only supplies what the phone asks for. If a bank delivers power badly or develops a fault, recent phones will slow down or stop charging and warn you. Q: Should a portable charger get hot? Warm is normal, because some energy is lost as heat while charging, especially wirelessly. Hot is not. If a bank or your phone gets too hot to hold comfortably, unplug everything, move the bank away from anything flammable, and stop using it if it happens again. Q: How long does a portable charger last? Most power banks keep useful capacity for a few years of regular use, and many makers rate their cells for several hundred full cycles. Storing a bank about half charged in a cool place helps it age more slowly. Replace one that swells, no longer holds a charge, or gets unusually hot. Final thoughts on the best portable chargers Best overall: Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) , 300W and a fast refill, for nearly everything you carry Best for travel: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 20,000mAh 130W , a 20,000mAh bank with a display, at a quarter of the Prime’s price Best MagSafe: Anker MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro , 25W magnetic charging for the iPhone 16 and newer, with a kickstand Best multipurpose: Anker Power Bank (10K, Fusion, Built-In Cable) , a wall charger and battery in one, with a built-in cable Best for laptops: UGREEN Nexode Power Bank 25,000mAh 145W , our long-term tested pick for keeping a laptop running Best with AC outlet: Goal Zero Sherpa 100AC , a real AC outlet in a bank you can still fly with Best for hiking: Nitecore NB10000 Gen 4 , 5 ounces and waterproof, for the trail Best budget: Anker Zolo Power Bank (10K, 30W) , a $30 bank from a brand you know A dead phone at the wrong moment is more than an inconvenience. It can leave you unable to call for help, find your way home, or pull up a boarding pass. Pick a bank sized for what you actually carry, check its model number against recent recalls, and charge it before you need it. Then stop worrying about the battery icon. title: The best pizza ovens
author: Carla Sosenko
content: The best pizza oven for most people is the Gozney Arc ($799.99 at Gozney as of October 2026), a 14-inch propane oven with a thermometer in the box that I’ve cooked on myself. If space or budget is tight, its smaller sibling, the Gozney Arc Lite ($399.99), heats quickly, holds its heat, and packs away easily. If you’d rather cook over live fire, the Ooni Karu 2 ($449) burns wood or charcoal out of the box. Plenty has changed since our last update: Gozney replaced the Dome we tested with the Dome Gen 2, Ooni renamed the Karu 12G to Karu 2 and put our old favorite, the first-generation Karu 12, on clearance, Ooni now sells a stone that rotates your pizza for you, and the ALFA oven we recommended for big pies is discontinued. This guide covers outdoor ovens plus one indoor pick; if you only cook inside, our guide to the best indoor pizza ovens goes deeper. Best overall: Gozney Arc Best compact: Gozney Arc Lite Best wood-fired: Ooni Karu 2 Best premium: Gozney Dome Gen 2 Most versatile: Ninja Woodfire 8-in-1 Outdoor Oven Best budget and best for beginners: Nexgrill Ora 12 Best for large pizzas: Ooni Koda 2 Max Best automatic rotating stone: Ooni Koda 2 Rotating Stone Bundle Best indoor: Ooni Volt 2 How we chose the best pizza ovens I’ve cooked on the Gozney Arc and Arc Lite myself, and PopSci tested the Ninja Woodfire, the Nexgrill Ora, and the original Gozney Dome for earlier versions of this guide. The rest of the picks are research-based. We didn’t run a new comparative test round for this update. Instead, we combined our earlier hands-on testing with current manufacturer specs and measurements from named independent reviewers, and we focused on heat-up time, cooking consistency, ease of use, capacity, and fire management. For the researched picks, we read the manufacturers’ spec pages and help centers, checked every price at a named retailer on October 21, 2026, and read reviews from TechRadar, T3, Livingetc, and Bob Vila, crediting their measurements by name. Maximum temperatures are labeled as manufacturer ratings because a stone rarely reaches them in use. We also checked each brand’s lineup for successors and discontinued models, which is how the old Dome, the first-generation Karu 12, and the ALFA 4 Pizze ended up reworked or cut. We favored ovens you can buy new from the manufacturer or a major retailer today, and we cut picks that only turned up through third-party sellers, which is what happened to our old countertop pick. The best pizza ovens: Reviews & Recommendations Pizza ovens split along fuel lines. Propane is the easiest to live with, wood and charcoal require more attention but give you a live-fire cooking experience, and electric models trade top-end heat for convenience. Our picks range from $149 to $2,299.99 and cover all three, plus an indoor oven. Maximum temperatures are manufacturer ratings, and each card’s specs list how we evaluated it: tested, researched, or predecessor tested (we tested the previous version and researched the current one). Prices and availability were checked from October 21 to October 26, 2026, at the retailers named and may change. Best overall: Gozney Arc Why it won: The Gozney Arc keeps the rolling side flame of the Arc Lite but adds room for 14-inch pies, a thicker stone, and a thermometer in the box. Gozney See It Pros Takes pizzas up to 14 inches Thermometer included in the box Thicker 20mm stone than the Arc Lite’s 12mm, plus two-layer insulation Rolling side flame with adjustable flame control Cons $799.99, twice the Arc Lite’s price 47.5 pounds, nearly double the Arc Lite Propane only Specs Best for: Most people How we evaluated it: Tested (Stan Horaczek) Fuel: Propane Max temperature: 950°F (Gozney’s rating) Pizza size: Up to 14 inches Weight: 47.5 pounds, oven only Price: $799.99 at Gozney I’ve cooked on both of Gozney’s compact Arc ovens, and the regular Gozney Arc is the one I’d recommend first. It costs $799.99 at Gozney, twice the price of the Arc Lite below, and the extra money addresses the Lite’s two biggest limits: the Arc takes a 14-inch pizza instead of a 12-inch one, and it comes with a thermometer, so you’re not guessing at the oven’s temperature. On paper, the rest of the upgrade is about holding heat. Gozney lists a 20mm cordierite stone, thicker than the Arc Lite’s 12mm, inside a two-layer insulated body, and that extra stone mass is what you want when you’re launching pizzas back to back. The heat comes from a lateral gas burner on one side that Gozney says recreates a wood-fired rolling flame, the same layout as the Lite, with an adjustable flame control. The box also includes a hose and regulator for a standard propane tank, a burner guard, and a stone adjustment tool. The tradeoff is bulk. Gozney lists the Arc at 47.5 pounds and about 19 by 22 inches, nearly twice the Arc Lite’s weight, so it’s still a tabletop oven but less of a grab-it-and-go one. It runs on propane only, and Gozney extends the warranty from one year to five if you register within 60 days. The built-in thermometer reads the oven, not the stone, so an infrared thermometer is still useful. If you want 16-inch pies, the Arc XL costs $999.99. Best compact: Gozney Arc Lite Why it won: The Arc Lite heats fast and holds its heat in a 26.4-pound body that costs half as much as the Arc. Gozney See It Pros Heats up quickly and holds heat well between pizzas Compact 26.4-pound body is easy to store Cools down relatively quickly once you shut off the gas Gozney sells a deep lineup of high-end accessories for it Cons No built-in thermometer, so plan on an infrared thermometer Tops out at 12-inch pizzas Propane only Specs Best for: Small spaces and tighter budgets How we evaluated it: Tested (Stan Horaczek) Fuel: Propane Max temperature: 950°F (Gozney’s rating) Pizza size: Up to 12 inches Weight: 26.4 pounds, oven only Price: $399.99 at Gozney I’ve been cooking on the Gozney Arc Lite too, and it’s the one I’d pick if storage space or budget matters more than pie size. It heats up quickly, it holds that heat well from one pizza to the next, and it cools down relatively quickly once you turn off the gas, which matters when you’re the one waiting to put it away. It also feels like a much more expensive oven than it is. Gozney launched the Arc Lite in March 2026 at $399.99, which is still its price (it dropped to $349.99 during Gozney’s Labor Day sale). Size is the reason it gets its own slot. Gozney lists it at 26.4 pounds and about 17 by 19 inches, with a half-inch cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pies and a rolling flame along one side of the chamber, controlled by a dial on the front. It fits on a small patio table or a shelf in the garage between cooks. That footprint may also suit some balconies, provided your building rules, local restrictions, and Gozney’s clearance requirements permit a propane oven. Bob Vila’s reviewer, writing in May 2026, needed 20 to 30 minutes of preheat and finished most pizzas in 2 to 3 minutes. My one real gripe is the missing thermometer. The Arc Lite has no built-in temperature readout, so you can’t see when the stone is ready, and an infrared thermometer is strongly recommended if you want repeatable results. Gozney sells its own infrared thermometer for $49.99, and our guide to the best infrared thermometers has other options. Gozney offers an extensive accessory lineup (covers, a stand shared with the bigger Arc models, peels), although the extras add up quickly. If you want 14-inch pies and a thermometer in the box, step up to the Arc above; the Arc XL goes to 16 inches for $999.99. Best wood-fired: Ooni Karu 2 Why it won: The Karu 2 burns wood or charcoal out of the box and takes a $120 gas burner later, so you don’t have to pick a fuel up front. Ooni See It Pros Burns wood or charcoal out of the box Optional gas burner (a $120 add-on at Ooni) adds propane Built-in thermometer tracks oven temperature Same oven as the Karu 12G, renamed, so older reviews still apply Cons Live fire takes practice to keep steady Gas costs extra 33.6 pounds is heavier than the first-generation Karu 12 Specs Best for: Wood-fired cooking How we evaluated it: Researched Fuel: Wood or charcoal; propane with the optional burner Max temperature: 950°F (Ooni’s rating) Pizza size: Up to 12 inches (13.3-inch stone) Weight: 33.6 pounds Price: $449 at Ooni; $569 with the gas burner Propane is the easy way to make pizza. Wood is the more involved way, and the Ooni Karu 2 is the oven we’d buy for it. It burns hardwood or charcoal right out of the box, and the optional gas burner (a $120 add-on) gives you propane for weeknights when you don’t feel like tending a fire. Ooni lists it at $449. If the name is new to you, it shouldn’t be: Ooni’s own FAQ says the Karu 12G and the Karu 2 are the exact same oven, so the Karu 2 is a rename, not a redesign. Wood takes more attention than gas. You’re feeding small splits into the rear tray, watching the flame, and adjusting airflow to keep the stone hot, and how close you get to Ooni’s 950°F rating depends on dry fuel and a well-fed fire. The Karu 2’s built-in thermometer tracks the oven temperature, but an infrared thermometer is still useful because it tells you when the stone itself is ready for a pizza. Live fire can add some smoke character, especially on longer cooks, though for a pizza that bakes in about a minute or two the difference versus gas may be subtle. Most of the appeal is the fire itself. Our previous best overall, the first-generation Ooni Karu 12 , is still on sale at Ooni for $249 (down from $349). At 26.5 pounds, it’s lighter and $200 cheaper than the Karu 2, and it’s a good buy while the clearance stock lasts. Best premium: Gozney Dome Gen 2 Why it won: The Dome Gen 2 adds a built-in air-and-floor temperature console and room for a 16-inch pie to the design we tested. Gozney See It Pros Sold in propane and natural gas versions, and also burns wood or charcoal Built-in console reads air and floor temperature and takes two meat probes Fits one 16-inch pizza or two 10-inch pies Thick 30mm stone holds heat for back-to-back pies Cons $2,299.99 before the stand 136.7 pounds, oven only Gozney’s powered Wood-Fire Control Kit costs extra 40 to 45 minutes to heat, per TechRadar’s review Specs Best for: Outdoor kitchens How we evaluated it: Predecessor tested; current model researched Fuel: Propane or natural gas, depending on the version; also burns wood or charcoal. Gozney’s optional Wood-Fire Control Kit adds powered airflow and finer live-fire control. Max temperature: 950°F (Gozney’s rating) Pizza size: One 16-inch or two 10-inch pizzas Weight: 136.7 pounds, oven only Price: $2,299.99 at Gozney We tested the original Gozney Dome for an earlier version of this guide, and it impressed us. In gas mode it passed 930°F in under 20 minutes without any tending, and it took us three or four pies to dial in a classic Neapolitan, after which it was easy to repeat. That Dome is gone now. Gozney replaced it with the Dome Gen 2 in fall 2025, its old product link now forwards to the Gen 2 lineup, and Gozney’s help center says the cheaper Dome S1 is no longer made. What follows about the Gen 2 comes from Gozney’s specs and other outlets’ reviews, not our own testing. The Gen 2 is a bigger, smarter oven. Gozney’s specs call for one 16-inch pizza or two 10-inch pies on a 30mm cordierite stone, 136.7 pounds for the oven alone, and a built-in digital console that shows air and floor temperature, runs a cook timer, and takes two meat probes. It comes in separate propane and natural-gas versions and can also burn wood or charcoal. Gozney’s optional Wood-Fire Control Kit ($199.99, sold out when we checked) adds powered airflow and finer control over a live fire. Gas mode works a lot like a propane grill : light it, then manage the pizza’s distance from the flame. It’s a project, though, and the stand is extra. TechRadar’s December 2025 review lists a 40- to 45-minute heat time, says the oven does best with little or no wind blowing into the mouth, and notes that the Gen 2 drops the original’s steam injector attachment for bread. T3’s reviewer couldn’t get the igniter to spark even after two battery changes and lit it with a match instead. It was $1,999.99 during Gozney’s Labor Day sale, and the Dome XL Gen 2 fits an 18-inch pie for $2,799.99. Most versatile: Ninja Woodfire 8-in-1 Outdoor Oven Why it won: We tested the Ninja Woodfire, and it’s the only pick here with a built-in pellet smoker and a dehydrate mode. Ninja See It Pros Easy to use: set it, preheat, and close the door Pizza, roast, broil, bake, smoke, dehydrate, and keep-warm modes Pellet box adds smoke flavor for low-and-slow cooks Runs on electricity, so no propane tank or wood Cons 700°F max (Ninja’s spec) is cooler than the gas and wood ovens here A 12-inch pizza barely fits Out of stock at SharkNinja when we checked Specs Best for: Pizza plus smoking and roasting How we evaluated it: Tested Fuel: Electric (wood pellets for smoke flavor) Max temperature: 700°F (Ninja’s spec) Pizza size: Up to 12 inches Weight: 33 pounds, unit only (per Ninja) Price: $329.99 at Best Buy We love pizza as much as the next person, but you have to eat something else occasionally, and the Ninja Woodfire 8-in-1 Outdoor Oven handles most of it. It’s about the size of a microwave and runs on electricity. You plug it in, add the right rack or the pizza stone, set the temperature, and let it preheat. Next to the gas and wood ovens on this list, it’s close to hands-off. It has five pizza settings: thin crust, pan, New York, Neapolitan, and frozen. In our testing, the Neapolitan and New York modes took about 15 minutes to hit max temperature, then we slid in the pizza and closed the door. There’s almost no learning curve and no turning or babysitting, and when we opened the door we had a well-cooked pie. The chamber is snug, though. Our roughly 12-inch pizza just barely fit and took some nudging to keep it from oozing over the sides. The stone lifts out, but Ninja says not to get it wet : let it cool completely, scrape it gently with a nonmetal tool, and wipe away debris with a soft cloth. Once you’re done with pizza, it roasts, broils, bakes, dehydrates, and smokes. It held a steady 225°F to 250°F in our testing, and the pellet box on the side adds smoke flavor the way a pellet grill does. SharkNinja’s own store showed the Woodfire out of stock at its $399.99 list price, while Best Buy had it for $329.99 with a 4.1-star average across 864 ratings. SharkNinja’s newer Ninja Artisan MO201 ($249.99 on sale, down from $299.99) keeps the 12-inch capacity and 700°F ceiling but drops the pellet smoker. Best budget and best for beginners: Nexgrill Ora 12 Why it won: For $149, the Nexgrill Ora’s rotating-stone knob gave us a more even bake than turning pies by hand. Nexggrill See It Pros Knob rotates the stone for even cooking Easy setup: drop in the stone pieces and connect propane Compact design $149 at Nexgrill Cons No thermometer A couple of Home Depot reviewers say the knob occasionally sticks Specs Best for: Budget buyers and beginners How we evaluated it: Tested Fuel: Propane Max temperature: 900°F (Nexgrill’s rating) Pizza size: Up to 12 inches Weight: Not listed by Nexgrill Price: $149 at Nexgrill Cooking homemade pizza in a 900°F oven can be intimidating, and the Nexgrill Ora 12 makes it easier to get good results on your first try. A knob on the right side rotates the central pizza stone, turning your pie for an even cook. With most ovens, you turn the pizza yourself with a peel, and at these temperatures 10 seconds can be the difference between a well-cooked pizza and a charred one. Setup was easy. The oven comes fully assembled; all we had to do was drop in the five pieces of its stone, which felt like a big, easy puzzle, then connect a propane tank. Gas is beginner-friendly because the heat is steady without feeding wood. A chamber on top can hold wood if you want a little smoke. Turning it on was as simple as twisting the power knob to the flame icon. The flame sits toward the back, so rotating matters, and the oven was ready in about 10 minutes in our testing (Nexgrill rates it to reach 900°F in about 20). Our one complaint is the lack of a built-in thermometer. Pizzas went in and out the same way as in other ovens: flour the dough on a peel, top it lightly, launch it, and pull it after about 90 to 120 seconds. The difference was a more even cook every time, thanks to the knob, which has enough resistance that you won’t send the pie spinning. Nexgrill sells it for $149 , though The Home Depot listed it at $206.12 the same day, where it averages 3.9 stars across 116 reviews and a couple of owners mention the knob occasionally sticking. Best for large pizzas: Ooni Koda 2 Max Why it won: The Koda 2 Max is rated for a 20-inch pie or three 10-inch pizzas at once for about $1,000 less than the Dome Gen 2. Ooni See It Pros Rated for one 20-inch pizza, two 12-inch, or three 10-inch pies Two independently controlled burners Includes Ooni’s Connect digital temperature hub Sold in propane and natural gas versions Cons 95 pounds, so it needs a sturdy table $1,299 Out of stock with preorders open when we checked Specs Best for: Big pies and crowds How we evaluated it: Researched Fuel: Propane or natural gas, depending on the version Max temperature: 950°F (Ooni’s rating) Pizza size: One 20-inch, two 12-inch, or three 10-inch pizzas (Ooni’s rating) Weight: 95 pounds Price: $1,299 at Ooni Feeding a backyard full of people one 12-inch pie at a time gets old fast. The Ooni Koda 2 Max is our pick for that party. Ooni rates its 24-by-21-inch cordierite stone for one 20-inch New York-style pie, two 12-inch pizzas, or three 10-inch pizzas at once, and two independently controlled burners let you run the two sides at different heat. It’s gas only, in separate propane and natural-gas versions, and Ooni includes its Connect digital temperature hub and a food probe, so you’re not guessing at stone temperature the way you are with the Arc Lite. We replaced the ALFA 4 Pizze with it in this slot. The ALFA we used to link is discontinued, and the current wood-fired top ran about $2,800 to $3,000 at BBQGuys and Embers Living, before you build a base for it. At 95 pounds, it needs a permanent spot on a stout table. Ooni lists it at $1,299, though the page showed it out of stock with preorders open, so check the delivery estimate before you plan a party around it. It also works with Ooni’s rotating stone , sold separately or in a $1,649 bundle. Best automatic rotating stone: Ooni Koda 2 Rotating Stone Bundle Why it won: This is the least expensive way to get Ooni’s motorized stone, which turns the pizza so you don’t have to. Ooni See It Pros Stone turns continuously or in 90-degree steps Wave a hand or peel at the sensor to start and stop it About 7 hours of rotation on four AA batteries, per Ooni Bundle includes the regular stone too Cons Rotating stone fits only Ooni’s Koda 2 ovens Base Koda 2 has no thermometer (Ooni’s hub is sold separately) Out of stock with preorders open when we checked Specs Best for: Hands-off turning How we evaluated it: Researched Fuel: Propane Max temperature: 950°F (Ooni’s rating) Pizza size: 12 inches on the rotating stone; 14 inches on the standard stone Weight: 35.27 pounds, oven only Price: $799 at Ooni (regular $828) Turning the pizza is the skill that separates a leopard-spotted crust from a scorched one, and Ooni’s rotating stone takes it off your plate. Launched in March 2026, it replaces the standard stone in Ooni’s Koda 2 ovens with a motor-driven one powered by a battery pack under the oven floor. Wave your hand or a peel in front of its sensor and it starts or stops. Ooni says it can spin continuously or turn 90 degrees at timed intervals, and that four AA batteries last about seven hours of rotation. We picked the bundle with the standard 14-inch Koda 2 because it’s the least expensive of Ooni’s three rotating-stone bundles: $799 (regular $828), versus $499 for the oven alone and $329 for the 12-inch stone on its own. You still launch the pizza yourself. Livingetc’s reviewer, writing in May 2026, got an uneven first pie because she moved it too soon, then got even results by turning the flame down to about half; each pizza took 90 seconds to two minutes. The rotating stone caps the base Koda 2 at 12-inch pies (the standard stone that’s also in the box handles 14), and the base Koda 2 has no thermometer. The cheaper way to rotate is the Nexgrill Ora’s manual knob for $149. Ooni showed the bundle out of stock with preorders open, so check the ship date. Best indoor: Ooni Volt 2 Why it won: The Volt 2 is the successor to the indoor oven we tested and liked best, and Ooni rates it for 850°F from a standard outlet. Ooni See It Pros Ooni says it’s made for indoor use Rated to 850°F Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan presets, plus a Boost mode Dough-proofing mode and a dishwasher-safe grease filter Cons $699 Heavy and bulky at 38.8 pounds Charcoal Grey was sold out when we checked Specs Best for: Indoor cooking How we evaluated it: Predecessor tested; current model researched Fuel: Electric (120V, 1,600W) Max temperature: 850°F (Ooni’s rating) Pizza size: Up to 12 inches Weight: 38.8 pounds Price: $699 at Ooni No yard, no balcony, or no interest in standing outside in February? The Ooni Volt 2 brings high-heat pizza indoors. Ooni says it’s made for indoor use only, plugs into a standard 120-volt outlet, and reaches 850°F. It replaced the original Ooni Volt, which PopSci tested and named the top pick in our guide to the best indoor pizza ovens . We haven’t tested the Volt 2 itself, so this pick is research-based. Ooni calls the control system Pizza Intelligence. In practice, it’s presets for Neapolitan, thin-and-crispy, and pan pizzas that manage the top and bottom elements for you, plus a Boost mode that Ooni says drives the top element hard enough for a 90-second Neapolitan. A proofing mode drops as low as 70°F for dough, and the smoke and grease filter goes in the dishwasher. It costs $699 at Ooni, and Ooni extends the warranty to three years if you register it. The Charcoal Grey version was sold out when we checked, while Polar White was listed at the same price. At 38.8 pounds, it wants a permanent spot on the counter. What to consider when buying a pizza oven Every oven on this list can make a good pizza. The differences come down to fuel, size, and how much help you want while you learn. Fuel Propane is the default for a reason. You turn a knob, wait for the stone to heat, and the flame stays steady all night. Wood and charcoal take more attention, since you’re feeding the fire and managing airflow; some people want that ritual, and live fire can add some smoke character, though on a pizza that bakes in a minute or two it may be subtle. Electric ovens like the Ninja Woodfire and Ooni Volt 2 are the easiest of all, though Ninja rates the Woodfire to 700°F, below the 900°F to 950°F ratings on the gas ovens here. The Dome Gen 2 and Koda 2 Max are sold in separate propane and natural-gas configurations, so choose the version that matches your setup. Size and weight A 12-inch pizza capacity is enough for most households, and it’s what keeps the Arc Lite and Karu 2 portable. The 14-inch Gozney Arc is the middle ground at 47.5 pounds. Bigger stones let you cook larger pies or several at once, but the weight climbs fast: their makers list the Koda 2 Max at 95 pounds and the Dome Gen 2 at 136.7 pounds. Measure your table, and decide whether the oven lives outside full time or goes back into storage after each cook. A thermometer Stone temperature is the key measurement for deciding when to launch a pizza, and several ovens here don’t show it. The Arc Lite, the Nexgrill Ora, and the base Koda 2 have no built-in readout, so budget about $50 for an infrared thermometer. The Karu 2, Gozney Arc, and Arc XL have built-in thermometers, the Dome Gen 2 has a digital console, and the Koda 2 Max comes with Ooni’s temperature hub, but an infrared reading of the stone is still useful on all of them. Turning the pizza Most outdoor ovens put the flame on one side or at the back, so the side nearest the fire cooks faster and you have to turn the pie regularly with a turning peel. If that sounds stressful, the Nexgrill Ora’s manual rotation knob and Ooni’s motorized rotating stone handle it for you. FAQs How hot does a pizza oven need to be? Neapolitan-style pizza needs intense heat to cook in a couple of minutes or less, which is why most gas and wood ovens here are rated to 900°F or 950°F. Those are manufacturer ratings; the stone itself usually reads lower in use, especially on wood. In our testing, pies on the Nexgrill Ora took about 90 to 120 seconds. New York-style and pan pizzas do better a bit cooler and a bit longer. Is a gas or wood-fired pizza oven better? Gas is better for most people because the heat is steady and it takes almost no fire management. Wood and charcoal are more hands-on and can add some smoke character, though on a fast-baking pizza the difference may be subtle. Multi-fuel ovens like the Ooni Karu 2 burn wood or charcoal out of the box and take an optional gas burner, so you don’t have to choose up front. Do I need an infrared thermometer for a pizza oven? It’s strongly recommended for any oven without a built-in readout, including the Gozney Arc Lite, the Nexgrill Ora, and the base Ooni Koda 2, and it’s still useful on ovens that have one. An infrared thermometer reads the stone’s surface temperature, which is what tells you when to launch. Gozney’s costs $49.99 as of October 2026. Can you use an outdoor pizza oven indoors or in a garage? No. Propane, wood, and charcoal ovens burn fuel and produce carbon monoxide, so they belong outside with open air around them. Follow your oven’s manual for clearances. If you want to cook indoors, use an electric oven designed for it, like the Ooni Volt 2, which Ooni says is for indoor use only. What’s the difference between the Ooni Karu 12, Karu 12G, and Karu 2? The Karu 12G and Karu 2 are the same oven; Ooni’s FAQ says so directly, and the Karu 2 is the current name. The Karu 12 is the first-generation model, which Ooni was selling for $249 (down from $349) as of October 2026. Is the Gozney Dome discontinued? The original Gozney Dome has been replaced by the Dome Gen 2, which launched in fall 2025 starting at $2,299.99, and Gozney’s old Dome product page now forwards to the Gen 2 lineup. Gozney’s help center says the Dome S1 is no longer manufactured. A larger Dome XL Gen 2 costs $2,799.99. Has a pizza oven been recalled recently? Yes. On July 9, 2026, the CPSC announced a recall of about 12,660 Cuisinart Propel+ Four Burner 3-in-1 Gas Grills with a pizza oven (model CGG-6331), because the oven’s tempered glass window can shatter. They were sold at Lowe’s, Walmart, and Cuisinart.com from December 2024 through May 2026. A search of the CPSC recall database on October 21, 2026, found no recalls for the specific models recommended here. When do pizza ovens go on sale? The deepest discounts we documented in 2026 came during holiday sales. During Labor Day 2026, Gozney cut the Arc Lite to $349.99 and the Dome Gen 2 to $1,999.99, and Ooni’s Memorial Day 2026 sale had the first-generation Karu 12 at $249. We’ll update this guide after Black Friday. Final thoughts on the best pizza ovens The Gozney Arc is the best starting point for most buyers: it takes 14-inch pies, comes with a thermometer, and costs $799.99. If space or budget is tight, the $399.99 Gozney Arc Lite heats quickly, holds its heat, and stores easily; add a $50 infrared thermometer. Choose the Ooni Karu 2 if tending a live fire is part of the appeal, the Nexgrill Ora 12 if price and easy turning matter most, or the Ooni Volt 2 if your pizza oven has to live in the kitchen. For crowds, the Ooni Koda 2 Max handles 20-inch pies, and the Gozney Dome Gen 2 is the one to build an outdoor kitchen around. The post The best pizza ovens appeared first on Popular Science .

title: Parents of premature newborns can have more skin-to-skin contact with new device
author: Andrew Paul
content: For infants struggling in a neonatal intensive care unit (NICU, incubators dramatically lower premature infant mortality. However, these neonatal-specific incubators create their own challenges for skin-to-skin contact. This kind of touch is more than an emotional moment for a family—it helps regulate the baby’s body temperature, stimulates their immune system, encourages breastfeeding, and even reduces issues of postpartum depression . The World Health Organization recommends every infant born before 37 weeks old receive at least eight hours of contact every day. Incubators make reaching this goal practically impossible, but that doesn’t negate the equipment’s own medical benefits. Doctors and parents have struggled to balance the two options for decades, but a new device may finally provide a bridge between both needs: the Skincubator . As the word-combo implies, the Skincubator is a wearable machine that functions as a portable neonatal incubator, while still offering prolonged skin-to-skin contact. The device includes all the necessary, lifesaving equipment featured in a neonatal unit including ventilator tubes, catheter, and arterial lines. It also maintains a stable microclimate with 70–90 percent humidity at 84.2–87.8 degrees Fahrenheit, while keeping the child in a safe, secure, and stable fetal position. A specially designed, retractable pad then carefully slides beneath the infant to facilitate skin-to-skin for hours at a time. Skincubator’s creators designed the device over four years and have already reported successful trials in countries like Germany. In December 2025, the company received a Breakthrough Device designation from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) allowing them to quickly begin similar efforts in the United States. “This is a great invention,” Tiffany Ikwuagwu, a new mother of twins and the first U.S. trial participant, recently said in a video from Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston . “I think the fact that I can help regulate the babies’ heart[s] and help the babies relax, and just have that connection to them, is very special.” Moving forward, the device’s creators hope to collaborate with more hospitals around the country while offering parents a chance to leverage the benefits of both advanced medical devices and skin-to-skin contact. title: Read censored texts from around the world at this Minecraft library
author: Andrew Paul
content: High-end graphics, cinematic plotlines, and challenging boss battles aren’t what made Minecraft one of the most popular video games of all time. After nearly 15 years, millions of people still play it every day because it doesn’t offer any of those features. Instead, Minecraft hinges exploring, building, and experimenting inside a virtually infinite digital universe. For many players, logging onto a server provides a sense of freedom that the real world sadly denies them. It’s not symbolic, either. Minecraft ’s digital freedom produces tangible benefits that extend far beyond the game itself. In 2020, the international press advocacy organization Reporters Without Borders (also known as Reporters Sans Frontières, or RSF) announced the Uncensored Library , an online repository filled with books, essays, and articles by individuals routinely silenced by their authoritarian governments. But instead of stashing the collection in an unassuming corner of the game, RSF and the Minecraft design collective BlockWorks built a massive, gorgeous neoclassical library located on a picturesque, pixelated island.  “Freedom of expression is a fundamental human right, and yet, there are countries that seek to censor their citizens or prevent them from accessing certain information,” RSF explais . “This is why The Uncensored Library exists; a grand digital library meant to combat censorship – and it’s all accessible through Minecraft.” Even six years after its debut, the project regularly goes viral on social media, and receives routine updates from RSF and BlockWorks. There is even a map to guide visitors through the digital institution’s multiple wings that are organized by country. Until recently, the library hosted materials from writers contending with particularly repressive governments across eight nations, including Iran, Saudi Arabia, Russia, and Egypt. Earlier this year, RSF added a section for the United States following the Trump administration’s pushbacks on the press. “Often, suppressing stories takes a less overt form than direct censorship,” RSF North America executive director Clayton Weimers said at the time , adding that the decision to include the U.S. was intended to highlight that “fully authoritarian regimes do not have a monopoly on free press violations.” The Uncensored Library is accessible either by downloading the files to your personal computer, or accessing the visit.uncensoredlibrary.com server while playing Minecraft .
