title: The 2026 Mama Bear Award goes to a black bear with a mullet
author: Laura Baisas
content: While Fat Bear Week has come and gone, there is another group of Alaskan bears currently getting their due. The United States Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest are doling out the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in southeastern Alaska. Black bear Goblin at Anan Wildlife Observatory Site dining on salmon. Image: USDA Forest Service. Meet the Anan Bears Tongass is the nation’s largest national forest and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. It is home to Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises ), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, which is home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.  According to Friends of Anan , there are 39 known bears that feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. Thirty-one are black bears ( Ursus americanus ) and eight are brown bears ( Ursus arctos ). Like their counterparts further to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return here every summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits.  The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org ’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics. And the 2026 Mama Bear Award goes to… Osso! The adult female black bear was first spotted in 2022 and has a white chest patch shaped like the letter I. She usually has a mullet of hair on the top of her head at the end of the summer season. Her name is spelled either Osso (Italian for bone), because her chest patch also resembles a bone or Oso (Spanish for bear). She had one cub in 2019, two in 2024, and three this year.   Mother bears show fearless aggression when sensing any danger to their young, and the Forest Service says Osso is a prime example of this tenacity. “Feeding and watching out for three cubs was more than a full-time job, especially with so many other bears about,” the team writes . “Scuba Sue, a female brown bear, got too close for comfort on this occasion and Osso didn’t hesitate before sending her cubs up a tree and taking a swipe at Sue. Not all heroes wear capes, some pop their jaws and raise their claws.” Unfortunately, Osso was only seen with two cubs in August. While it is not clear what happened to her third cub, the Forest Service assumes she did her best to protect the cubs.  The post The 2026 Mama Bear Award goes to a black bear with a mullet appeared first on Popular Science .

title: Earth’s first fully-marine amphibian stalked the seafloor with a chunky, bony body
author: Laura Baisas
content: Nearly 237 million years ago, a spiky and toothy bottom dweller skulked the Late Triassic oceans that once covered present-day China. What sets this newly discovered giant salamander -sized prehistoric amphibian apart is not its impressive body–it’s that it lived in the ocean. The newly described Gerrothorax maritimus is the first example of a fully marine amphibian in the fossil record, according to a study published today in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution . There are currently over 8,000 species of living amphibians, and none have been known to live in fully marine (salt water) environments. Less than two percent like crab-eating frogs ( Fejervarya cancrivora ) and some spotted salamandars have any degree of salt tolerance. Other four-limbed animals, including birds, reptiles, and mammals, all have species who can survive without any food or water from land. There was also no evidence of a fully marine amphibian in the fossil record. Until now. In this study, a team from the University of California, Davis in the United States and Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou in China analyzed two nearly complete skeletons found in southern China’s Guizhou Province. The fossils were found in an area once covered by ocean and hundreds of miles from any large land mass.  “This area is part of an ecosystem that we’ve been looking at and trying to reconstruct,” Ryosuke Motani , a study co-author and paleontologist at UC Davis, said in a statement . “We’ve been mostly studying marine reptiles and the fish from this place, but now we also have this amphibian and it’s a sort of very unusual member of the lineage.”    The well-preserved skeletons helped the team reconstruct what Gerrothorax maritimus looked like and offer clues to its marine life. Notably, it had a flattened body covered in bony armor. This armor likely defended it against predators like the 10-foot-long ichthyosaur that stalked these seas millions of years ago. Gerrothorax maritimus itself was roughly three feet long with a disc-shaped body. New fossil evidence reveals the first fully marine amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus, which dates to the Late Triassic period nearly 237 million years ago. The animal had a flattened body that was covered in bony armor, a potential defense mechanism against predators like ichthyosaurs. Image: Ryosuke Motani, UC Davis. Ryosuke Motani “If you think about today’s amphibians, this animal is unusual because it’s big,” Motani said. “It’s probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what’s different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky.”    Based on Gerrothorax maritimus’   bony armor and the shape of its skull, the team believes that it was a bottom-dwelling suction feeder, similar to the wobbegong, a family of 12 bottom-dwelling carpet shark species alive today.  “They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in,” said Motanti. Modern amphibians can’t live in marine environments because their skin does not tolerate salt. The skin is permeable, and allows them to use it for multiple purposes like respiration . Amphibians don’t drink or breathe through the same mouth opening since they can do both just using their skin.  The fossilized left hand of the newly discovered prehistoric marine amphibian Gerrothorax maritimus . Image: Ryosuke Motani/UC Davis. Ryosuke Motani Due to this salt-intolerant biology, they must live in or near freshwater. While some modern species like the crab-eating frog have some degree of salt tolerance, they will lose weight in brackish waters and must recover in freshwater. The researchers propose that bony armor and a more fish-like body helped Gerrothorax maritimus circumvent this limitation. The armor would have kept its skin from absorbing water, meaning that it needed to drink salt water with its mouth, and then absorb it through its digestive tract. The creature’s gills would have allowed it to filter out the salt. Other species in the Gerrothorax also have gills.  According to the team, the fossils’ location within deep sea sediments and the fact that they were nearly complete led them to believe that Gerrothorax maritimus was an ocean-dweller.  “Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” said Motani. “But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived.”  The post Earth’s first fully-marine amphibian stalked the seafloor with a chunky, bony body appeared first on Popular Science .

title: Family finds World War II grenade in grandfather’s basement
author: Andrew Paul
content: A family near Kalamazoo, Michagan was in for a surprise while cleaning out their grandfather’s basement. Amid the dusty storeroom clutter, the Paw Paw Township residents discovered a vintage, possibly live grenade from World War II apparently forgotten after decades in storage. Unsure what to do with their newfound, potentially deadly device, family members quickly contacted local emergency services. According to the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office , first responders confirmed the grenade’s authenticity and estimated that it dates back to 1945. However, they couldn’t immediately determine if the weapon remained functional after more than 80 years tucked away in the cellar. For that, officials needed to call in the Kalamazoo Department of Public Safety Bomb Squad. Peering inside the grenade required specially designed X-ray equipment, which lets explosives experts examine internal components from a safe distance before handling the weapon. Thankfully, the process remained relatively straightforward and the team confirmed that the veteran wasn’t a reckless wartime collector—someone already had decommissioned the grenade long ago. That doesn’t let history buffs off the hook, however. “The Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office reminds residents that old military ordnance, ammunition, and other potentially explosive devices can remain dangerous for decades, regardless of their age or appearance,” officials cautioned. Unexpected, military-grade finds are more common than it may seem. Recently, a late WWII veteran’s neighbors located a trove of files related to Stalag Luft 3 , the infamous Nazi prison camp depicted in The Great Escape . Researchers are regularly rediscovering long-lost shipwrecks from the era, while restoration specialists are even bringing vintage aircraft back to life. First responders also offered some standard guidelines for anyone else who might stumble across unexpected incendiary devices, but they all basically boil down to one simple rule: do not mess with them. Any suspected explosives—no matter how old—should always be handled by trained professionals, so it’s best to immediately retreat to a safe distance and call the proper authorities. “Even items believed to be military souvenirs or decommissioned equipment should be treated as potentially hazardous until examined by qualified professionals,” the sheriff’s office added. title: Celebrate the flavors of fall with three spicy recipes
author: Priya Mani
content: Adapted from Spiced: Recipes Celebrating Spices from Around the World by Priya Mani. (Phaidon, US $54.95, 2026) Kimchi transforms in flavor and texture as it ferments. Image: Priya Mani. Kimchi / Baechu kimchi Makes: about 2 1/4 lb / 1 kg kimchi Preparation time: 30 minutes, plus 2 hours standing and 8–16 days fermenting Cooking time: 8–10 minutes In Korea, families gather each fall (autumn) for kimjang , to make and share large batches of kimchi to sustain them through the winter. This version is classic baechu kimchi made with napa (Chinese) cabbage. Seek out fermented shrimp, saeujeot , at a Korean grocery, while glutinous rice flour, coarse gochugaru flakes, and dashi (powder and concentrate) are available in Asian stores.  Kimchi transforms in flavor and texture as it ferments. Fresh kimchi, baechu geotjeori , is crisp, with a bright gochugaru flavor; it pairs with steamed rice, salads, or bibimbap . After a month, kimchi is sour and piquant; add it to pancakes, kimchijeon , soup, kimchi guk , and Korean Fried Rice ( Kimchi-bokkeumbap , page 154). When the kimchi has aged and soured, use it to make rich stews such as kimchi jjigae or mukeunji jjigae , a slow-braised pork stew. INGREDIENTS 1 large napa (Chinese) cabbage ( Brassica pekinensis ), about 2 1/4 lb / 1 kg 1/ 8 cup (1 oz / 30 g) coarse sea salt 2 tablespoons glutinous rice or all-purpose (plain) flour 1 cup (8 fl oz / 250 ml) dashi or vegan dashi 1 tablespoon turbinado (demerara) sugar 5 cloves garlic, minced 3/4-oz /20-g piece fresh ginger, minced 1 small yellow onion, halved 1/4 cup (2 fl oz / 60 ml) fish sauce (optional, or replace with soy sauce for a plant-forward version) 2 tablespoons fermented shrimp (Korean-style saeujeot , see Glossary, page 481), minced (optional) 1 cup (4 oz / 120 g) finely milled gochugaru 1 small Asian pear ( bae ), grated, or a small apple (optional) 3 scallions (spring onions), cut into rings 1 small Korean radish or daikon, cut into thin matchsticks, 2 inches (5 cm) long 1 small carrot, cut into thin matchsticks, 2 inches (5 cm) long DIRECTIONS Score the base of the napa (Chinese) cabbage and tear it in half lengthwise. Submerge it in a large bowl of cold water for a few minutes. Remove, and rub the coarse sea salt between the cabbage leaves and set aside to weep in a large bowl for 2 hours; toss the cabbage occasionally.  To make the kimchi paste, whisk the rice flour with the dashi in a small saucepan, making sure there are no lumps. Place it over medium-low heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring constantly until it thickens into a translucent paste. Stir in the sugar, remove from the heat, and let cool for about 15 minutes.  In a blender, combine the cooled paste, garlic, ginger, onion, fish sauce (or soy sauce), and minced fermented shrimp, if using, until smooth. Scoop it into a large bowl, add the gochugaru, Asian pear, scallions (spring onions), radish, and carrot and mix well. This is called yangnyeomjang . Set it aside while you prepare the cabbage.  Drain the cabbage and wash well in multiple changes of cold water. Taste a leaf, it must be well salted and crispy. If it is too salty, let it soak in a bowl of fresh, cold water for 30 minutes more. With very clean hands (or wearing food-grade gloves), spread the yangnyeomjang paste between the cabbage leaves, ensuring an even coating. Fold each half cabbage tightly and pack into suitably sized sterilized glass jars (see page 479). Leave at room temperature for 1–2 days to start fermenting, then store in the refrigerator. For the best flavor, let it ferment for at least 1–2 weeks before eating. Properly stored, kimchi lasts for months in the refrigerator, developing deeper flavors over time. Cheongyang gochu / C. annuum / 8,000–10,000 SHU In Korean, gochu simply means chile. Gochugaru, or chile powder specifically used for kimchi, can be milled from several varieties of local chile to suit regional preferences, though the mild, dried, red hong gochu is a good base chile. Another variety, Cheongyang gochu , grown in Cheongyang in South Korea, is a cross with spicy Thai chiles that yields a more pungent product, which can be added to the gochugaru to taste. Red hong gochu are harvested at full maturity, then dehydrated mechanically, but in traditional practice, they are laid out under the clear fall (autumn) sun for several days in a method called taekyung (or taeyangcho ). The peppers are then split open and the stems, seeds, and pith are removed, leaving a brilliant red fruit behind. This is milled to produce flakes or a coarse powder, shiny and full of luster. Gochugaru is sold as coarse or finely milled powder. Kimchi Fried Rice / Kimchi-bokkeumbap Serves: 4 Preparation time: 15 minutes, plus 3 hours for cooling the rice  Cooking time: 20 minutes Kimchi fried rice is a quick dish to make with matured kimchi. You can use leftover rice, or cook it for the dish as this recipe describes, though as with most fried-rice dishes, day-old rice works best. You can let the rice dry out for a few hours or refrigerate it for the best results. Gochujang is stocked in the Asian pantry aisle of supermarkets. INGREDIENTS 1 cup (7 oz / 200 g) short- or medium-grain rice, or 1 lb 5 oz / 600 g cooked rice 2 teaspoons toasted sesame oil, plus extra for drizzling 1 tablespoon neutral oil 3 1/2 oz / 100 g ground (minced) beef or firm tofu, cut into bite-sized pieces 1 clove garlic, minced 2 scallions (spring onions), green parts only, cut into thin rings 7 oz / 200 g well-fermented Kimchi (page 152), chopped 1 tablespoon gochujang (Korean red pepper paste, see Glossary, page 481) 1 tablespoon soy sauce 1 teaspoon granulated sugar (optional, to balance acidity) 2 tablespoons kimchi juice (from the kimchi container), optional To serve 1 teaspoon white sesame seeds, toasted 2 tablespoons toasted seaweed, cut into thin strips 4 eggs, fried DIRECTIONS Cook the rice (see page 479), drizzle with sesame oil, and turn to coat well. Spread the rice out on a baking sheet, cover with a net or cheesecloth (muslin) and dry it out for at least 3 hours or overnight. You can also refrigerate it. The next day, fluff the rice with a fork to separate the grains.  Heat the neutral oil in a large skillet or wok over medium heat. Add the beef or tofu and stir-fry for 8–10 minutes, until well cooked, or the tofu cubes have taken on some color. Increase the heat to medium-high, then toss in the garlic and half the scallions (spring onions), and cook, stirring for 2 minutes, or until fragrant. Add the kimchi and cook for a minute more, stirring occasionally, so it softens and releases its juices. Stir in the gochujang, soy sauce, and sugar and mix well.  Add the rice and toss again until evenly coated. (Add some of the juices from the kimchi jar for some moisture and extra tang to the rice if you like.) Cook for another 3–4 minutes, pressing the rice down so it sizzles and crisps in the oil. Drizzle with sesame oil and mix. Garnish with sesame seeds, seaweed, and the remaining scallion greens. Divide among serving plates and serve with a fried egg on top. Kimchi Tofu / Dubu kimchi Serves: 4 Preparation time: 15 minutes Cooking time: 30 minutes This is a very popular anju , or bar snack, in Korea, served alongside soju or makgeolli . INGREDIENTS 1 lb / 450 g firm tofu 12 oz / 350 g Kimchi (page 152), chopped 2 Asian scallions (spring onions), sliced thinly, reserve the green parts to garnish 1 small onion, thinly sliced into half-moons 1 teaspoon grated fresh ginger 2 cloves garlic, minced 2 tablespoons gochujang (see Glossary, page 481) 1–2 tablespoons soy sauce 1–2 tablespoons toasted sesame oil, plus extra to finish 1 teaspoon granulated sugar 2 teaspoons sesame seeds (ideally a mix of black and white) salt DIRECTIONS In a saucepan of salted water, place the tofu, and simmer it over medium heat for about 15 minutes. Remove carefully with a slotted spoon and cut into 1/2-inch (1-cm) thick slices.  Place the kimchi and the remaining ingredients in a mixing bowl (reserving half of the mixed sesame seeds to garnish) and let them marinate for 10 minutes. Transfer to a skillet (frying pan) and bring to a simmer over medium heat. Let the liquids sizzle and nearly evaporate, then turn off the heat. Arrange the tofu pieces fanned in a ring on a plate. Pour on the warm kimchi mixture, drizzle with more sesame oil to finish, and scatter the scallion (spring onions) greens on top, to serve. Calabrian Chile Paste / Bomba alla calabrese Makes: about 3 cups (25 fl oz / 750 ml)  Preparation time: 45 minutes, plus 30 hours resting Bomba alla calabrese is often sold in small jars playfully packed like a “firecracker,” nodding to the condiment’s assertive heat from fresh red, peperoncini a mazzetti chiles. Toss some bomba with pasta, serve it atop bruschetta, or dip your crackers in it—its heat is very moreish, tempting you to dip into it one more time, every time. Chop all the vegetables into 1/4-inch (5-mm) dice. INGREDIENTS 1 large eggplant (aubergine), diced 1 large red bell pepper, cored, seeded, and diced 1 stalk celery (about 8 inches / 20 cm), diced 1 carrot, diced (optional) 1 small bunch basil, leaves picked 2–3 tablespoons coarse sea salt, as needed 20 fresh peperoncini a mazzetti chiles, diced (or fewer, if you prefer) 1/4 cup (2 fl oz / 60 ml) white wine vinegar, plus extra if needed 2–3 cloves garlic, minced 1 1/ 2 oz / 40 g anchovies or sardines in oil, finely chopped (optional) 1 cup (8 fl oz / 250 ml) extra virgin olive oil, plus extra as needed DIRECTIONS Place the eggplant (aubergine), bell pepper, celery, and carrot in a large bowl.  Rinse the basil leaves and pat them dry with a paper towel. In a large mixing bowl, sprinkle coarse salt at the bottom, then add alternating layers of vegetables and basil, generously sprinkling salt between the layers. Cover with a plate, place a heavy weight, such as a small stone mortar on top, and let it rest for 24 hours. Meanwhile, place the chopped peperoncini chiles in a separate bowl and add 1/4 teaspoon of coarse salt. Wearing food-safe gloves, massage well, then cover with plastic wrap (clingfilm) and let stand alongside the salted vegetables. After 24 hours, squeeze the vegetables thoroughly to remove as much liquid as possible. A potato ricer or sieve works well for this step. Transfer the drained vegetables to a clean, non- reactive bowl (like glass), add the vinegar, cover, and let it rest for 6 hours. Then, squeeze them again to remove the excess vinegar. Place the drained vegetables and salted peperoncini in a food processor and pulse in short bursts until coarsely chopped, avoiding making a smooth purée. Add the garlic and anchovies, if using, then taste to check if the salting is optimal. The condiment’s flavor has not yet developed, this is just to ensure it is not too salty. I like to add the briny liquid from the peperoncini to retain its burn, but you can skip it to moderate the heat level. Spoon the mixture into sterilized glass jars (see page 479), leaving space at the top. Pour enough olive oil to cover the vegetables completely, then seal the jars tightly. Store in a cool, dark place for up to a month. The condiment will mellow and become very flavorful as it sits in the spices and aromatics for a week. After opening and using, always push down any vegetable matter from the sides and top off with more olive oil to keep the surface sealed from air. Peperoncini a mazzetti / C. annuum / 15,000–30,000 SHU In Calabria, at the toe of the Italian peninsula, flanked by the Ionian Sea to the east and the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west, hot, dry winds sear over the Calabrian coast from North Africa. Many feisty chiles thrive in the region’s clay soil, the spirit of many of Italy’s iconic condiments including ’nduja, sardella, and bomba alla Calabrese. Peperoncini a mazzetti are a local Calabrian chile pepper whose fruits grow in tight clusters ( mazzetti means “little bunches”). Because of their curious appearance, many gardeners grow them as decorative plants as well as for culinary use. They tend to be pungent but not excessively fiery, with a fairly direct chile heat that works well fresh, cooked, or dried. They are sold in bundles, fresh or sun-dried, still perched on their stems. A crisp green chile with nearly no heat also goes by the name peperoncini (or frigitelli or Campanian friarelli peppers). In Italy, they are served pan-fried as a snack with a little salt. She founded Appetite Studio, based in Copenhagen, and is the author of, and contributor to, several food books articles for the BBC, and journals, including Bloomsbury Handbook of Indian Cuisine (Bloomsbury Academic, 2023). In 2022 she won the prestigious Guild of Food Writers Award (2022) and the International Association for Culinary Professionals (IACP) award. She is a trustee of the Oxford Food Symposium, and a director at the British Guild of Food Writers, leading the committee on Diversity. title: In 1934, a doctor brought a dog back to life. He tried to do the same with humans.
author: Shoshi Parks
content: Under the harsh glare of overhead lights at a laboratory at the University of California at Berkeley, Lazarus II lay motionless . Dr. Robert E. Cornish, who’d asphyxiated the rangy white fox terrier with ether and nitrogen, watched the clock. Six minutes after the final heartbeat, the scientist gathered up the dog and strapped him to a teeterboard, a see-saw-like invention whose back-and-forth, up-and-down motion Cornish believed was key to restoring the blood’s circulation.  He pushed a saline solution primed with oxygen, heart-stimulating adrenalin, and the liver extract heparin into a vein in Lazarus’ thigh, then lowered his head over the patient. As his assistant rocked the teeterboard and rubbed the little body vigorously, Cornish exhaled deep breaths into the dog’s mouth and lungs. Long seconds turned to minutes and then, suddenly, Lazarus gasped and jerked his leg. Slowly, his heart began to beat. Lazarus II had returned from the dead. Dr. Cornish’s real-life zombies With the invention of modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) still a quarter century off , resurrecting Lazarus after his heart stopped was something of a miracle in 1934. But while the fox terrier lived for another eight hours and 13 minutes, he did not live well, stuck in a restless zombie state punctuated by the occasional whine, bark, and panting. “Irreversible damage occurs to either the heart or the brain after a period of time, making a good recovery impossible,” Samuel Tisherman, professor of surgery and director for the Center for Critical Care and Trauma Education at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, tells Popular Science .  Lazarus II wasn’t Cornish’s first attempt to revive dying patients using his teeterboard. He wasn’t even the first Lazarus. The young scientist, a former child prodigy who’d earned his doctorate from UC Berkeley at age 22, became obsessed with resuscitation sometime around 1933.  Dr. Cornish feeds one of his dog subjects named Scooter. Image: Getty Images / Contributor / Bettmann Dr. Cornish tried to resurrect people, too Before working on dogs , Cornish began his reanimating work on people. A 62-year-old printer who died of cardiac arrest was the first to receive Cornish’s reanimation treatment. Four-and-a-half hours after his death, Cornish arrived at the hospital to strap the man’s heating pad-swaddled body to a teeterboard. After see-sawing the patient up and down for 90 minutes, Cornish failed to revive the subject—although Cornish noted a point at which the printer’s “face seemed to warm up suddenly, sparkle returned to the eyes, and soft pulsations were observed in the soft tissue between windpipe and sternum,” according to science journalist Frank Swain’s How to Make a Zombie: The Life (and Death) Science of Reanimation and Mind Control . Two weeks later, Cornish tried the same treatment on a 22-year-old machinist who’d been pulled dead from the San Francisco Bay three hours before, working his body on the teeterboard for a full four hours. It, too, failed, along with a third attempt the following day in which Cornish submerged an electrocuted cadaver in a warm bath instead of using heating pads before placing the body on the teeterboard. Dissatisfied with the outcomes, Cornish decided it would be wise to perfect his methodology on fox terriers before returning to human subjects. He named each one Lazarus after the biblical man Jesus brought back to life. How a doctor brought dogs back to life Cornish’s biggest breakthrough came with Lazarus IV . Though blind and unable to stand on its own, within 13 days the dog could crawl, bark, and sit up. Its appetite, too, had returned. Over the few months of his life after death, Lazarus IV went through almost a pound of meat each day.  The next patient, Lazarus V, recovered even more quickly. It took just four days for the dog to resume some normal behaviors despite suffering blindness and brain damage. Like his predecessor, he too lived only a few months. Despite their mixed outcome, Cornish was praised for his Lazarus experiments. In the press, the scientist who’d often been considered an oddball by his peers for pursuing projects like underwater reading glasses was hailed as a celebrity. A movie about his work, Life Returns , was released in 1935. The 1935 film Life Returns follows Dr. Kendrick (played by American actor Onslow Stevens) as he tries to bring a dog back to life. Video: Life Returns (1935) | Full Movie | Onslow Stevens | Lois Wilson | Valerie Hobson, TriCoast Worldwide But Cornish’s resuscitation experiments were not without controversy. Dogged by animal rights protests and other outcries from the public, UC Berkeley’s administrators had him removed from campus. Cornish continued his work from home, turning a garden shed into a laboratory that neighbors claimed stunk up the street.  How does CPR bring people back to life The science behind resuscitating a dying patient has come a long way since the Lazarus experiments. These days, “how to restore a pulse depends upon the cause of the cardiac arrest,” says Tisherman.  “The first, most important intervention is assuring good chest compressions,” he continues. How quickly intervention begins also plays a role. “It’s generally been considered that if the period of no blood flow at all, before someone starts CPR, is greater than five minutes, the outcome will likely be poor,” says Tisherman—though that idea has been challenged and “no one knows for sure.” While drugs and medications similar to those used by Cornish to improve blood flow and return heart rhythms to normal in his Lazarus experiments play a part in modern resuscitation protocol, emergency medical practitioners have never adopted the teeterboard he believed was key to restoring life. Cornish never had the opportunity to prove that his teeterboard worked, despite appealing to the governors of Nevada, Arizona, and Colorado for permission to revive criminals executed by the gas chamber shortly after completing his Lazarus experiments. Their refusal didn’t stop Cornish from making one final attempt in 1948, sending multiple requests to the warden at San Quentin State Prison to resuscitate kidnapper and murderer Thomas McMonigle following his upcoming execution by gas chamber—all of which were rebuffed.  Once news of Cornish’s plan for McMonigle became public, more than 50 other “mostly single men” volunteered to be brought back to life by his teeterboard but by then, it seems, Cornish had moved on to something a little less extraordinary: formulating and marketing toothpaste to the American public. title: 6 stellar images of the early universe
author: Popular Science Team
content: Millions of miles away from Earth, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope are revealing the early days of our vast universe in extraordinary detail. A team at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian have developed Lumina , one of the largest and most detailed simulations ever created of the early universe . The new model is detailed in a study published today in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society . It recreates how ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation all interacted during the universe’s first 2 billion years. This gives scientists a new tool to test out their theories about how the cosmos evolved after the big bang . Comparing observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes with Lumina’s predictions, also can help astronomers determine whether their understanding of the laws governing our universe remain accurate or if new discoveries require them to reconsider existing theories. Creating Lumina required more than 15,000 graphics processing units. Take a peak at some of Lumina’s stellar images and videos in the gallery below. (Click to expand images to full screen.) A rendering of the cosmic web about 650 million light-years across, produced by the Lumina simulation. The fine filaments represent dark matter, and the warm orange and yellow tones highlight where gas is moving the fastest between galaxy clusters. Image: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. A view of helium during the early universe, developing into the form we know today, represented by the Lumina simulation. This view encompasses a stretch of the cosmic web 650 million light-years across, as represented by the Lumina simulation. The helium is blue where it’s only singly ionized (its primitive form) and where it’s doubly ionized (its modern form). Image: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. The cosmic web structure as simulated by Lumina. Image: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” study lead author Oliver Zier , a computation astronomer and ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, said in a statement . “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.” The cosmic web structure as simulated by Lumina, showing where hydrogen has changed to its modern form in the early universe (gold regions).. Image: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. Lumina is the largest cosmological radiation-hydrodynamics simulation ever created. This kind of simulation models how the universe’s fundamental ingredients interact to form stars and galaxies. These ingredients include dark matter, light, and gas. Lumina is tracing how the earliest galaxies emerged and transformed the vast regions of gas between them over the universe’s first 2 billion years. The cosmic web structure as simulated by Lumina, showing where helium has changed to its modern form in the early universe (cyan regions). Image: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. A cosmic map showing the composition of dark matter across the Lumina simulation. Image: Oliver Zier, Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina,” added Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and study co-author. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation.” To view the entire project, visit the Lumina Project. title: Why do dead bodies move and make noise?
author: Sarah Kuta
content: Death is supposed to be the end of the road. The lights are out, the curtain has fallen. No breathing, no heartbeat—end of discussion, right? Not quite. In some cases, corpses twitch, flex, shift, change positions, or even make noises that could easily be mistaken for messages from beyond the grave. But before you call the Ghostbusters, take a deep breath. The explanation is less zombie apocalypse and more basic biology .  Even after the heart stops beating, the body still has a few tricks left up its sleeve. The results can be creepy, sure, but experts say they’re perfectly natural. Here’s why corpses sometimes move and make noise. How much does your body move after you die Our bodies can continue moving long after death . When researchers in Australia used time-lapse cameras to keep tabs on a decomposing human body, they discovered that it continued to shift for at least 16 months, with some parts moving as much as 20 total inches over the course of the study period. Researchers call this “post-mortem movement”—and it’s a lot less dramatic than you might imagine.  “A body can move, but not necessarily in the way that I think most people envision,” Derek Boyd , a biological anthropologist who co-directs the Forensic Anthropology and Bioarchaeology Laboratory at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, tells Popular Science .  “The movements are very subtle—you’re not going to see a body sit up or turn its head.” Why do dead bodies move so much After death, the human body moves through a pretty predictable series of decomposition stages . One of the earliest is rigor mortis , when the muscles stiffen and the body becomes rigid. As this process unfolds, a corpse may shift, creating the appearance of movement—but it’s easy to miss, Boyd says.  “You’re not necessarily going to see [the movement] unless you’re laser-focused on the body for the first 48 hours—and even then it’s just going to look like tension, just the body stiffening,” he says. The next stages in which movement might occur are boat and post-bloat, says Boyd. When someone dies, the body’s own enzymes begin breaking down its cells, a process known as autolysis.  Green burials, and specifically human composting , is an environmentally conscious, life-sustaining burial option that allows bodies to decompose naturally. Image: Return Home Meanwhile, bacteria and microbes start spreading throughout the body, digesting tissues and producing gases. This process, known as putrefaction, can “cause the body to become distended or start to bloat, and that bloating can result in a dramatic expansion,” he says. “The body inflates in various places. But, again, this is something that happens gradually.” Eventually, those gases escape—and the body gradually deflates, sometimes causing small shifts in its position. Finally, in the advanced stages of decomposition , the body’s soft tissues begin to dry out, a process known as desiccation. “We have ligaments that are attaching bones together, tendons connecting muscle to bone, and in these later stages of decomposition, those connective tissues can shrink and tighten—and, in doing so, they can pull on our skeleton in various ways,” he says. Of course, not all postmortem movement comes from decomposition itself. Outside forces can also cause a body to shift or change position. Scavengers may drag or disturb remains while feeding, for example, while insects can move small body parts or contribute to the breakdown of tissues. Environmental factors, such as wind, flowing water, or shifting soil, can also displace remains over time. Our bodies also make noises after we die While we’re alive, our bodies are constantly making noise—burps, farts , stomach gurgles, and growls, creaks, and cracks. Considering how noisy our living bodies can be, it shouldn’t come as much of a surprise that they can continue making noises after death .  As gases build up during putrefaction, for instance, the body can produce gurgles, bubbles, groans, or even noises that sound like sighs, Sarah Chavez , executive director of the Order of the Good Death , a nonprofit that aims to change how people think about death and make end-of-life care and funeral options more accessible and equitable, tells Popular Science . Fluids and gases can also get pushed through the mouth or nose, which can sometimes create surprising sounds, she says.  “It can be startling if you’re not expecting it, but there’s nothing supernatural happening,” Chavez adds. “The body is just continuing to do what bodies do—break things down, move fluids and gases around, and occasionally make unintentional noises.” At Greenwood Burial Ground cemetery, near Suffolk, England, bodies are laid to rest amongst the trees. Despite human composting’s promise of a more sustainable burial option, the most eco-friendly option is a placing bodies in a shroud or wooden box and letting nature do the work . Image: Geography Photos / Contributor / Getty Images / IANMURRAY Corpses are a ‘beautiful ecosystem’ Ultimately, the fact that bodies can move or make noises after death is a reminder that the human body is “a beautiful ecosystem of its own,” says Boyd. In life, our bodies are home to countless microorganisms that interact with one another and help keep us alive. After death, those same microorganisms continue to play a role in the body’s breakdown, creating the conditions that can cause a twitch, a shift in position, or an unexpected sound.  The body no longer has thoughts, feelings, or aspirations, but it remains a complex biological system in its own right. “We are walking ecosystems , and we remain ecosystems even after death,” says Boyd.  And scientists are still learning what these postmortem ecosystems can tell us. For example, Boyd says researchers are exploring whether changes to the body’s microbial communities could help forensic investigators estimate how much time has passed since someone died—a “ microbial clock ” of sorts. In other words, the very same processes that can make a corpse move or make noises may also offer valuable clues about the biology of death itself.  In Ask Us Anything , Popular Science answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions, from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. title: 6 ways bats are surprisingly human
author: Laura Baisas
content: Bat Week officially begins today. It’s the one week where Earth’s only winged mammals get top billing. Often associated with disease, vampires , and other generally unpleasant things, bats are actually important pollinators and play critical roles in our ecosystem. “They’re just so cool and so interesting. During first forays into bat studies, it was just one question after another,” Rachel Page , an evolutionary biologist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute in Panama, tells Popular Science . “The more I sort of scratched the surface, the more interesting it became—which is the fun part.” One reason bats are so interesting to scientists like Page is that they are surprisingly similar to humans. Here’s how.  Sharing food with friends  Sharing a meal with good company brings immense joy for us humans. For many vampire bat species (subfamily Desmodontinae), sharing food is a matter of survival . They survive exclusively on blood and can only go about two nights without a blood meal before they die. To get around this, they rely on their social networks. “They have the equivalent of friends. Basically, if a bat comes back from a night of foraging and has not been successful, other members of that social group will share food,” Page explains. “They’ll regurgitate blood for the bat that came back hungry.”  If that donor bat has difficulty getting food later, the one recipient will often become the donor. “So there’s this very reciprocal relationship,” says Page.  The common vampire bat ( Desmondus rotundus ). Image: Wirestock via Getty Images. Wirestock Not being afraid to punch above their weight  According to Page, bats will have their distinctive personalities just like people. It’s present across species, but also individual bats as well. “You have some species that are very feisty, and they’ll go out of their way to pick a fight, and then other ones that are much more passive, calm, and very gentle,” she says.  At the edge of Panama’s Soberanía National Park, tiny, fruit-eating bats will take over the roost of larger, carnivorous bats. The Seba’s short-tailed bat ( Carollia perspicillata ) weighs roughly the same as a strawberry. By comparison, the frog-eating, fringed-lipped bat ( Trachops cirrhosus ) weighs roughly as much as an apricot and twice as much as the short-tailed bat.  Page and her colleagues in Panama have witnessed fights between the two species from roosts set up throughout the forest.  “Basically, it was the male Seba’s short-tailed bat who was instigating the fight. He was coming over and was kind of boxing and threatening much larger bats with wide open mouths and lots of teeth,” Page recalls. “And he just kept at it, and then finally, this group of fringed-lipped bats left.” Figuring out their prey’s trick through problem solving Even in the thick jungles of Panama, bats can find motionless insects on leaves. Initially, scientists believed that the thick tree cover would give small insects an “acoustic camouflage” that would confuse a bat’s echolocation system. But they were wrong.   The bats can see through this acoustic camouflage by changing the angle at which they approach the still insect. “If you approach a flat leaf at just the right angle, you can actually get an echolocation signature,” Page explains. “You can get an echolocation signal that jumps back at you, but only if you direct your echolocation call at just the right angle.” That’s exactly what the bats were doing in order to find insects who tried to hide in leaves. Pushing their kids out into the world—literally  When it’s time for the babies to wean or leave the roost, mother tent-making bats ( Uroderma bilobatum ) will physically prod their young with their forearms. “There is this interesting tug that you see across so many different species. For birds, when they’re ready to fledge, there’s this sort of uncertainty.” Tent-making bats and their babies.  Image: Merlin Tuttle. Changing our behavior when someone is sick When sick, humans and even non-human primates change their behavior. We isolate so that the disease does not spread, and will look to plants and other sources of medicine for relief. Bats appear to change their diet to less nutritious leaves. While this may sound backwards, it’s in the hope that they have medicinal properties.  In an ongoing study with a team from the Ukrainian Bat Rehabilitation Center , the Smithsonian team is looking at the bats from Barro Colorado Island in Panama.  “We have fecal samples from these bats, so we were able to see exactly what they are eating,” says Page. In addition to changing their diets, vampire bats will self-isolate when they are sick and others will act in a way familiar to any human parent—continuing to care for our young, even when sick. “You don’t do as many of the normal behaviors unless it’s taking care of your babies,” says Page. “And again, it’s like a human relationship. If your little kid has a fever, you’re not going to shut them in a room and leave them. You’re not going to desert them.” Learning by listening To find dinner, the fringe-lipped bat ( Trachops cirrhosus ) will listen in on their prey’s mating calls . These frog-eating bats eavesdrop on the mating calls that the male frogs use to attract females. They then use the calls to assess if the frog is edible or poisonous before going in for the kill.  “They’ve really cracked this communication of another entire group,” says Page. According to Page, it’s similar to being in a quiet room and hearing someone open up a bag of potato chips and is loudly eating. The noise makes everyone pay attention. “Bats attend to those acoustic signals of other bats, and that attention then helps them learn,” Page says. “They can learn those distinctions of palatable versus poisonous, and they can learn that socially as well from observing the other behaviors with bats.” To learn more about bats and how to help protect them, visit Bat Week’s website .  The post 6 ways bats are surprisingly human appeared first on Popular Science .

title: Why volunteers are gluing seeds to clam shells in Connecticut
author: Margherita Bassi
content: Environmental restoration sometimes requires out-of-the-box thinking. Along the waters of Long Island Sound in New York and Connecticut, experts are tackling the challenge of restoring crucial eelgrass habitats by gluing the plant’s seeds to clams .  Eelgrass ( Zostera marina ) is an important member of the ecosystem. It provides foraging areas and shelter for young fish and invertebrates, diminishes coastal erosion, draws in excess nutrients, filters water, and releases oxygen, for instance. Compared to the 1930s, eelgrass meadows in and around Long Island Sound have decreased by more than 90 percent, according to regional environmental action group Save the Sound . To make matters worse, eelgrass is difficult to restore and there have been a lot of failed attempts, Bill Lucey , a Long Island Soundkeeper from the organization, tells Popular Science . In 2025, the team tried a different approach—recruiting clams as underwater gardeners. The strategy was originally ideated by Robert Vasiluth, the founder of Submerged Aquatic Vegetation EngineersEnvironmental (SAVE) . The approach consists of attaching eelgrass seeds to the clam’s shells. When the clams are released into the sound, they bury into the sediment, taking the seeds down to the bottom and effectively planting them. When they conducted drone imagery to check in on their results this year, they found that the eelgrass meadow coverage had increased by 178 percent.  The clams take the seeds with them into the sediment, where they can grow into eelgrass. Image: Courtesy of Save the Sound. “It needs to survive for three years before we can really trumpet our horns and say it’s working, but the actual method of putting clams out and seeds attached to them really worked. The generation of the plants was incredible,” Lucey explains.  During their 2025 planting, the team used glue typically used in coral reef restoration to attach seeds to the clams. But then Connecticut College biologist Maria Rose yielded better germination rates when she used wet pieces of rice paper (the kind you make spring rolls with) to seal the seeds against the shell. The Save the Sound team asked its volunteers to do the same earlier this week.  The team is using wet rice paper to help seal the seeds against the clam shell. Image: Courtesy of Save the Sound. “The problem with the spring roll wrappers is yesterday [Monday, October 19], when we deployed them for the first time in scale, they weren’t all staying on,” says Lucey. “So what we’ve started doing today [Tuesday, October 20] is putting a little pocket of seeds, 10 to 20 eelgrass seeds on the top of the clam, putting a little circle of this [coral] glue around it, and then putting the spring roll wrapper stamp over that and wetting it. And so it keeps the seeds moist, and the glue holds the spring roll wrapper to the clam till it dissolves, and then it’ll release the seeds next to the clam.” Save the Sound is aiming to release 10,000 claims and 300,000 seeds this season. title: How to turn your smartphone into a mobile video editing suite
author: David Nield
content: With so many smartphone apps in the modern age locked (or partially locked) behind paywalls, it’s important to grab the free ones when they become available—and on rare occasions, it’s the biggest software companies on the planet offering apps free of charge. Adobe Premiere for iOS launched back in September 2025, and a year later, we got Adobe Premiere for Android too. You don’t need an Adobe account or a subscription to use these apps (unlike the desktop equivalents)—the only paid components are credits for AI image and video generation , if you want to use those tools. With these apps available, there’s really no excuse for sharing sub-standard video. You get a wealth of editing features right on your mobile screen, all optimized to suit the smaller display and the more limited capabilities of a phone versus a full computer. We’re going to concentrate on the Android app here, as it’s the one most recently launched, but the features are the same on the iPhone too. You can even use Premiere across multiple Android and iOS devices. The video editing timeline A wealth of edits and filters can be applied from the timeline. David Nield It’s easy enough to get started with Premiere: From the main screen, tap the + (plus) button to choose a saved video clip or image to use as the starting point for a new project, or select New blank project . Either will take you to the timeline view, and you can then use the + (plus) button on the timeline to load in more content. The layout is going to be familiar if you’ve used a video editor before. Photos and videos make up the main timeline, and if you select them, you get handles around them—use these handles to shorten or lengthen the clips. Select a video on the timeline, then tap Split to cut it in two at the current playhead position (that’s wherever the long vertical white line is in the timeline). Your video project is previewed above the timeline, and you can use the playback controls to go backward and forward through it. The other options you’ll see on the toolbar include Audio (for dropping in a voiceover or some stock music), Text (for titles and overlays), and Generate (for producing generative AI content). You can also select Files to load local files (such as audio snippets) from your phone. Select anything on the timeline to get more options for it. For a video clip, these will include Retime (for changing the speed of a clip or freezing it), Filters (for adjusting the look of a clip), Effects (tweaks like glows or shakes), and tools to mirror, flip, or duplicate whatever you’ve got selected. To change transitions, tap on the borders between scenes. Then there are the generative AI tools, which you can get to by tapping on the Generate button underneath the timeline. This part of the app requires an Adobe account—the account itself is free, but you’ll be restricted in terms of your AI usage before you have to start paying for credits. Working with templates Templates and export options are easy to access. David Nield If you want a quicker, easier way to make content, there are plenty of ready-made templates to use. You’ll see these on the front screen, under headings like Lifestyle and Beauty. Tap on a template to view it, then choose Use this template to start making it your own. Making it your own means picking images and videos from your phone’s library to add to the template you just viewed. As you make your selections, you’ll see the template slots fill up underneath (you don’t have to use all of them)—when you’re done, choose Next to see the finished product. This will have the same transitions, timings, titles, and audio as your template, and if you’re happy with that, then tap Export to send the video somewhere else. There are some basic editing tools here as well: Select one of the images or videos you’ve dropped in, and you can trim them or replace them with the buttons at the bottom. To customize the clip even more, choose Full editor to return to the fully featured interface we looked at above, complete with filters, effects, and everything else. Note that once you’ve converted your template-based video to work with the full timeline interface, you can’t go back into template mode with the same project. It’s an app that works well for quick video creations and more detailed projects you want to do on your phone, and you’ll also get numerous settings (resolution, frame rate, quality) when it’s time to export your work. If you do sign up for an Adobe account and pay for the Creative Cloud suite, you can easily sync your projects with Premiere on the desktop. The post How to turn your smartphone into a mobile video editing suite appeared first on Popular Science .

title: 12 striking images from European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
author: Popular Science Team
content: For 13 years, photographer Imre Potyó has ventured into restricted-access mine tunnels in the Börzsöny Mountains of Hungary to capture images of hibernating lesser horseshoe bat ( Rhinolophus hipposideros ). Despite their deep slumber, the bats occasionally wake to hunt insects that enter the dark caves. “In doing so, the bat leaves behind droppings that gradually accumulate into a continuous dark layer,” Potyó explains. “And this is where the real wonder begins: in the beam of a torch, a whitish coating can be seen on the guano —a small pin mould thriving in this unusual habitat. Using a macro lens, I captured the mould in the foreground with the hibernating bats visible in the background. The photograph—a long exposure incorporating a focus shift—was taken during a controlled bat count and without disturbing the animals.” That effort paid off. Potyó’s image, titled “Hidden Worlds,” (seen below) took home top honors at the European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 awards . “Hidden worlds” Overall winner I have been photographing hibernating bats for 13 years in restricted-access mine tunnels in the Börzsöny Mountains of Hungary, and yet this particular composition was novel for me. A key characteristic of the lesser horseshoe bat ( Rhinolophus hipposideros ) is that, during hibernating it occasionally wakes and leaves its roost to hunt flying insects. In doing so, the bat leaves behind droppings that gradually accumulate into a continuous dark layer. And this is where the real wonder begins: in the beam of a torch, a whitish coating can be seen on the guano—a small pin mould thriving in this unusual habitat. Using a macro lens, I captured the mould in the foreground with the hibernating bats visible in the background. The photograph—a long exposure incorporating a focus shift—was taken during a controlled bat count and without disturbing the animals. Credit: Imre Potyó – Hungary / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 The European Wildlife Photographer of the Year ( EWPY ) competition is now in its 26th year. Amateur and professional photographers in 46 countries submitted more than 26,000 images, from which 107 were selected as winners across nine categories and two special categories. “All the photographers taking part in this competition share a common outlook: they move through the world with open eyes and are committed to a harmonious coexistence of people and nature,” Sabine Riewenherm, President of the German Federal Agency for Nature Conservation (BfN), said in a statement. Through their work, they draw attention to the beauty of our planet, but also to its vulnerability. I am deeply grateful to these photographers for their outstanding contribution, as they play a vital role in raising awareness for nature and its protection.” “Evolution” Winner, Humans and Nature Travelling to Thailand, my hope was to see a Malayan sun bear ( Helarctos malayanus ) in the wild. I got my wish – though not quite the way I had imagined. A bear had taken to dropping by the visitor centre at Kaeng Krachan National Park, wandering fearlessly behind the rangers’ kitchen in search of food scraps. On this day, it climbed into the waste incinerator and fell asleep inside. And this despite having some 3,000 square kilometres of habitat at its disposal within the park – its behaviour, in other words, had nothing to do with habitat loss or a degraded environment. What struck me was the contrast between this magnificent animal and one of humanity’s uglier inventions. The irony was complete when I noticed the manufacturer’s label: “Evolution”. Credit: Petr Bambousek – Czech Republic / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 “Little housemates” Highly commended, Mammals I was on my way home from school when, just a few minutes from my house, I suddenly came face to face with a young red fox ( Vulpes vulpes ). We were both caught off guard and stood motionless for a moment. I then hurried home to fetch my camera. Four fox cubs and their mother had moved into an abandoned barn right in the middle of my village. Two of the cubs poked their heads out of the barn door and watched me curiously. A few days later, I learnt that the barn’s owner felt disturbed by their presence. He threw stones at them and eventually chased them away. The foxes moved on, in search of a safer place. Moments like these remind me how important it is to look out for the wild animals that share our world with us. These animals are not intruders – they are our neighbours, seeking safety just as we do. Credit: Marc Siegle – Switzerland / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 “A seal’s worst nightmare” Highly commended, Mammals For many years, I had been planning to photograph the most common hunting technique of polar bears ( Ursus maritimus ) from a seal’s perspective. In the dense pack ice at 83° N, I drilled a hole next to a seal’s breathing hole, installed my camera beneath it, and positioned a motion sensor on the ice above. Eight hours later, I spotted a polar bear in the distance heading straight for the breathing hole. By then, a thin layer of ice had formed on the water. The bear pushed its head through the ice to see what was going on below and looked straight into the camera. The bear then lay down and slept for nine hours, leaving me unable to retrieve my camera. When the animal finally moved on, I rushed over and was over thrilled to discover that I had captured my dream photo of a polar bear. Credit: Audun Rikardsen – Norway / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Audun Rikardsen “Turbulent feeding patch” Runner-up, Underwater World Marine iguanas ( Amblyrhynchus cristatus ) are endemic to the Galápagos Archipelago, Ecuador. They are most often seen basking in the sun, their dark bodies perfectly camouflaged against the black lava rocks. As ectothermic reptiles, they rely on external heat to regulate their body temperature. This is particularly important as they dive into the cold waters surrounding the archipelago to forage, primarily on marine algae. I followed this individual into the water and watched with fascination as it propelled itself swiftly and purposefully through the powerful surf with the aid of its muscular tail. While I was tossed about by the waves, the marine iguana clung firmly to a rock with its sharp claws and began methodically grazing on algae. Despite its dragon-like appearance, the marine iguana is remarkably placid: a herbivore that shows no aggression, even when approached closely on land or underwater. Credit: Henley Spiers – United Kingdom / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 HENLEY SPIERS “The florist” Highly commended, Mammals Every year between April and May, vast amounts of water from Angola inundate the floodplains of the Chobe River in Botswana, creating ideal conditions for numerous water lilies to flourish. In spring 2023, a combination of early flooding and unusually high water levels resulted in a truly spectacular display of white and purple flowers. I spent each day out on a boat, hoping to photograph wildlife feeding on the nutrient-rich floating vegetation. One afternoon, in perfect light, everything came together: an African elephant ( Loxodonta africana ) strolled leisurely through the shallow water, plucking flower after flower. Lying flat in the boat, I managed to capture this unique scene. Credit: William Steel – United Kingdom / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 William Steel Photography “Exit stage right” Highly commended, Mammals End of a performance in Lake Clark National Park, Alaska: the scene is over, and the grizzly bear ( Ursus arctos horribilis ) has had its moment in the spotlight. The animal leaves the stage without a bow, without a backward glance. Fog hangs like a flowing curtain, and the bokeh glows like fading stage lights. A gull remains behind, watching the main actor’s exit and perhaps wondering what it should do next. The image was deliberately composed with the protagonists positioned in the upper part of the frame to create the impression of a grand stage. Credit: Preeti John, GDT – United Arab Emirates / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Composing the Wild “Barbecued golden eagle” Highly commended, Humans & Nature For years I photographed a pair of golden eagles ( Aquila chrysaetos ) living on a mountain above the small coastal village in northern Norway I call home. One morning, working from home, I lost power for about five minutes. While walking the dogs a few hours later, I discovered why. One of the eagles I had watched and photographed from my hide for years had struck the power lines behind my house – the current had burned clean through its body. Large raptors, with their enormous wingspan, can bridge two power lines at once and be killed instantly. Sadly, this hazard does not just exist here in Norway — it affects large birds across the world. Credit: Audun Rikardsen – Norway / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Audun Rikardsen “Helping hands” Runner-up, Humans and Nature During the mating season, capercaillie ( Tetrao urogallus ) sometimes lose their wariness of people, seeing them instead as rivals. That is exactly what happened at a ski resort near my home, where a capercaillie took up position on the ski slope every day throughout the lekking season to defend his patch. The bird soon became something of a local celebrity, even making the news, and crowds came daily to watch and film him. Then, one day, a ski race was held – and the bird chose the middle of the course to display. Not the safest spot. Several people stepped in, gently steering him behind the safety fence and out of harm’s way. A year later, the same bird was accidentally killed by a skier who failed to notice it. Some people care. Others simply don’t. Credit: Lukas Schaefer – Italy / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 luki schaefer “Peaceful European bison” Highly commended, Rewilding Europe By the early twentieth century, the European bison ( Bison bonasu s) had been declared extinct in the wild across Europe. Reintroduction has since rebuilt the population of the continent’s largest land mammal to more than 7,200 animals. Travelling with friends last autumn to Białowieża National Park, in eastern Poland on the Belarusian border, we encountered both wolves and European bison — in the latter case, two bulls grazing in a meadow on the edge of a village. As powerful as they are, the animals accepted our presence without concern, settling down to rest undisturbed. That kind of coexistence is possible here because the bison are given room to roam, through forests and meadows alike. Approach these primeval-looking creatures with respect, and you can feel the calm they carry with them. Credit: Fabian Thorand, GDT – Germany / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 “We are family” Highly commended, Plants and Fungi In northern Poland, in the area around Gdańsk where I live, extraordinary species of animals and plants are rare. Most subjects in the region have been photographed countless times. Thus, it requires a good deal of imagination to take an unusual photograph. Over the years, I have made many attempts to capture the large-flowered hemp-nettle ( Galeopsis speciosa ) in an interesting way. Most of the time, the results have been disappointing, but every now and then, the effort pays off … Credit: Marek Mierzejewski – Poland / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 The post 12 striking images from European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 appeared first on Popular Science .

title: The 5-Second Rule is scientifically false
author: Eric Alt
content: Since elementary school, we’ve all been taught the “5-Second Rule.” The idea is simple: Food dropped on the floor is still perfectly edible if retrieved in under five seconds. The logic behind the theory, such as it is, is that germs and dirt and pet dander are somehow caught by surprise by the sudden arrival of food and need a few seconds to get their bearings. If you snatch the food up quick enough, they won’t have time to get it “dirty.” Even as kids, we were skeptical but admit it–you still roll the dice on it every now and again. It’s like shouting “shotgun” before getting into the passenger seat even if it’s only you and the driver. It’s instinctual. But is it true?  “Let’s go with ‘No,’ there is no truth to the ‘5-second rule’,” says Gillson Sciences Director of Operations Erin Thane. “But I would argue that specifics matter.”  Wetness matters As Thane explains, variables such as comparative wetness of said food and type of flooring can swing things one way or another. “Food dropped on a carpet will likely pick up less contamination than food dropped on a smooth surface with the same microbial loads. Sticky or wet foods will likely pick up more contamination than dry foods dropped on the same contaminated surfaces.” Sticky food will pick up more contamination. Image: Getty Images Patrick Strattner And that’s not all. “There are actually a lot of nuances to this question,” says Thane. “Is it the floor of Windsor Castle or a public bathroom? Was sticky gum dropped and then put back in the mouth, or was it a goldfish cracker? Am I a healthy adult eating something off the ground or an immunocompromised individual?” Your floors are dirtier than you think Perhaps more surprising, according to Thane, is that the floors in your home and floors in public spaces actually don’t vary in cleanliness as much as you’d like to think. As Thane puts it, “We all wear the same shoes–or socks hopefully in the home–across the floors we encounter daily, like the kitchen and bathroom, to other areas or spaces. We are constantly picking up hitchhiking germs and depositing them from one floor to the next.”  Specifically skin-inhabiting bacteria such as Staphylococcus (which puts the “Staph” in “Staph Infection”) and Corynebacterium (which can cause diphtheria) to gut bacteria such as Bacteroides . Shoes, clothing, and bags can also carry Bacillus or mold or yeast that can cause nausea and vomiting.   While there are mitigating factors, it’s safe to say that in terms of grossness, the “5-Second Rule” is pretty high up there.  “I would certainly stay away from any wet, moist or sticky foods which act like a sponge and will immediately cling to any and all dirt, debris and contamination that it comes into contact with,” advises Thane. “However, after everything we have discussed so far, I refer back to the best practice or rule of thumb which is to just not eat any food off the floor.” The post The 5-Second Rule is scientifically false appeared first on Popular Science .

title: Play ‘Doom’ on this tiny, uterus-shaped period tracker
author: Andrew Paul
content: Doom is much more than a classic, bloodsoaked first-person shooter known for its chaotic action, over-the-top weapons, and challenging boss fights. For some odd (but very enjoyable) reason, it’s served as a benchmark for testing basic computing capabilities for well over 30 years. Name a device ——calculators, ATMs, digitally enabled tractors, and even biochips built with E. coli bacteria —and someone has likely coded it to run Doom . The latest entry in the ever-growing list of Doom compatible contraptions is a double-dose of DIY ingenuity, however. The Linux software engineer known as Miss Molerat recently began tinkering with a pocket-sized medical gadget made specifically to keep track of her menstrual cycle . But unlike many similar commercial products , “Clotty” keeps all personal data strictly on the device itself. It never connects to an external cloud or offloads sensitive information to a company’s servers, thereby preventing any unwanted data harvesting. And it does all this on a custom, uterus-shaped minicomputer running on a Raspberry Pi microcontroller. Clotty includes a Tamagotchi-like sprite players must maintain and keep happy. Credit: Miss Molerat “I have one thing that has been bothering me for as long as I’ve been menstruating: despite my cycle being very regular, I somehow manage to get surprised by PMS each and every month anew,” Clotty’s inventor wrote on her website’s blog . Clotty “does the boring stuff” for her by tracking her period via a Tamagotchi-like digital pet that requires attention and maintenance throughout each month. The pixelated creature’s mood shifts depending on the cycle phase, but it also can go on little quests and offer various minigames in the meantime. “[It’s] basically some sort of adorably shaped mirror version of my own moods that serves as a reminder that I, too, am just some sort of creature that tries to stay alive and happy,” explained Clotty’s creator. But why stop there? Clotty is powerful enough to run Doom on its itty-bitty LCD screen, which is thematically perfect given the project’s overarching, bloody motif. This means that, when not keeping up with personal health, a user can also blast through wave after wave of space demons using small onboard sensors. The inventor admitted that Clotty is still in its “fetal stage,” but she plans to add more features like a menstrual cycle history archive, more games, and even some reproductive health trivia. It’s also a completely open-source project , so anyone can follow her online tutorials and download files for Clotty (and Doom ).
