title: This robot exists solely to bounce ping-pong balls
author: Mack DeGeurin
content: In a world where tech leaders are racing to build autonomous machines that can do almost anything, one hobbyist is going the complete opposite route: an over-engineered   robot that does exactly one thing and one thing only.  T-Kuhn’s Hexa-Bouncer only bounces a ping-pong ball, but looks like it’s capable of far more. The six-armed, metal machine was first designed  in a simulated environment and then brought to life with a CNC milling machine. Custom-built joints let it rise, fall, and tilt, and even bob up and down while tracing a circle. A pair of cameras, set 120 degrees apart, track the ball’s position and send that data to a computer over USB. The computer then builds a 3D picture of the scene, then calculates when the paddle should strike the ball and at what angle. All of this happens in a fraction of a second. Hexa-Bouncer keeps balls in the air remarkably well. In a video , Kuhn holds a ping-pong ball above his creation, and the machine moves up and down in sync with his hand. When he drops the ball, the robot immediately reacts, striking it back into the air and keeping it aloft bounce after bounce, all the while making small adjustments. After a few more bounces, the device eases off its swing and the ball starts bouncing lower and lower. It’s unclear exactly how long Hexa-Bouncer can keep the ball in the air, it never misses—at least in the video posted online..  Kuhn describes his ball juggler as the latest in a series of, “useless but mildly interesting ball bouncing machines.” Prior to this, he released his Octo-Bouncer , a similar design that keeps a ping-pong ball bouncing in the air using a four-sided flat plate. Some might say all this over-engineered ball bouncing is unnecessary, but Kuhn would disagree. For him, solving the design puzzle is a journey in itself.  “Building a thing like this is like bashing your way through a jungle,” he said . “It’s an adventure. You’re not completely sure if you can make it through or not, and that’s exactly why you do it.” The post This robot exists solely to bounce ping-pong balls appeared first on Popular Science .

title: New comet accidentally discovered by space telescope
author: Andrew Paul
content: Launched in 2023, the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid space telescope observes some of the most distant regions of the visible universe for signs of dark matter and dark energy . But even while focused on the “big picture,” Euclid’s onboard equipment is surprising astronomers by capturing tiny photobombers like errant comets . Its recent portraits of one specific dusty space rock are especially impressive, however. Euclid spotted a never-before-seen comet sailing through space more than 807.7 million miles from Earth. The telescope isn’t designed to automatically flag an image interloper. Instead, the bright blemish seen in multiple images was spotted by a moving object detection program designed by Mikko Pöntinen , an astronomer at the University of Helsinki in Finland. “I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images—the result of a fast-moving object,” said Pöntinen . “Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.” Comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) seen in a wide VIS image for context (left), with a zoom in (right). Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026 Pöntinen quickly relayed his findings to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC), which then passed the news along to researchers around the world. On October 8, the MPC confirmed the newly discovered comet, which is now classified C/2026 S1 (Euclid). C/2026 S1 was seen from five different fields of view over multiple days in the Euclid Deep Field North region of the telescope’s scans. Astronomers now know the comet’s trajectory isn’t located on the same horizontal plane as the planets. Instead, its path is technically taking it over the solar system along a multi-thousand-year orbit. Euclid’s discovery is particularly striking because the telescope’s six-year mission is specifically mapped to avoid areas of the sky that are laden with comets and asteroids. “Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid, so it was a happy coincidence,” added Euclid archive scientist Bruno Altieri . title: Bat Beauty Contest returns October 24
author: Laura Baisas
content: With Alaska’s fat bears done packing on their winter weight and spooky season in full swing, it’s time to turn our collective animal-loving attention to a smaller mammal— bats . The Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) annual Bat Beauty Contest returns on October 24 and promises “plenty of batty puns.” Beginning Saturday, October 24, BLM will post photos of the competitors to their Facebook and Instagram accounts and ask you to vote for the best-looking one. All of the competing bats are part of wild populations that live on land managed by the public agency and are photographed by wildlife technicians. The winner will be announced (appropriately) on Saturday, October 31. The bats in this competition are known for their squishy faces and clever names. In 2024, a hoary bat ( Lasiurus cinereus ) from Oregon named Hoary Potter took the crown . Other contestants included a long-eared myotis ( Myotis evotis ) named Honey Bunches of MyOtis, a myotis bat ( Myotis myotis ) named Robert Battinson, and western small-footed bats ( Myotis ciliolabrum ) named Batt Damon and Batlor Swift. The contest was not held in 2025 due to the 43-day-long federal government shutdown.  A hoary bat at Isle Royale National Park in Michigan. Image: NPS Photo/Bat Conservation International. The contest is not all bat puns and a way to keep the spirit of Fat Bear Week alive. It falls during Bat Week (October 24-31). Bat Week raises awareness about the Earth’s only flying mammal . More than just a Halloween symbol, bats play a critical ecological role as plant pollinators and through eating insects that can threaten crops and forests around the world. According to Bat Week , one bat can eat up to its body weight in insects every night. Only three species of bats eat animal blood, with two specializing in bird blood. Female lesser long-nosed bats even make tequila possible . Every spring, they migrate from south-central Mexico up to the southwestern United States, following “nectar corridors” of columnar cacti and agave plants. They pollinate agave plants, which are then used to make tequila and mezcal. When they feed on cactus fruits and nectar, they may also help disperse cacti seeds. Other bats eat pollen, nectar, or fruit. Bats are increasingly threatened due to habitat loss, light pollution, and diseases like white-nose syndrome . This fungal disease infects the skin of the muzzle, ears, and wings of hibernating bats. In about 20 years, it has killed millions of bats across North America and affects about half of the species on the continent. Bats also are often misunderstood as carriers of diseases such as rabies.  The planet is home to over 1,400 species of bats, and they make up almost 20 percent of all mammal species. Bats also can be found almost everywhere on Earth, even in desert and polar regions. To look up which bat species live near you, you can use Bat Week’s state bat database . Stay tuned for more Bat Week updates! The post Bat Beauty Contest returns October 24 appeared first on Popular Science .

title: The mysterious dancing plague that killed people in 1518
author: Sarah Kuta
content: In the summer of 1518, people in Strasbourg couldn’t seem to stop dancing—some even danced themselves to death. It all started with one woman, who stepped into the street and began moving uncontrollably. Soon, dozens of other residents followed suit, overcome with the inexplicable urge to hop, jerk, and sway. Within weeks, the outbreak had spread throughout the city, leaving officials, physicians, and religious leaders scrambling to figure out what was happening—and, more importantly, how to make it stop. Five centuries later, the dancing plague of 1518 remains one of history ’s strangest medical mysteries. Historical records confirm that a bizarre episode turned a medieval city into a very unwilling dance floor that summer, but exactly why it happened remains a matter of debate.  A bizarre outbreak takes hold The dancing plague began on July 14, 1518, when a woman named Frau Troffea started dancing in Strasbourg, then part of the Holy Roman Empire and now a city in northeastern France. Though her husband begged her to stop, Troffea kept moving as day faded to night, while a crowd of onlookers gathered around to watch. Eventually, she collapsed and fell asleep, but when she awoke the next morning, she resumed her solitary jig.  Troffea’s uncontrollable dancing, known as choreomania, seemed to be contagious. Dozens of other people were soon gyrating in the streets of Strasbourg and, by late August, as many as 400 individuals had succumbed. At the time, the leading theory was that St. Vitus, a fourth-century Sicilian martyr believed to punish sinners by making them dance , had cursed the afflicted. Then, once St. Vitus decided his victims had suffered enough, he would relieve them of the curse. St. Vitus was martyred in 303 during the persecution of Christians by the co-Emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Image: Contributor / Getty Images / Print Collector City leaders determined that the best course of action was to keep the dancers dancing, so they cleared the outdoor grain market, built a stage, and hired musicians. They didn’t explain their rationale in any known, surviving documents, so historians don’t know exactly why they did this. But John Waller , associate professor of the history of medicine at Michigan State University and the author of The Dancing Plague: The Strange, True Story of an Extraordinary Illness , suspects they had two reasons: They believed dancing could help people purge physical impurities from their bodies, and they viewed it as a form of penance.  “If people were believed to have been cursed by God or a saint for some kind of immorality, well, dancing was associated with hedonism and that was fundamentally immoral,” he tells Popular Science . “A way of basically punishing oneself would be to dance to the point of exhaustion and pain and potentially even death. It would make sense with that penitential framework.” In other words, from the leaders’ perspective, if dancing was their punishment, let them be punished. Dancing themselves to death Regardless of their motives, the authorities’ decision had “very, very clear consequences,” he says. It was a hot summer, and the dancers were likely under the full glare of the sun. They weren’t eating or drinking much, and they weren’t resting.  “This is certainly going to be extremely dangerous for a large number of people, particularly anybody with any kind of susceptibility to heart attack or stroke,” says Waller. The historical records are murky on exactly how many people died—one writer claimed as many as 15 per day, at least for a time—but it was enough to make city leaders completely change course.  “They essentially banned dancing, except for some people in the privacy of their own homes, and then instituted a program of penance and prayer,” says Waller. “They clearly realized that what they’d been doing before was causing harm and I suspect they got the impression that it was making things worse.” Eventually, the authorities transported the remaining dancers to a shrine dedicated to St. Vitus about 30 miles away, where religious leaders went to work praying and leaving offerings. As days and weeks passed, the dancers overcame their choreomania and returned to their normal lives—traumatized and tired, but otherwise fine. Strasbourg’s dancing plague in 1518 wasn’t the only such incident of its kind. Image: Getty Images / Contributor / Bettmann The dancing plague of 1518 wasn’t the only such incident of its kind. Numerous other outbreaks of uncontrollable dancing occurred in western Europe between the late 1300s and mid-1500s—and Waller thinks it’s no coincidence that many were clustered along the Rhine River and its tributaries.  “ Rivers are very good for, obviously, transporting trade goods, but they’re also very good for spreading ideas,” he says. “From the headwaters in Switzerland all the way down to where the Rhine flows into the North Sea, you’ve got this belief in a saint who curses with a dance.” Theories behind the dancing Now that we have the benefit of hindsight, what might explain the dancing plague of 1518 and others like it? One theory is that the dancers were sickened by ergot, a fungus that can contaminate grain . Another holds venomous spiders bit the afflicted. Demonic possession, epilepsy , typhus, and encephalitis— brain inflammation caused by an infection or autoimmune response—have also been put forward as possible explanations. But after considering all the evidence, Waller thinks there’s only one plausible theory that truly makes sense. He suspects the dancers of Strasbourg were all victims of mass hysteria , also known as mass psychogenic illness, brought on by intense psychological distress.  The years leading up to 1518 were rough, particularly for the lower classes, with failed crops, bad weather , economic issues, social unrest, religious tensions, and illnesses like smallpox , leprosy, and syphilis taking a toll on peoples’ psyches. They were hungry, anxious, sad, scared, and worried that God had abandoned them.  Waller suspects the people living in Strasbourg simply reached their breaking point, then entered into a trance-like state that rendered them largely insensitive to their extreme fatigue and sore feet. They danced, Waller argues, rather than weeping, fighting, praying, or engaging in some other behavior because of their belief in St. Vitus and his dancing curse. Related 'That Time When' Stories In 1976, a college paper blamed the Salem witch trials on moldy bread. It wasn’t true. Ancient Romans thought drinking gladiator blood could cure epilepsy In medieval France, murderous pigs faced trial and execution 4 times drinking coffee was illegal—or even punishable by death The British author who harvested mutant, jumbo peanuts from her atomic garden The radioactive ‘miracle water’ that killed its believers Modern takeaways  Given the period-specific cultural and religious underpinnings, could something like the dancing plague of 1518 happen today?  Waller shares several modern examples of mass psychogenic illness that, although they don’t involve dancing, he finds to be similar in nature. More than 300 students in Blackburn, England, suffered from a mysterious fainting fit in 1956, for example, and hundreds of people succumbed to alternating fits of laughing and sobbing in East Africa in 1962. In 2007, students at a Catholic boarding school near Mexico City came down with a mysterious sickness that made walking difficult . A year later, 20 female students in Tanzania suffered a mass fainting episode during their final-year national examinations. And although the dancing plague of 1518 took place more than 500 years ago, Waller says we can still learn plenty from it. For him, the most important takeaway is “the way in which our expression of severe distress can be culturally conditioned and channeled.”  When Waller initially started researching the dancing plague of 1518, it was such a “wild phenomenon” that his inclination was to think “as strange as the past can be, this was simply too strange to have actually happened,” he says. But as he dug deeper—and, more importantly, began to understand the context within which it arose—it started to make more and more sense.  In other words, he says, it reminds us that psychological distress is not expressed in a vacuum. The culture, beliefs, and circumstances around us can shape how our inner turmoil manifests—and, in some cases, how it spreads from one person to another.  In That Time When , Popular Science tells the weirdest, most surprising, and little-known stories that shaped science, engineering, and innovation. title: Scientist tattoos himself with disappearing ink
author: Andrew Paul
content: Tattoos are pretty permanent decisions , and laser removal is often described as more painful than actually getting them in the first place. But what about a design that can only be seen when you want to see it? Engineers at the University of Colorado Boulder are working on a new type of tattoo ink to answer that question. Their dye is specifically concocted to physically alter depending on exposure to visible or ultraviolet (UV) light. The team described their invention in a study published earlier this month in the journal Matter & Light , and they didn’t only demonstrate the capabilities in the lab on silicone and pig skin. One of its creators, Carson Bruns , has already tattooed himself with the ink. “[It’s] almost a tradition,” the study co-author recently told Nature . Bruns, a nanoscientist at UC Boulder, previously developed a now-commercialized tattoo product called “Magic Ink” that turns magenta depending on its exposure to UV light. To highlight its efficacy, Bruns gave himself “solar freckles” as a method to track his exposure to sunlight. In similar fashion, he recently completed a similar session on his leg using the disappearing ink. The formula currently comes in three colors—yellow, blue, and magenta—and essentially relies on the same principles behind transition lenses and some textiles. Each dye is composed of tiny spheres of acrylic glass. These beads contain photochromes, which are chemical compounds engineered to absorb specific light wavelength photons. In this case, the photochomic dye’s spheres begin in their original color, but then flatten into transparency after absorbing corresponding light photons exposed to UV rays. The dye remains this way until it absorbs visible light photons, which destroys the chemical bond and allows the spheres to return to their original shape. Aside from the lab tests, Bruns tattooed his own leg over about 12 months using various dye combinations, all of which responded as intended to UV and visible light exposure. The ink also remained effective for over two years—but the team’s intention is go beyond a nifty parlor trick. Future ink iterations may be particularly useful in medical procedures, such as temporary markings to help maintain accuracy during direct radiotherapy sessions. For now, however, the photochromic tattoo dyes remain for laboratory (and Bruns’) use only until further safety assessments are completed. title: Roman child’s grave contains coin to pay afterlife entry fee
author: Andrew Paul
content: Not far from the Black Sea, a child’s grave uncovered in present-day Bulgaria has provided archaeologists a somber look at Roman funerary practices . Flagged in the city of Stara Zagora during a site survey for a new apartment complex and parking garage project, the burial contained stunningly preserved gold earrings as well as a single, small coin known as an antoninianus . But while the currency’s age is traceable to within a year of its minting, the bronze piece may also represent a grieving family’s hopes for their child’s safe passage into the afterlife. The grave is one of about 135 located in the cemetery. Credit: Regional History Museum – Stara Zagora Martin Kolev The Roman empire at its height included over 1.9 million square miles of territory, including much of central Europe and central Asia. Rome annexed the region of Thrace in 46 CE, and eventually renamed the city of Stara Zagora as Ulpia Augusta Traiana in honor of Emperor Trajan (98 to 117 CE). Augusta Traiana quickly grew into one of Thrace’s most prominent urban hubs, becoming so prosperous that Rome ultimately granted permission to build its own coin mint during the second and third centuries CE. Over 1,750 years later, Augusta Traiana’s remnants exist underneath a city once again known as Stara Zagora. Ruins of the Roman empire are regularly unearthed through the town, including the recent discovery of a large cemetery used for nearly three centuries outside Augusta Traiana’s original walls. Among the 135 graves, researchers identified a child buried with a pair of gold earrings and one of Thrace’s bronze coins. Although details about the young individual’s death and identity remain unclear, the coin clearly dates to either 274 or 275 CE. Archaeologists assume the child likely died either around that time period, or soon after. The coin was minted in either 274 or 275 CE. Credit: Regional History Museum – Stara Zagora While researchers may never learn the precise circumstances of the burial, ancient Greek and Roman funerary beliefs suggest the coin served a specific purpose. It’s possible the child’s family intentionally placed the currency with the deceased as payment to Charon, the ferryman who brought souls to the afterlife. Knowing this, it may be that grieving relatives hoped to impart one final gift to their loved one. title: How to watch Japan’s mission to Mars
author: Popular Science Team
content: Japan launches a ground-breaking mission to the Mars moon Phobos today, and you can watch live. The JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission aims to collect samples from Phobos , the larger of Mars’ two moons, and deliver it back to Earth for analysis. If successful, the samples could help solve long-standing mysteries about Mars’ moons, including their origin. In 1877, US astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and its smaller sibling, Deimos. The moons have arguably the most bad-ass names in our solar system: Phobos comes from the ancient Greek word φόβος (phobos), meaning “fear,” and Deimos originates with the ancient Greek word Δεῖμος, which translates to “dread.” Despite increased attention on Mars in recent decades, astronomers don’t know exactly how the celestial bodies formed. Theories include asteroids or debris leftovers from way back when the solar system formed about 4.5 billion years ago. “The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator and Science Mission Directorate at NASA, said in a statement . While a JAXA mission, NASA worked with the agency to provide instruments and technologies to assist. The MMX spacecraft launches on top of an H3 rocket at Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (4:41 a.m. Japan Standard Time on October 20). You can watch it live on JAXA’s YouTube page . The mission will get to Phobos in August 2027 and spend at least 16 months surveying the surface before collecting samples. The samples will not return to Earth until at least 2031. The post How to watch Japan’s mission to Mars appeared first on Popular Science .

title: This snake cartwheels to escape danger
author: Andrew Paul
content: Snakes will bite, rattle their tails, and even spit venom to escape danger. But of all the world’s species, southeast Asia’s dwarf reed snake ( Pseudorabdion longiceps ) relies on an especially fascinating escape method. When threatened, the diminutive serpent rolls away like a speeding wheel. An adult dwarf reed snake typically measures less than 12 inches long, but its unique locomotive maneuvers allow it to retreat as fast one foot per second—about four times faster than it travels by simply slithering on the ground. It’s not a flailing getaway, either. The snake also easily rolls along a straight path while somehow keeping its head both stable and facing forward. Now, researchers finally have a better understanding of how the dwarf reed snake achieves such dizzying acrobatics. In a study published today in the journal Current Biology , a team at Japan’s Toho University detailed the specific physiology that enables its locomotion after filming the snakes with high-speed cameras. Essentially, the snake doesn’t rotate its entire body in a singular, forward motion—it whips one side of its body forward towards the ground while an arched portion swings down by its head in what the study’s authors call a “stroke.” The snake then alternates between its left and right side coming into contact with the ground for each successive stroke. Essentially, it’s like twirling a rope in a lateral circle while holding one end in your hand—except that end is the snake’s head. The cumulative efforts bypass the traditional idea of a wheel requiring something like a central axle. Instead, this ingenious, highly controlled movement allows the animal to keep its head and sensory organs upright and facing ahead while traveling at such high speed. This is compounded by the dwarf reed snake directing regions of its body to engage in large, alternating rotations while stabilizing its head. By gaining better insight into these biological mechanisms, researchers also highlight the difficulty in trying to predict an animal’s capabilities based solely on its physiology. A snake may have primarily evolved to slither—but that doesn’t mean it can’t get creative when necessary. The post This snake cartwheels to escape danger appeared first on Popular Science .

title: Expert ‘bat wranglers’ put GPS trackers on California’s bats
author: Margherita Bassi
content: October is officially Bat Appreciation Month . In the spirit of the season and conservation, a team of biologists in California recently spent time finding bats at Muir Woods National Monument and Samuel P. Taylor State Park. And while Halloween is fast approaching, the activity had nothing to do with spooky festivities and everything to do with tracking hoary ( Lasiurus cinereus ) and western red bats ( Lasiurus blossevillii ).  The goal of their survey was to put GPS trackers on bats from the two migratory species. Hoary bats have grey-white fur and are the most widespread bat species in North, Central, and South America. Western red bats , also known as southern red bats, sport a reddish fur and are found in parts of South America. In redwood forests, bats like nesting within holes inside large trees.  “When they migrate, those little guys can cover a LOT of ground!” the Golden Gate National Recreation Area writes , referencing both species. “By learning about these migratory patterns, we can better understand entire ecosystems like Muir Woods.” The bats were released back into the wild after getting their trackers. Image: NPS / Emily Pellegrini. Bats are important members of such ecosystems. They are pollinators , they spread seeds, and they help manage insect populations. To catch these helpful agents, scientists set up a sheer, delicate net called a “mist net” over a creek at dusk. All bats are nocturnal , and when they went searching for their next meal—bugs—they flew into the net.  It was a bit of a trick for the winged mammals, but a treat for the human team. “Expert bat wranglers” carefully took them out of the nets, noted their weight and size, presumably attached the GPS tracker, and then returned them to the wild.  The Golden Gate National Recreation Area’s shared pictures of tiny, disgruntled looking bats carefully pinched between gloved fingers. In one image, an expert holds a bat wing up to the light of a colleague’s headlamp. In fact, illuminated wing membrane patterns literally shed light on the bat’s age and developmental stage. A bat’s membrane can tell biologists how old the animal is and what developmental stage it is in. Image: NPS / Emily Pellegrini. While this survey focused on two bat species, researchers at the Muir Woods National Monument have previously spotted 10 different species . title: The remarkable bond between a man and a deer
author: Paul Bochner
content: Excerpted from PENELOPE by Paul Bochner . Copyright © 2026 by Paul Bochner. Published in the United States by Crown, an imprint of the Crown Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC.  On the evening of March 18, as it was growing dark, I went to the window, not knowing what was drawing me. Next to the house stood a shadow, ghost-like, shrunken, at one with the dusk, almost translucent, and I recognized The Girl with the Broken Foot. I walked out into the falling wet snow, slowly approaching her, and she allowed me to come close. Nine months old, she was the size of a fawn half that age. Starkly emaciated, her body seemed to be collapsing inward, her head held low. Literal hunger and a deeper starvation were palpable. She bore the haunted look of terminal solitude seen in souls driven to the margins of society, among the liv-ing, yet apart. She seemed so frail that I couldn’t imagine she would live more than another day or two. Going inside and returning with a bowl of apples, I cut them into pieces and placed a few on the ground between us. She was raven-ously hungry and I gave her a few more apples, and still more, until she had eaten a total of eight. After she had finished eating, she stayed with me. We stood about a foot apart. She showed no fear of me, a fact which I would later come to recognize as meaningful. The moment had the compelling quality which has been present at the onset of many enduring connections in my life, of being un-bound by linear time. “I am watching over you,” I said softly. “If you come here, I will take care of you. You are not alone.” It was fully dark when we parted, having been together for an hour. I expected that she would recede into the woods, yet the next morning she was sleeping against the house, directly beneath the window closest to where I sit all day to work. Save for the wall separating us, she could not have gotten any closer to me. Paul feeding Penelope. Image: Paul Bochner. When I went around to the front of the house, she struggled to her feet and approached. In the morning light, I was better able to assess the state of her health. Months of solitary survival had taken a severe toll. Her body seemed hollowed, her ribs and pelvis sharply visible beneath her skin, and it felt a miracle that she was alive. On her right flank was a hemispherical mass the size of a cantaloupe, which I took to be a tumor, yet it had an open, running wound at its center, which she periodically craned her neck to lick. Her eyes were running and had congealed masses at their inner corners. I bent to get a look at her injured foot. From not being walked on, the backward-facing cloven hoof had grown to an abnormal length and was curling upward. The wrist, which unnaturally bore her weight, had a flattened forward surface, an oval about two inches across, worn raw, without hair or skin, only pale pink–grey flesh, which, at its center, appeared to have been further abraded to the bone. Her right front foot, forced to compensate, was splayed and rockered, her right scapula protruded, and her front quarters were substantially lower than her hips. I again placed apple pieces on the ground between us. I spoke very gently to her, saying, “You are the best one of all the deer. You are the most beautiful. You are good.” I continued to talk to her while she ate her apples, and when she had taken all she could, she returned to her resting spot under the window. I went inside to work, keeping periodic watch, pleased that she seemed to have claimed a place. But in a few minutes, from around the corner of the house came the twins, followed by their mother who immediately and ag-gressively charged at her. The Girl with the Broken Foot lurched upright and hobbled down the embankment, across the road and into the woods. She was once again alone, but a step had been taken. Since the previous evening, things had changed. Even before her second feed-ing she had recognized me on sight. She had approached and had again allowed me near. Although I had seen her fewer than half a dozen times in the preceding months, from the night of our first connection, she began to come to the house every day. She slowly gained strength and I would watch for her and thrill to the sight of her slow approach. It was our private time. We stood together, and I placed her food on the ground between us. After she ate, she would stare into my eyes for long periods, seemingly entranced. I told her stories. I sang softly to her. I told her she was my beauty. So began our journey, and one of the greatest loves I have ever known. Penelope walking into the house. Image: Paul Bochner. About the Author Paul Bochner  began his professional life early, as a working musician through his mid-teens in Los Angeles, then moving to Montreal at the invitation of the National Film Board of Canada. He has won several international awards for his films and is the recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in painting. He has written for  The New Yorker  and  The Atlantic . title: Wash your hands. There’s probably poop on them.
author: Eric Alt
content: You would think, post- COVID , that we would all understand the importance of frequent and thorough handwashing . And yet, spend any time in a public restroom and you’ll see an alarming number of people who still see it as optional. We know it can help curb the spread of illness when you’re sick, but on an average day, just how gross is it to not wash your hands?  “Your hands have a microbial flora that is always present. These are mostly good bacteria that help protect your skin,” Allison Pappas, PhD, Director of Business Development at Gillson Sciences , tells Popular Science . “On unwashed hands, your normal flora is going to be the most abundant group of inhabitants and they’re nothing to worry about. If you’re not washing your hands, they won’t become overgrown by deadly bacteria. However, your hands will accumulate an increasing number of pathogenic bacteria and viruses from your environment.” Pappas explains that eating a sandwich or wiping your nose after exposure to these pathogenic bacteria are quick ways to then introduce those germs into your body. She describes it as a “tug-of-war,” with germs pulling one way and handwashing your only way to tug in the opposite direction. There are also physical characteristics that come into play as well. People with longer fingernails or rough, coarse skin give bacteria more places to hide. And it’s not always visible. As Pappas puts it: “Your hands can look clean but be utterly disgusting from a microbial perspective.”  According to the Center for Disease Control (CDC) , germs like Salmonella , E. coli, and norovirus that cause diarrhea, as well as some respiratory infections like adenovirus and hand-foot-mouth disease can all be present on unwashed hands. Why? Because there might be…wait for it…invisible poop.  “It’s extremely gross, but assume you’ve got poop on your hands,” says Pappas. “That sounds crazy, but studies have found fecal bacteria on children’s hands and toys and on the hands of 28 percent of commuters in the UK. Even if you don’t have a child and don’t commute via subways, you’re still touching all the same door handles and common utensils as the people who do. That poop is transferring to your hands, you just can’t see it.”  So how gross is not washing your hands? It’s “you have poop on your hands” gross.  “Yeah,” says Pappas, “Please wash your hands.” What is the right way to wash your hands ? Recent studies suggest that most people wash their hands too briefly to actually kill germs . So, if you want to avoid getting sick and spreading illness, it’s time to forget everything you thought you knew, and follow these instructions for proper hygiene: Wet your hands with water at a comfortable temperature. You can’t actually get the water hot enough to kill microbes without burning your skin, so just do what feels nice. The CDC actually recommends shutting the tap off while you lather your soap to conserve water . Lather your hands with soap. Don’t worry about buying something with anti-microbial ingredients; research shows that outside of a hospital setting, these additives don’t provide a significant benefit , and their use contributes to the rise of antibiotic resistance. Make sure you lather the backs of your hands, between your fingers, and under your nails, as dangerous microbes can lurk on any part of your skin. Continue scrubbing for 20-30 seconds before you start rinsing. It’s longer than you think. One study showed that most adults lather for just six seconds . Try singing “Happy Birthday” twice in your head (or out loud, if you’re feeling fun) to help keep time. Turn the tap back on and rinse. The CDC notes there’s little evidence that using a paper towel to turn the tap on and off after washing will improve your health. Dry your hands with a clean towel if possible, or with an air dryer. The CDC says that wet hands more easily transfer microbes. Plus, you don’t want to walk around with clammy hands all day. The post Wash your hands. There’s probably poop on them. appeared first on Popular Science .

title: New water lily can be seen from space
author: Margherita Bassi
content: One cold December day in 2021, Colorado carnivorous plant grower Jeremiah Harris shared some pictures of wild Amazonian giant water lilies ( Victoria amazonica ) plants in the Inírida River in Guainía, Colombia to Instagram. There’s just one problem. No known Victoria water lily species grow there.  When water lily expert Carlos Magdalena saw the post on Instagram, he suspected a new plant species could be involved. To investigate the matter, he used satellite imagery to remotely search the Inírida River and its surrounding lakes and confirmed the presence of Victorias. And yes, you can see these enormous plants from space. Victorias grow the world’s second largest single plant leaf.  Victoria colombiana is the fourth Victoria water lily to be described. Image: Carlos Magdalena. Magdalena is a botanical and scientific research horticulturist at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew in the U.K. Along with his colleagues, the team went on a five-day expedition to Inírida. The team included members of the Indigenous reserves del río Atabapo, one of whom had seen the lilies during his childhood.  However, the trip didn’t exactly go according to plan. By their last night, they had found only two water lily plants, neither of which had flowers. This was a problem, because botanists need a flower to differentiate species. As if that wasn’t bad enough, the water lilies they found seemed to be struggling with a late rainy season.  But when Magdalena described their situation to the expedition’s boat captain, Gustavo Melo, he said he knew where they could find more of this water lily. They didn’t have much time to do so, with the team’s flight back to Bogotá was at 9:00 a.m. the next morning. Thus at 1:00 a.m., Melo, a member of the Indigenous Tucano community, led them to a small lake. There, they found five more Victorias, one of which was blooming.  Horiculturalist Carlos Magdalena holds up a giant lilypad. Image: Mauricio Bernal. “This is one of those extraordinary stories where indigenous and horticultural knowledge with the help of social media and technology came together to uncover a truly extraordinary botanical achievement,” Magdalena said in a statement .  The  researchers were able to collect what they needed to start the official scientific description of the new species: Victoria colombiana . They even managed to make that early flight. In their recent study published in the journal Phytotaxa , he and his colleagues also announced the discovery of another new Victoria species, Victoria mattogrossensis .  A Victoria colombiana bud. Image: Nilo Rodriguez. The team estimates that there are only between 30 and 50 wild V. colombiana plants, and is extremely vulnerable to extinction. They are currently working to get the plant officially categorized as Critically Endangered by the IUCN Red List.  “Now that we know this water lily exists, our responsibility is to understand it better and protect it. With so many plants in the wild threatened with extinction, we simply cannot wait any longer to take action,” Magdalena added. Experts are considering starting a naturalized population in a more accessible lake in Indigenous territory and researchers also are hoping to cultivate the species in Bogotà. title: Real-life vampire birds hunt and drink blood in remote Ecuador
author: Clarissa Brincat
content: When zoology professor Daniel Baldassarre traveled to the remote Galápagos Islands of Wolf and Darwin with two other researchers, getting there proved quite a challenge. With no beaches to land a boat on, they had to approach the islands’ cliffs in a small dinghy and wait for a lull in the waves before jumping onto sharp, black lava rocks. But their efforts paid off. On that trip, they saw a bird that very few people have ever set eyes on in the wild: the vampire ground finch. These finches are only found on Wolf and Darwin , and feed on the blood of much larger birds called Nazca boobies that also live on the islands.  Up close, Baldassarre and his colleagues noted the vampire finches’ blood-stained bills and their throats visibly engorged with blood. They also saw them in action.  “We observed scores of vampire finches clamouring all over the backs, tails, and wings of boobies, opening up substantial wounds with their sharp beaks, and drinking their fill of blood,” they wrote in an article for The Conversation .  Why only some birds drink blood “ Blood is a notoriously difficult food source to process and extract nutrients from, which probably partly explains why so few animals have evolved to feed on it,” Baldassarre tells Popular Science . He suspects that on these islands where freshwater is extremely rare, blood might serve as a water source for the finches.  Two Nazca boobies perform their species’ mating call. Vampire ground finches feed on Nazca boobies on the remote Galápagos Islands of Wolf and Darwin. Image: Getty Images / inthedark72 It’s not the only component of the vampire finches’ diet, however. Based on unpublished data collected by Baldassarre and his colleagues, blood makes up about one-tenth of the vampire finches’ diet.  “These finches are quite opportunistic, so they will eat just about anything they can find,” Baldassarre says. “We observed them feeding on everything from seeds to insects to broken seabird eggs.” One theory is that vampire finches rely more on blood feeding in periods of extreme drought, when other resources are scarce. But more research is needed to see if this idea holds up in practice. How this strange behavior evolved Vampire finches weren’t always vampires , scientists think. The relationship between vampire finches and boobies probably started off with the finches eating parasites found on the skin and feathers of the boobies. This would have been mutually beneficial because it provided a cleaning service for the boobies and food for the finches. But at some point in evolutionary history , in the process of picking off parasites, the finches started to create lesions on the boobies’ skin, and eventually began feeding on their blood . Over time, their bills became more scalpel-like, perfect for making skin incisions. Their digestive system also changed. When Baldassarre and his colleagues studied the microbes found in vampire finches’ guts, they found that their gut microbiome was very different from that of other, non-blood-consuming finches on the Galápagos Islands, something they attribute to their unique diet. Until recently, vampire finches were considered a subspecies of the sharp-beaked ground finch ( Geospiza difficilis ).  “But they have now been designated as their own species [ Geospiza septentrionalis ] because of the differences they have evolved because of blood feeding,” Baldassarre notes.  Vampire ground finches on Wolf island have been seen drinking nectar from Galápagos prickly pear flowers and other flowers. Image: Peter Wilton / CC BY 2.0 How the boobies cope  Baldassarre and his colleagues have seen vampire finches gang up on and kill nestling boobies,“but that was quite rare,” he points out. “In most cases, the finches seem to inflict just enough damage to break the skin and extract some blood, but not too much to harm the boobies significantly.” This is similar to many parasite-host relationships, such as fleas , ticks , and mosquitoes on mammals. “You can kind of think of the vampire finches as giant mosquitoes,” Baldassarre says. As seen in a segment on vampire finches in David Attenborough’s documentary A Perfect Planet , the boobies seem to tolerate the vampire finches rather than chasing them away. There are likely a few reasons for this, Baldassarre says.  “For one, as in large animals being bitten by mosquitoes, often the damage is minimal and not noticeable, so it doesn’t elicit a strong reaction. Also, the boobies sometimes have a vested interest in staying put and guarding their spot in the colony, or perhaps nest or nestlings, so may not want to fly away. Finally, the finches seem to target hard-to-reach areas on the boobies like the base of tail feathers, so it’s likely difficult for the boobies to deter them.” I, for one, was feeling very sorry for the boobies being constantly hounded by these small vampire birds. Until I learnt that Nazca boobies practice something called “obligate siblicide,” which essentially means that the first-hatched chick routinely attacks and kills its younger sibling. It’s a harsh, bird-eat-bird world in the Galápagos Islands. title: WhatsApp like a pro with these 7 expert tricks and hidden features
author: David Nield
content: When it comes to the mobile app heavyweights, few can beat WhatsApp. It’s estimated that around 3 billion people now use the cross-platform messaging tool at least once a month. And it’s important to remember there are only 8 billion or so people on the planet, so there are no signs of its popularity waning anytime soon. Beyond being a hugely successful app, it’s also packed with features. You can use it to chat, make voice and video calls, share files, broadcast your location, and more. Even if you’ve used WhatsApp for years, you might not have discovered everything it’s capable of—which is where these tips come in. 1. Set a timer for messages to disappear You don’t necessarily want everything you say on WhatsApp to be remembered forever, and the app includes a timer feature that will automatically expunge messages in a chat 24 hours, 7 days, or 90 days after they’re read, unless you specifically keep them. This is set on a chat-by-chat basis, and affects everyone in a conversation. To change the setting for one of your chats, tap the contact or group name at the top of the screen, then pick Disappearing messages to select your time limit. This is applied until you turn it off or select a different period, but doesn’t affect the conversation history. 2. Lock away your most sensitive chats Put certain chats behind a lock. David Nield Another way of protecting sensitive information in chats is to add an extra lock to specific conversations. Even if someone should gain access to your phone and your apps, they won’t be able to see your locked chats. From inside a conversation, tap the contact or group name at the top, then pick Chat lock ( Android ) or Lock chat ( iOS ). You can then use a specific PIN code to block access to the conversation, or use the same biometric scan technology (such as Face ID) that already protects your phone at the lock screen. 3. Edit a message after sending it Have you noticed you can edit messages after sending them? It’s handy for those typos you only spot after dispatching a message—long-press on whatever you just sent, then tap the three dots and Edit (Android), or just Edit on the pop-up menu (iOS). Modified messages have an ‘Edited’ label visible to everyone in the chat, but they won’t be able to see what the original message said. 4. Stop specific contacts from seeing when you’re active Take control of who sees your activity on WhatsApp. David Niel WhatsApp can tell your contacts whether you’re currently using the app and when you were “last seen,” but this might not be information you want to share with everyone. As well as disabling the feature entirely, you can also turn it off for specific contacts. Open the You tab, then tap Privacy > Last seen and online , then select My contacts except … under the Who can see my last seen heading. You can then pick the contacts you don’t want to give this information to, and set the Who can see when I’m online option to match the same list. 5. Pin important messages you need to refer to or remember Important details can quickly get lost in WhatsApp conversations, especially in busy group chats. But there is a way to pin specific messages to the top of the chat so they’re easy to get back to—someone’s address or the start time of an event, for example. To pin a message on Android, long-press on it, then tap the three dots (top right) and Pin . On iOS, long-press a message and choose More > Pin . You can have up to three pinned messages per conversation, and select from three options for how long they’re pinned for: 24 hours , 7 days , or 30 days . 6. Give contacts their own notification sound Your contacts can have their own alert sounds. David Nield WhatsApp lets you assign specific notification sounds to specific contacts, which means you know who’s calling or messaging without picking up your phone. It gives you a better idea of whether something needs attention right away or can be safely ignored for a while. Tap the group or contact name at the top of a chat, then pick Notifications and Notification tone or Ringtone to make changes. You can also select Vibrate to customize vibrations for each chat, though there are only four options here. The option to mute the conversation is on the same screen—you can set mute separately for calls and messages. 7. Message yourself with notes and reminders Not all messaging apps let you have a conversation with yourself, but WhatsApp does. This might seem like a rather pointless (and lonely) way of using the messaging app, but it can be really useful for jotting down things you need to remember on the go, leaving yourself voice notes of ideas and thoughts, and so on. From the main conversation list, go to start a new chat, then search for “you” as the contact (or just enter your own username or phone number). title: Orphaned walrus calf rescued from nearby polar bears in Alaska
author: Margherita Bassi
content: Some animal rescues are more complicated than others—especially when the creature in peril is about to become a snack for a seagull on a remote Alaskan beach with polar bears lurking nearby.  That was the sticky situation an orphaned Pacific walrus (a subspecies of Odobenus rosmarus ) calf was in when two researchers found it on an island in the region of Point Lay, Alaska. U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) research walrus biologist Tony Fischbach and Ilisaġvik College student and Point Lay local Violet Anniskett stumbled upon the young male while investigating walrus carcasses on a remote beach. They found the orphan between the remains of two adult walruses, which was a first in Fischbach’s long experience working with walrus herds there.  The researchers requested permission to rehabilitate the walrus from the local Inupiaq community and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Once the approval arrived, the next hurdle was getting the mammal to the Alaska SeaLife Center . The center is the only marine mammal rehabilitation facility in Alaska, and was over 800 miles away. As if things could get any more difficult, stormy weather left Anniskett, Fischbach, and the walrus stuck on the island for days. In the meantime, the researchers guided the calf to an abandoned building to shelter from predators. “When we found him, a determined flock of gulls was intent on scavenging him. He was in immediate peril of suffering this fate had we not gotten approval to intervene. Two polar bears were also active on the island,” Fischbach said in a statement .  “He bonded with us fast and wouldn’t sleep unless one of us were in the room. It was just us two for three days, stuck in a storm with the young walrus,” Anniskett added.  The calf was finally transported to the local airport, and made it to Alaska SeaLife Center on September 14 after a flight and van ride. The 200 pound baby arrived dehydrated, but in good physical condition. They treated some superficial wounds, gave him fluids, and applied other stabilizing treatments.  But the calf’s journey wasn’t over. In fact, orphaned Pacific walrus calves are one of the most specialized patients in marine mammal rehabilitation.That’s because in the wild, calves are very attached to their mothers, with whom they usually stay for one to two years. Close physical contact both with their mothers and others of their king is a crucial element in a calf’s early life. In the case of an orphaned calf, humans (who are authorized specialists) can act as surrogates, but it’s a tough babysitting job. Someone has to be around all the time to provide physical contact, social interaction, feeding support, and any veterinary care.  Caring for a Pacific walrus calf is not for the faint of heart, but can be pretty cute. Image: Kaiti Grant/Alaska SeaLife Center. “Caring for an orphaned walrus calf is truly a team effort and requires around the clock commitment,” said Jane Belovarac, an Alaska SeaLife Center wildlife response curator. “At least two staff members have been working shifts around the clock to stay with him and provide the care he needs. This means long days and some unusual sleeping schedules for our team.” It also means that the calf becomes comfortable with humans and thus cannot return to the wild. Now in a new long term home (whose location hasn’t been announced yet), he will be an ambassador for his species by teaching people about Pacific walruses.  The post Orphaned walrus calf rescued from nearby polar bears in Alaska appeared first on Popular Science .

title: 15 uplifting images from Dog Photography Awards 2026
author: Popular Science Team
content: Sometime between 32,000 and 11,000 years ago , dogs domesticated. Since then, these four-legged friends have provided companionship, assistance, and protection for people. Whether you favor a squished-face potato dog or a determined and smart working dog, you likely understand how dogs got the designation of “man’s best friend.” The Dog Photography Awards celebrate dogs of all shapes and sizes. The annual competition awards prizes across six categories (Studio, Action, Portrait, Dogs & People, Documentary, and Open) in addition to naming an overall winner. “City Lights” 2026 Portrait Outdoor, Honorable Mention Credit: Maddie Newton / Dog Photography Awards This year, Katie Brockman took the prestigious title of Dog Photographer of the Year. The St. Louis-based photographer’s winning entry, titled “Loved and Hated” (seen below), captures the duality of feelings around pitbulls and similar breeds. “I started photography after my dog Caldwell ended up at the emergency vet on Christmas Eve 2020 for an obstruction surgery” Brockman said. “I suddenly realized that I didn’t have enough photos of him, and I wanted a way to document our adventures together. So I saved up for a camera, and in 2021, I officially started my dog photography journey.” “Loved and Hated” Dog Photographer of the Year 2026 Credit: Katie Brockman / Dog Photography Awards This year’s competition drew 1,900 entries from photographers in 50 countries. A judging panel of photographers, dog experts, and industry professionals decided on the winners. content: I’ve been in the bag world so long that I remember a time when logos were very, very, very out. The idea of carrying a logo bag was not only not a trend, but also seen as tacky in a way. But then, the logo came back, and it feels like that non-logo era was a blip of time that will never fully take hold again. Because logos are very in, in various manners. Gucci was the first brand that I started to learn to re-love the logo. The classic GG monogram feels subtle enough; the tan-on-brown comes off as a neutral, while remaining iconic. And as a forever Gucci girl, I am always perusing the site to see what might catch my attention next. However, a few months ago, my friend was in Italy and sent me a photo of a bag. I hadn’t seen it before, and once she shared it, she and I both texted our adoration for it. It instantly made its way to the top of my wishlist, and I decided it just might be the best Gucci bag I’ve ever seen. Meet the Gucci Aperitivo Crystal Shoulder Bag And here she is, in all her glory! This is the Gucci Aperitivo Crystal Shoulder Bag , and she is stunning. She is everything I love from Gucci, from the classic GG monogram to the Piston closure (think Gucci Jackie ) to the all-over crystal finish. The base is sand and dark brown GG canvas, a combination that already has my heart, but the clear crystals covering it are what sent me over the edge. You can still see the monogram underneath, and I love that Gucci didn’t lose that familiar feeling when adding all this sparkle. The gold-toned hardware and Piston closure finish it off, and honestly, there isn’t a detail here that I would want to change. A photo of the bag my friend sent me when she spotted it in Italy! The sparkle picking up the light is what sold me on it Gucci’s crystal pieces are some of the best: the best I’ve seen, the best as far as aesthetics go, and the ones you love most when I share them. So this bag? It is the best of the best. Part of Gucci Primavera, the Aperitivo is meant for evenings and pre-dinner drinks, which feels very fitting for both the name and the bag. But I am also very much of the belief that you don’t need to save a bag like this for a special occasion. Jeans, a simple top, and this bag? That would do it for me. What Fits Inside the Gucci Aperitivo? The bag measures 10.2 inches wide by 5.7 inches high by 1.4 inches deep, so this is a slim shape with room for the essentials. Gucci lists an iPhone Pro Max or Plus, AirPods, a small wallet, and lipstick among what fits inside. The interior is lined in dark brown leather and includes one zip pocket. There is a chain strap, along with a detachable, adjustable leather strap that allows you to wear it crossbody. I appreciate having that option, even if the chain is what I am immediately drawn to with this particular bag. Made in Italy, it weighs approximately 0.7 pounds. I haven’t had this one in my hands yet, so the real-life what-fits test will have to wait. For now, I am admiring it from afar, zooming in on the details, and finding absolutely no reason to move it down my wishlist. I’ve seen a lot of Gucci bags over the years. I’ve loved a lot of Gucci bags over the years. But this one? This one has me doing the thing that got me into bags in the first place: thinking about it long after I’ve closed the tab. Shop the Gucci Crystal Apertivo for $4,150 via Gucci.

title: One Bag, Two Ways: Kelsey Merritt Quietly Favors The Row’s Margaux Bag
author: Kaitlin Serio
content: If you’re not one of Kelsey Merritt’s 2M Instagram followers , then you might not have heard of the model, who made history in 2018 as the first model of Filipino descent to walk in the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show. Merritt sat this year out, handing over the torch to model Christina Nadin, who became the second model of Filipino descent to walk the Victoria’s Secret runway. Instead of gym-hopping around LA for show prep, Merritt touched down in New York to celebrate her 30th birthday. A Lesson in Low-Key Luxury The Row Margaux East-West Clutch The model was spotted heading to and from New York’s Bowery Hotel multiple times over the past week—because where else would a model-turned-influencer stay for a milestone birthday? Merritt gave us a lesson in quiet-luxury dressing, opting for The Row’s chic, if entirely impractical, Margaux East-West clutch for a couple of effortlessly polished evening looks. Simple but entirely sophisticated, Merritt’s outfits prove the power of great staples. The perfect black bootie, a statement pair of sunglasses, or an It bag can do all the talking, even when the rest of the look is intentionally under the radar. After all, sometimes the most understated pieces make the biggest statement.

title: Dior’s Iconic Newsprint Is Back for Cruise 2027
author: Kaitlin Serio
content: Jonathan Anderson continues to shape a distinctive identity for Dior, bringing together the House’s rich heritage and a contemporary perspective. For his Cruise 2027 debut , he explored this connection through Christian Dior’s longstanding fascination with cinema and his close association with Hollywood glamour. Revisiting Dior’s Cinematic Heritage This cinematic influence has remained an enduring part of Dior’s legacy, and Anderson revisited the archives for the collection, drawing inspiration from a jacket featured in Christian Dior’s Spring/Summer 1949 Haute Couture collection. The design was worn by Marlene Dietrich in Alfred Hitchcock’s Stage Fright, reflecting the actress’s celebrated affinity for the House. Dietrich famously declared to Warner Bros. executives, “No Dior, no Dietrich!”—a statement that captured her unwavering loyalty to the designer. Dior Lady D-Joy Bag , $5,900 Dior Mid-Length Asymmetrical Dress , $7,700 Another archival reference in Anderson’s Cruise 2027 collection takes a more contemporary turn, paying homage to John Galliano’s era at Dior. Enter Galliano’s iconic Fall 2000 Dior newsprint, which made its return to the runway this season. Anderson isn’t the first Dior designer to revisit the motif, however, with Maria Grazia Chiuri offering her own interpretation for Pre-Fall 2024 . Jonathan Anderson Looks Back to Galliano Anderson reimagines the iconic newsprint across a range of accessories, including the classic Saddle bag, a mini Saddle pochette dubbed the Saddle Rodeo that feels like a nod to the archives, as well as Anderson’s signature Bow Bag and the Lady D-Joy. For Dior collectors who have never quite managed to get their hands on Carrie Bradshaw’s infamous Dior newsprint dress—now a highly coveted piece that commands exorbitant resale prices—Anderson’s take offers a new way to wear the iconic motif. The catch? It’ll set you back $7,700 . Dior Saddle Rodeo Mini Bag , $2,450 Dior Newspaper Square Scarf , $620 Dior Bow Bag , $5,000 Dior Saddle Bag , $4,800

title: The Handbag Trends to Watch for Spring 2027
author: Kaitlin Serio
content: With Fashion Month Spring 2027 officially behind us, it’s time for our twice-yearly look at the handbag trends that stood out most on the runways this past season. Through a microlens, Fashion Month offers a glimpse into the direction each of our favorite brands is headed for the season ahead. From the continued evolution of established creative visions to the latest collections from fashion’s most talked-about Maisons, the Spring 2027 shows gave us plenty to unpack. Taking a step back, Fashion Month as a whole offers a broader look at where the industry is headed. Which styles are gaining momentum? What are we likely to see less of? And, most importantly, which handbag trends are poised to be everywhere in the coming months? Today, we’re taking one final look at the Spring 2027 runway shows to bring you six of the biggest handbag trends we spotted this season. We considered both the collections we covered in greater detail here on the site and those we didn’t review in full. Without further ado, let’s get into it! It’s What’s On the Inside that Counts This season, a less ubiquitous but still noteworthy trend was bags with colorful interiors. Building on last season’s relaxed, open interiors, designers took things one step further for Spring 2027, introducing colorful linings and contrasting hues that made the inside just as interesting as the outside. Givenchy Jil Sander Chanel Celine Balenciaga Altuzarra On the Wild Side Animal skins are set to continue their reign come Spring 2027, with everything from croc and python to ostrich popping up on the runways. Both faux and real exotic finishes made an appearance, often in unexpected, colorful hues that gave these familiar textures a fresh feel. Miu Miu Prada Chanel Marni Valentino Dior Loewe Mulberry Khaite Dries Van Noten Gucci Louis Vuitton From East to West To all the east-west bag haters out there, we apologize in advance: the elongated, divisive silhouette is here to stay. For Spring 2027, it appeared across a range of styles, from shoulder bags and top handles to the ever-popular baguette-inspired clutch. Prada Louis Vuitton Khaite Ferragamo Chanel Chanel Celine Bottega Veneta Balmain Gabriela Heart Pretty in Purple Purple lovers (raises hand) rejoice! After making waves last season, purple is continuing its reign into Spring 2027, appearing in everything from bold, royal hues to softer, muted lilacs. The color made such an impression at Miu Miu that the Maison even transformed its show space with a royal purple runway. Balenciaga Miu Miu Tory Burch Prada Givenchy Valentino Chanel Dior Really Into Red For every runway where purple was absent, red was sure to make an appearance—and sometimes, the two came together. Color is having a moment again, and if purple isn’t quite your speed, red is another standout shade worth considering. Bold enough to make a statement yet surprisingly easy to work into your wardrobe, it’s a trend that feels just as wearable as it does eye-catching. Loewe Givenchy Celine Marni Chanel Chanel Bottega Veneta Maison Margiela Courrèges Fendi Jil Sander Proenza Schouler Bigger Is Better Looking to jet-set or simply run around with everything you own? Spring 2027’s biggest bags have you covered. From exaggerated duffels at Miu Miu to oversized takes on classic silhouettes at Mulberry and Proenza Schouler, this season, bigger is definitely better. title: The Ultimate Guide to the Coach Nolita Bag
author: Megs Mahoney Dusil
content: Certain bags stay with you, and my first Coach bag holds the top spot for me. It was a little Coach Pochette, the bag that got me hooked on handbags, and I still own it to this day. I smile thinking of all the girls who will start their own handbag collections with one little bag, without knowing where it might lead. Mine led me here. For many of them, that first bag will be the Coach Nolita . The Coach Nolita has that kind of appeal. It’s a going-out bag, a little bag to pack for a trip, a gift you’re excited to give, and a place to start a collection. And even if you’re well past your first bag, as I very clearly am, there’s always room for a little Coach. Coach Nolita at a Glance Nolita 19 in black leather The Coach Nolita 19 is a mini shoulder bag that can also be carried as a wristlet , with a zip-top closure and two interior credit card slots. It’s compact, keeps the essentials close, and comes in enough materials, colors, and prints that choosing your favorite might be the hardest part. The built-in card slots mean you can leave your cardholder behind if you want to save space. Or, if you’re like me and prefer moving a card case from bag to bag, you have that option, too. Dimensions: 7.5″ L × 4.5″ H × 2″ D Materials: Options include leather, Signature coated canvas, denim, and seasonal finishes Closure: Zip-top Interior: Two credit card slots; additional pockets vary by version Carry options: Mini shoulder bag or wristlet Price: $119–$129 for the styles featured in this guide Prices and availability checked 10/21/26. What Sizes Does the Coach Nolita Come In? Style Dimensions Carry options Price Coach Nolita 19 [7.5″ L × 4.5″ H × 2″ D] Shoulder carry or wristlet $119 – $129 The Coach Nolita is currently offered in the Nolita 19 , measuring 7.5 inches long, 4.5 inches high, and 2 inches deep. Coach has offered other sizes in the past, including the smaller Nolita 15 and larger Nolita 24 wristlet and crossbody designs. For me, the appeal of this size is simple: I don’t always want a bag that gives me an excuse to carry more. Sometimes, having room for just the necessities is exactly the point. What Fits Inside the Coach Nolita 19? The Coach Nolita 19 is designed for small essentials. Coach lists room for keys, a card case, and an iPhone up to the iPhone Pro Max . Your phone case and the other items you carry will affect how comfortably everything fits. The two interior card slots are useful here. You can carry your cards directly in the bag, leaving more room for the things you don’t want to go without. If you prefer a separate wallet, a slim card case will take up less space than a bulky wallet. With a bag this size, fitting everything inside is only half the equation. You also want to be able to get your phone or keys out without unpacking the entire bag. Leaving a little breathing room makes a small bag much easier to use. Coach Nolita Sizes, Colors, and Materials One of the best parts of the Nolita is the variety. The shape stays familiar, but a different material or color can give it an entirely different feel. Signature coated canvas is a classic Coach choice, especially if you love the house’s recognizable pattern. There are neutral combinations as well as seasonal colors, so you can decide how much you want the bag to stand out. The leather versions offer another direction, from the texture of pebbled leather to crinkle finishes and crocodile-embossed leather. The latter gives you the look of a croc pattern embossed onto leather. Denim holds a special place in my heart because it reminds me of the Coach bag my sister chose when I got my first Pochette. Her bag feels nearly as much a part of my handbag memories as mine does, even though it wasn’t mine. I also love the leopard-print haircalf version. A small bag is a very good place to have a little fun. Colors and finishes change with the assortment. If you’re choosing between versions, check the individual listing for the exact exterior material, lining, hardware, and interior details. Signature Canvas/Gold/Walnut/Black Signature Canvas/Gold/TanBrown Signature Canvas/Silver/Sand/Taupe Signature Canvas/Gold/White/Chalk Signature Canvas/Gold/Navy Signature Canvas/Gold/Black Currant Pebbled Leather/Gold/Black Pebbled Leather/Gold/Chalk Crinkle Leather/Gold/Poppy Haircalf With Leopard Print Signature Regenerative Cotton Denim Signature Canvas/Gold/Sand/Tan Signature Canvas/Gold/Sand/Chalk Embossed Crocodile/Gold/Maple Embossed Crocodile/Gold/Black How Does the Coach Nolita Carry? Coach Nolita carried as wristlet Coach Nolita carried over shoulder The Coach Nolita can be worn as a mini shoulder bag or carried as a wristlet . For the wristlet configuration, you simply detach one end of the strap and clip it to the opposite side. That gives the same little bag two useful roles: over your shoulder when you want your hands free, or around your wrist when you’d rather keep it close. Coach lists a 6.25-inch handle drop on the current refined pebble leather Nolita 19 . This won’t fit over the top of most jackets, and will even fit snugly on different people, something to keep in mind. The shoulder-to-wristlet conversion is also different from crossbody carry. You could opt for a shoulder extension strap to turn this bag into a crossbody, or make it a longer shoulder strap. Coach Nolita in Action The Coach Tabby tends to get the spotlight, but the Nolita has its own appeal. It’s familiar without demanding attention, the kind of little bag you can picture fitting right into your wardrobe. @c.assie @avagracelaurie @bran_bran1984 I always love seeing how people actually carry their bags, and the Nolita is no exception. Over the shoulder or around the wrist, with jeans or dressed up for dinner, it makes a good case for keeping things small. Is the Coach Nolita Right for You? If your daily necessities are a phone, cards, keys, and a few small extras, the Coach Nolita is worth a look. If your essentials include a full-size wallet, a large sunglasses case, and several just-in-case items, its compact dimensions deserve a closer look before you buy. I like the idea of the Nolita as a smaller bag to pack inside your travel tote, ready for dinner once you arrive. It also makes sense as a gift, especially for someone choosing her first Coach bag. I’ve seen so many young girls receiving little Coach bags lately, and it brings me right back to where my own collection began. At $119–$129 for the versions featured here , the Nolita offers plenty of choice without the price of a much larger bag. You can go classic with Signature canvas, keep it simple with leather, or choose a print because it makes you smile. That’s part of what I’ve always loved about Coach. Your first bag can feel like a very big deal. And years later, even with a closet full of bags, you can still understand exactly why.

title: The Savette Symmetry Chain Pochette Is Back for Fall—and Better Than Ever
author: Kaitlin Serio
content: Some designs need little introduction, and by now, this rings true for the Savette Symmetry Pochette. Despite its quiet appeal and under-the-radar feel, the Savette Symmetry Pouch has become a celebrated signature of the brand, beloved for its architectural lines, distinctive turn-lock closure, and effortless elegance. The Savette Symmetry Pochette: a Modern Classic Launching as part of Savette’s debut collection, the Symmetry Pochette has become a staple of the brand. Its signature turn-lock is evocative of sculptures found in modern art, while its lines are clean and geometric. Incredibly pared down and sleek, it’s elegant in all its simplicity. The Symmetry Pochette’s simple design and clean lines allow the bag’s quality and craftsmanship to shine through—and shine it does. The bags are crafted just outside the Italian city of Florence, an area known for its traditional leatherwork and attention to detail. Made by hand with an exceptional focus on the finer details, Savette’s bags feel worth the investment, particularly in a luxury market where prices seem to climb ever higher. Savette Symmetry Chain Bag , $1,690 Savette Symmetry Chain Bag , $1,690 A Little Chain Goes a Long Way Now, the shape we know and love—and one I return to time and time again —returns in its newest iteration that offers a fresh perspective on the original. We immediately took notice of the Savette Symmetry Chain Pochette when it first launched in 2024, thanks to the added hands-free functionality it brings to a shape we know and love, all without compromising on elegance. Furthering its sleek appeal, the chain is delicate and refined rather than chunky or cumbersome, making this a bag deserving of a second (OK, third) look. New for the fall season, the Savette Chain Pochette arrives in a fresh range of suede hues alongside classic black leather and timeless neutrals, giving us yet another reason to turn our attention to the Savette Symmetry family.
