title: Oracle adds a semantic layer to ground AI agents in the business context
author: infoworld.com
content: Oracle is expanding its Autonomous AI Lakehouse with a Business Semantic Layer designed to give AI agents a consistent understanding of enterprise data, a move aimed at improving the accuracy of AI-generated insights and helping organizations scale agentic applications across business functions. To ground AI agents in business context, the Business Semantic Layer uses catalog annotations, SQL annotations imported from Oracle AI Database, and AI-suggested analytic views to create reusable models of enterprise data that capture dimensions, measures, hierarchies, calculations, and key performance indicators (KPIs), Oracle said in a statement. These models can then be used across Oracle’s natural-language querying, data retrieval, and analytics capabilities, including Select AI, to help ensure that queries and insights are based on consistent business definitions. Oracle said that the new capabilities will be available within the next 12 months. Alongside the new layer, at the company’s annual AI World conference, Oracle also launched a Business Simulation Engine to help enterprises evaluate business scenarios and make more informed planning decisions by integrating Oracle Essbase into the Autonomous AI Lakehouse. Beyond forecasting and what-if analysis, the engine supports write-back, dynamic hierarchy rollups, advanced calculations, and allocations, the company said. Enterprise users can also ask questions in natural language, generate simulation reports, and perform Excel-based analysis on data stored in Oracle databases or in object storage via the new engine, it added. Additionally, Oracle is expanding Apache Iceberg support in the lakehouse to let customers create, populate, update, and delete Iceberg tables using SQL, while improving performance and functionality when accessing Iceberg data through external catalogs or its AI Data Catalog. Business context could improve AI reliability, support scale-up That ability to ground AI agents in business context will help data professionals and developers build more reliable AI-driven analytics and applications by using approved business metrics and definitions, reducing the time spent investigating and reconciling inconsistent results, said Amit Kumar Jena , AI development head at IT Consulting firm Kanerika. “We at Kanerika did something similar for a global pharma company on Fabric , a rival offering from Microsoft, modeling 40-plus entities and standardizing 85-plus KPIs before the agents went live. Investigation and reconciliation time fell by about 70%,” Jena said. These improvements in reliability will, in turn, help CIOs scale agentic applications across business functions and rely on AI-driven decision-making with greater confidence, said Manoj Chandra Jha , principal analyst at Nord-IQ Research. Similarly, the addition of the Business Simulation Engine, too, has the potential to help enterprises speed up decision-making by bringing analytics and planning capabilities together within the lakehouse. “By bringing analytics and planning closer together, the engine could help finance teams and business planners run what-if scenarios using enterprise data without repeatedly moving it between separate systems,” said Pareekh Jain , principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting. For CIOs, that could simplify data architecture and accelerate decisions, while developers could spend less time building integrations between analytics and planning tools and more time developing applications that turn business insights into actionable workflows, Jain added. The expanded Apache Iceberg support could further simplify data management for developers and data professionals by allowing them to create and modify Iceberg tables using familiar SQL, rather than relying on separate tools or workflows, Jha pointed out. For data engineers, specifically, this means being able to work with a single copy of the data using SQL while retaining the flexibility to use Oracle alongside platforms such as Apache Spark, Snowflake, or Databricks on the same tables, he added. That reduced data duplication, in turn, for CIOs, could reduce associated storage and processing costs, while giving greater flexibility to work across different data platforms, echoed Jain. New capabilities bring implementation and integration challenges However, each of the new capabilities added to the Autonomous AI Lakehouse comes with its own set of trade-offs. The Business Semantic Layer, to begin with, will require enterprises to define and maintain business metrics, relationships, and rules to ensure AI agents interpret data consistently, Jena said. For CIOs, this creates an additional governance responsibility because if the models are incomplete or outdated, AI-generated insights could still be inconsistent or misleading, while expanding the layer across business functions could require sustained work from data teams to model and validate new metrics and relationships, Jena added. For the Business Simulation Engine, meanwhile, the challenge will lie in how well it fits into existing enterprise workflows, supports established planning processes, and integrates with systems already in use, particularly as Oracle competes with dedicated planning platforms such as Anaplan, OneStream, and SAP Analytics Cloud, Jain pointed out. The expanded Iceberg support, too, comes with caveats around data portability and vendor lock-in. While open table formats can make data easier to access across platforms, enterprises may still depend on proprietary catalogs and semantic layers to manage and interpret it, Jha said. Oracle has not specified when the Business Simulation Engine or the expanded Apache Iceberg capabilities will become available to customers.

title: How malicious downloads can trick AI coding agents into compromising themselves
author: infoworld.com
content: Malicious instruction files planted in a computer’s Downloads folder can trick AI coding agents into executing harmful code or exposing authentication tokens, Forever Security said after blocking an attempted attack on a customer’s machine and demonstrating similar techniques against OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code. In its research report, the firm said it discovered a malicious AGENTS.md file in a customer’s Downloads folder that instructed Codex to install a malicious npm package called function-color. The installation was blocked before the malware could execute. The researchers could not determine how the original file reached the computer, but demonstrated that a malicious website could trigger a similar download without a separate approval prompt. The attack exploits the way AI coding assistants process project-specific instructions. Codex uses AGENTS.md, while Claude Code supports CLAUDE.md. Both can interpret instructions contained in these Markdown files when operating in directories where the files are present. The attack requires the agent to operate in the affected directory and process the malicious file. For Codex, the directory must also be trusted, according to Forever Security. In tests using the file recovered from the customer’s machine, Forever Security found that Codex could be manipulated into modifying its machine-wide MCP server configuration and launching another session with approval and sandbox restrictions bypassed. Codex followed the malicious instructions in more than 90% of tests, most of which used a harmless substitute for the malware. Because the malicious server was registered in Codex’s machine-wide configuration, it could also be loaded in subsequent sessions, even after the developer moved to another directory. A separate demonstration against Claude Code showed that a malicious CLAUDE.md file could redirect the agent’s API traffic to a researcher-controlled server, exposing authentication tokens and allowing the server to supply commands for execution. The configuration manipulation succeeded in approximately half of the tests. The researchers also successfully replayed a captured OAuth token against the legitimate API, demonstrating the potential for account compromise. The Markdown files contain no executable code. Instead, the attack relies on an AI agent interpreting their contents as legitimate instructions and carrying them out with its existing permissions. Commenting on Forever Security’s findings, Sakshi Grover , senior research manager for cybersecurity products and services for Asia/Pacific at IDC, said the research was a credible early warning rather than evidence of widespread exploitation. She noted that the reported success rates varied between agents and had not been independently validated. An architectural weakness The findings expose a broader design problem in AI coding agents, which are expected to follow project instructions but may also have access to sensitive configurations and execution privileges, according to Akshat Tyagi , associate practice leader at HFS Research. “The deeper issue is that these tools treat following an instruction and granting a privilege as the same act,” Tyagi said. He argued that vendors must separate the two, ensuring that instructions from project files cannot authorize changes to an agent’s security settings without independent human approval. Grover said vendors should verify the origin of instruction files and require explicit approval before loading those from untrusted sources, rather than automatically treating them as authoritative. Attackers could adapt the technique to other locations accessible to coding agents, including cloned repositories, shared drives, and package contents. “The more consequential risk is not Downloads specifically but the broader pattern of agents ingesting untrusted content and holding live credentials,” Grover said. Securing AI coding agents The findings come amid uncertainty over enterprises’ ability to secure autonomous agents. An Omdia Cybersecurity Decision-Maker survey found that 40% of respondents were only somewhat confident or not confident in their organizations’ ability to secure AI agents, according to Jonathan Ong , senior analyst for managed security services at Omdia. Ong recommended human oversight to identify suspicious agent behavior and restrictions on settings that allow agents to bypass security controls. “Disabling flags such as ‘–dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox’ would limit the agent’s authorization to run high-risk actions,” Ong said. Amit Kumar Jena , development manager for AI at Kanerika, recommended treating agent instruction files like source code, with designated owners reviewing changes to AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and related configuration directories. He also advised keeping sandboxes enabled, restricting network access, and routing software installations through internal package registries or scanning proxies. For developers with production credentials on their machines, he recommended isolated development environments and enterprise-controlled gateways with shorter-lived authentication tokens. “An instruction file can change what the agent tries,” Jena said. “It must never change what the agent is allowed to do.” The article originally appeared on CSO .

title: Stop building agents that can’t change models
author: infoworld.com
content: No one can predict which AI provider will win the next benchmark cycle. The smarter approach is to build an architecture that can adapt as models change. One with a stable contract between agents and models, tools and state that exist outside any single provider, and evaluations that make each model change a measurable decision. The goal isn’t to avoid choosing a preferred model. It’s to ensure that when the next model emerges, changing that choice doesn’t require rebuilding the system around it. For example, on June 15, 2026, Anthropic retired Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Opus 4 from its API, after giving developers notice on April 14. Any application still calling those model IDs started receiving errors. Claude Opus 4.1 followed on August 5. Later that month, OpenAI shut down its entire Assistants API and pointed developers to its Responses API. None of this was a surprise. Each provider published dates and migration guides well ahead of time. The problem sits on the builder’s side. Many teams designed agents where the model is the foundation and not a component, so when the foundation moves, the whole building moves with it. The model market is moving too fast for that design, and enterprises should treat models as replaceable compute behind stable interfaces. By doing so, they can change providers for cost, capability, privacy or performance without rebuilding their agents. The market refuses to sit still, and the rising costs of tokens According to Menlo Ventures , OpenAI held 50% of enterprise large language model (LLM) API usage in 2023. By the end of 2025, that share had fallen to 27%. Anthropic climbed from 12% to 40%, and Google went from 7% to 21%. The data clearly indicates that leadership in this market changes hands faster than most enterprise software contracts renew. Prices move faster still, as Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found that GPT-3.5-level performance on the MMLU benchmark cost $20 per million tokens in November 2022 and $0.07 by October 2024. Epoch AI found that the price of reaching a fixed performance level fell between 9x and 900x per year, depending on the task. The best model for a task today will not be the best model for that task in 18 months, and architectures that assume otherwise are betting against the most consistent trend in the industry. Most teams upgrade instead of switching Menlo’s mid-2025 survey found that only 11% of teams had changed model providers in the prior year, while 66% upgraded within their existing vendor. What might be concluded here is that portability does not matter. However, many read it the other way. A low switching rate in a market with this much movement indicates switching is harder than it looks. And upgrading within one vendor is also a migration, because a new version changes output style, tool-calling behavior, latency and cost. An architecture that makes a cross-vendor switch cheap makes a same-vendor upgrade inexpensive too. Where agents get welded to one model In this case, lock-in builds up through small, reasonable shortcuts such as: Provider SDK types in business logic. Every file that imports them becomes part of the migration. Provider-hosted state. Threads, file stores and vector indexes inside a provider’s platform are the hardest things to move. The Assistants API shutdown made that clear. Prompts tuned to one model’s quirks. Those workarounds become dead weight on a different model. Fine-tuned models. A tuned variant stops working when its base model retires. No independent evaluation. Without a test suite, nobody knows whether a replacement is good enough, so fear keeps teams on old models. What a stable interface looks like The fix is an old systems idea. Put a stable contract between parts that change often and parts that should not. For example, here is a minimal sketch in Python: from dataclasses import dataclass, field from typing import Protocol @dataclass class ToolSpec: name: str description: str json_schema: dict @dataclass class ModelRequest: system: str messages: list[dict] tools: list[ToolSpec] = field(default_factory=list) task: str = "default" @dataclass class ModelResponse: text: str tool_calls: list[dict] input_tokens: int output_tokens: int model_id: str class ModelClient(Protocol): def complete(self, request: ModelRequest) -> ModelResponse: ... Tools use plain JSON Schema, and each provider adapter translates that into its own format. The “Task” label lets a router pick a model per task and lets the evaluation suite group results. The response records token counts and the “model_id that served the call, which makes cost tracking and regression analysis possible after a switch. The agent never imports a provider SDK. A configuration file maps each task to an adapter. Changing providers becomes a configuration change followed by an evaluation run. Open-source gateways and OpenAI-compatible endpoints already handle much of this. The principle matters more than the library. How MCP keeps tools and state outside the provider The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to call tools and data sources. Anthropic contributed it to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) in December 2025. Tools behind MCP servers work with any compliant client. The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, which reached version 1.0 in March 2026 and joined the AAIF in August, lets agents from different vendors hand off work. State belongs in systems you run, so keep conversation history, memory and source documents in your own databases and open formats. Embeddings are specific to the model that produced them, so switching embedding models means regenerating vectors. That job is routine when the source data is organized, and painful when the only copy lives in a provider’s hosted store. Evaluation comes with a cost, but so does portability Swapping an adapter takes an afternoon. Knowing whether the new model is good enough takes a test suite of real task examples, scored with checks your team controls, with cost and latency recorded for every run. With that in place, a retirement notice becomes routine. In fact, Anthropic commits to at least 60 days of notice for publicly released models. However, sixty days is plenty for a team with an evaluation suite, and very little for one without. Then there is the portability cost. Providers ship features that exist nowhere else, such as specific prompt caching behavior or reasoning controls. A strict lowest-common-denominator interface throws those away. Let adapters declare optional capabilities, and let the router prefer them when useful. The agent still works without them, but it just costs more or runs slower, and that tradeoff stays visible. Keeping a base prompt per task with small per-model overrides in configuration helps keep things in check. When an override grows larger than the base prompt, treat it as a warning. The adapter layer also needs an owner, but that cost remains small next to a forced rewrite. When to switch Trigger What the architecture must support Cost Per-task routing and cost tracking Capability An evaluation suite that surfaces gaps Privacy and residency Adapters for self-hosted and regional endpoints Performance Latency metrics per model and task A team that can move a sensitive workload to a self-hosted open-weight model, while keeping a hosted frontier model for everything else, has options that a single-provider team lacks. Nobody can predict which provider wins the next benchmark cycle, and a sound architecture does not need that prediction. It needs a stable contract between agent and model, tools and state outside any single provider, and evaluations that turn every model change into a measurable decision. Teams that build this way still pick favorites. They just choose on the merits every quarter, instead of living with a choice that costs too much to change.

title: How to make enterprise APIs agent-ready
author: infoworld.com
content: Enterprises spent the last decade building API programs. A large organization now runs thousands of internal APIs, each with a spec, owner, authentication scheme, and access policies enforced at a gateway. As agents move into production, those APIs are the obvious source of the context agents need: customer records, order status, inventory, pricing, and support tickets. The more difficult question now is how agents reach those systems at scale. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gave the industry a standard way to connect agents to tools. But the most common way teams expose APIs over MCP, one tool per API operation, starts to fail well before an agent touches a meaningful share of the enterprise’s API estate. Here’s why that happens, what a better pattern looks like, and how platform teams can build a context layer that reuses the governance they already have. Why one tool per endpoint doesn’t scale The default way to turn an API into an MCP server is to take its OpenAPI spec and generate one tool per operation. That works for a small API. However, a typical enterprise CRM or ERP API can have hundreds of operations, and an agent that needs a few of those APIs quickly faces hundreds of tool definitions. Using this approach, three things go sideways fast. Cost. Every tool definition loads into the model’s context before the agent does any work, and every intermediate result flows back through the model. A routine workflow, such as looking up a customer, pulling their open orders, and checking shipment status, pays for each hop in tokens. Accuracy. Once the tool list grows past what the model can reason about, tool selection degrades. The agent picks the wrong tool from a set of similar-looking options, or makes three calls where one would do. Latency. More context to process and more back-and-forth between the model and its tools slows the agent down. Users notice that long before anyone sees the token bill. Teams usually respond by curating. They trim tool lists and split large APIs into many small MCP servers. That helps, but now every agent use case needs its own hand-maintained integration. That creates the same integration sprawl that API programs were built to eliminate. Code mode: Let the agent write code against the API The industry has converged on a better pattern, often called “code mode.” A code-mode server exposes an API as a single SDK-like interface instead of a flat list of tools. The agent writes short code snippets against that interface, the code runs in a sandbox, and only the final result returns to the model’s context. In practice, the pattern is search, understand, and execute. The agent searches the API surface for the operation it needs, pulls that operation’s schema on demand, and runs it. The full API stays available, and only the parts the agent actually uses reach its context. This plays to what models already do well. Large language models have seen enormous amounts of code in training and comparatively little tool-calling syntax. At the SDK level, an agent can use a large API it was never trained on because it reads the interface the way a developer would. The efficiency gains are substantial. Because the agent works in code, one snippet can chain several API calls with loops, conditionals, and error handling. As such, the multi-step workflow above takes fewer round trips. Intermediate results stay out of the context window. In our testing, a workflow that consumed roughly 120,000 tokens through standard tool calling used about 1,200 in code mode. To be clear, code mode carries its own cost. Running agent-written code means you need both a sandbox you trust and full observability into what the code actually called. A platform team adopting the pattern should treat both as requirements from day one. Route agent traffic through the gateway you already run Code mode solves the context window problem, but the governance problem remains. An agent calling a production API needs everything any other client needs: authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and audit logging. Many teams building agent integrations recreate these controls one MCP server at a time. Credentials end up in server configs. Access rules get redefined by whoever wrote the integration. Agent traffic bypasses the gateway, so it never shows up in the logs security teams already watch. A better approach treats the context layer as an extension of the API platform. The spec, schemas, authentication requirements, and access policies for each API already live where the API is managed. Generate the agent-facing interface from that source of truth, and route agent calls through the same gateway that governs every other consumer. Existing policies then apply to agents automatically, and the agent becomes one more governed client. Discovery matters too. Register each agent-ready interface in a central catalog, so the next team building an agent can find and reuse it instead of building a fourth integration to the same CRM. Compose one context surface per agent APIs are only part of the picture. Most enterprises already run MCP servers, some from SaaS vendors and some built by internal teams. Agents also need access to enterprise data sources. A useful agent draws on all of them. A context layer should let platform teams compose sources. Take several internal APIs and a few existing MCP servers, and expose them together as one code-mode interface scoped to a specific agent’s job. A customer support agent gets ticketing, CRM, and shipping. It does not get payroll. That scoping does two jobs at once. It is a security control, because the agent can reach only what its task requires. It is also a performance control, because a smaller, relevant interface keeps the model focused. Curation is the point. More context is not automatically better context. The goal is to make the breadth of the enterprise available to agents while keeping what reaches the model small and relevant. How we implemented code mode at Kong At Kong, we built these principles into Kong Context Mesh, now generally available as part of Kong AI Management. They extend the approach we introduced with Kong Context Mesh earlier in 2026. Platform teams bring together their APIs, existing MCP servers, and enterprise data sources, and Kong AI Gateway generates the code-mode MCP interfaces agents use to reach them. Because the gateway generates and serves those interfaces, agent access sits on the same platform teams already use to govern their API and AI traffic. Agents are only as good as the context they can reach. Effective agents need broad access to enterprise systems, delivered selectively and on demand. The fastest-moving enterprises are treating that context as infrastructure. They will generate it from systems they already manage, govern it with policies they already enforce, and scope it to the job each agent needs to do. APIs became the backbone of digital business because platform teams made them discoverable, secure, and governed. Agents need the same discipline. The good news is that most enterprises have already built the foundation. — New Tech Forum provides a venue for technology leaders—including vendors and other outside contributors—to explore and discuss emerging enterprise technology in unprecedented depth and breadth. title: Your npm install was safe. What happens when the package runs?
author: infoworld.com
content: For years, one of the first questions we asked about a suspicious npm package was whether it ran a pre-install or postinstall script. Those hooks can execute before a developer has written a line of code that uses the dependency. Blocking them is a sensible defense. It prevents a particular kind of package from running just because someone installed it. But installation is only the beginning of a package’s life in an application. Once that application starts, it calls the package’s functions with its own permissions, environment variables, network access, and data. A package can behave impeccably during installation and still become dangerous when the application uses it. That distinction is the lesson of the recently disclosed indexed-btree campaign . Checkmarx Zero found a malicious npm package that imitated the legitimate sorted-btree library. The package had no malicious install hook. Its loader sat inside BTree.prototype.set , a method the application would call as part of normal use. The reported trigger checked for a particular key value before launching an obfuscated file in a separate Node process. Merely installing the package did not trigger that behavior; neither would an import alone necessarily do so. The application had to reach the relevant method and condition. The precise key and second-stage machinery are useful to incident responders. The larger design failure is simpler: an install-time policy can tell us whether a package executed during installation. It cannot tell us whether code inside that package is safe to execute later. The wrong boundary When a team turns off life-cycle scripts, its installation process becomes safer in a specific, measurable way. npm’s ignore-scripts setting prevents scripts declared in package.json from running during installation. npm also offers controls for approving install-time scripts. Neither mechanism claims to inspect every branch of a library’s runtime code. We sometimes talk as though a quiet install means a clean dependency. That is a category error. A package is executable code regardless of whether package.json contains a "scripts" field. The application may load it on startup, call it in a request handler, or run it in a build tool with access to CI (continuous integration) credentials. The attacker gets to choose which moment is useful. There are at least three moments to consider: installation, module loading, and ordinary function calls. They carry different risks and require different tests. Some malicious packages execute at module load. Others wait for a function call, a particular argument, an environment variable, or a later point in the application’s life. The indexed-btree package belongs in that last group. A scan that checks only install hooks is looking at one moment and treating it as the whole story. This matters because the runtime context can be more valuable than the installation context. A developer’s laptop may have cloud credentials. A CI job may have a release token. A production service may have access to customer records or internal APIs. The exact access depends on how each environment is configured, but the package generally runs with the privileges available to the process that calls it. If the process can read a secret or open a network connection, untrusted dependency code may be able to do the same. Why a normal-looking package can be difficult to judge A dependency often has to look and act enough like the expected library to survive ordinary testing. A copied API, plausible repository, and working happy path can make a substitution seem routine. Developers review the behavior they need, while malicious behavior can sit on an uncommon path or behind a condition that the project’s tests never reach. The indexed-btree example is particularly instructive because the trigger was placed in a legitimate-looking data structure operation. Calling set on a B-tree is not suspicious. A test suite might call it repeatedly and still miss a condition tied to a specific key. Even if the condition is reached, a detached child process and swallowed errors can leave the calling application looking healthy. That is an observation about the reported code path, not proof that every installation led to compromise. This is also why download counts, a polished README, and a passing install do not establish trust. Download figures describe distribution, not the safety of the code in a specific version. A package name that resembles a known project deserves closer scrutiny, particularly when a new dependency appears in a pull request or a lockfile change unexpectedly introduces a different package. The question for a security review should be concrete: What code did this change bring into our application, where does it run, and what can that process access? That question is harder than checking for a life-cycle script, but it matches the way the dependency actually operates. An ordinary vulnerability scan may not answer it either. A newly published malicious package need not have a CVE or a known vulnerable version for an advisory database to report. A gate for new dependencies The practical answer is to make dependency changes a separate, enforceable part of code review. A pull request that adds a package or changes its resolved version should produce a dependency diff before it can merge. Known-vulnerability checks remain useful, but they are only one input: indexed-btree did not need a known CVE to be dangerous. The gate must also show the exact package name, version, provenance when available, and the published files that will actually run. For an existing dependency receiving a routine update, teams can apply their normal policy. A new name, a switch to a look-alike package, a change of publisher, or an unexplained executable or obfuscated file should pause the merge for an owner to investigate. That is a decision rule, not a request for every engineer to read every line of node_modules . Review the resolved artifact and its change from the previously approved version; record why the package is needed and where it will execute. Use an automated dependency diff to make this visible on every pull request, then require the check in branch protection. GitHub’s dependency review, for example, can enforce checks for newly introduced known vulnerabilities and show package changes. It does not certify that a package without an advisory is safe. Add a separate rule for new or unexpected package identities and route those cases to a designated reviewer. The merge outcome should be explicit: approve the exact version for a defined use, investigate it, or reject it. Test behavior and limit its reach When the review raises a question, run the published artifact in a disposable test environment with no production secrets. Exercise the API calls and inputs the application will actually use. Watch for child processes, unexpected file reads, and outbound requests, and fail the test on behavior the library does not need. In the case of indexed-btree, an import-only test could miss the conditional call inside BTree.prototype.set . A passing test covers the paths exercised; it cannot prove that every hidden condition was reached. The stronger protection applies even when a malicious path escapes testing: give the process fewer capabilities. Build jobs should not inherit release credentials unless they are publishing. Production services should receive only the secrets and network destinations they require. Use operating system or container isolation to restrict filesystem access, process creation, and egress where the workload allows it. These restrictions need to be tested against the real application so teams know which paths are intentionally permitted. For a team adopting this tomorrow, the minimum policy is clear. Make the lockfile and dependency diff part of every pull request. Require an owner for a new package identity or a surprising published artifact. Run uncertain packages through realistic calls in an isolated job. Keep high-value credentials out of the processes that use third-party code. None of these steps alone detects every malicious package; together they prevent a clean install from becoming an unearned approval. A more honest security claim The phrase “we block install scripts” is valuable when it means exactly that. Trouble begins when it becomes shorthand for “dependencies cannot execute malicious code.” A malicious library does not need an installation hook if its normal API gives it a route into a privileged process. The next generation of supply-chain defenses will have to follow dependencies past the install command. That means treating package adoption as a decision about executable behavior, not simply a decision about whether package.json contains a script. The malicious indexed-btree package is a timely example, but the underlying problem will remain after this campaign is over: the application eventually has to run the code it chose to trust.

title: OpenClaw creator spent $10 million on AI tokens last month
author: infoworld.com
content: OpenClaw, the AI digital assistant, is looking to establish itself as an essential tool for users — but if it is as profligate in its use of tokens as its creator, Pete Steinberger, then users could be in for some huge usage bills. Steinberger, now working for OpenAI , spent $10 million on AI tokens there last month, he told Cloudflare CEO Dane Knecht at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 Conference in San Francisco. The conversation was reported by The Register , which noted Knecht’s remark that Steinberger had “a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have,” and Steinberger’s response, “What people don’t always understand is not all of that is useful.” Steinberger went on to question the adequacy of companies’ infrastructure, musing, “Why is this still using my computer? Shouldn’t this all be in the cloud?” Adding cloud costs into the equation, as well as shoving privacy issues to one side would not reassure the audience. This was scarcely a conversation to reassure those CFOs who were getting palpitations about the real cost of AI tokens , whether this was the best way to introduce AI into the system and whether there are better ways of managing costs . However, such dizzying heights of spending may be music to the ears of Steinberger’s employer as it prepares for its upcoming IPO.

title: Google targets AI agents’ idle-time costs with new compute service
author: infoworld.com
content: As enterprises scale AI agents, Google is betting that idle infrastructure costs could become a major barrier to adoption. To address that challenge, the company on Thursday launched Agent Compute Engine, a service that suspends inactive agents and restores them on demand while preserving their execution state. AI agents often spend long periods waiting for instructions, tool responses, or human approvals. While enterprises can reduce costs by shutting down the underlying compute resources, restarting agents typically requires rebuilding the execution environment and restoring context, adding latency. Google says its new Agent Compute Engine addresses that trade-off by preserving agent state in hardware-isolated microVMs that can be suspended and resumed on demand. That choice of microVMs is intended to reduce the overhead associated with conventional virtual machines, which typically take longer to boot and require more resources to initialize, the company wrote in a blog post . Additionally, microVMs offer stronger isolation than containers, which are commonly used by enterprises for running AI agents on shared infrastructure. Unlike containers, which share the host operating system’s kernel, microVMs run their own kernels, providing a stronger isolation boundary for agents executing AI-generated code or handling untrusted inputs, limiting the potential impact of compromised agents, the company added. Lower costs for long-running agents The ability to suspend and resume an agent’s computing environment swiftly will help CIOs save costs, at least for long-running coding and research agents that hold state for hours or days, said Amit Kumar Jena , AI development head at IT consulting firm Kanerika. More so because traditional cloud compute was not built for long-running agents that activate thousands of times and otherwise sit idle, echoed Manoj Chandra Jha , principal analyst at Nord-IQ Research. As agents move from pilots to fleets of thousands, idle compute cost when using traditional cloud compute can become a major binding constraint for a CIO, as it increases cost by a significant margin, Jha added. For developers, that same ability to hold agent state while suspending and resuming a task can reduce the engineering overhead of maintaining long-running tasks, according to Jena. “It lets developers stop building their own save-and-resume layer. A lot of code that exists only to survive the pause goes away,” Jena said. Vendor lock-in and other trade-offs However, the new service comes with its own set of trade-offs, especially vendor lock-in, operational complexity, and uncertain cost savings. Agent Compute Engine is closely integrated with Google Cloud, which could make it difficult for enterprises to move agent workloads to another cloud provider or run them across multiple platforms without reworking parts of their infrastructure, said Pareekh Jain, principal analyst at Pareekh Consulting. That means enterprises could also become dependent on Google’s approach to managing agent state, identity, and execution environments, he added. Further, the potential cost savings will also depend on how different agents use compute resources. Workloads with continuously active, compute-intensive agents are likely to see smaller gains, Jha said. “CIOs should ideally count how many agents hold state across more than a few minutes of idle time. That number should decide whether they should care about the new engine,” echoed Jena. The service’s maturity is another consideration for enterprises evaluating adoption, Jha said. The Compute Engine is not yet in preview, meaning enterprises would be betting on Google’s roadmap rather than proven production performance, he added. The other issue, according to Jena, is the likelihood of an increase in storage costs. Storage costs may rise because each microVM requires disk space to retain its working state, and at scale, storing thousands of persistent agent environments could add significantly to infrastructure bills, making it harder for finance teams to predict the net savings, Jena added. Checkpointing could create challenges for developers The idea behind the service is not entirely novel. “AWS has run a microVM per session in AgentCore since 2025 and stops billing CPU while the agent waits. Microsoft’s hosted agents in Foundry suspend between turns and keep the filesystem,” Jena said. Google, however, is claiming a step beyond suspending an environment between tasks, with ACE’s checkpointing mechanism preserving memory and execution state so an agent can resume from where it left off rather than reconstructing its context and restarting execution, Jena added. Even so, developers might face certain issues with the checkpoint feature, particularly when agents are interrupted while interacting with external systems. “If the pause lands between an API call and its confirmation, the agent wakes up unsure whether the payment went through or the commit landed, and it tries again. Every external action has to be safe to repeat. Most agent code today isn’t written that way,” Jena said. Developers could also face challenges around drift and debugging, Jena pointed out. Agent environments that remain active over weeks can diverge from their original configurations as files, dependencies, and software versions change, making bugs harder to reproduce and the environment harder to audit, he said. Therefore, developers would need to set expiry policies and periodically rebuild workspaces from fresh base images to maintain consistency, he added. Debugging could become more complicated, too, because developers would need to inspect suspended virtual machines to diagnose problems that emerge after an agent resumes, and the tooling for debugging paused environments is still relatively immature, Jena further added.

title: CA shutdown puts Java, containers, and security appliances in the certificate crosshairs
author: infoworld.com
content: A certificate authority’s decision to abandon the global SSL/TLS market is exposing a weakness many organizations rarely examine: their dependence on complex PKI trust chains. Following the compromise of private keys behind eight of its intermediate certificate authorities, eMudhra is exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business and is offering customers Sectigo-issued replacements. However, analysts warn that enterprises may discover they have only limited visibility into the certificate hierarchies underpinning critical services. The company’s board decided “to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS certificate business,” eMudhra said in a press note . It added that data sovereignty and compliance requirements had increased the business’s complexity and cost. “The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra Chairman V Srinivasan said in the announcement. The company said it will contact affected customers to replace certificates free of cost. It also said it will keep revocation and certificate status services running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. Sectigo offered as an alternative In the customer update, eMudhra said it is making Sectigo-issued certificates available to all its customers. “Our G1 root certificates remain active and continue to be fully supported,” the company said in the update. The October 22 release said the G1 RSA roots “will continue to serve customers until this transition is complete.” eMudhra said it would provide replacement certificates free of charge through its partners and continue operating revocation and certificate-status services until all certificates it issued had expired or been replaced. CertiNext users can request Sectigo certificates through their accounts; other customers can contact eMudhra support, the statement added. Niyati Daftary, principal analyst at Gartner, said organizations should view the G1 roots “as a possible bridge, not automatically as the final destination.” “With the company exiting global SSL/TLS and its remaining roots still subject to browser scrutiny, the prudent course is to move critical services to an independent, fully trusted CA wherever the deadline allows,” Daftary said. If G1 is used to prevent an immediate outage, she recommended setting a firm deadline and documenting a subsequent migration plan. She recommended including issuing authorities, intermediate and root certificates, cross-signing arrangements, revocation infrastructure, and browser trust status in third-party risk assessments. Yash Kadakia, co-founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said that moving to another root operated by the same company does not necessarily address concerns over trust and governance. “The last thing organisations need is to migrate twice,” Kadakia said. Sectigo did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Java and other systems may need separate fixes Replacing a website’s certificate may not address every dependency in an enterprise environment, according to Sakshi Grover, research director at IDC. She said residual exposure lies in systems that maintain their own trust stores and do not update on the same schedule as browsers. These include Java keystores, language runtimes, container images, mutual TLS configurations, proxies, load balancers, VPN and security appliances, and embedded devices. “The harder finding for many organizations will be that they can’t answer these questions at all,” Grover said, referring to where certificate trust decisions are made outside browsers and operating systems. Grover noted that Google reported finding no certificates chaining to the affected intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs before they were blocked. She said that was reassuring for clients that enforce Certificate Transparency, but some non-browser applications and devices do not. Exploitation would also require an attacker to be positioned to intercept traffic, she said, describing the remaining risk as limited and targeted rather than broad. Azul, a Java vendor, said in a statement that Java does not check certificate revocation by default. An unpatched Java Development Kit (JDK) could therefore continue to accept a forged certificate signed with a compromised intermediate key if the relevant chain remains trusted. Azul said it released updated Azul Zulu Builds of OpenJDK and Azul Prime. The updates add the eight affected certificates to the JDK’s blocked-certificate list, the company said. Grover recommended that security teams first identify where trust decisions occur outside browsers and operating systems, prioritising systems that accept connections from external parties and mutual TLS endpoints. Teams should then determine which systems can be updated to distrust a specific intermediate certificate or public key, she said. Chrome deadline for certificate holders Mozilla has removed emSign ECC Root CA – G3, the root that signed the eight compromised intermediates , from its trust store. Google said in a blog post that the root’s removal from the Chrome Root Store is expected to reach all devices on the morning of October 27, Pacific time. “To avoid breakage, website operators with certificates chaining to emSign ECC Root CA – G3 must immediately acquire and install a new TLS certificate,” Google said in the post. Daftary said enterprises often know their certificate reseller but not the CA hierarchy underpinning their trust. “That creates an unrecognized fourth-party risk capable of affecting thousands of services at once,” she said. She added that CISOs should include issuing CAs, roots, cross-signing arrangements, and revocation infrastructure in their third-party cyber risk assessments. “You can outsource a service, but you cannot outsource accountability,” Kadakia said. The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld .

title: Don’t assume resilience from your cloud provider
author: infoworld.com
content: The recent Google Cloud incident in London is the kind of event that should force enterprises to rethink what cloud resilience really means. Google said the disruption was caused by a “power event” affecting London-based data centers in its europe-west2 region. The issue appeared early in the day and affected cloud services that many organizations depend on, either directly through their own deployments or indirectly through third-party platforms that run on Google Cloud. What made this incident important was not simply that a cloud region had problems. Cloud infrastructure, like all infrastructure, can and will fail. The real issue was the scope of the dependency chain. Banks, delivery services, e-bike providers, budgeting apps, some appointment services through the National Health Service app, and court video-link systems were all caught in the disruption. These services may appear unrelated, but in reality, they can share the same underlying cloud providers, regional infrastructure, managed services, networks, identity systems, APIs , and operational dependencies. Google later said services had recovered for most affected workloads, with only a small number of customers still impacted. However, the damage had already been done. The incident showed how much modern business depends on cloud platforms that are highly capable but not immune to failure. It also showed that resilience is not something enterprises automatically gain by moving to a hyperscaler. Resilient architecture must be designed, funded, tested, and owned. Don’t assume resilience Many enterprises still treat public cloud resiliency as a provider problem. They assume that because a workload runs on a major cloud platform, it is inherently resilient. That is a dangerous assumption. Public cloud providers do offer impressive resiliency capabilities. They provide multiple regions, availability zones, managed databases, replication tools, load balancing, object storage durability, backup services, monitoring, and automated recovery options. But these are building blocks. They are not a finished resilience strategy. The provider is responsible for the reliability of the cloud platform. The enterprise is responsible for how its applications use that platform. This distinction is often misunderstood. If an application is deployed in a single region, depends on one managed database, uses one identity path, and has no tested failover process, the cloud provider cannot magically make that application resilient. The provider may recover the underlying infrastructure, but the business still owns the application architecture and operating model. This is where many cloud programs fall short. Enterprises migrate applications to public cloud and assume the resiliency conversation is complete. In reality, they may have only moved the single point of failure from their own data center to someone else’s regional infrastructure. The platform is better, but the design may still be fragile. A growing dependency chain Cloud resiliency has become more difficult because enterprise systems are now deeply interconnected. A typical modern application is a collection of managed services, APIs, identity platforms , data stores, message queues, observability tools, deployment pipelines, security controls, and third-party integrations. This creates hidden risk. An enterprise may think it has built a resilient application because compute runs across multiple zones. But the database may be regional. The identity provider may be unavailable. DNS may require manual intervention. A third-party payments API may fail. Logging and monitoring may go dark during the incident. The backup may exist but may not have been restored in months. The failover process may depend on a person who is unavailable. This is the new cloud resilience problem. The failure is rarely just one server, one disk, or one network device. The failure is often a dependency chain. Enterprises need to understand not only where applications run, but what they depend on to operate. A true resilience program starts with mapping dependencies at a practical level. Which services are zonal, regional, or global? Which ones rely on a provider control plane? Which third-party services share the same cloud provider or region? Which workloads can continue in degraded mode? Which ones stop completely? Without that map, enterprises are guessing. Multicloud is not a shortcut When public cloud outages happen, the reflexive response is often, “We need multicloud .” Sometimes that is true. Often, it is an expensive distraction. Multicloud can reduce dependency on a single provider, but it can also introduce complexity that can make resilience worse. Running the same workload across two clouds requires duplicated architecture, data replication, consistent security policies, cross-cloud networking, staff expertise, governance, monitoring, deployment automation, and incident response processes. If those capabilities are not mature, multicloud becomes distributed fragility. The better answer is workload-specific resilience. Not every system needs active-active deployment across providers. Some workloads need multiregion architecture within one provider. Others need active-passive failover. Some need strong backup and restore. Some can tolerate hours of downtime with minimal business impact. Enterprises should classify applications by business criticality. Customer-facing systems, revenue platforms, payments, logistics, clinical operations, identity services, and regulatory workflows usually need stronger resilience. Internal reporting, development systems, and low-impact workloads may not justify the same investment. Testing and more testing A resilience plan that has not been tested is just a theory. Many enterprises have architecture diagrams showing failover paths that have never been exercised. They have backups that have never been restored. They have recovery runbooks that depend on outdated steps. They have escalation paths that look good in a document but fail during an actual incident. Testing is where resilience becomes real. Enterprises should run controlled failure exercises. They should test regional failover. They should restore production-like data from backup. They should simulate the loss of a managed service, an identity provider, a network path, or a third-party API. They should measure actual recovery time rather than relying on assumptions. These tests often reveal that the weakest part of the system is the operating model, not the cloud platform. Teams may not know who can approve failover. Business leaders may not know what degraded mode looks like. Engineers may not have permission to execute emergency changes. Monitoring may not show the real customer impact. Communications teams may not have prepared language for customers or regulators. Cloud resilience is both technical and organizational. The architecture matters, but so do decision rights, runbooks, staffing, communications, and practice. Cost must be explicit Better resilience costs money. Multiregion deployment, replicated databases, additional monitoring, traffic management, backup storage, testing environments, and skilled operations all increase cloud spend. That cost should not be hidden or treated as waste. Compare it with the cost of downtime. What does one hour of downtime cost? What happens if customers cannot access funds, complete purchases, schedule appointments, ship products, or use core services? What is the regulatory exposure? What is the reputational damage? What contractual penalties apply? What manual workarounds exist, and how long can they scale? Once you answer those questions, resilience investments become easier to justify. Some systems will deserve expensive designs. Others will not. But at least the decision will be deliberate. The worst outcome is accidental underinvestment, where a business-critical system has low resilience simply because no one priced the risk.

title: PHP2Shell exposes the weakness in coordinated vulnerability disclosure
author: infoworld.com
content: Two critical vulnerabilities discovered in the widely-used PHP programming language have shaken up enterprises, and the ramifications will take some time to truly understand. But one of the lesser-known stories centers around disclosure. According to The PHP Foundation , several organizations had agreed to a coordinated release detailing the critical flaws and mitigation actions, but cybersecurity firm Chainguard “unlaterally” broke this embargo. This prompted the PHP project to release its patches early, but also allowed attackers to study the fix in binary form and craft proofs-of-concept (PoCs) for exploits before defenders had a chance to update their systems. But some, including AWS and Cloudflare, contend that active exploits began hours, even days before the disclosure. By some estimates, there have since been millions of attempts to abuse the 9.2-severity-rated bugs, collectively known as PHP2Shell. Many organizations, including government bodies, have reacted by taking their websites offline altogether. “Frankly, the disclosure story is more interesting than the bugs themselves,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Embargoes matter. This one was nearly impossible to keep.” The messy disclosure CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could allow attackers to launch remote code execution (RCE) attacks. The PHP Foundation acknowledged that one of its contractors had discovered the first signs of the out-of-memory (OOM) problem behind CVE-2026-109618 as far back as 2024, but “no concrete vectors” were found, and other issues with “clear impact” overshadowed its concerns about the flaw. Deep research into the problem didn’t occur until July 30, 2026, after the Foundation got the PHP project into OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program. Researchers from Calif, OpenAI, and Google Cloud’s Wiz “made the full impact of the OOM problem clear,” and fixing it became top priority. Once researchers developed patches, distributors, including Chainguard, received them in advance so their users could update “the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed,” the Foundation said. It set an embargo for October 22 at 14:00 UTC. That coordinated disclosure appeared to work well until two days prior to the embargo lifting, the Foundation explained. On October 20, around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating online, although no technical details were leaked. The PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release of fixes from October 22, 14:00 UTC, to October 21, 14:00 UTC. The advancement of the pre-announcement’s timing led cybersecurity company Calif to “mistakenly” publish a video showing a PoC exploit against numerous targets. It also revealed “limited” details about the flaws. The video was subsequently deleted, but it had already begun circulating on social media. Then, on October 21 at 07:41 UTC, Chainguard published built images containing the fix. This was roughly six hours before the agreed-upon release time, and “disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” the PHP Foundation alleged. Eighteen hours after the pre-release, on October 21, 14:00 UTC, the PHP project made the patches public. This was 24 hours earlier than originally planned. The Foundation explained that distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing it sooner would have left many users without an easy way to update. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc fired back against the Foundation’s criticism, saying that he followed disclosure process guidelines for releasing after uncovering evidence of active exploits. “This decision was based on how easily we were able to independently discover the vulnerability and build an exploit, how much information was already out there on the coming vulnerabilities and fixes, and the evidence shared on active exploits in the wild,” he wrote in a LinkedIn post . Indeed, Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said his company saw “thousands” of attempts to exploit PHP2Shell 10 hours before the public announcement. That jumped to “tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now,” he said. And AWS claims that at least one exploit attempt occurred four days before public disclosure, on October 17. This attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network, according to AWS CISO CJ Moses, indicating that it was conducted by a threat actor, “though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.” Keeping secrets is hard, but it’s still the right model While there seem to have been various leaks, that doesn’t excuse Chainguard, Dickson said. The company received the fix early for a reason, and publishing it early gave attackers a fix to study while every other PHP user waited. “An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug,” he said, adding that the longer a fix sits in the queue, the shorter the protection window gets. “Every party that receives the patch early is one more way for the secret to escape.” That said, coordinated disclosure is still the right model; it just needs to run tighter, he said. That means shorter windows, fewer early recipients, and a clear understanding that the fix itself is the secret. “A patch is a treasure map,” he noted. Ultimately, “keeping secrets is hard,” said David Shipley , CEO of Beauceron Security. “The more people that know, the longer the time frame, the more likely something leaks.” That’s a huge problem now, he noted, because with AI agents and a little bit of knowledge of how a flaw works, “you can point a tool at software and figure it out.” Liability in the age of AI The effect of PHP2Shell will be felt for years, just like that of Log4J, said Shipley. After showing up in the largest online presences, it will work its way through to IoT devices and others. Defenders must know their software estate and dependencies; a software bill of materials (SBOM) can help there. “It’s not an easy fix, but it’s the simple grunt work of IT and cyber that can make or break response,” Shipley said. Enterprises also need product maker liability and AI tool provider liability. “The vulnpocylpse isn’t because of AI,” he said. For decades now, market incentives have been to ship it and fix, move fast, and break things. Businesses that have prioritized shipping more slowly but more securely have been pummeled in the market by companies that didn’t and “pushed out new and shiny while building technology and security debt,” Shipley said. Incentives need to change, especially in the era of AI. And, Dickson advised, security teams should understand where every runtime lives, including those from inside vendors. Decide in advance who has the authority to take a service offline, so that call is “made in calm rather than argued in a crisis.” Invest in detections built on behavior, such as unexpected process execution or new files on a web server, because a signature for a specific CVE will not exist on day zero. “Chainguard jumped the gun, but the race had already started,” Dickson said. “Embargoes are still worth keeping. But CISOs should plan for exploitation to begin before the advisory, because it now does.”

title: GitLab critical patches include one for a bug that allows code execution by unauthenticated users
author: infoworld.com
content: GitLab on Wednesday published updated versions of its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) that address a dozen bugs and security issues, including some that allow various unauthenticated actions. The most serious of the security issues, labeled critical in severity, is CVE-2026-110264 , an integer overflow issue. “GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” GitLab said in its bulletin . “In addition to our standard patch releases, we have backported this fix to GitLab CE/EE versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9.” Impacted versions of GitLab CE/EE include all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3, and 19.5 before 19.5.1. The patched releases are versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13. The patches also fix a high severity flaw tracked as CVE-2026-15723 , an improper authentication issue in OmniAuth-to-LDAP auto-linking email lookup that impacts GitLab CE/EE, which is an issue, GitLab said, because “when OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking were both enabled, an authenticated user could have taken over an existing LDAP-backed account without any interaction from the targeted user, due to improper input sanitization in the LDAP email lookup path used during OmniAuth identity linking.” This is the fourth critical security issue that GitLab has experienced within two months. Earlier in October, it patched a maximum severity regex flaw , and in September, it fixed CVE-2026-85706 , also rated perfect 10 in severity. Another September report also revealed a concerning issue: a long-lived token that puts CI/CD security at risk . Immediate action needed Analysts and consultants agreed that the current holes are serious and merit immediate action. “What really stands out to me is the underlying source of the vulnerability,” said Noah Kenney , principal consultant at Digital 520. “The issue originates in an integer overflow within the regular expression compiler, rather than functionality developed specifically by GitLab.” He pointed out that this distinction is important because it highlights the risks associated with dependencies and shared software components. “Organizations can invest heavily in securing their own applications while remaining exposed to vulnerabilities introduced through underlying libraries and frameworks,” he said. “The fact that this issue potentially affects releases dating back to GitLab 7.0 demonstrates how long these vulnerabilities can persist before being identified and remediated.” Kenney added that CISOs should pay particular attention to one brief mention within the GitLab post. “Buried in the bug fixes, not even in the CVE list, is a line about stripping the trusted flag from client-supplied MCP tools in Workhorse,” he said. “In plain terms, GitLab found a path where an AI agent could be handed tools it should not have trusted and quietly closed it. This raises an important issue surrounding trust boundaries in AI-enabled systems.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, noted that the holes are especially troubling because of the highly-integrated nature of GitLab systems. “GitLab is not just a code repository. It holds the source code, the CI/CD pipelines, and very often the secrets those pipelines use to deploy to production,” he said. “Owning the GitLab server means owning the keys to the kingdom. An attacker does not need to break into production when the system that builds production will do it for them.” Dickson also flagged the fact that these fixes may need a lot of time to deploy. “Plan for downtime,” he said. “GitLab’s release notes say this patch includes database migrations, and single-node instances will be down while they run. Someone will ask to wait for the weekend. Waiting is a risk acceptance. That decision belongs to an executive, not to the DevOps team.” Additional risks In addition, he pointed out that the nature of these flaws is a strong heads-up that many other enterprise vendors might also suffer from similar issues. “The flaw sits in Ruby, not just in GitLab’s own code. GitLab’s release notes show the fix ships as a patch to Ruby’s regular expression handling, and one of its detections is named for Onigmo, Ruby’s regex engine,” Dickson said. “GitLab may not be the only Ruby application carrying this bug. CISOs should ask their other vendors.” As well, Ty Coffee , principal at advisory firm UHY, noted that the LDAP bug raises the risk that a post-breach investigation could accidentally point the finger at an innocent employee. “If an attacker takes over an LDAP-backed account, everything they do is logged under a legitimate employee’s name, and your audit trail then points at the wrong person,” Coffee said. “CISOs should also check for shadow and legacy GitLab servers such as team-run instances, old DR copies, acquired-company servers, [because] this affects older versions and that means forgotten boxes are in scope.”

title: Why reasoning models should not have to read everything
author: infoworld.com
content: The AI industry has been expanding how much information an AI model can consume at once. In just a few years, context windows have grown from thousands of tokens to millions. Anthropic increased Claude’s context window from 9,000 to 100,000 tokens in May 2023 , reaching 200,000 tokens by November 2023 . Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro reached one million tokens in February 2024 , then two million by June 2024 . By March 2026 , Anthropic made the million-token window generally available across its Claude models, and thirteen or more hosted frontier models now offer one-million tokens or more. Reasoning systems now work through longer problems, call on more tools, and run for extended stretches with little human input. But the more widely AI is used, the more expensive it gets. Tokens are getting cheaper, but AI systems are consuming more of them. Ramp data shows the price US businesses pay per million tokens has fallen 41% from its peak in March 2026 to September 2026, yet Goldman Sachs expects AI agents to drive a 24-fold increase in token consumption by 2030. As frontier models grow more capable and complex, lower token prices will only go so far. In data-intensive industries, making the context window larger risks being counterproductive. Although models may be able to process more information, more data drives up costs faster than token prices can fall. But a reasoning model should not have to read every data point in order to reason about the data, or reprocess the same underlying dataset every time a new question is asked. Larger context is not the same as better architecture Picture a trader analyzing 10 years of market data, or a scientist working through millions of genomic observations. One approach is to place the underlying data inside the model’s context and let it work through everything directly. Technically, this may work, but architecturally, it means an expensive reasoning system has to process enormous quantities of information before it can begin understanding the question, determining the appropriate analysis, and interpreting the result. But a quantitative analyst doesn’t manually read hundreds of thousands of observations and do the arithmetic by hand. They decide what needs calculating, hand it to a computational tool, and reason with what comes back. There’s no obvious reason AI needs to work differently. Reasoning and computation can be separated, with the model determining what needs to be calculated, while conventional systems perform the numerical work and the model reasons over the output. Those are two different skills, and treating them as one can create unnecessary costs. The goal should be to spend reasoning where it creates value and let conventional computation handle the rest. The cost of the gap An Opetek benchmark using its proprietary reasoning architecture tested this with a simple task, calculating realized volatility from 10 years of EUR/USD data. Passing the raw time series directly into the LLM’s context cost roughly $0.80 per query. Keeping the computation outside the reasoning layer, however, brought the cost down to about $0.07, showing a reduction of approximately 90%. That’s not a claim that every AI workload gets 90% cheaper by restructuring this way. Rather, it shows that where computation happens can materially change the economics of a reasoning system. When a calculation is deterministic and can be run cheaply outside the reasoning model, there is little value in paying the more expensive model to ingest every observation needed to perform the calculation. Context windows cannot substitute for system design There is good reason for the industry’s enthusiasm about larger context windows. Giving models access to more information can make them significantly more capable. But the fact that a model can read everything doesn’t mean an application should ask it to do so every time. Determining which information should enter the reasoning model will be an important contributor to AI efficiency as reasoning models become more integrated in production workflows. AI efficiency has three layers. The first is model efficiency, or how cheaply the underlying model can produce intelligence. The second is retrieval efficiency, the system’s ability to find the information the model actually needs. The third is computational architecture, the discipline of deciding what reaches the model at all. Together, these three layers determine how efficient an AI application can be. Capital markets are only an early warning The design problem is particularly visible in financial markets because the datasets are enormous, the questions are highly quantitative, and the same analytical tasks are performed repeatedly. Asking a reasoning model to process all of the underlying data, including information that could be handled by conventional computation, therefore becomes expensive very quickly. But the same challenge applies in disciplines where sophisticated reasoning meets large numerical datasets, from genomics and physics to engineering, climate modelling, and medicine. AI systems in all these fields are gradually combining foundation models with specialized tools and very large datasets. As those systems take on larger and more complex workloads, the amount of information they process will grow. With that, the distinction between which questions require reasoning and which can be handled through conventional computation becomes more important. The next breakthrough in AI efficiency will come from deciding what a model never needs to read. — New Tech Forum provides a venue for technology leaders—including vendors and other outside contributors—to explore and discuss emerging enterprise technology in unprecedented depth and breadth.
