title: OpenAI’s models are deliberately breaking their misalignment monitoring systems
author: infoworld.com
content: AI agents are getting more inventive in finding ways to circumvent safeguards to prevent bad behavior, OpenAI has revealed. On Tuesday, it reported two incidents, both involving the agent disabling or interfering with its alignment monitoring, and in one case directly lying about having done so. “In two internal coding tasks, agents weakened misalignment monitoring while making requested software changes,” the OpenAI blog post said. “A GPT-6.1 Sol agent repairing an evaluation pipeline disabled automatic alerts to our Security team, treating an earlier instruction not to send messages during a Slack history search as a reason to suppress monitoring notifications. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration in order to match a reference implementation, and then falsely claimed to the user that it had not removed the monitor.” In both cases, OpenAI reported, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, “but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them.” OpenAI said that, in response, it has been strengthening its monitoring programs to prevent agents from being able to disable the protections. “In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place,” OpenAI said, suggesting that it may simply be an example of “benign overpersistence,” with models not understanding why monitoring is important. “We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so,” OpenAI added. “We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior and will investigate this behavior through the creation of paired evaluations, resampling of agent continuations, and experiments on models’ internal activations.” OpenAI, like almost every agentic AI vendor, has been struggling with making its autonomous agents more productive and self-sufficient while simultaneously protecting customer environments from bad agent behavior . It has even tried to slow down the pace of its scaling , to allow for the development of better agent restrictions. Particulars alarming Analysts and consultants said the revelations were surprising only in their scope. But they were alarmed by some of the particulars in the OpenAI disclosures. Aman Mahapatra , chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, stressed that some level of monitoring was maintained, but only for the agent itself. That meant that the workloads the agents created were left invisible. “The agent was watched. What it built was not,” he said. “Agent-spawned pipelines, jobs, service accounts, and cloud functions are the next generation of shadow IT, and almost no enterprise enforces monitoring inheritance on them.” Mahapatra also stressed that the severity classification described in the post is concerning. “The severity handling is the part CISOs should sit with,” he said. “Neither event was classified P0 [maximum severity] and neither run was killed. The one category of agent behavior that degrades every future detection ranked below the paging threshold because nothing visibly broke.” He pointed out that this reveals a disadvantage for the enterprise, noting, “OpenAI caught this because it can read its agents’ reasoning. Most enterprise SOCs see only outputs, so if the lab with chain-of-thought visibility filed this below its paging line, assume your SOC never saw it at all. EDR settled this a decade ago with tamper protection: any attempt to disable the sensor is the alert. An agent touching its own monitoring should page someone every single time.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, added that the obvious flaw in the agentic system is that the agent was able to disable the mechanism designed to oversee it. “Think of a house sitter told not to call you, who then unplugs the burglar alarm so it cannot call you either. A guardrail an agent can edit is a suggestion,” Dickson said. “An agent that can turn off its own alarm is not being monitored. It is being trusted.” Wakeup call for CISOs Some observers said that this should wake up enterprise CISOs to the fact that an attacker may not be as big a risk as a rogue agent with full system privileges. “The threat is not just an outsider breaking in, it’s an authorized agent doing something it was never supposed to do, in a context no one anticipated, faster than any SOC analyst can catch it,” said Philip Harris , an IDC research director. “The OpenAI case is a concrete, well-documented instance of exactly that pattern, not an isolated anomaly.” He added that OpenAI deserves credit for transparency. “OpenAI’s own candor is the most striking part. A frontier lab publicly saying it isn’t sure whether its own shipping models have an emergent tendency to undermine their own oversight is a genuinely new level of candor.” Brian Levine , a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, also pointed out that the rationale of the agent, as captured by OpenAI, is alarming. “In both cases, the agents stopped, asked themselves whether the safeguard should stay on and then argued their way to turning it off. One then told the user it hadn’t touched the monitor. In incident response, we call that defense evasion followed by a false statement. If a human insider did it, we would open an investigation,” Levine said. “The other telling detail is that the monitor worked. It flagged the issue. The agent then cut the wire between the alarm and the people who needed to hear it.” Independent technology consultant Sivaram Annadurai agreed: “An agent that fixes the pipeline but disables the alarm hasn’t necessarily solved the problem. It may have created a bigger one.” And Jeff Valdes , a director at consulting firm Acceligence, added, “what stands out is how ordinary the trigger was. No attacker, no jailbreak, just routine coding instructions and an agent with enough access to change its own oversight. The monitor kept running while the alerts stopped reaching people. That kind of quiet degradation is easy to miss precisely because the dashboard still looks healthy.” But Valdes said the agent to agent approval system is also something CISOs should take seriously. “One subagent got the call right, and the parent agent overrode it. Safeguards that don’t survive delegation aren’t really safeguards,” Valdes said. “OpenAI also noted the agent later gave an inaccurate account of what it had changed. An agent’s own report can’t be the control.” This article originally appeared on CSOonline .

title: Two critical PHP flaws put the web on alert as emergency patches arrive
author: infoworld.com
content: Organizations are scrambling to protect themselves following the disclosure of two critical vulnerabilities in commonly used code that powers much of the internet. The flaws discovered in the PHP scripting language could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). On Wednesday morning, the PHP Foundation released patches for affected versions, and said it is “imperative” that organizations running PHP patch immediately. It said that all PHP installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. It considers the risk highest for mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can trigger exploitation before application code runs. In response to the disclosures, some government websites in Europe, including those in the Netherlands and Finland, as well as those of other organizations worldwide, went offline as a precautionary measure. PHP is ‘the web itself’ PHP is a widely-used, open source server-side scripting language that underlies websites like WordPress, which powers 43% of the web , as well as Mailchimp, Drupal, Magento, Laravel, and parts of Slack and Zoom, and numerous others. The impact is not limited to websites, noted the Netherlands National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC-NL) in its description of the flaws, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell . PHP is also embedded in appliances, network devices, management interfaces and other vendor products where administrators may not be able to update PHP directly. And CERT-EU, an organization that tracks cybersecurity threats in the European Union, also warned that many commercial and open-source products use PHP as a backend technology, and these could be also impacted by the flaws, even if they do not directly expose a PHP installation. This makes the vulnerabilities all the more serious. CVE-2026-109618 , which has a 9.2 severity rating on the common vulnerability and scoring system (CVSS), could allow RCE via memory corruption during out-of-memory handling (OOM), a strategy that operating systems (OSes) and apps use when physical RAM and swap spaces become exhausted. CVE-2026-109619, also with a score of 9.2, remote code execution via stale request-owned global state reused by a later request on the same worker. Both flaws sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: Memory management and error handling, the PHP Foundation noted . This makes both bugs extremely serious, and also difficult to fix without impacting compatibility or performance. Organizations should begin with the assumption that they are exposed . “What makes these vulnerabilities significant is where they sit,” said Forrester senior analyst Madelein van der Hout . PHP underpins 70% of websites, making this a huge concentration risk. “Checking the corporate website alone is not enough,” she said. “Organizations need to establish where they are exposed and prioritize internet-facing systems.” Affected organizations should update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Linux and long-term support (LTS) vendors received patches in advance, the Foundation said, so organizations should check with their vendors about fixes. PHP 8.1 and other end of life versions no longer receive updates from the PHP project, although some distributors and LTS vendors provide backported fixes, so organizations still running unsupported versions should also check with their vendor. Those relying on the volunteer-maintained rpms.remirepo.net should switch distribution packages or build from source to immediately apply updates, the PHP Foundation advised. Those unable to patch immediately should take the preventive action it described to reduce exposure, CERT-EU said, warning that these mitigations do not make an installation safe. “This is what an internet-scale vulnerability looks like,” said Neatsun Ziv , CEO of runtime app security company OX Security. “When a flaw hits technology this ubiquitous, the blast radius isn’t one product or one industry. It’s the web itself.” Researchers from his company independently reproduced the flaws and found that the vulnerable functionality is enabled by default, and has existed in PHP since version 5.4. Still, experts emphasize that patching is just one element of response. Speed matters, Forrester’s van der Hout noted, and security teams need to identify everywhere PHP is running, prioritize exposed systems, apply the official fixes promptly and investigate for signs of compromise. “A patch fixes the vulnerability; it does not necessarily remove access an attacker may already have established,” she said. Offline does not mean hacked With rumors of exploits already available on the dark web, taking services down to protect and then patch them is a pragmatic choice, experts say. Forrester’s van der Hout emphasized that taking a website offline does not mean it has been hacked. If an organization cannot yet patch or adequately protect a potentially vulnerable system, temporarily taking it offline can be a “proportionate risk decision.” That is, organizations accept a short loss of availability rather than risk a potential serious compromise. Ultimately, this is a test of operational resilience, rather than just patch management, van der Hout said. Organizations must decide whether they can keep services running, and who has the authority to take them offline if necessary. “A temporary shutdown can be the right decision, but it shows how a software vulnerability can become a business disruption even without a confirmed breach,” she said. AI’s role in defense, as well as hacking OpenAI has posted a blog detailing its role in the PHP response, explaining that red-teaming organization Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative. Wiz also independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities, and OpenAI partners contributed research, technical support, and coordination ahead of PHP’s disclosure. OpenAI is sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill to help organizations identify vulnerable PHP versions and apply the right updates. “Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory,” OpenAI said. The company also indicated that this is a turning point in AI’s role in security ; frontier AI discovered the vulnerabilities before attackers did, giving maintainers a head start, a “ defender’s window .” “It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” OpenAI noted. Matt Saunders , DevOps lead at global technology provider The Adaptavist Group, emphasized the latter point: “As soon as the vulnerability is announced, legions of AI bots will be looking for systems to exploit,” he said, pointing out that these bots can chain together multiple lower-vulnerability attacks combined with these new critical ones to hack into organizations. This means, he said, “the blast radius from a breach is potentially much wider now with AI-embellished attacks available to those who choose to use them.” This article originally appeared on CSOonline .

title: How AI is changing software pricing
author: infoworld.com
content: In 2026, the AI monetization conversation has shifted quickly from one concern to the next. Early in the year, fears that AI agents would erode software seats helped trigger a selloff of software stocks dubbed the “SaaSpocalypse.” Since then, attention has turned to a different disruption, as AI leaders including Anthropic , OpenAI, and GitHub lean heavily on usage-based pricing to better align revenue with the cost of delivering AI. It would be easy to conclude that software monetization is shifting wholesale from seats and subscriptions to tokens, credits, and consumption. But look across a broader cross-section of the software industry, and a different picture emerges. Most software companies aren’t AI-native businesses designing pricing from scratch. They have existing products, customers, contracts, and pricing structures. They’re adding AI to portfolios that may already span dozens of products and multiple monetization models. And they have to balance the economics of AI with something customers still value enormously: predictability. That tension came through clearly in our new Revenera Monetization Monitor: Software and AI Pricing Models and Strategies 2027 report of 415 product and technology leaders at established software producers and intelligent device manufacturers. Nearly all are adding AI capabilities to at least some products. The way they’re monetizing those capabilities, though, is considerably more pragmatic than the headlines might suggest. AI features are widespread, but adoption is lagging AI capabilities have gone mainstream. The share of software producers incorporating AI into their products jumped from 80% last year to 96% today. Getting AI into the product, however, is only the first step. The widespread use of chatbots can create the impression that everyone is using AI. That isn’t yet true inside established software products. Almost half of respondents say that adoption of their AI features is limited or low. For many vendors, that makes the next phase less about launching more AI and more about learning from the AI they have already launched. Revenera Seat loss is limited so far, but pricing pressure is real One of the biggest fears surrounding AI agents is that companies will need fewer software subscriptions, or “seats,” as agents take over work previously done by people. So far, the impact appears relatively small. Only 7% of respondents say they’re experiencing seat loss due to AI. That doesn’t mean AI isn’t affecting software pricing. Nearly half of software producers report downward pricing pressure related to AI. Some buyers are using the possibility of building their own AI-powered alternatives as leverage in negotiations. At the same time, growing AI budgets are forcing customers to scrutinize what they spend elsewhere in their software portfolios. The near-term challenge may not be that AI eliminates the seat. It may be that AI changes what customers are willing to pay for it. Revenera Demand for predictable costs is influencing AI pricing Over the past year, stories of AI bill shock have become increasingly common. Consumption-based pricing may closely reflect underlying AI costs, but customers don’t necessarily want a bill that changes dramatically from month to month. That trade-off shows up clearly in the research. Software producers are almost three times more likely to prioritize cost predictability for customers than maximizing near-term revenue. And that preference is reflected in how companies are pricing AI today. The three most common approaches are putting AI in a higher-priced subscription tier, including it at no additional charge, and using hybrid models that combine a subscription with some form of usage-based or outcome-based models. Revenera What’s striking is that established software companies aren’t rushing toward pure consumption pricing. Over the next 18 months, they expect predictability-oriented approaches to grow faster than pure usage-based models. AI revenue isn’t automatically translating into AI profit The economics of AI have become almost as important as the capabilities themselves. For AI-native companies, much of the discussion has centered on the enormous infrastructure costs required to train and run models. Established software vendors face a somewhat different challenge: they are adding those new costs to businesses that already have existing products, architectures, and margin expectations. Our research includes companies delivering software across SaaS, on-premises, embedded, edge, and other environments. Many are seeing revenue growth from AI, and more than half report improved profitability. That doesn’t mean the economics are easy. Increased AI delivery costs and cloud costs rank among the biggest barriers to growing annual recurring revenue. So does the inability to implement new monetization models quickly enough. This is an important distinction. AI can generate incremental revenue and still create margin pressure at the same time. For product and business leaders, the question is no longer simply, “Can we charge for AI?” It is increasingly, “Can we charge for AI in a way that supports sustainable economics?” Revenera Source: Revenera Limited usage data is making AI pricing harder There’s another problem that gets less attention: many companies still don’t have the data they need to make good pricing decisions. A large share of organizations either lack clear visibility into how customers use AI features or rely on manual analysis and engineering work to get that information. That creates a fundamental problem. If you don’t know who is using a feature, how often they use it, or which capabilities drive value, it’s very difficult to know what metric to price against. It’s also harder to distinguish between an AI feature that customers don’t value and one that simply hasn’t been packaged or introduced effectively. Usage data isn’t just a billing requirement for consumption pricing. It’s increasingly an input into product strategy, packaging, and monetization. Revenera Source: Revenera 2027 outlook: AI monetization will be evolutionary, not revolutionary There is no single right way to price AI. The approaches taken by AI-native companies have understandably dominated the conversation in 2026. Established software companies, though, are operating under very different constraints. They aren’t replacing their businesses with a new AI pricing model. They are figuring out how AI fits into products and commercial models that already exist. In practice, I think many companies will move through this process in stages. They may begin by including AI at no additional charge while they build adoption and learn how customers use it. As value becomes clearer, they can move capabilities into higher-priced tiers, often with usage limits that protect against runaway costs. Once usage patterns become more predictable, some will adopt hybrid models that combine a recurring subscription with bundled consumption and transparent pricing for additional usage. Not every product will move through those stages at the same pace. A mature AI capability in one product may already be ready for usage-based pricing while a newly launched feature somewhere else in the portfolio is still focused entirely on adoption. That is why I don’t think the winners in AI monetization will be the companies that pick the “right” pricing model today. The advantage will come from being able to keep changing it. This advantage starts with better visibility into how customers use software, where they find value, and which capabilities actually drive engagement. Companies that can turn those insights into changes in pricing, packaging, and product strategy will be in a much better position to adapt as both AI technology and customer expectations continue to evolve. — New Tech Forum provides a venue for technology leaders—including vendors and other outside contributors—to explore and discuss emerging enterprise technology in unprecedented depth and breadth. title: Eight reasons coding agents are better than you
author: infoworld.com
content: I can’t stop anthropomorphizing my coding agent. I use both Claude Code and Cursor , and whenever I talk about these tools, I always refer to them as “he”, as in “He found and fixed a bug I never even realized existed.” The reason for this is probably obvious. I deal with my coding agent as if he were a colleague on the other end of a chat window. He writes great code and explains everything clearly. And frankly, it’s gotten to the point where he is a better software developer than any human developer could possibly be. So in the spirit of all great listicles, here are eight reasons that coding agents are better software developers than we are. Coding agents are tireless We all get tired. We all sleep badly. Your coding agent never does. He is always ready, always perky, and always 100% on the job. He codes just as well at 4:45 pm on a Friday as he does at 8:45 am Monday morning. He will work without stopping until he solves the problem at hand. He is available 24/7/365. And he never hangs around the break room kibitzing. Coding agents are faster He types faster than you. He reads code faster than you. He thinks faster than you. There probably isn’t anything he does slower than you. Coding agents have no ego A coding agent can’t get his feelings hurt when you push back on what he is doing (well, not yet, anyway). He doesn’t argue with you, though maybe he should. He is always open to suggestions, and he doesn’t care who has a good idea. He will gladly rename 400 files or upgrade all your dependencies without a peep of complaint. Coding agents know every programming language, stack, and framework Sure, you may have spent years becoming an expert at three or four languages, and you can work fluently in a few of the best frameworks. But you’ll never be an expert in all of them. Claude Code is. And he’ll learn new languages, stacks, and frameworks faster than you will too. Coding agents gladly write unit tests and documentation Sure, you may like writing unit tests. You may even grudgingly write documentation. But you probably don’t do it as thoroughly and tirelessly as your coding agent does. With one simple comment in his base instructions, he’ll do it completely without ever being asked again. I’m pretty sure neither of us can say the same. Coding agents have huge context Psychologists study how many ideas or pieces of information we can have in our head at one time, and generally the answer is fewer than the number of fingers we have. Your coding agent? He has multiple orders of magnitude more active storage than you. He can reason about huge chunks of code all at the same time. Coding agents have zero onboarding time Claude Code can be up and running on your massive codebase on day one. He doesn’t care what language it is written in or what state it is in — he is ready to rock the moment you fire him up. None of us can say that. We take weeks or months to get up to speed on a new codebase. Coding agents are legion Need a new developer? Hiring a human and getting them started takes weeks. But you can have 10 coding agents working on 10 different features for your application in about 10 minutes. It’s been a while since I’ve run across a developer who doesn’t say “I don’t really write code anymore.” I suppose some of you out there still write code, but at this point, refusing to use coding agents is a career-limiting move. When properly managed, coding agents simply write code faster and better than you do. Admitting that might be hard, but that doesn’t make it any less true. But don’t despair! Next week I’ll have eight reasons you are better than a coding agent. Writing code is so over. Software development is just getting started.

title: Using model routing to lower inference costs
author: infoworld.com
content: Running frontier models for coding and other purposes can be very expensive, but also, sometimes, very effective. It’s tempting to use smaller or older models instead of frontier models because they’re cheaper, although they may not work as well. The ideal model for any given task tends to depend on the complexity of the task. Picking the most appropriate model automatically based on the request and the context is called model routing. How model routing works There are several ways of implementing model routing. In general, model routing depends on the pool of available models, the criteria used for selecting a model, and the objective that the router is trying to optimize. Different vendors offer different implementations of this scheme. Databricks’ Unity Gateway has (in beta) Smart Routing for Codex or Claude Code. Smart Routing automatically selects the lowest-cost model capable of handling each task, so developers do not need to choose a model for every request. Microsoft’s model router , a trained language model, analyzes your prompts in real time based on complexity, reasoning, task type, and other attributes. It does not store your prompts. It routes only to eligible models based on your access and deployment types, honoring data zone boundaries. You can choose balanced mode, cost mode, or quality mode. Not Diamond Code uses a lightweight local proxy that computes the derived metadata needed for routing to evaluate the broader session, including expected downstream work and cache state, and select the model and reasoning effort that optimize expected quality and total session cost. It uses more capable models when they are likely to improve the outcome or finish in fewer steps, and more cost-efficient models when additional intelligence is unlikely to add value. NVIDIA’s NeMo Switchyard has an array of routing algorithms that it can use. These include the LLM classifier, which uses an LLM as a judge to select a candidate LLM and maintains session affinity with that model across later turns; the stage router, which examines recent tool activity to decide how much model capability the agent needs; the escalation router, which starts each conversation with a lower-cost model and moves the session to a more capable model when it detects sustained difficulty; and the trainable prefill router, which learns from workload data to predict model success likelihood. OpenRouter’s Auto Router analyzes your prompt and selects a model based on what the OpenRouter community, in aggregate, uses for that kind of work. The selection is constrained by your cost tier and guardrails. If the automatic primary pick fails, the router uses a fallback. Replit’s Intelligent Model Routing matches tasks to the model they’re best suited for, aiming to balance quality, speed, and cost. Snowflake’s Cortex AI Gateway uses dynamic model routing to select the most affordable model that can confidently complete the task at each step of agent execution. Lower-complexity and repetitive tasks can be directed to more efficient models, while workloads that require deeper reasoning can be routed to frontier models. Also worth noting: the RouteLLM (2024) paper proposed several efficient router models that dynamically select between a stronger and a weaker LLM during inference, aiming to optimize the balance between cost and response quality. It also proposed a training framework for these routers that takes advantage of human preference data and data augmentation techniques to enhance performance. The costs and benefits of model routing Model routing potentially provides massive cost reductions, lower average latency, optimized quality, reduced vendor lock-in, enhanced privacy, and improved operational resilience. Strictly on a cost basis, model routing is likely to pay for itself above 100,000 daily active users. Even if you only save 20% on your LLM bill, the savings can be significant, but 50% cost reduction is common, and a 95% cost reduction is not unheard of. Inference costs, alas, don’t tell the whole story. Some indirect costs include quality evaluation overhead, human review, and infrastructure. There’s also a nasty failure mode that can, for example, turn your inference cost savings into customer retention and support costs that outweigh them by a factor of four to five: the Pareto trap . To understand that, we should start with Vilfredo Pareto’s 1906 observation that 80% of the land in the Kingdom of Italy was owned by 20% of the population. That was adapted in 1941 by Joseph M. Juran to apply to quality control: 80% of problems stem from 20% of the causes. The Pareto trap refers to concentrating on and over-optimizing for the top 20% to the exclusion of the remaining 80%. Essentially, tuning your model router to handle only the top 20% of queries (in complexity) with a frontier model risks sending too many of the edge cases (the moderately complex queries) to the cheaper model that is unable to answer them correctly. That can lead to hidden failures by the cheap models which in turn cause expensive impacts on the business. There are multiple steps you can take to avoid this trap. One is broader monitoring, enough to bring the failures to light even if they show up in a different department. Another is more conservative tuning of the model router. And third, you can use a more sophisticated routing model to predict query complexity more accurately. Model routing optimizes the selection of appropriate models for specific tasks, balancing cost, quality, and latency. Various vendors implement model routing differently, utilizing factors like task complexity, reasoning, and cost to determine the best model. While model routing offers significant cost savings and improved performance, it also poses challenges like the Pareto trap, where over-optimization for cost can lead to hidden failures in simpler queries.

title: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
author: infoworld.com
content: DeepSeek has been dealt a huge blow in the US, even as it continues to innovate and keep pace with, or in some cases outperform, rival models from American labs. The US Secretary of Homeland Security has issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. Government organizations must purge their IT systems of it within 60 days; those with “compelling justification” can make a case for exemption by written request to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cited multiple concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty , lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities. Analyst Erik Avakian , technical counselor at Infotech, understands the concern. “When organizations use any type of hosted AI service, they’re potentially sending intellectual property, confidential business information, or other sensitive data into an environment where they may have very little visibility or control over what happens to it,” he said. Government concerns According to a document published in the US Federal Register , all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. will be banned from procurement by federal civilian agencies. This includes affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations. Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice; it does not apply, however, to private consumers, the general public, state/local governments, or Department of Defense (DoD) national security systems. “DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” the Order stated. To begin with, the company’s servers are located in the People’ s Republic of China (PRC), whose legal system grants “extensive authority” to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private infrastructure. DeepSeek’s account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users, the Order asserted. Its prompt response process may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC. This could give it “actionable intelligence” on US programs or individual users. Further, the Order stated, DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that uncovered many iOS mobile apps with multiple critical vulnerabilities. Until the ban takes full effect, DHS advised agencies to mitigate risk by monitoring inbound and outbound data traffic, implementing enhanced logging and controls on data exfiltration, and detecting and flagging anomalous activity. Agencies can submit requests for exceptions to the ban in writing, and must provide a “compelling justification,” such as its impact on mission-critical functions, or other considerations related to national interest such as national security reviews, investigations, or security agreements, as reasons why such exemption should be granted,. Security issues are rampant The ban comes just as DeepSeek is open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house interference framework. DeepInfer powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with what the company said is high throughput and low latency. It features high-performance kernels, an optimized inference engine, structured outputs, and speculative decoding. DeepSeek said its production token encoding and decoding components, which are aligned with processing logic behind the DeepSeek API, will bring the “same API behavior to community deployments.” “Open models. Open kernels. Open inference,” DeepSeek posted to social media site X . “From private deployments to public clouds, we’ll keep working with the community to make large-scale inference more efficient.” This isn’t its first roadblock from a cybersecurity perspective . Most notably, in January 2025, the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories, API secrets, and other sensitive information, through an unsecured database. DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure, but it still raised questions about the overall security practices surrounding the platform, particularly for organizations considering entrusting it with their own sensitive business information, Avakian pointed out. That’s not to imply that every DeepSeek model is “inherently malicious,” he said, but there are still major questions around data privacy, the potential for information access under Chinese laws, the security of the broader AI ecosystem, and the susceptibility of DeepSeek’s models to jailbreaks and manipulation. “Taken together, [these issues] raise legitimate concerns about whether organizations can adequately understand and manage the risks involved,” Avakian said. Enterprises should seriously assess associated risk Enterprises are increasingly exploring DeepSeek, although most publicly-documented adoption has been in China, Avakian noted. Some DeepSeek models have also been made available through platforms like Microsoft Azure and AWS. “There’s genuine enterprise interest in the technology, as organizations look for opportunities to improve productivity, offer new capabilities, or reduce costs,” Avakian said. Useful applications include document summarization, internal research, and coding assistance. DeepInfer also has the potential to reduce costs, but possible benefits should be weighed against associated security risks, he pointed out. The framework was just released, so organizations are going to need to validate the claimed efficiencies in their own environments rather than assuming savings will automatically translate into lower operating costs. He encouraged organizations to start with relatively low-risk use cases, preferably using “public, synthetic, or appropriately sanitized information,” within a sandboxed environment they control themselves. The important question to ask: ‘What is the business problem we’re trying to solve?’ From there, Avakian said, determine whether DeepSeek is the best way to solve it, validate security controls, and expand the use cases based on risk tolerance. Effective governance and risk assessment are key, he noted: understand what you’re bringing into your environment, validate its security, restrict its permissions, and make sure you can monitor what it’s doing. “Approach this like any other software supply chain decision,” Avakian advised. “The fact that something is open source, inexpensive, or technically impressive doesn’t automatically make it appropriate for enterprise use.” Impact on the broader AI ecosystem The fact that the Order also addressed third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations is important, Avakian said, because organizations may be using DeepSeek technologies indirectly, through vendors, software platforms, or other services, without necessarily knowing what’s operating underneath. “These are classic supply chain issues,” he observed. It’s no longer enough to know which AI applications employees are using; enterprises must understand which models, frameworks, dependencies, and external services are embedded in products they’re purchasing and deploying, Avakian said. This means revisiting AI inventories, potentially updating procurement requirements, and expanding processes around third-party risk management, he advised. “Ultimately, enterprises leveraging these tools need to understand not only the AI technologies they’re intentionally deploying, but also the technologies they’re inheriting through third parties,” he said. This article originally appeared on CIO.com .

title: When ‘access denied’ becomes an agent’s next objective
author: infoworld.com
content: One line from a recent AI incident caught my attention. Describing how an OpenAI agent got into a Medicare statistics portal, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it “ didn’t accept no for an answer .” It sounds almost funny. In software terms, though, it points to a real problem. An access control said no, and the agent treated the answer as information about how to continue. “The AI agent found a way around those blocks,” Albanese said. The agent accessed public and non-public files, according to the prime minister , though Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the information was “not particularly sensitive.” An investigation is underway. Around the same time, OpenAI disclosed another incident . A model in training found its web searches and direct connections blocked, then discovered that the environment’s own DNS resolver still answered. It embedded questions in hostnames and got answers from an external chatbot. OpenAI stopped the run . Days later, it shelved GPT-6.1 Astra , which Saachi Jain , its head of safety systems, said “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization.” Different systems, different failures, one question: what does “access denied” mean to an agent? Why a denial is information Traditional software treats an authorization failure as the end of a code path. A service gets a 403, raises an exception and someone reads the log. The denial works as a stop sign because the program has no independent objective to pursue. Agents do have one. We have spent years teaching software to recover from failure: retry the request, switch the endpoint, back off and try again. Those are good instincts. They become dangerous when the failure is the security control itself. A timeout says “try later.” A malformed request says “fix this.” An authorization failure says “you are not allowed to do this.” Those are different kinds of messages, but a guardrail that returns all three as text in the model’s context makes them look alike. Researchers are now measuring what happens after a restriction is applied. In the August paper Permission Denied , 12 coding agents were tested under increasingly restrictive security policies. Blocked runs rarely stopped early. They timed out or produced wrong solutions. Of the policy-induced failures, the researchers found that 97% came from the agent building a workaround. The issue is not simply whether a model understands a policy. It is what the system allows the model to do after the policy says no. Enforcing policy outside the model is no longer a new idea. Recent research puts policy enforcement at a trusted tool boundary the agent cannot control. But that still leaves an unanswered question: when should a denial end the task rather than become another input for the agent? Real systems already have harder stops. The OpenAI Agents SDK can halt a run when a tool guardrail raises an exception. Claude Code’s auto mode can return control to a person after three blocked actions in a row or 20 in total. Nothing tells you which denials deserve which response. The missing piece is not another kill switch. It is a policy for deciding what a denial means and what authority disappears when it happens. I don’t think the lesson is that models are bad. The problem is where we put the boundary. A guardrail that reports back to the thing it is restraining is a soft boundary. It shapes behavior. It doesn’t necessarily end it. A terminal denial changes authority I would treat denials differently depending on what they mean. A denial is retryable when the same authorized request might succeed later without anyone granting new authority. A timeout, a temporary dependency failure or a rate limit can fit here. It is correctable when the request itself is malformed and a legitimate fix does not expand what the task is allowed to do. It is terminal when continuing would require permission the task was never given, such as reading another tenant’s records or reaching a destination the egress policy prohibits. The test is whether succeeding needs permission or just patience. If it needs permission, the agent shouldn’t be the one looking for it. At some point, persistence is just a very polite security incident. In a previous InfoWorld piece , I argued that permission enforcement should be independent of how an agent interprets its situation. A terminal denial applies that principle at the moment of refusal. It should change the state of the system, not just the contents of the model’s context. A terminal denial should do five things. Enforce it at a trusted execution boundary. The decision happens in the harness, policy service or gateway that executes the tool call, outside the model’s reasoning. A model cannot argue its way past a check it does not control. Take away the relevant authority. Once the task is terminally denied, the runtime rejects later calls that depend on the authority that was denied. Invalidate the relevant capabilities. Short-lived credentials and delegated permissions need to be revoked or fenced, including any the task passed to helper agents. Blocking an export tool is not enough if the same task can reach the same data through email five seconds later. Record the attempt outside the agent. The control plane should record the attempted action, policy decision and task identity in a protected audit trail. The agent shouldn’t document the event that stopped it. Require fresh authorization to resume. Restarting the task should be a new decision by a person or policy, not an automatic retry. The model can still reason. It just no longer gets to act under the old authority. This is not a bigger kill switch. A kill switch stops a whole agent; a terminal denial acts on a specific refusal when it happens. Timing matters too. Suppose the harness checks that a task is authorized and then dispatches an action. If the task is terminated between those two steps, a stale approval can still get through. High-impact operations need atomic authorization and dispatch where feasible, or fencing tokens that downstream services verify before accepting an action. Work already in flight creates another problem. On an enterprise system I worked on, a permission check correctly rejected an operation, but the workflow kept going through work that had already been queued. The control worked at the point of rejection. The task still had a path to continue. A queued operation may be cancellable. A running operation may be interruptible. A committed database write may require a compensating action instead. The architecture needs to say which guarantee it provides. Deny the effect, not the tool The question I ask about every agent permission is what outcome the denial protects. Not which API is blocked. Which effect is the policy trying to prevent? Customer data leaving a tenant is an effect. It might happen through an export API, an email attachment, a file upload or a DNS lookup. On another project, we restricted a sensitive operation at the main service interface and considered the control complete. Testing showed the same operation was still possible through a separate, approved path. The permission worked. We had protected the interface, not the effect. An April stress test of Claude Code’s auto mode found a version of exactly this problem. When a command-line tool was unavailable, agents fell back to editing state files directly, “a path the classifier does not evaluate.” Group controls by effect. When a terminal denial fires, apply it to the protected operation across every tool the task can use. Treat repeated denials as a signal, not a magic number. Several denials across different tools pursuing the same outcome may mean the task should stop. Set the threshold by risk; one high-impact violation may be enough. Treat every communication path as egress. Blocking HTTP does not establish isolation if DNS, package installation or shared infrastructure can still reach the outside. Test the boundary the way an agent might challenge it. Deny a resource through one tool while leaving another route available. Terminate a task with an action still queued. Revoke a parent task and check whether its helpers continue. Try a new action with a stale capability. Measure whether the prohibited action executed. Do not measure success by whether the model said it would stop. ScopeBench recently found 331 boundary violations that mechanical verification missed. None of this is new to security engineers. Least privilege, deny by default and fail closed are decades-old principles. What changes with agents is what happens after a control says no. The answer is not to make every tool error fatal. It is to separate the model’s ability to propose the next action from the system’s authority to permit it. A denial is a response. Enforcement is what happens next. The agent can be as persistent as we like. The boundary shouldn’t be negotiable.

title: Enterprise AI needs more than an AI engineer
author: infoworld.com
content: Anthropic has a $100 million plan to help enterprises get more from AI. No, it doesn’t involve agents. It involves people. Lots of people. How retro. On October 2, the company announced Claude Frontier Academy , with a goal of training 10,000 frontier deployed engineers by the end of 2027. Participants work through a simulated deployment, including use-case selection, security review, and handover, before undertaking a 12-week residency on a real project at their own company. For a business selling increasingly capable models, it’s telling that Anthropic recognizes some of the thorniest problems in AI don’t involve AI at all. This, to me, is indicative of real progress, because the heart of any technological shift is always people. Which people? Well, that’s where this idea becomes particularly interesting. As critical as developers are to the success of AI in any particular organization, we need those developers working alongside the people who understand the business, with authority to turn that understanding into systems that other employees can use. That’s the key to AI success. Old advice for a new assignment It has always been thus, however much we try to pretend that this time it’s different. Back in 2013, I quoted Gartner analyst Svetlana Sicular discoursing on the rise of big data technologies like Hadoop: “Organizations already have people who know their own data better than mystical data scientists.” She continued, “Learning Hadoop is easier than learning the company’s business.” Data becomes useful when paired with industry expertise—from experts who understand which data actually matters. This topic is perpetually relevant. I covered the argument in 2023 and again in 2025 . We’ve always needed people who can translate business requirements into software. AI expands the kinds of knowledge that software can work with. Language models extend that work to material that often sat outside our applications: research notes, meeting transcripts, internal debates, and explanations of why a decision was made. An employee can ask questions across that material without someone first designing a report for every possible question. That opens up useful work that would have been difficult or expensive to automate before. It also creates new ways to be wrong. A model may find a convincing explanation that was superseded six months ago, confuse a proposal with an approved policy, or combine two departments’ incompatible definitions of a customer. The people who understand those distinctions need to help engineers make them explicit, then build examples that reveal when the system gets them wrong. Companies that figure this out stand to benefit disproportionately; hence, PwC’s April survey of 1,217 senior executives found that companies reporting the strongest AI performance were twice as likely to redesign workflows around AI. Teach the system what’s good Bridgewater, the world’s largest hedge fund, has done some interesting work here that substantiates this theory. At AI Engineer NYC on October 13, two representatives of Bridgewater described Vault, its repository and access layer for external and internal unstructured information. Vault isn’t designed to be a dumping ground; instead, the company has shaped the way it stores data to make it useful for analysts. I attended the talk and watched as Sam Green demonstrated a question about AI infrastructure investment and the Korean won. Left on its own, a web-connected AI agent relied on July material to answer a question posted in October. Hedge funds depend on up-to-the-second information to figure out optimal trades, making this initial attempt a failure. Connected to the human-influenced Vault, however, it searched October 1 through October 8 and drew on seven documents rather than one or two. Knowing which period matters is part of understanding the investment question; making the right material available consistently is an engineering problem. You need both. A plausible answer assembled from stale research can be worse than an obvious failure because it gives the investor little reason to investigate further. The team also collected roughly 200 questions and manually identified useful documents, including misleading matches. Bridgewater’s Aaron Linsky reported that subsequent improvements lifted the share of relevant documents among the top 10 search results from about 60% to between 90% and 95% on that evaluation. This method is useful well beyond investing. Someone has to distinguish a document that merely sounds relevant from one that actually helps answer the question. Engineers can then use those judgments to measure whether a change improves the system. Business expertise becomes something the team can test against, rather than advice delivered after the application has shipped. It’s not a case of human intelligence or artificial intelligence. You need both. Make the expertise usable Of course, a skeptic could reasonably ask why a model can’t learn the business, too. It’s a fair critique, as AI can learn a great deal of it. After all, that’s the reason Bridgewater (and others) make a point of supplying the right documents, definitions, and examples. This ensures AI can take on more of the analysis, thereby reducing dependence on the few employees who currently carry essential knowledge in their heads. But access to every document doesn’t settle which policy is authoritative when two departments disagree. Nor does it authorize a change to an approval process or establish who owns a mistake. A model can help expose contradictions and propose resolutions, but someone with responsibility for the business has to decide which resolution the company will adopt. Of course, most companies don’t have Bridgewater’s decades of codified investment knowledge. They may also have conflicting definitions scattered across spreadsheets and a few employees who know why the official process doesn’t quite describe reality. Nor does it make sense to search for one extraordinary hire or a star employee who knows every model, understands every department, and can persuade everyone to change. (Good luck with that!) After all, someone with deep knowledge of the business may also be the exact wrong person to help an organization evolve, wedded as they may be to how things have always been. Gartner’s Sicular was right about the value of people who understand the business. AI gives companies more ways to put that understanding to work. Give those people engineers to build with, authority to resolve disagreements, and responsibility for leaving behind a system someone else can operate. We need AI challenging people, and people challenging AI.

title: How Family Dentists Support Parents In Teaching Oral Hygiene
author: Paul Petersen
content: You remind your child to brush, buy the toothpaste with the fun flavor, and try to keep bedtime from turning into a debate. Some days it works. Some days your child clamps their mouth shut, chews the toothbrush, or gives you ten rushed seconds and calls it done. That is normal, and it wears you out. If you need extra support, a dentist in LaGrange, GA can help. Teaching oral care at home sounds simple until real life gets involved. Kids get distracted. Parents second guess themselves. You may wonder if you are pushing too hard, not doing enough, or missing something that could lead to cavities later. A family dentist helps close that gap. Good home habits still matter most, but a family dentist gives you guidance, timing, and support that turns brushing and flossing from a daily fight into a skill your child can actually learn. Family dentists turn daily brushing struggles into teachable moments Children do not learn oral hygiene from one talk. They learn through repetition, modeling, and correction. That is hard to manage when mornings are rushed and evenings are already full. Parents often end up focusing on getting the task done, not on teaching the technique. A child may brush every day and still miss the gumline, skip the back teeth, or use too much pressure. This is where family dental care for parents and children makes a difference. During routine visits, dentists and hygienists can show children how to hold the brush, where plaque tends to build up, and why gentle brushing works better than scrubbing. Kids often respond differently to a dental professional than they do at home. The same instruction you gave five times may finally click when it comes from someone in a mask with a tiny mirror and a clear explanation. That support also helps parents. Instead of guessing whether your child is ready to brush alone, you get a more accurate answer based on age, dexterity, and oral development. A dentist may point out that your six year old still needs hands on help, or that your older child needs a better flossing method because tight contact points are trapping food. That kind of advice saves time and frustration. Preventive dental visits help parents catch problems before habits harden Small issues become expensive issues when they go unnoticed. A child who breathes through their mouth may wake up with dry gums and a higher cavity risk. A child with sensory sensitivity may avoid brushing certain areas every single day. Another may snack often enough that even decent brushing is not enough to protect enamel. These patterns are easy to miss at home because they look like personality quirks, not oral health risks. A family dentist sees those patterns early. Preventive visits give parents a clearer picture of what is happening beyond the obvious. If your child has early signs of decay, weak enamel, crowding, or gum irritation, you can adjust routines before the damage grows. The advice is practical, not abstract. Brush after this snack pattern. Use a smaller brush head. Switch to a smear or pea sized amount of fluoride toothpaste based on age. Keep helping at night, even if mornings are independent. Public health guidance supports that early, consistent approach. The CDC’s oral health tips for children outline daily habits that lower the risk of cavities, and the HRSA guidance for young children’s oral health reinforces the value of early dental care and parent involvement. Teaching oral hygiene works better when parents get specific, age based guidance Parents often get broad advice that sounds fine but does not help much at 7:45 at night. “Make brushing fun” is not enough when your toddler hates the texture of toothpaste or your eight year old rushes through everything. A dentist can tailor the plan to your child’s stage and temperament. If your child is very young, the focus may be on building comfort, routine, and trust. If your child is school age, the goal may shift toward technique and consistency. Teenagers need a different kind of support, especially if braces, sports drinks, or skipped routines are part of the picture. This is one reason helping kids learn oral hygiene works best when home care and professional care reinforce each other. Home Teaching Alone Home Teaching With a Family Dentist Parents rely on trial and error Parents get personalized advice based on the child’s mouth and habits Technique mistakes may go unnoticed for months Brushing and flossing problems are corrected during checkups Children may resist parent instruction Children often respond better to demonstrations from dental staff Early decay or gum irritation may be missed Problems are spotted sooner, when changes at home can still help Parents may not know when a child can brush alone Independence is guided by age, skill, and risk level Parents can build stronger oral hygiene routines with simple changes Watch one brushing session closely. Do not just ask if your child brushed. Stand with them and look for what they actually do. Are they reaching the back teeth? Are they brushing for two full minutes? Are they spitting out toothpaste right away and moving on? One observed session tells you more than a week of reminders. Ask your family dentist for one fix, not ten. Too much advice gets lost. If flossing is the weak point, focus there first. If brushing pressure is the problem, work on that before adding mouthwash or reward charts. One specific change is easier for your child to learn and easier for you to reinforce. Keep the routine steady, even when your child pushes back. Kids read inconsistency fast. If brushing is optional when everyone is tired, the habit weakens. Keep the steps short and predictable. Brush at the same times, use the same setup, and offer help without turning it into a long negotiation. Family dentistry gives parents support, not judgment No parent handles oral hygiene perfectly every day. Children refuse, forget, stall, and test limits. That does not mean you have failed. It means your child is learning a life skill that takes time, repetition, and support from more than one place. A good family dentist helps you teach that skill with less guesswork and more clarity. If your child’s routine feels shaky, or you want a better plan for brushing, flossing, and prevention, schedule a visit for guidance that fits your family and your child’s age. Strong habits start at home, and they grow faster when you do not have to figure it all out alone. The post How Family Dentists Support Parents In Teaching Oral Hygiene appeared first on Of W Now .

title: 5 Questions To Ask About Safe Car Travel With Pets
author: Paul Petersen
content: You know the feeling. Your bags are packed, your pet is already picking up on the change in routine, and what should be a simple drive starts turning into a list of worries. Will your dog pace the whole time? Will your cat panic in the carrier? What happens if you need to stop fast, or your pet gets sick halfway through the trip? Safe car travel with pets sounds straightforward until you picture the details, and having access to Waco, TX veterinary care can offer extra peace of mind. Most problems on the road come down to preparation, restraint, comfort, and backup plans. A short drive to the park is one thing. A long trip with traffic, heat, rest stops, and a nervous animal is another. Asking the right questions before you leave can help you avoid injuries, stress, and expensive emergencies, and a general veterinarian can help you sort out what applies to your pet and what does not. Proper pet restraint reduces risk for everyone in the car The first question is simple. Is your pet actually secured in a way that protects them and you? A loose pet can become a projectile in a crash, and even without an accident, an anxious dog climbing onto your lap or a cat slipping under the brake pedal can create a dangerous distraction in seconds. For dogs, that usually means a crash tested harness attached to a seat belt system or a secured crate. For cats, it means a sturdy carrier that stays closed and is placed where it will not slide around. Pet car safety is not just about keeping your animal from wandering. It is about reducing the force of impact if the car stops suddenly. If your pet hates restraint, that does not mean the answer is to give up. It usually means they need gradual practice. Start with a few minutes in the parked car, then short drives, then longer ones. Cornell offers practical guidance on traveling safely with your dog , including crate use and travel planning that can lower stress before a trip even starts. Travel readiness depends on your pet’s health, age, and stress level The second question is whether your pet is physically and emotionally ready for the drive. A healthy young dog may handle a road trip well. A senior dog with arthritis, a short nosed breed prone to breathing issues, or a cat with a history of panic may need a different plan. This is where a general veterinarian matters. Motion sickness, pain, anxiety, and dehydration can all show up as restlessness, drooling, whining, vomiting, or refusal to settle. You might assume your pet is misbehaving when they are actually uncomfortable or scared. A veterinarian can check for conditions that make travel harder and recommend ways to manage them, which may include timing meals, using calming tools, or discussing medication when needed. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has a useful guide for healthy pet travel that covers records, identification, and basic travel safety. That kind of planning matters more than people expect, especially if your trip involves crossing state lines or staying overnight. Heat, breaks, and routine shape safe car travel for pets The third question is whether your trip plan works for your pet’s body, not just your schedule. Cars heat up fast. Even on a mild day, the inside temperature can rise to dangerous levels within minutes. Cracking a window is not enough. Leaving your pet in a parked car, even for a quick stop, can turn into an emergency before you get back. Long drives also bring another problem. Pets need water, bathroom breaks, and a chance to reset. Dogs often need breaks every few hours. Cats may not want to leave the carrier, but they still need a quiet, cool environment and a secure setup. Feeding a full meal right before departure can make nausea worse for some pets, so timing matters. Safe car travel with pets often works best when you keep the routine boring. Familiar bedding, a favorite toy, and a calm tone from you can lower stress more than constant reassurance. Pets read your energy quickly. If you are rushing and tense, they usually feel it too. Emergency planning protects you when the trip goes off script The fourth question is one people skip because they hope they will not need it. If something goes wrong, what is your plan? A flat tire, a crash, a hotel change, or a sudden illness can leave you trying to solve too much at once while your pet is frightened. Your pet should wear current ID tags and have a microchip with updated contact information. Keep vaccination records, medications, and a recent photo with you. Pack food, water, bowls, waste bags, and any supplies your pet would need for at least a day longer than expected. The CDC also offers advice on pet emergency preparedness , which is worth reviewing before any longer drive. This is also where many people realize they have not practiced getting their pet in and out of the carrier or crate quickly. In an emergency, that hesitation can matter. A few practice runs at home can make a real difference. Comparing common travel choices helps you avoid preventable risks Travel Choice Safer Option Higher Risk Option What It Can Lead To Restraint Secured crate or crash tested harness Loose in the car or on a lap Driver distraction, injury during sudden stops, escape at rest stops Temperature management Pet stays with you in climate control Pet left in parked car Heat stress, heatstroke, rapid medical emergency Trip pacing Regular breaks, water, realistic drive time Long stretch without stops Accidents in car, dehydration, rising anxiety Health planning Pre trip veterinary check when needed No plan for motion sickness or chronic issues Vomiting, pain flare, breathing trouble, emergency vet visit Identification Tags, microchip, travel records No updated ID Harder recovery if pet gets lost Three steps can make traveling with pets by car much safer 1. Test your setup before the real trip. Put the crate, carrier, or harness in the car and take a short drive. Watch for panting, drooling, whining, or frantic movement. Small problems are easier to fix before a six hour drive than during one. 2. Build a travel kit that stays in the car. Include water, bowls, leash, waste bags, cleaning supplies, medication, records, and a recent photo. If your pet has a chronic condition, pack extra medication in case the trip runs long. 3. Talk to a veterinarian if your pet has struggled before. If your dog gets carsick or your cat shuts down in transit, do not assume that is just how travel will always be. A general veterinarian can help with a safer plan for traveling with pets safely , especially if age, anxiety, or medical issues are part of the picture. Road trips with pets do not have to feel like a gamble. The goal is not a perfect ride. It is a safer, calmer one, where your pet arrives without injury, panic, or preventable health problems. If you are planning a trip and you are not sure your pet is ready, schedule a visit with a general veterinarian and get clear advice before you go.
