title: Top 10 Fruit Tree Suppliers for Community Orchards in the UK
author: Paul watson
content: The planting day is the easy event to imagine. People arrive, spades appear, someone takes photographs and the new orchard finally looks real. The more revealing question is who will water the trees during a dry week in June, when the original organiser is away. A community orchard needs a supplier that fits the work the group can sustain. Some projects already have an experienced grower and want well-specified trees. Others need help with the site, species, training or the first years of care. These ten UK suppliers offer different routes into that decision. Choosing between them becomes easier once the group has agreed which parts of the project it can handle itself. Make the quote useful to the next organiser A committee comparing quotes needs to know what each one will achieve. The suppliers here have relevant fruit-tree ranges, with different forms of guidance, orchard support and fulfilment. Their published service descriptions determine where extra help is available. The list gives those differences room, so the group can match a purchase or a separately agreed service to the work it needs done. A useful enquiry includes a site sketch, soil observations, access to water and the number of people likely to maintain the planting. It should also say who will take delivery. Bare-root trees arriving while a site is inaccessible create work that a well-attended planting day cannot retrospectively solve. Record the agreed varieties, rootstocks, spacing and aftercare responsibilities somewhere the next organiser can find them. That document may be more valuable in three years than the original shopping list. If the supplier is providing design, a visit or training, the quote should identify that service separately from the trees. “Advice available” can mean several very different things. 1. Chris Bowers & Sons A community group assembling a UK orchard can use the fruit trees for sale range at Chris Bowers & Sons to turn a general wish for shared harvests into a specified order of trees. Apples, pears, plums and other fruit types can be considered alongside rootstock and form, with growing information and direct contact available for questions. The useful work here is making the order legible. “Six fruit trees” leaves too much for a future volunteer to unravel; named varieties with their rootstocks, expected roles and planting positions give the group something it can maintain. The nursery’s range allows those choices to be made across several fruit types without making one fashionable variety the organising idea. Young material intended for later training also needs to be described accurately. It is a starting point for a framework the group will develop, with work attached. Chris Bowers is relevant where the committee can agree the site and maintenance plan, then wants a broad specialist source for the plants. A general enquiry should not be assumed to include a designed orchard or a supervised planting service. 2. Sheffield Fruit Trees Sheffield Fruit Trees brings education and orchard design into the same conversation as the plants. The social enterprise raises its own stock and offers a particularly tangible route for projects within reach of its local collection and delivery arrangements. That combination matters when enthusiasm is plentiful but horticultural experience is uneven. A group may need fewer trees than first imagined and more shared understanding of how they will develop. Design and educational work can address that need directly. Its local S8 arrangements make geography part of the choice. A nearby project can discuss the practical support it requires without treating a national mail-order comparison as the only way to buy. The scope, dates and cost of any additional service still belong in the agreement. 3. Tom Adams Fruit Tree Nursery There is an advantage to learning around actual trees before deciding what an orchard should become. Tom Adams has a demonstration orchard, visits by arrangement, consultancy and propagation courses, alongside its nursery stock in the Shropshire and Welsh Borders area. For a group with one or two volunteers keen to build lasting skills, that can be a more useful starting investment than increasing the order. Someone who understands formative growth and can explain it to the next cohort gives the project continuity. The nursery’s consultancy and courses are identifiable services, so a committee can decide which to commission and budget for them. A tree purchase by itself should not be read as an open-ended commitment to train or manage the volunteers. 4. Scottish Heritage Fruit Trees An eight-tree pack sounds as though it might settle the shopping quickly. Scottish Heritage describes a typical mixture of four apples, two plums and two pears, while inviting discussion of the site and photographs. The important word is “typical”. A community orchard on a difficult site benefits from a selection shaped around the conditions, rather than loyalty to a convenient number. The nursery also describes site visits, design and planting supervision by arrangement. For a project that needs help defining the orchard, this is a route to discuss both the trees and the support around them. The group should leave that discussion with the actual agreed mixture and service scope recorded. That prevents a useful example pack from becoming an accidental specification. 5. The Heritage Fruit Tree Company Some community orchards begin with trees already on the ground. The Heritage Fruit Tree Company’s local pruning and maintenance work, together with limited survey and design services, makes it relevant to that less tidy starting point. An existing orchard may have gaps, unidentified trees or a maintenance backlog. Adding new stock immediately can make the shared workload larger before the group understands what it has inherited. A local assessment can help establish which work comes first and where new planting would contribute. Availability and service area matter here because practical work on a site is different from delivering a box of trees. The company’s fruit-tree range then becomes part of a broader decision about the orchard’s future, rather than a separate shopping exercise. 6. Adam’s Apples Young feathered maidens give volunteers trees whose early structure is still theirs to develop. Adam’s Apples combines that nursery stock with wholesale enquiries, collection options and consultancy or site visits by arrangement. This is a useful fit for a group prepared to invest in establishment. The catalogue also includes planting accessories such as stakes, ties, guards and shelters, allowing the quotation to address some of the supporting materials alongside the trees. Quantities and suitability should follow the planting plan rather than a standard bundle. A modest order can still create a full season of work. The nursery’s young stock makes that visible: the first success is sound establishment, followed by a developing structure, with future cropping given the time it needs. 7. Walcot Organic Nursery The stakes provide a small but revealing logistical detail. Walcot makes them available for collection rather than delivery, so a group planning an entirely delivered order needs another arrangement for that part of the planting. Its own organically produced trees are attractive to a project that values the production method. Bought-in fruit bushes have a different status, and the distinction should remain clear if the orchard includes a soft-fruit area. Walcot therefore suits a committee willing to specify the whole planting operation. The trees, support materials and delivery or collection plan must meet on the same day at the same site. Sorting that out in the quote is far easier than discovering a missing component with volunteers already waiting beside open holes. 8. Ian Sturrock & Sons A named regional variety can give people a reason to take an interest in a young orchard. Ian Sturrock’s work with Welsh fruit, including Bardsey, offers that point of connection alongside a practical nursery range. The interest is most useful when it leads to lasting identification. A label, planting record and short account of why a variety was chosen can help future volunteers understand the collection. Regional history should sit beside the site’s suitability and the fruit’s intended use, with no assumption that a Welsh association makes every variety right for every Welsh garden. Bare-root trees can be posted; potted stock has more limited collection arrangements. Those differences matter when planning who will receive the order and when the group can plant. 9. R.V. Roger A community orchard need not consist entirely of identical young trees. R.V. Roger’s nursery production in North Yorkshire includes a wide choice of rootstocks and forms, including trained trees developed in the field. That gives an established project room to specify a tree for a particular position. A trained form may serve a designed space differently from an open-grown orchard tree, but it also needs people who understand its continuing care. The nursery is useful when the group can describe that position accurately. Crown shape, access and the work required after planting deserve as much attention as the variety name. A more developed tree changes the starting point; it does not remove the need for a shared maintenance plan. 10. Orange Pippin Trees Online pollination information can make a committee discussion more concrete. Orange Pippin combines variety descriptions, compatibility tools and orchard packs, helping a group move from favourite fruit names towards an order that has been thought through. The tool is only as useful as the identities entered. An unidentified apple over the fence is a question to resolve, rather than a reliable component of the pollination plan. Its retailer route also distinguishes ordinary tree deliveries from more restricted arrangements for trained forms. Orange Pippin is particularly helpful where someone in the group is comfortable collecting the information and returning to the committee with a clear proposal. The shared decision can then concern an actual selection, rather than ten competing recollections of what might grow well. After the planting photograph Assign the first summer before placing the order. Someone needs responsibility for checking water, someone for maintaining labels and records, and someone for noticing when guards or ties need attention. These responsibilities can rotate; what matters is that they are visible. The final supplier choice should make that plan easier to carry out. An experienced group may need a precise plant order. A new group may gain more from a smaller planting with agreed training or site support. Either approach can produce an orchard worth sharing when the purchase reflects the people who will still be caring for it after the event. Source note: Published supplier ranges, service descriptions and fulfilment information underpin this comparison. No customer interviews or assessments of completed community orchards are claimed. title: Best 10 Dealers for Bicentennial License Plate Collections
author: Paul watson
content: Two hundred years from what starting point? That is the first useful question in a Bicentennial license-plate collection. The national anniversary of 1776 and a state’s own bicentennial can produce equally interesting plates, but they belong to different commemorative stories. A later validation date can add a third timeline: the design may remain in circulation after the anniversary it celebrates. US collectors choosing dealers for this subject therefore need more than a search for license plates dated 1976. The offers below include national and state commemorations, later-dated survivors, individual plates, and two-plate purchases. Each merchant has actual collectible stock relevant to the theme. The comparison keeps the anniversary, the date assigned to the particular plate, and the quantity being sold separate. Which anniversary, which object? The anniversary design, the identity of the offered plate, and its purchase format supply the three comparison criteria. They explain why the list includes later-dated bases alongside 1976 objects, and why a named pair can be useful even when the same design is available singly. ShopLicensePlates leads in the promoted position. DAZ and Automobile License Plate Store offer direct routes to named commemorations; the sequence then develops choices among representative designs, particular specimens, later validation, and pairs or sleeved sets. These are editorial purchase comparisons based on the sellers’ offers. Best 10 Bicentennial License Plate Dealers 1. ShopLicensePlates 2020 and 2021 have different jobs on Missouri offer LB8L3T among the US license plates for sale at ShopLicensePlates. The former is the seller’s listed year for the plate; the latter closes the 1821-2021 statehood interval celebrated by its Bicentennial design. Both dates belong in the record. Dropping either would lose the distinction that makes this a useful addition to an anniversary collection. Placed beside a national Bicentennial design, the Missouri plate would change the display from one anniversary into a comparison of commemorations. The red-white-and-blue palette may connect the objects visually, while the 1821-2021 interval gives Missouri its own historical subject. That relationship is the reason to add it to a collection already rich in 1976 material: the two-century idea continues, but the event being remembered changes. For a display, the Missouri state seal provides a clear visual center. Compare its visibility and the anniversary wording in the offered photograph before choosing the specimen. Those features carry more of this collection’s meaning than an otherwise attractive registration number would. 2. DAZ PL8S DAZ PL8S is especially useful when the collection includes more than one anniversary. Its Tennessee 555 GST offer carries the BicenTENNial design and a 1996 sticker date, while Montana entries identify the national Bicentennial theme. The compact inventory lets a buyer pursue those separate commemorations without treating their shared keyword as the whole history. The Tennessee example is graded very good minus. That condition may be quite acceptable when the aim is to represent the state’s anniversary design, especially if the distinctive wording remains the principal interest. A display requiring uniformly clean faces would place more emphasis on the exact specimen. DAZ’s “s” suffix denotes the sticker year. Read in that way, the Tennessee offer sits comfortably beside the Missouri statehood example while the Montana stock returns attention to the national anniversary. The collector’s table supplies a route through those separate subjects, allowing the group to grow through deliberate commemorative contrasts instead of another plate chosen only because its date reads 1976. 3. Automobile License Plate Store Automobile License Plate Store explicitly identifies an Indiana Bicentennial example in its 1976 inventory. That named variant is the reason to search the merchant for this project. A year filter alone could return plenty of plates whose date is correct but whose design does not serve the intended commemorative comparison. The dealer’s state and year organization can be helpful once a collector has chosen the anniversary and wants to locate a particular issue. Begin with the named Bicentennial offer, then examine the condition and quantity attached to that product. The store’s broader practice of selling expired collectibles gives the purchase an appropriate collecting context. 4. RusticPlates RusticPlates offers a 1976 Nebraska Bicentennial design attributed to Dixon County. Its supply format is important: the image is representative and the registration letters and numbers can vary. The purchase is a specimen of that offered design, not a reservation of the photographed serial. For a design-based Bicentennial group, that flexibility can be entirely reasonable. The buyer gains the Nebraska representation without making an incidental number part of the requirement. A collector pursuing a specific serial or an exact pictured wear pattern needs a different arrangement. 5. Plate Dog Plate Dog’s Illinois inventory makes the condition and completeness choice visible within one national Bicentennial design. Current 1976 listings include separate numbered singles and pairs, including pair HW9455. Instead of immediately moving to another state, a collector can decide which physical version of the Illinois contribution belongs in the group. A single may be sufficient for a wall arrangement with one face per design. A pair can be preferable when the collecting unit is the complete offered set, even if only one member will normally be displayed. The dealer states that the photographs show the actual items supplied, so this is a comparison of particular offers. 6. Brandywine General Store Brandywine General Store supplies a clearly identified Oklahoma 1976 national Bicentennial plate, with commemorative wording and the 1776-1976 interval described on the design. The store offers several condition selections, including unused-stock grades and a lightly used option. This gives a buyer a direct budget-versus-condition decision within one design. The important qualification is that the photographs represent the condition classes; they are not a promise of the precise numbered plate shown. A collector can choose the stated grade while accepting that the individual serial may differ. Oklahoma’s printed 1776-1976 interval also brings the national anniversary into direct view beside Missouri’s statehood dates. That comparison can carry the display even when the supplied Oklahoma serial differs from the illustration. The grade selection is therefore enough for a design-led purchase, while a collector interested in one particular worn survivor would have a different requirement and might prefer Plate Dog’s individually photographed Illinois stock. 7. LicensePl8s.com LicensePl8s.com illustrates the long life a commemorative base can have. Its current Virginia product is titled as a 1985 passenger plate, number 293 508, on the Bicentennial base. That later date does not remove the design from an anniversary collection; it changes the story the specimen can tell within it. The aluminum Virginia plate belongs to the part of the collection concerned with a commemoration’s afterlife. title: Why Some Children Gag During Toothbrushing Even Without Dental Anxiety
author: Paul watson
content: You stand at the sink, toothbrush in hand, and brushing should take two minutes. Instead, your child gags the second the brush reaches the back teeth, pulls away, cries, or refuses to try again. That can feel confusing, especially when your child is not scared of the dentist and does not seem anxious in other situations. You are not imagining it, and your child is not being dramatic. Gagging during brushing can happen for several reasons that have nothing to do with fear. If this keeps happening, talking with a kids dentist in Reseda, CA can help you understand what may be causing it and what to try next. In many cases, the issue is a sensitive gag reflex, mouth breathing, nasal congestion, enlarged tonsils, texture sensitivity, or the simple fact that a child has a small mouth and is still learning how to tolerate brushing. Why Some Children Gag During Toothbrushing Even Without Dental Anxiety often comes down to body mechanics and sensory response, not behavior. The good news is that small changes at home, and support from a pediatric dentist when needed, can make brushing much easier. Gagging during brushing often starts with a sensitive reflex, not fear The gag reflex is a normal protective response. It helps keep objects from going too far back into the throat. In some children, that reflex is stronger. A toothbrush that seems small to you can feel huge to them, especially if they have a tight mouth, a low tolerance for certain sensations, or trouble breathing well through the nose. This is why children gagging while brushing teeth can happen even in calm kids who do fine at checkups. If your child gags most when the brush touches the tongue, the back molars, or the roof of the mouth, the reflex may simply be easy to trigger. If gagging gets worse during allergy season, colds, or at bedtime, congestion may be adding to the problem. Some children also have enlarged tonsils or a crowded oral space. Others are highly sensitive to taste, foam, or the feeling of bristles. A strong mint toothpaste, too much paste, or a brush head that is slightly too large can set off the whole cycle. Your child braces, gags, panics, and then expects it to happen again the next night. Sensory issues and mouth discomfort can make toothbrushing harder You may notice that your child dislikes certain food textures, covers their ears in noisy places, or resists hair washing and face wiping. That pattern matters. Gagging can be part of broader sensory sensitivity. The mouth has many nerve endings, and some children feel brushing much more intensely than others. Physical discomfort can also play a role. Loose teeth, erupting molars, mouth sores, dry mouth, reflux, and postnasal drip can all make brushing feel unpleasant. If your child says, “It feels weird,” that may be the most accurate description they can give. Younger children often do not have the words to explain whether the problem is pain, pressure, taste, or the fear of gagging itself. When this keeps happening, brushing can turn into a nightly standoff. Parents may start rushing, skipping the back teeth, or avoiding brushing altogether because the struggle feels too big. That is understandable, but it can also raise the risk of cavities and gum irritation. MedlinePlus offers a helpful overview of children’s dental health , including why daily care matters even when routines are hard. Small technique changes often reduce gagging during toothbrushing The first fix is often the simplest one. Try a smaller toothbrush head, less toothpaste, and a slower pace. A smear or pea sized amount is usually enough, depending on age. If foam is part of the problem, changing toothpaste flavor or brand may help. Some children do better with unflavored or mild fruit options than mint. Position matters too. Brushing while lying flat can make gagging worse. Standing upright, leaning slightly forward, and encouraging your child to breathe through the nose can reduce that throat trigger. If nasal breathing is hard because of congestion, brushing may improve once that is addressed. It also helps to avoid going straight for the back teeth. Start with the front teeth, keep the brush on the outer surfaces first, and work in short passes. Over time, your child may tolerate more. MedlinePlus has practical guidance on brushing your child’s teeth that can support these adjustments at home. Home strategies and a pediatric dentist serve different needs Approach Best For What It Can Help Limits Smaller brush head and less toothpaste Children with a strong gag reflex or foam sensitivity Reduces triggers at the back of the mouth May not help if enlarged tonsils or pain is the main issue Upright posture and slow brushing sequence Children who gag when brushing starts too fast Improves control and lowers panic Needs consistency to work Sensory desensitizing at home Children with texture or touch sensitivity Builds tolerance over time Progress can be slow pediatric dentist evaluation Children with frequent gagging, pain, or brushing refusal Checks for oral crowding, tonsil issues, cavities, and behavior supports May lead to referral if the cause is medical rather than dental A pediatric dentist can often spot patterns parents cannot easily see during a rushed bedtime routine. That includes bite issues, sore gums, erupting molars, or signs that the child needs a gentler behavior approach. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry outlines behavior guidance that supports children who struggle with care routines in a respectful, child centered way. You can read that guidance here . Three steps you can start tonight Use less brush and less paste. Pick the smallest soft brush you can find and use only the amount of toothpaste your child needs for their age. If mint causes problems, switch flavors. This one change helps many kids with gagging during toothbrushing . Change the order and the position. Brush while your child is upright, not flat, and start with the easiest areas first. Leave the inside back molars for last. Keep strokes short. Pause before your child gets overwhelmed instead of pushing through a gag. Track patterns for one week. Notice whether gagging is worse in the morning, at night, during congestion, with certain toothpaste, or on one side of the mouth. That record is useful if you need to talk with a pediatric dentist or your child’s doctor. Consistent support usually makes brushing easier If your child gags while brushing, it does not automatically mean fear, defiance, or poor cooperation. Sometimes the mouth is sensitive, the airway is blocked, or the routine needs a different approach. When you adjust the tools and technique, many children improve. When they do not, a pediatric dentist can help sort out whether the cause is sensory, dental, or medical. You do not need to force your way through this every night. A calmer routine and the right support can protect your child’s teeth without turning brushing into a battle. title: Four Safety Nets Between Your Air Conditioner and Your Ceiling
author: Paul Petersen
content: An air conditioner does two jobs at once. It cools the air, and it pulls moisture out of it. On a humid summer day, that moisture adds up to a surprising amount of water, sometimes gallons over a day of heavy running. It collects on the indoor coil, drips into a pan, and is supposed to flow quietly away through a drain line. Most of the time it does. When it doesn’t, the water goes looking for somewhere else to go, and that somewhere is often a ceiling, a wall, or a finished floor. The good news is that a well installed system has several layers of protection against this, and you can check most of them yourself. Net one: the drain line The first line of defense is the simplest. A drain pan sits under the indoor coil, and a pipe carries the water from the pan to a safe place, such as a floor drain, a utility sink, or the outdoors. Gravity does the work, which means the pipe needs a steady downward slope and a clear path. The trouble is that the inside of a drain line is warm, wet, and dark, which is a perfect place for algae and slime to grow. Over a season they build up, and add dust, insects, and debris, until the line slows to a trickle or stops. The most common signs are water around the indoor unit, a musty smell near it, or an air conditioner that simply shuts off in hot weather. Check where your drain line ends. If your system has an outdoor outlet, look for a small stream of water dripping during a hot, humid afternoon. If it’s dry on a day when the system has been running hard, that’s worth a call. Net two: the backup pan and drain Because drain lines do clog, building practice calls for a second layer. The American Society of Home Inspectors notes in its article on understanding condensate that HVAC equipment producing condensate must have a secondary drain line, a condensate overflow switch, a secondary drain pan with its own drain line, or some combination of them, to prevent overflow if the primary drain blocks. This matters most when the air handler is in an attic, closet, or above a finished ceiling, where a spill lands on drywall. Anyone arranging air conditioning in Basking Ridge , particularly with the indoor unit above living space, should ask the installer to point out the backup pan and where its separate drain line ends. That secondary line should discharge in a conspicuous place, such as over a window, so that water dripping from it gets noticed. If it ever drips, that’s your sign the main line has failed. Net three: the float switch The third layer is an electronic one. A float switch sits in the pan or the line, and if the water rises too high, it shuts the air conditioner off so it stops producing more condensate. The ASHI article lists the overflow switch as one of the required options for preventing overflow, and it’s a common reason a system suddenly quits in the middle of summer. That shutdown can feel like a malfunction, but it’s the switch doing its job. If your air conditioner stops and the thermostat still calls for cooling, a tripped float switch is a likely cause, and the right response is to find the clog, not to bypass the switch. Defeating a safety switch to keep the system running is how a minor drain problem becomes a flooded ceiling. Ask the technician to show you where the switch is and to test it during maintenance visits. Net four: you The last layer is a habit, and it costs almost nothing. Once a season, look at the indoor unit and the area around it. Check the pan for standing water, look at the drain line for sagging or kinks, and confirm the outlet is clear. Keep the area around the unit free of stored items that would hide a leak. Replace the filter on schedule, because a clogged filter can make the coil freeze and then drip heavily when it thaws. Some manufacturers recommend periodically flushing the line with a cleaning solution, and some suggest diluted white vinegar. Check your equipment manual before pouring anything in, since the right product and amount can vary, and don’t use harsh chemicals that could damage the pan or pipes. A professional tune up usually includes clearing the drain, which is the most reliable way to keep the first net working. What to do if you see water If you find water near the indoor unit, turn the system off at the thermostat first, so it stops making more. Mop up what you can, and put a towel or container under any drip. Look for a visible clog at the outlet, but don’t cut into pipes or take apart the equipment unless you know what you’re doing. If water has soaked drywall, insulation, or flooring, remember that wet materials should be dried quickly, within a day or two, to reduce the risk of mold. Then call a technician, and ask what caused the problem, not just what they cleared. The fourth net is a habit The first three nets are built into the system, and they work well when they’re installed properly and maintained. The fourth is the one only you can supply. Know where your drain outlet is, know where the backup line ends, know what the float switch does, and look at all of it once each season. Do that, and the water your air conditioner makes stays where it belongs: in a pipe, headed outside. It’s a small routine that protects some of the most expensive surfaces in your house. title: 5 Ways Family Dentists Help Ease Dental Fear In Kids
author: Clare Louise
content: You know the look. Your child stiffens in the waiting room, hides behind your leg, or starts crying the second they hear the word dentist. For some families, it starts after one rough visit. For others, the fear shows up before a child has even sat in the chair, fed by stories, sounds, and the simple fear of the unknown. That stress can build fast, and it often leaves you wondering whether pushing through a visit will make things worse, especially if you are also trying to find an emergency dentist in Cave Creek . Dental fear in children is common, and it can affect how often they get care, how they behave during treatment, and how they feel about oral health for years. A good family dentist does more than clean teeth. They help your child feel safe, understood, and more in control. That is where 5 Ways Family Dentists Help Ease Dental Fear In Kids becomes more than a catchy idea. It is often the difference between a child who dreads every appointment and one who learns that dental care does not have to feel scary. Family dentists reduce fear by making the visit feel familiar Kids tend to fear what feels unfamiliar. A family dental office usually sees patients of different ages, which helps create a calmer, more normal setting. Your child sees siblings, parents, and other children getting care, and that can lower the sense that something strange or threatening is about to happen. That familiarity matters because anxiety often grows in silence. A child may not be able to explain why they are upset. They just know the chair looks big, the tools look sharp, and they do not like someone working so close to their face. A family dentist is trained to notice those reactions early and slow things down. Instead of rushing into treatment, they often start with a gentle exam, simple language, and a steady tone that tells your child they are safe. This is one reason many parents look for a dentist for kids with dental anxiety rather than focusing only on the procedure itself. The emotional experience shapes what happens next. Clear, child-friendly communication helps children feel more in control Fear gets worse when a child feels trapped or surprised. Family dentists often use age-appropriate explanations before they do anything, which lowers the chance that your child will feel caught off guard. They may show a mirror first, count teeth out loud, or describe a cleaning in simple words. That small step gives a child time to process what is happening. Control also matters. A dentist may agree on a hand signal so your child can pause the appointment if they need a break. That can completely change the mood in the room. A child who knows they can stop for a second is often more willing to keep going. Research continues to show that children’s oral health is closely tied to access, trust, and positive early experiences. The CDC shares practical oral health tips for children that support regular preventive care, which is much easier when fear is managed early. Gentle preventive care lowers the chance of painful dental visits Many children are not afraid of the dentist at first. They become afraid after pain enters the picture. That is why prevention matters so much. A family dentist focuses on regular exams, cleanings, fluoride treatments, and early cavity detection so small issues do not turn into bigger, more uncomfortable ones. When visits stay simple, children build a memory bank of neutral or positive experiences. That makes the next visit easier. It also lowers the odds that your child will need urgent treatment, which is where fear often spikes. National data in the Oral Health in America report shows that oral disease still affects many children, especially when preventive care is delayed or inconsistent. This is one of the clearest benefits of working with a family dentist . The goal is not just fixing problems. It is preventing the kind of experiences that teach a child to be afraid. Behavior guidance gives anxious kids support without shame Some children need more than reassurance. They need a dentist who understands behavior, sensory overload, and the way anxiety can show up as tears, refusal, or anger. Family dentists often use behavior guidance techniques such as tell show do, positive reinforcement, short appointments, and pacing that matches the child’s tolerance. That matters because shame makes fear stick. If a child feels judged for crying or struggling, the next visit becomes harder before it even begins. A calm dental team can help your child feel that being nervous is allowed, and that they will still be treated with patience. Evidence also supports nonpharmacological approaches for managing dental anxiety in children. A review in this published study on pediatric dental anxiety management describes methods such as distraction, communication, and behavioral support that can improve cooperation and reduce distress. Parents can support anxious children better when they know what to expect Children read your face fast. If you are bracing for a battle, they often feel it. Family dentists help parents prepare in a way that does not add pressure. They may suggest simple phrasing before the appointment, a morning visit when your child is rested, or bringing a comfort item from home. They also help you avoid common mistakes, like promising there will be no discomfort or using the visit as a threat. If your child hears “it won’t hurt” and then feels even mild pressure, trust drops. A better approach is honest and calm. You can say the dentist will count teeth, clean them, and help keep their mouth healthy, and that you will stay close by. Approach What It Often Leads To Better Option Waiting until pain appears Urgent visits, stronger fear, harder treatment Regular preventive visits with a family dental provider Using vague reassurance Loss of trust if the child feels discomfort Simple, honest explanations about what will happen Rushing through tears More resistance at future appointments Slow pacing, breaks, and child-friendly behavior guidance Skipping visits after one bad experience Fear becomes stronger over time Return with a plan focused on calm, shorter visits Small steps can change how your child sees dental care 1. Talk about the visit in calm, plain language. Keep it short. Tell your child the dentist will look at their teeth and help keep their mouth healthy. Avoid loaded words and long explanations. Your tone matters as much as the words. 2. Schedule before problems grow. Do not wait for pain. A routine checkup is usually easier, shorter, and less stressful than a problem visit. That helps your child connect dental care with prevention instead of discomfort. 3. Choose a dental office that welcomes anxious kids. Ask how the team handles fear, whether they use gradual introductions, and how they support children who need breaks. If a practice treats anxiety as normal instead of inconvenient, your child will feel the difference. Fear around dental visits can feel bigger than it should, especially when you are trying to protect your child and still get them the care they need. The good news is that the right support changes the experience. A trusted family dentist can make visits feel safer, gentler, and more predictable, and that often helps children build confidence one appointment at a time. title: How CPAs Assist With Estate and Inheritance Planning
author: Danny White
content: You may already have a will, a few account statements in a drawer, and a vague plan to “get everything organized soon.” That usually means one thing. This has been sitting in the back of your mind for a while, and every time you think about it, it feels heavier. Estate planning brings up money, family, aging, control, and the fear of leaving a mess behind. Inheritance planning adds another layer because even close families can struggle when details are missing or taxes catch them off guard, which is why many people seek CPA services in White Plains . A Certified Public Accountant helps bring order to that stress. A CPA does not replace an attorney, but they do play a major role in the financial side of the process. They help you understand what you own, what may be taxed, how gifts and transfers work, and where small mistakes can create expensive problems later. When people ask about how CPAs assist with estate and inheritance planning , the short answer is simple. They help you protect assets, reduce confusion, and make the numbers match the plan. Estate and inheritance planning often breaks down at the financial level Most estate plans do not fail because someone did not care. They fail because life got busy, records were scattered, beneficiary forms were outdated, or no one understood how taxes would apply. A parent may assume a home, retirement account, business interest, and life insurance policy will pass smoothly to children. Then one account names an ex-spouse, another has no beneficiary at all, and the business valuation creates tax issues no one expected. This is where a CPA becomes useful fast. They review account structures, ownership, basis, income tax exposure, prior gifts, and expected estate value. They can help identify whether your estate may trigger federal estate or gift tax concerns, using current guidance from the IRS estate and gift tax rules . For many families, the issue is not a federal estate tax bill. The issue is poor coordination, missed tax elections, and records that are too thin to support decisions after death. You also may be caring for a parent and trying to make sense of their money while respecting legal limits. That situation gets emotional quickly. One sibling thinks bills should be paid from one account, another wants to sell property, and no one knows who has authority. Clear financial documentation matters here as much as legal paperwork. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau offers practical guidance on managing someone else’s money , and a CPA can help turn that guidance into a workable system. A CPA supports the tax, recordkeeping, and transfer side of estate planning A good CPA starts with facts. They gather a full picture of assets, debts, income sources, business interests, retirement accounts, real estate, and past gifts. That creates the financial map your attorney needs to draft or update documents that actually fit your life. They also help with cost basis records. That matters more than many families realize. If heirs inherit stock, a rental property, or land, the tax result often depends on records that may be decades old. Without those records, beneficiaries can end up paying more tax than necessary or spending months trying to reconstruct history from old files. Business owners need even more care. If you own part of a company, your estate plan should address valuation, buy sell terms, successor ownership, and the tax effect of transferring those interests. A CPA can model different outcomes before anything is signed. That kind of planning is a core part of estate tax planning services , especially when family members expect fairness but the assets are not easy to divide evenly. Families also use CPAs for trust and estate income tax filings after death. Many people do not realize that estates and certain trusts become separate tax entities. Deadlines continue, income still gets reported, and distributions can affect who pays the tax. Those are not details to guess at. DIY estate organization and professional CPA support produce very different outcomes Approach What It Usually Includes Common Risk Likely Benefit DIY estate organization Basic asset list, informal instructions, downloaded forms Missing beneficiary updates, poor tax records, unclear transfer plan Low upfront cost Attorney only Will, trust, powers of attorney, legal transfer structure Financial details may be incomplete or not coordinated with tax records Strong legal framework Attorney and CPA together Legal documents, tax review, basis tracking, gift strategy, filing support Higher upfront planning cost Better alignment between legal intent and financial reality The difference shows up later. If your heirs receive clear records, current account titles, and a tax aware transfer plan, administration moves faster and conflict tends to stay lower. If they receive a binder full of partial notes and outdated statements, they spend time and money sorting through avoidable problems. Many families benefit from a simple affairs checklist before they do anything else. Penn State Extension has a practical guide on getting your affairs in order . A CPA can use that kind of checklist to spot gaps in records, ownership, and tax history. Practical steps make inheritance planning easier to manage Build a clean asset inventory. List bank accounts, brokerage accounts, retirement plans, real estate, insurance policies, business interests, debts, and digital assets. Include how each asset is titled and who the beneficiary is. This is the backbone of inheritance planning , and without it, every later decision gets harder. Match your documents to your tax reality. Review your will, trust, beneficiary forms, and gifting history alongside your financial records. If one document says assets should be divided equally, but most of your wealth sits in a retirement account with one named beneficiary, your plan is already off course. A CPA can help reconcile those gaps before they become family disputes. Prepare the people who may step in. If a child, sibling, or trusted friend may manage finances during incapacity or after death, give them a clear contact list, location of records, and a general map of what exists. You do not need to hand over every detail today, but silence leaves people guessing when the pressure is highest. Certified public accountant support can reduce confusion and protect your family You do not need to solve every estate issue at once. You do need a plan that reflects your actual finances, your family dynamics, and the tax rules that apply to your assets. A Certified Public Accountant helps turn scattered information into decisions you can trust, and that can spare your family stress when they are least able to handle more of it. If estate or inheritance planning has been hanging over you, this is a good time to gather your records and schedule professional support. Clear numbers lead to clearer choices, and clearer choices leave less for the people you love to untangle later. title: What mass spectrometry confirms about wolverine stack compound identity?
author: Paul Petersen
content: Mass spectrometry confirms wolverine stack compound identity twice over, establishing that the BPC-157 is the fifteen-residue sequence it claims and the TB-500 is the thymosin beta-4 fragment it claims, through two separate analyses; no single run can replace. Identity for a stack is a paired question, and the instrument answers each half on its own evidence. Buyers sourcing the wolverine peptide stack for identity-critical research ask for both reports before ordering, since a confirmed BPC-157, besides an unconfirmed TB-500, leaves the pair half-proven. Two compounds, two runs, two confirmations, and the doubled structure change how the reading works. The sections below cover the twice-run analysis, each compound’s own confirmation, and what the paired results settle. Spectrometry confirms identity Spectrometry confirms a stack’s identity through a run structure that single-compound buyers never meet. Each material passes through its own analysis, weighed intact against its own calculated mass and fragmented against its own reference sequence, because the two peptides share nothing analytically; they have different lengths, different masses, different fragment maps, and a result for one says precisely nothing about the other. Twice-run analysis, therefore, doubles every part of the identity file. Two intact readings, two fragment tables, two reference comparisons, and the buyer’s question shifts from whether a report exists to whether both reports exist for the specific lots offered. Suppliers serving stack researchers understand the double ask and hold both files ready, which itself becomes a quiet marker of who supplies pairs seriously and who supplies two compounds that happen to share a parcel. Buyers who ask for both reports in their first enquiry sort the market on that market alone, before any certificate is even opened. Wolverine stack compounds Wolverine stack compounds each face the instrument with their own identity questions, and the first analysis belongs to the shorter chain. BPC-157 analysis – Compounds of this length give clean intact readings, and the run confirms the fifteen-residue chain at its calculated mass before fragmentation maps the residue order end to end. Terminal chemistry closes the check, since truncations cluster at chain ends, and full coverage here confirms that the synthesis completed the way its documentation claims. Mass analysis confirmation Mass analysis for the second compound asks a longer question, and its run completes the pair. TB-500 analysis – Confirmation here works the forty-three-residue fragment against its reference, with the intact mass separating the true fragment from shortened variants and the fragment table confirming the actin-binding region, the mechanism depends on, sits intact within the sequence, since a fragment missing that region would pass a casual check and fail the research. Confirmed together, the paired reports settle the stack’s identity as a documented fact, each lot tied to its analysis and both analyses filed beside the purity certificates, so every study drawing on the pair inherits proof rather than assumption, and every reviewer who later asks meets a file that already answered. Mass spectrometry confirms wolverine stack compound identity by answering two separate questions with 2 separate runs: the BPC-157 is proven as its full sequence, and the TB-500 as its intact fragment. The doubled analysis doubles the file a careful buyer collects, and research built on both confirmations starts from measured ground, lot after lot. title: HSBC set to launch $1bn buyback despite revenue miss
author: Samuel Norman
content: HSBC has unveiled plans for a bumper buyback despite its third-quarter revenue missing market expectations, after banking net interest income and its wealth division lagged behind expectations. The FTSE 100 bank said it would return $1bn to shareholders through a buyback programme after it scored a $9.63bn profit for the quarter. This was broadly in line with the consensus expectations of $9.69bn. But revenue missed the mark after HSBC reported $18.6bn for the period, below the forecast of $18.9bn. The over $300m miss followed underperformance in banking net interest income, which delivered about $11.6bn, some $247m below expectations. Revenue in the bank’s wealth division was also softer than expected at $2.7bn, compared to a $2.8bn consensus. Shares in the bank slid seven per cent in early trading to 1,269.0p – putting the bank on track to lose its crown as the biggest listed firm by market value. The firm also revealed an interim dividend of $0.1 per ordinary share, which equates to around $1.7bn being dished out to investors. Along with the buyback, this could bring returns for the quarter to around $2.7bn. “Our performance shows that in a more complex world clients continue to turn to us to navigate uncertainty and seize new opportunities. It also reflects consistent execution of our strategic priorities with pace, precision and discipline,” Georges Elhedery, group chief executive, said. “As we simplify HSBC, we are creating greater capacity to invest, grow and deliver strong returns for our shareholders.” HSBC set to fall in UK tax grips Operating expenses at the bank dropped 12 per cent to $8.8bn, mainly due to the absence of a major legal charge that dragged up the previous year’s figure. HSBC made a $1.1b provision in its third quarter results in 2025 following a Luxembourg court rejecting the bank’s appeal in regards to an investment fraud case associated with the Bernie Madoff scandal. The legal claims against the bank revolved around allegations that it breached its supervisory duties by failing to properly safeguard or verify the existence of the assets and thereby facilitating the continuation of the fraud. Just over a year ago, the bank also revealed plans to buy out minority shareholders in Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Bank. The group paid a 30.3 per cent premium on the deal, and said it would be funded by suspending its buyback programs. It said it would resume buybacks in August following a second-quarter profit jump. The update from HSBC – which is Europe’s biggest lender by market value – comes less than a week before Chancellor John Healey delivers his maiden Budget, where banks are expected to be targeted with a punishing tax raid. Healey has faced fierce lobbying from the left of the Labour party and trade unions to slap higher taxes on the sector following the bumper profits reaped by the industry this year. A five per cent hike to the UK banking surcharge, which sits on top of corporation tax, is expected to raise some £2bn a year.

title: Why The Reeds at South Lodge is long weekend heaven
author: Steve Dinneen
content: Waking up to the sunrise streaming through the floor-to-ceiling windows in the calm, modern luxury of my biophilic lodge ranks among my favourite moments of the year. The Reeds is a relatively new addition to the South Lodge estate, a series of six two storey cabins perched over a lake, into which the brave can dash for a bracing morning swim.  I was content to relax in the morning glow with a cup of coffee and a copy of City AM The Magazine , the bustle of the main South Lodge estate feeling like a world away. Available in various sizes – mine was a roomy one-bedroom called “Damselfly” – these are impeccably put together structures, the word “cabin” utterly failing to do these louche, curvy residences justice. Downstairs is a chic living space with sofas overlooking a terrace. There you can enjoy the hot tub as you gaze out at the gently rolling countryside, or warm up within your own private sauna. Upstairs on the mezzanine you will find the giant bed. The amazing spa at South Lodge Where is The Reeds at South Lodge? This is ideal long weekend fodder, with South Lodge sitting right in the Goldilocks Zone just outside of London, far enough from the City to feel like a proper change of scenery but close enough that you’re not going to spend half your trip on the motorway. Located a short drive from Horsham in West Sussex, it’ll take you as little as an hour to get there by car should the traffic gods smile upon you, and less than two hours all-in by train. What is there to do? Seriously, when you check out this cabin, you’re not going to want to leave – but South Lodge is a stunning estate worth exploring. Beside the cabins you’ll find a young vineyard, which will eventually supply wine to the restaurants (you’ll find a bottle of local fizz in your cabin, which is a nice touch). Further afield lies the estate itself, a stunning country pile that’s been tastefully modernised by the Pecorelli family’s Exclusive Collection . Before you make your way through the grand entrance, cast your eye over the manicured lawn to the largest rhododendron in Europe, an absurdly vast shrub that is said to be impossibly beautiful when in bloom. The hotel is rather easy on the eye, too, all ornate carving, marble floors, heavy wood panels and botanical wallpaper. You can feel the history here, whether you’re relaxing in the chandelier-lit Billiard Bar with a dram of whisky or sitting on the stepped lawn, which is so precisely manicured it must be maintained with nail scissors. Ant then there is the spa, which is half the draw at South Lodge, made up of a sprawling collection of pools and tubs, both indoor and out. Loungers circle the pools, giving the impression you’re somewhere warmer than the UK and when I was there, the weather duly obliged. Should you wish to cool down, there’s a ‘wild swimming’ pool that will get your heart thumping before you hop back in the hot tub. The South Lodge estate What about the food at South Lodge? The food, you ask? Oh, let me tell you about the food. There are three restaurants here as well as the aforementioned bar, of which I ate at two. Let’s start at the top: The Pass earned a Michelin star in 2023 under head chef Ben Wilkinson (just seven months after his arrival) and you can see why. With just 28 covers, it’s an intimate affair, with many of the tables overlooking a kitchen that would be the envy of most London restaurants. You know what to expect here – incredible lamb and oysters and turbot – but that doesn’t make it any less enthralling to eat. Book a table here, you won’t regret it. There is also the only-slightly-less-fabulous Camellia, situated in the sun-filled room in which you’re served breakfast. Expect innovative twists on classic country dishes: rabbit loin and venison and a brilliant take on Sussex beef tartare, including oyster emulsion, crispy capers and pickled shallot. And the main hotel? The rooms in the main building are the equal and opposite of the cabins: traditional affairs with the kind of idiosyncratic layout typical of such estates. Mine featured exposed beams, a double-width ‘stable’ door downstairs and a chimney stack sprouting from the centre of the room. Very quaint. • For more information and to book  go to the website here

title: Private equity-backed Unity Advisory hits 120 clients as former Big Four chiefs target rivals
author: Rosie Harris-Davison
content: Having shaken off early legal threats from PwC, secured 120 clients, and already won work from traditional rivals , two former Big Four heavyweights told Rosie Harris-Davison that their advisory firm, Unity Advisory, is not a challenger but a contender in the evolving market. Marissa Thomas, former chief operating officer and managing partner at PwC UK for 32 years until 2025, and Steve Varley, former chairman and managing partner of EY UK and Ireland, founded the private-equity-backed firm Unity Advisory to “modernise” the advisory model. “I had strongly held views on how advisory needed to be different, by putting talent and expertise at the heart of the model, and leveraging technology and AI responsibly to accelerate delivery,” Thomas told City AM . “I just wanted to be part of creating something that was the next chapter versus trying to update something that needs retrofitting.” Since Unity Advisory took on its first client in November last year, after two Big Four veterans founded it in April, the advisory firm now has 120 clients on its books, serving primarily private-equity-backed businesses and private equity firms, alongside some listed companies, and shows no signs of slowing down. “We’re not a challenger, we are a contender,” Thomas said, adding that the firm is “winning work from a broad range of competitors”. However, the firm’s early journey hit some bumps after its debut when reports said PwC sent legal threats in February to senior members of the advisory firm who had jumped ship from the Big Four giant. But months later, the heat seems to have cooled, as Thomas told  City AM  that there is “no ongoing litigation or legal battle with PwC, or any of the Big Four [firms].” “I’d say the relationships are appropriately cordial,” Thomas added. Firm targets outcome-based billing Varley said after he left EY, his previous clients asked what he was doing next, and when he shared the idea of Unity Advisory, his former clients were “really interested in continuing a relationship”, as he stated with an advisory firm that focused on “outcomes” instead of the traditional advisory model of billing by the hour, which “got him thinking” even more about the business idea. He said the firm is now “a viable alternative” to the Big Four and other mid-market advisory firms, and compares its conflict-free business model to being “like a speedboat rather than an oil tanker”, able to move faster and adapt quicker than large, well-established legacy firms. The Mayfair-headquartered firm uses AI and proprietary software to increase client-facing time and reduce administrative work, which Varley said makes Unity an “AI-powered” firm, enabling it to speed up delivery while retaining human judgement. “We want to work out the value we’re going to create together, and then we’d rather be paid on the value creation rather than the billable hours ,” he said. This comes as the Big Four and the wider professional services sector increasingly invest in stronger ‘human skills’ as AI reshapes the industry. PE backer expectations ‘exceeded’ Unity Advisory signed a deal with US private equity backer Warburg Pincus for up to $300m (£224.8m) in funding last April. “It’s really unusual for a big private equity house to back a startup,” Varley said. “A lot of startups end up hand to mouth every week. We’ve had a little bit more luxury of space.” After Varley and Thomas agreed to the deal with Warburg, they said they hired an independent firm to talk to prospective clients and gauge market sentiment for a firm like Unity. “The phrase that stuck in our mind was they were looking for something that was a modern advisory business,” he added. “That confirmed our confidence, and also, I think for Warburg, it confirmed their confidence in the proposition.” James O’Gara, managing director and partner at Warburg Pincus, told City AM the “significant client demand that Unity Advisory is experiencing in its first year” has “confirmed our investment thesis that there is a global opportunity for a new and modern advisory firm.” “The success of Unity Advisory to date has exceeded our expectations,” O’Gara said. Last week, Unity opened its second office in Manchester, as the firm sets its sights on expanding its advisory footprint beyond the City and to “service the whole of the North-West,” according to Thomas. The chief executive added there are “two reasons” for the Northern expansion, which are for “talent and clients”. “We’ve got a growing book of business locally, a lot of clients that love our model and want something different, and we’ve got some very, very talented people that have joined us. It’s a really good market for professional services talent,” she added.

title: Four in five London homes shed value as mortgage costs soar
author: Felix Armstrong
content: The vast majority of homes in London are losing value, prompting calls for John Healey to cut stamp duty at the Budget later this week.   Across the capital and the south east of England, 85 per cent of homes have fallen in the last year, according to property portal Zoopla, compared to 35 per cent in the UK as a whole.  London’s property market has borne the brunt of rising mortgage costs and falling demand for homes since the Iran war, as housebuilders urge the government to boost affordability.  The average home in the capital is worth £5,400 less than it was a year ago, according to Zoopla, while house prices in the north west are £6,600 higher.  Londoners are bearing the brunt from stamp duty because house prices are so much higher in the capital. Prospective homeowners are forced to lower their asking prices because buyers cannot afford the tax, according to Zoopla. The homes portal said extending the two per cent stamp duty band would save home movers up to £7,500, while similar action for first-time buyers could save up to £6,000 in every transaction.  Top housebuilders, including Berkeley, Bellway and Barratt Redrow, have urged the government to abolish stamp duty altogether for first-time buyers in order to stimulate the housing market.  Last month, Andy Burnham revived George Osborne’s Help to Buy scheme , which offers equity loans to help first-time buyers afford a deposit. Housebuilders welcomed this programme but property experts voiced fears that it would not be enough.  Housing market ‘becoming localised’ Mortgage rates have soared since the Iran war broke out in February. The resulting weight on demand has combined with rising build costs to make construction increasingly unviable, housebuilders say. Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, said: “Buyers’ budgets are being squeezed as the Middle East conflict sends borrowing costs higher, but the overall number of mortgage approvals has also fallen, which has weakened demand further.  “Price growth has effectively ground to a halt this year and we expect the downward pressure to continue in the final months of the year, which may be aggravated by this week’s Budget.” Nathan Emerson, chief executive of estate agency trade body Propertymark, said the UK’s housing market is becoming “increasingly localised,” making it harder for the government to intervene. He said: “Despite regional price falls, demand remains, but buyers are increasingly selective and focused on value.  “Ultimately, market confidence will depend on improved affordability, access to suitable housing and the ability of buyers and sellers to move with confidence.”

title: Exclusive: Prem Rugby CEO set for US trip to woo banks and private equity
author: Matt Hardy
content: Prem Rugby chief Simon Massie-Taylor will embark on a Stateside schmooze next month in a bid to drum up investment into the English game, City AM understands. The chief executive is set to use the break in play provided by November’s international schedule to head to the United States, just weeks after holding talks with Eddie Hearn’s Matchroom about a formal marketing collaboration. It is understood that Massie-Taylor, the former Rugby Football Union chief commercial officer, will speak to private equity houses and family offices about investing in the seven Prem Rugby teams who are yet to secure big-name backing following stake sales to energy drinks giant Red Bull, British billionaire Sir James Dyson and AFC Bournemouth owner Bill Foley. He will also meet US banks about potential sponsorship of Prem Rugby, which counts US-headquartered insurance firm Gallagher as its long-standing title partner. Massie-Taylor is expected to sell the domestic top flight as a stable investment, despite three clubs going under in recent seasons and millions in taxpayer cash being owed to the government after a series of loans kept clubs afloat during the Covid-19 pandemic. Prem Rugby’s Stateside jaunt Exeter Chiefs (Foley), Newcastle (Red Bull) and Bath Rugby (Dyson) have seen inward investment over the last two seasons, while current table-toppers Gloucester Rugby are understood to be just months away from joining them in gaining fresh capital. It is understood Northampton Saints and Leicester Tigers, too, are also subject to investment interest from a number of domestic and overseas suitors. Prem Rugby’s decision to remove relegation from the league is seen as a key selling point for the league, aligning itself with cricket’s The Hundred and US sports leagues rather than the riskier football pyramid. Prem Rugby continues this weekend before a four-week break to accommodate the first Nations Championship finals series, which will take place across Europe before a concluding weekend at London’s Allianz Stadium. The development Prem Rugby Cup will take place across England during November.

title: There can be no Big Bang 2.0 – investors need hard incentives to revive the City
author: Charlie Conchie
content: The idea of another sudden, transformative burst of Big Bang-style deregulation is a fantasy. The City needs long term policy that encourages and incentivises investment, writes Charlie Conchie In an essay to mark the 20th anniversary of his sweeping reform of London’s financial markets in 1986, Nigel Lawson made several things clear: one was that the package of measures known as the Big Bang was initially drawn up to avoid a damaging antitrust probe into the London Stock Exchange. Another was that the structural issues threatening to drag the exchange into a regulatory mire were not the primary issue – rather it was their consequences. “The problem was that these restrictions in practice ensured that the stock exchange was woefully under-capitalised,” Thatcher’s former chancellor wrote in 2006. His proposed changes were technical remedies on the face of it – scrap fixed commissions on trades, ditch single capacity rules restricting the roles of brokers, open up membership of the London Stock Exchange to foreign firms – all delivered alongside a major automation programme led by the LSE. But they were reforms designed with an overarching aim: get more money flowing into the market. After a mass retreat by pension funds from the domestic stock market, a wave of take-private deals from cashed up foreign buyers, and a dearth of IPOs, Lawson’s comments are more prescient than ever. Lawson’s warning The idea of a ‘Big Bang 2.0’ has been invoked by several ill-fated Prime Ministers and Chancellors in the past decade to pledge fast and lucrative reform. It is a neat and tempting rhetorical device. But it’s also a redundant one – the easy levers have been pulled and the simple deregulation has been done. What is needed now are incentives to get capital flowing into the country’s great growth engine again. As a starting point that means removing tax breaks for pension funds investing in equities overseas, slashing the punitive stamp duty on shares and incentivising retail investors to back London-listed stocks. But more importantly it means a long-term philosophy of market reform and tax policy that encourages and rewards investors for backing London’s markets in the decades to come. Few are holding their breath in expectation that John Healey will be the man to set that philosophy in motion with his maiden Budget on Wednesday. But he would do well to at least heed another of Lawson’s comments in 2006. “Britain’s good fortune is that its most successful industry is one of the fastest growing on the planet. But it is also one of the most mobile,” he said. “Take care not to take it for granted.”

title: Does the government realise the rich aren’t leaving on a whim?
author: Yorke Eaton
content: From experience advising high net worth individuals, the “exodus of wealth” is rarely a decision taken lightly, writes Yorke Eaton Much has been reported about the departure of wealthy individuals from the UK and the impact this will have on tax revenues. A recent analysis suggested that ultra-high net worth residents collectively worth £121bn have either left or loosened their ties to the UK in recent years. Tax changes and uncertainty about what’s to come have often been cited as factors behind the trend. From experience advising high net worth individuals, the “exodus of wealth” is rarely a decision taken lightly. For anyone seriously entertaining the idea, the process tends to begin months, or even years, before anyone boards a plane. And, contrary to popular opinion, it is not always the tax they face today that leads wealthy families to relocate overseas; it also tends to be the uncertainty over what their bill will be in the future. The benefit of affluent individuals and families to the UK isn’t just the tax they pay. It is the money they spend and invest here, the people they employ and the knock-on benefits for tax revenues and consumer spending. So, how do we retain high net worth individuals? The government needs to understand what might prompt UK residents to consider becoming non-resident and provide a compelling answer to why they should remain. The UK has an enormous amount going for it and many wealthy families want to live here for personal, family and business reasons. The opportunity is to provide sufficient stability and certainty for them to make long-term decisions here with confidence. HNWIs are looking for certainty In its submission ahead of the Autumn Budget, TheCityUK makes a compelling case for a tax roadmap and simplification of the regime to support growth and competitiveness.  The government may also wish to review its recent changes to Business and Agricultural Relief for inheritance tax purposes, with a view to a system that better targets the behaviours the changes were designed to address, while allowing genuine business owners to invest knowing that the business can continue after their death. Various credible alternatives have been discussed within the tax industry. The UK is currently one of the only major European countries without a favourable regime to encourage the internationally mobile affluent to make the UK home. The UK could look to schemes such as those Greece and Italy have put in place to attract internationally mobile affluent people to invest in the UK and make it their home. Leaders in the tax field have already worked on a suitable Investor Visa structure and recent reports suggest this is something the government is now considering. Where people choose to live depends heavily on their circumstances. Age, family make-up and what people want for their children all play a part. For some, this is about their own residence in the relatively near term. For others, the concern is much further ahead: ensuring what they have spent years building can continue to provide for future generations. There is no room for complacency. Traditionally, children’s schooling has been one of the barriers to wealthy families leaving the UK. Yet this is being made easier by the growing number of prestigious UK school brands opening in favourable tax jurisdictions. Becoming non-resident is a major personal and financial decision, and many won’t leave even if there is a significant financial advantage in doing so. The challenge for the Treasury is to understand what influences these decisions and what can be done to encourage wealth to remain in the UK. The numbers tell us what has already happened; announcements in the Budget and conversations in the coming months will determine what comes next. Yorke Eaton is head of private wealth at Addleshaw Goddard

title: John Healey is a beer man. Does this spell good news for pubs?
author: Felix Armstrong
content: Geoffrey Howe sipped a gin and tonic, Nigel Lawson quaffed a wine spritzer, while George Osborne and Gordon Brown stuck to mineral water. Ahead of his first Budget, one of the many decisions weighing on Chancellor John Healey’s mind will be whether to get a little squiffy at the despatch box. If he does, it could be an early signal of what lies in Healey’s red box. The Chancellor has made much of his love for ale, and pub industry lobbyists are watching to see whether he brings a pint with him on Wednesday. The thought process is that if the Chancellor delivers the Budget nursing a beer, he won’t hike costs on the pub industry while doing it. The hospitality sector is in a unique position ahead of this week’s Budget: the main tax cut they had been hoping for has already been announced. Just days into his premiership, Andy Burnham unveiled a 20 per cent cut to the business rates bill paid by pubs, clubs and music venues.  Burnham, who used his first photo-op as PM to get a round in at the Hare, a McMullen’s pub in Harlow, said the move would protect pubs, which he called “the beating heart of our communities,” adding that the tax cut was “just the start.” Burnham was right to acknowledge that this tax cut was not the end of it, hospitality industry figures said, though they suggested pub companies are getting their hopes up that any more substantial support will come out of this Budget.  The industry has urged the government to reform the business rates system for good – a pledge in Labour’s election manifesto – and help employers curb the rising number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).  With Healey set to deliver a “steady-as-she-goes Budget” in a bid to restore the UK’s fiscal credibility, hospitality figures have accepted that these issues will not be solved in one session at the despatch box.  But this hasn’t stopped some pub bosses calling for another round. Some in the industry hope for an increase to tax breaks for draught beer, which the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) says could create 7,100 jobs , including 3,400 for workers under 25, and knock 10p off the price of a pint. Chris Jowsey, chief executive of Legal & General-owned Admiral Taverns, which runs about 1,350 pubs in the UK, said the beer duty paid by British landlords is among the highest in Europe. “With costs continuing to rise and many pubs working hard to simply keep their doors open, there is often little choice but to pass the cost on to customers,” he said. VAT is ‘elephant in the room’ Freezing beer duty and increasing the draught discount, so beer served on tap is liable for less tax, from 13.9 to 30 per cent, would “give pubs much-needed breathing space,” Jowsey said. Luke White, managing director of the UK arm of Estrella brewer Damm, said a freeze to beer duty would “help pubs manage the continued pressure on their margins, keep pints affordable and give businesses greater confidence to invest and plan for the future”.  Action on beer duty at the Budget would leave a bitter taste for some pub bosses, who claim that the real way to slash hospitality costs is a cut to VAT. A campaign led by celebrity chef Tom Kerridge has been pushing for the current 20 per cent rate to be halved. Sir Tim Martin, chairman of JD Wetherspoon, has long bemoaned the premium punters pay for pints at pubs compared to supermarkets. He claims cutting VAT could give pubs a leg-up by drawing more punters away from Sainsbury’s and Tesco. “Reductions in beer duty and business rates would be warmly welcomed, but VAT is the elephant in the room,” Sir Tim said. The Wetherspoon boss said he will also be on the lookout for “sleight of hand” increases to pubs’ costs at the Budget, including hikes to sugar taxes or climate levies.  While Burnham’s business rates cut was welcomed, some pub landlords still haven’t forgiven Labour for the hikes to their tax bills that followed last year’s Budget. Andy Lennox, who led hundreds of pubs in barring Labour MPs from their premises late last year, said a change to beer duty would be “completely and utterly the wrong thing to do”. The sector needs a cut to VAT and any other tax changes billed as a boost for pubs are “all just noise,” he said.  While pub landlords would toast the sight of John Healey clutching a pint of ale at the Budget on Wednesday, they will hope his efforts to revive Britain’s hospitality industry are not all froth.

title: Amir Khan’s union the GFA hires £500-an-hour silk to probe fighters’ rights
author: Frank Dalleres
content: Amir Khan’s trade union for combat sports, the Global Fighters’ Association, has hired top barrister Jonathan Caplan KC to lead an investigation into boxing and MMA. The GFA is aiming to raise £500,000 through crowdfunding to complete its certification as a union and launch the three-month inquiry into the safety, governance and treatment of fighters in all combat sports. Caplan, whose hourly rate for legal work is more than £500, is regarded as an expert on health and safety and regulatory justice inquiries, and will produce a report setting out what changes are needed to give fighters the same protections and rights as other athletes. “Over the last decade or so, professional sports such as rugby, football and horse racing have raised their game when it comes to the welfare of the participants,” said GFA chair designate Simon Bazalgette.  “They recognise that the brand of the sport increasingly depends on demonstrating that best-in-class welfare underpins any aspiration to grow the audience and the commercial value of the sport. “It is striking that combat sport is one of the last workplaces with no professional representation for its workers, meaning little protection, no minimum health and safety standard, no independent pension scheme, no insurance floor, and no single body a fighter can turn to when something goes wrong.  “The GFA has been formed to rectify this, to help the sport create a stronger bond of trust with its participants and its audience, and thereby give a stronger foundation for growth.” Ali Act moves ‘should be wake-up call’ for combat sports British boxers Khan and Paul Smith set up the GFA in 2022 in response to concerns that fighters lacked protections against financial and health and safety risks.
