Their latest move comes amid efforts to amend the Ali Act in the US, which was established to afford more rights to combat sports participants. “What’s happening to the Ali Act in the US right now should be a wake-up call for every combat sport worker, everywhere,” said GFA Acting General Secretary Paul Maloney. “It’s the one piece of legislation anywhere in the world that gives fighters a level of workplace protection, and it’s currently being rewritten in a way critics say favours the promoters and networks that already hold most of the power.  “If it can be stripped back there, it can happen anywhere else that lacks its own independent, respected voice for fighters – which is exactly why the GFA exists.”

title: Healey warned ‘the dam is breaking’ on shop price inflation
author: Felix Armstrong
content: The Chancellor has been warned that the “dam is starting to break” on surging shop price inflation, which retailers had kept at bay with heavy discounting. Shop prices rose by 2.1 per cent in the year to October, according to new data from the British Retail Consortium, ahead of September’s 1.4 per cent and the three-month average of 1.6 per cent.  Retailers have said the long-feared spike in inflation caused by the Iran war’s knock-on effects on energy and supply costs is beginning to take hold.  Rising prices of long-life goods are behind this uplift. Fresh food inflation remained steady at 2.6 per cent, while overall food prices rose 2.9 per cent in the year to October, up from 2.5 per cent the previous month.  Price inflation among non-food goods almost doubled, from 0.8 per cent in September to 1.7 per cent in the year to this month.  Shortly following the US and Israel’s first strikes on Iran, food industry experts warned that the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz would cause food prices in the UK to surge, as they did following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Food and Drink Federation (FDF) had tipped food inflation to surge by as much as 10 per cent by the end of this year, but later adjusted its forecast to eye up a peak of 6.4 per cent by next summer. Chancellor urged to slash costs on retailers Food inflation has remained steady at 1.3 per cent in recent months, prompting bosses at top supermarkets, including Sainsbury’s and Tesco, to question whether these cost increases would pass through. Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at data firm NIQ, said retailers had managed to delay some of the impact of these price rises by working hard to discount products. “High street retailers, faced with consumers becoming more cautious in the face of higher energy and fuel costs, will now be more reliant on promotions to drive discretionary non-food spend,” he said.  Helen Dickinson, the BRC’s chief executive, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years. “The message to the Chancellor ahead of tomorrow’s Budget could not be clearer: act now or prices will keep on rising. Without a change of course, October’s jump in inflation is only the beginning.” The trade body has urged Chancellor John Healey to follow a “simple recipe” to halt food inflation, including cancelling hikes to business rates, slashing the cost of employment, and ditching costly packaging taxes.

title: ‘You can walk in the road!’: Inside Oxford Street’s first day without traffic
author: Anna Moloney
content: The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street felt like the dream that could never come true, but this morning the first phase of the mayor’s transformation project began. Anna Moloney rushed to Selfridges to soak up the first day atmosphere It’s only day one of Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation, but its place as a pivotal moment in the history of the street is already being memorialised. In the middle of the newly cordoned-off stretch, I stop to read a series of museum exhibit-style boards, narrating the history of the road from the Romans to today: “Long before Oxford Street became London’s busiest shopping street, and ahead of its transformation into a traffic-free space,” the chronicle begins – harking back, then, to all of yesterday. It’s a confident launch for the long-mooted and highly contested project (possibly rushed through to give Sadiq Khan his legacy project), but if the mood of shoppers on the street is anything to go by, it’s already going down as a success.  A celebratory atmosphere Indeed, as I proceed past the first batch of neon-green bollards signalling the start of the traffic-free zone, the mood is decisively celebratory. “You can walk in the road!” one balding Brit exclaims, springing from the pavement to the tarmac. Elsewhere, despite the drizzle, almost everyone is snapping pictures, while a number even stop to pose in front of the bollards. Two women, wanting to document the moment together, interrupt a security worker to take their photograph, while further up I spot a row of six men, hands soberly clasped in front of them, poised for their picture of this momentous day.  Pepe Velo, a wine importer for Spain who I interrupt taking a picture of the bollards on his way to a meeting, says he thinks it’s a great initiative. “It’s extremely difficult with the amount of people to go shopping with just two pavements, my wife and I always end up travelling up the middle,” he tells me, referring to the islands that stand between some of the traffic on the street. He compares it favourably to Las Ramblas, though adds that the weather is a crucial differentiator. Further up the street I come by Daniel Te, a young artist perched on one of the street’s shiny new green benches, sketching the car-free scene ahead of him. “I love a good pedestrianised street, it’s so crazy to see no cars here,” he says, adding that he would definitely be more likely to come shopping on Oxford Street now. “I do find myself intuitively staying on the pavements though,” he laughs, and indeed it is notable as I stroll along that the crowding is still concentrated at the edges, presumably out of habit as everyone gets used to the novelty of walking slap bang down the middle. Daniel Te poses with his sketch of the newly pedestrianised Oxford Street Aside from the biggie – no traffic – the transformation of the street design-wise is still in its early stages, and no doubt some will be determined to scoff at the opening as a damp squib compared with the sunny, tree-lined scenes promised by the shiny renderings pumped out by the mayor’s office. Indeed, other than the bollards and one central street mural, the street is unchanged in look, with pedestrians currently just welcomed to walk down the still road-marked tarmac. Currently, it’s just the Orchard Street to Great Portland Street stretch marked off (the Selfridges end), though further extensions are in the works, and the current trial period will seek to identify and mitigate potential issues. The Oxford Street naysayers Naturally, removing traffic from one of London’s busiest thoroughfares does not come without downsides. When I approach one security woman stationed by the bollards to ask about her role in this pedestrianised utopia, she barks the reply: “We’re doing HMVs”. When I ask what HVMs are, she looks at me like I’m an idiot before a three-word explanation: hostile vehicle mitigation.  Another key job of the security personnel is scolding cyclists . I watch one flag down a Deliveroo driver, who proceeds to dismount his bike, walk a few steps, and promptly get back on again. Cabbies, too, are not happy about the change. One taxi driver tells me through his window that today, a half-term Monday, should have been the easiest day for the change, yet it was “already carnage” down the side roads. He says he’s keeping his fingers crossed the initiative will be reversed.  A key driver of the project has been to give London’s retailers a shot in the arm by rejuvenating the city’s flagship high street. A worker at the big Boots tells me it’s been a little bit busier today already, though the rain was partially driving more people to shelter inside anyway. A worker at a nearby shoe shop tells me she thinks the surge will come next week, when more people realise the change has happened, but says she’s not excited about it – she doesn’t want it any busier before Christmas. She may then wish to consider a job at one of the many vape or tackier souvenir shops that populate the street, and that Sadiq Khan has expressed a particular distaste for. When I go into one such establishment to ask if they are excited about the change, the manager says not. He says business has been completely dead today, which he attributes to the lack of buses. For the mayor, who has said he wishes to see the loss of Oxford Street’s “dross” shops as a result of the change, that may well be a victory. Anna Moloney is City AM’s deputy comment and features editor

title: Deloitte hikes pay for top boss while headcount shrinks
author: Rosie Harris-Davison
content: Big Four giant Deloitte hiked pay for one of its chief executives last year by almost half while overall headcount at the firm fell, in part tied to targeted job cuts. According to the firm’s latest accounts, Deloitte’s chief executive of EMEA, Richard Houston, saw his pay increase to £7.1m, almost fifty per cent more than the £4.9m he was paid in 2025 . Houston led Deloitte’s UK business for seven years prior to being promoted in June to head his role in the EMEA division, a new entity which oversees Deloitte’s operations in more than 80 countries following a restructuring this year which he led. Houston’s pay package for this financial year included a “one-off award” granted “under a long term incentive plan” by Deloitte’s North and South Europe (NSE) board. In the pay report, the Big Four firm said the award “had a number of strategic and financial performance metrics”, including for his work for the firm’s broader operations in Europe. Houston’s hiked pay was 93 times Deloitte’s median pay for its UK employees in its most recent financial year, whilst the year prior it was 65 times the higher. Deloitte declined to comment. Headcount drops as bosses paycheck almost doubles Houston’s paycheck comes as Deloitte’s headcount has fallen over the past year. According to Deloitte’s latest companies house filings, last year, the Big Four firm’s average number of employees in its UK workforce was reduced by 1,360 from 17,264 in 2025 to 15,904 in the end of the 2026 financial year in May. In June, the firm sought to cut nearly 200 jobs across its audit business in the UK, the latest in a series of cuts at the accountancy giants, due to low staff attrition. The firm said it was offering voluntary redundancy packages to a number of employees in response to low levels of staff attrition in its audit practice. A Deloitte UK spokesperson confirmed, at the time, it was a result of the low attrition rates across the audit and assurance business. “We have taken the decision to offer voluntary redundancy on enhanced terms to some of our people in the impacted areas. We do not take these decisions lightly and will do everything we can to provide support to those who are considering this option.” City AM revealed in July competitor KPMG, had also offered its UK staff bumper redundancy packages as the firm looked to slash its headcount and trim costs. Deloitte announced last week it is set to create up to 100 new jobs across the North of England with the launch of a specialised regional deals unit.

title: Healey to ‘increase minimum wage by 3.9 per cent’
author: Maurício Alencar
content: Chancellor John Healey will reportedly hike the minimum wage by nearly four per cent at the Budget, setting the floor for wages for all over 21-year-olds at £13.20 for the next year. Healey is expected to deliver a huge pay increase of 3.9 per cent to low-wage workers on Wednesday, according to The Times .  However, the increase will also mark the end of the government’s desire to equalise wages for under 21-year-olds with other adults.  The national living wage could rise from £12.71 to £13.20 while the national minimum wage, which applies to younger workers, will also only rise by 3.9 per cent from £10.85 to £11.27.  The policy is popular among voters although business chiefs have long warned that extra staff could add to pressures in the jobs market and force them to raise prices. Increases in the minimum wage by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves were cited as a reason for rising unemployment. The unemployment rate is at 4.7 per cent, rising from around 4.4 per cent in the last two years.  Labour’s manifesto promised to end a “discriminatory” minimum wage for young people. The party said it would bring wages in line with the living wage by 2030.  The government takes recommendations by the Low Pay Commission, which is an independent body. It sets the commission a mandate on pay increases. Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak said the quango should be abolished in May.  Healey’s plan to balance risks Business chiefs have said a rapid rise in the minimum wage had deterred bosses from hiring younger people given added costs. The unemployment for those aged between 16 and 24 surpassed 16 per cent for the first time in over a decade.  Healey and Andy Burnham have also made solving a crisis among ‘Neets’ , which are young people out of employment, education and training, a top priority.  Alan Milburn, whose review on youth joblessness is set to be completed next month, linked a rise in unemployment to additional costs on employers from higher wages in a report over the summer.  Kate Nicholls, the chair of UK Hospitality, said equalisation of wages between younger and older workers “would damage job opportunities at entry level” as she welcomed the decision.  The Treasury declined to comment on “speculation”. The measure is expected to come alongside a host of “everyday fixes” on the cost of food and family life. A day before the Budget, the Treasury announced that the UK would remove import tariffs on products including chocolate, banked beans and some fertilisers used by farmers. Burnham said that policies to make tax-free mileage rates permanent for care workers and extending parental pay to self-employed dads would “make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket”. Healey said: “Today’s everyday fixes are just a small part of what we are doing to give families a bit of breathing space. “Conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting families here at home through higher everyday costs. We can’t control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference.”

title: Meta unveils $95bn share sale as AI spending drains cash reserves
author: Saskia Koopman
content: Meta has announced plans to raise up to $95bn (£71bn) through share sales to fund its AI expansion, as soaring infrastructure costs put pressure on the Facebook owner’s cash flow. The tech giant said on Monday it would raise $35m through public equity offerings, followed by a further $60bn through a programme allowing it to sell shares at the market price at the time of the announcement. Chipmakers Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have expressed interest in buying up to $5bn of shares between them, as Meta races to secure the computing power needed to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The fundraising, Meta’s largest to date, will support its investment in AI data centres, its Muse AI agent and what chief executive Mark Zuckerberg has described as “personal superintelligence”. Meta shares fell around 1.4 per cent following the announcement. The move comes just days after the firm raised its full-year capital expenditure forecast to between $135bn and $145bn, having previously earmarked $130bn. Meta’s beat Wall Street expectations over its third quarter, posting a 26 per cent jump in revenue to $64.6bn, but spending increased significantly faster. Total costs and expenses jumped 68 per cent to $51.6bn, while free cash flow turned negative at $2.12bn, compared with a positive $10.63bn a year earlier. The company has also disclosed around $825bn in future spending commitments, largely linked to data centres and infrastructure. Despite its growing AI bill, Meta held $82.45bn in cash and cash equivalents at there end of September, alongside $80.92bn in long-term debt. AI spending fuels fundraising boom The share sale highlights how even the world’s largest tech firms are increasingly turning to external financing to fund the AI infrastructure race. Meta is building four computing clusters with capacity exceeding one gigawatt each, and expects to nearly double its infrastructure capacity this year. The company said its AI investments were already improving ad performance and engagement across Facebook, Instagram and Whatsapp, while opening opportunities in AI agents and smart glasses. But the scale of its spending has raised questions over how quickly those investments will generate returns. “We expect investors to continue to question the financing and potential for future capital raises”, analysts at William Blair said. They added that the fundraising demonstrated both Meta’s confidence in AI’s long-term potential and the increasing cos of competing in the sector. The involvement of Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom has also drawn attention to the circular nature of AI investment, with chip suppliers potentially helping finance one of their biggest customers. It comes as Google parent Alphabet recently outlined equity fundraising plans worth around $85bn, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX has secured a $40bn financing arrangement for AI computing equipment. Anthropic filed for a blockbuster stock market listing on Monday, revealing a first-half net loss of $80.7bn as it prepares for a potential valuation of up to $2 trillion. Goldman Sachs estimates that global AI-related capital expenditure could reach $7.6 trillion between 2026 and 2031, covering data centres and chips.

title: Farage: ‘Loathsome’ banks should not be hit with new tax
author: Maurício Alencar
content: Nigel Farage has said that banks should not be hit with new taxes at this week’s Budget in a partial U-turn on his previous position. Earlier this year, the Reform UK leader vowed to scrap interest payments lenders receive on deposits at the Bank of England, a move that would be widely regarded as a banking tax. Asked by City AM on whether he would support reported plans by Chancellor John Healey to increase taxes on banks, Farage said that lenders already faced a larger burden in the UK than in other countries and that he did not want banks to leave Britain, even though believed the sector’s practices were “loathsome”. “I hate the banks,” he said in a press conference on Monday.  “The fact is that they are already taxed at about 46.5 per cent, which is the highest out of any other competitor nation.  “You might as chancellor be able to squeeze a bit more out of them. But you have got to be jolly careful.” ‘I do not want a tax rate that makes banks leave London’ Farage accused lenders of failing to pass on gains from higher interest rates to customers and said that de-banking was “still very painful for individuals and businesses”.  However, he said he would “put that aside” as he called for Healey to spare lenders.  “I do not want a tax rate that makes the banks leave London. That will make all of us poorer,” he said. Farage has been at odds with banks for years, with Natwest’s private bank Coutts de-banking the former Ukip and Brexit Party leader over a claim he failed to meet eligibility criteria of holding at least £1m in his account.  It was later found in a report that he was prevented from accessing his account due to his political involvement, leading to the resignation of Natwest chief executive Dame Alison Rose.  Reform UK’s deputy leader Richard Tice has also long been a critic of the Bank of England’s interest payments to commercial lenders as costs are directly incurred by taxpayers. Governor Andrew Bailey said a removal of payments could undermine financial stability and cost taxpayers through extra borrowing costs.  At Reform’s party conference in September, Jenrick said there were no party plans to increase taxes on banks although he admitted Farage was concerned about the profits that lenders made from the Banks’ interest payments. Farage’s speech on Monday was designed to present an alternative Budget to Healey’s on Wednesday.  A list of 64 policy proposals included approving oil drilling at Rosebank, abolishing the energy profits levy, repealing the renters’ rights act, reviewing capital requirements on banks and re-legalising the use of Imperial units.  Some City figures welcomed the plans. Peel Hunt’s deputy research chief Kallum Pickering said some of the reforms would lead to a “much greater improvement in growth and fiscal balances”.

title: The anatomy of a bank tax: what can the UK learn from Europe?
author: Samuel Norman
content: With days to go until John Healey delivers a Budget expected to target banks with a cash raid, Samuel Norman looks at the UK bank tax framework and other experiments across Europe. For years City lobbyists managed to bat away demands for a bank tax hike. As Chancellor, despite delivering two tax-heavy Budgets, Rachel Reeves successfully saw off a clamour from her own backbenches to target the sector. But under Andy Burnham’s government and John Healey’s Treasury, times have changed. Analysts now expect a raid on the banks to be the base case in Wednesday’s Budget – and the City is bracing for impact. Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM, told City AM an increase to the bank levy was “probably the most likely option”. He added, depending on the remnants of Healey’s fiscal headroom and spending commitments, it may be the only major tax-raising measure introduced in the Budget. The UK banking sector paid a record £47.8bn into Treasury coffers in the year to April 2026, according to a report from trade body UK Finance. The industry already faces a raft of different levies, from the typical employment tax to sector-specific charges. These include the UK banking levy, an annual tax on balance sheet liabilities, and a three per cent surcharge on corporation tax. The two taxes are expected to have generated around £2.6bn for the Treasury purse in the last year, according to PwC analysis. The total bank tax contribution is expected to be around 4.3 per cent of government tax receipts. How far Healey seeks to push ahead with a tax increase will depend on his political appetite as much as the fiscal crunch he is faces. Some campaigners have urged the Chancellor to maximise the opportunity and opt for a windfall tax on the booming profits of the largest institutions. But it is a tried and tested experiment across Europe – and in some cases, it may give rise to caution.  Trial and error  Italy attempted an aggressive 40 per cent levy on its banking sector back in 2023 following interest rate hikes from the European central bank.  A coalition government led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said banks would be taxed on net interest income earned in 2022 or 2023 that exceeded the prior years’ baselines by five to 10 per cent. It was expected to raise up to €3bn (£2.5bn) but would go on to raise …almost nothing.  Markets were caught off guard by the initial announcement, sending bank stocks plummeting. Italy’s banking index dropped nearly eight per cent in a single day after news emerged, wiping out billions from valuations and panicking investors.  Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni supported a bank windfall tax. (Image: PA) Facing fierce lobbying, the government added an opt-out clause where banks could avoid the tax entirely if they kept 2.5 times their tax bill locked on their balance sheets as capital reserves instead of paying it out to shareholders.  Nearly all major banks – including Unicredit and the country’s biggest by total assets, Intesa Sanpaolo – opted to build up their reserves. It gave the government some political points, allowing it to claim it took on big banks and forced them to strengthen the financial system, but the initial tax plan proved to be a colossal misfire. In a more moderate instance, Spain introduced a 4.8 per cent levy on banks’ net interest income and fee revenues for 2023 and 2024. Pedro Sánchez’s government left no loopholes and succeeded in raising €1.3bn in 2023 and €1.7bn in 2024. The levy hit banks earning over €800m, which left a majority of smaller lenders and international banks outside the target range.  The levy was originally planned to be a two-year tax but the government would later extend it to 2027 and replaced the flat 4.8 per cent with a sliding scale between one to seven per cent tied to revenue earned.  While more successful than Italy’s bank tax bid, Spain faced harsh consequences. Top banks Santander and BBVA adamantly fought the tax. The initial announcement in mid-2022 wiped some €5bn off the value of Spanish banking stocks and triggered a wave of legal rows. It also tightened lending criteria for risky borrowers and restricted credit growth as lenders adapted to the increased cost. Tax to spend  Both Italy and Spain framed their taxes under a patriotic mandate, to help cushion households against soaring inflation and rising living costs. Lithuania introduced a bank tax in 2023 after it faced an eerily similar scenario to John Healey with a significant funding gap for defence. The government launched the ‘Temporary Solidary Contribution’ marking the introduction of one of the most uniquely focused windfall tax models across Europe. It took the form of a 60 per cent rate applied to net interest income that exceeded a 40 per cent jump over the bank’s average net interest income from the previous four years. It followed rising interest rates, causing half-year profits across commercial banks to grow 150 per cent in the first half of 2023. The government legally restricted the tax revenue to the state defence fund and military infrastructure. It brought in over €240m in its first full year and €220m the year following, a major sum relative to the size of its economy.  The highly concentrated nature of Lithuania’s banking sector – where three Scandinavian institutions control nearly 90 per cent of the market – made the tax simple to monitor and left incumbent lenders unable to simply pick up and leave without surrendering valuable market share. Comparatively, in the UK the biggest five players control around 80 per cent of the deposits, but a thriving middle layer exists. Challenger institutions , building societies, and digital-first banks, such as Nationwide, Virgin Money, Monzo, and Starling, offer viable switching alternatives, ramping up competition. Healey has kept tight-lipped on the scope of a bank tax, telling industry bosses only of the fiscal “challenges” the country faces. But if Europe’s misfires prove anything, it is that squeezing the banks is rarely straightforward. How much he leans on the industry will depend on how deep those fiscal holes run – and how much political heat he can take.

title: Activist investor revives Auction Technology Group campaign
author: Ali Lyon
content: The notorious activist investor behind a failed bid to buy Auction Technology Group has revived its campaign against the FTSE 250 firm’s management, calling for a new chair and a strategic review that could result in a sale. Fitzwalter Capital, which is Auction Technology’s (ATG) largest shareholder, called on investors to oust incumbent chair Scott Forbes who has overseen “five years of value destruction” at the online auction platform, it said in a statement on Monday. Under the proposal, Fitzwalter’s nominee to replace Forde, Richard Campbell-Breeden, would launch a strategic review exploring a buyback programme or a sale. The calls come just six months after the investor abandoned an attempt to buy the FTSE 250 constituent off the stock market. Fitzwalter has called a general meeting where investors will vote on the plans. The activist investor, which backs a combination of private and publicly listed firms, had nearly a dozen bids for ATG rebuffed during a hostile takeover campaign in which it accused its portfolio company’s management of “disastrous oversight”. Many of the bids were made place behind closed doors before ATG disclosed the offers to investors, arguing the 33 per cent premium implied in Fitzwalter’s final bid “fundamentally undervalued” the company. ATG said it was “disappointed” at Fitzwalter’s latest broadside, branding it an “unnecessary and unwarranted distraction” from the delivery of its strategy. “The board believes this does not reflect the significant progress and momentum in the business, with the share price having risen 72 per cent since the start of the year.” Auction Technology’s shares remain in doldrums ATG’s shares have shed more than 65 per cent of their value in the past five years, amid a barrage of structural headwinds and a struggle to integrate the loss-making US rival Chairish which it acquired in 2025. But so far this year, shares have rallied more two thirds in a sign of a recovery. In the group’s update on Monday, Fitzwalter partner Andrew Gray accused incumbent chair Forbes of overseeing “five years of value destruction”. “Replacing him clears the way for an independent strategic review, including a potential sale. Most importantly, shareholders will have the final say,” he added. As part of its latest salvo, Fitzwalter is angling for the strategic review to explore both a buyback programme or for directors to offload the company to a new owner. It added it was not committed to a sale should it not receive any offers that deliver “appropriate value”. It also vowed not to bid for the company should the review lead to a sale process, and promised to throw its weight behind any bid the board recommends to shareholders. Cambell-Breeden, a former investment banker at Goldman Sachs, said he was independent of Fitzwalter had “not prejudged the outcome of any strategic review”. “What matters is that the review is rigorous, open-minded and focused on delivering the best outcome for ATG and all its shareholders,” he added.

title: Fifa election twist as Prince Ali drops ‘coercion, threats and bribes’ claim
author: Frank Dalleres
content: Infighting in Asia over the future of Fifa has taken a fresh twist after Prince Ali bin Hussein of Jordan appeared to retract claims of “coercion, threats” and “bribes”. Prince Ali spoke out in a social media post on Sunday, days after the head of the Asian Football Confederation, Bahrain’s Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, used an extraordinary congress to pledge the region’s support to under-fire Fifa president Gianni Infantino. “Confederation presidents have no say: the vote is by each and every member association,” Prince Ali, a long-standing critic of the current Fifa regime, wrote on X. “So any claims that have recently emerged that confederation or Fifa Council members have a part in the vote is not relevant. “Having recently come back from Tokyo where the AFC Congress took place, the first two days were about football, which we all serve. The last day was pure politics at the behest of Gianni Infantino. “There were reports that Asia has a united position when it comes to electing the next Fifa President. In fact, nobody was allowed to speak, question, debate or talk with the media. “Lack of transparency leads to lack of accountability. No amount of coercion, threats or bribes should be allowed.” Challenger to Infantino yet to emerge as deadline looms The post has since been deleted by Prince Ali, who previously accused Fifa of “blackmail” for allegedly withholding funding unless he endorsed Infantino. Sheikh Salman told Infantino last week that the AFC was “ready to move forward, united in your support”, just weeks after co-signing a letter with European and North American chiefs calling for his removal over “a fundamental breach of trust”. Prince Ali, like Sheikh Salman, ran against Infantino in the 2016 Fifa presidential election that immediately followed the corruption scandal that led to Sepp Blatter ’s ousting. He withdrew after forcing a second round of voting and has given no indication that he will stand again. Infantino looks set to be re-elected unopposed in March, with no serious challengers having yet come forward ahead of next month’s deadline despite widespread criticism of his now-dropped plan to partially privatise the World Cup . Fifa was approached for comment.

title: Anthropic reveals $80bn loss as AI giant files for blockbuster IPO
author: Saskia Koopman
content: Anthropic has revealed an $80.7bn (£60bn) first-half loss as the AI giant filed for a blockbuster US stock market listing that could value the company at up to $2 trillion. The Claude developer published its long-awaited IPO prospectus with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, offering investors their first detailed look at its finances ahead of what could become one of the largest flotations in history. Revenue surged to $16.3bn in the six months to June, up from $1.1bn a year earlier, as businesses ramped up spending on its AI models and coding tools. However, the company reported a net loss of $80.7bn over the same period, including around $72bn in non-cash accounting adjustments linked to convertible debt and other financing instruments. It lost $42bn in 2025. Anthropic also spent $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of 2026, compared with $7.3bn across the whole of last year, underlining the mounting costs of developing and operating advanced AI models. The company has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing infrastructure in the coming years, including cloud agreements with Amazon and Google. Anthropic targets record-breaking valuation The San Francisco-based company plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading the offering. Its market debut could come as early as November, although the company has yet to confirm a listing date or offer price. Investment bankers have reportedly targeted a valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion, although recent market volatility has raised questions about investor appetite for richly valued AI companies. The listing would provide Anthropic with access to public capital markets as it competes with OpenAI and Google to develop increasingly powerful models. Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic has built a substantial enterprise business through its Claude chatbot and coding products. Its prospectus also highlighted the risks associated with developing advanced AI, including potentially harmful model behaviour and an increasingly complex regulatory environment. The company has faced scrutiny over its safety practices in recent months after former researcher Jacob Coxon accused Anthropic and OpenAI of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence”. The IPO comes amid growing investor concern over whether the enormous sums being invested in AI infrastructure will deliver sufficient returns. Jared Carmel, co-founder of Manhattan Venture Partners, an early Anthropic investor, said a $2 trillion valuation was not unreasonable given the company’s rapid revenue growth. “The market isn’t pricing a chatbot. It’s pricing an infrastructure layer for how every business is going to run”, he said.

title: Revolut founder accused of hatching a ‘scheme’ to avoid fees in superyacht row
author: Samuel Norman
content: The billionaire founder of Revolut has been accused of hatching a “scheme” to avoid paying brokerage fees in a row over a superyacht said to cost €350m. In new legal filings, seen by City AM , Nik Storonsky is accused by a luxury superyacht broker of “secretly negotiating” to buy the vessel “behind the back” of the company. Cecil Wright & Partners (CWP) claims the fintech chief sidelined the company by entering direct talks with the yacht’s owner, even while an aide was actively liaising with brokers. The firm accuses Storonsky’s representative, Alexander Chapchaev, of stringing the firm along with calls to discuss “next steps” while a direct deal was being hammered out behind the scenes. In the new filing, which labelled Storonsky’s defence as “lengthy and repetitive”, CWP alleges the Revolut founder’s camp continued “pretending to the claimant that the defendant was not secretly negotiating… behind the Claimant’s back” as part of a “scheme to try to cut the Claimant out of the deal”. Storonsky has argued he never indicated he wanted CWP to negotiate on his behalf and maintained he was free to strike a deal directly.  Revolut boss found superyacht’s ex-owner on ChatGPT The superyacht, which is named Nixie, was originally commissioned by Canadian billionaire and former professional ice hockey player Patrick Dovigi, before being sold to a Brazilian individual. The buyer was arrested for alleged fraud in 2025 leading to the yacht’s ownership reverting back to Dovigi. When Storonsky purchased the yacht directly from Dovigi, the broker argued it was cut out of the standard five per cent commission rate for a vessel of that scale. CWP estimates Storonsky paid €350m for the yacht, which means its fees would equate to €17.5m (£15m). Storonsky’s defence says the sum paid is confidential. Storonsky’s defence contends that no brokerage contract existed and said CWP explicitly told him in writing that “commissions are always paid by the seller”. When Dovigi insisted the broker show written proof that Storonsky had hired them and would cover their fee, CWP agreed but never asked Storonsky to sign anything, the bank boss’s lawyers said. The broker said Storonsky had already struck a deal with the seller before such a stage was reached. Storonsky’s legal team also argues CWP acted for the seller and marketed the vessel to rival buyers.  Filings claim the Revolut boss identified Dovigi via ChatGPT and secured his direct contact through a mutual acquaintance without CWP’s help. Storonsky’s family office declined to comment.  A spokesperson for Cecil Wright & Partners said: “We stand by our account of the events leading to Mr Storonsky’s purchase of Nixie and look forward to presenting the evidence in court.”

title: Financial advisers feel the effects of Reeves’ final tax raid as Healey’s Budget looms
author: Maisie Grice
content: Financial advisers are feeling the effects of Rachel Reeves’ final Budget, as families brace for billions of pounds of tax rises regardless of what chancellor John Healey announces at the despatch box later this week. From April next year, the sweeping shake up to the tax system announced by Reeves in 2025 will come into force. Financial advice firms say they have been hit by a deluge of requests and inquiries as Brits scramble to prepare. Two thirds of firms said they had seen an increase in enquiries over inheritance tax (IHT) and estate planning, according to the Personal Investment Management & Financial Advice Association (PIMFA). Under Reeves’ overhaul of IHT, pensions will be pulled into the tax’s scope, meaning families who inherit unspent pots will be required to pay tax on them. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), estimates it to raise £1.5bn annually by 2030. Advisers have previously warned the change, coupled with frozen tax thresholds , will subject ordinary working families to the death duty, despite not considering themselves wealthy. Richard Paddle, director at Isio wealth planning, said: “The decision…has already fundamentally changed how many people need to think about passing wealth to future generations. “What was previously a relatively straightforward approach to retirement planning has therefore become considerably more complex.” Pension taxation Elsewhere, firms have been hit by an influx of questions surrounding pension taxation, with nearly 60 per cent reporting an increase, according to the survey. In her final Budget, Reeves capped salary sacrifice contributions and extended the freeze on national insurance and income tax thresholds, which is expected to generate £7bn annually, leaving many workers questioning how to avoid being pulled into higher bands. While advisers have noted they have not seen the “panicked rush” to withdraw tax-free cash that took place last year following “unfounded leaks”, many are still worried about how their savings could further be impacted. Healey’s Budget has heightened concerns on taxation, following reports he will implement Reeves’ plan to shield low-income retirees from paying income tax on the state pension as it is set to rise above the £12,570 allowance threshold in the 2027/28 tax year, costing taxpayers £200m per year. Tom Selby, director of public policy at AJ Bell, said: “While details remain thin on the ground, there is a danger in attempting to fulfil his predecessor Rachel Reeves’ promise not to apply income tax to those who only receive state pension income, Healey creates a mess of complexity, odd incentives and obvious unfairness in the tax system.  “Those who have saved could understandably argue their diligent behaviour has effectively been punished.” The cash ISA ceiling will also be cut from £20,000 to £12,000 for under 65s. Nearly 50 per cent of firms confirmed that clients have increased or maxed out their ISA contributions in a bid to beat the 2027 shakeup, while all taxpayers will experience a two percentage point rise to income tax. Healey’s headache Healey is facing a fiscal headache in his Budget, as he looks to raise revenue to offset the blow of rising interest rates and defence spending. He is expected to slam the banking sector with a wave of hikes as his main-revenue raiser, but family businesses have also found themselves in the firing line. The Chancellor is reportedly considering proposals to levy income tax when business owners hand down to their children, potentially almost doubling the bill. Under current rules, transfers can be structured in a way that allows them to attract capital gains tax (CGT) which is charged at a lower rate, but Healey is debating a shake-up in a bid to increase revenue in his maiden Autumn Budget.

title: Sheikh Mansour doubles down on Manchester City with £100m injection despite legal row
author: Frank Dalleres
content: Sheikh Mansour has reaffirmed his commitment to City Football Group despite Manchester City’s ongoing legal battle with the Premier League by investing a further £100m. Filings at Companies House show that 11,327,163 new shares in CFG were allotted on 14 October, raising the nine-figure sum. A spokesperson for CFG confirmed to City AM that the shares were bought by Sheikh Mansour’s Newton Investment and Development, marginally increasing his majority holding. The transaction came two weeks after the Premier League announced that Manchester City had been found guilty of more than 100 counts of breaking financial rules in order to increase their spending power, helping them to become England’s dominant team. City chiefs have appealed the verdict, which they said “contains clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”. If upheld, they could be relegated, fined and Sheikh Mansour forced to sell the crown jewel in the CFG network. Describing the cash injection as “equity from our largest shareholder”, a City Football Group spokesperson added: “The proceeds will be used for normal corporate purposes against our strategic plans, funding planned investments into the City Football Group.” City Football Group valued at just under £6bn CFG is football’s biggest multi-club ownership group, with mostly majority holdings in 10 teams across Europe, North and South America, Asia and Australia. They include New York City, Melbourne City, Palermo, Girona, Troyes, Montevideo City Torque and Bahia. Following the share issue, Abu Dhabi royal Sheikh Mansour owns around 81 per cent of CFG, with US private equity firm Silver Lake holding most of the remainder. The transaction implies a valuation of CFG of £5.9bn. CFG and Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said earlier this year that CFG would fetch “$10bn [£7.3bn] minimum” if sold on the open market. He added that there was no desire to sell, calling the organisations “jewels”. That valuation could be affected by City’s fight with the Premier League, however. The Independent Football Regulator has powers to force owners found guilty of wrongdoing to divest by a certain deadline , after which the IFR can take the matter out of owners’ hands. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been forced to insist he will not apply any pressure to the Premier League or IFR over City’s treatment, having previously admitted he would be concerned to see Sheikh Mansour sell up given Abu Dhabi’s investment in the wider Manchester area.

title: The Big Bang transformed the City of London – 40 years on, can it happen again?
author: Charlie Conchie
content: The City of London was changed forever by a sweeping package of deregulation in 1986, known as the Big Bang. Forty years on – and facing existential threats – can the Square Mile reinvent itself again? When Alasdair Haynes left work as a young options trader on Friday 24th October 1986, he didn’t know what world would await him when he returned on Monday morning. For months technicians had been wiring up futuristic-looking machines in offices around the Square Mile. Haynes’s bosses had been running practice sessions on new electronic trading systems and briefing staff as best they could in preparation for the sweeping change ahead. The reality, he says, was more drastic than anyone could have imagined. “Everybody thought on Friday that there would be a few people off the [stock exchange] trading floor working in offices, and everybody else would come in. But we came in and the trading floor was practically a desert,” Haynes, who went on to found challenger stock exchange Aquis, tells City AM .  “Everybody else had gone off on Friday, never to come back ever again. It was a mind-blowing experience.” On that Monday, 27th October 1986, the sudden deregulation of financial markets known as the Big Bang took effect, transforming the City of London and catapulting Britain’s financial industry into the modern age.  The bustle and life of the London Stock Exchange floor were swapped for the screen-based Stock Exchange Automated Quotation system. Strict rules dividing work between brokers – who bought and sold shares on behalf of clients – and jobbers – who made markets and held shares – were ditched. Fixed commissions were abolished, allowing transaction fees to be negotiated freely, as were rules prohibiting international firms from owning London’s stockbrokers. International firms piled into the City and consolidated London’s fractured broking market. Americans arrived in droves – and with them came their hard-charging, cut-throat ways of working. The City’s clubby and cosy ways were changed forever.  “In the morning of the old days at the London Stock Exchange, you used to walk around the boxes around the edge of the exchange, and talk to everybody and find out what they thought about the market,” Haynes says.  “You’d meet people after work in the Arbitrager or Greens, or go out to lunch. All that changed, literally as if somebody turned a light switch off.” Speaking at the Lord Mayor’s banquet two weeks after the changes took effect, even Margaret Thatcher acknowledged her reforms were a death knell to a certain way of life. “The new technology does have a disadvantage: the people who are making deals need never meet,” she said. “You can’t look a computer in the eye and shake its hand to close a bargain.” The train timetables shifted too to accommodate the earlier starts and longer hours of new international arrivals coming in from the home counties, Sir Philip Augar writes in his book the Death of Gentlemanly Capitalism. The result though was a sudden rise in jobs in Britain’s financial services sector. In early 1986, the City employed around 1m people. By 1990 that had swelled to 1.18m, according to government figures. The deregulation drive, ushered in by Thatcher and Chancellor Nigel Lawson, triggered an explosion of activity in the Square Mile and thrust London back to the forefront of global finance. A string of huge privatisations of state-owned utilities added to a sudden influx of investment and jobs in the Square Mile. While the day itself delivered a shot in the arm, London’s markets had been internationalising for years prior thanks to the rise of the Eurodollar market – the global banking market for dollar deposits held in banks outside the United States – and the abolition of exchange controls in 1979, which ended strict limits on moving money in and out of the country. Duncan Weldon, the financial historian and author of Two Hundred Years of Muddling Through, argues those changes were just as significant as the sudden overhaul on that Monday in October 1986. “The City was in this sort of funk from the 1920s, all the way up to the 1950s. And then in the 50s, ’60s and ’70s you see this rebirth in international finance in London in debt markets, because of the Eurodollar market,” he says.  Dropping exchange controls in 1979 too was “just as big a deal as the changes to the market structure in the mid-80s”, he adds. A trading floor after the Big Bang took effect. Big Bang 2.0? Politicians have for years nostalgically invoked the Big Bang to pledge another wave of quick and transformative deregulation. Jeremy Hunt, Rishi Sunak , Liz Truss and Kwasi Kwarteng all promised various forms of Big Bang 2.0, claiming that slackened solvency buffers for insurance firms and an overhaul of listing rules would thrust London back to the centre of global finance. But Weldon says the reality is more complex. “Rhetorically, the idea of the Big Bang, and the idea there are some regulatory levers you can pull and it will turbocharge your financial sector, is clearly a very appealing one to policy makers,” he adds. “But it helps to put this in a longer context. It wasn’t just that the policy unit in Number 10, and Nigel Lawson as Chancellor, did these reforms and it turbocharged the financial sector in London.” Weldon’s warnings point to the challenge now facing the City as it is battered by a wave of foreign takeovers and a historic dearth of initial public offerings. While there have been signs of life for London’s listing market in recent weeks, a slew of reforms made to the rules governing UK capital markets have so far failed to yield a meaningful uptick in deals. Changes to the buffers of insurance firms and calls for pension funds to pump more cash into domestic equities are also yet to shift the dial on domestic investment. The London Stock Exchange has faced a wave of takeovers and a dearth of listings in recent years Policymakers and regulators point to a retreat of domestic capital as among the primary reasons for London’s market malaise. Just four per cent of the domestic stock market is now held by UK pension funds, down from 39 per cent around 20 years ago, according to think tank New Financial. Like the rebirth of the City in the 1980s, that trend has been decades in the marking. Steven Fine, boss of City investment bank Peel Hunt, says: “The problem we’ve got is that the IPO Market hasn’t come back, and the bigger problem we’ve got is the almost complete lack of domestic demand and the hollowing out of the domestic asset management industry. “That I think is something that is more in need of [another] Big Bang than regulatory change for listed companies.” Few are looking at the Budget on Wednesday as a moment likely to deliver solutions and reignite the City’s animal spirits. Banks are set to be hit with higher taxes despite warnings from international bosses that such a move will force them to reallocate capital away from the UK. While a capital gains tax hike has been ruled out, the City’s calls for an end to stamp duty on shares and tax breaks for domestic investment from pension funds look set to be unheeded. Is another Big Bang possible? Not in Haynes’s view. Rather than search for another deregulatory transformation to revive the Square Mile’s former glory, he says policymakers should learn from the principles that inspired it. “There’s no magic wand, but the Big Bang wasn’t a magic wand. It was thought through for a long time beforehand” he says. “It was about many things which a strong, powerful government at the time was able to push through. And that is what we need today. It’s not Big Bang 2.0 – you can’t electronify something again. But what you can do is take the same principles to make it work better.”

title: Tech bosses warn Chancellor UK risks surrendering to foreign AI giants
author: Saskia Koopman
content: Britain risks becoming dangerously dependent on foreign tech giants unless the government develops a comprehensive strategy for its own AI, industry leaders have warned the Chancellor ahead of his Budget on Wednesday. UKAI, which represents more than 270 AI businesses, has urged John Healey to commit substantial funding to a national sovereign AI strategy, warning that the country could become a “vassal state” reliant on overseas powers for critical technology. The warning comes just days after the Treasury unveiled more than £600m in AI investment , including additional funding for British startups and domestic chip design. However, the trade body argued that successive funding announcements had failed to address the broader problem of Britain’s dependence on foreign companies for the AI models, computing infrastructure and services underpinning its economy. “The UK has some of the world’s best AI companies, yet no Sovereign AI strategy to help them thrive”, said Tim Flagg, UKAI’s chief executive. “The AI Opportunities Action Plan , the Sovereign AI Fund and the AI Hardware Plan are all welcome steps, but nothing joins them together. On their own, they are building blocks. Joined up as a strategy, they would be transformative”. He warned that without immediate action, Britain risked becoming a “vassal state, dependent on countries that control the AI infrastructure our economy increasingly relies on”. Pressure builds over Britain’s AI dependence The warning follows major disruptions from a recent Google Cloud outage , which UKAI said affected banks, businesses and courts, proving the risks of relying on a small number of overseas providers. It also comes amid growing concern over Britain’s exposure to geopolitical tensions and the dominance of American tech companies in the global AI market. Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cybersecurity firm Check Point, said the government needed to move beyond individual funding commitments. “Without a dedicated sovereign plan in place, the UK will continue to be at the mercy of overseas tech firms, subjected to damaging outages and major cyber security scares”, she said. “Piecemeal funding announcements are tactical at best, and we need a detailed strategy about how the country will build and design a new wave of AI tools to support critical national infrastructure”. Wilson argued that developing domestic AI capabilities should also form part of Britain’s defence spending plans, especially as cyber threats from hostile states intensify. The calls follow a warning from the government’s Council for Science and Technology that Britain risks becoming a “high-value AI customer” rather than a producer of critical technology unless ministers strengthen domestic capabilities. The government has already established a £500m Sovereign AI Fund to help British startups scale, with the Treasury announcing a further £60m for the programme on Saturday. Another £60m will support research and procurement of British AI technology, while £18m has been earmarked for a new advanced chip-design academy. The wider package includes £165m for a national AI biosecurity initiative, backed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, alongside £130m for AI-powered cybersecurity projects. Healey said the investment would help deliver a “distinctively British approach to AI” that protects national interests while supporting economic growth. AI minister Kanishka Narayan also acknowledged the risks of overseas dependence, warning that Britain could not “afford to rely entirely on technology built overseas”. However, UKAI wants the government to bring its existing initiatives together under a single strategy, backed by dedicated funding and changes to public procurement that would give British AI companies greater access to government contracts. Flagg said Britain had the entrepreneurs, research and talent to compete but that these remained “fragmented and disconnected”. “The government can change that by uniting and championing British AI businesses and reforming public procurement, so that taxpayer money builds British growth and British jobs”, he said. “Next week’s Budget is the moment to act”.

title: Plus500 finance chief says US listing ‘always on table’
author: Samuel Norman
content: The finance boss of Plus500 has said a US listing is “always on the table” as the fintech firm turns to North America for its next phase of growth. Elad Even-Chen, chief financial officer at Plus500, told City AM: “We always keep assessing all the opportunities. It’s our duty as a public company.”  “It’s something that is always on the table, but in order for us to say it’s the right thing… it needs to come also with substance of a bit more and greater kind of level of performance,” he said. Even-Chen tied the listing considerations to the group’s medium-term targets around revenue for the US. He said in the next three to four years the US will “be at least the level of 30 to 35 per cent” of the group total. The fintech boss said it would be able to “consider” a US listing “properly” when a “considerable” amount of revenue and profit was driven from the region. “It may be applicable in the future, we’ll continue to assess it. But for the time being, we’re very much focused on the UK.”  The London market has faced criticism over a lack of investor appetite for high-growth technology companies. Money transfer firm Wise ditched its primary listing last year in favour of New York citing deeper liquidity and London-based AI infrastructure firm Nscale confirmed last month it would look to list on the US market.  “I think that it goes without saying that yes, indeed, there is a gap within certain kinds of verticals to fully understand areas of technology that may be associated with different businesses,” Even-Chen said. But he added the firm had done a “good job” to educate the market and was seeing “very established blue-chip parties within our register”. Plus500 gears up for US super-app launch The remarks follow Plus500 upgrading its full-year guidance targets to “ahead of current market expectations”. The FTSE 250 firm’s revenue rose 11 per cent in the third-quarter to $203.2m after new customer sign-ups surged by over a quarter. US expansion continued to play a dominant role with its non-OTC business, which includes futures and physical share dealing, accounting for 16 per cent of group revenue and 31 per cent of new customers. Earlier this month, the group confirmed it had begun development of a super-app that will offer “sophisticated trading capabilities” and new features for US users. It followed its acquisition of retail investor platform Hedge, which holds a US broker-dealer registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). “From a strategic perspective, we said that yes, the US would be the first location,” Even-Chen said. “However, we also identified Europe and the UK more specifically to be the second leg of the issuance of that super-app.” Plus500 began operations in the UK shortly after it was founded in 2008. It expanded into the US nearly fifteen years later following the acquisition of Cunningham Commodities in 2021.

title: Sadiq Khan urges banks to stay in London as tax raid looms
author: Samuel Norman
content: Sadiq Khan has urged London’s biggest banks to keep investing in the UK, days away from an expected tax raid on the sector. On Monday, the Mayor of London said the City’s banking sector is “really important” but refused to say whether he opposed the tax raid, adding that “those with broader shoulders carry the greatest burden”.  Chancellor John Healey is expected to target the sector with a tax grab when he takes to the despatch box on Wednesday. A hike to the UK banking surcharge, which sits on top of corporation tax, is expected to be one of the Budget’s largest revenue-raisers. The surcharge currently sits at three per cent, taking banks’ total corporation tax rate to 28 per cent, but raising it to eight per cent is expected to raise about £2bn. The Chancellor has been cautioned that a raid on banks could threaten the City’s global status. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JP Morgan, has previously warned that higher taxes could make him “reconsider” building his bank’s new megatower in Canary Wharf. But the Mayor urged banks not to scale back investment in London. He said: “The financial sector is really important to London. The City of London area is very important to London.  “Hundreds of thousands of jobs are created in the financial sector, including the banks. I want them not just to stay here, but I want banks to come here as well. “I’m really pleased that JP Morgan Chase are investing in a huge new building in Canary Wharf. We’ve seen Goldman Sachs move here, and others move here as well. That’s really important,” he added. The Mayor’s office is among signatories of a memorandum of understanding that paves the way for JP Morgan to receive a sweeping business rates discount on its tower. The project is expected to pump £10bn into the local economy.  The capital ‘could pay more tax’ This week’s Budget is expected to lay the groundwork for Andy Burnham’s pledge to drive growth in the UK’s regions, prompting concerns that London’s economic role could be overlooked. But Khan believes London “could pay more” in tax. He said: “It’s not London versus the rest; it’s London with the rest as well. As a capital city, every year we contribute net between £40bn and £50bn.  “I think we could do even more with the right support from the government. But I think our ecosystem relies upon everyone doing well in this city,” he added. On Sunday night, Oxford Street was closed to traffic for the first time in its centuries-long history. Khan said City Hall’s longer project to rejuvenate the high street will boost flagship stores like John Lewis and drive out “dross” American candy shops.  High street retailers say the business rates system unfairly taxes them compared with online shopping giants like Amazon, Shein and Temu.  During his campaign to become Makerfield MP, Burnham said he would hike taxes on “out of town” warehouses to fund tax cuts for high street shops.  Healey has since ruled out a tax raid on warehouses, after industry bosses warned that this would push up costs for retailers and end up in higher prices for shoppers. But the Mayor of London said online retailers should pay more tax. He said: “It’s not a level playing field, and so I’m looking forward to the Chancellor addressing that. “It can’t be right that you’ve got a shopkeeper having to pay business rates, rent, salaried staff, people to serve customers, and those who are warehouse retailers don’t,” the Mayor added.

title: Healey’s state pension shield could create ‘messy £200m cliff edge’
author: Maisie Grice
content: The Treasury’s plans to shield low-income pensioners from income tax could lead to a “messy” cliff edge and a ballooning bill for future governments, a former pensions minister has warned. Chancellor John Healey will use his maiden Autumn Budget this week to protect nearly one million retirees who are dependent on the state guarantee by announcing they will not pay income tax. The plans to shield them from income tax was first announced by then chancellor Rachel Reeves in last year’s Budget and the policy is expected to run until the end of this Parliament. Healey is anticipated to confirm that the full state pension will rise by £489 to £13,036 on Wednesday, but the rise will push those who rely solely on the state benefit above the £12,570 personal allowance threshold, meaning they will be dragged into the income tax net. Pulling them down This could leave them paying tax on nearly £500. To prevent them from paying, Healey is expected to announce a hike in the tax-free allowance for this group to £13,036. But this will cost taxpayers £200m a year by 2030, according to calculations by Steve Webb, a partner at pension consultant LCP who served as pensions minister during the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government. “This scheme is being developed because the repeated freezing of the personal allowance has dragged more and more retirees into the tax net.  But the proposed solution looks messy and increasingly expensive,” said Webb. “The gap between the new state pension and the tax threshold is set to grow every year, which will make the policy hard to switch off.  But if it continues, the cost will grow and grow.” Despite the tax allowance being frozen for the remainder of this Parliament, the gap between the new state benefit and tax threshold will continue to grow, even if it only rises by the 2.5 per cent minimum guarantee, according to Webb. In the 2027/28 tax year, the state guarantee is expected to rise to £250.70 per week, leaving it £466.40 above the threshold, meaning the scheme would have to ignore £93.28 in tax at the 20 per cent basic rate. By the 2029/30 financial year the pension is anticipated to climb to £263.35 per week, equal to £13,694 per year, exceeding the allowance by £1,124.20. This pushes the tax ignored up to £224.84. £1 drag Webb added that the new tax allowance is set to apply only to those whose income matches the new state pension, meaning those who find themselves with just £1 of taxable income above this level would lose the protection. Meanwhile, the Treasury is yet to clarify how the policy will affect those with a “modest” state pension who have accumulated small private pots. He said: “At present, income tax would be collected through a PAYE tax code on the private pension. In future, would these individuals be taxed first and then have to claim back a tax rebate every year? “If the extra allowance is available only to those on a low income, there could be a growing ‘cliff edge’ problem where those with very small amounts of private income lose the whole allowance and end up worse off than those with nothing”.

title: Oxford Street pedestrianisation is a win for London
author: Andrew Busby
content: The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will create a new a public realm where it is anticipated that people will enjoy the new space, stay longer and spend more, says Andrew Busby The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street is the most radical project to hit the West End in decades. Almost a kilometre of the nation’s high street, from Orchard Street to Great Portland Street, will be closed to all traffic, including buses and taxis. After years of debate, it happens just in time for the busiest Christmas shopping period.  Retail veteran Peter Ruis highlights the need, pointing out that surrounding streets have stolen much of the footfall from Oxford Street. He told City AM , “Now with the pedestrianisation, I think for all retailers, there’s going to be lots and lots of opportunity to do more innovative things because I think it was just so difficult before, with issues around theft, traffic, and safety”.   The economic theory is simple. Nabeel Khan, chief executive of the Oxford Street Development Corporation (OSDC), told City AM : “By pedestrianising the nation’s high street, we’re going to make it a much more walkable, much more accessible, much greener space that Londoners and visitors are more likely to dwell in, to sit in, to admire the beautiful architecture. And as a result, we know there’s a direct correlation between dwell time and spend with retailers.” The greening of Oxford Street , with plenty of opportunity for people to sit down and relax are both a large part of the plans. What Khan is describing is a vision of a public realm where it is anticipated that people will enjoy the new space, stay longer and spend more. More than a shopping street Here is the thing many people miss: Oxford Street is no longer just a shopping street. Khan points out that there are now more office workers than retail workers along it, a shift driven by the pandemic and the opening of the Elizabeth Line. The OSDC has three million square feet of commercial office space in its pipeline, with more coming forward over the next three to five years. Hence the ambition; in his words: “the ambition around Oxford Street is to turn it from being a primarily retail corridor to being a much more mixed-use experiential destination.” A John Lewis spokesperson, speaking for a business that has traded on the street for over 160 years, said: “We continue to invest in our flagship store, and believe pedestrianisation will create a vibrant, thriving shopping environment enhancing the area’s appeal as a top retail destination.” Other retailers, such as Selfridges are investing too. And a huge new Harry Potter flagship, with a food counter inside, is due to open at the eastern end shortly. The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, sees a wider prize. “Revitalising Oxford Street will help to super-charge regeneration, boosting jobs and economic growth in the capital and beyond,” he said. Ruis makes the same point in plainer terms. “Let the country’s premier shopping street dwindle, he says, and it causes challenges for everyone, because its footfall and innovation filter into the rest of the retail economy”. None of this means the scheme is without critics. Some local residents are unconvinced, and the obvious worry is what happens when buses, taxis and bikes are diverted onto the roads surrounding Oxford Street. The OSDC acknowledges as much, hearing those concerns is very much part of the scheme. This first phase is deliberately temporary, so that real-time feedback can be gathered from residents, accessibility groups, businesses and workers. Traffic on the nearby roads will be closely monitored, and what is learned will shape the permanent design, with a transitional scheme in place by the end of spring 2027. Christmas first, construction later The scheme is being delivered at pace with the first phase involving temporary, event-style safety measures went in at 8pm on Sunday, so traffic can be diverted from today. Construction of the semi-permanent safety measures then runs to the end of November, stops to protect the Christmas Golden Quarter, and restarts in January. From April, the carriageway in front of Selfridges and John Lewis will be raised to create two new public squares, alongside more trees, seating and street furniture. A trial dining area beside the alleyway to St Christopher’s Place will let people bring their lunch and watch street life unfold. Ruis is realistic. The street will need proper public realm, with cafes and experiences, and it will take a good 24 months for the benefits to be fully felt. “We spend years talking about something and everyone complains,” he says. “But I think in five years’ time no one will be looking back.” Today, Oxford Street begins to find out. Andrew Busby is founder of Redline Retail, which helps retail technology companies build visibility, credibility and pipeline.

title: Andy Burnham doesn’t listen to anyone but himself
author: Eliot Wilson
content: Burnham strives to appear inclusive but he ignores the voice of industry and defence. Signs are emerging that this is a government which doesn’t listen at all, says Eliot Wilson This week will see Chancellor John Healey deliver his Budget. At 66, he will be the oldest Chancellor of the Exchequer to present a first Financial Statement and Budget Resolutions to the House of Commons. Since his appointment in July, the veteran frontbencher, first given a ministerial post in 2001, has seemed quietly resolute, even content. Chancellor and Prime Minister alike know how important this Budget is. With Burnham taking office after the House of Commons had adjourned for the summer, and with a break for the party conferences, the government has only really had four weeks of “normality”. Burnham’s overall rating is still positive, but the margin has fallen sharply. As his honeymoon inevitably fades, voters may want to know what sort of leader he really is, what – apart from Everton FC, the Labour Party and the Catholic Church – are his lodestars and how he steers by them? However inclusive and welcoming Burnham may strive to appear, however much he repeats his technocratic false dilemma of “problem-solving, not point-scoring” or talks about “collaboration”, the Prime Minister is not throwing open the doors of Whitehall to seek rigorous challenge or alternative policy. He knows what he thinks. Signs are emerging that this is a government which doesn’t listen at all. It started as soon as Burnham took over. He made several substantial machinery of government changes , a habit of new premiers to show dynamism. The department for science, innovation and technology, created in 2023, was dismantled. Rishi Sunak had set it up to develop the UK’s scientific, research and technological outputs: in essence to put the future under one ministerial portfolio. Burnham reversed that approach, returning digital policy to the department for culture, media and sport (where it had never really set comfortably); hiving off artificial intelligence to a small “taskforce” in the Cabinet Office; and merging science and innovation with business and trade in a sprawling, baggy department for business, innovation, science and trade. When a department has four titular focuses it has no focus at all. The disappearance of a department dedicated to technology, research and innovation was mourned by many in the sector who warned that policy would be less coordinated and less high-profile. It was criticised by techUK, the Startup Coalition, Baroness Lane-Fox, Lord Vaizey of Didcot, the Institute for Government, the president of the Royal Society, Solarwinds, Tom Loosemore of Public Digital and Matt Clifford, Chair of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency. Burnham remained unmoved. Warnings Last week, Rain Newton-Smith, head of the CBI, warned the Chancellor on behalf of her organisation’s members that increasing the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge, currently three per cent, would damage not just banks but the economy as a whole. “When London thrives,” she said, “it creates jobs across the UK. The strength of London sustains supply chains, attracts investment and supports growth in every part of the country.” But banks are popular targets, and the surcharge is expected to rise. Meanwhile former cabinet minister Liam Byrne was incandescent. The House of Commons business, innovation, science and technology committee, which he chairs, issued the government’s response to a report on investing in the UK economy published by its predecessor business and trade committee in June. The government accepted 16 of its recommendations, partially accepted 18 and rejected 13. The committee felt this “falls short of the coordinated reform needed”. Byrne was more emphatic. Having spent five years as a minister, he damningly pinpointed an institutional weakness: “I fear ministers have yet to grip the scale of reform needed. Too often, proposals for the next stage of reform are met with a defence of what is already being done.” No sign of listening mode. There was another decision which must have provoked dissenting voices behind closed doors in Whitehall. Luke Pollard, minister for defence readiness and Industry, revealed in response to a written parliamentary question that the repair and recovery version of the Boxer armoured fighting vehicle was “no longer being pursued” (which is how the MoD says “cancelled”). There is a simple equation. If an armoured vehicle breaks down, you need a vehicle of comparable size and weight to recover it. Boxer weighs just shy of 40 tonnes. But with the armoured vehicle programme due to be cut from £7bn to £5bn, the recovery version has fallen to the spending axe. This potentially makes it much more difficult to retrieve stricken Boxers in combat. It is crude cost reduction and no-one in uniform is likely to have advised this course of action. But the government has chosen other priorities. If we had paid careful attention, we could have foreseen this disinclination to listen. Burnham presents himself as a fanatically reasonable everyman, living in a world in which good people have ideals and bad people have ideology. But his first speech as Labour leader was significant. After his bromides of “a new politics” and “seeking more consensus”, he declared: “We will work with other parties… from the clarity of knowing where we stand… we win by being us. Boldly, confidently, authentically us – Labour. That’s how we win.” Burnham wants consensus and problem-solving, but he already knows what he wants to do. Labour represents “unity at the service of people”. This is no less doctrinaire than Margaret Thatcher, and it is much more dishonest: Thatcher never pretended to prioritise consensus. “The Old Testament prophets,” she maintained, “didn’t say, ‘Brothers, I want a consensus.’ They said, ‘This is my faith, this is what I passionately believe. If you believe it too, then come with me.’” Burnham has no room for that ‘if’. “I know what I want to do,” he told his colleagues at his coronation. It follows that he had nothing to learn from tech bodies or the CBI or the armed forces or any parliamentary committee. The course is set, and, to coin a phrase, there is no alternative. But socialists should know by now that there is always an alternative. That’s the point of freedom. Eliot Wilson is a writer
