title: High Waves and Winds in the Panamanian Pacific Until October 31. A Warning Issued By SINAPROC.
author: Newsroom Panama
content: The National Civil Protection System (SINAPROC) issued a prevention notice in response to the forecast from the Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology of Panama (IMHPA) regarding high tides and winds on the Pacific coast, valid until October 31, 2026.   The measure covers the Western Pacific, including the Gulf of Chiriquí; the Central Pacific, which includes the Azuero Peninsula and southern Veraguas; and the Eastern Pacific, which includes the Gulf of Panama and the Darién province. According to the IMHPA, waves between 0.6 and 1.2 meters are expected, accompanied by sustained winds of 15 to 35 kilometers per hour and gusts of up to 40 kilometers per hour.  These conditions are compounded by waves with periods of between 13 and 18 seconds, factors that could generate rough seas and cause flooding in coastal areas.  For this reason, the authorities recommended exercising extreme caution during maritime activities, with special attention to swimmers and operators of artisanal vessels.  Given this scenario, the agency urged the public to “avoid entering the sea when waves and currents pose a safety risk,” as well as to check weather conditions before setting sail and heed the instructions of security officials.  He also suggested taking extra care during walks and fishing trips, not staying in coastal areas prone to flooding, and staying informed through official channels.  “SINAPROC reiterates its call to the public to act responsibly and prioritize the protection of life,” the official statement emphasizes. title: What Panama’s Shift Off the EU Tax Blacklist Teaches Property Owners
author: Newsroom Panama
content: The European Union took Panama off its list of non-cooperative jurisdictions for tax purposes, and half the emails I got that week came from property owners who read the headline as “everything is fine now.” It isn’t. A blacklist removal changes how banks and counterparties look at you. It does nothing about the appraisal notice sitting on your desk with a number you don’t recognize. Here’s what that gap actually looks like in practice. Cross-border ownership means you’re juggling two, three, sometimes four separate valuation systems, each with its own filing calendar, its own definition of market value, and its own idea of what counts as evidence. Miss one window because you were busy with the other country’s paperwork, and you’ve handed away a year of savings without a single phone call. That’s the part nobody puts in the press release. Fifty years of combined market cycles is roughly what it takes to read a Latin American valuation the way locals do, which is why owners with holdings in Texas and abroad tend to hand the domestic side to property tax consultants texas while they wrestle with their offshore filings. Splitting the workload that way isn’t laziness. It’s triage. Why a Blacklist Removal Is a Signal, Not a Deadline People treat these lists like a switch that flips from danger to safety. They’re closer to a credit score. Getting removed takes you out of the penalty box with banks and institutional counterparties, but it doesn’t revalue a single square meter of what you own. A warehouse in Houston and a rental in Panama City both get assessed on local rules that were written long before any EU council meeting happened. According to the OECD , tax transparency standards have been tightening across most major economies for years, which is why jurisdictions keep adjusting their disclosure and filing expectations rather than standing still. That’s the real takeaway. The paperwork gets more demanding, not less, even when your country’s reputation improves. So what do you do with that? You stop reading list news as a plan and start reading it as a reminder to recheck your calendars. I’d take a boring spreadsheet over a triumphant press release any day, because the spreadsheet is what actually protects your cash. What Cross-Border Owners Keep Getting Wrong The single most common mistake is assuming value travels. It doesn’t. A property that appraises at one figure in one jurisdiction can land at a wildly different number next door, using the same building, same tenants, and same income. Local assessors weigh income approach, sales comparables, and replacement cost differently, and the weighting shifts by property type. You’ll also hit these recurring problems: Filings stacked on top of each other across two or three deadlines in the same quarter Notice letters going to an address you stopped using two ownership changes ago Business personal property returns filed in the wrong jurisdiction, or not at all Appeal windows that are shorter than the time it takes to gather your own records Notice how none of these are about tax law. They’re logistics. The owners who save money aren’t the ones who know the most statutes. They’re the ones who never miss a date and never show up to a hearing with a shoebox of receipts. I’ve watched owners win an appeal on a strong income argument, then lose the next cycle purely because the notice went to a decommissioned PO box. That’s not bad luck. That’s an address list nobody updated. The Two-List System I’d Actually Use Here’s a framework I’ve found holds up across jurisdictions. I call it the two-list system, and it’s deliberately unglamorous. List one is your deadlines. Every jurisdiction where you hold property, every filing date, every appeal window, every payment due date. One row per property. No exceptions, no “I’ll remember.” List two is your evidence. For each property, the documents that prove your value argument: leases, occupancy records, repair invoices, comparable sales, income statements. Filed before you need them, not the week a hearing gets scheduled. The two connect in one place: the moment a notice arrives, you check list one for the appeal deadline, then check list two for what you can actually prove. If list two is empty, you don’t have an appeal. You have a complaint. A concrete example. Say you own a mid-size office building and a residential rental in two different states. Your office notice arrives with a value increase you disagree with. Under the two-list system, you’ve already got current leases and a vacancy history on file, so your protest goes in with real numbers attached. Meanwhile your residential notice arrives three weeks later, and because the residential deadline sits outside the window you planned for, you would have missed it entirely without the calendar. That’s the entire value of the system. It catches the thing you weren’t looking at. This is also where most owners underestimate how much the professional side costs versus saves. A consultant who already knows the local assessor’s methodology and hearing process is worth more than a stack of generic templates, because the argument has to fit the forum. Where Stability Actually Comes From Reputation shifts and rule changes get the headlines, but the underlying conditions that protect property owners are boring and slow. According to the World Bank , property registration systems and legal certainty are among the strongest predictors of whether an owner can defend their investment across borders over time. Strong registries, clear title, reliable records. That’s what you’re really betting on. Which means your own record-keeping is part of the same story. If your title documents, ownership structure, and valuation evidence are all current and in one place, you’re operating like a well-run registry. If they’re scattered across three email accounts and a storage unit, you’re operating like a jurisdiction nobody trusts. The European Union publishes the criteria behind its tax lists, and reading them once tells you something useful: these reviews reward consistency and disclosure, not size or geography. The same trait rewards property owners. Consistency in filing, consistency in records, consistency in showing up on time. Your Practical Checklist Before Next Assessment Season Pull every notice and confirm the mailing address on file for each property. Build the deadline list for every jurisdiction you own in, current year and next. Gather income, lease, and occupancy records for each property into one folder. Identify which properties have a defensible value argument and which don’t. Decide, property by property, whether you handle the protest or bring in someone local. Set a reminder thirty days before each filing window opens, not the day it closes. Do those six things and the blacklist headlines stop mattering so much. You’re no longer reacting to news. You’re running a schedule. What to Do With This Panama coming off the EU list is genuinely good news for anyone holding assets there, and it may loosen some doors with banks and institutional partners. It won’t lower a single assessment, and it won’t extend an appeal deadline by one day. Those two jobs belong to your calendar and your records. So here’s the question worth sitting with this week: if a notice arrived tomorrow for your most valuable property, could you name the appeal deadline and produce your evidence within the hour? If the answer is no, the list news isn’t your problem. The gap between list one and list two is. title: On the Move From Andorra to Playacar, ‘El Panameño’ Wanted for Extradition by Panama Since 2022.
author: Newsroom Panama
content: The man arrested last week in Playa del Carmen, Mexico, accused of using the financial system of several jurisdictions to launder money from alleged illicit activities, has been wanted for extradition by Panama since October 28, 2022.  Sergio Rafael De Marco Cruz, nicknamed “El Panameño” (although he was born in Guerrero, Mexico), is under investigation by the Specialized Prosecutor’s Office against Organized Crime for alleged money laundering and crimes against public trust. As part of this process, an order was issued on October 28, 2019, to seize assets and funds in his name totaling $18 million.  However, despite several attempts, De Marco has never been charged in Panama, as his whereabouts—until now—were unknown. His lawyer claimed that his client was being prevented from returning to Panama, but never provided evidence to prove that the National Migration Service had actually denied him entry into the country.  The case began with a “spontaneous” communication from the Principality of Andorra, which informed the Panamanian authorities of information “that could be relevant” in relation to “The Panamanian”.  On October 28, 2022, the same day that a judge granted the extradition request for De Marco, another judge, in a separate hearing, suspended the precautionary measure of asset seizure imposed since 2019. The assets remained seized because the prosecution took the case to the Superior Court of Appeals, which on November 11, 2022, overturned the judge’s decision and upheld the asset seizure in the amount of $18 million.  This decision was subsequently confirmed by the Plenary of the Supreme Court of Justice, which on March 23, 2023 did not admit an appeal filed by De Marco’s defense.  It is not known what assets were seized from De Marcos, but news media found that in 2018 he imported a used Rolls Royce Ghost vehicle, whose declared CIF value is $174,264.85.  His name is also linked to a private foundation called RDM Holding, registered in 2017. Its president is De Marco. It has been suspended since 2021 due to the resignation of its resident agent, the firm Williams & Williams.  Although he was born in Mexico, De Marco is nicknamed “The Panamanian” precisely because of his reputation for using the country’s financial and corporate system to commit his misdeeds. De Marco was arrested at the exclusive Playacar residential and tourist complex, Phase 1 in the Mexican resort town of Playa del Carmen. According to the Mexican Attorney General’s Office and the Mexican Navy, he was the subject of an Interpol alert and wanted by five countries. title: The Reality of Homelessness in Panama.
author: Newsroom Panama
content: In certain areas of Panama City, one cannot ignore the fact that more people are living on the streets. In the capital alone, the estimate is over 1000 people in this situation. The homeless population in Panama City faces significant challenges related to extreme poverty, lack of affordable housing, and substance abuse. During one year dating from 2023 to 2024, the number of homeless people had more than doubled. Of this number, men were in the larger percentage and the majority of the homeless population suffered from substance abuse disorders. The areas of Panama City that have the highest concentration of unsheltered and displaced people is Curundú, Calidonia, Santa Ana, 24 de Diciembre and Tocumen. In response, the local government and humanitarian groups have established a network of care, recently marked by a historic milestone in social infrastructure. The Municipality of Panama City opened the “Comprehensive Care Center for the Homeless” (CAIPHAC) located in Las Garzas. The shelter has a capacity for 150 men and 100 women. This is Panama’s first comprehensive care center which offers a safe place to stay, alongside with medical care, psychological evaluations and substance abuse rehabilitation. The center operates through a partnership with the Mayor’s office, the Catholic Archdiocese, The Ministry of Health and The Ministry of Social Development. In Panama, local laws protect individual liberty therefor entry into treatment centers or shelters is voluntary. Those who enter must agree to a detoxification process of about three months as part of the treatment plan. Social workers use digital facial recognition tablets to create electronic medical and social files on-site, offering primary hygiene, food, and options for voluntary shelter. On the national level, the Exectutive Decree 11 of July 23 (2026) created the Inter-institutional Commission for the Guarantee of Rights and Comprehensive Care of People Experiencing Homelessness in Panama. This decree was published in the Official Gazette. The commission centralizes state action to move away from isolated municipal responses and toward a cohesive national strategy rooted in human rights and social inclusion, coordinating temporary accommodation programs, promoting physical and mental health services, promoting rehabilitation processes, and strengthening opportunities for training, education, and job placement. The decree also recognizes the participation of civil society organizations, foundations, churches, and community groups, with the purpose of joining efforts to serve this vulnerable population. title: Why Broken Promises Weaken Financial Confidence
author: Newsroom Panama
content: Financial Confidence Is Built on Trust Before Math People often talk about financial confidence as if it comes from spreadsheets, income, or investment knowledge alone. Those things matter, of course. But confidence with money usually begins somewhere more personal. It begins with trust. If you trust that your paycheck will arrive, your plan feels possible. If you trust that you will follow your budget, your goals feel realistic. If you trust that a financial institution, partner, employer, or even your own habits will hold steady, then making decisions feels less stressful. Confidence grows when the future feels somewhat dependable, even if it is never fully certain. That is why broken promises hit harder than people expect. They do not just disrupt a single plan. They weaken the feeling that your financial life is stable enough to navigate. You can see how important dependable guidance becomes when people search for options like Student Debt Relief , because what they often need is not only a solution, but a renewed sense that financial decisions can still lead somewhere useful.  A Broken Promise Changes More Than One Outcome When a promise breaks, the immediate consequence is usually obvious. A payment was missed. A deal fell through. A partner did not contribute what they said they would. An employer changed the terms. A lender’s offer looked different once the paperwork was final. Something concrete happened. But the deeper effect is often psychological. Broken promises make people question the reliability of the systems around them. They also make people question themselves. If a plan failed because someone did not follow through, you may become more hesitant the next time you need to make a decision. You may save less aggressively, delay investing, avoid budgeting conversations, or stop trusting your own projections. This matters because the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes financial well being as having control over day to day finances, the capacity to absorb a shock, and a sense of security about the financial future. When promises break, those exact conditions are damaged. Control feels weaker, shock feels more threatening, and the future feels less secure.  Self Trust Is Part of Financial Stability One of the less obvious sources of financial confidence is self trust. Not self esteem in a broad sense, but the quieter belief that you will do what you said you would do. If you promise yourself you will stop overspending, build an emergency fund, or finally open that retirement account, and then repeatedly break those promises, your relationship with money changes. Even if no one else knows, you know. That knowledge starts to affect your behavior. The problem is not just the missed action. It is the erosion of credibility. After enough broken promises to yourself, even a reasonable financial goal can start to feel fake. You stop believing your own plans. You create budgets you do not expect to keep. You tell yourself next month will be different, but part of you does not buy it. That kind of internal distrust weakens confidence in a very specific way. It makes financial planning feel performative instead of real. You may still go through the motions, but without belief behind them, execution gets weaker. Broken Promises Make Risk Feel More Dangerous Financial life always involves some level of uncertainty. Saving for a goal, changing jobs, starting a business, paying down debt, or investing in the market all require some tolerance for risk. But broken promises increase the emotional cost of taking that risk. Once trust has been damaged, uncertainty no longer feels like a normal part of decision making. It starts to feel like danger. That shift can make people overly cautious in ways that hurt them long term. The Securities and Exchange Commission’s Investor.gov explains that stocks can rise and fall, that investors can lose money, and that market fluctuations can be unnerving. But it also notes that long term investors have generally been rewarded over time. When trust is weakened, however, people often cannot access that long term mindset. A broken promise somewhere else in their financial life can make every uncertain move feel less tolerable, even when the underlying decision is sound.  Trust Between People Shapes Money Decisions More Than We Admit Money is rarely just individual. It is relational. Couples share expenses. Families lend and borrow. Business partners divide responsibility. Friends make plans around budgets and commitments. In all of those cases, financial confidence depends partly on whether people mean what they say. If one person keeps promising to contribute and does not, the issue is not only the missing money. The issue is that every future plan becomes harder to believe in. Conversations become defensive. Timelines become vague. The person carrying the uncertainty starts building around disappointment instead of around possibility. This can shrink someone’s financial world. They may stop setting bigger goals because they no longer trust the support system around them. They may become controlling because unpredictability feels too costly. Or they may disengage completely because hope starts to feel naive. Broken promises in shared financial life create a climate where caution replaces confidence. Institutions Matter Too People often think of trust as personal, but institutional trust matters just as much. Banks, lenders, employers, servicers, and financial programs all shape confidence. When those systems are clear, consistent, and transparent, people are more likely to participate fully. When they are confusing or unreliable, people pull back. The FDIC says its mission includes maintaining stability and public confidence in the nation’s financial system, and its Money Smart program is designed to help people enhance financial skills and create positive banking relationships. That language is revealing. Financial confidence is not treated as a bonus. It is treated as essential to a functioning system. Confidence depends on both knowledge and trustworthy structures around that knowledge. FDIC Money Smart resources make that connection very clear.  When institutions overpromise, hide terms, or create experiences that feel inconsistent, they weaken more than consumer satisfaction. They weaken participation. People who do not trust the system are less likely to use it confidently. Repair Starts With Smaller Promises, Not Bigger Speeches Once confidence has been damaged, the instinct is often to make a grand promise. This time I will stick to the plan. This time we will communicate better. This time the budget will be perfect. But big promises are often the wrong medicine for broken trust. Confidence usually repairs through smaller promises that are actually kept. A realistic transfer into savings every payday. A weekly money check in with a partner that really happens. A spending cap that is modest but consistent. A timeline that matches reality instead of wishful thinking. This works because trust does not rebuild through intensity. It rebuilds through evidence. Each kept promise gives your brain a reason to relax a little. Each follow through makes the next decision feel less shaky. Over time, confidence returns not because uncertainty disappears, but because reliability starts to reappear. Why Follow Through Feels So Powerful At its core, financial confidence is not about feeling certain all the time. It is about believing that your plans have enough honesty and follow through to be worth making. Broken promises weaken that belief. They turn planning into doubt, risk into fear, and goals into something that feels fragile before they even begin. But the reverse is also true. Kept promises strengthen confidence in quiet, practical ways. They make budgeting feel less like restriction and more like direction. They make investing feel less like gambling and more like strategy. They make financial conversations feel less threatening and more productive. That is why follow through matters so much. It is not just a character trait. In financial life, it is infrastructure. And when that infrastructure is weak, confidence wobbles with it. When it becomes reliable again, financial confidence has something solid to stand on. The post Why Broken Promises Weaken Financial Confidence appeared first on Newsroom Panama .
