As calls to pace the frontier abound , let us not lose sight of the fact that the AI frontier isn’t what each model can do in isolation—it is what a colony of them can accomplish together.

title: Israel's Choice
author: Eric Cortellessa
content: An election campaign banner featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hangs on a store ahead of Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. An election campaign banner featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hangs on a store ahead of Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, Monday, Oct. 12, 2026. —Oded Balilty—AP The Israeli settlement of Neve Daniel sits south of Jerusalem, atop one of the highest ridges in the West Bank, nearly 1,000 meters above sea level. The view to the east stretches to the mountains of Jordan, and to the west across the Mediterranean coastal plain—where most Israelis live. But the tranquility of the landscape belies the political fervor animating the Oct. 27 election, a contest with stakes as great as any in the 78-year history of the world’s only Jewish state. When I ask three residents what will ultimately determine their votes, one responds with particular ferocity. “Seven hundred trucks were delivered to Hamas today by Israel,” says Barak Moore, who has lived in Neve Daniel for 14 years. He’s referring to commercial goods and international aid entering the Gaza Strip. “We’re paying a terrorist organization that committed the greatest atrocity against the Jewish people since Auschwitz.” While much of the world has come to define Israel by its military actions in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, Moore’s views reflect the passions coursing through a society still traumatized by that day. Israelis tend to be less preoccupied by the nearly 75,000 Palestinian fatalities in Gaza since the war began, than by the 1,200 people killed in Israel and 251 hostages taken by Hamas—the women subjected to sexual violence, the children shot at point-blank range, the families burned alive in their homes. In a country so small and intimately connected, scarcely anyone was untouched by events that shattered the assumptions of a people whose nation was founded to give Jews a safe haven in their ancestral homeland. Both the Hamas massacre and the wars that followed loom over a vote shaping up not only as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, but also the nature of the country that, as Israel’s longest serving prime minister, he has done so much to shape. Arrayed against Netanyahu is a fractured field of challengers. There is Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief whose reputation for honesty, sobriety, and competence contrasts with Netanyahu’s polarizing leadership; Naftali Bennett, the right-wing former prime minister seeking a comeback; Yair Lapid, the centrist former premier who has spent years trying to dislodge Netanyahu; and Avigdor Lieberman, the hawkish secular nationalist who has become one of Netanyahu’s fiercest adversaries. Also on the ballot: Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, far-right extremists whose parties made possible Netanyahu’s current coalition, and whose ambitions to annex the West Bank and resettle Gaza constrain his room to maneuver while damaging Israel’s standing abroad. The next government will either push Israel further down the path of religious nationalism, permanent conflict, and international isolation—or toward a new generation of leadership. According to the polls, Netanyahu’s strongest challenger is Eisenkot, a soft-spoken, heavyset career soldier running as a centrist. His son, Gal, was killed fighting Hamas in Gaza, and one of his nephews also died in the war. Eisenkot is campaigning on a promise to restore public trust in government, rebuild Israel’s security, and heal the divisions that have fractured the country. “This election is about the identity of Israel,” Eisenkot told TIME in an interview on Oct. 20. “What will be Israel two weeks from now, 10 years from now, 20 years from now? This is the main question.” Gadi Eisenkot walks past memorial displays honoring victims at the Nova music festival site as Israel marks the third anniversary of the Oct. 7th 2023 attacks. —Erik Marmor—Getty Images Three years after Netanyahu’s political obituary was being written, pre-election polls show him running in a dead heat. On the eve of the vote, the nation is suffused with a sense of uncertainty; political analysts say almost anything can happen. Netanyahu and Eisenkot could form a unity government. Netanyahu could cobble together another right-wing coalition, dragging Israel further right. Eisenkot could join forces with Bennett, Lapid, and the Arab parties (20% of Israeli citizens are Palestinian) to oust Netanyahu, producing the closest thing Israel could muster to a center-left government. Or perhaps no bloc will manage to pull together the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority, plunging Israel into another round of elections and a reprise of the paralysis that produced five contests between 2019 and 2022. “The most probable scenarios currently are either there will be some sort of unity government, which again is very complicated politically because all of the opposition parties swear they don’t want it under Netanyahu, and I don’t see how Netanyahu is going to sit under them,” says Nimrod Nor, an expert on Israeli politics at Hebrew University. “The other is we’re going to have another election after this one.” According to two sources familiar with Netanyahu’s thinking, he would prefer to form a unity government with Eisenkot. One reason is legacy. He believes such an alliance offers his best chance to transcend the worst security failure in the nation’s history, and to be remembered not only as the leader who emerged from the slaughter of Oct. 7 to decimate Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon and persuade an American president to wage war against Iran, but also as the statesman who helped to reconcile a divided nation. The other reason, the sources say, is personal. Netanyahu has little desire to form another right-wing coalition that would leave him beholden to the radical and uncompromising parties led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, both of which he brought into government four years ago to reclaim power. “He thought that he could control Ben-Gvir,” one Netanyahu aide says. “Now he knows that he can’t.” That is precisely what the Israeli right fears he’s thinking, and what brought me to Neve Daniel. The settlement of capacious red-tiled homes is just across the Green Line that defined Israel’s borders before the Six-Day War of 1967. It was built on land that was a Jewish farm even before Israel was founded in the crucible of the 1948 war. Settler violence against Palestinians has risen sharply during Netanyahu’s tenure, but the militant settlers who make headlines by terrorizing their Palestinian neighbors tend to live on hilltops deeper into the West Bank than this. But few, if any, of the 700,000 Israelis who live in settlements are leftist. Many regard Netanyahu as a cynical opportunist—a political chameleon who parrots their convictions but will do whatever it takes to survive. Among his many heresies, they say, is a long history of accommodating American presidents: signing the Wye River Memorandum under Bill Clinton to advance the Oslo peace process that aimed to create a Palestinian state; voting for the disengagement from Gaza under Ariel Sharon and George W. Bush; endorsing, at least rhetorically, a two-state solution and imposing a moratorium on settlement construction under Barack Obama; and, under Donald Trump, accepting a ceasefire and hostage-exchange agreement to end the war in Gaza. Three people in Neve Daniel offer a revealing glimpse of the forces pulling Netanyahu rightward. Each plans to vote for a different party, but they all share an overriding objective: a right-wing government with Netanyahu at its center, constrained by allies who will keep him from drifting toward the middle. Barak Moore is supporting Zehut, a libertarian nationalist party founded in 2015, whose eclectic platform combines tax cuts, the dismantling of monopolies, and cannabis legalization with an uncompromising vision of Israeli sovereignty and the removal of Palestinians from Gaza. It is something of a right-wing hipster party, blending free-market economics with religious nationalism. Avi Abelow, 52, an activist who runs the website Pulse of Israel, is voting for Netanyahu’s Likud Party. His complaint is not that the prime minister has gone too far in Gaza, but rather that he has not gone far enough, hamstrung by a security establishment and governing coalition insufficiently committed to the nationalist cause. “We should have conquered all of Gaza and made sure it’s Jewish again,” he says. The youngest of the three, Hershey Kellner, is a 19-year-old Orthodox Jew who moved to Israel from New Jersey just months before Oct. 7. He is supporting Otzma Yehudit, the far-right party led by Ben-Gvir, whose confrontational politics and open contempt for established norms have made him a hero to some of Israel’s most fervent ideologues. Helner admires Ben-Gvir’s push to expand civilian gun ownership, permit Jewish prayer on the Temple Mount, and introduce the death penalty for terrorists. To explain his thinking, Kellner invokes one of the most consequential decisions in recent Israeli history: the 2011 deal that freed the Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit in exchange for more than 1,000 Palestinian prisoners. Among them was Yahya Sinwar, who would go on to mastermind the Oct. 7 massacre. Helner believes that sparing Sinwar’s life was a catastrophic mistake. “If you hanged him or put a bullet in the back of his head, not sure how the world would be now,” he says, “but it would definitely be better.” For three years , Israel has been a nation at war, not only with its enemies but with itself. The extraordinary solidarity that followed Oct. 7 has given way to recriminations and ideological divisions, intensified by the trauma of war, the anguish of the hostage crisis, the pain of deepening antisemitism worldwide, and the unresolved question of who bears responsibility for such a stunning security lapse. Though Israel rejects the charge, critics accuse the country of committing a genocide in Gaza, where the dead include both uncounted Hamas fighters and 20,000 children—and of countenancing a thuggish brand of ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. On Oct. 16, masked settlers were filmed attacking Palestinians and European diplomats in the West Bank, and injuring a Washington Post photojournalist. Smoke rises above Gaza after and Israeli air strike on Sept. 8, 2026. —Moiz Salhi—Anadolu/Getty Images The fault lines run through nearly every aspect of Israeli life. Secular and religious. Liberals and nationalists. Those obliged to serve in the military and the ultra-Orthodox who are not. Those who believe Israel must reach an accommodation with the Palestinians and those who want permanent Israeli control over the West Bank and Gaza. And, not least, those who regard Netanyahu as the indispensable guarantor of Jewish security and those who see him as the principal threat to the country’s democratic character and reputation abroad. The fear increasingly voiced across Israel’s political and cultural establishment is that another Netanyahu victory could push those divisions toward a societal rupture. After Netanyahu’s coalition moved in early 2023 to restrict the power of the Supreme Court, the prospect of another government dependent on religious and ultra-nationalist parties has raised the specter of an exodus of young Israelis, who see the country’s liberal and democratic traditions slipping away. In a recent survey by the Agam Institute, an Israeli research firm, and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, 59% of Israelis said they believe internal threats are greater than external ones, while 64% said they were considering leaving Israel, citing insecurity, living costs, and political instability. In a nation of roughly 10 million, even the departure of tens of thousands of highly educated citizens could have consequences far beyond their numbers, draining the country of the talent and investment on which its economic and military strength depends. There is a deeper irony. Israel was founded as a refuge, a place where a people long subjected to persecution and exile could finally determine their own destiny. Some Israelis now contemplate leaving, not because they have lost faith in the necessity of a Jewish state, but because they fear the political direction of the state created to provide one. For those contemplating a future abroad, there is an unsettling question: Where, exactly, would they go? Antisemitism has surged across much of the world, with 2025 marking the deadliest year for Jews in the diaspora in more than three decades, according to Tel Aviv University. Israel has become increasingly isolated, condemned in international forums, denounced in the streets of European capitals, and regarded by many critics as a pariah state. The result is a profound paradox: Israelis who fear for their country’s future wonder whether they would be any safer, or more welcome, anywhere else. It is this siege mentality, the sense of a small nation standing alone against a hostile world, that Netanyahu is counting on to sustain his political survival. He has spent much of his career presenting himself as a leader hardened by history, experienced in diplomacy, and ruthless in the exercise of power. His message: Whatever Israelis think of him personally, whatever blame they assign him for Oct. 7, the world is too dangerous to entrust their security to anyone else. The chasm between how Israelis see themselves and how much of the outside world sees them has rarely seemed wider. In the new documentary NAZA , Israeli filmmakers draw on the anonymous testimony of 24 soldiers and intelligence officers to expose what they describe as the military’s systematic use of artificial intelligence to identify Hamas targets in Gaza, even when commanders knew that bombing them would kill women and children. Inside Israel, meanwhile, the fifth season of Fauda , the country’s enormously popular television thriller, recreates the atrocities of Oct. 7 in harrowing detail, immersing viewers once again in the terror, grief, and vulnerability of that day. One production focuses on the suffering Israel inflicted, the other on the suffering Israelis endured. Together, they illuminate the competing narratives of a war that has left Israel increasingly estranged from the world, and many Israelis feeling more besieged than ever. Indications from polls and analysts are that even after voters have their say, no one bloc will have mustered a legislative majority. At that point the leading vote-getter will have weeks to try to gather a coalition, a test of the kind of political leadership at which Netanyahu has long excelled. For nearly three decades, Netanyahu has been the dominant figure in Israeli public life, his political fortunes rising and falling with the country’s anxieties and ambitions. He has survived scandals, indictments, electoral defeats, and repeated attempts to engineer his ouster. The question is whether a political system he has spent so long mastering can produce a future that no longer revolves around him. In a country not yet 80 years old, many are ready to chart a new era. “I think that Eisenkot is the one,” says Livna Savir, 72, at a rally for the challenger on a basketball court in Kibbutz Netzer Sereni, outside of Tel Aviv. “It’s a change of direction.” With her children living in the U.S., she laments the impacts of the last three years on a once unified group: “What happened now in our country—it’s not good for the family.”

title: In Maine, a Toss-Up Senate Race Is About the Incumbent and Not Much Else
author: Julia Terruso
content: Sen. Susan Collins directs a question to Troy Jackson during a debate at Husson University in Bangor, Maine, on Oct. 15, 2026. Sen. Susan Collins directs a question to Troy Jackson during a debate at Husson University in Bangor, Maine, on Oct. 15, 2026. —Gregory Rec—Portland Press Herald Susan Collins had just laid out her receipts. The five-term Republican senator was standing on a debate stage in Portland earlier this month, explaining how she deserved credit for ensuring concrete and road salt were exempted from President Trump’s Canadian import levies . The move saved one small town in northern Maine $10,000, Collins said. It helped a concrete business owner avoid a $150,000 hike. It was an updated version of the same argument Collins has been making for decades to win re-election in a state that hasn’t backed a Republican President since George H. W. Bush. When it was her opponent’s turn to respond, Troy Jackson shrugged. What about everything else going up in price, he asked her, before adding, “We can’t eat road salt.” For Jackson, the comeback was a hit. It sparked “let them eat road salt” memes of Collins depicted as Marie Antoinette and assuaged some fears among Democrats about how the last-minute replacement candidate would fare in the spotlight. The viral moment also brought into focus the race’s defining issue: Collins herself. Amid a handful of Senate races that will decide which party controls the upper chamber for the last two years of the Trump era, the race in Maine has emerged as the one most decisively about voters’ view of the incumbent. “He’s got a unique challenge because this race really isn’t about him,” says Emily Cain, a former Maine legislator and Democratic political strategist in the state. “This race is about Susan Collins and asking the people of Maine whether or not it's time for change. He just happens to be the alternative.” Given the candidate they ended up with, some Democrats are thrilled with this dynamic. Jackson became the nominee after a tumultuous summer in which the state’s Democratic primary winner, Graham Platner, withdrew from the race int he wake of being accused of sexual assault, which Platner has denied. While Platner and Jackson have nearly identical progressive, populist policy platforms, there’s a clear contrast between them in style. Platner is a charismatic, at times gripping, campaigner . Jackson is not. His speeches tend to be more subdued and matter of fact, and he often wears an expression of utter boredom despite being at the center of one of the highest-stakes contests in the country. His affect matches his typical attire on the trail—a Red Sox cap, a fleece vest, his cell phone on a belt clip. “Troy’s a salt of the earth guy. His biggest strength is his authenticity,” says Toby McGrath, who ran President Barack Obama’s campaign in Maine in 2008 and 2012. With polls showing Jackson ahead but within the margin of error, both sides have sharpened their attacks. Jackson has repeatedly highlighted a recent report that the FBI and Justice Department had previously sought to open a pay-to-play bribery probe into Collins, allegations, which she denied. And a super PAC aligned with Senate Republicans released an ad calling Jackson a “freak” and a “creep” over his relationship with his second cousin, with whom he has two sons. Last week, Collins distanced herself from the ad and called for it to be taken down. Yet it’s unclear if any of that is breaking through with voters in a race that could ultimately come down to how Collins ensures Maine isn’t forgotten by Washington. On the stump, she warns voters all that could all disappear if Jackson replaces her. "He'll be 100 in seniority,” she told Fox News digital earlier this month, “And all of that essential federal funding targeted for the state of Maine, virtually all of it will go away." Collins’ hold on Maine For years, Collins has been the immovable stateswoman. She is both Maine’s longest-serving member of Congress and the longest-serving Republican woman in Senate history. Astoundingly, she’s never missed a roll-call vote since taking office in 1997. A self-described centrist, she has cultivated a deep connection with Maine’s independent-minded electorate. In 2020, she was reelected by 9 points as Joe Biden carried the state by the same margin. Collins, 73, has increasingly found herself on the defensive over years of controversial votes, including those confirming Trump cabinet members like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. She also cast votes elevating Justices Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. Her 2018 vote on Kavanaugh, in which she said she trusted he wouldn’t endanger the right to abortion access, became a flashpoint after the court overturned Roe v. Wade in in 2022. (Collins is also the only Republican senator to vote for all three Democratic-appointed justices currently on the court.) Most towns in Maine have felt the benefit of Collins’ role as chair of the powerful Appropriations Committee, with which she has steered funding for community centers, railroad improvement projects and shipyards. Her campaign puts the total at $1.5 billion in congressionally directed spending and targeted investments since 2021. “Even Democrats acknowledge her work to bring funding and support back to the state is just off the charts,” says Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine. “So people are going to have to make a decision, ‘Do I hate Trump more than I appreciate and need the support Susan Collins has brought to the state over the years?’” That argument faces more pushback this year given wider dissatisfaction with Republicans and the state of the economy. Jackson has capitalized on those economic anxieties. One of his final ads references high heating oil costs. It’s hitting airwaves just as residents fill their tanks for winter in the nation’s fourth-coldest state. He repeatedly points to Collins' votes related to the conflict in Iran for driving up fuel costs and her vote to advance the Big, Beautiful Bill, a major Republican budget and tax package, for slashing Medicaid in the state. Last month introduced another chink in Collins’ armor, as a ProPublica investigation revealed that FBI and Justice Department agents sought to open a pay-to-play bribery probe into Collins related to allegations she’d rewarded a campaign donor with millions of dollars in federal naval defense contracts. Collins has denied the allegations, and no charges were ever filed against her or her campaign. Several Republican and Democratic strategists told TIME they question how effective the corruption argument is landing in tight-knit Maine. “Susan goes to the grocery store, does her own shopping, doesn't live in a lavish house,” Dutson, the GOP strategist said. “People may disagree with her, but I think it’s a big stretch for almost everybody up here to get their head around her being corrupt.” But the investigation cuts at the core of Collins’ Maine-first brand, McGrath argued, so even a small erosion of support could be the difference in a close race. ‘Troy is not a smooth talker’ Jackson, left, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York, during a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall in Portland, Maine, on Oct. 22, 2026. —Sophie Park—Bloomberg via Getty Images As Jackson’s campaign keeps the spotlight on Collins, it’s kept its own candidate somewhat hidden away. Up until recently, Jackson had done very few on-camera interviews, and it was rare for him to take many unscreened questions at campaign events. Local and national campaign staff have feuded over how to showcase Jackson from the early days of the campaign, infighting detailed in an August New York magazine story. “He has a nationalized campaign team, and these are folks who are generally only comfortable with smooth talkers, and Troy is not a smooth talker,” says a Maine Democrat who worked with Jackson in the state legislature. The Democrat, who supports Jackson, thinks there’s wisdom in trying to avoid gaffes that distract from Collins. Jackson has struggled at times to talk about foreign affairs or federal policy issues, like detailing how to pay for Medicare for All in a conversation with CNN’s Dana Bash in mid-October. But other allies of Jackson say an overcautious campaign is impeding the Bernie Sanders progressive and stalwart labor champion from connecting with voters. “A lot of folks don’t know anything about him except that he’s a logger. He has a charming and funny side, and you don't get to see it,” says Betsy Sweet, an activist and political organizer who ran for U.S. Senate in 2020. “The D.C. folks are sure they know everything, and I feel like in so many of our national races they don’t listen to us and they screw it up.” Jackson has a compelling working-class backstory. His mom was 16 when she had him in Aroostook County, on the rural northern tip of Maine. He grew up poor in Allagash, a frontier town near the Canadian border where he started logging at age 19, taking after his dad, his grandfather and his great-grandfather. When Canadian loggers started crossing into Maine and taking work away from locals, he helped lead a blockade, driving his truck to the border to halt temporary workers from coming into the state. The protest made headlines but did little to change the situation, and a frustrated Jackson turned his attention to the state legislature. He first ran unsuccessfully as a Republican and eventually got elected in 2002 as an independent. He became a Democrat two years later and rose through the ranks to become Senate president. Over decades in state politics, Jackson’s opinions on abortion and LGBTQ rights have evolved. Sweet, who lobbied for women’s groups, recalled pushing him to back abortion-rights legislation in the state. “I think it finally clicked for him after us telling him abortion is health care. It’s not whether women are gonna have one, it’s whether low-income women have the same access as rich women.” His reputation for having a gruff demeanor, Sweet says, is accurate, but attack ads that portray him as antagonistic toward women go too far. “He will go toe to toe with you. He’s not genteel. You know where you stand with him, but you work it out.” A shade of that temper came out in the final debate before the election. Jackson told Collins to “shut up” after she accused a protester of being one of his supporters. “It was a stupid thing for him to say,” the Democrat who worked with Jackson in the state legislature says of the debate moment. “Collins is known for her decorum, her civility. He’s courting 55- to 65-year-old women who are all about not being talked down to.” Maine’s population is the oldest in America and the race will likely come down to older, moderate voters who have split their ticket in past elections. Collins' campaign has argued Jackson has run to the left of the electorate, drawing liberal figures like Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York to rally with him. “That they are all campaigning in Maine for Troy Jackson tells voters exactly how he would govern,” Collins campaign spokesperson Blake Kernen said. For all the debate about whether Jackson’s makeshift campaign has positioned him for victory, it will largely be Collins’ race to win or lose. A September CNN poll of voters backing Jackson found 29% said theirs was a vote for Jackson, while 71% said it was a vote against Collins. Her future in the Senate may not come down to Jackson at all but whether she gives voters enough confidence in what the next six years would look like. “She’s got an amazing record in the past, but people need to hear from her what she’s gonna do in the future and what the game plan is,” Dutson, the GOP adviser, says. “They need to know, if we send Susan Collins back to Washington, how is that gonna help alleviate the anxiety this administration has been causing me right now?”

title: Exiled Opposition Leader María Corina Machado Returns to Venezuela
author: Chad de Guzman
content: Opposition leader María Corina Machado greets the crowd gathered around her vehicle amidst supporters in Caracas, Venezuela on Oct. 25, 2026 Opposition leader María Corina Machado greets the crowd gathered around her vehicle amidst supporters in Caracas, Venezuela on Oct. 25, 2026 —Jesus Vargas—Getty Images “I am here. With you.” Venezuela’s popular opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado posted the message on social media platform X Sunday morning local time, announcing her return to the country after more than 10 months in exile. Machado, who was briefly detained in January 2025 following a protest against autocratic then-President Nicolás Maduro ’s swearing-in despite a dubious election victory, went into hiding in Venezuela and emerged in December that year in Norway. Since then, she has been fighting for a return to democracy in her own country, demanding that, following the extraordinary American military operation that captured Maduro , Venezuelans get to have free and fair elections. The social media accounts of her political movement, Vente Venezuela, as well as her campaign, posted images and videos of Venezuelans crowding the streets of Caracas to welcome her return. The New York Times reported that Machado entered Venezuela from Colombia, citing two anonymized government officials. https://x.com/ConVzlaComando/status/2114539789047517605 Edmundo González Urrutia, another key opposition figure, also posted on social media Sunday that Machado is “on Venezuelan soil” and that he would soon be with her “so that our country truly advances toward freedom.” Machado’s return adds some urgency to the country’s democratic transition—which the interim Venezuelan government under acting President Delcy Rodríguez , as well as its apparent overseer, the U.S., have both promised. Rodríguez, who was formerly Maduro’s deputy, and U.S. President Donald Trump have both said that elections will be held in the country, but a date has yet to be finalized. The 59-year-old Machado, meanwhile, has called for elections by July 2027, telling the Financial Times that there was “more than enough time” to prepare for one. She has also said she will contest the presidency. A majority of Venezuelans want her to be President, according to a poll from AtlasIntel and Bloomberg. Following Maduro’s ouster, Venezuela’s highest court said Rodríguez’s interim presidential appointment could last for up to 90 days, with the National Assembly potentially extending her term for another 90. But the assembly, controlled by the ruling party, did not vote on extending her term, which officially expired in April . It remains unclear how Machado could hasten elections, given the Venezuelan government is in talks with a different U.S.-backed faction of the opposition. A third round of talks ended this month without reaching a firm election schedule. Venezuelans have since grown impatient and have taken to the streets to protest the delays. What the U.S. has said about Machado’s return Asked about Machado’s return to Venezuela, Trump said Sunday he was unaware of it. “I think she's a very nice woman,” Trump told reporters . “She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe.” Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal earlier this year in what appeared to be a push to hasten Venezuela's democratic transition. But since Maduro’s arrest and the U.S. elevation of a new Venezuelan government under Rodríguez, tensions between Trump’s Administration and Machado have increased. The opposition leader has tried to return to the country multiple times, but she has claimed Venezuelan authorities have repeatedly blocked her. Machado has denied suggestions that the U.S. was blocking her return. But her insistence on returning reportedly roiled some in the White House who worry it could spark a political crisis. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X that the conditions that allowed Machado’s return to Venezuela were “the direct result of the U.S. supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile.” But Rubio also hinted that the U.S. expects no further interference in the ongoing discussions: “The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected. Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.” Machado said earlier that, despite not being a part of the discussions between the Venezuelan government, legislative opposition, and the U.S., her movement will not hinder initiatives that “produce real progress.” The U.S. has argued that Venezuela must ensure political and economic stability before it can hold elections. But critics and other observers have pointed out that the Trump Administration’s approach has instead prioritized doing business with Venezuela over facilitating democratic transition—with Washington announcing a major oil deal with Caracas amid the talks. “She’s a very nice woman,” Trump said of Machado Sunday. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”

title: Politeness Has Changed. Our Language Shows How
author: Valerie Fridland
content: —Carol Yepes—Getty Images The next time someone does you a favor, take a minute to note how they respond to “thank you.” You’ll likely find that the traditional “you’re welcome” is fast fading and being replaced by “no problem” or “no worries.” We often treat politeness as a set of rules that people either follow or ignore. But the rules themselves are changing. In the time of Old English (5 th to 11 th centuries), acting according to one’s rank and station was simply expected. Linguistic analysis shows very direct request forms, for example, “Thou shalt do X,” rather than the more modern, “Would you mind doing X?” And routine thanking, or saying “you’re welcome,” would have seemed odd in a time when people simply did what was required. When Norman French started to enter English around 1066, the idea of courteous behavior also entered the language. An example would be the move toward switching between “you” and “thou” to appropriately show respect or intimacy, modeled on the French tu/vous distinction. This concept of courtesy was central to how one expressed gratitude and, by the time we arrived in the early modern era (the time of Shakespeare), thanking was firmly established. However, routinely responding to those thanks was not common. If uttered at all, we’d more often hear something like a deferential, “I am but your humble servant.” In the 18 th century, elaborate complimenting routines became popular, and by the late 19th and early 20th century, English-speaking society had a greater focus on treating all people as equals. As a result, being aware of how one’s actions might impose upon others became increasingly important. Requests that were once directly stated as imperatives were now couched with indirectness as merely suggestions or questions: “Shut the window,” became “Could you please shut the window?” And, in addition to saying “thanks,” responding with an acknowledgment of that thanks, such as “you’re welcome,” became routine. This brings us to modern times. Today, “you’re welcome” is becoming less common. Instead, when someone says “thank you,” we reply with “not at all,” “no problem,” or “no worries.” This assures the person who expresses gratitude that no imposition was involved. In this way, we attempt to offset any social imbalance. As a result, Americans who say “no problem” and those who always respond with “you’re welcome” can tend to believe the other camp sounds rude. Those who prefer “no problem” often feel that “you’re welcome” has a condescending tone, while “you’re welcome” traditionalists feel like “no problem” suggests the favor could have been a problem. For instance, the sense that “you’re welcome” can have a bit of a smug, haughty tone has been played up by comedians like Will Ferrell in his 2009 Broadway show, You’re Welcome America , satirizing George W. Bush’s presidency. Research confirms this shift toward expressions like “no problem” or “no worries” over “you’re welcome” is a generational one. In the norms of how we respond to thank you across generations , linguist Aaron Dinkin found that young Americans increasingly preferred “no problem” as the go-to polite response to “thank you.” Older speakers still felt “you’re welcome” was more appropriate, particularly when a favor required more than perfunctory gratitude. So, the way someone responds to “thank you” is much more than a simple return on someone’s gratitude. These small words help us understand how politeness—and our expectations of one another—have changed over time.

title: A New Way to Think About Women’s Heart Health
author: Sadiya S. Khan
content: —J Studios—Getty Images Women are speaking more openly about periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause , bringing once-taboo topics into public conversation. Clinicians and health systems need to now connect these experiences with what the science is telling us about how they influence a woman’s cardiovascular health throughout her life. A woman may see a gynecologist for her irregular periods, a therapist for her depression, and a primary care doctor or cardiologist for her high blood pressure. Each clinician may focus on an important concern. But what is often missing is a shared understanding of how those concerns fit together and what that means for her lifelong cardiovascular health. A narrow lens has too often been applied to women’s health, defining it as care of reproductive organs and pregnancy. Reproductive health is essential to a woman’s well-being, but women’s health is much broader. We now know that menstrual patterns, pregnancy, and menopause can provide important information about cardiovascular health. Our approach to care should reflect this. These missed connections matter because cardiovascular disease is the greatest threat to women’s health today. Approximately 1 in 3 deaths in women are due to cardiovascular disease every year. Yet fewer than half of women knew that heart disease was the leading cause of death for women, according to a 2019 survey performed by the American Heart Association. As a preventive cardiologist and epidemiologist, I study how women’s life events shape cardiovascular disease risk. We now know that unique signals of cardiovascular risk in women can be identified years and decades before heart disease develops. The challenge is making sure that this information changes the care women receive. This is what led the American Heart Association to bring together the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. Our three-part series , published today in Circulation , establishes a new framework for cardiovascular health in girls and women. The papers and accompanying videos introduce the new Female Life Stage tool , provide clinical guidance, and outline how health systems can deliver coordinated care throughout life. This framework gives clinicians a shared approach to cardiovascular disease prevention across specialties, interconnected areas of health, and life stages. What one clinician learns should inform the care a woman receives in different settings and from different clinicians. For example, pregnancy can act as a natural stress test, revealing cardiovascular risks that may otherwise go unrecognized. A history of preeclampsia should inform cardiovascular preventive care long after delivery. The 2026 Cardiovascular Kidney Metabolic Syndrome Guideline now explicitly recognizes pregnancy complications, as well as premature menopause, as one of the factors that can inform personalized prevention. Menstrual cycle patterns can also provide information relevant to cardiovascular care. A first period before age 10, irregular menstrual cycles, or menopause at a younger age can each serve as signals of higher cardiovascular risk. In a study of more than 10,000 women that my colleagues and I recently published, menopause occurring naturally before age 40 was associated with an approximately 40% higher lifetime risk of coronary heart disease. Mental health is also linked to hormonal and cardiovascular health. Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) can frequently disrupt sleep, physical activity, and eating patterns, which are relevant to cardiovascular health. These symptoms are common, but being common does not make them inconsequential. Mood symptoms during the menopause transition likewise deserve assessment and treatment as part of comprehensive care. A woman and her care team need to anticipate that her health needs will change from adolescence through older adulthood. The framework defines four Female Life Stages: the transition around the first period, the years of ovarian cycling (including pregnancy), perimenopause, and postmenopause. It gives clinicians and patients a shared language for recognizing changing health needs so everyone can know what to expect, identifying cardiovascular risk earlier, and guiding prevention across a lifetime. Recognizing perimenopause as a distinct life stage acknowledges that its symptoms can disrupt daily life, persist for years, and deserve treatment. Hormone and nonhormonal treatments can help, with decisions guided by symptoms, age, cardiovascular and cancer history, and a woman’s preferences. The same visit offers an opportunity to assess cardiovascular disease risk and address changes in cholesterol and cardiometabolic health. Women may spend nearly 40% of their life in the postmenopause stage. Yet conversations of hormonal health and their enduring impact often end with the last period. Hormonal health history should continue to inform cardiovascular care. But documenting information in the medical record will not be enough. We also need to change how care is delivered. An instructive historical example can be drawn from Vienna. In 1991, an art exhibition documented the daily lives of eight girls and women, including an eight-year-old, a student, a nurse, and a retiree. This resulted in the city incorporating women’s everyday needs into urban planning, including street lighting on walking routes for women’s safety. Health care should apply this principle; women’s experiences should shape how care is organized and delivered. But this redesign must be paired with structural change that addresses the barriers, bias, and discrimination that contribute to symptoms being dismissed , delays in care, and unequal access to health care and treatment for women. A shared framework—like the one we developed—can support implementation of existing evidence, but we also need better evidence for women. In 1993, the NIH Revitalization Act made women’s inclusion in NIH-funded clinical research a requirement. Yet underrepresentation in research persists. A 2025 systematic review of cardiovascular trials registered from 2017 through 2023 found that women comprised 41% of participants but only 22% in trials studying acute coronary syndromes, including heart attacks. Women’s health research also remains underfunded, though there may be some recent signs of progress. In October, President Trump signed an executive order to create a new division for women’s health in the National Institutes of Health, but no funding has been allocated at this time. These efforts are part of a larger movement that builds on decades of public advocacy for women’s health. Since its launch in 2004, the American Heart Association’s Go Red for Women campaign has helped bring women’s cardiovascular health into public view. Melinda French Gates’ investments through Pivotal are directing resources toward understudied areas in women’s health. Katie Couric and Dawn Porter’s forthcoming documentary “ HORMONAL! ” will add to this momentum by sharing women’s experiences. Girls and women represent half the population, and every clinician, every specialty, and every health system has a role to play in their health. Women can do much to protect their health, but they should not have to connect the dots in their care alone.

title: Intrinsic CEO Wendy Tan White on ‘Democratizing’ Robotics
author: Ayesha Javed
content: Wendy Tan White, CEO of Intrinsic Wendy Tan White, CEO of Intrinsic —Courtesy Intrinsic Wendy Tan White leads robotics software and AI company Intrinsic, which is focused on making industrial robots easier to use and train. Intrinsic initially sat outside of Google at Alphabet, as part of its “Other Bets” group, which includes businesses such as Waymo. But in February this year, Intrinsic was brought into Google as a separate entity, working closely with DeepMind and using Google’s Gemini models and cloud services. In September, Intrinsic announced that it would be making its basic software—needed to build and operate industrial robots—freely available, or open source. The aim is to give smaller manufacturers the ability to use robots without having to spend vast sums on custom technology. In the longer term, Google and Intrinsic hope to become the providers of the platform that powers what gets built on top of that software. Tan White sees this as the “Android for robotics and AI.” Tan White has experience as an entrepreneur, investor and operator. She co-founded U.K. website-building platform Moonfruit, later becoming a partner at the British Growth Fund’s £2.5 billion growth capital fund, and general partner at Entrepreneur First, a global tech talent investor in AI, robotics and biotech. Tan White was then recruited as a vice president at Alphabet’s X, the moonshot factory , and in 2021 launched Intrinsic, which spun out of X. She spoke with TIME about how she sees robotics helping small manufacturers, Intrinsic’s relationship with Google, and what skills young people need in the AI age. This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. Tell me about the history of Intrinsic. The manufacturing process hasn't really changed much for many years [since the Industrial Revolution and the advent of the Henry Ford model]. And the problem with it is, you’ve got to make it cost effective. It has to be high volume, and it has to be very similar in product. And so, from a customer's point of view, you can't always have something very specific customized to you at a price point you can afford. And also, from a production point of view, the lines are very brittle and very standardized. One of the things we were looking at is if you brought in robotics, could one let's say robot cell do more than one task? Could you get a robot cell that's more intelligent to make a phone and a server and it's not it's not as sophisticated as this yet, but maybe a whole other type of product in one line. Could you customize it, and could you only actually build a few items? The reason that's important is you don't waste inventory; you actually build what you really need. And a factory can actually effectively be much more flexible. The other advantage to something like that might be there are certain tasks that humans do in these line production, things that actually they shouldn't do. There are dangerous tasks. Through COVID, a lot of skilled labor workers in manufacturing retired because they don't want to do those jobs. In food production, there are some people who have to sit there deboning chicken. It's not a job humans should be doing, and there are just lots of dangerous and dirty and very repetitive jobs like that. So, I think with robotics and AI, what that brings is the ability to have much more flexible making and production more intelligently, so actually that's really what most of my team cared about. How can you democratize access to that type of technology and tooling so that both small and big businesses can have access to it? How do you make sure humans don't have to do those sorts of jobs? But also how could you bring some of this manufacturing back more locally as well, because otherwise, what we also do is we ship a load of raw materials to China, build it there because it's cheaper, and bring it back again. That seems like a real waste from both an economic and climate point of view, but also, it's a crazy supply chain to be relying on. So at that insight, actually, we proved that we could do cell and robotics with AI that could be more flexible and also could be a smaller unit or even in a small town or a small warehouse, but also could be used in a modular way in larger factories too. So that was the insight. We did a prototype, and then Alphabet got behind and said, "Actually, we think you're ready.” I think the way Google saw it was, it was like the Android for robotics and AI. They've been very good with innovating Android as a platform to democratize building applications for mobile phones. So I wanted to do the same. Intrinsic was brought into Google in February. What impact has that had? The reason we were brought back in is that robotics and AI come very front and center. So far, it's been about generative AI and agentic tools, but it's still very much in the digital world only. So it's for video, for images, for language. The next bastion is what we would call physical AI, which is: Can you bring the same ability to create intelligence around vision and touch and mobility, which we take for granted as humans. And that's what robotics really is. What we can do with AI now is add vision, touch, and mobility to robotics, and democratizing that, making it open in a software sense, is something we had proven we could do, and in a way, given Gemini and given where Google is going, it was a very natural way for them to go. There's going to now be a platform for AI into the physical, and they thought we would become a very core part of that. We had a lot of other partners, so we ended up doing a joint venture with Foxconn, the biggest electronics manufacturer in the world, with collaboration with Nvidia, and a lot of people started wanting to invest in us, and I think Alphabet felt this should be a core part of our next generation of software for physical AI, so they brought us back in. It's been helpful because we work very closely with DeepMind as well. It's given us more certainty to really focus on the democratization of the tooling rather than worrying about somebody wanting to invest in us. So far so good, but it's obviously psychologically a change, I think. How does that change how you approach things like day-to-day decision making? They've actually unusually kept us separate, so in a way, we've been brought in a bit more like DeepMind was when it was first acquired, and they've kept me CEO. They've kept our brand as Intrinsic. We've got two buildings of our own that are not in the core campus. So we have our own identity, and the reason they've done that is they know that we're still scaling and incubating. And if you just try and squeeze us in, it's a back to innovator’s dilemma. You put us back into a standard product area within Google. It may not get the airtime it needs to breathe and to keep innovating. Now we're innovating the business itself, not just the technology. So I think that's been really helpful. But the advantage we do have is we have much more line of sight to the senior level itself, and so they understand what we're trying to do, and we get decisions made faster, and that's been really helpful for us. The flip side is we also have to consider now that if we're representing part of the Google family as such, we can't just run. We can't just think “oh, we're just a startup, we should just take the risk and break something over here.” We actually have to consider the impacts that might have as well. What will be the initial tasks that we will see your technology being used for? There's a lot of hype at the moment around [whether it’s] going to be humanoids being at home with you. The thing about robots and AIs is the development of their senses so that they can be adaptive and safe within the home—there's still innovation to go there. So we made a choice to do this within manufacturing because it's a semi-constrained environment, and they've already got some understanding around safety and how to organize that. So we started there. Smaller machine workshops [that] do things like make a part of a phone, they'll use a CNC [computer numeral control] machine to do that. Typically, they haven't been able to afford things like robotics and AI, and we've already started working with a couple of different companies in the U.S., machine shops who effectively need their machines tending because it's a quite a boring job for humans to do, but also some of them have so much demand now for things like computers, the servers that produce the processing for the AI chips, and then they get put into data centers. So increasingly, that some of the machine shops in the U.S. are being asked to build component parts of these machines. They don’t have the skilled labor anymore to do it. They don't necessarily have the space to do it. [We provide] small cells for them, so that they can actually run an extra production run overnight themselves, without that labor. So suddenly they can meet that demand. But what's interesting is the same cell can do more than one type of task. It can tend a machine, but it can also inspect [a part] and do other tasks. So getting something that's cost effective and able to be flexible for a small machine shop like that is a game changer for them. It's a platform, so the same cell can be configured through software to do a different task, and so you don't have the cost of actually building another cell. We've also found we can plug them together and orchestrate them, and if you build up a whole set of flexible cells like this, you have a whole factory, and that's what we're doing with Foxconn. So the same cells that are going into small machine shops are now also able to go into whole factories as well, with the same platform and the same sort of structure, and that's really where we're starting to democratize it. So, the sort of task we're talking about is machine tending, polishing. We can look at inspecting. Some of the more innovative stuff we're looking at is things like assembly. So the thing that robots and AI haven't traditionally been able to do so far today is dexterous tasks. It's what we're good at, humans, like plugging things together, inserting things, screwing things. All those sorts of tasks are now more possible with AI, and so we're adding that in too Can you tell me more about the Nvidia partnership? With Nvidia, they do a lot of work in their site called Omniverse , which is simulation. So we're working with them and looking at how we do more of the orchestration of the cells I was talking about in factory. They also have some what we would call specific things like how do you grasp something? The Gemini team also have some of those. We are an agnostic platform. So we're a bit like Lego. We can wrap everything into a skill. So we can take a grasping skill from Nvidia or a grasping skill from Gemini, or we have some ourselves. So we have a world-class vision model at the moment that you can basically see with it very quickly, can look at a new part, see where it is, and pick it up. That sort of thing wasn't possible in the past. We can wrap those in skills and add them to a platform, so that people effectively can assemble skills. Like, can you pick this up? Can you move it here? Can you plug it together? All those become like Lego bricks within our platform, and we can use it on different types of hardware. So, we're working with several partners now. Nvidia, but also our own team, Gemini, and many other startups now doing these different models. We can also wrap different pieces of hardware like that too. So we've got a big partnership with the biggest robot manufacturer in the U.S., called FANUC [headquartered] in Japan. We've been able to add software and AI capability to their robots, which is the vision, touch ability to start to do things like insertion assembly that they've never been able to do before. So, in a way, we're a massive enabler. We wanted to make this open to many different types of people to access, and we also have a user interface layer that makes it easier for people who are more like operators to be able to use our tooling. This was again the democratization point. If you can get a standard operator within a factory or a machine shop to really use our tooling, it's a bit like using apps on phones. They can do things they've never been able to do before either. You give them access to that technology, so we're trying to provide that too at the moment. Do you have any specific rules or guardrails around what your products can't or shouldn’t be used for, like defense? We've always taken quite a strong view on where we can make the biggest difference and I think when I'm in the way, I'm mostly interested in helping the land of smaller suppliers. How can they actually have access to this? Whether it's U.S., Germany, Japan, we work in different countries in that way. If you take Germany’s economy, most of it is driven by the Mittelstand , which is that whole supply chain machine shop group in the middle suppliers, but we're also trying to understand what is needed at the bigger factory end as well. That's why we've got a partnership with Foxconn. But we just work in the factories right now in the U.S. with that to learn how to do that. I think we've stayed there because there's enough of a need around production. I think people forget just how hard it is to meet demand. In the U.S. 53% of skilled labor jobs are not fillable anymore, and the young are not coming into it, and the old have retired. A lot of what we do is more in that educational space. What's interesting is the next gen will come back in if they believe the tooling is more sophisticated, more like an application or it's got AI, and you get that a lot with the mom and pop shops because often they're family-owned businesses and they're finding they can't get their kids back in it [if] it looks really old-fashioned. Whereas, as soon as you bring a bit more technology in again, they'll come back in, so we're focusing more at that end of it, to be honest. There's been a lot of conversation around how AI is going to impact the labor market, particularly at the entry level, and what skills people should be learning. How would you advise a young person? My son's actually 21. He's an industrial designer, which, if I'm honest, is a great place to go, because he can code, he's a good engineer too, and he chose industrial design because he wanted to make, physically. And the design thinking process is really about your unique take on a problem solve or a product design. And actually, I think in a world where [AI can do] the coding for you, the design thinking process and the editing and the curation is going to become more important as the direction, to some extent. I think that matters for all the next gen. If that tooling is available to you, your unique taste and ability to direct it is going to become more important. And do you know that process of how to make that consideration in your own mind? I think that's going to happen to every industry. I think taste-making is going to become the thing to really hone. In my daughter's case, she's gone for neuroscience. So, same thing. She could have gone blank coding, and my husband and I encouraged her to go more down a creative route, again, because she's gone down a more science creative route, which is, how do you do the breakthrough thinking? So I would say for all the next gen, it's more about what do you love and are you great at, is what's going to become super valuable because that's all there's going to be, in some ways. It's what makes us human, and I think we're building things for other humans. That's the other thing people forget. What other humans that are interested in buying—things [or] having experiences—that resonate for them, that somebody else has designed. So that's what makes the connection. There's been discussion about women lagging behind in terms of AI adoption. What do you make of that conversation? I've been in tech my whole career. When I did computer science, [it was] with seven women on our course at Imperial College London, out of 120—it's got better. It is important, though, that I actually think this new world should suit women. I don't want to overgeneralize but we are very multi-hybrid in our skills, and often what happens is that we put and integrate things better together. Coding, for example, or pure technology is often quite focused, and sometimes the women on my team find that either too low level or they tend to like to do broader [work], so they make great product managers. I think we've got a media marketing problem in really putting it out there. I genuinely think women are going to be very good at using the tooling. The way I tend to use it now is, it's almost like a collaborator. So it's somebody. I tend to solve problems by talking to people, interacting. So what I'll do now is use an agent or something to actually just talk to it. And I test it too, like another person—I know another person has a perspective, I think you're an interesting person, I know you've got this information, I don't necessarily think you know everything, and that you're right. So what I want is a sort of debate. So, I think we can have better tools where it's more collaborative interaction. I think we'll all get more out of it, and I think then there'd be better adoption. I think the user experience side of it is going to become critical. The adoption won't be there otherwise, but I think it's coming. Is there anything that you definitely wouldn't use AI for? I'd never use it as a definitive answer. I know there's a lot of debate about critical thinking at the moment, but, even when I talk to one of my mentors, a human being, I will take the information and still try and think about it within my own context, and is it actually relevant or valid? Same thing here. Don't think it's a definitive answer. I think you need to use your own wisdom and brain and intuition if this is OK or not. I. I think it's the same as normal life. It's just a tool, right? So don't do anything with it that you don't feel fits with your moral compass. Just don't do it. I think these things are always going to be challenging. So, what's possible with it? I would just make sure you use it as an enabler, stay creative with it so that you don't sort of atrophy your own brain. You've worn many hats over the course of your career. What are some of the most important lessons that you've learned about leadership? I probably matured in that, because I was a CEO at 28 the first time round, I think I was hungrier then, and it kept me moving. But now I'm more patient, and I'm better at trying to get a full picture of information before I make a decision, but within constraint. So, one of the things about having done startups is you learn that some decisions are like 48:52 probability. You make a decision, that's your job as a leader, but I've got much better at fast trying to really get as wide a purview as I can in the time constraint I have before I make that choice. And then when I make that choice, I make it knowing that I may not have all the information. And so I'm also prepared that if something turns out not to be right later, to adapt to that, iterate on it, and be OK if I'm wrong [and] to admit it. I think a lot of people struggle in leadership or don't know how to own it and then to iterate, and that can cause more damage over time, or it can actually slow down, ultimately. What that's about is, you need to learn to drop your inner ego, for the outcome.

title: Brazil Re-Elects Lula for Historic Fourth Term, Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede
author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
content: Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for the Workers' Party (PT), waves a Brazil flag during a rally ahead of the presidential runoff at Avenida Paulista in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Oct. 24, 2026. Luiz Inácio Lula Da Silva, incumbent president of Brazil and presidential candidate for the Workers' Party (PT), waves a Brazil flag during a rally ahead of the presidential runoff at Avenida Paulista in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on Oct. 24, 2026. —Alexandre Schneider—Getty Images Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has been re-elected to a historic fourth term as Brazil’s President after a tight race with far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President and Donald Trump ally Jair Bolsonaro . Lula won with 51.8% of the vote to Bolsonaro’s 48.2%, Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court announced. Sunday’s vote was a rematch after neither reached an outright majority in the first round on Oct. 4. Lula had trailed then, becoming now the first presidential candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 to finish second in the initial vote and win the run-off. The election also marks a remarkable win for the global left, as it bucks a trend of right-wing electoral victories across Latin America. Lula will serve for another four-year term beginning on Jan. 5, 2027. “I want to thank the generosity of the Brazilian youth who took to the streets, who went to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night. “I want to thank the elderly. I saw scenes today of people being carried by their grandchildren to vote, people unable to move around, people with cancer and other illnesses. And people went to vote because we managed to convince them that voting was very important to ensure democracy in the country.” “This election was a defeat for denialism, a defeat for lies,” he continued. Bolsonaro, however, said late on Sunday that he would not concede defeat to Lula and would seek an annulment of the result. The senator for Rio de Janeiro said a ruling by the Supreme Court to extend voting for two hours , citing public transport issues, was “unacceptable.” Nevertheless, several liberal leaders around the world have already lauded the result. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said . Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney posted , “The relationship between Canada and Brazil has flourished under our partnership. Let’s seize this opportunity to make it even stronger, together — to create major new trade opportunities, protect ​the environment, and build greater prosperity for both our peoples.” Several U.S. lawmakers have also congratulated Lula on the result, including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders , Rep. Ro Khanna (D, Calif.) , California Gov. Gavin Newsom , and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani . A former metalworker and union leader, Lula co-founded the Workers’ Party in 1980 and continues to serve as its honorary president. He served as Brazil’s President between 2003 to 2011, before he was jailed from 2018 to 2019 on corruption convictions that were later annulled . He went on to defeat incumbent President Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, winning his third presidential term . Lula’s campaign focused on labor reform, welfare benefits, and affordability. At a time when public debt as a share of GDP has risen to its highest level since the pandemic, Lula cited his achievements in lowering poverty rates , as well as reducing unemployment , illiteracy , and deforestation to record lows. He pledged to make public transit free on the weekends, a program that would need congressional approval. He also increased benefits under his signature Bolsa Família program and championed a landmark constitutional amendment shortening the working week , which Congress approved. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, campaigned on harsher criminal penalties, tougher policing, lower taxes, and cuts to government spending. His campaign highlighted a corruption investigation involving Lula’s son and a pension fraud scandal that spanned both Lula’s and Jair Bolsonaro’s administrations. Bolsonaro also called for amnesty for his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence under house arrest after being found guilty of plotting a coup to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election. In his election night speech, Lula pledged to strengthen federal involvement in public security, expand education and healthcare, and develop Brazil’s technological and artificial intelligence industries. “This country will not be built by me,” he said. “But by you.” A blow to the right Lula’s win pumps the brakes on the broader political shift towards the right in Latin America. Colombia, Peru, Costa Rica, and Chile elected right-wing presidents in recent election cycles, reversing an earlier “pink tide” of left-wing governments. Lula’s victory also denies Trump another political ally in Latin America, which include Argentinian President Javier Milei and Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele . Bolsonaro had portrayed himself as an ally of Trump, courting closer ties with Washington and backing U.S. terrorist designations for Brazil’s major criminal gangs. Reuters reported on Saturday, citing current and former U.S. officials, that two U.S. State Department officials had pushed sanctions and other measures intended to weaken Lula and help return the Bolsonaros to power. The State Department did not comment specifically on the reported efforts but told Reuters that “all actions taken by the United ⁠States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections.” Trump previously expressed support for Jair Bolsonaro and labelled Lula a “radical left lunatic” during Brazil’s 2022 presidential election. He also criticized the criminal prosecution of Bolsonaro, calling it a “witch hunt” and demanding it end. Trump has not reacted to the election results as of early Monday. After Bolsonaro led in the first round on Oct. 4, Trump called the result “close, but a very, very big victory.” His son, Donald Trump Jr., posted earlier criticizing the Supreme Court’s decision to extend voting hours and what he described as the lack of American mainstream media coverage of it. Lula had warned that Bolsonaro would surrender Brazil’s sovereignty to Trump. Lula has publicly sparred with Trump on multiple occasions. He accused the Trump Administration of interfering in Brazil’s election and imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil under alleged pressure from the Bolsonaros. The Bolsonaro family and the U.S. State Department denied the allegations. At the same time, Lula has pursued closer ties with China, Brazil’s largest trading partner and the U.S.’s geopolitical rival, although he rejected subordination and said Brazil was not choosing between the two countries. “This country will not accept being anyone’s backyard,” Lula said on Sunday night. Analysts, however, warned that Lula’s political influence could wane despite his re-election. Earlier this month, Brazil elected its most conservative National Congress since the 1980s. Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) and allied parties could control majorities in both chambers, with more than 280 of 513 seats in the lower house and up to 50 of 81 seats in the Senate. That could make it difficult for Lula to pass his legislative agenda, analysts said. But Lula shrugged off those concerns and promised to work with the more conservative Congress to govern for all Brazilians. “The day after tomorrow, the 27th, I turn 81 years old, and I want to make a commitment in front of the press and in front of you,” Lula said. “I will have the best term a President has ever had in the history of this country”

title: What Does Trump’s Declining Latino Support Mean for Florida?
author: Rebecca Schneid
content: Voting booths are seen at Supervisor of Elections Office in Orange County, Florida, on the last business day before early voting begins for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections. Voting booths are seen at Supervisor of Elections Office in Orange County, Florida, on the last business day before early voting begins for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections. —Paul Hennessy—SOPA Images/LightRocket William Diaz has a mantra: His only political party is his Venezuelan community. He doesn’t abide by strict partisan rules, and doesn't believe in only voting for Democrats or Republicans. He supported Republicans Sen. Rick Scott and Secretary of State Marco Rubio when they were running for office in Florida , where Diaz has lived for 37 years. For these midterm elections, however, the Orlando resident hopes to make a clear statement: He does not support President Donald Trump’s immigration policies and is unhappy with how Republican-backed initiatives have affected his community. Read More: An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates “I voted already, and what I did when I was voting and when I was with my ballot, I was really thinking and praying for all those that has no voice, those that can not vote, those immigrants that are right now victim of actions on the streets,” Diaz tells TIME, referring to Trump’s mass deportation agenda and the expansive influence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “My people have been suffering that much.” Diaz is one of more than 2.6 million people who have already cast ballots in Florida, either by mail or through in-person early voting, according to state figures released Sunday. In-person early voting began in some counties Oct. 19 and expanded statewide Oct. 24. Diaz’s community is one part of a Florida Latino electorate with varied national origins and political loyalties. Taken together, however, Latino voters are a swing vote in several closely watched races statewide. They were key to Trump’s Florida victory in 2024, with 56% supporting him over Kamala Harris, according to the 2024 American Electorate Voter Poll . But new polls ahead of Election Day suggest that Latino support for the GOP may be on shaky ground—a shift that could put Republicans to the test in Florida and shape the political landscape beyond November. Why Florida’s Latino voters are frustrated with Trump Dissatisfaction among Florida’s Latino voters reflects a broader national mood, according to Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, an organization that studies Latino voting behavior. Concerns about the economy and immigration enforcement tactics are fueling dissatisfaction among Latino voters, who “make up a huge part of the electorate in Florida,” she says, pointing out that both of these issues are “disproportionately impacting” them. A Univision/YouGov poll, conducted Oct. 2–15, showed that 41% of registered Latino voters in Florida were “very or somewhat worried” that they, a family member, or someone close could be detained or otherwise directly affected by immigration enforcement, compared with 27% of Florida voters overall. The same poll showed that 4 in 10 Latino voters in the state felt that their finances had worsened over the past year, with 70% disapproving of Trump’s handling of the cost of living in the U.S. That stands in comparison to a 63% disapproval rate from Florida voters overall. Read More: Midterm Ad Spending Has Surpassed $10B. Where Is the Money Coming From? For Johanna Chavez, a Dominican immigrant living in Kissimmee, Florida, the economy is top of mind. “Many people are concerned about the economy and the price of gasoline … and then there’s the cost of rent, it’s become incredibly, overwhelmingly high,” Chavez, who speaks Spanish, tells TIME through a translator. “All the things they promised would be done—nothing has happened.” In the past few years, Chavez says it has felt like the United States has started “regressing,” and the opportunities she was looking for when she arrived here have not materialized in the way she had hoped. “It’s starting to feel just like the situation back in my home country, the Dominican Republic,” she says. “We all came here hoping for change, seeking a better life, but it’s ending up being the same thing all over again. Things just aren’t what they’re supposed to be.” Jared Nordlund, the Florida State Advocacy Director at UnidosUS, the largest nonprofit Latino rights organization in the U.S., says this is a common refrain among Floridian Latinos; people are upset over how the economy has been affected by tariffs and the war in Iran . Florida was hit particularly hard by rising gas prices after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz squeezed the global energy supply, he says. “Florida is not a state friendly for public transportation, so people are highly reliant on the cars, and so what they would be paying for food now is having to kind of get broke between … paying to get the gas and then going to get food,” Nordlund says. The question now is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Republicans—and whether it will be enough to tip the state’s close races. Trump’s declining Latino support puts Florida Republicans on notice Trump’s approval rating has plummeted with Latino voters in Florida, dropping from 58% approval at the start of his term to 36% ahead of midterm elections, according to Equis Research. According to an AP-NORC poll from October, about 6 in 10 Latino voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, and more than 7 in 10 disapprove of how he is handling the economy. A Pew Research Center poll found that Trump’s job approval rating among Latino voters dropped from 38% in February 2025 to 24% in September and October. Of those who backed him in the last election, approval dropped to 57%—down from 93% in early 2025. The shift may be resonating with Republicans like Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who is seeking re-election in Florida’s 27th District in Miami-Dade—a majority Latino district that Trump carried by some 15 points in 2024. She publicly broke with Trump in her campaign and criticized his immigration policies. In one ad in September, Salazar said that Trump has “gone too far" with his deportation agenda. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she notes in the ad. “Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” Salazar continues, addressing Trump. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.” Why Latino frustration may not translate into Democratic votes Guillermo Grenier, a Cuban American professor of sociology at Florida International University (FIU), agrees that many Latino voters are “ticked off” at Trump. “The population, if you look at the whole Latino conglomerate, is turned off pretty strongly with Trump,” he says. But South Florida’s Latino electorate is unique; Grenier points out that the state is home to 1.9 million Cuban Americans—the largest concentration in the United States. As a voting bloc, the community has significant sway. In 2024, FIU’s Cuba poll found that 68% of likely Cuban American voters in Miami-Dade County supported Trump, compared to 23% for Harris—representing his highest-recorded support level in the poll's history. A shift away from Republicans among Cuban American voters could therefore have significant consequences in South Florida. But disillusionment doesn’t always turn into action, according to Grenier. “I think a lot of Cubans are pissed off at Trump, but they're still Republicans,” he says.
