title: Bring The Holiday To You: How To Have Your Euro Summer At Home
author: Saacha Neilson
content: In partnership with Some of you lucky buggers spent June and July soaking up Europe’s rays, while the rest of us were freezing in share houses ‘cos we used all our savings on Meredith tickets. Can you guess which one I was? Well, to help avoid the same fate hitting us all next year, I’ve rounded up the best Euro-esque spots around Aus so you can see the sights without spending big.  The best European eats Europe boasts many incredible cuisines, so where do you find the crème de la crème?  French and Italian are classics and, as such, are readily available. France-Soir in Melbourne is an iconic restaurant which has been open for more than 30 years and will make you feel as if you’re sitting kerbside on a Parisian street. Similarly, Sydney’s Neptune’s Grotto will transport you to a cosy Sardinian restaurant — if you’re lucky enough to get a table. This could be you. (Image source: Getty) If you’re after a sweet treat, indulge in the Swedish tradition of Fika at Manly’s Fika Swedish Kitchen. With a bakery straight out of Gothenburg, you’ll be hard-pressed to stop at one.  And of course, who can forget Melbourne’s Eat Pierogi Make Love? If I can get my hands on a dumpling, especially a Polish one, best believe I’ll be there once a week.  But if you want the real taste of Europe at a moment's notice, grab yourself a bag of Kettle Ridge Cut European Style Sour Cream & Chives chips . They’ll have you thinking you’re on a holiday north of the equator, treading a cobblestone street and wishing you had started Duolingo earlier.  What every woman wants. (Image source: Getty & Kettle) Settle in for a drink For a casual drink, why not head to any of the million Irish pubs dotted around every city? Buy a Guinness, fail at splitting the G, and settle in for a cosy afternoon.  But if you want to soak up something a little more substantial, skip Tuscany’s vineyards and instead head to the Barossa Valley. It's an hour from Adelaide and boasts world-famous vineyards, so a sunny afternoon here will do you every bit as good as a day spent trawling the Italian countryside.  Finding Germany in Aus  Melbourne is always said to be similar to Berlin, what with our coffee culture and fun nightlife. I suppose that would make Revs our Berghain, though that's a sad thought. However, if you really want to land yourself in Germany, the little-known town of Hahndorf is the perfect place. The oldest surviving German settlement, this town in the Adelaide Hills made the choice to maintain its buildings’ facades and cultural ties. Now a hotspot for tourists, you can score a pretzel and a beer at just about every establishment. What could be more German than that? European-style beaches  European beaches are famed for their pebbles and lack of waves. Why someone would prefer this to our soft sand and lively waters is beyond me, but if that’s something you’re after, there are spots you can head to.  Western Australia’s Elephant Rocks, located in William Bay National Park, is the perfect example of a European beach here in Aus. With turquoise waters and boulders, it’ll transport you to a Mediterranean grotto. Not to mention, it’s literally in Denmark, WA. Couldn’t be more perfect if we tried.  Me the second the sun is out. (Image source: Getty) There are more ways to enjoy a little holiday, of course. I'd even bargain on a holiday-esque surprise hitting a Sydney or Melbourne street any minute. But until you spot that or manage to get overseas for real, we recommend hitting a gallery to see the Impressionists or simply buying a baguette.

title: Glee Is Getting A Reboot, So Which Cast Members Are Returning? Let's Unpack The Clues
author: Lachlan Guertin
content: Check in on your musical theatre friends. After being threatened teased by creator Ryan Murphy just last month , it’s now official: Glee is getting a reboot. It was announced on Thursday morning that Disney+ and Hulu had greenlit a revival series of the infamous musical dramedy, which ran for six seasons between 2009 and 2015 and featured countless covers of popular songs and show tunes that were better than the original (fight me) For those who never got on board or simply blocked out what the show was about, Glee followed a group of outcast students in a high school Glee club who competed in choir championships, faced bullying from their cohorts and sang about the highs and lows of adolescence. The series was groundbreaking at the time for dealing with a range of complex issues, including sexuality, disability, race, body image, teen pregnancy and domestic violence, although viewers have retrospectively criticised the often problematic ways it tackled the subject matter. Glee is getting a reboot. (Credit: FOX) Who is returning for the Glee reboot? Ryan Murphy — who went on to create the hit shows American Horror Story , Monster and Love Story after Glee — first told Entertainment Tonight last month that he’d written a reboot script with collaborators Brad Falchuk and Ian Brennan . He said he’d been in touch with “around 10 of the original cast members”, who had a lot of questions but were “very enthusiastic” about the idea. While it’s yet to be confirmed who will be returning to the series, there have been plenty of clues on social media since the reboot announcement was made. Unsurprisingly, Lea Michele is tipped to reprise her role as Rachel Berry, with multiple sources confirming her casting to Variety . The actress is no doubt already rehearsing “Drivers License” by Olivia Rodrigo and “Good Luck, Babe!” by Chappell Roan for the reboot, as well as hiring someone to read her scripts to her (IYKYK). Heather Morris , aka Brittany S Pierce, posted a photo of her character on Instagram following the announcement, seemingly confirming her return. “Yes ladies and gentle men of women, rumours are true. Brittany S Pierce was in fact lost in the sewers for all these years. But I’m here to inform you that she is alive and well… And back for more,” she wrote. Former cast members Josh Sussman (Jacob Ben Israel) and Damian McGinty (Rory Flanagan) both commented on the post, which suggests they’ll both appear in the reboot if they get asked back. Interestingly, Dianna Agron also posted on Instagram at the same time as the announcement. Although the post made no reference to Glee or her character Quinn Fabray, it hasn’t gone unnoticed that Michele and Jenna Ushkowitz (Tina Cohen-Chang) both liked the post. A few hours later, Agron appeared in a suspiciously timed TikTok with Ben Platt and Myha'la performing the viral “I Say A Little Prayer” dance trend from Glee , which fans have taken as a clear sign that she's returning. Jane Lynch (Sue Sylvester) reposted the casting news on her Instagram Story, and over on X (formerly known as Twitter), Kevin McHale (Artie Abrams) replied to a 2020 post from Genius announcing that Drake had passed the cast of Glee to have the most Billboard Hot 100 hits of all time. “Challenge accepted,” he wrote. Chord Overstreet (Sam Evans) also confirmed his casting by posting “Reunited and it feels so good!” on X, and replied “Blam” to a photo of himself with Darren Criss (Blaine Anderson). Meanwhile, according to Deadline , Matthew Morrison is not in talks to appear in the Glee reboot, but the actor is “hopeful that he will be part of the project”. There's also a strong chance Gwyneth Paltrow ( Holly Holliday) could return, as she married the show's co-creator, Brad Falchuk, in 2018 after meeting on the set of Glee . As for the other original cast members, Amber Riley (Mercedes Jones), Chris Colfer (Kurt Hummel) and Harry Shum Jr (Mike Chang) have yet to react to the news — although the trio remain close and Riley and Colfer both attended a taping of Dancing With The Stars last month to support Shum. Stay tuned for more updates, and start making your list of Glee plot and song predictions now.

title: Aussie Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Addresses Her Kikiva Ties After Founder’s Sister Uses Racial Slur On Livestream
author: Simran Pasricha
content: Content Warning: This article discusses the use of racial slurs.  Dallas Cowboys Cheerleader Faith Ward has spoken out about her connection to Kikiva after the activewear brand’s founder, Kia Buckley , livestreamed her sister using a racial slur. Ward, who viewers will recognise from Netflix’s America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders , previously released a collection with the Perth label. She’s now ruled out any future work with the brand. What happened on Kia Buckley’s livestream? Buckley was doing her make-up on TikTok Live when her younger sister arrived home and used the N-word off camera. After warning her sister she was live, Buckley denied the slur had been said, claiming she’d heard “what’s up sissys”. The footage was reuploaded online, drawing criticism of the slur and Buckley’s response. Several models who worked with Kikiva, including Vimbayi Hakutangwi , Evie Graves and Madison Meyerhoff , have since cut ties. What did Kia Buckley say in her apology? Buckley later acknowledged the slur in a statement shared to her TikTok story, which expired after 24 hours. “During the live, a family member arrived home and used a racial slur in the background off camera. I was deeply shocked, disappointed and upset by what was said,” she wrote. “I want to sincerely apologise to everyone who heard it and anyone who has been hurt by that language. The use of racial slurs or any other derogatory words is completely unacceptable under any circumstances. “I want to make it clear that I do not condone racism in any form.” (Image: TikTok / Kia Buckley) What has Faith Ward said about Kia Buckley? When someone questioned her association with Kikiva in a TikTok comment, Ward said their working relationship had actually ended four months earlier. Faith Ward launched her "It Girl" collection with Kikiva Activewear in May of this year. (Image: Kikiva Activewear) “I want to make it extremely clear that I do not condone or support any type of racism, discrimination or behaviour of that nature,” she wrote. “It does not align with me or my values, and I take things like this extremely seriously. My relationship with the brand stopped four months ago, and I will not be working with the brand again. I want to be clear about where I stand, as this is something I will never support.” (Image: TikTok) Kia Buckley has received waves of backlash online Beyond the brand partnerships, creators have questioned how readily people excuse racist language. Creator and activist Jeffrey Kissubi pushed back against the suggestion that anyone would be cancelled if their private behaviour were filmed. “Because not all of us are using racial slurs and dehumanising language for funsies,” he said. For TikToker Sinit Taab , the response points to a bigger problem with how casually racism is treated in Australia, particularly when conversations turn to defending someone’s intentions. “Anytime we have discussions about racism, people love to give benefit of the doubt to the perpetrator. And I've never understood this," she said. "Black people, people of colour, they shouldn't have to continuously justify the seriousness of racism for you , for you to understand it . Like, if your first response in these kind of situations is to be like, 'Oh, they didn't mean it like that, that wasn't their intentions', like, 'Oh, they shouldn't get all this backlash'. I think that's a very ill-informed response a nd you need to do better." Help is available. If you require immediate assistance, please call 000 . If you're in distress, please call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or chat online . Under 25? You can reach the Kids Helpline at 1800 55 1800 or chat online . You can also report instances of racism or discrimination to the Australian Human Rights Commission on 1300 656 419 or lodge a complaint online .

title: Linda Cardellini On Going Full Psychotic Mama Bear In Crystal Lake & Her Favourite Kill In The Series
author: Rebekah Manibog
content: If there's one thing folks love about horror, it's definitely the blood, guts and gore of it all. However, sometimes, the genre sets the foundations for in-depth exploration of grief, rage and loss, and in Crystal Lake 's case — which follows Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees — it's the perfect campground.   Fresh from the Friday The 13th universe, Crystal Lake explores the untold backstory of Pamela ‘Pam’ Voorhees, a single mother and cook at Camp Crystal Lake, as she grapples with the loss of her son, Jason Voorhees, while her mysterious, dark past resurfaces.  From solving mysteries to being the mystery. An icon. (Image source: Stan / Crystal Lake) Transforming into a major part of a legacy horror franchise, Cardellini admitted the role was “daunting”, knowing how fans are so protective of Jason, as well as following up Betsy Palmer , who played the OG Pam in the first movie, and her performance. “ I t has such an incredible fan base, and they love it so much,” she told PEDESTRIAN.TV.  "W hat Betsy Palmer does at the end of the movie — the first movie — she's, you know? There are sprinklings of her throughout. It's so wild and fun and amazing, and you can't really duplicate that.  “ But I do think that there is an opportunity to expand on that. S he makes such an impression with such a small amount of time on screen that it is fun to go back and imagine what the rest of that character's life could have been like."  Would only eat Ms Voorhees' food to NOT DIE. (Image source: Stan / Crystal Lake) And while the legacy franchise is known for its kills (my favourite being the sleeping bag slam Friday the 13th Part VII: The New Blood ) ,  Crystal Lake explores the pain caused by loss, and hyper-focuses on Pam's mother bear rage. Taking on Pamela Voorhees' motherly rage Being a mother in real life, Cardellini said there were definitely heart-sinking moments where she felt protective of her fellow child co-stars such as Callum Vinson , who plays Jason, and Gwendolyn Sundstrom , who portrays Grace.  “W e shot a scene where [Jason] has a medical emergency on the floor, and watching, just even being witness to a child actor doing something that is so difficult, and then you know why you just can't help but feel for him,” he said.  “ Calum was incredible in his part, and so was so was the Gwen who plays Grace, and so they brought so much they brought so much to it that it wasn't hard to imagine wanting to try to protect them, you know?”  Cardellini also referenced a scene in the first episode, where Pam drops off bodies in a bear cave, and shared that it's the perfect symbol for where Crystal Lake goes.  Never trigger the mama bear. (Image source: Stan / Crystal Lake) “ I think it's funny that she comes face to face with a bear, and I think there is that mama bear aspect to her that everybody is kind of aware to stay away from a bear if the cubs are around,” she said.  “ I think it's really the way that Brad Caleb Kane , our writer, set it up so that you see Jason and her willingness to do anything to protect him. I think it sets the show up and honours the franchise because the franchise is about Jason and everything that Pam does is for Jason."  Reflecting on the whole scope of the role, the DTF. St. Louis star said she was drawn to Pam's role mostly because it was “something [she] hadn't done before". 'I 've worked for a long time, luckily, and it was something that I just hadn't done before," she added.  “I hadn't sort of taken a turn like this, and there's a lot to do in the character, and she has a really wild ride, and she walks this line between sanity and insanity.”  Linda Cardellini's favourite Camp Crystal kill  Getting into the real slasher of it all, the scream queen admits her favourite kill of the whole series was the first one, in which Pam slashes Ed Shabani (played by Aaron Serotsky ) in the head with the iconic machete, then covers it with a bag that quickly fills with blood.  “ It took us a week. We planned out just to do the last 15 minutes of the first episode, which in TV time is a lot. Yo u don't always get that much time, and it just was a lot of choreography, a lot of stunts , a lot of special effects , a lot of blood,” she recalled.  “ I feel like when we completed that, we really felt like we had done something. W e had something that we could hold on to, and then I had just never seen anything like what happens with that bag. So although it was not very comfortable, it definitely put you in the world of Friday Th e 13th ."  Season Two of Crystal Lake has not been confirmed. However, Cardellini acknowledged there's a “long runway” until the first Friday The 13th movie, as the series takes place 10 years before it. So who knows where that will take us…  Stream all eight episodes of Crystal Lake on Stan now.

title: Ruby Rose Has Now Gotten Involved In The Kelly Clarkson Bird Drama: 'I Feel For Molly'
author: Lachlan Guertin
content: Ruby Rose has officially entered the conversation surrounding Kelly Clarkson ’s unsuccessful attempt to buy a $15,000 animatronic singing bird named Molly from a Brooklyn games and puzzles store — aka one of the most iconic celebrity stories of 2026. For the uninitiated, the American Idol winner started beefing with the New York City store Art of Play on social media earlier this month when she claimed she was treated like Julia Roberts ’ character in Pretty Woman  and “looked at as if [she] couldn’t afford” to buy anything. She and the store exchanged a series of public statements online and the security camera footage of Clarkson’s visit leaked online a few days later, and now Ruby Rose has said she “feels for Molly” amid the hullabaloo. “I know what it’s like to be Molly the bird,” she wrote on Threads . The actress went on to detail her experience meeting Kelly Clarkson in 2009 when she was a host on MTV Australia , and she was “so smitten by how down to earth and funny she was”. “After the interview I got up and left the room. But right before I closed the door, I heard Miss Clarkson say, ‘She was adorable, I just want to put her in my pocket and take her with me’, a reference to me,” she detailed. Ruby Rose interviewed Kelly Clarkson in 2009. (Credit: MTV Australia) Rose joked that the overheard comment has allowed her to empathise with Molly, the $15,000 bird, as it was something Clarkson also wanted to take home with her. “I asked my producer if I could find a way to become really tiny so that I could live in Kelly’s pocket. My producer laughed. We left and went on to another interview, but for years I wondered what my life could have been,” she remarked. “I feel for Molly, I really do.” Clarkson and Rose reunited on The Kelly Clarkson Show in 2021, where they reminisced about their first interview together and the Breakaway singer said she was “mesmerised” by the Aussie star. “You have the coolest spirit, you were so chill, and your hair was really crazy cool. I felt so inadequate as a cool person,” Clarkson joked. Ruby Rose and Kelly Clarkson reunited on The Kelly Clarkson Show in 2021. (Credit: YouTube) Rose’s post comes after Art of Play co-owner Adam Rubin did a series of media interviews and told USA Today that the online backlash has made them “afraid for the security of [their] shopkeepers”. “Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger,” he said. “Not just people showing up in person, but our neighbours are being doxxed and review-bombed, people are getting threatened on the street, and the worst part is: we didn’t know this was gonna happen, but Kelly Clarkson did.” He went on to invite Clarkson to attend the store again, attend one of their magic shows and give them another try because “this is an insane misunderstanding”. “If it is this intense to be merely mentioned by Kelly Clarkson, I can only imagine how intense it is to be Kelly Clarkson every single day, but things changed when she used her platform to attack us,” he continued. “It’s asymmetrical social warfare.” We promise to keep you updated on this absolutely insane celebrity news story.

title: Everything We Saw At Call Of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's Sydney Pop-Up Experience
author: PEDESTRIAN.TV
content: OK, OK. You’ve clocked me. I’m a massive gamer. I love escaping through a console and spending my adult money on virtual cashola for skins, exploring new maps and waiting for drops. So when I was invited to the Sydney  Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare® 4 pop-up, I moseyed on over, and honestly, I didn't expect to be launched into the game. For folks who’ve yet to feast their eyes on anything  MW4 , the next instalment of the legendary franchise explores a fictional full-scale North Korean invasion of South Korea that threatens to de-stabilise the world. Alongside that major plot, series icon Captain Price returns as an outlaw as he’s dragged into the middle of the conflict.  Tapping into that fresh storyline — alongside the return of a beloved, familiar face — Activision transformed Sydney’s Carriageworks into  MW4 ’s DMZ. And when I say transformed, I mean it. Walk with me, soldier. Exploring  Call of Duty®: Modern Warfare® 4’ s Sydney DMZ  From the jump, the atmosphere was intense, with a large barbed wire fence dividing the room into the North and South. Heading to the ‘Draft Station’, my silly goose self waddled into the North.  I've never been so impressed and stressed at the same time. (Image source: Supplied) Passing the barrier, which was also guarded by a soldier, I was fully launched into the  MW4 conflict zone and was assigned multiple missions in order to get stamps. This included conducting a contraband sweep, getting a state portrait (where I got in trouble for smiling and serving face), and installations where you can wear night vision goggles to find hidden clues to an escape room, which was pretty frkn cool.  But my favourite part — which I did not partake in — was the compliance cuts, which emulated the real-life 28 government-approved haircuts in North Korea. However, in Sydney we only got three, and I did ZERO because there was no way I was trading my golden locks for a bob!  I refuse to get a bob, sorry! (Image source: Supplied) Punters could also defect to the South, which had separate activities including a pressure test, a bomb defusal, and a bug hunt.  While the activities made me feel like an actual, playable character in the world of COD, it was the opportunity to play the Campaign in the new MW4 that got my blood pressure pumping.  In my little gamer gal moment, I got to play a Campaign mission where North Korea was taking over the South, and I had to defend my city. As someone who deeply appreciates world-building and graphics, I decided to take the easiest mode so I could run around freely and see what the new MW4 was about.  50 points for me for not rage-quitting on stage! (Image source: Supplied) The gameplay made me extremely excited for the full drop, and the fresh storyline of a fictional, full-scale invasion had me hooked from the start.  However, I will not be commenting on how many times I might’ve… failed…  Verdict?  The whole event in itself was something I’ve never seen before. From the soldiers and the activities and the haircuts (still shook about this, BTW)  — it really got me gee’d up for all the new campaigns, missions, characters and maps we’re about to see in  MW4 . To step beyond the screen and into a place that’s actually tangible, that engaged all five senses and more, was incredibly mind-blowing. Like, a COD conflict zone in Sydney is something I would never envision in my entire life, but here we are!  That being said, I will be sat for the next  MW4 , and with all that ‘training’ I’m ready to take other players down, specifically on Shipment.  Pre-order Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 before 23 October to play Campaign and DMZ Early Access from the very first minute.

title: Nicole Kidman's Daughter Sunday Rose Finally Addresses Nepo Baby Claims As She Lands Vogue Cover

title: Wearing This Sunflower Lanyard Helps Others Understand My Hidden Disability
author: Rachel Choy
content: In 2024, my life turned upside down with no warning. My chronic illness flared up to the point where I wasn’t able to leave the house for weeks on end; I had to leave a job I really loved, missed Christmas with my family, and trips overseas were off the cards. After trialling new treatments and working closely with my neurologist , I finally felt like I was ready to fly overseas to visit family. The only problem? I was getting anxious about the thought of navigating the airport by myself, and knew I’d be too nervous to request extra help when I needed it. I’d heard about the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower Lanyard , so I ordered one and wore it for my trip from Sydney to Auckland. The Hidden Disability Sunflower first originated at Gatwick Airport in the UK, and was brought to Australia and New Zealand by Melbourne not-for-profit organisation Bayley House . The Sunflower is a symbol that indicates the wearer may need assistance or understanding. In Australia, there are 4.4 million people who live with disability , and it’s believed that around 80% of them have invisible disabilities. They can include ADHD, autism, neurological conditions, chronic pain, depression, anxiety, cognitive and learning disabilities, and more. The first thing I noticed when putting the lanyard on before my trip was a sense of calm. As a Sunflower Business Member, Sydney Airport’s staff are trained to understand what the Hidden Disability Sunflower symbol means, so I knew I’d have the confidence to approach workers if I needed an extra hand.  The Hidden Disability Sunflower first originated at Gatwick Airport in the UK. (Credit: TfW) At Sydney Airport, there was a separate security line for business class passengers, crew, wheelchair users and those with accessibility needs marked by the Sunflower. The area where you go through security seemed to be separate from the regular section. While it can often feel hectic and rushed getting your bags scanned, this time around, I could take my time. The area was less crowded, and the friendly staff were definitely taking note of the lanyard around my neck. By the time I navigated the airport and arrived at my gate, I was a bit flustered. The airline crew were extremely kind and allowed me to slowly board the plane. While I didn’t expect special treatment on the plane, another flight attendant also put my bag up in the overhead locker for me, which was greatly appreciated.   While it may not seem like much, using the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower Lanyard to travel put me at ease during such a turbulent time in my life. With my neurological disability, I can have good and bad days — I only use the lanyard on days I need it — but it really makes a difference just knowing I have it in my travel pack.    Sandee Facy , Head of Business Development for Hidden Disabilities Sunflower Australia & New Zealand, says their goal is simple. “We want to normalise non-visible disabilities in the public eye, to remove stigma, improve accessibility, and create a culture where everyone feels comfortable asking for or offering support,” Facy told Refinery29 Australia . “The Sunflower is more than just a lanyard — it’s a conversation starter, an education tool, and a symbol of solidarity. We’re proud of how far it’s come in Australia, but we know there’s still work to do. The more people who understand it, the more inclusive our world becomes.”   The non-profit works closely with councils, transport providers, businesses and the community to implement the Sunflower in everyday situations. “We’re seeing remarkable growth. More organisations are joining the movement, and more individuals are wearing the Sunflower with confidence,” she added. The use of the Sunflower isn’t limited to just travel. If you take a look around, you might start to see them pop up at concerts, on public transport, at restaurants, or just on the street. A video of Havannah Vera ’s nine-year-old daughter Chloe wearing the lanyard at Taylor Swift’s MCG concert went viral on TikTok in 2024 . The mother-daughter duo have ADHD, and Vera’s daughter has a sensory processing disorder, so she was apprehensive about how overstimulating the experience could be. However, using the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower Lanyard completely changed their concert-going experience. “The staff and venue were amazing and accommodating. We actually had seats in the middle of the row, and my daughter was very overwhelmed, so we stood by the area where they have seats and open spots for people who have wheelchairs or cannot get up the stairs due to disability,” Vera told R29 . “[An] amazing staff worker… asked me if everything was okay and went above and beyond to make it [so] we could stay in the more open space so my daughter could enjoy the concert without being more overwhelmed and anxious.”   Vera believes the symbol is helping remove stigma from invisible disabilities, but acknowledges we still have a long way to go. “I’ve always been one to speak up and bring awareness but mostly understanding to others when it comes to hidden disabilities, because even the most empathetic individuals can be unaware of how certain comments can make it that much harder and depressing for someone with any form of hidden disabilities,” she explains. “I think it’s good to just make people aware that someone may struggle especially in social outings or experiences that yes, they may love [it], but can get overwhelmed and anxious a lot more quickly than others.”   Isabella Fantasia , a neurodivergent Melburnian, is a passionate advocate for the Sunflower and what it represents. She uses it when she attends concerts, on public transport, and at other events, and tells R29 it can be particularly helpful as a way to explain why she’s using a disabled space and avoid conflict. “I will pop it on just so I don’t get any confused looks or people kind of challenging me for why I might be using the disabled bathroom instead of waiting in line for the women’s bathroom, for example. I just find it easier to wear [the lanyard] so I don’t have to deal with potential questions and other bits and pieces that come with having a completely invisible disability,” Fantasia says.    “My biggest drama that I’ve had on public transport [is] I always need a seat. I can’t stand, especially when it’s like trains or trams are packed,” she adds. “Sometimes I’ve used it as a way of being able to give myself that boost of confidence for if I need to ask someone for their seat, or to insist that I get a seat… it’s been really great for me in that way, where I’ve been able to insist on my access needs and really persist with them.”   Hidden Disabilities Sunflower Australia and New Zealand hope to continue signing up businesses and increasing awareness of the Sunflower and invisible disabilities . Although it has only been operational in Australia for five years, it has already changed many people’s lives. “The lanyard is a powerful tool that helps foster a more inclusive and compassionate society. It’s not about labelling someone — it’s about recognising and respecting different needs,” Aspect’s Autism Consultant Emma Beardsley says.   “Importantly, it also plays a role in educating the broader community. When people see the Sunflower symbol and understand its meaning, it opens the door to greater awareness and acceptance of invisible disabilities, including autism. We see the lanyard as part of a broader shift towards universal design and neuro-inclusive environments where support isn’t just available on request, but a core part of the way we plan, design, and deliver experiences.”    The Sunflower is also recognised in Belgium, Canada, Ireland, Latin America, the Netherlands, the UK, the UAE, the USA, and Denmark, and it was even made the legally recognised national symbol for hidden disabilities in Brazil . With major companies like Hilton, NSW Parliament, CommBank, MasterCard, Qantas and more joining the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower network, it’s a relief to see the community becoming more aware of the 4.4 million Aussies who live with invisible disabilities every single day. And while it’s currently Invisible Disabilities Week, we should continue talking about hidden disabilities long after this week is over. You can pick up a lanyard free of charge from organisations and businesses that are part of Hidden Disabilities Sunflower or order one from their website if you are unable to travel.   This article originally appeared on Refinery29 Australia

title: Insider Trading: From $10 Op Shop Fits To The Runway: How Ebony Noire Made It To Melbourne Fashion Week
author: Simran Pasricha
content: Ebony Rose Kruger aka the brain behind Ebony Noire, has spent enough time backstage at fashion week to know exactly how chaotic a runway can be. She started out as a dresser, moved into styling, and eventually decided she’d rather be the one sending looks down it. Now, barely two months out of RMIT, the Arrernte and Māori designer is bringing a refreshed version of her debut collection to Ganbu Marra at Melbourne Fashion Week 2026. Between working at a fabric store, interning in alterations and training at the boxing gym, she’s also figuring out what kind of designer she wants to be. In this edition of Insider Trading, we spoke to Ebony before her M/FW debut about starting at the bottom, being told she was “too sensitive” for fashion, and why persistence has gotten her this far. Hi! Tell us a little bit about yourself and what you do.   My name is Ebony Rose Kruger, an Aboriginal and Māori fashion designer. I’m Arrernte from Mparntwe, with Māori whakapapa to Te Ātiawa and Ngāti Kahungunu in Aotearoa. I just debuted my first collection in march this year for MFF and about to show a refreshed version of the collection with some added pieces I have flat patterned and constructed by hand. I had just completed a side gig in costume design which was a challenge for me coming from fashion design to adapting to movement and comfortability for the performers.     I recently graduated from RMIT in June and now work at Rathdowne Fabrics, where I have the privilege of being surrounded by beautiful fabrics and building my knowledge of them. I’m also interning at Stitch House Alterations, learning more about garment construction and complexities of alterations. When I’m not working on fashion, I’m usually boxing.   How long have you been in your role for?   I studied full time for two years, and for the past couple of months I’ve also been working at Rathdowne Fabrics. Before that, I interned with master tailor Adriano Carbone , where I got to see the process of high-level tailoring firsthand from made-to-measure to construction. I hope to become skilled at suit making and bring my own twist to it. In my latest collection, I’ve made a hybrid double-breasted blazer-bomber, which I’m excited to showcase. I’m also currently interning at Stitch House Alterations on Sydney Road.    My mentor, Jenny Tran , is showing me the ropes of running a business and how complex alterations can be. Sometimes it feels like watching someone solve an intricate puzzle, which makes it a fun challenge. I can’t wait to develop that eye and build my own skills for it.   What does the day in the life of Ebony Kruger look like?   If I’m not working on a fashion project, I’m usually getting a head start on my next collection. I’ve already been saving ideas and researching which includes watching Gallianoflix [a free, fan-made digital archive that organises 132 runway shows from fashion designer John Galliano ] and practising new techniques. I often get sent home with alteration homework, which keeps me motivated, too.   I want to become well-rounded in upcycling. There are already so many clothes in the world, so alterations feel like an important direction for the future. I’ve also been inspired by Vivienne Westwood , who talked about taking apart old clothes to teach herself how to make garments. I love the idea of learning from what’s already there and using that knowledge to create something new.   One project I have coming up is helping a friend make her wedding dress, which will be a great opportunity to develop my couture techniques. And if I’m not doing anything fashion-related, you’ll probably find me at the boxing gym most afternoons.   What’s your favourite part about what you do? Bringing my ideas to life. I love the whole design process, although you’ll sometimes catch me cursing at my machine or asking myself why I chose design when things get tough.   But, in all seriousness, nothing beats seeing all those hours of work come to life on someone especially when you see a change in their confidence, or the garment brings out a side of them they get to tap into. That’s the golden stuff right there. What has been the biggest learning curve so far? The biggest learning curve has been realising how much determination and perseverance it takes to bring a design to life. Things don’t always work the way you imagined, especially when you’re figuring out construction and fabrication, so you have to problem-solve, keep going and sometimes start again.   I can be a perfectionist, so I’ve been lucky to learn from my mentors, who remind me to make the garment exist first and perfect it later. Through that process, I’ve learned that I’m more persistent than I gave myself credit for. When you were starting out in your career, what was your dream job? How did you end up in your current role? I’ve always been an op shopper, long before it became what it is today. People would ask where I got my clothes, and I’d proudly say, “This whole look was under $10”. Op shops were much cheaper back then! That love of putting outfits together eventually led me to give fashion design a go.   It wasn’t until I watched the Alexander McQueen documentary that I thought, “Maybe I could actually do this ”. Lee hadn’t come from a wealthy family, and hearing about his journey made a career in fashion feel possible for me, too. A few years later, I’ve assisted on shows across Melbourne Fashion Festival and Melbourne Fashion Week, returned to study at RMIT, and debuted my first collection. Now I’ve been invited back to M/FW to show as a designer, which feels pretty special. What was the journey to Melbourne Fashion Week like? I worked for Ganbu Marra as a styling assistant in 2022 and from there gained more opportunities to assist on other shows for MFW. Moth design reached out for MFW and now we’re here and from what has been mentioned to me we are all in for an exciting show. Backstage at M/FW. (Image: Supplied) What’s your advice for people who want to work in your industry and type of role? When I was starting out in fashion, someone told me I’d be too sensitive for the industry because my anxiety had too much control over me. My advice is: don’t be afraid to put yourself out there. When you open yourself up to different people and experiences, you’ll find your crowd.   I started as a dresser, then became an assistant, and now I’m a designer. I always knew those behind-the-scenes roles were helping me build confidence and get used to the chaos of a runway.   I’ve pitched myself for all my jobs, including my roles in alterations and at the fabric store. There were plenty of rejections along the way. Even Adriano Carbone initially turned me down, but I went back and asked again. His wife, Maria , told me, “See, Ebony? Persistence is key”. It shows that the romanticism of simply asking is still alive. What's something you love about the industry and something you hate about the industry? I love that the fashion industry is big enough to hold so many different voices and perspectives from all walks of life. I understand that you have to earn your place, but being paid in “exposure” in this economy really sucks. Backstage at M/FW. (Image: Supplied) Okay, let's get into the quick fire round. If you weren’t doing your current job, what would you be doing? Probably living in New Zealand or up north living a slower life maybe have kids who knows. Do you have a work uniform? I never understood why big designers always showed up wearing the most basic things, but I can only speak for myself: when I’m locked in on creating my collection and sewing up looks, I have no space in my mind to care about curating a look for myself. So catch me literally wearing the same clothes every day until it’s done and, of course, it’s usually black. What’s the most unhinged thing you’ve seen at work we can legally publish? I mean, tailored suits are usually for people who have the money to spend on handmade garments. Some of these fabrics are $500 a metre! The conversations you hear are informative, but it’s also a whole other world. Who do you admire in your industry? I admire my sister, Savannah Kruger. She’s a model, and I love getting to see her in her element. We’re each other’s rocks out here in the industry. Describe your inbox in three words. DND How do you sign off your emails? Thanks, Ebony

title: Miley Cyrus Claps Back At 'Clickbait' Concert Critics Who Flamed Her Hollywood Bowl Performance
author: Rebekah Manibog
content: Sweet niblets! Miley Cyrus has clapped back at “clickbait” critics who flamed her recent Hollywood Bowl performance.  After four years, Cyrus returned to centre stage with a full concert last Friday at California's Hollywood Bowl.  While it marked a massive comeback for the teen-pop-star-turned-icon , reviews of her performance weren't too stellar, with some claiming that she wasn't fully committed to performing, as she reportedly made the audience sing along to a majority of her hits.  "There was a part in the show where she was on the B-stage and started performing 'We Can't Stop.' This was a running theme throughout the show where these old nostalgic hits—'Party in the USA', ‘Flowers’,'Wrecking Ball', 'We Can't Stop'—she would outsource to the crowd to sing for her, and even kind of acknowledged it at one point," TikToker Tyler Wells ( @ttylerwells ) said in a video that has more than 736.8K views.  On Sunday, after criticisms of Cyrus' performance went gangbusters online, the star decided to address the “clickbait” head-on.  “I’ve never heard that I don’t put my heart into something,” Cyrus began.  “I don’t know if any of you heard that somebody was doing commentary to get clickbait on their video talking about my show on Friday night, but I’m a lot of things, and we’re not even going to entertain that.” Cyrus addressing the “clickbait” during Sunday night's performance. (Image source: X)  The Bangerz artist acknowledged that every move she makes has been “controversial”.  "The controversy it used to be a lot of fun, and it still can be, and I can be pretty melted . I love that about me is I actually used to live my life pretty hard, 'cos life's hard, so I thought I had to get hard," she continued. "But I didn't enjoy my life as much when I was living hard . I love pouring myself into something ."  Cyrus went on to admit that returning to the stage was “hard”, especially after four years, sharing that things change, and that “we evolve, we grow, and we find what gets to come with us” and “what continued to fit”.  "I'll be honest… it is hard for me to stand up here and do the show . It does not come as naturally as it once did to me before," she said.  Towards the end, Cryus took aim at critics who questioned where her heart was when it came to her first Hollywood Bowl performance, confirming she was “fully present” on stage. " I can take a lot, but one thing I will not stand for is any question about where my heart is when I'm on this stage . I am fully present ," she said.    Mama's Mad! (Image source: X)  " Every bit of our fears, they live in the future, and I have no business even questioning that right now, because the only thing that I have is this moment with all of you.  "S o to make it clear, I am all here with you right now . Nowhere else I'd rather be . And rumour has it that the Sunday crowd is gonna show the Friday crowd what's up."  Cryus hit back at critics a second time — this time with that snazzy sass we all know and love — during her performance of “Bass Persuades”.  “Oh, I forgot, I'm supposed to sing every f*cking line,” she said.  The internet reacts to Miley Cyrus' clap back at concert critics While many were cheering for the Hannah Montana icon during her speech, her words received a mixed bag of emotions from punters online.  “ We pay so much money for these concerts; we are allowed to have opinions and standards,” one person wrote under Erik David 's TikTok account.  “We pay so much money for these concerts, we are allowed to have opinions and standards,” another wrote.  “I can't with the passive aggressiveness okay, diva,” another wrote.  Other fans gave Cyrus grace, highlighting that she'd lost her godmother, country music icon Dolly Parton , two months earlier. She also broke down in tears during her Friday performance, reflecting on her loss.  “Me and Dolly, we are eternal. Nothing in this life could ever tear us apart," she tearfully shared.  Cyrus has no upcoming dates, but honestly, I wouldn't be surprised if she took another couple of years off following the hullabaloo of these two gigs.

title: These High-End Marshall Headphones Are Under $200 Right Now
author: Pradershika Sharma
content: We may earn a commission from links on this page. Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication. Marshall’s Monitor III ANC headphones have the kind of design that makes you want to show them off. The textured earcups and gold logo lean fully into the amp-inspired look, and at $199.99 (down from $379.99 at launch), they’re finally priced in a way that feels competitive. It's their lowest price ever, according to price trackers . Marshall Monitor III ANC over-ear Bluetooth headphones $199.99 at Amazon $279.99 Save $80.00 Get Deal Get Deal $199.99 at Amazon $279.99 Save $80.00 These are over-ear Bluetooth headphones with active noise cancellation, and they’re clearly aimed at people cross-shopping Bose and Sony. The difference is that Marshall is selling a vibe along with the sound. The build feels sturdy, and small details like replaceable ear cushions and a swappable silicone headband strap suggest they’re made to last longer than most. They fold down neatly into a compact hard case (included), but they’re not water-resistant, so they’re better suited for travel and home listening than sweaty workouts. Living with them day to day is mostly smooth. The small gold joystick handles volume and track controls in a way that feels intuitive after a few minutes. There’s a separate button to toggle noise cancellation and transparency, plus a customizable shortcut button you can set up in the Marshall app. The app itself is simple, with a five-band EQ and a few presets, though it’s not especially deep if you like fine-tuning every frequency. Bluetooth 5.3 keeps connections stable, but you’re limited to AAC and SBC codecs, so there’s no hi-res audio support. You also can’t charge and listen through a traditional 3.5mm cable at the same time, since the single USB-C port handles both charging and wired playback. Battery life is where these headphones truly stand out. Up to 70 hours with ANC on is more than enough for long trips, and turning ANC off stretches that to an almost excessive 100 hours. As for sound, they deliver strong bass and crisp highs, with enough punch to make hip-hop and electronic tracks feel lively. Noise cancellation reduces plane engine rumble and city noise well, but it does not match leaders like Bose in blocking midrange chatter, notes this PCMag review .
