title: COLUMN: Students through a microscope
author: Melanie Knapp
content: Carter Durst, a newly appointed ASUI Senator, is an avid proponent that everyone should get involved in their university and strive to improve their economic, political and media literacy. Durst is a freshman majoring in political science and minoring in economics.   On top of his involvement with ASUI, he’s also a member of UI’s Economics Club. In a recent interview, Durst dived into his involvement with the Economics Club and ASUI, shedding light on various important topics. To begin, Durst discussed the Economics Club’s recent trip to Washington, D.C., which spanned from Oct. 7 to Oct. 10.   Students had the opportunity to meet with representatives from the Security and Exchange Commission (SEC), Cato Institute, Department of Labor, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and various Vandal alumni.   Durst’s key takeaway from the trip was that “the federal government does a lot more than you’d think.”   Relatedly, his favorite part of the trip was getting to know the federal government and the complex ways in which it functions.  “You really don’t know the sheer size of the federal government until you’re really in the mouth of it. Out here, we really don’t see it,” said Durst. “The people there, especially the civil servants, care so much about their jobs. I feel like a lot of times today people are trying to disparage federal workers when, really, they’re the live stream that gives us what we are.”   The trip also helped prepare Durst for his professional future by making him more aware of the hiring process, the growing presence of political appointees and how AI is being implemented in the federal government.   The Economic’s Club is planning another trip to Portland within the coming months. Durst noted that clubs offer opportunities to travel for students who’ve never done that before; get involved, and opportunities arise.   Durst also noted that every individual should get involved with economics, whether that’s joining the club or taking an entry-level class. Economics Club also discusses serious topics such as immigration and the effects immigrants have on the economy.   “If you don’t have a basic understanding… you’re not gonna be as educated when you make economic decisions,” said Durst. “Economics Club definitely adds a secondary perspective that I feel would be helpful for every student on campus.”   From there, the conversation became more focused on ASUI and the current political landscape through Durst’s eyes. According to Durst, the main goal of ASUI is to speak for the common student and bring positive change to UI.   Celebrating diversity–in everything from race, political ideology, and basic opinions–is especially important to ASUI, and Durst in specific.   “I like college because I feel like here you’re pushed with conflicting opinions, and I feel like University of Idaho is in a very unique position where I feel like we get a very interesting core of students,” said Durst. “I think having conflicting views and being able to have conversations is very important.”   However, Durst did note that he believes politics are shifting from getting things done to attacking people with differing opinions.   He’s noticed this in Congress and feels that it’s bleeding down into ASUI “because a lot of people here are very passionate, which means they, a lot of the time, think emotionally, not necessarily logically.”   On top of that, he believes the country is falling away from merit and instead prioritizing loyalty and money. “[We’re] two wings of the same bird, right? I feel like the biggest thing that I wish people would realize… [is that] a house cannot fall together, but it can only fall from within,” said Durst.   One reason he proposes is the divisive nature of the media, which is contributing to a lack of media literacy and an us-versus-them mentality. It’s not uncommon for people of opposing political parties to immediately distrust views from anyone outside their party, potentially leading to a refusal to even engage with the other person.   “I see that in my own family,” said Durst. “Political divides have gotten that sharp, and I feel like that’s almost their intention, because if they do get that sharp, people vote just off a letter instead of policies.”   Durst encourages everyone to expand their media diet and make educated voting decisions. When it comes to student government, Durst has several ideas he’s trying to implement at the university. This includes repealing the ban on tasers, making parking tickets cheaper for students and improving quality at the Eatery.  “I’m gonna try my best to bring change this year through ASUI. That’s my biggest goal,” said Durst. For more information on UI’s organizations and events, visit the Engage UIdaho website.   Melanie Knapp can be reached at arg-life@uidaho.edu .

title: Fruit Bats perform at University of Idaho
author: Melanie Knapp
content: The Fruit Bats, an indie folk-rock band, performed on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at the University of Idaho’s International Ballroom.  The concert showcased the band’s newest album, “The Landfill,” which came out June 12 of this year through Merge Records.  According to Eric Johnson who leads and founded The Fruit Bats, the core concept of “The Landfill” is to use the image of a landfill as a metaphor for the “mountain dominating the landscape of [his] heart.”  Johnson, originally from the Midwest, describes his home region as a large, vacant expanse dotted with landfills that symbolize the past as well as prospects for the future, balancing a mournful and emotional tone in his music.  According to Johnson, “It’s both a very personal record, and my most collaborative to date.”   When it comes to instrumentals, David Dawda is on bass, Josh Mease is on guitars and synth, Frank LoCrasto is on piano and synth and Kosta Galanopoulos is on drums.  The opener for the concert was Matthew Logan Vasquez. Vasquez got the audience charged through his passion for indie rock, which was evident through classic head banging, screaming into the mic, and loud instrumentals.  After a brief intermission, the Fruit Bats took the stage.  Their music distinctly crossed genres, combining indie rock, folk rock and alternative country.   On top of their unique musical approach, their songs offered a chance to reflect on serious topics such as life, love and anxiety.  The room was a dark but colorful haze, the simple lighting and setting contributing to a small-town feel. This made it easy for the band to truly connect with the audience.  Johnson talked to the crowd throughout the show.  Near the start of the performance, Johnson revealed that this was his first ever performance in Moscow–however, he’s played several times in the neighboring town of Pullman.  The crowd booed in response, to which Johnson laughed and apologized for being unaware of the small-town rivalry.  Later, he shared a story about when he was a senior in high school. At one of his shows, he was asked if he could play two hours’ worth of music. He said yes, despite having only five songs in his pocket.  Now, he has over two hours of music to perform with.  One such song he performed resembled a waltz, during which Johnson encouraged audience members to find a partner and dance. The audience responded in kind.  Johnson also wished one eventgoer a happy birthday, to which everyone cheered.  Students and adults of all ages attended the concert. For students, the concert offered an opportunity to relax during a busy week of midterms.   According to Nashwa Khan, a UI student who attended the concert, “the vibes were like a low lit, neon haze indie-folk groove session with strangers. And I felt that bass in my chest.”  Khan also noted that the venue gave audience members flexibility in how they enjoyed the music.  “You could be in the crowd if you wanted to or enjoy it intimately by just stepping back a little.”  The band performed for nearly two hours. Before the finale, the crowd chanted “One more song,” their love for the band and their music evident.  Melanie Knapp can be reached at arg-life@uidaho.edu .

title: What to expect at the Kenworthy in late October
author: McKinley Forth
content: The Kenworthy’s October calendar is lined up with many movies and events for and by the local community. There are horror and thriller showings in anticipation of Halloween, theater productions, live shows, and some lighthearted movies as well. Here’s an overview of the many types of things going on at the Kenworthy throughout October.  From Colleges   These events are from colleges and campus clubs, with some being free for UI and WSU students.  Palouse French Film Festival – Oct. 13, 20, 27, 2026 at 7 pm  From WSU and UI, the Palouse French Film Festival will show French-language films The Stranger on October 13, In His Own Image on October 20, and Colors of Time on October 27. Entry is free for WSU and UI students; tickets are $5 or $12 for a Festival Pass.  Events   There are more than just movies at the Kenworthy; there are live performances and music as well.  Moscow Community Theater: Nosferatu – Oct. 29-31, 2026 at 7:30 pm and Oct. 31, 2026 at 2 pm  The Moscow Community Theater will be performing Nosferatu by John Faust. A link to purchase tickets is on the Kenworthy website.  Overall, there are many movies and events to see at the Kenworthy this October but as for what the Kenworthy staff is looking forward to Ben Ramalingam, whose worked at the Kenworthy for eight years, says “October has a lot of good things: between Rocky Horror Picture Show, which we do every year, we’re ending with a live play of Nosferatu I’m excited for that. But this year’s been our 100th year, and we’ve been doing centennial movies each month, and I am looking forward to Little Miss Sunshine; that one’s going to be a lot of fun.”  McKinley Forth can be reached at Fort8237@vandals.uidaho.edu

title: The Palouse French Film Festival returns to the Kenworthy
author: Cooper Molinengo
content: Started in 2010, the annual Palouse French Film Festival is back for its 16th iteration, with a notable roster of recent French films for audiences to enjoy, this year’s titles including Dossier 137 (Case 137) showing Tuesday, October 6, L’Étranger (The Stranger) showing Tuesday, October 13, À son image (In His Own Image) showing Tuesday, October 20 and La venue de l’avenir (Colours of Time) ending off the festival with its showing on Tuesday, October 27.  The first film of this season, Dossier 137 (Case 137), follows the story of an internal affairs investigator, Stéphanie Bertrand, played by Léa Drucker, whose job is policing the police. Following a civilian riot in the streets of France, Bertrand takes up a case in which a projectile fired by an officer in the riot struck a protester in the head, causing significant brain damage and a lifetime of struggle for the victim and his family. As Bertrand investigates, she deals with pressure from the police to lay off on her investigation, including from her divorced husband, confronts the realities of the public’s negative perception of law enforcement, including within her own family, and discovers she has a personal connection to the victim, pressuring herself to work harder to solve the case despite her personal bias being against investigation policy. The film was extremely relevant as the opening film of this year’s festival considering the current major riots taking place within France.  Sara Nelson, co-organizer of the festival, discussed how the festival is a continued collaboration between the University of Idaho and Washington State University, as well as with the Kenworthy, to bring French culture and language to the Palouse. “Our first priority was to provide a vehicle for cultural education to the students of our two universities, and for that reason, we made sure to offer free admission to students,” she stated while talking about the history of the event.  “It was also very important to us to be a resource for the broader communities of Moscow, Pullman, and the Palouse, and so we committed to keeping general admission prices low and to offering a very affordable festival pass.”  As a result, the festival has grown to be attended each year by a blend of roughly 40% students and 60% community members.   Sara Nelson explains how herself and the event’s other organizer, Sabine Davis of WSU, go about choosing a variety of films from such a large pool of potential selections. “We watch the French and American press for films that gain critical acclaim, we pay attention to the films that appear at various significant film festivals… We look for films that have something interesting to show about the societies they represent, something that audiences can learn as they watch.”  Layla Grace, French tutor and student at UI, provided her input on the value of the event to students.  “It’s important to have events centered around other cultures and people so that we widen our perspectives- not just French films but any foreign films! We are so used to focusing on what’s popular on Netflix or showing at the movies that I think sometimes we can lose track of the importance of learning and consuming media outside of our “bubbles”. À son image (In His Own Image), is the showing Grace is most interested in because of the various topics she anticipates the film will discuss and its setting in Corsica.  “People can expect to learn something from each film they attend, and to come away with interesting questions to think over. We help to amplify this effect by including some brief remarks before each film—remarks delivered by faculty members from the two universities in fields that connect with the content of the films,” Nelson adds.  Films will be showing through Tuesday, October 27, each Tuesday at 7pm at the Kenworthy in downtown Moscow.  Nelson concluded that “People can also expect a great communal experience when they attend the festival. Watching and reacting to the films while in the company of a diverse mix of other spectators is an enriching experience all in itself. And finally, audience members who attend the first and last films in each year’s festival will be treated to receptions with delicious food and drink and the chance to rub elbows with other French film fans!”  Cooper Molinengo can be reached at arg-life@uidaho.edu .

title: Regional Theatre of the Palouse presents the Addams family
author: Grace Boehland
content: The Regional Theatre of the Palouse delighted audiences with the opening night of The Addams Family, directed by John Rich. A sold-out house erupted with laughter and applause as spectators were welcomed into the delightfully deathly world of everyone’s favorite eccentric family.  The Addams Family is the story of the beloved, wicked family many know and love. This production focuses on the family’s daughter, Wednesday Addams, who was played by Ecuadorian actress and singer Beatriz Coronel.  Wednesday falls in love and keeps it a secret from the rest of her family: Gomez Addams played by Andre Felipe, Morticia Addams played by Lauren Carolyn Jones, Uncle Fester played by Travis Tingvall, Grandma played by Tina McClure, Lurch the butler played by Ethan Shaw and her little brother Pugsley played by Henry Weldon.  The Addams, being who they are, do not take well to the fact that their little Wednesday has fallen in love with a boy from Ohio, named Lucas, played by Braydon Simmons. His family, Mal Beineke and his wife Alice, played by Micheal Todd and Shannon Payette Seip, joins him in meeting the Addams in their spooky home in New York.  On the night that the Addams host the boy’s family, the Addams ancestors are trapped from returning to the dead realm they belong in by Uncle Fester. He is determined to make sure Wednesday and Lucas are happy, ever after, and wants help from the ancestors.  The production was well put together and created a spooky place in such a small theatre.  RTOP is not the biggest theatre but has the biggest heart; you can feel one with the play with how close the stage is to the audience. They constructed the family home with such creepy, pernicious elements and helped us be one with the scene with different backgrounds.  The costume department created the looks for each of the characters. Each ancestor was from a different decade of the Addams family’s past. They were given a white appearance of ghostly figures helping the young Wednesday to find her love.  A great scene that made the audience swoon with love was Uncle fester portraying his love to the moon. The background was light by a black curtain with lights to simulate the stars, the moon because a ballerina and danced into festers heart.  The production was expertly directed and choreographed, bringing energy, precision, and personality to every scene. Each department made a memorable impact, with the makeup team standing out for their incredible transformations that made the cast look as though they had stepped straight out of the Addams Family universe.  Under the director’s vision, the show embraced the beloved spirit of the original while adding a unique Regional Theatre of the Palouse touch, creating a production that felt both familiar and plainly its own.  Opening night was a great success with little pitfalls of nerves and forgetfulness, but overall, the night opened the show to greatness. Each of the Addams were portrayed in a unique way, and each had voices that could wake up all ancestors with a smile.  The Addams Family will continue its run from Oct. 15 through Oct. 25, with most performances beginning at 7:30 p.m. Select dates also feature a 1:30 p.m. matinee. General admission tickets range from $33 to $36, with discounted rates available for groups of 10.  Audiences are invited to spend an evening with the amusingly eccentric Addams family as long-buried secrets come to light; relationships are tested, and love takes center stage in a twister of passion, humor, and tango.  Grace Boeland can be reached at arg-life@uidaho.edu

title: Vandals shut out Southern Utah and keeps the Kibbie Dome undefeated
author: Star Stephans
content: The University of Idaho women’s soccer team delivered a memorable performance Sunday afternoon, defeating Southern Utah University 4-0 at the P1FCU Kibbie Dome. The victory capped Homecoming weekend as the Vandals finished their home schedule unbeaten and gave their graduating players a memorable final appearance in front of the home crowd. Idaho established control early, scoring three goals in the first half before adding another in the final seconds of the match. Makenna Stuart and Hallie Prinos-Grumbach led the offensive charge, combining for two goals and four assists. Senior Calli Chiarelli capped the afternoon with a late goal to seal the victory. The win improved Idaho’s overall record to 8-3-5, including a 2-1-3 mark in Big Sky Conference play. The Vandals also finished their home schedule with five wins and three draws, remaining unbeaten at the Kibbie Dome throughout the season. Idaho wasted little time establishing its offensive rhythm. In the 11th minute, Stuart opened the scoring with a goal assisted by Prinos-Grumbach, giving the Vandals an early 1-0 lead. The connection between the two players proved effective again just minutes later. Before the 15-minute mark, Stuart scored her second goal of the afternoon, once again finishing a pass from Prinos-Grumbach. The quick pair of goals put Southern Utah under immediate pressure and gave Idaho a 2-0 advantage. The Vandals continued to attack rather than settle into their lead. In the 30th minute, Mia Boltz found the back of the net following another assist from Prinos-Grumbach. The goal extended Idaho’s lead to 3-0 and capped a first-half performance in which the Vandals consistently created scoring opportunities. Idaho entered halftime with a 13-3 advantage in shots. The three-goal lead allowed the Vandals to approach the second half with confidence while maintaining their defensive discipline. Although Idaho’s offensive production attracted much of the attention, its defensive performance was equally important. Southern Utah attempted nine shots but could not find the back of the net against the Vandal defense. Senior goalkeeper Paula Flores played all 90 minutes and recorded four saves to preserve the shutout. Idaho finished with a 21-9 advantage in total shots and a 9-4 edge in shots on goal. The Vandals also earned six corner kicks compared with Southern Utah’s one. The shutout marked Idaho’s 10th of the season, highlighting the defensive consistency that has helped the team remain competitive throughout the campaign. Sunday’s match also carried significance beyond the final score. Homecoming provided an opportunity to recognize the players who have contributed to the program throughout their collegiate careers. The celebration received a fitting conclusion in the final moments of the match. With five seconds remaining, Chiarelli scored Idaho’s fourth goal, finishing an assist from fellow senior Tori Peters. The late goal capped the 4-0 victory and an unbeaten home campaign for the Vandals. With its home schedule complete, Idaho will turn its attention to the final stretch of the season. The Vandals are scheduled to travel to Portland State on Thursday, Oct. 29, as they continue their Big Sky Conference campaign. The challenge moving forward will be maintaining that level of execution on the road. Conference matches will be important as Idaho looks to strengthen its position in the standings and finish the regular season on a high note. As the Vandals prepare for their remaining conference matches, they will carry the confidence of a dominant Homecoming performance and an unbeaten home record into the final stretch of the season. The Vandals will next march into Portland State to take on the Vikings this Thursday, October 29 at 1 p.m.

title: Forsman’s 53-yard walk-off field goal lifts Idaho past Southern Utah
author: Liam Bradford
content: Idaho’s junior placekicker, Owen Forsman, came to Moscow as a highly-touted local recruit from Lakeland High School in Rathdrum. He earned his first chance to kick extra points and field goals last season in the first year under head coach Thomas Ford Jr., who recruited Forsman in 2023 when he was Idaho’s special teams coordinator.  Forsman made his first nine collegiate field goal attempts and had not yet been tested with any adversity. Two weeks ago against Weber State, Forsman faced his first real bump in the road. In the cold afternoon wind of Ogden, Utah, Forsman missed all three of his field goal attempts.  Against Montana, he made six PATs, and he has now made the first 33 extra points of his career. Saturday, he lined up with one second remaining on the clock and the game tied. He delivered, sending a 53-yard kick through the uprights as time expired to give the Vandals (3-5, 3-2) a 31-28 Homecoming victory over Southern Utah (3-5, 2-3) at the P1FCU Kibbie Dome. Forsman’s kick capped a frantic finish to a game in which Idaho built a 10-point fourth-quarter lead, watched Southern Utah erase it in the final minute, and then won it on a walk-off field goal.   The victory continued Idaho’s turnaround after an 0-4 start. The Vandals have now won three of their last four games, including victories over No. 1 Montana State and No. 7 Montana. “The heart rate is a little bit high after that,” Ford said.  Forsman’s decisive kick came after a six-play, 40-yard drive in the final 42 seconds. Joshua Wood found Zack Card for a 10-yard completion and then connected with Gus Donnerberg for nine yards to move the Vandals across midfield. After a pass-interference penalty against Southern Utah extended the drive, Wood found Card again for six yards to the 35-yard line. That set up Forsman, who completed a perfect afternoon on field goals to move to 15-for-19 in his career.  “I had no doubt when he took the field that he was going to make that kick,” Ford said.  “Everyone on that sideline knew that if we could get a field goal attempt anywhere inside of 55, he was going to make it,”  Despite a good defensive showing from Idaho, Southern Utah’s final stats benefited from a handful of explosive runs from their quarterback Will Burns.  The Thunderbirds finished with 450 total yards, including 245 rushing yards. Burns accounted for 392 yards of total offense, throwing for 205 yards and rushing for 187. Despite Burns’ production, Idaho’s defense made limiting Southern Utah running back Floyd Chalk a priority. Chalk entered the game among the FCS leaders in rushing but finished with 58 yards on 17 carries, his first game of the season below 100 yards. “I thought our defense played their best game of the season,” Ford said. “Coach Stalker put together a phenomenal plan that allowed our guys to play really fast.” The defense was dominant early on, but the Thunderbirds eventually found their rhythm. Burns broke a 37-yard run during a scoring drive in the second quarter, setting up Chalk’s 19-yard touchdown run that gave Southern Utah a 7-3 lead. On the ensuing drive, Damonte Bias broke loose for a 37-yard run, and Wood followed by finding Markel Taylor for a 19-yard touchdown pass. The score gave Taylor his first Division I touchdown.  On Idaho’s final drive of the first half, Wood scrambled for 36 yards to put the Vandals near the goal line, and Hayden Kincheloe finished the drive with a 1-yard touchdown run. After a Southern Utah penalty on the extra-point attempt, Idaho went for two, with Wood connecting with Donnerberg to make it 18-10 at halftime. The Thunderbirds needed little time to respond after the break. Burns took off scrambling for a 76-yard touchdown run on Southern Utah’s opening possession of the second half and tied the game at 18.  Early in the fourth quarter, Donnerberg joined Taylor by catching his first career touchdown as Idaho took a 28-18 lead. Ford said Idaho’s physical approach on the ground was central to the offensive performance. The Vandals rushed for 227 yards, averaging 5.8 yards per carry. Bias led the ground game with 89 yards on 11 carries, and Kincheloe added 46 yards and a touchdown. “Our offensive line really did a great job being physical, really dominating the line of scrimmage,” Ford said. Southern Utah drew within seven with under five minutes remaining on a 32-yard field goal. Idaho went three-and-out, giving the Thunderbirds the ball with under four minutes to go.   Isiah Bivins came up huge with a fourth-down pass breakup, giving Idaho the ball back; Idaho needed just one first down to end the game. Kincheloe fumbled on the second play of the drive, giving the Thunderbirds one final chance.  Trailing 28-21 with less than a minute remaining, the Thunderbirds converted a fourth down as Burns connected with Mark Bails Jr. for a 57-yard touchdown pass with 42 seconds left. It was a strong comeback effort, but Forsman’s field goal negated all of it.  Idaho travels to face Portland State on Oct. 31, looking to extend its recent run of success. The game kicks off at 1 p.m. on ESPN+.

title: Idaho volleyball defeats Southern Utah in four sets on Homecoming weekend
author: Sage Larson
content: The University of Idaho volleyball team defeated Southern Utah University in four sets Oct. 24, earning a second win over the Thunderbirds during Homecoming weekend. Southern Utah entered the match with an 0-8 Big Sky Conference record, while Idaho began the game at 2-7 in conference play. Looking to build momentum at home, the Vandals delivered a strong performance through the first two sets before Southern Utah responded in the third. Idaho regrouped in the fourth to secure the victory and improve to 12-10 overall. Idaho opened the match with an efficient offensive performance, recording 13 kills and a .391 hitting percentage in the first set. The Vandals established an early advantage with a six-point run that put them ahead 13-6. They maintained control for the remainder of the set, winning 25-16. The second set followed a similar pattern. Idaho built an early lead and put together an eight-point run to create separation. Southern Utah attempted to close the gap but remained at least four points behind for much of the set. Kills from Anika Hudson and Kiana Greer helped Idaho finish the second set 25-17, putting the Vandals one set away from the match victory. Southern Utah responded in the third set, finding more consistency and taking control of the game. Idaho recorded nine kills and committed six errors, while the Thunderbirds finished with 10 kills and five errors. The Vandals struggled to regain their earlier offensive rhythm as Southern Utah maintained its lead. The Thunderbirds eventually took the set 25-22, forcing a fourth set and keeping the match alive. Idaho entered the fourth set looking to close out the match. The Vandals limited their errors to two and played with greater efficiency, regaining control after Southern Utah’s third-set win. Greer helped lead the way offensively as Idaho pulled away to secure a 25-17 victory in the fourth set. The win gave the Vandals their third conference victory of the season and capped a successful Homecoming weekend for Idaho athletics. Greer led the Vandals with 18 kills, two service aces and three blocks. Her return to the lineup provided a significant boost after she was absent from Idaho’s match against Utah Tech earlier in the week. Hudson contributed five kills and a team-high seven blocks, helping strengthen Idaho’s defense at the net. Sarah Sullivan and Allie Ferrin also recorded five kills apiece, with each adding three blocks. On the defensive end, libero Kiera Kleidon led Idaho with 15 digs. Setter Csenge Krakoczki added nine digs and recorded 25 assists, helping the Vandals distribute the ball throughout the match. Idaho’s ability to limit errors proved important in closing out the victory. After struggling with mistakes in the previous match against Utah Tech, the Vandals showed improved consistency, particularly in the fourth set. Southern Utah also received a strong performance from junior Audrey Atwood, who finished with 12 kills, four blocks and 10 digs. Setter Uruena Jensen added 15 assists and eight digs for the Thunderbirds. Despite Southern Utah’s third-set response, Idaho maintained its composure and finished the match with a decisive fourth-set performance. The victory provided the Vandals with momentum as they prepared to return to conference play on the road. Idaho will travel to Flagstaff, Arizona, next week to face Northern Arizona University and Portland State University. The Vandals will look to respond against Northern Arizona after losing to the Lumberjacks in Moscow two weeks earlier before taking on Portland State, whom Idaho recently defeated.

title: Vandals finish scoreless against Utah Tech
author: Star Stephans
content: The University of Idaho women’s soccer team welcomed students, alumni and community members to the P1FCU Kibbie Dome on Thursday night for a Homecoming matchup against Utah Tech. Despite creating several offensive opportunities, the Vandals were unable to find the back of the net, and the contest ended in a 0-0 draw. While neither team managed to score, the match provided plenty of action on the field and energy in the stands. Nearly 900 fans attended the game, making it one of Idaho’s highest-attended matches of the season. The university also incorporated Homecoming festivities into the event, hosting its “Most Vandalized Fan” and “Yell Like Hell” activities. Student groups showcased Vandal-themed outfits and competed through spirited school chants, while the presence of Greek life helped bring additional excitement to the Kibbie Dome. Idaho entered Thursday’s contest looking to use its home-field advantage against a competitive Utah Tech team. The Vandals wasted little time creating offensive pressure, recording three shots during the opening eight minutes as they attempted to establish control of the match. Sophomore forward Mia Boltz helped lead the early attack with a shot in the second minute. Payton Oelkers followed with an attempt less than a minute later as Idaho continued looking for an early breakthrough. The Vandals maintained their offensive pressure throughout the match, finishing with an 11-7 advantage in total shots. Idaho also recorded five corner kicks compared with Utah Tech’s three, giving the Vandals additional opportunities to challenge the Trailblazers’ defense. Despite Idaho’s statistical advantage, neither team could convert its chances into a goal. Both defenses held firm throughout the opening half, keeping the match scoreless heading into the break. The second half continued in a similar fashion, with Idaho searching for a breakthrough while Utah Tech worked to limit the Vandals’ attacking opportunities. Although Idaho generated more shots and corner kicks, the Trailblazers remained organized defensively and prevented the home team from taking the lead. As the match progressed, the Vandals continued to push forward in search of a winning goal. However, Utah Tech’s defensive resistance proved difficult to overcome, and Idaho could not capitalize on its offensive advantage before the final whistle. The result moved Idaho to a 7-3-5 overall record and a 1-1-3 mark in conference play. Utah Tech left Moscow with a 7-6-3 overall record and a 3-2-2 conference record. Although the Vandals were unable to secure a victory, their advantage in shots demonstrated their ability to create opportunities against a challenging opponent. The next step will be turning those chances into goals as the team continues its push through conference play. Thursday’s match also highlighted the importance of the support surrounding the program. With nearly 900 fans in attendance, the Homecoming crowd provided a strong atmosphere for the Vandals as they competed in front of students, alumni and families. The combination of Homecoming activities and a competitive conference matchup gave the evening significance beyond the final score. While the Vandals would have preferred a win, the crowd’s energy helped create a memorable setting for the team and its supporters. Idaho will have another opportunity to compete at home Sunday, Oct. 25, when the Vandals host their Senior Night. The match will recognize the team’s graduating players as they approach the end of their collegiate careers. With conference play continuing, Idaho will look to build on its offensive production and find ways to finish scoring opportunities. The Vandals have demonstrated an ability to generate chances, but converting those opportunities will be important as they pursue their postseason goals. As the season moves forward, the team will aim to carry the energy from Thursday’s Homecoming crowd into its next match. Senior Night will provide another opportunity for the Vandals to compete in front of their home supporters while working toward a strong finish to the season. The Vandals next test will be up against Southern Utah on Sunday, Oct. 25 at 1 p.m.

title: Vandals swept by Utah Tech on the road
author: Sage Larson
content: The University of Idaho volleyball team hit the road this week to take on the Utah Tech Trailblazers in St. George, Utah. Following a difficult matchup against Northern Arizona last week, the Vandals entered the game with a 2-6 conference record, looking to rebound against a Utah Tech team that had gone 9-0 in conference play and 16-3 overall. The Trailblazers continued their winning streak against Idaho, earning a sweep in three sets. The first set opened competitively, with Utah Tech scoring three consecutive points. However, Idaho responded and kept the score close as both teams battled for the lead. Halfway through the set, the Vandals used 10 kills to build a 17-13 advantage, giving themselves an opportunity to close out the set. Utah Tech responded with several kills, while Idaho struggled with unforced errors. The Trailblazers eventually pulled ahead, taking the first set 25-22 in a closely contested matchup. Despite the loss, Idaho recorded 15 kills, matching Utah Tech’s offensive production in the opening set. Idaho carried its offensive momentum into the second set, recording another 15 kills. However, the Vandals struggled to overcome Utah Tech’s blocking and fell behind early. The Trailblazers maintained control throughout the set, using their attack to keep Idaho from closing the gap. Utah Tech’s senior outside hitter helped lead the offense before a service ace secured a 25-17 set victory and gave the Trailblazers a two-set advantage. Utah Tech carried that momentum into the third set, taking control as Idaho struggled to regain its footing. The Vandals had difficulty maintaining consistency, and their errors continued to accumulate. Idaho committed nine errors in the final set, allowing the Trailblazers to finish the sweep. The 25-14 final set gave Utah Tech the straight-set victory and handed Idaho another conference loss. Errors remained a significant issue for the Vandals throughout the match. Idaho finished with 25 errors compared with just six for Utah Tech, a difference that made it difficult for the Vandals to capitalize on their offensive production. Although Idaho kept pace in several statistical categories, the Trailblazers limited their mistakes and took advantage of Idaho’s struggles to secure the win. Despite the loss, Idaho found success in several areas. Sophomore setter Csenge Krakoczki led the Vandals with 32 assists, finishing with twice as many as Utah Tech setter Marley Roe, who recorded 16. Idaho also outperformed the Trailblazers defensively in the back row, recording 41 digs to Utah Tech’s 31. Both teams finished with 39 kills, showing that Idaho could match the Trailblazers offensively. However, the Vandals struggled to produce points from the service line and at the net. Idaho finished without a service ace, while Utah Tech recorded seven. The Trailblazers also finished with eight blocks, giving them an advantage in a category where Idaho struggled to find answers. Graduate student Anika Hudson led Idaho at the net with 11 kills, followed by junior Allie Ferrin with 10. Ferrin recorded half of her kills in the second set, helping the Vandals remain competitive offensively despite falling behind. Although Idaho finished with more digs as a team, libero Kiera Kleidon recorded 12, her lowest total across the team’s previous five games. Idaho also played without sophomore outside hitter Kiana Greer, who has been a consistent contributor in passing, hitting and serving throughout the season. Her absence presented another challenge for the Vandals as they attempted to keep pace with Utah Tech. The Trailblazers were led offensively by Kennedi Knudsen, who recorded eight kills. Nana Asiata and Tessa Treanor each added seven kills, while Treanor contributed four of Utah Tech’s seven service aces. Defensively, Mya Laufiso finished with 14 digs, and Reese Sydney led the team with three blocks. The victory extended Utah Tech’s winning streak and kept the Trailblazers undefeated in conference play at 9-0. Their ability to remain composed and capitalize on Idaho’s errors helped them maintain control, even as the Vandals kept pace in kills and digs. For Idaho, the match highlighted the importance of limiting errors and finding more opportunities to score at the service line and at the net. The Vandals will return to Memorial Gym to host the Southern Utah Thunderbirds on Saturday, Oct. 24, looking to regroup and get back on track in conference play.

title: Stegner against overpoliticization in Idaho
author: David Galindo
content: The Argonaut interviewed John Stegner, a candidate running for Governor of Idaho, at an open house on Sept. 29. Stegner is a former justice on the Idaho Supreme Court. In the interview, he discusses why he ran as an independent and how perceived overpoliticization has affected the position.  John Stenger | Courtesy, stegnerforidaho.com “I was dissatisfied with the political system as it existed and thought throwing my hat in the ring as an independent would give people an alternative that wasn’t being presented in any other way,” said Stegner. He mentioned his dissatisfaction with Governor Brad Little’s State of the State address as his final inspiration to run.  When asked about the experience he had as a justice could bring, he said that “you deal with the governor and the legislature in very real ways … I listened to the facts and the law.” Stegner also said that the position of governor has moved away from fact and evidence-based governing and towards overt politicization.  Stegner mentioned healthcare, education and nuclear waste as his three campaign priorities.   “We’ve lost 35% of our OB/GYNs and half of our maternal fetal medicine specialists … I think directly related to the fact that we have laws that don’t address women’s healthcare in ways that it should,” Stegner said on healthcare. He also said that he would veto a legislative attempt to overrule Prop 1 if it passed.   On education, he brought up a quote regarding the funding of schools: “I heard about a former governor, [who said] ‘we’re not fulfilling our constitutional obligation to the students, but we’re doing the best we can.’” He pointed out the inherent contradiction and how he said he believes public schools are not being properly funded.   Regarding nuclear waste, he stated his concern with efforts that would turn the Idaho National Laboratory into a site for such waste and radioactive material. He called back to former governors Cecil Andrus and Phil Batt, who both fought against efforts in the 90s to store waste in Idaho. “I’m very worried that we’re rushing into this, I haven’t seen why … if we don’t get this right, we can be paying the price for the rest of existence,” Stegner said.   When asked about what he has learned during his campaign, he praised what he learned about American Falls superintendent Randy Jensen, who achieved universal preschool in the town of just over 4,500. “That strikes me as a very good idea,” he said. He also thanked his social media coordinator, a University of Idaho graduate.  Stegner is facing off against incumbent Brad Little (R) and Terri Pickens (D). In his closing remarks, Stegner reflected on Idaho “I’m in this race because I think Idaho is worth fighting for. I think we’ve been on the wrong path for several years, if not, more than that. I’d like to get Idaho back to the Idaho that I grew up in, one that let people live their lives … That’s what I’m fighting for,” he said.  David Galindo can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Governor, U.S. Senator, U.S. Rep. positions up for reelection
author: David Galindo
content: Idaho voters will cast their ballots for the governor of the state and two seats in Congress when they go to the polls on Tuesday, Nov. 3.  Issues on voters’ minds in this mid-term election include high gasoline and diesel prices stemming from the U.S.’ conflict with Iran, higher food prices, tariffs placed on imported goods, and housing affordability. Another issue for Idahoans is public land; the Trump administration has suggested selling off some federal land in western states. All Idaho candidates are generally opposed to that effort, while maintaining that the federal government needs to better support staffing in federal public land agencies that was decimated by the DOGE cuts in 2025 led by Elon Musk.   Currently Republicans hold a 53-45 advantage in the Senate (with two independents) and a slim 218-214 majority in the House of Representatives, with two vacant seats and one independent. Democrats hope to flip enough seats nationwide to regain majorities in Congress.   Left to right: Jim Risch (R), Matt Loesby (C), Natalie Flemming (D), Todd Achilles (I), At the top of the ballot are the federal races for U.S. Senate and U.S. representative for Idaho’s First congressional district. Republican incumbent Jim Risch is running for his fourth term in the U.S. Senate; his main challenger is independent Todd Achilles, a veteran and former representative in the Idaho Legislature. Independent Natalie M. Fleming and Libertarian Matt Loesby are also in the race. Achilles is considered to have the best chance to unseat Risch, but statewide polls, which have widely varied, mostly show Risch with a commanding 10- or more point lead.  Left to right: Sarah Zabel (I), Russ Fulcher (R), Kaylee Peterson (D) Not Pictured: Brendan J. Gomez (C)  For representative, Republican incumbent Russ Fulcher is running for his fifth term. He is being challenged by Democrat Kaylee Peterson, independent Sarah Zabel and Constitution candidate Brendan J. Gomez. Polls indicate a 20- or more point lead for Fulcher over Peterson.  Left to right: Brad Little (R), Pro-life (politican) (C), Terri Pickens (D), John Stenger (I) Republican Brad Little is running for his third term as Governor. He is being challenged by Democratic lawyer Terri Pickens, independent and former Idaho Supreme Court justice John Stegner (see page 12 for interview with Stegner), Libertarian candidate Paul Sand, and the perennial anti-abortion candidate who goes by the name Pro-Life. A Democrat has not held the governor’s position for 30 years. The race for Lieutenant Governor is a head-to-head between incumbent Scott Bedke (R) and Democrat Eric Myricks.  Left to right: Shawn Keagan (D), Phil McGrane (R) For Secretary of State, the race pits Republican incumbent Phil McGrane against Democrat Shawn Keenan. The Secretary of State is responsible for administrating and regulating elections, registering businesses among other authorities such as notarization and liens. Left to Right: Brandon D Woolf (R), Rakesh Mohan (D) The race for State Controller is between Republican incumbent Brandon D. Woolf and Democrat Rakesh Moran. The State Controller manages Idaho’s fiscal affairs. The position is not to be confused with the separate State Treasurer, who performs as Idaho’s head banker and head of investments. That race is contested between Republican incumbent Julie A. Ellsworth and Democrat Kevin A. Jones.  Left to right: Lori Hickman (D), Raul Labrador (R) For Attorney General—the state’s chief legal officer—incumbent Raúl Labrador (R) is being challenged by Democrat Lori Hickman. (See page 12 for interview with Hickman.) Labrador is seeking his second term as attorney general, while this is Hickman’s first run for public office. She has said Labrador has “politicized” the attorney general’s office, while Labrador has countered that he is simply aggressive in enforcing the law.  Labrador served two terms in the Idaho legislature and four terms in Congress as a U.S. representative, and unsuccessfully challenged Little for the governor’s seat in 2018.   Left to right: Debbie Critchfield (R), Becky Sundin Mitchell (D) Not Pictured: Teresa Roundy (C) The last statewide office on the ballot is for Superintendent of Public Instruction, the head of the state Department of Education. Republican incumbent Debbie Critchfield faces off against Democrat and teacher Becky Sundin Mitchell and Constitution Party candidate Teresa Roundy.  David Galindo can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Latah County Commissioner candidate pledges accountability
author: Olivia Maggs
content: Dan Schoenberg, a Latah County Commissioner candidate, acknowledged his mistake in a 2006 petit theft case and said he will be accountable and humble if elected to the commission.   On Aug. 23, 2006, Schoenberg was charged with misdemeanor petit theft for $970 in unauthorized expenditures made by Schoenberg from the year 2000 through 2004 while working as the auxiliary services director at the University of Idaho.  He used money from his auxiliary services budget to make personal purchases. These purchases included tools, supplies, and building materials for personal home renovations. Auditors found other questionable charges but found them to have no criminal concern.  Schoenberg, also a partner at Palouse Properties in Moscow, has been dealing with some concern among voters and in online forums about his credibility and trustworthiness as a candidate.   Schoenberg, in an Argonaut email interview, said that voters deserve a direct answer.  “I made a mistake, accepted responsibility, and learned from it. It was a difficult experience for me and my family, but it reinforced the importance of accountability, humility, and earning trust through actions rather than words,” he said.   Schoenberg was originally charged with a felony count of misuse of public funds for $970 of personal purchases, but State v. Pruett in 2006 changed that. The case followed two Hagerman police officers who used the company credit card to purchase hunting licenses. The Idaho Supreme Court ruled that they could not be charged with misuse of public funds because they were not the ones directly in charge of the money. When applied to the case of Schoenberg, it meant that he too would not be charged with misuse of public funds, since he was technically not in direct control of public funds.   In light of State v. Pruett and the fact he was accused of spending less than $1,000 of school funds, Schoenberg pleaded guilty to the misdemeanor. Prior to sentencing, Schoenberg served 15 days in jail before being put on one year of probation. He had paid back more than $4,700 to the university and resigned from the UI position.   Olivia Maggs can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Voting as a Vandal
author: Maddie Wright
content: Q. Can I vote in Idaho as a non-Idaho resident?  A. Out-of-state students can only be registered to vote in one state. If they have lived at least 30 days in Idaho, an accepted form of ID along with proof of said Idaho residence can be used to register. To participate in elections, non-students must be residents of that state. For more information on becoming an Idaho resident, view https://www.uidaho.edu/registrar/residency-requirements .  Q. What can I bring for voter ID?  A. A valid Idaho driver’s license or ID card, a U.S. passport or federal photo ID card, a tribal ID card, or an Idaho concealed weapons license can be used for voter ID. Student identification cards are no longer accepted as valid forms of voter ID.  Q.   What do I need to bring to register?  A. Valid photo identification and proof of residence must be provided to register.  Photo identification includes a valid form of voter ID (as listed in the question above). Proof of residence includes, but is not limited to, utility bills, bank/credit card statements, current enrollment letters from an Idaho college, and paystubs or paychecks.   Q. Is there a same-day voter registration in Idaho?  A. Yes and no; voters may register at the polls when voting in person, at early voting or on Election Day. However, online voters must register 11 days before an election.  Q.   Can I vote at any voting location in my county?  A. No. voters must visit their assigned voting location which is based upon their physical address. This voting location can be found voteidaho.gov on the Where Do I Vote page.  A new general election is upon Idaho residents, occurring on November 3 rd and with polling locations open from 8:00 am to 8:00 pm. Some polling locations include the Bruce Pitman Center, Hamilton Indoor Recreation Center, and Latah County Fair & Event Center. Early voting and absentee locations are open from Oct. 13 to Oct. 30, located at the Idaho Student Union Building and Latah County Fairgrounds. Absentee ballots must be requested by 5:00 pm on Oct. 23.   Candidates include those for United States offices, state offices, legislative offices, and county offices. Four ballot measures are also on ballots this November, including Proposition 1, House Joint Resolutions 4 and 6, and a nonbinding advisory question over what should be named Idaho’s official state gun. Sample ballots can be viewed at voteidaho.gov .   Voters may register in a variety of ways, including in person, online and through mail. Online registration can be done through the https://voteidaho.gov/voter-registration/ page. Cooper Feldtman, a freshman at the University of Idaho, described registering online as “very easy, only needing [his] driver’s license and that was it.” Another alternative to in-person registration can be done by mailing a registration form to the country clerk at the Latah County Courthouse. Registering in person can be done at your polling location on Election Day. Cora Crawford, a Moscow local, remarked that the process was “super simple and everyone was very helpful.” In person, registration may be done before Election Day by visiting the county clerk during business hours, with current photo ID and proof of residence.   For more information about candidates and ballot items, see the Argonaut’s 2026 Midterm coverage starting on page 9.    Maddie Wright can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: State representative candidates for District 6 seat A
author: Maddie Wright
content: State Representative Seat A in District 6 is up for election on Nov. 3 rd , with two new candidates. The would-be incumbent, Lori McCann, ran instead for state senator and lost the Republican primary to Dan Foreman, leaving two new faces to run for District 6A.  Trish Carter-Goodheart   Trish Carter-Goodheart | Courtesy, trishforidaho.com Trish Carter-Goodheart is running as the Democratic candidate for state representative Seat A. Her plans in the Idaho legislature and for District 6 are to be “of hope, unity, & progress,” as she is quoted on her online campaign page . Carter-Goodheart’s primary areas of policy are investing in rural Idaho, as well as sustainability and protecting public lands.  Carter-Goodheart is a member of the Nez Perce tribe, raised in the Lapwai community. There, she and her husband are raising their two children. She has been a board member of the National Indian Child Welfare Association, also known as NICWA, since 2008. Carter-Goodheart is described as a small business owner and a nonprofit grant writer on her campaign page. She studied at Arizona State University at the Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and received her certificate in communications and media. Along with Arizona State, she studied at Lewis-Clark State College.   The main policy concern of Carter-Goodheart is to support rural Idaho. On her campaign website, she proposes investing in early education, increasing rural access to health care, and increasing the minimum wage to back working families. Protecting public lands and promoting sustainable agriculture is also part of Carter-Goodheart’s intentions for Idaho. Her slogan is “Community First, Solutions that Last.”  Colton Bennett   Colton Bennett | Courtesy, bennettforidaho.com Colton Bennett is running as the Republican candidate for state representative Seat A. He describes himself as a “dedicated Christian, conservative, Army veteran, husband, and father,” as stated on his online campaign page . Main policy concerns of Bennett include reducing property taxes, protecting Idaho hydroelectric energy production and water resources, advocating for pro-adoption, anti-abortion policies as well as issues concerning illegal immigration.   Bennett grew up in Indianapolis, Indiana. After graduating high school, he served six years, both active and reserved duty. He received the rank of staff sergeant and was deployed overseas in 2022 as a combat medic. In 2021, he received his associate degree in health sciences from Purdue University. Currently, he resides in Troy, Idaho with his wife and two children.   An area of policy concern for Bennett is property taxes, as well as constitutional rights. He is described on his campaign website as calling for a permanent property tax cut and as an advocate for secondamendment rights. Bennett also intends to preserve dams on the Snake River, and their clean energy production. He is a 100% Right-to-Life candidate. This rating is given by the National Right to Life Committee, one of the oldest pro-life organizations in the United States. Bennett advocates for increased cooperation between state and federal law enforcement to remove illegal immigrants from Idaho.  Maddie Wright can be re ached at arg-news.uidaho.edu

title: Candidates running for Latah County office
author: Maddie Wright
content: County Commissioner District 1    Carole Wells | Courtesy, caroleforcommissioner.com Carole Wells: Wells is the Democratic candidate running for Commissioner of District 1. She currently works as a real estate agent in Moscow but retired from her position as Director of Admissions at the University of Idaho’s College of Law in 2020. He now serves on the Latah County Zoning Commission, and his main policy goal is infrastructure growth that respects property rights and transparent operations.   Laura Hiense | Courtesy, lauraforlatah.org Laura Heinse: Heinse is the Democratic candidate running for county commissioner of District 2. She plans to support reliable infrastructure, expand high-speed internet, as well as improve wildfire preparedness.   Clerk of the District Court   Julie Fry | Courtesy, fry4latahid.com Julie Fry: Fry is the current clerk of the district 6 Court and is running again as the Republican candidate. Her intentions include well-organized elections with shorter polling lines, as well as making county services and records more easily accessible online.   Coroner   Debby Carscallen: Carscallen is running uncontested, as the Democratic candidate for Coroner. She served thirteen years as the deputy coroner, became a paramedic in 2009 and the Division Chief of EMS Operations in 2017.   Maddie Wright can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Dan Schoenberg runs for Latah County Commissioner
author: Olivia Maggs
content: Dan Schoenberg, a partner in Palouse Properties and a former University of Idaho executive, is running for Latah County Commissioner this November.  Dan Shoenberg | Courtesy, electdan.vote As a Latah County resident for nearly 50 years, he has experienced and watched the county grow and change. “Latah County faces significant decisions that require thoughtful leadership and long-term planning,” he said. Schoenberg wants to run for Latah County commissioner to give back to the community that he built a life in. “After years of serving people, solving problems and leading organizations. I finally felt it was the right time to give back to the community that has given so much to me,” Schoenberg said.  Schoenberg aims to focus on the issues that matter most to Latah County’s future with a campaign built around “responsible leadership, thoughtful planning and a commitment to serving all residents in the community.”  Before running for county commissioner, Schoenberg worked as the director of auxiliary services for UI and as a partner in Palouse Properties. He feels as though these experiences give him a unique perspective on challenges in both the public and private sectors. Over the last 20 years he has managed budgets, facilities, operations and employees while working with people of many different backgrounds and viewpoints. Through these experiences, he said he has learned that leadership starts with listening, informed decisions and accountability.  As a UI graduate, Schoenberg recognizes many of the challenges that students face today. These challenges include but are not limited to education, housing, employment and deciding where to build a future. He believes that students are an important part of the community and wants to include them in discussions about Latah County’s future.   Schoenberg said he wants the voters to know that he cares deeply about this community, and he is “committed to serving it with integrity, respect, and common sense.” He said his approach has always been to listen first, bring people together, and focus on finding practical solutions.  Olivia Maggs can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Ballot measures on 2026 midterm for Latah County
author: Josie Adjanohoun
content: In addition to proposition one, there are four other Idaho ballot measures in the 2026 midterms, including house joint resolutions four and six, the Moscow School District levy, and the Idaho advisory question on the state gun.   House Joint Resolution Four has the ability to give the authority to the state to legalize marijuana. In no way does the passing of this constitutional amendment legalize marijuana in the state, but in passing, legislators in the Idaho Senate can bring a bill to the floor in Senate to then pass or fail. This will also give exclusive authority to the Senate, which would mean that only the Idaho Senate would have the authority to legislate on weed or narcotics, removing the chance for citizen ballot measures. If this house resolution was to pass, there would be an adjustment to section 26, article three of the Constitution of the State of Idaho, adding the words “Psychoactive substances,” and a subsection stating that the state will have the power to legalize the growth, production, manufacture, transport, sales, delivery, dispense, prescription, distribution, process or use of marijuana.  To make English the official language of Idaho, House Joint Resolution Six, would create a new article in the Idaho state constitution, making English the language used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and in the acts of any public institution in the state. A “yes” vote for the joint resolution will support adding this provision to the Idaho constitution, and a “no” vote would oppose the addition of the provision. The ballot measure also states that this amendment would also allow for languages other than English to be used when required by federal law.  Requiring a 60% vote, the Moscow School District has a levy on this year’s ballot, which will authorize a tax of $280 per $100,000 of taxable assessed value per year, per taxpayer, for a total maximum of $9,370,000 per year, for 7 years. The purpose of the levy would be to renovate and expand the current middle school campus to serve as a high school, and adding technical education and preforming arts spaces, renovating the prior John Russell Elementary School building for admistrative offices and alternative high school programs, as well as replacing the HVAC system at Lena Whitmore Elementary School. In this measure, you can vote in favor of, or against the levy.   On the ballot, there is an Idaho advisory question, asking voters what gun should be designated as the state gun of Idaho. Guns listed include the Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30), Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40), 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver “Peacemaker” (.45 Colt), M1 Garand rifle (.30-06), Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt Pistol (.45 ACP), and the Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06).   For more information about ballot measures, and see a sample ballot, click here .   Josie Adjanohoun can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Argonaut sit-down with Lori Hickman: seeking accountability in AG office
author: Josie Adjanohoun
content: Lori Hickman, a candidate for Idaho Attorney General running as a democrat, had an in-person interview with the Argonaut News Team on Sept. 15. Hickman is running a campaign that tries to differentiate the role of attorney general from the political atmosphere of the state.   “This is my first run for a political office … I choose to step into this race because the current attorney general has lost the trust … as the chief legal officer of the state, trust between your clients and being a reliable attorney that will provide sound, independent legal advice is paramount,” said Hickman.   When asked how she would operate outside of the party system, Hickman said, “You practice law, not politics, and so I would like to restore the office back to the way it used to be, which had Republican and Democrat Attorneys General who just gave out solid legal advice to their clients, the boards, the agencies, the legislature and weren’t worried about how it looked politically.”   When asked by the Argonaut, about how her campaign can connect to students specifically at the University of Idaho, “As all Vandals are coming into adulthood and figuring out your lives … whether you want to remain in Idaho, or you’re just here to go to school in Idaho … It’s the direction of our country, it’s the foundation of our democracy, it’s the rule of law and as the attorney general remaining true and steadfast to the rule of law and keeping that.”   Hickman has also listed protecting federal lands, Idaho water protections, preserving access to safe healthcare, protecting women’s access to healthcare and providing support to law enforcement as campaign priorities. In the interview, Hickman touched on a bill passed last session, House Bill 752.   “It’s highly controversial for a lot of reasons … Law enforcement came in and testified in the debates about that bill saying there is no teeth to this … As attorney general, I would be doing two things in the legislature, saying whoa … there is some deficiencies here, you’re going to face some challenges, and … if the law enforcement community is coming in and testifying against it, I would also be supporting them,” said Hickman.  Hickman’s webpage also promotes the “right to have a free, uniform and thorough” public education, and protect students from “unwarranted attacks that seek to undermine our public schools and interfere with the ability of our students to learn and succeed.”   Hickman has worked in both corporate and state law, and is currently practicing at McFarland Ritter PLLC, where she has worked since 2014. She has a bachelor’s degree in finance from Brigham Young University and graduated from the J. Reuven Clark Law School at BYU. Hickman also provides pro bono legal counsel in child protection cases, and is licensed to practice in Idaho, Utah and New York.   Hickman is running against incumbent Raul Labrador, who is seeking his second term this November.   Josie Adjanohoun can be reached at arg-news@uidaho.edu

title: Proposition One seeks to restore limited abortion rights
author: Paige Wilton
content: Proposition One has been at the center of statewide debates this election season due to its controversial subject matter, as it seeks to repeal the near-total abortion ban Idaho currently upholds by changing the verbiage of the law.   Idaho’s current abortion law, which can be found on the Idaho Legislature website, states that “every person who performs or attempts to perform an abortion as defined in this chapter commits the crime of criminal abortion,” and is eligible to serve between two and five years in prison while incurring fines. As outlined by the law, the only instances when an abortion may be performed is when the life of the mother is at immediate risk, or during the first trimester in cases of rape or incest, though the individual receiving the abortion had to have filed a police report of the crime beforehand.   Prop 1 seeks to largely decriminalize abortion. As stated on the VoteIdaho website, Prop 1 is a, “measure creating right to abortion before fetus viability, and post-viability to protect health; right to privacy; healthcare provider liability protections.”  In more specific language, it would allow women the “right to abortion up to the point of the fetus’s ability to survive outside the womb. After fetal viability, there would be no general right to abortion except in cases of ‘medical emergency,’” as stated on VoteIdaho.   A citizen-ballot initiative championed by the organization Idahoans United for Women and Families (IUWF), Prop 1 seeks to amend the current abortion law that was established in 2022 after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision triggered Idaho’s abortion ban.  A list of pros and cons for passing Prop 1 is listed on the VoteIdaho website, providing a platform for organizations across the state to voice their opinion on the subject.   The pros IUWF gave for passing Prop 1 include but are not limited to: Restoring the medical standard that Idaho operated on for nearly 50 years, protecting healthcare providers from being criminally prosecuted for providing standard medical care and protecting reproductive care that Idaho families count on daily.   The cons were provided by Idaho Family Policy Center, Idaho Chooses Life, Right to Life Idaho, Too Extreme for Idaho, and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise. Their reasons for opposing Prop 1 include but are not limited to: It’s a “backdoor attempt” to legalize late-stage abortions, it redefines fetal ‘viability’ and it would allow healthcare providers to perform abortions on minors without parental consent.   Each group’s rebuttal to the other’s points are listed on the same web page.   Many candidates running for a variety of positions this election season have voiced their opinions on Prop 1 publicly, both in interviews and on their campaign platforms.   Those who have publicly supported Prop 1 include independent Governor candidates Terri Pickens and John Stegner, as well as US Senator candidate Todd Achilles among others. Their stances on the subject can be found on their candidate websites.   “Women, not the government, should be able to make their own choices related to family planning. The state has no business telling doctors what to do,” Pickens says on her website.  Those who have publicly voiced opposition to Prop 1 include Governor incumbent Brad Little, US Senator incumbent Jim Risch and US Representative incumbent Russ Fulcher. Their opinions can be found across their campaign platforms, as well as on the Idaho GOP website.    “I am voting no on Proposition 1,” Gov. Little is quoted on the GOP website. “It would allow girls under 18 to receive abortion without parental consent, and it would make abortion far more accessible in Idaho. Proposition 1 simply goes too far.”  In Moscow, UI students hold their own opinions on Prop 1.   Connor DeFrain, a senior in finance, explains his perspective on the proposition is rooted in “the actual data and consequences of the current policies, and the circumstances that occur to the people living under them,” rather than moral and religious reasoning.    “Logically, I think we’re missing half the picture here. At some point, you have to separate what a law is intended to accomplish from what it’s actually accomplishing,” DeFrain stated. “There’s a difference between making sure a child is born and making sure that child and their mother have a decent shot at a good life.”  Another student, civil engineering major Lucia Cummings, says she wishes to “protect all women,” but claims that Prop 1 will have the opposite effect by removing medical safeguards for women and parental consent for minors.   “Current Idaho law already allows for abortions for cases of ectopic pregnancy, saving the mother’s life, rape and incest. Prop 1 does not protect women,” said Cummings. Her extended Letter to the Editor can be found in the Oct. 22 Argonaut print. In an anonymous poll of 229 UI students, 79% (181) said they will be voting yes on Prop 1, and 21% (48) said they will be voting no. By voting yes for Prop 1, a voter is agreeing to largely decriminalize abortion and amend the abortion law as it currently stands in Idaho. By voting no, a voter is agreeing that the abortion law should remain untouched.   More information about Prop 1 can be found at voteidaho.gov/idaho-general-election . A sample ballot for Latah County can be found at latahcountyid.gov/auditor/elections .

title: Brandon Mitchell, Kathy Dawes run for Idaho House District 6, Seat B
author: Sam Walsh
content: Republican incumbent Brandon Mitchell and Democratic nominee Kathy Dawes are running for Idaho House of Representatives District 6, Seat B, on the Nov. 3 ballot. The district covers the Moscow area, including Latah and Lewis counties and part of Nez Perce County.  Mitchell, a three-term incumbent, won the May 19 Republican primary unopposed with 6,036 votes, according to certified results from the Idaho Secretary of State. Dawes won the Democratic primary with 2,394 votes, or 90.82%, defeating Kenneth Williams, who received 242 votes, or 9.18%.  The candidates previously faced each other in the 2024 general election, when Mitchell received 16,157 votes, or 58.1%, to Dawes’ 11,649 votes, or 41.9%.  Brandon Mitchell (R) Brandon Mitchell | Courtesy, Mitchell for Idaho Mitchell was raised in Syracuse, Utah, and graduated from Clearfield High School in 1988. He studied criminal justice at Weber State University and later completed a business degree at Brigham Young University-Idaho.  In 2012, Mitchell purchased two retail stores, becoming a small business owner, one in Moscow and one in Pullman, Washington. He has co-owned the business with his wife since January 2013. According to his campaign website, the business has grown to six locations. Mitchell and his wife have three children and have served as certified therapeutic foster parents. Mitchell also served as a Boy Scouts of America leader from 2006 to 2018.  First elected to the Idaho House in 2020, Mitchell is seeking his fourth term. He holds several high-profile committee positions, being the vice chair of the House Transportation and Defense Committee and a member of the House Appropriations Committee.  Mitchell sponsored House Bill 621, which would have allowed concealed carry permit holders to bring firearms into public areas of county buildings while maintaining the existing ban on carrying firearms inside courtrooms. Mitchell told Boise State Public Radio that the bill would allow people to carry firearms while conducting their normal activities in county buildings. The bill passed the House but died in the Senate State Affairs Committee.  On his Idaho Republican Party candidate page, Mitchell lists property taxes, education and voting rights as his top three priorities. He supports working with local governments to provide tax relief and greater accountability, writing that “we must work collaboratively with local governments…while bringing greater accountability, transparency, and long-term tax relief to Idaho homeowners.” His support for education is geared towards “quality, free, and public education built on core subjects” as well as career and technical education programs. He also writes that parents should have a strong voice in their children’s education. Concerning voting rights, Mitchell wrote that, “every legal vote matters” and that he remains committed to election integrity.  Mitchell also describes himself as firm in his support for the pro-life position and protections under the First and Second Amendments.  Kathy Dawes (D) Dawes and her husband moved to Moscow in 1973 to attend graduate school at the University of Idaho, where she earned a master’s degree in zoology.  After graduate school, Dawes worked as a lab technician, started a scientific illustration business and taught eighth-grade science in the Moscow School District for many years. After retiring, she began following legislative sessions closely and providing testimony.  Dawes has been heavily involved in several local organizations. She is a founding member of the Moscow Arts Commission, Moscow Community Theatre, and Palouse Discovery Science Center. As an AmeriCorps volunteer at the science center, she developed hands-on science programs for rural schools in north Idaho and eastern Washington. She and her husband continue to run programs for rural libraries in the district.  She also served 13 years on the Latah County Parks Board and is active with the Palouse Chapter of the Citizens Climate Lobby. Dawes has worked to reduce political polarization and led workshops that bring people with differing political views together to find common ground. In 2024, the Latah County Human Rights Task Force presented Dawes with its Community Award, the Rosa Parks Human Rights Achievement, citing her as “Volunteer and author of ‘New Years Challenge”  Dawes describes her campaign as an effort to empower Idaho communities to develop solutions to local problems. She believes communities need resources for schools, childcare, health care, and housing and has also emphasized reducing political polarization.  In the Idaho Capital Sun’s 2024 candidate survey, Dawes listed increasing public education funding, including funding for facilities maintenance and construction, lowering property taxes by increasing the homeowner’s exemption, and eliminating the sales tax on food as her top state budget priorities.  Dawes also opposes using public tax dollars for private education, arguing that doing so would reduce funding for public schools, particularly rural districts without private school options.   On climate and wildfires, Dawes has called for a state plan to prevent wildfire spread and incentives for forest stewardship. She pointed to a personal example of her family’s 26 acres of woodland north of Moscow, which they maintain through thinning and controlled burns.  Dawes also supports adding health exceptions to Idaho’s abortion law. She has said the current law creates risks for pregnant patients and is “among the strictest in the nation.”

title: GALLERY: Fruit Bats performance helps boost energy on campus
author: Jaelynn Durels
content: On October 13, Fruit Bats, an indie folk and folk-rock band, performed at the Bruce M. Pitman center. Students and members of the community enjoyed a night full of fun lively music with the opener Matthew Logan Vasquez Band. They began the night with fan favorites, involving the crowd, and having fun with in each other throughout their chemistry on stage. The brought the power from crazy vocals, insane guitar moves to insane rock head bobs. They enjoyed the engagement the audience was giving them and after a 45 minute set they invited fans to go buy merch and to come talk to them. The Fruit Bats then came on with a smooth transition. It began with the guitar and piano, then bass and electric guitar came in. The drums kept a steady swinging beat for the artists to play along to. The crowd swayed and sang a long to the songs they knew. The Fruit Bats gave a good sense of environment for students to relax and reset before hitting the books during midterms. As they began their set many students yelling and calling out favorites. The main singer assured them that there was many to come in the night. This put the crowd at the edge of their seat, as the stood near the stage, eagerly waiting for what is the next song to be sung. As the night came to an end, the crowd created memories to last with listening to the musicians and hanging out with friends and family. Though it is the start of midterms, a fun night with rock music to sweet jazz sounding music keeps the motivation there as those memories store in their lives to start the week off strong and finish strong with midterms happening.
