title: Idaho State Gun question on ballots is a waste of voters’ time
author: Christopher Sprague
content: One of the items appearing on the November Midterm Ballot is Advisory Question: House Bill 932. This item lets voters cast their opinions on what the Idaho State Gun should be. This is a non-binding measure, so the legislature would still have to vote on it for it to become official during the next legislative session.  The advisory question gives several options on what the state gun should be, from Vote Idaho: the Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30), the Winchester Model 1873 “Gun that Won the West” (.44-40), the 1873 Colt Single Action Army Revolver “Peacemaker” (.45 Colt), the M1 Garand rifle (.30-06), the Colt M1911 .45 automatic Colt pistol (.45 ACP) and the Remington Model 700 bolt-action rifle (.30-06).  All-in-all this voting measure is not something that will impact the everyday voter. Most Idahoans already know and own their preferred gun(s), so this will just be voters voting for their favorite firearm, and which one they think best represents Idaho.  The “Idaho State Gun” will not change anything about the availability or price of the chosen firearm and will end up as just another “fun-fact” that elementary schoolers have to learn during their Idaho history year, and that pops up on internet lists of compiled facts about the states.  This will not lower the costs of gas or everyday items for the people of Idaho, nor will it improve Idaho healthcare, or schools or everyday quality-of-life. This advisory question will do nothing to make the lives of Idahoans cheaper or easier.  This voting measure is just political theatre appealing to the stereotype of “gun-toting Idahoans,” and costs the legislature nothing to look like they are doing something, on our dime during legislative session.  This is so your representatives can look you in the eye and tell you they are fighting for the “Idaho way of life” while simply passing a piece of legislation that just says: “Idaho likes guns.” Something that is well-known and part of the Idaho stereotype already.  Also, voters can only choose one option, forgoing to opportunity for voters to rank their choice from favorite to least, allowing the legislature to actually collect a more meaningful review of Idahoans opinions.  Because what if a voter is stuck between gun A and gun B, and likes both, then wouldn’t it make more sense for the voters to be able to rank the choices?  At the end of the day, this advisory question is a waste of the paper it will be printed on and adds nothing of value to the lives of everyday Idahoans; which is what the legislature should actually be focused on, not empty political points.  Christopher Sprague can be reached at arg-opinion@uidaho.edu

title: First Jazz Bands & Jazz Choirs concert of the school year
author: Melanie Knapp
content: The Lionel Hampton School of Music had their first Jazz Bands & Jazz Choirs concert on Friday, October 9. The event lasted from 6:30-9:30 pm at the Administration Auditorium of UI’s main campus.  The concert featured Jazz Band I, II and III, as well as Chamber Jazz Choir and Jazz Choir I.  Valentina Bailey, a member of Jazz Choir I, said: “I think the performance went, overall, pretty good. I think our blend was really nice… and every group did very well.”  The songs followed no particular theme, giving the audience a look into the broad genre of jazz and all its possibilities.  The bands performed first in reverse number order. Each group performed several songs, all of which included solos from various student musicians.  Jenny Kellogg is the director for Jazz Band III. They featured “Sagebrush” by Annie Booth, “Blue Bossa” by Kenny Dorham and “But Beautiful” by Van Heusen and Burke and arranged by Bill Holman.  Vanessa Sielert is the director for Jazz Band II. They featured “Time After Time” by Kahn and Styne and arranged by Don Schamber, “Yearnin’” by Oliver Nelson, “Back in Time” by Pat Metheny and arranged by Bob Curnow and “Strasbourg St. Denis” by Roy Hargrove and arranged by Vern Sielert.  Sielert is the director for Jazz Band I. They featured “South of the Border” by Kennedy and Carr and arranged by Billy Byers, “Lonely Carousel” by Bob Florence, “Little Minor Booze” by Willie Maiden, “To Be Yourself” by Ryan Acheson and “The American Express” by Bob Brookmeyer.  Chamber Jazz Choir, directed by Daniel Bukvich, followed suit. They featured “Almost Like Being” by Lerner and Loewe and “Moonlight” by Suessdorf, Blackburn, Miller and Parish. Each song contained a student solo.  Jazz Choir I performed following a brief intermission. They featured “Overture 2026” and “The River” (“Song of” and “Of Dreams”) from the traditional era of jazz, and “Bella Note” by Burke and Lee.  The choir began their performance in the auditorium, shocking the audience by running through the aisles onto the stage. Attendees were later ushered to the exit of the Administration Building, where the choir continued to sing until the night came to a close.  Concert tickets were $12 for students and seniors or $14 for general admission.  “You’re really getting your money’s worth,” said Sielert. With how many songs were performed, there’s no doubt his statement was true.  For a complete program of the concert, visit the Jazz Bands & Jazz Choirs program .  Sielert also showcased a poster recently designed by Reinaldo Gil Zambrano, marking the 60th Anniversary of the Lionel Hampton Jazz Festival. This event will take place April 15-17 of 2027.  For more information on the festival and other events, visit UI’s events website .  Melanie Knapp can be reached at arg-life@uidaho.edu .

title: Homecoming week is here
author: Melanie Knapp
content: University of Idaho Homecoming 2026 is set to take place from Sunday, Oct. 18, to Saturday, Oct. 24. This annual tradition involves a week of lively events, a chance to show off your school spirit, and opportunities to connect with Vandal students, teachers and alumni. This year’s Homecoming theme is Vandal Odyssey: Homecoming of Heroes.  The celebration began at 3 p.m. this past Sunday, Oct. 18 with Homecoming Kickoff, where student groups will competed in friendly competitions on the Tower Lawn.  At 3 p.m. on Monday, student groups painted windows of Main Street businesses with artwork representing the Homecoming theme.  From Tuesday through Thursday, there will be a blood drive and school supplies drive from 9 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. The blood drive will be held in the ISUB’s Clearwater-Whitewater Rooms. Donations for the school supplies drive can be dropped off near the information desk in the Bruce Pitman Center, Student Recreation Center and the ISUB.  At 7 p.m. on Wednesday, Jingles gave students the opportunity to perform skits combining their Vandal spirit with the Homecoming theme.  At 7 p.m. on Thursday, Most Vandalized Fan/Yell Like Hell at Women’s Soccer game will take place. Student groups will wear their best Vandal gear and create their own school spirit chant.  From 8 to 9 p.m. on Friday, Serpentine, Vandal Rally and Bonfire will be held.  For Serpentine, Vandals will gather at the UI Golf Course parking lot, where they’ll be led throughout campus by the Vandal Marching Band and Homecoming Committee, picking up people from residence halls and Greek housing.  At 8:30 p.m., the group will arrive at the P1FCU Kibbie Dome parking lot for Vandal Rally. Homecoming royalty court will be announced and President Scott Green, along with athletic-coaches and athletes, will get the audience charged. The night will end at 9 p.m. with an ICCU Fireworks show.  On Saturday, the day will be filled with parades, tailgates, and football. Parades will begin at 9 a.m. in downtown Moscow, with the 118 Annual Homecoming Parade beginning at 10 a.m. The Vandal Fan Zone tailgate starts at noon on the ICCU Arena Plaza. Finally, Vandal Football vs. Southern Utah will kick off at 2 p.m. in the P1FCU Kibbie Dome.  For more information, visit UI’s Homecoming website .  Melanie Knapp can be reached at arg-life@uidaho.edu .

title: Brennan earns OpenAI Select Partner designation
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Brennan has been designated as an OpenAI Select Partner in the AI giant’s OpenAI Partner Network. As a global program, the OpenAI Partner Network is designed for partners to build, sell, and deliver AI solutions with the vendor. It aims to find partners with deep industry expertise, delivery capabilities, and customer relationships, and gives them resources, enablement, and support for enterprise product adoption. As part of the designation, Brennan will maintain its working relationship with OpenAI in helping customers build, deploy, and scale AI. In a statement, the systems integrator (SI) said it will assist customers with implementing OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra model, utilising deeper reasoning and computer use to complete complex workflows. Brennan said it also brings its AI engineering, systems integration and managed services capabilities to the table as part of this relationship, which represents being a significant step in the SI’s focus on helping Australian organisations see returns from AI investments. “The opportunity for our customers is to bring OpenAI’s frontier technology together with Brennan’s engineering, integration and managed innovation capability to solve real business problems and get solutions into production,” Brennan founder and managing director Dave Stevens said. “Too many organisations are still working out how to move beyond AI pilots and experimentation. The challenge is identifying the right opportunities, integrating solutions into existing operations and delivering measurable business value.” To address this challenge, Stevens continued, the SI created the Brennan Innovation Foundry earlier this year to help organisations systematically capture, test and scale ideas. Since April, Brennan said the offering has delivered over 450 ideas, which range from smaller improvements and automations to six substantial business systems. Three examples include a whole-of-business platform for turning the SI’s strategy into owned and trackable actions, a product lifecycle management platform, and a Brennan-built system to replace a software-as-a-service human resource information system. In the future, Brennan said it plans to expand its OpenAI skillset with continued investment into AI engineering, skills development, and customer solutions. “Becoming an OpenAI Select Partner reinforces our commitment to helping Australian organisations move from discussing AI’s potential to actually delivering on it,” Stevens added.

title: DTA launches whole-of-government cloud computing guidance
author: arnnet.com.au
content: The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) has released whole-of-government guidance for cloud computing to support government agencies in making informed decisions through the cloud lifecycle. The guidance is focused on agencies implementing the federal government’s cloud computing policy, which came into effect from 1 July, and helps them surpass common challenges, manage risk, and build capability as required. Areas covered by the guidance include cloud strategy development; balancing contemporary cloud tech with legacy system management; bolstering security, privacy, and operational resilience; optimising AI and cloud service consumption; procurement, cost, and provider dependency management; and building up cloud service management skills. “Cloud is fundamental to how government operates and delivers services,” said DTA acting deputy CEO of strategy, planning, and performance Ramsey Beydoun. “Getting it right means looking beyond the technology and making choices that support better services, stronger resilience and long-term value.” According to the DTA, the cloud computing policy prioritises cloud for new digital and ICT initiatives and upgrades while also acknowledging some approaches will need to be altered to fit specific situations. By looking at both migration and legacy systems together, the Agency said this helps in deliberate decision-making around the future of existing systems as opposed to viewing a move to the cloud as a standalone exercise. “There is no single pathway to successful cloud adoption. The guidance gives agencies practical advice to navigate trade-offs and make informed decisions at every stage of their cloud journey,” Beydoun said. The guidance also highlights cloud cost management, with focus on FinOps practices to connect cloud consumption with business value. It also offers advice on AI-enabled cloud services cost management. “ As agencies adopt AI capabilities, expenditure can vary significantly depending on usage,” the DTA noted. “Understanding consumption patterns early can help agencies implement appropriate controls, manage costs proactively and ensure expenditure on AI services delivers the intended outcomes.”

title: Cisco 360 links partner profitability to secure AI and infrastructure services
author: arnnet.com.au
content: As Cisco’s 360 partner program moves from strategy to execution, the vendor used Partner Summit 2026 to outline how it will support its channel in capturing opportunities created by AI-driven changes across security, infrastructure and operations. This is creating new opportunities for partners to deliver advisory, implementation and managed services as customers move AI workloads into production while also driving cross-sell opportunities across the broader technology stack. To support this shift, Cisco is introducing dedicated pathways for different partner types across its ecosystem, alongside broader program changes unveiled at its 30th annual Partner Summit in Vancouver. These initiatives include ecosystem deal registration, a framework that formally recognises advisors and developers for their contributions to customer transactions, giving greater visibility to partner influence across the customer lifecycle. For newer growth paths, Cisco has introduced advisor and developer Partner Value Indexes (PVIs). It will also bring out a unified Distributor PVI scheduled to launch in spring 2027, with Cisco seeking to measure partners based on the value they contribute to customers. The vendor has also increased annual contract value (ACV) growth rewards by 50 per cent and has doubled Adopt incentives across use cases and introduced new adoption incentives tied to Cisco IQ. According to Cisco executive vice president and chief customer experience officer Liz Centoni, Cisco IQ gives partners a shared, current view of a customer’s environment such as uncovered devices, vulnerabilities, and equipment nearing or past end of support. “For every customer you onboard to Cisco IQ, we will pay you an adoption incentive,” she said. “We want to reward the motion, not just the outcome. Starting today, you also get that 6 per cent deal registration, but it’s on standard and signature on top of hire Cisco partner incentive rebates already.” That insight can help partners prioritise risks, propose services, and plan refresh or modernisation projects rather than relying on manual discovery. Modernisation path Beyond incentives, Cisco is also looking to create new services and modernisation opportunities for partners. One example is Cisco Capital, which is designed to help customers fund modernisation and security projects while giving partners a way to expand deal sizes and create budget for that work with deferred payment and step-up payment options. During the keynote, the vendor’s executive vice president and chief financial officer (CFO), Matt Patterson, said the vendor will help partners address customers’ technical debt. “To be more competitive … build more into the deal, upsize the size of the deals, and then let Cisco Capital really handle some of the complexities around foreign exchange, credit, payments, and things like that,” he said. For an additional cross-sell bonus, preferred and portfolio partners can earn an extra 2 per cent rebate on top of existing cross-sell incentives when expanding customer accounts into newer Cisco architectures, including Splunk. Cisco IQ adoption incentive will also be made available to partners who adopt it as well as for onboarding customers to the platform’s telemetry capabilities. The networking vendor also continues to position Cloud Control as the platform that brings together partners, IT professionals and AI agents to manage, secure and operate infrastructure supporting AI workloads. These initiatives are aimed at improving partner experience, profitability and enablement. “We’re in an equally significant challenge that resembles that in this way: trying to keep up with AI and frontier AI model threats,” said Cisco SVP global partner Tim Coogan to media and analysts at the Summit. “It’s a challenge to keep up, and we simply won’t be able to do it with humans that are badged employees of Cisco. “We know that the channel is the route to the customer. Customers have very sophisticated buying processes. They might transact with one, or a very small number of, partners, but they use a tremendous number of partners to run their businesses, and I think that’s really key. “We also understand that the mechanics of buying has changed. While we’re very good at many things, it’s not necessarily something that we’re good at, nor do we want to be good at.” According to Coogan, value is important, but just as important is speed to value. “[With] the way things are changing, that speed is even more critical,” he said. “Then there’s scaling efficiently, being big without finding a way to bring efficiency to that. “Whether it’s through the distribution model or through our ability to bring resources together to build new products or launch new products … I think it’s absolutely crucial.” That has influenced the evolution of Cisco 360 , which Coogan said was designed to reward partner capability and investment rather than scale alone. “One of the things that we enjoyed is that we did get feedback from partners, both large and small, in various geographies on things they didn’t want or things that they wanted us to change,” he explained. “That was important because the goal of 360 was many things – it was to reward investment and to align incentive to capability, and that shouldn’t necessarily be based solely on size.” For example, if a partner was at the Gold tier, there was a “lazy assumption” that they were great at everything, and that may or may not have been true, Coogan explained. “It may have been more based on that partner’s ability to deliver volume,” he said. “The idea behind 360 is to align a partner who wants to sell broadly across the portfolio with PVI scores that reflect that investment. “Also, to nurture a partner who may be very, very specific to a particular piece of the business.” According to Coogan, partners who specialise in security, collaboration, or even Splunk have found it difficult to compete with larger partners based on price. Meeting scale All these initiatives give partners the ability to compete based on capability — not just on price — with larger partners. When it comes to those smaller partners, distributors will also remain critical to helping them access certifications, specialisations and support resources as well as enabling them to build capabilities and participate more fully in the Cisco 360 program. “We have to have success up and down the stack, across all geographies,” said Coogan. “Quite honestly, we could probably sell to a certain number of customers with the resources that we have, but we’ll never have the scale that we need. “Distribution is fundamentally important because it enables partners that may not have the resources to achieve certification A or specialisation B. “From a pure scale standpoint, distributors remain critically important.” That’s why that’s one of the reasons why 2026 is heavily focused on bringing distributors even more into the 360 and the PVI models, explained Coogan. “Distribution, quite frankly, becomes the engine for long-term growth,” he said. The focus on distributors, partner capability and customer outcomes forms part of Cisco’s broader push to create what Coogan described as “durable growth”. This would be built on profitability, predictable performance and the ability to capture emerging opportunities in AI, security and infrastructure modernisation. Global channel bookings for fiscal year 2026 were approximately 90 per cent of Cisco’s total bookings. That strategy is already reflected in Cisco’s channel performance. For the fiscal year, global channel growth was slightly over 17 per cent. Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) were slightly over 19 per cent, while Asia Pacific Japan and China were over 11 per cent, and the Americas were over 20 per cent. Its observability arm, Splunk, finished the period strong. The performance update comes as Cisco continues to move forward with one of the largest overhauls of its partner program. “Last year, we began the biggest move we’ve had in decades,” said Cisco CEO Chuck Robbins during his keynote. “I do mean decades, because I was there when we did the last move. He recounted light heartedly that a partner on the morning of the keynote said, “congratulations on where you are with Cisco 360″. “I can tell you that when you first started it, I thought it was going to be a shit show,” Robbins said. “The team’s worked really hard, and what I would just tell you is that I’ve told you this on stage so many times over the years: we’re not perfect. “We’ll screw it up, but we’ll fix it. The program was built around the fact that most of our customers are leveraging six to seven different partners, so we needed to recognise the ecosystem.” Cisco wants to create “predictable profitability for the value and the life cycle management of things” that partners are doing, Robbins added. Lilia Guan attended Cisco Partner Summit in Vancouver as a guest of Cisco.

title: AirTrunk locks in $4.25B green loan for SYD3 campus
author: arnnet.com.au
content: AirTrunk has secured a $4.25 billion green loan to continue developing its SYD3 campus in Sydney. The funds will go towards infrastructure for cloud, AI, and other digital services, with more than 10,000 jobs estimated to be supported in construction, trades, engineering, logistics and safety. In a statement, the hyperscale data centre specialist said the facility is structured as a green loan with margin adjustments. Additionally, any contributions from the margin savings on the facility will go to AirTrunk’s social impact program to local charities focused on STEM education, digital equity, biodiversity and conservation, sustainable innovation and disaster relief. A consortium of 32 local and international financial institutions backed the loan, with the specialist noting this makes it one of the largest lending groups assembled to finance a data centre in Australia. AirTrunk is tapping into a 25,000-square-metre strategic buffer zone in Western Sydney for SYD3, covering the storage, staging, and pre-commissioning of critical data centre equipment, supporting just-in-time deliveries to the campus. The construction of SYD3’s expansion is underway, with completion due by mid-2028 “SYD3 is a long-term investment in Western Sydney and Australia’s digital capability, backed by the confidence of leading Australian and international banks,” said AirTrunk vice president of origination and market expansion Tom Mackellar. “As the campus develops, it’s building a regional ecosystem through active hiring, sustained project activity and strategic supply chain partnerships, creating opportunities for local workers, contractors and businesses while delivering infrastructure Australians increasingly rely on. “The green financing also reflects our view that sustainability should be built into how digital infrastructure is funded and delivered. We’re focused on responsible growth that creates lasting value for communities in the regions where we operate.” Including the new loan, AirTrunk’s total committed debt financing is now around $38.4 billion globally, with more than $19.8 billion stemming from Australian projects. The loan was underwritten by 14 lead banks, which were Banco Santander, S.A.; BNP Paribas; Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank; DBS Bank Ltd.; Deutsche Bank; ING Bank N.V.; Mizuho Bank, Ltd.; MUFG Bank, Ltd.; National Australia Bank Limited; Royal Bank of Canada; Société Générale; Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation; The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited; and United Overseas Bank Limited. Meanwhile, the loan coordinators were Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation Limited, and United Overseas Bank Limited. Legal advisers for the transaction were Mallesons for the borrowers’ counsel and Gilbert & Tobin for the lenders’ counsel. The expansion of SYD3 comes close to a year after AirTrunk purchased a site back in December 2025 in Melbourne’s north-west for MEL2 , its planned second campus in the city.

title: NextDC unveils board renewal measures following revised FY27 guidance
author: arnnet.com.au
content: NextDC has announced a series of board and governance changes ahead of its AGM on 20 November, as the company responds to investor concerns following delays to the M3 Melbourne project and its revised FY27 earnings guidance. The ASX-listed data centre operator said chairman Douglas Flynn will step down once a successor has been appointed and a short transition period has been completed. Executive search firm Spencer Stuart has been tasked with expanding its board renewal process to identify both a new chair and an additional independent non-executive director. Director Stuart Davis intends to retire once the board renewal process is complete and new directors have been appointed. In a further move aimed at addressing shareholder concerns, NextDC has withdrawn its proposed increase in the maximum aggregate remuneration pool for non-executive directors. Incumbent directors have also agreed to an immediate voluntary 10 per cent reduction in board fees. CEO Craig Scroggie has agreed to forgo both his FY27 short-term incentive and long-term incentive opportunities. Flynn acknowledged investor frustration following the company’s updated FY27 outlook and recent share price performance. “We recognise and share the disappointment of investors resulting from our revised FY27 guidance and share price performance,” he said. “The board and management are focused on two priorities: minimising the impact of the M3 Melbourne power delay and rebuilding the confidence of investors and other stakeholders.” As part of the renewal process, NEXTDC is seeking directors with expertise in data centres, energy, infrastructure development and capital management, reflecting the company’s significant capital investment pipeline. Subject to identifying suitable candidates, the board expects to appoint the two new non-executive directors during the first quarter of calendar year 2027. NextDC recently revealed the Melbourne M3 data centre has been delayed because of electricity network distributor Jemena partially suspending construction work due to “community and stakeholder opposition”. NextDC said M3 has been impacted by delays to Jemena’s 66kV line augmentation works.The distributor suspended parts of those works in September and formally told NextDC that it doesn’t expect to resume them until February 2027. In addition to the grid delays, NextDC is also facing an extended wait for a decision on its planning permit for stages six and seven. NextDC’s 2027 financial year guidance was updated to exclude M3 contracts, with net revenue previously forecast of between $615 million and $640 million now falling to between $475 million and $500 million.

title: Oracle pledges US$1B investment for partner growth
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Oracle has committed to spend US$1 billion over the next four years to help partners meet customer demand for AI solutions and services. Announced during the vendor’s AI World 2026 conference in Las Vegas, the investment is focused on expanding partner opportunities around solution development, selling alongside Oracle, training and tools, and longer-term customer support. The investment includes new and updated Oracle PartnerNetwork benefits and incentives, which cover planned investments in training and certification, technical enablement, development, testing and demonstration environments, cloud migration funding, go-to-market collaboration, and commercialisation through Oracle Marketplace. “Our partners extend our sales reach, expand our delivery capacity, and bring their own innovation and investment to help customers address evolving business needs,” said Oracle global field operations president Mark Hura. “Through the Oracle PartnerNetwork, we’re strengthening our ability to reach more customers, deliver solutions at scale, and accelerate innovation and business outcomes.” The vendor’s senior vice president of partner, sales, and operations strategy, Leah Yomtovian, said the investment has been designed to support the diversity of its partner base, accommodating different business models, capabilities, and growth ambitions. “By giving partners greater choice and flexibility in how they build, sell, and deliver with Oracle, we’re helping them grow their businesses while bringing more innovation, specialised expertise, and value to our customers,” she added.

title: AI transformation starts within the technology services workforce
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Customer zero is the foundation of any artificial intelligence (AI) strategy, but before taking AI to customers, transformation within the business is needed first. Cultural and operational change matter in completing a successful internal implementation. For digital AI consultancy firm V2 AI, that means applying AI transformation principles internally before taking them to clients, as it recognises that change affects people, processes, and technology. “When we go out to organisations and do AI transformation, we understand it’s as much about the people as it is about the processes and uplifting the technology capability,” chief executive officer (CEO) Craig Howe told ARN . “If we want to build the internal capability of our clients, then we understand they’re going through change. “How do we move with that change, upskill, and keep that internally?” V2 AI built internal dojos for learning, which not only found AI is moving rapidly, but also there is a lot of empathy for people who have completed certifications, as they build rich industry knowledge and gain experience only to then be faced with an AI juggernaut – whether internally or through customer engagements. “The more I saw the need in the market, the more we started to look internally as well,” Howe said. As part of this, V2 AI partnered with Cornerstone Workforce AI, a workforce agility platform that helps organisations identify skills gaps and development opportunities, retain and engage top talent, and provide multimodal learning experiences to meet the diverse needs of the modern workforce. “How we partner with Cornerstone both internally and externally … helps organisations understand what the skills are, what the learning needs are, and how to build fluency,” explained Howe. “For us to keep up internally, we also have external support for employee mental health and other services people can access, and you’ll always need that.” That requires a level of self and awareness of others – which is huge, he added. “At a high level, this isn’t just about the team,” Howe said. “It’s about how I can learn and how they’re learning too. “These are very high-skilled individuals who are very good at AI and very good technically. “How do we broaden their horizons, not just down the technical path they can go, but through leadership skills, commerciality skills and further delivery skills?” As a leader, these initiatives give employees awareness and help them with the teachings and also helps the player-coach going forward. “If I can get the data — we work with data over opinion — and show them that data — because they’re very data-orientated themselves being in AI — then it’s a much easier conversation to have with them,” Howe said. “They may think they’re a 10 out of 10 around commerciality when they’re probably not, and the data shows that. “We can have that conversation and build a plan and a learning program around that. That takes a lot of burden off as a leader when trying to guide your team.” Leading customers While organisations can create learning and career pathways, employees need a clear understanding of where they sit on that journey to make the most of those opportunities. Awareness of individual strengths, capabilities, and development areas are critical to building meaningful goals and career plans. “This is a huge part of that for me. It helps our HR [human resources], it helps our talent acquisition, and it helps from a leadership perspective,” noted Howe . “There are numerous benefits, in my opinion, to putting Cornerstone into organisations early, rather than leaving it until you’re in the middle of any type of high-growth build — or any transformation activity — with a client.” That focus on understanding workforce capabilities early becomes increasingly important as organisations faced the rapid pace of AI-driven change, said Cornerstone Workforce Intelligence leader for Asia Pacific and Japan, Marc Thompson. He told ARN the answer lies in giving businesses greater visibility into the skills they already have and the skills they will need in the future. “[Recognise] that AI transformation, tech transformation, or whatever transformation you’re putting in place has humans at the centre,” Thompson said. “It’s humans who will execute it, no matter what. “When you have a realisation like that, you take the learnings from each other about your own organisation. “From our organisation, we’ve spent 27 years focused on learning, talent management and helping organisations be ready through their people. In the early days, it was compliance, and everyone did the same training.” According to Thompson, delivering a learning program around 15 years ago, for a financial services organisation for example, meant going through processes for training. “We had to study the best performers, conduct focus groups and gather data to work out who the best was,” he added. “There were subjective reviews. Then, a program had to be developed, signed off and rolled out. “Today, there’s no chance. Everything has changed. The needs of individuals, businesses and teams have changed. That’s how far things have come.” Today, for an organisation like V2 AI , Cornerstone used visibility as the first step to enable organisations to use AI, while gaining a clearer understanding of the skills within their workforce, as well as assessing proficiency levels and identify the capabilities required to support work now and into the future. “Once you’ve got that visibility, the next part is hyper-personalisation, rather than putting everyone through the same program and waiting for data to be pulled from multiple sources,” Thompson explained “AI can determine what your skills are, what projects are available tomorrow, in three months or six years, how roles are evolving and take ownership of career development rather than waiting for HR.” There’s a number of challenges for organisations looking at how they can go through the shift from human resources to hybrid resources. This includes using AI as part of the solution rather than seeing it as a challenge. The other issue for organisations is how they can be structured differently to support speed, hyper-personalisation and greater visibility. Often people can see themselves in the future rather than feeling uncertain about where they fit. “A lot of people are asking what AI is going to do to their jobs,” Thompson said. “We keep hearing that everywhere. But I think if that’s the question we’re answering, we’re probably asking the wrong question. “A better question is how the tasks underneath a job are changing. A job is made up of decisions, skills, tasks and interactions … AI will change elements of that.” As that shift increasingly becomes cemented into organisations, Howe felt channel partners had an opportunity to lead workforce adaptation. AI is likely to increase the value of human decision-making rather than replace it entirely, even as some technical tasks become automated. While roles may evolve, Howe said that shift presents an opportunity for businesses to rethink how they engage employees, adapt their go-to-market strategies and prepare for ongoing change. As a professional service provider, workforce planning and skills development should be treated as business imperatives rather than employee benefits. This ensures they are able to demonstrate a long-term commitment to change while reducing uncertainty and anxiety among staff. “[For] the channel, I feel like this is one of those change paradigms that people think is optional but is becoming more and more mandatory,” he added . “Organisations can do nothing…everyone has that option. ‘Alternatively, organisations can follow this type of lead. In the channel, they can leverage [tech from] Cornerstone as well and get ahead of this more than they are today. “It drives a conversation with everybody and reduces the anxiety because organisations can say, ‘Here are the agents, here are the people, and here are the skills you have. This is what the agents are going to do.’ While external support for employee mental health and wellbeing remains important, the focus has also shifted to becoming more proactive. According to both Howe and Thompson, identifying patterns before they emerge and recognising when people may be approaching their limits is important – whether in learning, communication or other skills, before they hit a wall.

title: SUSE strengthens NVIDIA AI Factory ecosystem
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Enterprise open-source vendor SUSE is making a play around sovereign AI through a partnership with NVIDIA to help organisations run private enterprise AI in their own environments. The integration of NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture into SUSE AI Factory will allow customers to deploy private enterprise AI, reducing their reliance on public AI services. Organisations should be able to run AI agents safely inside their own walls, so sensitive data and IP don’t end up where they shouldn’t. It would also mean no more surprise per-token API bills, with costs that are much easier to plan for. SUSE also introduced SUSE Linux Enterprise Server (SLES) for NVIDIA, which sees customers run AI workloads on the chip maker’s hardware. It also provides a support model spanning the operating system, GPU drivers and Kubernetes environments. Along with this announcement, the open-source vendor has also introduced a two-tier independent software vendor (ISV) certification program for SUSE AI Factory and SUSE AI Factory with NVIDIA to validate software compatibility, simplify integration and provide clearer support pathways. The program includes a “Ready for” certification based on partner self-validation and a “Certified for” designation for jointly validated deployments with automated lifecycle management. These initiatives come as enterprises and government departments in Australia and New Zealand (A/NZ) are asking more of vendors to de-risk, standardise and certify otherwise complex AI infrastructure stacks . “For our national channel partners, this represents an important and massive opportunity to guide customers through this transition via offering pre-validated, sovereign AI infrastructure stacks,” said SUSE A/NZ general manager Ben Henshall. “This overall helps eliminate integration headaches, align with Essential Eight and SOCI Act requirements, and support enterprises as they look to scale production safely. “

title: Versent’s Tim Hope joins DX1 to help enterprises adopt AI with confidence
author: arnnet.com.au
content: After over a decade with Versent helping regulated organisations adopt cloud and AI, Tim Hope has joined Sydney-based engineering consultancy DX1 Australia to help customers connect technical solutions to business value while maintaining security and governance. In his new role as group chief technology officer (CTO), Hope will help enterprise customers connect DX1’s technical and engineering work to their business strategies. He told ARN that this will give them a practical business value from AI while maintaining security and governance. Hope will also support customers’ AI acceleration and help DX1 practice internally managing its own risks so it can demonstrate a responsible approach to customers. “AI has been building for some time, but toward the end of the year the conversation changed to, ‘Agentic is here.’ It’s got a lot of business value, he said. “I felt enterprises were ready for it, but … they need a confidence layer. “That confidence comes from security, automation and experience working with enterprise customers. “That’s what I saw in the DX1 team, coupled with a strong culture as well.” For Hope the other element is that, with AI and adopting new technologies, specialisation is important. “You become really focused on customers,” he noted. “With my role and background in enterprise, I’ve spent a lot of time talking to business stakeholders about how to get technology working within their ecosystem.” That background comes from nearly 12 years with Australian technology consultancy Versent, where he started as a principal consultant in DevOps and cloud before moving into the role of general manager for the north region (NSW and Queensland) in 2015. After four years in that position, he was promoted to CTO, solution engineering and GTM technology leader, which he held before joining DX1. “I joined under the founders off the back of the work we did for a financial services organisation,” Hope said. “We drove a lot of the Amazon adoption, bringing new technology into a regulated environment. “From there, we took that conversation into consulting to help other industries and regulated enterprises get value from the cloud.” With DX1, Hope sees a similar opportunity emerging around AI. While cloud was largely a technology conversation with technologists, AI is reaching business users directly. This creates new needs around education, costs, and choosing the right tool. “I’ve spent a lot of time talking to business stakeholders about how to get technology working within their ecosystem,” Hope said. “The team is really strong in engineering, which is awesome, because you want that solid outcome. “I can help connect that to enterprise strategy, make sure we’re driving the business value of AI, and bring through the security and governance needed to achieve those outcomes.” According to Hope, DX1 is able to demonstrate its approach by applying the same AI and risk management practices internally that it recommends to customers. This provides enterprises with real-world examples of balancing innovation with risk management. “AI is operating right in the business space,” he said. “It’s bypassing technology. It’s straight in with the end users, end customers in the business, and their customers … it’s a lot wider in impact. “As an enterprise, you really need to be able to adopt AI. If you don’t do it well, it takes confidence away. “You end up going too slow, or you don’t take enough options to get your team to understand it and adopt it well. It really does become an enterprise-wide conversation.” Hope noted that organisations need to invest in their security layer. “You’ve got to invest in your automation because you will probably get rogue things in your network,” he said. “As long as you’ve got the right security constructs and you’re secure internally, you’re going to be in a better position. “You can talk with your business about what they’re actually needing to do, and generally business stakeholders will want to do it the right way.” This is different from traditional technology procurement where IT owns the conversation. “You’re talking to technologists, and they understand they’ve got to manage the cost within a budget,” he said. “Technologists are quite used to managing the variable cost of cloud. They’re quite used to setting up cloud properly. “One thing I see with AI is it’s jumped past technology and straight into the business. Suddenly, business users are having to deal with variable token costs. “Asking a business user to tune their prompt for cost or use the right model is a difficult conversation. We’ve got to approach it differently because we’re not talking to technologists now.” DX1 CEO Alex Rea said Hope’s appointment comes at a pivotal time for the company, following a year of 20 per cent growth and the acquisition of Innablr last year . “DX1’s strong background in devOps and devSecOps, combined with Innablr’s data expertise,” he said. “Our work with AWS and Databricks, and the capabilities we are developing through our AI Labs, gives us a strong foundation to deliver for the Australian market. “Tim has spent his career helping enterprise leaders turn emerging technology into real, practical business value. That expertise is critical as Australian organisations move beyond AI experimentation and start thinking seriously about how to put emerging technologies into production. “Our focus is on helping local organisations adopt, govern and secure new technology while working closely with their businesses to engineer solutions that deliver meaningful outcomes.”

title: GTIA to advance MSPs’ AI service capabilities with Managed Intelligence Alliance
author: arnnet.com.au
content: The Global Technology Industry Association (GTIA) has created the vendor-neutral Managed Intelligence Alliance program to help IT service providers deliver artificial intelligence SMBs securely, responsibly and at scale through a common framework. “There are excellent international frameworks for AI governance, risk management and responsible technology development,” said GTIA vice president of industry standards and director of managed intelligence alliance Carlo Tortora Brayda. “What is missing is a common, practical framework for delivering AI as a managed service, particularly to small and midsize businesses. “Market demand for AI within SMBs is at an unprecedented high and thousands of MSPs are being asked to deliver AI solutions.” According to Brayda, the industry has yet to establish a common framework, agreed service specifications or a shared understanding of what a capable managed intelligence service provider (MISP) should be delivering . “This problem is exacerbated by the fact that most SMBs don’t have a clear picture of what AI can do for their business in terms of an interwoven agentic workforce – they are generally parked on implementing chatbots companywide,” he said. “Our aim is to close that gap and to enable business end users to be able to buy with confidence from solution providers that work to a quality standard with access to all the research information and enablement playbooks to deliver cutting edge AI that will genuinely deliver business outcomes.” The Alliance brings together four essential disciplines: open specifications, capability standards, accreditation and research. “We want to establish a common foundation that enables providers to develop reliable, repeatable and commercially viable services, while giving customers greater confidence in whom they can trust,” he said. “We are not trying to reinvent the work of ISO, NIST or other established institutions. “We want to translate and adapt that work to the operational reality of the channel, creating practical requirements that service providers can implement.” The Alliance is a community driven initiative, governed by a strict charter with strong antitrust measures. Pax8 is the Alliance’s charter member, with its corporate vice president of community and ecosystems Rob Rae , leading it as chair. In this role, Rae will help guide the group’s work and foster collaboration across the industry. Other founding members include CMIT Solutions, CrowdStrike, Cynet, F1 Information Technologies, Lyra, Microsoft, New Charter, NinjaOne, Rev.io and Sourcepass. “We are establishing an executive council and a technical steering committee, with technical work developed through collaborative working groups and consensus-based processes,” Brayda told ARN . “Importantly, our published standards and frameworks will be openly accessible, without fees. Every GTIA member already has a voice in this work, and organisations that want a more active role can join as Alliance Partners. “Our first year will focus on establishing our governance, identifying priority areas through member consultation, defining taxonomy, and developing our initial open specifications and capability frameworks.” The “acid test” will see how service providers will be able to deliver quality service to an understood standard, with business outcomes in mind, added Brayda. “The world has moved beyond just servicing tickets. MSPs will be able to embark on a fast track to becoming the partners that the customers of the future really need,” he added.

title: Pax8 takes next steps to guide MSPs into MIPs with AI offerings
author: arnnet.com.au
content: In the next step to help managed services providers (MSP) evolve into the managed intelligence providers (MIP), cloud marketplace provider Pax8 has launched AI offerings 8os and 8bot. Labelled as one of the first operating systems for the agentic workforce, 8os provides MIPs with a place to govern the fragmented AI landscape across every SMB customer they serve. Announced at the Beyond EMEA conference in Copenhagen, Denmark, the operating system is designed to address the growing challenge of deploying AI securely and can help partners turn a solution built for one customer into a service that can be repeated across others. This will connect usage, cost and outcomes within a recurring service model. It also gives partners greater visibility and governance over usage and costs, helping them manage customer environments as they scale and identify opportunities to build additional services around AI. Meanwhile, 8bot — Pax8’s packaged, managed AI coworker — provides an accessible starting point. It gives partners a ready-to-deploy AI service for individual employees, helping customers that want to embrace AI but may not know where to begin or how much to invest. A partner can start with one 8bot for a customer and, as their needs grow, use 8os to manage and govern an expanding AI workforce – whether that’s ten, a hundred or potentially thousands of AI workers. Many businesses will rely on technology partners to help govern, optimise and manage AI deployments, said Pax8 Asia Pacific executive vice president and general manager Lindsay Keating. “As partners begin managing hundreds or even thousands of AI tools and agents across multiple customers, 8os brings deployment, identity and access, governance and oversight, usage and cost tracking, support, billing and monetisation into a single operating model,” she told ARN . “For partners, the opportunity is to move beyond individual AI projects and build a repeatable way of delivering and managing AI services. That’s where 8os becomes important to Pax8’s vision for managed intelligence, giving partners an operating and commercial foundation as they evolve into managed intelligence providers. “As businesses adopt more AI tools and agents, the challenge is shifting from whether to adopt AI to how to manage it effectively.” According to Keating, 8os ensures a governed AI workforce, where partners know what AI workers can access, what work they perform, and where human decisions are required. “By bringing that AI workforce into one governed operating model, 8os is designed to help partners strengthen AI governance, reduce the risks of shadow AI, better manage usage and costs, and give customers greater control as AI adoption scales,” she added. “Many medium and small businesses don’t have the resources or skills to manage an AI workforce and need the support of a trusted partner.”

title: Swoop continues to divest with $4.5M Sydney fibre sale
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Swoop has maintained its divestment strategy with an agreement to sell its Sydney-based fibre assets to Xenith IG Australia Holdings for around $4.5 million. Proceeds from the potential sale have been earmarked for debt reduction and general working capital requirements, according to a statement published by the telco to the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX). The deal is subject to customary conditions and expected to be completed by the third quarter of the 2027 financial year. The divestment follows Swoop’s sale of its Melbourne Fibre project for $11 million in June this year , which it also sold to the dark fibre provider. It is also in line with the telco’s overarching goal to focus on its core broadband and mobile operations following the departure of then-CEO Alex West on 7 July . In mid-July, interim chair Tony Grist told ARN that he didn’t expect many more divestments to take place as, in his own words at the time, “there’s not really a lot more to divest”. “There’s some … fibre assets from the previous leadership’s acquisitions in Melbourne and Adelaide that could be divested,” he noted. “They’re not material in terms of our revenue and emerging cash flow profile with the focus on consumer.” While Grist did not mention its Sydney fibre assets, Swoop’s latest ASX statement about its divestment mentioned that it did not expect the Sydney fibre sale to adversely affect Swoop’s ongoing operations or service continuity.

title: DyFlex’s growth journey leads to Cognizant deal
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Australia’s mergers and acquisitions market is heating up once again, with Cognizant looking to strengthen its SAP play through the proposed acquisition of Perth-based DyFlex Solutions. The managed service provider (MSP) specialises in SAP transformation, including AI-led process advisory, across finance, digital supply chain, asset maintenance, human capital management, data and analytics. DyFlex spans the full SAP portfolio with capability across SAP public and private cloud. Its work is supported by proprietary delivery methods, accelerators and reusable assets, which the MSP is increasingly enhancing with AI. This will go towards strengthening Cognizant’s domain expertise in mining and resources, energy and utilities, manufacturing, logistics, and the public and mid-market sectors. Founded in 2011, DyFlex has grown to over 300 people, making it one of the leading employers of SAP talent across Australia and New Zealand, with multiple office locations in the region and a delivery presence in the Philippines. In October last year, DyFlex made its move to enter the New Zealand market through its recent acquisition of local SAP partner Bluetree Solutions. The acquisition, backed by private equity firm Five V Capital , would help further the SAP capabilities of both IT service providers. In an interview with ARN at SAP’s Now event on 7 August, DyFlex co-CEO Jason Heaney said at the time the acquisition complements its SAP capabilities, providing a one-stop shop for the vendor’s product services. “We were already moving into New Zealand as DyFlex,” Heaney said at the time. “The acquisition means we now have a presence there — an office and customer base — so that kickstarts us in [the country]. “We had signed a big manufacturing company for ERP [enterprise resource planning], and we had been resourcing that totally out of Australia.” Its breadth of expertise will provide Cognizant’s frontier and enterprise capabilities and global delivery at scale, helping clients derive greater value from AI across their business. “DyFlex brings deep SAP consulting capabilities that are key to reimagining SaaS, modernising clients’ business landscapes and driving operational performance,” said Cognizant senior vice president and head of intelligent enterprise platforms Roshan Subudhi. “This proposed acquisition would bring together DyFlex’s SAP expertise with Cognizant’s frontier and autonomous enterprise capabilities and global delivery at scale, helping clients derive greater value from AI across their business.” Following completion of the proposed transaction, Cognizant expects to combine DyFlex’s regional SAP expertise and proprietary accelerators with its global industry experience and AI platforms, including Neuro AI Enterprise Core, the Cognizant SAP Agentic AI Platform and Frontier offerings. “Clients across Australia and New Zealand are seeking practical pathways to modernise core platforms while adopting cloud, data and AI capabilities,” said Cognizant managing director Carla Ramchand . “This proposed acquisition would bring DyFlex’s deep local SAP talent and strong understanding of Australia’s major industries together with Cognizant’s AI capabilities and global scale. “For DyFlex’s clients and the organisations we look forward to working with, it would mean the trusted people they know today, with even more ways to accelerate their transformation ambitions.” The service provider’s clients would continue to work with the people and expertise they trust, backed by Cognizant’s global reach, industry experience and AI capabilities to help them go further. “DyFlex has grown by building enduring relationships with our clients, investing in our great people and developing deep expertise across our core industries and the SAP ecosystem,” said its CEO, Evan Mantis . “Joining Cognizant would be an exciting next chapter for our clients and colleagues.” That next chapter for DyFlex has long been a part of the MSP’s growth strategy. “Over the last three years, we’ve had 300 per cent growth in our employee numbers and 350 per cent growth in revenue,” Mantis told ARN in August. “The Bluetree team brought in just over 50 people, so our data and analytics team is around 70 people at the moment. “Of our 300 employees, what’s interesting is that this makes us one of the biggest investors in SAP talent across Australia and New Zealand.” The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to required regulatory approvals and the satisfaction of other customary closing conditions. Until closing, Cognizant and DyFlex will continue to operate as separate businesses. Financial details were not disclosed.

title: Dicker Data’s Ben Johnson: The role partners need to play in market demand
author: arnnet.com.au
content: The role of a partner should be to act as a leader for their customers to guide them from what they think they need to what they really need, which is particularly true for demands around AI adoption and device modernisation. This is according to distributor Dicker Data’s Australia and New Zealand general manager of marketing and strategy Ben Johnson, who said partners play a vital role in helping their customers realise what they want out of their technology stack, even if they don’t initially themselves. During the distributor’s TechX conference keynote, Johnson said partners are being placed in difficult positions when a customer tells them, “we want some AI”. “The scary thing is customers don’t actually know what they’re asking for when they’re asking for this,” he said. “What they mean is they want access to an AI-ready foundation. “So, the next time one of your customers says, ‘We need some AI,’ they mean they want access to the readiness, the governance, the compliance, the security, and so forth that comes with building an AI-ready foundation.” Johnson elaborated on his keynote, adding that partners are facing pressure to deliver AI solutions that they may not have access to the right frameworks for. As such, he said to ARN that AI should be viewed in the same way cloud was during its peak. “The future of AI … is quite similar to what the industry experienced with cloud, where everyone rushed to the public cloud, and then worked out that it may not have been the most appropriate place for every workload,” Johnson said. “When consumption costs were turned on, there was the bill shock phase, and then we landed somewhere in the hybrid environment, which is what we have today. At the moment, everyone is rushing towards public AI. “We’re at that same tipping point now, where they’re about to turn on consumption or have turned on consumption in many cases.” Just like cloud, Johnson said he sees the future of AI being both hybrid and sovereign, because “sovereignty equals control and reliability over your own data, and we need to move to a world where you can control your token costs based on the infrastructure that you have”. As a result, users become less budget dependent on workloads and more on infrastructure, he added. “You become less budget dependent on the workloads that you’re going to be running, and more dependent on the infrastructure stack that powers your AI solutions,” Johnson said. Millions of outdated devices yet to be updated Last year was also significant for refresh cycles, with Windows 10 reaching end of life in October 2025. Johnson highlighted during his keynote that while there are still 500,000 devices in the wild to be updated to Windows 11, the more alarming figure was that there are over three million Windows 11 commercial devices that are over four years old. Although these devices are still technically modern and compliant, they still run the risk of being outdated. “Businesses have had it tough in both Australia and New Zealand in that four-year period. Now, we’re starting to see customers investing again,” Johnson said. “We’re getting to that next investment cycle on the curve, and we’re starting to see positive turns in the economy where businesses are starting to invest again.” Attempting to keep pace with recent advancements in AI requires tapping into modern technology. Relying on outdated devices puts partners at a clear disadvantage when trying to meet demand. “There was a lot of hype around AI when it first came out,” Johnson said. “Our industry took on the majority of that hype and had to deal with customer expectations and the question of, ‘We need some AI’, … so now, the impact of AI is very real. “You even don’t have to look too far – even just as far as Microsoft, [which] has just announced hybrid intelligence, where Copilot will now run on the device, and it will work out where the right place to run each query is, depending on what you’re asking. “That is a really key piece of how partners and customers will manage cost.” To get the last of those holdouts towards hardware refreshes, partners should be emphasising the productivity benefits available to customers. “Applications haven’t slowed down,” Johnson added. “The amount of load on a PC is growing every day. “Edge intelligence and edge workload[s are] increasing at a pace that we haven’t seen before. So, if you’re running applications that are modern day today on PCs or devices that are four years old, your user experience is not going to be at the level where you need it to be. “Employee experience is actually becoming a real deciding factor for the generation that’s now entering the workforce. They want new, modern, and compliant devices that enable them to do their best work. They don’t want to sit there and wait for a minute while you log in. They want long battery life, [and] access to all of the features that modern devices bring to not only make them more productive but to deliver better outcomes for the businesses.”

title: Telstra enterprise experiences ordering and fulfilment issues
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Telecommunications service provider Telstra is experiencing issues with its Telstra Order Exchange platform for enterprise customers. It is understood by ARN that this could be impacting business customers, resellers and sales teams during a key period for device upgrades and contract renewals. According to reports, the disruption has delayed the processing and fulfilment of orders, leaving customers, dealers and account teams awaiting resolution. In a statement to ARN, a spokesperson from Telstra said earlier this week the telco had completed a planned upgrade to the Telstra Order Exchange platform used by enterprise customers. “Following the upgrade, we’ve identified some issues that are affecting ordering for some customers,” they said. “Our teams are working through those requests manually while we resolve the issue, and we expect normal service to resume soon. “We apologise for the inconvenience and thank our business and enterprise customers for their patience while we work to get things back on track.” However, Telstra did not confirm full scope of the outage, the number of customers affected and the timeline for restoration. This comes a month after an external review found Telstra failed to treat network timing as a critical network capability during its July outage , with unclear ownership and insufficient expertise and weak process controls contributing to the outage. The external review, conducted by Technology Audit Partners (TAP), found the outage was triggered when incorrect date information spread through parts of Telstra’s mobile network following planned maintenance on its network timing system. The firm’s findings were submitted to the Senate inquiry examining the Triple Zero disruption.

title: blueAPACHE lays out its redesign of managed services in the AI era
author: arnnet.com.au
content: blueAPACHE has redesigned the way it delivers managed and professional services as demands of AI, cyber security, compliance and digital transformation continue to put constraints on its customers. At the launch of its “re-engineered managed services strategy” in Sydney in mid-October, its chief executive officer (CEO) Michael Zuppa said governance, security, observability, operational integration and executive-led cultural change must be in place before organisations accelerate automation and AI initiatives. “Our customers want better experiences, and our regulators want assurances,” he told attendees at the event. “Then you’ve got security threats evolving at pace. “All of this is happening at the same time, and these demands are competing for the same organisational capacity … that’s the challenge.” The real hinderance to customer innovation isn’t “ambition”, but complexity – which is “outpacing organisational capacity”, Zuppa noted. “It’s a challenge of scale, capacity and an organisational shift to a new way of working,” he said. “That is what I mean by the mid-market innovation gap. “Innovation isn’t constrained by ideas; it’s constrained by capacity. The conversation needs to change.” According to Zuppa, the path forward is to “simplify, reduce complexity, avoid connecting disparate systems, and focus on processes that are controllable”. “Partnering is key … partnering with platforms, skilled providers and an ecosystem that is connected,” he said. “Driven together on a common foundation, then amplifying from there. “This is where we use the embedded capabilities of those platforms and partners to amplify outputs and multiply the impact of our current resources. It must be focused on outcomes and use cases that deliver tangible benefits back into the business and ensure technology is aligned to those objectives. “That’s going to allow mid-market organisations to differentiate, move faster and surpass what the market would otherwise expect.” A broader example of this approach is blueAPACHE running approximately120 inbound customer routes across its customer base. It uses the Zoom Contact Centre platform to automatically recognise callers and connect them to the right team regardless of which number they dial. Native integration with ServiceNow means interaction records are created automatically. This gives technicians customer context from the first second, while real-time dashboards provide visibility into staffing requirements throughout the day. “A key component of this whole integration stack was bringing it into the core ITSM [IT service management] platform so that our service agents don’t have to swivel-chair,” he told ARN . “They don’t need to look into three different applications. “They’re working out of one service workspace where they’re doing the ticketing, voice and troubleshooting analysis. It all comes together and is connected within their one service workspace. “That was the most important thing: making it streamlined and seamless in the way communication happens.” According to Zuppa, blueAPACHE didn’t know that it could adopt certain capabilities within the budgets and complexities of how it runs its contact centre solution. “We evaluated, through our partner ecosystem, options that could not only do what we were currently doing with our legacy-based communication platform, but also where we saw the market going,” he explained. “We wanted to ensure there was full AI capability embedded from the ground up. “It could handle transcriptions, recordings, voice and real-time sentiment on every single call.” Customer experience Those were the things blueAPACHE was evaluating, which proved the MSP had the ability to have full sentiment analysis across every single call, as well as summarised transcriptions automatically populated into each interaction. This is valuable when considering details for professional teams or when looking at interactions at a later date, explained Zuppa. “What we found during these assessments was that other elements within contact centre management, particularly the quality management side, are generally delivered through third-party OEMs or integrations and usually come with a very different cost profile,” he said. “One area that people often avoid is workforce management because it is generally expensive, hard to implement and time-consuming. “The way Zoom brought it in was at less than a tenth of the cost of anything else we looked at and probably a tenth of the complexity to implement.” “It wasn’t really something we would bring in, but because it was available, it has made a massive difference; tying in automatic scheduling and skill-based routing enhanced the level at which we can route and manage communications beyond what we were hoping to achieve.” The next evolution of contact centres is being driven by AI-powered interactive voice response (IVR) capabilities, particularly for handling structured and repetitive customer interactions. “These are sophisticated agents that can talk in any language, translate it and transcribe it into any language in real time,” Zuppa explained. It follows very structured workflows, which is typically what many contact-centre agents are doing. “They also have the ability to reference large knowledge bases curated for a specific service in seconds,” he said. “What that means is higher-quality first interactions in many cases. “They’re more accurate and more consistent. It is creating concerns at the lower level of structured work.” However, because blueAPACHE deals with complex IT-based issues, there is still a need for human interaction. “It’s about how we surface all of that information to our agents in real time as quickly as possible, while also deferring lower-level work that isn’t a good use of their time,” he said. “A simple password reset, a service request or similar task can be handled through natural language interaction. “The IVR agents can populate the ticketing systems with those details automatically.” Running fast Service interactions are likely to shift towards customer-side agents, with users increasingly talking or chatting directly with an AI agent on their device rather than relying on voice calls. Although organisations will still need to accommodate customers who prefer voice, he expects autonomous endpoints capable of self-healing, self-diagnosing problems and making recommendations to resolve issues in real time. However, Zuppa noted that successful AI adoption requires more than technology. Without executive sponsorship, organisational buy-in and cultural change, transformation efforts are unlikely to succeed this change won’t happen. “This is not just a technology problem to solve. It is an organisational and cultural shift, and a new way of working that we all have to adopt,” he said. “This is a completely cultural change, meaning that we have to enable our staff. We’ve got to change the way we allow and think and work. Some of our customers are moving at a much faster pace than others, but we are running just as fast as they are.” As a mid-market organisation, the MSP also looks to adopt a framework that has been tested on itself; as well as operationalised and learned internally. “Every capability that will be part of this platform has been built on those foundations,” Zuppa said. “We are not experts in everything. We have partnered well and integrated platforms well. “We are also learning and are probably only two to three months ahead of everyone else, especially those on the forefront of this. It is a fast-moving space. “You’ve got to connect with the right partners, learn together and get those foundations right. That’s why I talk about foundations. Speed without foundations will only compound risk.” Before organisations can become AI-ready, they first need to become operationally ready, Zuppa added. “That means concentrating on key domain pillars around governance to ensure the right policies and processes are aligned to security, cyber security coverage, regulatory requirements and other obligations,” he said. “You need visibility. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Organisations need visibility not only across traditional IT stacks but across this new and evolving landscape.” Another key area is financial observability and measuring actual outcomes and experiences, particularly in the world of tokenomics and AI usage. “You need that visibility and the ability to measure,” Zuppa added.

title: Equinix creates EPIC path to AI challenge
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Data centre operator Equinix is looking to help enterprises move their AI projects to production with the launch of its Equinix Enhanced Performance Innovation Centres (EPIC). In these centres, now live Sydney, Frankfurt, London, Osaka and Paris, enterprises will be able to test, build and deploy high-density AI infrastructure with the confidence and support of Equinix experts and technology partners. More locations are expected to open in 2027. For Equinix, these centres play a role in helping to ensure infrastructure is cooled, powered and connected. Those factors have become a strategic imperative that determines deployment speed, cost and performance. “Liquid cooling is an essential component of modern enterprise infrastructure and a hard requirement for customer’s deploying AI,” said Equinix senior vice president infrastructure products and services Brian Stein. However, few enterprises have the expertise to integrate cooling, power, networking and facility operations effectively, with shortcomings in any areas potentially delaying deployment. This delay creates growing pressure on organisations to ensure their AI infrastructure is ready to keep pace with adoption. EPIC looks to address those challenges by giving enterprises a place to prove it out inside live Equinix data centres , with enterprises being able to trial the latest liquid-cooled GPU and CPU platforms with leading hardware partners and test AI training and inference workloads under real-world conditions. Alongside Equinix experts , they can identify infrastructure and operational issues before production and make informed decisions as they scale. EPIC builds on Equinix’s existing innovation spaces, which started with the announcement of one of its first co-innovation facility in 2022. Two years on, the global data centre provider rolled out Solution Validation Centres for customers to validate deployments and see how Equinix supports distributed environments. EPIC brings that same experiential approach to liquid cooling and high-density AI deployments, noted global advertising company Criteo. “Liquid cooling was new territory for us, so we built our confidence step by step,” said its SVP of engineering infrastructure security internal IT and CISO, Matthieu Blumberg. “Our AI runs across a distributed footprint, and the infrastructure must perform the same way wherever it sits,” he said. “We saw how liquid cooling performed in practice, learned what it took to run it well, and then committed to scale.”

title: Zoom updates Up Partner program with simplicity, incentives, MSP specialisation
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Zoom is updating its partner program over the next several months with a streamlined structure and new incentives for improved partner enablement and a deeper focus on AI-powered offerings. Announced at Zoomtopia Partner Connect event, the updates include a simplified incentive structure, new partner specialisations, expanded self-service tools, and additional AI services. “When our partners succeed, we succeed, and we want to give our partners every opportunity to win,” said Zoom head of global channel GTM Nick Tidd. “In just two years, we’ve invested heavily in our program, tools, and the breadth of our platform to build a channel-first strategy squarely around our partners’ success.” The simplification of the program sees Zoom replace its legacy points bonus system with a net monthly recurring revenue (MRR) growth metric, with partners earning one point for every $1,000 in MRR growth during the relevant period. Additionally, newer customer MRR will count separately, enabling partners to earn points in both categories for eligible new customer growth. Meanwhile, on the program’s Participation track, the vendor is replacing asset shares and campaign leads with a flat five-point credit for every customer-facing activity, including events. Partners are also potentially eligible to earn points for qualifying AWS Marketplace deals and participating in quarterly marketing campaigns. Later this month, Zoom will launch a business process outsourcing program to grant eligible business process outsourcing providers access to Zoom Contact Center under usage-based terms. From next month, partners can view their not-for-resale (NFR) product availability by partner level. Additionally, the process to request incremental NFR licences will be made self-service via Zoom’s partner portal by the first quarter of 2027. By December, the vendor will introduce a managed service provider specialisation, with expected benefits to include advanced delegated account access, direct tier 2 support, incentive benefits and enhanced service levels. Meanwhile, in 2027, Zoom will introduce new sales performance incentive funds (SPIFF) and rebates to scale on contract length, with additional visibility into partners’ reward structures.

title: Evergreen co-founder Ramsey Sahyoun credits Warren Buffett for business model
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Since its entry into the Australian and New Zealand (A/NZ) market, Evergreen has made its mark on the surging mergers and acquisitions (M&A) landscape through the purchase of A/NZ MSPs via a long-term, decentralised ownership model inspired by Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway buy-and-hold approach. The company now counts around 140 MSPs globally within its portfolio, including 20 across Australia and New Zealand – a figure that is expected to rise to 23 in the near term.
