In September, it purchased of Adelaide-based technology consultancy, managed services and business communications provider Concept Data and its sister business Voice Select. Over the last two years Evergreen has made strides to become a part of the A/NZ channel, questions abound about its growth plans and what its expanding presence means for the local channel. In an interview with ARN , Evergreen co-founder M&A partner Ramsey Sahyoun explained the strategy behind its approach. “Berkshire Hathaway was really the inspiration for me and Jeff [Totten CEO and co-founder] when we started Evergreen,” he said. “Berkshire Hathaway is Warren Buffett’s holding company, and what we saw that was unique with Berkshire is that it’s structured as a holding company. “They buy companies, and they’re a permanent home for those businesses. They don’t buy companies with the intent of reselling them.” The idea to start a similar venture came to Sahyoun and Totten when they were both working at private equity firm Alpine Investors in 2015. “Jeff and I were previously working in private equity, and we loved it,” he noted. “We didn’t like the part where you sell businesses on a five-year time horizon because you never get to really build something. “You never get to see kind of the compounding effects. We’re nine years into building Evergreen, in traditional private. That’s like two different private equity hold periods.” That long-term mindset has also shaped how Evergreen funds its growth. Alpine Investors — the firm where Sahyoun and Totten used to work — is Evergreen’s majority backer. According to Sahyoun, the equity firm has been supportive of the holding company’s growth and helped to give them its start. “Today, what funds Evergreen is the cash flow from the existing companies, and that’s what we use to buy new businesses,” he told ARN during Evergreen Elevate. “Alpine put us in business nine years ago. “They gave us the initial capital to buy businesses, and when we proved this [worked], they doubled down on it. “They’re very long-term focused. They manage money for pension funds, endowments and foundations, so they’ve been a great partner and will continue to be for a long time.” That outlook is shared by Evergreen’s founders, with both Sahyoun and Totten focused on building an enduring business rather than chasing short-term outcomes. “We’re going to be doing it for a long time. You have to have that mindset at the top of the company to pursue a strategy like this, otherwise everybody just wants to flip,” Sahyoun said. While long-term holding companies are starting to become a little more popular in the US, by and large, roll-ups with five-year time horizons are still the most common type of investments for equity firms. “The incentives are set up so there’s more to gain by flipping a business in five years than by patiently compounding over 20 years,” Sahyoun said. “I don’t see a lot of people rushing into this. I don’t think people have the time horizon for it. “People want to make a quick buck and get out. Warren Buffett calls it the ‘get rich slow’ plan. “That’s how he’s referred to building Berkshire. He’s compounded the business at 20 per cent a year for 60 years and built one of the biggest companies in the world. It hasn’t been that slow, but he’s stuck with it for so long.” Long game For Sahyoun, the long-term strategy of Evergreen “is a ground game”. Ultimately, the business the holding company is in is providing guidance and support related to technology to small businesses. “Our business is buying small businesses,” he added. “You don’t do that through centralisation or from a distance. You do it face to face, you do it locally, conversation by conversation.” “There was a point four or five years ago where we started to get good at helping businesses grow.” Initially, Evergreen was a good home for companies. Sahyoun said eventually it helped the businesses become the best version of themselves. “We just didn’t screw them up, which is great. We’ve gotten a lot better at that, and that’s been really rewarding. I remember writing down the pitch I would make to business owners when we started Evergreen … it’s essentially the same today.” That pitch has been adjusted and Evergreen has improved its tactics over time. “The idea of operating a company independently and buying it to hold, not to flip, hasn’t changed,” said Sahyoun. “I’ve been making that pitch for 10 years and haven’t had to change it because nobody else has done it.” That philosophy remains key to the trust owner-led businesses have in selling to Evergreen. According to Sahyoun, founders spend decades building their businesses and deserve an outcome that preserves what they created. Through its model, Evergreen aims to provide a fulfilling path for business owners while generating financial returns by growing the revenue and profitability of the companies it acquires. “The companies we have bought, from an organic growth standpoint — excluding acquisitions and just looking at the growth of the individual companies — makes New Zealand our fastest-growing region, which is really cool,” Sahyoun said. “I think that says a lot about the quality of the companies we’ve partnered with here. “The conversations I’ve had with people that we haven’t yet acquired are often centred around goals for what they want to sell their business for, and the business is not there yet.” That is one of the reasons why Evergreen created its Elevate conference. Many of the MSP owners attend with a target valuation in mind, despite their businesses not yet being worth that amount. Sahyoun said the event was designed to provide practical strategies that owners could apply to increase the value of their businesses over time, helping them move closer to their long-term goals. “Most people, when I talk to them, aren’t like, ‘Glad you reached out. I want to sell my business right now’,” he said. “Nobody says that. It’s usually like, ‘I’ve got this goal. I’m not there yet, but let’s develop a relationship, and could you help me get there?’ That’s the bulk of the conversations I end up having.” The other side of the equation, Sahyoun continued, is the MSPs that have already sold to traditional roll-ups. He added that for founders who have spent 20 or 30 years building a company, it can be “a sad ending” to see it ultimately sold as an asset to a larger consolidator. “I think a lot of companies, they get rolled up and the customers leave, the employees leave, the business is a shell of itself or kind of no longer exists,” Sahyoun. “The people running the individual businesses … building the company, serving the customers … [and] building a culture of that individual business — that’s what it’s all about. “We try to keep the bureaucracy above the operating company to a minimum because we want to empower other people running the individual businesses.” Balancing demands To support that decentralised approach, Evergreen has built a regional operating model. The holding company is organised into eight regions overseeing about 130 MSPs, with each region led by a regional CEO responsible for between 15 and 25 companies. Its A/NZ MSP portfolio, Lyra Technology Group, is run by regional CEO Waruna Kirimetiyawa . He was the managing director of New Zealand-based MSP Lancom Technology , and one of the first MSPs in the region to sell to Evergreen. Having that experience enables them to support leaders from firsthand experience while helping preserve the company’s decentralised approach. The structure is designed to keep bureaucracy to a minimum, empower local leadership and allow operating companies to maintain their independence and culture, added Sahyoun. However, not every leader at Evergreen comes from an MSP background. Sahyoun said Evergreen vice president Sydney Hockett doesn’t have a channel background but has immersed herself in the industry. “One of the things I really like about our team is that it’s a mix. We have people who have run MSPs for 20 years,” he said. “We also have people for whom it’s their first time in the industry, and we’re having to teach them. “The people that do the best are the ones that really try to immerse themselves in the industry. You’ve got to go to all the events. You’ve got to meet with all the people…make it part of your identity.” For Sahyoun, that people-first approach is one of the most rewarding aspects of building Evergreen. Although being a global business means frequent travel, he said the greater challenge is balancing those demands with family life. “We’re a global business – I feel like I’m travelling practically every week,” Sahyoun said. “That’s been the hardest part. I have a family, balancing that has been hard. “I do relish the fact that people are counting us to deliver on something that’s important to them. I don’t get overwhelmed by that. I get overwhelmed by trying to juggle everything, but I don’t get overwhelmed by the responsibility. “We want to be old guys still loving what we’re doing and building the business, so hopefully we can do that.” Lilia Guan travelled to Evergreen Elevate in Melbourne as a guest of Evergreen.

title: Cohesity appoints Matthew Johnston as APJ senior partner sales director
author: arnnet.com.au
content: Security vendor Cohesity has appointed Matthew Johnston as senior director of partner sales for Asia Pacific and Japan (APJ) to lead its partner and channel go-to-market strategy across the region. According to Cohesity, Johnston’s appointment underscores its investment in strengthening its partner ecosystem in the region. This comes as organisations are prioritising data resilience and security as core parts of their digital transformation strategies, the company said. Based in Perth, Johnston will report to Cohesity’s APJ vice president of sales and general manager Peter Hanna and will be responsible for driving the delivery of data resilience and security solutions across Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Korea, Japan, Hong Kong and Taiwan. He will also expand new go-to-market partner programmes and partnerships to maximise alignment with customers’ most pressing cyber resilience challenges. “Matthew’s appointment reflects our continued commitment to deepening Cohesity’s partner ecosystem across one of our fastest-growing global regions,” said Hanna. “He brings a rare combination of regional expertise, executive sales leadership and deep channel relationships with our most significant multi-national partners. I’m confident he will play a pivotal role in developing our channel ecosystem and helping our customers strengthen their data resilience and security capabilities.” Johnston has more than two decades of leadership experience across Asia Pacific, most recently as chief revenue officer at data platform Odaseva where he led global sales, marketing, business development, solutions engineering, and alliances. Prior to that, Johnston held senior regional leadership roles at VMware, Commvault, Dell Software and Quest Software. “I’m looking forward to building on Cohesity’s clear market leadership momentum across Asia Pacific and Japan, by working strategically with our partners to help our joint customers strengthen their data resilience and security posture,” said Johnston. “As agentic AI deployment accelerates, the ability to protect, and secure, the data that drive those new, business critical workflows, will only become more essential to how our customers maintain secure, compliant and efficient operations.”

title: How to Get More Likes on Instagram Posts
author: Business Review Usa Team
content: Instagram is one of the most popular social media platforms in the world, with more than one billion active users each month. Having such a huge population on Instagram means it is the ideal place for businesses and entrepreneurs to establish their brands. The trick to being successful on Instagram is ensuring your posts are getting as many likes as possible. People gravitate towards accounts with a lot of likes, as they want to be in on the latest trend or interesting product. Getting more likes also means your account is rated better by the Instagram algorithm, which makes the account more visible to users who search related topics and keywords. Below are some ways to ensure you are getting more likes on your Instagram posts. Create Quality Content The basis for any quality Instagram account is having very good content. You have to ensure that what you are posting is authentic, relevant, interesting and unique. If your posts are boring, all the tricks in the world are not going to help your account become more popular. Focus on making each post unique in its message and aesthetic, while ensuring all your posts look as though they were done by a professional. Taking such steps to improve your content will ensure it catches the eye of people when they are scrolling through different posts. Your goal is to ensure people see your post and immediately want to click on your account, and then follow you for the foreseeable future. Leverage Hashtags To Your Benefit One of the most interesting ways to gain traction on Instagram is through hashtags. If you are ever on the platform and you notice a hashtag on a post, click on it and you will see an entirely new page open. The hashtag will allow you to see all posts that are made using that hashtag. You are likely to see the most popular and trending posts from the past day, which is why you want your account to be seen as popular and trendy by people and the algorithm. Ensure you are using all relevant hashtags, such as the category of your posts, area where you are doing business and anything else that may be relevant. But do not add too many hashtags either. Some people make the mistake of putting 20 hashtags on their post. Going in that direction is overkill, and will make people think your post is spam by a bot. Ensure you are using the most relevant hashtags, and not filling up your post with many variations of the same few words. Create Fun Captions The days of people solely looking at pictures on Instagram are long gone. The platform will always have a photo-first approach, but the captions on your posts matter a great deal as well. People can say a lot within those captions. You can write entire essays, make passionate speeches, or write witty one-liners to excite your audience. The captions you are putting on your posts should be relevant to the picture and your business. Think about the brand you want to build. Your captions should fit within that brand. Having a singular voice on all your posts will help you attract the type of audience you want. Another tip is to respond when people comment on your post or caption. Do not be afraid to engage, but always remain friendly. Post All The Time Posting infrequently is the worst mistake you can make on any social media platform. If you are making a single post a week, you are not going to gain any traction, regardless of how good that post may have been. While you should not be spamming people’s feeds with posts, you should be posting at least a couple of times a day. Try to keep a regular schedule for your posts, such as posting at a similar time each day. By creating a schedule for your posts, you give your audience something to expect each day. They will know that you are putting up a new picture or video at a certain time each day, which will drive them to visit your account page on Instagram more often. Considering Buying Likes Even if you try all of the above strategies, you may not see the substantial increase in likes you are seeking. Another issue is that creating the ideal posting strategies and schedules is time consuming. Not everyone has hours to dedicate to Instagram, especially if they are running a business at the same time. If you want to find a faster way to get more likes on your post, you may want to consider buying likes. There is a legitimate reason to purchase likes, even if you are taking those other steps to improve organic likes as well. Think of buying likes as an accelerant. The purchase will not take your account from anything to greatness, but it will speed up your rise on the platform. Use a Reputable Source for Likes If you do choose to purchase likes on Instagram , make sure you are doing it through a reputable seller. There are far too many websites that sell very cheap Instagram likes because they are low quality. These likes are easily detected by the algorithm and may be removed within a few days. When you are paying money for likes, you want them to remain in place and have a positive impact on how the algorithm views your account. Only reputable sellers can get these high quality likes for you. Purchasing likes will ensure your account rises in popularity very quickly. People will see your account in their feed and search results pages a lot more often, and the quality of your posts will ensure they follow you as well. To Conclude By using the above tricks, and then purchasing likes at strategic moments, you can ensure your account is getting as many likes on Instagram as possible. Within a few months, you will have a much more prominent account, which will improve your entire digital marketing strategy.

title: Supreme Court to hear case on division of retirement, disability pay in military divorces
author: Claire Barrett
content: The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to consider a case that challenges whether divorce settlements are enforceable if they agree to protect a former spouse’s share of military retirement pay and the amount is later affected by disability compensation. Under federal law, former spouses may receive up to half a service member’s time-based military retirement pay. But medical-based military retirement pay and any Veterans Affairs disability pay is protected and not divisible. In Marschner v. Marschner, which was accepted by the high court earlier this month, Roxane Marschner, who married North Dakota Army National Guard soldier Richard Marschner, is seeking to enforce a clause in her divorce settlement in which Richard agreed to pay her the equivalent of her portion of military retirement pay if any of it was offset by disability compensation. The couple married in 1994 and divorced 22 years later. In their settlement, Roxane was to receive a percentage of Richard’s military and federal civilian benefits when he retired. But Richard later was medically retired as a result of service-connected injuries and received medical retirement pay and VA disability compensation — neither of which is divisible under the Uniformed Services Former Spouses Protection Act. Roxane then took Richard to court, arguing that he had agreed to pay her if she did not receive her share of benefits. The lower court ruled in her favor. Richard then petitioned the North Dakota Supreme Court, which said the provision was unenforceable. Roxane Marschner then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to consider the case, saying that the law and a previous Supreme Court ruling only limited courts from instating provisions that divided disability compensation and did not apply to private agreements negotiated by spouses. She also argued that other states, including Virginia, Illinois, Nevada and Alaska, have allowed enforcement of such agreements, known as indemnification provisions, in divorce settlements, and a decision by the U.S. Supreme Court was necessary to ensure equity across the legal system. Richard Marschner’s attorneys have said the state courts don’t have the authority to divide federally protected benefits and the North Dakota district courts order to Richard to pay Roxane is invalid as a result. Marschner’s attorney, Johanna Clyborne of Minnesota-based Brekke, Clyborne and Ribich, told Military Times that divorce agreements such as the Marschners’ happen “more than people realize” because veterans — and attorneys — often don’t understand federal protections of disability benefits and medical retirement payments. “Congress has spoken on this issue, right, and it is non-divisible. There’s going to be different sorts of interpretations, but Congress thought that the veterans were entitled to disability benefits and basically prioritized, and to allow them to be stripped by a state court in very narrow circumstances is not what was intended,” Clyborne said in an interview. Several previous cases have addressed the division of retirement pay and disability benefits in military divorces. In Howell v. Howell, the Supreme Court ruled in 2017 that state courts cannot require a veteran to compensate his spouse half his retirement pay when he waived a portion of it to receive non-taxable VA disability compensation. The Court has not scheduled a date for Marschner v. Marschner, although the case could be heard as early as January. Clyborne said the case has the potential to affect divorce agreements for veterans who receive Combat-Related Specialty Compensation, Concurrent Retirement Disability Pay and other benefits. “Hopefully it will settle a lot of questions folks have been wrestling with,” Clyborne said.

title: US Army fields new system for sweeping munitions planning, management
author: migration
content: The U.S. Army released the initial modernized munitions system meant to be the official source for the service’s upgraded munitions requirements and expenditure reporting. The Total Army Combat and Training Munitions Information System, or TACTMIS, is meant to replace the previously used Total Ammunition Management Information System, or TAMIS, once it retires on Oct. 30. TACTMIS aims to update how the Army plans, manages and reports munitions for training, testing, operational and combat activities, according to a recent release . “TACTMIS is a foundational step in modernizing how the Army manages the munitions that enable readiness and warfighting,” Army Chief of Munitions and G-3/5/7 Deputy Chief of Staff John C. Hinnant said in the release. “It gives the Total Army a more authoritative, integrated and accountable way to generate requirements, manage authorizations and maintain trusted visibility of munitions data across the force.” TACTMIS, developed under the Software Acquisition Pathway, was built using the Appian Platform to be a cloud-enabled, low-code “Software-as-a-Service” capability, the announcement says. The system supports a variety of inputs such as requirements calculations, authorization management, request processing and enterprise reporting. Using a common organizational framework, the system is meant to reduce manual workload, improve data integrity and increase the visibility of munitions demand and fulfillment across the service and its joint partners. The upgraded system can coordinate workflows across enterprise systems while maintaining the commanding role of the Army systems and data sources it interacts with, per the statement, supporting readiness planning while providing timely data to inform decision-making for senior leaders and defense industrial base requests. “TACTMIS moves the Army from fragmented and manual munitions-management processes toward a modern digital capability built for the scale and speed of today’s force,” CW3 Deidre Burgos, TACTMIS program manager, said in the release. “Our focus is ensuring commanders and staffs have reliable tools to manage munitions requirements, authorizations, forecasts and expenditures with greater accuracy, transparency and confidence.” The system is also aligned to support the Army’s broader modernization efforts such as Ammo360, which is a software initiative meant to boost ammunition accountability and unify the operating picture within the service’s network. TACTMIS is designed to support over 10,000 users across the globe and operate without dedicated unit-level administrators. The system’s platform allows for TACTMIS to evolve in increments as the Army’s requirements, policies and mission needs change so redesigns are unnecessary for future enhancements. Planned enhancements include a classified capability intended to support real-time combat munition requirements and expenditure reporting for readiness and logistics operations, the announcement reads. “Delivering this initial release is an important milestone, but it is also the beginning of an enduring modernization effort,” Burgos said. “TACTMIS provides the digital foundation the Army needs to evolve alongside future operational requirements while maintaining uninterrupted support to the force’s ability to arm, train, and sustain.”

title: Lockheed invests $300M in Texas plant to feed missile surge
author: migration
content: Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand its plant in Grand Prairie, Texas, which supports all programs across its Missiles and Fire Control business, including the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors, the Precision Strike Missile and the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile. The company said Oct. 14 that the expansion will help the plant reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites, including Camden, Arkansas and Troy, Alabama. The project expands the plant’s manufacturing footprint to more than 735,000 square feet. The expansion adds 100,000 square feet of new space and converts 85,000 square feet of office space into factory floor space for automated, high-precision machining. Nearly 800 production employees work at the plant, which produced 250,000 parts in 2025. Lockheed said it has added more than 30 high-precision machines in recent months and expects to install nearly 100 additional machines by the end of 2026. Lockheed also said Hadrian, a California-based manufacturing startup, will install 24 automated machines at the Grand Prairie facility to produce missile parts. Lockheed employees will operate the equipment, which is expected to be up and running by early 2027. The project follows a memorandum of understanding the two companies signed in December 2025. “The warfighter can’t wait on peacetime timelines,” Hadrian CEO Chris Power said in the release. “Rebuilding the Arsenal of Freedom at the scale America needs will take partnerships that combine expertise and speed, and this is what that looks like.” The buildout supports a series of framework agreements the Defense Department has signed with Lockheed since January, designed to boost missile production and lead to long-term contracts. The first aims to increase PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 to roughly 2,000 interceptors per year over seven years. The Army followed with a $4.7 billion contract in April, then converted it in July into a seven-year production contract worth about $58.6 billion in total. A separate THAAD framework , signed in January, led to a June contract from the Missile Defense Agency worth more than $35 billion to quadruple interceptor production. Lockheed and the Pentagon announced similar agreements for the Precision Strike Missile on March 25 and for the AIM-260 on Sept. 17. “Lockheed Martin has brought together commercial speed and combat-proven performance because America needs both,” said Jim Taiclet, Lockheed’s chairman, president and CEO. “By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we’re transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale.” “This expansion is more than just a new facility; it is a stronger supply chain and a more resilient industrial base,” said Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment. The Grand Prairie investment is part of Lockheed’s plan to spend $8 billion to $9 billion through 2030 to increase munitions production and modernize or expand more than 20 U.S. facilities. The company said it plans to create 6,000 jobs nationwide, including 2,000 in Texas.

title: Pentagon needs $50B for mass drone production, Hegseth says
author: migration
content: The Pentagon wants to build its stockpile of autonomous weapons from thousands of units to the millions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed AUSA attendees at the Project Agincourt panel on Wednesday, sharing that the Pentagon is requesting roughly $50 billion in reconciliation funding to support the push to scale autonomous and robotic systems. This request is part of an effort to make the technology available in far greater numbers. The figure is separate from the Pentagon’s fiscal 2027 budget request, which includes $53.6 billion for the Drone Dominance initiative . That request covers $16.9 billion for unmanned-system procurement, $14.4 billion for counter-unmanned systems, $13.5 billion for contested logistics, $4.5 billion for collaborative autonomy and $4.3 billion for institutional systems and personnel. The budget request does not establish that the reconciliation funding Hegseth cited is the same money or that it is dedicated entirely to drone purchases Hegseth characterized the funding as a one-time investment rather than a recurring annual allocation, intended to accelerate the development and production of autonomous and robotic systems. “Ultimately we will be dealing with hundreds of thousands of one-way attack systems this year and into the millions in years to come at a pace that this department’s never ever seen before.” The Defense Secretary said the Pentagon must make it easier for new companies to compete in a defense market long dominated by established contractors and costly platforms. Traditional defense firms remain important, he said, but the department also needs lower-cost systems that can be manufactured at scale. The Army’s Drone Dominance program offers a concrete measure of that ambition. In a December 2025 announcement, the Army said a $1 billion initiative would fund approximately 340,000 small unmanned aircraft systems for combat units over two years. The service said it expected to deliver tens of thousands of drones in 2026 and hundreds of thousands by 2027. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the service is broadening access to its programs for companies outside the traditional defense industrial base. The Army, he said, must make room for new entrants while continuing to work with established suppliers. Telle also described plans to coordinate the Army’s autonomous-systems efforts while distributing capabilities to operational units. The service is developing an approach that incorporates drones, autonomous ground systems, autonomous fires and autonomous lift into future combat operations. “We have an MOS in the Army, 390A, where warrant officers could keep the speciality and the skills over the duration to teach our soldiers how to do robotics,” Telle added. Expanding access to Army test ranges is another part of that effort, Telle said. Greater access gives developers more opportunities to test systems and receive feedback from military users. He also described efforts to share lessons across the force rather than have individual units and organizations solve the same problems independently. Hegseth said the department must remove bureaucratic barriers that slow the adoption of new technology, telling the panel, “I want you to tell me which rules can be signed away.” He urged officials to identify rules and directives that could be changed without involving new legislation to accelerate progress.

title: Stanford outpaces elite colleges in faculty-to-student ratio
author: Trilby Schmidt
content: Stanford University has the lowest faculty-to-student ratio, at 2:1, among 11 peer institutions of comparable size and prestige, according to an analysis by The Daily using data from the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). The dataset includes Stanford and 14 other universities. Faculty-to-student ratio is a comparison of full-time instructional staff and the undergraduate student population. In 2024, Stanford employed 20,394 individuals: a staggering number compared to other Silicon Valley colleges but comparable to peer institutions like Harvard, Columbia, the University of Pennsylvania and Yale. This analysis expounds on statistics previously reported on by The San Francisco Business Journal, which stated that Stanford “employs nearly five times as many staff” compared to other Silicon Valley colleges. Using data from the NCES, The Daily tested if Stanford’s inflated staff population remained a trend when examined against other universities of similar student population, staff population and endowment size. Based on these characteristics, The Daily compared Stanford to the universities in the Ivy League and the University of Chicago. The Daily’s analysis showed that Columbia University and the University of Pennsylvania employ similar amounts of staff as Stanford, Harvard and Yale despite having significantly smaller endowment. The average salary of the instructional staff at these universities is comparable. It remains unclear how much federal funding, or other forms of funding, may impact these schools’ yearly budget. Data from the (NCES) reveals the university’s administrative bloat – an issue in higher education involving inflated administrative populations when equated to teaching faculty and students – is comparable when analyzed against other elite private universities. Administrative bloat is not a new concern for Stanford. In 2024, The Daily published data indicating the school’s staff-to-student ratio had doubled since 1996. This concern can also be seen at the national level, with a 2025 congressional hearing on the issue, which included a current Brown student using administrative bloat as a sub-argument to call attention to the issue of inflated tuition costs and fixed pricing among Ivy League institutions. Each school was compared using a fixed set of characteristics. Some characteristics measured university population, including the number of total staff, full-time staff, full-time instructional staff, full-time non-institutional staff, undergraduate students and graduate students. Other characteristics measured financial metrics like the average salary of instructional staff, size of endowment and whether or not the school guarantees housing for all four years. In this analysis, instructional staff is defined as an occupation where the primary role is teaching, research or public service. Four universities — the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC), San Jose State University (SJSU) and Santa Clara University (SCU) — were included in the original San Francisco Business Journal piece, selected based on proximity to Stanford.  University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) was not included in the Business Journal’s analysis because it did not fall within the nine counties that the publication covers. However, The Daily included UC Berkeley because of its comparable reputation with Stanford.   The other nine schools included in The Daily’s analysis were California Institute of Technology (CalTech), University of Chicago, Brown University, Columbia University, Cornell University, Dartmouth College, Harvard University, Princeton University, the University of Pennsylvania and Yale University. Each of these schools were selected as peer institutions to Stanford, in terms of school rank and prestige. The data presented in this article demonstrates the possibility that all elite universities face the issue of administrative bloat, and that some are better equipped with financial resources to reduce the impact on tuition paying students.  Disclosure: This article is not a comprehensive analysis of these universities’ employment characteristics, but an overview of areas of note. title: Student protestors express solidarity with demonstrations in India
author: Charlie Goldberg
content: Students, faculty and supporters gathered in White Plaza on Wednesday to protest Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government.  The Stanford protests come in response to large protests that have shook India’s capital, New Delhi, after the country’s National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) was cancelled following a leak of the exam questions. The protest movement grew to encompass a wider critique of the incumbent, right-wing BJP government. The solidarity gathering was originally scheduled for Oct. 16, but was rescheduled after organizers said they were told by a professor at the last minute that tabling was not allowed during Reunion Homecoming. Pete Cerneka, Associate Director of Student Organizations, told The Daily that protests are not discouraged during New Student Orientation (NSO) or Reunion Homecoming. He said, however, that “[the university] wouldn’t allow a protest to bump an event that had already booked White Plaza.” When Cerneka communicated to the organizers that White Plaza was being used on Oct. 16, organizers mentioned rescheduling the event for Wednesday. He told the organizers that the space would likely remain unbooked on that day. The protest at White Plaza opened at noon with protest chants in Hindi and drumming. Organizers and attendees brought signage — some handmade, some seemingly AI-generated — which criticized the Modi government. Protesters particularly focused on election minister Gyanesh Kumar, who has come under fire for expunging names from India’s voter roll. One sign read, “Modi Gov’t illegally deletes 133 million – restore the voters, resign Gyanesh Kumari.” Ankita, an organizer who requested her last name be omitted citing fears of retaliation against international students, thanked the 30 or so attendees.  “Just showing up is an act of resistance. We are gathered here today to express our solidarity with the protests ongoing in New Delhi, against the [Special Intensive Revision (SIR)] electoral process, which has been recognized as disenfranchising millions of eligible voters and undermining the electoral process in India,” Ankita said to the crowd. The SIR is Kumar’s process of updating the electoral rolls, a change which has led to more than 130 million Indians being removed from the voter rolls. Another organizer, a San Jose resident named Raj Pariyar, came swaddled in a U.S. flag and sporting a baseball cap that read “America.”  “I came because we have to stand up for democratic rights and because the U.S. and India need to support each other as fellow democracies,” he said. Ankita told The Daily that the protest hadn’t been organized by a formal group but rather by concerned South Asian students looking to express solidarity. Though the protest was specifically in support of the Indian “cockroach” movement, Ankita said that “we feel these issues of oppression and discrimination are global issues and that fascism is a global issue.” Confusion over scheduling led the protest to be delayed from its original date. One student organizer, who asked not be named out of fear of retaliation against international students, said that organizers made the decision to reschedule the protest after a professor told him that tabling was not allowed during Reunion Homecoming. On Oct. 16, the day scheduled for the original protest, organizers found White Plaza was being used by a DJ. Protestors who had traveled to Stanford from other areas in the Bay Area had to be turned away.  After communicating with a representative from the Office of Student Engagement (OSE) the following Monday, organizers decided to reschedule to Wednesday. The representative explained that the space was free for protests or vigils as long as it was not booked. One organizer explained that the representative said he would put anybody who might book the space in touch with the student organizers. The student told The Daily that while he was grateful for the support of the representative of the OSE, “it was interesting that the practice of free speech in the dedicated zone for free speech is not unconditional.” Ankita told The Daily that she hoped that “the rescheduling challenges do not overshadow the larger purpose of this initiative” to “express solidarity with those fighting for democratic rights and resisting state oppression in India.” The post Student protestors express solidarity with demonstrations in India appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Egg Donation: $10,000–$100,000 After a Successful Match
author: Third-Party Advertising
content: California Baby Surrogacy’s egg donor program offers compensation of US$10,000–US$100,000 after a successful match, alongside the opportunity to help someone take a meaningful step toward building a family. For adults in the Stanford community exploring donation, the financial terms and the potential family impact are both worth understanding. Screening is required. Individual compensation and payment terms are set out in writing; applying does not guarantee acceptance, a match or the maximum amount. Explore the egg donor program What the egg donor program includes After a successful match, the program includes one trip to the California clinic’s location, with an approximate two-week stay. Travel, accommodation and meal expenses are reimbursed separately from compensation. Before booking, ask how travel arrangements, eligible expenses and reimbursement work. The two-week stay is not the full process. Screening, preparation, appointments, recovery and follow-up may require additional time. The participating clinic should explain the medical process and risks relevant to you, so you can consider the full commitment alongside classes, research, work and other plans. A meaningful purpose alongside compensation Donation may help an individual or couple move closer to becoming parents. That possibility gives the program a personal meaning beyond the financial terms. It is an opportunity to contribute to someone’s family-building journey, not a promise of a particular outcome. Your own priorities belong in that decision, too. You can be interested in the compensation and the chance to help while taking time to understand the responsibilities. Asking questions about your health, schedule, privacy and personal boundaries is part of exploring whether donation fits your life. A separate sperm donor program California Baby Surrogacy also offers a sperm donor program with compensation of US$10,000–US$40,000 after a successful match. The arrangement includes one trip to the California clinic’s location and an approximate two-to-three-day stay, with travel, accommodation and meals reimbursed separately. That stay does not cover the entire screening or follow-up process, and one trip does not necessarily mean one appointment. Screening and written payment terms apply; acceptance, a match and the maximum amount are not guaranteed. Start with the details that matter to you Adults age 21 and over are invited to explore the program information. Age and student status alone do not establish eligibility; additional program and clinical requirements apply. Start with the program that interests you and ask what the compensation covers, when payments would be made and what happens if plans change. Discuss privacy and future-contact arrangements before sharing sensitive information. Medical and legal questions belong with appropriately qualified advisers. Please do not send medical records or identity documents in public comments or social-media messages. Learning more is a first step, not a commitment to participate. Meaningful compensation. Meaningful impact. A decision that remains yours. title: Reel Classics: ‘A Man for All Seasons’ is a movie for our time
author: Ada Huang
content: In her column Reel Classics, Ada Huang ’30 reviews and analyzes classic films. Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques.  What defines you as a person? Is it your career, your hobbies or your loved ones? All of these things are subject to change, hostage to circumstance. Is there anything you would never compromise, no matter the cost? If no such thing exists, if you are capable of being molded into anything under the right conditions, are you anyone at all?  “A Man for All Seasons” (1966) is a historical drama about a man who knows exactly who he is. Directed by Fred Zinnemann, the film follows Thomas More, a renowned Renaissance humanist best known for his sociopolitical satire “Utopia.” It chronicles the events leading up to his execution after he refused to recognize King Henry VIII as Supreme Head of the Church of England. The film makes no mention of “Utopia , ” neglecting to include his scholarly side at all. Instead, it focuses on More’s unwavering religious convictions, which ultimately cost him his life. .  “A Man for All Seasons” is a movie now largely forgotten. Upon its release, the film swept major awards ceremonies, earning eight Academy Award nominations and winning six, including Best Picture, Best Director and Best Actor. It is a film radiant in its wisdom and wit while remaining genuine in its convictions — much like the man it portrays. The actors do a nearly perfect job of delivering their roles, especially Paul Scofield, who plays Thomas More with a quiet, humble dignity. Wendy Hiller’s performance as More’s wife, Alice, brings a refined quality to her character, an uneducated woman in no way her husband’s intellectual equal, but supportive and helpful nonetheless. The dialogue is in equal measure sharply cunning and emotionally impactful, which allows it to inspire the mind and touch the heart. The film features witty one-liners which cannot fail to amuse, such as More’s chiding remark: “Richard, it profits a man nothing to give his soul for the whole world, but for Wales?” Such scenes of light cleverness only serve to enhance the truly emotional moments. At Henry VIII’s wedding to Anne Boleyn, he believes he sees More, his former friend and mentor, and races toward him with a look of genuine affection and happiness. When he sees that it isn’t More, the disappointment on his face is poignant, as the weight of his condemnation of More finally dawns on him. He realizes the validity of his marriage and his own happiness will never be complete without the blessing of More and his conscience. Robert Shaw, who plays Henry VIII, does a fantastic job of portraying this emotional transition, from his desperate, almost childlike desire for More’s approval to his visible deflation upon realizing his mistake. In a powerful scene at the start of the film, More attempts to teach a valuable lesson to his young acquaintance, Richard Rich. Driven by his desire for wealth and fame, Rich is blind to the consequences of his relentless pursuit of material success. In response, More offers Rich a silver cup that he received as a bribe, then says “But Richard, that’s a little bribe. At court they offer you all sorts of things, home, manor houses, coat of arms. A man should go where he isn’t tempted.” More instead offers a separate path for Rich: education. He suggests that a better path for Rich is to become a teacher, where he may never be widely recognized for his efforts, but his integrity will remain intact. Rich, however, rejects this plea to his soul and ultimately betrays More in his critical moment of need. You do not need to be religious to enjoy this film. In fact, what Thomas More believed in as a Catholic is not important at all. Regardless of their religion, convictions or political beliefs, everyone holds the right to keep the little space between their two ears private, and the right to uphold their integrity. Additionally, the message that More imparts to Rich seems particularly poignant in the current landscape of Stanford. Students here are often pressured to pursue careers considered “prestigious” or prioritize professional success, so how do we grapple with that? I say More’s answer rings truer to us than ever before: education. We may not all become teachers, but as students, it is our duty to participate sincerely in our own education, which goes beyond the development of practical skills. Stanford is a place where we are tempted, but it is also where we can uncover our personal truths that keep us from selling our integrity for our equivalent of Wales. Watching “A Man for All Seasons” was a necessary reminder for why I am here: not for fame, not for wealth, but to understand who I am. Only once I have found that can I become someone who stays true to their principles, or “a man for all seasons.”  The post Reel Classics: ‘A Man for All Seasons’ is a movie for our time appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Stanford Sonar: Students’ taste in music confirmed awesome
author: Micah Chung
content: In her hopefully long-lasting column “Stanford Sonar,”Micah Chung ’30 interviews random Stanford students about their favorite artists and most pressing recommendations. Hello ladies, gentlemen and all in between, and welcome to the “Stanford Sonar,” your bi-weekly stop for music recs courtesy of the Farm!  I begin this inaugural edition with my first foray into the wondrous world of spontaneous interviewing …. a foray which, sadly, turned into failure. I picked my subject from the bustling crowd at Old Union — only to find that the young adult typing furiously into a laptop was not actually a Stanford student.  Why would someone choose to LARP as a stressed-out undergrad? That’s a question for another column to answer. Luckily, though, I was able to ambush my peer tutor, Sam Kraus ’29 by Tresidder. As with all my subjects, I asked him three questions:  Who is your current favorite artist? What is your favorite genre?  Any music recs for the Farm?  Kraus — who’s currently on a Vienna Philharmonic Orchestra kick — recommended the 1982 recording of Mahler’s “Symphony No. 9 in D Major,” conducted by Herbert von Karajan. “The last movement, it fades to absolute nothing, which I think is perfect,” Kraus said. If it wasn’t immediately obvious, Kraus’ favorite genre is classical music, specifically late Romantic and impressionistic jams. While searching for an activity to justify procrastinating my Japanese homework, I happened across Nic Chesterman ’30. Chesterman’s pick for number one favorite music artist was Hozier! “[Hozier is] goated … the lyrics of his song can be written out, in my opinion, as poetry,” they said.  Chesterman then qualified their statement by adding that their favorite genre is “Weirdly, rock, which is not Hozier.” As for their recommendation, the indie pop band MUNA is currently their must-listen! After that wonderful interview, I found myself, like many writers for The Daily, in the unenviable position of having too few sources. To fix this problem, I decided to go to the one place on campus that I know people with good music taste hang out at, Florence Moore Hall. The fact that I live there is just a coincidence. Vedika Arora ’30, a distinguished member of Stanford’s very own Axe Committee, has a love of music that’s roughly comparable to her hatred of UC Berkeley!  Arora couldn’t decide on a favorite artist (“There’s too many good ones!”), but narrowed her favorite genres down to house and R&B music. She suggested fellow students listen to “Free Your Mind” by Prospa, Cloonee and Sybil and Doja Cat’s “Planet Her” album. Young Thug’s general discography also got a shout-out. Satisfied that I had spent enough time wandering around the edges of campus, and intimidated by legions of put-together students who seemed too locked in to approach, I got on my bike and fled to Main Quad, hoping to find another interviewee. But all I found was a legion of tourists, none of whom were particularly inclined to talk with this scrawny reporter with a bad hairdo …  … that is, until I spotted a figure in a red hoodie toting an electric scooter! My keys jingling from my carabiner like some kind of lesbian early warning system, I hurried to catch up to Peyton Vincent ’29. With my masterful timing, I caught her right before she had to clock in for her job. All the same, she left me with a few high-quality recommendations before blitzing away, presumably to do something productive with her time — something probably unrelated to harassing students for music recs.  After learning Vincent was a neo-soul fan, I wasn’t surprised R&B artists claimed top spots on her playlist. SZA took the title of favorite artist; Vincent also recommended checking out Kelela. Satisfied with my reporting for the day, and with the spectre of a Japanese test looming over my head, I once more hopped on my Hurley and zoomed back to Florence Moore to get some rest.  At Thursday morning breakfast, with my deadline fast approaching, I capped my interviews by talking to Sophia Gomez ’30. Saving me from certain obliteration by The Daily’s arts and life editors, she agreed! Gomez anointed the ever-provocative band Jockstrap as her current favorite artist, and added that her favorite genres are alternative, rock and pop. As for recommendations, there were a litany: Talking Heads, Japanese Breakfast, Michelle Zauner, Caroline Polachek, Black Country New Road and last but not least, Björk. And with that, that’s all for the first edition of the Stanford Sonar! Thank you very much for reading, and for my own shoutout, I’d like to recommend you give a listen to Shane Malone and Sprig! These two indie artists released the very catchy and very good single “Waiting” in 2022, and they are extremely underrated.  If you’d like to be interviewed for the Sonar, reach out at micah.h.chung@stanford.edu , or ambush me at FloMo, where I am often found daydreaming about finally being good at drums. title: Stanford’s band deserves better than AI slop
author: Micah Chung
content: Stanford recently published an AI-generated image of an ensemble of all white, all-male musicians performing in front of the Stanford Bookstore, in an obvious imitation of the Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band (LSJUMB). This is now part of a recurring pattern of Stanford staff using AI — whether that be to race swap students or make portraits of Black people — getting called out and then having to furiously backpedal. Frankly, it’s embarrassing to watch. More than that, it’s actively insulting. The implication, whether or not Stanford staff intend it, is that reality is not good enough. Black art isn’t as good as what an AI can make; real students aren’t as appealing as their artificial counterparts. The LSJUMB can’t be shown as it actually is. The Band deserves better from the university. We all do. The AI image sends the message that the university is too ashamed of its band to celebrate it, which is a baffling notion. Look: As a member of the Band, I can understand, in concept, why the university might want to distance itself. The Band has had its fair share of controversies. We were banned from the State of Oregon for 15 years for criticizing the logging industry’s destruction of spotted owl habitats in the Pacific Northwest. When UCLA football players were exposed for illegally occupying handicapped spots, we rolled the Stanford Tree out in a wheelchair and assumed a disability placard formation. More worryingly, and of particular concern to me as a survivor of sexual assault, the university once cracked down on the Band following years of institutional hazing, sexual harassment and alcohol use. It wasn’t the first time. But the Leland Stanford Junior University Marching Band of today is a far cry from the LSJUMB of even just ten years ago. Posters with sexual assault hotlines line almost every wall in the Band Shak, our home away from home away from home. It’s common for “I Consent” pins to be worn on members’ hats as we run around performing. In spite of any prior reputational issues, you’ll find members today coveting Cherry Coke more than alcohol.  In other words, the band is human — the opposite of what Stanford made it out to be in their post. It’s an active symbol of the immense power of individual people, bonded by love for music and each other, to change things for the better, and also to wear ugly hats while doing so. Perhaps in recognition of this growth, the university has publicly promoted the Band, with framed photographs, social media posts, and orientation events that all put the spotlight on the LSJUMB. That’s why it’s so hurtful that this insulting AI post would be allowed to slip through the cracks. I am particularly offended because of how the Band has created a safe space for me. I am a transgender student and have to deal with the assorted baggage that often brings. It’s normal for me to move through life operating under the assumption that my very presence is going to make other people uncomfortable or disgusted — assuming, of course, that they don’t simply become violent. It’s a necessary assumption, one that has kept me from brushing up against too many incidents of violence and unwanted attention in my life, but not one I want to have to make. Stanford, for all of its progressive values, hasn’t shattered this mindset — whether out of need or out of habit, or both. The band has been maybe the only place on campus where that simple assumption that I am, by default, unwanted has been proactively proven wrong. My attempts to put walls up were swiftly disarmed by a community of people whose sole mission in life seems to be to rock out and have as much fun doing so as possible. Fun(k) and vibrancy practically bleed from the Band. Any number of shenanigans can and do happen every week, from members hurling saxophones into the air during performances to linking arms with each other and frolicking in the middle of a song. Only the Band would ritualistically crucify an effigy of Oski every year on top of the Claw, or scream “I GOT IT! I GOT IT!” to distract the opposing women’s volleyball teams unfortunate enough to play in Maples. LSJUMB embodies such a distinctly human sense of joy and whimsy, which makes the AI version of the band that much more soulless. Gone is the multiethnic composition of the Band, replaced by a vision of a monochrome ensemble that hasn’t been accurate for years. In a supposed image of an organization with people from all genders — in my section alone, women and nonbinary people consistently match or outnumber the men — only men are shown. Regardless of how or why that image was put up, the university needs to do better. The band deserves to be portrayed just like it is in real life: a group of people from all ethnicities, all genders, all backgrounds, having fun — and rocking out. title: Men’s basketball transfer Nick Townsend looks ahead to regular season
author: Grace Pratt
content: Stanford men’s basketball has a lot of new faces on the court this season, but one of them is no stranger to Division I collegiate basketball. Fifth-year forward Nick Townsend traded the gothic towers and gloomy skies of New Haven for the sunshine and palm trees of Palo Alto when he transferred to Stanford to finish out his eligibility as a post-baccalaureate. After four years of playing with Yale, Townsend looks back on his time as a Bulldog with fondness. “I had a great experience at Yale,” he said. “It felt like a very special place to me. I thought the coaching staff helped me develop on and off the court, and I really loved all of my teammates.” At Yale, Townsend was a three-time Ivy League Champion, two-time Ivy League Tournament Champion, and two-time finalist for the Lou Henson Award, an honor presented annually to the top Division I mid-major men’s player of the year. As a senior, he started in 30 games and averaged 16.3 points, 7.4 rebounds, 4.3 assists and 1.1 steals per game. In addition to serving as team captain, he was named the 2025-26 Ivy League Men’s Basketball Player of the Year.  Townsend’s ties to the Ivy League extend beyond his athletic achievements. His older brother, Matt, played basketball at Yale 10 years earlier, and his sister, mother and grandfather were all athletes at Harvard. “In my early recruiting process coming out of high school, my family and my brother never really pressured me,” he said. “I guess I get the best of both worlds now, since I’ve gotten to follow in my brother’s footsteps and then branch off and come here.”  Although the Ivy League and ACC are very different conferences, Townsend sees many similarities between the Yale and Stanford programs, particularly in the vision of head coach Kyle Smith. “I think a lot of what drew me to Yale drew me to Stanford,” said Townsend. “Not only do you have a great school and great athletic program, but Coach Smith and the coaching staff are building something really special here.” He is equally enthusiastic about the potential of Stanford’s new roster, which is a mix of four-star recruits and veteran transfers.  “We have a lot of new guys, but it feels like the team is a really great group that’s very bought in and very committed to improving,” he said. “I’m excited to see how much better we can get over the course of the season.” The forward is focused on doing whatever he can to contribute to the team’s success, whether that means drawing on his experience as an older player or providing stability during a time of transition.  “I feel very grateful to be here in this position,” he said. “I just want to maximize the time that I’ve been given and help everyone take a step in the right direction.” Beyond individual aspirations, Townsend has a larger team goal in mind: returning Stanford to the NCAA Tournament, a feat that the Cardinal have not accomplished since the 2013-14 season.   In his Stanford preseason debut against Oregon (0-0, 0-0 Big Ten) on Sunday, he made an immediate impact, recording 11 points, six rebounds, five assists and two steals. As the Cardinal (0-0, 0-0 ACC) head into the regular season, Townsend’s performance offers an early glimpse of what he could bring to Stanford, helping a new roster find its footing while pursuing a return to the NCAA Tournament.  Townsend and the Cardinal will face off against Eastern Washington at Maples Pavilion on Nov. 2 at 7 p.m. The post Men’s basketball transfer Nick Townsend looks ahead to regular season appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Who to sit with
author: Anagha Iyer
content: Most days, around 2:45 p.m., I walk into Arrillaga for a late lunch and scan the room for a familiar face. As I hold a full plate in my right hand and a cup of hot chocolate in my left, I pray — for a moment — that I recognize someone to sit with at the dining hall. Arrillaga is almost closing; by then, the room is nearly empty. Upon realizing no one I know is here, I take a seat at the end of a long table, accompanied by three to four other students who also find some solitude in eating lunch alone. If you told me in high school that I’d be sitting by myself at least once a day, I’d have been devastated. What happened to the friend groups that got together every day under the glaring Florida sun? What happened to the feeling of knowing I’d always have someone to talk to? But if you ask me now, I’d have no complaints. Although it feels awkward at first, I’ve come to accept — and even love — the independence of eating on my own. It’s the one part of my day when I’m not rushing to class or answering anyone. In this isolation, I’m finally able to relax and catch up on my latest Youtube recommendations. Sometimes, though, I want someone to talk to, so I call my friends from home. I’m 2,600 miles away, and I’m hearing my Model UN partner talk about her new relationship, or my other friend enthusing about the internship he got as a result of our nonprofit work back home. I’m happy for them, and I’m glad to hear about it.  And when our schedules line up, my Stanford friends and I plan lunch together. It feels like we have an infinite number of things to catch up on, from the latest Nobel Prize winners, to my friend’s obsession with “10 Things I Hate About You,” to the simple question “what’s for dinner tomorrow?” But even when I don’t have plans, I don’t always end up alone. Some days, right on cue, someone I know from my dorm catches my eye across Arrillaga and ushers me over. I sit down, my hot chocolate still warm, ready to dig in.
