title: Amy Goodman of ‘Democracy Now!’ makes case for independent media, overcoming campus talk disruption
author: Clara Dunne
content: “Democracy Now!” host Amy Goodman held a conversation on journalism and independent media following a screening of her documentary at CEMEX Auditorium on Friday. The event was interrupted by Palo Alto City Council candidate Henry Etzkowitz, when he abruptly took center stage. “Steal This Story, Please!” a documentary detailing Goodman’s life, has toured cinemas and film festivals since its release last year. Friday marked the first time the film has been screened on a college campus. Goodman was accompanied by her brother Steven Goodman, associate dean of clinical and translational research at Stanford School of Medicine; Tia Lessin, one of two producers of the documentary; and Janine Zacharia, the Carlos Kelly McClatchy lecturer in Stanford’s Department of Communication. The group formed a panel that discussed and answered questions about media and journalism following the screening of the documentary. Lessin prefaced the documentary’s importance by explaining the difficult conditions that journalists currently face in the U.S., setting up the theme of journalistic integrity and perseverance that the documentary focused on. “Journalists are under attack on a daily basis under this administration,” Lessin said, introducing the screening. She characterized Goodman as a journalist who persisted despite such adversity. Fittingly, the documentary opens with footage of Goodman chasing down Wells Griffith, an energy advisor for the Trump administration, as he ran away from questioning. The sequence set the tone for the documentary, drawing laughter from the audience throughout the interaction with Griffith. The audience laughed and clapped during the screening as the film oscillated between Goodman’s “perfect comedic timing” (as Lessin put it), and depictions of her various journalistic achievements. The documentary highlighted perseverance in journalism, showing Goodman as she survived the East Timor massacre, marched into Chevron’s headquarters in Nigeria to make its chief spokesperson admit that Chevron facilitated the murder of protestors and turned a get-out-the-vote call to her radio station from Bill Clinton into a 30-minute interview that grilled the president. The film concluded with a warning about the current state of journalism and media in the current day, urging journalists to speak out on prescient issues regardless of consequence. “The media has to reflect on itself,” Goodman said in the final section of the film. “‘We will not be silent’ should be the Hippocratic Oath of the media.”  After the credits rolled, Goodman came out in person alongside the panel for a conversation about the film. But the conversation could not start as Henry Etzkowitz, a Palo Alto resident running for city council, started protesting near the stage. Etzkowitz stood up from his front-row seat immediately following the screening, waving around a piece of paper. He was protesting being banned from Stanford’s campus, he said. Despite the interruption, the panel tried to start the on-stage conversation. The effort was not successful.  “I will not leave here unless I’m arrested,” Etzkowitz repeatedly said. “I want to be arrested,” he later added. The crowd booed and heckled him as he spoke. “We want to hear Amy,” one audience member shouted. “We don’t want to arrest you,” said another. When it became apparent that Etzkowitz would not leave, Goodman tried to placate Etzkowitz. “I’d like to have a conversation here, and then in 25 minutes I’ll talk to you,” Goodman said. Etzkowitz refused. As a compromise, Goodman allowed Etzkowitz on stage for a five-minute interview, in the process moving him away from the crowd and near an exit. Goodman asked Etzkowitz about his presence at the event and his candidacy for city council. Goodman kept keen track of Etzkowitz’ five minutes, updating him as his time depleted. When Goodman noted that Etzkowitz had used all of his time, he refused to end the interview. “I’m going to treat you the same way I treat people on the show,” Goodman said, laughing, “you have 30 seconds to go.” Shortly after, authorities entered the auditorium and Etzkowitz was grabbed by a group of event staff that had surrounded him during the interview. As he was taken backstage, Goodman kept her microphone near his face with one hand, and held her dog Zazu’s leash with the other. Henry Etzkowitz and Amy Goodman took the podium, which event staff and onlookers surrounded. (CLARA DUNNE/The Stanford Daily) After Etzkowitz was removed from the venue, Goodman quickly returned to her seat and began her scheduled conversation. PhD student Sarah Chow, who was sitting next to Etzkowitz, told The Daily that the city council candidate was asleep during the screening of Goodman’s documentary. “He was snoring through the whole thing,” Chow said. During the on-stage conversation, Steven Goodman confirmed that Etzkowitz was not arrested at request of the event staff. He praised his sister’s role in placating and calming Etzkowitz. “We saw the peak of Amy’s powers there as a peacemaker,” Steven Goodman said.  Amy Goodman was then asked about the tension between prioritizing free speech and Etzkowitz’ removal. “I agree with freedom of speech,” Goodman said, “which is why I talked to Henry [Etzkowitz].” The remainder of the conversation focused on topics of journalism, corporate versus independent media and the importance of fighting for democracy. Goodman lauded The Stanford Daily for its journalistic work and for its work suing the U.S. government to protect international students. “I want to thank you and the student newspaper here,” Goodman said, speaking to The Daily’s editor-in-chief George Porteous ’27, who appeared on Democracy Now! last month. “You did something so important.” “These are issues we’ve been covering for years now,” Goodman said of the lawsuit, which focuses on first-amendment rights for student publications. “The paper here has shown how important a student paper is,” she later added. Goodman also advised student journalists to “follow your passion, be dogged.” Speaking more broadly, Goodman encouraged the audience to always stay aware and resistant of threats to democracy. “You never achieve democracy,” she said, “you have to fight for it every single day.” Goodman also emphasized how journalists who represent everyday people can be agents of peace. “When you hear someone speaking from their own experience, whether it’s a Palestinian child or an Israeli grandmother, an uncle in Iran or an aunt in Afghanistan, it changes,” she said. “It makes it much less likely that you will want to destroy the person.” “I think media can be the greatest force for peace on earth. Instead, all too often, it’s wielded as a weapon of war,” Goodman added, “which is why we have to take the media back.” The post Amy Goodman of ‘Democracy Now!’ makes case for independent media, overcoming campus talk disruption appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: ‘A civil rights issue’: New proposal for license plate cameras sparks concern over privacy
author: Natalie Tu
content: Public scrutiny over privacy concerns on campus was reignited as Stanford released its new General Use Plan (GUP) for public comment on Oct. 15. The plan calls for the expansion of automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology in tracking traffic flow in and out of campus, replacing a manual counting system used since 2000. According to the GUP, automation using cameras would “significantly reduce the risk of human error,” despite both student and local worries over privacy.  The GUP’s inclusion of ALPRs comes as the technology has been the subject of controversy nationwide. In August, following continued criticism and a petition , Stanford ended a contract with ALPR provider Flock Safety citing “data security issues,” opting for Genetec cameras instead. The move followed similar contract terminations with Flock by local jurisdictions including Santa Clara County, Mountain View, Santa Cruz and Campbell. Critics are worried about data security and privacy. “We have a concern about scope creep,” said Cara Silver, a member of Safety Over Surveillance Palo Alto, a coalition of local advocacy groups focused on ALPR usage. “If ALPRs are kind of enshrined in the GUP, we have a concern that the functionality may increase over time and that the use categories may increase over time.” Students harbor similar concerns over the implementation. “I think it’s important for us to understand what it means to continue using technologies that have shown and face public distrust,” said Angela Nguyen ’27. “Once a technology is used, whether that’s on campus or beyond, it’s super hard to revert from using it.” The University maintains that these traffic data cameras, however, remain distinct from public safety cameras. According to Stanford Transportation executive director Lesley Lowe, the overarching goal of the ALPRs was to “modernize some old technology.” She described issues with the cordon system ranging from road safety concerns, inaccuracies in counting and simple inefficiency as reasons for necessitating a change. “What we put forward is the opening to a conversation about trying to modernize [cordon counting],” StanfordNext Project Executive Whitney McNair said. “We’re open to working with the community and working with the county on determining what is the best approach or best tool.” Both Genetec and Flock have both come under scrutiny around their data storage policies. In Montreal, a Genetec camera was removed in August following a report by CBC Radio-Canada raising concerns over a lack of transparency with regards to their origins and potential uses. Genetec was also the target of a 2024 complaint alleging the company had done business with firms tied to the Iranian government, “enabling adverse impacts on human rights.”  Meanwhile, Flock has faced criticism for sharing camera data with federal groups like U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), as well as enabling stalking by police officers. Flock is also the subject of a pending lawsuit in the Eastern District of Virginia, alleging that the company’s technology contributed to a Fourth Amendment violation. While the new GUP does not specifically address the particular vendor these cameras will be contracted from, it does emphasize that “ALPR data used for traffic monitoring is different from Flock Safety or similar law enforcement data systems.”  Some critics say a potential alternative to ALPR usage could already exist. “What we suggested at the GUP hearing […] was self-reporting and using data sets that Stanford already has,” Silver said, specifically mentioning data on parking permits and employee numbers. ALPR usage needs to be avoided, she said, in situations where the cameras are “just not necessary.” “It’s civil rights more than anything,” Silver said. “I think it’s a Fourth Amendment issue, [and] a violation of privacy.” An earlier version of this article had Angela Nguyen as ’26 instead of ’27. The Daily regrets this error. The post ‘A civil rights issue’: New proposal for license plate cameras sparks concern over privacy appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: ‘Dilapidated but beloved’ Palo Alto community center at core of fight over taxation
author: Natalie Tu
content: At Palo Alto’s Cubberley Community Center, an average weekday afternoon can be hectic.  “There’s dance schools down there, these rooms are typically Chinese schools, and these are actual schools over here,” said Bella Urizar, a behavioral technician with Play ABA, a behavioral therapy center located at Cubberley.  On election day, Palo Alto residents will vote on Measure J, which would place a half-cent sales tax within city limits to fund the purchase of Cubberley Community Center’s land and renovate the facility. The Cubberley facility first opened in 1956 as a Palo Alto Unified School District (PAUSD) high school and reopened as a community center in 1990. Twenty-four businesses currently have long-term leases at the community center, ranging from a used bookstore to a Taekwondo school to a local historical society. Today, the building has begun to show its age. “People tend to go instead to Mitchell Park in that area […] especially people studying in the library there,” said Samhita Laxman ’30, who attended nearby Henry M. Gunn High School. “Cubberley just doesn’t have enough events.”  The measure would raise $15.6 million annually for Palo Alto to purchase PAUSD’s portion of Cubberley, appraised at $65.5 million, as well as subsequent retrofits. The building “requires extensive repairs to meet modern-day earthquake, fire safety and accessibility standards,” according to the City of Palo Alto’s Cubberley project webpage .   “This dilapidated but beloved destination known as Cubberley, which has been home to so many organizations for young children through seniors for decades, is in danger of falling apart,” said Palo Alto city councilmember Julie Lythcott-Haims ’89. “These buildings, we’re told, are nearing the end of their useful life.” However, Palo Alto voters have already expressed their hesitation this year to pass new taxes. In the June 2 primary elections, Measure B, a parcel tax directed towards funding PAUSD operations, narrowly missed the two-thirds threshold for passage, sending the district into a $33 million budget crisis. The measure would have renewed an already-existing parcel tax to fund local schools for four more years at a slightly lower rate than present.  Chris Robell, a board member of the Silicon Valley Taxpayers Association, said people are becoming “more sensitive to tax increases,” as well as towards “trust in government and that they’re managing the money wisely.” He specifically described Measure J’s language as “deceptive,” saying its structure as a general tax as opposed to a special tax meant revenue could also flow to non-Cubberley projects. Cubberley faces a crowded ballot this year on taxation and taxation policy. Among the other measures on this year’s Santa Clara County ballot is Measure RTM , a sales tax going towards regional public transit funding. Within Palo Alto, passage of both Measure J and RTM would leave the city at a 10.75% sales tax, among the highest in Santa Clara County. At the statewide level, tax reform is taking center stage. Proposition 43 seeks to overhaul how citizen-initiated local special taxes are approved, raising the required passing threshold from a simple majority to a two-thirds majority. Robell pointed to a California Supreme Court ruling, “California Cannabis Coalition v. City of Upland,” for allowing “bogus citizens’ initiatives,” as he described Measure RTM, to enter the ballot. The city insists, however, that this exchange with PAUSD is necessary for the community center. A 2024 Memorandum of Understanding between PAUSD and the City of Palo Alto set terms for the City’s eventual purchase of the land by 2027. The memorandum explicitly calls for a measure to fund the land purchase to be placed on the ballot in 2026, with both parties returning to the drawing board if it doesn’t pass. Part of the difficulty in maintaining Cubberley, Lythcott-Haims said, was the space’s ownership between two parties. “How do you deal with the wiring that cuts across and the plumbing and the seismic upgrades when you have two completely different owners who have different interests?” they said. “The buildings are 70 years old. They are not up to code seismically, [with] plumbing, wiring and [have] two owners!” “Ultimately, government is tasked with the role of caring about the things that bind us all together, the things that we all need,” the councilmember said. “A proper functioning community center that is a destination is what is needed to support humans in thriving in an era of loneliness.” An earlier version of this article had the sales tax rate as 10.25%, instead of 10.75%. The Daily regrets this error. The post ‘Dilapidated but beloved’ Palo Alto community center at core of fight over taxation appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Stanford defeats NC State in crucial ACC-after-dark matchup
author: Eli Zerr
content: An explosive first quarter with 234 yards of offense and two Davis Warren touchdown passes set the tone for a game that was always in control for the Stanford Cardinal (4-4, 2-3 ACC), lofting them 31-28 over the North Carolina State Wolfpack (3-4, 1-3 ACC) on Friday evening. This marks the first time Stanford has won back-to-back games since 2024 and the first time they have earned a .500 winning percentage through eight games since 2019. Bowl eligibility is even in sight for the Cardinal, who have not played in the postseason since 2018. Despite the stat sheet and final score giving the impression of a much closer game, the Wolfpack looked relatively anemic for long stretches in a game where they were favored to win by a touchdown and had a 75% chance of victory per the Football Power Index. NC State’s last win came in a narrow 31-28 decision over Louisville (4-3, 3-2 ACC) on Oct. 3, and Friday’s game marks its second consecutive ACC loss after a beatdown by No. 15 Wake Forest (6-1, 4-1 ACC). NC State head coach Dave Doeren, who was in his 14th season with the team, was fired upon returning to Raleigh.  Stanford’s offense got going early behind a surgical opening drive. Senior wide receiver Caden High alone had 63 receiving yards as the Cardinal marched down the field for a touchdown. A defensive stop would allow the Cardinal to again drive the ball downfield for a commanding 14-0 lead by the end of the first quarter.  Those first two Stanford drives saw five different players catch passes, showcasing the offensive schemes the Cardinal had drawn up to collectively create holes in the Wolfpack defense. “[We] knew they were going to play a lot of man [coverage] [and] we knew they were going to play a lot of cover three,” senior wide receiver Nico Brown said postgame. Actually hitting those receivers was enabled by a strong performance from the offensive line, with sixth-year quarterback Davis Warren crediting them for allowing receivers “time to go get open” and enabling the explosiveness in the pass game. The Wolfpack would finally respond with a deep 58-yard touchdown from sophomore receiver Deandre Desinor. One failed Stanford fourth-down conversion later, a quarterback keeper from junior CJ Bailey set the Wolfpack up for a goal-line touchdown dive, completely neutralizing Stanford’s early lead. Receiving the ball with only one minute and 49 seconds left in the half, Warren and company then put on an offensive clinic from deep within Stanford territory. Seven plays and 90 yards later, Warren would cap off the half with a 26-yard back-shoulder touchdown strike to High.  When asked about the Cardinal’s offensive control over the Wolfpack, head coach Tavita Pritchard stated that the team worked to “punch first” and “sustain through the ebbs and flows of [the] game.” A main point of improvement for the offense, he said, is “balanced football and a balanced offense.” Given that Stanford’s run game and offensive line have been much improved in recent games, it is continued consistency that will determine the future of the season for the Cardinal. “I thought a lot of our success early on was complementary run and pass, staying in manageable third downs, and just a sustained execution,” said Pritchard. Through the first quarter, Stanford had neither a 3rd-and-long nor a punt on its two scoring drives. Defensively, the Cardinal clamped the Wolfpack to a mere eight first downs in the first half. The Wolfpack would do a better job matching the Cardinal in the second half. Entering with only a seven-point lead, Pritchard said, “we knew we needed to keep scoring because [NC State] wasn’t a team that was going to go away.” The Cardinal would tack on more points in the third quarter with a 43-yard run by junior running back Micah Ford and a 4th-and-goal touchdown by Brown.  While NC State would retaliate with a nine-minute long touchdown drive of their own, a subsequent 31-yard field goal from sixth-year senior kicker Emmet Kenney once again extended Stanford’s lead to two possessions. At that point, it proved to be too late for NC State. With just under five minutes left, a last-gasp 89-yard drive simply burned too much time as the Cardinal defense sat back and forced the Wolfpack to make 14 plays before finding the end zone. After recovering the ensuing onside kick attempt, Stanford bled out the remaining 82 seconds in victory formation. Next Saturday at 12:15 p.m. PDT, Louisville will host Stanford in an all-Cardinal matchup against a top-five conference opponent. Victories away from Stanford Stadium have eluded the Cardinal for over two years, but will be necessary to sustain their postseason hopes.  Coach Pritchard is confident that the Cardinal can continue their success away from home. “I think it’s really about our continued growth as a program to be at our best and perform at our best no matter where we are, and we’re going to keep working towards that,” he said. title: Stanford recognizes 2026 Bass University Fellows
author: Miley Elle Weiner
content: The University announced the appointment of eight Bass University Fellows for their outstanding contributions to undergraduate education on Oct. 7. The professors will serve a five-year term and are invited to join the Bass Council of Fellows, which meets every quarter to advise Jay Hamilton, the vice provost for undergraduate education.  Chris Piech ’16, associate professor of computer science, said he is “very grateful” to have been appointed as the Dunlevie Family University Fellow.  “Stanford undergrads are the reason I love this job, so being recognized for undergraduate education in particular means a lot,” Piech wrote in a statement to The Daily.  Anne T. Bass MLA ’07 and Robert M. Bass MBA ’74 established the Bass University Fellows in Undergraduate Education Program in 2001. Each of the fellows’ appointments is named after major University donors, specifically ones that heavily contributed to the Stanford Endowment for Undergraduate Education during the Campaign for Undergraduate Education, a five-year fundraiser for undergraduate initiatives.  The 2026 fellows in undergraduate education are Nicole Ardoin, Adrian Daub, Lynn Hildemann, Tomás Jiménez, Lianne Kurina, Karla Oeler, Chris Piech and Ross Shachter.  Professor of Sociology Tomás Jiménez, who was reappointed as the Robert and Ruth Halperin University Fellow, said that learning and teaching are shared endeavors. “As faculty, we do only two things: learn and teach,” Jiménez said. “Our research is just an effort to learn. What I enjoy most about teaching undergraduates is the opportunity to learn with students.” Jiménez’s research and teaching focus on immigrant integration, immigration policy, race, ethnicity and national identity. He is the founding director of the Stanford Institute for Advancing Just Societies and Joan B. Ford professor of sociology.  Karla Oeler, associate professor of art and art history, is the William R. and Gretchen B. Kimball University Fellow. A graduate of Oberlin College, Oeler said she had many opportunities to interact with professors inside and outside the classroom.  “I try to bring this small-college experience to undergraduates at Stanford — which is a much bigger school — by requiring students in my classes to attend office hours and, when I was part of ITALIC, regularly eating lunch and attending field trips with students,” Oeler told The Daily. In the fall, Oeler said she enjoys taking new students to the Stanford Theatre and to boba or ice cream after. Oeler said she looks forward to serving on the Bass Council of Fellows and advising on the humanities at Stanford. Similar to Oeler, Piech aims to give students a more intimate learning experience, specifically through his project Code in Place. Code in Place is a free online version of CS106A where Stanford undergraduates volunteer as section leaders for a small group of students. The program has reached more than 150 countries, connecting almost 100,000 students with approximately 7,000 volunteer section leaders, according to Piech.  “The most defining part of my undergrad years was being a section leader,” Piech said. “It meant a lot to me, and it shaped my whole career.” He said his appointment feels like a team award: “Every class I teach is built with an amazing crew of TAs, section leaders and students.”  Lianne Kurina ’98, the Duca Family University Fellow, will also join the Bass Council of Fellows. Kurian is the senior associate vice provost of undergraduate education and a professor of human biology, epidemiology and population health. She co-leads the Promoting Academic Communities and Engagement (PACE) initiative , which will inform her advising on the council.  “The issues I’ve been thinking about most with PACE relate to the classroom and elevating its role in the self-transformation that students experience while at college,” Kurina said.  Ross Shachter, associate professor of management science and engineering, has been reappointed as the John A. and Cynthia Fry Gunn University Fellow. Alongside teaching courses in decision analysis, Shachter spent two decades as a Resident Fellow (RF) in Stern Hall.  His kids, raised on The Farm, studied abroad, served as Resident Assistants (RAs) and were involved in public service. “There are so many wonderful people and opportunities at Stanford, and I encourage students to be open to learning beyond their chosen field of study, ” Shachter wrote to The Daily. Nicole Ardoin was reappointed as the Barbara and Buzz McCoy University Fellow. An Emmett Family Faculty Scholar, Ardoin has been teaching at Stanford since 2008. She is a professor of environmental social sciences in the Doerr School of Sustainability and a senior fellow in the Woods Institute for the Environment. Ardoin teaches EBS325: “Foundations of Political Ecology” and EBS 308: “Qualitative Inquiry: Theory and Practice of Qualitative Environmental Social Sciences” and leads the Stanford Social Ecology Lab, where she tackles pressing sustainability issues.  Adrian Daub, director of undergraduate German studies and the Michelle R. Clayman Institute for Gender Research, was reappointed as the Thomas W. and Susan B. Ford University Fellow. He is the J.E. Wallace Sterling Professor of the Humanities and a professor of German studies and comparative literature. Daub has researched and written books on gender’s connection to German literature, music and philosophy. Civil and environmental engineering professor Lynn Hildemann was reappointed as the Gerhard Casper University Fellow. During her 37 years as a Stanford faculty member, she served as department chair for civil and environmental engineering, senior associate dean for the Doerr School and senior associate vice provost for undergraduate education. Hildemann’s research focuses on indoor airborne particulate matter and humans’ interaction with air pollutants. The Daily reached out to Ardoin, Daub and Hildemann for comment. title: Research Roundup: Scientists restore bleached coral, engineer protein-based material, use AI to simulate drug effects
author: Abigail Chan
content: Stanford scientists discover a strategy to restore bleached coral In the Doerr School of Sustainability, the Oceans Department’s Palumbi Lab found that bleached corals, when paired with healthy counterparts, could recover fully in record time. Bleached corals are corals that have turned ghostly white due to the expulsion of symbiotic algae living inside their tissues. The ejection of the beneficial algae is a distress signal caused by warming waters, according to the Doerr School of Sustainability.  The discovery represents the first time scientists have observed bleached corals completely recover through physical contact with healthy clones. The team, led by Danny Collins, a third-year Ph.D. student in the Oceans Department, published their findings in “Science Advances” on Oct. 14. “Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” Fiorenza Micheli, Collins’ faculty advisor and co-director of the Center of Ocean Solutions, told the Doerr School. “Once a coral has bleached, what can we do?” Collins said.  The team used a powerful microscope that led to the discovery of microscopic channels in coral tissues. When bleached coral tissue is fused with healthy tissue, the algae is transferred between corals through this pathway, restoring the bleached coral’s health in weeks. “Once beneficial algae enter bleached corals, they don’t just spread out,” Palumbi told the Doerr School, “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals.” The team observed that algae moved from healthy to bleached fragments in as quickly as three days. “These new insights into how corals can naturally recover give us hope for the future,” Fiorenza said. “They open the door to what’s possible and may lead to the breakthrough we need to accelerate reef restoration.” The restoration requires a genetically identical, healthy copy of every bleached coral and physical contact to jumpstart recovery. The research team aims to explore algae delivery methods and alternative solutions to coral restoration, including deeper insights into temperature’s role in the system. Researchers engineer protein-derived material for environmental and medical applications The Feig lab, run by Assistant Professor of Mechanical Engineering Vivian Feig, Ph.D. ’20, developed a flexible glycine-based piezoelectric material. Piezoelectric materials have the ability to generate electricity when physically manipulated. This newly developed material has potential applications in medical and environmental sensors.   The new biomaterial is made of glycine, the simplest amino acid. Glycine is pervasively found in the body, the environment and has even been traced to outer space. “Glycine is really interesting because it’s so abundant,” Feig told Stanford Report. “We know how to process it, our bodies know how to break it down and it’s cheap and really accessible.” The lab’s research expands consideration of glycine’s engineering potential in next-generation materials. Scientists had already acknowledged glycine’s potential, but noted its drawbacks: glycine disintegrates within seconds when in contact with water, and the crystalline state the glycine is more responsive to cannot generate electricity. The research team led by postdoctoral scholar Zhuomin Zhang successfully discovered a tactic to cultivate and fix glycine in its higher-performing form and protect it from degradation.  “When we are making new materials, we think about the entire functional lifetime for a device, as well as practical constraints about how it will be deployed,” Feig told Stanford Report.  The lab hopes to test their inventions under extreme temperature and pH conditions that closely simulate bodily environments. AI-backed model of the immune system helps identify drugs to prevent premature labor A Stanford Medicine research team constructed an AI-driven model of immune system changes in pregnancy, enabling scientists to test medications to avert premature birth. The team was led by Jakob Einhaus, a postdoctoral fellow in the department of anesthesiology, perioperative and pain medicine. Premature birth can lead to short-term and long-term health complications ranging from cardiovascular problems and learning impairments to neurological disabilities, according to the National Institutes of Health. Prematurity is the leading cause of death in children under age 5. Scientists trained AI to use a comprehensive atlas of the immune system. This atlas is accurate to a cell-by-cell level, successfully generating “digital twins” of the immune systems of individual pregnant women for virtual drug testing. The twin system, Simulated Immune Modeling of Clinical Outcomes (SIMCO), uses machine-learning techniques to integrate data on the body’s immune cell behavior during pregnancy. The system informs how individual immune cells will respond to various drugs. The researchers, equipped with AI tools, identified two common drugs that may mitigate delivery complications: aspirin and lansoprazole, taken together. Low-dose aspirin has a modest ability to prevent premature births, and Lansoprazole is occasionally prescribed to treat acid reflux during pregnancy. The findings published in Science Advances build on two decades of research on how the maternal immune system fluctuates during pregnancy. “In the digital twin system, these two drugs in combination had a large effect on the delay of labor, 15 times higher than aspirin alone,” senior author Brice Gaudilliere, professor of anesthesiology, perioperative and pain medicine, told Stanford Medicine. “We’re on the brink of having a real impact for the treatment of preterm birth, a global health problem that affects 10% of pregnancies worldwide.” These findings bridge a decades-long gap between previous solutions and modern pharmacological interventions for premature births, Gaudilliere said. title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ harshly interrogates a broken tech ecosystem
author: Mirabelle Lee
content: Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques. My hands delightfully slick with the buttery goodness of movie theater popcorn, I watched a woman triumphantly berate two Black police officers in the opening prologue of Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” (2026). The screen read in bold white letters: “White Girl Wasted.”  “This is what happens when you’re white in America!” she screamed. The officers took a deep breath, visibly perturbed by her racist remarks but determined not to give her the reaction she wanted for her Facebook audience. Moments later, a horrified and mousy Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) watched the confrontation play out on that woman’s Facebook page. The post’s provocative caption? “ Watch Me Own DEI Cops.” Later, we learn that the woman — “White Girl Wasted” Kaylee (Portia Doubleday) — was once Haugen’s progressive friend, recently radicalized by Facebook’s algorithms who guided her to extremist alt-right hate groups. Haugen, a Facebook data scientist, attempts to point out the platform’s radicalization algorithm to her colleagues.  Her warning falls on deaf ears. Based on true events, this companion piece to Sorkin’s acclaimed Facebook drama “The Social Network” (2010) directed by Dave Fincher, follows the unlikely but resilient duo of Haugen, a consummate technophile, and Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a technophobe investigative journalist. When Haugen turns whistleblower, they attempt to expose Facebook’s frightening desire to turn human behavior into engagement and profit by publishing “The Facebook Files” in The Wall Street Journal. “The Social Reckoning” does a hauntingly good job of highlighting the dangers lurking behind our most beloved social media platforms as well as the corporate rhetoric and PR machines used to disguise what motives truly operate the system. Madison gives a stellar performance as Haugen, a morally-conscious worker bee devoted to Facebook’s mission of bringing the world together — a philosophy it has strayed from in practice. She gives Haugen an untapped intensity that makes her difficult to look away from. Meek and awkward in most social situations, Haugen is nonetheless searingly passionate as the film unveils Facebook’s indifference to fact-checking, bullying and leniency towards hate groups. In a world where the loudest voice wins the room or algorithm, Madison’s soft-spokenness becomes a rebellion against the boisterous.  White complements Madison’s performance with his obstinate portrayal of journalist Horwitz. His performance occupies familiar territory for the actor, recalling the stubborn smart-alecks of his previous roles as Carmen Berzatto in “The Bear” (2022), a tortured culinary genius, and Lip Gallagher in “Shameless” (2011), an unruly STEM prodigy. Here, however, that headstrong, wise-guy persona underscores the self-assuredness of Silicon Valley at large.  Another performance worth noting is Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Mark Zuckerberg. Strong and Sorkin build on Jesse Eisenberg’s automaton-like interpretation of Zuckerberg in “The Social Network,” emphasizing the character’s almost alien estrangement from typical human interaction. The film even depicts his crisis-PR consultant Raya Akinola (Wunmi Mosaku) giving him detailed instructions on how to nod his head like a normal person. Strong’s Zuckerberg has been hardened by VC wealth and the press into a cold CEO who seems unable to redirect his devotion from profit toward the betterment of society. Sorkin deftly exhibits the differences between Zuckerberg and his colleagues, using cold, ashen lighting to make the CEO appear strangely alien and distant from those around him. But Zuckerberg’s most alien quality is not his apparent inability to perform humanity. It is his ability to recognize human behavior as something worth being monetized, while remaining seemingly indifferent and holier-than-thou towards humans themselves. In Sorkin’s screenplay, Facebook’s offices become less of the intended epicenter of human connection than a laboratory for the commodification of attention. The company’s great achievement is not connecting people — a mission Haugen returns to throughout the film, as if repetition alone would restore her faith in it — but learning which emotions will keep them connected and coming back for more.  I was most struck by a montage towards the end of the film, where Sorkin depicts the Facebook offices during the Jan. 6 riot at the Capitol. Dozens of Facebook employees are cramped into a room filled with live videos of the riot on the news, and a clueless Zuckerberg stands in the middle. The audience is transported back-and-forth between the bloody riot — officers pelted with metal barriers and furious bodies, their blood soaking into the Capitol carpet and concrete — and the Facebook offices, scrambling as employees beg their leader to do something. The contrast between the two scenes took my breath away and allowed the impact of digital voices online to be completely revealed in all of its bloody possibilities. For the first time in the film, danger was no longer simply talked about amongst the characters like a distant possibility, but shown in full, physical and brutal force. Leaving the theater, I found myself looking at my phone a little differently. I opened Meta’s Instagram — Facebook having been deleted long ago (sorry, not sorry) — and felt the platform’s incessant chatter of information blaring at me like an alarm: political advertisements for the upcoming midterm election; reels of “news” articles that, now that I look closer, are positively false; provocative and frankly annoying influencers yelling buzzwords that they know will generate views.  I thought of Haugen’s concluding testimony before the U.S. Senate, where she begs America’s leaders to confront the growing dangers of social media. I thought of Sorkin’s montage of the Jan. 6 riots, triggered by the president’s online behavior. I thought of Zuckerberg’s cold silence before the news screen, unable to say, “Shut it down.” I thought of “White Girl Wasted” Kaylee and who she was before Facebook’s algorithms invited her to some of the most fierce right-wing hate groups on the platform.  I looked back down at my phone, wondering what it wanted me to become. title: David Gorin and Jiachen Wang bring elegy, laughter to Stegner Fellow reading
author: Shaphnah McKenzie
content: Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques.  “What can poetry offer us today, living as we do in an era of spectacular difficulty?” asked Bhion Achimba, a second-year Stegner Fellow, as he introduced fellow poet David Gorin at the first Stegner Fellow reading of the academic year. In addition to Gorin’s poetry, Wednesday night’s reading also showcased fiction by Stegner Fellow Jiachen Wang. The fellows are part of two-year artist-in-residence program for emerging writers in fiction and poetry. A crowd composed of students and faculty alike had filled the Margaret Jacks Terrace Room in anticipation of the showcase. Many attendees chose to sit at the speakers’ feet on cushions and threadbare rugs — giving the night a casual, almost intimate ambience.  Gorin gave Achimba a long hug, thanking him for his flattering introduction, before addressing the audience. “It’s magic that a university building can give me the vibes it gives right now,” Gorin remarked, referring to how the Terrace Room was illuminated by orange string lights and glowing LED candles on the floor. The ambience had provoked immediate reactions of awe from the public as they streamed in. One attendee even exclaimed that the room was “so vibey.” Prior to the reading, Gorin spoke about his love for performing poetry with The Daily. “I really like having a stage, because I don’t like to grab attention for myself from a room full of people just with no excuse,” he said. “But I love having an excuse — because I’m a Leo.”  Gorin, who believes that poetry can be as fun as pop music, also remarked that while readings can be boring, he hoped to create a more enjoyable experience for his audience.   “Many of the readings with my peers are not boring at all,” he said. “They’re incredibly alive experiences. And I like being able to bring something like that to other people.”  Gorin kicked off his reading with the titular poem of his 2025 chapbook “To a Distant Country.” Described by Gorin as an “elegy without a name” for critic and activist Liu Xiaobo, the piece transported the audience into an airplane in which the speaker has visions of Liu.  “At such a speed clouds feel like sandpaper,” Gorin read. “The teeth of tiny frozen fish / When the cabin lights came on he disappeared from view.”  Despite the literary and introspective nature of many of the poems Gorin read, there were also moments of levity throughout.  “I have twisted with jealousy over a lover’s ex and learned, years later, she had made him up,” Gorin read from “I Have Never Disappeared for Even a Single Instant.” The line sent waves of laughter through the room. Following a round of applause, Gorin turned the floor over to first-year Stegner Fellow Jiachen Wang. Wang was introduced by second-year Stegner Fellow Adams Adeosun, who described Wang’s work as “brutal yet tender, personal and political.” Wang took to the podium to read an excerpt from the titular story of his collection “Stealing Fire.” Telling the story of  a 12-year-old boy living under the 1943 Japanese occupation of Manchuria, Wang vividly described the “purple toes sticking out of the rag” in which the narrator’s little brother was wrapped up to be buried.  Prior to the event, Wang told The Daily that his enjoyment of readings comes from their usefulness to him in honing his craft.  “It helps me hear my work out loud,” he said. “It’s more helpful to myself [than it is to] the audience.” More than anything else, Wang also hoped the audience would enjoy the reading. “I hope they won’t find it boring,” he said with a chuckle. “I hope they don’t yawn and fall asleep.” Like Gorin, Wang brought elements of humor to his reading. The room rumbled with laughter at Wang’s description of a teacher known as the “Tigress,” and the narrator’s remark that it was “a wonder how anyone would want to marry her.” The reading was followed by a Q&A session, during which those sitting on the rug snacked on complimentary SkinnyPop.  Both writers offered insight on their craft. Responding to a question about how to know when a poem is finished, Gorin recommended the book “Poetic Closure: A Study of How Poems End” by Barbara Herrnstein Smith. Wang received many questions about being a bilingual writer. He revealed that he first started writing in English because he had no choice. Later he discovered that writing in English was actually beneficial to him, since it made everything he was writing “so exotic.” Present in the audience was Alice Cao ’27, a regular attendee of the Stegner readings. “I go to these ‘cause they make me sane,” she said when asked what had brought her out to the reading. “I am mostly here for the atmosphere, to be among other people who want to listen.” Cao also expressed appreciation for Wang’s self–translated work, which she says she could tell had been translated from Chinese because of its cadence. “I like hearing words. I like in general just feeling that words still matter to people, even if they’re not necessarily as in the cultural zeitgeist as they were in the 1920s or as they are in Chile or as they are in China,” she said.  First-year Stegner Poetry Fellow Daniel Lurie said that while readings are easy for Stegner poets to attend, since they take place right after the group workshop, he would have come out to support the Stegner artistic community regardless.  “It’s incredible to just be in a space like that, in a space with people who take their writing and their craft so seriously, where you kind of just get swept up in their writing,” Lurie said.  As the evening ran late and the Q&A wrapped up, the candle-lit room hummed with voices, painting a picture of the Stanford community drawn together by the power of fiction and poetry. It was a sight that would’ve made Wallace Stegner himself proud.  The post David Gorin and Jiachen Wang bring elegy, laughter to Stegner Fellow reading appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: ‘Life’s so fun’ when MUNA comes to town
author: Madisyn Cunningham
content: Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques. Thousands of fans, from Stanford students to Bay Area locals, filed into Frost Amphitheater on Oct. 18 to witness indie pop band MUNA’s “Gets So Hot” tour. As the sun set and its warmth went with it, the crowd’s excitement for what was to come — a raunchy, sensual display of queer joy — grew so strong you could almost see it floating over their heads. Prior to MUNA taking the stage, Hemlocke Springs opened the show with a bang. The alt-pop artist played hits like “girlfriend” and “sever the blight,” the first of which went viral on TikTok in 2022 and has somehow beaten the app’s curse of weak staying power. Even though most of the crowd couldn’t sing along to Springs’ songs word-for-word, her infectious energy gave everyone no choice but to clap, or at the very least, bounce side-to-side.  Springs’ voice was so resounding that it was easy to imagine someone laying in their bed all the way in GovCo, hearing every one of her high notes or giggles. By the end of her set, she’d taken to commanding the crowd with a grand sword, and I was already searching the internet for the setlist so I could add her to my playlist. As the lights went out on stage, the crowd compressed towards the barricade, eager yet still refreshingly polite. The conversations happening around me — about lesbian dating trends in the Bay, about polyamory and all its offshoots, about regrets over not bringing appropriate outerwear — slowly faded as MUNA came out with a bang. A bright, white graphic of a fan (an homage to one of their most streamed songs, “Number One Fan”) lit up the stage screen, followed by flashing lights and a teaser of “It Gets So Hot,” the first song on MUNA’s setlist and the tour’s titular track.  The show was practically non-stop from there. MUNA’s music managed to strike the perfect balance between rock and pop, combining bone-chilling guitar solos and a blatant disregard for the norm with earworms that embody the unbridled joy of dancing with a stranger in a club (or a gay bar, an experience they explicitly reference in their 2022 song “What I Want”). All of MUNA’s members — Naomi McPherson, Josette Maskin and Katie Gavin — have a thrilling approach to stage presence. Despite freely admitting that they could barely see anything or anyone in the crowd, that didn’t stop them from taking upwards of 10 minutes to try to read messages off of faraway phones, or to simply converse about their hatred of AI and love of trains. At one point, Maskin chased the others onstage; later, Gavin danced against McPherson while the latter tried their hardest to focus on simultaneously singing and playing the keyboard.  I think that’s my favorite thing about MUNA, really. They’re just three lesbians who happen to be best friends and are, not to mention, extremely talented. I vividly remember the summer of 2023, when my friend first introduced me to their music beyond their hit “Silk Chiffon.” I was instantly hooked. Rarely ever before had I seen my brand of queerness — the gender non-conformity, the familial friendship structures — represented on such a stage. I vowed to myself and to my friends from home that I’d replicate their story: go off to college, find some other lesbians and start a trio. Not a musical one, necessarily. Just anyone I could find to keep me afloat 3,000 miles away from home.  I’ve always been awkward about going places alone, but hearing hits like “Eastside Girls” and “Kind Of Girl” left me too excited to worry about how I looked or what the people behind me thought of my jumping and screaming. One moment, I was watching Gavin and Maskin flirting playfully midstage; the next, I was pumping my fists to “Big Stick,” a song about government surveillance and American imperialism. Somehow the excitement coursing through my veins stayed consistent throughout, even as the songs’ themes went from serious to euphoric to strangely sad, despite their energetic backing tracks. “Stayaway” might have been the highlight of my night. It’s a truly devastating song about how the hardest part of a breakup is often not the initial split, but the tedium of going through the motions without the person with whom you once shared them. It’s about avoiding the bar because the bar means drinks, which means thinking about them; it’s about staying in because every road seems to lead back to this person. “Stayaway” is a song I’ve loved since the first time I heard it.  I’ve never felt it as potently as I did last Sunday, though. The bridge carries that perfect kind of heartbreak that makes you want to listen over and over again, blurring the line between masochism and pure artistic appreciation. This was really when all my inhibitions melted away. My head snapped back and I screamed every word. It felt like everyone was doing the same. For two hours, it didn’t matter what midterms were coming up or how messed up just about everything else was; all that mattered was dancing. MUNA, of course, ended with “Silk Chiffon,” their perennial hit with a simple message: “Life’s so fun.” And man, if it wasn’t fun before, it certainly was after this show. title: Malcolm Todd earns his rising star on the ‘Do That Again’ tour
author: Hayden Thompson
content: Malcolm Todd earns his rising star on the ‘Do That Again’ tour By Hayden Thompson Photos by Hayden Thompson Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques. Four years ago, Malcolm Todd was scooping ice cream at Cold Stone Creamery during his gap year and making music on the side. On Wednesday, the indie pop artist sold out the Fox Theater on one of the final stops of his “Do That Again” tour. A young audience composed of what seemed to be mostly high schoolers added an extra layer of frenetic energy to the concert. Leading up to the performance, a sea of concertgoers dressed in red  — the same color as the cover of Todd’s newest album — wrapped around the block, creating special buzz in Downtown Oakland. Their excitement reached a crescendo two hours later when Todd hit the stage. By the end of the night, it was hard to distinguish between fan favorites and skip tracks because the audience sang the words to every single song, including the ad libs. Todd, a 22-year-old singer-songwriter from Los Angeles, is having a breakout year. After the release of his sophomore album “Do That Again” in June — which follows a theme of complicated relationships, heartbreak and loneliness — Todd embarked on his North American tour in September. A self-taught guitarist, Todd’s unique chords have not only drawn in fans but also the attention of other artists. Rapper Don Toliver sampled Todd’s “Chest Pain (I Love)” on “EE72.” Toliver brought Todd to perform the song live at Madison Square Garden in June. Those listening in New York sang every word — and so did the Oakland crowd. The night opened with a performance by Johnny Rodriguez (stage name 54 Ultra), who brought a blend of pop and Latin soul to Fox. With his Freddie Mercury-style mustache, aviator sunglasses and a vintage Pittsburgh Pirates tee to match, 54 Ultra looked like he was pulled straight from the 70s. He engaged the crowd early, getting them to wave their hands from side-to-side and clap in unison. After 54 Ultra’s last song, he asked if the audience was ready for Todd. The screams in response left no doubt that they were. One-by-one, Todd’s band members were brought onstage in an NBA-style pre-game intro. Then — capitalizing on the surging hype —  Todd finally ran out to a roaring crowd. He started with “Jean Skirt,” “Breathe” and “Malcolm In The Middle,” all of which were accompanied by the chorus of the audience.  The visuals playing on the screen behind Todd complemented the music while also telling their own story. During “X’s & O’s,” a song about relationship uncertainty, Todd expressed confusion about where he stands with his partner a voicemail-style outro: “It’s, uh, it’s Malcolm, your boyfriend / Or honestly, don’t, I don’t even know what I am to you anymore actually,” he sang.  At the same time, the stage screen cycled through famous movies where characters in relationships are on the phone, pulling clips from films such as “ Ferris Bu e ller’s Day Off ” (1986) and “Good Will Hunting” (1987). His performance captured the core elements of typical teenage angst: falling in love, ambiguous relationships and general uncertainty about the world. Many of the young fans seemed to resonate with his lyrics, belting out song after song with deep emotion.   But Todd also put his whimsical side on display. Before “Obsessicia,” he started a call-and-response game with the audience, promoting them with “Who let the dogs out?” and “Marco?” Random as it was, the audience happily played along. After “Make Me a Better Man,” the music slowed for “Gun to My Head,” and Todd swapped out his guitar for a keyboard. Fans continued to sing along as their faces went red. At this calmer point in the show, Todd took a moment to engage with the crowd more, reading fan made signs aloud: One audience member’s poster shared it was their first concert. All night long, Todd’s talent was thoroughly appreciated — and he made sure to share the spotlight with his band. On “Goodbye,” band member Miles Tobel took to the saxophone for an excellent solo performance that even made the venue staff pull out their phones to record. The transitions between songs also featured small moments of comedy After “Chest Pain (I Love),” Todd suddenly stopped. “What the f—k?” he said. “Sorry, I’ve been looking for these all day.” The camera then panned down to a pair of earrings on the stage as the band transitioned into “Earrings.” When Todd and his band walked off stage, everyone stayed in place. A black screen with red lettering appeared with a series of questions. “Should I go back to scooping ice cream?” one read, calling back to Todd’s Cold Stone days. The crowd vehemently shouted “No!” “Should I sing another song?” then popped up. “Should I??” “Yes!” they all yelled back. Todd then returned to play “Do That Again,” closing the show out with “Roommates.” During the encore, the whole floor section (and most of the balcony) started jumping — moving hard enough to physically shake Fox Theater. Capping off a night of high engagement, strong live vocals and skilled instrumentals, it was the perfect way to go out with a bang. title: A love letter to T-charts
author: Sanya Gupta
content: Dearest T-charts, How do I love thee? Let me count the ways. You are the most beautiful blend of positivity and negativity, optimism and pessimism. The way you can seamlessly offer every possible perspective to any situation leaves me breathless. You walk me through my options without being impatient or callous. To me, you are perfection. I first learned of you at age ten, when my parents told me we were moving to the other side of the country. I was furious, consumed by the unfairness of it all. How could they do that to me? Then came you, my knight in shining armor. You met me at the intersection of the horizontal and vertical and guided me, hand held, to the exciting prospect of living in a new place. Without you, I wouldn’t ever have known how magnificent a Seattle sunset can be. Over the years, we’ve exchanged glances from across the room — deciding what to eat for dinner, what to wear in the morning, what movie to watch. You were always in the back of my mind. I needed you when I rephrased words in essays, I needed you when I decided what clubs to join. I felt a magnetic pull, a desire to do right by you. It was exhilarating to need something so deeply. All the while, it felt unnatural.  The prospect of what could have been felt too overwhelming, and I got scared. Scared of what we could be together. Deep down, I was scared I was asking too much of you. I was scared of being too clingy. If I called to you for every single inconsequential thing, would our love have become one-sided? Perhaps. But then again, perhaps life would’ve been easier if I had just written you right then and there, if only I didn’t overthink everything. Did you know once I almost wrote to you to decide if I should write to you? Life took the shape of an endless ouroboros.  At last, we met on a stormy night when I saw you from across the room. But happily ever after never comes easy. It was a hot and humid April rainstorm, and I had to decide where to spend the next four years of my life – where I should go for undergrad. Plagued with indecision, I ran into your arms, safe in your warm embrace. You said you would go with me wherever I ended up, of course you did. We compared costs of attendance, the cities either school was in and general culture. You were critical in a way I didn’t know you were capable of, it was endearing. You cared so much that I would find my place. Is it facetious to say heartbreak was inevitable? I know I wronged you. It was the coin flip. That was the final straw. When I went behind your back and flipped a coin to make my decision, I know that’s what hurt you most. For that I will always be so exceptionally sorry. You didn’t deserve my infidelity.  Ever since, I’ve been trying to make it up to you, to show you how much you mean to me. You know, I still talk about you with all my friends. “We can T-chart sometime if you’d like,” I’ll offer when they’re making the most important decisions of their lives. They know how great you are for me. To those who don’t know you like I do, I’ll ask “Would a pros and cons list help?” I can’t help it, I love talking about you. I love introducing you to new friends (they all always adore you). Best of all, despite my shortcomings, you’re still right there when I need you. When I needed to once again figure out where to move for grad school, you were waiting for me, flowers in hand. I’d hoped you’d take me back, that we could cross lines together once more.  We really are meant to be together. You’ve always known; I’m sorry it took me so long to realize. It just felt too good to be true. I long to be faced with another dilemma so that I may be reunited with you very soon.  All my love, Sanya The post A love letter to T-charts appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Women’s basketball dominates Pacific in first exhibition game
author: Natalie Tu
content: Stanford women’s basketball (0-0, 0-0 ACC) took a sound 72-45 victory over Pacific (0-0, 0-0 WCC) in their first preseason exhibition game on Saturday. The Cardinal entered this game coming off a 21-14 season, in which they fell to Miami in the first round of the ACC Tournament and missed the NCAA tournament. Pacific finished the previous season 11-19. Stanford took an early lead, with two early three-point shots by sophomore guard Hailee Swain securing the Cardinal a 13-point lead at the end of the first quarter. Swain’s performance amounted to 18 total points, with eight points coming in the first quarter alone. The momentum stayed with the Cardinal side throughout the first half, finishing 20 points over Pacific with a score of 37-17 going into halftime. Junior guard Shay Ijiwoye also played a well-rounded game, recording three assists and three steals with her physical style on defense.  The Cardinal lead never faltered, reaching as high as 26 points by the end of the third quarter, thanks to an impressive half-court shot from sophomore transfer forward Charlotte Tuhy to close out the period. Stanford would finish the game shooting 45.8% from the field, compared to Pacific’s 28.1%. Despite their success, however, the team struggled with free throws and turnovers. “We turned over the ball way too much. I think we got a bit careless with it,” said head coach Kate Paye after the game. Defensively, the spotlight fell upon Tuhy, who recorded 15 rebounds throughout the course of the game. She joins the Cardinal side after a strong freshman season at American, where she was one of only two freshmen nationally to average a double-double per game. When asked what makes Tuhy’s game so strong, Paye simply said, “effort.”  “When we were looking at the portal, [we noticed] she averaged a double-double last year as a freshman, [and] she was the second leading freshman rebounder in the country,” Paye said. “Things like that translate.” Swain and Ijiwoye were joined by junior transfer forward Inés Sotelo Míguez to record double-digit points, seeing 18, 15 and 12 respectively. Swain expressed her excitement and confidence in this year’s revamped Cardinal roster, consisting of three transfers and four freshmen joining the fold. She credited a preseason retreat for helping build chemistry among the team, especially as both she and Ijiwoye adapted into new leadership roles. Paye noted that, along with the win, there were many points for improvement in the coming games and into the season. “I think for our team, we know we can play much better than this,” Paye said. “But we’re excited to build on it.” Women’s basketball returns to Maples Pavilion Wednesday, Oct. 28 at 6 p.m. for the second and final exhibition game against U.C. title: Faculty Senate reviews AI disciplinary policy, honors late faculty members
author: Trilby Schmidt
content: The Office of Community Standards (OCS) invited the faculty senate to examine Stanford’s disciplinary policies on artificial intelligence (AI) and class credit at the faculty senate meeting on Thursday. Senators also remembered three past faculty members.  In a presentation about OCS’s response to AI policy violations, interim OCS Director Larry Marshall told the senate about the office’s approach to student discipline and goal of providing students with “a sense of love.”  “They [might] have stumbled, but it does not define their time at Stanford, or their worth,” Marshall said.  Stanford’s class retake policy allows students who received no credit in a class due to an academic violation to retake the same class for full credit. Upon retaking the class, the no credit (NC) is removed from their transcript and replaced with repeated course (RP), removing any indication that there was a violation and raising a possible signaling concern. Stanford is one of three universities with this retake policy.  But signaling is a significant issue for enforcing academic violations, Marshall said. He noted that if the University indicates that violating AI policies is not a “big deal,” then the issue will continue to permeate among students. Marshall invited the senate to study the policy but did not propose any immediate changes. The senate also passed memorial resolutions for late faculty members Clayton Wilson Bates Jr., Jonathan Bendor and Gerald Ernest Paul Gillespie.  Vice Provost and Dean of Research Arthur Bienstock remembered Clayton Wilson Bates Jr., former professor of materials science and engineering, who passed away on Feb. 18, 2024. He was memorialized for his contributions to X-ray research and planning of the Stanford Society of Black Scientists and Engineers (SBSE). He was also the first Black person to hold a tenured position in the School of Engineering. “This kind, gentle and productive gentleman will be a sad loss to the nation and our community, having made his mark as a very able scientist/engineer, mentor and encourager of aspiring African-American STEM students and great family man,” Bienstock and other professors wrote in Bates’ memorial resolution.   Jonathan Bendor, the Walter and Elise Haas Professor of Political Economics and Organizations, Emeritus (1950-2025) at the Graduate School of Business (GSB), passed away on Nov. 6, 2025. He was memorialized by GSB professor Ken Shotts.  Bendor is remembered for his “contributions to the study of bureaucracies, collective action and elections,” according to his memorial resolution. He also helped create “stimulating and generous spaces” in the classroom. Gerald Ernest Paul Gillespie, a professor of German studies and comparative literature, was remembered by his colleague Russell Berman for his work on the Baroque period in Germany, romanticism and 20th-century modernism. Gillespie passed away on July 20, 2025. Berman and other German studies faculty members wrote in Gillespie’s resolution about his “heated debates at Stanford and beyond concerning the changing character of American higher education.” The post Faculty Senate reviews AI disciplinary policy, honors late faculty members appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Oct. 7 survivors recount hostage experiences at Hillel
author: Bella Kim
content: Eliya Cohen barely spoke English when Hamas took him into Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023. He learned it in the tunnels, reading “Shadow and Bone,” a novel gifted to him by a fellow hostage, over a dozen times.  He recounted this story among others on Thursday at Stanford Hillel, using his newly learned English to tell a room of students and community members about surviving as a captive of Hamas. He left them with a simple but powerful message: “Don’t ask G-d what you want, ask him for what you need,” he said. Many Jews write G-d rather than God, out of reverence for the divine name. Cohen spoke alongside his wife, Ziv Abud, who survived the same terrorist attack on the Nova Music Festival on Oct. 7. For over 505 days, neither knew whether the other was alive. In their conversation, Abud and Cohen chronicled their experience on Oct. 7. Abud said they noticed initial signs of the attack at 6:29 a.m. Eventually, the couple took refuge in a bomb shelter near Kibbutz Re’im. Although it was meant to hold 10 people at most, 29 people crowded in — including Abud’s nephew and his girlfriend — as Abud noted. According to the couple, Hamas quickly broke into the shelter and began throwing grenades inside. After killing Aner Shapira, an off-duty Israeli soldier who lobbed the grenades back, Hamas fired into the shelter killing Abud’s nephew and his girlfriend. While Cohen was able to hide Abud under a pile of dead bodies, he was dragged out of the shelter at gunpoint with a bullet in his leg. As Cohen was driven into Gaza, people beat and spat on him, he said. In Gaza, his captors disguised him as a Muslim woman, and brought him to a large house before performing surgery on his leg without anesthetic. After being moved through tunnels beneath a mosque, he licked the tunnel walls for drops of water and bargained for food. He lost about 60 pounds in captivity. For Cohen, faith kept him going. He credited his survival to “choosing life,” despite having a “1% chance” of surviving. He also noted that hostages caught pieces of the outside world. For instance, Cohen said he learned that Donald Trump had won the presidential election and had promised to bring the hostages home after overhearing the TV. Once, after asking God for a sign, he heard an Israeli radio broadcast. Cohen also spoke about meeting other hostages, including Hersh Goldberg-Polin, an East Bay native who gave him the book after being told by Hamas that he was going home (Goldberg-Polin was later killed by Hamas in August 2024). Hamas also told Cohen that he and other hostages would be killed if the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) attempted to rescue them.  In an email to The Daily, Rabbi Jessica Kirschner, executive director of Hillel at Stanford, said the couple has “something precious and life-affirming” to teach the community.  “Eliya and Ziv provide pretty remarkable examples of resilience and growth in the face of adversity,” Kirschner wrote. The audience at Hillel at Stanford listens to Cohen and Abud speak on Thursday. (Photo: NICK MILLER/The Stanford Daily) Cohen’s captivity ended on Feb. 22, 2025, when Hamas released him as part of a hostage deal, upon which he met with Omer Shem Tov . On the stage Hamas set up in Gaza, Cohen smiled and flashed a victory sign.  He had survived, and to him, that meant he had won. Abud described her campaign to free Cohen, traveling the world to press for his release and tell their story. In March 2024, she stood in Tel Aviv’s Hostages Square in a yellow dress, the color for hostage liberation, instead of a wedding gown. On Valentine’s Day, she wore a red dress and set up a date for two, with only a photo of Cohen in his seat. Each week, she watched freed hostages come home. “They looked like Holocaust survivors,” she said. Freedom brought its own weight. Cohen said he felt guilty even eating or drinking until the remaining living hostages came home, about eight months after his release. When he campaigned in Washington D.C., people told him his story was propaganda. But the couple said that telling their story helped them remember details they had forgotten. According to the couple, they do not expect to change the minds of people who hate them, but they try. They have since told their story at a San Francisco synagogue and spoke at the United Nations on Oct. 6 this year. Both came back home changed. At first, they didn’t know whether they were still a match, so they started over and dated again from zero. Cohen proposed on Oct. 23, 2025, after the last living hostages returned home. They married on Aug. 19, 2026, before more than 1,000 guests at Ronit Farm in Israel, under a wedding canopy made from Ben Avida’s prayer shawl. During the question-and-answer session, an audience member asked whether any captor ever showed him compassion. Cohen said he wished one had. It never happened, he noted. He described everyone he encountered in Gaza, children and women included, as having evil in their eyes. Ultimately, Cohen and Abud said that they carry not post-traumatic stress, but post-traumatic growth. title: Appeal in Daily’s free speech lawsuit now on expedited schedule
author: Clara Dunne
content: The Trump administration’s Ninth Circuit appeal of The Stanford Daily’s free speech lawsuit victory is now on an expedited timeline. The case is projected to be briefed and argued faster than a typical Ninth Circuit appeal. The Department of Justice (DOJ) requested an expedited appeal process last week, which was quickly agreed upon by The Daily’s representation, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). Without expedition, the oral argument on the appeal could have taken place nine months to a year after filing. The expedited timeline now places the oral argument roughly three to six months in the future. The Daily filed the initial lawsuit in August 2025 after the Trump administration used the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) to threaten and revoke the visas of international students at multiple universities who engaged in pro-Palestinian speech. The lawsuit alleged that the administration’s actions chilled student voices and discouraged international students from interacting with The Daily. District Judge Noël Wise previously ruled the INA provisions used by the federal government unconstitutional in a 90-page decision. The decision, which the DOJ appealed last week, currently only has jurisdiction within the Northern District of California. With the appeal, the Ninth Circuit will weigh whether the ruling should be overturned or expanded to the entirety of nine states and two territories, including California. Editor-in-Chief of The Daily George Porteous ’27 holds a positive view of the expedition. “We see this case as an important one that should move quickly through the courts,” Porteous said. “Our lawyers are fully prepared to defend Judge Wise’s ruling.” The Daily is being represented pro bono by FIRE. According to the modified schedule, the opening and amicus briefs in support of the DOJ must be submitted before the end of the year. All briefs required to begin oral argument are due before the end of January, according to the court’s official order. “The appeal creates an opportunity for this ruling to protect international students in a broader area,” Porteous said. title: Frosh constructs Noah’s Ark to weather Crothers flood
author: Micah Chung
content: Editor’s Note: This article is purely satirical and fictitious. All attributions in this article are not genuine, and this story should be read in the context of pure entertainment only. This past Saturday, as sprinklers flooded Crothers Hall, Noah de la Cruz ’30 managed to escape the worst of the flooding thanks to divine intervention. Appearing to de la Cruz in a dream with a radiant flash of light, the Lord God declared that the inhabitants of Crothers Hall had been nursing thoughts of joining private equity and consulting firms after graduating, which was corrupt in God’s sight. De la Cruz, thanks to his virtuous rejection of the Stanford-to-consulting pipeline, would be spared. “Make yourself an Ark of bed frame wood; make it three cubits long, five cubits wide, and put the door in its side,” boomed the Creator of the Universe, as de la Cruz bolted awake in a cold sweat. “Bring with you into the Ark two of every cheat sheet, two of every homework assignment, two of every brand of mobile phone, and seven clean sets of underwear.” “What’s a cubit in football fields?” de la Cruz muttered in a daze, tossing aside his blankets as the dream faded. His roommate, Jason Caldwell ’30, helpfully informed him that a cubit was roughly half of a mini fridge, and then inquired as to why his mystery project would be wider than its length. Disguising his activity by informing his roommate that he was simply lofting his bed, de la Cruz assembled a boat to the exact specifications of the God of the Israelites, taking a hacksaw to his bed frame and tearing apart his desk and dresser.  As de la Cruz made a burnt offering of his Math 61 homework to the Almighty God, unleashing a storm of dust particles that floated their way up to the Lord, the fire alarm system coincidentally went off throughout the halls. “The day of reckoning is upon us!” de la Cruz screamed, rousing a confused Caldwell from his sleep. Though the original Noah was accompanied by his wife and children, de la Cruz, a math major, had neither, and boarded the Ark alone just prior to the flooding. Caldwell, due to not having taken out the trash the week prior, was not invited. As the raging waters in the Hall blotted out all homework assignments, notes and electronic devices from the face of the Earth, only de la Cruz’s items survived unharmed in the Ark. Caldwell, meanwhile, burst into tears upon learning that Stanford would not compensate him for lost or damaged items. However, RD&E generously offered a free pack of rice to lay his wet electronics in. This was a small consolation to Caldwell, whose floppy discs had become floppier due to the water. The rain was ordained to fall for forty days and forty nights. However, as the Bible was originally written on a semester system, the Stanford flood was shortened to around twenty minutes to fit the quarter schedule. True to myths that unicorns went extinct following their failure to get on the Ark, multiple Y Combinator hopefuls found their futures dashed as the hard drives containing their billion-dollar ideas were banished to the big Crungeon in the sky. Following the flood, the Lord God was pleased and promised de la Cruz that He would never again flood the dorms during midterms, turning the colors of de la Cruz’s Canvas courses rainbow as a sign of his covenant.  At press time, God accidentally leaned on the “RAIN” button in His heavenly office, causing this morning’s downpour.
