title: Stanford offers new courses in AI prompting and vibecoding
author: Charlie Goldberg
content: Amidst the normal fanfare at Stanford’s 136th Convocation, Vice Provost for Undergraduate Education James Hamilton made an unusual request during his remarks. Hamilton recommended students enroll in a new course, CS193T: “Thinking With AI,” so they could learn “agentic workflows.” Along with CS193V: “Effective Vibecoding,” CS193T is part of the computer science (CS) department’s push to ensure students with non-technical backgrounds can engage with large language models (LLMs). According to the class’s website, CS193T aims to teach “advanced prompting skills,” where students are instructed to apply AI to the work they normally do, but with “layers of reflection, analysis and comparison.” CS193V teaches students without coding experience on how to “vibecode” — the new art of getting an LLM to code for you, without review of the code itself. Keith Schwarz, who leads teaching in CS193V, said that Chris Gregg, associate professor of CS and the department’s associate chair for education, approached him last spring about teaching an AI-assisted coding class “aimed at a general audience.” CS193T has no prerequisites, unlike most courses the department offers. CS193V’s only prerequisite is CS106A or an equivalent level of a few months of programming experience. Even so, the syllabus starts from the basics.  “The vision of the course I’m trying out this quarter doesn’t involve reading or writing code,” Schwarz said. “Having a basic knowledge of coding is nonetheless helpful for understanding certain concepts we’ll cover.” Amari Porter ’27, a teaching assistant (TA) for CS193T, said that the class attracted a wide range of students, from “incoming frosh who might not know much, to mature Distinguished Career Institute fellows, who also might not know much.”  She said that CS senior lecturer Cynthia Bailey and the TAs are developing assignments as the class progresses. According to Porter, the assignments included “looking at differences between the major three [AI] models and having models infer life details when given writing samples.” Bailey had previously worked in AI safety and was chosen by the CS department because she is “very big on thinking about the impacts of AI usage,” as Porter noted. TAs, too, came from a range of experiences with AI as well.  “When I was a frosh, ChatGPT had just started to get popular, and during sophomore and junior year, I had felt overly reliant on AI and questioned how much of my own agency was being automated away,” Porter said, adding that she “tries to teach how to use AI without relying on it like a crutch.” Haowen Chen ’28, an environmental engineering major, decided to take CS193V after seeing projects his friends had vibecoded. “I also saw a lot of interesting things people were building on Instagram,” Chen said. “I have several projects myself, but I felt like I was lacking some of the basic technology and pipelines.” Schwarz told The Daily that vibecoding is “absolutely” a teachable skill. Even if students weren’t going to write the code themselves, he said, students would still want to have a basic understanding of the technology in order to evaluate costs and maintainability and determine if software works correctly.  “I’m hoping CS193V will equip students to think critically about these questions and make appropriate decisions,” Schwarz said. In a previous version of this article, Schwarz’s name was misspelled. The Daily regrets this error. title: Student organizations mobilize ahead of midterm elections
author: Grace Dong
content: From hosting astronaut Steve Smith to running weekly voter registration drives, student organizations are working to increase civic engagement and awareness in preparation for the midterm elections next month. One new initiative, Civics Week, hosted by StanfordVotes last week, featured speaker events that explored the current implications of the 1965 Voting Rights Act. StanfordVotes co-chair Maria Rueda ’28 said that beyond exploring current issues in voting rights, one of their priorities for the fall quarter was to ensure students properly completed voter registration and mail-in ballot applications, based on issues StanfordVotes observed with last-minute registrations this past spring. “Voting rules are very difficult to understand. They’re complex. They’re different for every single state,” Helen Scarborough ’28, a co-chair of StanfordVotes, said. Beyond Civics Week, the group also aims to help students overcome such organizational barriers through their 50-state voter guide, and hosted weekly voter education and registration drives at On-Call Cafe. Stanford students plan to vote in and out of California, with many opting to register for races closer to their hometowns.  “I’m keeping up with a lot of the very contentious races. Namely [in] the Senate,” said Sanjana Vadlapatla ’29, a public service co-lead for Stanford Women in Politics. With plans to mail her ballot to her hometown in West Texas, Vadlapatla emphasized the importance of staying educated and participating in elections at all levels, from local to federal positions. Other students echoed this sentiment. “Even in a state like California that is pretty predictably blue, it’s really important to vote for down-ballot races,” said Supriya Patel ’28, who plans to vote in her hometown of Sacramento. “I think that we underestimate how important local elections are.” In anticipation of election day and Stanford’s Democracy Day, various civic organizations are preparing events. The Stanford Political Review is moderating a student debate, the Stanford American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) is hosting a workshop on exercising student free speech, and The Stanford Daily’s opinions section will lead a workshop on free expression writing. “I think the true genius of Democracy Day is seeing all of these different civic organizations from a broad spectrum of sectors in society come together on this one day,” said Jadon Urogdy ’27, who chairs Democracy Day. He noted one of the main goals of the event is to take advantage of the varied backgrounds and ideologies that Stanford students bring to their shared civics organizations, enabling them to learn about citizenship in a way that persists beyond a single election cycle. On the ground, the Stanford Democrats have taken students on canvassing trips throughout the Bay Area for state and federal representatives, with phone-banking events planned for elections across the United States. “What I’m really big on emphasizing is making sure that Stanford students are able to break out of Palo Alto and get involved in real grassroots civics work,” Waleed Haider ’29, co-chair of the Stanford Democrats, said. “At Stanford Democrats, we want to make sure that we are winning elections for Americans that empower them, that make their lives better, and that we’re also looking forward towards the issues that we know are coming out of this campus in particular.” Haider noted that the 2026 election would shape America’s future. Urogdy made a similar point, noting that the consequences of voting extend beyond just policy. Other students have identified the stability of democratic institutions as a primary concern going forward.  “There’s a lot of tension that builds up around election day,” said Urogdy. “But I think most importantly, we should recognize election day as a moment where we can celebrate the democratic process and come together and make sure that our friends and family show up to vote.” The post Student organizations mobilize ahead of midterm elections appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: What does your dorm room say about you?
author: Coco Zhou
content: I’ve recently noticed that guys seem to be getting into perfume, skincare and even putting noticeable effort into decorating their dorm rooms in college. Having come from a boarding high school, I thought I had a good sense of what to expect in a teenage boys’ dorm room: a container of some sort for snacks, a carpet, occasionally LEDs and maybe some scattered posters or figurines. So when and why did this transformation to organization and aesthetic intentionality occur?  To me, dorm decorations are not just for aesthetics and to create a comfortable living space, it also encapsulates a personality. I suppose that some guys (and girls) have taken advantage of the summer after high school to reinvent themselves, presenting new versions of who they are for the first time during NSO room tours. Broadly speaking, maybe we all possess this desire to give visitors a glimpse of ourselves through what we choose to “display.” I don’t mean this in merely a performative sense, where the sole purpose is to impress with something that possesses material value or signifies achievement. The things I put up around my room are little pieces of my life I want to keep close because they remind me of where I come from, the people I hold dear and what I value. There’s a collection of keychains hanging from the wall that remind me of my friends. Over the past few years, I have received more keychains than I have bags to put them on — hence this collection. I figured people like gifting keychains because these little dangly things are physically carried around and even make noises to grab attention. Since they want to be thought of, hopefully my friends approve of how I’m putting them to use. If you’ve ever taken AP Art History, you would recognize elements of the pieces you’ve studied scattered throughout the room: a magnet of the Delphic Sibyl from the Sistine Chapel, my Smiskis Museum Series collection, a miniature print of Paul Cézanne’s Mont Sainte-Victore, some Japanese Ukioy-e postcards, etc. Each piece brings back astonishing moments of visiting art museums and landmarks around the world. And there’s my matcha and coffee cart! Though I’m not super proud of my caffeine addiction, I will always be a proud tea party host. Caffeine to stay up late studying or catching up is on me. Right above are my plane ticket and pin collections from more side-hustles and adventures.  My high school banner and teddy bear are also hard to miss. I loved my four years in high school and am still extremely grateful for how it has shaped me in every imaginable way. Compared to my high school room, the current setup has more traces of my travels abroad. I like to think that this “reinventing” process doesn’t mean becoming someone entirely new, but rather making small, intentional choices about the person we want to be. It’s similar to how we all set aspirational yet attainable goals for ourselves, then find ways to keep ourselves accountable to them. I come to college with the intention of traveling to more destinations beyond where I have already set foot. Maybe it is this desire to keep modifying and becoming that brought us all here in the first place. The post What does your dorm room say about you? appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Stanford football prepared, optimistic for NC State matchup
author: Eli Zerr
content: After a homecoming weekend win against Elon (4-4, 2-2 CAA), Stanford football (3-4, 1-3 ACC) looks to keep the momentum rolling this Friday against North Carolina State (3-3, 1-2 ACC). This game is pivotal as the Cardinal prepare to go back on the road for games at Louisville (4-3, 3-2 ACC) and Virginia Tech (5-2, 2-2 ACC) in the upcoming weeks. If Stanford is to position themselves as bowl game contenders, this game is even more of a must-win. The University has not played in a post-season game since 2018. Junior linebacker Sam Mattingly, fresh off a career game two weeks ago and another team-leading defensive performance against Elon, said that the win has upped the energy in the locker room. “Guys are excited. Obviously we know that NC State is a good team… the intensity the last two days of practice… it’s been way up,” he said after practice on Wednesday. While Stanford finally has some momentum, NC State is coming off an Oct. 10 drubbing by Wake Forest (6-1, 4-1 ACC) and a bye week. The Wolfpack failed to get much going offensively in the second half against Wake Forest, giving up a slightly higher-than-average 387 total yards despite key defensive contributors Popo Aguirre and Jackson Vick registering 12 and 8 tackles, respectively. Junior Stanford running back Micah Ford, who tied the school record in rushing touchdowns last weekend, will be looking to exploit NC State’s middling run defense, which gives up an average of 133 yards on the ground per game. For a Stanford rushing attack that had a breakout game last week, Friday will be critical to determining whether they can see sustained success. The goal is to be a complement to Stanford’s predominantly aerial offense. Up to this point in the season, the Cardinal have averaged 233 yards per game through the air compared to just 103 yards on the ground. Ford alone produces nearly three-quarters of Stanford’s ground yards. Ford also appeared in the injury report for the first time on Wednesday, where he is listed as probable to play. This comes after he said postgame on Saturday that the injury two weeks ago against No. 4 Notre Dame (6-1) was just a “spasm” and he felt fully recovered after a week. Whatever it may be, the mild injury characterization bodes well for Stanford’s offensive picture, which will certainly look to feature the standout running back. On the defensive side of the ball, Stanford’s focus will be on stopping Wolfpack junior quarterback CJ Bailey. “He’s been a good quarterback in this league for a while,” Mattingly said, though he is confident in the defensive game plan the coaching staff has devised. On his own recent success and defensive leadership, Mattingly attributed it to the coaches’ preparation. “They’re just putting me in good spots,” he said. He largely schedules his day around film and meetings at this point in the season, fitting it in both before and after his block of classes in the middle of the day.  On the field, preparation is what has allowed Mattingly to step into a leadership role in the absence of senior linebacker Matt Rose, who was injured in the Cardinal’s Sept. 26 victory over Georgia Tech (2-4, 1-2 ACC) and has yet to play since. Yet, Mattingly still credits Rose as a key mentor and contributor. “Rose is still [our] leader… It’s always next man up, that’s what we preach on defense.” One variable that the Cardinal must contend with as opposed to the Wolfpack is the short week of preparation due to a Friday game. While Monday would typically be an off day for the team, the schedule had to compress a bit. Mattingly didn’t think it was cause for any concern: “It kind of looks the same as every other week, starting a day earlier.” If the Cardinal are to get back to .500 this Friday, they’ll need to stay in rhythm with the offensive and defensive strides that led to victory last week. Reaching that mark would be a big milestone in the first year of this rebuild under new head coach Tavita Pritchard. But the one goal Mattingly has in mind is simple: “I think we just come out and execute,” he said. Kick-off is set for 7:30pm Friday. title: Lance Oppenheim’s ‘Primetime’ makes me ashamed to be online
author: Charlie Goldberg
content: Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques.  Scrolling TikTok, X or even the front page of the news, it’s easy to think that the United States has slipped into a uniquely cruel era of endless gawking and thinly-veiled pornography. Across the country, slack-jawed viewers toggle between videos of Ukrainian drones slamming into huddled soldiers, attempted or realized political assassinations and “pick-up” videos filmed with secret cameras and obviously disturbed girls. But as “Primetime” (2026), Lance Oppenheim’s compelling thriller based on television host Chris Hansen’s life, reminds us, American society has long thrived off public humiliation. The movie recounts the years up until Hansen’s infamous pedophile-hunting show, “To Catch a Predator,” came to an end after one of the “predators” committed suicide — a story originally told in a lengthy 2009 “Esquire” article. Hansen appears as a self-convinced hero, played by a frightening Robert Pattinson. He is matched by Andie Bender (Merritt Weaver), a slightly more sympathetic but ultimately ruthless producer who—perhaps even more than Hansen—is driven by pressure from NBC executives. Hansen also mentors a boyish actor nicknamed “Decoy Dan” (Skyler Gisondo), who draws the show’s predators into the stage-set houses, where a well-rehearsed Hansen confronts them. The movie is a vivid time capsule of the 2000s, a period when liberal and conservative America alike were far more confident in their self-righteousness. Besides “To Catch a Predator,” the other major entertainment on offer was the ongoing Iraq War, played on TV as a remote-controlled shooter game or as a triumphant courtroom drama. Self-righteousness is backed up by the creeping militarization of American life, seeping in from abroad: police toting assault rifles and riding in armored vehicles.  Hansen’s show is the apotheosis of the wider cultural landscape. Not so much lurking but leaping out of “Predator” is the tendency towards life-as-content; the confusion of acting with the real thing; everyday life lived in bad faith. This sort of willful existential confusion leads Hansen to believe his job is not so much exposing small-town perverts as it is unveiling the ultimate evil of the world. He doubles down on his career as his personal marital troubles compound. This delusion leads Hansen into dangerous territory. Oppenheim does a masterful job of entertaining Hansen’s megalomania as the TV host pursues a politician he suspects is a predator. Eventually, “Decoy Dan” is drawn into the deadly serious fun of it all and grows into Hansen’s role. In one memorable scene, the Manichaean struggle takes on an undeniably Lynchian tenor: we are thrust into a dreamlike world of strange, pitiful predators; toy blues and oranges caught in dark shadow; voyeuristic camera angles; and an overwhelming dread of unknown, possibly universal, origin. Hansen has convinced himself that the source of this dread is out somewhere in the world. He is egged on by his assistants to believe that vicious pedophiles lurk at every level of society. Every community has its outcasts and perverts, but they don’t emerge (as Hansen believes) out of some primordial gash in the earth. Darkness does not exist out of space and time, but it does multiply before our blinking, blinded eyes as we root around for it.  “Primetime” is larger than life, but only because Chris Hansen was determined to portray himself as larger than life. It is not really a pleasurable watch, or at least not in the voyeuristic, addictive way that “To Catch a Predator” is. Everybody —  from Hansen to his cronies to the pedophiles they chase — evinces a desperate discomfort. Oppenheim does not want us to wring the same guilty pleasures we do out of reality TV. I didn’t leave the theater feeling implicated — I don’t spend my time stitching together TikTok edits, and I stopped watching clips of “Predator” a long time ago. But as the credits rolled, I did feel perturbed and victimized. One of television’s — and, eventually, the internet’s — effects was to render private life impossible. We constantly exhibit ourselves. Occasionally, a movie like “Primetime” comes around and reminds us of the punishment of our constant exposure. It’s not dissimilar from the monotonous, nervous misery of being online. In “Primetime”‘s funhouse world, the possibility of turning away from the spectacle is never on offer. title: The Secret Lives of Poets: The Stanford writing war waged between the ‘Dean of Western Writers’ and the ‘Junkie Renegade’
author: April Yu
content: In “The Secret Lives of Poets,” April Yu ’30 investigates the absurd habits, wacky relationships, and creative practices that past and modern writers use to stay grounded or take flight. “I took LSD and he stayed with Jack Daniels,” writer Ken Kesey once said . “The line between us was drawn.” The year was 1958, and at the heart of Stanford’s Cecil H. Green Library, in one of the most coveted classrooms of the decade, a battle was brewing. On one side, Wallace Stegner: the dean of Western writers, literary traditionalist, the man Edward Abbey deemed “the only living American writer worthy of the Nobel.” On the other, Ken Kesey: spiritualist technophile, the father of the Merry Pranksters (a 60s counterculture group), the classmate Larry McMurtry called the instant “alpha male.” The conflict: the future of Western literature. To most English majors today, opponent one is a household name. Stegner founded the Stanford Creative Writing program 80 years ago and created the Stegner Fellowship, which has brought more than 600 emerging writers to campus to create art and gives lectures. As a professor, his roster of students was world-class: Pulitzer Prize winner N. Scott Momaday Ph.D. ’63, Supreme Court Justice Sandra Day O’Connor ’50 LL.B. ’52 and Poet Laureate of the United States Robert Haas M.A. ’65 Ph.D. ’71. The live culture of theory instruction, literary immersion and pure talent Stegner cultivated in the Jones Room of the Bing Wing thrived. What most students do not know, however, is that from 1958 to 1961, Stegner taught a college writer who became his in-class rival: Ken Kesey. In writing content, the two men were similar. They were both interested in the contours of the American West, in Nebraska and New Mexico. In every other way, they were completely different. Stegner was straight-laced and strictly coralled. He imagined the American West as a beautiful space that needed preserving, and his “Wilderness Letter” was used to establish the National Wilderness Preservation System in 1964. He taught sustained work, constant revision and carefully honed perspective in prose. Meanwhile, Kesey was subversive and prophetic, using drugs as emotional flights through Western geography in his works. He allowed manuscripts to flow from his typewriter unedited, shifting between time and perspective in his novel “Sometimes a Great Notion . ” Bob Stone, a writing fellow at Stanford, told Stegner’s first biographer, Jackson Benson, that “Stegner saw Kesey and what he represented as a threat to civilization and intellectualism and sobriety.”  So, who was right? Should art undergo scrutiny and endless revision, or is it best experienced at its rawest and newest? Was Stegner correct in his fear of the anti-intellectual next generation?  At today’s Stanford, which benefits from the writing both Stegner and Kesey produced, art has entered a complicated conversation about creativity in an age of unprecedented technological growth. Artificial intelligence has the power to shape both the raw material Kesey preferred and the revision process Stegner valued. It has the power to convert the most intelligent learner into a consumer that can only process synthesized, digestible summaries. It has the power to algorithmically predict what the future of Western literature could be and spew that, word by word, onto a student’s screen. In the modern climate, both men’s opinions contribute to an ethos of creation that resists shortcuts. Stegner’s push for revision is arguably a push for human inefficiency: the friction of reading every line in a piece of writing to make it more concise, accurate and authentic. Kesey’s drug-induced emotional journeys also supported the idea that bewildering and overpowering emotion is at the center of a piece, that the urgency of the human can never be replaced. Stegner and Kesey’s feud may have been buried with time and publications, but their debate grows ever more relevant. In an interview with The Paris Review, he made amends by celebrating that the program that Stegner arranged “ruled literature in California and, in some ways, the rest of the nation for a long time.” Kesey still embodies LSD, and Stegner lives on as the Jack Daniels, but we can realize that both arguments centered on an obsession with craft: an ideological war over how to make writing touching, intimate, incisive. The two men fought for two concepts of art that will always surpass one shortcut to the final product.  The post The Secret Lives of Poets: The Stanford writing war waged between the ‘Dean of Western Writers’ and the ‘Junkie Renegade’ appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: STEWARD project seeks to create oversight for AI in healthcare
author: Simon Vuong
content: As AI agents take on more responsibilities in healthcare, Stanford researchers are working to ensure these systems are safe and practical. The Safety, Trust, Evaluation and Watchdog for Embedded Agentic Care Delivery (STEWARD) is an independent, three-stage AI supervisory agent that evaluates the accuracy of medical recommendations of other clinical agents deployed in cardiovascular care.  The system first ensures that patients’ information and the agent’s recommendation are comparable to clinical trial data. When data is not available, STEWARD relies on past decisions and existing guidelines. It then verifies the information behind those recommendations, including patients’ medical history, medication dosage and drug interactions.  In stage three, STEWARD conducts a thorough evaluation of agents’ reasoning and treatment decisions, then provides feedback to improve system accuracy over time. Researchers hope STEWARD will help physicians provide those with limited access to medical services the care they need.  The demand for healthcare exceeds physician capacity, said radiology professor Akshay Chaudhari. When simpler cases are managed autonomously or efficiently, he noted that physicians could focus their efforts on patients with more complex needs. Chaudhari co-leads the initiative with medicine professor Euan Ashley and biomedical data science professor Roxana Daneshjou in collaboration with partners including OpenAI and the University of Washington. Stanford Medicine announced the funding of the STEWARD initiative on Sept. 30. with the research team receiving $14.9 million from Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) to develop a regulatory-grade monitoring system. The initiative falls under their Agentic AI-Enabled Cardiovascular Care Transformation (ADVOCATE) program, which has a broader objective of creating the world’s first FDA-authorized clinical agentic AI system, bringing 24/7 holistic cardiovascular care. For patients with cardiovascular issues, this could open up the possibility of more thorough and responsive care. One possible application would be in changing drug doses, Ashley said. Treatment recommendations often vary, he said, since most decisions are made based on how different patients respond. As such, STEWARD’s responsibility is not to find a single answer but rather to eliminate incorrect ones generated by the clinical agent. “There [are] multiple potential correct answers,” Ashley said. “But our focus is on the smaller number of potential wrong answers and detecting those.”  While applying a layer of oversight to the decisions of clinical AI agents might improve accuracy in their recommendations, researchers don’t plan for STEWARD to automate the medical process. Instead, it is meant to be an assistive tool that allows physicians to spend more time on specialized decisions, Ashley said. Before the agent is implemented, the team must work with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and conduct clinical studies to test the system’s reliability. A major milestone for the project would be to achieve Medical Device Development Tool (MDDT) status, which would allow STEWARD to serve as a generic framework for other monitoring systems, facilitating broader use, Chaudhari said. Even as the effort remains in its early stages, researchers are optimistic about its potential. “It’s usually harder to be an artist than to be the critic, right?” Chaudhari said of the oversight role. “We are mostly being the critics. Someone else is creating that art already, which is the hard part.” The post STEWARD project seeks to create oversight for AI in healthcare appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: 650,000,000 words about me
author: Angikar Ghosal
content: Starting January 1, 2026, I tried an experiment. Every day around 9 p.m., I forced myself to type 1,000 words of pure stream of consciousness — the conversations I had, the people I met, the thoughts I had, the thoughts about the thoughts, the various things that reminded me of other things, the stochastic associations making up consciousness. If I could continue this for a year, I would have written 365,000 words. In four years, 1.46 million words. By the end of college, I would have a corpus longer than all of Proust’s In Search of Lost Time . Suppose this finite body never felt tired, never needed food and could type for twenty-four hours a day nonstop at roughly one word per second. That’s 31.5 million words per year. Twenty years and still under a billion. GPT-3 was pretrained on roughly 400 billion tokens of filtered internet data from Common Crawl. At about 0.75 words per token, that gives around 300 billion words. The finite, limited body despairs. When I write anything, there are aspects, quirks, idiosyncrasies, stylistic marks that I can recognize as my own. Eschew, vicissitude, thereby, hitherto, weltanschauung — I know exactly which words are my signature, where brain-attached-to-finite-body diverges most from a typical language model. I would have loved to keep believing that this “style” is something that resides in me as my unique fingerprint. But no! All our mannerisms, all our behavioral patterns, the phrases we reach out to, the analogies we use to explain other analogies, our ideologies and our personalities — are they not the product of the various people we have met, the events we have experienced, the tokens we have processed and fine-tuned on top of our genetic pretraining? With a sufficiently large corpus of text, can you not reproduce the essential features of all the data that created my sense of “I?” What’s that? You argue that an individual piece of text is an incomplete representation, a limited projection of consciousness? Sure, then keep adding more text, keep getting a better and better approximation of reality! Humans may be high-dimensional but they are still finite -dimensional. In four years, at human speed, I can match Marcel Proust. If I start writing now, in say twelve years, can I not capture both the two dozen years I’ve lived and the years spent writing them? Are the twelve years spent writing not themselves twelve years spent living? Can Achilles catch the tortoise, if every thought recorded generates another thought about the recording? Fret not! The number of points in a vector space should not be confused with the number of dimensions to span the vector space. My thoughts may be innumerable, but the underlying generative structure is finite and learnable. Hence, I do not need to enumerate every possible thought for someone to reconstruct the process producing them. The Common App college application asks you to frame your life-purpose-goal-achievements in 650 words. It’s true, narratives are always artificial and constrained. I cannot exhaustively enumerate myself within even 65,000 words. But 650,000,000 words? Then I can not only recall with perfection the text of the Panchatantra, but also the thoughts I had while reading the Panchatantra for the first time at the age of six and the sixth time at the age of sixteen, the event at twelve that reminded me of the book, the event at twenty that reminded me of being reminded at twelve, and so on. If only I could output this corpus all at once right now! I could then fine-tune GLM-5.3 on this!  Would I not then have successfully cloned myself by uploading my entire Self to silicon? Would He not think like me and feel like me? What is the entirety of me? What exists that cannot be described by text? Perhaps there is no independent vantage point, no pure, unmediated reality describing me beyond text. There is no outside-text, no indivisible essence beyond text. Actually, a well-detailed map is the territory. One must dare to think of existence beyond flesh and blood! There can only be one biological version of me at any given time. But imagine copying over the weights of such a fine-tuned language model. Arbitrary duplication! A panoply of souls that are distinct persons but one essence! Indeed, there are forms of existence, there are forms of human flourishing, that are inhuman. The post 650,000,000 words about me appeared first on The Stanford Daily .

title: Q&A with Jennifer Laine, Executive Director of the San Benito County Arts Council
author: Michael Moore
content: This story was provided courtesy of the Monterey Bay Economic Partnership . The Monterey Bay Economic Partnership presented the following Q&A with San Benito County Arts Council Executive Director Jennifer Laine. MBEP recently celebrated the region’s arts industry with the Oct. 22 Creative Economy Summit in Watsonville. According to Laine, the county’s creative and cultural sector generates millions in annual revenue, attracts visitors to the region and supports employment. The latest available tax filings for the five largest local nonprofit arts and cultural organizations indicate approximately $2 million in combined annual revenue—just the tip of the iceberg for a much broader creative economy, according to MBEP.  Laine shares her perspective with MBEP and local readers on what the creative economy looks like, its potential and why intentional investment is vital to our regional economy. Q. What value can we assign to the creative economy in San Benito County? How do we quantify economic output and employment for a creative economy? A. San Benito County’s creative economy is an important but currently undermeasured component of our regional economy. It includes nonprofit arts and cultural organizations, independent artists and culture bearers, performing arts, visual arts, arts education, cultural heritage and tourism, and creative businesses working in design, media and related fields. Employment: The county’s 2023–27 Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy reported approximately 125 jobs in arts, entertainment and recreation in 2021. This provides a documented baseline, but it does not capture the full creative workforce, including freelance artists, self-employed creatives, designers, arts educators and creative professionals employed outside traditional arts industries.  A preliminary planning estimate of 400–700 creative jobs in 2025 has been identified, but additional occupational and industry-level data are needed to validate that range. Economic output: The latest available tax filings for the five largest local nonprofit arts and cultural organizations indicate approximately $2 million in combined annual revenue.  The San Benito County Arts Council, the largest arts organization and arts employer in the county, accounts for $1.2 million of this total, and over the last 10 years, has brought in more than $12 million to the region.  These data points demonstrate the operating scale of part of the county’s cultural infrastructure but are not a measure of the entire creative economy or its total economic impact, especially when you factor in tourism and for-profit cultural activities, such as the annual Hollister Concerts series put on by Guerra Cellars Winery, for example.  A comprehensive assessment would also include creative-business revenue, artist and contractor earnings, payroll, cultural tourism and spending at local businesses associated with cultural events and activities. In the simplest terms, what are we talking about when we use the term “creative economy”—what does that encompass, and how broadly can we apply that definition? Loosely, the creative economy is defined as the businesses and individuals involved in producing cultural, artistic and design goods and services. In San Benito County, that includes nonprofit arts and culture organizations, creative businesses and cultural tourism, amongst other activities. What are we doing well as a region in terms of supporting our creative economy? What can we improve upon to cultivate a creative economy here? A few strong examples of how we are supporting our creative economy in our region are through the emergence, growth and collaboration around local and regional film festivals, such as the Watsonville Film Festival, Popper Jasper Film Festival and others, through support and building cultural infrastructure around public art and the establishment of California-designated Cultural Districts; and through grant-funded workforce development projects, like the Pathways for Arts Educators Project funded by California Jobs First, to identify and establish pathways for sustainable careers in arts education.  To improve our creative economy here, we need more local government support in terms of funding, awareness and education and being included and embedded as a strategy in local and regional economic development planning. MBEP is a regional member-supported nonprofit organization consisting of public, private and civic entities located throughout the counties of Monterey, San Benito and Santa Cruz. Founded in 2015, MBEP’s mission is to improve the economic health and quality of life in the region.

title: More details emerge about Oct. 17 stabbing, carjacking, self-harm incident
author: Staff Report
content: Hollister Police offered more details last week about an Oct. 17 incident in which a woman who stabbed her partner before carjacking two victims. The woman ultimately fled into San Jose, where she died of self-inflicted stab wounds, according to authorities.  New details from the Hollister Police Department also reveal that the suspect, Vanessa Garcia, 34, of Hollister, is the same woman from a Sept. 26 incident in which a suicidal knife-wielding person was in an hours-long standoff with police near Apricot Lane at Summer Drive. On that day, Garcia was eventually safely detained and transported for treatment.  Police responded to the 1100 block of San Benito Street about 9:46am, after receiving a report of a stabbing. Before officers arrived, the victim, later identified as the suspect’s domestic partner, left the scene and called 911, says an Oct. 22 press release from the Hollister Police Department.  Officers found the victim at a local carwash, suffering from two stab wounds to his chest and neck, authorities said. A second victim, later identified as the suspect’s sister, was also at the carwash and reported being carjacked at knifepoint.  After stabbing her partner and carjacking her sister’s vehicle, Garcia fled the area armed with two knives, says the press release. Police obtained the vehicle’s license plate number, and with assistance from the Flock surveillance system learned the vehicle was last seen leaving Hollister. Due to the severity of the crime and concerns for officer safety, police issued an alert for nearby law enforcement agencies to be on the lookout for the woman, authorities said.  Within minutes, Hollister Police received a report that a vehicle matching the suspect’s description had been driving recklessly eastbound on Highway 152 near Casa de Fruta, says the press release. A second update reported that the suspect vehicle collided head-on with another car, causing one vehicle to overturn. Officers later learned Garcia had exited the crashed vehicle and carjacked another motorist at knifepoint, police said. She then fled westbound on Highway 152 toward Gilroy.  Using the Flock system again, Gilroy Police located the suspect vehicle as it entered the city limits, police said.  Officers from the Gilroy PD, Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office and California Highway Patrol pursued the vehicle—using spike strips and other tactics—to attempt to stop the vehicle. Their pursuit was unsuccessful and the vehicle entered San Jose, where officers lost visual contact, says the press release.  Police said they later learned that Garcia had abandoned the vehicle after it became disabled, and attempted to carjack more motorists at knifepoint.  San Jose Police officers located Garcia, who was still armed with a knife. With officers on the scene, Garcia then severely injured herself, according to Hollister Police. Earlier police reports said she used a knife to hurt herself repeatedly.  Officers provided medical aid and Garcia was transported to a nearby hospital. She was pronounced dead, police said.  Anyone who feels suicidal or is suffering from a mental health crisis can call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988, or the San Benito County mental health support hotline at 831.902.2911.

title: Hollister Council fires City Manager Ana Cortez
author: Michael Moore
content: The Hollister City Council voted in closed session on Oct. 21 to fire City Manager Ana Cortez, who has been the subject of increasing criticism for her approach to cutting costs and issuing layoff notices to dozens of city employees in recent weeks.  After the council returned to the City Hall chamber after the closed session, City Attorney Dayna D. Louie said the council voted 3-2 to terminate Cortez’s contract “for convenience.” Vice Mayor Priscilla de Anda and Councilmember Rolan Resendiz voted against Cortez’s firing.  It is unclear if the “for convenience” reasoning protects the city from having to pay Cortez for exiting her contract.  Louie added that the council also agreed to appoint Hollister Airport Director Jeff Crechriou as the acting city manager. Crechriou will serve as City Hall’s top staff person while the council considers its options for permanently filling the city manager’s position.  The council did not discuss a timeline or the next steps in a potential search for a new city manager.  Cortez’s firing comes after she issued layoff notices on Oct. 14 to at least 36 city employees, and has faced mounting accusations that she did so without consulting the city’s labor unions, department heads or other city officials.  Shortly after those layoff notices were issued, members of the Hollister Police Officers Association and the local chapter of the Service Employees International Union reported votes of no confidence in Cortez, and demanded that the council terminate her employment as city manager.  The layoff notices informed the affected employees that they were to be placed on administrative leave, with their employment with the City of Hollister set to end on Nov. 13. The affected employees included nine civilian police staff members, as well as employees in the city’s public works, airport, parks and recreation and finance departments.  The council hired Cortez in February, at an annual salary of $265,000.  The council called the Oct. 21 meeting as a special session, after taking actions at the Oct. 19 meeting that reversed previous decisions recommended by Cortez to address the city’s ongoing financial challenges.  Specifically on Oct. 19, the council voted to reverse a declaration of “financial emergency” that it approved on Oct. 2. The council also voted to end the laid-off employees’ administrative leave and “continue to meet and confer regarding impacts of the workforce reductions.”  But during the Oct. 21 meeting, some of the affected employees and their union heads said they remain in the dark about the fate of their future with the city. Speaking during the public comment portion of the meeting, some asked the council to rescind the layoff notices entirely.  Hollister SEIU President Frank Garcia, who works in the city’s stormwater division, said city employees are still concerned that they will be unemployed as of Nov. 13. Garcia added that city officials have acknowledged errors in City Hall financial reporting that may have influenced the recent layoff notices.  “Your employees should not bear the pressure of that deadline while the city sorts out its errors,” Garcia said. “Please rescind the layoff notices. Give us a fair opportunity to reach an agreement based on accurate financial information.”  City officials have said the current financial state is the result of years of inattention and mismanagement by previous councilmembers and city staff. At the Oct. 2 meeting, Cortez claimed the city had only $178 in its general fund bank account, and would not be able to pay employees’ next paycheck.  Also on Oct. 2, the council approved a loan of $18 million from its impact fees fund to the general and water funds in order to make payroll.

title: Survey shows 57% drop in San Benito County homelessness
author: Staff Report
content: The 2026 Point-in-Time Count of unhoused residents identified 267 people experiencing homeless in San Benito Couty—a 57% decrease from the 621 counted in 2024, according to the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers (CHSP). Officials from the CHSP conducted the count in partnership with the county, local governments, community organizations, service providers and volunteers. The PIT count is conducted every two years.  Of those counted in 2026, 69 people, or 26%, were sheltered, and 198 people, or 74%, were unsheltered, says a press release from CHSP. Unsheltered homelessness decreased by about 60%—from 496 people in 2024 to 198 in 2026.  The PIT Count provides a snapshot of homelessness on a single night, including people staying in emergency shelters and transitional housing, as well as those living outdoors, in vehicles or in other places not intended for human habitation, CHSP officials explained. The count helps inform local planning, funding priorities and efforts to strengthen the homelessness response system.  “This decrease is encouraging and reflects the dedication of our county partners, service providers and community members working to connect people with housing and support,” said Katrina McKenzie, Executive Director of CHSP. “At the same time, the survey findings remind us that many residents continue to face serious barriers to housing.  “Our shared responsibility is to build on this progress through prevention, affordable housing and services that help people achieve lasting stability.”  San Benito County and its partners have continued to expand housing and service resources, including shelter, rapid rehousing, transitional housing, rental assistance, permanent supportive housing and outreach, says the press release.  The results should also be considered alongside factors that may affect count coverage, CHSP said. The 2025 river cleanup may have reduced the number of people present in known encampment locations during the count. Changes in encampment locations, accessibility and participation may also have affected the number of people counted. In addition to the PIT count, 99 people completed the PIT survey, providing insight into their experiences and barriers to housing. These findings reflect survey respondents and should not be interpreted as representing everyone counted, says the press release.  Among respondents:  • 82% were living in San Benito County when they became homeless.  • 74% experienced homelessness for one year or longer.  • 48% reported that their current episode was their first experience of homelessness.  • 61% first experienced homelessness at age 25 or older.  Affordability and income were the most frequently reported barriers to obtaining housing, officials said. Seventy-seven percent reported being unable to afford rent, and 74% reported having no or insufficient income. Other barriers included housing costs (40%), missing documents (34%), prior eviction or housing-related history (30%) and difficulty finding suitable housing (30%).  Health challenges also remained significant. Fifty-four percent reported at least one disabling condition, says the press release. Self-reported conditions included depression (40%), substance use disorder (36%), physical disability (33%), post-traumatic stress disorder (31%), chronic health conditions (26%) and psychiatric or emotional conditions (22%).  Eleven percent of respondents were employed. Among those who were unemployed, 55% were looking for work. Seven percent reported prior involvement in foster care, and 26% reported having spent time in jail, prison or juvenile detention.  “The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development-required Point-in-Time Count is vital for understanding homelessness in San Benito County,” said Tracey Belton, Director of San Benito County Health & Human Services Agency. “The data helps guide policy decisions, resource allocation and our collective efforts to ensure that individuals and families experiencing homelessness have access to the housing and services they need.”

title: Authorities charge Turlock man in killing of Javier Becerril Jr.
author: Staff Report
content: Police arrested a Turlock man for the killing of Javier Becerril Jr., the Hollister resident who was found dead in the trunk of a Tesla July 9 on Highway 152 in Merced County. Manual Salceda, 39, was arrested Oct. 11 following a three-month investigation into Becerril’s death, the California Highway Patrol said in an Oct. 21 press release. The investigation was conducted by the CHP’s Central Division Major Crimes Unit.  CHP detectives determined that Becerril had been physically assaulted before his body was placed in the trunk. The vehicle was found parked on Highway 152 near Lower Cottonwood Road, after police responded to a report of a missing person.  Investigators used physical evidence, surveillance footage and other leads to identify Salceda as a suspect in Becerril’s killing.  Police said they also learned during the investigation that Salceda may have used multiple false identities to evade capture.  On Oct. 11, police found out that a vehicle believed to be transporting Salceda was located near Dublin, says the press release. Investigators tracked the vehicle through several counties in the Bay Area.  The investigation led police to a gas station on Road 8 near Interstate 5 in Woodland, where they arrested Salceda without incident.  Salceda was charged with murder on Oct. 20 in Merced County Superior Court.  “As California’s state police, the CHP is committed to pursuing violent offenders and working with our law enforcement partners to bring those responsible to justice,” said CHP Chief Damon Gilmore. “Our detectives tracked the evidence across multiple counties to locate and arrest the suspect in Javier Becerril Jr.’s killing.”

title: Hollister woman assaulted spouse, caused collision before stabbing herself
author: Staff Report
content: A Hollister woman stabbed her spouse Oct. 17 before recklessly driving the wrong way on a busy highway, left the scene of an accident before carjacking another victim, and continued to lead police up the valley to San Jose where she died after repeatedly stabbing herself with a knife, according to authorities.  The California Highway Patrol began receiving calls about 9:56am about a wrong-way driver on Highway 152 just east of the Highway 156 interchange, according to CHP Sgt. Robert Lehman. The driver, allegedly the same woman who had stabbed a male victim in Hollister, was driving a Chevrolet Cruze recklessly eastbound in the westbound lanes of 152.  The reckless driver collided head-on with another vehicle, causing the Chevrolet to overturn, Lehman said. The woman then carjacked a passerby who had stopped to check on the people involved in the crash.  She fled the scene, and the driver of the car she hit was transported to a nearby hospital, authorities said.  The woman drove toward Gilroy, where local police located her vehicle traveling on Monterey Road, Lehman said. Gilroy Police began to pursue the woman, but soon lost sight of her.  The reckless driver ended up in San Jose, where she exited the vehicle near the Highway 101 intersection with Highway 85. She walked across multiple lanes of traffic on both freeways before stopping on the southbound shoulder of Highway 101, Lehman said.  The woman then repeatedly stabbed herself in her shoulder with a knife. San Jose Police responded and located the woman, who was pronounced dead.  Lehman added there are “unconfirmed reports” that the woman vandalized other vehicles while she was walking across the highway in San Jose.  Anyone who thinks their vehicle was damaged by the suspect can call the CHP Hollister-Gilroy Area office at 408.427.0700.

title: Hollister City Council begins process of giving jobs back to 36 employees who received layoff notices
author: Michael Moore
content: The Hollister City Council emerged from a late-night closed session Oct. 19 without City Manager Ana Cortez, and with a unanimous vote to ask dozens of city employees back to the negotiating table after Cortez gave layoff notices to them last week.  The council approved the “emergency resolution,” which could result in all 36 laid-off city employees returning to work after being notified of the layoffs Oct. 14. The layoff notices had placed the affected employees on 30 days of administrative leave before their employment ends.  But now, Mayor Roxanne Stephens said those employees will soon hear from the city’s human resources staff to discuss coming back to work. A motion by City Councilmember Dolores Morales said the human resources director will “meet and confer with the unions” to negotiate on their employment, which includes an effort to find financial savings for the city.  The Oct. 19 vote—which took place just before 11pm and after hours of impassioned, and at times boisterous public comment from residents and city employees—also rescinded a declaration of financial emergency that the council had approved at an Oct. 2 meeting.  Among those likely to be affected by the latest decision are nine civilian police employees who had received layoff notices. Hollister Police Sgt. Bo Leland, president of the Hollister Police Officers Association, welcomed the council’s decision.  “For you guys to ask those employees to come back to work…and to rescind the financial emergency so we can get to the actual work of solving this city’s problems—I am in agreement with that,” Leland told the council.  Hollister Police Sgt. Bo Leland, president of the Hollister Police Officers Association, joins a rally in support of city employees outside City Hall Oct. 19. Photo: Michael Moore Cortez, who had advised the council to declare a financial emergency in the first place, did not return to council chambers when the five city councilmembers came out of closed session Oct. 19.  Two of the city’s largest union groups had taken votes of no confidence in Cortez in the days after she issued layoff notices. The HPOA and the Service Employees International Union called on the council to fire Cortez, offering a laundry list of grievances and allegations.  The council did not say why Cortez did not return to council chambers. One of two closed session items on the agenda was titled a “public employee performance evaluation” for the city manager. Stephens said she did not have “anything specific to report” from the closed session.  The council scheduled a special meeting for Wednesday, Oct. 21, “to finalize some decisions that we preliminarily made tonight,” Stephens said. She said for legal reasons, the city needs “a couple of days” to agendize the Oct. 21 items.  “Just know that the discussion that we started today about your concerns about the city manager will be part of the agenda item on Wednesday,” Stephens said.  The employees who received layoff notices Oct. 14 included nine civilian police employees, a police captain and 25 employees in the city’s public works, finance, senior services, parks and recreation and airport departments.  HPOA and SEIU representatives have said the employees who received pink slips perform critical “behind-the-scenes” responsibilities—such as answering phones, maintaining records and keeping storm drains clear—and possess unique experience and knowledge that are difficult to replace.  The layoffs would have had significant impacts on city services. Some of the civilian police staff even returned to work after Oct. 14, despite being on leave, according to union representatives.  Unions allege financial shenanigans Union presidents said Cortez did not consult with them or department heads to attempt to find other options to save money for the city. Leland and Frank Garcia, president of the local SEIU, claimed that Cortez and city finance staff have reported inconsistent and incorrect numbers when trying to explain the City of Hollister’s dire situation.  Garcia said he recently noticed some numbers in city financial reports that were incorrect, and notified city officials  “The city replied, and admitted that there were some incorrect numbers,” Garcia said before the Oct. 19 meeting. “That’s accountability. How are you going to lay people off when you openly admitted to me that you’ve miscalculated? How is that even possible?” Frank Garcia, who works in the City of Hollister’s stormwater department, speaks with a concerned resident outside City Hall, just before the Oct. 19 city council meeting. Photo: Michael Moore Garcia has worked in the city’s stormwater department for about nine years.  Leland said he had reached out to Cortez last week to discuss his ideas to save money in the police department, but the city manager refused to talk or meet, and has not been transparent about city finances.  “Ana Cortez’s history here can only be described as irrational, inconsistent and ineffective,” Leland said. “Depending on the day, the deficit around here is $3.8 million, $6 million, $16 million, $11 million and $20 million. Those are all the different numbers we’ve received from her. That’s out of control.” At the Oct. 2 council meeting, Cortez urged the council to declare a financial emergency after describing a dire situation in which City Hall only had $178 in its general fund bank account, and officials had no way of paying employees the following week.  Also at that meeting, the council approved an interfund loan of $18 million from impact fees to the general and water funds in order to make payroll.  The city’s deteriorating financial situation is due to years of mismanagement and inattentiveness by previous city officials, according to Cortez and the current councilmembers.  The meeting drew hundreds of people, with a standing-room-only crowd spilling out the back of council chambers and into the City Hall lobby. Union members and their supporters—many wearing purple SEIU T-shirts—gathered outside to rally the public before the meeting, and continued to demonstrate with signs and flags inside City Hall during the council session.  Most of the 50-plus speakers during a public comment period at the beginning of the meeting expressed their support for city employees.  Raucous audience Cortez, who the council hired on Feb. 2, did not appear to look in the direction of the individual speakers or the audience at any point during the 2.5-hour public comment period.  Some of the affected employees shamed the council for hiring Cortez in the first place, despite allegations of employment mistreatment and other grievances earlier in her city management career. Others said they have tried to reach out to their supervisors and Cortez for more information, but have not received any responses.  Some admonished city officials for letting go of longtime city employees with an apparent disrespect for decades of service and commitment to their jobs.  Stephens tried but failed to control the audience, asking them to hold their applause when they agreed with an individual speaker, often leading them to applause louder. Some speakers continued talking after a two-minute timer signaled the end of their time, even after Stephens told them to stop speaking.  At one point, Councilmember Rolan Resendiz loudly urged Stephens to “let them speak,” resulting in a brief shouting match with the two officials yelling over each other.  Animosity among city officials and audience members reared its head as well. When former Mayor Mia Casey stood up for her turn to speak, Resendiz displayed a handwritten note accusing her of bankrupting the city.  Casey told Resendiz to remove the note, and her husband Jon Casey, who is running for Hollister City Treasurer, approached Resendiz at the dais with a stern expression and pointing his finger at the councilmember.  Dee Jimenez, an SEIU member, speaks to concerned residents as she supports City of Hollister employees outside City Hall Oct. 19. Photo: Michael Moore

title: San Benito County seniors enjoy a day at the casino
author: Staff Report
content: On Oct. 3, a group of 55 San Benito County seniors boarded a bus for a day of laughter, friendly competition and good company at Table Mountain Casino Resort in Fresno County.  The outing was sponsored by Martha’s Kitchen, a nonprofit that provides meals and groceries to people facing food insecurity in six area counties.  The travelers are regulars at the Martha’s Kitchen congregate meal program, which serves free, nutritious lunches to older adults every weekday at the Pauline Valdivia Memorial Community Center in Hollister, and on Mondays in San Juan Bautista, says a press release from Martha’s Kitchen.  Martha’s Kitchen staff said the seniors enjoyed spending the day with friends, and several are already lobbying for the next destination, with Chukchansi high on the wish list. The fun has a serious purpose. For many older adults, especially those who live alone, chances to get out and socialize grow harder to find each year, and in a rural county, distance and limited transportation can deepen that isolation, says the press release.  “A good meal matters, but so does having something to look forward to and people to share it with,” said Bill Lee, Executive Director of Martha’s Kitchen. “These outings do not replace the meal. They make it matter more. When 55 seniors come home laughing and already asking about the next trip, we know we are doing something right.” The outing is one piece of a growing calendar of special events for the seniors Martha’s Kitchen serves in San Benito County, which also includes holiday gatherings, themed parties, and cultural celebrations with music, food, and fellowship.  San Benito County residents age 60 and older are invited to join Martha’s Kitchen for lunch Monday through Friday at the Pauline Valdivia Memorial Community Center, 300 West St., Hollister. For more information, call 831.636.4390.

title: High school district appoints Elaine Zuniga Galdos as new superintendent
author: Staff Report
content: Hollister High alumna and longtime employee of the San Benito High School District Elaine Zuniga Galdos has been named the district’s new superintendent.  The SBHSD board of trustees unanimously appointed Galdos to the new position on Oct. 13. She will take over the superintendent’s post from Dr. Shawn Tennenbaum as of Feb. 1, 2027.  Galdos is currently the district’s Assistant Superintendent of Academics and Instructional Programs. She has spent 30 years working in the Hollister education community, including the past 11 years at SBHSD, the district said in a press release.  “I’m honored to be selected as the next superintendent and grateful for the board’s confidence in me,” she said. “Having grown up in Hollister and graduated from Hollister High School, this opportunity is especially meaningful.”  Board of Trustees President Miguel Sahagun, Jr. said, “The board’s unanimous decision reflects our collective confidence in her leadership, her outstanding record of service to the District, and her unwavering commitment to the success of our students, staff and school community.”  Sahagun also emphasized Galdos’s collaborative approach to leadership, dedication to improvement and passion for public education, the district said. He also recognized the appointee’s commitment to professional growth as she pursued a doctoral degree.  “Her dedication to lifelong learning exemplifies the values we strive to instill in our students,” Sahagun said. “The board is confident that Elaine possesses the experience, vision and leadership qualities necessary to guide our District into the future.”  In an endorsement letter to the board, Tennenbaum praised Galdos’s leadership, integrity and commitment to placing students at the center of her decisions.  “Above all, she is deeply student-centered,” Tennenbaum wrote. “Every policy she advocates for and every decision she makes is guided by a singular, unwavering priority: doing what is best for our students.”  Galdos’s annual salary as superintendent is $266,414, according to district staff.  Tennenbaum announced his retirement at the Sept. 8 board meeting. He has been SBHSD superintendent for 11 years.
