title: Hundreds of students protest gun violence in downtown Bend Monday
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: Hundreds of high schoolers thronged all four corners of the intersection at Wall Street and Greenwood Avenue in downtown Bend Monday afternoon. Students walked out of school and staged a protest against gun violence in the wake of the Silver Rail Elementary shooting Oct. 15. Kids jumped up and down and screamed every time a passing car honked, creating a raucous and excited atmosphere. Kids climbed light fixtures, stood on benches and even climbed onto the roof of the restaurant Yoli, all holding signs proclaiming that students should feel safe in school. High schoolers organized the walkout and protest after the Silver Rail Elementary shooting Oct. 15 that left a teacher and three students dead. Adelyn Johnson, a 14-year-old Caldera High student, has a sister in third grade at Silver Rail Elementary. Her sister lost her best friend on Oct. 15, and Adelyn lost her volleyball coach, Megan Lambert. “I was just praying my sister was alive (on Oct. 15),” she said. “I found out she was okay and I just hope everyone can recover from this. I hope students are safe in the future.” Caldera High student Hannah Patton, 16, joined to protest against gun violence. Gun laws should be stronger, she said, and minors and those with “bad histories” should be banned from gun ownership. Signs ranged from “The scariest thing in school should be my grade” to “Your politics, our funerals.” One read “He was 16. How is that legal?” referring to the shooter. Another read “Thoughts and prayers don’t save lives.” Matias Kalberg, a 16-year-old Caldera High student, said he was showing up for his community. He skipped out of biology to be there for the protest. He thought the police responded well on Oct. 15, and said he believes in the city of Bend. “I’m doing my part to make sure everyone feels seen,” he said. “It’s inspirational that we can stay strong.” Student organizers led the crowd through chants against gun violence and protecting children. De-escalators stood at each corner of the intersection, ensuring traffic could cross safely and keeping an eye on the crowd. Several Bend Police Department vehicles made the rounds through the intersection as well. Gavin McCoy, a 16-year-old Caldera High student, skipped photography for the protest and said he was there to support “the young people of the world,” as he put it. Nancy Stevens, who said she’s “old but young at heart,” biked to the protest to stand with students against gun violence. She was glad the police were supportive and hoped the students felt heard. “I came to support the kids,” she said. “I hope it makes a difference.” “After Silver Rail, shootings feel real. It’s terrible, and someone needs to do something,” said Leilani, a 17-year-old Mountain View High student who declined to give her last name, “It’s never felt so real, and we shouldn’t have to have the fear of being shot,” said Ayla, a 16-year-old Mountain View High student who declined to give her last name. Leilani advocated for officers in every school, and Ayla for awareness before shootings happen. “Silver Rail Elementary did everything they should have,” said Ayla. “And people still died.” Kaimana Stanley, a 17-year-old Caldera High student, said that people want gun bans as the solution to gun violence, but that no one’s figured out how to make bans work. She believes guns should be permitted for specific purposes such as hunting or competitions. It’s legal, she said, to buy a long gun and give it to your child to use without supervision, while that’s not the case with pistols. “There’s too much emphasis on mental health, and you can’t take away rape and bullying entirely,” she said. Stanley skipped her government class and dual immersion senior seminar to come to the protest. Her grandfather, she said, owned a lot of guns and her family hunted and shot recreationally. Having access to guns, she said, is what’s killing people.

title: ELECTION 2026: Your guide to the Nov. 3 ballot in Deschutes County
author: none
content: Voters in Deschutes County will have plenty to think about they fill out their ballots this year. Need help learning about the candidates or the issues? Refresh yourself with our reporting from earlier this election season. Deschutes County district map measure Shall Deschutes County elect Commissioners by geographic district using the included five district map? Our coverage: The Deschutes County measure that would split the county into districts Deschutes County Commission Position 3 Lauren Connally and Amy Sabbadini are running against each other for Deschutes County Commission position 3 this November, after a crowded primary winnowed the field. Current Commissioner Patti Adair will end her term in January. Our coverage: Educator, administrator vie for Deschutes County Commission position 3 Deschutes County Commission Position 5 Rob Imhoff and Morgan Schmidt are competing for position 5 on the Deschutes County Commission. Our coverage: Deschutes County Commission Position 5: Imhoff vs. Schmidt Deschutes County Sheriff The Deschutes County Sheriff’s race has transformed into a soap opera, pitting two candidates against each other while each faces an internal investigation. There is also mudslinging and complaints of campaign law misconduct. It’s nothing new to the citizens of Deschutes County, after through the 2024 sheriff’s race and countless others. But both candidates — Ty Rupert and James “Mac” McLaughlin — said they hope to make a difference in the culture of the office to prevent the soap opera from entering another season. Differences lie, however, in how they believe that shift can be done. Our coverage: Investigations, accusations pepper another sheriff’s race Deschutes County Treasurer Two Deschutes County finance employees are running against each other for the office of Deschutes County Treasurer. Our coverage: Election 2026: Deschutes County Treasurer race pits two county employees against each other Deschutes County Clerk The race for Deschutes County Clerk will see incumbent Steve Dennison squaring off against challenger Jonathan Curtis. Dennison has been county clerk since 2021. Curtis says he is a sales manager with a company that cleans homes and businesses. Our coverage: 2026 Election: Incumbent Dennison faces outsider candidate for Deschutes County Clerk Officials condemn clerk candidate over inflammatory videos House District 53 Central Oregon’s race for state representative of House District 53 will pit incumbent Emerson Levy against Redmond school board chair Michael Summers. Our coverage: Election 2026: Levy, Summers face off for Central Oregon’s House District 53 ——— Redmond voters will decide several local races this November, including contests for Redmond mayor, three city council seats and a psilocybin treatment services moratorium. Local voters will also have a say in the county commission, sheriff, state representative and governor races as well as a county district map measure, county clerk and treasurer. Below is our coverage on local races: Redmond Mayor Incumbent Ed Fitch is running for re-election. It would be his fourth and final term, if elected. Longtime Redmond City Councilor Jay Patrick and returning candidate Charles Webster Baer will challenge for the mayoral position. The mayor of Redmond is a volunteer position that receives a $900 monthly stipend. Our coverage: • Meet the three candidates running for mayor Redmond City Council November’s election will see five candidates vie for three seats on Redmond City Council. Incumbent Kathryn Osborne will look to retain her council seat. She is joined on the ballot by challengers Tobias Colvin, Raven Hansen, Barbara Tate and Paul Povey. City council is a nonpartisan position that carries a four-year term. Councilors, along with the mayor, set city priorities and policy, vote on local laws and manage public resources. As at-large positions, voters in the city of Redmond can choose three candidates on their ballots. The top three vote-getters will fill the three open seats. Councilors are paid a $500 monthly stipend. Our coverage: Meet the candidates running for Redmond City Council Psilocybin moratorium measure Redmond voters will decide in November whether businesses can provide psilocybin treatment within city limits. Our coverage: Redmond voters to decide on psilocybin treatment centers Drop-boxes are located at the Deschutes County Expo Center and Fairgrounds and Redmond Public Library. Drop-boxes close by 8 p.m. on election night. Ballots must be mailed and postmarked by the United States Postal Service by 8 p.m. Nov. 3 and received by the clerk’s office by Nov. 10 to be accepted. Postage is not required. If ballots are received late, they are not counted. If you don’t receive your first ballot, you can go to the clerk’s office and request a new one. The first ballot is invalidated. You can also vote in person at the clerk’s office in the Deschutes County Services building. More information on how to vote is available here .

title: Friends, family remember teacher who died at Silver Rail as a ‘spark of joy’
author: Sydney Seymour
content: Megan Lambert was adventurous, bubbly, compassionate and funny, with a deep commitment to education, mental health and children with special needs, according to close friends and family. The 25-year-old special education teacher and volleyball coach was killed in the Oct. 15 shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School along with three children. The community celebrated her with numerous events last weekend, beginning with a memorial service Saturday at Caldera. Hundreds gathered in Bend’s Old Mill District on Sunday, walking and carrying Lambert’s favorite flower, carnations, in remembrance of Lambert and the children who lost their lives in the Silver Rail tragedy. “To tell you about Megan would take 25 years,” her family said in a statement. Born and raised in Bend, Lambert attended Juniper Elementary, Pilot Butte Middle School and Mountain View High School. After graduating from Boise State University in 2023, she taught English in Barcelona, Spain, for almost six months. She planned to return next summer to see Harry Styles in concert. Lambert ultimately wanted to teach in the district she grew up in. She started as a substitute teacher for Bend-La Pine Schools, often spending time at Silver Rail and its special education classroom. She landed her first full-time teaching job this year. Andy Young, a Mountain View High School science teacher and Lambert’s colleague, taught her chemistry about a decade ago. He remembered her as “a spark of joy.” “She was boisterous, gregarious, kind, a good soul,” Young said during the memorial. “She was a leader and people were drawn to her.” Lambert babysat for local families and worked at children’s camps and summer programs, helping connect hundreds of young kids to nature. Chance Caruso, owner of R.A.D. Camps for teens, said the packed auditorium at Caldera was evidence of the the impact Lambert had on her community. “Knowing how much she’s touched my life, how much she’s touched the rest of our teams’ life, I cannot imagine the impact that Megan has made across her entire life and I think this room is an example of that,” said Caruso. Friends cherished Lambert’s long-winded stories, sentimental gifts and impromptu visits. They described her as a product of Bend’s community: welcoming and loving. She enjoyed reading, picnicking at Drake Park, floating the river, listening to live music, crafting, playing cozy video games, visiting the Oregon Coast, spending time with her cat Spiderman and hiking with her puppy, Juniper. But she was more than that, friends said. “Megan is being narrowed down to fit into a nutshell,” close friend Somer Eckert said at the memorial service. “Nothing I tell anyone about Megan feels like enough.” The Lambert family created the Megan Lambert Memorial Fund to support the causes she believed in — education, mental health, services for children with special needs and Oregon schools. Central Oregon Volleyball Club created the Megan Lambert Volleyball Scholarship to help cover fees for low-income families, honoring how she once turned down pay to give families who couldn’t afford to play an opportunity to participate. Impact on students In college, Lambert was a residential assistant. She brought that same kind of care to teaching, friend said. She had the patience and willingness to educate kids who needed extra support. “She cared for her students, and it was down to details,” said Cadance Donlon. “She listened, she paid attention.” Lambert often added jewels to her nails because they provided something tactile for students to touch. While student teaching, she decorated her classroom in a Mario theme for state-test review, then switched to Sonic the Hedgehog the next day. “She was extra in the best way,” said her college roommate, Hannah. “She wasn’t just a teacher. She wasn’t just what she did. It was also who she was. She was such a light in every room that she walked into.” An athlete and reader Lambert grew up playing volleyball. “I’ve just never seen someone, especially at that early of an age, know how to show such kindness to people who aren’t kind,” said Mahryahna Callegari, who played volleyball with Lambert in middle school and high school. “She was showing me how to be kind when others aren’t kind. She never grew out of that.” In 2023, she started coaching high schoolers for the Central Oregon Volleyball Club. Coaches and players described her as selfless. “She’d give the shirt off her back,” said Heidi Wood, the club director. Wood saw Lambert as more than just a volleyball coach. “She was a mentor,” Wood said. “I would always talk to her at tryouts and point a kid out and say, ‘Hey, this kid’s going through this, and I need somebody to take them under their wing.’ And she just looks at me and says: ‘Okay.’” After working together at Camp Fire Central Oregon, Logan Betts, Eckert and Donlon bonded with Lambert over books. They called themselves the “book club.” “There are so many series that we were in the middle of, and there will be more of those books coming out that she’ll never get to read,” said Eckert. The friends plan to travel and read in Lambert’s honor, including visiting Barcelona — where Lambert had hoped to show them around. Betts also plans to read all of the books on her “To Be Read” list. “With only being 25, she didn’t get to experience the world that she was just tapping into,” Betts said. “She had so many places that she wanted to go, and so many places that we wanted to go together as a group.” Impact reached across the globe Half a dozen of Lambert’s friends from her time abroad traveled from as far as Canada, Australia and Spain to attend her memorial service. Although some had not seen each other in two years, they stayed connected through one-minute videos Lambert encouraged them to send every Wednesday. Abby Pierce said Lambert showed love through big and small acts, from “Waffle Wednesdays” to planning events that brought communities together. Lambert “craved” adventure, Pierce said. She kept a spreadsheet titled “Vacations” with travel plans, budgets and dream destinations. “Her life was just beginning, and it was already so full,” Pierce said. Shaelyn Daase said Lambert “was a dreamer, but she didn’t just dream. She made them happen.” Jessica Pasia, Lambert’s roommate in Spain, said Lambert made others braver by pushing them beyond their comfort zones. “However long you knew her, she made everyone feel seen and safe,” Pasia said. Esther Duka remembered Megan’s comforting presence while in Spain. “Whenever I was overstimulated, I would find Megan,” she said. Friends said people can honor Lambert by remembering her smile and laugh and by slowing down to appreciate the moment. “She just wanted to experience all there was,” said Jacynda Carmichael. “She inspired me to want to live like she did, and it would be as bold and courageous and curious about the world as she did.” A fierce advocate Lambert’s loved ones remembered her for her warmth and positivity but also for her determination to stand up for what she believed was right. “With Megan, that’s the only thing there was,” Phia Ringo said. “There is no part of her that would be hurtful to anyone. Every part of her was just like, ‘How can I do service in the world?’” Friends said Lambert was vocal about protecting children and would be outraged by the tragedy. “She would be devastated over what happened,” Donlon said. “She was very aware of the world and wanted to do whatever she could to make an impact, small and large.” Betts said, “She would be so mad that this happened, like so upset. She would just truly be screaming from the mountains, ‘This has to stop.’” Betts plans to continue advocating for the causes Lambert cared about. “I’m speaking twice as loud now,” Betts said. “I don’t want people to forget about this. I don’t want everybody that’s talking about this and all of the movement that’s happening behind this to stop there. When it comes down to it, she should still be here. Those three kids should still be here.” – Bulletin reporter Brian Rathbone contributed to this report.

title: Mountain View, Bend, Caldera all get IMC football victories
author: Brian Rathbone
content: REDMOND — There was a 15-day gap between Mountain View’s 42-19 win over Caldera on Oct. 8 and the Cougars’ 28-12 victory over Ridgeview on Saturday night. Those 15 days offered time to grieve, reflect and come together as a football team. There was also time to draw up trick plays. The Cougars hit on three trick plays for big gains against the Ravens: a halfback pass, a hook-and-ladder and a reverse pass. “When you have four extra days with nothing to do, you have a chance to work on some things,” said Mountain View coach Brian Crum. “It is something that we had been working on the week before and were able to put them in.” Before kickoff, both teams walked to the middle of the field and shook hands before holding a moment of silence for those affected by the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting on Oct. 15 in Bend. Both teams had Silver Rail stickers on their helmets, while Mountain View also had an “ML” stickle in honor of Megan Lambert, a 2019 Mountain View grad who was killed in the shooting. “It really brought us together,” said Mountain View senior running back Ryder Carpenter. “We had each other’s back after the tragedy. A lot of the kids were affected. But we all stayed together.” When Carpenter took a toss then threw a pass to a wide open Krew Harrison for a big gain on the game’s first offensive play, it knocked Ridgeview off balance. And the Ravens never fully recovered. With the win, Mountain View (6-1 overall, 3-1 IMC) moved ahead of Ridgeview (5-2, 2-2) in the Intermountain Conference standings and is in possession of the IMC’s second guaranteed 5A playoff spot heading into the final week of the regular season — and is also in prime position to host two playoff games. The Ravens are still in good position to reach the playoffs as an at-large team, but their chances of hosting a playoff game took a hit with their second loss of the season. “After the Summit game, we knew this was going to be our next big game,” said Carpenter, who had 75 yards rushing, two touchdowns and an interception on defense. “We just had to respond. After that Summit game, we got a chip on our shoulder. And I play best with one on my shoulder and our team does as well.” The Ravens were able to move the ball well throughout the game, finishing with nearly 400 yards of offense. Junior running back Bronx Lick had 73 yards rushing and a touchdown while also catching 10 passes for 122 yards. However, Ridgeview senior quarterback Jordan Rodriguez, while passing for more than 300 yards, threw four interceptions, two of them in or near the end zone. Coming down with two of those interceptions was Harrison, who was a difference-maker Saturday night. Along with the two interceptions, he led the team with 76 receiving yards. He also threw a 44-yard touchdown pass to senior wideout Brayden MacRostie on a reverse pass. Senior linebacker Tanner Loch also has an interception while blocking a punt. In the final week of the regular season both teams will play in rivalry games on the road Friday night. Mountain View will face Bend High, while Ridgeview will take on Redmond. In other Friday and Saturday night prep football action: Willamette 21, Summit 20 With senior quarterback Andrew Guthrie out with an injured knee, Summit (4-3, 4-0) nearly beat 6A Willamette of Eugene Saturday evening but its comeback effort came up one point short in the nonleague game at Summit. Summit senior running back Casey Westerhoff had two rushing touchdowns, while junior quarterback Curren Stilson connected with senior wideout CJ Scott for a fourth-quarter touchdown. The Storm, who have already locked up the IMC title, will play at Caldera in its regular-season finale on Friday. Bend 33, Redmond 23 Sophomore running back Sean McDonald scored four touchdowns to help Bend (2-5, 1-3) pick up its second win of the season at Redmond (2-5, 0-4) on Saturday night. The Panthers dropped their fourth game in a row. On Friday, Bend will host Mountain View while Redmond will play at Ridgeview. Caldera 27, Crook County 21 Waylon Clarke’s 26-yard touchdown with just over two minutes left in the game gave Caldera (5-3, 3-2) the IMC win over the Cowboys (2-5, 2-3) in Prineville on Saturday night. Clarke finished with three rushing touchdowns. The Wolfpack will close their regular season at home against Summit on Friday, while the Cowboys will close out their season with a nonleague home game against Hood River Valley. • Madras (3-5, 2-2) picked up its second win in a row when it knocked off Creswell Friday evening, 43-28, and is now in position to reach the playoffs with a win in its final regular-season game. The White Buffaloes will play at Sisters on Friday. • Sisters (2-5, 1-3) dropped its third straight game and was shutout 40-0 against undefeated Klamath Union. The Outlaws will host Madras on Friday in their final regular-season game. • Culver (8-0, 4-0) continued its unbeaten season and secured the 2A Special District 5 title with a 60-8 win over Lakeview on Thursday. The Bulldogs will play their final regular-season game on Friday against Rogue River at 7 p.m. • La Pine (5-2, 2-1) boosted its playoff chances with a resounding 52-21 win over Rogue River on Saturday. The Hawks will travel to Medford to take on St. Mary’s on Friday with the winner taking over second place in the district standings.

title: Kotek pledges state support in wake of Silver Rail shooting
author: Michael Kohn
content: Gov. Tina Kotek issued an executive order declaring a state of emergency for the Bend-La Pine School District and High Desert Education Service District on Monday. She pledging sustained state support for the community as it recovers from the Silver Rail Elementary School tragedy. Speaking at a press conference in Salem, Kotek announced a coordinated response involving multiple state agencies, including assistance with recovery funding, mental health services, paid leave and staffing. She also called for renewed efforts to keep firearms out of children’s hands. “What happened at Silver Rail should never happen to any school, to any community,” Kotek said. Community faces recovery The Oct. 15 shooting incident left four victims dead, including a teacher and three students, aged 5, 8 and 11. A fourth child and a second teacher are recovering under medical supervision. Kotek said the needs of students, families and educators will continue long after the immediate response ends. “The community is hurting” she said. “Their needs are immediate and the recovery will take time.” The executive order gives the two education districts administrative flexibility to address urgent needs. Kotek also said she is working with legislative leaders to request state funding through the Emergency Board, which meets in December, to help cover substitute educators, building repairs and recovery coordination. “We shouldn’t wait to invest in this community’s recovery,” Kotek said, adding that the district should not have to wait for federal reimbursement to receive financial support. State agencies mobilize Oregon Department of Education Director Charlene Williams said her agency is assigning full-time staff to help the district secure federal recovery funds and navigate administrative requirements. Williams visited Bend last week to meet with education leaders and see the work underway at the Family Assistance Center, where families and community members were connecting with mental health professionals, first responders and other organizations. Williams said the response from educators across Oregon has been substantial. When Bend-La Pine requested 90 substitute teachers for its first day back in session, she said that every position was filled within minutes. “Schools become more than buildings,” said Williams. “They become places of healing, connection and care.” Oregon Employment Department Director Andrew Stolfi announced that staff would be available in person at the Bend Workforce Center to help affected residents understand and apply for Paid Leave Oregon benefits. Eligible workers may receive up to 12 weeks of paid leave for qualifying serious health conditions or to care for a family member. Eligibility depends on individual circumstances. The Employment Department can answer questions and help other affected community members navigate their options. “No one should have to choose between receiving a paycheck and receiving the care they or a loved one needs,” Stolfi said. Lawmakers pledge action State Sen. Anthony Broadman and Rep. Jason Kropf also pledged support. Broadman said the outpouring of goodwill has demonstrated the strength of the community, even as residents grieve. “While the world saw Bend on our worst day, the world has also seen the best of Bend in our people, in our heroes and our angels,” he said. Broadman referenced the Saturday memorial service for educator Megan Lambert at Caldera High School, noting that conversations with parents, students, teachers and law enforcement underscored the desire to restore confidence in the safety of schools. “We will listen to and follow the lead of the Silver Rail community,” Broadman said. “We will heal together, and we will act together.” Kropf, speaking through tears, also thanked the people and organizations that have stepped forward to help. He cited the work of health professionals, volunteers and first responders, along with educators who have returned to school while working through their own grief. “Our town and our region is grieving, but there’s also been incredible displays of love and caring,” Kropf said. He thanked Kotek and her administration for addressing immediate needs while working to understand what support the community will require in the future. “The strength of our town is that we always show up for each other,” Kropf said. Firearm safety efforts Kotek also called for stronger efforts to prevent future tragedies, saying her office will direct school districts statewide to remind parents of Oregon’s firearm safe-storage requirements. She urged gun owners to use secure options, including lockboxes and cable locks, to keep firearms away from children. “Every family should know and be reminded of their responsibilities under Oregon law,” Kotek said, adding that she would continue reviewing the state’s gun violence prevention laws to identify needed improvements. Kotek added that recovery from the Silver Rail tragedy will take years and called for continued discussion of ways to prevent future shootings. “We know from other tragedies that (recovery does not take) a year. This is three years of making sure the community can come back to where they were before,” she said. “We will stand with them.”

title: Mobile home burns in northeast Bend, two cats die
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: A home at the Rock Arbor Villa Mobile Home Park off NE Purcell Boulevard in northeast Bend burned Sunday evening. Damage to the home and contents is estimated at $50,000. The resident, who called 911, was able to safety evacuate. Two cats died in the fire. Bend Fire & Rescue arrived to find the home engulfed in fire. Crews knocked down the blaze within minutes and prevented it from spreading to other homes. Smoke alarms alerted the resident to the fire. The Red Cross is assisting the resident with housing and other resources. Investigators determined that the fire started behind the wall where the fireplace flue was improperly connected. Bend Fire & Rescue reminded people to make sure their smoke alarms are working, and to have stoves and furnaces inspected.

title: Bend driver arrested twice in 7 hours for DUIIs
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: A Michigan woman was arrested twice by the Deschutes County Sheriff’s Office for allegedly driving under the influence of intoxicants over the weekend. Danielle Cox, 34, of Michigan, was first arrested at 6:20 p.m. Saturday after police allege she crossed into oncoming lanes and drove onto the shoulder several times on Deschutes Market Road near Pioneer Loop Drive. She was charged with DUII and reckless driving. Her blood alcohol content was allegedly over the legal limit, according to the sheriff’s office. She was lodged at the Deschutes County Jail and was released to an acquaintance at 10:30 p.m. Saturday. A dog in the car was brought to the Humane Society of Central Oregon at the time of the arrest. At nearly midnight, Cox called the sheriff’s office to get her dog back. The same deputy who arrived at the Humane Society to help with the transfer said that Cox was still impaired. Shortly after 1 a.m. Sunday, Cox was again arrested for driving under the influence of intoxicants. Due to being arrested for the second time for DUII within 12 hours of her last arrest for the same charge, Cox will remain in jail pending arraignment. From Oct. 20-27, the sheriff’s office and Bend Police Department are concentrating on DUII enforcement in honor of Bend native and La Mesa, Calif., police officer Lauren Craven. Craven was struck and killed by an impaired driver while assisting at a crash site in 2025.

title: Parents protest, ask for more safety from Bend-La Pine Schools
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: A small group of parents protested outside the Bend-La Pine education center, which holds the school district’s administrative offices, on Friday afternoon. The parents, who numbered less than 10, asked for more school resource officers in schools and additional security. A shooting at Silver Rail Elementary Oct. 15 killed three children and a teacher. Another teacher and student were injured and the shooter was also killed. Parents said they considered pulling their children out of school until changes were made and that they are tired of hearing the same arguments around mental health and gun control. Parents are planning to speak at the Nov. 10 Bend-La Pine school board meeting. A Change.org petition , which now has over 3,000 signatures, asks for school resource officers in every school, comprehensive school security assessments, creation of a parent-led school safety committee and a review of emergency response plans.

title: Southern Oregon drive-through animal park loses key national accreditation
author: Buffy Pollock
content: Wildlife Safari officials in Winston say they are working to remedy issues directly related to cheetahs and fencing; wildlife advocacy group expresses ongoing concerns over leashed big cat encounters Southern Oregon-based Wildlife Safari has been denied accreditation status for the first time in four decades through the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. The 600-acre, drive-through animal park was one of three facilities in the U.S. — of 33 reviewed this fall — announced Sept. 29 during the AZA’s Annual Conference in Portland. Tucked into the tiny burb of Winston, the park has billboards and other advertising positioned up and down the Interstate 5 corridor in Southern Oregon and attracts tens of thousands of visitors from around the Pacific Northwest each year. As one of two national accreditations, AZA accreditation is considered the more stringent, compared to the Zoological Association of America, and had been previously held by the wildlife drive-through park near Roseburg for over 40 years, according to park officials. Park representatives declined to offer a statement regarding the loss of accreditation but told the Rogue Valley Times this week that they are working to regain certification and that the loss of accreditation was not related to the level of care provided to animals. An employee who spoke to the Times but declined to be identified said one of the main reasons for denial of accreditation was a change to AZA standards on cheetah fencing habitat. The employee said fence height was not an issue, but that changes were being made to cantilevers located at the top of cheetah fencing intended to prevent escape. The employee, who said loss of accreditation had not impacted park attendance, pointed out that the facility had maintained its ZAA accreditation. Loss of accreditation In addition to Wildlife Safari, the AZA denied accreditation to Baylor University Bear Habitat in Waco, Texas, and Indianapolis Zoological Society in Indiana. According to a news release, any existing member denied reaccreditation has a 30-day window to appeal to the AZA Board of Directors. AZA President and CEO Dan Ashe, in the Sept. 29 release, wrote that each new facility accredited by the AZA’s Accreditation Commission “demonstrates how this program helps organizations prepare to meet AZA’s rigorous accreditation standards.” The accreditation process, according to the AZA release, includes a “detailed application and a meticulous multiple-day on-site inspection by an independent team of zoological and aquarium professionals. “The inspecting team analyzes all aspects of the facility’s operation, including animal care and wellbeing, veterinary care, staff training, educational programs, conservation efforts, financial stability, risk management, governance and guest services,” Ashe said in the statement. According to accreditation standards posted to the AZA website, changes between 2022 and 2026 included revisions to elephant management and care; changes to recommendations for developing a facility ambassador animal policy; and new polices on animal program engagement Animal welfare advocates speak out Keeping Wildlife Wild, an animal welfare advocacy group, challenged claims that accreditation loss was due to fencing and said it had expressed concerns for the past six or more years about the growing cheetah breeding program and public appearances provided, during which the cats are walked on a double leash setup and taken to community events such as local business grand openings or fundraising events. The park, which opened near Roseburg in 1972 and is officially named Safari Game Search Foundation but does business as Wildlife Safari, hosts a cheetah breeding research center — more than 250 cheetahs have been born at the park since it opened — and an international veterinary medicine program. Jeff Kremer, an animal welfare advocate with KeepingWildlifeWild.org said his concerns about Wildlife Safari extend beyond enclosure fencing. Kremer has raised concerns over the past decade regarding public safety and animal welfare implications regarding Wildlife Safari’s cheetah breeding and ambassador programs. Kremer cited examples including “taking leashed cheetahs to breweries, concerts, baseball games, business openings and fundraisers,” as well as the “conservation rationale for the park’s daily $49 cheetah photo opportunities,” which he said did not demonstrate a direct benefit to conservation of animals in the wild. Kremer pointed out that accreditation standards through AZA are more stringent than through ZAA. Comparison lists also are posted to various sites online. AZA cites confidentiality Contacted by the Times, AZA officials declined to comment specifically on Wildlife Safari, citing confidentiality of the accreditation process . AZA Vice President Sarah Fedele, responding to a list of general questions, said AZA had not yet been notified whether Wildlife Safari planned to seek AZA accreditation in the future. “They are still within their window of time to appeal their accreditation decision. If Wildlife Safari chooses to join AZA’s Pathway Toward Membership program, our team would be excited to help them continue to strive for excellence and regain their AZA accreditation status,” Fedele wrote to the Times. Loss of accreditation with AZA, Fedele confirmed, impacts the ways in which a facility can participate in Species Survival Plan programs. ‘Concerns for years’ Kremer applauded AZA’s denial of Wildlife Safari’s accreditation and said he was hopeful to see changes to Wildlife Safari’s ambassador program, including the volume of public appearances for profit. “I have been voicing concern for years. This is not an anomaly. It is systemic,” Kremer said. “In addition to be able to go on-site and engage in paid photo-opps with Cheetahs at the zoo, the animals are exhibited on leashes for events at breweries, concerts and baseball games. And more. “It is befuddling. I don’t know how much of Wildlife Safari’s budget is derived from exotic animal encounters, but I would suspect that it is substantial,” he said. “In my view, Wildlife Safari stands apart from other U.S. zoos in the extent to which it uses cheetahs for paid encounters and public appearances.” Reach reporter Buffy Pollock at 458-488-2029 or buffy.pollock@rv-times.com. Follow her on Twitter @orwritergal.

title: Three horror classics to stream this Halloween
author: none
content: I am not a huge fan of horror, but I’ve been trying to change my ways, and I’ve found a nice way to ease into the genre: Tiptoeing into its classic era. These are your favorite horror directors’ favorite horror films, which they have, no doubt, drawn inspiration from at some point in their careers. Not only that, these classics have often ventured back to the big screen through re-releases and remakes. Best of all, they’re usually blissfully —for other chickens like me — short. Here are just three you can stream for some spookiness this weekend. Night of the Living Dead (1968) —Director George A. Romero birthed the modern zombie movie we know today with the ultimate classic. It’s rough, unpolished and features a cast of unknowns that grounds the film. Watching it today, there are some clear tropes — which weren’t tropes yet — and styles are indicative of filmmaking at the time, but with several genuinely horrific moments that still manage to linger, it’s no wonder why it continues to inspire. It’s such a pivotal movie that spawned sequels and remakes, including the widely panned 2014 version. It is also where the line “They’re coming to get you, Barbara” comes from. Stream it on HBO Max, Prime Video, Starz or Tubi. The Last Man on Earth (1964) — Based on the book “I am Legend” by Richard Matheson (which has a couple of other versions including “The Omega Man” in 1971 with Charlton Heston and in “I am Legend” with Will Smith in 2007), about a global pandemic that wipes out the entire population and turns them into vampiric zombie creatures of the night. Vincent Price stars as the titular last man, Robert Morgan, who is on the hunt for vampires by day while dealing with his grief at night in his boarded up, garlic-laden house. A spaghetti-horror film with backing by an Italian production company and featuring mostly overdubbed, Italian castmates, Price really shines in this thrilling, post-apocalyptic horror. Stream it on Prime Video or on Tubi. Nosferatu (1922) — Considered the first horror film, this unauthorized version of Bram Stoker’s “Dracula” gets the silent German expressionist treatment in this forboding film that was almost lost to time and legalities. The Stoker estate ordered that every print of the movie be destroyed, as they didn’t approve of its likeness to “Dracula.” Over the next 100 years, prints in other countries were discovered, and it eventually was brought back to life and has continued to terrify audiences, specifically with Max Schrek’s performance as Graf Orlok, the menacing and obsessive vampire at its core. F.W. Murnau’s work also continues to terrify and spark inspiration and is credited as one of Guilmero del Toro’s favorite films. Stream it on Prime Video or Tubi.

title: Bend-La Pine students plan afternoon school walkout to protest violence at schools
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: Bend-La Pine schools students are planning a walkout Monday afternoon to protest against violence at schools after the Oct. 15 Silver Rail Elementary shooting that killed three children and a teacher. Students plan to leave school around 1:45 p.m. Monday and arrive at Peace Corner, at the corner of Greenwood Avenue and Wall Street in Bend, shortly after 2 p.m. An off-campus rally is not a school- or district-sponsored event, said officials. “We recognize and honor student voices in our community, and we respect their First Amendment rights to free speech and peaceable assembly,” said school district officials in a statement. “District and school administration and staff are to remain neutral on student demonstrations and refrain from encouraging or discouraging student participation. The District does not provide supervision for students who choose to leave campus for this event.” Students who leave campus before the end of the school day will receive unexcused absences for the classes they miss. Families will be notified after 4:30 p.m. of any absences. An unexcused absence may affect a student’s ability to participate in after-school activities, events or competitions.

title: Editorial: Bend should move ahead on defensible space
author: none
content: No community has fully adopted the state defensible space code to reduce the dangers of fire. But some are moving closer and using it as a guide, including Bend. A defensible space code is a big change in how many people landscape their properties. It would basically mean keeping flammable things — bushes, tree limbs, groundcover — away from homes. Of course, for many, those kinds of things near a home are the ideal. Complying with what’s smart to do to reduce wildfire danger could come with a high cost for property owners, too. On the more extreme end, it could cost even tens of thousands of dollars. And who wants to spend the money to take down a prized tree? Bend City Councilors discussed the tradeoffs recently and want to move ahead both quickly and slowly. The quick might be a kind of demonstration project. The city may pick a part of town at particularly high risk and also take into consideration if the neighborhood is less likely to be able to afford a cleanup themselves. Volunteers could do wonders. They would need professional coordination and direction. The city may be able to do a lot without too much expense. It would be ideal to get it done before the next fire season comes along. The longer term goals are probably two: Come up with a defensible space code Bend residents would support. Come up with a way to pay for getting more homes in compliance. Mayor Melanie Kebler wants to take the time to work with the community to develop that code. Parts of it may be less than popular. But there is a need. The city’s fire levy expires in 2029. The city will likely go out for a new fire levy in 2028. Beyond the need to continue to pay for excellence in Bend’s fire and rescue services, part of the levy may provide a source of money to do more wildfire prevention. Don’t wait for the city to take action. Take a look at the state’s model defensible space code and see what you can do. And if you would like, you can tell Bend City Councilors what you think they should do by emailing council@bendoregon.gov. Editorials reflect the views of The Bulletin’s editorial board, Editor Jody Lawrence-Turner, Editor Tim Trainor and Editorial Page Editor Richard Coe.

title: Antelope man dies in crash north of Madras
author: none
content: An Antelope man died Sunday after police say he turned in front of oncoming traffic on Highway 97 north of Madras. Thomas Derrig Jagels, 77, died at the scene. According to Oregon State Police, he was traveling southbound on the highway about 3:03 p.m. when he turned left across the path of a northbound van driven by Ronald Lee Jensen, 67, of The Dalles. The van crashed into the Honda, killing Jagels. Jensen was not injured, according to police. The highway was not impacted during the crash or investigation. Oregon State Police was assisted by the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Office, Jefferson County Fire and EMS and the Oregon Department of Transportation.

title: 10:30 a.m. UPDATE: Saylor Graham, injured in Silver Rail shooting, moved out of intensive care
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: Saylor Graham-Poarch, the 7-year-old injured in the Silver Rail Elementary shooting, has been moved out of the intensive care unit, said her family in a statement Monday morning. “She has a long recovery ahead, and right now all we want is to be with her through it,” said the family in a statement. Saylor was injured in a shooting Oct. 15 at the elementary school. Three children, a teacher and the shooter were all killed, and another teacher was injured. Teacher Becky Drury is recovering at St. Charles Bend. A memorial service was held for teacher Megan Lambert Saturday at Caldera High School. Saylor was initially taken to St. Charles Bend and was moved to Oregon Health & Science University Hospital for treatment. “Even as we’re grateful for Saylor’s progress, our hearts are broken for the families of the three children and the teacher who were killed. We are holding them close, and we grieve with them,” said her family. Saylor has a gene mutation disorder called CASK, which disrupts brain development and causes cognitive and physical challenges. She was chosen as Bend High School’s “Sparrow” during the 2024-25 school year. Nonprofit Sparrow Clubs match children with life-altering medical conditions with schools who fundraise to support the Sparrows and their families. “Thank you to everyone who has reached out, prayed for Saylor, sent messages, and shown our family so much love during the hardest time of our lives,” said the family. “We can’t respond to everyone individually, but please know that every kind word, prayer, and act of support means more to us than we can say.” There are two GoFundMe fundraisers to support Saylor’s recovery, which have collectively raised over $1 million. Sweatshirts designed by Saylor’s mother are also for sale to support her recovery. Nearly 250 have been sold as of Monday morning. “Above all, please keep Saylor in your thoughts and prayers as she heals,” said her family. “We are beyond grateful that she is still here with us.”

title: Bend Pilates studio becomes safe haven for breast cancer survivors
author: Emily Rogers
content: Jamie Skuse, owner of Club Pilates Bend and an ambassador of Heaven Can Wait, has become the first person Pilates members and their friends and family reach out to when they get a breast cancer diagnosis. “We have five people who just got diagnosed with breast cancer this month alone,” Skuse said. “We’ve had at least four to five phone calls of somebody who’s just gotten a cancer diagnosis.” Skuse was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2012. Since 2025 she has been an owner of Club Pilates Bend, never shying away from sharing her story and how early detection, exercising and finding community aided in her recovery. “We have had people join our studio just because they know it’s a support group, and we have quite a few breast cancer survivors,” Skuse said. “Because it really helps to have somebody who you know has been through it and ask questions and know that you’re a safe place.” Skuse hosts free Pilates classes throughout the year for different breast cancer groups. This year the Pilates studio closed on the day of the Heaven Can Wait 5K to benefit breast cancer education and patient support and had staff and Pilates members participate in the event. Skuse found Club Pilates after going through three types of chemotherapy and 34 rounds of radiation after her first breast cancer diagnosis in 2012. “The pain is unreal during chemo. At the end of it, it was like: “Allright what can I do to make myself healthy again?” Skuse asked. “For me that’s where Pilates came in. Because I knew I wanted to be here longer. I was told I may never see my kids graduate from high school, and I have.” Chemotherapy can weaken bones and cause significant bone density loss over time. But resistance training commonly used in Pilates can help protect bone density, according to Skuse. Skuse moved to Bend in 2019 and instantly got involved in opening a Pilates location in town. Just a few months after doing so, she went in for a mammogram where doctors found six tumors. All tested positive for breast cancer. The need for Pilates in her recovery became even more prevalent after her second diagnosis, which resulted in her needing a double mastectomy. “It’s great for your bones that resistance with both the reformer and the mat, but also being able to use every single part of your body again,” Skuse said. “When you have a mastectomy, you lose quite a bit of feeling in your chest, and so for me being able to move my arms and my shoulders and not get frozen shoulder and stiffness and achiness like so many people get was important.” After the surgery Skuse remembers her physical therapist releasing her from the hospital early due to the strength she had gained from doing Pilates up until the surgery. In 2024, Skuse became a certified Club Pilates instructor and a year later she bought the Club Pilates studio. Since then she has formed the studio into a safe space for breast cancer survivors to come and find community. Gina Kadow, a three-time survivor of breast cancer, has been attending Club Pilates Bend for the last year and half. Kadow was without cancer for past seven years until being diagnosed for a third time in August. However, Kadow has been able to find community support with the many breast cancer survivors who frequent the pilates studio. “There’s actually a lot of people that are at Club Pilates I have found that have gone through or are going through breast cancer,” Kadow said. “Pilates is mind/body experience as far as it just gives you an overall calming effect, relaxes you and at the same time, it’s strengthening your body to get through what you’re going through.” Skuse has offered to go with people to their first mammogram appointments and participated in food trains for clients who are currently undergoing cancer treatment. Despite not having cancer for six years, Club Pilates remains an important part of Skuse’s healthcare routine. “It (Club Pilates) gives me everything, especially right now as the owner,” Skuse said. “I feel like I have such a great platform to reach people. But to be in a support group, I think that’s all people want. They want somewhere where they can belong, and somewhere where they have a group of people.”

title: Sawyer Park parking lot closes for improvements
author: Michael Kohn
content: The Sawyer Park parking lot has closed as part of an improvement project to upgrade several areas at the park situated along the Middle Deschutes Deschutes River. The park, one of the oldest in Bend, will remain open to pedestrians and bicyclists using the Deschutes River Trail. Pedestrian access from O.B. Riley Road will be maintained along the park’s southern edge. The project includes relocating the parking lot closer to O.B. Riley Road, adding accessible parking, restoring habitat, improving trail accessibility and constructing a permanent restroom, picnic shelter and river overlook. Visitors should follow posted fencing, detours and closures during construction. The project is funded in part by grants from the Land and Water Conservation Fund and the Local Government Grant Program. Completion is expected next summer.

title: Column: How the federal debt happened
author: none
content: The federal government is drowning itself in red ink, caused by its spending far more than the revenues it collects. Economists agree that the debt explosion raises Americans’ borrowing costs, inhibits economic growth, and makes us all poorer. Yet our citizenry is rarely provided with detailed information about what drives this problem and what laws must be changed to correct it. To answer these questions, in 2013, I began quantifying the leading contributors to the federal fiscal imbalance, periodically updating the findings. This year’s update shows that nearly three-quarters of the problem is caused by spending growth in just a few areas of the budget: Medicare, Medicaid, Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace subsidies, and Social Security. This is roughly consistent with previous results. Until recently, the problem was almost entirely on the spending side, but that has since changed. With the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in 2025, roughly one-quarter of the imbalance now derives from tax cuts. Remarkably, over 87% of the worsening shortfall was legislated in just two concentrated periods of fiscal irresponsibility: the first from 1965 to 1972, the second beginning in 2010 and continuing through the present. Less than 13% of the problem was created in all the intervening years, encompassing the combined presidencies of Ford, Carter, Reagan, Bush 41, Clinton and Bush 43. The earlier period can be thought of as a time of legislative hubris, when lawmakers enacted massive new mandatory spending obligations with little appreciation for the cost growth they were unleashing. Specifically, there were the creations of Medicare and Medicaid in 1965, followed by expansions of both programs and Social Security in the early 1970s. Whatever the merits of these programs, the stubborn fact remains that Washington has yet to determine how to keep their cost growth at sustainable levels. The second period of deficit-expanding legislation, from 2010 to the present, began similarly with new mandatory spending: the ACA’s dramatic expansion of Medicaid and its new subsidies for health insurance coverage. Any single year’s deficit usually has a much longer list of contributors and tends to be more greatly affected by recent legislation. The 2026 deficit is no exception. Still, the vast majority of it — nearly 85% — was created by legislation enacted during the same two pivotal time periods of 1965-1972 and 2010 through the present. Nearly two-thirds of this year’s deficit is attributable to spending exceeding historical norms, while a little over one-third stems from recent tax cuts. On the spending side, the biggest contributors are growth in Medicaid and ACA spending, Medicare and Social Security, in that order, followed by recent expansions of veterans’ benefits and military retirement spending. The OBBBA tax cuts alone are responsible for roughly 30% of the deficit, by far the leading contributor on the tax side. Politicians will always blame the other party for rising debt, but there is plenty of blame to go around. Neither party has a compelling claim to superior fiscal responsibility. Rarely are American voters told the truth: that we won’t fix the problem until we moderate the growing costs of Medicare, Medicaid, the ACA and Social Security, and until we stop cutting taxes in the absence of spending restraint. Charles Blahous is the J. Fish and Lillian F. Smith Chair and Senior Research Strategist at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University and a former public trustee for Social Security and Medicare.

title: Letters: Imhoff, Connally for commission; Leitz for judge
author: none
content: Don’t add to the echo chamber Do we really need a bigger echo chamber? Commissioner Phil Chang is on a roll. In April, his Bulletin column went after a sitting commissioner. This week, me. Two races, two columns, each landing before voters decide. In January, Chang will be joined by Jamie Collins and Rick Russell. He doesn’t need a fourth reliable vote. He wants one anyway. Look who’s backing Morgan Schmidt: Chang, every member of the Bend City Council, Congresswoman Janelle Bynum, Sen. Anthony Broadman and Rep. Emerson Levy. Voters made this race nonpartisan in 2022, yet the Deschutes Democrats endorsed Collins, Russell and Schmidt as a slate. Same names, same endorsers, same votes. We know where echo chambers get us. That council put Greenwood Avenue on a road diet and approved a multi-million dollar footbridge. This year it voted 7-0, then 6-0, to stop requiring public comment at committee meetings, with no recorded discussion. It added a 20% “climate impact fee” on new homes with gas service, where young families can’t afford to buy. When everyone agrees, nobody asks hard questions, and residents pay the bill. For six years, Chang was the lone dissenter on a 2-1 board, forcing debate. I respect that. Now his side holds the majority, and he wants no one playing that role for the other half of the county. I’m running to be that voice: for rural residents, working families, and neighbors who testify and deserve to be heard. A five-member board should look like the county it serves. I’d be honored to have your vote for Position 5. Rob Imhoff, candidate for Deschutes County Commission Connally for Deschutes Commission As a Gold Star Father I have a deep personal perspective on service, sacrifice, public accountability and how local governments should support families and veterans. Lauren Connally understands my views because she has taken the time to listen to me and others. It all comes naturally for Lauren whose entire life has been dedicated to serving others as an officer in the Marine Corps, an executive-director at a Veterans nonprofit, mental health advocate and caregiver, and small business owner and employee. Lauren has taken a deep dive into learning about and understanding the issues that we all face, through study and thoughtfulness. Lauren’s thoughts are her own and not just political party lines. All of Lauren’s experiences along with that of being a mother have prepared her to be a stand out county commissioners who will be a good steward of our taxpayer dollars, make hard and good decisions; strengthen the county’s ability to serve us and bolster and relieve burdens for businesses that support local families and provide opportunities for workers. As we continue to face off against a mental health crisis and dangerous wildfires; Lauren knows that early proactive investments and interventions are needed to mitigate these public health issues and community safety threats. That’s why I’m voting for Lauren Connally for Deschutes County Commissioner. Peter Ostrovsky, Bend Leitz for judge My name is Jim Slife and I retired from the US Air Force after 36 years of service last year as a four-star general officer. I’m writing to let you know what a wonderful candidate you have for your Deschutes County Circuit Court Judge in Keith Leitz. I met Keith over 20 years ago when I served as his commander in a heavily deployed Special Operations assault helicopter squadron in the years following 9/11. Keith was a helicopter flight engineer and we flew combat missions in Iraq together. In those years, he was known for his meticulous attention to detail, his unflappable calm under fire and his bulletproof integrity. None of that has changed in the intervening decades. Keith left uniformed service for the first time to attend law school at the University of Oregon. Upon graduation, he rejoined the Air Force, this time as a Judge Advocate General. His legal career blossomed, both inside the Air Force and out. He prosecuted cases for the federal government and has served as a Special Assistant US Attorney, Coos County Counsel, and the City Attorney for Redmond. In short, his experiences have prepared him for elected office as your Circuit Court Judge. But beyond his experiences, his judicial temperament, attention to detail, calmness under pressure, and unassailable integrity make him the ideal candidate. Elect him! Jim Slife, Hartselle, Alabama

title: Fire at Newport seafood plant forces evacuations amid fear of ammonia exposure
author: none
content: Residents and visitors in Newport were evacuated Sunday when a fire erupted at a seafood production plant and it was feared ammonia tanks could rupture and send dangerous amounts of the chemical into the air. The fire at Pacific Seafood closed off the popular Bayport section of the coastal city. Firefighters swarmed the plant and were able to keep flames from the tanks, but continued to battle the fire Sunday evening. The City of Newport initially issued an evacuation order for a 1-mile radius around the plant due to concerns that smoke from the fire contained ammonia. Officials later decreased the evacuation zone to a couple of blocks surrounding the plant after they determined the ammonia tanks were stable. The city, located about 132 miles southwest of Portland, has a population of about 10,000 people. Its bayfront is a popular tourist attraction featuring restaurants, shops and tours. Ammonia is a colorless gas with a sharp odor. High levels of exposure can cause skin, eye and throat irritation, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. John Fuller, the public information officer for the city, told The Associated Press it is not clear what caused the fire. Approximately 30 to 40 people were in the building when the fire broke out, Fuller said in a Sunday afternoon news conference. One firefighter was taken to the hospital for exhaustion, Fire Chief Rob Murphy said, but no other injuries were reported. Pacific Seafood is a wholesaler and manufacturer that handles fishing, processing and the distribution of seafood across the country. One of its processing plants sits along the city’s Yaquina Bay, near a dock where sea lions gather. Ashton Meier, Pacific Seafood’s vice president of resource sales and processing, said the company expects a major loss. “We are incredibly thankful and glad to report that all of our team members on site are safe and accounted for and that at this time we are not aware of any injuries to others in the area,” Meier said in a Sunday evening statement. Fuller said the initial 1-mile radius included businesses as well as residences and made up a “pretty good chunk” of the small town. A shelter originally set up at the Sam Case Elementary School was moved further north away from the plant to the Atonement Lutheran Church as a precaution. Shelly Heim was at her home in Newport when she heard sirens and saw smoke coming from the nearby seafood plant. Flames were shooting from the roof, she said. She and her husband didn’t smell anything off in the air and didn’t evacuate, but were monitoring the wind to make sure it didn’t change direction and blow the smoke toward them. “It’s heartbreaking,” the 59-year-old real estate agent said, adding that Newport has a strong working port and fishing community and that Pacific Seafood serves as a big place of employment. “It’s a big asset. Hopefully they can rebuild.”

title: Ducks’ season teeters on the brink after 21-10 loss at Illinois
author: Wade Evanson
content: Oregon’s rollercoaster season continued on Saturday, and it isn’t going up. After narrowly pulling victory from the jaws of defeat last week against Nebraska, this week they turned a 10-point lead into an 11-point loss in a 21-10 defeat at the hands of Illinois on Oct. 24, in Champaign, Illinois. The Ducks moved the ball seamlessly on the opening drive of the game en route to a 7-0 lead, then tacked on a field goal late in the second quarter to make it 10-0. But a 75-yard touchdown run by Illinois’ Aidan Laughery late in the second half turned the tide, and it led to 21 unanswered Illini points and another disappointing loss for an Oregon team circling the drain. “Credit to Illinois,” Oregon head coach Dan Lanning said. “Thought they were the tougher team today. That definitely showed up in the second half, kind of a tale of two halves.” Laughery finished with 123 yards on 13 carries, and was part of an otherwise anemic Illinois offense that averaged 5.8 yards per carry against the Ducks defense, while throwing for a measly 89 yards. Outside of Laughery’s 75-yard jaunt, Oregon’s defense was solid in the first half, holding the home Illini to 127 total yards of offense. That changed in the second half where Illinois disguised nothing, and instead lined up and ran it right at the once vaunted Duck defensive line. “Yeah, I don’t think we had the same relentless effort in the second half,” Lanning said. “We weren’t winning the line of scrimmage. I think when we turn on the tape, we’re gonna see some technique that wasn’t there that needs to be there, and we’re gonna see some opportunities where guys are counting on someone else to make a play, and not running to the ball like their hair’s on fire.” Oregon’s offense finished with 426 total yards, but much of that felt like empty calories. Gage Hurych — who had been perfect coming into the game — missed three field goals, all of which were from distance. Oregon quarterback Dylan Raiola started his second game after leading last week’s late comeback, but was mediocre at best, completing 27 of his 41 pass attempts for 246 yards with two fumbles. Raiola rarely challenged the Illinois defense downfield, instead relying on quick-hitters or dump-offs to backs in an effort to gain yardage. You could argue that part of his hesitation to throw the ball down the field was due to the Ducks playing without four of their top-5 receivers in the game, but Lanning wanted nothing to do with that narrative afterwards. “That certainly would be an excuse, right?” Lanning said. “Not an excuse for us.” The Ducks were able to run the ball with some success, tallying 180 yards rushing, led by Jordon Davison and Dierre Hill Jr. who combined to carry 27 times for 175 yards. But beyond that it was just another disappointing performance for a team whose season is teetering on the brink. “Their response will be their choice, right?” Lanning said. “They gotta decide what they’re made up of and what that looks like. It’s hard in that locker room, right? Everybody’s disappointed. You can do something about disappointment with the way that you work.” That might be easier said than done for a group many thought would contend for college football’s biggest prize. But Lanning said such prognostications — while warranted due to recent success — came from outside the program, and now no longer exist based on how they’ve performed over the season’s two months. “Yeah, I mean, those expectations were created by previous performances by us,” Lanning said. “I don’t think I ever said we were gonna be something other than what we create, right? And football is about what you go to do every single day, what you do, your body of work. We don’t have the body of work as a team right now to be anything other than who we are.” And that’s a football team that’s not playing very well, compromised due to injury, and searching for answers that the coach said can only come from putting in the work. “We haven’t stacked days the way that we need to build stacked days, so it’s gonna be about how we attack tomorrow, how we’re gonna attack the rest of the night,” Lanning said. “And then what next week looks like, and a lot of that’s gonna be up to our players. It’s gonna be up to our own coaches, right? And, again, we’ll find ways to make sure that we’re continuing to improve and build.” Oregon hosts Northwestern at 12:30 p.m. next Saturday, Oct. 31, at Autzen Stadium.

title: Five knee-jerk reactions from Oregon’s 21-10 loss to Illinois
author: Wade Evanson
content: Below are five knee-jerk reactions from Oregon’s 21-10 loss to Illinois on Saturday, Oct. 24, in Champaign, Illinois. Dylan Raiola cannot be the starting quarterback in Eugene next season. I’m sure that was the plan when the Oregon coaching staff — along with a good amount of money — convinced the Nebraska transfer and former 5-star recruit to join the Ducks, but over the last four games he’s looked closer to a stop-gap signal-caller than one you hand the reins to. He consistently throws off his back foot, rarely if ever completes a pass on time, and doesn’t protect the ball. For as good as Oregon’s defense was in the first half (minus a 75 yard touchdown run), they were equally unimpressive in the second half. They allowed nearly 200 yards over the final two quarters, and 225 total yards rushing despite virtually no threat of the pass. Illinois true freshman starting quarterback Michael Clayton II completed 11 of his 18 pass attempts for 84 yards. In other words, they weren’t fooling anyone, but rather lining up and whooping the Oregon defensive line at the point of attack. So much so, television analyst Jake Butt referenced it on multiple occasions, speaking also to the team’s apparent lack of urgency. Oregon offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer doesn’t trust Dylan Raiola, and I don’t trust either one. Mehringer’s playcalling could only be described as conservative at best, scared to death at worst. Yes, the Ducks were without four of their top-5 receivers, but Mehringer’s inability to establish any rhythm via playcalling, and Raiola’s inability to see the field and attack the defense beyond the line of scrimmage results in little to no faith in the offense to move the ball. Oregon had 90 yards through 28 minutes of the second half. Don’t let the final numbers fool you, this offense was a slightly improved version over what we’ve seen in recent weeks and the lack of improvement is damning. The team is averaging 14 points per game over their last three games, and put up 10 points on an Illinois team that was allowing 27.8 points per game — 105th in the nation. In other words, Illinois’ defense isn’t good, but was too good for the Duck offense. This isn’t a good football team, but I’d argue that’s less on the players and more on the coaching staff at this point. Circumstances are such that Oregon is without their starting quarterback, along with — at least in this game — a bevy of starting receivers, but coaching is the difference between decline and ineptitude when it comes to circumstances unbecoming, and the drop off from what was and what has recently been is gigantic. No one is asking this team in its current state to be great, but somewhat capable isn’t a lot to ask of a roster that prior to the season was dubbed by many to be the deepest in the country. Where does Oregon go from here? The College Football Playoff has gone from unlikely to a pipe dream with the loss to the Illini, and with little to play for beyond a run-of-the-mill bowl game to be named later, we’re inching closer to some of the esteemed players making business decisions opposed to ones with the team’s chances of winning in mind. Additionally, the coaching staff has to start pitching star returners on why they should hang around next season opposed to finding a better situation with their future endeavors in mind.

title: ICE affirms in court documents there are no plans to build detention center in Newport
author: none
content: The Department of Homeland Security agreed in a settlement with the state to alert city officials at least 30 days before environmental permitting would get underway. No new Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers are slated for construction in Newport, Oregon, anytime soon, and the federal government will provide at least a month’s notice to city officials before any environmental permitting would get underway. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security agreed to those terms through Aug. 1, 2027, as part of a settlement with the Oregon Department of Justice filed in federal court in Eugene on Friday. “ICE doesn’t get to skirt the law to build a facility for locking up and deporting our neighbors,” said Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, in a news release. “Oregon stood up, we made the federal government answer for its plans in court, and now they have to follow the law.” The possibility of a new ICE detention center coming to Newport arose last fall amid concerns that federal immigration authorities were scouting the Oregon Coast for a long-term holding facility, including at Newport’s U.S. Coast Guard municipal airport site. Newport’s city leaders went public with their concerns shortly after, and strong opposition grew from residents and the state’s Democratic leaders, who also took issue with the temporary removal of a life-saving rescue helicopter from the city’s Coast Guard facility. Rayfield successfully sued the Homeland Security Department over the helicopter’s removal, securing a court order that it be returned to Newport, and asked a federal judge to halt any construction on an immigration detention facility at the site. In that case, which is behind the recent settlement, lawyers for Oregon’s Justice Department argued that the federal government had been skirting federal environmental and coastal land use regulations by trying to build a facility on the municipal airport site without providing advanced notice to state and local leaders. The Oregon Justice Department agreed to drop the case following the federal government’s commitment to providing advance notice should efforts to build a detention center in the area resume. The notice period required in the lawsuit does not apply to other Oregon cities, though the settlement notes ICE is not planning to expand or create any detention facilities or processing centers in the state. This article was originally published by Oregon Capital Chronicle and used with permission. Oregon Capital Chronicle is part of States Newsroom and can be reached at info@oregoncapitalchronicle.com.

title: Motorcycle adventurer from Bend reflects on his time in South Africa
author: none
content: Editor’s note: Bend’s Elijah Callan embarked on a two-year, 70,000-mile-plus motorcycle journey around the world on Aug. 31. He is sending The Bulletin stories and photos from the road, which we plan to publish every other weekend during his trip. Finishing my run, I opened the first of two security gates to enter the home I was staying at and thought to myself: “If a zombie apocalypse ever happens, South Africa is going to be the last country standing.” After seeing dozens of neighborhoods in Cape Town, I found it impossible to ignore the fact that nearly every home was not just a home — but a compound. A mini-fortress with 8-foot-high walls, security gates, barbed wire, electric fencing, and a placard from one of the dozens of security companies stating “WARNING: ARMED RESPONSE.” Due to a series of shipping mishaps and delays, I had been in Cape Town for nearly a month and had developed something of a routine while waiting for my motorcycle to arrive. I had come to enjoy my morning runs, as they were not just exercise but journeys into two human realities that coexisted in the span of a mile, though separated by an invisible boundary. Beyond the extraordinary contrasts in wealth, something else had become impossible to ignore during my time in Cape Town: the unmistakable presence of fear. Whether this feeling is justified or not, the infrastructure reinforces it, and more concretely, the statistics support it. From April 1, 2026 to June 30, 2026, the South African Police Service (SAPS) recorded 5,427 murders, 6,958 attempted murders, 9,201 reported rapes, 42,491 cases of common assault, and 26,839 aggravated robberies. During the reporting year ending March 2026, South Africa recorded approximately 36.6 murders per 100,000 people, placing it among the countries with the highest homicide rates in the world. And according to Gallup’s 2025 Global Safety Report, South Africans were the least likely among residents of 144 countries and territories surveyed to feel safe walking alone at night, with just 33 percent of adults reporting that they felt safe. Despite the staggering statistics, from the darling penguins at Simon’s Town to the spectacular sea cliffs at the Cape of Good Hope, my time in Cape Town remained trouble free until an unexpected encounter brought the topic of violence much closer to home. After a pleasant evening over bangers and mash, a few pints, and interesting conversation with my new friend, Erwan (a French expat who had ridden the west coast of Africa on a Royal Enfield Himalayan), he excused himself to the restroom. While I waited for Erwan, a tall, smartly dressed, black waiter from Zimbabwe named Joseph approached me with the bill but seemed more interested in me than my credit card. “You are from the United States?” Joseph asked without paying attention to the card reader in his hand. “Yeah, what gave it away?” I joked. Smiling back at me, he asked, “How do you like living there? What is it like?” “Oh well, you know, it’s got its pros and cons,” I said. “Yes, but what about the violence? And guns. I hear a lot about guns. Why are there so many people with guns? Can you be shot easily?” he pressed. Even though I didn’t show it, I suddenly found myself annoyed and was hoping Erwan would get back quickly. It was a topic that, when traveling, I desperately try to avoid, as explaining the Constitution, guns, and the Second Amendment to a non-American is akin to explaining the sanctity of a religious relic. “Well, the U.S. is a really big country. About 330 million people, and every state has different laws and every state is different.” It was a non-answer, and I wasn’t in the mood to discuss it with a non-American, yet it was clear that Joseph was not satisfied with my response. “I have a friend from Florida. She is visiting me here soon, and yesterday, she sent me an article about kids being killed at a school in America a couple days ago. How is this possible?” In the moments after he asked his question, I immediately recognized what he was referring to, and the only words I could muster were “That was my hometown.” Seemingly unaware of the significance of what I had just said, Joseph continued: “That does not happen in South Africa or Zimbabwe.” I felt an intense mixture of sadness, bewilderment, and anger. Here I was, sitting in a restaurant in South Africa, discussing a school shooting that had just happened in my hometown with a man from Zimbabwe. The entire situation felt surreal and for several moments, I lost track of what Joseph was saying. Interrupting him, I asked, “In Zimbabwe, if somebody walked into a classroom and shot a bunch of kids, what would happen?” Slightly taken aback by my question, he responded, “Firstly, there are no guns in Zimbabwe. The government took them, house to house, and they are very difficult to get. So, this wouldn’t happen. There are benefits to dictatorships.” “Yes, but what would happen if it did?” I pressed. Joseph paused thoughtfully as Erwan returned. “Well, let me give you an example. A couple years ago, outside the city, way out where they farm and there are very few people, a man shot a farmer. Several months later, he was tracked down in Mozambique, and we killed him.” For several more minutes, the three of us continued to discuss life in Zimbabwe and South Africa, as well as politics in the USA, though by that point, I had mentally checked out of the conversation and let Erwan take on the remaining heavy lifting.
