Relieved that the conversation ended when we split the bill, I said my goodbyes to Erwan and Joseph and took a 35-minute Uber ride back to Hout Bay. Despite my driver enthusiastically greeting me and trying to strike up a conversation, I sat in the back seat, morose and withdrawn. I later felt guilty for not engaging more, and may have even come across as rude, yet was in no mood for another conversation about anything, let alone America. Sitting in the dark back seat on the ride back to Hout Bay, I thought of home, the kids —just babies, really — and the parents from Silver Rail. And rather than reflecting on a nice evening with Erwan, who shared invaluable information with me about my upcoming ride up the west coast of Africa, I felt a wave of rage at the situation. Although the winding mountain road was making me nauseous, I pulled out my phone and began not just fact-checking Joseph, but looking up statistics on school shootings in South Africa and Zimbabwe. Arriving home, I could see the lights of Imizamo Yethu across the valley through my bedroom window. Crawling into bed, I continued my research. That night and throughout the following morning, I could not verify a single instance in which an individual, let alone a minor, entered a school with a gun, and indiscriminately targeted and murdered children. I found isolated instances of violence occurring at the individual level, or even specific teachers being targets of violent and deadly attacks by resentful students. But the phenomenon of an individual — of any age — obtaining a gun, entering a school, and killing en masse was absent from any data I could source on South Africa and Zimbabwe. South Africa has a serious problem with crime. Moreover, it faces immense difficulties with poverty, food insecurity, widespread mental-health problems, access to medicine, and a dark legacy of racial discrimination that has persisted well beyond the end of apartheid. There is pervasive substance abuse. It has one of Africa’s highest suicide rates, with a national study finding that more than one in four South African adults showed signs of depression. Some 2.7 million children have lost one or both parents. There are slums with unimaginable living conditions in every city. Across South Africa, violence, murder, rape, and robbery are seen at rates that dwarf those in most Western countries. However, despite the extraordinarily high crime rate and mental health crisis, the uncomfortable truth is that, according to the data, children in South Africa and Zimbabwe were safer sitting at their classroom desks than children in Bend.

title: Yesteryear: Survey indicates Bend has 10,400 residents in 1926
author: none
content: 100 YEARS AGO For the week ending Oct. 31, 1926 Survey Indicates Bend Has 10,400 Now Bend now has a population of 10,400 people, an increase of 92.2 per cent over the 1920 federal census. This was the information obtained today from J.L. Gaither, local manager of the Pacific Telephone & Telegraph Co., who has just received from his company’s engineers population data gathered in Bend in recent months. The data were obtained in a survey here which included an actual count of families, dwellings and business firms. Each section of Bend was carefully studied. “In 1920, the telephone company’s study showed a population of 5,650,” Gaither stated. “United States census taken five months earlier for the same year was 5,415. The closeness of the estimate is typical of the care and exactness with which the engineering forces work. The survey made this year embodied the same careful attention to detail as was exercised in 1920.” Four Streets In Bend Have Stop Signs Bend auto drivers faced a new traffic problem for the first time today when “stop street” rules went into effect at four intersections. Small orange half buttons were placed at the intersections, and all vehicles are required to come to a full stop before passing the markers. “Stop streets” designated today are Franklin at the intersection with Hill, Wall at Greenwood, Broadway at Delaware and Broadway at St. Helens. One of these intersections, that at Broadway and St. Helens, is a “four way stop,” with all cars coming to a stop before entering the intersection from any of the four streets. Early this afternoon, shortly after the new buttons were placed, practically all motorists were ignoring the new rules. After a short warning period, in which officers will be on duty at the stop crossings, fines will be levied for violations of the stop rules. Fifteen Million Trout Eggs to Be Taken in Central Oregon With 15,000,000 trout egg record of last fall as the goal, eastern brook egg taking operations are to start in the mid-state country in the immediate future. A crew of nine or ten men will be used in the work of taking the trout eggs from Elk and East lakes, and should there be a fall of snow before the work is completed, this number will be augmented. From Elk and East lakes, the eastern brook eggs are to be taken to one auxiliary station on Fall river where the water is more equable than that used in the Tumalo hatchery. There are over 1,000,00 young trout now at the Fall river station. Where they are to be kept until spring. Should the Cascades and Paulinas remain free from snow for several weeks, the work of taking the eggs from the trout and of hauling them out of the mountains to the Fall River hatchery will not be difficult, but should there be a heavy fall of snow it will be necessary for the hatchery employes to haul the eggs from the lakes to the hatchery on sleds. Egg-taking operation a year ago was very successful, some 13,000,000 out of the 15,000,000 eggs taken having reached the eyeing stage. 75 YEARS AGO For the week ending Oct. 31, 1951 Chase Over Desert Ends in Crash Here A 180-mile chase, across the high desert from Burns, ended near a local church about 10:30 o’clock this morning when a car operated by Norman Battey, 15, Astoria, crashed into parked cars on a one-way street. Injured in the crash, as he attempted to out-distance pursuing state and city officers, Battey was taken to St. Charles Memorial hospital. His injuries were not considered serious. The youth’s long-distance run, in an attempt to elude Officer H. A. Larson of the state police, ended here suddenly when he crashed head-on into cars parked on St. Helens by Mrs. Ray Forrest and Mrs. Thompson Taylor, who were preparing for a rummage sale in the Episcopal church. All three cars, two unoccupied were extensively damaged. The chase through Bend, west on Greenwood then down Wall to St. Helens, attracted wide local attention. Officers’ sirens were sounding as the cars roared down Wall street. Dams on Deschutes River Recommended Central Oregon’s spring-fed Deschutes river, described by the speaker as the jugular vein of the region, came in for major attention yesterday when the state natural resources committee, headed by Governor Douglas mcKay, held its all-day meeting in Bend. Construction of new dams on the Deschutes and its tributaries was recommended. Diversion of the entire flow of icy-cold Tumalo creek for mid-Oregon cities was suggested. Abandonment of the Crane Prairie reservoir was proposed. Construction of a power dam at the Pelton site was strongly backed. The Bend conference was devoted to a discussion of problems in the Deschutes and Crooked river basins. Similar river basin meetings will be held in all parts of the state. The committee created at the 1951 session of the state legislature, is composed of heads and representatives of the various state departments. Local Ghosts, Goblins Given Warning by Chief of Police Ghosts and goblins who will be aboard tonight with soap and sacks were cautioned today by city police that there must be no destruction of property. Youngsters making the rounds tonight on “trick or treat” missions were assured they would not be bothered by patrolmen, who will make runs only when calls relative to vandalism are received. Chief Casiday pointed out today that Bend has been singularly free of vandalism. Last year, several boys got in trouble when they turned on hydrants and tore down some street signs. They were required to pay for the damages. Nine officers have been alerted for duty tonight, and patrolmen will be abroad in three cars and a motorcycle. An officer is on duty in the local station at all times to receive calls, and relay these to patrols. Trick or treaters are expected to start their rounds about dark this evening, and apparently most homes in Bend are prepared for the visits, which are expected to continue until lights in residential areas go off for the night. 50 YEARS AGO For the week ending Oct. 31, 1976 Tetherow Bridge to be site of historical society marker The Deschutes County Historical society will place a historic marker at Tetherow Crossing, on the Deschutes River northwest of Redmond, Saturday at 1 p.m. The public is invited to attend and to participate in a picnic which will follow, weather permitting. The location, site of the present Tetherow Bridge, is now a county park. It is the spot where as early as 1879, immigrants camped en route to the Ochoco meadows on the trip from the Willamette Valley. It is also the location of the county’s oldest home, which is still occupied. The crossing was named for A.J. Thetherow, a pioneer stockman and a member of a prominent early Willamette Valley family. Thetherow had a farm on Crooked River, and operated a store and a cable-drawn ferry at the Deschutes River site. Jack Myers, society president, will trace the history of the crossing in a brief ceremony preceding the dedication of the marker. The society’s historic sites committee has placed several similar markers at historic locations in recent months. The Redmond Jaycees are assisting the historical society in preparing the area for this occasion, according to Perry Hereford, general chairman. After the dedication, there will be time for activities such as arrow-head hunting, hiking nearby trails and fishing, he said. He encouraged visitors to come prepared to spend the afternoon. Ribbon markers will be placed from O’Neil Junction and Highway 97 north of Redmond to the old ferry site. 25 YEARS AGO For the week ending Oct. 31, 2001 Internet use booms at local libraries Randy Handen visits the Crook County Library about three times a week, but not necessarily to check out books. “I don’t have a computer at home, and I’m moving,” she said, scrolling through online classifieds on a rainy Monday afternoon. “If this wasn’t here, I would probably just drive to Redmond or Bend.” Internet accessibility is one reason why the Crook County Library, as well as others in Central Oregon, has seen a jump in people using the facilities. Annual reports from the state’s libraries were due at the beginning of the month, and Oregon State Librarian Jim Scheppke said he expects the growth to continue into next year. In the two years the library has been wired, the number of Crook County people logging onto the Internet has nearly doubled — from 9,807 last year to more than 18,000 this year. “It’s created a whole new constituency,” Library Director Rick Chrisinger said. “I never thought the Internet would change the book-oriented people. Instead, it’s brought in a new crowd.” Local library directors say the internet attracts locals, as well as people traveling through the area. Todd Dunkelberg, manager of the Redmond library, said the Internet at his branch attracts international climbers on their way to Smith Rock. “On a rainy day in the summer, you can hear four or five languages in here,” he said. And while the new crowd may come for the technology, many still leave with a good old-fashioned book. In the Deschutes Public Library District, 60 percent of people using the Internet had never had a library card before, Director Michael Gaston said. At the Crook County Library, total circulation in the last two years has grown by 30 percent. Around the state, check-outs at Oregon libraries grew 8.9 percent in 2000, the most in a decade and double what was checked out in 1985. Oregon ranks third in the nation in check-outs per capita, according to 1998 data from the National Center for Educational Studies. And about 11 books per person were checked out last year by Oregonians with access to a library. While the library business may be booming, offering so many services has posed some new issues for local libraries. For example, Chrisinger, the Crook County Library director, said he want to get more computers, but may need to sacrifice book space to do so. In the Deschutes Public Library District, Director Gaston said providing electronic databases and Internet services means also employing people trained in those areas. The Deschutes district has hired people with database and Internet expertise and is continually sending other employees to classes on the advancing technology, he said. But for Gaston, launching libraries into the world of technology is a worthwhile endeavor. “Access is part of overcoming the digital divide,” he said. “And the public library is a key place to do that.”

title: Column: Stop school shooters before they get to school
author: none
content: The most sorrowful thing I saw for a long time was a woman running down the road, her Sunday dress whipping in the wind. Her dress was covered in blood. A tornado had struck the Goshen United Methodist Church near Piedmont, Alabama, during the Palm Sunday service more than 30 years ago. A weather warning had been issued. Nobody in the church heard it. The roof came down. Twenty people were killed. The woman was running away from it. I was a reporter then and arrived right behind emergency vehicles. The first responders ran out of body bags. The funerals of children were the hardest to deal with. I never thought I would experience something worse. The shooting at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend feels worse. Partly because it was human caused. Four universes of life, family and community unraveled by a teenager. So many more lives are horribly altered. There have been at least 2,300 gun incidents in schools across the country since 1966 . It can happen here, again. One solution evades us too often — a commitment to mental health. People have called and written The Bulletin’s newsroom telling us the shooting occurred because people have turned away from God. That seems blind to common sense. People at Bend’s City Council meeting this week called on Mayor Melanie Kebler to resign for not having enough police in the schools. That hardly seems fair. More school resource officers in schools could help. Would one in every Bend school be better? Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Wednesday he doesn’t know if that is the right solution. It’s understandable why some parents don’t like that response. It deserves debate. School lockdowns have been questioned. Shooters will know that students will be huddling in classrooms and not getting away. Better fortifying schools may help. It’s hard to know what level of reinforced steel or bulletproof-ness would ever be enough. Researchers say school shootings are often public suicides. They occur after a long string of failures. Shooters don’t snap. There are often points where intervention is needed and obvious. Shooters needed help that they didn’t get. Often people see something that is wrong. Sometimes they say something. Sometimes they do not. Maybe not all shootings can be prevented. Many could. Mental illness, behavioral health issues are treatable. Even today, that idea gets resisted. Mental health is not viewed as important as physical health. When the Bend-La Pine Schools and Deschutes County’s behavioral health first wanted to team up in the schools, it was questioned. The cost was questioned. The effectiveness was questioned. It’s reasonable to ask questions. Behavioral health interventions won’t work every time. The problem will always be that you won’t hear about the times it works. Last lines of defense at schools are necessary. But the goal should be prevention on the front line. The goal should be to stop shooters before they arrive at a school with a gun. The goal should be to ensure they don’t have access to guns. The goal should be to ensure young people are connected with behavioral health services. Seeking help for mental health is a sign of strength, not weakness. Richard Coe is editorial page editor at The Bulletin newspaper, in Bend. He can be reached at richard.coe@bendbulletin.com.

title: Bend schools, police have security measures to consider
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: Since the Silver Rail Elementary gutted Bend on Oct. 15, there has been plenty of anger and concern over school safety in Central Oregon. Future security ideas run the gamut — from having more school resource officers to putting bulletproof glass in schools. Parents organized a protest at the district administration building Friday afternoon to voice their concerns around school safety and security. Police officers in schools Bend-La Pine Schools, Bend Police Department and the Deschutes County Sheriff’s Office all collaborate to staff and fund the school resource officer program. The school district currently has eight school resource officers who rotate between six or seven schools each. Officers also cover schools for other school resource officers on days off. Officers typically serve three to four years in the role before they return to patrol, said police spokesperson Sheila Miller. Officers also return to police patrol during the summer when schools are no longer in session. “They might start a day at an elementary school welcoming kids, attend a meeting at a middle school, respond to a fight or disregulated student at the high school, then pop over to another elementary school for recess or to just say hi,” wrote Miller in an email. “Some days, they might spend an entire day at the high school taking case reports of abuse, harassment, sexual assault — you name it.” There is no requirement for how long officers must spend at one school. Officers are “actively investigating and managing a caseload of incidents that take place in schools, serving as mentors and trying to build trust with students, and doing a ton of work beyond simply standing guard at a school each day,” said Miller. “That’s just the thing that most members of the public see.” Adding more school resource officers would have to be a joint decision between Bend-La Pine schools and the Bend City Council. The latter controls the police department’s budget, said Miller. Salaries for school resource officers are split 50/50 between the school district and the police department. Bend-La Pine Schools also pays overtime for officers if they are asked to present for evening events. Each school resource officer makes an annual salary of roughly $90,000-$125,000, depending on Oregon Department of Public Safety Standards and Training certification level and years of service . “We realize the importance of presence and visibility at our schools. Many of you saw that today, and we were happy to be there with the staff and children as they came back to school,” said Mike Krantz at Wednesday’s city council meeting regarding school resource officers. “Why can’t there be an SRO at every school? While I appreciate that sentiment, that’s not something we can accomplish.” There are 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine School District. Adding 24 more SROS — one for each location — would cost at least $2.4 million a year. A school resource officer’s job includes mentoring, investigating crimes in the schools and more. Krantz said they are not full-time security guards. Bulletproof and safety glass Each school’s security vestibule already has shatterproof glass in place — layers of glass with a resin or plastic layer in between, so glass shards stick to the plastic instead of shattering. Shatterproof glass can cost anywhere from $5 to $10 per square foot. Bulletproof glass can cost anywhere from $100 to more than $450 per square foot. There are several types of bulletproof glass, some of which aren’t glass at all but hard acrylic plastic. Bulletproofing the main security entrance of a school can cost anywhere from $30,000 to $100,000, while bulletproofing all ground-floor doors and windows could bring the cost up to millions of dollars per school. More eyes on schools Parents have suggested setting up a volunteer watch around schools. The organization WATCH D.O.G.S. (Dads Of Great Students) , which began in 1998, organizes parent volunteers for extra security. After the Sandy Hook Elementary shooting in 2012, numerous parents stepped up to help, according to prior reporting from NPR . There have been nationwide discussions of arming teachers with guns to protect students and staff. Guns are not allowed on school campuses per Oregon state law. Oregon is an open-carry state. Though Silver Rail’s fencing did slow the shooter down, razor wire fencing that could more-seriously limit entry would cost anywhere from $25 to $45 per roll, with a roll covering 45 to 50 feet. The Oregon Legislature provided $2,000 in grant funding for a wireless panic alarm system in 2023, which Rep. Emerson Levy (D-District 53) was involved in. “According to the grant information from ODE, the intent of the wireless panic alarm system is that a teacher or other staff member can activate an alarm immediately upon observation of an incident that requires emergency response so that both the emergency responders are notified and the whole school can respond simultaneously,” according to the January 2025 after-action report created by the district after a student brought a loaded gun to Pilot Butte Middle School in 2024. The district ultimately decided the amount of funding was not enough to purchase a wireless alarm system. The district already uses Raptor Technologies for visitor and volunteer management, behavioral threat assessment and early intervention technologies, according to the report. Bend-La Pine Schools already uses cameras throughout the district. Officials have found that cameras are better used as a reactive tool after something has happened. “Cameras could serve as a deterrent to unsafe behavior, but historical incidents show that students know there are cameras in schools and still carry out unsafe behaviors such as fighting or vaping, and even take out their own mobile devices to record themselves conducting these behaviors,” said the January 2025 after-action report.

title: Martin Perry Rakich
author: none
content: Martin Perry Rakich May 20, 1953 – September 16, 2026 Marty Rakich, a beloved husband, father, brother, and friend, passed away peacefully at his home on September 16, 2026, after a courageous battle with cancer and dementia. Born on May 20, 1953, in Fontana, California, Marty was the cherished son of Peter and Patricia (Vogan) Rakich, who preceded him in death. Marty’s life was a testament to resilience, devotion, and kindness. He grew up in Ontario, California, and graduated from Chaffey High School in 1971. He went on to build a successful career in the HVAC business, where his expertise and problem-solving abilities were widely recognized. Marty was known for being able to fix anything and was always ready to offer a solution to whoever needed it. His work ethic and integrity left a lasting impact on those around him. In 1991, Marty married the love of his life, Bev, in a beautiful ceremony in Rancho Cucamonga, California. Together they shared 35 wonderful years of marriage, filled with love and laughter. Marty was a dedicated father to his daughter, Shannon Rose, a loving step father to Chris and Carey Cravens and a supportive brother to his siblings, Dave, Tim, Juli, and Janie. Throughout his life, Marty was an active member of several churches in Central Oregon. His faith was a cornerstone of his life, and he found great joy in daily Bible study. Marty was also deeply committed to supporting Alcoholics Anonymous, celebrating 42 years of sobriety with a spirit of gratitude and humility. Marty found relaxation and fulfillment in his hobbies, which included golfing, fishing, working on his classic car, and planting a garden. Yet, his greatest pleasure came from helping others. Known for his generosity, Marty never charged for his time, believing in the simple joy of lending a helping hand. His kindness and warmth touched countless lives, leaving a legacy of compassion and love. Marty’s family invites those who knew him to join in a celebration of his life on November 7, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. at the Crossing Church in Redmond, Oregon. In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations be made in Marty’s memory to Vern Baardson Ministries, 2501 55 Street S, Unit 316, Fargo, ND 58104. All donations are tax-deductible and will honor Marty’s spirit of giving and service. Marty will be deeply missed by his loving wife Bev, daughter Shannon Rose, brothers Dave and Tim, and sisters Juli and Janie, along with numerous friends and extended family. Though he has left this world, Marty’s kindness and generosity will continue to inspire those who were fortunate enough to have known him.

title: Trump DOJ to send federal monitors to Oregon’s Multnomah County on Election Day
author: none
content: It’s not the first time elections monitors have been sent to Oregon, but the move follows unusual monitor behavior in other states, Oregon election officials said. Federal lawyers on Thursday alerted Oregon officials that they will send election observers to Multnomah County for the Nov. 3 midterm, prompting Oregon’s secretary of state to remind voters about the limited powers those individuals have. It’s not the first time election monitors have been sent to Oregon and to counties in other states. But the type of monitors being deployed, President Donald Trump’s recent attempts to assert federal power over state elections and his continued denial of the results of the 2020 election where he lost to former President Joe Biden are heightening concerns among state leaders. Oregon is, so far, one of at least 10 states that have received notices from the Civil Rights Division of the U.S. Department of Justice notifying election officials that observers will be deployed. The others are Colorado, Florida, Indiana , Maine , Minnesota, Michigan , Texas, Utah and Washington. Harmeet Dhillon, the head of the division, told Fox News last month that the department planned to send 1,000 observers across the country . She characterized it as the “largest monitoring effort” in the agency’s history. Dhillon has repeatedly denied the 2020 presidential election results. DOJ spokespeople did not immediately respond to Oregon Capital Chronicle questions Friday morning regarding how many monitors would be sent to Multnomah County and why the county was selected. Typically monitors are civil lawyers and department support staff who are sent to areas to ensure civil rights laws are enforced at polls. But under Trump, the agency is also deploying criminal prosecutors as monitors for the first time. In a statement Friday, Oregon Secretary of State Tobias Read reminded voters that Oregon’s counties have clear rules for election observers to follow. Monitors are not allowed to talk to election workers, interfere in conversations between election workers and voters, take photos or videos of sensitive information, or handle any ballots or official election materials. Monitors are not allowed to enter restricted election facilities and cannot inspect voting equipment. They also can’t handle ballots or demand access to any election records under state rules. Monitors sent to Wyoming during a primary election earlier this year acted irregularly and aggressively, according to the state’s Republican Gov. Mark Gordon, who asked the Wyoming attorney general’s office to investigate the monitors’ behavior, including requests to examine voting machines. “Oregon’s elections are secure, accurate and fair, and we always welcome observers to watch our American election process unfold,” Read said. “But let’s be clear: It is not legal for these observers or anyone else to interfere with Oregon’s elections — even the Department of Justice. We are prepared. We will follow the law, and we will make sure the Department of Justice does the same.” This article was originally published by Oregon Capital Chronicle and used with permission. Oregon Capital Chronicle is part of States Newsroom and can be reached at info@oregoncapitalchronicle.com.

title: Bend man who killed school shooter says he regrets there were children he didn’t save
author: none
content: The Bend man who fatally shot a teenage gunman to end a deadly rampage at an elementary school last week says he was the children’s “last line of defense” and that he regrets not arriving soon enough to save them all. Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary, where the Oct. 15 attack occurred, said he feels like he failed the families of those who died. “I want to apologize for not saving their babies, that’s probably the biggest thing for me right now,” Giamanco told Oregon Public Broadcasting in an interview published Friday. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome. But there were ones that I didn’t save.” Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the school in Bend, Oregon, last week when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, blasted his way through locked doors with a shotgun and attacked a special needs classroom. Another student was critically injured and a teacher was injured and hospitalized. Police say another teacher threw her phone at the attacker and wrestled with him before Giamanco shot and killed him after following the gunman into the building. Giamanco said he dropped off his daughters at the school that morning before driving to work. A few hours later, the 36-year-old carpenter was passing the school again as he was heading home for lunch. He said he spotted someone wearing black and carrying a long gun fire shots into a pickup truck and at a person mowing the school’s lawn before the shooter climbed a fence and headed toward the school building. Giamanco said “panic fled into my brain.” He grabbed a .40-caliber handgun from his truck’s center console and went after the gunman as he dialed 911. He asked the dispatcher to send help before hanging up his phone. “I said ‘I’m sorry I have to go in. People are going to die,'” Giamanco said in the interview. `This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do’ As he got closer to the building, Giamanco said, he lay on his stomach and used his elbows to crawl across the ground. “That’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives,” he said. “And then I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster. And I told myself: ‘This is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do.'” Giamanco said he entered the school through a window that had been shot out. Peeking into a nearby classroom, he saw a teacher grappling with the shooter. He said he faced them both in profile, giving him an open shot. “I felt like I was the last line of defense between him and the rest of the children,” Giamanco said. He swung the door open, stepped into the room and fired his gun. Both the gunman and the teacher dropped to the floor. The teacher bolted from the room as the shooter reached for his shotgun. “He was scrambling for his weapon,” Giamanco said. “I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move, because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else.” ‘I was supposed to be there’ Police have said Giamanco was carrying his gun legally in his truck and have credited him and the unarmed teacher who confronted the gunman with saving lives. A day after the shootings, President Donald Trump said that Giamanco was a “great hero” who “took care of business.” A second teacher in the classroom, Becky Drury, said in a statement Wednesday that she lay on the floor, helplessly playing dead, after being struck at close range by a shotgun blast that nearly severed her left hand. The teacher who struggled with the shooter hasn’t been publicly identified. Giamanco told the public broadcaster that she’s “a real true hero” whose actions gave him an opening to kill the attacker. “I can’t tell you what it feels like to take a life … but I can tell you that I genuinely feel like I was supposed to be there,” Giamanco said. “If I wasn’t there, I just don’t know what would have happened.”

title: Donations to Silver Rail families, community hit $2 million — and still growing
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: Fundraisers for the Silver Rail community and the families of victims of the Oct. 15 shooting have raised well over $2 million — and that number continues to climb. Oregon Community Foundation is raising funds through two fundraisers: Rapid Response Fund and the Megan Lambert Memorial Fund. There are ten verified fundraisers through GoFundMe , as well as a Meal Train for the Summer family. GoFundMe launched a central hub for verified fundraisers for Silver Rail, which all go through a review process where “technical tools designed to catch misuse” and GoFundMe employees ensure the fundraiser is set up by people who are directly connected to an incident and help set them up as beneficiaries. Donations are processed and only released to the beneficiary. The beneficiary’s personal information must be verified before funds are released, said GoFundMe officials. People across the country have donated more than $685,000 as of Friday for “Support Saylor’s Recovery,” which is directed to 7-year-year-old Saylor Graham-Poarch. She was shot and critically injured and is currently recovering in a hospital. Another $214,000 has been donated to the family of 5-year-old Rhoam Summer, who died in the shooting. Funders have sent more than $413,500 to the family of Kaylub Giamanco, the man who entered the school after the shooter and shot him dead. The Silver Rail community is also collecting donations through Bend-La Pine Schools , as well as the Silver Rail Parent Teacher Organization . Local businesses have matched donations and supported the Silver Rail community as well. And more are in the works as well. Over 130 Dutch Bros. locations will donate $1 from every drink sold Friday to the Silver Rail PTO. Kefi Fast Fresh Mediterranean is donating all of its Friday sales to Silver Rail. 350 Deschutes is donating donations to Silver Rail made between now and Oct. 31. A Shevlin Crossing Art Gallery show starting Oct. 29 will donate proceeds to Silver Rail. The Lot Food Carts and Taproom will host a fundraiser on Sunday with 100% of proceeds going directly to Silver Rail families and students. Key Creative, a boutique design and environmental experience studio based in Bend has raised $10,000 for the Silver Rail PTO by selling prints of the city. The prints include 10 Bend-themed folded notecards and envelopes and can be purchased for $25. Dilly Dally Coffee and Porchllght Coffee donated all proceeds Monday to Silver Rail. Jackson’s Corner provided free sack lunches to any Bend-La Pine Schools students Monday and Tuesday. Mimi’s Bagel Deli, El Rancho Grande, Luckey’s Woodsman, Mountain Burger, Stacks Deli and others have all provided meals for first responders, families, students and school district staff. The Teal Tea & Art Lounge offered space to gather and activities. Dakota’s Brick Shop offered space to play with Legos and Fancywork Yarn Shop offered space for creativity. McMenamins offered free family movies and the High Desert Museum opened its doors as well. Steve Augustyn, the co-owner of Silver Moon Brewing, has a fourth grader who attends the school. Silver Moon held a donation event Wednesday night, where GoodLife Brewing and Cascade Lakes Brewing Co. offered to match all donations. Webfoot Home Improvements, a Central Oregon contractor, also donated $10,000 at the event, according to prior Bulletin reporting. Hawkeye & Huckleberry Lounge hosted a fundraiser Wednesday to support the school, with chef Brian Malarkey matching all donations. The day after the shooting, one aunt brought her nephew, a fifth-grader at Silver Rail, to the restaurant and also offered to match all donations that evening, according to prior Bulletin reporting. Its not just in Bend, either. The Dry Canyon Club in Redmond will host its second annual Pumpkin Painting Party on Saturday and all proceeds from the event will go toward families affected by the Silver Rail shooing in Bend. GoFundMe donations are verified, and a transaction fee is taken out. Meal Train includes both a calendar to set up meals as well as a donation option, which includes a transaction fee. Both organizations require a bank account number for the beneficiary to transfer funds.

title: One serve caps incredible comeback for Crook County volleyball player
author: Brian Rathbone
content: PRINEVILLE — Nerves were high on Senior Night at Crook County for everyone except one person. Hannah Nizich was certainly nervous as she watched her younger sister stand on the baseline, preparing to serve in Wednesday night’s volleyball match against Ridgeview. Nizich even told her as much while they were preparing for the Senior Night ceremony before the match. “I told her I’d be nervous,” Nizich said. Paige Wood, however, was completely calm. Excited, even. “At the end of the day,” Wood said, “it just felt natural.” She tossed the ball over her head and served it across the net, officially starting the match. The Ravens returned the ball and scored the first point. And just like that, Wood, a once-promising volleyball player who was involved in a near-fatal car accident 14 months ago, was subbed out, bringing her high school volleyball career to a close. Her time on the court this season lasted less than a minute. But making it back to the court at all was a triumph. Those handful of seconds in her No. 7 jersey, knee pads and pink Nikes represented months of hard work — and will stay with her long after Wednesday night. “I couldn’t give up on something just because I wasn’t playing,” she said. “That feels like defeat to me, and I said I was going to play this season, and that is what I intended to do.” Wood comes from a volleyball family. Her older sister, Hannah Nizich, formerly Hannah Troutman, was Oregon’s Gatorade Player of the Year and a four-time state champion with the Cowgirls. She was recently inducted into the University of Portland’s Hall of Fame and went on to play volleyball professionally overseas. Wood’s other older sister, Rylee Bales, was part of Ridgeview’s 2019 state championship team before earning All-American honors while playing for Corban University in Salem. Wood once envisioned a similar path, with volleyball taking her to the college level. “Growing up, people are always gonna be better, and you are going to outgrow them,” Wood said. “So this season has been really hard, knowing that I didn’t outbeat their talent. But the way they just showed up for me throughout this journey allowed me to put all of that to the side.” Over the past 14 months, there has been no quit in Wood. She survived the car accident, returned to competition in the javelin and shot put last spring, and, aside from missing practices here and there for various surgeries, remained a regular presence at volleyball practices and games. “She did so much work,” Nizich said. “She had all the physical ailments, but then you’ve got the mental side of it, and you’re talking about taking something from a 17-year-old. It was heartbreaking. “And then to watch her pull herself out of that, and work hard and figure out how to handle things mentally and physically,” Nizich added. “She’s gone through something that most people will never have to go through, thankfully, but she’s handled it with grace.” On Aug. 10, 2025, Wood fell asleep at the wheel while driving home to Prineville from Eugene on state Highway 126, just south of Santiam Pass. The crash left her with devastating injuries. She was trapped for hours before rescuers freed her and she was airlifted to St. Charles Bend with fractures in both legs and her left elbow, retinal damage, a lacerated kidney and a punctured lung. She also suffered multiple strokes after emboli traveled to her brain. Wood underwent extensive surgeries and spent time in a medically induced coma while receiving treatment at Doernbecher Children’s Hospital and OHSU in Portland. Grant Branam, an orthopedic surgeon, happened to be on call the day of the crash. He and his team at St. Charles were tasked with reconstructing Wood’s severely injured legs, with amputation of her left leg a very real possibility. “There was a second when I thought those were threatened limbs,” Branam said. “My goal was to help keep her legs and save her extremities. It is one thing to put bones back into place and realign limbs, but having a functional limb is the other portion. It was a lot of work by a lot of people.” Branam was in attendance at Wednesday’s match, like many others, wearing a Paige Wood volleyball T-shirt. “He’s quite honestly my hero,” Wood said of Branam. “He’s like a family member. He’s one of my biggest supporters.” Much like the track and field season last spring, this volleyball season was, at times, a challenge for Wood. Although she was on the team, she wasn’t able to play the game she loved and had once thrived in. At times, during three-hour practices, she wondered whether getting on the court for a single serve was even worth it. But after she took in the atmosphere of the packed gym, family, friends and supporters quickly put an end to every doubt she might have had. “The amount of love and support I had from each and every person that showed up (Wednesday) night meant everything,” Wood said. “And that’s why I played this season. I was pushed to go further, and I couldn’t give up.”

title: Summit soccer earns wins over Bend after tributes to Silver Rail
author: Brian Rathbone
content: During warmups, it looked as if two teams from the same school were preparing for a scrimmage. One team wore purple, the other white. Both teams wore warmup shirts bearing the Silver Rail Elementary School name. And during player introductions before Thursday night’s matchup between Bend High and Summit girls soccer, a sign reading “Silver Rail Strong” stood in the middle of the field at Summit High. As each player’s name was announced over the PA system, the player placed a rose against the sign. Then, with both teams preparing to play their first match since the Oct. 15 tragedy at Silver Rail (a game that could very well decide the Intermountain Conference title) the teams came together as one. Players interlocked arms in the middle of the field before holding a moment of silence. Players and coaches from both teams worked together to make the tribute possible, honoring the three children and one teacher killed in last week’s shooting. “It was very special that we have such a great community,” said Summit senior captain Coco Skovborg. “Obviously, the rivalry with Bend High is huge, and it always has been. But in this moment, being able to come together and support each other and lean on each other means so much more than the game of soccer.” Then there was a soccer match to be played. A massive one, at that. The Storm once again prevailed over the defending IMC and state champions, earning a thrilling 1-0 victory behind senior Nina Taft’s game-winning goal in the second half. “That one was pure heart and grit,” said Summit coach Kourtney Parks. “It has obviously been a really long week for everyone. We just came together and said, ‘Play with your heart and have some fun.’” And have fun the Storm did. Especially Taft, who broke the scoreless tie midway through the second half when she dribbled around Bend goalkeeper Brooklyn Mettler and buried the ball in the back of the net. Taft then sprinted to the corner with her teammates and kicked the flag in celebration. As much as it was a celebration of a pivotal goal, Taft also wanted to challenge the stereotype that girls soccer players don’t know how to properly celebrate a goal. “That was a big goal, so I needed to make it a big celebration,” Taft said. “I was happy to be able to do it because when the boys do it, it is so hype. When I scored that goal, I couldn’t hear anything. The crowd was so loud, and it was an amazing feeling.” With the way the Storm have defended this season, one goal was all they needed. Summit has conceded just two goals all season and none in eight IMC matches. Kate Mitchell’s performance in goal against the vaunted Lava Bear attack was a huge part of the victory. Bend has scored 54 goals this season, the most of any Class 5A team, but the Lava Bears have yet to get one past Mitchell in two matches against Summit. “I don’t think, I just do,” Mitchell said. “When you get so worked up, the adrenaline makes you feel like you can do anything.” Summit (8-0-3 overall, 6-0-2 IMC) is the only IMC team without a conference loss heading into the final week of the regular season. Bend will host Mountain View on Saturday at 11:30 a.m., while Summit will host Crook County at 2:30 p.m. Summit boys on a scoring tear There was a two-match stretch a couple of weeks ago when the Summit boys soccer team struggled to put the ball in the back of the net. First came a 2-1 win over Bend High on Sept. 29, with both of the Storm’s goals coming on penalty kicks. Then came a 1-0 loss to Redmond on Oct. 1, when Summit was shut out for the first time and suffered its first loss to a conference opponent since 2019. “It was a wake-up call,” said Summit coach Tom Bunnell. “All these teams are going to give you their best.” In the three matches since then, the Storm have outscored their opponents 21-0, including a 5-0 win over Bend in a matchup between two of the state’s top-ranked teams Thursday afternoon at 15th Street Field in Bend. The Storm now stand alone atop the IMC standings heading into the final week of the regular season. “We have to hold ourselves to a super-high standard,” said Summit senior defender Max Pagano. “We know what we are capable of, and we just need to continue to put that together. We can’t let our foot off the gas. Every team in our league is super solid.” Five different Storm players scored against the Lava Bears. In the 15th minute, junior Nash Orton broke the scoreless tie by slotting a shot off the post and into the net on an assist from Pagano. Orton’s goal proved to be the game-winner. But the Storm weren’t done. Junior Will Newton blasted a shot from just outside the box in the 50th minute to give Summit a 2-0 advantage. Minutes later, senior Owen Gassner made it 3-0. After winning a quick game of rock-paper-scissors with a couple of teammates for the chance to take a free kick, senior Phoenix Page converted his opportunity into another Summit goal. Junior Cole Carter got in on the scoring action in the closing minutes to cap the Storm’s dominant win. “We have never had a problem creating chances,” Orton said. “I think we have had to do a better job finishing, and we proved that we can.” Both the Storm and Lava Bears will return to the field Saturday. Summit will play at Crook County at 2:30 p.m., while Bend will visit Mountain View at 11:30 a.m.

title: Letters: Readers write in about Oregon’s 2026 election and shooting
author: none
content: Betz for judge I have been a long-time resident of Bend since 1994. I got to know Thad several years ago in a professional setting as an attorney. I found him to be a good listener, well prepared, competent, and focused on fairness. These are the attributes of an impartial and fair Judge. I highly recommend and encourage people vote for him as it would help Deschutes County be a better place. Victoria Smith, Bend Betz for judge I have worked on both sides of the courtroom, serving 17 years as a Public Defender in Seattle/King County followed by 14 years as a Special Assistant United States Attorney in seven federal judicial districts. Thad Betz has spent much of his career as a defense and civil rights attorney. Experience matters. I have known Thad for 13 years. In that time I have seen in him the qualities that matter most in a judge: he prepares relentlessly, he listens before he speaks, and he treats everyone in the room with respect, whether they’re a victim, a defendant, a police officer, or a fellow lawyer. A good judge doesn’t hear a case with a predetermined view or bias, but rather examines the facts, applies the law and makes sure every person leaves the courtroom knowing they were heard. Thad has argued in courts at every level, from circuit courts across Oregon to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and the Oregon Supreme Court. He knows how a courtroom should work because he has seen it from every angle. It’s no surprise that prosecutors, defense attorneys, and judges across Oregon, including so many justices of the Oregon Supreme Court, support him. Please join me in voting for Thad Betz for Deschutes County Circuit Court Judge, Position 3. Nancy Mishalanie, Bend No on commission map One of the bedrock principles of democracy is majority rule. Any districting map should respect this principle; the makeup of an elected body should reflect the will of the majority of voters. Unfortunately, the county commissioner district map proposed in Measure 9-185 fails this critical test. If we look at precinct-by-precinct 2024 election results for offices where all voters in the county had the same choices and total the votes according to the proposed map, we find that although the Republican party candidate received a minority of the votes countywide for each of those offices, the party would have won three of the five commissioner seats. As an example, the 2024 Republican presidential candidate received 54,850 votes countywide (43% of votes cast), while the Democratic candidate received 68,108 votes (53%), yet when broken down by proposed commissioner district, the Republican candidate would have received more votes in proposed districts 3, 4, and 5. Whether or not the committee that drew the district lines intended this result is beside the point; the end result is that one party can gain a majority of the commissioner seats with a minority of the votes cast, a decidedly undemocratic result. Reasonable minds can disagree on the best method of electing commissioners, but I would hope that we could all agree that the vote of the majority should be respected. Please vote No on Measure 9-185. Scott Stevenson, Bend District failed students James Baldwin thought us that all of the children are ours but in Oregon, we don’t see superintendent Steven Cook talk about the how the Bend-La Pine School District failed to identify a youth at risk and provide the intervention needed to prevent the horrific incident at Silver Rail Elementary. During the leadership of Ron Wilkinson or Shay Mikalson we didn’t hear of as many gun related deaths of minors like we see now under Steven Cook’s leadership. I can’t help to notice how post pandemic the emphasis has being on academic achievement, rather than developing social-emotional skills. Cutting support staff and having resource officers with zero pedagogy background around vulnerable youth creates an oppressive culture rather than a culture of acceptance and belonging for youth struggling to find their place in a world that easily discards of humans without social, political and economic power. Those who we trust to lead our youth need to take accountability for the road they have let us on. Joanne Mina, Bend Huntsman for judge Why am I voting for Sonia Huntsman? Because I care deeply about Deschutes County and about justice. A judge hears a wide variety of cases, and Sonia is well prepared to show up on day one. She has 20 years of legal experience in many areas, giving her a broad and deep understanding of the law that stands out among the other candidates. Sonia’s experience in criminal law includes service as both a deputy district attorney and a public defender. She’s worked hundreds of cases including major felonies, Measure 11 offenses, misdemeanors and child dependency cases. She understands the justice system from both sides of the courtroom and as a judge, she will treat everyone in her courtroom with fairness, dignity, and respect. Sonia is the only candidate with deep experience in family law. For a large part of her career, she focused on child welfare and domestic violence. She also navigated emotional and complex cases around custody, parenting time, property issues, and estate planning. Sonia pursued a custody and spousal support case all the way to the Oregon Court of Appeals, earning a rare win. There are a range of qualified candidates on the ballot, but none have Sonia’s balance of depth and breadth of legal experience. She’s the right choice for us, and I encourage you to vote Sonia Huntsman for Deschutes County Judge. She’s the best qualified for the job and will serve our community well. Susan Gregory, Bend Guns and Measure 114 Following the tragedy at Silver Rail, there have been multiple news organizations that have cited Everytown’s ranking of Oregon having the “12th” strongest gun laws in the country. Similarly, Giffords grades Oregon as a B+. These grades are incorrect because they rank Oregon on laws that aren’t in effect. In reality, Oregon’s gun laws remain a C+. In 2022, Oregon passed Measure 114, which required permitting, banned high capacity magazines commonly used in mass and school shootings, and required safety training before purchasing a firearm. This was brought to the ballot by Oregon voters, passed, and should be in effect today. Research from Johns Hopkins University has shown that hundreds of lives would have already been saved in Oregon had Measure 114 been in place. Instead, the law is still tied up in court, with the lawsuits backed by out-of-state gun industry lobby groups. When you report on Oregon gun laws, please reflect actual laws in effect today. Many Oregonians believe Oregon already has a waiting period and full background checks. In reality, we have no waiting period and today, a gun can be transferred from a dealer to a buyer after 3 days if the background check hasn’t been completed. The data show repeatedly that states with stronger gun laws have fewer school shootings. Without Measure 114, Oregon’s gun laws have long been ranked a C+ (Giffords Score Rank). This is where we remain today. Kat Baviera, Bend Abbie says yes on commission map My dog Abbie is very smart. Despite being an obedience school dropout, she has a set of highly developed analytical skills. That came apparent as I was going over the ballot and the voter’s pamphlet. I had them both out of the coffee table for review. She came and sat beside me as I was reading the candidate’s statements and the Measure 9-185 statements. I read them aloud so Abbie could assess each statement. If the statement supported voting for electing county commissioners by district, a yes vote, she would give out a small bark; if the statement opposed the measure, a no vote, she growled. Later Abbie somehow noticed that the pamphlet had city council candidate statements for La Pine, Redmond and Sisters but they were missing from my ballot. I told her that they are not on my ballot because we don’t live near there and should not be involved in their decisions. They have their own concerns and interests, and it is best that they choose their own officials. It is an example of why measure 9-185 should be approved. Abbie barked a twice. Abbie dozed through the Bend mayor and council candidate readings. She knows from my grumping about squeezed traffic lanes and costly bike lanes, that I am not enthralled with our city leadership. She agrees with me that rural residents should be wary of letting Bendites set their priorities. Abbie hopes measure 9-185 will pass because if it does she expects extra treats. Jared Black, Bend Thank you Allan Jet Blanchard We should all be thankful for young people like Allan Jet Blanchard. In the aftermath of tragedy, and in the midst of mourning, his Guest Column thoughtfully and rightfully calls out our individual and collective apathy. What action will we take after the prayers have ended and the candles are extinguished? If all we do is fortify our schools or blame our gun-owning neighbors, and then fall back into our mindless apathy, then we have missed another chance. Why can’t we lift the scales from our eyes, and start caring about the troubled kid next door? Why won’t we dip into our comfortable incomes and give our teachers and schools the resources and training they need to recognize and help the needy ones in our midst? Vigils and murmured ‘thoughts and prayers’ aren’t enough. Let’s look beyond the physical and mental fences we’re erected, and beyond the locked doors of our schools, and recognize that the difficulties facing all young people in our community are inherently our own troubles. It’s time we started caring, and time we started acting tangibly and personally. Thank you, Allan Jet Blanchard, for helping to open our eyes. Paul White, Bend Oregon needs governor who cares about prevention Our community is devastated by the heartbreaking tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary. No words can truly capture the magnitude of this loss. In the coming months, our state must come together and focus on what matters most — keeping our kids safe. Who we elect for governor will have a major impact. Christine Drazan is an extremist backed by the gun lobby. She has consistently voted against gun safety throughout her time in the legislature, including laws supported by most Oregonians. Drazan is endorsed by the NRA and has an A rating from their organization. No single law or policy can prevent every single shooting, but over and over, research shows that states with stronger gun laws have fewer school shootings and fewer gun deaths. At a time when the leading cause of death for American children is firearms, we must look at the actual evidence and data. We’re not asking legislators to take away guns. We’re asking them to implement laws that actually work. Oregon’s ERPO law prevents mass shootings — and in 2023, an ERPO helped prevent a tragedy right here at Smith Rock. Prevention works. But it requires leaders willing to act. Drazan has made her priorities clear, and Oregon deserves a governor who respects firearm ownership while prioritizing our children’s safety. Molly Winters, Bend No Kings and Silver Rail The October 20th Bulletin had an article titled “Bend residents at ‘No Kings’ protest mobilized by shooting”. What kind of twisted reasoning would think that the No Kings protest had anything to do with the Silver Rail tragedy? Perhaps, they think that President Trump was somehow responsible for Silver Rail? If that is the case, prove it! Just maybe, the people/party who think that we can actually control the weather/climate of the earth and has the majority support of the national media are the actual King wannabees? All they need now is political power and a figure head as leader. History tells us that to be a king/dictator one must have control of the national media. President Trump doesn’t have that and never will. Let’s not use the tragedy at Silver Rail grade school to push a political agenda of any sort. Tom Clark, Redmond

title: In Bend, across state, voters have approved hundreds of millions for school safety as shootings rise
author: none
content: Oregon voters have agreed to school bonding measures to pay for secure entries, cameras and fences to mitigate the risk of a tragedy like the Silver Rail shooting. More than 100 of Oregon’s 197 school districts have asked voters in the past eight years to agree to local property tax increases to raise money for school safety upgrades. That’s according to a Capital Chronicle analysis of ballot referrals to the Oregon Secretary of State’s Office, available online only through 2018, and a database of bond results provided by the Oregon School Boards Association. In 53 of those districts, voters have said yes — sending more than $6 billion to schools for infrastructure projects that also include hundreds of millions of dollars for school modernization and security investments such as automatic locking doors, fences, gates, hardened glass windows, alarm systems and other measures meant to mitigate the risk of a tragedy like last week’s shooting at Silver Rail elementary in Bend. A teen gunman entered the school building on the afternoon of Oct. 15 after climbing a fence and shooting through the windows of a locked side door — two security measures that slowed but did not stop him from getting into a classroom, where he then opened fire. He killed three children and a teacher before he was stopped by another teacher and an armed parent who followed the shooter inside and shot him. Voters in the Bend-La Pine School District are among those who approved school safety spending in bond votes taken in 2017 and 2022, and Silver Rail was a beneficiary of those dollars. The school has a secure front door and shatter-proof glass vestibule where guests are vetted before being able to enter the school halls, and updated door locks among other security measures, The Bulletin reported . “In my own experience, just about every school has a locked door and some sort of electronic doorbell, and that wasn’t the case 10 years ago,” said Oregon School Boards Association spokesperson Jake Arnold. “Pretty much every bond campaign I’ve looked at since at least 2020 mentioned safety improvements.” Nine more school districts are asking voters in November to approve school bonding projects that include school security and safety measures. They include the Gladstone, Glide, Grants Pass, Harney County, Hillsboro, North Clackamas, Reynolds, Silver Falls and Siuslaw school districts. Installing a single secure entrance at all school buildings is among the most common investments districts have made in recent years, Arnold said. Many schools have also invested in fences and exterior doors that can only be opened with key cards. In nearly half of all approved bonds that included safety measures, districts sought funding to replace and upgrade security cameras, which are now seen across schools from the elementary to high school level in much of the state. Voters in Lake Oswego passed two bonds that paid for school safety upgrades in 2021 and 2025. The 2025 bond was, of the two, most centered on school safety investments, and included plans to install new secure classroom doors, hardened glass, expand the number of security cameras in district schools and upgrade its emergency communications systems. West Linn-Willsonville, Oregon City and Redmond school districts have all passed two voter-approved bonds each to cover security spending in the last eight years. But just as home hardening against arson does not guarantee a house won’t burn down, security investments can only reduce the possibility or severity of a tragedy, school officials said. “While no system can 100% prevent determined acts of violence, thoughtful and modern security features can help lessen the chances and the impact of terrible situations,” said Kelly McIver, a spokesperson for the Eugene School District, in an email. McIver cautioned against the public seeing these investments as preventing a tragedy like the one at Silver Rail. Instead, people should think of them as risk reduction. “They also can help lower the odds of more common, less dire threats like vandalism, theft and unauthorized visitors,” he said. Voters in Eugene approved a 2018 capital bond measure that raised more than $319 million. Nearly $8.5 million of that went to school safety upgrades, including secure entry vestibules, security cameras, fencing and anti-shatter window film that is hard to break through. The district will in the next few years have invested in safety improvements at every one of its 32 instructional sites, McIver said. 2018 was among the worst years for school shootings in the U.S., according to the K-12 School Shooting Database . It was also among the worst years for mass shootings in American schools — where three or more people are killed — according to The Violence Prevention Project , the largest database of mass shootings in the U.S. run by Metro State University in Minnesota. The number of shootings at K-12 schools in the U.S. about doubled between 2017 and 2018, going from 60 to nearly 120. The number dipped during COVID when schools were closed in most of the country and has since risen dramatically since 2021, when a record 257 incidents of shootings at K-12 schools in the U.S. occurred, according to the School Shooting Database. A record 36 mass shooting incidents occurred in 2022, and 35 more followed in 2024, according to the Violence Prevention Project. A record number of fatalities also occurred in 2022, with 59 people killed and another 49 injured in mass shootings at schools. So far this year, the School Shooting Database researchers have recorded 155 shootings at schools and 118 wounded or killed victims. Most school shootings occur in parking lots outside of the buildings themselves, and in front of doors before anyone ever enters. Most school shootings in the U.S. occur at high schools, and most perpetrators are former students. This article was originally published by Oregon Capital Chronicle and used with permission. Oregon Capital Chronicle is part of States Newsroom and can be reached at info@oregoncapitalchronicle.com.

title: Commentary: What people and computers say about the Northwest power supply
author: none
content: When you use an artificial intelligence system like ChatGPT, what it gives you depends on the prompt you enter. The answer is likely to be most useful if the prompt is carefully crafted. This underlies a concern recently raised at the Northwest Power and Conservation Council. That regional planning agency uses computer modeling (think AI-adjacent) to analyze data to help develop its proposals and policies for matching electric power resources with need. But some of the outputs raise questions about inputs. The council’s computer tools include the GENESYS (Generation Evaluation System) model, as well along as OptGen/SDDP, AURORA and Itron. Use of such tools is likely to become much more common soon in government and corporate planning and management. And the council, based in Portland, describes its latest power and conservation plan (its ninth) as “a regional strategy for new, cost-effective resource additions to meeting growing power needs over the coming years … recommending new conservation, demand response, voltage regulation, renewables, storage, and natural gas to the system.” There’s a lot at stake here: Power bills, water supply, economic development, power outages, fish runs. The plan went public earlier this year and comment on it closed Oct. 16. At the Portland public hearing on Sept. 9 , Margaret Hoffmann, a council member from Oregon who chaired the meeting, said the plan “does put forward a mix of demand-side resources. … Renewables are key to the strategy, particularly combined with storage that can provide energy and capacity while meeting the clean goals. The draft plan does include new natural gas that can provide energy to the system, particularly in times of low hydro conditions where there’s just less water coming down the system. And all of these are supported by some additional recommendations around how to think about transmission.” The council’s longstanding goals have been to plan for adequate power for the region while also protecting the environment, notably including salmon runs. That second element seems a little downplayed in the new plan. One of the speakers at the hearing suggested how this might have happened. Patti Kramer with the Climate, Energy and Environment Team of the Consolidated Oregon Indivisible Network, a coalition of left-leaning activist groups, was concerned that the plan didn’t engage with calls for breaching the four lower Snake River dams in Washington state. “I am concerned that there is no explicit reference to dam breaching in the text of the plan,” Kramer said. “The Northwest Power Plan requires the council, as we know, to provide an analysis of cost-effective methods to provide electric power at the lowest cost. It also mandates the council to develop the power plan while taking into account fish and wildlife impact. The council uses the computer modeling tool, GENESYS, to simulate the operation of the regional power system to assess the adequacy of the power supply, given uncertain future conditions.” It could have been used to fully calculate the various costs and advantages of various dam options, but “It has not been used to do this, however.” She said the issue also arose during development of plan eight about five years ago, but then too “it is our understanding that the — this analysis was not carried out. We respectfully request that the council run GENESYS models without the four lower Snake River dams and include plans for this analysis in the 9th Power Plan.” The request was not to avoid using the tools, but to expand the data and parameters fed into them. Council staff have acknowledged the need for adjustments. A March 3 memo from a system analyst to the council, for example, said that “as part of final testing and preparation for the OptGen analysis, staff identified a need to reconfigure the GENESYS setup to further align model assumptions. The resulting change focused on updating balancing reserve alignments, and it required rerunning the needs assessment to calculate new adequacy reserve margins for all sensitivities included in the Ninth Plan.” Using these computer-driven models makes sense. The mass complexity of the Northwest power system, its inputs and outflows, make new ways of tracking and analyzing immense amounts of data become necessary. But it also highlights the role of the humans involved in overseeing the system, who have an even larger responsibility and a harder task in watching the inputs, assumptions and directions given to the programs, so the region gets the end result it wants. And as other governments (and private entities too) move in the direction of getting help from computer models, AI and otherwise, as they will, they should start developing human guidelines to ensure the models don’t run off in directions unwanted or unforeseen by the people who will have to live with the policy results that emerge from them. Randy Stapilus has researched and written about Northwest politics and issues since 1976 for a long list of newspapers and other publications. A former newspaper reporter and editor, and more recently an author and book publisher, he lives in Carlton. This article was originally published by Oregon Capital Chronicle and used with permission. Oregon Capital Chronicle is part of States Newsroom and can be reached at info@oregoncapitalchronicle.com.

title: Cascade Natural Gas abandons Knott Landfill renewable gas project
author: Michael Kohn
content: Cascade Natural Gas has decided not to move forward with a proposed renewable natural gas facility at Deschutes County’s Knott Landfill, citing rising development costs and changes in the company’s projected demand for the fuel. The company and the county have worked together since 2023 on a project to capture methane produced by decomposing waste at the Bend landfill and convert it into renewable natural gas. The project had reached the final design stage, and construction was expected to begin soon, said Jeff Merwin, director of Deschutes County Solid Waste. Equipment, including a compressor skid, a thermal oxidizer stack and large electrical panels, had already been delivered to the landfill in preparation for construction. All development and equipment costs incurred so far were paid by Cascade Natural Gas, Merwin said. Plans also called for installing 45 additional vertical gas extraction wells this spring, with further phases planned over the next five years as the landfill continued to fill. Cascade notified the county last week that it would discontinue the project, Merwin said. The company cited higher-than-anticipated construction costs and changes to Oregon’s Climate Protection Program that affected the timing and volume of its renewable natural gas needs. Cascade said projected development costs had increased significantly over the past three years, making the project no longer a prudent investment for its customers. “Bend is an important community to Cascade, and we value Deschutes County’s partnership,” said Hart Gilchrist, the company’s vice president of business development and external affairs. “While we are disappointed this project will not move forward, our commitment to Bend and our customers has not changed,” Gilchrist said. The project was intended to put landfill gas now burned off through flaring to productive use. Captured methane would have been cleaned to remove contaminants and then sent through a pipeline for local consumption. Deschutes County Solid Waste is evaluating alternatives for making productive use of the methane generated at Knott Landfill, Merwin said. Cascade said it will continue working with the county to take the steps needed to conclude the project.

title: Low-flying helicopters to survey region’s geologic resources
author: Jayson Jacoby | Baker City Herald
content: BAKER CITY — Helicopters equipped with an unusual accessory will be flying at low altitudes over parts of Baker County and other sections of Eastern Oregon helicopter this fall to measure tiny changes in the Earth’s magnetic field that can help geologists find underground deposits of valuable and rare elements and minerals. The flights, which are scheduled to start Oct. 26, weather permitting, also can pinpoint groundwater sources, geothermal potential, and faults that can generate earthquakes, according to geologists. The sensors attached to a proboscis-like probe that extends in front of the helicopters allow geologists to create maps of underground features that can’t be mapped accurately based on traditional ground surveys. The device that extends from below the helicopter’s nose is a sensor that measures the magnetic field 10 times per second. The project, which started in the fall of 2025, will continue this fall until significant snow falls, then resume in the spring of 2027 once the snow melts. Snow reduces the quality of the data collected, said Alex Lopez, public affairs coordinator for the Oregon Department of Geology and Mineral Industries. The state agency is partnering with the U.S. Geological Survey on the latter agency’s Earth Mapping Resources Initiative. The project is designed to modernize the nation’s maps of geology and mineral resources. “Partnership with state surveys helps accomplish national goals like mapping the critical minerals the U.S. needs” Jamey Jones, science coordinator for the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, said in a press release. “The Oregon Department of Geology & Mineral Industries is helping with the work of the nation — and adding to state knowledge crucial to water resources, hazards and the resource economy.” “This 2026 airborne geophysical survey is of significant scale and in an area that has been a department focus for some years,” Oregon State Geologist Ruarri Day-Stirrat said in the press release. Although the survey covers parts of six counties, the vast majority is in eastern Grant County and far western Baker County. According to the state geology department, historical mining records in the area show the presence of critical elements such as antimony, chromium, cobalt, copper, nickel, silver, tungsten and zinc, in addition to precious and base metals. Some of those elements are needed for rechargeable batteries used in electric vehicles and many other products. The region also has the most potential in Oregon for natural hydrogen sources, according to the geology department. Flights will be based from several airports and rural airstrips, including Baker City Airport. Helicopters will fly on weekdays and weekends, weather permitting, and only during daylight, Lopez said. The sensors attached to the helicopter are passive, meaning they don’t emit energy, according to the geology department. The helicopter will not take any photographs or video images during the surveys, according to the agency. The helicopter will fly about 330 feet above the ground in most areas, flying a pre-planned grid pattern with flight paths spaced about 660 feet apart. The U.S. Geological Survey hired New Sense Geophysics and the Merrick-Surdex Joint Venture to provide the AS350 helicopters. Different types of rocks have different effects on the magnetic field, so the aerial survey data can help geologists interpret rock formations below the ground, Jason McClaughry, geological survey and service program manager at the geology department’s Baker City office, said in a 2025 interview. Another sensor attached to the helicopter estimates the concentrations of radioactive elements potassium, uranium and thorium in the underground rocks by measuring the natural gamma radiation those rocks emit. McClaughry said geologists can compare those results with lab tests of rock samples collected on the ground to further refine geologic maps.

title: Redmond concerned about irrigation pipeline’s impact on groundwater
author: Michael Kohn
content: Redmond is shifting from a potential legal challenge to a collaborative effort to address groundwater concerns as the Central Oregon Irrigation District moves ahead with plans to pipe 18.5 miles of the Pilot Butte Canal between Bend and Redmond. The Redmond City Council decided this week not to pursue a legal challenge to the project’s environmental impact statement, instead seeking to work with irrigation districts and other basin partners on a program to replenish groundwater, according to a letter from Mayor Ed Fitch to irrigation district officials. ShanRae Hawkins, a spokesperson with Central Oregon Irrigation District, confirmed to The Bulletin that there is no legal dispute between the irrigation district and the city. The proposed approach could involve directing some winter water releases from the Deschutes River to areas where the water could seep into the ground and replenish the aquifer that supplies Redmond and rural residents with drinking water. The proposal remains in its early stages, however, and its feasibility has not been evaluated by the state. “We are involved in ongoing discussions with basin partners,” said Jason Cox, a spokesperson for the Oregon Water Resources Department. “An application for this project has not yet been filed so we have not yet done the analysis needed to assess the project’s feasibility.” Piping impacts The city’s decision follows weeks of discussions with Central Oregon Irrigation District, North Unit Irrigation District and other regional partners about the potential effects of piping the canal, which currently loses water through seepage into the ground. That water does replenish the underground aquifer that many residents and the city of Redmond taps for drinking water. Redmond relies on groundwater and has raised concerns that reducing seepage — caused by piping the canal — could seriously affect the aquifer. The city has also been working to address state requirements related to groundwater management. In his letter, Fitch said representatives from Redmond, COID and North Unit met Oct. 13. The City Council later heard public comments from North Unit patrons, and a city delegation met with state representatives in Salem.
