Fitch described that meeting as positive and said the city was cautiously optimistic about the discussions. Redmond has also discussed the issue with other Central Oregon cities, the Deschutes River Conservancy, the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs and commissioners from Deschutes and Jefferson counties. The Central Oregon Cities Organization and consultants from GSI Water Solutions are expected to work with irrigation district representatives and other basin partners to develop a memorandum of understanding, Fitch wrote. The city hopes the agreement will help the partners pursue grant or legislative funding for an aquifer recharge study. Under the concept discussed by the city, some water that North Unit is required to release during winter to support Oregon spotted frog habitat could potentially be routed to locations where it would infiltrate the ground and help replenish the aquifer. Fitch estimated that the effects of canal piping could emerge over three to five years. The city hopes a recharge effort could help stabilize groundwater levels, protect domestic wells in Deschutes and Jefferson counties, and help Redmond meet its obligations under state law. Delay warning The canal modernization project is intended to reduce water losses and improve the efficiency of irrigation deliveries. But North Unit Irrigation District officials have warned that delaying or halting piping could affect farmers who depend on conserved water from projects in the Deschutes Basin. North Unit serves more than 950 irrigators and about 59,000 acres of farmland in Jefferson County. Its growers produce specialty crops, including hybrid carrot seed, according to district General Manager Josh Bailey. As a junior water-right holder, North Unit relies heavily on Wickiup Reservoir and is vulnerable to water shortages. Earlier this month, Bailey told Redmond City Council members that conserved water from COID piping projects, along with piping in other districts, is expected to be shared with North Unit and other junior water-right holders. The water savings will improve water availability for farmers. It also helps North Unit make more water available for winter flows in the Upper Deschutes River, which are required under the Deschutes Basin Habitat Conservation Plan, intended to protect the Oregon spotted frog and fish. North Unit must increase winter releases from Wickiup Reservoir under the plan regardless of whether additional conserved water is available. Without that water, Bailey said, farmers could face greater shortages while the district’s environmental obligations remain unchanged. “We do believe there are solutions worth exploring, including opportunities for aquifer recharge, and allocating conserved water to help meet municipal needs,” Bailey told the council. “These changes require collaboration, not litigation.” Bailey urged the council not to pursue litigation that could halt or delay COID’s piping projects, saying farmers, communities and the environment all depend on continued progress. Farmers, ranchers and Jefferson County Commissioner Seth Taylor also raised concerns to city council at the meeting earlier this month. Millions secured COID has secured $66.9 million for the Pilot Butte Canal Modernization Project, including $25 million through the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service Regional Conservation Partnership Program. Another $5.9 million is sourced from the state of Oregon and $21 million comes from the Inflation Reduction Act funding, according to Hawkins, the COID spokesperson. The district also has $15 million in USDA funding, pending final contract execution, which Hawkins said was anticipated within 90 days. COID General Manager Craig Horrell said the district has already spent $42 million on Pilot Butte Canal piping that has been installed. That work has been completed near Redmond. “As with all grants, we need to spend what we have before we can ask for additional funds,” Horrell said. “We continue to work hard to ensure that the funds we have been utilizing continue to be available.” The project’s final environmental impact statement was published in August. The Natural Resources Conservation Service was expected to issue a record of decision before the end of the year, Hawkins said. COID anticipated ordering pipe for the project in November or December and beginning portions of construction as approvals allow.

title: Election 2026: Investigations, accusations pepper another sheriff’s race
author: Emily Rogers
content: The Deschutes County Sheriff’s race has transformed into a soap opera, pitting two candidates against each other while each faces an internal investigation. There is also mudslinging and complaints of campaign law misconduct. It’s nothing new to the citizens of Deschutes County, after through the 2024 sheriff’s race and countless others. But both candidates — Ty Rupert and James “Mac” McLaughlin — said they hope to make a difference in the culture of the office to prevent the soap opera from entering another season. Differences lie, however, in how they believe that shift can be done. James ‘Mac’ McLaughlin McLaughlin has 19 years of experience at the Deschutes County Sheriff’s Office, working as a task force officer, SWAT team commander, detective and patrol sergeant on the major incident team, street crimes detective and currently as detective lieutenant leading the detective division. Before working for the sheriff’s office, McLaughlin served in the U.S. Marine Corps, worked as a production supervisor at Nosler Inc. and was an ordained Christian minister at Eagle Mountain Church in Bend. On June 5 McLaughlin was placed on administrative leave by Rupert due to an independent internal investigation into McLaughlin covering up his own and other officers’ alleged misconduct related to a SWAT team arrest on Feb. 25. Jim Band, an independent investigator hired by Rupert, sustained five allegations against McLaughlin, including dishonesty, misconduct, lack of integrity and insubordination. Since Sept. 3, McLaughlin has been on medical family leave, putting any discipline from the investigation’s findings on hold until he returns to work. If elected in November, McLaughlin could decide his own discipline. “I look forward to ardently defending myself against the majority of these allegations,” McLaughlin said. “I have no problem being corrected. I have no problem owning my mistakes. I do have a problem when I believe my honor is being used against me, and I believe that things are untrue, and there are things inside this investigation that I do believe are untrue.” McLaughlin believes that the investigation and paid administrative leave Rupert put him on are a part of political theater that recall past elections in the long-troubled department. Rupert, on the other, said he has no political motivation for his actions. “Just because you’re running for office or you’re a certain person or whatever it is, does not mean that you are exempt from being held accountable, including myself,” Rupert said. In light of the pattern of an increase in internal investigations during election season, McLaughlin’s top priority if elected is to introduce a community advisory council and an independent ombudsman to oversee external and internal complaints. “I think those two tangible pieces can piggyback into a more ethereal culture building and change the direction of the agency as a whole,” McLaughlin said. The sheriff’s office balances a $72.2 million budget, which is 16% of the county’s $446.1 million budget. McLaughlin emphasized long-term planning over short-term savings and focusing on reducing recidivism to save taxpayers money. To lower recidivism, McLaughlin wants to expand the inmate work crew program by partnering with small businesses, construction outfits and unions in Deschutes County to certify inmates once they complete specialized technical skills. “We can start doing that with our work crews, get them certified in wildland firefighting or different things like that so that there is purpose for them when they leave, instead of just a brown paper bag when they walk out the door without a place to stay, with no transitional housing,” McLaughlin said. McLaughlin would also like to focus on crime prevention by establishing specialized units for digital forensics and street crimes, as well as an internal exchange program to move personnel between corrections and patrol. “Instead of me having to reinvent the wheel and go outside all the time for some of these specialty groups, I’m now training within,” McLaughlin said. “That is not a 100-day model at all. That would take years (but) I ca take some corrections deputies who are interested in digital forensics, and I exchange program them. That doesn’t cost us dollars. It’s body for body.” McLaughlin says he has a more intelligence-based approach and openness for new technology. “I think it’s part of the future of law enforcement in that we do have technology at our fingertips,” he said. “It’s the matter of utilizing it and dispersing that information that makes us more effective.” McLaughlin would like to see a more technology-forward approach, noting that there’s been “too many near misses” with preventing crimes against children, elder fraud and drug trafficking when not adapting to new technologies. “We have to develop a deeper level of speciality when it comes to intercepting drug traffickers through Highway 97 through the Highway 20 corridors … be able to interdict those and look for the signs that we quite frankly don’t do,” McLaughlin said. “Operationally, we do not have a ‘check-the-box’ search warrant for reasonable suspicion on interdiction to get into a vehicle with a canine alert for narcotics … that’s a problem. That means that those traffic stops that we normally would have had, where we could use basic techniques, right now we can’t because of law.” McLaughlin supports the sheriff’s office in using license plate reader cameras in exigent circumstances like Measure 11 crimes, protecting children and addressing imminent threats to life. “I don’t believe law enforcement should be without (technology), but I believe that it has to be restrained very tightly, and it has to be restrained by people with the operational skill set and understanding, and people outside of law enforcement that can mitigate some of those decisions and get very clear lines in the sand,” McLaughlin said. “And right now, I think those lines are very gray.” Ty Rupert Interim sheriff Rupert has 21 years of law enforcement experience and 15 years of private sector experience focusing on budgeting and management skills. Rupert started as a reserve deputy in 2005 and has risen through every rank at the sheriff’s office. Prior to working in law enforcement, Rupert was the vice president of Redmond-based auto parts manufacturer Fuel Safe Systems and served in the U.S. Marine Corps. Rupert’s experience in both the private sector and throughout the sheriff’s office is one of the main things he believes sets him apart as a candidate. “As a sheriff, I need to know the operation of the entire agency,” Rupert said. “It’s like being a captain of a ship. I need to know everything from the top of the ship all the way to the engine, the operations, everything. Because when I make decisions, it’s going to affect the entire organization.” Prior to being appointed interim sheriff by Deschutes County Commissioner, Rupert wrote in his letter of interest that he intends to restore morale and trust, address staffing needs, foster community engagement and ensure fiscal responsibility. In the last 15 months, Rupert feels he has made good on his promises, highlighting new body-worn cameras, new evidence system, hiring new laterals, hosting town halls, introducing a health and wellness coordinator, and balancing the budget throughout his interim. “A lateral employee is a certified police officer from another agency; they get to pick and choose where they want to work,” Rupert said. “They’re coming to our office for a reason. They’re not coming there because of the culture that used to be there. They’re coming there because they see that shift in culture and they want to be a part of the change.” Rupert also believes he changed the culture by hosting the office’s first award ceremony to recognize excellence among employees and hiring the first female canine deputy in the office’s history. “Just trying to change that perception of this club,” Rupert said. “There is no club. We’re all on the same team.” Rupert would like to introduce a citizen advisory board within the next year made up of seven or nine community members. “I want people to better understand our office,” Rupert said. “It’s another way for me to hopefully help rebuild the trust of the community.” In his first nine months, Rupert saved over $1 million in the 2026 to 2027 fiscal year, allowing him to repurpose the money to hire more patrol and jail staff. When Rupert introduced Axon body-cameras to the sheriff’s office, he chose not to enable license plate readers for two reasons: the public concern of personal privacy and the cost to the office. Axon cost $2.4 million, and adding on license plate readers would take away from money needed to hire more jail and patrol deputies. “I’m always going to put the concern of privacy first because there are really ways to try and track people besides license plate readers … because it’s been done for years without that technology,” Rupert said. In the same vein of privacy, Rupert discussed sanctuary laws and how he would not give U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement information on immigrant inmates. He mentioned the local case of a non-American man who was arrested and charged with a serious crime in Deschutes County. “He ( Rajinder Kumar ) was in our custody, and for weeks federal agents were swarming this area, waiting for him to get released to be picked up,” Rupert said. “They were camped out in my parking lot. They were hoping that we would tell him when he was going to get released, and I won’t tell them. My staff won’t tell them because we can’t.” In 2025, Ty Rupert signed a letter with 34 other Oregon sheriffs seeking legal clarity on their legal obligations under the Oregon Sanctuary Promise Act and Oregon Public Records Act in conjunction with federal laws. “I’m local and state law, and my job is to protect the citizens of the county,” Rupert said. “The letter I signed was for clarification of what our rules are, what we can do. Sheriffs have different opinions, right? And I’m a sheriff, and I get beat up on this from the right side because they’re like ‘Well, you have a constitutional duty.” Well, I have a state law duty. I took an oath to the state law and the Constitution, but I don’t get to violate the law, and I won’t violate the law.” Rupert is also currently under investigation for allegedly violating two state statutes regarding prohibited use of official position or office and methods of handling conflicts during his campaign. On Jan. 27, Rupert used the sheriff’s office public information officer to send out an email announcing his election campaign to news outlets. The complaint also alleges that Rupert used county resources to conduct a series of town halls while running for sheriff. The commission found that there was no substantial evidence that Rupert used county resources to conduct town halls, but did move to investigate the email. Rupert appeared in front of the Oregon Government Ethics Commission regarding the misconduct on Sept. 11 and apologized, stating it was a mistake. The commission voted 5-0 to move forward with the investigation, with some members noting they felt the case could be resolved with a letter of education for Rupert.

title: Police seize 69 guns from south Bend home
author: Emily Rogers
content: The Central Oregon Drug Enforcement Team seized 69 “ghost guns” from a residence in south Bend Thursday evening. Detectives began investigating a report of a person manufacturing and selling ghost guns in October, identifying Eric Testerman, 66, of Bend as the alleged manufacture and seller. Ghost guns are often self-assembled or 3-D printed and can bypass background checks making it difficult for law enforcement to investigate the guns when used in a crime. CODE seized 69 firearms from the residence on Winnebago Lane in the Deschutes River Woods neighborhood in Bend, with a majority being unserialized, short-barrel rifles and automatic firearms. Officers also seized manufacturing tools used to craft unserialized firearms from the residence. Oregon House Bill 2005 prohibits the sale, transfer, or manufacture of untraceable, unserialized and 3-D printed firearms or unfinished frames and receivers for firearms made after October 22, 1968. Testerman is not currently in the area and was not present while officers searched the residence. Officers will present the investigation to a Deschutes County grand jury for consideration on charges of the manufacturing, importation, sale or transfer of undetectable firearms, and unlawful possession of machine guns, certain short-barreled firearms and firearm silencers.

title: What we know about Bend teen who killed 4 at Silver Rail
author: Emily Rogers
content: The 16-year-old Bend resident who killed three kids and a teacher and critically injured two others at Silver Rail Elementary on Oct. 15 came from a violent home, had long absences from school and suffered from social and behavioral health issues. Still, there is lots of information the public and investigators are trying to find out about Griffin John II. He was born in Newport in 2010 to Griffin Jay John and Shauntai Nickerson. Four years later the couple divorced, with Nickerson being awarded majority custody. Griffin John Sr. has a long history of run-ins with the law. His recent rap sheet includes 14 misdemeanor crimes and three violations committed in Benton, Lincoln and Clatsop counties, and one felony in 2003 in Lincoln County for assaulting a public safety officer, resisting arrest and harassment. Since 2017, he has been charged three times for being a felon in possession of a weapon. A day after the tragedy at Silver Rail, local police and the FBI were searching for the shooter’s father, who lived 250 miles away from Bend in Astoria. Griffin Jay John Sr. has been homeless, living in the woods near the river town for years. Police had some difficulty locating him, according to Astoria Police Chief Stacy Kelly. But on Saturday morning, two days after the shooting at Silver Rail, police located John and delivered information to him that his son had died. He told police said he had not been in contact with his son for about a year, according to Kelly. According to oregonlive.com, two journalists later found his encampment in the woods. He told them: “I’m going through a lot right now” and asked the journalists to leave. Mary Rose Eng, a homeless advocate in Astoria who has interacted with the shooter’s father, said the man had a history of violence, sexual abuse, intimidation and drug activity. “I was told that he sexually assaulted numerous of my friends,” Eng said. “I was told that he strangled them, or I would be present as a horrified survivor was describing this to a family member. One of the most vociferous victims told me he beat her within an inch of her life.” Meagan Gauthier, a former girlfriend of John Sr., said he was an absent father, but if he had known there were any signs of his son struggling or being violent he would’ve “been there in a heartbeat.” “He would’ve done whatever he could have, whatever was in his power to get there and help,” Gauthier said. “He’s just broken about this. But on the other hand he did have a temper, but his son was always his number one most important thing.” Life in Bend At the time of Thursday’s school shooting, Griffin John II lived with his mother several blocks away from Silver Rail in an apartment on Brosterhous Road. Nickerson had previously lived with Griffin John Sr. in Toledo, Oregon before moving to Bend in 2008. Nickerson lived in both Bend and Redmond, but has been living on Brosterhous Road since at least 2018. On Thursday, Bulletin reporters visited the home but found all the shutters closed and all the lights off. Nickerson has not responded to the Bulletin’s requests for comment. Nickerson pleaded guilty to DUII and careless driving charges in Deschutes County in 2018. The DUII charges were dismissed in April after she completed a diversion program. In 2023, Nickerson was booked into the Deschutes County Adult Jail for alleged harassment and assault in the fourth degree of a Bend woman. Those charges were later dismissed. Education history Griffin John II had lengthy absences from school from fourth grade through his sophomore year of high school. The last time he showed up to school was at what was then-called Bend Tech Academy in November 2025. He attended Elk Meadow Elementary in kindergarten and Silver Rail Elementary for first through fifth grade, but he had multiple periods of unenrollment or inactivity, according to Bend-La Pine Schools. He didn’t show up for a month in fourth grade, from Dec. 5, 2019 through Jan. 9, 2020. He eventually matriculated to Pilot Butte Middle School and continued to take part in special education programs until the end of eighth grade. But he had major absences in middle school too, including no attendance from Feb. 23 through April 6 in 2023 and again from May 9, 2023 through the end of seventh grade. He then was inactive during his freshman year at Bend Tech Academy from May 12 through the end of the school year, and a week in his sophomore year before dropping out for good on Nov. 20, 2025. In third grade he began taking part in special education programs like Nurturing Empathy Safety and Trust (NEST) for students with intensive behavioral and social skill challenges. He also took part in another special education program while in the district. Bend-La Pine schools are not able to comment on if John faced any disciplinary actions or threatened anyone in the school district due to the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act. The rights to his education records are held by his mother due to Griffin John II being a minor. Police action Bend Police detectives secured warrants and searched the home where Nickerson and her son lived. They also searched his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms. Police also confirmed Wednesday that the firearm used in the Oct. 15 shooting, a Maverick 88 pump-action shotgun, was purchased legally. Police and the FBI have declined to comment on who bought the gun and how the shooter obtained it. They said that was still under investigation. A 16-year-old could not legally buy the gun. Investigators are continuing to look into a possible motive and if other people were involved. Federal and state law enforcement are investigating connections between violent online extremist groups and the shooter, according to reports from OPB. In Feb. 19, 2026 the Boston Division of the FBI warned parents, guardians and caregivers about the increase in the activity of “violent online networks targeting and exploiting children and other vulnerable individuals across the United States,” according to Kristen Setera the spokesperson for FBI Boston. Subjects can be motivated by nihilistic violent extremism, according to the FBI. “They want to sow chaos and facilitate the destruction of society,” Setera said. “These extremists often emerge from decentralized online networks and subcultures that glorify violence, mass killers, and self-harm.” Investigators have not confirmed if the teen who shot and killed three students and a teacher at Silver Rail was a part of one of these violent online networks nor has a motive for the shooting been determined yet. “There are still a lot of pieces to this case that we are unable to share at this time and we appreciate your patience as we ensure the integrity of the investigation,” said Sheila Miller, a spokesperson for the Bend Police Department.

title: Ducks set to start QB Raiola at Illinois with Moore still out
author: none
content: EUGENE — All signs point toward Oregon Ducks quarterback Dylan Raiola starting on Saturday at Illinois. Dante Moore is out, according to the Big Ten’s availability report released at 5 p.m. Wednesday. Earlier on Wednesday, Raiola met with the media shortly after coach Dan Lanning spoke. Officially, Raiola is still competing with Brock Thomas for the start. Lanning refused to tip his hand. However, Thomas started Saturday’s 17-14 win over Nebraska before being replaced in the fourth quarter by Raiola, who led the team on two scoring drives to win the game. Raiola transferred to Oregon (4-2, 2-1 Big Ten) after two seasons at Nebraska to back up Moore and continue his development. Raiola, a former five-star recruit, is not used to competing for playing time, but he said he welcomed the process Lanning set up over the past two weeks. “Competition brings the best out of everybody and I believe that,” Raiola said. “That’s why you come to Oregon. That’s why you come to a place like this. And it only gets you ready for the adverse moments in the game.” How did we get here? Moore suffered a concussion on Sept. 26 at USC. Raiola replaced him and passed for 289 yards and two touchdowns in the 41-27 win. Two weeks later, Raiola started at home against UCLA but struggled, completing 6 of 19 passes for 43 yards and throwing two interceptions through three quarters of the 17-15 loss. Thomas replaced him and played well in the fourth quarter. Last week, Thomas beat out Raiola to start against Nebraska, only to struggle through three quarters, leading to Raiola’s heroics. Lanning said the competition remains fluid as the team works to identify which quarterback gives the Ducks the best chance to win until Moore returns — if he does. Moore has been in concussion protocol for four weeks. “Every week’s week-to-week,” Lanning said. “And I think that’s the best thing that those guys have recognized is we gotta go out and work again. It’s your body of work. It’s what you do in practice. They’re attacking it and both getting reps and doing a great job of that.” Lanning and the staff are evaluating each quarterback’s practice performance, how they have performed in certain game situations, and which of them best fits the game plan against Illinois (3-3, 1-2). But aside from Raiola’s inexplicably poor play against the Bruins, he is clearly the most accomplished quarterback on the roster after Moore. Raiola was at a loss to explain what happened that day, but believed that the performance was in the past and not worth dwelling on. However, he did learn from the experience. “I did go back and look through that week of preparation that I had and I kind of tweaked the little things in my routine,” he said. “I think that made a big adjustment in how I was able to play free and play clean (against Nebraska). So, making those tweaks gives me a lot of confidence going forward.” Starting Raiola, who passed for 59 yards and the game-winning touchdown against Nebraska, makes more sense than Thomas, a former walk-on from Sheldon High School. Raiola has made 23 career starts, including one against Illinois as a freshman in 2024. That day, Raiola passed for 297 yards, three touchdowns and one interception in a 31-24 overtime loss. Raiola said that performance doesn’t matter much today, given that he is on a different team and most of Illinois’ players from that day are gone. However, he could draw on that performance, along with his preparation, for confidence. “I always fall back to the level of my training,” he said. “The offseason, you make it really hard on yourself. You make things extremely challenging. So it gives me the ability to go out there and be free.” That wasn’t the case against UCLA. Raiola appears confident that such a poor performance won’t happen again. Lanning praised Raiola for how he handled the demotion and for how he responded when called upon to help bring the team back against the Cornhuskers. How Raiola handled that situation could prove valuable moving forward. He didn’t sulk. He remained engaged and did all he could to help Thomas and the offense. Raiola said he listened in on every play, stood behind the offense to see the field from the quarterback’s vantage point, discussed plays, strategies, and adjustments with Thomas, and kept himself mentally sharp just in case he had to take over. “Being able to help, obviously, with knowing the game plan helps,” Raiola said. Having Moore involved has also helped. He’s been helping Raiola and Thomas in practice, meetings and games. “It kind of helps us speed up the process so we’re not learning in the game …” Raiola said. “We kind of have that peace of mind going into the game.” Oregon (4-2, 2-1 Big Ten) at Illinois (3-3, 1-2) When: Saturday, noon Where: Gies Memorial Stadium; Champaign, Ill. Latest line: Oregon by 8.5 points TV: Big Ten Network

title: Silver Rail Elementary memorials moved to storage
author: Noemi Arellano-Summer
content: Memorials to three slain Silver Rail Elementary students and one teacher were taken down and moved to Bend-La Pine Schools safe storage early Thursday morning. People have spent the past week leaving hundreds of flowers, signs, crosses, balloons and other materials to several memorials around the perimeter of the school. Superintendent Steve Cook said during Wednesday’s Bend City Council meeting that most mental health professionals suggest leaving school memorials up for about five to seven days after a tragedy. “Right now, the Silver Rail school community is seeing that as a tribute to all of the actions of the last six days,” said Cook. “Part of our next steps now are can people see that again as a place of learning and a place where students go to seek out their futures?” There may be future conversations about the memorials, said Cook. Bend-La Pine Schools, with the exception of Silver Rail, returned to classes on Wednesday. Silver Rail Elementary students will not be back in school at least through the end of next week. The Boys and Girls Clubs of Central Oregon has offered free space for 150 Silver Rail students during schools days. Bend-La Pine Schools nutrition is offering free grab-and-go meals for Silver Rail students from 10:45-11:45 a.m. Wednesday through Tuesday at R.E. Jewell.

title: Fire damages Bend’s Black Bear Diner
author: none
content: A kitchen fire caused heavy damage to the Black Bear Diner in Bend early Thursday morning. According to Bend Fire & Rescue, crews were called by an on-duty Bend police officer who notice flames coming from the roof of the restaurant, located at the corner of Third Street and Northeast Olney Avenue. Firefighters arrived at 12:51 a.m. to find flames reaching 15 to 20 feet above the roof. Crews extinguished the fire within minutes of arriving at the scene. The fire was determined to have started when a faulty safety switch on the stove failed to shut off the gas as intended. The fire spread from the stove into the wall behind it and then into the attic. The diner sustained water and smoke damage throughout the restaurant. Damage to the structure and contents is estimated at approximately $250,000 Bend Police forced entry into the building and confirmed it was unoccupied before assisting incoming crews with traffic control around the scene. Bend Fire & Rescue inspectors inspected the diner’s kitchen hood suppression system, which is designed to detect and extinguish flames within seconds, two weeks before the incident. Firefighters said the system activated successfully during the fire and credited it with minimizing damage to the structure.

title: Football returns as teams unite in wake of Silver Rail tragedy
author: Brian Rathbone
content: A week after tragedy struck Bend, and following a week of schedule reshuffling, sports have returned, with high school football set to be played once again. Across the Intermountain Conference, each team will hold moments of silence to honor the victims of last week’s tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary in southeast Bend. All seven teams will wear some form of Silver Rail helmet sticker. Mountain View will also wear an “ML” sticker in honor of Megan Lambert, a 2019 Mountain View graduate who was killed in the shooting. “Many of our coaches had her (as a student),” said Mountain View football coach Brian Crum. “My oldest daughter was really good friends with her. We’re going to have those stickers to remember those people who dealt with tragedy and who tried to keep our kids safe.” Crook County has painted a Silver Rail symbol on its field ahead of Saturday night’s matchup against Caldera. Summit will have players from every level of its program, from freshmen to varsity, suit up for the varsity game as a show of unity. “We think it will be a great way for our community to come together on Saturday night,” said Summit coach Corben Hyatt, whose team will host Willamette. Friday and Saturday nights will be about communities coming together in the wake of tragedy and, perhaps for a couple of hours, finding a distraction from the events of Oct. 15 that took the lives of three children and Lambert. “It has been an incredibly tough week for our community,” Crum said. “You can never ignore or try to deny the terrible tragedy that happened at Silver Rail and how that affects every person in a different way. “On Saturday at 7 o’clock, we’re going to line up,” Crum added. “(Ridgeview is) going to be on that side in their purple, and we’re going to be on our side in our whites. And we’re going to go freaking play a game against a really good team.” “It’s obviously uncharted waters, kind of going through what the community’s gone through the last week,” said Ridgeview coach Pat Pillegi. “And so we’re kind of navigating that like everybody else. We’re trying to keep our focus as much as we can. But the kids are excited.” Saturday’s matchup features two teams battling for second place in the Intermountain Conference standings. Mountain View and Ridgeview share identical records (5-1 overall, 2-1 IMC). The winner will head into the final week of the regular season in position to claim the conference’s second automatic playoff berth, while the loser will likely need an at-large bid to reach the Class 5A postseason. But with both teams having high OSAA rankings (Ridgeview No. 2, Mountain View No. 7 as of Thursday morning) both are positioned to get one of the five at-large playoff bids. The Cougars-Ravens winner will also likely earn at least one home playoff game, and potentially two, when the postseason begins on Nov. 6. “This is another huge opportunity for us,” Pileggi said. “Us and Mountain View are pretty high up in the standings. We’re setting ourselves up for a great seed and, you know, hopefully a good draw, and take this thing as far as we can. The kids are motivated and they’re focused.” Because of the school and sports cancellations across Bend-La Pine Schools from last Friday through Tuesday, teams were unable to practice together until Wednesday. Mountain View, for instance, used an online video application to share game film with players, with Crum narrating the video as he would during a normal film session. Players also organized their own practice session without coach supervision. While Bend-La Pine teams had to cram a week’s worth of preparation into just a couple of days, other IMC teams from different school districts were able to practice throughout the week. “We were not given a choice, our voice was not heard,” Crum said. “I can find a way to go ahead and push that out on a video for them to watch. And then our leaders stepped up, and that’s why we have leaders. That’s why you build a culture. They were able to organize some of their own practices. And that’s my job as a head football coach, is to create kids who can go out into the world and do things on their own without having to be asked.” Friday and Saturday prep football games • Willamette at Summit (Saturday, 7 p.m.) • Caldera at Crook County (Saturday, 7 p.m.) • Bend High at Redmond (Saturday, 7 p.m.) • Klamath Union at Sisters (Friday, 7 p.m.) • Creswell at Madras (Friday, 7 p.m.) • Rogue River at La Pine (Saturday, 7 p.m.) • Lakeview at Culver (Thursday, 7 p.m.)

title: Oregon Disc Golf Championships set for River’s Edge in Bend
author: Mark Morical
content: The Oregon Disc Golf Championships are set for River’s Edge Golf Course in Bend on Saturday and Sunday. The tournament is at capacity with 160 players, including a handful of touring pros, but spectators are welcome, according to tournament organizer Andy Wade. “We had a tournament at River’s Edge last year, which was awesome,” Wade noted. “This year it’ll be the state championship.” Tee times are schedule from 8 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on both days, with state titles on the line. Divisions are based on age and skill level, and amateurs can self-select advanced, intermediate or novice. The temporary disc golf course will be set up for this weekend only. But there are numerous permanent courses in Central Oregon. The popular Pine Nursery Park course in northeast Bend boasts a full 19 holes. In west Bend, Skyline Sports Complex, Central Oregon Community College, Cascades Academy, and Seventh Mountain Resort each offer short but technical 9-hole courses. Rockridge Park in northeast Bend has a 9-hole putting course. Sisters, Redmond, Crooked River Ranch, Madras, La Pine, Sunriver, and Prineville also have disc golf courses. The Central Oregon Disc Golf Club hosts events all year, from weekly leagues in the summer in Bend and Redmond, to the Central Oregon Winter Series (COWS), nine tournaments from December to March all over the region. The club also runs juniors events and women’s leagues. For more information, visit www.codgc.org. — Bulletin staff report

title: Visiting Idaho’s ‘weird and scenic’ Craters of the Moon National Monument
author: none
content: Traveling east out of Boise along I-84 can quickly wear on you. The vast expanse of relatively flat fields and open spaces drones on to the sound of your car whizzing along at 80 mph. I recently found myself driving into the rising sun as the vastness of Idaho’s Snake River Plain bore down as I made my way to Wyoming. The interstate pulls away from the inviting hills to the east as it curves slightly southward. I decided that it would be far more interesting to drive through those hills along U.S. Highway 20 instead of going around them, knowing that way route passes Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve and at least has some curves in it. Not only was the way out varied and beautiful, but the monument that sat along the route was worth the extra miles on my already long road trip. Cones, caves, broken crater Admittedly, I was hesitant to stop at the park 127 miles east of the I-84 turnoff because we have loads of lava fields in Central Oregon. What could be so different about this one? The rock is basalt, the same as lava fields at home; what sets it apart is how much of it there is and how many different formations visitors can explore. At 750,000 acres, the monument’s bounds include cinder cones, fissures, caves and spatter cones that cover the 620 square miles of lava fields, the largest in the region. The monument has several hiking trails from easy to moderate difficulty and from half-mile jaunts to full-day commitments, each one showing off some of the many geologic features here. Since my recent trip was meant as a driving break, my sister, Heather Kelly, and I opted to explore one of the very short, very easy paths just past the fee station — the North Crater Flow Trail. The one-way, paved, elevated path loops for 0.3 miles, taking visitors on a quick journey through time. Several interpretive signs are placed along the short trail with information on the geological history and processes that created some of these staggering features, most notably the rafted blocks that tower above the trail and surrounding lava field. These rocks, according to signage, most likely are sections of a broken crater that were carried here by the lava flow during the last eruption, around 2,000 years ago. The monument also features a short loop drive that connects to the various trails and features, as well as gives visitors a quick overview of the lava fields. Volcanic geology, early peoples Another thing that sets Craters of the Moon apart is its origins. Formed about 15,000 years ago during the Great Rift, a volcanic event that pulled the Earth’s crust apart, forming a 52-mile crack that led to the eruptions at the current monument. These fissures that formed spewed lava far and wide, then continued to erupt eight more times until about 2,000 years ago at the aforementioned North Crater. In all, these events formed 25 cinder cones, including one of the largest basaltic cinder cones in the world, lava tubes, tree molds, a special blue-hued basalt known as the Blue Dragon Flow (the largest flow in the park), along with hundreds of square miles of lava fields covering the flat landscape below the Pioneer Mountains with rugged, dark rock. Humans have been taking in the vast lava fields for thousands of years too, with members of the Shoshone and Bannock tribes calling this area in the Snake River Plain home for 12 to 14,000 years. Given the known archeological sites on younger lava fields and oral traditions from the Indigenous peoples, it is highly likely they witnessed some of the volcanic events that occurred here throughout history. More recently, European settlers started settling in the plain in the 1840s, some skirting the edges of Craters of the Moon using Goodale’s Cutoff to reach Boise from the Oregon Trail. It wasn’t until the 1920s that word of the lava fields started causing a stir. Robert Limbert was a big fan of Idaho and wanted the world to know it too, and Craters of the Moon was just one of the things to boast about. On his third trip to the area, he brought a camera. Those photos and his field notes got the proverbial ball rolling, making more expeditions with scientists in the following years. In 1924 Limbert wrote an essay for National Geographic and sent a letter to President Calvin Coolidge advocating that Craters of the Moon be made into a national park. Within two months, Coolidge proclaimed it a national monument. Take the trip While quickly taking in all that Craters of the Moon has to offer, I couldn’t help but imagine what this place would look like in the spring, with flowers popping up through the cracks in the rock, or in the winter, when the north end of the park can see over twenty inches of snow and the roads are open to snowshoeing or skiing, or simply stargazing at this designated International Dark Sky Park. This “weird and scenic” place, as Calvin Coolidge once opined, is really something to see, with twisted trees dotting the expanses of rock and monolithic features that seemingly rise out of nowhere. Craters of the Moon is a place you can spend two hours or two days exploring, and either one is worth the longer trip east. If You Go What: Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, Arco, Idaho When: Open year-round; visitor center is closed December-January; Loop Road is closed November-mid April. Cost: $20 per vehicle, $10 per person when visiting on foot; America the Beautiful passes accepted. Contact: 208-527-1300 or nps.gov/crmo GETTING THERE: From Boise, Idaho, take Interstate 84 East for 40 miles, then take Exit 95 towards Mountain Home. Turn left at the stop sign to continue onto U.S. Highway 20 and drive for 100 miles until you reach the town of Carey, then turn left to continue onto the highway towards Arco. Go an additional 25 miles and turn right to reach Craters of the Moon.

title: Downtown Nashville generates a big tax surplus. The mayor hopes to nudge the group deciding how to spend it.
author: Daniel Potter
content: A nine-member board that state lawmakers created earlier this year is now deciding what to do with millions in surplus tax dollars from downtown Nashville. While some officials have floated giving money back to businesses around Broadway facing high tax bills , other proposals are in the works. Two decades ago, the Tourism Development Zone was created for hotel and sales taxes to help pay for Nashville’s new convention center. That arrangement has overperformed, leading to tension between the city and state officials over the surplus. This spring, state lawmakers created a board to decide how to disburse those funds. Earlier this month, former governor Bill Haslam, a member of the new Joint Capital Tourism Board, suggested that just giving it to business owners could prove uneven. Another board member, Nashville Mayor Freddie O’Connell, says he hopes to steer funding in other directions. “For instance, we have a very small Central Precinct despite the number of calls they get. And we may look at potential for some kind of public safety expansion there that could include police, fire and OEM,” Nashville’s Office of Emergency Management, O’Connell said. Details of those proposals are still pending. The exact amount of excess revenue is not yet clear, but it could be in the tens of millions — and should be settled by the end of the year.

title: Dollar General is sued by the FTC and 20 states over ‘deceptive’ pricing
author: Tony Gonzalez
content: The Federal Trade Commission has sued the Tennessee-based bargain chain Dollar General for what it characterized as “long-running deceptive pricing practices” by charging customers more once they reach the register than the prices that are displayed on shelves and in advertisements. Twenty states joined in the complaint, filed by the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee. It said that Dollar General failed to correct the issue despite what it said was “extensive corporate knowledge of the problem.” “Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” wrote Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection. Dollar General, based in Goodlettsville, did not immediately return a request for comment from The Associated Press. The states joining the FTC lawsuit include: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin, according to the FTC. Americans have become frustrated with higher prices, and also what they perceive to be new methods used by restaurant chains and major retailers in setting prices including the use of artificial intelligence tools.

title: Nashville SC clinches trophy, No. 1 seed in MLS Playoffs
author: Alexis Marshall
content: Nashville Soccer Club has earned the trophy for having the best record in Major League Soccer in the 2026 regular season, and there are still three matches to go. The Boys in Gold defeated CF Montréal 2-0 on Saturday, making it impossible for any other team in the league to catch up to their winning record. It’s the first time in club history that the team has won the Supporters’ Shield. Nashville SC has dominated Major League Soccer this season. In its first 31 games, the team has earned 70 points, with a 21W-3L-7D record. That’s the best record at this point in the season for any team in league history. And Nashville SC is within striking distance of the MLS record for most points scored in a single regular season. Inter Miami currently holds the record with 74 points. They won the Supporters’ Shield in 2024 before taking home the MLS Cup. View this post on Instagram The top prize in MLS works differently than in many major European soccer leagues. Elsewhere, the team with the best regular season record is the champion, but in MLS, teams go on to battle for the cup in knockout-style bracket competition. “For one, two weeks we can be European, celebrate the championship,” star midfielder Hany Mukhtar joked in a quote to MLS . “But then we have to get back to how the system is here, the playoffs and all that. We need to be ready. We know that it’s a new season in the playoffs, and we will make sure that we are all ready.” The Supporters’ Shield isn’t just a pretty piece of hardware — it comes with serious perks in the postseason. With it, Nashville SC receives the No. 1 seed and home field advantage throughout the playoffs. Only one of the team’s matches in the best-of-three opening round will be played on their opponent’s home turf. This win also automatically qualifies the team for international competition in the Concacaf Champions Cup.

title: Faith leaders urge voter turnout in Bordeaux and Edgehill neighborhoods
author: Camellia Burris
content: Faith leaders in Nashville are working to increase voter turnout for the midterm elections. Members of Nashville Organized for Action and Hope – an interfaith group also known as NOAH – sang and chanted before casting their ballots at voting sites in Bordeaux and Edgehill on Saturday. Their mission was to bring “souls to the polls” — based on the belief that people of faith are called to not only welcome strangers and feed their neighbors, but to participate in the decisions that affect their collective future. Tennessee has among the lowest voter turnout rates in the country , and, in Davidson County, many of those who are registered to vote never make it to the ballot box . Reverend Kelli X, pastor of the Village Church in Madison and one of NOAH’s founding members, said getting people registered is only the first step. “Folks need to have a plan to go vote and to know that there are locations and availability,” she told WPLN News. “We’ve been knocking on doors, canvassing, encouraging folks to know that voting is happening and their votes matter.” The local chapter of the NAACP is also offering free rides to voters who need transportation to polling sites. Camellia Burris/WPLN News Sen. Charlane Oliver, D – Nashville, spoke to attendees of the march in Bordeaux to provide some background on the three constitutional amendments on the ballot. The proposed amendments focus on bail, property taxes, and the rights of crime victims. While voter turnout in Nashville has improved since the last midterm election in 2022 , NOAH chose to rally voters in Edgehill and Bordeaux to make sure residents who may feel disenfranchised know that they have a place in the political process. “The question is does our state government see the people who live in Bordeaux? Do our local elected officials and federal government see Bordeaux?” asked Rev. Alicia Smith-Haddock, the chairperson for NOAH’s transformational task force. “We wanted to make it very clear that we see the people in Bordeaux,” she told WPLN News. Speakers at the event also addressed concerns about problems with voting machines – encouraging voters to take their time, check their ballots and report any issues to poll workers Early voting ends Oct. 29 and Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Amid financial turmoil, whiskey maker Uncle Nearest seeks a buyer
author: Daniel Potter
content: If you’ve always dreamed of owning an acclaimed Tennessee whiskey company, now might be the time to snap off a deal. Uncle Nearest — the brand named for the once-enslaved man who later taught Jack Daniel the art of whiskey-making — is looking for a buyer. Since last summer, the company has been in receivership, meaning a court-appointed attorney, Phillip Young, has been in charge. His job is to shepherd Uncle Nearest through huge financial problems: over $100 million in debt and years of unpaid taxes. Young has to make regular reports on how it’s going, and the latest update is not stellar. The company remains insolvent, and he’s been looking for someone to buy its assets. This summer, there was speculation that an investment firm tied to rap mogul Jay-Z might step in, but that hasn’t happened. Part of the problem is people just aren’t buying as much booze these days. Young’s latest report says he’s on track to offload some French vineyards, but then there’s a chateau — one of many Cognac chateaus languishing on the market because the thirst for cognac is down even worse than whiskey due to tariffs. Other problems include key employees leaving for steadier work elsewhere, as well as ongoing financial investigations. Still, the latest report says the company has a future. A buyer could come through. And for Uncle Nearest, sooner would be better.

title: NDOT will ban right turns on red lights at these Nashville intersections
author: Alexis Marshall
content: Turning right at a red light will soon be banned at seven Nashville intersections. The Nashville Department of Transportation will also make changes to signals at several more intersections to improve pedestrian safety. The changes are much narrower than a proposed blanket ban on right turns at red lights, which Metro Councilmember Sandra Sepulveda filed this summer. She later dialed back the proposed ban to a few dozen stop lights. Then Tuesday, after weeks of debate, Sepulveda withdrew the legislation after assurances that NDOT would implement the ban at a handful of intersections and study the issue at others. The push for improved pedestrian safety comes as the city has seen a high number of pedestrian deaths this year. In a statement to WPLN News, NDOT public information coordinator Brendan Scully wrote, “Right turn on red restrictions are one of the many tools in NDOT’s toolkit for making streets safer for people walking.” He wrote that NDOT’s engineers use data to determine on a case-by-case basis what restrictions are needed to improve safety at intersections across the city. “Pedestrian safety is a top priority for the department and we will continue working to make streets safer for people walking, biking, rolling and driving,” Scully wrote. NDOT will be banning right turns at red lights at these seven intersections in the next couple of weeks: Third Avenue North and Commerce Street Fourth Avenue South and Korean Veterans Boulevard 12th Avenue North and Broadway 25th Avenue South and Children’s Way Nolensville Pike and Welshwood Drive Rosa L. Parks Boulevard and Church Street Smith Springs Road and Old Murfreesboro Pike NDOT will also alter the traffic and walk signals at seven intersections to add leading pedestrian intervals. That gives pedestrians a head start to establish control and visibility in a crosswalk before vehicles may begin turning. One intersection, at 25th Avenue South and Children’s Way, will get both the right-turn-on-red ban and the updated signals. title: Tennessee joins ‘Bird City’ network to conserve species, habitat
author: Caroline Eggers
content: Tennessee has joined a bird conservation network that spans the Americas. Any city or county across the state can now apply for the Bird City Network, a program from the American Bird Conservancy, Environment for the Americas and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The network’s aim is to build programs for education. That includes opportunities for citizen science, reducing common threats to both resident and migratory birds, and protecting parks and green spaces. “This really just gives you an on-the-ground, local-based grassroots opportunity to start to make a difference and conserve birds in their habitats,” said David Hanni, the bird conservation coordinator for the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency. About a third of the nation and Mexico, Columbia and Brazil are involved in the program. Multinational cooperation is beneficial, given that many birds’ ecosystems extend across continents as they make long migratory journeys each year. “It’s important to conserve these birds through their full annual cycle,” Hanni said. Nashville has already signed up. The city is now part of two efforts to conserve local bird habitat and species, having joined the Urban Bird Treaty in 2023. “This collaboration allows us to combine resources and advance Nashville’s conservation agenda, broadening the tent and launching new initiatives to engage the public and conserve our birds and habitats,” said Nathan Heath, who will serve as the Bird City Nashville coordinator. Nashville has wrestled with its own goals in recent years. In 2023, the Nashville Symphony cut down its trees to forcibly remove a roost of purple martins from its doorstep. The next year, after the city committed to conserving habitat for migratory species, Metro Nashville opted to cut down 10 city trees to further evict the songbirds from the symphony. Caroline Eggers WPLN News Purple martins gather in front of the Schermerhorn Symphony Center in downtown Nashville on August 15, 2023. Since then, the city has enacted some voluntary measures, like guidelines for downtown developers to design bird-friendly windows. Re flective glass kills as many as a billion or more birds in the U.S. each year. Other key threats to birds include feral cats — which the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service estimates kill another 1 to 4 billion birds per year — climate change and habitat loss, which is considered the greatest long-term threat to birds.

title: Fears over ballot switches spread every election. Here’s what Nashville is doing about it
author: Marianna Bacallao
content: Democratic voters have reported problems with Nashville’s voting machines. When they select the Democratic candidate for governor, Jerri Green, the machine will sometimes select Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn instead. The problem stems from the voting machine’s sensitivity. Since the Republican option is first, selecting the Democratic option too close to the boundary on the screen can make the machine choose the wrong candidate. To help ensure the machine picks the right option, Davidson County Election Commissioner John Richardson said polling sites are bringing back plastic straws. MORE: Tennessee’s next governor might not break 50% as independent gains traction Nashville first used the coffee stirrers in the 2020 election to limit the spread of COVID-19 at the polls. The election commission had initially opted to retire the straws this election over environmental concerns. Since rolling the straws out Thursday, Richardson told WPLN News that he’s gotten fewer calls about the issue. To date, Richardson said all ballot errors have been caught before the voter officially cast their ballot. “Each and every person I’ve spoken with that’s called into our office and has expressed their concern, I’ve called them back. I’ve had a meaningful conversation with each of them,” Richardson said. “Every voter I’ve spoken with has been very confident that their vote counted.” Any ballot error can be corrected before it goes through the scanner. After it enters the scanner, it has been tallied and cannot be changed. Early voting runs through Oct. 29. Election Day is Nov. 3

title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: ‘He has peaked’
author: Megan Jones
content: BENSALEM, Pa. – When the Trump merchandise store here announced it was closing earlier this year, Wes Alker, a Trump superfan and retired auto mechanic, came by for some nostalgia and the going-out-of-business deals. They included everything from “Trump Won” caps for $9.99 to Trump pool floats for $19.99. Trump stores first emerged during the 2016 campaign. But with the president now in his second and final term, store owners say there isn’t as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened. At least four stores have closed this year. The MAGA Mall , a big online retailer and wholesaler, reports sales of MAGA gear are down 30% compared to a presidential election year when Trump is on the ballot. Trump fans Wes Alker and Joseph Flanagan pose at a going-out-of-business sale at a Trump store in suburban Philadelphia. Flanagan lives nearby and said he visited the store more than 25 times. (Frank Langfitt/NPR) “He’s no longer a viable business model for entrepreneurs because he has peaked,” said Alker, who wore a gray T-shirt with a photo of former President Joe Biden and former Vice-President Kamala Harris which read, “Dumb and Dumber.” Trump’s lame duck status isn’t the only drag on demand. When the Bensalem store closed – it still maintains an online presence – Trump’s average approval rating had already fallen from 50 % when he took office to 44 %. Nine months later, when Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside of Knoxville, Tennessee, the president’s approval rating had fallen five more points. This Trump store in a suburban Philadelphia strip mall is one of at least four that have closed this year as the president’s merchandising appeal has dimmed. (Frank Langfitt/NPR) Hays said unpopular policies – such as DOGE’s massive government staff cuts – have had an impact. He noticed that instead of immediately putting on their new Trump gear, more buyers asked for bags. “People were not wearing their colors, so to speak, like they did before the (2024) election,” said Hays, 80. Trump merchandise has been big business. The MAGA Mall, a retailer and wholesaler, sells over a 1,000 MAGA, patriotic and religious products, including 400 different kinds of hats. (Frank Langfitt/NPR) When Hays opened his store in April 2024, business boomed. One day, he said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month. “After the inauguration, I think a lot of people felt that their job was done,” said Hays. “They didn’t have to promote MAGA or Trump.” Hays still has a Trump store in the Tennessee tourist town of Gatlinburg. He’s waiting to see how Christmas sales go before deciding its future. Trump stores are a phenomenon. Other charismatic presidents such as Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama developed ardent followings, but didn’t inspire brick-and-mortar merch outlets in red and blue states. Hays says Trump created such demand because he’s a salesman – and he tells people what they want to hear. The Trump Store in Bensalem, Pa., sold a wide variety of products before it closed early this year. Items included an “Alligator Alcatraz” T-shirt, “Trump Won” caps and this patriotic Trump bear. The store continues to sell online. (Frank Langfitt/NPR) Ron Solomon, president of the MAGA Mall, says there are about 20 stores that specialize in Trump merchandise still in operation. In Myrtle Beach, Rick Kligman sells items out of two stores, but he’s trying to get rid of older material, stuffing $40 worth of merchandise into a grab bag that he sells for $9.99. He’s concerned about the mid-terms and thinks a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate could turn off the more casual Trump consumer. “I don’t want to be sitting holding thousands and thousands of dollars of Trump merchandise and absolutely no possibility of selling it,” said Kligman, 69. Given term limits and Trump’s age, retailers are diversifying beyond the Trump brand and embracing more patriotic products, including hats that say “We the People.” Solomon says this is a natural progression. Eventually, Trump will leave the national stage. Unless a family member picks up the mantle, Solomon says the Trump merchandise business “will fade away.” Research by NPR’s Susie Cummings.
