title: Jay-Z to headline Super Bowl LXI halftime show in 2027 in historic first
author: Manjusha Radhakrishnan
content: Dubai: Rapper Jay-Z has been announced as the headline performer for the Super Bowl LXI halftime show, marking his first appearance as the main act at one of the world's biggest sporting events. The National Football League (NFL), Apple Music and Roc Nation, Jay-Z's entertainment company, announced on Monday, 26 October, that the Grammy-winning artist would perform at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, on 14 February 2027. The announcement was made during halftime of a Monday Night Football game between the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys. A landmark year for Jay-Z The announcement comes after a busy period for the rapper, who recently completed his Jay-Z 30 concert series with two performances in Los Angeles on 23 and 24 October. The series also included three concerts in his hometown of New York in July, two performances in London in September and a show in Paris on 10 September. He also recently premiered an HBO documentary series, Jay-Z in 8 , at a star-studded event in New York. Speculation about his involvement in the Super Bowl halftime show had grown in the days before the announcement, amid renewed attention surrounding his recent performances and projects. The 2027 appearance will be Jay-Z's first time headlining the Super Bowl halftime show, although he has been involved in shaping the event's musical programme for several years. Jay-Z's role in the Super Bowl In 2019, Roc Nation entered into a partnership with the NFL to advise on live music entertainment, as part of the league's Inspire Change initiative. The initiative was launched amid controversy surrounding the NFL's treatment of former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick, who began kneeling during the national anthem in 2016 to protest racial injustice and police brutality. Jay-Z had previously declined an opportunity to perform at the Super Bowl halftime show in 2017. He later described his decision as a matter of principle, amid reports that the NFL had asked him to bring Kanye West and Rihanna on stage. Lady Gaga ultimately headlined that year's show. Since its partnership with the NFL began, Roc Nation has played a central role in selecting performers and producing the halftime entertainment, including shows featuring Jennifer Lopez and Shakira, Rihanna, Usher and Kendrick Lamar. Beyoncé's Super Bowl appearances Jay-Z's wife, Beyoncé, has performed at the Super Bowl twice. Her first appearance came in 2013, when she headlined the halftime show at the Mercedes-Benz Superdome in New Orleans. She was joined by her former Destiny's Child bandmates Kelly Rowland and Michelle Williams. The performance attracted approximately 110.8 million television viewers in the United States, making it one of the most-watched halftime shows at the time. Beyonce performs with Kelly Rowland, left, and Michelle Williams, right, of Destiny's Child, during the half-time show of the NFL Super Bowl. Beyoncé returned to the Super Bowl stage in 2016, joining Coldplay and Bruno Mars at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California. Her performance of Formation drew attention for its references to Black identity and pride, prompting debate among politicians and audiences. A history of major musical performances The Super Bowl halftime show has evolved from a largely traditional entertainment programme into a major platform for international music stars. Michael Jackson's performance at Super Bowl XXVII in 1993 is widely regarded as a turning point in the event's history, helping establish the halftime show as a headline attraction in its own right. Since then, performers have included Prince, U2, Madonna, The Rolling Stones, Paul McCartney, Bruce Springsteen, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Usher and Kendrick Lamar. The 2025 show featured Kendrick Lamar and SZA, while Bad Bunny headlined the 2026 edition. Jay-Z's scheduled appearance in 2027 will add another major name to the event's history, while bringing his long-standing relationship with the NFL into the spotlight. title: Sachin Tendulkar congratulates niece on major achievement, receives sweet response
author: Abdul Bari Khan
content: Dubai: Cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar has congratulated his niece Karishma Tendulkar after she received an award for her contribution to surgical research in ophthalmology. Karishma shared the news on Instagram, revealing that she had won the Bell Pharma Award for the Best Surgical Research Paper by a Young Ophthalmologist at the Maharashtra Ophthalmological Society Annual Conference (MOSCON) 2026 in Mumbai. She received the award from Dr Farokh Udwadia and thanked her mentors at Narayana Nethralaya for their continued encouragement. “Taking this forward, with much more to learn and give the best to my patients,” Karishma wrote in her post. Karishma is the daughter of Nitin Tendulkar, Sachin’s older half-brother as per online reports. The Indian cricket legend was quick to celebrate the achievement, sharing a congratulatory message on his own Instagram account. View this post on Instagram “A big congratulations to my niece, Karishma! It’s lovely to see your hard work being recognised,” the former India captain wrote. He added a playful touch to his message, saying: “By the way, I hope you know that this achievement comes with an uncle who’s going to be telling everyone about it. So proud of you!” Karishma responded warmly in the comments, calling him “Sachu kaka” and thanking him for his support. “Means a lot coming from you. You have always been an inspiration for me,” she wrote. The achievement also drew congratulatory messages from Sara Tendulkar, Sachin’s daughter, and Saaniya, who joined the family in celebrating Karishma’s success. While Sachin is celebrated worldwide for his cricketing records, his latest post showed the pride he takes in his family’s achievements beyond sport.

title: Huawei unveils wearable tech for cardiovascular health at MEA Innovation Talks
author: GN Focus Report
content: UAE: Huawei held its MEA Tech Innovation Talks conference in Dubai at Grand Plaza Movenpick today. The conference, highlighting the brand’s innovations across the wearables and smartphone segments, has featured several researchers and experts from the healthcare and technology sectors. Held on the sidelines of the ISH-ECS 2026 annual conference, where Huawei unveiled the new Huawei Watch D3 medical-grade blood pressure monitoring smartwatch, the conference focused on wearable-based cardiovascular health management technology and early diabetes risk identification. As a major international gathering dedicated to hypertension, ISH-ECS 2026, taking place in Dubai from 22 to 25 October 2026, brings together leading organisations and experts from around the world to discuss the latest research and developments in hypertension prevention and management. Showcasing its newly launched Huawei Watch D3 at the conference, Huawei, which is also a member of the International Society of Hypertension (ISH), was a notable presence. International experts presented findings from their research using Huawei Watch D Series wearable blood pressure monitors, highlighting the potential of wearable technology to support blood pressure monitoring and management. Underpinning Huawei’s innovations is a sustained commitment to long-term research and development. In 2025 alone, the company invested $28.62 billion in R&D, equivalent to 21.8 per cent of its annual revenue. To support further research in the study of hypertension, Huawei has established the Wearable Blood Pressure Technology Innovation Fund in collaboration with ISH. Attended by representatives from several major media networks and technology experts based in the UAE, the event provided deeper insights into innovations developed by Huawei Health research labs worldwide, as well as the company’s extensive global health research collaborations. The presentations highlighted three key areas of progress in wearable-based health management, namely blood pressure monitoring, coronary heart disease risk research, and diabetes risk assessment. Experts participating in the conference spoke about the potential of wearable technology to transform cardiovascular health management by making blood pressure monitoring more seamless and accessible. Professor Jiguang Wang, Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the Shanghai Institute of Hypertension, noted that the Huawei Watch D3 could point towards a future in which blood pressure monitoring is integrated more naturally into everyday life. "Innovations like Minimally Disruptive ABPM and environmental monitoring reminder by Huawei Watch D3 may be inspiring for shaping a new direction on how future blood pressure management is automated and seamlessly embedded into daily life, via wearable devices," he stated. Professor George Stergiou, President of the International Society of Hypertension, described the Huawei Watch D3 as a novel, reliable wearable device that provides insights into blood pressure profiles and patterns. He also noted that the European Society of Hypertension (ESH) and the ISH encourage the clinical use of validated wrist-cuff blood pressure monitors, while calling for further research into their implementation in clinical practice. The discussions also explored the broader potential of wearable technology in advancing preventive and personalised healthcare. Professor Datin Yook-Chin Chia, Professor and Senior Consultant at Sunway University, Malaysia, emphasised that reducing disruption and the number of required measurements could make comprehensive ABPM more practical for patients. Professor Maryam Al Saeed of Mohammed Bin Rashid University of Medicine and Health Sciences commented, "Dubai Health and Huawei are collaborating on a clinical research initiative to evaluate non-invasive wearable technology for earlier diabetes risk, leveraging real-world health data to advance personalised prevention, enable proactive healthcare, and improve long-term health outcomes across diverse populations." Attendees also had the opportunity to try the blood pressure monitoring capabilities of the Huawei Watch D3 across different scenarios, offering a closer look at how advanced wearable technology can make blood pressure monitoring more convenient and accessible in everyday life. As part of the brand’s broader innovation focus, Huawei’s latest smartphone innovations were also presented during the conference. Huawei’s leadership in the foldable smartphone market and smartphone camera technology was showcased through recent models. Edwin You, Chief Technology Officer at Huawei, also spoke about the company’s latest Tau Law technology, which could revolutionise the way microprocessor chips are designed and manufactured. This technology provides a new approach to semiconductor development, shifting the focus from shrinking transistor dimensions to reducing signal propagation delays. Through technologies such as LogicFolding, Tau Law can dramatically improve transistor density and system performance.

title: Abu Dhabi’s Zayed National Museum tells a human story in a futuristic space
author: Hamna Iqbal, Reporter
content: The Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi Abu Dhabi : You see the sturdy white wings. Five of them, rising from a green hill on Saadiyat Island, Abu Dhabi, curved and still, as if the wind has just paused them mid-flight. A falcon does not hurry before it flies. It opens its wings, listens to the wind, and waits. The Zayed National Museum holds that moment in steel. Gulf countries used a traditional method of catching cool breezes from above and directing them indoors to cool rooms naturally. They called the tower ‘barjeel’. Now imagine that mechanism converted into modern architecture. Inspired by the falcon wings, Foster + Partners architecture firm, designed the Zayed national Museum, where they built the five aerodynamic towers harnessing the principles of barjeel wind tower. Two visitors, two impressions While the visitors walk through the boundaries of the museum, the architects wanted the image of a falcon in flight, storming in pride and standing sturdy, 83 to 123 metres into the sky. “I found myself wanting to pause and capture the details from different perspectives, because the building offers so many interesting compositions,” said Mohammed Ajmal, a Digital Marketing Manager, visiting the museum. Mohammed Ajmal describes the architecture of Zayed National Museum feels powerful yet graceful. Norman Foster hand-sketched the initial conceptual designs, and the museum opened to the public on December 3, 2025, the day after UAE National Day, after roughly 15 years of construction . For Ajmal, it is a place where architecture becomes an experience rather than simply something to look at. The thoughtful use of space, natural light, materials, and architectural details made the experience immersive for him. For Advait Bal, an Abu Dhabi resident working as a solutions Consultant, capturing the moments on his camera, he said, “Being inside the museum gives me a sense of calmness, admiration, and pride.” Inside the museum The structure of the place creates an interplay of light and shadow, which, according to Ajmal adds depth to its interiors and makes exploring the museum a visual experience in itself. Picture used for illustrative purposes. “As you move through the museum, the changing perspectives encourage you to slow down and appreciate your surroundings,” he added. When Advait walked through the white floors of the monument, he said, “there is something powerful about being surrounded by a design that reflects the identity of the UAE The effect comes from the space itself. The interiors are mostly white, the rooms are wide and open, and the lighting is carefully designed. Together they create what he called a clean, futuristic atmosphere. What stayed with him was a contrast. The building looks like the future, but the story it tells is deeply human. “The museum tells a deeply human story about the UAE, its roots, its people, and its journey,” he said, “The architecture feels like a vision of the future while the exhibits connect you to the nation’s past and identity.” Zayed National Museum That story belongs to the national museum of the United Arab Emirates, a tribute to the nation’s founding father, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, and to the ancient and modern identity of the country he united. The technology carries that story forward inside the museum. Much of what visitors see is interactive, he added, with holograms and advanced technology bringing the exhibits to life. Heritage is not placed behind glass but something you can step into. Standing beneath the dome Asked for one moment he would carry home, Advait described standing in the centre of a circular theatre and looking up at its beautifully shaped dome. Advait Bal sharing his best moment at Zayed National Museum. “I felt almost abducted by a stronger force,” he said. “Feeling the beauty of modern architecture and cultural heritage inside you.” Advait needed only one word for everything he felt: “Breathtaking.” For Ajmal, it was the museum’s soaring towers. Their striking form against the sky creates a powerful visual impression in his memory. title: What Nobel economics can teach the UAE about recovery
author: Damyana Bakardzhieva
content: Dubai shopping stock By Damyana Bakardzhieva, Special to Gulf News This year Stockholm awarded the economics Nobel prize to Robert Hall of Stanford and Michael Woodford of Columbia for the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” The phrase sounds a long way from the tankers loading at Fujairah. It is not. Their shared insight is that economies are steered less by what policymakers do today than by what households and firms expect them to do tomorrow. Families spend according to the income they expect over years, not this month’s pay slip. Firms set prices with an eye on where costs and policy are heading. Get those expectations right, and a shock passes. Get them wrong, and it compounds. That insight matters more for the UAE than for most countries, because the current crisis is unusual. Most of the world faces an oil-price shock. The UAE faces high prices for the oil it can sell, lost volumes for the oil it cannot ship, and a non-oil economy of tourism, trade and property shaken by a war on its doorstep. Hall and Woodford do not hand the country a script. What they do is show where its leverage lies. A strong balance sheet, a constrained toolkit The shock is real. The International Monetary Fund’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects that the UAE economy will shrink 3.9% this year (IMF). Petrol prices crossed Dh4 a litre in October, its highest in more than four years Dubai’s timely stimulus sends strong signal of confidence Yet the country entered the crisis with enormous buffers. S&P puts sovereign wealth and foreign reserves at about 200% of GDP. Fitch still expects the UAE to run a budget surplus of 4.5% of GDP, helped by high prices and pipeline exports through Fujairah, which bypass the strait and by July handled about two-thirds of UAE crude exports. What the UAE lacks is a monetary policy lever. The dirham’s peg to the US dollar ties local interest rates to the US Federal Reserve, and the Fed is under pressure to tighten as the oil shock feeds into American inflation. Hence, the UAE imports tighter monetary policy that helps it fight inflationary pressures, yet this happens just as its own economy contracts too. That leaves the country two main tools for economic management: the budget, and the government’s word. Those are exactly where Hall and Woodford have the most to say. Hall: People spend on the future they expect Hall’s best-known result, from 1978, is that household spending tracks expected lifetime income. A shock people believe is temporary barely changes consumption; they borrow or draw down savings. A shock they believe is permanent changes behaviour at once. Advantage UAE and Gulf economies in changed investment environment? In the UAE, that logic applies with special force, because so much demand rests on bets about the future: whether an expatriate family renews its lease, whether a company keeps its regional headquarters in Dubai, whether a developer starts the next tower. Fitch expects Dubai’s output to stay below its 2025 level even in 2027, partly because investment, tourism and expat inflows return slowly. That is Hall’s point in practice. The lasting damage comes from doubts about tomorrow, not today’s lost income. The implication is to spend in ways that make the future credible. Worried households save rather than spend much of any one-off cash handout. Visible, multi-year commitments work better: bypass ports, pipelines and rail that reduce Hormuz exposure; credit guarantees that keep small firms alive; residency and visa stability that tell families the UAE remains a place to build a life. Hall’s later work on fiscal multipliers adds a further point. Government spending does the best when monetary policy cannot cushion the blow, which is precisely the UAE’s position under the peg. Woodford: Say what you will do, then do it Woodford’s 2003 treatise, Interest and Prices, recast stabilisation policy as the management of expectations. His framework also separates two kinds of inflation in a supply shock. The first round is the direct jump in fuel and freight costs. The second round is what follows if wages, rents and service prices start chasing those costs. The first can be tolerated; the second must be stopped. Five things to know about the Nobel Prize The UAE has handled the first round sensibly. Monthly fuel pricing passes global costs through transparently and preserves the necessary signal. Dubai inflation reached 5.54% in August, its highest since 2022, as transport costs kept rising. The second-round risk lies in rents, school fees and services, where contracts get written with crisis premiums that can outlast the crisis. Woodford’s answer is commitment, clearly communicated. The government should publish how administered prices such as utility tariffs, rents and school fees will move over the next year or two, so firms and landlords do not bake in worst-case assumptions, he says. The rent freezes announced across the country did just that. If any household support is to be distributed, it should target lower-income workers, who feel transport costs hardest, and it should carry an announced end date tied to shipping returning to normal. A rule people can see beats discretion they must guess at. What the UAE should do, and what economics alone cannot solve Three government moves follow from the theoretical work of Woodford and Hall. First, use the fiscal space boldly and visibly, front-loading investment that reduces dependence on the strait. Speeding up the construction of the second ADNOC pipeline, the Green Corridor with Oman, increasing storage capacity in Fujairah, launching full-fledged Etihad Rail cargo and passenger operations all embody this strategy. Second, publish a stabilisation framework stating what support exists, who gets it, and what will end it. Third, protect the anchors: keep the peg, keep fuel pricing transparent, and contain second-round inflation through predictable administered prices. Nonetheless, there are limits to what using economic science can achieve. Hall and Woodford built tools for fluctuations around a stable path. If Hormuz becomes a permanently tolled or obstructed waterway, that is a structural change, and the right response would be adjustment, not stabilisation. The UAE’s push to cut its long-term reliance on the strait is the right instinct for that scenario. The Nobel committee noted that the laureates’ models now guide central banks and governments worldwide. The UAE is already implementing their discipline: decide what the country is committing to, say it plainly, and let households and firms plan around it. Damyana Bakardzhieva Damyana Bakardzhieva is Senior Research Fellow, Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy

title: Diwali 2026 in the UAE: Festivals, temples and where to celebrate
author: Areeba Hashmi
content: India Palace Dubai: Diwali falls on Sunday, November 8 this year, and celebrations across the UAE begin the week before. There's a riverside festival at Souk Al Seef, temple prayers in Abu Dhabi and community events in Dubai's residential neighbourhoods. Here is where to mark the Festival of Lights. Dubai's Festival of Lights Dubai's official Diwali programme runs citywide from November 2 to 12 as part of the emirate's retail calendar. It is organised with Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment. The programme includes: Diya painting and rangoli workshops Music and dance performances Festive offers across malls and gold retailers Visit Dubai also lists prizes including gold coins, gold bars and vouchers. Most activities are free. Venues and timings are expected to be announced closer to the date. When: November 2 to 12 Where: Citywide, Dubai Price: Most events free Noor: Festival of Lights Noor returns for its third edition at Souk Al Seef, beside Dubai Creek. It is produced by Teamwork Arts with Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment and the Consulate General of India in Dubai. The programme includes: Live music, dance and storytelling Cultural processions Stand-up comedy Rangoli workshops Traditional drumming Previous editions have been free to attend. When: November 7 and 8 Where: Souk Al Seef, Dubai Global Village The India Pavilion at Global Village usually marks Diwali with a festive mela, rangoli and weekend fireworks. Last year, vendors there sold gold-plated jewellery, bangles, saris and Kashmiri textiles, and a group of UAE-based artists created a large rangoli on site. Season 31 opened on October 14, and this year's Diwali dates are yet to be announced. When: To be announced Where: Global Village, Dubai Celebrations in your community Dubai Holding Communities is hosting Diwali events across 17 neighbourhoods, including Al Furjan, Jumeirah Village Circle, Jumeirah Village Triangle, Discovery Gardens, Villanova, Remraam, Dubai Wharf, Bay Square and Jumeirah Islands. Dates and timings vary by community. Details are available from Dubai Holding Community Management on 800 DubaiCM. When: Varies by community Where: Dubai Holding communities Price: Free View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dubai Holding Community Management (@dubaiholdingcommunities) BAPS Hindu Mandir, Abu Dhabi The Mandir will hold Diwali celebrations from November 6 to 10. The programme includes: Pujas Maha Annakut Darshan, a display of food offerings traditionally prepared for the Hindu New Year Cultural performances and festive activities The Mandir is normally closed on Mondays, but it will open on Monday, November 9 for the festival. Meghan on keeping her distance The reports have brought renewed attention to Meghan’s estranged relationship with her father. title: WKU Football returns home, seeking third-straight win against Delaware
author: Jonah Moore, Sports Reporter
content: WKU Football returns home to take on Delaware on Oct. 27 after an almost two week hiatus, looking to crest three-straight wins for the first time this season. In their past two games, the Hilltoppers outscored both opponents by a combined 34 points, securing blowout wins over Missouri State on Oct. 8 and Sam Houston on Oct. 14. Senior quarterback Brock Glenn started both those games, racking up a combined 178 yards on the ground and a touchdown, leading the team in rushing against Sam Houston. “They make use of every single rep and that’s what you want in a quarterback and that trickles down to the rest of your team,” Head Coach Tyson Helton said. Senior running back Ajay Allen has also gotten in on the action, recording his fourth career 100-plus yard performance against the Bears. Although the run game has been potent, the Hilltoppers passing attack has lacked efficiency, with Glenn completing just over half of his passes over the past two games. Even with the struggles, freshman wide out Jonathan Stafford Jr. marked four-straight games with 60-plus receiving yards– a streak that ended against the Bearkats. “To be 18 years old and to be as mature as he is to go out there and contribute to this football team the way he has… he’s a guy that has a tremendously bright future,” Helton said. WKU is a perfect 2-0 on the season at home, outscoring their opponents by 66 points, as the Hilltopper faithful have shown up and shown out in support of the Hilltoppers. As WKU closes the month of October, they prepare for two difficult matchups against Jacksonville State on Nov. 14 and Liberty Nov. 21, both of which sit atop the Conference USA standings. “This is a highly competitive conference,” Helton said. “It’s anybody’s game, and we’re all about the same. It just depends on who plays the best.” Helton and the Hilltoppers will look to end the month on a good note, hoping to take advantage of a struggling Delaware squad at the Houch. Stream the game on CBS Sports Network , kicking off at 6 p.m. The post WKU Football returns home, seeking third-straight win against Delaware appeared first on WKUHerald.com .

title: Potions aren’t the only toxic waste to watch out for this Halloween
author: Lauren Sexton, News Reporter
content: Warren County’s Division of Stormwater Management invited residents to “get rid of hazardous waste the right way” on Oct. 31. The division partnered with many businesses to host Household Hazardous Waste Day on Saturday to teach Warren County residents the most environmentally friendly way to dispose of hazardous waste in their homes. The event will take place at 999 Lauren Avery Drive from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. According to the Warren County website , hazardous waste can range from paint, ant-freeze, oil or e-waste, such as TVs, phones or computers. There will also be an on-site shredder for community members to bring any personal documents they need to shred. “By participating in Household Hazardous Waste Day, you and your family may get rid of those extra household items cluttering up your garage, cabinets and closets and protect the environment at the same time,” the website said. title: BG community and local politicians celebrate ‘A Decade of Pride’
author: Abigail Vickers, News Reporter
content: Circus Square Park transformed into a lively scene of vibrant colors and high-energy drag performances on Saturday to celebrate the 10 th annual Bowling Green Pride Festival, organized by Bowling Green Fairness . Bowling Green Fairness is affiliated with the statewide Fairness Campaign , headquartered in Louisville. The Fairness Campaign aims to pass Fairness Ordinances in cities across Kentucky, banning discrimination against the LGBTQ+ community. Doug Lowery, vice chair of the Fairness Campaign, said the organization lobbies in Frankfort, endorses candidates and helps people become more politically active, among other efforts. Lowery said the Fairness Campaign typically endorses candidates that align with the organization’s values. The Fairness Campaign has helped 24 municipalities across the Commonwealth enact LGBTQ+ discrimination protections through endorsements and political activism, according to the organization’s website. Bowling Green celebrated the LGBTQ+ community during the Decade of Pride event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, at Circus Square Park in Bowling Green, Ky. The event featured live music, vendors and drag performances by Queen Venus Knight, Geneva LaDiva, Kara Belle, Mykul J Valentine, Kassandra Hilton, L’Zayna Zahara, Serenity Sweets, Miss B, Dahlia Blake and Calvin Brooks. ( Kylee Holt ) Louisville and Lexington, Kentucky’s two largest cities, have already enacted Fairness Ordinances. Bowling Green is the largest city in Kentucky without a Fairness Ordinance. Patti Minter, a Bowling Green Fairness leader and WKU professor, has helped organize BG Pride since it first began in 2017. Minter said this year’s festival was themed around “A Decade of Pride” in the city, becoming the largest festival in BG Pride’s 10-year history. Local vendors sold pastries, jewelry, crocheted accessories and other goods at tables scattered across Circus Square Park. Patrons could also get tarot card readings, see live drag performances and donate to different causes and organizations like Bowling Green Fairness. The annual Pride Crawl following the festival also enticed patrons to spend a night out enjoying deals on drinks and cocktails from local businesses across downtown Bowling Green. Since Bowling Green doesn’t have a Fairness Ordinance, Minter said these annual events give those in the LGBTQ+ community a day and night to fully express themselves. LGBTQ+ community members write “Sorry Mom” in chalk during the Decade of Pride event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, at Circus Square Park in Bowling Green, Ky. The phrase shows themes of identity, self-expression and family acceptance within the community. ( Kylee Holt ) “This is a day where people can wear their colors, feel proud of who they are and support others who are showing up and showing out,” Minter said. “It’s a beautiful day every single year.” In support of Bowling Green Fairness, Fairness Campaign representatives tabled at BG Pride. The organization helped people register to vote and sold $20 shirts that went toward supporting the organization. A city commission needs three votes to pass a Fairness Ordinance, according to Bobbie Glass, board chair of the Fairness Campaign. The majority of Bowling Green’s five City Commissioners repeatedly rejected the ordinance over the years. While Bowling Green Fairness is still working on getting a Fairness Ordinance passed, Glass said BG Pride exceeded her expectations. “There is nothing like having an annual event as something that keeps growing and getting bigger,” Glass said. “I’m just really impressed.” Jessica Faine, a Bowling Green resident, attended BG Pride for her first time on Saturday. She said events like BG Pride create a sense of belonging for her and others in the LGBTQ+ community. Faine said her favorite parts of the festival were the performances. Some of the performers included local favorites like Queen Venus Knight, Serenity Sweets of The PrimaDonnas and Calvin Brooks, Bowling Green’s longest performing drag king. “People can come together that feel alone and know that there are others that are just like them and that everyone is supportive,” Faine said. Attendees watch a drag performance by Geneva LaDiva during the tenth annual Decade of Pride event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, at Circus Square Park in Bowling Green, Ky. ( Kylee Holt ) Chick Falcon, a lead singer of the Daddy Sisters , has performed at BG Pride for the past six years. The Daddy Sisters are a punk duo from Bowling Green, and Falcon said the community has always been very supportive of the group. She said community events like BG Pride have also helped her in coming out as a transgender woman. “I feel like a smaller community like Bowling Green really needs queer people to lift it up because we don’t even have a Fairness Ordinance,” she said. Several local city and state politicians running in the upcoming election spoke at BG Pride. These candidates garnered support from the LGBTQ+ community with the promise of creating and passing more fair laws and ordinances that will benefit everyone within the Commonwealth, regardless of their gender or sexual orientation. Candidates included U.S. Rep. candidate Megan Wingfield, Bowling Green City Commission candidate Thomas Morris and current Bowling Green City Commissioners Dana Beasley-Brown and Carlos Bailey. U.S. Sen. candidate Charles Booker spoke at BG Pride as Election Day approaches. Booker showed his support for the LGBTQ+ community and took photos with fans after his speech. He said BG Pride was one of most beautiful events he has been to in a long time, and he wants to help support everyone in Bowling Green if elected. “When we begin to choose love, that’s when we begin to choose freedom,” Booker told the crowd. title: Spirit of Riverview still strong 60 years later
author: Miles Davis, News Reporter
content: Members of the Bowling Green community came together on Friday night dressed in various costumes. Despite its silly appearance, the gathering served an important purpose of helping preserve a part of the city’s history. Riverview at Hobson Grove hosted its Spirit of Riverview Costume Gala at the Corvette Museum. The event served as the main fundraiser for the only historic house and museum in Bowling Green. It also celebrated the 60th anniversary of the Hobson House Association . Donated items for the event’s silent auction filled the tables, such as a Mad Men’s Gentlemen’s Package, which included a cigar box and ashtrays. Auctioneers from Progressive Auction Group hosted the live auction for vacations, condo stays and other prizes. Proceeds collected from both auctions and admission costs, $100 per person or $720 for a table of eight, benefited the Hobson House, a historic Civil War-era property. It was used as a munitions magazine in the 1860’s by the Confederate army before construction was finished. “It takes a lot to keep a house that old running,” Tia Tabor said. Tabor was the main organizer for the silent auction and a board member for Friends of Riverview, the non-profit support organization for Riverview at Hobson Grove. The group supports restoration efforts for the Hobson House and organizes its fundraising events. Patrons dressed up as TV characters, the theme for the event. Costumes ranged from Wednesday Addams from “The Addams Family” to Margaret “Hot Lips” Houlihan from “M*A*S*H.” Michael Trapasso dressed up as Spock from “Star Trek,” donning the iconic blue uniform and pointed ears. Trapasso is a former Friends of Riverview board member and city commissioner. He moved to Bowling Green in the 1980s, and donated to the Hobson House project ever since. He said he’s happy with the progress that it’s made in its physical restoration. “It was a wreck when I first got here,” Trapasso said. “Now it’s a wonderful house museum.” Trapasso is a former professor at WKU, where he taught meteorology for over 35 years. Current students on the Hill also attended the event. A group of Spirit Masters, the university’s official student ambassadors, volunteered, welcoming guests and helping serve dinner. “I’m making sure if they (guests) have questions, they can ask me,” said Spirit Master Emaun Riley, a junior and human resource management major. The evening concluded with a costume contest. The winner took home a painting of the Hobson House made by board member Claire Aldrige, who dressed up as Bob Ross for the event. Friends of Riverview Executive Director Brooke Westcott-Peterson expressed her gratitude for guests’ support through a written statement in a handbook distributed at the event. “You enable us to carry on the Spirit of Riverview,” Westcott-Peterson said. title: WKU Men’s Basketball falters in 79-74 loss to Indiana
author: Jonah Moore, Sports Reporter
content: WKU Men’s Basketball made the trek to the Hoosiers’ backyard, taking on Indiana in Evansville for their final exhibition game of the season. The Hilltoppers put together an inspiring performance against one of the nation’s best, falling in the final minutes, 79-74. WKU led for the majority of the second half, however, Indiana came storming back with an 8-0 run fueled by multiple turnovers and missed opportunities by the Hilltoppers in the final two minutes that propelled the Hoosiers to a narrow victory. Indiana received considerable contributions from their bench, racking up 57 points off the bench compared to just 17 from WKU. Fifty-three of the team’s 74 points were split between redshirt junior guard Teagan Moore, sophomore guard Armelo Boone and junior guard Sharron Young, which inhibited the Hilltoppers’ ability to sustain their efficiency down the stretch. Entering the game, WKU came off a 65-62 win in their first exhibition game against Bowling Green State Oct. 20, where Moore recorded 22 points, hoping to carry over his successes against Indiana. Moore was outstanding against Indiana, knocking down four threes en route to his first-career 30-point game, including a half-court heave to beat the buzzer in the first half. His stellar shooting performance was infectious, as the Hilltoppers’ were making it rain, shooting 40% from three. The Hoosiers entered the matchup with ample momentum, coming off back-to-back wins over North Carolina and Butler, where they dominated in the paint, outrebounding both teams by 42. Without a true center on their roster, WKU relied on Boone, who was a force down low for the Hilltoppers, scoring 13 points and hauling in seven rebounds. His partner in crime, senior guard LJ Hackman, also chipped in with four points and eight rebounds, marking the second consecutive game where both Boone and Hackman combined for 15 or more rebounds. The Hilltoppers were much improved in comparison to their last matchup, largely thanks to their defense that recorded 10 steals and held the Hoosiers offense to just 79 points. Despite the improved play, WKU was unable to get the upset win, but still has something to build on as the season swiftly approaches. With the loss, the Hilltoppers will look ahead to their season opener against Morehead State on Nov. 2, hoping to live up to their expectations and kick off the season with a win. title: WKU Soccer undefeated at home with New Mexico State takedown
author: Zoe Cristy, Sports Reporter
content: WKU Soccer took down New Mexico State 2-1, securing an undefeated season at home for the first time since 2020. This is just the fourth time in program history that the Hilltoppers have not fallen on their home pitch for a season. “The players take a lot of pride in wearing the uniform and defending their home turf, and I’m really proud of them,” Head Coach Jason Neidell said. The Hilltoppers established their power on the field from the first kick, keeping the ball in their control for most of the half. Their consistent pressure led them to nine shots, and two shots on goal before the half. After the half, the pressure lapsed and the Aggies gained more control, holding the Hilltoppers to six more shots and three on goal. WKU struggled to connect with the net, with five shots on goal to their fifteen total shots. Sophomore midfielder Mya Jackson brought the Hilltoppers their first goal in the 18th minute, assisted by junior midfielder Alyvia Walls. The Aggies struggled to keep up initially, only managing two shots in the first half, with one on goal. NMSU opened the second half determined to bring the Hilltoppers an answer, with graduate forward Sydnee Johnson tying the match in the 49th minute. With 13 fouls for the Aggies and seven for the Hilltoppers throughout the game, it was a power struggle to the very end. Walls scored in the 79th minute, assisted by graduate forward Danielle Lewin. From there, the end of the game was a brawl, with both teams receiving yellow cards in the last 11 minutes. The Hilltoppers will next be traveling to MTSU on November 1. title: WKU Men’s Basketball on the road against Indiana
author: Jonah Moore, Sports Reporter
content: WKU Men’s Basketball will play their first road game of the season on Oct. 25, taking on the Indiana Hoosiers at the Ford Center in Evansville, Indiana for their final exhibition game before the season opener. The Hilltoppers kicked off the season with a 65-62 win at home against Bowling Green State on Oct. 20. Junior guard Teagan Moore led the charge for the Hilltoppers, recording 22 points and shooting 50% from the field. Behind Moore was an entourage of brutes down low, with sophomore guard Armelo Boone and senior guard LJ Hackman recording 16 combined rebounds. “I do think we put a lot of pressure on the rim,” Head Coach Hank Plona said. “It just kind of is naturally who we are.” Despite a late flurry by the Falcons, WKU maintained control of the game defensively, limiting Bowling Green State to just one shot from beyond the arc in the first half, propelling the Hilltoppers to a hard fought victory. WKU now turns their attention to their last true test before the season gets off and running, facing off against an Indiana Hoosiers squad that defeated the likes of North Carolina and Butler by 46 combined points. After a low scoring affair against the Falcons, Plona will look to up the offensive efficiency and make a statement against one of college basketball’s most storied programs. “It’ll be great for our guys,” Plona said. “We’ll know where we currently stand against one of the best teams in America.” Stream the game on BIG TEN+, tipping off at 3 p.m. The post WKU Men’s Basketball on the road against Indiana appeared first on WKUHerald.com .

title: WKU Volleyball remains perfect in CUSA with wins over Kennesaw State
author: Morgan Larkins and Zoe Cristy
content: WKU Volleyball defeated Kennesaw State in back-to-back four set matches, improving to 10-0 in Conference USA and 16-6 overall. Sophomore rightside hitter Kaira Knox continues to impress, finishing the weekend with 34 kills, four blocks, and two service aces. “We moved sets inside for her and that got her on the right track,” Head Coach Travis Hudson said. “Just a special talent, we are very fortunate to have her.” The Hilltoppers continued to be inconsistent from the service line, finishing the weekend with 16 service aces and 26 errors. Despite the inconsistency, WKU were much more composed in game two, finishing with eight aces. Sophomore defensive specialist Kennedy Cherry especially made her presence known, keeping Kennesaw State out of system when she was at the service line. Game one The Hilltoppers opened their weekend against KSU with a four set win. WKU attacks, serves and defense were riddled with errors which the Owls took advantage of. WKU took set one 25-21. The Hilltoppers opened strong with a kill from Knox, but couldn’t keep the momentum up. The Owls capitalized on critical Hilltopper errors, allowing them to keep the lead until a service ace from libero Tayler Baron. A kill from junior middle hitter Faith Young put the set away for WKU. The Hilltoppers took set two 25-17. A strong start from WKU was not enough to keep them in the lead. Kennesaw State predicted every Hilltopper move and once again capitalized on critical errors to tie them up. A kill from Young firmly put the Hilltoppers ahead of the Owls 16-13 and the energy did not stop. An attack error from Kennesaw State put the set away for WKU. WKU fell in set three 25-23. The Hilltoppers found their missing piece and started with a strong offensive push, but didn’t last forever. Despite Kennesaw State initially struggling to keep up with the Hilltopper’s, the team quickly caught on and tied the game. The end of the match became a battle for points — the Owls clawing for a fourth set and the Hilltoppers looking to end the game. The Owls got their wish after a kill from Kennesaw State’s junior rightside hitter Ashlyn Anderson ended the set. The Hilltoppers took set four 25-21. An early battle broke out for points, with WKU coming out on top after a kill from Young. The Owls once again figured the Hilltoppers out, managing to tie up the set, 14-14. Instead of keeping a steady lead, the court once again became a battlefield for points to get ahead. A kill from junior outside hitter Alivia Skidmore put the Hilltoppers in the lead and a kill from Knox put the set and match away. Game two WKU fell in set one 25-22. The tumultuous opening set saw a struggle to maintain a lead, with both teams making critical errors. The score changed consistently with six lead changes, and 11 ties as the battle for the set raged until the very end. Eventually, Kennesaw State found themselves on a 3-0 scoring run, ending the set with a kill by freshman outside hitter Ashley Theiss. WKU took set two 25-19, after a power struggle that defined the set. While both WKU and KSU made several errors in the opening, the Hilltoppers eventually took control with a 3-0 scoring run that brought the score to 12-9.The Owls’ continued errors as well as WKU’s renewed determination led to a quick end to the set. A service error from Senior middle blocker Maggie Byrd ended the set in the Hilltopper’s first win of the night. The Hilltoppers took set three 25-9. WKU freshman defensive specialist Cali Foster took complete control from the service line, opening with a 6-0 run. Throughout the set, continual errors from the Owls allowed the Hilltoppers to further stretch their lead to 24-9. Knox brought the Hilltoppers to their second set win. “It was two really good service runs that kind of put us in control,” Hudson said. WKU won the fourth set 25-18, leading to another 3-1 victory against the Owls. WKU remained largely in control, taking a 21-13 lead. However, Kennesaw State came to life, going on a 4-0 run, closing the deficit to four. The surge was too little too late, as a kill by Skidmore gave the Hilltoppers the set and match. WKU hits the road to face off against Florida International University Oct. 30 at 5 p.m. on ESPN+. title: Boots on the ground: Charles Booker brings campaign to WKU
author: Maha Salem, News Reporter
content: Students and Bowling Green community members frenetically packed the Downing Student Union to hear U.S Sen. candidate Charles Booker speak. WKU Democrats president Jacob King explained that he was honored to host and endorse Booker to replace U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell. King introduced Booker emcee-style, like a basketball announcer announcing the most valuable player at a high-profile game. “We are very glad that he’s here,” King said. Booker then spoke about his mission to represent his constituents “from the hood to the holler.” “The hopes that we have, in a lot of ways, have gone unheard,” he said. “And the status quo in Washington has really shown us that they don’t care whether we live or die.” He compared his campaign to “Avengers Endgame”, Kentuckians banding together like superheroes to fight President Donald Trump’s administration. “I think it speaks to who we are right now,” he said. “Because we’re up against it. We’re in a fight for our future, our humanity and for democracy.” Booker also explained his feelings toward billionaire politicians. “I believe we deserve better than a government that gives tax breaks to Elon Musk and gives us the middle finger,” Booker said. This sentiment was met with applause from the audience, who cheered him on throughout his speech. Booker then opened the floor to the audience members, citing his Kitchen Cabinet initiative. This program, he said, is an amalgamation of grassroots advisory committees from different backgrounds. He gave examples of the people in these groups: teachers, college students and religious leaders. Senior political science major Jaden Marshall asked U.S. Sen. candidate Charles Booker about rising costs inside the Downing Student Union on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. The event, hosted by the WKU Democrats, is part of a larger campaign initiative. (Photo provided to the College Heights Herald by Christian Pastura.) Senior political science major Jaden Marshall asked the candidate about his plans to resolve rising costs, citing general inflation. Booker explained that he believes inflation is a result of the war in Iran, and that holding Washington leadership accountable will stop the war. “There has to be accountability across the board,” he said. “And I will continue to say this: Pete Hegseth has to go.” Pete Hegseth is the U.S. Secretary of Defense, though he refers to himself as the Secretary of War. Booker also said his opponent, U.S. Rep. Andy Barr, is against this anti-war notion. “My opponent has essentially said that this president doesn’t even need to come to Congress to get authorization,” he said. “That what’s happening is a success. That’s scary.” Sophomore film student Jackson Meade shared similar thoughts. “I came here because, I’ll admit, I don’t know enough about politics,” he said. “But I know I don’t like Andy Barr.” Booker continued and told the attendees that he had breaking news. “We will win this Senate race,” he said. “How poetic would it be?” In an interview with the College Heights Herald, Booker talked about his plans to decrease student debt. He shared that he is still paying off loans after attending the University of Louisville, and intends to eradicate loan debt by raising wages. “This is a holistic conversation,” he said. “We need more money in our pockets to address rising costs.” Booker concluded with a group photo and a group chant. “The people united will never be divided,” the crowd said. “The people united will never be divided.” The post Boots on the ground: Charles Booker brings campaign to WKU appeared first on WKUHerald.com .

title: Migrant workers find strength in each other amid Israeli strikes in Lebanon
author: Shirin Jaafari
content: It was 3 o’clock in the morning last March when Israeli strikes hit Dahieh, in the suburbs of the Lebanese capital Beirut. The attacks sent families fleeing their homes. Myra Aragon’s phone started ringing. “They were asking, ‘Where are we going to go?’” she recalled in an interview this month. “Because they don’t have any place to go, and they were just walking, so I kept monitoring them. Also, I was at a loss. We were not at all prepared.” The people calling her were terrified. They were mostly women domestic workers who, like her, had traveled from the Philippines to work in Lebanon. Some had children with them, Aragon said, and they were on the streets, looking for somewhere safe to shelter. By the time the families reached Aragon, they had been walking for three hours, she said. She had nowhere to put them. “[One] family has two children, the other has four. The other one has three. It’s chaos.” Aragon is 52 and from the Philippines. She said the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah has brought an entirely new level of desperation to the migrant workers in Lebanon. “Before, only [specific] areas were targeted by Israel, but this time it’s widespread,” she said. The workers were already struggling with discrimination and few legal protections in Lebanon. They come from various countries, but most are from the Philippines, Ethiopia, Bangladesh and Sudan. They clean homes and care for children or the elderly. They also work on farms or as drivers. Many have left their own families behind, hoping to earn enough money to send back home for a chance at a better life. When Israeli strikes forced families across Lebanon to flee their homes, many migrant workers faced the especially difficult choice of where to go. Some were left behind by their employers. Others found themselves shut out of shelters, with little money and no way to leave the country. St. Joseph Church in Beirut became a temporary shelter for displaced migrant workers when Israel struck the city back in the spring. Shirin Jaafari/The World “The migrants here are very much marginalized. There is [little] protection,” explained Father Henry Ponce, a Filipino Jesuit priest, who works with migrants in Beirut. He said that last spring, his church became an emergency shelter. People arrived hungry, exhausted and frightened. “A lot from the south evacuated to Beirut, and there were shelters, Lebanese shelters of the government, but they do not accept migrants. They only accept Lebanese,” Ponce said. Lebanon’s kafala , or sponsorship system, ties many migrant workers’ legal status to their employers, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation. Most can’t just leave the country if things aren’t going well. They often don’t have the money to pay for flights, and if they’re undocumented, they can be arrested and jailed. They also don’t want to give up an income that helps their families back home. Ponce and his team sheltered about 200 people at the St. Joseph church in Beirut. All three floors of the church were packed, he added. The church provided hot meals and a place to sleep for the displaced migrants. But more kept coming. “Our shelter was full already,” Ponce said, “but I [couldn’t ] just let them go.” The situation in the south of the country was even worse. Rescue worker Hussain Fakih in the city of Nabatiyeh said when the airstrikes came, some families fled, leaving behind their employees. “A large number of them were still there,” Fakih said, “and some were injured in the strikes.” He described evacuating Sudanese and Ethiopian workers from farms. They were hungry and frightened; he said they could barely think straight. Myra Aragon, who helped the migrants in Beirut, said she jumped into action because she knows what it feels like to have nowhere to turn. Like many migrant workers in Lebanon, her presence in the country and her movement were dependent on her employers. She arrived in the country in 2004, expecting to work as a nurse. Instead, she was cheated by a recruitment agency. A couple promised her they would get her residency papers, but she said they also took her money and disappeared. She was forced to live in the shadows as an undocumented worker. Myra Aragon traveled to Lebanon in 2004 with the hope of working as a nurse. Instead, she said she was cheated and forced to live in the shadows as an undocumented migrant. Shirin Jaafari/The World At one point, Aragon said, she ended up caring for an older woman in a city in northern Lebanon. But the woman’s son sexually assaulted her. “He [was] a civil engineer. Even if I am a registered nurse in the Philippines, in Lebanon, I am just a house maid. So, who will believe me?” she recalled. The abuse went on for a while. “I [felt] like I’m an animal,” Aragon said, “no respect at all. How could I face my family? I was already trafficked. I was cheated with the contract. And now I go home with this story of being subjected to sexual abuse? I cannot.” Aragon felt she could no longer stay in that house. She came up with an elaborate plan to escape. Today, she helps migrant workers learn about their rights. She organizes training for women who’ve experienced exploitation and abuse. “I don’t want to be bitter about all the things that have happened,” she said, “because of all the challenges that I have suffered in Lebanon, this is how I became an advocate. Because I want to stand up for my community so that what I have experienced, I hope they will not experience.” She has also been pushing for changes to Lebanon’s labor laws, but progress has been painfully slow. A meeting with lawmakers planned for March was postponed when the war escalated. Still, she isn’t giving up. “Working on this is not a quick and easy job,” Aragon said, “but at least the seed has been planted. I may not benefit [from] it, but maybe the future [workers] will benefit [from it]. This is important for me.” On a sunny October day, a group of migrants gathered at the St. Joseph church in Beirut for mass. Music echoed through the church’s high-ceilinged hall. The church has become a place for the migrants to see each other, exchange stories and commiserate. Aragon, who was among the crowd, said she knew she couldn’t solve everyone’s problems. But at least the people who turn to her know they’re not alone. And that there’s someone they can count on when they need help. This story was reported with support from the Pulitzer Center. title: Brazil’s presidential election has two very different soundtracks
author: Tibisay Zea
content: Ahead of Brazil’s presidential runoff, some of the country’s biggest musicians are making their political preferences known. At a concert in Paraná last Sunday, country music superstar Gusttavo Lima waved a Brazilian flag and endorsed Flávio Bolsonaro . “God willing, Oct. 25 will be number 22,” he said, referring to the election date and Bolsonaro’s ballot number. Lima is among several stars of sertanejo — Brazil’s version of country music — backing the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Others include Leonardo, Zezé Di Camargo and Amado Batista. Meanwhile, musicians have also been mobilizing behind President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. On Oct. 12, samba musicians and Carnival groups gathered in Rio de Janeiro for a demonstration called “ Samba Won’t Be Silent .” Days later, thousands gathered on Copacabana Beach for a concert featuring Brazilian music legends Caetano Veloso and Djavan. Supporters of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is running for reelection, wave campaign flags and play samba music during a rally called “Samba com Lula” ahead of Brazil’s presidential runoff election in Brasilia, Brazil, Oct. 22, 2026. Eraldo Peres/AP Organizers called it a demonstration in defense of democracy, not an official campaign rally. But many attendees openly supported Lula. Kjetil Klette Bøhler, a music professor at the University of South-Eastern Norway, has studied Brazilian political demonstrations. “It’s everywhere,” he said of music. “And any kind of political slogans that they say, it has a rhythm. And through that rhythm, people can sing along.” Samba and traditional Brazilian popular music are often associated with the left, while sertanejo has become linked to conservative politics. But researchers say the divide isn’t so simple. The history behind the music Samba emerged from Afro-Brazilian communities in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, becoming an expression of Black identity and resistance to inequality. Samuel Araújo, an ethnomusicologist at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, said samba’s history is closely tied to Brazil’s Black working class. Initially subjected to discrimination and police repression, samba eventually became a national cultural symbol. Later, música popular brasileira (MPB) artists like Caetano Veloso and Chico Buarque became prominent voices against Brazil’s military dictatorship, from 1964 to 1985. Today, some Afro-Brazilian artists and activists support Lula over concerns about racial equality and setbacks they say occurred under Jair Bolsonaro. Sertanejo followed another path. Rooted in rural Brazil, it developed a huge domestic following while samba gained international recognition. Its visibility grew alongside Brazil’s increasingly powerful agricultural industry. Araújo said agribusiness helped bring sertanejo into the mainstream, even reaching the presidential palace. Bøhler says the genre also developed connections to conservative values. “There’s a strong historical legacy between conservative values, family, sometimes religion, the importance of these businesses and the music.” Opposition presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro holds a campaign rally near Copacabana Beach in Rio de Janeiro, Aug. 16, 2026. Bruna Prado/AP Beyond political stereotypes Historian Gustavo Alonso, at the Federal University of Pernambuco, cautioned against dividing musicians into opposing political camps. “The reality is more complex,” he said. Many sertanejo singers supported Lula in earlier elections, he noted. And their audiences extend well beyond wealthy farmers. “ Sertanejo music represents a huge portion of the Brazilian population,” Araújo said. “I’m not talking only about the elite, but also about the working class, just like samba.” That broad popularity makes musicians attractive to politicians seeking millions of potential voters through concerts and social media. But Alonso doubts endorsements necessarily influence votes. “They used to have a lot of influence, but not nowadays,” he said. “Nowadays, everyone has a cell phone, everyone thinks with their own head.” With Sunday’s runoff approaching, musicians have made their choices. Whether their fans follow them to the ballot box is another question. The post Brazil’s presidential election has two very different soundtracks appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: Ghana’s malaria vaccine success faces a sustainability test
author: Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman
content: Adeline Ahiatrogah carries her seven-month-old twins to a vaccination session in Ghana’s Volta Region, where mothers wait beneath a sprawling tree for health workers to call their children’s names. One twin is strapped to her back. The other rests against her chest. Ahiatrogah, 27, has brought them for their second dose of a malaria vaccine. Her older children have had malaria, and she remembers the fevers, the weakness and the fear that their illness might become fatal. Adeline Ahiatrogah, 27, holds one of her seven-month-old twins as he receives his second dose of the malaria vaccine.The RTS,S malaria vaccine, developed after more than three decades of research, targets Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite responsible for the deadliest form of malaria. Ghana, Kenya and Malawi launched the vaccine’s pilot program in 2019. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World “I was always afraid they could die,” she said. “As a mother, you just wish you could take the sickness away from them.” According to the World Health Organization,  malaria killed 610,000 people worldwide in 2024, about 95% of them in Africa. Young children remain particularly vulnerable. Since her twins began receiving the vaccine, she said neither has developed malaria severe enough to require a hospital visit. She hopes they will remain protected as they receive the remaining doses. Ghana has made substantial progress against malaria. Ghana’s Health Service estimates that malaria deaths fell by 98% between 2011 and 2025, with 52 deaths recorded nationally in 2025. The country has also seen a significant decline in child malaria fatalities, which have fallen by 76% in just three years. The progress reflects years of prevention, diagnosis and treatment, including insecticide-treated mosquito nets and improved access to healthcare. Mothers bring their children for routine health checks during a community outreach in Adaklu, Ghana’s Volta Region. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World In October 2021, the WHO recommended widespread use of RTS,S, or Mosquirix, the first malaria vaccine to receive such a recommendation. Ghana, Kenya and Malawi had already begun a pilot program in 2019 to assess how vaccination could be delivered through routine health services. Today, malaria vaccination is offered in 25 African countries as part of national childhood immunization programs and malaria-control plans. Five years after that landmark recommendation, Ghana’s experience illustrates both the potential of vaccination and the challenge of sustaining its benefits. A complex target for vaccine science Malaria has long challenged vaccine developers because Plasmodium falciparum , the parasite responsible for the deadliest form of the disease, has a complex life cycle and can evade the human immune system. When an infected mosquito bites a person, it introduces parasites called sporozoites into the bloodstream. These travel to the liver, multiply and then enter red blood cells. The resulting infection causes malaria symptoms and can progress to severe anemia, organ failure and death. RTS,S targets the parasite during this early stage. It trains the immune system to recognize the parasite’s circumsporozoite protein, helping prevent some infections from progressing to the blood stage. Researchers work in the immunology and vaccine biology laboratories at the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research in Accra. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World Developed by GlaxoSmithKline with research partners, RTS,S emerged from decades of scientific work. It does not provide complete or lifelong protection, but it reduces the risk of clinical malaria during childhood, when the disease can be particularly dangerous. Under Ghana’s RTS,S schedule, children receive doses at six, seven, nine and 18 months of age. The fourth dose requires caregivers to return months after the first three. At the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research in Accra, immunology professor Kwadwo Asamoah Kusi said completing the schedule helps extend protection. Kwadwo Asamoah Kusi, an immunology professor at the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research in Accra, researches malaria, vaccine biology and immunity. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World “If you just do one or two, it will protect you for a few weeks to a few months and then it’s gone,” he said. “But doing all the four extends how long that protection lasts for them. So, it’s very important that we finish all of it.” Protection varies, but the schedule presents practical challenges for families living far from health facilities or struggling with transport costs. Missed appointments can mean children do not receive the full intended protection. In Adaklu, 32-year-old Dope Kulafe took her two youngest children, aged four years and 23 months, through all four doses. She initially worried about side effects. Her children experienced symptoms that she said resolved after about three days. Dope Kulafe, 32, takes her child for weighing during a community health outreach in Adaklu, Ghana’s Volta Region. She says her two youngest children have completed all four doses of the malaria vaccine without suffering from severe malaria. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World “From my experience, the vaccine is helping my children, and I’d encourage other mothers to get their babies vaccinated,” she said. Building trust in vaccination In Adaklu, health workers say misinformation remains an obstacle to vaccination. Emelia Tanyeva, a health worker involved in community outreach, said some caregivers have carried suspicions from the COVID-19 pandemic into the malaria vaccination program. Some believe the malaria vaccine is being introduced because parents refused COVID-19 vaccination, while others suspect it is part of a Western effort to reduce Africa’s population. “Some caregivers believe that it is a way of reducing their population. They want to kill their children or wipe out the children they are giving birth to,” Tanyeva said. Emelia Tanyeva, a community health worker, says mistrust of the malaria vaccination programme sometimes complicates efforts to reach caregivers. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World There is no credible scientific evidence supporting these claims, but health workers say such rumors can undermine confidence in vaccination. Some parents also question why children need four malaria vaccine doses on top of routine childhood immunizations. Health workers are responding by taking vaccination services and information into communities, explaining the schedule and addressing concerns about side effects. Yet, misinformation is not the only obstacle. Transport expenses, time away from work and competing family responsibilities can also cause missed appointments. Health Worker Emelia Tanyeva explains to a mother that malaria vaccination should be complemented by other preventive measures, including sleeping under insecticide-treated mosquito nets. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World The Adaklu District Health Directorate said nearly 70% of eligible children had completed all four doses. It also reported that annual malaria cases among children under five had fallen from about 6,000 to 2,000, with no deaths recorded since the vaccine was introduced, alongside existing malaria-control measures. Evidence of an effect on child survival A 2026 study published in The Lancet , examining malaria vaccine implementation in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi, reported a 13% reduction in deaths from all causes other than injury among children eligible to receive three doses.  “So basically, in these communities, the malaria vaccine prevented approximately 1 in 8 deaths of children that were non-accidental, non-injury-related,” said Dr. William Moss, a professor of epidemiology and deputy director of the Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute. A health worker examines a child during a community health outreach in Adaklu, Ghana’s Volta Region. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World Moss explained that the data strengthens the case for vaccination. But he said sustaining those gains will require the vaccine to complement — not replace — existing malaria-control measures. “If funding for bed nets and surveillance, testing and treatment all decline, we’re going to see more people, unfortunately and tragically, infected with the parasite, developing disease,” he said. “And even in the face of the vaccines, we’re going to see a larger disease burden.” Moss added that sustaining these gains will be critical as Ghana confronts the spread of the invasive Anopheles stephensi mosquito, emerging insecticide and diagnostic resistance and growing pressure from other mosquito-borne diseases, all of which threaten to complicate malaria control even as vaccination expands. Who will pay for the gains? That creates a financial challenge for Ghana as international health assistance comes under pressure. Disruptions to United States foreign assistance, including the dismantling of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), have contributed to a $78 million health financing gap for Ghana, affecting several interventions, including malaria programs. A researcher examines blood samples and prepares specimen slides for analysis in a laboratory at the Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research in Accra, Ghana, as part of scientific work supporting research into malaria. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World The shortfall raises questions about whether Ghana can sustain the procurement, distribution and community outreach needed to protect children against malaria while maintaining other essential health services. Ghana is also gradually assuming a greater share of its immunization costs through co-financing arrangements with Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance . Official figures for Ghana’s obligations put its contribution at $54 million next year, rising to $60 million by 2030.  Ghana’s rollout covers more than 130 of the country’s 260 districts. The national program includes RTS,S and, more recently, R21 , another WHO-recommended malaria vaccine. The R21 malaria vaccine, also recommended by the World Health Organization, is part of Ghana’s national malaria vaccination program. Ridwan Karim Dini-Osman/The World Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh said the government would find the resources needed to finance the program fully when Gavi’s support ends in 2030. Delivering on that commitment will require clear budgets for vaccine procurement, distribution, cold storage, trained health workers and outreach to families whose children miss appointments. Gladys Damalin, programs manager at Hope for Future Generations , a civil society organization advocating better health policies, said sustaining the vaccine’s impact requires clearer financing plans and accountability. “The question is sustaining and ensuring that every district is covered,” she said. Damalin wants a dedicated immunization budget that would make allocations and disbursements easier to track. Without predictable funding, she warned, the services needed to keep vaccination programs functioning could weaken even when vaccines remain part of national policy. Back in Adaklu, Ahiatrogah’s twins still need to complete their doses. She said she is holding on to the promise that the protection they have begun receiving will help spare them the illness that frightened her when her older children contracted malaria. But experts say whether that promise translates into lasting progress will depend not only on getting vaccines to children, but also on Ghana’s ability to finance the program and sustain the wider measures that keep malaria in check.
