title: Mexico’s Korean wave goes from K-pop fandom to trade and diplomacy
author: Tibisay Zea
content: At the 2026 K-Expo in Mexico City, 17-year-old Fanny Mendez moved from booth to booth, surrounded by everything Korean. The expo — held Sept. 24-27 — brought together K-pop, food, beauty, entertainment and other Korean industries. She moved among booths selling Korean food, beauty products and pop-culture merchandise, stopping at games where fans could win cards featuring their favorite singers. “I’m absolutely loving it,” Mendez said. She came with her mother after discovering the expo on TikTok. “My favorite part right now is the games where you can win photo cards.” Visitors interact with digital displays at the K-Expo in Mexico City, a showcase of Korean culture, entertainment, food, beauty and consumer products. Jiroko Nakamura/The World She doesn’t speak Korean and knows little English. But she said that doesn’t keep her from connecting with Korean pop music. “I got goosebumps,” she said. “I think that’s the magic of it. You don’t have to understand the language to feel it.” The expo is an example of the growing popularity of Korean culture in Mexico. But that trend has now extended beyond music and merchandise, leading to a deeper economic and diplomatic relationship between Mexico and South Korea. Mendez, who is 17 years old, may have gone to the K-pop (Korean popular music) expo but found herself drawn to Korean skincare, as well. Visitors gather around Korean beauty displays at the K-Expo in Mexico City, where skincare and cosmetics were among the products featured. Jiroko Nakamura/The World At one booth, a woman sat down for a quick demonstration as a specialist examined her skin and recommended products. Nearby, tables were stacked with cleansers, creams, serums and makeup. Korean cosmetics have become increasingly popular in Mexico. Exports of Korean cosmetics to the country jumped 51% between January and July of 2024 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency, or KOTRA. Entrepreneurs have noticed. Jason Bae, a Korean social media creator known as “Jason Coreano,” has built a large Spanish-speaking following online. At the expo, he was promoting his Korean skincare brand, Clever Steps. And he chose Mexico as its first market. “Korea is my first country, but Mexico is my second country,” Bae said. “There’s something about Mexican people that made me fall in love. That’s why we are launching our skincare brand first in Mexico and then the United States.” Little Seoul, before the K-pop boom Mexico City’s connection to South Korea predates the current K-pop craze. In the city’s Zona Rosa, a pocket of Korean restaurants, grocery stores, cafés and karaoke spots is commonly known as “ Pequeño Seúl ,” or Little Seoul. The neighborhood began taking shape in the mid-1990s, as Korean residents and businesses concentrated in the area . It initially catered largely to the Korean community, but that has changed as Korean culture has become more popular among Mexicans. A display of Korean instant noodles and food replicas at the K-Expo in Mexico City, which featured Korean food alongside music, beauty and other cultural products. Jiroko Nakamura/The World At Surasang, a Korean barbecue restaurant, employee Abby Gallín has watched that shift firsthand. “There are always Koreans here — always, always, always,” Gallín said. “But lately, a lot of Mexicans have been coming in, especially after the BTS concert this year.” The cultural exchange goes both ways. Surasang’s chef is Mexican, from the southern state of Chiapas. Gallín said he learned to cook Korean food from a Korean chef. Korean dishes are displayed at the K-Expo in Mexico City, part of a broader showcase of Korean food and culture. Jiroko Nakamura/The World Nearby supermarkets have entire aisles devoted to ramen, snacks and Korean ingredients. And karaoke bars draw Mexican K-pop fans who sing songs in a language many of them don’t speak. In public spaces around Mexico City, fans gather for another K-pop ritual: the “random play dance.” Short clips of K-pop songs play one after another. When dancers recognize a song and know the choreography, they jump in. When the music changes, a new group takes over. For Mendez, gatherings like these are also a way to meet people. She said fans can arrive alone and leave with several new friends. Cans featuring characters from the Japanese anime Dragon Ball are displayed outside a shop in Mexico City’s Zona Rosa, near the city’s Korean business district. Jiroko Nakamura/The World From niche fandom to the mainstream Lizette, another fan at the expo, and who only shared her first name, has been listening to K-pop for more than 15 years. “It really wasn’t that well-known before,” she said. “I’d say it started getting really big around 2017.” Social media helped accelerate that growth. Today, major K-pop groups can draw enormous crowds in Mexico, and tickets can sell out quickly. The phenomenon has even reached Mexico’s presidential palace. Earlier this year, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said she wrote to South Korean President Lee Jae-myung asking whether BTS could perform additional shows in Mexico after fans complained about the difficulty of getting tickets. Then, in May, Sheinbaum hosted BTS at the National Palace. Nearly 50,000 people filled Mexico City’s Zócalo, the city’s historic main square, as the group appeared on a palace balcony to greet fans, according to the Mexican government. Members of the South Korean band BTS wave alongside Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum from a balcony of the National Palace in Mexico City, May 6, 2026. Marco Ugarte/AP Culture meets economics and diplomacy That cultural connection is developing alongside a much larger economic relationship. Trade between Mexico and South Korea reached nearly $29.7 billion in 2025, according to Mexico’s Foreign Ministry, and more than 2,000 Korean companies operate in Mexico. In September, President Lee made the first state visit to Mexico by a Korean president in 16 years. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, left, and Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum pose for photos during a welcoming ceremony at the National Palace in Mexico City, Sept. 24, 2026. Eduardo Verdugo/AP Lee and Sheinbaum agreed to deepen cooperation in trade, technology, science, education and culture. The presidents also discussed creating a K-pop cultural center in Mexico. During the visit, Sheinbaum pointed to Mexican enthusiasm for Korean culture as another link between the two countries. In some ways, the diplomatic relationship is catching up with a cultural connection fans have been building for years. For long-time fan Lizette, Korea’s presence in Mexico no longer feels temporary. “I feel like Korea came here to stay,” she said. “The culture, the food, the K-dramas, the music — all of it. It’s already really embedded in Mexico.” Jiroko Nakamura contributed to this report. The post Mexico’s Korean wave goes from K-pop fandom to trade and diplomacy appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: Why funding scientific research overseas matters
author: Joshua R. Ehrlich
content: The Trump administration is proposing a 12% cut to the National Institutes of Health’s 2027 budget. The proposed cuts are unlikely to pass Congress. But scientists still feel the need to advocate for the value of their work abroad. Host Carolyn Beeler speaks with Josh Ehrlich, associate director of the Center for Global Health Equity at the University of Michigan, about the importance of funding research overseas. Click on the player above to hear the full interview. Below is Ehrlich ‘s article on the importance of global health research, first published on The Conversation . Recently, a middle-aged woman came to see me in my ophthalmology clinic because her eyes felt gritty and uncomfortable. She had seen another doctor a month earlier who diagnosed her with eyelid inflammation and wrote her a prescription. As I examined her eyes, she mentioned in passing the prescription medication she’d been using — ivermectin. This was the first I’d heard of this drug being used for itchy, uncomfortable eyes . I knew researchers had studied and rejected ivermectin as a cure for COVID-19 , and that the medication treats onchocerciasis , a condition more commonly known as river blindness, mostly seen in rural sub-Saharan Africa. River blindness is caused by a parasitic worm that’s transmitted when people are bitten repeatedly by infected blackflies. A long-neglected tropical disease, it’s mostly known for causing severe skin disfigurement and permanent blindness. So why was this patient with itchy eyes in the US using the same drug used to kill a blinding parasitic worm? This is just one instance where decades of investment and collaboration to fight a disease that affects the global poor had yielded an unexpected benefit — a treatment for eyelid inflammation, dry eyes and rosacea. This medicine is just one data point in a pattern worth billions of dollars. As a population health researcher , I see firsthand the benefits of investment in global health research. Global health research has a long history of producing treatments, knowledge and economic benefits that advantage wealthy countries in unexpected ways. While ivermectin is used to treat river blindness in Côte d’Ivoire, the same drug is used to treat itchy eyes and rosacea in the U.S. Issouf Sanogo/AFP via Getty Images (via The Conversation) Economic investments paying off Global health research — whether it’s vaccine and drug development, large-scale population data collection or comparative policy studies — demands considerable investment. The results consistently show that this investment makes good economic sense. A 2012 report from the US National Institutes of Health estimated that every US$1 the agency invests in global health research will have a return on investment of $2.21 and that each research grant creates seven American jobs. This report proved true. Between 2008 and 2024, US governmental institutions like the NIH spent around $46 billion in three key global health areas — neglected diseases, emerging infectious diseases, and sexual and reproductive health — an investment that catalyzed $104 billion in economic activity and created 600,000 jobs in the US. Beyond the economics The benefits of global health research go far beyond economic gains. This work also improves health and medicine in the US and worldwide. As I saw in my own clinic, research into a disease half a world away led to treatment for a patient in the US — and this is not unusual. The nonprofit research organization Impact Global Health tracks what it calls innovation spillover . It details a host of global health research innovations that have led to health and economic benefits in the US and other high-income countries. From COVID-19 tests to vaccines for HPV and rotavirus, to breast cancer risk reduction and pediatric cancer treatments, the direct benefits are impressive. One example is a research partnership from the 1980s between GlaxoSmithKline and the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research that yielded a life-saving malaria vaccine . That vaccine now prevents up to 1 in 8 childhood deaths in malaria-affected areas of sub-Saharan Africa. On top of that, the technology behind that malaria vaccine is also the basis for the shingles and RSV vaccines used in the US and globally. The shingles vaccine alone is expected to prevent over 9 million cases of shingles in the US and save the healthcare system $55 billion by 2050. An even older example of this innovation spillover is the tuberculosis vaccine . Over 100 years ago, French scientists developed a vaccine for tuberculosis, a lung infection that still kills over 1 million people each year, 80% of them in low- and middle-income countries. As it happens, in 1990, the US Food and Drug Administration Food and Drug Administration approved the medication used in the tuberculosis vaccine as a treatment for bladder cancer. Researchers estimate this medication will prevent more than 300,000 cancers from recurring and save nearly 100,000 lives and nearly $12 billion in the US by 2050. Improving the healthcare system itself Beyond essential medications, global health research also produces vital and actionable knowledge about healthcare delivery. Studying the health of populations around the world can provide unique insights that researchers can use to improve care in the US and strengthen its healthcare system. Most Americans, regardless of political beliefs, are dissatisfied with the U.S. healthcare system . Many other wealthy countries spend less money to get better outcomes — fewer premature deaths, longer health and life expectancies, more equitable access to care and so on. US researchers have been studying those countries to understand what works about their systems and what doesn’t to inform ways to improve American healthcare. One example of this is Washington state, which borrowed key lessons from Germany’s experience with long-term care to design the first publicly operated long-term care insurance program in the US. This program, Washington Cares , is funded through a small payroll tax of less than 0.6% of wages and can be used to cover long-term care costs such as home care, installing ramps or grab bars, compensating informal caregivers, and nursing home expenses. Economists estimate that unpaid caregivers in the US provide care valued at trillions of dollars per year. A robust long-term care system could enable caregivers to make larger contributions to the formal economy. This would benefit the US economy as the American population ages . Looking forward Proposed cuts to NIH’s 2027 budget threaten to undermine the benefits of global health research. In a time when many Americans feel overwhelmed by the cost of living , it may be tempting to consider cutting research aimed at helping people outside the US . But the data suggest that the kind of global health research the NIH funds gives Americans a big bang for their buck. Any investment that yields these kinds of financial returns, while also delivering new drugs, vaccines and useful knowledge, seems worth holding onto. Global health research is an area where the US can do well by doing good. The post Why funding scientific research overseas matters appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: As the climate changes, loneliness grows
author: Hannah Chanatry
content: Climate change is reshaping nearly every part of our lives — even human relationships. Researchers are increasingly exploring how the impacts of climate change can contribute to feelings of loneliness and sometimes also combat those feelings. The World is breaking this down for The Loneliness Diagnosis, our series on solutions to loneliness and social isolation around the globe. Samia Akhter-Khan , a psychologist who studies climate change and loneliness at Brandenburg Medical School in Germany, told Host Carolyn Beeler that there are multiple links between the two that are largely overlooked. “We think, for example, about a flood or a hurricane that separates people from families and communities,” she said. “So, we might not be able to go outside and enjoy activities we want to do, but also not visit our neighbors or our friends and families. So, that may isolate us physically or objectively.” An aerial view of the San Rafael neighborhood inundated by the Paraná River after heavy rains caused it to overflow in Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, Oct. 16, 2026. Jorge Saenz/AP Carolyn Beeler: So, just simply that the roads are cut off, things like that, like you can’t physically reach people for a while. Samia Akhter-Khan: Yeah, totally. That’s one pathway that’s possibly leading from climate change to loneliness. And another one might be migration. So, just increasing climate change around the world leads to increasing migration, which results in loss of place and identity for many people who migrate to a new culture and then maybe feel isolated, as well, because they don’t share the same cultural norms and values as they’re used to at home and also miss their home, of course. So, when people are displaced as a result of climate change, that contributes to loneliness because they have to leave their homes and communities. They’re uprooted. That’s right. And there’s also a term called solastalgia. If you leave your home and you see your home being destroyed, you might feel this sense of loneliness that you cannot go back to the places where you shared many memories with your friends and families, and you are sad about losing that physical place, as well. Interesting. Those sound like they are both linked somewhat to extreme weather events. Is there any link here between the slower-moving impacts of climate change, like rising heat or rising drought to loneliness? Of course. Yeah. Heat is a big one, as well, where we know that heat is very much related to increasing conflict and violence. So, if there are hotter days, then there’s more violence in the city, as well, and more crime. But also, within families, there is more interpersonal violence as well, for example, directed at children. So, there’s more child abuse during hotter days, which makes sense if we think about it, that people are then confined to their homes. Maybe more stressed, maybe more agitated during heat, but then also not being able to leave because perhaps your home is air-conditioned and outside it’s just far too hot to do anything. I know that’s true in some places for domestic violence, intimate partner violence, as well, worse on hotter days. Yeah, totally. A home burns in the Eaton Fire in Altadena, Calif., Jan. 8, 2025. Nic Coury/AP/File photo There’s another phenomenon here that you talk about in your research, which is something called “climate loneliness,” which is a little bit different than the other things we’ve been talking about. What is that? Climate loneliness is very much related to pluralistic ignorance, which is a shared misperception of how others think or behave. And that poses a challenge to collective action. And I’ll give you one example. In the US, a study found that 80% to 90% of Americans underestimate how much people support climate change mitigation policies and climate concern. So, if I feel very strongly about climate policies and mitigation, but I believe that my family and people around me don’t believe in climate change and don’t believe in policies and action that concerns them, then I might feel isolated because of that difference between me and my close relationships. And that is what we call climate loneliness. All right, so we have these different types of loneliness, these different ways that climate change drives social isolation, but we also want to talk about the solutions here. I know that’s something you’ve looked into. What are some ways that have been shown to actually work to combat the loneliness that can be caused by climate change and natural disasters? In research, we see a natural tendency to look for social bonds and reconnect with people who we’re maybe not so attached to after an extreme event or during a heat wave when there’s something special. We saw this a little bit during COVID-19, as well, where people were checking in on their neighbors to see if they’re feeling all right. And some of these programs have really implemented that natural tendency to go back to these bonds by, for example, in Italy, creating a neighborhood check program where volunteers or just neighbors checked in on older people who are living alone because they’re some of the most vulnerable people in the context of climate change. And throughout a summer of multiple heat waves in Italy, these people checking in on other people could reduce the mortality rates of these older people living alone by 13%. Wow. And that’s a really impactful way, an easy way as well, to check in on your neighbors who live alone, who may not get the medication they need, or may not be able to get the groceries they need because they’re supposed to stay at home during a heat wave. A woman shelters from the sun with an umbrella during a heat wave in central Nicosia, Cyprus, Aug. 21, 2026. Petros Karadjias/AP Or they might not know where to go or be able to go somewhere cooler if they need it, maybe, and folks can help them do that. What about the isolating impact of migration that you’ve outlined? I mean, is there a way to solve that? If you’re displaced from your home, what can help? I mean, many things could help. It’s always useful for people who have migrated to connect with others in the community and strengthen those social bonds, so you’re not the only one who migrated and can share that feeling. But then also connect with people from the local culture. So, there are, like, buddy programs, or we also just conducted a study using a World Café method with migrant students and older adults in Germany, where we brought people together to think about climate solutions, but also issues around climate change and social isolation and loneliness in the city of Berlin. And these ways of connecting between generations, as well, and talking about something that’s meaningful to everyone and affects everyone in the world, as well, that could really help strengthen that social connection and also create new social ties and bonds. Does it matter why people are displaced, or do some fixes apply to everyone? So, if you’re trying to address social isolation in a city where people come from all over, does it matter that some of them have been displaced due to the impacts of climate change, or can we just think about addressing loneliness for the whole population as the fix? It makes sense to think about different reasons and different situations and contexts that people are in. If you come from a place where you were displaced because of a flood or a storm or an extreme weather event, you might have post-traumatic stress, as well, associated with that, as well as with conflict. And these often go together, like political conflict and climate change. They’re also very much connected in a way. So, these folks are dealing with a very different experience than people who migrate for economic reasons, for example, and might have a difficult journey as well, but not this extreme traumatic event that they experienced. Interesting. I think you mentioned that the link between climate change and loneliness is not something that is at the forefront. It’s not super well-known or super studied. Do you see that changing? Well, I hope so. Our lab in Brandenburg is really dedicated to making this a more prominent issue of looking at social infrastructure and social relationships in the context of climate change, as well, next to just physical and mental health outcomes, which most researchers and policies have focused on. So, I think they’re really nice integrative points in policy as well, as well as research to look at solutions that address both loneliness and climate change, basically having these co-benefits for social relationships and climate change mitigation adaptation. This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity. The post As the climate changes, loneliness grows appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: Lessons learned from Portugal’s decriminalization of drugs for personal use
author: Robert Glover
content: During the 1990s, Portugal experienced a devastating heroin epidemic accompanied by a surge in HIV/AIDS infections. Instead of cracking down on drug possession, Portuguese authorities tried a public health approach focusing on harm reduction. This year marks the 25th anniversary of that policy change. The World’s Host Carolyn Beeler spoke to Robert Glover, who teaches political science at the University of Maine and co-wrote a piece in The Conversation about this Portuguese approach. Click on the player above to hear the full interview. Below is Glover and colleague Karyn Sporer ‘s article on Portugal’s drug decriminalization, first published on The Conversation . Nearly 70,000 Americans died of a drug overdose in 2025. While that is a decline from the nearly 108,000 deaths recorded in 2022, these grim figures distinguish the US from other high-income countries. At the peak of the opioid crisis, the US overdose death rate was 68% higher than Canada’s and nearly five times that of Australia. And death is only the starkest indicator: Substance use disorder imposes hundreds of billions of dollars in healthcare, criminal justice and lost productivity costs each year — to say nothing of the incalculable disruption to families and communities. For decades, US drug policy has aimed to reduce drug use by disrupting supply, punishing possession and use, and promoting abstinence. But this isn’t the only approach to addressing drug use. 2026 marks the 25th anniversary of Portugal’s landmark decision to decriminalize the possession of all drugs for personal use. This is one of the world’s longest-running efforts to center public health and harm reduction in national drug policy. As a criminologist and a political scientist , we have spent the past three years teaching a course on drug policy and harm reduction in Portugal, bringing dozens of students to the country to study its approach firsthand. That experience has given us a close look at both the promise and the limitations of the Portuguese model. Surprising assumptions While in Portugal, our students meet with policymakers, health and law enforcement officials, treatment providers and practitioners. These experiences complement our research on how policies once considered unthinkable can gain acceptance among the public and policymakers. We also examine nonpunitive approaches to problematic drug use — that is, recurrent drug use that significantly interferes with a person’s health or quality of life. What always strikes us in our work here are the pragmatic and, compared with the US, surprisingly apolitical assumptions that underlie Portugal’s approach: People will use drugs, and public policy can reduce the harms associated with that use even when it cannot entirely prevent it. In practice, this means measures such as providing sterile equipment to consume drugs, expanding harm-reduction services that can help people better understand the substances they are using, and operating overdose prevention sites where substances can be used under medical supervision. These measures do not treat drug use as harmless, nor do they abandon recovery as a goal. Instead, they recognize that reducing harm has value in itself, and that keeping people alive and healthy can be the first step on a path away from disordered use. Providing sterile injection equipment has been an important part of Portugal’s harm-reduction approach and its efforts to reduce HIV transmission associated with injection drug use. Robert Glover, CC BY via The Conversation A devastating problem Portugal embraced this approach during a devastating heroin crisis in the late 1990s. Injection drug use was fueling one of Europe’s worst HIV epidemics , while problematic drug use was felt in Portuguese communities across social and economic lines. At that time, an estimated 1% of the population was addicted to heroin, with overdose deaths rising sharply. By the turn of the century, Portugal had the highest HIV incidence in the European Union among people who injected drugs. Even before formal decriminalization, police, healthcare professionals and other workers who came into contact with people using drugs had already begun directing them away from punishment and toward care. These emerging practices soon became the basis for a broader national response. In 1998, the Portuguese government appointed a multidisciplinary commission of experts , including physicians, psychiatrists, psychologists, legal experts and researchers, to rethink the country’s drug policy. Its recommendations became the basis for a national strategy integrating prevention, treatment, harm reduction and social reintegration that was adopted in 1999, followed by decriminalization in 2001. Decriminalization does not mean that possession simply goes unaddressed: People found to have small amounts of substances for personal use can be referred to multidisciplinary dissuasion commissions , which can connect them with services or impose minor administrative sanctions. But they cannot be criminally charged or incarcerated for possession. Drug manufacturing and trafficking, meanwhile, remain criminal offenses . Portugal’s financial investment in this strategy has remained in place despite financial crises and budget cuts . The country continues to provide multiple ways for people who use substances to access healthcare and treatment, while also addressing problems such as housing and unemployment that can make sustained recovery difficult. Dramatic results The results have been striking. Drug-related deaths fell sharply as Portugal adopted its new approach, and they remain low by European standards. In 2023, Portugal recorded 105 fatal drug overdoses , up slightly from 96 the previous year and 81 in 2021, but still far below the levels seen at the height of the country’s drug crisis. New HIV diagnoses associated with injection drug use, which still numbered in the hundreds annually in the mid-2000s, fell from 583 in 2005 to just 19 in 2024, a decline of roughly 97% . Treatment also remains central to the Portuguese model: In 2023, more than 24,000 people received care through the country’s specialized public outpatient system . This system consists of a nationwide network of multidisciplinary treatment teams providing medical care and connections to other health and social services. The use of cannabis – which, like all drugs in Portugal, is illegal though not a criminal offense – is now one of the leading reasons people enter this system. Portugal also experienced a broader shift in how problematic drug use was publicly understood. Although the Portuguese still hold negative views of substance use, problematic use increasingly came to be understood as a health and social problem rather than a moral failing warranting punishment. An international model — or one of a kind? These outcomes helped turn Portugal into an international model for drug policy reform. But its experience has proven easier to admire than to replicate. More recent experiments underscore a less celebrated lesson from Portugal: These policies depend on an integrated system of health and social services, sustained political support and buy-in from the institutions, including law enforcement , charged with making them work. British Columbia’s 2023 decriminalization pilot offers a more complicated example and an important contrast with Portugal. Despite Canada’s universal healthcare system and an established harm-reduction infrastructure, the province did not replicate Portugal’s integrated model. Police were not required to refer people to services, treatment providers received no additional funding, and waitlists persisted. The three-year pilot sharply reduced possession offenses and police drug seizures, but there was little evidence of broader health benefits. Amid growing concerns about public drug use, the province allowed the experiment to expire in January 2026 . If British Columbia illustrates the limits of reform even with a comparatively robust public health system, Oregon’s experience illustrates the risks of pursuing such a strategy without one. In Oregon, voters approved Measure 110 in 2020, decriminalizing drug possession while directing cannabis tax revenue toward expanded treatment and recovery services. But a December 2025 state audit concluded that implementation was plagued by unstable leadership, delayed services and poor coordination. Unlike Portugal, and to a lesser extent British Columbia, Oregon also failed to secure buy-in from law enforcement, leaving many officers opposed to the policy and skeptical of their role in implementing it. Rather than creating an integrated system of care, new services often operated alongside the state’s already fragmented behavioral health system. Meanwhile, highly visible drug use, rising fentanyl deaths and a citation system that rarely connected people to treatment fueled public frustration and political pressure to reverse the course. Oregon lawmakers recriminalized possession in 2024 , before the state had even developed reliable data to assess whether the experiment had improved access to care or reduced drug-related harms. Healthcare workers in Portugal take great pride in how they treat patients who use substances. Robert Glover, CC BY via The Conversation Building a sustainable policy Twenty-five years on, Portugal’s most important lesson may not be about decriminalization itself. Rather, its experience shows that reducing the harms of drug use requires painstakingly building and sustaining a system that connects people with treatment, healthcare and social support without making abstinence a precondition for receiving help. Changing drug laws can be part of that project. The harder work is building and sustaining the institutions that make a public health approach possible. The post Lessons learned from Portugal’s decriminalization of drugs for personal use appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: University students are leading the fight to reelect president Lula in Brazil
author: Michael Fox
content: On the campus of the Federal University of Santa Catarina in Brazil, it seems like just an ordinary day. The cafeteria is packed during lunch. Students walk back and forth to class. But things aren’t normal these days. “I don’t even know how to tell you how chaotic it is at universities right now,” said Carla Pereira, a 26-year-old pharmaceutical student. “There are a lot of demonstrations. It’s crazy.” Universities have become flashpoints for organizing around Brazil in recent weeks.  About a hundred students sit on the pavement in front of the university’s main administrative building. They’re making signs for a march this evening. A university student makes a sign to display at a student-led march for the reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Michael Fox/The World Tiago wears a red soccer jersey and holds a marker in his hand. That’s not his real name, though. He asked that it not be included, fearing attack from far-right supporters for speaking out. Students have faced this here in the past. “We’re here because we’re afraid that if Flávio Bolsonaro wins, he will dismantle the public infrastructure for education and health in the country,” he said. “And that will affect a large part of the population.” Roughly 2 million students in Brazil today study at one of the more than 110 federal and state universities around the country. That accounts for roughly 20% of the students studying at universities in Brazil. It’s an important section of the student body. “The best universities in Brazil are public universities. They either belong to the federal government or the state government,” said João Feres Júnior , a political science professor at Rio de Janeiro State University’s Institute for Political and Social Studies. “So yeah, they’re publicly funded. Students pay no tuition. There is no debt coming from tuition. And sometimes they can get a stipend too.” It’s perhaps the biggest difference between public universities in Brazil and the United States.  More than half of students at federal and state universities today are from working-class or poor communities. The Brazilian government also provides extensive federal funding for grants and research at both public and private universities. But President Jair Bolsonaro, the father of candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, cut billions of dollars from Brazil’s federal universities when he ran the country from 2019 through 2022. He also tried to defund humanities departments like sociology and philosophy, which he accused of being “Marxist, ” the Brazilian equivalent of “woke.” At the time, grants dried up and universities scrambled for private investment. Brazilian Students led some of the largest protests against his government. Today, they fear a Flávio Bolsonaro administration will mean a return to the policies of his father. A student holds a sign that reads “Education is the only path for emancipation.” Michael Fox/The World They have reason to be concerned. At the launch of his candidacy in July, Flávio Bolsonaro danced on stage with a large pair of scissors alongside Argentine president Javier Milei. Milei has overseen widespread budget cuts to education in his country, sparking rolling protests there from teachers and students. Flávio calls his plan, if elected, the “ tesouraço ,” which translates loosely to “The massive scissoring.” He has proposed transferring oversight of federal universities from the Ministry of Education to the Ministry of Science and Technology, as part of his promise to cut billions from universities and refocus higher education away from so-called “Marxist social sciences.” “We have to teach our youth to have their own businesses,” he said on a Brazilian program earlier this year. “To study IT, computer science, technology, math, Portuguese, sciences. That’s all we need.” Student signs read, “If Flavio wins, you lose” and “Get Out Trump.” Michael Fox/The World Guilherme Vargas says Bolsonaro is on the right path. Vargas, a mechanical engineering student at Santa Catarina Federal University, supports Flávio for the presidency and says Flávio’s promise to trim government fat and push for excellence won’t affect federal universities. “No, I don’t believe there will be big cuts,” he said. “There’s no way to end funding for the Federal University, because it’s a source of research for the country, and research and education is necessary anywhere.”  But many students are scared. And they’ve been organizing. Earlier this week, they held marches across Brazil, hoping to turn the tide in the election. “The student movement has woken up,” says Anderson Gheller Froehlich , a professor at UNEMAT, a state university in Mato Grosso. “And the youth are going to save the country. It’s the youth that are going to the streets to convince others to vote.” Students march in Florianópolis, Brazil. Michael Fox/The World Flávio Bolsonaro won the first-round election in early October by just over two million votes. Students have been leading the race, encouraging the 33 million people who didn’t vote to show up this time. They say this election is not just a fight over higher education in Brazil, but the future of other public services, like health and social security. ”I think that by going to the street and talking to the workers, the students absolutely have the ability to change this election,” said Ariadne Meneghel , a leader in the DCE student union at Santa Catarina Federal University. The runoff vote between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro is on Sunday, Oct. 25. The post University students are leading the fight to reelect president Lula in Brazil appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge
author: Hannah Chanatry
content: Former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay is the recipient of this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. The South Africa-born, Harvard Law School graduate dedicated her award to “all the survivors of international crime.” The World’s Host Carolyn Beeler spoke with Iva Vukušić, assistant professor of international history at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, who specializes in international courts, about Pillay’s work and legacy. Carolyn Beeler: Can you tell us more about Navi Pillay and the work that she is being recognized for today? Iva Vukušić: She’s really a towering figure in international law. She has been involved in some of the most important situations, cases, trials since the 1990s. She served as a judge, adjudicating cases at the Tribunal for Rwanda, and sat on some really important decisions. So, this is really somebody who deserves such a recognition, is highly respected and she really is such a role model. Former ICC judge Navi Pillay, who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, poses for a photograph at The Hague, in the Netherlands, Oct. 12, 2026. Patrick Post/AP What did the Nobel Committee say today about why they chose her, and why they chose her now? So, I think, the fact that they chose her is important symbolism, because the speech announcing this award was talking about courage, was talking about standing up for what is right for decades in these proceedings, in various institutions that concern war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide. There’s a lot of pressure on international judicial institutions, so it’s also, symbolically, an important way to show that the Nobel Committee, in this case, wants to support not only the person, but also the idea of accountability, of justice, of this universal approach to human rights and to protecting people all around the world — in a way that is equal, and not guided by double standards. That’s how I, and many of my colleagues, read this decision. Pillay’s most recent work, at least the most recent work that made headlines, was her role as the judge who oversaw the UN Commission of Inquiry that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza. That is getting a lot of attention after today’s announcement. What do you see as the significance of her being recognized, given that work and given the state of international affairs today? I think it reflects what is increasingly becoming a mainstream position, and the mainstream position is that the operation in Gaza, most likely, reached the level of genocide. I am aware that the conversation in the United States is different, due to political reasons and the political landscape, but in Europe, and generally in much of the rest of the world, there’s been quite a choir of voices that have analyzed the evidence, have analyzed the law and came out with that decision. Of course, we’re going to still see what judges at the International Court of Justice will say, because that’s a case that is underway here at The Hague, but there’s a significant body of scholars and analysts, and people who have really nothing to gain or lose by being political partisans — there’s no real reason for them to play politics. In that sense, there’s a recognition that the Commission of Inquiry was probably right in their finding. That’s at least what, among my colleagues and here at The Hague, is increasingly a very mainstream position. Then-UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay, center, arrives at a hotel in Colombo, Sri Lanka, Aug. 25, 2013. Eranga Jayawardena/AP/File photo Israel, of course, firmly denies this accusation of genocide. The Israeli Foreign Ministry had some very harsh words on social media today about the Nobel Peace Prize announcement, accusing Pillay of lies, hatred and blood libel. Right. I’ve been following trials and proceedings for 20 years. There’s never a state that is accused of similar things that is saying, “Yeah, sure, we recognize it.” So, that’s, to me, absolutely not surprising. The wording maybe is harsher than sometimes is the case, but it’s really not surprising. There’s no state in the history of the world that came out and said, “Yes, of course, we’re committing genocide,” in the modern era. So, I find that really predictable. As you mentioned, Pillay made her name internationally working on the Rwanda Tribunal . How successful was that tribunal and her work, and how was it viewed in your circles? So, from all the tribunals that we have — and by now we have quite a few — but two early ones, were the Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia and the Tribunal for Rwanda. Both of these prosecuted more cases than all the others put together. These are tribunals that were established by the UN Security Council, and they established facts to enable us to know what happened. All of this evidence was collected that otherwise would have never been collected. Witnesses, survivors were heard. There was an acknowledgement of harm, of something that was done to them. Some guilty people — not all, but some guilty people, and among them leaders as well — went to jail. All taken into consideration, I think these two tribunals were actually quite successful. Then-United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay, left, meets Zimbabwean then-President Robert Mugabe at the State House in Harare, May 23, 2012. Tsvangirayi Mukwazhi/AP/File photo Pillay then went on later in her career to work as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. What is her legacy in that role? One thing that is notable about her work as a High Commissioner, but also later on the Commission of Inquiry, is that she speaks very plainly. When she speaks, it’s like she’s not afraid, she just says what’s on her mind, based on the evidence and the analysis that she’s conducted. I think some of the other people serving in these high-flying jobs are, maybe, a little bit more calculating, and I think she is not. She is known as a very straightforward person, and that’s something that stands out. The Trump administration today announced that it would sanction the International Criminal Court, where Pillay used to work, as we’ve been talking about. Previously, it had imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges; this is an expanded sanction. What impact will this have on the work that that court is able to pull off? Right. So, this is not a surprise but this is different, because this is against the court itself. It has a chilling effect on any other institution that is trying to hold up some standards, in terms of international law and human rights, but also it could be potentially completely paralyzing for the court because many organizations, private companies — people who have cloud services and software services and do catering for the court and all of that — are not going to be able to do that. If they have any links to the US, it’s very important now to see what the EU is going to do, because there’s a set of measures that the EU can introduce. It’s called the blocking statute, but at this point, it’s very hard to say because this has never happened. Sanctions normally applied against terrorist networks and drug lords. We know that the US has never been particularly friendly to the ICC, but if somebody told me 10 years ago that this is what we would be discussing, I would call them absolutely irrational. So, we have to see, in the weeks that are ahead of us, how this looks in practice, and how effective the counter-measures that the court has been preparing for, for months already, have been. This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity. The post Nobel Peace Prize awarded to former ICC judge appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: The Beirut assassination that foreshadowed today’s Middle East crisis
author: Joyce Hackel
content: On a January morning in 1984, Malcolm Kerr, president of the American University of Beirut, stepped out of an elevator outside of his office for the last time. Reports said assassins gunned down the prominent American civilian and that a gunman from the [now defunct] pro-Iranian Shia militia group, Islamic Jihad Organization, claimed responsibility for his killing. Lebanese authorities never found Kerr’s killers. That left his family, including his son Steve Kerr , a future NBA player and coach, with many questions . American University of Beirut President Malcolm Kerr, 52, was assassinated outside his office on the campus of the University located in West Beirut in Lebanon, Wednesday, Jan. 18, 1984. AP/File Decades later, Lebanese journalist Kim Ghattas went searching for answers. Ghattas was a child growing up in Beirut when Kerr was killed. Now, in her new book, “ The Best Kind of American: A True Story of Murder, War, and America’s Undoing in the Middle East ,” Ghattas uses the assassination as a window into 1980s Lebanon. To help readers understand not only Kerr’s murder but the roots of the region’s current crisis, Ghattas spoke with The World’s Host Carolyn Beeler and explained why, among the countless violent deaths in Lebanon in recent years, she chose to focus on Kerr’s murder. “Malcolm Kerr stood out as the first political assassination by groups affiliated with Iran. And it was all spurred by an email that I received from his widow, Anne Kerr, who became a very good friend, asking me if in the research for my previous book, I’d come across any more information about her husband’s assassination. And it really got me thinking that even though there was a claim of responsibility … there were still many unanswered questions. And so, I set off on a quest to try to answer them.” Carolyn Beeler: So, take us back to the Lebanon of the 1980s. What is the backdrop for Malcolm Kerr’s murder? Kim Ghattas: The backdrop is a war in Lebanon that started in 1975 and is often described as a civil war. I reject the term because so many regional and international players were involved that Lebanon [became] a battleground for regional and international rivalries. The Syrians had invaded and sent thousands of troops. The Israelis had already invaded in 1978 and then invaded again in 1982. And they do that because Palestinian militants who came to Lebanon in the early ’70s are using the south of Lebanon as a launchpad to attack Israel with rockets. So, it makes for a combustible combination. And when the Israelis invaded Lebanon in 1982, in June of that summer, just a few days later, Iran shows up on the scene and sends hundreds of Islamic Revolutionary Guard [Corps] commanders and soldiers to Syria and then onward to Lebanon to fight Israel. And then also America — because America also shows up on the battlefield — sending in the Marines ostensibly to keep the peace, but, you know, they become a target. So, when Malcolm comes to Lebanon to take up his job as president of the American University of Beirut in the summer of 1982, he arrives in this very volatile situation. This Monday, June. 22, 2020 photo, a man walks on American University of Beirut’s campus (AUB,) one of the oldest and most prestigious education institutions in the Middle East region. Bilal Hussein/AP/File When he became president in 1982, he called that a dream come true. He was a scholar, and you describe him as writing about Lebanon with clarity and true empathy. And Kerr, of course, was living in the middle of that delicate situation. He was the high-profile leader of an American institution in a country in conflict, as you have outlined, where the US was not a neutral player. It had troops on the ground. How did Kerr try to navigate that as a very public American? Kerr knew Lebanon very well. He’d been born there to parents who worked at the American University of Beirut, who were part of this long tradition of educators and missionaries who’d come to the Middle East since the 1800s. He had grown up on the campus of the American University of Beirut. He spoke Arabic. Three of his children were born in Lebanon. He’d met his wife, Anne Kerr, in Beirut. He really felt at home. But as you heard in that clip [YouTube video below starting at 03:42], he understood the turmoil that was gripping Lebanon. He was not naïve when he took the job. And I have to point out that he took the job just before the Israelis invaded Lebanon. And at that point, he was wondering, “Is it still wise to go or not to Beirut?” But he felt so dedicated to the mission of leading this university. And he really represented the best of what America had to offer to the Middle East. Malcolm Kerr was sympathetic to the Palestinian cause, but also worried about what it meant for Lebanon. He was having to protect the university from Palestinian militants coming in and then from Israeli soldiers trying to come onto the campus. [He found himself] in a very difficult situation, which is why, as you heard in the clip, he tried to stay away from politics and focus on his mission as an educator and leader of an educational institution. I imagine that was almost impossible at the time though, to stay away from politics. No, he did that very well. He navigated it well, trying to [advance] Lebanese interests and bridge ideas between America and the Middle East, and to [present] what the American University represented at the time: not only the best of America, but the best of America as it blended with Middle Eastern ideas and culture. He very much believed in learning from the Middle East, not just coming to the Middle East to teach something about America. So, what got him in trouble, I believe, and what I unearthed in my research, was his dogged effort to find his colleague David Dodge, who had been the university’s acting president while Malcolm was trying to make his way to Lebanon after his appointment. David Dodge had also been kidnapped by groups affiliated with Iran. And it was Malcolm’s efforts to find him that I believe put him on the radar of both the Iranian groups [and] the Syrian regime next door, [then President] Hafez al-Assad, who was an ally of the Iranians. The phrase, the book’s title, “The Best Kind of American,” has a double meaning. It refers to the ways that Kerr was a good actor there in Lebanon, but also to the view that some Lebanese had at the time that the best kind of American was a dead American. At the time, Kerr put his own odds of being murdered at 50/50. Can you tell us more about how he was assassinated, how he died? Malcolm Kerr was described by some of his close friends, when he was murdered, as the best kind of American who came to the Middle East because he loved the region so much and spoke the language and so on. And so, why would anyone kill him? But yes, there were some, like those assassins who came for him on the morning of Jan. 18, 1984, and shot him point-blank from the back as he exited the elevator outside of his office, who thought that the best kind of American was a dead one because he did not fit the image of bad America … America the enemy, that countries like Iran and Syria and groups like Hezbollah wanted to paint America as. And so, he did not fit that image. But as I also write in the book, he simply knew too much about some of the workings of these groups and organizations and countries at the time because of his investigation of the Dodge disappearance. And, you know, there is a very facile accusation in the Middle East then and to this day that people like Malcolm Kerr or David Dodge or anyone who knows through their research — I mean, I could be accused of the same thing — “Oh, you must be a spy.” There’s this sort of fear of people who know too much. And that was an accusation that was also leveled at Michel Seurat , the French scholar. Today, I think a lot of people are wondering in the Middle East, but also in America, “What does America stand for? What is America? Who is the best kind of American?” And I think that’s why the title of this book will speak to so many people. But I also think that’s why Malcolm Kerr’s words about the need for empathy are so important. Some of the former American hostages held in Lebanon pose for photographers during the National Anniversary Celebration held in their honor in Washington, Dec. 2, 1992. From left are: Frank Regler, Benjamin Weir, Terry Anderson, Jesse Turner, David Jacobsen, Rev. Martin Lawrence Jenco, Jeremy Levin, David Dodge and Joseph Cicippio. Greg Gibson/AP/File There was never a full investigation of Kerr’s death, but you found in your investigation that his son, Andrew, carried a secret about his murder for many years that ended up being a key to solving it. How did he come across that secret? I found it really shocking that for 10 years, the Kerr family had no information, no real clues about what had happened, especially why. I mean, there was a claim of responsibility. But there were so many groups at the time making phone calls to claim things. And so, there was still doubt. “Was it the Islamic Jihad [Organization]? Was it Iran? And if so, why? Why would they kill a man who understood the Middle East, loved the Middle East and was sympathetic to the Palestinian cause?” What I found shocking was that the American government actually had information about it, which I reveal in my writing, but they never shared it with the Kerr family. And it is Andrew Kerr, the youngest son, who, during his work as a junior staffer on the National Security Council at the Clinton White House in the 1990s, came across a document with the names of people who admit in a phone conversation that they were the ones who shot Malcolm Kerr. And the most appalling part of it for Andrew was to read that they were boasting about this assassination. So, that confirmed to the family who … but it still was unclear why. And that’s what I also set out to uncover with my research. And I don’t know how much you want to talk about this in this interview, or how much you want to let readers discover on their own. But can you tell us who and why? Well, the Kerrs went to court, and they sued the Islamic Republic of Iran. And they won in court, although the terrible, unfinished part of this is that there was no one in the dock. And that is something that is a recurrent theme in the Middle East and impunity. There is no one who actually really goes to jail. And that also applies to the assassination of many Lebanese, including our very own former Prime Minister Rafic Hariri, who was also assassinated on the orders of Iran and Syria. There was a trial at The Hague, but there was no one in the dock. Rafic Hariri (right), then-Lebanese Prime Minister, walks with Jacques Santer (left), then-president of the EC, and Manuel Marín, Vice-President of the EC in charge of External Relations with Southern Mediterranean Countries, the Middle East, Latin America, and Asia, including Development Aid. Their talks then focused on the donors conference aimed at Lebanon’s reconstruction. © European Union, 2026, CC BY 4.0 (via WikiMedia Commons) Did any of this bring the family much closure? They had already found some closure, of course, with the trial, which took place around 2003. They felt that they had closed that chapter, but there was a sense of still unfinished business because there was no one in the dock. And they were, and especially Anne, very open and very eager to talk to me during the process of my research, as I helped place the Kerr assassination in the wider context and showed how the domino effect of an Israeli invasion, the arrival of the Iranian fighters, the arrival of the Americans led to the eventual assassination of Malcolm Kerr. You know, that all helped bring a sense of better understanding. We have had too many assassinations in Lebanon, and I’ve seen firsthand, because I’ve also lost friends to these assassinations, how it stays with you forever. I was also very grateful to the relatives of other characters in the book because I was also very keen to make clear how much other people were affected. There’s this whole chapter about the captivity and the death in captivity of a French hostage, Michel Seurat, who died in 1986. And I spoke to his widow as well, Marie Seurat, and she was very open. It’s almost cathartic to speak about these issues, even if they’re in the past. And of course, also the wife of a Lebanese who was forcibly disappeared by the Lebanese authorities of the time in 1982, Wadad Halawani, spoke to me about her husband’s disappearance , how he’s never come back, along with 17,000 other Lebanese who’ve never come back from whatever dungeons they were taken to. I think the human tragedy of everything that happened, and how we write about it, can [help] us better understand the geopolitics and the importance of connecting with these stories. Another point in the clip [4:10 ] from Malcolm Kerr on Arab American Television, shortly before his death, is how the country survived the conflict. That resilience we still hear so much about today because, unfortunately, there’s still so much conflict in Lebanon today, many years later. What about those three institutions that he outlined? How are they doing today? You know, the American University of Beirut is really a beacon of hope in the region, and it has not only survived but is thriving despite everything that has happened in Lebanon over the last few years. You know, we emerged from the Lebanese War in 1990 and had some good years, and then we had the assassination of Rafic Hariri in 2005. But the American University of Beirut has managed to thrive over the last few years despite a financial crash, the pandemic, the Beirut port explosion in 2020 and now two years of war since the Oct. 7 massacre by Hamas and the ensuing Israeli wars against, not just Gaza, but also Lebanon, Syria and Yemen. It is difficult for the Lebanese to keep talking about resilience because what we really want to do is to just live and not survive. Lebanese students hold banner during a protest inside the campus of the American University of Beirut to show their solidarity with the Palestinian people in Gaza Strip, in Beirut, April 30, 2024. Scores of students held pro-Palestinian protests at some of the largest universities in Beirut as Universities across the US are grappling with how to clear out encampments as commencement ceremonies approach, with some continuing negotiations and others turning to force and ultimatums that have resulted in clashes with police. Hussein Malla/AP/File Don’t want to have to continue being so resilient. But that is somehow the fate of this small country, a battlefield for regional and international rivalries. And we dominate the headlines with war and destruction, but we still produce so much beauty, with beautiful designers in fashion and interior design, and incredible authors, writers and universities, like the American University of Beirut, and an incredible diaspora around the world that is a vibrant community and produces so much wherever it settles. But we can only hope that somehow we and the region emerge from what I increasingly feel is a battle for survival between Israel and Iran. “The Best Kind of American: A True Story of Murder, War, and America’s Undoing in the Middle East” book cover Courtesy of Henry Holt & Company Kim, you were writing this book when missiles were flying over your head in Beirut. As you were doing that, what other connections were you drawing between Kerr’s murder and what is happening today in Lebanon? Writing this book was a very painful experience. I mean, writing generally can be painful, as many authors will know. But I was doing that while living through war and while being reminded very painfully of the importance of what had happened in the 1980s and how these three players —America, Iran and Israel — had collided on the shores of my country. But I really hope that it also illuminates the importance of empathy, the importance of understanding the region through its people and the importance of understanding the connection between America and the Middle East. You know, I begin the book with a quote from Malcolm Kerr himself, who says, “The truly civilized man is marked by empathy.” And in this age of division and polarization, I think those words have never been truer and more important. Parts of this interview have been edited for length and clarity. The post The Beirut assassination that foreshadowed today’s Middle East crisis appeared first on The World from PRX .

title: In your words: What the Kennedy Center means to you and the D.C. region
author: Alison Brody
content: The Kennedy Center has been mostly closed since mid September. And while members of Congress seek details from the administration about their plans, the future of the institution remains extremely unclear. As the fight over funding and renovations continues in the courts , we wanted to hear what the Kennedy Center means to you, your family and the D.C. region. Here’s some of what you told us. Kennedy Center tour guide Rosanne Russo welcomes a group of high school students to the performing arts center. WAMU / courtesy of Rosanne Russo Roseanne Russo, tour guide : For me, the Kennedy Center has been a welcoming place of vibrancy, joy, and wonder. I have so many memories of the remarkable and awe-inspiring performances that would transcend me to a wondrous world. Jeanne Jordan, audience member and singer with Encore ROCKS : For nearly 20 years now, the Kennedy Center has been my happy place. It’s where I went to immerse myself in music from around the world to find peace and happiness. Peter Russell (far left) in 1982 as assistant to stage director Peter Mark Schifter (at right) during a rehearsal for his production of Offenbach’s operetta Monsieur Choufleuri with Washington National Opera at the Kennedy Center Terrace Theater. WAMU / courtesy of Peter Russell Peter Russell, artistic director at Vocal Arts DC : In August of 1980, I was so excited to start working at the Kennedy Center, my first job out of college. I used to get goosebumps for years every time I would walk into the Terrace Theater on the upper level. Caitlin Wittig, audience member : One of my first memories of going to the Kennedy Center was when I was in the fourth grade and my grandmother, who was an opera fanatic, took me to my very first opera. I still remember the special skirt that I wore and what an incredibly special event it was for both of us to share. We always go to take beautiful pictures. My mother loves the Kennedy bust. Kristina Sracic on December 7, 2024 at A Holiday Pops! with Broadway star Jessica Vosk and The Heritage Signature Chorale. WAMU / David Sracic Kristina Sracic, audience member : When I moved to Washington, D.C., the Millennium Stage was my home away from home. Eva Reynolds, former usher : I used to be an usher at the Kennedy Center, first in the theater lab and then in the opera house. The difference between these two performance spaces alone under the same roof, one offering night after night improv comedy while the other one is more focused on musicals and operas, really epitomizes the breadth of programming that the Kennedy Center would offer in order to make the arts accessible to everyone. Dorothy Patton’s husband Jason and son Adam, who was learning to walk outside while his brother was inside at an NSO petting zoo. WAMU / Dorothy Patton Dorothy Patton, audience member: We have cherished the Kennedy Center at all phases of our children’s lives. The holidays would not have been complete without the Candlelight Christmas by the Washington Chorus. Clare Bennett, audience member : One time I went to go see this instrument on display called a life harp. I think that was on an early date with my now husband. We even had one of my dear friends, when she passed away, we had her celebration of life on the top level of the Kennedy Center. Ashley Smith poses with his son backstage before a performance of Giselle . His son got a part in the ballet, and he was asked to stand in as an extra. WAMU / courtesy of Ashley Smith Ashley Smith, father of a performer : My special Kennedy Center memory is from late January of 2020. It was just before the COVID lockdown, and I’d taken my eight-year-old son to the Kennedy Center to audition for American Ballet Theater’s production of Giselle . He got the part. We’ve taken our kids to many wonderful performances at the Kennedy Center over the years, ballet, theater, live music. What’s happening now to that beloved institution for us is truly heartbreaking. Margaret Waagner, parent and school field trip chaperone : I chaperoned our school field trips to the Kennedy Center, which gave schools free or low-cost tickets. Our buses would pull up alongside dozens of other school buses. My kids saw the Cinderella Ballet dress rehearsal at the Eisenhower Theater. They saw opera scenes from La Boheme in the Opera House, Junie B. Jones and Knuffel Bunny in the Family Theater. Alison Cooper in front of a sign at the Kennedy Center celebrating the 40th anniversary of the Choral Arts Society of Washington. WAMU / courtesy of Alison Cooper Alison Cooper, choral arts performer : For 41 years, I’ve been a chorister in one or both of the area’s two major symphonic choruses with most of our performances at the Kennedy Center. Every single time I’ve been on that stage singing a choral masterpiece with an amazing orchestra and looking out into that beautiful concert hall, I’ve said to myself, I cannot believe I’m getting to do this. Laura Collins, audience member : I was even able to snag a single ticket for Hamilton when that was such a big show for half price, and I was seated in between two other single women. We had a lovely conversation. The post In your words: What the Kennedy Center means to you and the D.C. region appeared first on WAMU .

title: WAMU’s Week Ahead: D.C.’s delegate race, Virginia’s reproductive rights amendment, Black Women Thriving East of the River
author: Jsinnenberg
content: Here are a few of the stories WAMU will be covering this week: Next Tuesday, voters in D.C. will have their chance to send a new delegate to Congress for the first time in decades. 89-year-old Eleanor Holmes Norton, who has held the seat since 1991, is not seeking reelection. While the D.C. delegate to Congress cannot vote on legislation, they do serve on committees and advocate on behalf of District residents in the House of Representatives. There are three official party nominees vying for the seat: Democrat Robert White, who currently serves as an At-Large member of the D.C. Council; Republican Denise Rosado, a lawyer; and Green Party candidate Kymone Freeman, a community activist. All three candidates are running with affordability proposals to counter D.C.’s high cost of living. Rosado is also emphasizing public safety concerns and proposing that D.C. police work more closely with federal law enforcement. Freeman is calling for greater community investment. White told WAMU after winning the nomination in June, he is laser-focused on the push for statehood. “People will see me in D.C., but also nationally. I plan to elevate this to a national seat … We have to build a national profile and national momentum for D.C. statehood because as the country realizes that we win the redistricting battle through D.C. statehood, they’re going to support it nationally.” As the Trump administration continues to threaten D.C.’s home rule, many voters are looking for a delegate that will fight hard on the District’s behalf. WAMU’s Matt Blitz will have an update on the delegate race. Virginia residents are voting on a handful of amendments to the state constitution, including enshrining reproductive health care access. Virginia is the most permissive state for reproductive care in the south and the only southern state that did not enact post-Dobbs abortion bans. It has become a destination for those seeking reproductive care across the south. According to the Guttmacher Institute , 8400 people traveled to Virginia for abortion care in 2025. Democrats took over the House of Delegates in 2023, promising to protect abortion access post-Dobbs. With a trifecta in Richmond, they are trying to fulfill that promise. However, critics say the amendment goes beyond current reproductive rights guaranteed under state law. Opponents like Amy McInerny of the Catholic Diocese of Alexandria say the language of the amendment is too broad and could cause regulatory issues in the future. Sara Sanatkar from the health advocacy group Repro Rising Virginia disputes those claims, she spoke with VPM News. “Is it too broad for Virginians to want to have access to birth control? Is it too broad for them to want to have access to abortion rights if they need one? Is it too broad? I would say no.” Charlotte Rene Woods of the Virginia Mercury will discuss the contours of the debate for this week’s Health Hub. WAMU’s Sarah Y. Kim will shine a light on a different health care story in D.C. Black women are disproportionately under-represented in the healthcare field and often face barriers to accessing healthcare. Kim will highlight Black Women Thriving East of the River , a group of working in Southeast D.C. to increase healthcare access and employment in the healthcare field. It’s the latest in our monthly series Voices of Wards 7 and 8.
