title: Cyber Monday: Centering accessibility in tech
author: wamu.org
content: Think about the last movie you watched. The look on someone’s face. The clue in the background. Something important happening just outside the main action. Now imagine having to put all of that into words. And you can only speak…when the actors aren’t talking. That’s the challenge of audio description — narration that accompanies a movie and explains key unspoken details. It’s a critical piece of technology, allowing people who can’t see to follow a movie’s on-screen action. But that tech sometimes misses the mark, leaving out key character and environment descriptions or condescending to its users by omitting risqué plot elements. This kind of garish gadget goes by a nickname in accessibility circles: disability dongles. And advocates say their creation can be avoided if the people they’re meant to serve are brought into the creation process earlier. Our “Cyber Monday” series returns and this time we talk about tech and accessibility. The post Cyber Monday: Centering accessibility in tech appeared first on WAMU .

title: Special ed diaries: Teachers tell NPR about their most joyous, most difficult moments
author: Dhackney
content: One of Kathleen Tejeda’s students began freshman year just trying to get by. High school can be tricky for any teenager, but she was navigating it as a blind person. By the end of her junior year, with support from Tejeda and other school staff, the student had gone from getting by to going big: She made the cheerleading squad and the school choir. She even sang the national anthem in front of the whole school. Tejeda, who has been a special educator for 20 years in Riverside County, Calif., said that kind of advocacy is just as much a part of her job as teaching her students. But teachers like her can be hard to find. There is a shortage of special educators in 45 out of 50 states , according to the Learning Policy Institute, an education research organization. That shortage is growing because the number of special education students is climbing: It’s now more than 8.2 million — about 1 out of 6 public school students. While turnover worsened sharply after the COVID-19 pandemic, the shortage isn’t new. It has existed since special education became embedded in federal law with the passage of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act in 1975. Half a century later, a fundamental question remains: Why is this shortage of special education teachers so persistent? Myths and realities about teaching special education Let’s start with a common misconception: The kids are hard to work with, so teachers don’t want to do the job. “That is not the case,” said Liz Bettini, a former special education teacher who is now a researcher and professor at Boston University. “That has not borne out in our research at all.” What Bettini’s research does show: Special educators can feel isolated from other school staff and feel they have too many student needs to manage. The volume of required paperwork can be crushing. These educators are often responsible for teaching across several subjects and grade levels. Many feel they don’t get paid enough to do this essential work. “That’s a very heavy weight to carry as a teacher,” Bettini said. NPR set out to hear directly from about a dozen special educators from around the United States’ public schools to learn what it takes to do their jobs day to day. They have been sharing snippets of their lives through voice memos since the start of the school year, and some will open their classroom doors to NPR in the coming months. “No teacher does this for the paycheck,” said third-year high school teacher Diana Swanson, who works in Vail, Ariz., as she sat at her desk the day before her school year began in July. “Just the students, that fulfillment, seeing them fill their cup a little bit, seeing them smile, be a member of society and part of their community. That’s what fulfills me.” “I feel like I was coming into this school year more prepared this time around,” fourth-year elementary school teacher Danalyn Garcia said late one school night from her living room in Chicago. “Yet, I feel the needs are even greater than the year before.” “Honestly, I had no life outside of school and outside of being a teacher,” said Kaori Anderson-Walker, looking back on his first year of teaching middle school in Philadelphia. Now in his fourth year, he said he has finally learned to manage his time more effectively but said the work is still never-ending. “When my students aren’t performing where I want them in the classroom, my mind is just constantly moving.” Much of the day isn’t spent on teaching Being an educator of any kind is demanding and requires immense skill. Research shows that burnout among all kinds of public school teachers is high, but it’s even more acute for special educators. These teachers work with students who have an incredibly diverse set of needs, including those with autism, learning disabilities such as dyslexia, developmental delays and physical disabilities. Special educators also do a lot more than teach — in fact, one study found that they spent only about a third of their day on instruction. They spend the rest of their time tracking student goals, coordinating specialized services for students (say, speech therapy or extra reading help), training support staff and writing individualized education programs (IEPs), which are legal documents that track each special education student’s needs at school. In many states, that means teachers must have specialized certification and training, but they typically aren’t paid more. In 32 states, teachers get no extra pay for the hardest-to-staff positions, including in special education, according to a recent study . While all 13 special educators NPR has spoken to said building relationships with students is their favorite part of the work, they also described the realities of those students’ needs being more complex than those of many general education students. “Special educators have reported, ‘I can’t teach this kid and respond to the student’s crisis simultaneously. So I’m abandoning instruction because the crisis has to take priority,'” Bettini said. For example, Grace Fitzgerald, who teaches elementary school in Peoria, Ill., shared on a drive home from school that one of her students had an emotional crisis that forced her to evacuate the rest of her class for their safety. “It’s been challenging mentally and emotionally to kind of go through that at the very end of the first quarter, my first year of teaching,” she said. “No one gets a road map to deal with that kind of situation.” Several teachers shared that behavioral challenges with individual students can make it harder to meet the needs of their many other students. “Our school doesn’t have walls. So we have six classes per grade level in one ginormous room, and it’s separated by dividers,” Garcia, in Chicago, said. “So when one kid is screaming and crying and begins to escalate, it disturbs the whole pod and then other kids react to it.” Getting students back on track can be difficult in these kinds of situations, she said. Essential but time-consuming paperwork Individualized education programs are a key part of special education. These written plans, required by federal law, are managed by teachers and other school staff and serve as a kind of road map for each special education student. IEPs outline the student’s unique needs and their annual goals. For example, a goal of a student with autism may be to maintain eye contact for a certain period of time. IEPs help families hold schools accountable, and they also help enforce a primary aim of special education: to teach students in the “least restrictive environment,” meaning students with disabilities are taught alongside students without disabilities as much as possible. But IEPs also require regular meetings with families, an understanding of special education law and time spent away from teaching students — time that teachers often don’t have. Then there’s the work of putting the IEP into practice in the classroom. Tejeda, of Riverside County, said when she’s “pushing in” to other teachers’ general education classrooms, she provides targeted support without singling out special education students. “We’re going to walk the classroom and check in with everybody, but at the back of our minds, we know that we need to make sure we’re [making] accommodations for that particular student.” For Anderson-Walker, in Philadelphia, “the biggest struggle” was feeling like he had to juggle IEP paperwork with teaching duties. Then, last year, his school, Boys’ Latin of Philadelphia, hired staff members who are responsible for the paperwork part of IEPs, leaving teachers more time for the classroom. “Not having that stress is amazing,” Anderson-Walker said. Searching for solutions In addition to the workload, at the core of the special education teacher shortage are pay and the sheer number of qualified people. Research shows that paying teachers more can help attract and retain them. For example, in 2020, Hawaii raised special education teacher salaries by $10,000 annually. That cut the state’s vacancies by 35%, but it wasn’t enough to keep many special education teachers in their jobs. Seventeen states now pay teachers additional money to work in hard-to-staff subjects, including special education. That’s down from four years ago, when 22 states did so. The pipeline of qualified special educators is another big problem. According to education policy researcher Chad Aldeman ‘s analysis of federal data a few years ago, about 46,000 special ed teachers leave public schools every year, while teacher preparation programs train fewer than 30,000 annually to replace those teachers. Aldeman calls it a crude estimate but said that the rapid increase in demand for special education teachers is outpacing the supply of people trained to do those jobs. Many schools end up resorting to hiring teachers who aren’t fully qualified for the work. But research has found that “grow-your-own” programs that focus on recruiting people who already live in the community may be effective at filling special education jobs. Bettini and her research partners also found that supportive administrators and adequate planning time can help make the work feel more sustainable for teachers. For example, Fitzgerald, the first-year teacher in Illinois, said she was feeling overwhelmed by her workload at the start of the year. So she worked with her school leadership to build more dedicated planning time into her day. “I think that’s going to be very beneficial and will hopefully lead to a decrease in time spent after school,” Fitzgerald said. She uses that time to focus on lesson plans, logging data and writing IEP goals. It allows her to be more present in the classroom, working with her students. title: Lula’s election win and the future of Brazil
author: wamu.org
content: The results of Brazil’s runoff election are in. Incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has completed a stunning political comeback, winning an unprecedented fourth term. His win is a shock result that defied polls, precedent, and anti-incumbent sentiment. He defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former jailed President Jair Bolsonaro. The younger Bolsonaro has, so far, refused to concede. After a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America, what does a win by Lula – an icon of the left – signal about the future? And what challenges could he face in his fourth term? The post Lula’s election win and the future of Brazil appeared first on WAMU .

title: If You Can Keep It: The DOJ’s midterm moves
author: wamu.org
content: Early voting for the midterm elections is underway all across America. And Election Day is just over a week away. Now the president, facing likely losses in the House and the Senate, is ramping up his campaign to intervene in midterm voting and vote counting like no other president ever has in history. The Department of Justice is alleging widespread non-citizen voting in California on flimsy evidence. The DOJ is also filing high-profile criminal charges alleging non-citizen voting. Department authorities are also threatening local officials in California, saying they could face legal action if the department disapproves of how they handle ballots. In this edition of “If You Can Keep It,” we look at what these unprecedented moves from the Justice Department mean for the midterms and for our democracy. title: Republicans are spending millions and still may not win districts drawn to favor them
author: Jsinnenberg
content: Starting last year, President Trump and his political team put pressure on Republican-led states to redraw congressional district lines to favor Republicans. It was supposed to build a firewall for Republicans hoping to avoid the historical pattern of heavy midterm losses for the president’s party. “It just has not turned out that way,” said Nathan Gonzales, editor of Inside Elections. Instead, Republicans are spending millions of dollars on House seats that were supposed to deliver easy wins and may end up losing them anyway. Among those districts is North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, which the state legislature aggressively redrew late last year to try to make it a reliably Republican district. Under the new lines, Trump would have won the district by more than 11 percentage points in 2024. Now it is widely considered a toss up. Trump recently headlined a rally in eastern North Carolina where former Republican Party chairman turned U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley got most of the attention. It was cold and getting late when Trump finally got around to mentioning two congressional candidates sitting in the VIP section. “Come up. The two of you, we have to get them in,” Trump said of Laurie Buckout, the Republican nominee in NC-01 and Jennifer Balkcom, the Republican running to represent NC-11 on the opposite side of the state. “We have to vote for them. These are two special people. Come on up.” On stage, Buckhout, a retired Army colonel, who ran and lost in the district two years ago, leaned into the partisan advantage Republicans should have in the district, saying it’s “simple math.” “There are more of us,” said Buckhout. “All you’ve got to do is get out the vote. God bless you. Mr. President.” But concern about turnout is exactly why Trump was in the state, begging voters to cast their ballots as if he were on it. Trump told the rally crowd that House Speaker Mike Johnson had asked him to give an extra boost to Buckhout and Balkcom, describing the situation as “tough.” “He said ‘if you could, give them a special call out tonight, because they’re going to have close races’,” Trump said. Buckhout and her team didn’t respond to requests to participate in this story. But, if this redraw was meant to notch an easy Republican win, it hasn’t worked out. This is now one of the most expensive House races in the country, with more than $42 million spent on advertising between Sept. 1 and Election Day, according to an NPR analysis of AdImpact data. New district lines, same issues A volunteer snaps a photo of Democratic Rep. Don Davis with Onslow County Board of Commissioner candidates Rebecca Cooper and Michel Leandre Jr. outside an early voting location in Swansboro, N.C. Onslow is one of six counties added to North Carolina’s 1st District in the latest redraw of congressional district lines. One recent morning, Democratic Rep. Don Davis, was greeting voters at an early voting location in Swansboro, at the far southeastern tip of the district, an area he hasn’t represented before. As Davis introduced himself to a voter walking out of the polling place, the man told him he wasn’t in his district. “Oh, I’m sorry,” Davis said, laughing and noting this has been happening to him a lot lately. “This is my third run on a third new map,” said Davis. Davis has been a top target for Republicans in multiple rounds of redistricting. This time his home county was drawn out of the district and he got all or part of six new counties. He says issues in eastern North Carolina, though, are universal. “You hear so much about affordability, inflation and costs but I believe this is becoming for many about survivability,” said Davis, referencing farmers, truckers and fisherman hit by high fuel prices. “Just how they’re able to make it and survive during these tough times.” Davis is a happy warrior, even joking about his predicament with a volunteer handing out flyers in front of the polling place. “I just don’t know how many other ways you could redraw it now, other than maybe, you know if you just start annexing Virginia or something or maybe taking it into the Atlantic Ocean or something,” he said adding with a laugh, “I’ll just swim and talk to the fish you know.” Republicans and Democrats alike acknowledge Davis is a formidable campaigner, making this race more competitive than it should be just based on the way the lines were drawn. “I think they believed that they had beaten Don Davis with the redistricting pen,” said Morgan Jackson, a prominent North Carolina political consultant, who is running Democrat Roy Cooper’s U.S. Senate campaign. “As it turns out, Don Davis has always been a tough out. He’s a local politician who runs really strong.” Incumbent Democrats in several redrawn districts around the country decided to stay in and fight and now look well positioned to win, said Inside Election’s Gonzales. “Republicans gained an advantage in 15 congressional districts nationwide but what we are seeing this close to Election Day is that some of those that were supposed to be easy victories are not turning out that way and the party is having to pour in millions of dollars to win districts that were supposed to be easy victories,” said Gonzales. A Republican strategist involved with midterm races, but who wasn’t authorized to speak publicly, pushed back on the idea that the redistricting push has been a bust, saying “redistricting creates new battlefields, it doesn’t create outcomes.” That’s a lot less confidence than Republicans were projecting about these districts just a few months ago. Two Florida congressional districts redrawn to boot democratic incumbents are nearing a combined $90 million in ad spending. In Texas, districts drawn to have a 10-point Trump advantage have shifted towards Democrats and a previously safe Republican district that had some Democratic voters added to it in the redrawn maps now appears to be at risk as well. “I think at the end of the day, this will go down as a dummymander rather than a gerrymander,” said Jackson. title: A D.C. park was made ‘for the pleasure of the people.’ Trump’s plan would change that
author: Dhackney
content: WASHINGTON, D.C. — President Trump’s express wish to take over the East Potomac Golf Links has thrust a municipal D.C. golf course into the national spotlight. But locals rely on that area for much more than golfing — and worry the district could lose an invaluable recreational oasis. The southern tip of East Potomac Park, known as Hains Point, is beloved by cyclists, runners, picnickers and birders for its waterfront views, cherry trees and Ohio Drive, the scenic three-mile loop around its perimeter. Runners use the wide, flat road to train; it’s even a fixture of several major race courses, including the Marine Corps Marathon on Sunday. “It’s such an important part of the fabric of this region, even though it’s not very well known [beyond it],” said Elizabeth Kiker, the executive director of the Washington Area Bicyclists Association. She herself took her now-husband on a bike ride on their second date 20 years ago. Locals describe Hains Point as a rare public resource in D.C. It’s easily accessible from the National Mall yet removed from the crowds, full of people but free of traffic. Congress created it in 1897 , “to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people.” And yet, under the president’s proposed golf course redesign, Hains Point as people know and love it may cease to exist. East Potomac Golf Links and Hains Point as seen from the top of the Washington Monument this week. (Saul Loeb | AFP via Getty Images) Trump said on Truth Social last weekend that renovations would keep the entire park closed for 15 months starting in November. But it’s not clear what would be left when it reopens: The rendering he posted shows an 18-hole course spanning the entire peninsula — including the current playground and picnic area on its southern tip — with no road visible around the perimeter. The White House referred NPR to the Department of the Interior, which did not respond to NPR’s questions about whether those features would be removed as part of the redesign. The proposed renovations have so far been the subject of mixed messages from the administration: Trump said last weekend that work would begin in mid-November, then “immediately.” But government lawyers said in court Monday that they were not aware of a final plan . Even so, the government abruptly downed hundreds of trees on the course with little warning earlier this month, which critics worry was a pretext for beginning renovations. (The government says it was following up on recommendations from a 2019 landscaping report.) Judge Ana Reyes held a hearing on Monday to learn more about the tree-clearing and decide whether to block further work on the golf course. But it’s not just the golf course that’s at stake, as a group called Hains Point Runners told Reyes in the courtroom and a written brief. In its 35-page brief, the group says federal law requires the National Park Service to identify and consider the “longstanding recreational uses of the Hains Point corridor” and ways to avoid harming those uses, before embarking on any work that would change it. “From the perspective of the running community, that did not occur here,” lawyers wrote. Ashley Hawkins of Prince George’s County, Md., runs at Hains Point every day, even in the snow. She especially loves the river view and people watching: the families with fishing poles, binocular-wielding birders, people taking a leisurely drive. “Running is so tied to my mental health,” Hawkins said on a recent sunny morning, stretching before she hit the road. “And no place in this area has given me the peace that Hains Point has.” Hawkins has been following the headlines about her beloved running route. While she says she’s still in denial about its potential closure, she sees the prospect as part of a pattern of Trump “bypassing” courts to advance his construction projects . “But to me, this feels the most egregious, because he’s taking away public space and trying to make it private,” she says. “It feels like one of the more king-like things that he’s done so far.” Trump’s proposal would combine the park’s three historic — and historically affordable — courses into one 18-hole “championship-style” course, which has already raised concerns about who will be able to play on it. Trump has said on Truth Social the golf course will “be open to the Public” while also able to host “world class tournaments” such as the U.S. Open and PGA Championship. He’s called the current course “dilapidated, and of no further use or effect,” dubbing part of it “ Trash Island .” What’s at stake Each spring, when D.C.’s iconic cherry blossoms bloom, Hains Point is a fan-favorite viewing spot for both locals and tourists. The annual Credit Union Cherry Blossom 10-mile run takes roughly 20,000 participants around the peninsula for that very reason. But race organizers are looking into backup options for next year given the rumored renovations, event director Rob Wolfe told NPR. In an email to prospective runners earlier this year, the organization said both the proposed golf course renovations and Trump’s planned arch on nearby Arlington Memorial Bridge could significantly alter the course. It urged people to share their concerns with lawmakers and the National Park Service. Hains Point is part of the course of several major road races, including the Credit Union Cherry Blossom ten-mile run each April and the Marine Corps Marathon every October. (Andrew Harnik | AP) Wolfe said the best race experience includes as many cherry blossoms as possible — ideally the ones that frame the park. But, he says, the park’s future is “more important than our Sunday in April or Marine Corps Marathon’s Sunday in October.” “It’s really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, hundreds, thousands of people on a daily basis would lose out,” he said. Luke Cancilla, a runner and physical therapist who works primarily with endurance runners and cyclists, said Hains Point is a particularly safe environment because there are fewer obstacles such as traffic, stoplights and sidewalks. He often recommends it for people who are starting out or returning after an injury. “It’s open to all of us, which makes it so unique,” he said. “You don’t have to have an experience level … or be intimated to go out there.” The park is a popular spot for fishing in the Potomac River. (Andrew Harnik | AP) Summer Delehanty, an avid birder, found out about Hains Point when she moved to the area for work about a year ago. She said it’s played a huge role in building her D.C. community. “I’ve only been here a year, but I still have so many fond memories of going there,” she said. “I was there January 1st looking for the snowy owl … I’ve been there on super hot days, I’ve picnicked there.” Delehanty has spotted all kinds of birds at that park, including rarities such as the fork-tailed flycatcher. She said Hains Point is a uniquely great birdwatching spot in the district because of its position right along the Potomac River: People have a 360-degree view of the migrating birds that fly overhead or take shelter in the trees. “There’s nothing else in D.C. like it,” she said, adding that she’s not sure where regular birders would go instead. They could perhaps get similar views from the Virginia side of the river, she said, but those wouldn’t count as D.C. bird sightings. The Trump administration cut down 430 of the park’s trees earlier this month, with less than a day’s notice. That means fewer places for tired birds to rest, Delehanty says, and potentially fewer birds stopping by altogether. And, if the park is closed to humans, there won’t be anyone there to track the species that do, which she said is important for conservation purposes. María-Elena Montero, president of the D.C. Bird Alliance, says the potential closure of Hains Point would mean a “devastating loss of habitat” for birds and humans alike. “It belongs to the people,” she said. “And to lose that aspect of being able to experience such a gorgeous space right in the middle of the city, right in the shadow of an airport and monuments … is a big loss for everybody.” How people are mobilizing Last October, the Trump administration started dumping debris from another controversial construction project — the demolition of the White House East Wing — on the grounds of the golf course. In February, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers sued the government in an effort to stop what they describe as an unlawful takeover of a public course. Fear and confusion grew this summer, when Trump was photographed touring East Potomac with a group including golf course architect Tom Fazio and staffers holding rolled-up renderings. Trump later announced that Fazio would design a new championship-level course, with work set to begin on September 1. When Delehanty saw that news, she realized “this involves me directly,” she said. She decided to put her design skills and sizable social media following to use, designing “Hands off Hains” T-shirts to raise awareness and money for the D.C. Preservation League. She says she’s sold around 200 so far, raising about $1,500. President Trump and officials toured the East Potomac golf course in June, fueling locals’ concerns that construction would soon begin. Trump said this week that work would close the park starting in mid-November, though a plan has not been finalized. (Mark Schiefelbein | AP) “In the grand scheme of things, against an administration, is that going to do anything in court? Not really,” she said. “But for me, it’s about [the fact] these are 200 people that care so deeply about this they’re willing to … wear a shirt, show up to these events and say ‘This is not something I’m happy about.'” The push to protect the park is grassroots – and growing. There’s Save East Po, a nonprofit started by a resident named Alex Rosen who works as a consultant and described himself to NPR as “just a guy who really likes a park and doesn’t want to see its fundamental characters change significantly, especially without any public input.” The D.C. Bird Alliance is leading a series of daily “Hold the Point!” bird walks next week. And the Washington Area Bicyclists Association has held several installments of a combined bike-ride rally called “ Hains Point Hoopla .” East Potomac Park is a fan-favorite spot for locals and tourists alike to enjoy the cherry blossoms each spring. (Alex Wong | Getty Images) The most recent Hoopla, held earlier this month, featured speakers including David Hearn , the former Olympian falsely accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool — and an avid cyclist. Critics see a throughline in Trump’s D.C. construction projects. “It goes to this overall theme of potentially taking away from the local communities, making things a little bit more challenging and having us modify things in order for something that no one really asked for in the first place,” said Cancilla, the running coach. He’s one of many who would like to see more input from the community about the changes to East Potomac. Critics of Trump’s plan say there are steps the government can take to improve the park — such as adding benches and fixing the crumbling seawall — without risking access to public resources. Amidst the court battle and confusion, locals are at least heartened to see their beloved park getting more national attention. At a time when its future feels out of their hands, they’re encouraging people to speak up and show up. That’s no problem for Hawkins, who says she plans to keep running at Hains Point every day “until they physically tell me that I can’t come anymore.” Where would she go then? “I’m not ready to answer that question,” she said. “I feel really tied to this place.” Transcript: JUANA SUMMERS, HOST: President Trump wants to make his mark on many parts of D.C. from the White House to the Kennedy Center. His latest focus is a municipal golf course. Locals worry the administration is not only trying to take it over but fundamentally change one of the city’s most beloved public parks without any public input. NPR’s Rachel Treisman reports. RACHEL TREISMAN, BYLINE: East Potomac Park is just blocks from the bustling National Mall. But on Thursday morning, the loudest sounds were the birds flying over the nearby Potomac River and the whoosh of cyclists rounding a turn. (SOUNDBITE OF WIND RUSHING) TREISMAN: The southern tip of the Peninsula is known as Hains Point. It has open green space, set off from the golf course. People come here to fish, birdwatch and picnic. There’s a three-mile loop around its perimeter that cyclists and runners love. ASHLEY HAWKINS: Running is so tied to my mental health, and no place in this area has given me the peace that Hains Point has. TREISMAN: Maryland resident Ashley Hawkins runs here seven days a week, even in the winter. She doesn’t know where else she would go if it closes down. HAWKINS: I’m not ready to answer that question. TREISMAN: But locals may have to. In the rendering President Trump shared last weekend of his proposed golf course redesign, there’s no public green space or perimeter road. The Interior Department did not respond to NPR’s questions about what that would mean for the park. Trump has said work would keep the entire park closed for 15 months, beginning in mid-November, though other administrations officials have said there is no final plan yet, and there’s still a lawsuit trying to block his golf course takeover altogether. Here’s Hawkins. HAWKINS: He’s taking away public space and trying to make it private. It feels like one of the more king-like things that he’s done. TREISMAN: Trump has criticized the state of the current golf course and said the new one will still be open to the public, but the future of Hains Point is unclear. LUKE CANCILLA: Even though it’s just a road and it’s just a park, it’s really, like, a safe place for us. TREISMAN: Luke Cancilla is a runner and physical therapist who primarily treats endurance athletes in D.C. He says Hains Point is one of the only places in the city with this kind of wide, flat loop free of stoplights and cross streets. CANCILLA: It’s open to all of us, which, again, makes it so unique. TREISMAN: Several major road races go through Hains Point, including the Marine Corps Marathon this Sunday. The Credit Union Cherry Blossom Ten Mile Run takes runners through the park’s canopy of cherry trees every April. Event director Rob Wolfe says organizers are looking for backup routes for next year, but he says the conversation is about much more than any one race. ROB WOLFE: It’s really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, thousands of people on a daily basis would lose out. TREISMAN: It’s not just runners and cyclists. Birders love Hains Point, which offers a 360-degree view of migratory birds flying over the Potomac River. SUMMER DELEHANTY: There’s really nothing else like it in D.C. TREISMAN: That’s Summer Delehanty. She’s a product designer by day, birder in her spare time. She has created and sold about 200 Hands Off Hains T-shirts. She’s donating the proceeds to the D.C. Preservation League’s lawsuit. Different groups are organizing their own protests, from bike ride rallies to bird walks. DELEHANTY: I feel like the only way to get things to stop is when actual eyes are on it and, like, it’s making headlines and people are there, people are watching. TREISMAN: Hains Point may not have the name recognition of the White House or the Kennedy Center, but the locals who use it every day want a say in its future. Rachel Treisman, NPR News. title: What’s behind the early voting surge? It’s more than voter enthusiasm, expert says
author: Nstarobin
content: As of Friday morning, nearly 21 million Americans have already cast ballots in the midterm elections, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, which tracks voting by mail and in person. But early voting numbers can be misleading. A surge in ballots cast before Election Day doesn’t necessarily mean more Americans will vote overall. That’s because many of those voting early would have voted on Election Day anyway, according to Charles Stewart, a political science professor at MIT and founding director of the MIT Election Data and Science Lab. Stewart told Morning Edition that the increase reflects both voter enthusiasm and the money campaigns are spending to encourage supporters to vote early. “It also kind of reflects the large amount of money that’s in this campaign that’s going into retail politics, going door to door, and just making sure that supporters are energized,” he said. Stewart also sees changes in how Democrats and Republicans are voting. Democrats still have an advantage in voting by mail, but that gap is smaller than in 2022 as more Democrats shift to early in-person voting. Republicans’ slight advantage in early in-person voting could also narrow. What stood out to Stewart was the early voting activity in Maine and Iowa, two states that haven’t been major battlegrounds in recent elections. He said the numbers reflect voter enthusiasm and campaign efforts to mobilize supporters in places that haven’t seen as much political activity in recent years. While speaking with NPR’s A Martinez, Stewart also discussed whether concerns about the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) and Trump’s opposition to mail voting are changing how Americans vote — and why polls still matter, even if they can’t predict exactly what will happen on Election Day.
