title: Zelenskyy Meets US Envoys in Norway as Russian Strikes Kill Civilians and Ukraine Seeks Urgent Military Support
author: Iris Vanea
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy travelled to Norway on Tuesday for high-level talks with US and European officials, seeking stronger military support and a renewed diplomatic effort to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. The meetings took place as Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least nine people across Ukraine, according to the Associated Press, and damaged infrastructure in several regions. The Oslo discussions brought together Zelenskyy, US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb. Jared Kushner, another member of the US negotiating team, was expected to participate remotely because of illness, according to the Norwegian government. The talks come at a sensitive moment for relations between Kyiv and Washington. Disagreements over military assistance, intelligence sharing and the direction of peace negotiations have raised concerns in Ukraine and across Europe about the future of American support. Renewed diplomatic efforts amid mounting pressure Norway and Finland are hosting the discussions as part of a broader effort to move negotiations towards a more constructive path. The Norwegian government said Zelenskyy had requested the meeting with the American envoys, reflecting Kyiv’s desire to maintain direct communication with Washington despite growing political tensions. Zelenskyy said the discussions would address strengthening Ukraine’s air defences and expanding joint weapons production. These priorities have become increasingly urgent as Russia continues to launch attacks against Ukrainian cities, energy infrastructure and logistics facilities. US President Donald Trump has recently criticised Zelenskyy and suggested that another person should negotiate on Ukraine’s behalf. His remarks have intensified concerns about whether Washington’s approach to the conflict is shifting in ways that could place additional pressure on Kyiv. For Ukraine, maintaining US involvement remains important not only because of military equipment but also because of American intelligence capabilities and access to advanced defence systems. European countries have expanded their support, but some critical military capabilities remain difficult to replace quickly. Russian attacks leave casualties and disrupt electricity supplies The diplomatic meetings coincided with another wave of Russian attacks across Ukraine. The Associated Press reported that at least nine people were killed, with additional casualties reported in the Kyiv region and the central city of Dnipro. The attacks also caused electricity disruptions in 12 regions, according to Ukrainian officials and the national grid operator. Damage to energy infrastructure presents a continuing challenge for a country already dealing with the cumulative effects of years of war. Russian forces have repeatedly used missiles and drones against infrastructure and urban areas. Moscow says its military operations target military and logistics facilities, while Ukrainian authorities report civilian deaths and damage to homes, warehouses and essential services. The latest strikes underline the difficulty of conducting peace negotiations while military operations continue. They also reinforce Ukraine’s argument that any diplomatic process must be accompanied by sufficient defensive capabilities to protect its population and infrastructure. Air defence remains a central priority One of Zelenskyy’s key objectives is to secure additional air-defence support, particularly Patriot interceptor missiles capable of countering certain ballistic and other advanced missile threats. Ukraine has repeatedly warned that shortages of interceptors limit its ability to defend cities and critical facilities against sustained attacks. Deliveries have also become a source of tension, with Kyiv expressing concern about delays affecting equipment needed for its defence. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has discussed Ukraine’s military requirements with Zelenskyy, including interceptors and early warning systems. Ukrainian officials have also raised concerns about access to satellite communications used in military operations. Washington has not accepted all of Kyiv’s characterisation of recent changes to intelligence and military support. The disagreements nevertheless illustrate how operational decisions can become intertwined with wider political negotiations. For European governments, the challenge is to help Ukraine maintain its defences while avoiding a breakdown in transatlantic cooperation. Additional European funding and weapons purchases can ease some pressure, but replacing American intelligence and certain advanced systems would be difficult. Europe faces a larger role in Ukraine’s security European leaders have increasingly emphasised that Ukraine’s future is closely connected to the security of the continent. Norway and Finland’s involvement in the Oslo meetings reflects a broader effort by European governments to keep diplomatic channels open and ensure that Kyiv remains involved in decisions affecting its future. The discussions also take place amid disagreements over possible terms for ending the war, including concerns that Ukraine could face pressure to surrender territory. Kyiv has maintained that any settlement must address its security and sovereignty, while Russia’s objectives remain a major obstacle to a lasting agreement. European assistance has become particularly important as uncertainty surrounds the scale and timing of future US support. However, European governments face their own budgetary, industrial and political constraints, meaning that increasing assistance requires coordination and sustained commitments. What the Oslo talks could mean The meetings are not, by themselves, evidence that a peace agreement is close. Their immediate significance lies in keeping communication between Ukraine, the United States and European partners active at a time of heightened tension. For Zelenskyy, the priorities are clear: secure the military capabilities needed to defend Ukraine, maintain international backing and ensure that negotiations do not exclude Kyiv from decisions about its territory and future security. For Washington, the challenge is to reconcile its diplomatic objectives with disagreements over military assistance and the terms of a possible settlement. European leaders, meanwhile, must determine how much additional responsibility they can assume if American support becomes less predictable. The outcome will depend on whether the participants can translate diplomatic contacts into concrete commitments on air defence, intelligence cooperation and the framework for future negotiations. As Russian attacks continue, the consequences of those decisions will be measured not only in diplomatic progress but also in Ukraine’s ability to protect its population and critical infrastructure.

title: Zelenskyy Asks Europe for €70 Billion as Ukraine Faces Russian Attacks and Uncertain US Support
author: Iris Vanea
content: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on European Union leaders to provide at least €70 billion in additional support for defence and national resilience, as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks and growing uncertainty over the future of American military assistance. Speaking during a European summit in Brussels on Friday, Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine must prepare for a difficult winter while continuing to defend its cities, energy infrastructure and front lines. The appeal comes at a sensitive moment for Kyiv. Relations between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump have deteriorated following disagreements over attacks on energy infrastructure, Washington’s approach to Russia and the future of peace negotiations. European leaders have publicly reaffirmed their support for Ukraine, but questions remain over whether the bloc can provide the scale of assistance Kyiv says it needs. The latest diplomatic confrontation is unfolding as Russian missiles and drones continue to strike Ukrainian territory, placing additional pressure on the country’s air defences and electricity network. Zelenskyy seeks a larger European commitment Addressing European leaders, Zelenskyy said Ukraine needed at least €70 billion to strengthen its defences and maintain the resilience of its economy and infrastructure. He described the request as a realistic assessment of the country’s needs as the war continues into another winter. The financial appeal reflects the enormous cost of sustaining Ukraine’s military operations while keeping essential public services functioning. Funding is required for weapons, ammunition, air-defence systems, repairs to damaged infrastructure and support for a population exposed to repeated attacks. European governments have already provided extensive military, financial and humanitarian assistance since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. However, the latest request comes amid growing concern in European capitals that Washington could reduce some forms of military or intelligence support. Replacing American capabilities would be difficult in the short term. Ukraine relies on Western equipment and intelligence to detect threats, coordinate operations and defend infrastructure against long-range attacks. European officials have acknowledged that some technologies, including satellite communications systems used by Ukrainian forces, cannot easily be replaced with European alternatives. The challenge for the EU is therefore not simply to approve additional funding. It must also determine how quickly money can be mobilised, which military capabilities are most urgently needed and how support can be sustained over the longer term. Russian attacks increase pressure ahead of winter The summit is taking place as Russia intensifies attacks across Ukraine. According to reporting by the Associated Press, Russian strikes hit nine Ukrainian regions, damaging property, disrupting electricity supplies and injuring at least 15 people, according to Ukrainian officials. The attacks have heightened concerns about the country’s ability to protect civilians as temperatures fall. Previous winters have demonstrated how damage to power stations, transmission networks and other critical infrastructure can disrupt heating, water supplies and essential services. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is preparing further missile attacks in the coming months. Strengthening air defences has consequently become a central priority for Kyiv, particularly as interceptor missiles and other defensive equipment remain in high demand. The consequences extend beyond the immediate damage caused by individual strikes. Electricity shortages can interrupt industrial production, increase costs for businesses and force public services to operate under difficult conditions. Prolonged disruptions can also increase the financial burden on the Ukrainian government, which must simultaneously fund the war effort and support civilians. For European governments, helping Ukraine maintain its infrastructure is therefore both a humanitarian priority and part of a wider effort to prevent the conflict from creating further instability across the continent. Tensions between Zelenskyy and Trump complicate diplomacy The Brussels meeting also exposes growing differences between Kyiv and Washington over how to approach the war. Trump has criticised Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that such operations risk increasing energy prices and complicating diplomatic efforts. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has accused Moscow of showing no genuine willingness to end the conflict and has questioned the effectiveness of current peace initiatives. The disagreement has become particularly sensitive following Trump’s announcement of a proposed ceasefire covering attacks on energy facilities. Ukraine has disputed aspects of the arrangement, while Russia has continued military operations. The two sides have not reached a comprehensive agreement to end the war. Zelenskyy’s criticism of a US agreement involving Russian diesel has added another point of tension. The Ukrainian president has argued that commercial arrangements that generate revenue for Moscow risk undermining efforts to pressure Russia over its invasion. European leaders have expressed support for Ukraine while navigating their own economic and political constraints. Energy prices, defence spending and disagreements over the EU’s longer-term budget are complicating decisions about how additional assistance should be financed. The summit therefore presents a difficult balancing act: maintaining support for Ukraine, managing relations with Washington and avoiding further economic disruption within the European Union. Europe’s security debate moves to the forefront The latest developments have renewed debate over Europe’s ability to defend itself and sustain military assistance without relying so heavily on American capabilities. European governments have increased defence spending and expanded support for Ukraine, but differences remain over funding arrangements, procurement priorities and the distribution of costs among member states. Satellite communications provide one example of the challenge. Ukrainian forces depend heavily on systems operated by private companies, and European officials have acknowledged that an immediate replacement for the American-controlled Starlink network is not available at comparable scale. The issue highlights how military resilience increasingly depends on commercial technology as well as conventional weapons. A larger European role would require coordination between national governments, EU institutions and defence manufacturers. It would also require decisions on whether new assistance should be delivered through existing programmes, bilateral agreements or additional common financing. For Ukraine, the urgency is immediate. For Europe, the debate concerns not only the future of the war but also the continent’s capacity to respond to security threats over the coming years. What happens next? The Brussels summit is expected to shape the next phase of European discussions on military assistance, financial support and Ukraine’s longer-term relationship with the EU. However, expressions of solidarity do not automatically translate into approved funding or immediate weapons deliveries. The key questions are whether European governments can agree on the scale and financing of additional assistance, whether critical military equipment can reach Ukraine quickly enough, and whether diplomatic channels with Washington can prevent further disruption to allied coordination. The coming weeks will be particularly important as Ukraine prepares for winter and European governments consider their next budgetary and defence commitments. Zelenskyy’s request places the financial and strategic stakes clearly before EU leaders. Ukraine is seeking not only the resources needed to continue fighting, but also assurances that its partners will remain committed while the military and diplomatic situation remains uncertain. For Europe, the decisions made now could influence Ukraine’s ability to defend its infrastructure, protect civilians and sustain its military operations. They will also help determine how much responsibility European governments are prepared to assume for the continent’s security as the war continues.

title: Houthis Strike Yemen Presidential Palace in Aden, Killing Two as Regional Conflict Escalates
author: Iris Vanea
content: Yemen’s Houthi rebels launched a missile attack on the presidential palace complex in the southern port city of Aden on Thursday, killing two security guards and injuring at least six people, according to Yemeni officials cited by Reuters and the Associated Press. The strike marks a significant escalation in the conflict between the Iran-aligned movement and forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government. The attack targeted the al-Maashiq palace complex, which serves as a key government headquarters. Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said Prime Minister and cabinet members present at the complex were safe following the incident. The Houthis claimed responsibility, saying they had targeted a military operations headquarters associated with Saudi forces. Their account of the intended target has not been independently verified. The attack came amid renewed fighting in Yemen and a broader regional confrontation involving Iran and its rivals. A direct strike on a government stronghold Witnesses reported multiple explosions in the vicinity of the palace, prompting panic among residents and security concerns across Aden. Officials said the attack involved missiles, while the government also reported the use of drones. The al-Maashiq complex is an important centre of authority for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. Although much of the country remains divided between rival forces, Aden has served as a principal base for government institutions and officials. The strike is particularly significant because it brought the conflict directly to a prominent government site in a city that has remained outside Houthi control. The deaths of two security guards underline the human cost of the escalation, while the reported injuries raise further concerns about the risks facing personnel and civilians near strategic installations. In its statement, the Houthi military leadership described the operation as part of a campaign against Saudi military deployments in Yemen. The group has increasingly framed its actions as an effort to pressure Riyadh over its role in the conflict. Saudi Arabia and its partners have accused the Houthis of expanding attacks against strategic infrastructure. However, claims made by the opposing sides regarding targets, weapons and responsibility for individual incidents require independent verification. Conflict spreads pressure beyond Yemen The attack in Aden comes as fighting intensifies around Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where government-aligned forces and Houthi fighters have been engaged in renewed clashes. The fighting has raised concerns about access to essential goods and the ability of humanitarian organisations to reach vulnerable communities. The wider conflict also carries implications for regional security. Yemen sits near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic maritime passage connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. The waterway is an important route for international shipping, including energy supplies and commercial goods moving between Europe and Asia. Any sustained escalation around the strait could increase shipping risks, raise insurance costs and complicate decisions by commercial operators. The consequences would extend beyond Yemen, particularly if attacks begin to affect maritime traffic or other critical infrastructure more directly. The conflict has also placed Saudi Arabia under growing pressure. The Saudi-led coalition has reported intercepting missiles and drones in Saudi territory, including near strategically important locations. The coalition has accused the Houthis of pursuing a wider campaign against Saudi infrastructure, while the Houthis have continued to present their operations as retaliation for Saudi involvement in Yemen. These developments increase the risk that the conflict could become more closely linked to the wider confrontation involving Iran and regional powers. They do not, however, establish that every attack in the region is coordinated or directed by a single actor. Humanitarian concerns deepen as fighting resumes For Yemen’s population, renewed hostilities threaten to worsen an already severe humanitarian crisis. Years of conflict have damaged infrastructure, weakened public services and left many communities dependent on humanitarian assistance. The situation in Taiz is especially concerning. The Associated Press reported that access to essential supplies has deteriorated, with residents facing shortages of food, fuel and other necessities. The World Food Program has warned that hundreds of thousands of people in the area are beyond its current reach for aid deliveries. Further disruption could increase prices, limit access to healthcare and make it harder for displaced families to obtain basic necessities. Civilians living near front lines or strategic installations face additional risks as fighting expands. Humanitarian organisations have repeatedly stressed the importance of protecting civilians and ensuring safe, sustained access to people in need. Any prolonged escalation would make those objectives more difficult to achieve. What happens next? The immediate priority is to establish the full extent of the damage, support the injured and determine whether further attacks are imminent. Regional governments will also be watching for signs of retaliation and any additional threats to airports, energy infrastructure or maritime routes. Diplomatically, the attack adds another obstacle to efforts to contain the conflict. Saudi Arabia and its partners face pressure to respond to attacks on their personnel and infrastructure, while the Houthis have signalled that they intend to continue targeting what they describe as Saudi military assets. A wider escalation is not inevitable, but the combination of renewed ground fighting, strikes against government-linked facilities and threats to regional infrastructure raises the stakes for all parties involved. For now, the confirmed facts are that the palace complex in Aden was struck, two security guards were killed and at least six people were injured. The Houthis claimed responsibility, while their stated explanation for the target remains unverified. Further developments will determine whether Thursday’s attack remains an isolated escalation or becomes part of a broader intensification of the regional conflict.

title: Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case as Health Authorities Expand Contact Tracing
author: Iris Vanea
content: Kenya has confirmed a second Ebola case linked to its first recorded infection, intensifying efforts to contain the virus after the initial patient died in Nairobi earlier this month. The newly confirmed patient, a 39-year-old close relative of the first case, had already been placed in quarantine and was isolated after developing symptoms, according to the country’s health authorities. Officials said the two infections are epidemiologically linked and that there is currently no evidence of wider community transmission. The second case nevertheless adds urgency to contact tracing, monitoring and infection-control measures, particularly because the initial patient had travelled across several countries before the infection was identified. The development comes as regional authorities continue responding to an Ebola outbreak associated with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kenya is now among the countries reporting infections connected to the wider outbreak, increasing the importance of coordination across borders. Quarantine and contact tracing remain central Kenyan authorities have identified 128 contacts linked to the first patient. As of the latest reported update, 113 had been traced, with 108 in quarantine in Kenya. Five contacts were outside the country, and authorities said the relevant health agencies abroad had been informed. Efforts to locate the remaining contacts were continuing. The second patient’s identification while already in quarantine is an important detail for public-health officials. Monitoring people who have been exposed to a confirmed case can help health workers detect symptoms quickly and isolate patients before further transmission occurs. Authorities are also assessing people who may have come into contact with the second patient after symptoms developed, including healthcare workers and staff at the quarantine facility. Such investigations help determine whether additional people require monitoring and whether infection-prevention procedures need to be strengthened. Kenya has tightened screening at airports and border crossings, including measures for travellers arriving from countries associated with the outbreak. Screening can help identify potential cases, but it cannot detect every infection. Early symptoms may be difficult to distinguish from those of other illnesses, making travel histories, contact tracing and prompt medical assessment essential parts of the response. Why the regional outbreak matters The wider outbreak is centred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where health authorities and international partners have reported thousands of confirmed infections and more than 4,000 confirmed deaths in the latest available figures. The outbreak involves the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola virus, for which there are currently no approved vaccines or specific treatments. Ebola is transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or with contaminated materials. Symptoms can include fever, fatigue, muscle or joint pain and, in more severe cases, vomiting, diarrhoea and bleeding. The disease can become life-threatening, making early clinical assessment and infection-control measures especially important. The absence of an approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain complicates the response. Healthcare teams must focus on rapid identification, isolation, supportive medical care, protective equipment and the careful monitoring of contacts. Public communication is equally important, as misinformation can undermine trust and delay people from seeking medical help. No evidence of community spread, but vigilance continues Kenyan authorities have urged the public to remain calm while following official health guidance. The confirmation of a second case does not, on its own, mean that the virus is spreading widely in the community. However, the situation will depend on whether further infections are identified and whether contacts can be traced and monitored effectively. The coming days will be important for determining whether the response can contain the infections within the known transmission chain. Health authorities will need to keep the public informed, support affected patients and healthcare workers, and maintain surveillance without creating unnecessary panic. For the wider region, the case also underlines the limits of relying on border screening alone. Cross-border coordination, transparent reporting and rapid communication between health agencies remain crucial when an outbreak moves across national boundaries.

title: BREAKING NEWS | UK Reaffirms Support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy Seeks Security Assurances Amid Strained US Ties
author: Iris Vanea
content: The United Kingdom has renewed its commitment to supporting Ukraine after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in London for high-level talks with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III. The visit comes at a sensitive moment for Kyiv, as intensified Russian attacks coincide with growing uncertainty over Ukraine’s relationship with Washington and concerns about access to critical military and communications capabilities. Burnham used the meeting to signal that British support would remain in place despite the shifting diplomatic environment. London has announced a new £45 million support package for Ukraine, including £10 million in accelerated deliveries of air-defence missiles intended to help counter Russian drones. British officials have also been working on additional sanctions and further military and financial assistance. The visit is more than a diplomatic gesture. It reflects a wider European concern that Ukraine could face mounting pressure if disagreements with the United States weaken coordination among its principal partners. Air defence and intelligence cooperation at the centre of talks Ukraine continues to face attacks involving missiles and drones, placing pressure on its air-defence systems and the infrastructure needed to sustain civilian life. British support for lightweight air-defence missiles is intended to strengthen Ukraine’s ability to respond to incoming threats, including newer types of jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy also raised concerns about difficulties involving intelligence sharing and access to Starlink satellite communications. These systems have become important to Ukraine’s military coordination and operational resilience during the war. Any disruption can have consequences beyond communications alone, affecting the speed at which information reaches units and the ability to coordinate operations. The issues are particularly sensitive because Ukraine remains dependent on external partners for several capabilities that are difficult to replace quickly. Kyiv therefore has an interest not only in securing additional weapons, but also in ensuring that existing cooperation remains dependable. The British government has presented its position as a long-term commitment rather than a response limited to the latest escalation. Burnham has also called for additional international pressure on Moscow, including measures targeting services that facilitate Russian liquefied natural gas exports. A diplomatic challenge involving Washington The London meetings are taking place against the backdrop of worsening tensions between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Recent disagreements have raised questions about the future direction of American policy towards the war, while Washington’s reported agreement concerning Russian diesel exports has added to European unease over the consistency of sanctions policy. For Kyiv, maintaining close relations with the United States remains strategically important. European assistance can provide substantial support, but replacing every American military, intelligence or technological capability would be difficult and potentially expensive. Britain’s effort to reinforce its relationship with Ukraine may also be intended to encourage other European partners to sustain their commitments. However, political declarations will need to be followed by deliveries, funding decisions and practical coordination if they are to make a meaningful difference on the battlefield. What happens next The immediate question is whether the latest British commitments translate into timely assistance as Ukraine prepares for further Russian attacks and the challenges of winter. The effectiveness of the new package will depend on delivery schedules, Ukraine’s operational requirements and the availability of complementary systems. The broader diplomatic question is whether London and other European capitals can help preserve a coordinated international response while relations between Kyiv and Washington remain strained. Zelenskyy’s visit demonstrates that Ukraine retains important partners in Europe. It does not, by itself, resolve the uncertainty surrounding American support or guarantee a change in the military situation. The next indicators will be concrete decisions on weapons, intelligence cooperation, sanctions and financial assistance.

title: Spain Moves Towards Centralised Gambling Risk Checks as Regulators Tighten Player Protection
author: Iris Vanea
content: Spain’s gambling regulator has reopened a public consultation on a proposed system designed to identify online gambling customers whose behaviour may indicate an increased risk of gambling-related harm. The proposal would introduce a standardised monthly assessment for operators licensed at national level, giving regulators a more consistent framework for identifying potentially harmful patterns across the market. The Directorate General for the Regulation of Gambling, known as the DGOJ, opened the consultation on October 13. Stakeholders can submit comments until October 22, 2026. The draft would require operators to assess customer activity over a 183-day period, using a mechanism intended to identify warning signs in account behaviour. The initiative could have significant implications for online casino and sports betting companies operating in Spain. It also reflects a broader regulatory trend in which player protection is increasingly being treated as an operational responsibility requiring systematic monitoring, rather than relying exclusively on customers to recognise and report problems themselves. How the proposed system would work Under the draft, licensed operators would run the assessment during the first seven calendar days of each month. The model would examine activity across the preceding 183 days, using indicators such as deposits, withdrawals, betting patterns, session duration and other account behaviour. The aim is to identify customers whose activity suggests elevated gambling-related risk. A common mechanism could make assessments more consistent between operators, reducing the likelihood that similar patterns are treated differently simply because customers use different platforms. According to industry reporting on the consultation, operators would be expected to notify customers identified by the system and explain the factors behind their classification. The proposal also addresses how risk-related information may be used, an important issue because behavioural data can be commercially sensitive and could otherwise be used for purposes unrelated to consumer protection. The consultation remains a draft regulatory process. Its final requirements, implementation timetable and operational details may change following feedback from industry participants, consumer-protection organisations and other stakeholders. What it could mean for operators For gambling companies, a centralised risk-detection framework could require changes to data processing, compliance procedures, customer communication and internal reporting. Operators may need to ensure that their systems can collect and analyse the relevant information consistently, document the results and demonstrate that appropriate procedures are followed when potentially risky behaviour is identified. Smaller operators could face proportionally greater implementation costs if they need to upgrade existing technology or introduce additional compliance resources. Larger companies may already have behavioural monitoring systems, but they would still need to assess whether those systems meet the regulator’s proposed methodology. There are also practical questions about how the model will perform. A system that identifies too many customers as high risk may generate unnecessary interventions, while one that fails to identify concerning behaviour could provide a false sense of security. The quality of the indicators, the treatment of unusual but legitimate activity and the process for reviewing classifications will therefore matter. Data protection will be another key consideration. Gambling activity can reveal sensitive information about a person’s financial behaviour and habits. Any framework using that information must operate within applicable privacy rules, with clear limits on access, retention and secondary commercial use. A wider shift towards measurable player protection Regulators across multiple markets have been placing greater emphasis on identifying harmful gambling behaviour earlier. The underlying challenge is that gambling-related harm rarely presents itself in the same way for every customer. Changes in spending, frequency, session length or betting patterns can be warning signs, but no single indicator necessarily establishes that a person has a gambling problem. A centralised model could help standardise the first stage of detection, but its effectiveness will depend on what happens after a customer is flagged. Clear explanations, appropriate support options and proportionate interventions will be important if the system is to deliver meaningful protection rather than simply generate compliance records. For operators, the direction of travel is clear: responsible-gambling measures are becoming more closely linked to data governance, product design and day-to-day business processes. What happens next The October 22 consultation deadline gives operators, industry groups and consumer advocates a short window to comment on the proposed framework. Their feedback could influence how the model is applied, what safeguards accompany it and how much flexibility operators retain in their own monitoring systems. Until the regulator publishes a final decision, the proposal should not be treated as an already implemented legal requirement. Nevertheless, operators serving Spain’s nationally regulated online gambling market have reason to review their existing systems and assess what changes might be needed. The outcome will be relevant beyond Spain, as other jurisdictions continue to consider how automated monitoring can support player protection while respecting privacy and ensuring that regulatory obligations remain workable.

title: Ukraine Says It Received No Warning Before Russian Missile Strike on Kyiv as Doubts Grow Over Proposed Energy Truce
author: Iris Vanea
content: Ukraine has received no advance warning from its international partners about a Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv that struck civilian infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday, October 13. The statement came amid a renewed wave of Russian aerial attacks across Ukraine and growing uncertainty over a proposed energy truce announced by US President Donald Trump. Kyiv says Russian strikes on critical infrastructure have continued despite the announcement, while Moscow has yet to confirm that a formal agreement is in force. The developments underline the difficulty of translating diplomatic statements into arrangements that can be verified on the ground. A missile attack raises questions about early warning Zelenskyy said five Russian missiles hit civilian infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital. He stressed that advance intelligence from partner countries could help Ukrainian authorities prepare for incoming ballistic missile attacks and protect civilians. Early warning is particularly important when dealing with ballistic missiles, which can travel at high speed and leave limited time for emergency responses. Even a short warning may allow people to reach shelters, emergency services to prepare and local authorities to issue public alerts. The Ukrainian president did not assign responsibility for the absence of a warning. His comments nevertheless highlight the importance of intelligence-sharing between Ukraine and its international partners as Russia continues to rely on missiles and drones to strike cities and infrastructure. The wider wave of attacks has also caused casualties elsewhere. Zelenskyy said Russian strikes had killed four people and wounded 41 in Kharkiv, where a residential building was hit. Other attacks were reported in the Kyiv, Lviv and Rivne regions. These figures reflect the situation reported on Tuesday and may change as rescue operations and damage assessments continue. The energy truce remains uncertain The attacks have also raised questions about the proposed energy ceasefire announced by Trump over the weekend. The US president said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to refrain from striking each other’s energy infrastructure. However, the announcement has not been followed by a jointly confirmed set of terms. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday that contacts on the matter were continuing, rather than confirming that a formal agreement had entered into force. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian oil refineries and other energy sites during the two days following Trump’s announcement. He accused Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure. The Ukrainian claim that its own attacks had stopped could not be independently verified at the time of reporting. However, neither Russian officials nor Russian media had reported Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries since the announcement, according to the Associated Press. The distinction matters because an announced truce is not necessarily an operational agreement. A functioning arrangement would require clarity over the facilities covered, the duration of the restrictions, how alleged violations would be investigated and how both sides would communicate during incidents. Why energy infrastructure matters Energy infrastructure has become a central part of the conflict because damage to power plants, distribution networks and fuel facilities can have consequences far beyond the immediate military situation. For Ukrainian households, attacks on electricity and heating systems can disrupt daily life and increase pressure on public services as colder weather approaches. Hospitals, water systems, transport networks and businesses also depend on reliable energy supplies. For Russia, attacks on oil refineries can affect fuel production and the operations of energy companies. A reciprocal halt to these attacks could therefore offer economic and humanitarian benefits, even without resolving the broader conflict. But a limited energy truce would not amount to a general ceasefire. Fighting elsewhere could continue, and the agreement would need to be monitored to establish whether it was being respected. The international diplomatic challenge The latest developments put pressure on the diplomatic efforts led by Washington. The United States has sought to encourage steps that could reduce hostilities, but the lack of clear confirmation from both governments complicates the assessment of progress. Ukraine’s partners also face questions about how intelligence-sharing can support civilian protection. Early warning is only one part of the response: air defences, shelter access, emergency services and resilient infrastructure all remain important. For European governments, the continued attacks reinforce the connection between military security and energy security. Damage to infrastructure can create additional economic costs, increase reconstruction needs and complicate preparations for winter. What happens next? The key indicators will be whether Moscow and Kyiv confirm the terms of an energy truce, whether attacks on energy infrastructure decline and whether mechanisms emerge to verify compliance. For now, the situation remains unsettled. Zelenskyy’s statement highlights both the immediate danger posed by continued missile attacks and the gap between diplomatic announcements and conditions on the ground. Any agreement that reduces attacks on civilian infrastructure could represent a meaningful step. Its credibility, however, will depend on observable changes in military activity rather than statements alone.

title: UN Adopts New Global Pandemic Declaration as Countries Face Pressure to Turn COVID-19 Lessons Into Action
author: Iris Vanea
content: The United Nations General Assembly adopted a new political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response on October 12, renewing international commitments to strengthen health systems and improve cooperation against future outbreaks. The declaration was adopted by 153 votes in favour, with the United States, Israel and Argentina voting against it and New Zealand and Paraguay abstaining, according to reporting by Global Issues citing UN information. The outcome comes as governments continue to negotiate how to share pathogen information, distribute medical products more equitably and ensure that countries are better prepared for the next major health emergency. A political commitment, not a new emergency power The declaration establishes a shared political agenda, but it is not itself a binding international treaty. Its adoption does not automatically create new enforcement powers or guarantee that governments will provide additional funding. Instead, it renews pressure on countries to strengthen the systems needed to prevent, detect and respond to outbreaks. These include disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, trained health workers, reliable supply chains and the ability to communicate risks to the public. The World Health Organization welcomed the decision, describing it as a renewed commitment to international cooperation. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged governments to fulfil their promises, particularly by completing negotiations on an important component of the WHO Pandemic Agreement. The declaration reflects a central lesson of COVID-19: an outbreak that begins in one location can quickly affect health systems, travel, trade and economic activity across the world. The unfinished question of sharing pathogens and benefits One of the most important issues is the proposed Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing system, known as PABS. The system is intended to help establish how pathogen samples and related information can be shared for research and development, while ensuring that the benefits of resulting products are distributed more equitably. Access to pathogen information can be crucial when researchers are identifying a new disease, developing diagnostic tests or designing vaccines and treatments. However, governments have different concerns about how such information should be used and how countries providing samples should benefit from the products developed from them. The negotiations are therefore about more than scientific cooperation. They also involve questions of fairness, manufacturing capacity, access to medicines and the distribution of responsibilities between wealthier and lower-income countries. WHO says the outcome of the PABS negotiations will be considered at the next World Health Assembly in May 2027, or earlier through a special session. Finalising this work is a key step towards enabling the broader Pandemic Agreement to enter into force. Why equitable access matters During a major outbreak, the ability to manufacture and distribute vaccines, treatments and diagnostic tests can determine how quickly health systems respond. Countries with strong research institutions and pharmaceutical manufacturing capacity may be able to secure supplies more quickly. Others can face delays, limited production capacity or difficulties financing purchases. The new declaration calls for stronger local and regional manufacturing, greater investment in research and development, improved surveillance and sustainable financing. These measures could help reduce dependence on a small number of suppliers during emergencies. However, building manufacturing capacity takes time, investment and technical expertise. Facilities must also be able to meet quality standards and remain useful between major outbreaks. Equitable access is therefore not simply a question of distributing products after they have been developed. It also depends on where research takes place, how information is shared and whether countries can manufacture or procure essential supplies when demand rises sharply. Preparedness must extend beyond hospitals Pandemic preparedness also involves coordination between health authorities, governments, communities and sectors such as agriculture, transport and education. Disease surveillance needs to detect unusual patterns early. Health systems need plans to expand capacity without abandoning routine care. Authorities need clear communication strategies so that people understand risks and can make informed decisions. The declaration also supports a broader approach that recognises the connections between human, animal and environmental health. This matters because some infectious diseases can emerge or spread through interactions between people, animals and changing environments. Preparedness requires investment before a crisis begins, when the immediate political pressure to spend money may be lower. The challenge of turning commitments into results The vote itself illustrates that international consensus remains difficult. While the declaration received broad support, three countries voted against it and two abstained. A political declaration can establish priorities, but implementation depends on national budgets, legislation, institutions and continued international cooperation. Countries may agree on the need for preparedness while disagreeing about funding, access to technology or the obligations attached to international agreements. The absence of automatic enforcement also means that progress will need to be assessed through concrete measures: stronger surveillance, improved emergency planning, more reliable supply chains and better access to essential health products. What comes next? The next major milestone is the continuing work on the Pandemic Agreement and the PABS system. Governments will need to resolve outstanding questions before the wider framework can become operational. For the public, the significance of the declaration will ultimately depend on whether it helps countries detect outbreaks earlier, respond more effectively and avoid the unequal access to medical products seen during previous emergencies. The vote renews a global commitment, but it is only one stage in a longer process. Preparedness will be measured not by the language of the declaration, but by the systems countries build before the next health emergency arrives.

title: Around 400 Scientists Call for International AI Oversight Body as Cybersecurity Risks Intensify
author: Iris Vanea
content: Approximately 400 scientists, including prominent artificial intelligence researchers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, called on Tuesday, October 13, for an international body to oversee safety standards for advanced AI systems capable of carrying out cyber operations. In an open letter, the researchers proposed common containment standards, independent oversight and a registry of significant security incidents that could eventually be made public. They argued that voluntary commitments by technology companies are not enough to address risks associated with increasingly capable AI systems. The appeal comes as regulators in the United States and Europe intensify scrutiny of AI use in banking and cybersecurity. Why researchers want international standards Advanced AI systems can assist with software development, identify weaknesses in computer networks and automate tasks that previously required substantial human involvement. These capabilities can have legitimate uses. Security teams may use AI to detect vulnerabilities, investigate suspicious activity and respond more quickly to cyber threats. The same capabilities, however, could also be misused. Systems that can analyse code, identify weaknesses or coordinate complex digital tasks may lower the technical barriers for malicious actors. Risks become more difficult to manage when a system can take multiple actions with limited human supervision. The researchers argue that safety standards should not depend entirely on the policies of individual companies. They want a more coordinated framework that establishes minimum expectations for containment, oversight and incident reporting across the industry. Their proposal is a call for action, not an international regulatory body that already exists. Establishing such an institution would require governments and other stakeholders to agree on its authority, membership and operating rules. The proposed role of containment standards One of the letter’s central recommendations is that advanced AI models should initially be isolated from external networks, a practice commonly described as air-gapping. The purpose is to limit the ways a system can interact with outside infrastructure while researchers evaluate its capabilities and potential risks. Isolation alone cannot eliminate every danger. AI systems may still produce harmful outputs, and security failures can occur through people, connected tools or weaknesses in the surrounding software. Nevertheless, restricting network access can reduce the number of pathways through which a system could cause harm during testing. The researchers also called for independent oversight. This would help ensure that assessments are not conducted solely by the organisations developing the technology, which may face commercial pressure to release products quickly. Independent evaluation could provide a more consistent way to test whether systems remain within defined limits and whether safeguards work as intended. Incident reporting could improve accountability The proposed incident registry is another significant part of the initiative. At present, information about AI-related security failures may be distributed across companies, cybersecurity researchers and affected organisations. Reporting practices can vary, making it difficult to compare incidents or understand whether particular weaknesses are recurring. A shared registry could help researchers and regulators identify patterns, assess the severity of incidents and improve safety practices across the industry. Making information public would require careful decisions about what can be disclosed. Detailed reports could help defenders understand vulnerabilities, but they could also expose technical information that malicious actors might exploit. A workable system would therefore need rules covering confidentiality, verification, severity thresholds and the timing of public disclosure. Regulators are already examining AI risks in banking The appeal coincides with a separate regulatory push involving financial institutions. Reuters reported on Tuesday that regulators in the United States, including the Federal Reserve, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, are questioning banks about their use of advanced AI systems. The inquiries include how banks use AI agents in cybersecurity, what limits are placed on their actions, whether decisions can be audited and how systems can be shut down if they exceed their authority. European supervisors, including the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, are also pressing financial institutions to improve recovery plans and prepare for AI-enabled cyber threats. The concern is not limited to the theft of customer data. A major attack affecting a bank or a critical service could disrupt payments, prevent customers from accessing accounts and undermine confidence in financial markets. Regulators are still gathering information and have not, according to Reuters, imposed a new uniform set of requirements through these inquiries. Innovation and control must develop together Technology companies face pressure to deploy increasingly capable AI products, while businesses want to use automation to improve productivity and strengthen security. However, the speed of adoption can outpace the development of appropriate controls. Organisations may introduce AI tools before they fully understand their dependencies, access permissions or failure modes. For businesses, this creates practical questions: Which systems can an AI agent access? Can its actions be reversed? Is a human required to approve sensitive decisions? Can the organisation continue operating if the AI service becomes unavailable or compromised? These are operational issues as much as technical ones. Effective AI governance requires clear responsibilities, testing, monitoring and plans for recovery. The challenge of global coordination An international oversight body could help establish common standards across countries, reducing the risk that companies face inconsistent expectations in different jurisdictions. But reaching agreement would be difficult. Governments have different approaches to technology regulation, national security and information-sharing. Companies may also disagree about the costs and scope of mandatory oversight. Some researchers and policymakers favour stronger international controls, while others argue that existing laws and technical safeguards should be improved before creating another institution. The debate is therefore not simply about whether AI should be regulated. It is about how to make oversight effective without unnecessarily restricting beneficial research and development. What happens next? The scientists’ proposal adds pressure on governments and technology companies to move from general safety principles towards more concrete standards. The next steps will depend on whether governments engage with the proposed framework, whether researchers can agree on practical containment requirements and whether companies are willing to disclose meaningful information about significant incidents. For businesses adopting AI, the immediate lesson is clear: security planning cannot be separated from AI deployment. As systems gain greater autonomy, organisations will need stronger controls, better recovery procedures and clear accountability for decisions made with automated tools. The call for international oversight does not settle the debate, but it signals growing concern that the governance of advanced AI must develop alongside its technical capabilities.

title: Cristiano Ronaldo Returns With a Goal for Al-Nassr Following Portugal Dispute, but His International Future Remains Uncertain
author: Iris Vanea
content: Cristiano Ronaldo returned to club competition on Friday, October 9, scoring the opening goal in Al-Nassr’s 3-0 victory over Diriyah in the Saudi Arabian league. The result, reported by the Associated Press and other international media outlets on October 10, came after a turbulent period for the Portuguese forward, who had left the national team’s training camp following a dispute over his role in the squad. The goal was reported as the 980th of his career. Meanwhile, the Portuguese Football Federation initiated disciplinary proceedings and announced a provisional suspension, with the duration of any final sanction still to be determined. A response on the pitch after a turbulent week Ronaldo opened the scoring in the first half after the opposing goalkeeper parried a shot from Kingsley Coman. The Portuguese forward followed the rebound and finished from close range. Al-Nassr continued to control the match, with Samu Costa extending the lead before half-time. Coman added a third goal in the second half to complete the 3-0 victory. The result was important for Al-Nassr as it continued its pursuit of the league title. The club moved level on points with leaders Al-Qadsiah, with goal difference separating the teams after the eighth round. Ronaldo remains an important part of the attack, and his scoring form will be a key factor in the club’s ambitions. The goal also attracted attention because it came after several days in which media coverage of Ronaldo focused more on his relationship with the national team than on his performances on the pitch. How the dispute with Portugal began During the latest international window, Ronaldo left Portugal’s training camp before the team’s next match in the Nations League. The forward said that newly appointed coach Jorge Jesus had failed to honour promises concerning the playing time he would receive. The coach disputed the existence of a formal agreement of the kind described by the player, and the disagreement became a major subject in international sports coverage. The Portuguese federation subsequently opened disciplinary proceedings and imposed a provisional suspension. A final decision on any additional sanction remains subject to the federation’s disciplinary process. Ronaldo apologised for the way he handled his departure and for failing to say goodbye to supporters and teammates. He also indicated that he was prepared to accept the consequences and wanted to remain available for national-team selection. A major player, but an institutional decision Ronaldo is one of the most prolific scorers in international football history. His record for Portugal stands at 146 goals in 234 appearances, according to figures cited in recent reports. His status means that any dispute involving his place in the national team attracts considerable attention. However, a player’s sporting achievements do not override team regulations or the disciplinary procedures of the governing body. The case highlights a familiar challenge in elite sport: managing relationships between high-profile players, coaches and the institutions responsible for selection. Coaches must choose teams according to tactical plans and sporting performance, while experienced players may have their own expectations about their roles. When those expectations conflict, clear communication and established rules become essential to preventing a disagreement from escalating. Al-Nassr remains focused on the title For Al-Nassr, the victory over Diriyah provided a positive result at a time when attention surrounding Ronaldo could have distracted from the league campaign. The club needs consistency throughout the season, and competition for first place remains close. The Saudi Pro League continues to attract international attention through the presence of prominent players and substantial investment by its clubs. Star performances contribute to the competition’s visibility, but sustained success depends on the entire squad rather than one individual. Ronaldo’s return to scoring form is therefore useful for Al-Nassr, but the club’s longer-term prospects will depend on results across the remaining fixtures. What comes next for Ronaldo? The next significant development will be clarification of the disciplinary situation within the Portuguese federation and the conditions under which the forward could return to the national team. Scoring on his return to club football does not resolve the institutional dispute, but it demonstrates that Ronaldo continues to contribute on the pitch. The situation will remain unresolved until the federation communicates a clear decision. For Portugal, the challenge is to manage a dispute involving one of its most important players while preserving the authority of the coaching staff and ensuring that team rules are respected. For Ronaldo, the task is to continue performing for his club and clarify his relationship with the national team ahead of future competitions.

content: ZURICH, Oct 27 (Reuters) – UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti ​said on ‌Tuesday his bank’s integration of fallen rival Credit ‌Suisse, ​which it ⁠acquired in ⁠2023, forced it to slow its deployment of ​AI somewhat, but now ⁠the lender ⁠can put ​even more emphasis ​on technology. title: NBA roundup: Cavs rally from 15 down, hand Wolves first loss in OT
author: Syndicated Content
content: By Field Level Media Oct 27 (Field Level Media) – Donovan Mitchell hit a tiebreaking midrange jumper with 48 seconds left in overtime as the host Cleveland Cavaliers rallied from a 15-point deficit to defeat the previously unbeaten Minnesota Timberwolves 127-125 on Monday night. Timberwolves superstar Anthony Edwards missed a wide-open 3-pointer with 3.9 seconds remaining that could have tied the game. Peyton Watson grabbed the rebound and made two free throws to push Cleveland’s lead to 127-122. Mitchell finished with 26 points and seven assists, while James Harden had 19 points and nine assists for the Cavaliers, who ​improved to 2-1. Evan Mobley added 18 points and 10 rebounds, and rookie Meleek Thomas scored 16 off the bench in his NBA debut. Edwards connected on a 3-pointer at the buzzer to finish ‌with a season-high 47 points, his seventh career regular-season game with at least Jaden McDaniels had 14 points and Rudy Gobert collected 20 rebounds and LaMelo Ball had 11 points and seven turnovers. Warriors 134, Nuggets 114 Steph Curry hit all eight of his field-goal attempts and scored 17 of his 24 points in the third quarter, leading visiting Golden State over Denver for its first win of the season. Curry made a trio of 3-pointers and all five of his free-throw attempts to complete his perfect night. Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg scored a career-high 31 points and added 12 rebounds, Brandin Podziemski scored 18 points, Gui Santos contributed 13 and Al Horford had 11 for Golden State. DeMar DeRozan scored a team-high 21 points, Nikola Jokic finished with 19 points and 11 assists, Jamal Murray also had ‌19 points ​and Bryce Hopkins added 13 points for Denver, which played the final 8:34 without Aaron Gordon after the forward was hit with two technicals. Bucks 110, ⁠Pacers 102 Tyler Herro compiled 23 points, 10 rebounds and seven assists ⁠as Milwaukee notched the first win of the Taylor Jenkins era, defeating visiting Indiana. Ryan Rollins added 19, Kyle Kuzma had 17 and Kel’el Ware paired 16 points with 14 rebounds as Milwaukee avoided its first 0-4 start to a season since 1976-77, 50 years ago. Tyrese Haliburton posted 22 points and nine assists for Indiana, while Pascal Siakam chalked up 20 points, 13 boards and six assists. Mavericks 113, Heat 109 Reigning Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg returned from a one-game absence to score 29 points and dish 11 assists as visiting Dallas defeated Miami. Flagg, who sat out Saturday due to a left shoulder injury, added six ​rebounds against the Heat. He shot 12 of 23 overall and 2 of 8 on 3-point attempts. Kyrie Irving, who was rested in Dallas’ previous game, posted 18 points, six rebounds and six assists. Giannis Antetokounmpo posted his first triple-double for the Heat — 29 points, 15 rebounds and 11 assists — but Miami fell to 0-4 on the season. Besides Antetokounmpo’s contributions, Miami got 21 points from Davion Mitchell. All-Star center Bam Adebayo was held to eight ⁠points and eight rebounds. Celtics 134, Bulls 99 Payton Pritchard came off the bench to score a game-high 28 points to lead Boston to ⁠a victory over visiting Chicago. Pritchard made 7 of 10 shots from behind the 3-point arc. Jayson Tatum added 23 points, seven rebounds and six assists for Boston, ​which made 21 of its 44 3-point attempts and had a 54-40 edge in rebounds. Norman Powell led the Bulls with 20 points. Caleb Wilson tossed in 17, and Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis each finished with 11. Leonard Miller ​had nine points and nine rebounds. Thunder 125, Suns 114 Ajay Mitchell scored 30 to lead Oklahoma City to a home win over Phoenix a day after losing a pair of ‌starters to long-term injuries. Oklahoma City was playing its first game since Jalen Williams suffered a fractured fibula and a dislocated left ankle in the closing minutes of a win over the Clippers. Earlier in that game, Cason Wallace suffered a torn labrum. Both will require surgery and will be out long term. In the win over Phoenix, Alex Caruso left after turning his right ankle. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scored 26 points on 11-of-18 shooting and Isaiah Hartenstein had 15 points and 13 rebounds. Phoenix’s Devin Booker had scored a combined 66 points over the first two games but finished with just three points on 1-of-7 shooting. Jalen Green led the Suns with 20 points while Dillon Brooks added 19. Rockets ⁠120, Hawks 110 Alperen Sengun scored a game-high 29 points, Jabari Smith Jr. added a double- double and Houston Rockets remained unbeaten by beating visiting Atlanta. Sengun added nine rebounds and nine assists to pace a balanced attack. Smith paired 16 points with 12 rebounds, while Kevin Durant added 22 points and nine boards. Tari Eason and Reed Sheppard scored 13 points apiece off the bench. Jalen Johnson paced the Hawks with 21 points and nine rebounds while ⁠CJ McCollum added 20 points and four 3-pointers. The Hawks dropped back-to-back games against ‌the Rockets. Grizzlies 110, Jazz 105 Ty Jerome scored eight of his 15 points in the final six minutes — including two clutch free throws with 11.6 seconds remaining — to ⁠lead Memphis to a victory over host Utah. The Grizzlies won their fourth straight game to open the season for only the second time in franchise history. ​Meanwhile, Utah lost ‌two starters in the first half. Jaren Jackson Jr., the former Grizzlies star, injured his right knee in the second quarter and did not return. Lauri ​Markkanen injured his right ⁠wrist early in the first quarter and did not return. Cedric Coward had 16 points and 11 rebounds, Jaylen Wells added 14 points and Cam Boozer and Jerami Grant each scored 13 for Memphis. Keyonte George had 26 points for the Jazz and Ace Bailey contributed 17 points and 10 boards. Mo Bamba added 14 points and seven rebounds off the bench. Hornets 110, Wizards 103 Brandon Miller scored a career-high 39 points and Charlotte held off visiting Washington for their first back-to-back wins of the young season. Miller made 15 of 28 shots from the field, including five 3-pointers. Naz Reid added 18 points and 12 rebounds for Charlotte, while Grayson Allen scored 15 off the bench, including seven from the free-throw line. Moussa Diabate chipped in 11 points and 17 rebounds. Anthony Davis scored 29 points and grabbed 10 rebounds for the Wizards, hitting three of Washington’s nine 3-point attempts. Trae Young added 22 points and 10 assists, Kyshawn George posted 20 ​points and Alex Sarr had 12 points. (–Field Level Media)

title: Meghan to join Australia’s Junior MasterChef next year
author: Syndicated Content
content: LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) – Meghan, the wife of Britain’s Prince Harry, will star in the next series of ​Australia’s Junior MasterChef in 2027, ‌returning to a franchise where she appeared as a guest judge on the adult version earlier this year. Meghan, an American actress before ‌she ​married Harry in 2018, ⁠has recently moved ⁠back to Britain from the US with her family, with media reports suggesting she was keen to find a ​new acting role. Channel 10 said on Instagram that Junior MasterChef Australia would ⁠return in 2027, hosted ⁠by Poh Ling Yeow and ​Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex. Australian website News.com.au ​said filming was expected to take ‌place in Melbourne early to mid-next year. Harry and Meghan have attracted global media attention since they stepped down as ⁠senior members of the royal family in 2020 before moving to the US, where they ⁠gave multiple ‌interviews criticising the institution. The couple ⁠returned to the headlines last ​week ‌after authorities in the Philippines ​said they ⁠were investigating whether Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, had possessed child sexual abuse images. She said she was “deeply distressed” over the allegations. (Reporting by Kate Holton, Editing by ​Paul Sandle)

title: India’s Cipla misses quarterly profit view on muted US sales
author: Syndicated Content
content: Oct 27 (Reuters) – Cipla, India’s third-largest drugmaker by revenue, missed second-quarter profit estimates on Tuesday, as muted sales of generic Revlimid ​and stiff competition weighed on its US ‌business. The company’s consolidated net profit fell to 8.78 billion rupees ($92.2 million) in the quarter ended September 30, from 13.51 billion rupees a year ago. Analysts, on average, had expected ‌profit ​to fall to 9.42 billion ⁠rupees, according to data ⁠compiled by LSEG. Cipla is facing mounting pressure in its key US market as sales of generic Revlimid – Bristol-Myer Squibb’s blood cancer drug – continue to ​taper amid rising competition, increasing its dependence on India where sustained growth in chronic therapies ⁠and newer launches are ⁠helping offset the drag. The company is ​also banking on obesity drug, Yurpeak, to support growth ​as weakness in the US business weighs ‌on overall momentum. Yurpeak is Cipla’s brand of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide, which it sells in India under a partnership with Lilly.Revenue from its India ⁠business rose 12%, while North America revenue decreased 19% during the quarter. Revenue from operations fell 2.4% to 74.04 ⁠billion rupees during ‌the quarter, partly due to ⁠a reclassification from April 1, 2026, ​that now ‌presents certain marketing and promotional expenses ​as a ⁠reduction from revenue rather than under other expenses, with no impact on profit or cash flows. India and North America together contribute about two-thirds of Cipla’s revenue. (Reporting by Kashish Tandon in Bengaluru; Editing by ​Jochelle Mendonca)

title: Attackers kill 60 people in Ethiopia’s conflict-hit Oromiya region, Orthodox church says
author: Syndicated Content
content: NAIROBI, Oct 27 (Reuters) – At least 60 people were killed in two separate attacks in Ethiopia’s conflict-hit Oromiya region in the ​past week, the Ethiopian Orthodox Church said. Church ‌authorities said the dead were all Christians, but did not go into details on how they died or who was behind the attacks. The Oromiya regional government and ‌a ​source linked to a rebel ⁠alliance fighting government forces ⁠in the northern Tigray region traded blame for the attacks. The Holy Synod of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church said 14 believers were killed ​in Merti Woreda on October 20 and 46 in Sherka Woreda on October 24. More ⁠than 20 homes were also ⁠burned and more than 20 people ​hospitalised with severe injuries, the church’s statement, issued ​on Monday, added. The regional government said the rebel ‌alliance launched the attacks to try to spark religious conflict, without providing evidence. The source linked to the rebel alliance said the Oromiya regional ⁠government had carried out the killings, citing conversations with two local residents. The Oromo Liberation Army rebel group, which ⁠the regional ‌government has blamed for previous attacks ⁠on Orthodox Christians, did not immediately ​respond ‌to a request for comment. The OLA ​is one ⁠of seven armed groups that announced last month that they had formed an alliance aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government. (Reporting by Nairobi newsroom;Writing by Vincent Mumo Nzilani;Editing by Alexander Winning and ​Andrew Heavens)
