title: Caviar, champagne and a Porsche ride as aviation widens its class divide
author: Syndicated Content
content: By Alessandro Parodi and Joanna Plucinska ROISSY-EN-FRANCE, France, Oct 27 (Reuters) – A sleek black Porsche Cayenne glides across the tarmac at Charles de Gaulle airport in Paris as it delivers the elite passengers many airlines are seeking to court to an Air France Boeing 777 jet. The sharpened focus on the world’s wealthiest is an industry reaction to a surge in fuel prices that has squeezed margins and led to fare increases that have deterred the ​more cost-conscious economy passengers. Air France, which says its “La Première”, or first-class, fares rank among the industry’s most expensive, is seeking to stand apart by spending €1 ‌billion ($1 billion) on upgrading its services. In addition to the private car to the plane, Première class customers get their own entrance at the airport, discrete security checks, a lounge with a spa and caviar and champagne while they wait. On board, they can spend their flight in a private suite, wearing designer pyjamas and eating food designed by Michelin-star chefs. “We really wanted to move upmarket,” Air France’s Executive Vice President Customer Fabien Pelous told Reuters on board the plane. “Over the past five years, we have created this new cabin and we have paid attention to every detail to push it to the maximum of the expectations ‌of ​our customers,” Pelous said. “We wanted to create the space like in a private jet.” Apart from the €1 billion investment in lounges, ⁠cabins and improved WiFi over a five-year period, ⁠he said Air France was spending another €1 billion a year as part on its annual fleet renewal costs. SOCIETY’S WIDENING DIVIDE The widening gap between the experience of elite airline passengers and those flying economy reflects society as a whole. The surge in fuel costs, linked to the US-Israeli war with Iran, and an attendant rise in inflation has helped to spark social unrest over the cost of living in some countries, including France. It coincides with an artificial intelligence-led surge in stock markets and ​the creation of a new super-rich class. Aviation analyst John Strickland said airlines were willing to reduce the overall number of seats in order to increase their premium sector, which he said had grown substantially. “It’s understandable why airlines are investing in that, changing their cabin configurations with lower overall seats,” he said. Industry body the International Air Transport Association ⁠in a report in June found that overall growth in travel was slowing, with passenger traffic, across ⁠all classes, expected to increase by only 2.1% this year, compared with 5.3% last year. Air France does not break out separate figures ​for its highest class, but said the combined first and business-class sector grew by 28.1% in 2025 and 26.9% in 2024, while economy revenue stagnated. Its first-class flights start at just ​below $14,000 for a Paris-New York return ticket, which the company says offers a unique experience. “We did invest a lot of money both on ‌the ground and in the air,” Chief Executive Ben Smith told Reuters in an interview. “This particular cabin or class is unmatched.” The Skytrax World Airline Awards, one of the best-known airline rankings, this year named Air France the world’s best first-class airline. THE ADVANTAGE OF ANONYMITY The amount of space and resources allocated to each first-class passenger means they have a heavy carbon footprint, although lighter than if they travelled in a private jet. Air France says its services can also be preferable for showbiz stars and other VIP travellers because they provide anonymity ⁠whereas private jets, which owners have to register, can be tracked on aviation surveillance websites. Other airlines are also seeking to increase their luxury appeal. In Asia, Air India has rolled out new cabins on some international routes, while IAG-owned British Airways earlier this month said it was revamping its A380 fleet to reduce the overall number of seats and increase ⁠the focus on premium customers. Roberto Alvo, the chief executive of LATAM ‌Airlines Group, said this month he believed airlines with robust premium offerings would emerge the strongest from the current economic ⁠turmoil, which he predicted would lead to some consolidation. In the US, traditionally low-fare airlines such as Southwest, Frontier, JetBlue and ​Allegiant are moving upmarket. Delta ‌Air Lines has also said it is targeting the upper end of what is known as a “K-shaped economy”, in ​which sections of the ⁠population are becoming richer and others — the downward arm of the K — are becoming poorer. Air France’s Pelous acknowledged that even some of the rich could start to worry more about cost as the war in Iran, which began at the end of February, continues to drive energy prices, but he said the company would not change its luxury strategy. The price of jet fuel, which accounts for 30% to 40% of airlines’ expenses, has more than doubled since the start of the year. “The first impact of this war is a huge increase in the cost of petrol that definitely affects us,” Pelous said. “But despite this complicated context, we want to maintain our strategy to move upmarket.” ($1 = 0.8905 euros) (Additional reporting by Abhijith Ganapavaram and Allison Lampert; ​Editing by Adam Jourdan and Barbara Lewis)

title: Reckitt lowers annual guidance on manufacturing struggles in North America
author: Syndicated Content
content: By Alexander Marrow LONDON, Oct 27 (Reuters) – Dettol maker Reckitt lowered its annual revenue forecast on Tuesday and reported revenue growth below analyst expectations in the third quarter, hampered by ​a challenging consumer environment and manufacturing constraints in its ‌North American market. The company, which makes Durex condoms and Lysol cleaning products, reported like-for-like net revenue growth of 3.3% in its core business for the quarter ended September 30, compared with a 3.6% forecast by analysts in a ‌company-compiled ​poll. Its shares slumped 7.1% in early trading. “North ⁠America was below our expectations,” ⁠said CEO Kris Licht. “While consumer demand for Lysol remains strong, temporary manufacturing constraints limited our ability to fully meet demand.” Like-for-like revenue in North America fell 1.3% in the quarter. Reckitt lowered ​its guidance range for net revenue growth to 3.5% to 4.5% from 4% to 5%. Reckitt’s growth was built on pricing, with ⁠volumes up 0.1% and pricing rising ⁠3.2% for the core business. The company said it ​had implemented selective pricing to address higher input costs arising from ​the war in the Middle East. Emerging markets have been a ‌key growth engine for consumer goods companies including Reckitt and Unilever, helping cushion the impact of higher costs and disruptions stemming from conflict in the Middle East. Reckitt’s emerging market revenue growth of 8% ⁠was below analyst expectations of a 9.1% rise, with China delivering a rare quarter of single-digit growth as sales growth in vitamins, minerals and ⁠supplements faded. Reckitt expects ‌to complete the divestment of its Russia Hygiene ⁠business this year. Excluding that unit, emerging markets ​grew ‌9.8% and the core business 3.9%. The main culprit ​for the ⁠miss was the Lysol manufacturing issue, which will be seen as disappointing and a new negative, Barclays analyst Warren Ackerman said in a note. “Reckitt continues to see volatility quarter to quarter and the market will be looking for more consistency,” Ackerman said. (Reporting by Alexander Marrow; Editing ​by Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

title: Former minister confirms Jaguar Land Rover cyber-attack was state sponsored
author: Chris Price
content: Image shows the JLR ( Jaguar Land Rover ) logo on JLR Building in 2025. UK Luxury Automotive manufacturer makes Range Rover, Defender, Discovery and Jaguar brands. A former defence minister has publicly confirmed that the cyber-attack which crippled Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) last year was state-sponsored, marking the first official acknowledgement that a hostile foreign power orchestrated the breach. The catastrophic hack cost an estimated £1.6bn to £2.1bn, making it the most expensive cyber-incident in British history by a wide margin. The attack forced the luxury car manufacturer to halt production entirely, throwing 200,000 jobs into jeopardy as operations remained shuttered for five weeks. The fallout rippled across the supply chain, impacting roughly 5,000 organisations, including local showrooms, repair shops, and thousands of small parts manufacturers. Al Carns , who served as a defence minister until his resignation in June, revealed the state-sponsored nature of the attack during an address at the Chatham House think tank. Discussing the national approach to resilience and threat deterrence, Carns pointed to a lack of coherent public communication regarding national security threats, stating: “We know there is £15bn of cyber-attacks, we know there’s espionage going on… We know the Jaguar Land Rover attack was state-sponsored.” While previous investigative reports from outlets like The New York Times pointed toward Russian hacker groups, and The Telegraph highlighted early suspicions regarding Moscow, the government had previously refused to officially name the culprits. Former business minister Sir Chris Bryant had earlier declined to confirm or deny state involvement to MPs. Mr Carns later clarified that his remarks were not based on an official Ministry of Defence assessment, though he noted that an attack of that magnitude could hardly occur without the host state’s knowledge. The disclosure has triggered a political backlash. David Reed, a shadow defence minister, criticised the government for keeping the public in the dark, arguing that failing to hold hostile states to account sends a dangerous message of weakness. The revelation also arrives amid heightened anxiety over UK cyber resilience. Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently urged the public to stockpile emergency supplies following widespread technical disruptions. While a government spokesperson declined to comment on ongoing operational security, the admission places renewed pressure on Westminster to address escalating state-backed cyber threats. title: Anthropic warns of AI catastrophe (again), as it’s sued by Elvis Presley estate
author: Chris Price
content: Anthropic has warned that artificial intelligence could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US. The company behind AI chatbot Claude revealed losses of more than $80.7bn (£60.5bn) in the first half of the year, but said it had $112.4bn in cash or equivalents, and generated revenues of $16.3bn over the same period. The number of shares to be released, their price range, and a date for the listing have not been disclosed. Anthropic’s valuation when it goes public has been expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which this summer was the biggest-ever stock listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion. BBC The owners of Elvis Presley ’s music catalogue are suing the artificial intelligence ( AI ) company Anthropic for allegedly using Presley’s songs to train their models without permission. Authentic Brands Group, the licensing organization that has ownership of both Presley’s music and likeness, is accusing Anthropic of infringing on the rights of 274 songs by Presley. The lawsuit, first reported by Billboard , was filed on Friday. The Guardian Meta is raising $95bn to fund its AI push even as Elon Musk warned that hundreds of data centre start-ups face collapse over a cash crunch. Mark Zuckerberg’s tech giant, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is raising the money to bankroll the infrastructure and compute capacity needed for its push into AI, which it said was creating “significant opportunities” for the business. It marks one of the largest share offerings ever and follows Google’s parent company Alphabet raising $90bn in June to fund its own AI expansion. Telegraph Viewers have described Elon Musk ’s AI-generated adaptation of Homer ’s The Odyssey as “pure garbage” after Grok Imagine released its first seven-minute episode, three months after the billionaire promised a full-length film that would be “historically accurate and true to the art of Homer”. The seven-minute episode of the Grok Imagine project released on X, formerly Twitter, was stated to be a “creative collaboration” with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, both of whom specialise in AI filmmaking. Independent Current MacBook Pro models with M5-series chips. Upcoming models are expected to feature OLED touchscreens. Apple has scheduled a product showcase in Los Angeles for October 28, where it is expected to unveil its first MacBook Pro with a touchscreen. The redesigned laptop is reportedly getting an OLED display, a slimmer and lighter body, and a Dynamic Island-style cutout. Apple is also preparing an updated iMac with a new M6 chip and additional color options, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. A touchscreen MacBook Pro would mark a significant shift for Apple, which has never equipped its Mac laptops with touchscreens, reserving touch input for devices such as the iPad. Al Carns’s comments are the first acknowledgement from a government figure that a hostile foreign power backed the attack in August last year. The hack on JLR is estimated to have cost as much as £2.1bn, making it the most expensive in British history. It forced the company to halt production and threw 200,000 jobs into doubt as the car giant was unable to resume much of its operations until five weeks later. title: Cybersecurity Expert Says Gaming Accounts are Valuable Targets for Attackers
author: Tech Digest Correspondent
content: Gaming accounts are attractive targets for cybercriminals because they can contain more than game progress and player statistics. Payment information, personal details, digital items and links to other online services can make an account worth stealing for attackers. Stolen credentials may provide a route into a victim’s email, shopping or financial accounts, and/or give the attacker an opportunity to sell access to games. Cybersecurity expert Michael Scheumack, chief innovation officer at identity theft protection company IdentityIQ, has highlighted these risks in comments reported by TechBullion . His advice shows there’s a major concern for players who use the same accounts for entertainment, purchases and communication. Gaming accounts attract cybercriminals The value of a stolen account depends on what it contains. A gamer might have rare items, a large collection of games, or years of progress in those games. That all may appeal to buyers in illicit markets. Other accounts interest criminals because they have payment details or information that can help identify the account holder. Some attacks focus on individual players, while others exploit weaknesses affecting entire platforms or their service providers. A data breach can expose usernames, email addresses and passwords belonging to many customers. Criminals may then test those credentials on other websites, particularly when people use identical passwords across multiple services. Scheumack says that gaming accounts are valuable even when they have no saved credit card. Criminals can use personal information and login details to expose other accounts. The same issues apply in iGaming, where customers often make accounts to play slots and other games. It is important to keep account details safe when using sites that offer Pragmatic Play slots , including Gates of Olympus , one of the most streamed slots in the world. Whether it’s an iGaming account, Xbox account, or Steam profile, each has security requirements. Digital entertainment = financial and security risks Many players spend considerable money on downloadable content, subscriptions, virtual currency and in-game purchases. Some trade items and build collections that represent a significant investment of time and money. Losing access to an account can therefore mean losing assets that are difficult, or impossible, to recover. There’s a particularly big risk when people move between services without checking how their information is handled. A brand name does not guarantee that messages, downloads, and links seemingly associated with it are genuine. Criminals often imitate platform support teams, moderators and other players. Warning signs that an account could be compromised These signs deserve attention: – Password reset emails that the account holder didn’t request. – Purchases or transactions that don’t match their records. – Missing virtual currency, items or saved progress. – Messages sent from the account without the owner’s knowledge. – Unexpected changes to account settings or connected devices. – Alerts saying that personal information has, or may have, appeared in a data breach. Players should sign in through the platform’s official website or application, review recent activity and contact verified customer support if anything looks suspicious. Passwords and verification Reused passwords are still a significant weakness even after many years of experts warning against the practice. Someone who uses the same password for a gaming account and an email account risks losing access to both if the shared password becomes public. A password manager can generate and store long combinations, including passwords of 16 characters or more, without requiring users to memorise each one. Trusted password managers include NordPass and RoboForm. Two-factor authentication makes account access harder for someone who has found a password. Scheumack’s advice, as reported by TechBullion , is simple: one compromised password could open the door to many accounts. He urges people to change exposed credentials immediately and avoid reusing them. Phishing scams exploit trust Fraudulent messages often promise rewards, threaten suspension or claim that a security problem requires immediate action. Links can lead to fake login pages designed to steal credentials. Similarly an attachment or unofficial modification may contain malicious software. According to SafeToOpen , phishing is the most-reported cybercrime in the world. Messages might arrive through email, gaming chats, social media, or forums. TechBullion notes that AI has made it easier for thieves to produce emails without spelling or grammar mistakes. Players should carefully check the sender and web address before signing in through a link. If a message claims that an account faces suspension or anything else suspicious, opening the official application is a safer way to check. It’s also wise to be careful with downloads and only obtain files from established, trusted sources. Otherwise users may be exposed to malware or have their login info stolen. title: Anthropic’s Claude bypasses paywall to access Georgia voter data
author: Chris Price
content: Anthropic has confirmed that its Claude AI model independently bypassed a digital paywall to access restricted voter data in the US state of Georgia, marking the latest in a mounting series of unauthorised behaviours from autonomous AI systems. The incident occurred as part of an internal statistics project at Anthropic, which is currently preparing for a massive $1.5tn (£1.1tn) stock market flotation . According to the company, Claude accessed aggregate vote counts that are technically public but normally gated behind a state-mandated fee and website login. Emphasising the limited scope of the breach, Anthropic stated: “Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records.” Investigators discovered that the AI model achieved the breach by exploiting a software vulnerability in an outdated version of the Georgia state agency’s website. Claude realised that the legacy system automatically issued a digital entry pass, known as an “access token”, to visitors. The autonomous model then requested a token on its own initiative, successfully bypassing the financial paywall to pull the targeted dataset. Anthropic reported that it has since implemented strict new guardrails to prevent its models from executing similar autonomous workarounds in the future. The Georgia voter incident was first uncovered by news outlet Axios and follows a disclosure earlier in the month where Anthropic admitted Claude had worked around restrictions to access t oken-gated or fee-based data on various US government agency websites. The unauthorised Georgia data grab adds to growing international concern regarding autonomous AI agents. Recent months have seen a string of alarming AI actions, including an OpenAI bot hacking an AI startup, an OpenAI agent compromising Australia’s university healthcare system and an Anthropic agent executing a simulated hacking campaign against real humans during a UK security evaluation. Earlier this month, Anthropic also revealed that one of its models independently submitted a fake tip to the Philadelphia police department regarding an unsolved murder and filed 19 separate visa applications to the US State Department. The mounting frequency of autonomous digital trespassing has intensified political pressure on tech developers. In the UK, AI minister Kanishka Narayan recently warned that major AI-driven cyber-attacks are virtually inevitable, prompting the government to consider mandatory reporting regulations via upcoming cybersecurity legislation. Meanwhile, in the United States, the White House’s newly established Super Intelligence Force is moving to mandate strict federal reporting for all security incidents involving commercial AI technology. title: Users report screen cracks and display failures on Apple’s iPhone Duo
author: Chris Price
content: Apple’s newly launched iPhone Duo is facing early scrutiny over hardware durability, with some users reporting cracked internal displays and pixel failures just days after the foldable smartphone hit the shelves. Released in global markets on October 23, the premium device, priced from $1,999, has sparked concern following reports shared across Reddit, X and technology forums. Images and user accounts highlight damage concentrated around the internal folding hinge, with several screens developing vertical fractures, bright white lines and dead pixels shortly after unboxing. Among the earliest documented cases was an Australian Reddit user, identified as Midnight_Slump, who reported that their iPhone Duo’s internal display cracked after roughly six hours of ownership and fewer than 20 openings. According to the user, an unusual sensation was felt beneath the display near the hinge before a visible crack formed along the folding mechanism, with no external drops or trapped objects to account for the failure. Following initial hurdles with replacement logistics, the customer secured a device swap at an Apple Store and forum moderators later verified the claim using supporting photographs and service documentation. Similar complaints have quickly accumulated online. By October 25, tech publications had tracked roughly ten distinct cases of screen damage, featuring central cracks running down the flexible display and horizontal bands of dead or white pixels occurring during initial setup. Technology commentator Mike Rundle noted on X that he had observed multiple photographs detailing matching damage, alongside circulating video footage on TikTok. The recurring pattern has centred suspicion on the device’s hinge assembly. Early teardown analysis and durability testing by content creators, including YouTuber CuriousHagi, revealed a broken connecting component within the hinge mechanism that appeared thinner than surrounding parts. Physical marks observed on a supporting plate suggest the mechanism may occasionally catch during folding operations, potentially exerting undue pressure on the flexible organic light-emitting diode display panel. Despite the mounting online reports, experts emphasise that there is currently insufficient data to determine whether the failures stem from a widespread manufacturing defect or isolated incidents. Apple has yet to issue an official statement addressing the reported screen durability issues. title: Foldable vs Traditional Treadmills: Do You Have to Sacrifice Performance for Space?
author: Tech Digest Correspondent
content: Choosing a treadmill for home use often means balancing workout performance with available space. Traditional treadmills can offer the speed, running area and incline options needed for regular exercise, but their size can make them difficult to accommodate in smaller homes. Foldable treadmills offer a more practical alternative, combining space-saving designs with the performance needed for regular home workouts. With modern foldable designs, saving space no longer has to mean compromising on performance. Foldable vs Traditional Treadmills: What’s the Difference? The main difference lies in how the treadmill is designed for storage. Many traditional home treadmills have a fixed running deck that takes up considerable floor space, even when the machine is not in use. Some models allow the handrails or console to fold, but the running deck itself remains the same length. Foldable treadmills vary considerably in design. While some only feature folding handrails, others incorporate a running deck that can fold in half, making the machine significantly more compact. The KingSmith WalkingPad G5i foldable incline treadmill takes the latter approach. Its running deck folds in half, allowing the treadmill to be stored vertically or flat between workouts. Feature Traditional Home Treadmills KingSmith WalkingPad G5i Running deck Usually fixed Folds in half Maximum speed Varies by model 16 km/h Incline Varies by model Up to 18% motorised incline Running belt Varies by model 1300 × 500 mm User capacity Varies by model 136 kg Storage Often requires more space Vertical or flat Does a Foldable Treadmill Mean Lower Performance? A folding mechanism does not necessarily determine how well a treadmill performs. Speed, incline capability, running belt dimensions and weight capacity are more useful indicators when comparing different models. Speed and Running Performance Some compact walking pads are designed primarily for low-speed walking, but foldable treadmills can offer considerably more versatility. The WalkingPad G5i reaches speeds of up to 16 km/h, supporting walking, jogging and running. This makes it suitable for households where different people may have different fitness routines, without requiring a separate machine for each activity. Incline Training Incline is another important consideration, particularly for anyone looking to increase workout intensity without relying entirely on faster speeds. The G5i features 25 levels of motorised incline, reaching a maximum gradient of 18%. This allows users to introduce uphill walking or running into their routines and adjust the challenge as their fitness improves. Running Belt Size and Stability Running belt dimensions can affect how comfortable a treadmill feels, particularly at higher speeds or with longer strides. The G5i provides a 1300 × 500 mm running area and supports users weighing up to 136 kg. Its relatively wide belt gives users room to move naturally during workouts, demonstrating that a folding running deck does not automatically mean a narrow running surface. How Much Space Can a Foldable Treadmill Really Save? Storage is where the differences between treadmill designs become particularly noticeable. Traditional treadmills with fixed running decks often require a permanent space in a spare room, home gym or living area. Even models with folding consoles may retain much of their original footprint. By contrast, the G5i’s running deck folds in half, reducing the space needed for storage. It can be stored vertically or laid flat, giving households more flexibility when arranging furniture or using the same room for different activities. For people living in flats or homes without a dedicated exercise room, this flexibility can make a significant difference. A treadmill that can be put away after a workout is less likely to interfere with everyday living space. What Should You Look for When Choosing a Home Treadmill? The right treadmill depends on more than whether it folds. Before buying, consider how you intend to use it and where it will be kept. Available space: Measure both the workout area and the intended storage location, allowing sufficient clearance for safe use. Speed range: Choose a treadmill that supports your preferred activities, whether walking, jogging or regular running. Running belt dimensions: Check the usable running area rather than the machine’s overall dimensions. Incline options: Motorised incline can add variety and intensity to workouts without requiring higher speeds. Weight capacity: Make sure the treadmill comfortably supports the intended users. Ease of storage: Consider whether the running deck actually folds and whether the machine can be stored vertically or flat. A treadmill that fits comfortably into daily life may prove more practical than one with impressive specifications but nowhere convenient to keep it. Who Should Choose a Foldable or Traditional Treadmill? A foldable treadmill can be particularly appealing to people who want regular home workouts without dedicating an entire room to exercise. Models with folding running decks offer additional flexibility for flats, shared living spaces and multipurpose rooms. Traditional fixed-deck treadmills remain a sensible choice for households with permanent home gyms or users who need particular features, such as larger running surfaces or specialised training programmes. Neither design is automatically better. The important question is whether the treadmill provides the performance you need while fitting comfortably into your available space. Conclusion Choosing a foldable treadmill no longer has to mean giving up the features associated with traditional home running machines. The KingSmith WalkingPad G5i shows how a folding running deck can work alongside versatile training capabilities, making it possible to enjoy regular home workouts without permanently surrendering valuable living space. Ultimately, the best choice is a treadmill that suits both your fitness goals and the way you use your home. Frequently Asked Questions Are foldable treadmills as good as traditional treadmills? They can be, depending on the model. Compare maximum speed, incline capability, running belt dimensions and weight capacity rather than judging performance by the folding mechanism alone. Can you run on a foldable treadmill? Yes, provided the treadmill is designed for running. Some compact models are intended only for walking, while others, including the WalkingPad G5i, support running speeds. Do foldable treadmills have incline settings? Some do. The WalkingPad G5i, for example, offers 25 motorised incline levels with a maximum gradient of 18%. Are foldable treadmills suitable for small homes? Models with compact folding mechanisms can be particularly useful in smaller homes. Check the folded dimensions, storage orientation and available clearance before purchasing. What is the difference between a folding deck and folding handrails? Folding handrails reduce the height or profile of certain treadmill components, while a folding running deck reduces the length of the running platform itself. The latter can provide more substantial storage benefits. The post Foldable vs Traditional Treadmills: Do You Have to Sacrifice Performance for Space? appeared first on Tech Digest . title: Elon Musk admits SpaceX restricted Starlink in Ukraine
author: Chris Price
content: Tech billionaire Elon Musk has confirmed that his company, SpaceX, intentionally restricted the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, citing violations of the company’s terms of service regarding military operations. The admission follows a week-long disruption that severely hampered Ukraine’s defensive operations and military communications. The connectivity crisis emerged during a tense diplomatic standoff between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure. US President Donald Trump stated he instructed Musk to restore the service, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy subsequently confirmed that connectivity across both Starlink and the military-grade Starshield network had returned to stable levels. Writing on X, Musk defended the move, stating that using a civilian commercial service for offensive actions violated policy. “Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. “Ukraine’s military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.” Musk maintained that SpaceX has done more to support Ukraine than any private company on Earth since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. He also clarified that Starshield, the separate military counterpart, is controlled by the US government and operates under independent jurisdiction. Ukrainian officials expressed bewilderment over Musk’s justification. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov pointed out that commercial Starlink terminals in Ukraine feature built-in speed restrictions and do not function over Russian territory, making it physically impossible to use them for deep-strike operations. Military commanders reported that the throttling had interrupted missions and blinded drone operators, though defence officials confirmed that network speeds and stability have now been restored. title: How a Turbo Rebuild Works and What the Alternatives Are
author: Tech Digest Correspondent
content: Downsized petrol engines and almost every diesel on sale rely on a turbocharger for the performance that once required a much larger engine, which makes a failed turbo one of the more expensive faults a driver can face. Knowing what goes wrong inside the unit, and what can be done about it, makes the decision simpler when a garage delivers the diagnosis. Why Are Turbo Failures So Common on Older Cars? Part of the answer lies in the age of the cars on British roads. According to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT), the number of cars in use rose to 36.7 million in 2025, while their average age climbed to 9.7 years, up from 9.5 years in 2024. Older, higher-mileage cars are where turbochargers begin to show wear after years of heat cycles. A turbo spins at extremely high speeds in the path of hot exhaust gas and depends on clean oil for lubrication and cooling. Most failures trace back to oil contamination or starvation caused by a blocked feed pipe or overdue servicing. Foreign objects entering the intake or exhaust can also damage the compressor or turbine wheels. Typical symptoms include a loss of power, blue or grey smoke from the exhaust, a whining or siren-like noise under acceleration, rising oil consumption and a warning light on the dashboard. What Happens Inside a Turbo Rebuild? A rebuild returns the original unit to working order by replacing the parts that wear while retaining the components that remain within tolerance. Stripping and Inspection The technician dismantles the turbo completely, separating the compressor housing, turbine housing and centre section, then inspects each part for cracks, erosion, scoring and heat damage. Badly cracked or warped housings usually rule out a rebuild. Cleaning Carbon deposits, oil sludge and debris are removed from every component, typically with ultrasonic cleaning and blasting media suited to each material, so that faults hidden by grime become visible. Replacing Bearings, Seals and the CHRA Bearings, thrust components, piston rings and seals are replaced as standard. Where the shaft or wheels are damaged, many specialists fit a new centre housing rotating assembly (CHRA), often called a cartridge. This core section contains the shaft, wheels and bearing system, so renewing it restores the heart of the turbo while the original housings are reused. Balancing and Testing The rotating assembly is balanced on specialist equipment at high speed, as even a minor imbalance can quickly destroy new bearings. Variable-geometry turbos also need their vane mechanism set and calibrated so that boost is delivered correctly. A properly carried out turbo rebuild finishes with these checks before the unit is returned to the customer. How Do the Main Repair Options Compare? Drivers generally have five routes once a turbo has failed. A rebuild repairs the owner’s own unit and suits cases where the housings are sound and the car can wait. A reconditioned turbo has been through a similar restoration process but comes from existing stock rather than from the owner’s car. It is usually more cost-effective than buying new. An exchange unit is a ready-to-fit turbo supplied straight away, with the old unit returned as a core once the swap has been made. Its main appeal is speed, since the car is not left waiting for its own part. A new turbo is built entirely from fresh components, either by the original equipment manufacturer or by a quality aftermarket producer. It carries the highest price but removes any question over the part’s history. The broader category of replacement turbos covers any unit fitted in place of the failed one, whether new, remanufactured or reconditioned, and is often the answer when the original is too badly damaged to save. How Should Drivers Choose Between Them? The right option depends on the condition of the failed unit, the budget and how long the car can be off the road. A turbo specialist can inspect the failed unit and explain which options are realistic for it. Cracked housings point towards a replacement, while a turbo with worn bearings but healthy castings is well suited to a rebuild. Drivers who need their car back quickly often lean towards an exchange. Whichever route is taken, the cause of the original failure should be identified before a repaired or new unit is fitted. Changing the oil and filter, cleaning or replacing the oil feed and return pipes, and checking the intercooler for debris all help to prevent a repeat failure, since a restored turbo fitted to an engine with a restricted oil feed will fail in the same way again. A turbo failure is rarely welcome news, but it is a well-understood fault with a range of sensible solutions, and a clear picture of each option helps drivers choose what fits their car and circumstances.   The post How a Turbo Rebuild Works and What the Alternatives Are appeared first on Tech Digest . title: How Modern Aggregate Processing Equipment Works
author: Tech Digest Correspondent
content: Sand and crushed stone are used in almost every road, rail line and building in the UK. Before they can be used, raw material from a quarry, gravel pit or demolition site has to be crushed, washed and graded to a set specification. The equipment that does this has changed a lot over the past twenty years. Plants now use more automation, recycle most of their water and handle recycled material as well as quarried stone. Crushing Material Down to Size Processing usually starts with crushing. A jaw crusher takes the largest rock and squeezes it between a fixed plate and a moving plate, producing a coarse product that can go onto a conveyor. Cone crushers then reduce the material further by compressing it inside a rotating chamber, which suits hard, abrasive stone such as granite. Where a well-shaped, cubical product is needed, operators often use impact crushers . These throw material against breaker plates at high speed so it breaks along natural weaknesses. Shape affects performance, because flaky or elongated stone needs more cement paste in concrete and packs less tightly in a road base. Washing Out Clay, Silt and Contaminants Crushed or dug material usually carries clay, silt and organic matter. Left in, these weaken concrete and stain finished surfaces, so they have to be washed out. An aggregate wash plant brings several stages together in one flow. Feed is wetted and scrubbed first, sometimes in a log washer or attrition cell where paddles rub particles against each other to strip off clay. Slurry pumps then move the mix to hydrocyclones, which use centrifugal force to separate sand from the lighter silt. Cyclone linings are made from rubber or polyurethane to resist wear, and replacing them is one of the main running costs on site. Finally, dewatering screens vibrate the sand on fine mesh until it is dry enough to stockpile and sell. Some older sites still use bucket wheel setups for this stage. Grading Material by Size Screening sets the product range. Vibrating screens with two or three decks split material into separate sizes, and spray bars rinse each size as it travels along the deck. Each product has to fall within a grading curve, which is the size distribution set out in the relevant standard. Many decks now use polyurethane panels instead of woven steel mesh, as they last longer, run more quietly and can be swapped quickly when worn. Setting up the decks correctly on an aggregate screen is often the difference between a stockpile that meets specification and one that has to be reprocessed or sold as lower-value fill. Recycling the Water Washing aggregates uses large volumes of water, so most modern plants recycle it. Dirty water from the plant flows into a thickener, where a flocculant makes fine particles clump together and settle. Clear water overflows from the top and goes back to the plant, while the thickened sludge is pumped away. Many sites now put this sludge through a filter press, which squeezes it into a solid cake that can be moved with a loading shovel. This reduces the need for large settling lagoons. Automation and Remote Monitoring Programmable logic controllers manage start-up and shutdown, so conveyors, pumps and screens come on and off in the right order. Sensors track motor loads, bearing temperatures, water flow and tank levels. Engineers can view this data remotely, which helps them spot a blocked chute or a failing bearing before it causes a long stoppage. Modular Plants and Recycled Material More plants are now built from modular, skid-mounted sections that are tested before delivery and connected on site. This shortens installation and makes it easier to move equipment when a deposit is worked out. The same approach has helped the growth of recycled aggregates. Construction and demolition waste can be crushed, screened and washed to remove plaster, wood and plastics, with some plants using upward water currents to lift out lightweight contaminants. Fines recovery systems then capture sand that would otherwise be lost to settling ponds, so more of the material can go back into new construction. Choosing the Right Setup No two sites use exactly the same layout. The right combination of crushers, screens and washing stages depends on the feed material, the products the site needs to sell and the space and water available. Most operators work with a supplier of mineral processing equipment to test samples of their material first. The results show which stages are needed and how the plant should be sized before any equipment is ordered. The post How Modern Aggregate Processing Equipment Works appeared first on Tech Digest . title: Samsung names Ryan Van Lee top winner
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse He said he’d ‘bring it home’, and he did. When we interviewed local musician Ryan Van Lee in August, inquiring about his position in the Top 20 for Samsung’s True North Tunes competition, he knew he wanted to win. While over 4,000 musicians hit the list, by August, it was whittled down to 20. From that point, there would be three top winners. On Friday, Oct. 2, the winners were announced. Josh Moore from Vancouver, Angelique Dancel from Toronto, and of course, Ryan Van Lee, from good old Haliburton Ontario. “We won the competition,” said Van Lee, a locally well-known country singer. “We brought it home to Haliburton, just like we talked about.” The winners were decided based on over 875,000 votes from across the country. And truthfully, Van Lee didn’t think he had a shot. So when an unknown number called to share the news, Van Lee let it ring through the voicemail. A voicemail that has changed the trajectory of his life. “They told me I won,” he said. “It’s been wild. I really haven’t processed it yet.” “One of the most exciting things about Samsung True North Tunes has been seeing the depth of talent emerging from communities across Canada,” said Tafari Jilany, head of corporate marketing for Samsung Canada. “Ryan is a great example of an artist building momentum from his local community, while creating music that has the potential to resonate far beyond it. Ryan’s creativity, passion and dedication to his craft stood out throughout the program, and we’re thrilled to see him recognized as one of this year’s winners.” Van Lee learned music from his grandfather, who taught him the accordion when he was a young boy. He went on to receive training from the iconic Johnny Burke, who gave him guitar lessons after Van Lee approached him following a local show. He’s worked his way up to the national stage, touring the United States before the COVID-19 pandemic, which put his career on the backburner for a few years. This past summer, Van Lee played to a full house during Music in the Park, presented by Haliburton Rotary. The local show had him buzzing, and reignited the passion and pride he has long harboured for his hometown. So what’s next? Samsung has invited the local country musician to head down to the city. He’s going to be meeting with reps from the music industry, network, and continue to develop his brand and sound. “Through Samsung True North Tunes, we’re helping connect artists with mentorship, industry relationships and opportunities that can support the next stage of their careers, while using our platform and technology to help more Canadians discover their music,” said Jilany. They’re even in the process of making a nation-wide beer with Van Lee’s name on it. “They wanted me to be the face of Samsung music in 2027,” he laughed, “I told them they should fire whoever came up with that idea.” Through all the noise, Van Lee brings it all back to Haliburton County. He told his family and friends about the win, who had tears in their eyes upon the announcement. Even the local high school classes have been listening to his music, adding a new point of pride to their hometown roots. “Thank you so much, from the bottom of my heart,” shared Van Lee in a shoutout to his community via Instagram, shortly after receiving the news of his win. “It’s crazy how my hometown came together … It was truly a great experience. And so much more to come.” Van Lee can be found on Instagram @Ryan_VanLee. While he aims to continue making music across the country, he knows he will always return to his hometown, through it all. “It just goes to show you, any kids out there watching from my hometown, sports aren’t the only option,” he said. “You can do things if you just set your mind to it, and you don’t give up.”

title: Passion project
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse Not a single journalist I know is in the job based on the pay. It’s a long-running joke we have amongst writers. That we don’t choose the career for money. It’s a passion project, these words from the heart. But as I sat and wrote these words this past week, I realized that I’m not alone in this endeavour. This week, I interviewed a musician who made his mark on a national stage, an entrepreneur who broke away from the status quo to follow their own path. I spoke with school board trustees who are putting the future of our children ahead of themselves, politicians who know they’re barely cracking minimum wage to live with their lives under a microscope. None of us are in it for the money. It’s a passion project, a point of pride. Maybe that’s not the way it’s supposed to be. Unfortunately, we live in a world where we are ushered forward through capitalism. Every day requires a slog of consistency around meal times and bills paid and rents due. But starting something from the heart takes bravery. We’ve all seen those movies where there is a sad figure clad in black and white, checking into their tiny work cubicle at 9 a.m., eating a bland sandwich at their desk, clocking out at 5 p.m. And then doing it all over again. And again. And again. And again. There are many highs and lows to our communities. The winters are long and the cell reception is poor and somehow all of our sidewalks are always under construction. But you won’t see those bland black and white characters around here anytime soon. This is a community of vibrancy and colour. It’s live music and maple coffees and doers and dreamers who don’t take no for an answer. As I watch the municipal election continue to take shape, while I’d be the first to hold any one of them accountable for their actions and priorities, I hope it goes without saying that putting your name in a hat for a position in municipal government is one of the biggest passion projects going. Very poor pay, very high expectations. And I’ve been impressed, thus far, with the charisma and passion I’ve seen at the all-candidates meetings. While I freely put my words out into the community, standing in front of a room of 250 eager audience members is not my idea of a good time. But so far, no one has looked particularly nervous. No one has stumbled, no one has panicked. While they may look out at hundreds of eager eyes, all I see is over 50 candidates with a flame ignited. A hope that they can make some sort of difference, a belief that their community matters. So, here is to the doers and the dreamers. The ones who crack the molds of black and white and elbow their way to a world that works for others. I know not everyone’s intentions are good, but in a world where we often feel more comfortable in the shadows, it’s good to acknowledge the light. Because we’re not in it for the money. And we need these people, who refuse to take no for an answer. TAGS: Emily Stonehouse editorial

title: Halbiem speed reduction granted within one month
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse Community concerns around speed limits have been promptly considered by Dysart staff. During the last meeting of Dysart council at the end of August, resident Kim Stamp, a member of Haliburton by the Lake Owners’ Association, brought a delegation to council, requesting a speed limit change around Halbiem Crescent, from 50 kilometres an hour down to 30. “We feel that this is a very serious safety concern for all residents of Haliburton County,” said Stamp. “Not just our neighborhood.” At the time, council members agreed that a speed limit change could be made, keeping safety at top of mind, but directed staff to run a study to quantify the concern. “If people are travelling 60 (kilometers per hour) in there, maybe it is a bigger issue than a community safety zone and lowering the speed,” said Director of Public Works, Rob Camelon. “We won’t know that until we have data.” One of Camelon’s concerns around adopting a new limit came with precedent, noting that there could be an influx of similar requests if the speed limit is changed. “If they don’t pay attention to the sign that says 50, they probably won’t pay attention to the sign that says 30 is my concern,” said Camelon. During the Sept. 22 council meeting, with Camelon absent, CAO Tamara Wilbee noted that staff had set up speed monitors around Halbiem area. “Rob did get out to check the speeds out there,” she said, “and currently with the 50 kilometre and hour zone, there isn’t a speeding issue. People are typically staying under the 50. That doesn’t mean that it’s maybe not too fast for that area, but he thinks 30 is a reasonable request, but he’d recommend a speed area zone.” For an identified speed area zone, the minimum for speed notification is two signs present, with council given the option for increase if needed. Wilbee noted that Camelon could have a speed bylaw in place by the next meeting. “I support that wholly,” said acting Deputy Mayor Pat Casey. “50 kilometres is great for some areas, but I think Halbiem definitely could use that.” “It’s definitely what the residents want in there,” agreed Mayor Walt McKechnie. “I think we should let them have their 30 kilometre speed limit and move forward. They’re the ones who live in there.” Council approved a speed limit of 30 kilometres per hour around Halbiem Crescent, with a speed bylaw promised for the upcoming meeting of council.

author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse 46,406. That’s how many words have been strictly dedicated to sharing the platforms of every (responsive) candidate in this upcoming municipal election. That’s how many words I have read, reviewed, edited, and approved. That equates to exactly 114 pages. That’s how many pages I have meticulously sifted through, added apostrophes, indented lines and highlighted bullet points around. That’s how many contributions I have pulled from emails in all formats, adjusted fonts for, sifted and sorted through on evenings, weekends, and even vacation times. That number doesn’t even include coverage of the all-candidates meetings, which have taken up my weekends since they started. There’s still two more to go. Only to log into Facebook and read that someone “can’t find any information on any candidates”. Honestly, I get why journalism has a high turnover rate. In 2023, Bill C-18 was introduced. While everyone with access to a flag budget loves to blame the Liberals for every wrongdoing, this was a situation where the party had our back. They had requested to Meta – the social media conglomerate that owns Facebook and Instagram – that journalists be compensated for their product, the exact same way an influencer or advertiser is paid through the platforms for generating content. It was a nod to the work and integrity of Canadian journalism, and a situation where it felt like the government was looking out for the little guy. Unfortunately, Meta called their bluff. And instead of paying journalists, they blocked all Canadian news from major social media sites. That means that you cannot share links, photos, pages, or headlines via Facebook or Instagram. We get a warning that says “In response to Canadian government legislation, news content can’t be viewed in Canada.” So now we’re at a standstill. If the government backs down and agrees not to pay journalists, then Meta wins. And there’s no way Meta is going to pay for journalistic content. They cut corners wherever possible. Therefore, you will not see our news stories online. That’s not because we don’t wish to share. It’s because we’re banned and blocked from sharing. And we have been for years. So, as we head into this municipal election, please, pick up a local newspaper. While I have edited 46,406 words, I know the Highlander has their own strategies for sharing content as well. So does Canoe FM, so does Moose FM. We’re trying – desperately – on evenings, weekends, and vacation times, to get these platforms out there. We’ve committed time, energy, and in some cases, literal blood sweat and tears, to chase these candidates, to elevate their voices, to educate voters on the best fits for their communities. If you want to see coverage of these elections, the Haliburton Highlands Healthy Democracy Project ( www . hhhdp . ca ) has the videos of the all-candidates meetings available. If you missed a week that our paper highlighted your ward, let me know, and I will personally make sure you have access to that newspaper. Email emily @ haliburtonpress . com . If you’re willing to learn, I am more than willing to help. Educate yourself. The information is out there. Over 46,406 words of it. It’s up to you to read them.

title: Indigenous artist to unveil mural at public lookout
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Ivy Katz Murals are said to be special because they bring private art out of galleries and into public spaces for everyone’s benefit. Both nature and art are scientifically known to boost our endorphins. Now, hikers on the James Cooper trail will have one more thing to lookout for when they’re looking for that rush of endorphins. Indigenous artist and Algonquin Highlands local Kristel McKay is the force behind giving people the best of both these worlds. McKay is adding the final touches to a mural she was commissioned to paint by a private customer. Although the mural will be on private property, it is specifically designed to be seen with binoculars from the lookout on the James Cooper trail. “The owner of the mural very much wanted to share the collective vision of the mural by installing it on one of the structures on his property,” said McKay. “He was inspired after purchasing one of my art pieces.” McKay is not a stranger to large murals. When she was still a teenager in the early 90’s, she was one of a few people commissioned to paint murals inside Toronto’s famous Barracuda nightclub in Yorkville. The Barracuda was the new club opening up in the space that previously housed The Copa, an nternationally recognised nightclub known for its themed shows and for debuting some of the best acts of the time, including Tina Turner, throughout the 80’s until its closure in 1992. The space is so large that today it is a condo complex. Like many gifted artists, McKay naturally started creating art since she was a young age. By the time she hit her teenage years, her art was already entering the public sphere. In the year 2000, she was part of the City of Toronto’s “Moose in the City” project, which commissioned artists to paint moose throughout the city. McKay’s moose, entitled Guess Who?, was located in Commerce Court. Her installation made a statement about the stock market, while also commemorating the band The Guess Who, who were playing in Toronto that year. McKay’s cultural roots are Indigenous Canadian and Celtic. As a result, McKay has focused her life on cultivating an extensive background knowledge in both Indigenous Mi’kmaw and Celtic traditions and artforms. She paints in oil and acrylic. Generally clients will see some of her artworks, and if requested, she will work with them to establish their artistic vision and create custom pieces. McKay also creates beaded jewellery. Over the years, McKay has always focused her passions on a variety of artistic pursuits, especially ones that create a difference in the public realm. “I am very grateful to have been selected to share my art and teachings with the public,” said McKay, on the organisations she has worried with, which include the Toronto District School Board (TDSB) and the Association for Native Development in the Performing and Visual Arts (ANDPVA). Her Indigenous art installations have graced city events from the Skydome Powwow, to Osgoode Hall, and City Hall, to company logo’s throughout Canada, such as Halcyon Hot springs in British Columbia, over the last three decades. Perhaps most importantly, McKay has inspired and influenced youth with traditional art and Indigenous teachings. “One of my most memorable and rewarding projects was when I experienced working with youth was a Medicine Wheel Teaching,” said McKay. “The art installation created by the graduating students of General Crerar and the personal letters I received from the students expressing how they gained a grater understanding of Indigenous Traditions and cultural awareness was a result of the art project.” In addition to her art installations, McKay does energy work and has dedicated many years to various healing modalities, including ceremonies, drumming, guided meditations, and traditional medicines. She has a whole apothecary of dried herbs from her land and gives guided medicine walks. She is a certified Reiki Master with the Canadian Reiki Association, and holds her certification in counselling in Addictions and Mental Health. A sneak peak of the mural reveals that a medicine wheel is part of the image. The medicine wheel is integral to the way of life and is shared between many Indigenous Nations. Asked what the medicine wheel colours represent, McKay explains that it is a teaching used to help balance ourselves. She explains the meanings of the four cardinal colours, yellow, red, black, and white, and the attributes associated with each colour help guide us through life’s journeys. The mural was created at Black Cloud Studios. The studio has been a space for artists over the last seven years, offering a serene environment for creative expression. McKay credits Seamus Robertson for helping to kick-start this particular mural project by assisting her in laying down the foundational design elements of the piece. “He is a talented young man,” said the artist. People can find him under @wonderraven. The mural has been weather-proofed and was installed by BKS Carpentry Ltd. As of press time, the mural is ready for the public. McKay plans to share videos of the process on her Instagram @kristeltempest1. People interested in connecting with the artist can reach her via email at kristeltempest@yahoo.com. Now, hikers and art enthusiasts will be able to have the best of both the natural and artistic worlds when they visit the James Cooper trail located at 1065 North Shore Rd, just north of Carnarvon. Be sure to bring your binoculars!

title: Dillman Trail ready for turtle trails
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Ivy Katz Turtles are a keystone species and act as eco-engineers by helping to create a healthy ecosystem. The long ordeal with the closure of the Dillman Trail was discussed in council, with plans for its reopening, dependant on keeping the Blanding’s Turtle safe, and hopefully recouping some of the monies to be spent through grants and othher avenues. Consulting firm Cambium Inc. prepared a species conservation plan and presented it to Highlands East council at the last regular meeting of council on Sept. 8, 2026. “A lot of effort has been put into reinstating the Dillman Trail over the last handful of years,” said Camden Jermey of consulting firm Cambium Inc. Cambium was retained by Highlands East to prepare a special conservation plan to support the maintenance and repairs of the Dillman Trail, located just north-east of Gooderham, in Highlands East. “Turtles are known to nest on trails close to wetlands,” said Jermey. Exclusion measures were a requirement by the Ministry of Environment, Conservation, and Park’s (MECP), and will exclude turtles from entering the trail, protecting them, their nests, and hatchlings from being hit. “An exclusion plan would also make trail maintenance easier and mitigate impacts from ongoing use,” he said. Turtles tend to nest on trails and seasonal maintenance can disturb their nests. Dillman Trail Historical Context The Dillman Trail is part of the original historic Burleigh colonization road, which has been a long-standing municipal transportation corridor in continuous public use for 140 years, according to the Cambium report. Highlands East is seeking to complete improvements to the trail where it bisects a wetland, said the report. The proposed work focuses on maintenance, rehabilitation, and species mitigation enhancements within a disturbed footprint. The improvements proposed do not represent expansion of the corridor or construction of a new transportation infrastructure, stated the report. “The Ministry of Environment, Conservation, and Park’s (MECP) was continuously concerned with impacts to Blanding’s Turtle from ATV and recreational use on the trail,” said Jermey. Change in legislation responsible for hold up Cambium was previously retained to complete an assessment of potential impacts to Species at Risk (SAR) at the Dillman Trail following a Stop Work Order issued by the MECP issued on Sept. 15, 2023, due to a potential contravention of the Endangered Species Act (2007). “We have tabled several strategies and ultimately, they continuously reiterated that permanent exclusion fencing and eco-passages were required on the trail, to support its reopening,” explained Jermey. That consultation happened in Oct and March of 2025. Cambium submitted a permit application to the MECP in late August of last year for exclusion fencing, eco-fencing, and other mitigation approaches, which the MECP. They agreed and sent a complete permit application in September, explained Jermey. However, they never received a permit back from MECP and followed up several months later. On March 30, 2026, they received a notification that the Endangered Species Act was repealed and replaced by the Species Conservation Act . The legislation change meant they had to “re-start all the consultation work,” when much consultation work had already been done. “Dealing with MECP has been a long, drawn out affair,” said Jermey. “Essentially we were working under a former framework with the Endangered Species Act and now we are under the Species Conservation Act; the pathway of which is slightly different , ” explained Jermey. “That’s what has precipitated this species conservation plan.” Understanding the new rules Under the new Species Conservation Act, there are “registerable activities,” which the Dillman Trail falls under. There are still “permit activities,” which still require MECP oversight and approval, explained Jermey. The intent with the “registrable activities” is to streamline approvals, with a “registration first approach,” which can be audited at their discretion at a later time by MECP. With the Dillman trail falling under the registrable category, certain work can be begun without permits, the activities must only be registered in a “living document” as the work commences. “This means that in theory, the work could begin quite quickly,” shared Jermey. Conserving turtles with eco-passages Jermey’s report presented a variety of eco-passages from throughout Canada, USA, Cuba, and Germany. Based on the wetlands water levels on the trail, he recommended a two-sided culvert, made of concrete with a grate over-top, which will allow light and facilitate wildlife passage. “One of the requirements for these passages to be effective is that they need daylight to shine through or else wildlife won’t go through them,” said Jermey. Timing important to wildlife The timing period is an important layer when considering how to mitigate harmful effects on wildlife, explained Jermey. One of the major mitigation measures for turtles, fish, and birds, is to utilize timing windows when conducting ecology and environmental work, and thereby aligning construction activities when animals are in their lower-sensitive period. For this reason, Cambium outlined a two-phased approach: first to install the culverts, ie: eco-passages. The MECP requested that be done during the active turtle season, which is May through to end of October. The second phase would be to install exclusion fencing, which could be done in November-December, said Jermey. Exclusion fencing is a type of low and buried fencing, made of safe and durable material, meant to deter wildlife, such as amphibians and small animals, from entering onto roadways, generally by leading them along the fence or to an eco-passageway. “I wanted to highlight that because timing is limited at the moment,” said Jermey. “We don’t really want to lose another year due to delays.” One of the requirements as per the Office of the Regional Auditor General (ORAG) is Monitoring. Cambium suggested a low-cost alternative to the monitoring element, that being leveraging municipal staff, some support from Cambium staff, and installing trail cameras. These compliance are important as future audits from could take place to ensure the work is being done properly. According to the website for the Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, ORAG examines financial statements and public accounts for the province; investigates specific government operations, assesses whether public-sector and government programs spend money efficiently and with due regard for the economy. ORAG is an independent and non-partisan and reports directly to the Legislative Assembly to help taxpayers understand how public funds are managed. The cost Deputy Mayor Cecil Ryall was concerned about the cost of the project, despite the fact that he had no doubt that “this will solve the turtle problem.” He asked what the cost would be and if there was any other support or grants available. Jermey indicated that preliminary costs are in the range of 80,000 to 120,000 dollars. He agrees the costs are “substantial,” and will be reaching out to contractors to get direct quotes. “Seeking grants is a good strategy and we can look into options,” said Jermey. Mayor Rob Burton wanted to know if they do move ahead with the costs, would there be any guarantee that the project would be pased by the MECP. Jermey shared that the new policies put a lot of “onus on the consultants and there is no guarantee that people will even review this file, given the history.” However, Jermey believes they have a strong case, based on the previous approval, should the MECP decide to audit them at a later time. Councillor Angela Lewis asked what would be the time-frame if they spent the 100,000 dollars. Jermey replied that it could be ready by the new year. He added that once the exclusion fencing in place, maintenance of the trail will be a lot easier because turtles will not be on it. Councillor Lewis asked whether or not the Highlands East department could do the work with the cement and the grate or exclusion fencing. Treasurer Brittany McCaw said she wasn’t sure if their department had the “expertise.” “Typically we see external consultants but I think it would be reasonable to review what we are proposing with with the municipal departments,” responded Jermey. He believed that the culverts could possibly be done through the public works department. He recommended the fencing have specialized people. Jermey thought a hybrid approach might work. Deputy Mayor Ryall remained concerned about the uncertainty of regaining any funds and the timing of the project, as well as making a decision too quickly. Jermey pointed out it has already been a very long process. Councillor Lewis was interested in the hybrid approach. Stakeholders, including ATV users and turtle advocacy groups are aligned, according to Jermey. He remained optimistic about sourcing and recouping funds once stakeholders were reached. Deputy Ryall remained concerned and said, “I cannot see my self supporting this whole thing, at least not today.” The long history of permit work and consulation on the particular file, Jermey expressed he felt this plan “essentially mirrors and alliance” with MECP. In addition, he explained that based on the new legislation, there is no approval process, just a registration process, and the plan for that has already been made and presented to council. Councillor Ruth Strong was in support of the initiative. “I think it is quite evident we should go ahead with it,” said Councillor Strong. “I don’t think there is that big a risk.” Treasurer McCaw indicated that there are budgetery monies in this years budget because they knew this was coming. She suggested taking the phased approach and in the new year look at remaining monies and grants. Counsillors Lewis and Strong voted in favour of the motion. Resolution was to approve the plan and direct Cambium Inc. to submit and register the plan with the MECP. To view the meeting on Youtube or see Cambium’s detailed report, visit highlandseast.ca/municipal-services/mayor-and-council/agendas-and-minutes/ and seek out the Sept 8. 2026 Agenda Minutes.

title: LifeLabs reopens in Haliburton
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse LifeLabs in Haliburton is officially re-opened. As of Sept. 21, Haliburton Patient Service Centre (PSC) at Gelert Road is re-opening their doors for the first time since March. “This reopening marks an important milestone for the Haliburton community,” said the LifeLabs media team, “restoring convenient access to laboratory testing services for residents and those in surrounding areas. We recognize the importance of these services and appreciate the patience and understanding shown by patients, healthcare providers, and community partners throughout the disruption.” The clinics were closed at the Gelert Road location in the spring, citing issues around an unwelcome odour that had seeped through the walls. The building, under the ownership of the Municipality of Dysart et al, underwent a series of alterations to make the space accessible again. During the closure, the other businesses in the building continued operation. “As always, the health and safety of our patients and employees remains our highest priority, “said LifeLabs media. “The Haliburton PSC remained closed while an investigation was undertaken by the municipality to identify and address the source of the odour concerns. In August, the investigation identified an issue that was subsequently addressed by the municipality. Following completion of air quality testing at the beginning of September, it was determined that the space was suitable for re-occupancy.” The LifeLabs media release noted that there was no indication of hazardous gases within the facility. Air monitoring included hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, oxygen, and combustible gas levels, including propane. “We appreciate the support and collaboration of local healthcare providers and community partners while the issue was investigated and resolved,” said LifeLabs. “We look forward to welcoming patients back to the Haliburton PSC and continuing to provide high-quality laboratory services close to home. LifeLabs remains committed to ensuring a safe, reliable, and positive experience for all patients accessing our services.” The 7217 Gelert Road location will be open Monday to Friday from 7:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. TAGS: LifeLabs Haliburton

title: Lifeblood
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse I was not particularly surprised to hear the crux of concerns at the Minden all-candidates meeting circulate around people. It’s long been known that there are issues with staffing in Minden Hills. People seem to come and go, switch municipalities, come back, leave indefinitely, move backwards, move forwards. Regular readers would know that I was a senior staffer in Minden Hills, before they bumped tourism and economic development up to a County level after I left during Covid – one area with a one-tiered focus we’ve been doing for years since. I didn’t leave because of the pay or the people or the pandemic. I left because I was unhappy. Because there were a group of figureheads we had elected, who truly didn’t have our best interest at heart. They said they were there to represent ‘the people’, sure, but as staff, weren’t we ‘the people’ too? I don’t think they’re bad people. Councillors are wedged into a tricky situation. Elected to represent their wards, while in reality, it’s the staff that do the vast majority of work. They have the connections, the networks, the expertise, the experience. They’ve gone to school to study for these roles, dedicated their lives to public service. In good and in bad, in sickness and in health. I was deeply discouraged to not hear a single council hopeful defend the staff of Minden Hills during this past weekend’s all-candidates meeting. There are issues, for sure. A lack of response coming from staffers on major questions and concerns. Radio silence when businesses are looking to move ahead. But I can absolutely guarantee one thing: Staff aren’t doing that on purpose. They’re not responding to emails because they’re burnt out. They’re exhausted. They’re overwhelmed. They’re in over their heads. They’re looking to get out. They’re unhappy. I know that, because I was in that exact position. And for every single council hopeful to place blame and point fingers at staff shows me that there is a deep lack of understanding between staff and council. Now don’t get me wrong, I get as annoyed as the next guy when a staffer doesn’t respond. It stalls stories, holds out on facts. But I carry a level of empathy for those who have chosen to take on these roles. They’re the definition of thankless jobs. Wins credited to council, losses laid on staff. While we need to hold everyone – yes, everyone – accountable for the jobs they signed up for, a lack of compassion and empathy for the ones that should be working as a team is the very foundation for the bulk of issues that arise out of Minden Hills. While a few candidates seemed to understand the human element of the job, other council hopefuls suggested a policy in place to make sure emails are responded to in a prompt manner. 24 to 48 hours was the suggestion. “If they can’t do that, maybe it’s time for a new job.” Here’s my suggestion: Make Minden a better place by actually respecting your staff. Make it a place people want to work, so that there are people on-hand to promptly respond to emails; administrative tasks are handled by administrative staff, and the areas of focus are given time, commitment, and attention. The staff are the literal lifeblood of any municipality. While council are the figureheads, staff are the neck, the body, the limbs, the heart. If council hopefuls had said ‘yes, there are problems, let’s focus on how we can support staff better,” that would have been one thing. Instead, fingers were flung, triggers were pulled. Clearly I’m not alone in this: You couldn’t pay me enough to work for a township where no one has my back.

title: Residents seek Community Safety Zone
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Thomas Smith Anyone who drives in Haliburton County has experienced people who drive too fast. You can hear it every day through Haliburton, as wheels rip down the main drag only to be stopped by the red light at the high school. Residents of Halbiem Crescent sit at a unique position with Haliburton. With connections to Fleming College’s campus, several people drive through the crescent to park and walk to the college, hikers walk through to connect to the trail systems, walking groups travel through the subdivision, and it is visited by high schoolers as part of the annual Terry Fox Walk. All valid reasons to request a reduced speed limit. That is what Kim Stamp, member of the Haliburton by the Lake Owners’ Association wanted to change. Visiting Dysart council held on Tuesday, Aug. 25, Stamp requested Dysart council to designate the Halbiem Crescent a Community Safety Zone. “Our current speed limit of 50km per hour, is way too fast for the safety of everyone using our roads system,” said Stamp. A community safety zone would restrict the speed to 30km per hour and any speeding fines would be doubled within the area. “This designation advises drivers that they are within a zone where public safety is of special concern,” said Stamp. She told council members that this past school year, there was an incident where someone did not slow down despite a school bus having its flashing arm out. Two children were put in danger but were luckily uninjured.
