She says that over time, the demographic of the Haliburton by the Lake neighborhood has increased to have many young families with kids who ride their bike to school and play around the neighborhood. “We feel that this is a very serious safety concern for all residents of Haliburton County,” said Stamp. “Not just our neighborhood.” “My opinion is we should grant you that speed limit in your area there,” said Dysart Mayor Walt McKechnie. “It just makes sense.” Dysart Councillor Nancy Wood-Roberts expressed the desire to implement slower speed limits in denser housing areas in Dysart. Rob Camelon, director of public works, expressed concerns that if a Community Safety Zone is designated, there would be an influx of similar requests. “If people are travelling 60 (km per hour) in there, maybe it is a bigger issue than a Community Safety Zone and lowering the speed,” said Camelon. “We won’t know that until we have data.” He suggested that a reduced speed bylaw should be drafted and presented to council in the future. “We also have no sidewalks,” said Stamp. During the winter and ice conditions, she says that people walk on the sand. Without sidewalks and lack of street lighting, the speed poses a safety concern during the winter. “Ideally, we’d like to see more than one speed sign,” said Stamp. “I think if we can get the speed limit reduced, that would greatly help with our concern.” Camelon says that after the speed limit is reduced, a study should be conducted to see what speeds are being reached in the neighborhood. If needed, a Community Safety Zone can be established. “If they don’t pay attention to the sign that says 50, they probably won’t pay attention to the sign that says 30 is my concern,” said Camelon. A speed tracker will be implemented in the area to collect data and direct council at a future date.

title: Lake Ontario
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse I spent the past week out of town. While I will be the first to fly the flag of the Haliburton Highlands, my husband and I realized it had been years since we had taken any trips across the borders. And no, I don’t mean hopping and skipping between Minden and Haliburton. We landed on P.E.I. as our destination of choice. A first major vacation for this blended and chosen family, and it was truly beautiful. Life changing in all the right ways. At the beginning of the week, my brother found an article, chuckling as he read through it before sharing with us over scrambled eggs and hot coffee. “Trump wants to change Lake Ontario to Lake America,” he laughed. We all did. Because, really, how could he do such a thing? The world isn’t run through temper tantrums and fist pounding. That’s how children operate, until they are given the tools to manage their emotions. So, to compare Trump to a child having a tantrum would be highly offensive to the child. By the end of the week, he did it. And instead of laughter, our blended and chosen family felt pain. A deep ache. A question, a worry, a wonder for tomorrow, as we watched our own children, laughing and splashing in the ocean. What can’t this man do, via temper tantrums and fist pounding? When will he stop? Who will stop him? We sat in this sadness for a while. Until the red sands from the castle on the beach started to crumble, damp little hands adding seashells to the miniature doorways. Normally, I’d say we should leave politics off the table during a family vacation. But this isn’t politics. This is personal. It’s hurtful, corrupt, manipulative bullying from a man with an ego the size of the continent. I am going to give credit to Mark Carney, who held his ground not only during trade negotiations, but when it came to the battle of Lake Ontario. “The name Lake Ontario comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io, which, appropriately, means ‘the lake is beautiful, the lake is big,’” Carney wrote on social media, noting that the name had been used for more than 400 years – predating Canadian Confederation and the signing of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. “We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he said. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.” It feels good to have someone in your corner. I watched a snippet of a Blue Rodeo concert this past week, where the band sang their Canadian anthem, Hasn’t Hit Me Yet . When they got to the iconic bit in the middle, belting out Out in the middle, of Lake Ontario , the crowd went wild. As Canadians, we feel proud of who we are. There is a time and a place for renaming pieces of our history, yes, but to be coerced to change through bullying is clearly something our country won’t tolerate. And as I sat on the red sands this past week, thinking about home, here, there, and everywhere, question, worry, and wonder abound, I felt a deep pride in this place we all share. And whether it be on a micro or a macro scale, small towns or whole countries, we will do our best, to stand up to bullies. TAGS: Emily Stonehouse editorial

title: Local musician to debut on national stage
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse It all started with an accordion. Local musician Ryan Van Lee found his passion for music at a young age, watching his grandfather play the accordion. Before long, he was right up there with him. “I started playing around at church and Midnight Madness,” recalled Van Lee, “then I started playing at talent shows, started making a little name for myself with the accordion.” Van Lee was born and raised in Haliburton. While he goes by Ryan Van Lee onstage, he’s proud of his vanLieshout family roots, with deep ties to the Highlands. The singer/songwriter has recently been named to the Top 20 in Samsung’s True North Tunes music competition, whittled down from over 4,000 musicians from across the country. Van Lee is making a name for himself nationally, but he stays committed to his hometown upbringing. While he spent his younger days touring around the community with his grandfather and their accordions, Van Lee shared that as he grew up, he decided to shift gears. “I think I got to an age where I probably wanted a girlfriend,” he laughed, “so I had to make some changes. I wanted to learn the guitar.” Van Lee has early memories of playing ‘air guitar’ in his room, rocking out to Elvis Presley. With the sudden interest in rock and roll and old country, Van Lee’s grandmother offered to bring him to a Johnny Burke concert in town. “And the rest is history,” said Van Lee. Burke originally hailed from New Brunswick, but called the Haliburton Highlands home. While he garnered a significant following and an induction into the Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame, Burke led a quiet life, and was recognized for his soft nature and pure passion for music. A perfect role model for a young guitarist, finding his footing in the scene. Van Lee was captivated by Burke, and during a break in his set, the young boy approached the well-known musician. “I said, Mr. Burke, I’d love for you to teach me guitar,’ and somehow, he agreed.” Guitar classes started with once a week, and eventually went to three times a week, as Van Lee caught the music bug. “He became my mentor,” recalled Van Lee. “He taught me everything.” The young musician dove deeper and deeper into the world of music. “I tried sports,” he said, “but they weren’t for me, I wasn’t into it. I was a different kid.” And just like that, Van Lee’s career in music started to take off. Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, he spent time in the States, playing in Florida and travelling around for various country shows. While the pandemic hindered his travel time, Van Lee has committed to local stages, performing and playing whenever possible. He recently played a hometown show as a part of Haliburton Rotary’s SummerFest in Head Lake Park, with a huge crowd cheering him on and celebrating his successes. Because at the end of the day, Van Lee ties it all back to his hometown roots. While the True North Tunes is ongoing, Van Lee hopes to make it to the Top Three, which will be announced in October. Voting is live now via the website www. truenorthtunesmusic . ca , and everyone is able to cast their votes leading up to the Top Three announcement this fall. “The town has been super supportive,” said Van Lee, “If I won, it would be cool to bring that home to Haliburton.” Van Lee wants to bring it back to the community that raised him, and prove that even the ‘different kids’ can make their mark. “Instead of just being a sports town, maybe I can show some kids that we can be a music town as well,” he said, “I want to do it for this community, and I want to do that for the kids.” And he’s not slowing down anytime soon. “The drive is to just continue to go forward,” said Van Lee, “I’m not quitting anytime soon.” TAGS: Ryan Van Lee

title: Bingo Kitty Marv rides the airwaves into our hearts
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Thomas Smith It has become part of my summertime routine to go for a swim on Monday evenings. After the hustle and bustle of our weekly production meetings, I like to unwind and get a swim in at a local lake. It was during these trips to the lake that I learned about Bingo Kitty Marv. With a high pitched, almost alien voice, Bingo Kitty Marv always calls in to Penny Randall-Mowbray’s show Locally Sourced on Canoe FM to chat after the first song on Monday evenings. Bingo Kitty also lets listeners know anything interesting happening across the county and the shenanigans that he gets up to with his nephew Spinach (another cat, not the vegetable). An outspoken lover of big band and swing music, Bingo Kitty Marv occasionally selects the music for the show on several occasions. When a musical guest will be joining, Marv is often the one to introduce them. “He loves to cut a rug with his ‘pawrents’ Jack and Jill,” explained Randall-Mowbray. Over the weeks I found Bingo Kitty Marv as a mysterious figure. How can a cat call the radio station? How did he learn to speak English? Who taught him how to dance? Most importantly, who exactly is Bingo Kitty Marv? Marv’s story (before his Bingo Kitty moniker) starts with his ‘pawrents’ Jack and Jill Spitz. It was a cold Toronto night in October of 2017 when the couple heard the tiny feline screams coming from their driveway. Looking through their car, the couple find a tiny orange kitten cuddled up next to their motor. From the kitten’s size, he could only have been a few weeks old, seeking shelter on that cold night. Initially, Jack and Jill had no intentions of keeping Marv. As longtime Airedale owners, the couple had no intentions of another pet after the passing of their beloved Brodie 16 years earlier. “We had only intended to foster him,” said Jill. “Nine years later, we can’t imagine life without Bingo Kitty Marv.” As ‘dog people’ Jack and Jill treated Marv like they would any dog, and leash trained him. Learning to go for walks since he was a kitten, Marv is a natural explorer on the leash. When coming to the cottage, Marv thrives while living his life in Haliburton. “He’s obsessed with bingo, pinball, backgammon, baseball, and hockey,” said Jill. “He loves life in Haliburton and spends much of his time in his ‘catio’ taking in the sights, smells, and ambiance of living by the lakeside.” During the COVID-19 pandemic, Marv’s family was playing Canoe FM’s radio bingo when their son Daniel, who was visiting from California, left his seat. Hopping up to join in on the fun of playing Radio Bingo, Jill snapped a picture. The photo of Marv playing radio bingo spread like wildfire. Thus, the moniker Bingo Kitty Marv was bequeathed by Randall-Mowbray. “It describes him perfectly and has stuck,” said Jill. “Marv has continued to play bingo and enjoy listening to Canoe FM radio with our family.” It was through listening to Canoe FM where Bingo Kitty Marv fell in love with big band and swing.Whether he is getting his favourite lint roller massage, sleeping in a blanket fort, or rough housing with his nephew Spinach, Bingo Kitty Marv always tunes in to Canoe FM (with the help of his ‘pawrents’, of course). “Bingo Kitty Marv is my biggest fan,” said Randall-Mowbray. “He is very encouraging of local musicians and sends me a photo, so I know he’s listening too.” Naturally, Bingo Kitty Marv also reminds everyone to buy their Canoe FM Radio Bingo sheet with the proceeds from their sales supporting the community radio station. “Listeners may not realize that not all of our audience is human,” said Randall-Mowbray. “Many are in fact various animal varieties, not just feline and canine. They enjoy the comfort of familiar voices when their owners have to leave them at home. Canoe FM is turned on and they can relax and enjoy the day until everyone comes home.” While Bingo Kitty Marv has a soft spot for female singers, Frank Sinatra remains one of his favourites. Marv is no stranger to reminding listeners that his mother Jill has an ‘over the top’ crush on James Taylor, so sometimes he sings Taylor’s songs for his mom. “Canoe FM is so much more than great music,” said Randall-Mowbray. “We are the ones you turn to in a crisis when the power is down, accidents when they happen, road repairs and so much more. We are that one link that listeners have come to rely on.” Naturally, Bingo Kitty Marv loves the Pet Detective segment, with cheers heard from across the county when beloved pets are found. “Canoe FM has become something you can rely on and that’s a comfort,” said Randall-Mowbray. “Each year we ask our listeners to help ‘keep us on the air’ by giving donations to our Radiothon and they don’t let us down. This tells us, community radio matters.” For Randall-Mowbray, volunteering with Canoe FM has been a gift, allowing her to meet Bingo Kitty Marv and have him join in as an occasional co-host. Under the leadership and guidance of station volunteers like Roxanne Casey, Ron Murphy, Scott Duggan, and Janice Andrews, she has been able to do things she would have never thought possible. “As a volunteer with Canoe FM, it has been nice to have someone to ‘bounce ideas with’ and he gives some great furry feedback,” said Randall-Mowbray. “We both feel volunteer roles are crucial to Canoe FM and many of the other wonderful organizations in the County and beyond exist due to dedicated volunteers.” Bingo Kitty Marv has become quite the local celebrity, with not only a human following, but furry, feathered, and hooved friends expecting to hear his voice on the radio on Monday evenings. “We are tickled by Bingo Kitty Marv’s status as a local celebrity,” said Jill. “We are honored to be his ‘pawrents’.” TAGS: Bingo Kitty Marv Canoe FM Thomas Smith

title: Elephant
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse I have watched a lot of council meetings in my day. Between working for a municipality and then jumping into local media, the meetings tend to be regular happenings. And truthfully, I’ve always liked them. While some may snooze through the agenda, I personally find the ebbs and flows of local government to be captivating. A small representation of us, gathered around a table, making decisions that impact our everyday lives, whether we like it or not. But in my many years of council viewing, I have personally never seen a meeting like the County council one last Wednesday. I’ve seen things get heated. I was a senior staffer during the great arena debacle in Minden Hills in 2019. I’ve also watched meetings that are calm, cool, and collected; my reporter brain pulling and prying any one councillor for a quote that could turn into a story. But last week’s meeting was different. It was bordering on uncomfortable. The main topic was amalgamation. There, I said it. The elephant in the room. EORN presented their report on the “County of Haliburton’s Community-wide Affordability and Governance Structure Study” to County council, and needless to say, there were some questions. With four options on the table, there was a visible discomfort amongst the sitting members of council; the weight of what’s next hanging like a heavy cloud. And through that sense of unease, I sensed sadness. Several members sitting at that table will not be the ones deciding on this project, on the future of the County of Haliburton. For some, that’s their choice. For others, there’s a level of uncertainty and fear as we wade our way towards election season. The energy in the council room last Wednesday felt a bit like the last day of school. When the teacher tries to find work to keep the students busy, but everyone knows it’s too late. Grades are submitted, report cards are on their way. And during that meeting, it was clear that nobody wanted to be the bad guy. Steadfast stances were not taken. Statements skirted around accusations and eye contact was shifted and avoided. It was fascinating to watch. And it reminded me that the people sitting at that table, the ones we’ve put our faith and trust in for the past four years, they’re only human. This elephant in the room is big to them, too, and they’re not sure which way it’s going to charge. Right now, they’re just sitting in its shadows, waiting for it to make a move. For the next step of the project, the County approved an additional $100,000 for EORN to bring back some financial details around each of the presented models. Which truthfully, feels a little bit like one of those scams we’ve all fallen for online, where we put our credit card in for a free sample, only to be told we get the final results with a charged card. Why weren’t these financial implications included in the original report, which already came with a price tag of $200,000? When all is said and done, that means we could be facing $300,000 for a few answers. Is that what we want? Maybe, if it means we will get some clarity on next steps; especially considering the decision will land on the shoulders of some very green councillors in the new year. And at this point, it’s all just a guess, as to where that elephant will charge.

title: Irondale church needs help
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Thomas Smith Stepping into Irondale’s St. John’s Church, you are teleported back 120 years in time. Looking outside through the church’s original windows, the trees are distorted with swirls and ripples, showing you exactly what the congregation saw a century ago. As its namesake suggests, Irondale has origins connected to the iron ore industry. Charles Pusey, an American iron magnate came to the Irondale area in 1879 and was influential in planning the layout of the town including a hotel, store, mill, and railway station. As a devoted Christian, Pusey’s wife Ruth was heavily involved with the Church of England. As an act of her devotion, she financed the building of the church in Irondale. Once completed, she donated the church to the local community to be a house of worship for all denominations. By 1900, Pusey’s mining operation was shut down after the iron proved not to be lucrative. By 1960, Canadian National’s abandonment of the IB&O railway was the final nail in the coffin for the town. Known today as a ghost town, the Irondale Church remains an attendant to Irondale’s boom. For Bark Lake Cultural Developments executive Douglas Rodger, Irondale’s Church is a time machine. It brings back memories of the one room churches he attended with his mother. Waking up early to light a fire, his congregation’s breath could be seen on the coldest of mornings. As the church sits today, original artifacts and wainscotting decorate the interior. The nonprofit group Bark Lake Cultural Developments Group (formerly the Irondale Historical Society) was formed to purchase the building from the Anglican Diocese of Toronto, battling for control of the church for two years before acquiring it in 2012. Several families from the local community contributed funds towards acquiring the church and paying for its mortgage, in addition to many fundraisers over the years put on by the BLCD group. The building was recognized by Minden Hills in 2011 as being culturally and historically significant, but is not recognized as a historical place provincially or federally. On July 9, Bark Lake Cultural Developments posted a plea for help on Facebook asking the public to help save the church. As a vibrant community hub, the Irondale Church has seen many weddings, funerals, celebrations, and has acted as the central cultural hub for Irondale. Carol Simmons has been leading the charge as president of the BLCD in preserving the Irondale Church for over 18 years. Last December, Simmons penned her resignation from the BLCD board. “We need a president,” urged their post. “Without that person stepping forward, BLCD will be forced to wind down its activities, liquidate its assets and donate the proceeds to other charitable entities as determined by the rules of the Canadian Revenue Association.” For Bark Lake Cultural Developments executive Douglas Rodger, he envisions the Irondale Church to become a known space for the arts in Haliburton County. “I would like to take the cultural development part of it and make that more of an active part of it, along with the history,” said Rodger. As a playwright, he sees potential in the space as a multi-use venue for the arts, in addition to providing non-denominational worship. With potential connections to improve the sound system, he says that the most crucial aspect of the church’s future is a president with a long term vision. With the church’s natural acoustics, Rodger says that the church is already uniquely positioned towards music and performance. While it will always look like a church,everything inside is movable and can be arranged to suit a variety of needs. “There would be enough money in the back to keep things going,” said Rodger. “Until they could come up with new and different ways for fundraising and more volunteers to do the work.” Beginning the process, Rodger has put up a lighting system and says that a sound system would not be difficult to acquire. “People’s imagination can fill the space,” assures Rodger. “This is a pretty important place and worth the effort to keep it alive.” As the population of Irondale and surrounding Minden Hills increases, Rodger hopes that the increase of full-time residents brings fresh faces to the group. To sustain the BLCD, a secretary, treasurer, and president is needed. Primarily, a president is needed in the future to sign papers and to continue to be a nonprofit in the eyes of the CRA. “I would really hate to see it go,” said Rodger. “There is something unique about it. The simplicity, the unadorned nature of it. I get a feeling of being back in time,” said Rodger. “To me, it is completely original.” To learn more about the organization and to get involved with BLCD, please email historical @ irondaleontario . ca . On Saturday, Aug. 22, the family folk trio Mystikana will be playing a concert at the Irondale Church. Hailing from Eastern Ontario, the group draws on classical training and their love of nature to create intimate, interwoven melodies and rich harmonies. For this concert, BLCD will be transforming the church to reflect the natural world and enhance the ethereal qualities of their music. Tickets can be purchased at irondaleontario . ca and cost $25. The show begins at 7 p.m.

title: Wrong door
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse When did things get so complicated? This past week, through the Community Safety and Well-being plan, a group of dedicated individuals brought a report to County council, outlining the importance of the No Wrong Door approach. Once used years ago, the initiative was developed to bypass the red tape of bureaucracy, and offer a helping hand to anyone in a state of crisis. And as was outlined in the presentation, crisis doesn’t just mean sirens and breakdowns. It can refer to anyone whose coping mechanisms aren’t sufficient for the problem they are navigating. And if that’s the definition, we’ve all been in a state of crisis before. No Wrong Door was a concept that humanized the clinically developed approach to community support. And I am not an expert on the sociological chapters of human history, but mental health seems to have gone from something that was seen as very taboo (closed door), to something that you spoke to your friends and neighbours about (open door), to an era of red tape and waitlists (wrong door), and finally, back to the beginning of the cycle (closed door). No one is talking, because no one knows where to turn. We’ve done a full circle, causing individuals in crisis to fend for themselves in the shadows of their own demons. No Wrong Door was introduced in an effort to allow anyone looking for support to open any door, and be met with a helping hand. That hand would then connect to perhaps another hand, then another, creating a chain of compassion to carry those in crisis. While I was listening to the presentation, all I could think about was how things are so complicated. The organizers behind No Wrong Door are simply expressing empathy, noting that quite literally every individual is deserving of dignity, support, and resources, instead of a door slammed in their face; a redirection, a shove of responsibilities. I felt this way when I worked for a local municipal township. When did things get so complicated? I asked myself that, every single day. And while it’s been years since I’ve dabbled in local politics, one of the core reasons I left was because I felt my sense of compassion dimming. I started to look at situations and presentations through a lens marred by red tape. Dreams and aspirations brought to me by those who didn’t understand the cobwebs in our closets would be shut down before they could ever take off. Each project needed criteria, composition, complications. And through that, we lost the compassion, the care, the community. I’ve seen initiatives take off at municipal levels since my departure that has shown me that some of the red tape has been torn down, but I remain hopeful that the many rights and wrongs and zigs and zags can be further simplified for those in need. Things don’t need to be complicated. I understand that there is a time and place for liability and logistics, but at the end of the day, no one should be told they’re at the wrong door. No one should be someone else’s problem, someone else’s project. Because we’re all human. And every door should be available, for whoever needs a helping hand.

title: Loon Lake residents meet another dead end
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse This is a story about nothing. Normally, we choose to write stories about updates and events, new businesses and recent developments. But this is a story about nothing. Because there are no updates. And perhaps, that’s a whole story unto itself. In September of last year, we wrote an article about the Loon Lake community seeking a speed reduction along their highway. The stretch of road is a hotspot for vehicular accidents, with the most recent occurring a few short weeks ago. For years, the Loon Lake Property Owners Association (LLPOA) has been making every effort to work alongside the Ministry of Transportation Ontario (MTO) to limit the speed down from 80 kilometres an hour to 50 kilometres an hour. But their pleas have fallen through the cracks. “We’ve been bounced around, everywhere you can go,” said Doug Harper, a resident of Loon Lake on the eastern side of Dysart, “but we still haven’t gotten anywhere.” In June, 2023, Harper went with the LLPOA to Dysart council, requesting support in connecting with MPP Laurie Scott. “Dysart et al Council supports the request from LLPOA to reduce the speed limit along the Loon Lake shoreline of Highway 118,” reads the now three-year old resolution. Council then directed the resolution to be forwarded to MPP Laurie Scott, and the former Minister of Transportation, Caroline Mulroney. At the time of press, the LLPOA have not heard of the resolution being received from either. Fed up with a lack of communications from the province, Harper sought support from the Ontario ombudsman, an independent official who investigates complaints, helps resolve disputes, and promotes fairness in organizations. He also put forth a Freedom of Information (FOI) request to see if the issue had been progressing at a provincial level. And once again, was met with a dead end. Through choppy communications, Harper noted that Laurie Scott’s office stated that the issue was out of their hands, and directed Harper and the LLPOA to take the issue up directly with the MTO. According to Dysart staff, an email was received from the MTO in May, noting that they will be installing ministry-owned portable speed message signs on Highway 118 in the area of Loon Lake. And while the signs have remained up, no effort has been made to change the speed on the stretch of road. The area in question houses 24 driveways, as well as three entry/exit points to roads, including Gregory Lane, serving 35 residents, Loon Lake Road, serving approximately 60 residents, and Trappers Trail, which the LLPOA believes supports over 200 individuals. But this story is about nothing. Years and years of dedication through their community, and nothing but dead ends. Kathy Jolivet and Adrienne Patterson are another two locals who call the stretch of 118 home. Jolivet has been coming to the cottage since she was young, and has been discouraged at the lack of interest in ensuring safety for the area. “It’s completely different than what it used to be,” said Jolivet, carrying in her years of experience in the area. “People are just racing now … we can’t even go for a walk (along the road) without feeling like we’re in danger.” Patterson is a longtime resident, and notes that the increased speed isn’t isolated to the summer months. “If I want to pull out of my driveway, I have to roll the window down,” she said. “That’s the only way we can hear if someone is coming, and coming in fast.” While the Loon Lake locals note that speed reductions merely provide guidelines for drivers, the consequences change based on the limits set. Last year, OPP Constable Hillary Newman noted that if the speed limit is set to 80 kilometres, drivers have to notch 50 kilometres over that limit to be considered stunt driving. But if the limit is set to under 80, anything 40 kilometres over that is considered stunt driving. “And the penalties for that are pretty severe,” she said. In 2025, according to the OPP Detachment Board annual report, there were 983 charges for speeding last year, down from the 1,030 in 2024. The OPP recorded 38 speed related collisions last year, with two fatalities in total. Alcohol-related collisions were up from the previous year, with 17 registered, and animal-related collisions remain the highest risk, with 211 noted in 2025. After following up with the MTO on July 9, 16, and 21, this paper never received a comment from the organization on the LLPOA’s request. Harper noted that they have never been assigned a specific contact within the MTO, and every request has ended in a dead end. A story about nothing. Years of work, and nothing to see. But the LLPOA will keep going. While they feel discouraged and disheartened by their requests falling flat, the group remains hopeful that some changes may be made in the future. “We have to do it,” said Harper, “we’ve come too far now. We’re a dog with a bone. We have to see it through.”

title: Trent students create map of invasive aquatic species
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Thomas Smith There needs to be action taken to cease the spread of invasive species in Haliburton County. Meagan Shier and Vidhushi Hatwal, students from Trent University have recently completed a project in Algonquin Highlands doing precisely that. Over the course of many months, Shier and Hatwal compiled and consolidated existing records of aquatic invasive species, identifying current and emerging risks to local lakes, and created a map to support awareness, monitoring, and prevention efforts. The project was supported by the U-Links Centre for Community-Based Research. Shier attended AH council on Thursday, July 16 to present on the project’s findings and future steps. “One of the concerns that we received from members of the public and from council was the lack of our overall understanding and awareness of the sorts of invasive species that are in our water systems,” said Deputy Mayor Jennifer Dailloux. “The intention was to try and create a map of that.” The area of study included cold water lakes such as Oxtongue, Maple, and Boshkung and three connected watersheds of Muskoka, Lake Simcoe, and Gull River. Past observation records were found using iNaturalist and EDDMapS. The abundance of the invasive species was calculated and mapped using ArcGIS. Vegetation, fish, and invertebrates were considered during the study. Overall, no prohibited species under Ontario’s Invasive Species Act were recorded. Some restricted species indicated were purple loosestrife, zebra mussels, spiny waterflea, and Chinese mystery snails. Shier noted that the majority of invasive invertebrates are found in the south end of Algonquin Highlands. One outcome of the project was the creation of a pamphlet for the public to encourage species reporting and information on how to stop the spreading of aquatic invasive species. “Algonquin Highlands is a headwater region and that means species introduced here have a very large potential to spread downstream,” said Shier. Hotspots included Boshklung Lake and Beech Lake. “Prevention and early detection remains the most effective of these management strategies,” said Shier. “Controlling established species is often really expensive and difficult.” Shier indicated that the next steps for Algonquin Highlands could include offering public education and outreach, prioritizing early detection at hotspots lakes, and continuing to grow the database from citizen science resources. Councillor Julia Shortreed encouraged AH council to distribute the brochure to lake associations. “I think the biggest threat is tourism in this area,” said Councillor Sabrina Richards. She noted that many people with boats keep them on the same lake throughout the year. While encouraging tourists to dump and wash their vessels, AH lacks pump stations for them to do so. Mayor Liz Danielsen says that communication needs to flow between the various lake associations and the municipality. However, she is unsure how to direct this work. “What this project helps to establish is a baseline,” said Dailloux. Parks, Recreation, and Trails Manager Chris Card said that the Coalition of Haliburton Property Owners Association already has put up signs encouraging people to stop the prevention of aquatic invasive species at all boat launches and landings. Looking forward, AH council hopes to increase its communications to assist with ceasing the spread of aquatic invasive species. Shier and Hatwal’s publication and other U-Links projects can be viewed at database.ulinks.ca.

title: Haliburton County faces the heat as wildfires rage on
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse While life ticked on this week, a heavy cloud loomed over the County of Haliburton. Quite literally. Rolling in on Wednesday, July 15, smoke from northwestern forest fires seeped into the communities, forcing air quality warnings from Lakelands Public Health. The alerts came on the heels of an extreme heat warning, prompting cooling centres to open up where possible, while temperatures lingered around 34 degrees Celsius. While the heat and humidity broke Tuesday evening, smoke rolled in through the night, with the community waking up to eerie yellow skies on Wednesday morning. As of Thursday, July 16, there were over 180 active wildland fires burning in Ontario. Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) originally noted Haliburton County as a yellow level on Wednesday, but by Thursday morning, the organization had shifted up to orange. “During heavy smoke conditions, everyone’s health is at risk regardless of their age or health status,” said Environment Canada. “Limit time outdoors. Reschedule or cancel outdoor sports, activities and events.” While normal levels of air quality range between one or two, Thursday morning levels were registering between eight and nine on the AQHI. Concerns with smoke exposure include but are not limited to symptoms such as eye, nose and throat irritation, headaches or a mild cough. More serious, but less common symptoms include wheezing, chest pains or severe cough. People aged 65 and older, pregnant people, infants and young children, people with an existing illness or chronic health condition, and people who work outdoors are more likely to be impacted by wildfire smoke. It was noted that individuals should avoid strenuous activities outdoors, and seek medical attention if experiencing symptoms. Haliburton Grassroots Soccer, a league that supports over 200 youth throughout the summer months, made the decision to cancel both the Tuesday sessions, as well as the Thursday night games. For an organization that prides itself on running rain or shine, the unprecedented weather left them in a difficult position. “As much as I’m gutted to cancel another soccer night, I don’t want to put any of our kids in harm’s way,” said Kathy Judson, the coordinator of the league. “Before 7 a.m. I already had a scratchiness at the back of my throat just being outside for a few minutes, so we can’t possibly do any high intensity cardiovascular activities in this.” Judson noted that traditionally, soccer is a mild weather sport, slated for the spring or fall seasons. But with limited local access to large fields, the venue is only available during summer months when school is not in session. “We have such a short window to access the only fields in town and it’s so sad when weather or environmental factors cut our time even shorter,” said Judson. “Cancelling soccer is not a huge deal if we consider what some of our northern neighbours are dealing with. It’s an inconvenience for sure, but things could be way worse.” While the wildfire smoke continued, social media users were taking to their platforms, curious about a fire ban. Currently there is no ban in place, but regulations outline that burning is only permitted before 7 a.m. and after 7 p.m. “The four fire chiefs of the county are checking conditions daily in conjunction with the Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry (MNRF),” said Dan Chumbley, the chief in Dysart. “We don’t make the decision lightly, and will implement for a one week minimum if/when we do.” Chumbley noted that overall, he has been impressed with the general public during this dry season, noting that the majority have been well informed, and are taking it upon themselves to be more cautious. MPP Laurie Scott noted the health concerns associated with the wildfire smoke. “Please don’t go outside if you don’t have to,” she said. “We have a good community here in Haliburton County, remember to check on your loved ones and neighbours.” Scott said that she feels the provincial government is doing everything they can to support the firefighting efforts. “Our government is sparing no expense and coordinating with impacted communities to ensure safe evacuation efforts where needed,” she said. “We will continue to dedicate all the resources necessary to respond to these fires and to keep people safe.” According to this year’s provincial budget, Ontario has spent $271 million on emergency firefighting. That original budgeted amount was $135 million, but went well over the allocated amount due to a difficult fire season last summer. Under the leadership of Premier Doug Ford, the province’s budget for 2026-2027 emergency firefighting has been set for $150 million. While the fires may seem far away, Carnarvon local Kim Switzer felt them near and dear to her heart. Switzer’s 14-year-old son, Memphis, has been backcountry camping with Keewaydin Camp since early this summer. Now in his fourth year of the canoe tripping camp, Switzer firmly believes in what the camp offers for youth. “It’s been such a need for a kid like Memphis,” she said during a recent interview. “Being in the outdoors is what grounds us. Being outdoors has become home.” But nothing could have prepared her for this season. During a routine multi-day trip, the fires surrounding the sites began to escalate. Switzer received a message from the camp, saying that they were putting an evacuation order in place. The campers were paddling an area around Armstrong and Collins First Nation. “I realized that things were getting very serious,” said Switzer. “As a mom, you’re feeling helpless. You’re trying not to have fear, or picture that worst case scenario in your mind. But I couldn’t even look out the window without seeing smoke here, and you can’t get away from it.” With the campers encouraged to go screen free for the duration of their experience, Switzer had no direct contact with her son. But she gives major credit to the camp for their professionalism and navigation of the difficult task. “Hats off to them,” she said. “I can only imagine what all these staff members are going through. What an amazing team of hardworkers.” While the camp worked diligently to remove the groups from the high risk zones, the first group was taken out by float plane, the second was removed via helicopter, but the last group – the one that Memphis was a part of – needed to take refuge at a small island for a night while they waited for evacuation. “I didn’t sleep at all that night,” said Switzer. By the next morning, parents had been notified that plans had changed. “The boys had to get back to the train station, to be dropped off at a small town to meet police, and get on a bus to Sioux Lookout.” Finally, Switzer got notice that Memphis had made the bus. “I was told that the boys are out of harm’s way,” she said, “and they are en route to safety.” Switzer hopes that this experience doesn’t instill fear in the hearts and minds of campers, rather, it teaches them resilience, and gives them confidence for navigating this ‘new normal’ of climate change. “I hope it gives them experience for the lands up there,” she said. “And I really do hope they can look back on this experience, knowing that it was something they overcame as a team, as a family.” At the time of press, the air quality has returned to normal levels, and there is not a full fire ban in place. Burning is only permitted between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., and further questions can be directed to local municipal fire stations.

title: The buzz on housing
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse I am going to say something that I doubt will win me many friends: I think we need to slow down on housing. Whoa whoa, keep reading. I promise I will explain this. To begin, I adamantly, wholly believe that housing is a human right. That every individual – regardless of background or financial status – is deserving of a roof over their head. Full stop. But that said, as someone who has waded many waters in this community, I think the term “housing” has become a bit of a buzz word. Something that often bugged organizations and committees I’ve been a part of in the past, was my dedication to using proper language. We say we need housing, sure, but there are countless homes on the market that haven’t moved for months, even years. A number of dorm units in the newly-built college residence are sitting empty. Landlords are advertising in newspapers and online, unable to find suitable candidates to rent their spaces to. The housing seems to exist. Okay, so let’s whittle it down. Maybe we don’t need housing, maybe we need affordable housing. And what does affordable look like? According to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, “affordable” housing is identified as living accommodations that cost less than 30 per cent of a household’s gross (before-tax) income. So the issue doesn’t really seem to be around the housing after all. The real problem lies within the challenges of affordability. Our costs of living are through the roof. That’s no secret. We’re not bringing in the same income we once did. Groceries, gas, childcare, taxes, they’re all increasing. And of course, a little inflation is expected, but with the West Wing becoming the Wild West, the future of financial stability is on the rocks. We also have to look to our own provincial leaders. While Ontario has the second highest minimum wage in Canada, coming in at $17.60/hour, it doesn’t come close to the required $22.20 living wage, which is the bare minimum locals need to survive. I’m not saying we need to kibosh the efforts made for housing. But I am saying that we need to take a look at the big picture. I do believe that the brick and mortar buildings exist in our community, so when we hear the buzz word of housing, housing, housing, and watch as these walls are built, I don’t believe it’s necessarily addressing the problem as a whole. The housing exists. We just need to unpack the layers around affordability. And there are many, many layers. Maybe it’s time to take away the buzz and focus on the words. In an election year, don’t just ask interested individuals whether they prioritize housing, ask them exactly how they plan on making it attainable for those in need. Because it’s not just about the buzz of the buildings. It’s about laying the groundwork for a sustainable model that will benefit the greater community. That’s something worth buzzing about. title: Dysart denies extra units to be used as STRs
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse It’s been a hotly discussed topic at Dysart council, but questions around an amendment to the zoning bylaw that would allow for additional dwelling units (ADUs) to be used as short term rentals (STRs) has come to an end. “Staff questioned whether the proposal is good planning,” opened Jeff Iles, director of planning for Dysart during their regular meeting of council on June 23, “and whether this benefits the community as a whole.” In March of 2025, staff were directed to bring forward a proposed amendment that would allow ADUs to be used as STRs on Dysart properties. Section 3.1 of the zoning bylaw indicates that additional units cannot be used for the purposes of rentals, and at the time, Dysart council requested that staff change those regulations. Yet, through careful consideration, staff have made the recommendation to deny the proposed bylaw, and direct interested property owners to a property specific zoning bylaw amendment. According to Iles, dwelling units refer specifically to a home or a residence on-site. “Staff question whether an ADU, being solely used for short term purposes, is a home or a residence of a family,” he said. Generally, an STR is a property used for 28 days or less. It was noted that neighbouring municipality, Algonquin Highlands, do permit ADUs to be used as STRs in rural areas, but not in settlement or waterfront areas. Minden Hills does not permit the units to be used for rentals, with the intention of the spaces to be used as housing as opposed to recreational properties. Highlands East follows suit. Iles noted that in 2019, the province broadened regulations around ADUs in an effort to expand availability for full-time housing, making additional units more readily available for those in need. The flags of concern were raised when it came to changing these ADUs to include an STR option, as it could limit the number of dwellings available for permanent rental purposes, therefore going against the priorities laid out by council when it comes to prioritizing housing in the area. In an effort to garner awareness around the topic, the bylaw department conducted two surveys in relation to short term rentals, aimed towards members of the public, as well as owners of short-term rentals. One of the questions asked was if ADUs should be used as short term rentals. In the public survey, 23 per cent are in favour of using the additional units as rental properties, with 73 per cent opposed. The short term rental owner survey showed drastically different results, with 49 per cent in favour of ADUs being used as STRs, and 41 per cent not in favour. “Based on that consultation and the public input, the proposed amendment does not appear to be desired,” said Iles. “And it doesn’t appear to benefit the greater public good, in staff’s opinion … Council may wish to consider whether a property specific zoning bylaw amendment would be a more appropriate solution in these cases as opposed to an overall policy change that would jeopardize rental and affordable housing in the municipality.” It is for these reasons that staff made the suggestion to deny the bylaw. Councillor Pat Casey questioned the locations of the survey respondents, noting that he personally does not support ADUs used as rental units on lakes, but is open to the idea of the additional units being used for rentals in residential areas. “Any housing is good housing in this market,” he said. “If we can add more housing, even if it’s short term, two weeks, two months, five months, it helps.” Iles confirmed that if residents are seeking individual amendments to the bylaw, the process would take four months to complete the approval, with a minor zoning bylaw amendment application is $1,500. At this time, ADUs are not allowed on lakefront properties at all. As per staff recommendation, the bylaw was denied. Councillors Pat Casey and Carm Sawyer did not vote in support of the denial.

title: One room
author: Sue Tiffin
content: By Emily Stonehouse If there’s one singular reason for amalgamation, please let it be fewer meetings. It’s a sticky topic. I get that. Over the course of five meetings as well as multiple conversations with township staff and members of the public this week, I am starting to understand more and more that there is no such thing as a one-size-fits-all solution. When I worked as a senior staffer at the Township of Minden Hills, I was adamantly in support of merging our municipalities. Namely because I carry a steadfast desire to get things done. I lack the patience for process, for red tape, for spinning in circles. And with items circulating in all corners of the county about who does what and when and how, streamlining the process seemed like the right box to check. But as I step away from that professional role and look at the system through the eyes of the average taxpayer, it becomes a multi-faceted issue. Concerns around identity, grant funding, cost savings, and infrastructure all bubble to the surface. Some municipal staff have worked above and beyond to create their brand, to maximize their budgets, while others aren’t working with the same priorities in mind. All this to say, I’m on the fence. What was once so clearly black and white has now been muddled. Colours and chaos elbowing their way to light. It’s significantly more complicated than removing the boundary lines and smacking the same name on every corner. But the irony of presenting nearly the exact same presentation five times on the efficiency of streamlining in the most inefficient way possible is not lost on me. We’re paying for each and every one of these presentations. A total of $200,000 for the study as a whole. Over the course of the five meetings (yes, I tuned into all five), a few councillors made the suggestion that this doesn’t need to be an all or nothing situation. County Councillor Cec Ryall brought up merging the planning departments, and what that could look like. But my suggestion, as a person who has watched an awful lot of meetings this week, is to start even smaller. Start with the meetings. Those five meetings very easily could have been one. And I’m not just saying this from the perspective of someone responsible for covering this content. This was an opportunity to get every single person involved into one room. And anyone who has been in a room of movers and shakers knows that when those people are in the same space, magic can happen. And while we sit together and say we all get along, I have never seen every member of our local councils in a room together at once. Wouldn’t this have been a prime opportunity? Blurring the boundary lines across the board, removing the upper and lower tier hats, and realizing that everyone in that room is there for the exact same reason. Because they care. In all five of those meetings, the exact same concerns came up. The exact same points of pride were shared. The exact same questions were asked. Sitting in one room and realizing we aren’t so different from our neighbours can provide an opportunity to take that first step into sharing services, crossing boundaries. Because it’s not just black and white. There’s colour and chaos added to the picture anytime change is afoot. And we need to start small, if we want to dream big. TAGS: Emily Stonehouse editorial

title: CNN’s “Have I Got News For You” Announces This Week’s Guests
author: joverstreet
content: NEW EPISODE PREMIERES SATURDAY, OCTOBER 24 AT 9PM ET ON CNN NEW YORK – (October 22, 2026) – Comedian Jenny Hagel and political commentator David Pakman will join as guests on this week’s episode of CNN’s Have I Got News For You , the American version of the long-running UK comedy series. Produced by Hat Trick Productions for CNN Originals , the ten-episode season will continue this Saturday, October 24 at 9pm ET on CNN. The episode will stream the next day for subscribers of CNN’s streaming offering . Always relevant and of-the-moment, Have I Got News for You serves up a smart and edgy take on the news of the week from host Roy Wood Jr. along with two illustrious team captains in Amber Ruffin and Michael Ian Black . The series joins CNN’s encore presentation of Real Time With Bill Maher on the network’s Saturday primetime lineup of topical entertainment programming. Jenny Hagel is a comedian and writer. She is currently a writer and performer on Late Night with Seth Meyers where she appears on the recurring segment “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell”. Hagel is also known for her work as Executive Producer and Head Writer on Peacock’s The Amber Ruffin Show. She has also written for Impractical Jokers , the Big Gay Sketch Show , and served as Head Writer for MTV’s 10 on Top . David Pakman is a political commentator, author and host of The David Pakman Show , an independent progressive news and political commentary program. He launched the show in 2005 as a local radio program before expanding to television, YouTube and podcasts. Pakman has appeared as a commentator on CNN and Fox News, as well as The Joe Rogan Experience and The Lex Fridman Podcast . He is the author of The Echo Machine and Pay Attention: How the Algorithms and Media Wars Are Suppressing Truth and Rewiring Your Brain . New episodes of Have I Got News For You broadcast weekly on Saturdays at 9pm ET on CNN and are available to stream the next day for CNN’s All Access subscribers and on HBO Max. This week’s episode will stream live for pay TV subscribers via CNN.com, CNN connected TV and mobile apps on Saturday, October 24. It will also be available on demand beginning Sunday, October 25 to CNN’s streaming subscribers and pay TV subscribers via CNN.com, CNN connected TV and mobile apps, and Cable Operator Platforms. ### About CNN Originals The CNN Originals group develops, produces and acquires original, long-form unscripted programming for CNN Worldwide. Amy Entelis, executive vice president of talent, CNN Originals and creative development, oversees the award-winning CNN Originals portfolio that includes the following premium content brands: CNN Original Series, CNN Films, and CNN FlashDocs. Since 2012, the team has overseen and executive produced more than 50 multi-part documentary series and 70 feature-length documentary films, earning more than 120 awards and 450 nominations for the cable network, including CNN Films’ first Academy Award® for Navalny . Acclaimed titles include the Peabody Award winning and 13-time Emmy® Award-winning Anthony Bourdain Parts Unknown ; five time Emmy® nominee, Apollo 11 , directed by Todd Douglas Miller; the Emmy® Award-nominated “Decades Series”: The Sixties , The Seventies , The Eighties , The Nineties , The 2000s , and The 2010s, executive produced by Tom Hanks and Gary Goetzman; Dreamland: The Burning of Black Wall Street , executive produced by LeBron James and Maverick Carter; Have I Got News for You , produced by Hat Trick Productions and hosted by Roy Wood Jr. along with Amber Ruffin and Michael Ian Black; I’m Chevy Chase and You’re Not directed by Emmy® winner Marina Zenovich; The Last Movie Stars , directed by Ethan Hawke about the lives and careers of actors and humanitarians Joanne Woodward and Paul Newman; Grammy® Award nominee Little Richard: I Am Everything , directed by Lisa Cortés; the Oscar®, BAFTA, PGA, and duPont-Columbia Award-winning, Navalny directed by Daniel Roher; This is Life with Lisa Ling ; Primetime Emmy® and duPont-Columbia Award-winning, RBG , directed by Betsy West and Julie Cohen; the Searching For travelogue franchise, which began with Searching for Italy , followed by Searching for Mexico in 2023, Searching for Spain in 2025, and Searching for France in 2026, and has earned 3 Primetime Emmy® Awards and 12 nominations; Space Shuttle Columbia: The Final Flight in partnership with the BBC; BAFTA nominee and Directors Guild Award winner, Three Identical Strangers , directed by Tim Wardle; and the five-time Emmy® Award-winning United Shades of America with W. Kamau Bell ; and the seven-time Emmy® Award-winning The Whole Story with Anderson Cooper . title: CNN hosts inaugural Asia edition of Global Perspectives: In Bangkok
author: manamehta
content: Influential leaders and bold thinkers convened to examine Asia’s expanding role in shaping the global economy, policy, technology and culture On 14 October, CNN hosted the inaugural Asian edition of its new events franchise, Global Perspectives , in Bangkok, Thailand. Graced by the presence of H.R.H. Princess Sirivannavari Nariratana Rajakanya and opened by H.E. Anutin Charnvirakul , Prime Minister of Thailand, the invitation-only event convened prominent leaders, decision-makers and influential voices from the region and beyond for insightful discussions on the forces shaping global transformation. More than 500 attendees joined the conversation at the Ritz Carlton in Bangkok, where distinguished speakers including President of the European Central Bank Christine Lagarde, Director-general of the World Trade Organization Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Grab CEO Anthony Tan , and Academy Award-winning Creator and Co-director of “KPop Demon Hunters” Maggie Kang, shared insights on leadership in an era of change, resilience of trade, and the future of AI. Conversations were moderated by CNN journalists Dr. Sanjay Gupta , Richard Quest , Kristie Lu Stout , Will Ripley and Hanako Montgomery , with panels exploring the ideas that shape belief, the power that shapes lives, and the futures we are shaping. CNN Global Perspectives: In Bangkok sponsors include B. Grimm, Dangote, JFOODO, Bank of America, Siam Piwat Group, Tencent, Central Pattana, Tourism Authority of Thailand and Thailand Convention & Exhibition Bureau. Interested audiences can catch up on the conversation and key takeaways from the event at cnn.com/globalperspectives A selection of images can be found here: https://bit.ly/3TRRUP6   Key Insights from the Event H.E. Anutin Charnvirakul, Prime Minister of Thailand, said “I am especially pleased to welcome CNN Global Perspectives , building on the success of CNN Countdown last year…CNN Global Perspectives gives us the chance to hear different views and discuss how economic decisions affect people’s daily life. I hope today’s program will bring different perspectives together and keep the discussions grounded in practical choices.” Christine Lagarde, President of the European Central Bank , said, “What we have at the moment is this recurring, infamous war of Russia against Ukraine, that is continuing and it’s putting pressure on refinery capacities, as you know. But since March ’26, we also have the war in the Middle East, which is also putting a huge strain on the supply and movement of oil and gas.” Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-general of the World Trade Organization , told CNN’s Richard Quest, “Trade is facing the biggest disruptions it’s ever faced in the 80 years history of … the World Trade Organization… But at the same time, Richard, what has really surprised us is the resilience of trade.” Grab CEO Anthony Tan , said “AI itself is not going to take your job … but who will take your job is somebody who knows and uses AI, they’re going to take your job… If you aren’t going to re-invest and self-invest and learn and embrace AI, I’m sorry, the person on your right, on your left who is embracing AI will take your job.” Maggie Kang, Academy Award-winning Creator and Co-director of “KPop Demon Hunters” , said “We had already, you know, as a culture, kind of cemented our place in movies and TV with ‘Squid Game’ and in music with Kpop, and I saw all of that, and you know growing up where my culture wasn’t so cool, I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, we’re cool now’. Maybe it’s time that we could do something cool in the animation space because Koreans have produced a lot of animation for a lot of other people, but we never really had like something that we could call our own.”   – Ends – About CNN Worldwide CNN is the most honored brand in cable news, reaching more individuals through television, streaming and online than any other cable news organization in the United States. title: CNN’s All Access Subscription to Launch Internationally in the U.K. and Canada on October 20
author: courtneyh
content: Subscribers Will Have Full, Multiplatform Access to CNN’s Award-Winning Global Journalism NEW YORK, NY – October 13, 2026 – CNN announced today that its All Access subscription will expand to the U.K. and Canada on October 20, 2026, providing international audiences for the first time with one direct, centralized destination for CNN’s programming and journalism, including live and on-demand video programming to stream. Subscribers in the U.K. and Canada will now be able to stream a selection of live channels from CNN’s portfolio of International and US programming, exclusive video-on-demand content, and a library of award-winning CNN Original Series and CNN Films. Subscribers will also have unlimited access to all text, audio and video content on CNN.com and the CNN app, including subscriber-only content such as exclusive distinctive reporting and feature stories. The subscription will be available across web and select mobile and connected TV apps. With the consequential U.S. midterm elections just a few weeks away, subscribers will have an unprecedented front-row seat as races heat up, culminating on Election Day. CNN’s award-winning live political coverage and election reporting, exclusive streaming content and in-depth analysis from political experts will help audiences stay across all the breaking developments. “CNN’s reputation as a premium, trusted name in news is unparalleled around the globe. We’re excited to provide these audiences with a simple way to access our live 24/7 channel and global reporting in one place,” said Alex MacCallum, Chief Operating Officer, CNN Worldwide. “Following the enthusiastic reception of this offering in the U.S., expanding first to the U.K. and Canada has been our top international expansion priority as we continue to invest in and grow our direct-to-consumer business.” The offering will be available in Canada for $7.99 CAD per month or $79.99 CAD annually, and in the U.K. for £4.99 per month or £49.99 annually. Subscribers will be able to take advantage of a special “welcome” offer at launch, with an introductory price of $59.99 CAD in Canada and £37.99 in the U.K. for the first year. author: amayastarkey
content: NEW YORK, NY – (October 12, 2026) – The Whole Story with Anderson Cooper , a seven-time Emmy® Award-winning CNN Original , returns with an examination of how, a decade after MAGA remade the right, President Trump’s second term has tested the movement’s faithful, from the Iran war and the Epstein files to the aftermath of Charlie Kirk’s death. “MAGA Ever After?” with CNN Senior Correspondent Donie O’Sullivan premieres Saturday, October 17 at 8pm ET/PT and will be available to stream the following day at CNN.com/watch and on the CNN app for CNN streaming subscribers . In this hour, O’Sullivan travels across the country revisiting people and communities he has followed for years, from the die-hard loyalists to the new generation who are moving even further to the right. With access built over years inside MAGA communities, O’Sullivan asks whether the movement’s loyalty to Trump can survive his second term. “From Tucker Carlson to Marjorie Taylor Greene, some of the president’s loudest supporters have turned on him this year. Many in the MAGA base don’t know where to turn or who to trust. We ask what comes next for the Republican Party in a post-Trump world,” said O’Sullivan. O’Sullivan speaks with Ashley St. Clair , a former MAGA influencer and the mother of one of Elon Musk’s children; James Fishback , a far-right political activist and former gubernatorial candidate in Florida; Gen Z streamer Sneako , a social media personality; and the prominent Trump ally Laura Loomer , along with other voices from across the political right. Together, they reveal a movement in flux, shaped by the contradictions of the online world where millions engage in politics, and raise the question of what comes next for MAGA. The series, which has been honored with three consecutive Emmy® Awards for Outstanding Recorded News Program, is executive produced by Susan Chun . title: Delta extends retirement age for clinical health workers to 65
author: The Nigerian Observer
content: Gov. Sheriff Oborevwori of Delta has approved an extension of the retirement age for skilled clinical health professionals in government hospitals from 60 to 65 years. The policy also extends the maximum length of service from 35 to 40 years, whichever comes first. Oborevwori announced the development on Monday in Asaba. He said the initiative was aimed at addressing manpower shortages, retaining experienced medical personnel and strengthening healthcare delivery in the state. The governor also said the policy covered 26 categories of skilled clinical health professionals actively engaged in clinical services in government hospitals. According to him, they include medical officers, nursing officers, pharmacists, medical laboratory scientists, physiotherapists, radiographers, optometrists, psychologists, dental officers, community health officers and audiologists. Others he said were dieticians, medical laboratory technicians, pharmacy technicians, X-ray technicians, dental technologists, dental therapists, prosthetic and orthoptist, among others. Oborevwori said the extension followed appeals by the Delta Council of the National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives and the state chapter of the Nigerian Medical Association. “The associations have sought the adoption of the policy in Delta following its approval at the federal level,” he said. The governor explained that eligible officers seeking the extension must apply through their respective chief medical directors six months before attaining 60 years of age or completing 35 years in service. “Applicants are also required to present medical certificates of fitness, while chief medical directors are expected to forward applications to the Ministry of Health for screening and approval by the commissioner,” he added. Oborevwori clarified that the policy does not cover skilled clinical health professionals serving in ministries and extra-ministerial departments. He said the extension was specifically designed for personnel actively engaged in clinical practice in government hospitals. He expressed confidence that retaining experienced and medically fit personnel would help preserve professional expertise and institutional knowledge within the state’s public hospital system. The governor added that the policy took effect from the date of approval, subject to the prescribed application, screening and approval procedures. (NAN)

title: Tinubu says Dangote Group performs excellently in driving economy
author: The Nigerian Observer
content: President Bola Tinubu has commended the Dangote Group for its significant contribution to Nigeria’s economic growth, citing the conglomerate’s strategic investments in key sectors as instrumental in boosting domestic production.Track Exec Orders Tinubu said it is also creating jobs, reducing dependence on imports, conserving foreign exchange and strengthening the country’s industrial capacity. The President gave the commendation during a visit to the Dangote Group pavilion at the ongoing 32nd Nigeria Economic Summit in Abuja, on Monday. He was represented at the event by Vice President Kashim Shettima. Tinubu praised the Group’s performance across its business operations, highlighting the critical role of private-sector investments in expanding productive capacity, stimulating economic activities and supporting national development. The Dangote Group has investments spanning cement manufacturing, fertiliser production, sugar refining, salt processing and petroleum refining. These investments contribute to local value addition, employment generation and the development of domestic supply chains, while supporting efforts to reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported products.Access Services He said his administration is creating conditions for public and private sectors to invest, expand and generate productive employment. Dangote Group is the second biggest employer of labour after the federal government. The 2026 Nigeria Economic Summit, themed “Growth That Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity,” was declared open by the President. The President, who used the occasion to defend the Federal Government’s ongoing economic reforms, emphasise the importance of industrial harmony and private-sector-led growth. The summit brings together policymakers, business leaders, investors and other stakeholders to discuss practical strategies for accelerating economic growth, improving productivity, generating employment and ensuring that the benefits of economic expansion reach more Nigerians.Nigerian news analysis The President’s commendation underscores the importance of sustained collaboration between government and the private sector in building a more productive, competitive and resilient Nigerian economy. He said Nigeria has performed below its potentials for far too long, but “there is no shortcut for economic development.” “We came to rewrite the story of a nation that has performed below its potentials for far too long,” he said. Through its investments in strategic industries, the Dangote Group remains a major private-sector participant in Nigeria’s industrialisation drive, with the potential to deepen local manufacturing, strengthen supply chains and support the country’s broader economic development objectives. Through the Dangote Group’s diversified operations, the conglomerate has established a substantial presence across critical sectors of the economy, providing products and services that support construction, agriculture, manufacturing, energy and other productive activities. One of its investments is the Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals complex in Lagos, which has the potential to transform Nigeria’s downstream petroleum industry by increasing domestic refining capacity and reducing the country’s reliance on imported refined petroleum products. (NAN)

title: Nosh vs Roqqu: Which Is Better for Converting Crypto to Naira?
author: The Nigerian Observer
content: If you hold crypto and want it converted to naira, you have probably noticed there are so many platforms that promise to do exactly that. Nosh and Roqqu are two of the best-known names Nigerians turn to for converting their crypto to naira. Both are widely used and trusted by a lot of people, so the real question isn’t whether they work. It’s which one works better for you. This guide compares them side by side so you can decide with confidence, whether you are cashing out for the first time or you have been converting crypto for a while. How to Know the Best Crypto Exchange for Nigeria? Before comparing platforms, decide what matters to you, like the final amount you receive, how fast it arrives, and the help you can get if something goes wrong. High rate and no hidden cost: A platform that offers you high rates and doesn’t have any hidden fees. Fast transactions: A platform that converts crypto to Naira fast without delays. Safety and regulatory standing: A platform that safeguards your money using features like two-factor authentication, data encryption, and fraud prevention measures. Customer support: A platform that has active customer support to handle issues when they arise. Easy to use: A platform you can easily navigate. How do Nosh and Roqqu compare? Feature Nosh Roqqu Main strength Turning crypto into naira quickly All-in-one crypto app for trading, saving, and more How selling works Send crypto to your wallet address, and your Naira wallet is credited automatically once the transfer is confirmed Sell or swap in the app, then withdraw to your bank Fees No hidden charges or extra fees for selling, with the rate shown in a live calculator before you send 2% on each buy, sell, or swap; naira deposits and withdrawals are free. Supported coins BTC, ETH, USDT, USDC, TRX, BNB, DOGE, LTC 100+ cryptocurrencies Ease of use Simple and user-friendly interface: pick your coin, choose Naira, check the rate, send Clean and beginner-friendly, with more features to browse Customer support 24/7 via in-app live chat, WhatsApp, phone and email 24/7 via in-app message, email and WhatsApp Security Data encryption, fraud prevention and two-factor authentication Strong encryption and fraud monitoring Countries Nigeria and Ghana Nigeria, Ghana and others Crypto conversion fees Nosh offers the best crypto trading rates with no hidden charges or extra fees for selling your crypto. You see the rate in the calculator before you send anything, so you know the naira amount upfront. Roqqu charges 2% each time you buy, sell, or swap, while naira deposits and withdrawals are free. That’s simple to understand, but 2% adds up on larger conversions. On ₦1,000,000 worth of crypto, that’s ₦20,000 before anything else. Crypto conversion speed On Nosh, the process is automatic. You send crypto to your wallet, and once your transaction is confirmed, your crypto is converted, and your Naira wallet is credited instantly. The process finishes in minutes. There’s no buyer to wait for, no order book, and no manual release. Roqqu is also quick. The app states that withdrawal requests are processed within 30 minutes, including weekends. Some in-app steps (selling, then withdrawing to your bank) add a stage compared with a wallet that credits naira automatically. Cryptocurrency coverage Roqqu has the larger catalogue. It lists over 100 cryptocurrencies, which suits people who want to trade, swap between coins, or hold smaller assets. Nosh supports Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, USDC, Tron, Binance Coin, Dogecoin, and Litecoin for naira conversion. That covers the coins most Nigerians actually cash out, including the stablecoins freelancers get paid in. Ease of Use Nosh is neat and easy to use for changing your crypto to naira. You pick your coin, choose Naira, check the rate, send your crypto, and your naira shows up in your wallet. This makes it quick, even if it’s your first time. Roqqu is also neat and easy for beginners to use. It works in several languages, including Igbo, Yoruba, and Hausa, which helps a lot of users. But it has more features, so there’s a bit more to look through before you find what you need. It is clean and beginner-friendly. Customer Support Nosh offers 24/7 customer support, so you can get help at any hour. Roqqu also lists 24/7 support on its website, and you can reach it through the in-app message button on the homepage, by email, or on WhatsApp. Since both are available around the clock, the better test is how quickly each one replies when you have a real problem. Security Nosh protects your account and money with data encryption, fraud prevention, and two-factor authentication. The extra login step means someone who gets your password still can’t get into your account easily. Roqqu also puts security up front, with strong encryption and tools that watch for fraud. Reviewers have described it as a highly secure platform, and it has built up a large user base over several years. Its larger set of features means more places where you manage money, so it’s worth turning on every protection the app offers. Which One Should You Choose? If your goal is to turn crypto into naira, Nosh is the better fit for most people. It suits you if you’re paid in USDT or Bitcoin for freelance work, you want to know what you’ll receive before you send anything, and you’d like to spend your naira on bills in the same app. Roqqu makes more sense if converting is only part of what you do.
