title: All four NFC North teams are playoff-caliber — and have fatal flaws
author: Patrick Finley
content: <p>Packers coach Matt LaFleur didn’t want to make a bad day worse by getting fined. Asked Sunday about the controversial calls during his team’s 20-17 loss to the NFC North rival Lions, he went full Marshawn Lynch.</p><p>“I can say what I really think, but I don’t think it does any good,” LaFleur said. “So it is what it is. You’ve just got to overcome it.”</p><p>The Packers had a chance to move beyond two roughing-the-passer penalties, including one on the Lions’ game-winning drive, and an unnecessary-roughness call in which the official threw the flag while lying on his back, having been knocked over by players after he believed the play had ended. It was as simple as making their field goals. However, the Lions tipped Trey Smack’s 35-yard attempt in the fourth quarter after he’d previously missed a 26-yarder in the first. He also missed from 43 and 47 yards two weeks ago against the Bears. No NFL kicker has more missed field-goal attempts than Smack’s five this season.</p><p>It’s the perfect encapsulation of the NFC North through seven weeks. This is the best division in football, yet each team — including the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> — has glaring flaws.</p><p>Glancing at the next three months, that’s both encouraging and a challenge to be solved. All four teams can, with a straight face, say they have Super Bowl aspirations. Whether it’s on the field or in the conversations their general managers will be having ahead of the NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10, they’ll be racing each other for position.</p><p>If the season ended today, all four teams would make the playoffs, with the unbeaten Vikings winning the division and earning a bye and the Bears, Lions and Packers holding the Nos. 5-7 seeds. Since the NFL switched to four-team divisions in 2002, no division has sent all four of its teams to the postseason.</p><p>None of these four is perfect, particularly the one on top. The Vikings (6-0), the last undefeated team in the league, also have the best defense. But their offense is more pedestrian than a crosswalk. They’re fourth-worst in the NFL in yards and passing yards, and their average of 20.8 points per game was the third-worst in the NFC through Sunday. Although quarterback Kyler Murray has improved, he has had a worse passer rating in each of the last two weeks than J.J. McCarthy, whom the Vikings traded to the Giants last month for a song.</p><p>The Vikings’ 16-10 victory over the Colts on Sunday was the fourth time this season an NFL team won with 16 or fewer points and 275 or fewer yards, and the Vikings have done it twice, with Week 2 against the Bears the other instance.</p><p>The Bears’ latest big flaw revealed itself Thursday, just as fans were celebrating what felt like the start of a blowout victory. Ahead by 13 points with three seconds left in the first half and the Patriots just past midfield, the Bears blitzed quarterback Drake Maye, who dumped the ball off to running back Rhamondre Stevenson for a sprinting touchdown up the right sideline. Stevenson was touched once when cornerback Jaylon Johnson nicked his undershirt.</p><p>Of 76 cornerbacks who have played at least half their team’s snaps, Johnson’s coverage grade was 72nd, according to Pro Football Focus. Rookie teammate Malik Muhammad ranked 62nd.</p><p>The Bears give up 20.4 points per game, ninth-fewest in the NFL. They can, at times, look dominant, thanks to a killer third-down package and coordinator Dennis Allen’s knack for unusual blitzes. But what happens when they can’t get to the passer? What happens when those blitzes don’t land? What happens when Allen’s gambles don’t pay off?</p><p>Lions coach Dan Campbell certainly knows that feeling. He decided to go for it twice on fourth down Sunday, costing the Lions points the first time and nearly costing them the game the second, spared only by some good fortune. With about a minute left in the third quarter and the Lions ahead by three, Campbell called a pass play on fourth-and-goal from the Packers’ 6-yard line rather than kick a field goal. It failed. Then, with about five minutes left in a tie game, Campbell got absolutely ridiculous. going for it on fourth-and-one from his own 24. Running back Jahmyr Gibbs was stuffed for a two-yard loss. Smack’s field-goal kick was tipped four plays later.</p><p>Campbell explained his two-point rationale for the second call: One, he thought they’d make it, and, two, he knew they’d get the ball back regardless. By that rationale, he should have just handed the Packers the ball and told them to score.</p><p>The Lions give up more yards per game than any team in the NFL. Their coach leads the league in hubris. If the former doesn’t doom them, the latter might.</p><p>Not that the Lions were apologizing after kicking a field goal as time expired to win their first NFC North game of the season.</p><p>“They all count the same, [whether] we play this game now or later in the year with the division on the line,” quarterback Jared Goff said.</p>

title: White Sox announce John Schriffen won't return as TV voice
author: Jeff Agrest
content: <p>For John Schriffen, it’s three seasons and you’re out.</p><p>The White Sox announced Monday that Schriffen won’t return to their TV booth next season. The team said it told Schriffen, 42, it won’t extend his contract. His three-year deal expired after the season, and the Sox won’t pick up the option year.</p><p>The move is no surprise after Schriffen’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2025/09/18/white-sox-john-schriffen-steve-stone-gordon-beckham-chicago-sports-network-mike-mccarthy-marquee-sports-network" target="_blank" >rocky run as the play-by-play voice</a>. His defense of the Sox during their record 121-loss season in 2024 was outlandish, and his lack of baseball-broadcasting experience and knowledge of the franchise were apparent. Still, his excitement endeared him to a segment of Sox fans, particularly during the playoff run this season.</p><p>‘‘John has been a true professional throughout his three seasons with the White Sox, bringing energy, enthusiasm and a distinctive style to our broadcasts,’’ Brooks Boyer, the Sox’ chief revenue and marketing officer, said in a statement.</p><p>‘‘As his contract comes to an end, we believe this is the appropriate time to evaluate the direction of our broadcasts and determine what is best for the organization and our fans moving forward. We are appreciative of John’s contributions and the connection he built with our fan base. We wish him continued success in his future endeavors.’’</p><p>‘‘I’m grateful to the Chicago White Sox organization for the opportunity to call games over the past three seasons,’’ Schriffen said. ‘‘Being part of this team’s turnaround and playoff run was truly special.</p><p>‘‘I want to thank White Sox fans for welcoming me to Chicago and for their support throughout my time here. I’ll always cherish the memories and look forward to what’s next.’’</p><p>Perhaps Schriffen saw the writing on the wall <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/10/15/john-schriffen-chicago-white-sox-tv-steve-stone-connor-mcknight-connor-onion-wayne-randazzo-len-kasper-darrin-jackson" target="_blank" >when he chose to call a UFC event</a> rather than be available for the Sox’ playoff clincher in September. He contractually was allowed a certain number of games off, but his decision to miss the Sox’ first clinching game in five years couldn’t have sat well with team brass.</p>

title: Why I can't figure out how seriously to take the Blackhawks' bad start — or what to expect next
author: Ben Pope
content: <p>I have a confession to make: I’m not sure how to analyze the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> right now.</p><p>Oh, they’ve been bad so far, I can tell you that. I could provide many stats as supporting evidence, too, but the standings suffice well enough. At 3-8-0, the Hawks have the second-worst record in the NHL.</p><p>I’m struggling to identify who deserves the bulk of the blame for their woes, though.</p><p>Is it general manager Kyle Davidson, who assembled this roster? Is it coach Jeff Blashill and his staff, whose systems don’t seem to be working well? Or is it the players, who have been universally mistake-prone on the ice?</p><p>I’m also struggling to determine how problematic it is that they’ve been bad. Perhaps these early-season struggles were inevitable with a roster this young and recently assembled, or perhaps they’re an indication this roster never will succeed.</p><p>And I’m really struggling to predict what will happen the rest of the season.</p><p>Perhaps Blashill’s seat will heat up by January or February. That then could heat up Davidson’s seat, given that not many GMs get the privilege to hire and fire more than two coaches.</p><p>Perhaps Hawks chairman Danny Wirtz’s confidence in Davidson — whom he just awarded a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/15/blackhawks-kyle-davidson-contract-extension-danny-wirtz" target="_blank" >contract extension</a> in April — and patience with the slow rebuilding plan will hold strong. That might allow Davidson to maintain his belief in and patience with Blashill and keep fans’ impatient (furious, in some cases) cries falling on deaf ears.</p><p>Or perhaps the Hawks are about to turn things around, like the equally young Sharks did around this time last season, and all questions about seat temperatures will fade away.</p><p>I would love to anticipate which hypothetical path will become reality, so I’ve been searching for any sorts of signals hidden in the first month of the season.</p><p>Every attempt to do so, however, ignites a tug-of-war between different thought processes in my brain.</p><p>Here’s how it usually goes:</p><p><i>The Hawks’ results need to be taken with grains of salt because their schedule has been brutal. Almost every opponent has been a Stanley Cup contender. Plus, they’ve only played one game with both their No. 1 forward (Connor Bedard) and presumptive No. 1 defenseman (Bowen Byram) in the lineup.</i></p><p><i>But in hockey, bad teams still should beat good teams sometimes. The Predators just walloped the Avalanche 6-2 on Sunday. The Hawks haven’t done that even once yet. Every team deals with injuries, too. And the Hawks haven’t actually had that many in terms of quantity.</i></p><p><i>But the Hawks have been snakebitten. Their last three games, in which they’ve scored three goals, have been laden with missed opportunities. That should even out over time.</i></p><p><i>But most teams think they’re unlucky because scoring is really difficult. The Hawks’ team shooting percentage (10.2%) is only one tick off the league average. Meanwhile, they’re 31st in shots on goal per game, and that’s not luck.</i></p><p><i>But Blashill is a smart coach. He has the right combination of intelligence and flexibility to succeed tactically and the right combination of empathy and assertiveness to succeed developmentally. Many fans have convinced themselves otherwise, but he’s impressive in-person.</i></p><p><i>But every NHL coach is smart and well-rounded. The bar is high in this league. And Blashill’s systems clearly aren’t working as intended, regardless of whose fault it is. The Hawks often look lost in defensive-zone coverage, have been awful with defensive-zone breakouts and haven’t been effective on the forecheck.</i></p><p><i>But young studs such as Anton Frondell, Roman Kantserov and Artyom Levshunov already have shown flashes of immense talent and should get more comfortable in the NHL over time. They have the potential to become stars alongside Bedard, and a few stars can change a team dramatically.</i></p><p><i>But it might take them a couple of more years to reach stardom, and nobody wants to wait a couple of more years — especially for outcomes that aren’t guaranteed. That would be excruciating.</i></p><p><i>But my own expectation bias probably influences my perspective. I’m so accustomed to watching the Hawks lose — after covering five consecutive terrible seasons — that it’s difficult for me to imagine them winning.</i></p><p><i>But that track record of losing genuinely can create a cycle that’s difficult to escape. Confidence is real, and not only do the Hawks lack it relative to their peers, but opposing teams have good reasons to feel extra-confident against them. Climbing a mountain is harder than defending it from the top.</i></p><p>I imagine most Hawks fans aren’t encountering the same endless mental loop. I’ve already heard from many with fully formed strong opinions.</p><p>Most fans are affected by emotions, however. Take emotion out, and the logic — at least to me — balances on both sides.</p><p>The brutal-schedule element isn’t about to stop complicating the evaluation process, either. After a brief respite against the Kings and Red Wings, the Hawks will enter another six-game murderer’s row against Cup contenders. Things won’t lighten up until the second half of November.</p><p>Conclusions generally become safer to draw as sample sizes get larger, however, so I’m hopeful the next few weeks will show me some light. In the meantime, I’ll keep searching for signals.</p>

title: Six Flags Great America’s Raging Bull to get additional restraints after deadly Georgia coaster accident
author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi
content: <p>Six Flags Great America’s Raging Bull roller coaster in Gurnee will have seat belts for riders following a crash involving a similar ride at Six Flags Over Georgia, where a 42-year-old man died after being ejected from a similar coaster.</p><p>Raging Bull is one of three Six Flags roller coasters that will add seat belts, along with the Nitro ride at Six Flags Great Adventure in New Jersey and the Goliath at the Georgia park, a company spokesperson said Monday.</p><p>Already in place on the Raging Bull and similar coasters are clamshell-like padded lap restraints which lock into place and have handles for riders.</p><p>The company also says it will have independent engineers and ride inspection specialists review safety procedures across its parks.</p><p>“Our focus remains on supporting and cooperating with the ongoing state investigation while taking meaningful actions to further strengthen safety across our parks,” the spokesperson said.</p><p>No date has been set to reopen the Raging Bull ride. The ride will reopen after the modifications and subsequent safety checks are complete, the spokesperson said.</p><p>Raging Bull opened in 1999. The tallest and longest roller coaster at the Gurnee amusement park, it stands 202 feet tall, spans 5,057 feet and hits speeds of up to 73 miles an hour.</p><p>In the incident Oct. 12 at Six Flags Over Georgia, an Atlanta man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was ejected from Goliath and died, according to police in Cobb County, Georgia. That police department said ts preliminary findings indicated he struck other patrons before falling beneath the ride. That investigation continues.</p>

</div><p></p><h3>“Eight Bridges”</h3><p>Every year festival programmer Sam Flancher gets one experimental film into the lineup. This time it’s the minimalist, meditative “Eight Bridges” by James Benning, who screened his first film at the fest in 1971. Eight 10-minute shots beautifully frame bridges from coast to coast. First is San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge, followed by others over the Alabama River, Columbia River, Hudson River, Mississippi River, Sheyenne River and the Rio Grande Gorge. Longest is the Seven Mile Bridge in the Florida Keys. Benning frees our imagination to interpret the engineering and environment on our own, minus dialogue, voiceover or score. Mindful of patrons overstimulated by cinema and crowds, fest organizers set aside a Quiet Room at the AMC NewCity theater. The serene “Eight Bridges” itself offered one such “sensory-friendly quiet room space” to reset.</p><p><i>“Eight Bridges”</i> <i>is not available for streaming at the moment.</i></p><div writer-director-cinematographer-editor-production designer Lav Diaz offers a tragic saga of Catholic colonizers quashing indigenous Malayan spirituality in 1617. Obsessed with building a church, a Spanish priest forces converts to haul a load of costly marble through 50 kilometers of dense jungle. Notorious bandits lurk. It’s all for an altar to complete a 15-year construction effort. Many men have already died to build this church. Shot in indelible black and white, this gripping tale excels as a work of anthropological history. Last year at the festival, Diaz’s “Magellan,” starring Gael García Bernal, covered similar themes. Both films were shot in scenic Sampaloc, Quezon Province.</p><p><i>“Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors” is making the film circuit rounds and is not slated for a wide theatrical release or is available for streaming at the moment.</i></p><h3>“Possible Love”</h3><p>The latest film by Lee Chang-dong is South Korea’s official Oscar entry for the best international feature film. The plot observes an upper-class woman making a documentary about survivors of a factory strike. Her focus is a working-class family in the aftermath of brutal anti-union violence. Inspired by a 2009 strike at a Korean car manufacturer, this deftly plotted drama incorporates some news footage of the clash. Besides critiquing the ethics of nonfiction directors, Lee scrutinizes class friction. Issues come to a head when the filmmaker and her husband invite her interview subjects for a weekend at their fancy summer house. Ironies and emotions erupt. “Possible Love” won the Ebert Director Award at the Toronto International Film Festival this year.</p><p><i>“Possible Love” comes to Netflix on Nov. 6.</i></p><div title: Federal appeals panel considers who can fire top federal prosecutors named by judges
author: Jon Seidel
content: <p>Chicago’s top federal prosecutor said he serves at the pleasure of the president.</p><p>But Andrew Boutros<b> </b>didn’t take the traditional route to office. Nor did many of his peers. Rather, when President Donald Trump returned to the White House, he employed a law that eventually let federal judges appoint U.S. attorneys<b> </b>across the country —<b>&nbsp;</b>including Boutros.</p><p>That raises a critical question: Who gets to fire a judge-appointed U.S. attorney?</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/05/30/andrew-boutros-interim-us-attorney-chicago-judges-role-pam-bondi" >Is Chicago’s interim U.S. attorney here to stay? Judges could play an unusual role in picking top prosecutor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>A West Coast legal fight might soon provide an answer. A 9th U.S. Circuit<b> </b>Court of Appeals panel<b> </b>in San Francisco spent nearly 90 minutes<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>considering whether to overrule a lower-court judge who<b> </b>concluded<b> </b>this month<b> </b>that “the president cannot unilaterally fire”<b> </b>such a prosecutor.</p><p>That judge got it wrong, Justice Department attorney<b> </b>Mark<b> </b>Freeman<b> </b>argued Friday. He said, “the power of a prosecutor is awesome. It brings the full power of the state against a citizen.</p><p>“That is why it is essential that the president be the one who can be blamed for it.”</p><p>But a U.S. attorney’s office is “supposed to be run by somebody who is confirmed by the Senate,” lawyer<b> </b>Donald<b> </b>Verrilli Jr. argued. That’s the judgment of Congress, he said, “and it is being evaded.”</p><p>The panel’s ruling will not be binding in Illinois. But it might offer guidance on a question that took on new relevance this summer. Local elected Democrats<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/06/04/trump-blanche-boutros-doj-broadview" target="_blank" >called on Boutros to resign</a> after his office was accused of misconduct in a high-profile case tied to Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>A judge is now considering whether to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/jon-seidel?p=00000198-1631-d49b-af99-df3def400000.2" target="_blank" >name a special prosecutor</a> to investigate Boutros and others for criminal contempt. The controversy revolves around a now-defunct conspiracy case Boutros’ office brought against a group of Midway Blitz protesters known as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“the Broadview Six.”</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Andrew Harnik/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Attorney General Todd<b> </b>Blanche<b> </b>has said the Justice Department “fully supports U.S. Attorney Boutros.”<b> </b>Blanche made that comment before he was confirmed to his job on a permanent basis.</p><p>U.S. District Chief Judge Virginia Kendall has declined to comment on the controversy, citing the judicial code of conduct.</p><p>The West Coast case was heard Friday by Judges<b> </b>Richard<b> </b>Paez, appointed by President Bill Clinton; Jay<b> </b>Bybee, appointed by President George W. Bush; and<b> </b>Jennifer<b> </b>Sung, appointed by President Joe Biden.</p><p>It’s unclear how they’ll rule, or when.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/donald-trump/2026/06/04/trump-blanche-boutros-doj-broadview" >Trump’s acting attorney general backs Boutros amid fallout from botched ‘Broadview 6’ case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Traditionally, U.S. attorneys are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. That hasn’t happened in Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2017/11/9/18363175/lausch-confirmed-to-be-chicago-s-next-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >since 2017</a>,<b> </b>when the Senate confirmed<b> </b>Trump nominee John Lausch.</p><p>Instead, then-Attorney General<b> </b>Pam Bondi<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" >appointed<b> </b>Boutros<b> </b>to the job</a> on a temporary basis<b> </b>in April 2025. Then, when that appointment expired<b> </b>four months later, Chicago’s federal judges <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/07/25/chicagos-federal-judges-choose-andrew-boutros-as-top-prosecutor" target="_blank" >chose<b> </b>Boutros</a><b> </b>to continue on a more permanent basis, using the same law at issue out west.</p><p>The controversy has caught the attention of former top feds from across the country, including ex-Chicago U.S. Attorney Scott<b> </b>Lassar. He and others filed a brief opposing the Trump administration’s interpretation of the law.</p><p>Lawful appointments matter, they wrote, because a prosecutor’s decisions<b> </b>carry<b> </b>“life-changing consequences.”</p><h3><b>A swift dismissal</b></h3><p>It took Trump less than an hour<b> </b>to<b> </b>fire<b> </b>Roger<b> </b>Rogoff, named<b> </b>July 15<b> </b>by judges<b> </b>in Seattle to be the top federal prosecutor<b> </b>there.</p><p>Shortly after he was sworn in, Rogoff<b> </b>learned<b> </b>by email<b> </b>that he’d been removed from the job — at the direction of the president.</p><p>Trump later sent the Senate a nominee for U.S. attorney, who has yet to be confirmed. The president also<b> </b>directed<b> </b>a former immigration judge<b> </b>to run the U.S. attorney’s office<b> </b>in the meantime.</p><p>Rogoff<b> </b>sued, arguing<b> </b>his dismissal by the president violated the law. On Oct. 1, U.S. District Judge Stanly Bastian<b> </b>agreed. In his preliminary injunction ruling, the judge<b> </b>posed the very question at issue: “Can the president fire a court-appointed U.S. attorney?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Alex Brandon/Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Then, he answered it:<b> </b>“No.”</p><p>Bastian said that would “upend the framework created by the Constitution,”<b> </b>which balances the president’s right to appoint a prosecutor and the Senate’s right to confirm one.</p><p>“Allowing the president to fire a court-appointed U.S. attorney also eliminates the incentive to nominate a candidate that can be conferred by the Senate — in other words, bypassing the requirement that the executive and legislative branches work together to nominate and confirm the U.S. attorney,” Bastian wrote.</p><h3><b>What does the law say?</b></h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/546" target="_blank" >The law</a> used to appoint Rogoff, Boutros and others allows the attorney general to name a U.S. attorney for 120 days. Then, if that appointment expires, it says the district court “may”<b> </b>appoint<b> </b>someone to that role.</p><p>Crucially, it says the court<b> </b>can appoint that person “to serve until the vacancy is filled.” That’s generally been taken as a reference to Senate confirmation of a presidential nominee.</p><p>“It does not say until that person is fired by the president,” Bastian pointed out<b> </b>in his order.</p><p>The Rogoff case is not the first to raise questions about the law.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Andrew Harnik/Associated Press</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Justice Department’s initial attempt<b> </b>to prosecute<b> </b>former FBI Director James Comey<b> </b>fell apart when a judge ruled that Lindsey<b> </b>Halligan<b> </b>had not properly been appointed U.S. attorney<b> </b>in Virginia<b> </b>under the law.</p><p>But the question in the Comey case revolved around who gets to choose the U.S. attorney once<b> </b>the attorney general’s initial<b> </b>120-day<b> </b>appointment<b> </b>expires. The Rogoff case<b> </b>turns on who can fire a judge-appointed U.S. attorney.</p><p>The Justice Department’s Freeman<b> </b>said a separate, but related, <a class="Link" href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/541" target="_blank" >statute</a> makes things clear.</p><p>It says, “each United States attorney is subject to removal by the president.”</p><h3><b>‘The president makes a choice’</b></h3><p>Freeman argued in court filings that Bastian’s ruling was "indefensible."</p><p>It means a top federal prosecutor “may wield the core executive power of criminal law enforcement however he pleases — without accountability to anyone, without risk of removal for any cause, and without regard to whether he is insubordinate, corrupt, incompetent, or malfeasant — for the foreseeable future, unless the Senate agrees to confirm a replacement,”<b> </b>Freeman and his colleagues argued.</p><p>Verrilli reminded the appeals panel<b> </b>that no one forced the president to use the law.</p><p>“The president makes a choice,” Verrilli said. “A voluntary choice to gain the benefit of [the law] and the fact that he can basically put anybody he wants in the office for that interim period. But it comes with a constraint. The president opts into the constraint.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/04/07/chicago-crime-justice-department-doj-boutros-trump-midway-blitz-corruption" >After rocky first year, Chicago’s top federal prosecutor says he isn’t taking orders from Washington</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The judges asked Freeman and Verrilli about prior court rulings and the practical implications of their arguments,<b> </b>including whether judges may remove the prosecutors they appoint.</p><p>Along the way, Verrilli acknowledged<b> </b>for Judge Bybee that a judge-appointed prosecutor has the same power as one confirmed by the Senate.</p><p>“Your contention is that he just can’t be removed under [the law] even though he is identical in authority, power and title?” Bybee asked.</p><p>That’s correct, Verrilli argued. Otherwise, the framework of the law has “basically unraveled,” he said.</p><p>“Congress made a judgment,” he told the panel, “that this is an office that should be subjected to the advice and consent power.”</p>

title: El desfile de Halloween Arts in the Dark regresa con 100,000 asistentes
author: Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ staff
content: <p>El desfile anual "Arts in the Dark" de Halloween se puso en marcha en la calle Balbo el sábado, atrayendo a un estimado de 100,000 asistentes con atracciones vibrantes y coloridas como un dragón que escupe fuego, alebrijes gigantes y un gusano luminoso de 60 pies.</p><p>El evento, que fue calificado por <a class="Link" href="https://10best.usatoday.com/lifestyle/best-halloween-parades-usa/" target="_blank" >USA Today</a> como "una de las mejores celebraciones de Halloween del mundo", tiene como objetivo incluir artistas de todos los ámbitos y de todos los distritos políticos de Chicago, dijeron los organizadores.</p><p>En su duodécimo año, el desfile contó con bandas marciales, grupos de baile y más de 1,000 intérpretes. Además de la inclusión de programas para jóvenes y organizaciones culturales, 11 distintas escuelas secundarias y tres universidades participaron en el evento de este año.</p><div title: Walter Koenig, Ensign Chekov on original ‘Star Trek’ series, dies at 90
author: AP
content: <p>LOS ANGELES (AP) — Actor Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov, the youthful Russian navigator on the “ <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/star-trek-60th-anniversary-plans-lego-6cab7180bc56ddb4255c5a7fb61cb6b7" target="_blank" >Star Trek</a> ” television series and several movies, has died. He was 90.</p><p>Koenig died Monday at his home in the North Hollywood neighborhood of Los Angeles, talent agent Zachery McGinnis said in a statement.</p><p>In “Star Trek,” Ensign Chekov was the sole Communist-bloc member of the spaceship Enterprise bridge staff. His friendly, supportive presence showed how the rival nations (in the far-off future in which the show was set) were capable of working together.</p><p>Speaking heavily Russian-accented English, Chekov embodied stereotypical Russian personality traits, including fierce pride, love of poetry and blind loyalty.</p><p>“Star Trek” ran on NBC from 1966 to 1969 and has had an almost unprecedented afterlife as fans, or Trekkies, kept interest in the show alive.</p><p>“My heart is heavy,” Koenig’s castmate, <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/george-takei-japanese-war-incarceration-book-07c2b803a951b766962ac029ce59da14" target="_blank" >George Takei</a>, said in a post on the social platform X. “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend.”</p><p>“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it,” McGinnis said. “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”</p><p>McGinnis said Koenig died surrounded by his daughter and niece.</p><p>Koenig was <a class="Link" href="https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/walter-koenig-dead-chekov-star-trek-russian-1236740088/" target="_blank" >born in Chicago</a> on Sept. 14, 1936, to Lithuanian immigrant parents. He played Chekov in seven “Star Trek” movies starting in 1979, as well as innumerable other spinoffs, including writing a “Star Trek” book, “Chekov’s Enterprise,” in 1980. The TV show has also inspired two spinoff TV series with new casts and conventions that draw thousands of fans.</p><p>He returned to the science fiction genre with occasional appearances in the syndicated 1990s TV series “Babylon 5.”</p>

title: Photo of man suspected of knocking down woman at Red Line stop released by police
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>Chicago police are searching for a man accused of pushing a 27-year-old CTA passenger to the ground earlier this month at a CTA Red Line station on the South Side. </p><p>The female passenger, who suffered minor injuries, was approached from behind and pushed to the ground before the man ran away Oct. 13 at the 95th/Dan Ryan station in Roseland, police said. </p><p>In a community alert, police issued a picture of the alleged attacker, described as a male wearing a green hooded sweater with yellow designs, black pants and green and white gym shoes. </p><p>Anyone with information is encouraged to contact public transportation detectives at 312-745-4447 or submit an anonymous tip at CPDTIP.com using reference RD No. JK449694.<br></p>

title: Second man dies after shooting at West Garfield Park gas station
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>A second man has died after a shoot-out late Saturday night at a West Garfield Park gas station, Chicago police said.</p><p>Antwon McCollum, 28, an unidentified 30-year-old man and another 28-year-old man were at the gas station in the 400 block of South Kostner Avenue around 10 p.m. when a white SUV pulled up and three armed men got out and started firing at them, according to police. The gunmen then returned to the car and fled. </p><p>The still-unidentified 30-year-old was shot in his neck and pronounced dead at Mount Sinai Hospital, and McCollum was pronounced dead at 5:28 a.m. Sunday at Mount Sinai Hospital, police said. </p><p>Another 28-year-old man was shot in his knee and taken in good condition to Stroger Hospital.</p><p>Police have not announced any arrests. </p>

title: Woman struck, critically injured by CTA bus in Lincoln Park
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>A woman was found lying in the road after a CTA bus hit her Sunday night in Lincoln Park on the North Side,police said. </p><p>Police found the woman, 40, just after 9 p.m. in the 2500 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive, according to Chicago police.</p><p>She was taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital, where she was listed in critical condition, police said. </p><p>No citations have been issued, and the the police department's major accident unit is investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash.</p>

title: Man, 26, gunned down in Greater Grand Crossing
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>A man was fatally shot Sunday night in Greater Grand Crossing on the South Side. </p><p>Around 9:40 p.m., a 26-year-old man was on the sidewalk in the 7000 block of South Eberhart Avenue when he was shot multiple times, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, police said. </p><p>Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

title: Dear Abby: Mom isn't keen on walk down memory lane with son
author: Abigail Van Buren
content: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am the mother of a beautiful 30-year-old son, "Caleb," who's married, employed and happy. We have a close relationship, and he thinks Mom and Dad (married 35 years) are awesome. He was also close to his "perfect" grandma, who died recently. He adored her, and she loved and spoiled him.</p><p>What he doesn't know is Grandma was a horrific parent who left my cold, heartless dad to marry another man, breaking up the family. Mom pushed me to graduate from high school early, forcing me into college when I wasn't prepared. I failed, and then she pushed me into a marriage at 20 to an abusive man so she could be alone with her new hubby. I divorced after two years of beatings, which she knew about before the wedding. She was manipulative and selfish even into her last days, which Caleb never saw.</p><p>Now Caleb wants me to do one of those "Mom, Tell Me About Your Life" books. I don't know what to say. Telling him I was previously married will be a jolt, but the "why" questions will be tougher. I don't want to lie, but I also don't want to ruin his image of his grandma. My husband says I should tell him only the basics, but I feel that would be a lie of omission. How do I proceed? — <i>TROUBLED PAST</i></p><p><b>DEAR TROUBLED PAST:</b> I'm sorry for the loss of your mother, even though you weren't on good terms. Caleb is old enough to understand your reasons for not wanting to participate in his project. Tell him you and your mom didn't always get along, and you'd prefer to spare him the unpleasant details. If he persists, add that these memories are painful and you don't care to relive them.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I thought I was having a private conversation with my husband on my daughter's porch. My daughter overheard some negative comments I made about her through her new home security system and was extremely hurt.</p><p>I have apologized and told her it wasn't meant for her to hear. I'm forgetful at 77, and I forgot she had told me about her new security system. We've had no contact since, even though I've sent birthday cards. She has no children but convinced her sister and her sister's kids to no longer have contact with us. What can I do? — <i>BIG MOUTH IN GEORGIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR BIG MOUTH:</b> I'm sorry you didn't mention what you said that caused you and your husband to become estranged from your children and grandchildren. Why you felt it was necessary to speak disparagingly about your daughter in her own home is puzzling, unless your relationship with her was strained to begin with.</p><p>You can apologize repeatedly for hurting her feelings, but there's no guarantee she will accept it. In the future, instead of opening your mouth, remember the words of Benjamin Franklin, who said, "I will speak ill of no man, and speak all the good I know of everybody." Especially family.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

title: Livestream execution plans may have pushed more Americans to rethink death penalty
author: Ben Jealous
content: <p>What if President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s push for more executions ends up helping America abolish the death penalty?</p><p>After this wild October, the question is not so far-fetched.</p><p>Hegseth wanted Americans to watch the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of murdering 13 people at Fort Hood. But some of the sharpest objections came from conservatives.</p><p>Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., called streaming the execution “beyond disgusting,” adding: “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do.” Sen. John Curtis, R-Utah, warned, “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b90000" name="module-b90000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos <a class="Link" href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/wide-majority-americans-oppose-livestreaming-nidal-hasans-execution/story?id=137263671" target="_blank" >poll</a> found 80% of Americans opposed the broadcast, including 64% of Republicans. Trump canceled the livestream on Oct. 15. The execution itself remains scheduled.</p><p>That distinction matters. Opposing a spectacle is not the same as opposing capital punishment. But look at what else happened this year.</p><p>On Oct. 20, Republican Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey commuted Toforest Johnson’s death sentence to life without parole.</p><p>Johnson was convicted of murdering a sheriff’s deputy. His conviction stands, but the local district attorney, former judges and others had questioned the evidence.</p><p>“I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death,” Ivey explained. She did not declare him innocent. She recognized that execution leaves no opportunity to correct a mistake.</p><p>Then there is Ohio Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. As a state senator in 1981, he voted to restore Ohio’s death penalty. After decades as a prosecutor, attorney general, U.S. senator and governor, he called for its abolition in June.</p><p>“The moral justification I had,” DeWine said, “no longer exists.” He concluded the death penalty does not deter murder and described the toll that decades of appeals exact on victims’ families. Ohio has not executed anyone since 2018. Bipartisan repeal legislation is pending, although legislative opposition remains.</p><p>Those are not identical positions. They do, however, raise questions conservatives have particular reasons to ask: How can we distrust government with ordinary powers yet trust it never to execute an innocent person? And what does justice require when punishment becomes a spectacle?</p><p>There is also a constitutional reason to pay attention.</p><p>Fifty years ago, in Gregg v. Georgia, the Supreme Court allowed executions to resume. But the Eighth Amendment still forbids cruel and unusual punishment. In Atkins v. Virginia, the Court prohibited executing people with intellectual disabilities. In Roper v. Simmons, it prohibited executing people for crimes committed before age 18.</p><p>Both rulings considered America’s “evolving standards of decency,” including the number of states rejecting those practices and the direction of change.</p><p>Today, 23 states have abolished the death penalty. Ten more retain it but have gone at least a decade without carrying out an execution. That is 33 states — two-thirds of the country — where executions have been abolished or absent for at least 10 years.</p><p>Just three more abolition states would make a majority. That would not automatically make capital punishment unconstitutional. The Supreme Court has no simple 26-state rule. But the growing rarity of executions is evidence future justices would have to confront.</p><p>The cruelty, meanwhile, is impossible to dismiss. In September, Tennessee’s attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection failed. She survived, and Republican Gov. Bill Lee halted the state’s remaining scheduled executions pending an independent review.</p><p>September also marked 15 years since Georgia executed Troy Davis. I stood outside that prison. Seven of nine key witnesses had recanted or changed their accounts. William Sessions, FBI director under Presidents Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush, urged Georgia to stop. It did not.</p><p>I helped lead Maryland’s successful abolition campaign in 2013, making it the first state south of the Mason-Dixon Line to end capital punishment. I learned then that this cause can unite people who disagree on almost everything else: believers in redemption, skeptics of government and people determined not to risk an irreversible injustice.</p><p>Virginia became the first former Confederate state to abolish the death penalty five years ago. More executions are taking place in some states now; today’s Court may be unwilling to overturn the punishment. Hope should not be confused with certainty.</p><p>But this October brought something real: Republicans rejected an execution broadcast, one governor spared a man amid doubts, and another is asking his state to end executions altogether.</p><p>Those are not the same steps. They are steps in the same direction.</p><p>Maybe Trump and Hegseth have inadvertently done something abolitionists could not: made more Americans look squarely at what government killing means.</p><p>Fifty years after executions resumed, that may help us finally bring them to an end.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7e0000" name="module-7e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

title: Sexual assault allegations arise from Country Thunder music festival, this time at Arizona locale
author: Robert Herguth
content: <p>Held each summer on the Illinois-Wisconsin border, the Country Thunder music festival has been the scene of sexual violence over the years, as young female concert-goers have come forward to say they were given alcohol and possibly knockout drugs — and then raped by men at the event.</p><p>As the Chicago Sun-Times reported earlier this year, there was at least one sexual assault reported in 2025, 2024, 2022, 2017 and 2015 at the event, which serves as a large draw for Chicago area teenagers and young adults as country music’s popularity surges in the Midwest.</p><p>Recently obtained records provide further evidence that such incidents have not been limited to the Kenosha County locale. Police have fielded reports of two possible sexual assaults involving women at the festival’s Florence, Arizona, location earlier this year.</p><p>On April 13, a 24-year-old woman went to a medical facility to report she “was possibly drugged and sexually assaulted at Country Thunder,” according to records from the Pinal County, Arizona, sheriff’s office.</p><p>Two days earlier, around 8 p.m., the woman indicated she “was near the main stage area and purchased alcohol at a white vendor tent,” according to a police report.</p><p>She “bought a White Claw and the vendor opened it in front of her,” and “she returned to where her brother and his friend were, and placed her drink on the ground while hanging out listening to music.”</p><p>“It is unknown how long the drink was out of her control before picking it back up to consume it. After finishing the drink, [NAME REDACTED] felt tired and a little out of it.”</p><p>Later, she went to buy more drinks and “on the way back to her brother, she stopped to talk to some unknown people” but does not remember much of “what occurred after that, and woke up the next morning naked in a random recreational vehicle at an unknown campground.”</p><p>Upon waking, “there were three men and a woman still partying in and outside of the RV,” according to the police reports.</p><p>“While at the RV she could recall being touched by two of the males and she could remember telling them ‘no thank title: In UK, police dogs are trained to sniff out date-rape drugs, but it's not something cops here have embraced
author: Robert Herguth
content: <p>Young women have reported being given what they believe were knockout drugs before being sexually assaulted at the Country Thunder music festival on the Illinois-Wisconsin border in past years, which begs the question:</p><p>How can organizers or police at the multi-day outdoor festival, or any other events, stop people from bringing in and using “roofies” or other date-rape drugs such as GHB?</p><p>There may be no single or easy answer, but overseas, police are trying a new tactic: training canines to sniff out drugs known to be used significantly in facilitating sexual assaults.</p><p>The Thames Valley Police in England have started training their dogs to identify such drugs and begun using them in patrols to not only catch offenders, but serve as a deterrent, officials said.</p><p>“These are planned offenses,” said the police department’s Sgt. Lath, who asked that his first name not be used. “So it’s really about turning the tables” on offenders, “going out and looking for them.”</p><p>Part of the aim is also to “let people know this is a new tactic,” and that “we’re out proactively,” Lath said. “We’ll quite often go into pubs and clubs.”</p><p>“The dogs have proven successful,” he said, adding they’re trained to detect an array of drugs, with the most common “spiking” substances now among them.</p><p>If an illegal substance is sniffed out, there’s “a change in behavior” with the dog that the handler watches for, Lath said.</p><p>His agency is discussing this canine program with other British police departments interested in possibly following suit.</p><p>In the United States, privacy laws and practices can differ, along with crime patterns, and police resources and priorities — and local policing agencies don’t appear to be embracing the concept, at least not yet.</p><p>“At this time, our canines do not sniff for drugs that may be used in sexual assaults,” a Chicago Police Department spokeswoman said.</p><p>“CPD’s canines are trained for various duties that include building searches for hidden offenders, locating missing persons, tracking suspects who have fled the scene of a crime, performing article searches, detecting narcotics or explosives, and conducting public service canine demonstrations.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5e0000" name="image-5e0000"></a> dogs, “of which a little more than half are certified by the state to detect the following four substances and their derivatives: cocaine, heroin, methamphetamines and cannabis. The first three substances are illegal with no carve outs for medical or therapeutic use, and cannabis has strict laws governing legal possession, quantity and use.”</p><p>“The sheriff’s office does not train its K9s to detect drug compounds that may be legally possessed for legitimate medical or therapeutic use. There are significant Constitutional and legal restrictions on how and when K9s may be used even when deployed to search for illegal narcotics they are certified to detect, and these restrictions would be even tighter if the substances K9s are asked to detect have legitimate legal uses.”</p><p>“Ketamine and GHB, which are two of the three drugs often considered ‘date rape’ drugs, can be legally prescribed in the U.S. The third, Rohypnol, cannot be prescribed, but is in the benzodiazepine class of therapeutic drugs and is chemically similar to Xanax, Valium, Klonopin, and other commonly prescribed drugs used to treat anxiety, sleeplessness and withdrawal.”</p><p>A spokeswoman for the Illinois State Police said: “ISP canines are not trained to detect ‘date rape drugs.’ Canines are currently focused on detecting (imprinted on) methamphetamine, heroin, cocaine and crack cocaine.”</p><p>“We are not aware of law enforcement agencies in the U.S. training and utilizing K9s to detect date rape drugs. ISP is consistently having discussions about how best to utilize the resources available to us in the pursuit of justice. Please note, ISP K9’s main jurisdiction and focus is on drug interdiction along highways and major routes across Illinois.”</p><p>The State Police has about 70 canines statewide.</p><p>Use of knockout drugs in sexual assaults has been a major concern for years. More recently, in at least one of the cases involving reports of sexual assaults at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >University of Chicago fraternity houses,</a> allegations surfaced that the victim drank alcohol that might have been spiked. In that case, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/21/university-chicago-sexual-assault" >a woman told Chicago police</a> she feared she was drugged before being sexually assaulted at the Alpha Delta Phi house in February.</p><p>Some experts say it’s worth exploring whether to broaden the drug menu the dogs are trained on, noting it’s not that difficult to add one or more compounds to the training mix.</p><p>Brandon Parker, founder and CEO of Rockford-based MPIK9 that trains police and security dogs, said: “Would it be effective here? Yes. Is it being used here? Not that I know of.”</p><p>He added, “It’s a good idea.”</p>

title: Music fans rally to support Dean Schlabowske of Waco Brothers after leukemia diagnosis
author: Mark Guarino
content: <p>Musician and songwriter Dean Schlabowske spent nearly 40 years building an audience by returning to their towns, sharing meals and drinks after shows, and connecting with people through a common love of music.</p><p>He is now witnessing the payback. Last month, after returning from playing shows in the United Kingdom with his band the Waco Brothers, Schlabowske received a surprise medical diagnosis: Acute Myeloid Leukemia, an aggressive cancer of the blood and bone marrow that leads to heightened fatigue, shortness of breath and easy bruising.</p><p>Suddenly, his life turned upside down.</p><p>Instead of writing his next record or playing shows around town, he is now facing full days managing multiple medications, specialist appointments and chemotherapy treatments. Looming on the horizon: insurmountable medical costs, heading into the six digits.</p><p>For a musician whose income is built through touring and side jobs, both of which were no longer possible, the shift left him facing a dire outcome: “Put everything on credit cards and go bankrupt,” he said.</p><p>But then a friend in Austin, Texas, launched <a class="Link" href="https://www.gofundme.com/f/donate-to-support-dean-and-jo-right-now?attribution_id=sl:a23b8578-708f-4e83-83f1-c2636551b681&amp;lang=en_US&amp;ts=1792437780&amp;utm_campaign=fp_sharesheet&amp;utm_content=amp30-treatment-3&amp;utm_medium=customer&amp;utm_source=facebook_story" target="_blank" ><u>a fundraising campaign through GoFundMe</u></a> to see if friends could help. Within a week, donors met the limit of $65,000 and it is now hovering around $80,000. Schlabowske said he does not recognize many of the donor names but suspects they all have a common trait: “They’re fans.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“You put that good karma out there for a lot of years, and it pays dividends when you need it,” said Schlabowske.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Dean Schlabowske</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“When I was super young and toured, me and the guys in the band thought it was cool to have this punk rock attitude where we were more cynical and not as outgoing and friendly, but I learned pretty quickly what you’re doing while you’re touring is creating goodwill,” he said. “You put that good karma out there for a lot of years and it pays dividends when you need it. I’m not going to lie. There are times I get pretty emotional about it.”</p><p>Schlabowske, 61, grew up in Milwaukee but moved to Chicago in 1987 where he got a job working at the legendary Wax Trax! record label. Through his noise rock band Wreck, he became a part of the city’s thriving post-punk scene for years. The trio recorded its debut EP with Steve Albini in 1990 and four years later hired Mekons co-founder Jon Langford, who had recently moved to Chicago from Wales, to produce its follow-up.</p><p>By then, Schlabowske had discovered country music and, with Langford and his fellow Welshman Tracey Dear, he formed the country punk band the Waco Brothers. The group performed its first show standing atop the bar at the Rainbo Club in Wicker Park. By 1995, the group released “To the Last Dead Cowboy,” their first recording which served as a pioneering statement for the burgeoning alternative country movement in Chicago.</p><p>With three principal songwriters — Schlabowske, Langford, and Dear — the Waco Brothers remain one of the most enduring bands out of Chicago that have tackled political and social injustice in their music for decades.</p><p>Over the years, Schlabowske released records with his side project Dollar Store and, in recent years, he collaborated with his wife, Jo Walston, who once headed the Austin band the Meat Purveyors, on playing bluegrass and honkytonk country.</p><p>Schlabowske received his diagnosis at an urgent care clinic where he went after a few weeks of feeling fatigued and nauseous. Not long after, Walston raced him to emergency care after his breath became dangerously short. After a week of procedures, he started his first round of chemotherapy. Complicating matters is the discovery of a weak heart valve that will require open heart surgery. He is commuting weekly from the couple’s Old Irving Park apartment to Lutheran General Hospital in Park Ridge.</p><p>Since his diagnosis, Schlabowske has put music on the back burner and is instead focusing on his regimen of appointments and medication, and taking a daily walk. He cannot see people for fear of an infection. At first, he had to board his two dogs, but they are expected home soon because he says he needs the emotional relief.</p><p>Despite the life change, he is taking everything in with a healthy dose of humor. “I’m 61. I’ve done a lot of cool [stuff]. Do I want to live to 100? Sure, but if that’s not meant for me, that’s not meant for me. This didn’t happen when I was 30. Any other way of looking at it leads to a dead end of depression,” he said.</p><p>Schlabowske and Walston recently relocated back to Chicago after living for a spell in Louisiana. He is insured through Walston’s job as a bookkeeper for a local business, but Schlabowske says the combination of a $10,000 deductible for this year and next, plus skyrocketing medical costs, make it not enough. </p><p>The response to the GoFundMe, he said, has been humbling, especially as he scrolls through donor names of people he knew or even briefly met five, 10, 20, 30 or more years ago. They are living proof of the community that music and audience can build together over years across cities, towns and even countries.</p><p>“A lot of those names that I don’t recognize are probably people I had a really pleasant conversation with at some point along the way,” he said. “I’ve always shied away from promoting myself. But I’m immensely grateful and incredibly touched that there are so many people who wanted to help out in such a big way. I never expected it.”</p>

title: The new transit authority has unprecedented power to develop land. How could this change your neighborhood?
author: David Struett
content: <p>When lawmakers passed the law creating the Northern Illinois Transit Authority nearly a year ago, they spoke about the new agency’s grand mission to transform Chicago-area public transit.</p><p>To make that happen, lawmakers concentrated power in NITA that its predecessor, the Regional Transportation Authority, never had. For the first time, the umbrella agency over the CTA, Metra and Pace could set fares, control construction projects and set rail and bus service.</p><p>But, tucked inside the thousand-page-plus law, they also granted NITA unprecedented power to buy and develop land near transit.</p><p>The technical term for this is transit-oriented development, or TOD. It’s the method for building on underused land near transit to boost ridership. The point is to make those areas more desirable places to walk, live, work and shop.</p><p>For years, transit agencies in other major American cities like Washington, D.C., have had powers to develop underused, transit-owned land.</p><p>The NITA Act catches Chicago up to its peers. But it goes further by granting power to buy and develop land for reasons unrelated to transit, said Yonah Freemark, an expert on the method at the Urban Institute, a DC-based think tank.</p><p>"There are some provisions that give NITA substantial power for undertaking transit-oriented development projects itself that virtually no other transit agency across the country has,” he said. "This could be a potentially massive change."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e40000" name="image-e40000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/90c8403/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/87d90d4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13a204f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Transit-oriented development 43G One opened in 2023 at 4308 S. Calumet in Bronzeville." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13a204f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/738ec9e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13a204f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F12%2F01%2Fe73f2e01453ab1a3aa30cf41f82f%2F43green-041923-18.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Transit-oriented development 43G One opened in 2023 at 4308 S. Calumet in Bronzeville.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The law gives NITA sweeping powers to build on land near transit. It allows NITA to undertake public-private partnerships, called joint developments. The agency can take on debt, offer incentives for developers and condemn land, so long as it has a municipality's approval.</p><p>NITA officials say they are committed to using these new powers. But there are challenges. The agency still has to create its own development office. Developing anything right now is difficult because of high loan and construction costs. And any NITA-led development could still be years away.</p><h3>Why do it?</h3><p>NITA’s new powers could accelerate development near transit, said Juan Sebastian Arias, who has been advocating for TOD for years as leader of Downtown nonprofit Elevated Chicago.</p><p>“It’s such a huge opportunity,” Arias said. “NITA doesn't have to do this on their own. There's opportunities to partner with the city or municipalities who have their own vacant land near stations.”</p><p>There are many potential benefits. Households can potentially save up to $10,000 a year in transportation costs, according to the Chicago-based Metropolitan Planning Council. TOD <a class="Link" href="https://metroplanning.org/projects/equitable-transit-oriented-development/" target="_blank" ><u>increases access</u></a> to jobs, especially among low-income families, and can also lead to higher home values, higher retail sales, lower obesity rates and less traffic congestion with fewer people driving, the council found.</p><p>Other cities have been pushing for developing land near transit for years.</p><p>The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority has built 10,800 new homes in the last five years. Los Angela's Metro is working to build 10,000 homes on agency-owned land in the next five years. The Bay Area Transit Authority in Northern California has built more than 4,200 homes near transit.</p><p>The city of Chicago has been encouraging TOD since 2013, when the City Council passed an ordinance removing some of the parking spot minimums for new buildings near train stations.</p><p>The city bolstered transit development again in 2021 when it passed an ETOD policy — for equitable transit-oriented development — that sought to push transit development while making sure low-income residents are not pushed out. </p><p>Since then, the city has made <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/12/chicago-progress-equitable-transit-oriented-development-5-years-policy-push-report" target="_blank" >substantial progress</a> developing city-owned land near transit, according to a May report from Elevated Chicago. More than 100 of those projects are <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/06/12/chicago-progress-equitable-transit-oriented-development-5-years-policy-push-report" target="_blank" >underway</a>.</p><h3>Win-win development</h3><p>But as the city pushed TOD-friendly policies, Chicago's transit agencies struggled to spur development themselves.</p><p>NITA's predecessor, the RTA, could help municipalities plan development but not lead it.</p><p>"We've been doing planning studies ... <a class="Link" href="https://nita.illinois.gov/communities/community-planning" target="_blank" >for nearly 30 years</a>," said Heather Mullins, NITA's division manager for local planning. "But that's really all we could do."</p><p>The NITA Act changes that. Now, NITA is in the driver's seat. </p><p>NITA can now partner with developers to build on transit-owned land, "something we've wanted to be doing for quite some time," Mullins said.</p><p>But first the agency must staff a new office to lead such projects. NITA is in the process of hiring a manager for that department, which will have about 10 employees, she said.</p><p>Mullins acknowledged that lawmakers have given NITA immense power to build up areas near transit, including the power to buy land. But first, Mullins said, NITA plans to build up unused land now owned by transit agencies.</p><p>Under the law, NITA must inventory all underused transit-owned parcels and publish the list by June 2027. That list isn’t public yet. But Mullins said the agency has identified 3,000 underused parcels owned by transit agencies. She said 91 of them are ripe for development. Most of them are in the suburbs. That's enough land near transit to build 8,500 homes.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" The agency should start taking proposals from developers in 2028, Mullins said. Building could start in 2029. After that, NITA hopes to be doing four or five TOD projects a year.</p><p>NITA plans to put $10 million toward these projects, many of which will be affordable housing, she said.</p><p>These projects benefit everyone, Mullins said.</p><p>"It's beneficial to the transit agencies. We're making it easier for people to access transit. It builds our ridership,” she says. “It's also beneficial to the communities. We can bring housing. We can bring more walkable communities."</p><p>Mullins said they found there’s not much money to be made from development. But NITA aims first to increase needed housing, she said. Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagobusiness.com/opinion/city-that-works/ccb-city-that-works-housing-crisis-needs-solutions-20261015/" target="_blank" >ranks last</a> among big cities for issuing new housing permits.</p><h3>Building supercharged</h3><p>The NITA Act also overhauls a major obstacle to building cheaper, dense projects near transit: mandatory parking spot minimums.</p><p>Called People Over Parking, the new rule eliminates all municipal parking spot requirements within half a mile of a rail station, and within one city block of bus corridors.</p><p>That's key for spurring development, said Audrey Wennink, a senior director of transportation policy with the Metropolitan Planning Council.</p><div class="Enhancement" Juicy, pink guava preserve from Michoacán and cheese are folded directly into the laminated croissant dough for a crispy, tropically sweet-salty all-day treat. ><b><u>Floriole Cafe &amp; Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>1220 W. Webster Ave., Lincoln Park</i><br>The mild-mannered answer to Good Ambler’s chocoholic pastry, Floriole’s chocolate croissant earns its spot for achieving sweet-salty harmony. Because the croissant is a little extra salty, the cocoa-sweetness of the chocolate shines through. Best case: Pick one up within two hours of opening, because when the chocolate is still a bit warm, it melts into gooey harmony with the innermost ring of pastry, like the inside of a soft-baked chocolate chip cookie.</p><h3><b>Ham and cheese croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://badbutterchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Bad Butter</u></b></a></h3><p><i>1655 W. Cortland St., Bucktown</i><br>Actor-turned pro baker Dan Koester moved from professional pastry kitchens to his home during the pandemic, hawking his sourdough creations as Dan the Baker before eventually <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/food-drink/2026/04/08/sourdough-bakeries-chicago-instagram" >debuting his brick-and-mortar storefront</a> in April. Bad Butter is known for creatively remixed, extra-crunchy croissants, zhuzhed into creations like Chicago-style hot dogs. Even the staple ham and cheese becomes pastry fine dining in Koester’s capable hands. The rich, flaky leaves encase sliced herbed porchetta from Tempesta Artisan Salumi, whole-grain mustard and Gruyère cheese, the latter of which melts into a cracker-crisp cheese skirt.</p><h3><b>Pain au raisin, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/guillotinebakery/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><b><u>Guillotine Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>1711 W. Chicago Ave., West Town</i><br>Open since June, this popular West Town newcomer channels Parisian baking with an edge, as its French Revolution-inspired name suggests. Boasting one of the best baguettes in town, the high-gloss pastries also lean classically French, as in pain au chocolat, plain croissants (both available in hilariously oversized, $40ish versions as well) and pain suisse with pastry cream. My go-to is the pain au raisin, a golden, buttery coil made from the same laminated croissant dough. Each layer of this crisp, chewy-tender revelation is swiped with sturdy custard studded with tangy sultana jewels.</p><h3><b>Banana pudding croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.sugarmoonchicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Sugar Moon Bakery</u></b></a></h3><p><i>3612 W. Wrightwood Ave., Logan Square</i><br>From owner Dina Cimarusti’s tiny Logan Square storefront, Sugar Moon slings high-concept yet rustic sweet and savory baked goods well worth the interminable lines. The staple banana pudding croissant, packing vanilla custard, just-caramelized banana, salty caramel, whipped mascarpone and vanilla-tinged crumb, is a balanced, light-yet rich textural marvel on its own. But its pastry vessel speaks just as loud via flaky, golden layers with a rustly crunch. Tip: You may have better luck on Fridays at this weekends-only shop. Regardless, plan to come early, and wait.</p><h3><b>Chocolate croissant, </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.misericordia.com/pages/hearts-flour-bakery-and-cafe" target="_blank" ><b><u>Misericordia Hearts &amp; Flour Bakery</u></b></a><b> </b></h3><p><i>6130 N. Ravenswood Ave., West Ridge</i><br>The third chocolate croissant entry on this list, Hearts &amp; Flour’s version suits the mornings that require an extra drizzle of indulgence. The golden, crackly exterior is squiggled with chocolate before giving way to a tender, buttery middle packed with more chocolate. While the weather cooperates, pair it with a floral, citrusy cardamom orange cold brew. In case you need another excuse to visit, this sunny cafe employs adults with developmental disabilities, matching responsibilities to unique abilities.</p><div class="Enhancement" Sedgwick St., River North</i><br>A crunchy, silken brunch fixture since this raucous neo-bistro opened four years ago, Obelix’s visually striking pistachio croissant began life as a special from then-pastry chef Antonio Incandela (now pastry chef/owner at Mariscos San Pedro). It became a brunch staple owing to its popularity. Now in the capable hands of executive pastry chef Courtney Kenyon-Snider, the green-striped, laminated dough envelops a cloud of satiny, not-too-sweet pistachio pastry cream that smacks of gelato. It’s available for pickup on weekends as part of the restaurant’s preorder pastry program.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a30000" name="module-a30000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>For more on Chicago dining:</h3><ul id="rte-0d956412-d14c-11f1-8cc2-2719644f60b0"><li>Art and food collide at singer and chef Lizz Wright’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/10/21/singer-chef-lizz-wright-monica-haslip-the-hunt-chicago-restaurant" ><u>new Woodlawn cafe</u></a></li><li>A new Chicago brewery is making Korea’s oldest alcoholic drink, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/10/19/yido-makgeolli-brewery-chicago-peter-chung" ><u>makgeolli</u></a></li><li>A foodie hot take: The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/04/01/onion-burgers-oklahoma-hot-take-smash-burger" ><u>onion burger</u></a> is criminally underrated</li><li>Is Chicago suddenly <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/food-drink/2026/06/03/popup-bagels-chicago-rosca-local-bagel-shops" ><u>a bagel town</u></a>?</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

title: Top movies we saw at this year’s Chicago International Film Festival: Reginald Ponder’s picks
author: Reginald Ponder
content: <p>The Chicago International Film Festival is a movie lover’s delight, showcasing more than 100 feature films and nearly 60 short films. While it was impossible to see it all, it was possible to curate a slate of films that piqued my curiosity. In addition to special events, red carpets and interviews, I saw 19 feature films and eight short films over 12 days. Here are the films that made my top five “most” list. Each is worthy of your viewing, so keep an eye out for opportunities to see them.</p><h3>Most Galvanizing: “14th”</h3><p>This documentary by Ava DuVernay takes a look at the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and what it means to exist in the world today and to the promise that America makes to its citizens. Through a series of interviews, DuVernay connects the 14th Amendment’s origins to today’s attacks on its protections, including birthright citizenship and the right to vote. The film also addresses the clause concerning disqualification from office for insurrection or rebellion. What might feel like a lecture becomes more of a call to action to participate and protect fundamental ideals of equality and justice. DuVernay does an exceptional job of weaving together interviews, commentary by politicians, educators and even comedians, historical material and current-day footage to illustrate the relevance of this discussion and simply why we should care. Powerful, personal and promising.</p><p><i>“The 14th” will premiere worldwide on Netflix on Dec. 4, following a theatrical release in select U.S. theaters beginning Nov. 27.</i></p><div The documentary takes a look at the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Paul Garnes/Netflix </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Most Inspiring: “Elsinore”</h3><p>This film follows the life of actor Ian Charleson, who finds himself in the middle of an opportunity and a tragedy. He has AIDS and is offered the part of Hamlet at the National Theatre of London after Daniel Day-Lewis drops out. Charleson’s struggle asks the question: Is it better to live to have life, or is it better to have life while you live, truly live? There is nothing more poignant than Hamlet’s existential investigation of “to be or not to be, that is the question.” This is a question Charleson, who died in 1990, confronts with vigor and valor. The filmmakers deliberately tie Hamlet’s plight to Charleson’s journey, elevating the play beyond a mere performance within a film. It becomes a commentary on mortality steeped in Charleson’s reality. Beautifully shot, excellently scored and personally piercing.</p><p><i>“Elsinore” will open in limited theaters Nov. 20.</i></p><h3>Most Intimate: “Once Upon a Time in Harlem”</h3><p>This film completes the work of famed filmmaker William Greaves. The documentary brings together Black luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance to discuss that time period and its impact. Greaves’ son David and granddaughter Liani embarked on the humongous task of taking hours of footage and allowing viewers to be a fly on the wall as these groundbreakers reminisced and debated what it meant to be Black and brilliant. You will laugh as they laugh, ponder as they pontificate, question as they challenge each other and marvel as they recount the memories of those who helped pave the way. “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” allows us to witness history and passes the baton for us to continue the conversation today.</p><p><i>“Once Upon a Time in Harlem” opened in theaters in October and is not available for streaming yet.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-840000" name="image-840000"></a> <picture
