“All of a Sudden”</h3><p>Marie, a nursing home director, struggles to convince her institution to revolutionize patient care from speed and profit to humane, self-affirming treatment. A chance encounter with Mari, a terminally ill playwright and director, sparks a bond that reshapes Marie’s quest to make the seemingly impossible possible, providing care that restores dignity and individuality.</p><p>“All of a Sudden” is loud in its protest against the mistreatment of the elderly, yet tender and quiet in the friendship and love Mari and Marie share. That bond extends to their approach to patient care. It is heartwarming to see residents viewed as people rather than profits or problems. The film asks what it truly means to live, proposing that everyone, including Mari, Marie and the elderly, deserves that chance. “All of a Sudden” is a powerful protest softened by life’s reality and affirmed through the dignity and humanity demanded by its finality. </p><p><i>“All of a Sudden” is scheduled for a U.S. theatrical release on Nov. 25.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" graduating from high school. Minnie, played by Katherine Mallen Kupferer, is Callie’s best friend who lives in the shadows of Callie’s talents and personality. A tragic accident leaves Helen and Minnie trying to find their place in this new world without Callie. Their need to stay connected to Callie in some form or fashion threatens boundaries and creates a dysfunction that is simply unsustainable. “Mouse” is an interesting exploration of grief through the eyes of both Helen and Minnie but also all the lives Callie touched. It is sad, funny and unnerving, but the range of emotions is necessary for these two to discover life after loss. Chicago directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson present a slice of life that feels real and thoughtful. And the lead actors bring an authenticity to the roles that says, “I know these people and I know this pain.”</p><p><i>“Mouse” in open in limited theaters Nov. 6, before expanding to wider audiences on Nov. 13.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-050000" name="module-050000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>For more film news:</h3><ul id="rte-132811b2-cc02-11f1-93e8-d7a4a3eaa479"><li>From film icons to NBA stars, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/15/chicago-international-film-festival-celebrity-movie-red-carpet-john-c-reilly-derrick-rose" ><u>these celebrities</u></a> are in town for CIFF</li><li>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/08/25/chicago-international-film-fest-2026-lineup-bob-odenkirk-curtis-duffy-martin-mcdonagh" ><u>2026 CIFF lineup</u></a> includes documentaries on Bob Odenkirk, chef Curtis Duffy</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/06/25/chicago-music-box-theatre-debuts-third-screen-lakeview-movie-expansion" ><u>Chicago’s Music Box Theatre</u></a> debuted its third screen earlier this year</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

content: <h2>Moon alert</h2><p>There are no restrictions to shopping or important decisions today. The full moon peaks in Taurus today.</p><h2>Aries (March 21-April 19)</h2><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p>Parents have to be patient with their kids today. All of you have to be patient with others when discussing shared property, taxes, debt and inheritances as well as social occasions and involvement with friends and groups. People are at odds with each other today! Mum’s the word.</p><h2>Taurus (April 20-May 20)</h2><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-290000" name="html-embed-module-290000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>so-so</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p>There's no way to sugarcoat this. The full moon is in your sign, plus the moon is at odds with Pluto and Mars. "Our options are limited, Captain. We cannot fire, and we cannot flee." Yes, the logic of Spock. Sit this one out. Don't add fuel to the fire.</p><h2>Gemini (May 21-June 20)</h2><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p>Arguments and disputes are classic today because a number of planets are at odds with each other. Plus, it's a full moon in Taurus. Simply put, this means don't go looking for trouble because it will easily find you. Your work might be hampered by delays and mistakes.</p><h2>Cancer (June 21-July 22)</h2><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p>Naturally, with the moon being your ruler, you will feel the energy of today's full moon. But more than that, today's moon is at odds with both Pluto and Mars, encouraging competition, confrontations, even jealousy. Quarrels about money and possessions might take place.</p><h2>Leo (July 23-Aug. 22)</h2><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-290000" name="html-embed-module-290000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>so-so</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p>This is a challenging day because the full moon is at odds with your sign, possibly triggering irritation and annoyance with others. Some kind of situation will likely come to a head. One upside is that secrets could be revealed, which might be a good thing.</p><h2>Virgo (Aug. 23-Sept. 22)</h2><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p>You might be quick to make a retort to someone today, and you will notice that others are a bit touchy as well. Fortunately, today's full moon is supportive of you; nevertheless, you will have to be patient with others. title: 1 critically wounded in Little Village shooting
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>A 23-year-old man was critically wounded in a shooting Sunday morning in Little Village, Chicago police said.</p><p>The shooting victim was outside along the 3100 block of West Cermak Road at about 10:25 a.m. when two people approached him on foot before a physical altercation took place, police said.</p><p>The 23-year-old, who police said has a valid concealed carry license and firearm owner’s identification card, pulled out a gun and fired toward the assailants, according to police.</p><p>One of them was shot and taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in critical condition. No other injuries were reported, police said.</p><p>Area 4 detectives were speaking with a person of interest.</p>

title: Ex-Blackhawks defenseman Seth Jones isn't exactly welcomed back, has no hard feelings
author: Jeff Agrest
content: <p>Defenseman <b>Seth Jones</b> wasn’t exactly welcomed back Sunday to the United Center, where he played his first game since the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> traded him to the Panthers on March 1, 2025. There was no video tribute and no cheers for Jones, who badly wanted out of Chicago when the going got rough.</p><p>The deal has worked out for both sides. The Panthers got a quality player, and the Hawks got a quality goalie in <b>Spencer Knight</b>, who has stabilized the position. The Hawks also got a first-round draft pick, one of three they have in 2027.</p><p>Former Hawks general manager <b>Stan Bowman</b> had big plans for Jones after acquiring him in a draft-day blockbuster in 2021 and signing him to an eight-year, $76 million contract. Jones was supposed to take over for <b>Duncan Keith</b> as the Hawks’ top defenseman. But almost halfway through the contract, his frustration with all the losing became too much.</p><p>Still, Jones said he has ‘‘nothing but love’’ for the organization.</p><p>‘‘Had an experience here for four years,’’ said Jones, who missed the Panthers’ visit to Chicago last season because of a broken collarbone. ‘‘I like where I’m at now, but I wish this organization nothing but the best.</p><p>‘‘It was a good trade for both sides. I’m sure they’ll be very successful in the future when all these picks grow up and get more experience. It was awesome to be back for the first time.’’</p><p>Jones assisted on the Panthers’ second goal, a power-play goal, giving him 11 assists and 12 points for the season, both second on the team. He also logged 24 minutes, 55 seconds of ice time, more than anyone in the game, and put a team-high-tying four shots on goal.</p><p>On the goal, which gave the Panthers a 2-1 lead in the first period, Jones skated into the high slot with the puck and shot it toward the net. It probably would have gone wide, but it deflected in off <b>Matthew Tkachuk</b>.</p><p>‘‘I had so much time, I was kind of shocked,’’ Jones said. ‘‘I was just trying to get it in there. Sometimes you need those.’’</p><h3>Forsling returns, too</h3><p>Jones wasn’t the only former Hawks defenseman on the ice. <b>Gustav Forsling</b>, who played for the team in 2016-19, has turned into a shutdown defenseman for the Panthers, helping them to back-to-back Stanley Cup titles in 2024 and 2025.</p><p>But the Hawks weren’t the only ones who gave up on Forsling. The Canucks drafted him in 2014 and traded him to the Hawks the next year. The Hawks traded him to the Hurricanes, who put him on waivers in 2021. That’s when the Panthers claimed him.</p><p>‘‘Gustav was a late developer,’’ Panthers coach <b>Paul Maurice</b> said. ‘‘He just had to put some size on his frame, and he became so focused on his fitness and his size. He worked himself into being an NHLer. We’re lucky on that one, getting a player like that.’’</p><p>Forsling played 23:12, including a team-high 6:23 short-handed. He helped the Panthers kill all seven Hawks power plays.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Having played one of the toughest schedules in the league to start the season, the Hawks finally will face an opponent in their weight class Tuesday, when the Kings come to town. Both teams have six points. It will be the second of back-to-back games for the Kings, who visit the Rangers on Monday.</p><p>• Before the game, the Hawks honored defenseman <b>Ian Cole</b> for playing in 1,000 career games, a milestone he reached Friday. In 17 NHL seasons, he has 233 points (38 goals) and won Stanley Cups with the Penguins in 2016 and ’17.</p>

title: Blackhawks' frustrations mount as breakdown leads to third straight loss
author: Jeff Agrest
content: <p>Nothing is going right for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>. They certainly haven’t helped themselves much during a frustrating start to the season, but they haven’t been lucky, either.</p><p>Case in point: Ryan Donato. He had five prime scoring chances Sunday against the Panthers and didn’t convert any. Among them, he couldn’t push a sliding puck into an open net in the first period, and his stick broke after he was set up perfectly in the third.</p><p>The Hawks also couldn’t capitalize on Frank Nazar’s partial breakaway or Cole Smith’s breakaway from the red line, both in the third period. And they allowed the winning goal with 2:23 left after a bad change, falling to the Panthers 3-2.</p><p>The player responsible for the screw-up was defenseman Kevin Korchinski, who otherwise played well in his first game back after being scratched for seven in a row.</p><p>After getting a boost from Connor Bedard’s return and winning his first two games back, the Hawks have lost three in a row and have fallen to 3-8. Their schedule has been a gauntlet, and they’ve had their top forward (Bedard) and top defenseman (Bowen Byram) in the lineup for one game. But the promise of last season and the return of Patrick Kane haven’t yielded positive results.</p><p>‘‘There’s going to be frustration; we’re 3-8,’’ Bedard said. ‘‘You’ve got to use that in the next game and try to dig ourselves out. When you play with that edge, you play a little better. If we can do that the rest of the year, that’d be great.’’</p><p>Scoring would help. The Hawks have three goals during their skid. And for all the excitement surrounding Kane, he has one goal and a team-worst minus-13 plus/minus. He’s on the Hawks’ five-forward power-play unit, an experiment that hasn’t exactly worked. Overall, the power play went 0-for-7 against the Panthers.</p><p>‘‘The power play is mirroring our five-on-five game: We can’t score,’’ coach Jeff Blashill said. ‘‘I can’t say that we don’t get any chances; I think we do. Power plays are funny animals. You can get [lousy] power plays and score and good power plays not.</p><p>‘‘We’re just not scoring easy at all, and we have really good players that are going to score goals that are not scoring.’’</p><p>Shooting would help. The Hawks put 21 shots on net, right at their average. And when they did that, good things tended to happen. Ryan Greene opened the scoring with his first goal of the season. Korchinski shot the puck wide, but it went off the boards to Andrew Mangiapane, who passed to Greene in front of the net.</p><p>The Hawks veritably peppered Panthers goalie Akira Schmid with a whopping nine shots in the second period. One went in when Roman Kantserov took a pass from Kane in the right circle and beat Schmid to tie the score at 2.</p><p>The game appeared headed to overtime until the Hawks’ change went bad. Aaron Ekblad sent a pass from the Panthers’ own end to Lars Eller at the Hawks’ blue line. Eller skated in and beat Spencer Knight to his blocker side.</p><p>‘‘He’s going to want the change back,’’ Blashill said of Korchinski. ‘‘But I thought he played solid in that pair with [Sam Rinzel]. Both of them did a lot of good things. It’s unfortunate that he had the tough change.</p><p>‘‘I thought we did a lot of good things through the majority of the game. I thought the last half of the first [period] was the only time I didn’t like us at all. That was the only time I thought we got pushed around. But we came back out in the second. I thought [we] had great pushback in terms of competing. I thought we had great, great compete.’’</p><p>That hasn’t been enough, however.</p>

title: Optimist vs. Pessimist: There's no limit to what the Bears can do over the final 10 games
author: Jason Lieser
content: <p><i>For Patrick Finley's pessimistic look at the Bears' next 10 games, </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/25/bears-next-10-games-optimist-vs-pessimist-dig-out-nfc-north-hole" target="_blank" ><i>click here</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>The current version of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> requires some rewiring of the brain for anyone who has watched this team the last four decades. It’s the same uniform, the same logo and the same field, but a very different operation.</p><p>It’s no longer inevitable, or even probable, that the Bears will fall apart. The annual tradition of a four-to-six-game losing streak is done. There’s competency across the board, as evidenced by their impressive win over the Patriots, managing well during quarterback Caleb Williams’ three-game absence and the fact that they’ve won 17 of their last 24 games.</p><p>There’s every reason to be optimistic about where the Bears are headed, and it starts with coach Ben Johnson.</p><p>The mentality of the entire organization changed when he arrived. Goals got greater, standards got stricter and doubt got demolished. There had been a feeling of resignation toward certain realities, like the Packers’ dominance, but it’s not there anymore.</p><p>At 5-2, the Bears are in position to chase everything they want this season.</p><p>The schedule certainly gets tougher, but none of their remaining 10 games are daunting enough to concede. Even in the Nov. 2 visit to the defending champion Seahawks, the early line has the Bears as a negligible three-point underdog.</p><p>At their best, they have every piece necessary to make a run at the Super Bowl: a savvy head coach who has a handle on both sides of the ball, a game-changing quarterback surrounded by weapons and a dynamic defense.</p><p>Are they flawed? Yes, but that’s true of every team. It comes down to how well they can scheme around their flaws and compensate for them. Johnson and defensive coordinator Dennis Allen have consistently shown that ability.</p><p>The starting point on discussing whether any team can win a title is the coach and quarterback. For the first time in recent memory, the Bears check those boxes.</p><p>Johnson’s credibility is high enough that he pretty much skated on a botched trick play Thursday in which Williams handed the ball off illegally to left guard Joe Thuney. He brushed it off with, “Shooters shoot,” and it’s hard to imagine any recent Bears coach getting away with that.</p><p>He has shown an uncommon ability to adjust, whereas previous Bears teams had no shot if Plan A crumbled. He’s fully engaged in the defense and special teams, even though they aren’t his areas of expertise. And, most of all, he’s developing Williams into a championship-caliber quarterback.</p><p>The high-end talent was obvious with Williams his first two seasons, but he lacked a foundation. Johnson has helped establish the essentials — throwing accuracy, coverage recognition, quick reads, precise timing — and blended that with his remarkable improvisational skills.</p><p>If that continues, the Bears will finish at least 12-5. They won’t necessarily sweep their road games against the Seahawks, Bills and Lions — a tough ask for anyone — but, at minimum, they’ll hold their own.</p><p>This is a team that nearly made the NFC Championship Game last season and is playing better this season. There’s no limit on who the Bears can play with and how far they can go.</p>

title: Optimist vs. Pessimist: Bears could struggle to dig out of NFC North hole
author: Patrick Finley
content: <p><i>For Jason Lieser's optimistic look at the Bears' next 10 games, click </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/25/optimist-vs-pessimist-theres-no-limit-on-what-the-bears-can-do-over-the-final-10-games" target="_blank" ><i>here</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>It’s easy to be optimistic about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ first seven games. It gets harder to do so when you look at their final 10.</p><p>For all their success this season — to be 5-2 after starting three different quarterbacks is nothing short of remarkable — the Bears have struggled where it matters most: against the rest of the NFC North. Both their losses have come to divisional opponents: the Vikings in Week 2 and the Packers in an embarrassing Week 5.</p><p>The Bears have four more divisional games to play, starting with a Thanksgiving game against the Lions at Ford Field. To take the NFC North for the second-straight season, they’ll probably need to run the table against the Packers, Vikings and Lions.</p><p>That’s a difficult hill to climb, one far tougher than anything they’ve accomplished to this point this season. But if the Bears have their eyes on the NFC championship&nbsp;— and they should, given the way they’ve played — they know they have to position themselves to play as many playoff games at home as possible.<br>The Bears proved last year what a tremendous impact both their home crowd and freezing temperatures — wind chill was 26 degrees in the first playoff game and 11 in the second — can have in January.</p><p>They can’t put themselves in the same position this year without winning the NFC North. And they can’t win the NFC North without winning head-to-head matchups. At the least, they can’t count on it happening again.</p><p>When the Bears won the NFC North last year, they did so with just a 2-4 record. That had happened only two other times in the modern history of the sport, provided you throw out the 1982 strike year. Since the AFL-NFL merger in 1970, just two other teams won their division despite going 2-4 within it: the 1971 49ers and the 2010 Chiefs.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson has never beaten the Lions. That needs to change for the Bears to get where they want to go. A Christmas Day matchup against the Packers looms large, too — if the Packers, win they’ll hold the tie-breaker against their rivals. And then there are the Vikings, the team that leads the NFC North. At the start of the year, the Bears could look at their season finale in Minneapolis and dream of a scenario in which the Vikings, eliminated from the playoffs and perhaps chasing a better draft pick, simply rolled over. A lot would have to go wrong for the Vikings, who had the best defense in the NFL entering Sunday’s games, to freefall into irrelevance by Week 18.</p><p>The Bears’ schedule the rest of the season features two of the best three teams in the AFC: the Jaguars at home and the Bills on the road. The defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks await the Bears next week in Seattle, where they’ve lost just one game the past two seasons to teams not named the 49ers.</p><p>But nothing will be more important than what they do against the NFC North. After starting the season 0-2 against the division, they don’t have any further margin for error.</p>

title: Bulls slowly figuring some things out, but schedule about to turn brutal
author: Joe Cowley
content: <p>Rookie Caleb Wilson didn’t really need the reminder as someone recited the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" target="_blank" >Bulls</a>’ upcoming schedule to him.</p><p>‘‘It’s rough,’’ he said before hearing about a second game against the Celtics this week.</p><p>‘‘Rough’’ is one word that comes to mind. ‘‘Gauntlet,’’ ‘‘daunting’’ and ‘‘brutal’’ do, too, heading into the first of the Bulls’ two games this week against the Celtics on Monday.</p><p>Throw in two against the defending NBA champion Knicks, two against the new-look 76ers and a home game Nov. 11 against Victor Wembanyama and the Spurs, and Wilson and the Bulls are about to be tested in the next couple of weeks.</p><p>‘‘Every matchup is its own thing,’’ Wilson said. ‘‘Not every team has a Wemby; not every team has a Jayson Tatum. So every game we go out there with the approach that we need to be great players and do what we need to do because it’s about us.</p><p>‘‘I feel like, with this team, we’re really well-rounded, and I feel like that’s going to be to our benefit. I like us, so I’m excited for the opportunity.’’</p><p>The silver lining coming out of the weekend is that the Bulls’ starting five finally seems to be coming together — enough so that coach Tiago Splitter believed in them enough to try to finish the game with them Saturday against the Wizards.</p><p>That wasn’t the case Friday against the Bucks, when Splitter benched Matas Buzelis and Josh Giddey in favor of hot hands Isaac Okoro and Tre Jones down the stretch. Against the Wizards, however, Giddey had six assists and was a plus-10 in the fourth quarter, and Buzelis scored nine points in the quarter.</p><p>Both contributed to the Bulls’ comeback, which fell short, but neither led it.</p><p>No, that was Wilson, who scored 11 of his 30 points, grabbed five rebounds and handed out two assists in the fourth. It was the second consecutive game in which Wilson was the focal point in crunch time.</p><p>‘‘I feel like it shows that we have fight, but we put ourselves in that [bad] position,’’ Wilson said of the late-game push. ‘‘I wouldn’t say I’d give us a moral victory, but it’s good to know the character of the guys we have on this team.’’</p><p>That character is about to be tested by the toughest stretch the Bulls likely will have this season. But if the starting unit can continue to build the connectivity it showed against the Wizards, that will go a long way in trying to navigate that stretch.</p><p>‘‘Just an unselfishness, being able to move the ball, being able to trust each other,’’ Wilson said about the starting unit growing. ‘‘That’s all that really happened, and it led to a really good start. But you’ve got to do it for 48 minutes.’’</p><p>One positive about facing the Celtics, Knicks and 76ers is that none of those teams starts a lineup with two big men. The Wizards started Anthony Davis and Alex Sarr and staggered in Deandre Ayton.</p><p>The Celtics start Mitchell Robinson in the middle, but they’re more about the versatility they have on the wings in Tatum and Paul George. The Knicks have length up front with Karl-Anthony Towns, OG Anunoby and Mikal Bridges, but they don’t start two true big men.</p><p>‘‘I’m really tall, but I’m on the thinner side, so I just try and run and be faster than everyone,’’ Wilson said. ‘‘But, honestly, I feel like the biggest adjustment in playing double-bigs is knowing you have to box out and be physical. That was one of my biggest things [against the Wizards].’’</p><p>Two bigs or no bigs, however, Wilson is going to have to be physical during the next few weeks, given what’s coming.</p><p>‘‘Like I said, it’s going to be rough,’’ he said.</p>

title: Arts in the Dark Halloween Parade returns for its 12th year
author: Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ staff
content: <p>The annual Arts in the Dark Halloween Parade stepped off on Balbo Street Saturday, drawing in an estimated 100,000 attendees with vibrant, colorful attractions such as a fire-breathing dragon, giant alebrijes and a 60-foot glow worm.</p><p>The event, which was dubbed by <a class="Link" href="https://10best.usatoday.com/lifestyle/best-halloween-parades-usa/" target="_blank" ><u>USA Today</u></a> as “one of the best Halloween celebrations in the world,” has a goal to include artists from every field and from every ward of Chicago, organizers said.</p><p>In its 12th year, the parade featured marching bands, dance groups, and over 1,000 performers. In addition to the inclusion of youth programs and cultural organizations, 11 different high schools and three colleges participated in this year’s event.</p><div class="Enhancement" title: Lake Street bridge closure for CTA Green, Pink lines extended 2 days
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>CTA Green and Pink line trains will continue to be rerouted this week as ongoing construction on the Lake Street bridge is behind schedule by two days. </p><p>The two train lines were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/12/lake-street-bridge-cta-green-pink" target="_blank" >rerouted two weeks ago</a> to accommodate the ongoing repairs to the Lake Street bridge over the Chicago River. Those repairs are behind, the Chicago Department of Transportation announced Sunday. </p><p>Green and Pink line trains were set to resume their normal routes on Monday, but CDOT says that won't happen till Wednesday at 4 a.m. </p><p>Pink Line trains are currently not running through the Loop. Instead, the train line terminates at Racine, where riders can transfer to the Blue Line.</p><p>The Green Line has been operating in two separate sections. The Lake Street branch ends at Clinton, where riders can take a free shuttle bus to the Clark/Lake station. The Green Line’s southern branch continues running to the Loop, but winds around stations in a clockwise direction before returning south again.</p><p>The bridge has been closed to pedestrians and vehicle traffic for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/09/28/lake-street-bridge-repairs-closure-chicago" target="_blank" >just over a year</a> for renovation. Construction is estimated to last until January 2028.</p>

title: Bears QB Caleb Williams fined $11,941 for wearing Tom Brady-backed Caddix cleats; another fine likely coming
author: Jason Lieser
content: <p>The NFL fined <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/30/caleb-williams-wins-bears-over-with-rare-talent-but-even-rarer-people-skills" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> $11,941 for the cleats he wore in his return from a hamstring injury Oct. 18 against the Falcons, and he likely will be paying another fine for wearing them again Thursday against the Patriots.</p><p>The league said it fined Williams for a uniform violation because he wore cleats made by Caddix, a relatively new company that says the studs it uses will reduce non-contact knee and ankle injuries.</p><p>The NFL has partnerships with only Nike, Adidas and Under Armour. If a player wears a shoe made by any other brand, he must cover the logo. Players can’t promote any non-partner on game days, from pregame warmups through postgame media availability, and the league noted in its letter to Williams that the policy was communicated to all players before the season.</p><p>Williams wore Caddix cleats during the preseason and in the first two games of the regular season, including when he suffered a hamstring injury against the Vikings. But they were all-white, so the logo wasn’t prominent enough to cause an issue. Against the Falcons and Patriots, Williams wore black cleats with the gray Caddix logo clearly visible.</p><p>Williams was tremendous in both games. He completed 75.4% of his passes for a combined 613 yards and threw three touchdown passes with no turnovers for a 116.4 passer rating. The victory against the Patriots pushed the Bears to 5-2 leading up to their game next Monday at the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks.</p><p>Williams hasn’t had a shoe contract since entering the NFL as the No. 1 overall pick in 2024, which is unusual. Most players of his status have one, but he hasn’t wanted to be boxed in and frequently has worn Nike and New Balance. He wore Nike cleats in his first two seasons.</p><p>Hall of Famer Tom Brady works with Caddix and wore their cleats in the Fanatics flag-football event this year. Williams has been friends with Brady since reaching the NFL, and Brady occasionally is on the Fox broadcast team for Bears games.</p><p>Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco and 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk also have worn the Caddix cleats, and the company said roughly 40 players are wearing them this season.</p><p>Caddix produced its first cleats in 2024 and has made inroads in football, soccer and lacrosse. The brand has jumped on the opportunity for publicity with Williams wearing the cleats, and CEO Jack Rasmussen said in a statement that the company will pay any fines he receives.</p><p>The NFL fines players $5,971 for having a foreign substance on their uniform, using noncompliant pads and face masks, using an unapproved visor or wearing a uniform improperly. The $11,941 fine applies to displaying personal messages or unauthorized logos.</p><p>Williams has until Friday to appeal the fine.</p><p>The NFL also fined Bears wide receiver Jahdae Walker $5,620 for each of his penalties against the Falcons. Walker was flagged for hitting punter Jake Bailey in the third quarter and ejected for head-butting wide receiver Chris Blair in the fourth.</p>

title: Bears' defense looks great one moment, shaky the next, so what exactly is this group?
author: Jason Lieser
content: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ defense has been all over the place this season, and it was as erratic as ever <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/22/bears-inactives-vs-patriots-lb-t-j-edwards-out-with-hamstring-injury" target="_blank" >in their 30-24 victory Thursday against the Patriots</a> at Soldier Field.</p><p>The defense opened by forcing a turnover on downs and two three-and-outs, then got an interception in the end zone by linebacker D’Marco Jackson to keep points off the board. It also was fantastic on third downs, holding the Patriots to 2-for-7.</p><p>But it allowed an exasperating, inexcusable 48-yard touchdown pass just before halftime on a throw underneath from quarterback Drake Maye to running back Rhamondre Stevenson.</p><p>The Bears shut down the Patriots’ running game but got torched by Maye for one of the best games of his career.</p><p>Kyler Gordon suddenly looks as though he’s going to make a run at Defensive Player of the Year, but Jaylon Johnson has struggled for weeks.</p><p>So what exactly is this defense? Even coach Ben Johnson had a tough time pinpointing that Friday as he sized up a unit that has allowed the most yards per play in the NFL (6.3) but ranks eighth in points allowed (20.4).</p><p>‘‘I hate to look back at last year, but we’re a better defense than we were a year ago,’’ he said. ‘‘[But] we’re not taking the ball away quite as much. If we can continue to harp on getting those takeaways, you’re going to see more consistent defensive play.’’</p><p>The Bears led the NFL with 33 takeaways last season; they’re on pace for 24 this season.</p><p>Johnson saw what he wanted in the defense’s ‘‘super-hot’’ start, but Maye started punching back in the second quarter and never stopped. He finished 24-for-31 for 321 yards with two touchdowns and an interception for a 117.8 passer rating.</p><p>While Johnson gives defensive coordinator Dennis Allen autonomy, he’s highly engaged in that side of the ball, even as the offensive play-caller. Whereas Matt Eberflus sounded lost when talking about offense and Matt Nagy struggled to discuss defense, Johnson has a clear vision of how he wants the Bears to play defensively.</p><p>‘‘Our play style is the most important thing,’’ he said, pointing to an aggressive, physical approach in which swarms of tacklers converge on the ball.</p><p>He called that last part ‘‘non-negotiable’’ and was dismayed by how badly the Bears failed in it on Stevenson’s big play. They faltered at every level of the defense, and Johnson vented that his staff had spent ample time practicing for situations just like that.</p><p>The Bears lined up in a prevent coverage with two safeties at the goal line, and there were five defenders between Stevenson and the end zone when he caught the ball at the Bears’ 46. Yet he barely was touched.</p><p>That play changed the game.</p><p>If the Bears had been able to close out the final 14 seconds of the first half, they would have come out of halftime with a 20-7 lead and the ball. They could have buried the Patriots at that point. Instead, the game went down to the final minutes, and they needed a career-long 58-yard field goal from Cairo Santos to ensure victory.</p><p>The week before, the Bears let a 31-7 lead in the fourth quarter dwindle to a one-score game in which the Falcons had the ball and a chance to tie the game with more than three minutes left.</p><p>The Bears know better than anyone not to play around like that. Their run of comebacks last season had as much to do with opposing defenses whiffing on chances to finish them off as it did with the offensive heroics of Caleb Williams and others, and they’re now leaving that door open for their opponents.</p><p>Six of their remaining 10 games are against teams in the top half of the NFL in scoring, so they’re unlikely to continue getting away with such inconsistency.</p>

title: Dear Abby: Neighbor's unruly granddaughter skates on thin ice
author: Abigail Van Buren
content: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My next-door neighbor, "Dee," has a granddaughter, "Sarah." A year ago, I was friendly with Sarah, but months later, she became disrespectful. She wouldn't listen when I asked her not to ring my doorbell for no reason or tease my cats. I told Dee, and she said she would try to talk to her. Dee said she can't make Sarah mind at times.</p><p>The misbehavior stopped briefly until about two weeks ago. Now Sarah skates back and forth in front of my apartment. I didn't think much about it until I caught her watching me when I'm outside. What do you do when you want to stay friends with a neighbor but she has a teen that won't stop acting up? I need some ideas. — <i>ANNOYED IN KENTUCKY</i></p><p><b>DEAR ANNOYED:</b> Stay friends with Dee by continuing to treat her as a friend — as long as Sarah behaves herself. Saying she "can't make Sarah mind" is no excuse. As the adult in the household, Dee is responsible for anything Sarah does, and you should react accordingly.</p><p>I don't think "watching you" is an offense worth risking your friendship with Dee over, but if Sarah's antics escalate to their previous levels, inform Dee and tell her you expect her to control her granddaughter. If Sarah ever resorts to outright criminal behavior, call the police immediately.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My mother-in-law moved in with my husband and me seven months ago. It has been difficult from the beginning. We got along pretty well before she came to live with us. It happened pretty quickly, and we really didn't get to discuss it.</p><p>She doesn't offer to help with the cooking or cleaning. Of course, costs went up — electricity, groceries and the water bill. We pay for everything. We take her to her doctors, but she doesn't do what they recommend. We even pay for her prescriptions with no offer from her to reimburse us. She is disrespectful toward me, and I don't like being around her.</p><p>My husband does everything for her. He helped her with her bills, packing up her house and putting everything in storage. I understand she is his mom, but she never acted like a mother. She has never sent birthday cards or acknowledged our children or grandchildren. She was and is all about herself.</p><p>My husband asks me, "What am I supposed to do, kick her out?" I feel this has gone on long enough and we three need to sit down and talk, which we should have done a long time ago. How can we sort this out? — <i>HEAVY-HEARTED IN MISSOURI</i></p><p><b>DEAR HEAVY-HEARTED:</b> You and your husband should have had a frank discussion about this before his mother was invited to move in. Because that didn't happen then, do it now. By all means, call for a meeting of the three of you because it is overdue. Before the meeting, make a list of the things you feel your MIL should be helping with so you can refer to it. That her things are all in storage may be a blessing, in case she needs to relocate again.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

title: Bulls fall to the Wizards as tough love lessons continue being learned
author: Joe Cowley
content: <p>The principles that coach Tiago Splitter has preached are easy to grasp: Play hard and you’ll play late.</p><p>Salary amount and contract length don’t matter. Experience alone need not apply. It is a simple ideology and one that the Bulls coach deems non-negotiable.</p><p>That was evident in Friday’s win in Milwaukee as crunch time came and the likes of Josh Giddey and Matas Buzelis were nowhere to be found. A night later in the home opener against the Wizards at the United Center, Giddey and Buzelis had a bit more urgency off the tip, letting their coach know that the message had been heard loud and clear.</p><p>Now the next lesson needs to be about staying power for 48 minutes, as the Bulls (1-2) overcame a disastrous third quarter in which they were doubled up 40-20, to make it a game late before falling 124-120.</p><p>And yes, Giddey and Buzelis were on the floor for closing time.</p><p>“We were very inconsistent with our coverages,” Splitter said of the third-quarter issues. “We didn’t take the best shots that third quarter. We’ve got to be smarter. It was really tough for us to score. For us to win basketball games we’ve got to play 48 minutes.”</p><p>Buzelis was more harsh with his assessment of the third, pointing the finger at himself.</p><p>“We gotta be ready to play,” Buzelis said. “Part of that is on me, being a leader on this team. We should have easily won that game.”</p><p>Call it baby steps.</p><p>The one player who is a baby in NBA years but continues to play anything like a 20-year-old rookie? Caleb Wilson not only finished with 30 points and 14 rebounds but also put on an aerial assault of the rim not seen by a Bulls player in quite a few years.</p><p>If the NBA Rookie of the Year campaign was waiting for a first-year player to move the needle, Wilson did more than jump-start it on Saturday with five first-half dunks.</p><p>“Just being aggressive,” Wilson said of his mentality to attack the paint. “The Wizards are really big, and our opportunities are in transition because they have so much size.”</p><p>With 30 points, 14 rebounds and two steals, Wilson became the third-youngest player in NBA history to put up those minimums, joining John Drew and Victor Wembanyama.</p><p>But the big picture through the first few games for the Bulls is the mentality that Splitter is trying to instill and the penalty for the players who don’t get it.</p><p>“In general players got to compete every possession and we’re not there yet,” Splitter said. “But that’s how I believe they get better. They need pressure. They need to have minutes as well, but they need to feel the pressure of when they’re not playing the way I want, you’re going to sit with me for a little bit.”</p><p>Buzelis actually sat with Splitter a lot in Milwaukee, like the entire fourth quarter. The two spoke before the Wizards game and that’s why the coach tried to downplay how big of a deal it was.</p><p>“We’re making it a bigger deal than it should be,” Splitter said.</p><p>Buzelis showed a bounce back, scoring 10 points in the first half against the Wizards and finishing with 21. And tough love for Buzelis was nothing new, considering that’s how former coach Billy Donovan handled the young forward in their time together.</p><p>Still, Year 3 for Buzelis was supposed to be different. Splitter wants to make sure it will be: “He’s a 22-year-old, he’s still learning.”</p>

title: The Fire knock off Atlanta United to earn second consecutive 50-point season
author: AP
content: <p>ATLANTA — Anton Salétros had a goal and an assist to help the Chicago Fire rally for a 3-2 victory over Atlanta United on Saturday night.</p><p>With the victory, Chicago (15-10-6) reached the 50-point plateau in back-to-back seasons for the second time in club history — also doing so in 2000-01.</p><p>Atlanta United took a 1-0 lead in the 4th minute when first-year defender Tomás Jacob took passes from Miguel Almirón and Mauricio Amaro and scored his fourth goal. Almirón's assist was his eighth of the season and Amaro collected his first in his ninth career appearance.</p><p>Chicago pulled even on the second goal by Salétros, unassisted in the 30th minute and the tie stood through halftime.</p><p>The Fire took a 2-1 lead in the 51st minute when Anzor Mekvabishvili stole the ball and scored his first goal in his third appearance in the league.</p><p>Chicago grabbed a two-goal lead in the 60th minute when Salétros notched his third assist in setting up Philip Zinckernagel for his sixth netter this season.</p><p>Breel Embolo used his head to score off a long assist from Elías Báez to cut it to 3-2 eight minutes later. Amaro was also credited with an assist on Embolo's second goal in his first nine MLS matches.</p><p>Chris Brady finished with one save for Chicago, which snapped a two-match skid.</p><p>Lucas Hoyos did not have a save for Atlanta United (8-17-6). The club's 10 losses at home this season are the most in the league.</p><p>The Fire beat Atlanta United 1-0 at Soldier Field in early April.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Chicago: Hosts Orlando City on Wednesday.</p><p>Atlanta: At New York City FC on Wednesday.</p>

title: Man, 18, shot multiple times in Little Village
author: Sun-Times Wire
content: <p>An 18-year-old man was in serious condition after a shooting Saturday afternoon in Little Village, Chicago police said.</p><p>The man was walking near the sidewalk in the 3300 block of West 31st Street about 3:16 p.m. when a vehicle approached and at least one person inside fired multiple shots at him, police said.</p><p>The man was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital in serious condition.</p>

title: Chicago Archdiocese clears retired priest accused of sexual abuse, approves return to ministry
author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi
content: <p>The Archdiocese of Chicago is allowing a retired priest to return to ministry after the church's independent review board found no reasonable cause to believe he had abused a minor decades ago.</p><p>In a letter distributed Saturday to six parish communities, Cardinal Blase Cupich said he had accepted the review board’s recommendation to close the case against the Rev. Kenneth Fleck.</p><p>The archdiocese received the allegation in July, more than 30 years after the alleged abuse occurred. Fleck served as pastor of Our Lady of Peace from May 1984 to August 1996, during which the abuse was alleged to have occurred.</p><p>Three months ago, Cupich asked the priest to step away from ministry while civil authorities and the archdiocese’s Independent Review Board investigated the allegation. The archdiocese also said it had been informed a lawsuit alleging sexual abuse of a minor would be filed.</p><p>Fleck strongly denied the allegation and cooperated with the investigation, according to Cupich’s letter. He said Fleck is a priest in good standing and expressed appreciation for his years of service to the archdiocese.</p><p>"It is important to stress that the welfare of the children entrusted to our care is of paramount importance," Cupich wrote. "For this reason, we take all allegations of sexual misconduct seriously. At the same time, we must restore the good name of anyone so accused when the allegations are found to be unsubstantiated."</p><p>Fleck also served at St. Barnabas, St. Josephine Bakhita and St. Katherine Drexel, all in Chicago, as well as St. Catherine of Alexandria in Oak Lawn, Christ Our Savior in South Holland and St. George in Tinley Park.</p><p>The archdiocese also encouraged anyone who has experienced sexual abuse by a priest, deacon, religious or lay employee to come forward.</p>

title: Bulls' Noa Essengue was back on the bench but out of the doghouse
author: Joe Cowley
content: <p>It’s tough for coach <b>Tiago Splitter</b> to guess how many minutes <b>Noa Essengue</b> was going to get on Saturday against the Wizards.</p><p>The second-year forward has emerged in that rotation mix of the No. 9 or No. 10 guy, based on matchup, according to Splitter, and he insisted that he planned to lean more on <b>Zach Collins</b>, anyway, because of his physicality in the paint counters what the Wizards bring to the floor.</p><p>By tip-off Essengue’s minutes weren’t an issue, however, with the medical staff deciding that the light sensitivity Essengue was experiencing after he took a shot in the head during Friday’s victory against the Bucks was enough to sideline him for a night.</p><p>Not exactly great timing since Essengue had by far his most productive minutes of his career against the Bucks, but again a reminder that the 19-year-old is still a project.</p><p>At least he’s one that Splitter and the organization feel a little better about.</p><p>Not the case in July, when Essengue’s effort and his habit of being overly emotional didn’t sit well with Splitter. What ended up sitting well with the coach was Essengue, benched throughout Summer League.</p><p>Message received.</p><p>“It was a strong message,” Essengue told the Sun-Times last week. “To see my playing time cut in Summer League because they said I don’t put any force or energy on the court, it was something where it just forces you to change it, to put that force out there.”</p><p>That mentality earned Essengue 10 minutes of work in the blowout to the Raptors, but saw that bump to 17 minutes against the Bucks. And his role is simple: Be a disrupter on defense with his length.</p><p>Splitter did reiterate that Essengue’s presence on the floor was match-up based from game-to-game, but at least the forward is seemingly out of Splitter’s doghouse.</p><p>“There’s a feel of course,” Splitter explained on Saturday when asked about handling Essengue with tough love. “From the first meeting I had with him, he asked me to be coached hard, that’s what I did. I told him the truth, I was honest with him, and he reacted.</p><p>“Kudos to him to approach it differently. Yes, he can make mistakes but at least he’s trying to do the right thing and he’s playing hard. That’s my take on him.”</p><p><b>Odd man out</b></p><p>It continues to be very clear that <b>Patrick Williams</b> has not only fallen out of the rotation but is not even a thought come mop-up time. He was the only active player to not get minutes in the blowout loss to Toronto on Wednesday and didn’t sniff the court in the Bucks win.</p><p>That wasn’t an issue Saturday, however, with Williams being ruled out with a sore groin. It was not believed to be serious.</p><p><b>For openers</b></p><p>Even going back to the preseason, the Bulls’ starting unit hasn’t looked connected for extended period of times. Maybe it’s the group still trying to figure out Splitter’s system and executing it more consistently or maybe it’s just growing pains because of all the changes.</p><p>Rookie <b>Caleb Wilson</b> didn’t sound overly concerned with the starting group.</p><p>“Sometimes it does [look stagnant] but that’s just basketball,” Wilson said of the slow starts. “We’re all playing together, we have a new coach, a new system, some of us are new to the team, and I’m one of the focal points of the team and I’m a rookie in the NBA trying to figure it out myself.</p><p>“It’s stuff we have to work on and get the chemistry on, get better and better.”</p>

title: Eric Couper to Peter Panagiotopolous connection sets records, drives Notre Dame deeper into the 6A playoffs
author: Michael O'Brien
content: <p>The quarterback-receiver chemistry driving Notre Dame’s high-powered offense began in a seventh-grade classroom at St. Juliana on the Northwest Side.</p><p>Peter Panagiotopoulos and Eric Couper didn’t play football together then, but they became best friends. When Couper decided to switch from defensive player to quarterback when he started high school at Notre Dame, the two friends made it happen together.</p><p>“We just kept hitting random fields that entire summer before freshman year,” Panagiotopoulos said. “We threw the ball around anywhere we could. That’s my best friend.”</p><p>Couper started as quarterback on the freshman team, but had to wait his turn before starting on varsity as a senior. Panagiotopoulos caught just one pass his freshman year.</p><p>No one expected this duo to earn local headlines and set school records. But they have. Panagiotopoulos is the school’s career leader in receiving yards (1,233) and receptions (85) and set single-season records this year in receptions (70), yards (1,015) and touchdowns (16). Couper set school season records for touchdowns (31) and passing yards (2,226).</p><p>“I can always trust [Panagiotopolous] to get open,” Couper said. “He’s not very tall, but he is fast, and he is smooth and will pretty much catch anything.”</p><p>Couper threw five touchdown passes, two to Panagiotopolous, in Notre Dame’s 44-0 win over Maine West in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class6a-illinois-2026" >Class 6A</a> opening round playoff game on Saturday in Niles.</p><p>“Eric is a major competitor and was right there with the two seniors that played last year,” Dons coach Dan DeFranza said. “So I knew he was going to play well this season, but the numbers have surprised me. I know he was very disappointed last year with that playing time. He is a real, real competitor.”</p><p>Couper was 9-for-11 for 207 yards against Maine West. Panagiotopoulos caught three passes for 103 yards. Nathan Nowak, JD Look and Deonte Macon also caught touchdowns.</p><p>“Couper never played quarterback growing up, and Panagiotopolous had one catch freshman year,” DeFranza said. “These kids put in the work. They are really good friends, and they work hard together and put in the extra time together, and that shows.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" title: Driver killed after dump truck overturns at Plainfield-area quarry
author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi
content: <p>A dump truck driver died Friday after the vehicle overturned at a rock quarry in unincorporated Plainfield, authorities said.</p><p>The Plainfield Fire Protection District was dispatched to the quarry at 22950 W. 119th St. about 4:08 p.m. Friday after receiving a report of an industrial accident, according to a news release.</p><p>Responders found the driver trapped inside the large overturned truck, and the driver was pronounced dead, fire officials said.</p><p>The Will County sheriff’s office and the Mine Safety and Health Administration are investigating.</p><p>The fire district said Saturday it had not yet been informed whether investigators had determined what caused the truck to overturn.</p>

title: Even with first-time starter at QB, Illini knock off visiting Ducks
author: AP
content: <p>CHAMPAIGN — Aidan Laughery ran for 123 yards and a touchdown and Collin Dixon made a diving catch for a 23-yard score late in the fourth quarter as Illinois defeated Oregon 21-10 on Saturday.</p><p>It was the Ducks’ first road loss in Big Ten play since they joined the conference in 2024. They had won 10 straight.</p><p>Michael Clayton II was 11-of-18 passing for 84 yards and two TDs for Illinois (4-3, 2-2), including the throw to Dixon in the corner of the end zone. Dixon had six catches for 65 yards.</p><p>“I have no idea how Collin made that catch,” Illinois coach Bret Bielema said about Dixon's game-clinching TD.</p><p>Dylan Raiola was 27-of-41 for 246 yards for Oregon (4-3, 2-2). Dakorien Moore caught nine passes for 70 yards. Jordon Davison had 14 carries for 92 yards and a TD and Dierre Hill Jr. had 83 yards rushing on 13 carries.</p><p>“Give credit to Illinois. They were the tougher team and that showed up in the second half," said Oregon coach Dan Lanning. “We have to evaluate who we are. Each person needs to look within and identify where they can improve.”</p><p>Illinois went in front for good at 14-10 early in the third quarter on a 9-yard play-action TD pass from Clayton to Christian Abney.</p><p>Laughery ran untouched 75 yards for a TD that trimmed the deficit to 10-7 with 2:15 to go in the half. Illinois had gained just 43 yards before Laughery’s score.</p><p>“I thought this team could do a lot better than what we've done,” Bielema said.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Oregon: Star quarterback Dante Moore was sidelined for a third consecutive game after suffering a concussion Sept. 26 vs. USC. The Ducks miss him. They've scored just 39 points in the games Moore has been out. The Ducks lead the nation in 30-plus points games (48) and TDs (312) since Lanning became coach in 2022.</p><p>Illinois: Clayton, a freshman, started at quarterback in place of fifth-year senior Katin Houser, who suffered a broken hand Oct. 10 vs. Michigan State. Clayton became only the sixth freshman in program history to start at QB, but he shared duties in the second half with Carson Boyd. Bielema called the rotation, orchestrated by offensive coordinator Barry Lunney Jr., “poetry in motion.”</p><p><b>Four Ducks down</b></p><p>Four of Oregon’s top wide receivers didn’t play. Evan Stewart, the Ducks’ leader with 27 catches for 352 yards and four TDs, had been suspended indefinitely following a DUI arrest early Sunday morning. Jalen Lott, Messiah Hampton and Jeremiah McClellan also missed the game due to injuries.</p><p><b>First misses</b></p><p>Oregon kicker Gage Hurych, the reigning Big Ten special teams player of the week after kicking three field goals in a win over Nebraska, missed two 52-yard attempts and a 39-yarder in the fourth quarter against the Illini. Hurych is 10 for 13 on field goals and 20 for 20 on PATs.</p><p><b>Up Next</b></p><p>Illinois: Plays next Saturday at Maryland.</p><p>Oregon: Hosts No. 24 Northwestern on Halloween.</p>

title: Why are pro-housing groups split on Proposition 45?
author: Gabriel Dillard
content: Housing developments under construction in the community of Goshen on Aug. 17, 2024. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local This story was originally published by CalMatters . Sign up for their newsletters. For nearly a decade, California’s Yes In My Backyard activists and other pro-development advocates have wanted to overhaul California’s signature environmental law to clear the way for more housing construction. Now Proposition 45 is on the ballot. Supporters say it would, among other things, overhaul that law, known as the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, to clear the way for — you guessed it — more housing construction. So why are YIMBYs divided? Assemblymember Buffy Wicks , an Oakland Democrat and one of the movement’s most stalwart champions in the Legislature, is for it. So is the bulk of the building industry , including many major for- and non-profit developers. Bay Area pro-housing advocates Eastbay for Everyone and the Greenbelt Alliance , two typical allies of Wicks, are emphatically against it. In the uncommitted middle lies the lion’s share of California YIMBYism: Abundant Housing Los Angeles , SPUR , and both California YIMBY and YIMBY Action — the movement’s two flagship advocacy organizations — have all taken neutral positions. “It’s been a weird campaign so far,” said Ali Sapirman, advocacy manager at the Housing Action Coalition, an urban building industry group that supports the measure. “The housing community has been a little bit fractured.” Those fissures aren’t over whether more homes should be built across California. Instead, it mostly boils down to a question of where . “The central question here is how you feel about sprawl,” Max Dubler of California YIMBY wrote in the group’s non-endorsement statement , referring to low-density housing development at the edge of metro areas. Though some exurban growth “will necessarily be part of solving our housing shortage,” he expressed concern about making it easier to build “car-dependent sprawl housing and the freeways and water infrastructure necessary to serve that sprawl.” To sprawl or not to sprawl For nearly a decade, the Legislature has been on a tear , passing “streamlining” bills aimed at speeding up the regulatory approval of new construction. Almost all of those laws have only applied to projects in places where homes and other infrastructure already exist. Prioritizing so-called infill development helped wrangle together a coalition of developers and construction labor unions , but also a diverse swath of Democratic-leaning advocates whose interest in seeing more apartments and condos goes beyond the cause of affordability alone. That includes climate activists who want to see less commuter car traffic; transit, bicycle and pedestrian advocates who want more riders and walkers and urbanists who want Los Angeles to more closely resemble Barcelona . In breaking from that urban focus, Prop. 45 is driving a wedge inside that coalition. If passed, the measure would speed up the review process required under CEQA (pronounced “see-kwah”) for all types of housing projects. That includes transit-adjacent downtown condo towers, but also freshly paved subdivisions at the metropolitan fringe. The measure is “a doubling down on essentially 75 years of land-use patterns that we know haven’t worked,” said Jordan Grimes, legislative director with Greenbelt Alliance, which opposes the measure. “It’s a return to the sprawl era.” Not everyone in the movement necessarily sees that as a bad thing. Among those who want California to build its way out of its current housing shortage , opinions differ over whether more environmentally-friendly infill development alone is up to the task. “I’m an ‘all of the above’ person when it comes to housing,” said Wicks, explaining her support of the measure. “I think we need housing of all different types, shapes, and sizes.” An earlier version of this rift first emerged earlier this decade when a handful of Bay Area tech investors announced plans to build a brand new city on Solano County farmland in 2023 under the banner of California Forever . Some YIMBY commentators applauded the plan as a welcome injection of much-needed supply . Others decried it as sprawl dressed in urbanist clothing . With Prop. 45, that regional debate is now playing out at a statewide scale. Housing front and center Prop. 45 is about much more than housing policy . CEQA requires public agencies to review the possible environmental consequences of the decisions they make, including the permitting of private projects. For decades industry groups, developers and, more recently, housing supply boosters have said the law makes it too easy for project opponents to jam up worthwhile projects by repeatedly demanding additional analysis. “The clock is endless and the number of people and entities who can challenge you are also endless,” said Linda Mandolini of Eden Housing, an affordable housing developer. Prop. 45 would not exempt any projects from environmental review outright. But for projects deemed “essential,” it would narrow the focus of these reviews and require them to wrap up within 365 business days. Any resulting litigation would also face a shot clock; Judges would have 270 business days to resolve them. Such lawsuits would also be made harder to sustain in court. Aside from housing, essential projects include roads, hospitals, schools, clean energy projects, water and broadband infrastructure. But housing has loomed large in the electoral debate. The Yes on 45 campaign has touted the support of affordable housing developers and housing advocates , while pointing to housing affordability concerns as the initial impetus for the measure. It’s easy to see why. Environmental challenges to often innocuous-seeming housing projects have regularly generated headlines for years, helping to cement the idea among lawmakers and many voters that CEQA is a major cause of the state’s housing woes. Environmental justice groups and their allies have spent years fighting against that argument in the Legislature. Though Prop. 45 does not exempt “essential” projects from environmental review outright — it just shortens and hems in the process — these groups have now lined up to oppose it for much the same reason: They reject the premise that CEQA needs fixing. But for opponents like Grimes, who supported many recent streamlining bills, the argument that the law is holding up desperately needed residential construction is a year out of date. Last year, the governor signed Assembly Bill 130 , a Wicks-authored measure that exempted most infill housing from the CEQA. Since becoming law in July 2025, developers have used it to entitle 17,913 units of housing, according to the Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, a state agency. “When you look at what’s left to do on urban housing, there are absolutely still barriers,” said Grimes, whose organization applauded last year’s exemption . “CEQA just isn’t one of them.” The task of the No on 45 campaign, he said, is to convince enough voters that “we’ve actually solved this problem.” Are we done here? Many developers and affordable housing advocates, even those working in urban areas, dispute that CEQA is no longer a major obstacle. Last year’s exemption does not exempt projects larger than 20 acres, which means supersized urban redevelopment projects are still subject to the old process. Prop. 45 also applies shot clocks to other permits issued later in the development process and which regularly slow a project more than environmental review. And while state laws like last year’s infill carveout may grant certain developers the right to ignore CEQA, there is nothing to stop a deep-pocketed opponent from suing anyway. Putting time limits on those lawsuits could be the difference between a project succeeding and being delayed to death, said Mandolini. She points to the planned 130-unit affordable housing project that Eden Housing has been trying to and failing to build in the Bay Area suburb of Livermore since 2018 as an example. In 2021, a nonprofit funded by a handful of well-heeled Livermore residents sued the city, arguing that it hadn’t done enough environmental analysis on a housing development that would be built on a former grocery store parking lot behind a row of downtown restaurants. A lower court ruled that the group’s CEQA arguments were “almost utterly without merit.” An appellate court agreed. The state Supreme Court allowed that ruling to stand. But by then two years had passed. “Every year you lose in litigation is real money for real projects and another year that 130 families don’t get to live in that housing,” said Mandolini. “It’s a great way to kill a project.” Even an infill project. But among some pro-housing supporters of the proposition, the infill versus sprawl debate isn’t much of a debate at all. “We’re not an urbanist organization,” said Mahdi Manji with the Inner City Law Center, a legal aid provider and housing advocacy group in Los Angeles’ Skid Row. The group supports Prop. 45 and doesn’t mind the concept of more housing far from the city’s core. “To the extent it results in housing that is a little more affordable in Lancaster and Palmdale, a lot of our clients live out in Lancaster and Palmdale.” This article was originally published on CalMatters and was republished under the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives license.
