Parents can track their child’s progress and receive insights into their learning journey. ABCmouse ABCmouse is a subscription-based app aimed at children aged 2 to 8, providing a comprehensive curriculum that includes reading, math, art, and music. With thousands of activities, it keeps children engaged while learning essential skills. The app offers a step-by-step learning path and rewards system, which motivates kids to complete lessons. It’s particularly effective for early learners who benefit from structured guidance. Endless Alphabet Endless Alphabet is an interactive app designed for preschoolers to learn vocabulary and word meanings. It features adorable monster characters that help children explore new words through fun animations and puzzles. This app is ideal for building a strong vocabulary foundation, as it introduces words in context and encourages children to use them in sentences. It’s a playful way to enhance language skills without pressure. Duolingo ABC Duolingo ABC is a free app focused on teaching young children the basics of reading and writing. It uses engaging stories and interactive exercises to introduce letters, sounds, and simple words. The app is designed for children aged 3 to 6 and emphasizes phonics and vocabulary development. Its game-like format keeps kids motivated and makes learning to read enjoyable. Osmo – Genius Starter Kit The Osmo – Genius Starter Kit combines physical play with digital learning, making it a unique educational tool for kids aged 6 and up. It includes interactive games that promote creativity, problem-solving, and critical thinking. Using a tablet and a special base, children can manipulate physical objects to solve puzzles and complete challenges. This hands-on approach enhances engagement and makes learning more tangible. How do educational apps enhance learning outcomes for kids? Educational apps significantly enhance learning outcomes for kids by providing engaging, interactive content that caters to various learning styles. These apps often incorporate features that promote active participation, making learning more effective and enjoyable. Interactive learning experiences Interactive learning experiences in educational apps allow children to engage with content actively rather than passively consuming information. For example, apps that use gamification techniques can motivate kids to complete tasks and challenges, reinforcing concepts through play. These experiences can include quizzes, puzzles, and simulations that require problem-solving skills. Such activities not only make learning fun but also help in retaining information longer by creating memorable experiences. Personalized learning paths Personalized learning paths in educational apps adapt to each child’s unique pace and style of learning. This customization can involve adjusting the difficulty level of tasks based on the child’s performance, ensuring that they are neither bored nor overwhelmed. For instance, an app might offer different levels of math problems, allowing a child to progress from basic addition to more complex equations as they master each stage. This tailored approach helps maintain engagement and fosters a sense of achievement. Immediate feedback mechanisms Immediate feedback mechanisms in educational apps provide instant responses to a child’s actions, which is crucial for effective learning. When a child answers a question correctly or incorrectly, the app can immediately inform them, allowing for quick adjustments in understanding. For example, if a child struggles with a particular concept, the app might offer hints or additional practice problems tailored to that area. This real-time feedback loop helps reinforce learning and encourages children to take ownership of their educational journey. What features should parents look for in educational apps? Parents should prioritize features that enhance learning while keeping children engaged. Key aspects include an engaging user interface, age-appropriate content, and progress tracking capabilities to monitor development. Engaging user interface An engaging user interface is crucial for maintaining a child’s interest in educational apps. Look for apps that use bright colors, intuitive navigation, and interactive elements that encourage exploration and learning. Simple animations and sound effects can also enhance the overall experience. Consider apps that offer gamified learning experiences, where children earn rewards or unlock new levels as they progress. This approach not only makes learning fun but also motivates children to return to the app regularly. Age-appropriate content Age-appropriate content ensures that the material is suitable for a child’s developmental stage. Apps should align with educational standards for specific age groups, covering topics like math, reading, and science in ways that are engaging and understandable for young learners. Parents should review the app’s curriculum and content to ensure it matches their child’s interests and learning needs. Many apps categorize content by age ranges, helping parents select the right material for their children. Progress tracking capabilities Progress tracking capabilities allow parents to monitor their child’s learning journey effectively. Look for apps that provide reports or dashboards showing completed activities, skills mastered, and areas needing improvement. This feedback can help guide future learning choices. Some apps also offer features that allow parents to set goals or customize learning paths based on their child’s progress. This personalized approach can significantly enhance the educational experience and ensure that children are challenged appropriately. How do educational apps compare in terms of quality? Educational apps vary significantly in quality, impacting their effectiveness for children’s learning. Key factors to consider include the content’s research backing, user feedback, and expert endorsements. Research-backed content Apps that incorporate research-backed content are more likely to enhance learning outcomes. Look for applications that align with established educational standards and utilize proven pedagogical methods. For example, apps that focus on interactive learning and adaptive assessments can better cater to individual learning styles. When evaluating an app, check if it references educational studies or has been developed in collaboration with educators. This can indicate a stronger foundation in effective teaching practices. User reviews and ratings User reviews and ratings provide insight into an app’s real-world effectiveness and engagement levels. High ratings often reflect positive user experiences, while detailed reviews can highlight specific strengths or weaknesses. Aim for apps with ratings above four stars, as these typically indicate a higher level of satisfaction among users. Pay attention to comments regarding usability and engagement, as these factors are crucial for maintaining children’s interest and promoting sustained learning. Apps that receive consistent praise for their interactive features are often more engaging. Expert recommendations Expert recommendations can guide parents and educators in selecting high-quality educational apps. Look for endorsements from educational organizations or professionals in child development. These recommendations often come from thorough evaluations of the app’s content and effectiveness. Consider resources like educational blogs, parenting websites, or academic journals that review and rank educational apps. This can help you identify apps that are not only popular but also respected in the educational community. What are the pricing models for popular educational apps? Popular educational apps for kids typically use various pricing models, including subscription-based pricing, one-time purchases, and free trials. Understanding these models helps parents choose the best options for their children’s learning needs and budget. Subscription-based pricing Subscription-based pricing requires users to pay a recurring fee, usually monthly or annually, to access the app’s content and features. This model often provides continuous updates and new material, which can enhance the learning experience over time. Prices for subscriptions can vary widely, ranging from around $5 to $15 per month, depending on the app’s offerings. Parents should consider whether the ongoing cost aligns with their budget and if the app consistently delivers value through new content. One-time purchase options One-time purchase options allow users to buy the app outright, granting permanent access to its features and content without ongoing fees. This model is appealing for parents who prefer a single payment without the commitment of a subscription. Prices for one-time purchases typically range from $1 to $30. While this option can be more economical in the long run, it’s essential to check if the app will receive updates or additional content after the initial purchase. Free trial availability Many educational apps offer free trials, allowing users to explore the app’s features before committing to a purchase. Free trials can last from a few days to a month, providing a risk-free way to evaluate the app’s effectiveness for a child’s learning. When considering a free trial, parents should take advantage of the opportunity to assess the app’s engagement and educational value. However, it’s crucial to note when the trial ends to avoid unexpected charges if a subscription is not canceled in time. How can parents ensure their kids stay engaged with educational apps? Parents can enhance their children’s engagement with educational apps by selecting high-quality content and actively participating in the learning process. Choosing apps that are interactive and age-appropriate, while also setting clear guidelines for usage, can significantly improve learning outcomes. Setting usage limits Establishing usage limits helps maintain a healthy balance between screen time and other activities. Parents should consider setting daily or weekly limits that align with their child’s age and developmental stage, typically ranging from 30 minutes to 2 hours per day. To effectively implement these limits, parents can use built-in features on the iPad, such as Screen Time settings, which allow them to monitor and restrict app usage. This not only helps prevent overuse but also encourages children to engage in offline activities, such as reading or outdoor play. It’s essential to communicate the reasons behind these limits to children, fostering understanding and cooperation. Parents might also consider creating a schedule that includes educational app time alongside other activities, ensuring a well-rounded approach to learning and play.

title: Creative Apps for iPad: Value, Features and User Experience
author: John Doe
content: Creative apps for iPad are designed to merge powerful features with intuitive interfaces, making them ideal for artists, designers, and students alike. With options like Procreate and Adobe Fresco, these applications leverage the iPad’s capabilities to enhance creativity and streamline workflows, allowing users to express their ideas with ease. When choosing an app, consider features such as collaboration tools and customizable options to maximize your creative potential. What are the best creative apps for iPad? The best creative apps for iPad combine powerful features with user-friendly interfaces, catering to artists, designers, and note-takers alike. Popular choices include Procreate, Affinity Designer, Adobe Fresco, Notability, and Paper by WeTransfer, each offering unique tools and experiences tailored to various creative needs. Procreate Procreate is a leading digital painting app known for its intuitive interface and extensive brush library. It allows users to create stunning artwork with features like layering, customizable brushes, and high-resolution canvases. Artists appreciate the smooth performance and responsiveness, making it suitable for both beginners and professionals. Consider exploring its time-lapse recording feature to showcase your creative process. Affinity Designer Affinity Designer is a vector graphic design app that excels in precision and versatility. It supports both vector and raster graphics, making it ideal for creating logos, illustrations, and complex designs. With tools for pixel-perfect editing and a one-time purchase model, it offers great value compared to subscription-based software. Users should familiarize themselves with its dual workspace to maximize efficiency in their design projects. Adobe Fresco Adobe Fresco is designed for digital painting and drawing, featuring a blend of vector and raster brushes. It is particularly favored by illustrators and graphic artists for its live brushes that mimic real-world painting techniques. Fresco integrates seamlessly with other Adobe products, allowing for a smooth workflow if you already use Adobe Creative Cloud. Users should take advantage of its cloud features to access their work across devices easily. Notability Notability is a versatile note-taking app that combines handwriting, typing, and audio recording. It is particularly useful for students and professionals who need to capture ideas quickly and organize them effectively. The app supports PDF annotation, making it easy to mark up documents. Users should utilize its search function to find handwritten notes quickly, enhancing productivity during study sessions or meetings. Paper by WeTransfer Paper by WeTransfer is a sketching and note-taking app that emphasizes simplicity and creativity. It offers a clean interface with tools for drawing, writing, and visual thinking, making it suitable for brainstorming and concept development. Users can create mood boards or visual notes easily, and the app’s export options allow for sharing ideas in various formats. Consider using its color mixing feature to enhance your sketches and improve visual storytelling. How do creative apps enhance user experience on iPad? Creative apps significantly enhance user experience on the iPad by providing tools that are both powerful and user-friendly. These applications leverage the iPad’s hardware and software capabilities to facilitate creativity, making it easier for users to express their ideas visually or audibly. Intuitive interfaces Intuitive interfaces in creative apps allow users to navigate and utilize features with minimal learning curve. Many apps employ familiar gestures and layouts, enabling quick access to tools and functions. For instance, apps like Procreate and Adobe Fresco use a simple toolbar design that helps artists focus on their work rather than getting lost in complex menus. When choosing a creative app, look for those that offer customizable interfaces, allowing you to tailor the workspace to your preferences. This can enhance productivity and make the creative process more enjoyable. Touchscreen capabilities The iPad’s touchscreen capabilities provide a tactile experience that enhances creativity. Users can easily manipulate images, draw, or edit with their fingers, which can feel more natural than using a mouse or trackpad. Apps like Affinity Photo take full advantage of this by allowing pinch-to-zoom and swipe gestures for seamless editing. Consider apps that offer multi-touch support, as this can significantly improve workflow. For example, being able to rotate and scale images with gestures can save time and make the creative process more fluid. Apple Pencil integration Apple Pencil integration elevates the user experience in creative apps by providing precision and control that is essential for detailed work. With pressure sensitivity and tilt recognition, artists can create varied strokes that mimic traditional drawing tools. Apps like Notability and Concepts fully utilize these features to enhance note-taking and sketching. When using Apple Pencil, explore settings that adjust pressure sensitivity to match your drawing style. This customization can lead to a more personalized and effective creative experience, allowing for greater expression in your work. What features should you look for in iPad creative apps? When selecting creative apps for your iPad, prioritize features that enhance your workflow and creativity. Key aspects include collaboration tools, customizable brushes, and cloud storage options, which can significantly impact your user experience and productivity. Collaboration tools Collaboration tools are essential for working with others on creative projects. Look for apps that allow real-time editing, commenting, and sharing, enabling seamless communication among team members. Features like version history can also help track changes and maintain project integrity. Consider apps that integrate with popular platforms such as Slack or Microsoft Teams, as this can streamline communication. Additionally, check if the app supports multiple users working simultaneously, which can enhance teamwork and creativity. Customizable brushes Customizable brushes are crucial for artists who want to create unique styles and effects. Look for apps that offer a variety of brush types and settings, such as size, opacity, and texture, allowing you to tailor your tools to your specific needs. Some apps even let you create and save your own brushes for future use. Experimenting with different brush settings can lead to discovering new techniques and artistic expressions. Ensure the app provides a user-friendly interface for adjusting these settings, so you can focus more on your creativity rather than navigating complex menus. Cloud storage options Cloud storage options are vital for safeguarding your work and accessing it across devices. Choose apps that offer integration with popular cloud services like Google Drive, Dropbox, or iCloud, ensuring your projects are backed up and easily retrievable. This feature is particularly important for collaborative projects where multiple users need access to the same files. Evaluate the app’s storage limits and any associated costs, as some may offer free tiers with limited space while others may require subscriptions for larger capacities. Regularly saving your work to the cloud can prevent data loss and provide peace of mind while you create. What is the value of using creative apps on iPad? The value of using creative apps on iPad lies in their ability to enhance productivity and creativity through a user-friendly interface and powerful features. These apps provide artists, designers, and content creators with tools that are both accessible and versatile, allowing for a seamless creative process. Portability iPads are lightweight and compact, making them ideal for creative professionals on the go. You can easily carry an iPad in a bag or even under your arm, allowing you to work from various locations, whether it’s a café, park, or client meeting. This portability means you can sketch, design, or edit videos anywhere, without being tethered to a desk. Many creative apps are optimized for touch input, which enhances the mobile experience and allows for intuitive interaction. Cost-effectiveness Using creative apps on an iPad can be more cost-effective than traditional software on a desktop. Many apps offer one-time purchases or subscription models that are significantly cheaper than full desktop software licenses, which can run into hundreds of dollars. Additionally, the iPad itself can serve multiple functions, replacing the need for separate devices like a laptop or drawing tablet. This consolidation can save you money in the long run, especially for freelancers or small businesses. Access to professional tools Creative apps on iPad provide access to a range of professional-grade tools that were once exclusive to high-end desktop software. Programs like Procreate for digital painting or LumaFusion for video editing offer features that rival traditional applications. Moreover, many apps are regularly updated with new features and improvements, ensuring that users have access to the latest tools and technologies. This continuous enhancement allows creators to stay competitive in their fields without needing to invest in expensive hardware or software upgrades. How do creative apps compare in pricing? Creative apps for iPad vary significantly in pricing, influenced by their features and business models. Users can expect to encounter subscription models, one-time purchases, and a mix of free and paid features, each offering different value propositions. Subscription models Many creative apps operate on a subscription basis, charging users monthly or annually for access to their full range of features. This model often includes regular updates and new content, which can be beneficial for users who need the latest tools and resources. Prices typically range from around $5 to $30 per month, depending on the app’s complexity and functionality. When considering a subscription, evaluate how frequently you will use the app and whether the ongoing cost aligns with your creative needs. Some apps offer free trials, allowing you to test before committing. One-time purchases One-time purchase apps require an upfront payment, granting users permanent access to the software without recurring fees. Prices for these apps generally fall between $10 and $100, depending on the features offered. This model can be more economical for users who prefer not to pay ongoing fees. However, be aware that one-time purchase apps may not receive updates as frequently as subscription-based ones, which could limit access to new features over time. Always check the app’s update policy before buying. Free vs. paid features Many creative apps offer a tiered structure where basic features are available for free, while advanced tools and functionalities require payment. Free versions can be a great way to explore an app’s capabilities before deciding to invest in the full version. When using free versions, consider the limitations that may affect your workflow, such as watermarks on exports or restricted access to premium tools. If you find the app useful, upgrading to the paid version can unlock additional features that enhance your creative process. What are user reviews saying about popular iPad creative apps? User reviews of popular iPad creative apps highlight a mix of satisfaction and areas for improvement. Users often praise the intuitive interfaces and powerful features, while also noting occasional performance issues and steep learning curves for advanced functionalities. Overall satisfaction ratings Overall satisfaction ratings for iPad creative apps tend to vary, with many users giving high marks for ease of use and functionality. Apps like Procreate and Adobe Fresco frequently receive ratings in the high fours or fives out of five, indicating strong user approval. However, some apps may have lower ratings due to bugs or limited features. Common praises and complaints Common praises for iPad creative apps include their versatility and the ability to create high-quality work on-the-go. Users appreciate features like pressure sensitivity and customizable brushes. On the flip side, complaints often revolve around crashes during intensive tasks and the lack of certain tools that desktop versions offer. Feature requests from users Feature requests from users often include enhancements to collaboration tools, improved file management, and more robust export options. Many users express a desire for better integration with other software and cloud services. Additionally, some users seek more tutorials or onboarding resources to help them utilize advanced features effectively.

title: Brant Frost IV Sentenced to 15 Years, $76.4 Million Restitution in First Liberty Ponzi Scheme
author: Ellie White-Stevens
content: Edwin Brant Frost IV was sentenced Monday to 15 years in federal prison and ordered to pay $76,454,374.39 in restitution to victims of the First Liberty Ponzi scheme, following a Newnan courtroom hearing where investors described losing retirement savings, financial security, and even the trust of their families. Chief U.S. District Judge Leigh Martin May imposed a sentence one year longer than the 14 years federal prosecutors recommended and 10 years longer than the five years Frost’s attorneys requested. The 69-year-old Newnan businessman must also serve three years of supervised release after completing his prison sentence. Frost has been given 30 days to surrender and is expected to report to federal prison in Montgomery, Alabama, on Wednesday, November 25, the day before Thanksgiving. The October 26 hearing took place in the federal courthouse in downtown Newnan, just doors away from the former First Liberty Building and Loan offices where Frost operated the business at the center of the fraud. Frost pleaded guilty May 12 to one count of wire fraud. Federal prosecutors said his Ponzi scheme caused more than $76 million in losses to more than 300 investors, many of them retirees who trusted him with their life savings. The courtroom was so crowded that some attendees were directed to an overflow courtroom, where they could hear the proceedings. Among those following the hearing were Coweta County Board of Education member Amy Dees, Georgia Assistant Commissioner of Securities Noula Zaharis, and victim advocate Lisa Deveraux. All three spoke with The Citizen afterward. U.S. Attorney condemns use of faith to attract investors U.S. Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg issued a statement following the sentencing, describing how Frost used religious and political associations to gain investors’ confidence. “Like a false prophet and ravenous wolf in sheep’s clothing, Frost used religion, politics, and promises of profitable returns to lure investors into giving him their hard-earned money. He wickedly exploited their faith to plunder their accounts and enrich himself,” Hertzberg said. “This was a stunning, sinful, and sacrilegious abuse of trust that wrecked hundreds of investors, including retirees and seniors who lost their life savings.” According to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Frost operated the fraudulent investment scheme from at least 2021 through July 2025 through First Liberty Building and Loan LLC. He promoted the company as a conservative Christian lender helping small businesses obtain short-term financing. Investors were promised annual returns of 8% to 18%, paid monthly, from high-interest bridge loans to businesses awaiting longer-term financing, often through the Small Business Administration. By 2021, numerous loans had defaulted, and First Liberty was no longer generating enough legitimate income to meet its obligations. Instead of disclosing the company’s financial problems, Frost continued assuring investors that their funds were being used for performing loans and that only a few borrowers had defaulted. In reality, he was using money from new investors to pay returns to existing investors, the defining characteristic of a Ponzi scheme. Federal investigators determined that Frost also diverted at least $5 million of investor funds for personal benefit. Expenditures included a $230,000 vacation home rental in Maine, more than $140,000 in jewelry, a $20,800 Patek Philippe watch, more than $335,000 paid to a rare coin dealer, more than $2 million in credit card payments, and more than $570,000 in political contributions. Marlo Graham, Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta, said the sentence reflected the FBI’s commitment to pursuing complex financial fraud cases. The investigation was conducted by the FBI and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of Inspector General, with substantial assistance from the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Angela Adams prosecuted the case. Victims describe financial and family devastation Amy Dees, who listened to the entire hearing from an overflow courtroom, described the investors’ testimony as the most significant part of the day. “Their testimonies preached a sermon,” Dees said. According to Dees, several investors described damage to relationships with spouses and children who had trusted their recommendations to invest with Frost. One father described the pain of having encouraged his children to invest, only to lose their confidence in his financial judgment. Others described marriages strained by the losses. The Baldwin family, including a father and two sons, was among those who addressed the court. Lisa Deveraux, who was seated in the main courtroom, said their testimony illustrated consequences extending across generations, including concerns about paying for children’s education. Some victims who had not intended to speak ultimately found the confidence to address the judge after listening to others, Deveraux said. Frost’s attorneys had submitted more than 80 letters from pastors, political associates, family members, business owners, and longtime friends describing his charitable activities and service to the community. Prosecutors, however, argued that Frost had exploited those same religious and political relationships to attract investors. Amy Dees: A day of accountability for Coweta County For Dees, Monday’s hearing carried significance beyond the federal criminal case. She has served on the Coweta County Board of Education through years of political activity involving the Frost family and attended the sentencing because she wanted to support the victims and witness the outcome. “It’s a good day in Coweta,” Dees said. Her comments reflect a history of political disputes involving the family and local Republican organizations. Brant Frost V, the convicted businessman’s son and a former First Liberty employee, previously served as chairman of the Coweta County Republican Party. He resigned as chairman in August 2025 amid controversy surrounding First Liberty’s collapse. The Citizen previously reported concerns from Republican leaders , including state Rep. Josh Bonner, about the family’s continued political influence after the scandal became public. Dees said she felt the family’s conduct toward her and the community over many years made it important for her to attend. “I went to see Justice come to a family that I feel has attacked this community for years,” Dees said. Her comments describe her personal experience and views. Monday’s federal sentence concerned Frost IV’s criminal conduct; it was not a finding of wrongdoing against his relatives. Dees also expressed admiration for the investors who addressed the court, describing their willingness to speak publicly despite painful financial and personal consequences. “I was so proud of these victims,” she said. At 95, James McMaster speaks for himself and other victims Among those addressing the court Monday was 95-year-old James McMaster, the oldest known victim of the First Liberty scheme. McMaster, whose story The Citizen previously reported , lost approximately $1.3 million after investing with First Liberty. His longtime friend Lisa Deveraux, who helped organize the First Liberty Victims Portal, described his courtroom appearance: “James McMaster was a rock star.” Because of health concerns, McMaster had prerecorded a victim statement in case he could not attend the hearing. According to Deveraux, arrangements had been made through the FBI to submit the recording if necessary. Instead, McMaster appeared in person. Deveraux said he walked the court through his investment, the research he conducted before trusting First Liberty, and his interactions with Frost. He also discussed a photograph Frost had sent him of himself and his daughter celebrating Christmas in New York. Deveraux said the personal connection was particularly meaningful to McMaster because he had lost his own daughter at age 50. McMaster raised questions about the roles of other individuals connected to First Liberty and efforts to recover investors’ money. Deveraux said his willingness to speak publicly has helped other victims overcome their reluctance to tell their stories. Some have felt embarrassed about losing money, particularly after encouraging friends or relatives to invest. His example, she said, has helped others come forward. Judge challenges Frost’s explanation After the victims and other speakers addressed the court, Frost had an opportunity to speak on his own behalf. According to multiple people who attended the hearing, Frost discussed business difficulties and an artificial intelligence venture he believed could have rescued First Liberty from financial collapse. The defense’s earlier sentencing memorandum had described his investment in MyHealthAI, a virtual healthcare company whose anticipated financial success never materialized. Several witnesses told The Citizen that Judge May described Frost as “delusional” in connection with this explanation. Zaharis recalled the judge telling Frost that his presentation sounded as though he were attempting to sell her an investment. Both Dees and Zaharis said they were struck by what they regarded as a lack of remorse in Frost’s courtroom remarks. Zaharis, who watched from the main courtroom, observed that Frost did not turn toward the victims while speaking. She said she had expected more warmth and humility from someone whose attorneys had emphasized his remorse. Dees described Frost’s remarks as an attempt to explain the business failure rather than fully confront the victims’ losses. These observations contrasted with the defense’s portrayal of Frost as profoundly remorseful and committed to making amends. According to attendees, the defense also requested that Frost be allowed 90 days before reporting to prison. May allowed 30 days. State investigation continues Zaharis attended the hearing representing Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger’s Securities Division, which has been conducting its own investigation into First Liberty and individuals associated with the operation. She addressed the court and emphasized the financial harm suffered by investors, many of whom are between 70 and 90 years old. Zaharis told The Citizen that more than 150 victims have filed complaints with her office and that investigators have spoken with approximately 90% to 95% of them. Some victims remain reluctant to speak publicly because of embarrassment or fear that family members, friends, or people in their churches will learn about their losses. Zaharis said her division has numerous ongoing administrative proceedings and active investigations connected with First Liberty. Three individuals associated with First Liberty have already been subjected to separate state enforcement actions: • Brant Frost V , former Coweta County GOP chairman and son of Frost IV. • Timothy Nathaniel Darnell , a former Bankers Life financial advisor. • Randy Hough , a member of the Fayette County Board of Education. The Secretary of State’s Office previously issued $500,000 civil penalties against each of the three and referred their cases for possible criminal prosecution. Those actions are separate from the federal criminal case against Frost IV. Zaharis said the state investigation is independent of the federal proceedings. Her office administers Georgia securities laws and can pursue administrative remedies and refer matters to prosecutors. “We made the decision that it was very important that we show the victims that we are in support of them, and that is why we went,” Zaharis said. Questions remain about recovering investors’ money The restitution order represents a substantial financial judgment against Frost, but it does not mean victims will immediately receive repayment. During Monday’s hearing, an attorney representing the court-appointed receiver questioned the defense’s description of Frost’s cooperation with efforts to recover investor assets, according to Dees and Deveraux. Dees said the receiver’s representative told the judge that the defense had only recently expressed a willingness to cooperate, like in the last day. Deveraux said she also had questions about that account, given earlier proceedings involving First Liberty’s loans and business records. Judge May directed attention toward continuing recovery efforts, and victims were invited to meet after the hearing with representatives involved in the investigation and receivership. Deveraux created the First Liberty Victims Portal to give investors a place to share their stories, obtain information, and connect with agencies involved in the investigation and recovery process. She said the portal will continue providing assistance without charging victims. One recovery effort has already produced a significant agreement. In April, the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office announced a $6.7 million settlement with Bankers Life Advisory Services and Bankers Life Securities to repay 46 investors who had been directed to First Liberty by Darnell while he was employed by Bankers Life. The agreement was intended to return those investors’ lost principal, accounting for any money they had previously received. According to a recent call with Zaharis, those funds have been repaid to Darnell’s victims. But that settlement covers only a portion of the people harmed by First Liberty’s collapse. Deveraux believes the next phase of the case must concentrate on recovering money for other investors and determining what additional action may be taken against individuals involved. “This man in jail is one thing, but the recovery is a whole another animal,” Deveraux said. Sentencing ends one chapter, but not the case Frost’s prison sentence brings a significant conclusion to the federal criminal case against him, but investors continue to face unanswered questions about their losses. The Secretary of State’s Office has confirmed continuing investigations. The court-appointed receiver is working to identify and recover assets. Victims and their advocates continue pressing for restitution and accountability. For McMaster and others who came forward, the hearing provided an opportunity to have their experiences heard by the judge responsible for determining Frost’s punishment. Deveraux said she was relieved by the sentence but remained focused on what comes next. “Everything is focused, has to be focused, on recovery,” she said. For the victims of First Liberty, the sentence has been imposed. The work of recovering their money remains.

title: Officer Knew Dorsey, Ordered Him to Drop Gun Before Fatal Shooting
author: Ellie White-Stevens
content: DNA Found on Handgun 42 Feet Ahead of Where Teen Fell; Mayor Says Body Camera Footage Is Inconclusive The Newnan police officer who fatally shot 18-year-old Zadarious Dorsey knew him from previous encounters and called him by his nickname, Dae Dae, during the foot chase that ended in his death, according to new information released Monday by Coweta Judicial Circuit District Attorney Herb Cranford. The October 26 statement also confirms that Dorsey’s DNA was found on a handgun recovered approximately 42 feet ahead of where he fell after being shot October 3. But the available video does not conclusively establish whether Dorsey was holding the gun when the officer fired, according to Newnan Mayor James Shepherd, who reviewed the body camera footage during an October 22 meeting with prosecutors. In an interview with The Citizen , Shepherd said the recording captures the officer repeatedly ordering Dorsey to drop the gun immediately before firing. Whether Dorsey pulled the gun to use it, threw it away, or was still holding it when the officer opened fire remains unresolved. Officer knew Dorsey from previous encounters According to Cranford’s October 26 statement, surveillance footage shows that the officer pulled his unmarked police vehicle alongside the car in which Dorsey was riding at approximately 1:11 a.m. October 3. The officer exited wearing a vest marked POLICE, with his badge visible. The vehicle had not been stopped by police, Cranford said. Its occupants began walking away, and the officer directed only Dorsey to stop. Shepherd said he believed Dorsey was wearing a ski mask on top of his head, rather than pulled down over his face. During the ensuing foot chase, the officer called out, “stop, Dae Dae,” using the nickname by which Dorsey’s family and friends knew him. Cranford said police records confirm that the officer had been present during previous encounters involving Dorsey. Those included arrests in October 2025 and May 2024, both involving allegations of unlawful firearm possession, and Dorsey’s removal and trespass from Newnan High School in August 2023. The October 2025 arrest was previously documented in records obtained by The Citizen through an open records request. That report described an encounter in which Dorsey, then 17, fled from officers after making an improper U-turn on a scooter near Taylor Street and Fair Street. Officers pursued and apprehended him, reporting that they found a handgun in his possession. He was arrested on a charge of possession of a firearm by a person under 18. Cranford’s latest statement establishes that the officer involved in the fatal shooting was present during that earlier arrest. Dorsey’s DNA found on handgun 42 feet ahead of his body Cranford said the GBI recovered a Canik 9mm pistol equipped with an extended magazine and containing one bullet in the chamber. The firearm was found approximately 42 feet from where Dorsey fell. Importantly, it was not behind him along the path of the chase. It was ahead of him, farther from the vehicle where the encounter began. Cranford described its location as approximately the 2 o’clock position relative to the direction Dorsey had been running—diagonally ahead and to his right. That placement raises questions about how the gun traveled beyond the point where Dorsey fell. Dorsey could have thrown it forward, but the available evidence does not establish precisely when or how the gun reached that location. On October 15, the GBI Division of Forensic Sciences completed a DNA typing report identifying a match between DNA found on the firearm and Dorsey’s DNA. The finding provides forensic evidence connecting Dorsey to the handgun. It does not establish when he handled it, whether he threw it, or whether he was holding it when the officer fired. The original purchaser told investigators the handgun had been stolen from him in Albany, Georgia, several years earlier. The distance between the firearm and Dorsey’s body has been a point of contention since his family reviewed the body camera footage October 9. Family members told approximately 100 protesters gathered outside the Newnan Police Department that they questioned how the gun came to rest so far from where Dorsey fell. Attorneys Ben Crump and Harry Daniels, representing Dorsey’s family, have argued that Dorsey was unarmed when he was shot. The GBI’s preliminary account stated that Dorsey pulled a firearm from his waistband before the officer fired. Mayor says body camera footage is inconclusive Shepherd, who attended the October 22 evidence presentation, said the officer repeatedly ordered Dorsey to drop the gun immediately before firing. However, he emphasized that the recording does not clearly establish what Dorsey was doing with the gun during the final moments of the chase. “The video is not conclusive,” Shepherd said. The mayor said the footage is too blurry to determine whether Dorsey pulled the gun, pointed it toward the officer, or threw it away. He emphasized that the recording does not provide definitive visual evidence supporting either the family’s position that Dorsey was unarmed when shot or the conclusion that he was threatening the officer with a firearm at that moment. The number of shots fired also remains to be conclusively established. During the October 9 protest, family members said they counted six shots while reviewing the footage. Shepherd separately described hearing five shots, with the possibility of a sixth. The GBI’s initial statement said the officer fired multiple times but did not specify a number. The uncertainty over what occurred in the final moments is significant because the legal justification for deadly force depends on the circumstances the officer reasonably perceived when he fired. Dispute over Dorsey’s final words The family has also questioned what Dorsey said after being shot. During the October 9 protest , relatives who had viewed the complete body camera recording said Dorsey asked the officer, “Why did you shoot me, bro?” Shepherd said the footage shown to community leaders October 22 stopped at the shooting, out of respect for the family. He did not hear Dorsey’s words afterward. According to Shepherd, prosecutors provided a transcript of the subsequent audio and believed Dorsey had said, “I dropped it, yo.” The mayor emphasized that he had not personally heard that portion of the recording and could not determine which interpretation was accurate. The difference between the family’s account and the prosecutors’ interpretation remains unresolved. Two meetings with attorneys and family Cranford’s latest statement followed two meetings he conducted Thursday, October 22, at the Coweta County Justice Center. During the morning, Cranford met with civil attorneys representing Dorsey’s maternal relatives. That afternoon, he met with relatives from Dorsey’s paternal side, state and local NAACP leadership, clergy, and elected officials. The afternoon meeting was requested by Dr. Cynthia Finney, president of the Coweta County NAACP, who helped arrange the attendance of paternal family members with whom the district attorney’s office had not previously been in contact. Public officials attending included Coweta County Commissioner Al Smith, Newnan Mayor James Shepherd, Newnan Councilwoman Cynthia Jenkins, and Coweta County School Board Member Andrew Copeland. Cranford presented evidence from the ongoing investigation and explained the legal standards prosecutors will use in deciding whether the officer should face criminal charges. He also emphasized that his office does not represent the City of Newnan or the Newnan Police Department. The district attorney declined to comment on the civil attorneys’ interpretation of the evidence. Why did the officer pursue Dorsey? Cranford’s statement establishes that the initial encounter was not a traffic stop. According to surveillance footage reviewed by prosecutors, the other occupants of the vehicle walked away freely. The vehicle itself was driven from Cliff Circle at approximately 1:23 a.m., 10 minutes after the shooting. The officer pursued only Dorsey. Cranford explained that Georgia law distinguishes between consensual police encounters, investigative detentions, and arrests. During a consensual encounter, an officer generally may approach and speak with a person without suspecting a crime, provided the person remains free to leave. An investigative detention requires reasonable, articulable suspicion of criminal activity. Cranford said his office has not determined whether the officer had sufficient legal grounds to detain Dorsey when he ordered him to stop. He also distinguished that question from the legal justification for the shooting itself. According to Cranford, prosecutors must ultimately determine whether they can prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the officer was unreasonable in believing deadly force was necessary to protect himself from death or great bodily injury. Cranford also confirmed that Dorsey was prohibited from possessing firearms under the terms of bonds issued in Coweta County on October 10, 2025, and Carroll County on February 16, 2026. Those restrictions establish that Dorsey was not legally permitted to possess a firearm at the time of the shooting. They do not, by themselves, resolve whether the officer’s use of deadly force was justified. Investigation continues The GBI has not completed its investigation, and the final autopsy report remains pending. Cranford previously announced plans to release the body camera footage, other evidence, and a presentation of the shooting timeline after receiving the autopsy report. The new forensic findings and confirmation of the officer’s previous familiarity with Dorsey answer some of the questions raised by his family and the community since the October 3 shooting. But the central question remains unresolved: whether Dorsey posed an immediate threat to the officer at the moment deadly force was used. Cranford said his office will continue providing updates as the investigation develops. No charging decision has been announced.

title: Follow the Money: Where Campaign Cash in Georgia’s 3rd District Goes
author: Kenneth Hamner
content: Last November, when Peachtree City residents were deciding who should be on City Council, a political committee run by Rep. Brian Jack sent $500 to one of the candidates. A month later, Jack’s campaign sent a far bigger check to the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC). Those two checks point to a part of campaign finance most voters never see. We already know congressional campaigns are expensive. We know corporations and wealthy people give a lot of money, and we know some of them seek greater access to elected officials. None of that is news. What I wanted to understand was something else: When someone writes a check to our congressman, where does that money actually go? A big share of the money raised in Jack’s name never goes toward his own re-election. Meanwhile, his Democratic challenger, Maura Keller, runs a much smaller campaign, and almost all of her money stays in her race. None of this is improper. It is how the system is built to work for a member in Jack’s position. But it means a donation to Brian Jack can also be a donation to something much bigger, and that says a lot about where money in politics stands today. I sent both campaigns questions by email, and both answered in writing. Jack’s campaign responded through a spokesperson and included a statement from the congressman. Keller’s campaign manager, Alex Waterson, answered for her. Their answers appear throughout this story. Following The Big Check Let’s start with the bigger of the two checks, the one Jack’s campaign sent to the national party a month after 2025’s Election Day. It was for $250,000 , and the campaign followed it with another $50,000 in February. If you are not familiar with the NRCC, it is the Republican Party’s national organization for winning seats in the U.S. House . It recruits candidates, helps pay for their campaigns, and spends heavily in the close races that decide which party controls the chamber. By the end of March, it had already raised $164.4 million this cycle . Those two checks were only the beginning of what Jack has sent. To understand where the money went, it helps to know how Jack raises it. Many candidates, like his opponent Keller, run their campaign through a single committee. Jack runs his operation through three: Brian Jack for Congress is his campaign. Peach State PAC is his leadership PAC and lets a member of Congress give money to other candidates and causes. Team Brian Jack is a joint fundraising committee and lets a candidate and a party collect one large check and split it. Jack shares his with the NRCC. That third committee is arguably the most important. The law caps what one person can give Jack’s campaign at $3,500 per election . The cap for giving to the NRCC is far higher, at $44,300 a year. So a donor who wants to give more than Jack’s campaign can accept needs another way to do it. That is where Team Brian Jack comes in. It lets a donor support Jack and the party with one much larger check. Its filings list three partners : Jack’s campaign, his leadership PAC, and the NRCC. When a check comes in, the committee divides it among the three using a formula set in advance, and no partner can receive more than its own limit allows. Because the NRCC’s limit is so much higher, the joint committee can accept checks far bigger than anything Jack’s campaign could take on its own. Several donors have written checks of $100,000 or more. Jack’s campaign told me the committee’s disbursements “adhere to the FEC’s disbursement limits, as prescribed by federal law.” So where has that money gone? Since the start of 2025, Team Brian Jack has raised about $1.1 million and handed out just over $1 million. The biggest share, $426,595 , went to the NRCC. Jack’s own campaign received $375,143, and his leadership PAC got $204,562. Add the $300,000 his campaign sent directly, and Jack’s committees have given the NRCC $726,595, a total his campaign confirmed to me. Jack’s campaign has also sent about $116,000 to other Republican candidates, and his leadership PAC has added $16,500 for federal candidates and the state party. A few examples: On a single day in March, the campaign sent $2,000 apiece to 15 House Republicans, including Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Mike Lawler of New York, Tom Kean of New Jersey, Jen Kiggans of Virginia, Zach Nunn of Iowa, and David Valadao of California. It voided 13 of those checks in June and reissued many of them later, which Jack’s campaign told me was “due to a clerical error.” Over the summer, it gave $95,500 to nearly 50 candidates , from Randy Fine in Florida to Nick Begich in Alaska, a total that includes the reissued checks. The leadership PAC gave $5,000 to Mike Collins’s U.S. Senate campaign and $2,000 to Michael Whatley’s in North Carolina. Add it all up, and the picture comes into focus. Not counting money moved between his own three committees, Jack’s operation has raised about $3.2 million this cycle. By my count, nearly $900,000 of that has gone to someone other than Jack. That is more than $1 of every $4 raised in Jack’s name. His campaign said its own count is even higher, above $950,000. And there is more where that came from. At the end of September, Jack’s campaign still had $1.21 million in the bank, and a report filed Oct. 22 showed $1.11 million by mid-October. Federal rules let a campaign move unlimited amounts to its party . When I asked his campaign whether more of that money would go to the party or to other candidates, the answer was one word: “Yes.” Following The Small Check Now back to the smaller check, the $500 that landed in a Peachtree City race on Election Day last November. It came from Jack’s leadership PAC, Peach State PAC, and went to Clint Holland when he was running for re-election to City Council . Peachtree City’s council races are nonpartisan. When I asked how the PAC decides which local races to support, a Jack campaign spokesperson said the congressman has built friendships with local officials across the district and is “delighted to consider any request for support from candidates who seek to also represent his constituents.” Holland is far from the only local recipient. Peach State PAC has given about $28,000 to state and local candidates and groups: Local Republican parties got $6,000 in Fayette County, $2,000 each in Carroll, Heard, and Lamar counties, and $1,500 in Haralson County. The North Spalding Republican Women’s Club got $2,000. State House candidates Daniel Cook, Jutt Howard, Tim Bearden, and Carmen Rice each got $1,000, and Rice got another $1,000 from Jack’s campaign. James Dutton got $1,000 for his race for Spalding County commissioner. The rest included $2,000 to the Fayette Shrine Club, $1,000 to Georgia Good Government, and $3,300 to a candidate in Texas. The PAC also spends a fair amount on itself. Its operating costs total about $95,000 , including $52,500 to a law firm called Elections LLC and about $30,000 to compliance consultants who handle the detailed reporting federal law requires. By my count, it has given away about $44,800. Jack’s campaign puts the figure at $73,800. Either way, the PAC has spent more running itself than it has given away, and it had $185,699 in the bank at the end of September. Why Raise Money For Everyone Else? Part of the answer is our district. Georgia’s 3rd stretches from Fayette and Coweta counties south to the northern suburbs of Columbus, and Jack won it by 33 points in 2024. Every major forecaster rates it safely Republican this year. In a seat like that, a congressman does not need millions of dollars to keep his job. That frees him up to use his fundraising for other things. The rest of the answer is the job itself. House members face fundraising targets for the party, known as party dues, on top of what they raise for themselves. No law requires members to pay, but in practice those dues are not voluntary . Former Rep. David Jolly, a Florida Republican, said he was handed an invoice for what he owed the party in his first week in Congress. He later wrote that a member of his party’s leadership told him his responsibility was to raise $18,000 a day to secure his re-election. In 2017, chairs of the most powerful committees, including the Rules Committee, were expected to raise at least $1.2 million for the NRCC. Jack sits on Rules but does not chair it. His campaign would not share his target, calling it part of internal party strategy, but said he has exceeded it. Jack also has a bigger role than most. He is deputy chair of the NRCC , and he leads the effort to recruit Republicans to run for the House across the country. Before Congress, he ran then-House Republican Leader Kevin McCarthy’s political operation , and in his first term he landed a seat on the Republican Steering Committee , which decides which committees other Republicans serve on. His supporters could argue that kind of influence is what our district gets in return. His Georgia colleagues do some of this as well, just not to the same degree. Rick Allen of the 12th District has given $320,700 from his campaign to other candidates and committees, and Rich McCormick of the 7th has given about $38,000, plus $89,000 in transfers to other committees. What really sets Jack apart is his reach. He has raised more than either of them, including about $246,000 from donors who gave $200 or less. Who Is Paying For It? That reach raises another question: Who is supplying the money? Nearly 300 PACs have given Jack’s campaign a combined $1 million . A few industries stand out because several of their PACs gave the $10,000 maximum: Peanuts: Four groups representing growers, shellers, and buyers gave $10,000 apiece, or $40,000 in all. They are the U.S. Peanut PAC, the Peanut Buying Points PAC, the American Peanut Shellers Association PAC, and the PAC of the Alabama Peanut Producers Association. That is no surprise in a state that grew 51% of the nation’s peanuts in 2025. Accounting: The four largest accounting firms and their national trade group gave $36,000. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants gave $10,000, Ernst & Young gave $8,000, Deloitte gave $7,500, KPMG gave $7,000, and PwC gave $3,500. Health insurance: Six large insurers and their trade group gave $26,000. Cigna gave $7,500, Elevance Health gave $5,500, Molina Healthcare gave $4,000, Centene gave $3,500, Humana gave $2,500, UnitedHealth Group gave $2,000, and the trade group America’s Health Insurance Plans gave $1,000. Aflac: The Columbus-based insurer gave $10,000 to Jack’s campaign and another $10,000 to his leadership PAC. The biggest checks go to Team Brian Jack, where seven donors gave $551,000 through June . Donors rarely explain why they give, and the filings do not say. Their backgrounds, though, show the kinds of interests Congress touches: Rick Yi of Suwanee gave $125,000, the most of anyone. He is president of STSC, a Gwinnett County company that provides technology and network systems to government agencies and corporations. Narasimhulu Neelagaru of Atlanta gave $101,000. A retired cardiologist, he founded Quantum National Bank in 1995 and joined the board of HomeTrust Bancshares when that company bought his bank in 2023. He was also appointed to the Georgia Student Finance Commission in 2024. Thomas Tull of Sewickley, Pennsylvania, gave $100,000. He founded Legendary Entertainment , the studio behind films such as Inception and Jurassic World, and sold it in 2016. Today he runs his holding company, Tulco, and chairs U.S. Innovative Technology , an investment fund that backs defense technology companies such as Anduril and Shield AI. He is also part of the Pittsburgh Steelers ownership group. Karmin Pace of Chattanooga, Tennessee, gave $100,000. FEC filings list Pace as founder of the Appalachian Conservation Institute , a nonprofit that protects nearly 11,000 acres in Tennessee’s Little Sequatchie Cove. Michael and Szana Marr of Sandy Springs gave $50,000 together. Michael Marr is an Atlanta personal injury lawyer who runs the Marr Law Firm. Michael Saylor and Phong Le each gave $37,500 in March. Saylor is the founder and executive chairman of Strategy, and Le is its CEO. Strategy is the world’s largest corporate owner of bitcoin , so federal rules for cryptocurrency matter a great deal to its business. Much of Jack’s money also comes from outside Georgia. By my count, only 16% of the money his campaign received over the summer from donors large enough to be listed by name came from people with Georgia addresses. For Keller, it was 82%. So does any of this influence how Jack votes? I looked, and I could not find evidence that donations changed his votes. On the votes he has cast this Congress, he has sided with his party about 97% of the time , and the crypto industry’s biggest checks came months after he voted for bills setting federal rules for cryptocurrency , not before. The one place where a donor’s business and his own work meet is the SALUTE Act , which sets up a Pentagon pilot program letting service members and their families buy supplemental cancer insurance. This is the kind of coverage Aflac pioneered. Its language became law in December 2025. Aflac lobbied on it , and most of the $49,000 that Aflac’s PAC and employees gave Jack’s committees came after the bill became law. Jack’s campaign said “constituents engaged Congressman Jack with an idea to better support our brave service members who are fighting cancer,” and that the bill has 32 cosponsors, 19 Republicans and 13 Democrats. The Other Way To Run While Jack is flush with money, Keller calls her operation the “coupon-clipping” campaign , and her filings fit the description. She has raised $237,866 through a single committee, Maura Keller for Congress , with no leadership PAC or joint committee behind it. Ninety-six percent of that came from individuals, and the typical gift over the summer was $50. Her top cities were Peachtree City, Newnan, and Fayetteville. Only three committees have given to her for a combined $10,000: March On PAC is a women-led group focused on reproductive freedom and voting rights. Hold the Line is a Democratic PAC founded by Marcus Flowers, who ran against Marjorie Taylor Greene in 2022. SCP Democrats for Action is a group of Democrats in the Sun City Peachtree retirement community in Griffin. Her spending is just as simple. Over the summer, her campaign spent $60,165 , and its biggest payments were $15,000 each to her communications director, AJ Flanigan, and her campaign manager, Alex Waterson. She had $114,762 left at the end of September. By mid-October, after raising another $8,755 and spending $29,996, she had $93,522. Keller has also expressed her own frustrations with how her party raises money. Her campaign said she has not decided whether she would pay dues to the DCCC (the Democrats’ version of the NRCC) if elected. Waterson said Keller is frustrated that the party’s spending always seems to react to races instead of building for the future. “How are we going to develop rural areas if we never give a dime to party-building because they’re not built up enough?” Waterson wrote me in an email. “It’s a Catch-22.” Is This A Healthy System? Not everyone thinks so. House members told NOTUS this summer that they or their teams spend about 10 to 20 hours a week on “call time,” phoning donors for money. One House Democrat described constant reminders to pay “your full dues.” Lauren Underwood of Illinois, who helps lead candidate recruiting for House Democrats much like Jack does for Republicans, put it simply: “We always have to make fundraising calls.” The watchdog group Issue One has argued that party dues pull members’ time and attention away from legislating, oversight, and constituent services, and some Republicans agree. Former Rep. Trey Radel, a Florida Republican, has described a tally sheet on display at NRCC meetings listing what each member had given, calling it “a huge wall of shame.” Former Rep. Zach Wamp of Tennessee called the dues system “a recipe for corruption that disconnects members of Congress from their constituents.” Watchdogs have also questioned the rule that lets campaigns send unlimited sums to their parties, especially after Michael Bloomberg moved $18 million in leftover campaign money to the Democratic National Committee in 2020. Party leaders see it differently. Former Rep. Rodney Davis, an Illinois Republican, has said the payments are not a requirement . Others argue that pooling money is how a party protects its most vulnerable members and holds a majority, and that a strong majority is how members deliver for their districts. Rep. Beth Van Duyne, a Texas Republican, recently compared a $25,000 fee to attend her party’s midterm convention to NRCC dues, calling it a way for “team members to help other team members.” What to do about all this is where people part ways. Some reformers want to change the job itself. The STOP Act, introduced in 2016 by Jolly, would have barred members of Congress from personally asking for money and left fundraising to their campaign staff. Democratic Rep. Rick Nolan of Minnesota signed on, but the bill went nowhere. Other reformers have pushed to lift up small donors so candidates depend less on PACs and wealthy givers. I asked both campaigns how much time their candidates spend raising money. Keller’s campaign said she spends about 20 to 30 hours a week on fundraising calls. Jack’s campaign did not give a number. Instead, a spokesperson pointed to his record and claimed he is one of only nine members of Congress who have never missed a vote and has visited local groups more than 100 times. What Should We Make Of This? Let’s go back to those two checks where one went to a city council race in Peachtree City and the other, 500 times bigger, went to Washington. Members of Congress who want to move up are expected to raise money for their party, and Jack has built an operation that does exactly that. The money raised in his name pays for his own campaign, but it also pays for House races across the country and for Republican candidates and parties here at home. Our district is not unusual in where its money comes from, either. In 2024, only 17.6% of the itemized money given to House campaigns came from donors inside the candidates’ own districts, according to an OpenSecrets analysis . A decade ago, it was closer to 30% to 40%. Online platforms like WinRed and ActBlue have made it easy for a donor in Dallas to give to a congressman in Georgia, and it’s just as easy for that congressman’s campaign to pass the money along to a race in New York. Voters have noticed. In a 2023 Pew Research Center survey, 72% of Americans said there should be limits on how much individuals and organizations can spend on political campaigns, and 84% said special interest groups and lobbyists have too much say in what happens in politics. Support for limits crossed party lines. Where you land probably depends on what you want from a congressman. Jack’s supporters could say a member with deep party ties and a big fundraising network may be able to do more for our district in Washington. Keller’s supporters could say a member who depends on her neighbors may feel more answerable to them. Either way, a check written to our congressman does not always stay with him. It might pay for his own race, help a neighbor running for City Council, or end up in a House race a thousand miles from here. Whether that is the system working or the system broken is a question only you can answer, and you get your say on November 3rd. Want To Dig Into The Records? title: Crabapple Lane Celebrates Dolly Day with Book Drive
author: The Citizen
content: Crabapple Lane Elementary followed the example set by Dolly Parton, raising more than 800 books for donation. To help honor the legacy of Dolly Parton, especially her Imagination Library that has donated more than 300 million books, the school embarked on a book drive leading up to Dolly Day on Sept. 25. Led by the Pre-K Hatchlings class, the school was asked to give new and gently-used books for Children Read Atlanta. All together, more than 800 books were collected. To celebrate the huge success, students and staff were encouraged to dress up on Dolly Day in their best rhinestones, cowboy hats, and “Dolly” items. Of course, they made sure to share some good books, too! Principal Erik Falkenhagen thanked Ashley Fannin and Mary Beth Thompson for organizing the event and for all the participants who helped make it special. “Dolly Day was a huge success!,” he said. “Their generosity will help put books into the hands of children and continue to build a love of reading in our school community.”

title: Gov. Kemp Extends Suspension of State Gas Tax
author: The Citizen
content: ATLANTA – Governor Brian P. Kemp, in consultation with Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones and Speaker of the House Jon Burns, today announced he is extending a state of emergency due to global market volatility and the corresponding suspension of the state’s motor fuel excise tax through November 30. With gas and diesel prices remaining high, this action will provide needed relief for Georgians through the Thanksgiving holiday travel period. “With a major holiday coming up and fuel prices still at high levels, I am proud to take this step to keep more money in Georgians’ pockets,” said Governor Brian P. Kemp. “Our commitment to fiscal responsibility and stewarding taxpayer dollars has allowed us to act when needed, whether by suspending the gas tax or returning billions to taxpayers through income tax refunds and property tax relief. I’m grateful to our partners in the General Assembly for their support and for standing with us to budget conservatively for times such as these.” This follows the Governor’s previous executive orders declaring a state of emergency, which also suspended state weight limits on commercial vehicles, and then extending that state of emergency and also suspending penalties for using off-road “dyed” diesel on roads. Read the Governor’s executive order here . Georgia’s current motor fuel excise tax is 33.3 cents per gallon for gasoline and 37.3 cents per gallon for diesel. Following the suspension of the state motor fuel tax on September 28, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in Georgia has remained well below the national average, according to AAA . Georgia’s average price for a gallon of regular gas is approximately 63 cents below the national average, and the average price for diesel is around 61 cents below the national average. The current average price for a gallon of regular gas in Georgia is $3.66, and the average price for a gallon of diesel is $ 5.72.

title: Crabapple’s Camp Read-A-Lot Sparks Literacy Fun
author: The Citizen
content: Crabapple Lane Elementary’s Camp Read-A-Lot kicked off their One School, One Book program with flair. This year, the Cardinals are all reading “Big Foot and Little Foot” by Ellen Potter. The school-wide literacy initiative encourages the entire school community to read the same book at the same time, fostering meaningful conversations and a shared love of reading both at home and at school. Camp Read-A-Lot was an evening was filled with interactive activities, literacy resources, family engagement, and a strong sense of community. During the “Camp Out With a Good Book” session, each family received the surprise book selection, enjoyed camping-themed snacks, and read together in tents. The “Night at the Library Campout” featured a living character museum where teachers dressed as their favorite book characters, inspiring students to discover new books and authors. Families also enjoyed an interactive “Readers Theater” session that brought stories to life through performance and audience participation. Parents attended the “Trailblazing Reader Detectives” workshop where they learned strategies for helping children think more deeply about what they read through critical-thinking discussions. “Reading Ranger” stations provided literacy resources for families, including Beanstack support and information about Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library. Staff from the Tyrone Public Library was on hand, registering students for library cards and sharing information about programs and events for families throughout the year. The night even included a surprise book character reveal, with students eagerly guessing the mystery visitor before Big Foot arrived. Principal Erik Falkenhagen was thrilled with the response from the Cardinal family. “Camp Read-A-Lot was an exciting evening that brought together students, families, staff, and community partners to celebrate the joy of reading while launching our One School, One Book program,” he said. “The event was a tremendous success, building excitement for reading and setting the stage for a year of shared literacy adventures.”

title: Coweta County Sheriff’s Win First in their Category at Governor’s Challenge Awards
author: The Citizen
content: (MACON) The Governor’s Office of Highway Safety today honored 33 different Georgia law enforcement agencies for their year-round work to save lives and reduce traffic crashes on our roads during the 27th annual Governor’s Challenge Awards held at the Macon Centreplex. An annual recognition program for statewide law enforcement agencies of all sizes, the program featured awards in eight different categories based on department size, as well as Campus and University Police, Military Police, Traffic Enforcement Network of the Year, Coordinator and Assistant Coordinator of the Year, HEAT Team of the Year and several specialty program area awards. The first ever Director’s Cup grand prize, in honor of Director Allen Poole of the Governor’s Office of Highway Safety, was awarded to Snellville Police Department. This coveted award is given to the top performing department among all categories. Snellville garnered a score of 237 out of 260, with judging done by highway safety experts in Tennessee and South Carolina. This is Snellville’s second overall win in three years. The Governor’s Challenge program honors law enforcement agencies for their work to prevent crashes, injuries and deaths in their communities, college campuses and military installations. Designed to award outstanding achievements in highway safety enforcement and education, the awards recognize agencies for the approach and effectiveness of their overall highway safety programs. Agencies are evaluated not just for enforcement initiatives, but for unique problem-solving in their communities, using public information activities, and creating departmental policies that support their traffic enforcement campaign efforts. “Hosting Governor’s Challenge each year is one of the ways we can express our sincere gratitude to the men and women in law enforcement who dedicate themselves to saving lives on Georgia’s roads.,” Governor’s Office of Highway Safety Director Allen Poole said. “We’re honored to highlight these officers, deputies and troopers for helping keep Georgia’s roads safe.” Another highlight of the awards program was the always-anticipated awarding of this year’s Governor’s Challenge vehicle, a fully-equipped 2026 Dodge Durango. To award the vehicle, 10 agency names are drawn out of a pool that includes any agency that won an award. Those agencies each choose a key and whoever has the key that illuminates a special law enforcement light bar wins. This year’s vehicle was won by the Donalsonville Police Department. “Georgia has law enforcement agencies large and small in all corners of the state and that’s what’s great about Governor’s Challenge.” GOHS Law Enforcement Services Director Roger Hayes said. “These awards recognize the efforts of all agencies, no matter their size, on working towards the ultimate goal of zero traffic deaths on our roads. That is a goal we will never stop reaching for and we do that by encouraging departments that urge their citizens to buckle up, slow down, drive sober and never drive distracted.” The full list of this year’s Governor’s Challenge winners is as follows: AWARD CATEGORY PLACE Category 1: 1-10 Officers Demorest Police Department 1st Place Boston Police Department 2nd Place McCaysville Police Department 3rd Place Category 2: 11-25 Officers Twiggs County Sheriff’s Office 1st Place Forsyth Police Department 2nd Place Cairo Police Department 3rd Place Category 3: 26-45 Officers Calhoun Police Department 1st Place Morrow Police Department 2nd Place Fort Oglethorpe Police Department 3rd Place Category 4: 46-75 Officers Snellville Police Department 1st Place Dalton Police Department 2nd Place Tifton Police Department 3rd Place Category 5: 76-100 Liberty County Sheriff’s Office 1st Place Rome Police Department 2nd Place Valdosta Police Department 3rd Place Category 6: 101-200 Coweta County Sheriff’s Office 1st Place Gainesville Police Department 2nd Place Warner Robins Police Department 3rd Place Category 7: 201-500 Hall County Sheriff’s Office 1st Place Savannah Police Department 2nd Place Newton County Sheriff’s Office 3rd Place Category 8: 501+ Richmond County Sheriff’s Office 1st Place DeKalb County Police Department 2nd Place Cobb County Police Department 3rd Place Category 9: Colleges & Universities Georgia State University Police Department 1st Place University of Georgia Police Department 2nd Place University of West Georgia Police Department 3rd Place Traffic Enforcement Network of the Year Coastal Area Traffic Enforcement Network 1st Place Middle Georgia Traffic Enforcement Network 2nd Place Mountain Area Traffic Enforcement Network 3rd Place Coordinator of the Year Captain Lee Smith Asst Coordinator of Year Dep.
