title: QTS Invests $14 Million in Energy Efficiency Program to Help Lower Energy Costs for Fayette County Household
author: The Citizen
content: Collaborative program could help more than 800 eligible homeowners access needed weatherization and energy-efficiency home repairs through partnership with Georgia Power As part of Energy Efficiency Month, QTS Data Centers today announced the Fayette County Community Resilience Program, an innovative partnership with Georgia Power designed to help eligible customers overcome barriers to energy-efficiency improvements through home assessments, repairs and community-based support. QTS is investing $14 million to support pre-weatherization for more than 800 homes in Fayette County. Pre-weatherization work will address critical structural, health and safety issues that can prevent a home from accessing energy-efficiency improvements. By helping households complete this foundational work, the program is intended to create a pathway to homes that are more energy efficient, comfortable, healthy and safe. “At QTS, we believe that being a good neighbor means investing in the things that matter most to the people who call Fayette County home,” said Brian Herlihy, chief development officer at QTS. “This partnership with Georgia Power is about making a real difference for residents and families by creating opportunities to access resources that can improve their homes, lower energy costs and deliver benefits that last well beyond a single project.” For some households, necessary health and safety repairs must be completed before weatherization or other energy-efficiency improvements can begin. The Fayette County Community Resilience Program is designed to help close that gap, creating a coordinated pathway from customer outreach and home assessment to needed repairs, energy-efficiency improvements and follow-up. Eligible upgrades, based on a program-specific home assessment, may include: Improving attic insulation Sealing air gaps, cracks and leaks Installing smart thermostats Sealing heating and air conditioning delivery ducts Servicing heating and cooling systems Upgrading gas furnaces, boilers and water heaters “We know that energy costs are an important part of every family’s budget and that’s why we work every day to connect our customers with tools, programs and resources to save money and energy,” said Latanza Adjei, senior vice president and chief customer officer for Georgia Power. “Developing new strategic partnerships that help meet customers where they are and move them closer to energy efficiency, alongside outstanding partners like QTS, is just one of the ways that we are keeping customers at the center of what we do and making growth work for Georgia.” QTS and Georgia Power are working with The Same House and Groundswell to connect eligible households with the program and help residents navigate the process. The Same House will support local education and outreach, helping build awareness and connect residents with available resources. Groundswell will serve as the Energy Navigator, providing personalized guidance, technical screening and application support as households move from initial engagement toward home repairs and energy-efficiency improvements. Eligible Georgia Power customers in Fayette County can learn more about the program, eligibility requirements and the enrollment process by visiting Groundswell.org/Soul/Soul-Fayette . Customers not eligible or not selected for the Fayette County Community Resilience Program are also encouraged to visit GeorgiaPower.com/Save to join the hundreds of thousands of customers who take advantage of savings programs from the company every year.

title: Senoia Optimists Host Blood Drive for Red Cross on November 2nd
author: The Citizen
content: The next Red Cross Blood Drive, sponsored by The Optimist Club of Senoia and the Senoia United Methodist Church (UMC), will be on November 2nd, 2026, from 1 – 6 pm at the church which is located at 229 Bridge Street. Donors who participate in the Senoia UMC blood drive on November 2nd will be eligible to receive a $10 Amazon gift card from the American Red Cross (ARC). Successful November donations will also get free A1C testing, commonly used to screen for prediabetes and diabetes. (One test result per donor in 2026; fasting is NOT required.) You’ll also be able to enjoy a “famous” grilled cheese sandwich along with snacks provided by the ARC during the blood drive. Sign up now for the blood drive using the link https://www.redcrossblood.org/give.html/find-drive or call the Red Cross at 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767). Who can you help by donating blood? Among others, you can help cancer patients, trauma patients, Sickle Cell patients, and burn patients, according to the ARC web site. The need is constant. The gratification is instant. Give Blood. If you would like to learn how you can help in this or another worthwhile project sponsored by the Senoia Optimist Club, please email the club at senoiaoptimistclub@gmail.com . or visit its Facebook page (“Senoia Optimist Club”) or its web site ( https://optimistclubofsenoia.org/ ). If you would like more information about the Senoia United Methodist Church, please visit its web site at https://senoiaumc.org/ , check its Facebook page (“Senoia UMC”) or call the church office at 770-599-3245.

title: Lula’s Victory Is Surprising Because He Has So Little to Offer Brazil
author: Bruna Frascolla
content: Latin America Lula’s Victory Is Surprising Because He Has So Little to Offer Brazil The left-wing incumbent’s fresh policies were largely reversals of those he implemented previously. Photo by Alexandre Schneider/Getty Images On the eve of the second round of Brazil’s presidential election, every major research institute believed that Flávio Bolsonaro would win. Even Lula voters were pessimistic. Things began to change when the Workers’ Party (PT) asked the Superior Electoral Court to extend the voting time by two hours (that is, until 7 p.m.) in Salvador and nearby cities, arguing that Bolsonarist mayors had made it harder for residents to vote by reducing the number of buses. This is not an unusual accusation, and the higher courts are generally seen as favorable to Lula. (Even though the president of the electoral court happens to be a justice appointed by Bolsonaro, his decisions were disregarded by fellow members.) Notably, Salvador votes heavily for Lula. But the transit difficulties were caused —at least in part—by the activity of Lula’s partisans themselves. Trade unionists glued PT stickers on buses while they were still in the garage; because such advertising would constitute a crime under Brazil’s election laws, city workers had to remove the stickers before the buses could start their routes. By 10:30 a.m., traffic was more or less back to normal. When the PT used this to ask the courts for an extension, Flávio’s campaign did the same, arguing that some southern cities whose voters tilt toward him should have their polling hours extended to account for weather-related issues. The surprise came when the PT went further, and asked not the Electoral Court, but the Supreme Court, to keep the polls open until 7 p.m for the entire country. The Supreme Court, operating under an unaudited system , picked Cristiano Zanin, Lula’s former personal attorney, to decide the matter. And Zanin ruled as his former client wanted. (The decision also created ambiguity around voting machines: Some machines had already been sealed in anticipation of a 5 p.m. closure, and the Court’s decision did not allow these to be reopened). Following this decision, Lula won the election, to the amazement of many Brazilians. What will happen next is unclear. It is worth noting that Brazil elected an opposition-controlled Senate with a penchant for impeaching justices. And we may also see appeals for help from outside Brazil, since Bolsonaro supporters are unlikely to get redress in their own country. Regardless of where such efforts go, it remains to explain why Lula’s performance was so poor up until the second round. A modest but persistent fact sums up Brazil’s political reality: Lula’s campaign appealed overwhelmingly to the elderly . After over 16 years of PT rule, Lula failed to persuade Brazil’s youth that a fourth term augured an auspicious future. In Brazil, presidents are limited to two consecutive terms but face no limit on the total number of terms. Thus, Lula served two terms between 2003 and 2010, handed things off to a PT successor, Dilma Rousseff, who served until 2016, and then himself returned to office in 2023. The interruption in PT governance consisted of Rousseff’s neoliberal Vice President Michel Temer (2016–19) and Jair Bolsonaro (2019–23), who currently is in prison and barred from running for office. In 2022, older voters compared the good times of Lula’s prior terms to the chaotic, Covid-hobbled Bolsonaro administration and concluded that the elder leftist could bring back the 2000s. Lula’s third term made it clear that he couldn’t. It’s well known in Brazil that Lula lucked out during his previous presidencies. During the 2000s, China became an economic powerhouse with 1.4 billion mouths to feed. Brazil, on the other hand, transformed into an agricultural dynamo, thanks in part to government-sponsored research conducted during military rule (1964–85). The country’s Central-West Region went from a barren land to a global breadbasket. Lula’s administrations have no comparable accomplishment; his most-celebrated feat was the reduction of poverty through an income transfer program called Bolsa Família , in which families received cash payments in exchange for sending children to school. Inspired by Milton Friedman’s negative income tax , the program has precedents in the neoliberal administration of Fernando Henrique Cardoso (1995–2003). The key difference between Cardoso and his successor was the latter administration’s more bountiful sources of funding. All things considered, one could argue that Lulismo is a neoliberal version of Chavismo . In both cases, the president relies on commodities to transfer income to the poor and win elections. Notably, each administration’s primary goal is maintaining itself in power, as opposed to spurring long-term development. But while Chavismo used Venezuela’s state oil company to raise funds, Lulismo depends on a cozy relationship with financialized agribusiness giants. Neither model worked, of course, and in Brazil the consequence has been the decimation of a once mighty manufacturing industry. The best the average Brazilian can hope for in 2026 is driving an Uber and complementing his income with Bolsa Família . Instead of doctors driving taxis as in Cuba, Brazil has engineers with student debt driving for Uber. In this regard, Brazil is similar to the United States, many of whose factories decamped for China and elsewhere, leaving behind a “basket of deplorables.” Of course, deindustrialization in Brazil came later, much of it happening during Lula’s first term. In 2004, Brazil signed an agreement recognizing China as a market economy, thereby dropping key anti-dumping barriers: a flood of cheap Chinese imports subsequently enraged São Paulo’s Industrial Federation . Decades later, Brazilian industry has suffered another blow from the EU-Mercosur agreement, which Lula approved in 2025. Naturally, it benefits Brazilian agribusiness at the expense of manufacturing. What, then, was Lula doing to entice voters? During the campaign, he improvised three big commitments: shortening the work week, ending the so-called “shirt tax,” and banning online gambling. The first was embraced only under pressure from the upcoming vote. As for the shirt tax—a 20 percent import duty on small-value foreign parcels coming into Brazil—Lula himself created it in 2024. The tax was imposed on imports from websites like AliExpress, and was aimed at favoring Brazilian retailers while increasing tax revenue. In effect, Lula lauded undoing his own work as a great victory. Much the same can be said of online gambling, since Lula himself tolerated and regulated the industry following its initial approval by Temer. (Online gambling, of course, was a much appreciated source of tax revenue.) By the end of the campaign, the incumbent was making increasingly desperate attempts to shore up his candidacy. Just twelve days before the first round, he announced a 15 percent increase for Bolsa Família . When asked why he had gone more than three years without raising Bolsa Família despite inflation, he said he hadn’t realized the program had lost buying power. Lula also proposed a $80-a-month stipend for university students, as well as debt forgiveness for micro-entrepreneurs. Who exactly qualifies as an individual micro-entrepreneur? Anyone, potentially; the category was created during Lula’s second term, as a way of recognizing individuals otherwise lacking labor protections. In the end, Lula had nothing to offer Brazilians uninterested in living off of welfare. Voters, moreover, were concerned with many noneconomic issues such as crime, corruption, woke ideology, and judicial abuse. It’s no wonder then that Lula resorted to fear-mongering against his opponent. His campaign went so far as to insinuate that the evangelical Flávio Bolsonaro would dethrone Our Lady of Aparecida as the country’s patroness. (The authority for such a move lies with the pope.) With the legal-electoral outcome somewhat in the air but clearly trending toward upholding Lula’s victory, the question is whether the younger Bolsonaro would have been a better alternative to Lula and the PT. After all, Flávio is a close ally of Argentina’s Javier Milei, whose administration’s economic policies have increasingly subjected Argentines to something approximating a vegan diet. (Brazilians had hoped, however, that Flávio would follow a different path from that of his anarcho-capitalist neighbor.)  The younger Bolsonaro’s candidacy also prevailed over that of São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas, who was favored by market-friendly Milei enthusiasts on the right. Naturally, that faction was supported by financial and agribusiness elites, many of whom embrace the environmental, social, and governance policies abhorred by Bolsonaristas. Adherents of this brand of market fundamentalism are also fond of financial jargon centered on spending cuts and “efficiency.” One such proponent, Flávio-advisor Daniella Marques, floated replacing civil servants with AI —a proposal which was subsequently seized upon by Lula’s campaign. While the elder Bolsonaro’s sons have no history of developmentalist politics, it seems this may have changed. Trump’s tariffs for instance have upended entrenched dogma over free trade on the Bolsonarista right. Last year, Eduardo Bolsonaro shocked both left and right by defending the legacy of the heterodox Brazilian dictator Getúlio Vargas, who, despite governing as an anticommunist, is often celebrated by leftists. More promising, however, was the backing of two of Lula’s former cabinet members, Aldo Rebelo and Roberto Mangabeira Unger, who broke with the president over his subservience to fanatical foreign and environmental lobbies. Rebelo is a former communist, while Unger is a Harvard professor and philosopher. The pair spoke with Flávio for over an hour, and all of them committed to a defense of Brazil’s sovereignty. The post Lula’s Victory Is Surprising Because He Has So Little to Offer Brazil appeared first on The American Conservative .

title: The Left Wants America to Look Like France
author: Taki
content: Politics The Left Wants America to Look Like France The Hexagon is reaping the consequences of socialism and mass migration. TakiMag (Pascal LACHENAUD / AFP via Getty Images) I think all writers, especially those writing about politics, have been guilty of getting their facts wrong at times, not on purpose, mind you, but in their eagerness to make their point. This one stuck out like the proverbial you-know-what. The writer, Rich Lowry, I used to know in the old Bill Buckley days. Last week he wrote about the troubles in France, prompting me to write this column. However incredible it may sound, I knew the French general involved in the story I’m about to tell you, the one that would reject an assertion made by Lowry.  Lowry writes, “In 1968, President de Gaulle himself briefly fled Paris for fear that student protesters were going to topple the government, before finding his nerve.” When I read this line, it was like hearing someone say that Leonidas and his 300 Spartans had fled before the Persians at Thermopylae. Although not particularly drawn to de Gaulle, I happen to know first-hand why he had left Paris, and it was not because he feared the spoilt and pretentious students who had risen against his government and were burning down the ancient city. De Gaulle had flown to Germany to meet with French General Jacques Massu, the tough-as-nails paratroop leader and veteran of Indochina and Algeria colonial wars. Massu was based in Germany with a French army group. De Gaulle wanted to know if Massu and his troops were ready to come to Paris if needed and to crack the whip. The start of the conversation went  as follows. De Gaulle: “ Alors Massu, toujours con ?” (So, Massu, still an a–hole?) Massu: “ Oui, mon General, toujours Gaullist .” (Yes, General, still a Gaullist.”) (The same exchange between the two men has been reported as occurring a decade earlier.) Army people talk like that, semi-tough, semi fun between them. Massu had first sided with the generals who had revolted against de Gaulle when he granted Algeria her independence. They formed the OAS and began a guerrilla war against the mainland. But Massu ultimately remained loyal to de Gaulle, who forgave him. How do I know what went on between Le Grand Charles and the toughie Jacques? That’s an easy one: The latter told me while we were watching tennis at Roland-Garros in the players section. That’s where we first met, back in the early Sixties, when I spotted Massu sitting alone and watching the matches. None of the players had a clue who he was. I introduced myself and he asked about various tennis players. Massu was very well read, like many Frenchmen, and was close to generals Salan, Challe, Jouhaut and Zeller, the OAS leaders who all eventually were locked up but retained the respect of the French people, who considered Algeria part of France. Well, we all know how it ended. France lost Algeria in 1962, but gained millions of its nationals over subsequent decades. Many of them have remained Arab, Muslim, and feeling foreign despite having been born in France. There has been no cultural assimilation whatsoever. (As the U.S. Congresswoman Ilhan Omar allegedly said, she and her compatriots are “Somalis first, Muslims second.” I predict Omar will be with us for the duration.) They have also remained anti-French, anti-Catholic, and anti-establishment. France today is what those nice socialist Democrats would like the U.S. to become one day, with open borders and welfare payments for everyone. One-hundred thousand Somalis in Minneapolis will one day turn into millions. The irony is that de Gaulle had foreseen all that when he headed the new Fifth Republic upon his return to power in the late ’50s. He broke with Israel because he knew the country’s policies would alienate the Arab world, and remained an independent member of NATO. De Gaulle was personally very brave. He had made his reputation when as a colonel he led a bold counterattack during the Guderian blitz in May 1940. When the OAS sprayed his presidential Citroen limo in Petit Clamart, he did not even flinch or bow his head, but miraculously escaped unscathed. Hence the idea that a bunch of publicity-seeking, smelly lefties drove him from Paris in 1968 is quite false. France at present is what our socialist friends would like America to become. For decades, despite apocalyptic warnings by both politicians of the right and writers such as Michel Houellebecq, France has taken the path to disaster. The warnings have been ignored, and those doing the warning have been persecuted as Nazis. What motivated the mob back in 1968 and still does is greed, laziness, entitlement, and envy. The rioters are not the weak and starving, but the indulged and ignorant children of a welfare state and woke culture. They smash windows, grab designer goodies, and the media headline them as revolutionaries.  And another thing. The deep-seated hostility toward free markets and enterprise derives from the French passion for philosophers, clowns like Michel Foucault, a pseudo-philosopher, and others who taught “nothingness” as a value system. Those clowns were venerated by leftist media and publications and taught that history was false, all lies in order to exploit the people. The only joy, according to those false prophets, was the criminal act.  The French state owns nearly all public services, public transport, energy interests, and utilities. Public debt stands at 120 percent of GDP, the highest since right after the Second World War. Pensioners enjoy a higher income than workers. If you wish to see the same thing over here, vote for those nice socialists next month. It will be a start. title: Russia–Ukraine Peace Compromise Is Necessary. It Won’t Be Fair
author: Ted Snider
content: Ukraine Russia–Ukraine Peace Compromise Is Necessary. It Won’t Be Fair Kiev will need to make painful concessions to guarantee its survival. Photo by Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto via Getty Images U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff flew last week from Oslo, where he had held talks with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, to St. Petersburg for a meeting with Russia’s President Vladimir Putin. Witkoff reportedly carried with him updated proposals for a framework agreement to end the war. Putin reportedly responded that he is ready, in principle, to resume talks with Kiev in November. It is time for the U.S. and Europe to put every effort behind those talks. The narrative of why the West supposedly needs to keep backing Ukraine’s war effort has evolved over the course of the conflict, from upholding international norms to regaining territory to defending democracy to protecting Europe against an imperialist Russia. But the time has come to stop creating narratives and start accepting the painful reality that Ukraine faces existential peril if the war continues. Each new narrative only provides more time for Ukraine’s crisis to become more acute. Ukraine is bleeding land, people, and money. Its ports, bridges, data centers, transportation, mining, agriculture, industry, and infrastructure are being annihilated. It can no longer defend itself from devastating attacks on the capital and elsewhere—so an end to Russian attacks must be negotiated. A compromise peace, rather than the total defeat of Russia, is not a fair outcome. Nor would the details of such a settlement be fair; Ukraine would have to make more concessions than Russia. But the peace cannot be fair because the war was never fair: It wasn’t fair that the more powerful Russian army illegally invaded Ukraine, and it wasn’t fair that the West used Ukraine as a proxy to fight against Russia, rather than settling the war in its early weeks when the opportunity arose. Despite the fact that a peace deal would not be fair, it would save Ukraine and stop the war from getting worse. And although Ukraine would have to make the more painful concessions, Russia too would need to give way on some things. Under any reasonable settlement, Ukraine would remain a sovereign country and keep most of its territory. It would be free to join the European Union and orient itself toward the West: the dream of the 2014 Maidan protests. And it would retain a large, well-equipped military to defend its borders. NATO membership, however, is probably off the table. At the close of the Cold War, Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev was told that NATO would not expand eastward. In 1991, Russia recognized the sovereignty of Ukraine on the basis of the Declaration of State Sovereignty of Ukraine, adopted when the latter withdrew from the Soviet Union. This document stated that Ukraine “solemnly declares its intention of becoming a permanently neutral state that does not participate in military blocs.” Ukrainian neutrality should be restored. To that end, NATO and Ukraine must both sign legally binding commitments that the latter will not become a member of the former. This concession is essential to ending the war because Russia will not stop fighting without it; indeed, it was the key reason Russia launched its invasion. For its part, Russia has made an important concession in dropping its objection to Ukraine joining the EU. Part of the reason for Moscow’s initial opposition to this is that the EU’s Association Agreement with Ukraine was also a security agreement. It committed Ukraine to “deeper involvement in the European security area” and “military and technological cooperation.” That is now a key reason why Ukraine must be granted EU membership: With the NATO door closed, EU membership may be the strongest security guarantee Ukraine can reasonably expect to get.  Ukraine will have to cede some territory for the war to end, though how much remains up for discussion. That would set a bad precedent for international order, yet Russian-speaking citizens of Ukraine in Crimea and Donbas do deserve full protection of their cultural, linguistic, and religious rights, and Kiev’s relinquishing these territories could facilitate this guarantee. The Minsk Agreements, which ultimately collapsed, had been intended to solve this problem in part by expanding autonomy for these regions. However, Ukrainian and European leaders appear to have seen these commitments more as a way to buy time for Ukraine to rearm than as a serious solution to the problem. The idea of increased autonomy within Ukraine is now off the table, and Putin will not stop the war without directly annexing as much of this territory as possible. By giving up NATO membership and some territory, Ukraine can survive, and eventually thrive, as an intact nation, aligned with Europe and boasting a strong military and adequate security guarantees. Any proposed security architecture should embrace not just Ukraine, but all of Europe, including Russia, finally putting in place the foundation for peace that was never established after the Cold War. Ukrainians are suffering through a conflict that their leader, and leaders in Europe, have had difficulty stopping because of promises they made to defeat Russia. But it is time to end this war—even if that requires an unfair peace. The post Russia–Ukraine Peace Compromise Is Necessary. It Won’t Be Fair appeared first on The American Conservative .

title: Iran War Day 241: IDF Chief Resists Push for Pre-Election Military Op Against Iran, Per Report
author: Luke Nicastro
content: According to Israeli media reports , an “unprecedented confrontation” occurred over the weekend between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israel Defense Forces (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir. Israel’s Channel 12 reported that Zamir resisted carrying out Netanyahu’s directive for unspecified military action against Iran, requesting proof of legal authorization and signed documentation before proceeding. Per Channel 12, Zamir was concerned that “the political echelon could lead Israel into a scenario of miscalculation facing Iran just before the elections.” Netanyahu has denied that such a confrontation occurred.  Senior representatives from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey—the three members of the newly-formed Mecca Pact— traveled to Tehran this week. The Saudi defense minister, Turkish intelligence head, and Pakistani army chief are in Iran for unusually high-level discussions with their Iranian counterparts. The talks are believed to be aimed at managing the conflict in Yemen and preventing a renewed escalation of the Iran war. Brent crude was trading at around $116 per barrel Monday morning, a slight pullback from Friday but still near six-month highs. AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline in the United States is $4.29 per gallon, and the average price of diesel is $6.35 per gallon. title: Vucic Concedes Defeat in Serbian Election
author: Luke Nicastro
content: In a speech Sunday night, former Serbian president and prime minister Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in his country’s parliamentary elections. Vucic, who has dominated Serbian politics since 2012, lost to a new student-backed political grouping called Student List-Students Win, which took around 140 seats to his party’s 103. Students have played an outsized role in the opposition to Vucic’s government. Following the 2024 Novi Sad train canopy collapse, they led street demonstrations demanding accountability for the disaster, which quickly snowballed into broader anti-corruption protests. Ahead of the election, Student List-Students Win cited ending corruption, protecting media independence, raising living standards, and improving relations with neighboring countries as its chief priorities. It is not yet clear who the bloc will tap to be prime minister. The post Vucic Concedes Defeat in Serbian Election appeared first on The American Conservative .

title: Lula Wins in Brazil, but Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede
author: Andrew Day
content: Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term on Sunday in a polarized runoff election against the right-wing candidate Flavio Bolsonaro. Lula won 51.8 percent of the vote with all the votes counted, according to results announced by Brazil’s electoral court. Bolsonaro refused to concede and asked for the election to be annulled, pointing to a last-minute decision from a Supreme Court justice to extend voting for two hours. He observed that the justice, Cristiano Zanin, is Lula’s former lawyer, but both candidates had requested extensions. The results defied preelection polls and marked a setback for the rising Latin American right. Bolsonaro is the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated in 2022. The elder Bolsonaro was sentenced to prison for plotting a coup to remain in power. The post Lula Wins in Brazil, but Bolsonaro Refuses to Concede appeared first on The American Conservative .

title: Biden’s Israel Catastrophe
author: Martin Di Caro
content: Foreign Affairs Biden’s Israel Catastrophe A veteran journalist reveals how a Democratic White House enabled Israeli atrocities in Gaza. U.S. President Joe Biden poses for a picture with Israeli President Isaac Herzog on July 14, 2022. Both sides vowed to deepen the Jewish state’s integration in the region as they face their common foe Iran. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images) Crossing the Red Line: Biden, His Advisors, and Israel’s War in Gaza, by Akbar Shahid Ahmed. W.W. Norton & Company, 368 pages When confronted with warnings that famine was spreading across northern Gaza in early 2024, members of President Joe Biden’s foreign policy team could not believe what they were being told. The alarming reports came from U.S. agencies and respected international humanitarian groups, but they starkly contradicted Israel’s version of events.  National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan and Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk doubted Palestinians were going hungry amid mountains of rubble and corpses because the “people in photographs from Gaza did not look skinny,” reports the investigative journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed, based on accounts from his anonymous sources. Not only were staggering numbers of Palestinians desperate for food. They lacked clean drinking water, medicine, and shelter. They were being torn to pieces—in many cases by U.S.-manufactured bombs—as the Israeli military  kept up its relentless offensive. Yet the president and his top aides failed to meaningfully exert their influence to alleviate the suffering. Instead, their response was shaped by credulous deference to the Netanyahu government and disregard for both U.S. and international law. “Biden’s stubbornness was one of his trademarks; Sullivan and others closest to him began to behave similarly, such as questioning the Palestinian casualty counts, even as they received more and more information from intelligence and humanitarian officials that showed how their policy had failed to ensure that aid reached Gazans,” writes Ahmed in Crossing the Red Line , his must-read reportage on the Biden administration’s refusal to restrain Israel from perpetrating what a growing consensus of scholars, jurists, human rights groups, and an independent U.N. commission now consider a genocide. A diplomatic correspondent at The Washington Sun , Ahmed made his name during twelve years working at HuffPost , where he won awards for his Mideast coverage. The book draws on this prior work, augmented by interviews with dozens of former officials and a careful review of the documentary evidence. The result is a meticulously reported, damning portrayal of a president and his tiny clique of decision-makers who, despite their pledge to uphold the “rules-based order,” found themselves enabling Israel to wage war against a civilian population and destabilize the region. Future historians will rely on Ahmed’s account, which reveals how highly credentialed, intelligent officials can close their eyes to what’s in front of them and make policy for an alternative reality. Among Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s staff, for example, a culture of what one official called “herd impunity” enabled the near-automatic approval of weapons transfers as veteran diplomats discouraged internal dissent. Ahmed reports that Blinken never asked the intelligence community to assess whether Israel was committing war crimes, and officials repeatedly slowed down or subverted internal inquiries. The resulting lack of information allowed the administration to claim, quite conveniently, that it lacked sufficient evidence to cut Israel off from U.S. weapons. Ahmed’s rendering of Biden’s team evokes nothing so much as President Lyndon Johnson and the “best and the brightest” who sank the United States ever deeper into the Vietnam War. Yet Biden faced an easier task than withdrawing hundreds of thousands of U.S. troops from an unwinnable war. The tools he needed were right in front of him. But time and again he refused to withhold weapons from Israel despite convincing evidence the IDF was indiscriminately leveling entire neighborhoods—even targeting schools, hospitals, and aid stations—in illegal acts of collective punishment. Moreover, Biden provided diplomatic cover for Israel at the UN, shielding Netanyahu from international consequences. Why did the Biden administration choose this course? Ahmed does not depict U.S. decision-makers as bloodthirsty monsters; rather, one gets the impression they simply wanted to ignore what was happening. Unlike their Israeli counterparts, who publicly declared their intention to render Gaza unlivable, top White House officials displayed callousness, ignorance, myopia, or the all-too-human instinct to blame others rather than oneself. As a consequence, they gaslit the country while licensing ever more Israeli violence.  Widening the historical lens, Ahmed underscores the importance of U.S. support for Israel and the casual dehumanization of Palestinians going back decades. Thus, after the October 7 horrors inflicted by Hamas, a president was ready to give Israel carte blanche. Biden’s Gaza policy also flowed from the disastrous experience of the Global War on Terror and “a refusal among policy elites to reckon with its flaws,” says Ahmed, which fostered “comfort with jaw-dropping atrocities and dehumanizing of people in the region.” “Within America’s system of checks and balances,” he writes, this “limited scrutiny of presidents and their aides, reversing progress toward transparency… while holding few liable for abuses or crimes committed in the name of U.S. national security.”  Biden’s approach was myopic, of course. He believed Netanyahu would repay his goodwill with restraint if asked. Instead, the Israeli prime minister bullied and humiliated him whenever a glint of daylight appeared between their governments. Beyond some tough talk, Biden rarely used the United States’ considerable leverage to curb his partner’s excesses. The exceptions proved the rule. It was easy to ignore the killings of hundreds of nameless, faceless Palestinian aid workers — or simply blame Hamas for every IDF misstep. But on April 1, 2024, Israeli drones incinerated an aid convoy belonging to the celebrity chef Jose Andres’ World Central Kitchen. Seven people, including a U.S.-Canadian citizen, were killed. This could not be ignored. The next day, “USAID experts privately made their most serious assessment yet of Palestinian suffering… famine was likely occurring in Gaza, the humanitarian analysts wrote in a message sent to the White House and U.S. diplomats globally,” Ahmed tells us. “The rapid spread of hunger was ‘unprecedented in modern history.’” On April 4, Biden called Netanyahu and demanded Israel let more aid into Gaza. For the first time in six months of war, the administration strictly adhered to the international standard that food, water, and medicine must be provided to civilians. Ahmed notes that the president’s newly stiffened spine encouraged “his aides to be more proactive about advice from experts they had discounted for months” out of fear of annoying the president and the Israelis. It worked: Israel opened new routes for supplies to enter Gaza, and as the mere talk of “either Biden or Congress restricting weapons continued… more changes in Israel’s behavior followed.” More trucks were suddenly allowed into Gaza, undermining past claims that aid wasn’t being deliberately restricted. But such episodes of moral courage were rare. Cowardice usually ruled the day; and indeed, the administration failed its next major test. After drawing a red line against an Israeli invasion of Rafah in southern Gaza, the Biden administration undercut its credibility and botched a pause on shipments of some 2,000-lb. bombs. Says Ahmed: They retreated to their pattern of sending more U.S. weapons to Israel as it committed apparent war crimes, and claiming Netanyahu would accept an American-brokered ceasefire — though his defiance of Biden and disregard for Palestinian survival were at their peak. For all their professed expertise and political skill, Biden and his circle failed to truly grasp that the Israeli political establishment had no interest in a peace deal that might somehow lead to a Palestinian state. “Focusing on Netanyahu as the source of Israeli obstinacy misread his country’s politics and the effect of decades-old norms in U.S.-Israeli relations,” Ahmed writes. Netanyahu and the fanatics in his coalition were bent on conquest and ethnic cleansing—and not in Gaza alone. They eventually expanded their war to southern Lebanon, while also giving free rein to rampaging settlers in the West Bank. Herein lies another disastrous Biden legacy. His failure to restrain Israel in 2023-24 dramatically accelerated the regional instability the increasingly enfeebled president said he and he alone was qualified to prevent. Put another way, Biden’s “ghastly and self-defeating Gaza policy” paved the road to Trump’s war, on behalf of Israel, against Iran.  There’s another galling continuity to consider here, too: the lack of accountability. When it comes to foreign policy, being colossally wrong rarely threatens one’s career. McGurk now opines about national security on CNN. Blinken and Sullivan hold positions at prestigious universities. But thanks to Akbar Shahid Ahmed, their failures will not remain hidden from history. What’s left to be uncovered are the bodies of thousands of Palestinians, buried under Gaza’s rubble, whom they did so little to protect. title: At Least One Dem Group Understands the Party’s Failings
author: Peter Van Buren
content: Politics At Least One Dem Group Understands the Party’s Failings The Rural Urban Bridge Initiative is giving good advice to blue politicians. Republicans should start worrying—and not just about a difficult midterm election season. A small Democratic organization may have figured out the reason for the party’s failures among rural, post-industrial, and non-college educated voters (shorthand here: the Midwest) and devised a way to win them back. In Ohio, I saw the Democrats’ failures happen in real time: their abandonment of the Midwest. Factories and mills closed down, and family farms were consumed by mega-agricultural concerns. The people who had made their livings in those ways were simply left behind, like the now-rusted machinery strewn across the landscape. Generations of solidly Democratic voters were bewildered. They had done the right thing. They had voted Democrat. Now, who in government even knew they existed? Not Hillary. On September 9, 2016, Clinton explained Donald Trump’s political appeal. She divided his supporters into two groups. One group felt the government and the economy had failed them. The other, she said, constituted a “basket of deplorables”—racist, sexist, homophobic, xenophobic, and Islamophobic, everything her coastal supporters and media champions were not. She added that some were “irredeemable,” leaving open the question of how they might fare under another Clinton administration (Midwesterners remembered what NAFTA—a legacy of her husband’s presidency—did to the region). Hillary argued Trump gave legitimacy to dangerous people and ideas. That was bad, but it was the succinctness of the term “deplorables” that for practical purposes ended Clinton’s campaign that afternoon. She and her supporters did not just hate Trump’s politics, they deplored his voters as people. Clinton changed politics by transforming a political disagreement into a judgment about the character of millions of Americans. Democrats did not suddenly abandon the Midwest. They gradually lost their cultural and political connection to large portions of it (recall Barack Obama’s 2008 remark that economically frustrated voters there “cling” to guns and religion). The Dems deprioritized most of the heartland, confident in their ability to win elections with just the coasts and some blue patches inland. It did not work. Vitriol toward Trump voters is the default attitude among the “resistance” and many progressive politicians today. Hypocritically, Democrats never held Obama to the torch for his murder of hundreds of civilians by drone, yet those same Dems blame Republican voters personally for drug boats being blown up in the Caribbean. They wish ill on the Midwest not only because of who they voted for, but who they actually are as people. The term “MAGA” as a pejorative has been expanded to all Republican supporters and construed to mean opposition to democracy and even basic decency. I should know. It is a helluva thing to be shunned at Thanksgiving by my own liberal relatives. But now, a political organization is seeing clearly how wrong the Democrats played all this—and wants to fix the problem. A newsletter from the group declares : “holding individual voters accountable for the egregious things Trump has done might feel like an act of justice, but it’s a strategic pitfall.” The Rural Urban Bridge Initiative (RUBI) is a Democratic organization which seeks nothing less than to transform the default position of most progressives. They know that personal animosity toward Trump supporters repels voters who might otherwise switch sides for a new-style Democrat, a no-nonsense heartland state governor perhaps. They see the hatred of the person, not the idea, as a failed moral posture, one that threatens our core rights of speech and debate. Albeit for selfish reasons (to get more Democratic votes), they abhor the banning of controversial speakers on campus, the one-sidedness of modern media, and the nasty glee over the assassination attempts on the president. Never mind the actual killing of people like Charlie Kirk. The founders and principals of RUBI are media unknowns, albeit with biographies that span from old-school Democrat to near-libertarian. Many are (or were) farmers. They are trying to produce handbooks and talking points to guide blue politicians looking to gain ground in red and purple districts. Their goal is not to turn the Midwest all blue again, but to turn the tide in elections where victory and defeat are separated by only a few percentage points. One of their products is the 2026 Rural and Factory Town Candidate Toolkit . The guide reminds Dems of some rough math. “Criticizing the opposition,” it says, is insufficient when only 39 percent of the electorate has a favorable view of Democrats. In most rural and factory-town districts, working-class voters are the majority…. It’s not possible to win without regaining working-class support and, as of July, only 31 percent of high school grads and 42 percent of voters with some college said they planned to vote for Democrats in the midterms. What to do? There’s a lot of general helpful information in the Toolkit, but a key point is this: Focus on what’s important to voters in your district. Talk like a neighbor, not like a politician or activist. Talk less about Trump/GOP/saving democracy and more about what you will do… Voters need a reason to vote for you. Democrats cannot win simply by getting more votes in cities and suburbs. Somebody has to build a bridge. That last one captures the group’s overall political strategy. Much of the guidance from RUBI is not new, albeit worthy of reiteration: Talk about local issues. Meet people where they live. Build trust. Hold community events, like park cleanups, at which Democrats and Republicans can work together. Don’t hold voters personally responsible for things politicians do. Respect free speech and viewpoint diversity. RUBI cites a poll of factory town voters which found that 59 percent perceived Democrats as being “obsessed with LGBT issues instead of focusing on kitchen table economic issues.” RUBI urges candidates to avoid bolstering that impression.  It seems like common sense until you look at the likely 2028 presidential candidates, like Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom, Pete Buttigieg, AOC, all of whom often seem to have not gotten the memo. So, will it work? Park clean-up projects can make pot-luck friends of political adversaries, but relationships do not automatically translate into votes. No amount of improved messaging, however sincere and clever, can entirely eliminate the genuine disagreements that divide us over guns, abortion, immigration, climate change, and traditional values. There is also the problem of scale. Creating a new form of political organization in thousands of rural communities requires money, buy-in from compelling candidates, volunteers, and sustained effort. It is much easier to spend millions on anti-ICE advertising in mostly-blue agreeable suburbs than to build relationships in small towns. There is clearly not enough time left before the 2026 midterms to do that, nor even before 2028 if you consider the heavy lift of winning back lost votes in the Midwest. It just may not be possible to build those bridges. Many national-level Democrats have lost the ability to talk to people they once knew how to represent. But for conservatives, it’s worthwhile to keep an eye on RUBI as, nearly alone among liberal groups, it has the right idea. title: The Write-In Stuff
author: Bill Kauffman
content: The Home Plate The Write-In Stuff Must all change always be for the worst? (DigitalVision/Getty Images) I was an election junkie at an early age. I stayed up late into the night of November 5, 1968, pulling for that old windbag Hubert Humphrey. (I’m told that I cried upon waking to his defeat the next morning, though maybe I just didn’t want to go to school.) I began collecting campaign buttons and political ephemera in 1972—anyone wanna buy a bag of 100 “Nixon Now” pinbacks?—and however deep my adult anarchist streak runs I have always enjoyed the act of voting: walking to the polling place, joking with the election ladies, and pulling the lever for friends or no-hope longshots. Ah, but those days are gone. The lever machines were junked as a result of the second President Bush’s tech-soiled Help America Vote Act, and the longshots were wiped out by the Aqualung-ish second Governor Cuomo’s election “reforms,” which made it nearly impossible for third parties and independents to achieve ballot access in New York State.  Must all change always be for the worst? In classic “arsenic or cyanide, sir?” fashion, New Yorkers are given the Hobson’s choice between a Democratic Party that has lost any connection to rural and working-class Americans and a Republican Party that is running this year on the Iran War and building more data centers. Whoopee! Ever Pollyanna, I tease out the silver lining in this assault on democracy by scribbling write-in votes, so on November 3, 2026, I’ll be doing just that. And y’know, it’s kinda fun. In the governor’s race, Donald Trump’s non-support chased Rep. Elise Stefanik, who might have given incumbent Kathy Hochul a run for her donors’ money, out of the race, making way for the charisma-deficient Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman. On one of Mr. Blakeman’s earliest forays Upstate he toured our lovely green and hilly Southern Tier, the northern tip of Appalachia. Dumbfounded by its lack of resemblance to Long Island, he remarked disapprovingly on what he saw as the life-worn people and shabby towns and rusted old pickups, speculating that if only the hicks would embrace fracking they’d be happy as clams, their prosperous asses perched on the seats of spanking new pickup trucks. Stay on Long Island, Bruce. My fervent friend Howard is writing in Jesus Christ for governor this year. “Sister” Jeanette Chin, street lady and holy fool of Manhattan, was beloved by Catholic Workers for her favorite saying: “I vote for Jesus because Jesus votes for everybody.” I agree wholeheartedly with the good sister, so I’ll go halfway and write in the Catholic Worker founder and saint-in-waiting Dorothy Day for chief executive of New York. “Our” congresswoman, the Republican Claudia Tenney, represents a hideously gerrymandered district into which the Democrats shoved as many of Upstate’s disproportionately Republican voters as could fit. How embarrassing is she? In 2025 La Tenney introduced legislation to make Donald Trump’s birthday a national holiday. There is probably no degrading act she would not perform for Forever War Don, up to and including calling the humble Great Lake thirty miles to our north “Lake America.” How, O Lord, did we fall so far and so fast? For the House I’ll write in my late friend and our ten-term congressman Barber Conable, a brilliant and witty and entirely honorable (he refused any individual campaign contribution of greater than $50, even in the Watergate-flooded year of 1974) decentralist rural Republican of a sort who existed in a better country. My pal Chuck, our retired county judge, a man of probity and intellect and humor, surely is superior in every respect to Attorney General Letitia James, whose lack of commitment to protecting the liberties of New Yorkers would make a Stasi apparatchik blush. He’ll still spend summers on the golf course, but Chuck would make a fine part-time AG. Few state governments are as profligate as New York’s, so for comptroller I’ll pencil in my late friend Jim, the cheapest man in Batavia, a guy who would call my dad crowing in triumph if he found a dime in the racetrack parking lot. The only vote I’ll cast for someone whose name actually appears on the ballot will be for our state assemblyman, Steve Hawley, ebulliently mischievous Republican tribune of rural New York. Picking up the mantle formerly lofted by William Randolph Hearst, Bella Abzug, and Norman Mailer, Steve has proposed the division of New York into two or more states, an idea so sane, so logical, and so much less bureaucratic and inhuman than the status quo that it appalls the power-lusters. (The first Governor Cuomo called the division of New York “divisive”—well, yeah, I guess it is….) A lot of air has gone out of the balloon since 1968. I don’t cry over election results anymore. Maybe I should. The post The Write-In Stuff appeared first on The American Conservative .

title: Iran War Day 240: Trump Says No Strikes on Iran Planned for Sunday
author: Jude Russo
content: President Donald Trump said Sunday that there would be no attack on Iran before the end of the weekend. “There will be no strike today,” he told reporters at a White House press gaggle. Before departing for a campaign event in Michigan, Trump commented to a separate gaggle at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland about a Friday intelligence memo about Iranian plans targeting Americans in the Middle East. “There are two very different sets of intelligence reports—I have them both,” he said. “We have very advanced sets of intelligence on Iran, and we’re doing very well with Iran, as you know.” The president’s recent rhetoric on Iran, along with recent measures like U.S. embassy evacuations, has led some to believe that he plans more strikes on Iran in the near future. “Do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off? That’s the only question,” he said in a phone call to Fox News’ Sunday Morning Futures . The president did not comment on the status of negotiations, but multiple outlets reported that a Qatari delegation was in Iran Sunday in an effort to restart diplomacy between the U.S. and the Islamic Republic. Direct U.S.–Iran military engagement remains relatively low-intensity. Admiral Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), visited the Strait of Hormuz per a statement on CENTCOM’s X account. Iran’s state-affiliated Tasnim news agency reported that Iran had downed an American drone over its port of Bandar Abbas. Yet fighting raged on other fronts throughout the region. Saudi Arabia claimed to have intercepted a missile barrage from Yemen’s Houthi rebels near Mecca. Israel continued offensive operations in Lebanon , the West Bank , and Gaza through the weekend. AAA reported national average prices per gallon of $4.29 for regular gas and $6.35 for diesel.
