title: The Differences Between SIM and VOIP Numbers
author: DonklePhant
content: At one time, the only option you had, if you wanted to make a phone call, was to pick up a landline and hope that someone else wasn’t already using the phone. Phone technology has changed radically over the past few decades, and you can call someone from pretty much anywhere. You can even have multiple phone numbers attached to one phone! That’s right, we’re talking about VOIP numbers. Curious how they differ from SIM numbers? Read on to learn everything you need to know about this awesome technology. What Is a SIM Number? You’ve spent a lot of time researching smartphones to figure out which one is the best for your needs. When you go to your cell phone carrier’s store and make the purchase, you might notice that they pop a little card into the phone before activating your service. That card is a SIM card, and it contains information about your account, including your phone number. Your cell phone carrier uses information from the SIM to generate your cell phone bill because they track all of the calls and texts that you make. If you want to swap devices, all you need to do is pop out the SIM card and add it to a new device. Easy, right? What Are VOIP Numbers? VOIP numbers are totally different from SIM card-based numbers. It stands for Voice Over Internet Protocol, and it’s a real phone number assigned to a person, but it’s not necessarily tied to a particular device. Instead, you utilize the internet to make and receive calls. Some common examples of VOIP numbers in real life include Google Voice and Skype. All you need to do is log into the app from any capable device, and you’re able to make and receive phone calls. Some services also allow you to make video calls and send text messages. Should You Use a VOIP Service? Depending on your needs, getting on board with a VOIP service is a great decision. This is especially true for people who are tired of lugging around multiple cell phones for work and home. With a VOIP service, you’ll have everything you need in one place, which is a time and space-saver. title: Small Business Management: 6 Tips for Running an Efficient Business
author: DonklePhant
content: Even though it’s easier and cheaper to start a small business today, that’s no guarantee of success. Believe it or not, 50% of small businesses fail in the first year. If you don’t have a solid plan to run your company, you won’t accomplish much and will fail. Small business management isn’t easy to do well, but there are a few things you can do to improve your management process. Follow the six small business management tips below to make your life easier and grow your business faster. 1. Learn to Delegate It’s tempting for business owners to try and handle as much as possible themselves. After all, it’s hard to hand off important work to people that may not meet your expectations. Doing this is a mistake. As a business owner, you don’t have the time to handle every task in your business. On top of that, you’re probably not an expert at everything you need to do. Delegating work to the right people interested in helping your business succeed will make your life much easier. You’ll have more time to do what you do best – running your business. You can focus on more critical work and rely on the experts to handle the other business tasks that need to be done. 2. Build a Technology Infrastructure You don’t have to handle everything by hand anymore in business. There are now countless tools available that give you a way to make communication and organization easier in companies. The good news is that it doesn’t cost much money to set up IT systems anymore. With the countless cloud tools available, you can get all the tools you need to run a business at a low monthly cost. However, setting up an internal IT system isn’t as easy if you have an office. It pays to reach out to a professional IT company like Velocity IT to get help setting everything up. It may cost some money upfront, but you’ll save a lot of time and energy in the future when you set things up correctly. 3. Automate Where You Can With the proper IT infrastructure, you can start taking advantage of the newest tech tools. One benefit that brings is the ability to automate many repetitive business tasks. Look at everything you do each day in your business to check for repetitive tasks. These aren’t tasks that require a lot of thought and creative input to accomplish. Think of things like data entry, regular emails, and reporting. Once you have those tasks, look for ways to automate them. There are countless tools out there that can talk to each other and perform tasks for you without any work on your part. Doing this will free up your time to work on more critical work that significantly impacts your business. 4. Limit Micromanaging It’s tempting when you delegate tasks to look over the shoulders of the people performing them. After all, you expect a certain level of quality when you assign work. It makes sense to want to ensure you’re getting quality work for the money you pay. However, this is a significant detriment to the people working. The people you hire are great at what they do. If you hover over someone’s shoulder, it signals that you don’t trust them. Take a step back and allow people to do what you hired them to do. You’ll spend less time and energy worrying about other people while giving people the confidence to handle their jobs. 5. Create Standard Procedures It’s hard to create an efficient workflow when people do things their own way. While this strategy may work when you’re small and have a few employees, it becomes much more challenging when you start growing. It pays to have your team start working the same way. If people handle the same tasks differently, it’s hard for people to help each other and pick up where someone leaves off. By creating standard procedures, you make one system for handling a task. That means everyone stays on the same page when working. This is also useful for new hires. You can pick up and use a documented procedure more quickly than having to figure things out yourself or have several different methods explained to you. 6. Only Hire the Best Talent It’s tempting to hire unqualified employees to save money. This is especially true if your business is just starting. You only have so much money to spare, so you need to squeeze every dollar you can. Unfortunately, this usually causes more problems than it solves. If you want an efficient business, you need to hire the best people. When you underpay your employees, they work slower and less efficiently. They may even quit before the job gets done if they feel undervalued. On top of that, you’re wasting precious time when training new employees and playing catch up on work that isn’t getting done. You can’t expect talented people to stick around when you underpay them, so losing employees and finding new ones is a constant battle. Hiring the right people and paying them what their worth is far more effective. You’ll get more work done and spend less time babysitting people. Don’t Underestimate the Importance of a Great Small Business Management Strategy You only have so much time to handle work as a small business owner, so you can’t afford to waste what little time you have. The right small business management strategy is critical to getting the most done. Keep the tips above in mind to manage an efficient business. title: How to Increase Cyber Hygiene in Your Business
author: DonklePhant
content: The amount of money the world loses to cybercrime is growing rapidly. In 2015, losses to cyberattacks amounted to $3 trillion per year. By 2025, that figure will reach $10.5 trillion annually. These figures are especially alarming to businesses, given that cybercriminals target enterprises more. It’s the reason cyber hygiene should be at the top of your list of priorities for your company. While you may have cyber insurance to protect your business in the event of a breach, it’s always better to prevent an attack from happening in the first place. This blog will give you tips on boosting cyber hygiene in your company so that you ensure business growth. Educate Employees on Cyber Hygiene About 88% of all cyber breaches are caused by employee error. This is why it is essential to educate employees on digital hygiene. There are a few ways to do this. First, provide cyber hygiene training for all new employees. This can be in the form of an online course or an in-person seminar. In addition, make cyber hygiene a part of your company’s culture by holding regular meetings and sending out monthly newsletters on the topic. You can also commit to offering incentives for employees who practice good digital safety habits. Finally, lead by example and make sure you are following all the best practices yourself. Use Antivirus Software and Firewalls Cybersecurity threats are always evolving, and it can be tough to keep up with the latest security risks. One of the best ways to protect yourself is to use antivirus software and firewalls. Antivirus software works by scanning your computer for known viruses and other malware and then removing any malicious files that it finds. Firewalls, on the other hand, act as a barrier between your computer and the rest of the internet, blocking suspicious traffic and helping to keep your data safe. Both of these tools can be essential in keeping your computer safe from attack. In addition, it’s important to keep your antivirus software and firewalls up to date. That’s because, as we’ve already pointed out, new cyber threats are constantly emerging. Implement Two-Factor Authentication Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) is an extra layer of security that requires you to provide two pieces of evidence before being granted access to an account or device. For example, you may need to provide your password and a code that is sent to your phone. This makes it much harder for cybercriminals to gain access to your accounts, as they would need to have both your password and your phone. Use Password Managers One cyber security tip that is often overlooked is using a password manager. A password manager is a software program that helps you create and store strong, unique passwords for all your online accounts. When used correctly, password managers can be a powerful tool for protecting your online information. When creating passwords, it is important to use a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols. However, it can be difficult to remember multiple complex passwords. This is where password managers come in. Password managers generate strong passwords for you and then store them in an encrypted database. When you need to log in to an account, the password manager will automatically fill in the correct password. This not only saves you time but also reduces the chances of you using a weak or reused password. Restrict Access to Sensitive Data Restricting access to sensitive data means keeping your most important files and folders locked down and only giving people the access they need on a need-to-know basis. There are a few different ways to do this, depending on the security measures you have in place. For example, you might use password protection or encryption to keep your data safe. Or, you might use physical security measures like keeping your computer in a locked room. Whatever measures you choose, the important thing is that you make sure only authorized people have access to your sensitive data. Back Up Your Data Regularly Losing digital files can be a nightmare. Whether it’s business financial documents or sensitive client information, the loss of digital data can be devastating. That’s why it’s so important to back up your data regularly. By making regular backups, you can be sure that your files will be safe in the event of a system crash or malware attack. There are many different ways to back up your data, including using an external hard drive or cloud-based storage service. Keep Your Software Up to Date Staying up to date with the latest software releases is essential for digital safety. By running the latest version of your operating system and applications, you can patch known vulnerabilities and close off potential entry points for cybercriminals. In addition, newer versions of software often include improved security features that can help to keep your devices and data safe. Of course, keeping your software up to date can also help to improve performance and compatibility, so it’s a win-win all around. Bolster Your Cyber Hygiene to Thwart Potential Threats Cyber hygiene is an important aspect of running today’s business, and taking it lightly is asking for serious trouble. Even a single breach can have devastating consequences. By following the tips in this article, you can help to increase cyber hygiene in your business and protect yourself from digital threats. title: Can You Hear Me Now?: The Big Benefits of Trunked Radio Systems
author: DonklePhant
content: 86% of employees and executives claim the lack of effective communication is the cause of many workplace failures. This is why so many companies are looking at trunked radio systems to improve company communications. You’ve probably heard of trunked radio systems, but you’re not sure what they are or how they work. Trunked radio systems are a critical part of many businesses but can be confusing to understand. Keep reading because, in this article, we’ll break down the key benefits of a trunked radio system for your business. What Is a Trunked Radio System? Trunked radio systems like the bkr 5000 , are networks that provide shared access to a group of users to a limited amount of radio frequencies. You use them in emergencies and important situations where communication is key. How Do Trunked Radio Systems Work? Trunked radio systems work by dividing the available radio frequencies into separate channels. These channels are then assigned to specific users or groups of users. When a user wants to communicate with another user, they will request access to a channel from the system controller. The system controller will then grant them access to that channel. Once the communication is finished, the channel will be returned to the pool of available channels for other users to use. What Are the Benefits of Trunked Radio Systems? There are many benefits to using trunked radio systems. Here are some of the key benefits to consider: Improved Efficiency In a traditional radio system, each user is assigned a specific frequency on which to transmit. However, this can lead to problems when multiple users are trying to communicate at the same time. Trunked systems address this problem by sharing radio frequencies among multiple users. When a user wants to transmit, they first search for an available frequency. If you find one they can transmit their message. Once it finishes, it makes the frequency available for other users. This system helps to reduce overall congestion and improve communication efficiency. In addition, it allows for greater flexibility in terms of frequency assignment, as users are not limited to a single frequency. As a result, trunked systems can provide better coverage and reduce interference. Increased Security As more and more businesses move their operations online, the need for secure trunked systems has never been greater. Trunked systems offer several advantages over traditional telephone lines. These advantages include having more space, better call quality, and being able to add more security features. Encryption protects unauthorized people from seeing sensitive information. This is important for businesses that handle sensitive data. You can change trunked systems can to meet the needs of a business. This makes them a good and flexible solution for businesses of all sizes. As the world becomes increasingly connected, the need for secure trunked systems will only continue to grow. Better Organization You can use trunked systems in a variety of settings, from small businesses to large-scale organizations. Trunked systems help to organize radio communications by separating different types of traffic. This can be especially helpful in emergencies when every moment counts. defined channels can help to reduce confusion and ensure that vital information is relayed. Also, by separating different types of traffic, trunked systems can help to improve the overall flow of communication. This can be helpful during special events when multiple agencies are working together. By using a trunked system, agencies can coordinate their efforts and make sure that everyone is on the same page. In short, trunked systems offer several advantages that can be beneficial for businesses and organizations of all sizes. If you are looking for a better way to communicate with your radio, trunked systems may be the perfect solution. Trunked systems make communication more efficient and secure. Improved Coverage They can provide radio coverage over a larger area than a conventional system. They achieve this by using many repeaters. This is especially beneficial for organizations that have workers spread out. You can also use trunked systems to connect multiple sites. This could be a chain of retail stores or a network of office buildings. This helps different locations work together and makes sure everyone is on the same page. As a result, trunked systems provide many advantages for businesses and other organizations. Increased Capacity Trunked systems are two-way radio systems that share a limited number of channels. This makes it possible for more people to use the radios and spectrum efficiently. Trunked systems also offer features such as call waiting and caller ID. This can be useful in business or other high-demand applications. In addition, trunked systems are often designed with built-in redundancy. This helps to ensure reliability in the event of a power outage or other failure. Increase Company Performance A trunked system can improve company performance. It does so by allowing employees to communicate more efficiently. Also, it can help to improve coordination between different departments. And can also help businesses save money by reducing the need for separate phone lines. This is because trunked systems use the same infrastructure as the telephone system. As a result, businesses can save money on installation and maintenance costs. Also, they offer features that help businesses be more responsive to customer needs. Ready to Invest in a Trunked Radio System? There are many different types of two-way radio systems available on the market. But trunked radio systems are becoming more popular. Especially for businesses and government entities. Trunked radio systems offer many advantages over other types of radio systems. These advantages include improved organization, increased capacity, and built-in redundancy. If you’re thinking about a two-way radio system, check out our blog for more information. Also, be sure to share this article with anybody you know who may be looking at investing in a trunked radio system. title: Identity Verification in Unemployment Insurance: What Works
author: Hailey
content: The nation’s system of unemployment insurance (UI)—a vital lifeline for workers as well as local and regional economies during an economic downturn—faced unprecedented levels of benefit fraud committed by criminal enterprises during the COVID-19 pandemic. While state efforts to eliminate fraud through programs such as ID verification (IDV) have made tremendous strides, states will need to continue to improve their IDV protocols, as criminal enterprises will continue to attack the UI system relentlessly. But as of yet, there has been scant research or consensus on which approaches have worked best, and which have been easiest to implement. Furthermore, states often struggle to maintain strong lines of communication with each other regarding combating fraud or even establishing a common terminology about the challenges they are facing. This report—the product of interviews with a range of UI stakeholders across the country—will review current state IDV processes and practices as well as emerging trends in combating fraud; it will then detail what is needed to ensure that all states can adequately protect the UI system from current and future threats. Why ID Verification (IDV) Still Matters At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, criminal enterprises found their way into pandemic unemployment benefits, which at the time had greatly enhanced payments but few requirements regarding identity verification. Congress had added a requirement to the Continued Assistance Act of 2020 to require states to “ include procedures for identity verification or validation and for the timely payment, to the extent reasonable and practicable, by January 26, 2021 ,” 1 but it took states months to use the allocated federal funding to shore up their ID verification efforts. At the end of the enhanced pandemic programs, state ID verification efforts were achieving results, but the criminals have not given up. Fraud is now a persistent and ongoing threat 2 to the unemployment insurance (UI) system. One of the most critical protections against fraud continues to be verifying that claimants are real people and who they say they are. Because of the robust work states already have done, ID fraud has fallen to nearly zero in almost every state. 3 Fraudsters continue to hone their tactics, so states have to respond in kind by improving their practices. For example, as artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more sophisticated, fraudsters can use this technology to make more convincing claims, invent more believable fake employers, and hijack legitimate claims more efficiently. The U.S. Department of Labor continues to communicate to states that it expects them to conduct robust, universal, and frequent ID verification. This current state stance on identity verification is dramatically different from the one prior to the pandemic. Before 2020, states would accept a claim application once it was submitted. In fact, most states would tend to encourage individuals to file a claim as soon as they were no longer working. In large part, this was based on state statute or policy, and the fact that claims-filed is directly tied to federal funding amounts. Also, in the years leading up to the pandemic, many states were steering individuals to electronic-only filing methods rather than through in-person filing, due to historically low staffing (due to historically low claim rates), decreased staff presence in One-Stop Centers, and state efforts to modernize their benefit system. Although states remain focused on serving legitimate claimants, they cannot go back to a pre-pandemic stance, as fraudsters are unrelenting in their attacks on UI systems. IDV is now core to state functions and has multiple impacts on state UI systems, ranging from speed of service delivery, benefit rights information that individuals receive and at which point during the claim-filing process, how and when other issues are adjudicated, the customer experience, staffing levels and use of staff within state agencies, workload distribution, and funding. Also, more government agencies and other entities are increasingly involved in combating UI fraud. ID verification also matters to claimants. It is important for UI to reach the right people, on time. That is why it is critical for IDV services to be user-friendly, accurate, and fair. Overly complex application steps can cause claimant confusion and excessive contacts to state agency contact centers. If IDV is not smooth, it can create workloads for state agencies that they cannot manage while also paying claims on time. A cumbersome process can also exacerbate the stress of a larger economic downturn on individuals and the economy. Project Overview: The Need for Information on the State of IDV While IDV is seen as a critical bulwark against fraud in UI programs, not enough is known about the impacts of identity verification on fraud prevention. Implementation of IDV varies widely across states, including which vendors are used, which claimants are screened and when, and what combination of digital and non-digital identity verification is used. U.S. Department of Labor policies and oversight of state operations are still based on a pre-pandemic reality and are not optimized to incorporate and comprehensively track identity verification, and states are eager for guidance that better fit their reality. While fraud prevention is dynamic, there is a need to establish standards and expectations for identity verification, by identifying and normalizing evidence-based best practices. This report gathers frontline information about the effectiveness of current practices, how states are measuring impact, and the implementation of compensating controls due to limits in IDV and cost considerations. In addition, the report discusses operational and policy issues, such as concerns about facial recognition for UI applicants with darker skin tones and ways states integrate IDV into their process in light of regulations. For the purpose of this analysis, representatives from UI offices in eleven states were interviewed, 4 as well as other experts in fraud prevention and technology, vendors, and claimant advocates. Interviews were conducted with state leaders with intimate knowledge of current and past program operations across five of the six Employment and Training Administration (ETA) regions among a mix of ten large and medium states and one small state. These UI programs represent a range of service delivery models, operational challenges, vendors contracted, quality of relationship amongst program stakeholders, identity verification tools, and strategies for detecting and preventing fraud. Current State IDV Processes, Practices, and Challenges As with every other area of UI, each state has different processes and practices for ID verification. This section covers the technology, processes, and practices states use, while protecting details that could aid fraudsters. To minimize the risk of providing useful information to fraudsters, this report avoids technical detail about some interventions that states use, as well as where and when they are used. As several stakeholders noted, there is no single solution or silver bullet for ID verification. As several stakeholders noted, there is no single solution or silver bullet for ID verification. IDV is a major component in a multilayered fraud prevention program, with states often engaging with multiple vendors that interact in different ways in different states. States utilize IDV at various points throughout the claims process and vendors also expressed the need to have anti-fraud capabilities and different tools across the claim lifecycle. Notably, even some vendors appear to believe that layering with other vendor products is part of the answer, as part of a belt-and-suspenders approach. Several states even credited the relatively lower number of system attacks on the use of multiple vendors. States and vendors vary in terms of at what point or points in the claims process they conduct ID verification. The U.S. Department of Labor issued guidance in early 2021 informing states that all claimants must be provided a written determination that can be appealed, 5 and most of the states interviewed said they allow applicants to file an application before ID verification is completed to ensure their ID verification process is not making a de facto eligibility determination. Some states treat a claimant’s nonresponse to ID verification requests as fraud while others issue appealable determinations or appealable failure-to-respond determinations. Still others have no way of knowing who has abandoned ID verification. Some states have implemented—or are expected to implement—a statewide login that necessitates ID verification before navigating to the UI application, or otherwise requires ID verification before starting a claim. This affects the entire claims process, including when claimants receive information about their benefit rights, when other eligibility issues are adjudicated, what the customer experience looks and feels like, how staff is deployed, what workloads look like, and how much funding states need to operate. Vendors have acknowledged this rethinking is ongoing, with multiple vendors noting that states continue to reassess pandemic-era IDV policies and practices. Other states allow claimants to start a claim but do not begin the employer notification process until the IDV is complete to avoid unnecessary workload or aggravating employers of workers who have been impersonated, but this negatively affects payment timeliness. Moreover, even though states acknowledge that the various IDV steps contribute to how quickly a claim is processed, they all agree that there is no negative impact on overall timeliness goals. The tools, tactics, and approaches best suited to effective IDV vary considerably, depending on factors such as claim rate, population characteristics, available funding, and the nature of the fraud threats a state faces. Smaller states can engage in a more personalized but labor-intensive approach. One small state reported that it has fifty-five internal fraud-prevention interventions it executes before ID verification to minimize burden on claimants. By contrast, another larger state has invested in automated tools that identified a particular fraud attack after approximately 150 claims were affected, compared to a previous attack identified by human staff only after several thousand claims had been impacted. Of course, interventions may need flexibility and a plan to scale in case of major economic downturn and dramatic increase in claims intake. Often, states do not require ID verification for all claimants. Several vendors provide sophisticated products that provide a risk score on each claimant, and claimants that meet a certain threshold of risk are then referred to an ID verification service. At least one state has built its own in-house risk identification solution. These risk scores vary across states and require continuous refinement. This can save both states and claimants time by sometimes reducing the number of claimants who must go through every IDV step. States also report that these flags need frequent intervention to narrow down overflagging. To that end, states reported the need to be able to make these adjustments on the fly based on operational needs and according to the unique profiles of the given state’s populations. This was especially important for states using vendor scoring models because they were concerned about the lack of flexibility of the vendor’s product. States have an expectation that the product should be maximally customizable to meet their specific needs instead of limiting their requested changes to meet the needs of all other vendor customers. Further, vendors tended to express high confidence in their ability to prevent fraud while being flexible enough to customize to state needs. Beginning in 2022, the U.S. Department of Labor set up a partnership with the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to provide in-person identity verification with participating state agencies. States report positive feedback on the USPS partnership because it is an established and trusted entity. At least one state indicated that it has served as a reliable alternative, particularly for claimants who are resistant to providing biometric data required by digital platforms. Access to USPS has also been particularly helpful to claimants in rural areas who may lack Internet access. In some states, it had been the front door for a significant percentage of claimants. Claimant advocates reported that it has been crucial for claimants who struggle with digital literacy. They also pointed out that anti-fraud protocol increasingly leans on claimants being able to access and maneuver an electronic portal. Further, several states reported that USPS locations can be easier to get to, especially in areas where there is little access to One-Stop Centers, and at least one state said the availability of USPS helps the state to successfully manage their timeliness measures. Another state requires all out-of-state claimants to go through USPS. Yet, new guidance from U.S. Department of Labor now requires that claimants establish a Login.gov account 6 before they can engage with USPS services. Meanwhile, maintaining USPS as a direct resource for claimants in the IDV process is a popular stance among states interviewed for this report. Also, at least one state expressed concern for whether expanded use of Login.gov could overload the Login.gov call center by claimants seeking IDV or claim resolution. Because ID verification alone cannot make a determination of eligibility for a UI benefit, states provide multiple opportunities to clear issues as they arise. Since the pandemic, state staff have received training in how to spot false IDs. One state said that they strive for 80 percent in-person verification, while at least two other states couple in-person verification with Reemployment Services and Eligibility Assessment (RESEA) program participation. In addition to in-person verification at either USPS or a state One-Stop Center, some states have a process for verification over the phone. One state’s process for failing the initial online ID verification step is referral to USPS and will ask for a selfie for the UI agency’s review. Claimant advocates also noted that in-person off-ramps should be more prevalent and more publicized. Advocate groups also said there needs to be more flexibility on acceptable document types. Vendor selection is a challenge, and states have been seeking help from the federal government in this regard, which is why several states appreciated the USPS partnership. Cost is a huge factor, as is mitigating friction for claimants and state agency staff. The public’s familiarity with the product also can sway an agency’s decision to adopt. Conversely, claimant unfamiliarity with a third-party verification entity and concerns about the privacy implications of engaging with yet another platform can create friction and erode trust. Stakeholder pressure can also shape vendor selection in significant ways. Claimant advocates have raised concerns about equitable access that steered states away from particular vendors. In general, states are sensitive to the potential downfalls of facial recognition technology, and multiple states cited the potential for racially disparate outcomes in making their decisions about whether to deploy that kind of technology. Others felt more confident in steps taken by vendors using facial recognition that they made a good faith effort to address those concerns. States are sensitive to the potential downfalls of facial recognition technology, and multiple states cited the potential for racially disparate outcomes in making their decisions about whether to deploy that kind of technology. States’ relationships with their IDV vendors are a significant factor in program effectiveness, and interviews revealed a complex dynamic. For example, one state raised concerns about their vendor’s reliance on historical identity data that may itself have been compromised in prior data breaches, raising questions about the reliability of that data as a fraud-detection signal. Interviews also revealed that states with the same vendor can have meaningfully different experiences depending on the specific product or service level they have purchased, which makes the case for greater communication and collaboration between states on vendor selection. This also demonstrates some of the reasons that states must meet with vendors regularly regarding flag accuracy and other performance conversations. Since interviews were conducted, the federal government has taken several steps to expand its role in IDV , 7 including by building the website unemployment.gov, so it may be the case that the vendor role and vendor selection process will shift dramatically in the coming years. However, states’ concerns about data security stemming from early efforts in this administration may cause reluctance in federal interventions involving data. One state specifically said that they do not like the concept of the federal government being the “end-all-be-all” in ID verification, as eligibility determination is the state’s role; rather, the federal role should consist of things like assisting with plain language and translations. Another state viewed having (up to) fifty-three front doors a strategic means of deterring fraudsters. Multiple states expressed a preference for receiving adequate federal funding with maximum flexibility to design their own IDV programs, rather than being steered toward particular vendors or standardized approaches. Most states use a wide variety of crossmatches, particularly within the offerings provided by the National Association of State Workforce Agencies (NASWA) Integrity Data Hub (IDH). States are now looking to streamline crossmatches, particularly as a part of broader technology modernization. Connections between agencies can be crucial. A couple of states reported that their staff have direct access to DMV records which they can review against submitted ID documents, and one noted that collaboration has caused a dramatic reduction in false positives. A significant gap identified across multiple interviews is the absence of reliable methods for measuring IDV-related fraud. Multiple stakeholders noted that states generally lack good tools for quantifying the scope of IDV fraud, making it difficult to assess whether their investments in IDV tools are achieving their intended effect. Most states do their best to gather and evaluate data about when claimants abandon the process during the ID verification stage, and some of the leading states use that drop-off data to inform how to update their efforts to improve accuracy. However, it is very difficult to draw conclusions from drop-off data as to whether those who abandon the process are frustrated claimants or fraudsters. Some states are not even able to access their drop-off data to analyze it. Vendors could provide better data to states about their product’s effectiveness, including important metrics such as demographics and drop-offs. It is critical not just to know whether a drop-off was a fraudster, but also to understand what segments of the population are legitimate claimants who are having the most difficulty accessing benefits because of the hurdles imposed by a fraud intervention. Emerging Trends in Combating Fraud As states have become more sophisticated at identifying fraud, criminals have turned to other social engineering methods to attack the UI system. A common manifestation is claim hijacking, in which a fraudster gains access to a legitimate claimant’s account and changes the bank account to which benefits are directed. In response, states often require claimants to go back through identity verification in order to change their benefit payment method. Also, NASWA has added a bank account validation feature to the IDH. Increasingly, sophisticated AI could also create more believable fake identification, which could require states to also develop a more sophisticated response to this. AI is also getting better at deep fakes, which means that fraudsters can use AI technology to create more believable “claimants” that are more difficult to distinguish from legitimate claimants. Increasingly, sophisticated AI could also create more believable fake identification, which could require states to also develop a more sophisticated response to this. As vendor contracts signed in response to the surge in fraud during the pandemic have been expiring, states are faced with whether to continue with their pandemic vendors, pivot to a new vendor, or focus on modernization and attempt to build in-house solutions. These decisions have broad implications on the state’s claim filing process and IDV protocol. Vendors interviewed indicated they are working with their state customers to help demonstrate current ROI. In addition, more states appear to be moving in the direction of statewide single sign-on (SSO) across participating state agencies. One vendor recommended having a statewide IDV front door, with a statewide fraud score, while also saying that statewide SSOs are better if they allow for different types of risk profiles, allowing the state UI agency to maintain control. This echoes one state that was concerned that having a statewide SSO would possibly not meet the more stringent validation needs of UI applicants. Moreover, the vendor suggested that SSO helps manage budget constraints via cost-sharing and noted the customer service value in having a statewide front door. On a similar topic, two fraud experts shared the opinion that claimants who already verified with one government entity should be able to carry that verification to another government entity. How to Make IDV More Seamless and Effective Establishing and communicating commonly understood terminology across stakeholders will help to avoid confusion amongst partners and claimants alike. The wide variations between state practices and terminology is a hindrance to collaboration. For example, the field lacks a shared vocabulary. Interviews conducted for this project revealed meaningful variation in how different stakeholders define and refer to the same concepts. This definitional inconsistency is not merely semantic. At the outset of one state interview, agency staff asked interviewers to define what “ID verification” meant. Even within the state UI community, practitioners may be working from different assumptions about the scope and purpose of identity verification. Interviews also suggested that terminology has different meanings among federal entities, including the U.S. Department of Labor and the National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST). Sustainability is a major concern. ID verification is a relatively new responsibility that states must plan and budget for, and some recent grants from the U.S. Department of Labor to fight fraud have been rescinded, while the department has recently threatened state administrative funding over fraud-prevention efforts. States need predictable ongoing funding to pay for and maintain current efforts to combat fraud. This is going to be increasingly important in light of any potential future economic downturn because, as claims increase, so does the potential for fraudulent claims. States with limited resources may find the need to redirect funds committed to combating fraud to crisis response in paying new claims instead. Importantly, states are still funded on the same model as before the pandemic, when the nature of fraud was far less pervasive and sophisticated. ID verification is a relatively new responsibility that states must plan and budget for. There will always be a tension between preventing fraud and paying benefits in a timely manner. While fraud prevention ideally would be seamless and instant, that is not the case with current technology and practice. The current timeliness standard was set in 1971, when technology and the claim filing method was far more limited. That standard should not slip in 2026, when we should be able to find technology solutions to help speed those processes. The problem is that ID verification failure can trigger a manual investigation that is onerous and time-consuming. A promising practice that emerged from these interviews is ensuring that claimants have enough opportunity to verify ID within twenty-four hours, so as not to slow the overall claims. Fortunately, many states are now reporting that IDV is no longer having an effect on timeliness. At least one state reported that working with U.S. Department of Labor Tiger Teams to adopt plain language and form simplification practices has helped to better sort actual claimants from fraudsters. When claimants do not understand what is being asked of them, why, or within what timeframe, they are more likely to get questions wrong, miss deadlines, abandon the verification process, and lose benefits to which they are entitled. Ironically, complicated forms are something that sophisticated fraud rings can master while filtering out first-time filers unfamiliar with jargon. To the extent that states can minimize how invasive their interventions are without sacrificing security, saving unemployed claimants time and effort that should be focused on reemployment activities, states should seek to minimize the time claimants spend on bureaucracy. To that extent, a few states raised difficulties in document submission and management, and a couple claimant advocates identified factors around electronic document submission as being among the most challenging requirements for claimants. Developing solutions for this challenge that multiple states could implement could be helpful. Security practices such as multi-factor authentication, CAPTCHA, device fingerprinting, and other interventions that are minimally cumbersome for claimants can help root out fraud without creating hurdles that will slow claim processing, particularly during a potential future economic downturn. One state noted that it would be helpful if third-party assistance, such as USPS, would retain a copy of IDs in case the state wants to further vet them. However, this could present an unacceptable liability on the behalf of those entities. Another state suggested that it would be optimal for states to build in-house services that are now purchased from vendors, which is unfortunately expensive at the outset but probably more cost-effective over time. To that end, when a state develops an effective yet cost-friendly fraud prevention and detection strategy, it should do its best to share that with other states. Collaboration amongst stakeholders is key to success. State agencies that have productive relationships with their DMV counterparts tend to have better access to data than states with limited or no relationship. Better communication across states would be helpful on a number of fronts. Trends have not slowed with regard to fraud. The emerging AI threat is a solid example of how states learning from each other is increasingly important. Similarly, information integration across state programs and systems could also spread out the cost and liability of identity verification. The same bad actors that attack UI systems are finding their way into other federal, state, and private programs. Just as sharing information across states is helpful, sharing information across state silos can be useful where it is legal and appropriate. Appeals of ID verification determinations should have their own expedited process, which appears to be the case in many states, but claimant advocates in more than one state have indicated that the appeals process for these cases are either not separated from more complicated denials or that they are otherwise protracted. Many also have processes that intercept a formal appeal by offering a re-determination, which can be a less adversarial path that may better serve claimants who simply missed a deadline or need additional assistance. In addition, one state discussed training staff for special situations, citing months when public sector employees are regularly laid off and the challenges that are presented by information about them such as their names and salaries being available to the public, making fraudsters’ jobs easier. Looking Ahead Combating UI benefit fraud during the pandemic presented an enormous new challenge for states. In the ensuing years, they have become more sophisticated at detecting and preventing fraud, and ID verification in particular has been a sweeping success. However, combating fraud has also created hurdles that legitimate claimants must clear to access their UI benefits. In order for states to establish resilient IDV systems that do not prove overly onerous to legitimate claimants, stakeholders should consider pursuing the following: Predictable funding. With the arrival of widespread UI claims fraud, states have a new fixed and ongoing cost that needs accounting for. States are going to have trouble being proactive and planning for the future without the acknowledgement of and support that meets this new reality. States are going to be increasingly skeptical of one-time or episodic funding after grants through the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) were rescinded last year. State leaders seem confident in their ability to protect state UI systems from IDV fraud, but maintain that federal funding support must match the ongoing threats. Sharing information within states. While multiple states raised the advantage of information sharing with the DMV, it might also be helpful for various state-level entities to share information, such as a suspicious actor repository, across various state programs. Data sharing could help decrease vendor-related dependencies and expenses. Sharing information between states. NASWA routinely convenes states to share patterns and things that states have learned. Importantly, sharing promising practices among states who share vendors is the most obvious use case that arose in interviews. States should be empowered to get feedback from other states who share the same vendor, whether they make a direct connection, or it is facilitated by the vendor or another third-party. Sharing definitions and processes across states. This is an issue more broadly with UI administration, but particularly when new issues arrive, it would be helpful to establish standards and definitions for states. Helping states understand what “good” looks like. At least two vendors noted that states often lack a clear picture of what effective identity verification looks like in practice, such as which metrics to track, which outcomes to target, or how to evaluate tradeoffs between fraud prevention and access. Federal technical assistance that helps states articulate and measure success could significantly improve program design. Improvement in pathways for legitimate claimants who fail IDV. Claimants should have multiple paths to proving they are who they say they are if the ID verification fails. This includes an easier appeal path if the only disqualification is failing IDV. Better data. State agencies need to have more information about who is abandoning claims and why, and also have demographic data about who is successfully navigating IDV and who is not; if vendors do not supply this data, agencies cannot know whether a claimant drop-off is a fraudster denied, or a legitimate claimant prevented from getting benefits. This information also would help states target outreach and assistance. Guardrails on IDV technology so states are not on their own in navigating. The UI program will continue to be exposed to rapidly evolving technologies and vendor products, particularly in regards to advancements in AI. States should have a clear understanding about data security standards, including how claimant data is stored, shared, and protected, along with a framework for ensuring accountability. States need these supports while maintaining operational flexibility in administering UI programs. title: Halloween Candy Prices Up 15%, Giving American Families a Jump Scare
author: Hailey
content: With Halloween just around the corner, mummies, zombies, and giant spiders have staked their claims on lawns across the country. However, the scariest thing Americans face this Halloween won’t be a haunted house, but price tags in the candy aisle. New analysis from Groundwork Collaborative and the Century Foundation finds Halloween candy prices up 15.3 percent—a staggering four times overall inflation. Wickedly inflated prices are hitting Americans’ pocketbooks at the same time as the effects of Trump’s disastrous policies are also straining families. In addition to tariff-driven price hikes, Trump’s costly war in Iran has disrupted supply chains and sent the price of gasoline and diesel skyrocketing, fueling higher prices for virtually any good that’s shipped to shelves. To make matters worse, price hikes come as families reel from ghoulish cuts to healthcare and food assistance programs, thanks to Trump’s budget law . There is simply no more wiggle room: 40 percent of households with young children plan to take on debt in order to cover this year’s Halloween costs. Thanks to Trump, this Halloween is frightening for all the wrong reasons. Spooky season should be about candy, decorations, and the shivers you get from a good costume—not scary price hikes. Jump Scare in the Candy Aisle Whether handed out to trick-or-treaters, shared during a scary movie, or simply bought to mark the season, treats are central to celebrating Halloween. More than 95 percent of Halloween shoppers plan to purchase candy this year, with holiday confection spending projected to pass $4 billion . Unfortunately for consumers, our new analysis finds that Halloween candy favorites cost more than 15 percent more than last year. Prices for candy variety packs—seasonal staples perfect for stocking up for trick-or-treaters or filling an office candy bowl—reached shudder-inducing highs this year. For chocolate lovers, the outlook is frightening: prices on packs from Hershey (maker of KitKat, Reese’s, and Heath bars) and Ferrero (maker of Butterfinger, Crunch, Baby Ruth, and 100 Grand) are up a whopping 19 percent. Fruity and gummy candy lovers will face even higher hikes: packs from Mondelez (maker of Sour Patch Kids and Swedish Fish), Hershey (maker of Jolly Ranchers and Twizzlers), and Wrigley (maker of Skittles and Starburst) have surged 39 percent, 21 percent, and 17.4 percent, respectively. Pumpkin-shaped treats will cost families a pretty penny: Hershey Seasonal Peanut Butter Cups will cost nearly one-fourth more. Table 1 Trump’s tariffs continue pushing prices up on everything from costumes to candy. Even toilet-papering a neighbor’s house or DIY-ing a mummy costume will cost more, with toilet paper prices surging due to Trump’s trade war with Canada. Aluminum tariffs put upward pressure on packaging costs, and plastic packaging prices are similarly rising thanks to Trump’s war in Iran disrupting global oil supplies—making candy wrappers more expensive, raising prices even more for those looking for a sweet fix. Candy lovers could have caught a break this year. While extreme weather in West Africa—where 70 percent of the world’s cocoa is grown—ravaged crops and sent cocoa prices upward in 2023 and 2024, cocoa prices have fallen by more than half from their 2024 peak. Furthermore, wholesale prices of sugar have fallen by 10 percent and corn syrup 4 percent over the past year. But, thanks to corporate profiteering, consumers will continue to face high prices in the candy aisle. While these input price decreases and last year’s tariff exemption on cocoa should have provided some relief for consumers, companies chose to keep sticker prices high and pocket the savings for themselves instead. Hershey’s gross profit margin reached 45 percent in the second quarter of this year, up from 30 percent a year ago with the help of a $9 million tariff refund that never made its way to customers. Fellow candy powerhouse Mondelez saw a similar trend, with gross profit margins jumping to 43 percent, up from 33 percent a year earlier. High consolidation in the candy market allows these corporate giants to increase prices without taking much of a hit on sales, as consumers have few alternatives to switch to for a bargain. Just five months ago, Hershey’s CFO bragged to investors it was well positioned to “rapidly recover margins.” Financial Tricks, Fewer Treats Despite frightening prices, Americans are determined to make the most of the season—even if that means stretching their budgets. Halloween is one of Americans’ favorite holidays, with 74 percent planning to celebrate and combined spending projected to reach $13.5 billion . Amid this year’s price hikes, consumers feel the pressure to strategize while making every purchase. Nearly one-third plan to comparison shop and 26 percent say they will prioritize finding coupons and sales to find the best deal, while 23 percent expect to buy fewer items overall. Many consumers start their Halloween shopping early, with nearly half beginning before October, in order to spread out purchases and ease the strain on their budgets. Similar to last year, when consumers also faced a brutal price environment thanks to Trump’s tariffs, discount stores remain shoppers’ go-to destination for Halloween purchases in 2026. This follows broader consumer shifts toward warehouse and discount shopping , with traditional outlet prices out of reach for many Americans. While Americans are forced to go out of their way to cut costs and find savings, celebrating Halloween in 2026 remains unaffordable for many. According to a LendingTree survey, 24 percent of Halloween consumers anticipate taking on debt in order to cover Halloween costs. For families hoping to share the holiday with their kids, the picture is even bleaker: 40 percent of parents with children younger than 18 plan to take on debt this Halloween season. Coming right off the heels of a painfully expensive back to school season , in which nearly half of parents shouldered debt to finance supplies and lunches, this high-cost autumn has continued to push families to the breaking point. Household debt haunts the American worker like the vengeful ghost of paydays past, with obligatory debt payments consuming 52 cents of every dollar of raise in real income they received . Consumer debt obligations are taking more and more out of workers’ earnings, now accounting for around 10 percent of working-age adults’ household incomes after taxes. It’s no wonder that consumer sentiment continues to fall: stalked by rising prices and mounting debt obligations, American households are feeling spooked. Conclusion With consumer sentiment sunk to the second-lowest level ever recorded—lower than at any point during the Great Recession—this Halloween season is shaping up to be full of more tricks than treats. As families navigate inflated prices and declining wages , many have stretched their wallets to the limit. If Trump does not end his war in the Middle East and his chaotic tariff agenda and reverse cuts to vital assistance programs, families will be pushed closer to financial ruin not just during Halloween, but throughout the year. title: What the Next Congress Must Do for Maternal Health
author: Kim
content: *Please Note: The livestream will begin on this page at the time of the event. For any questions please contact: events@tcf.org America’s maternal health crisis demands more than protecting the progress we’ve made. The next Congress will have an opportunity to chart a new course—and advocates closest to the crisis have a clear vision for what it should look like. Join The Century Foundation on Thursday, October 15, at 12:00 PM ET for a timely conversation about the maternal health priorities the next Congress should take up in 2027 and beyond. Speakers will highlight emerging opportunities for change, share lessons from the communities leading this work, and lay out a collective vision for building a more equitable maternal health system. Drawing on years of organizing, policy advocacy, and community leadership, members of the Black Maternal Health Federal Policy Collective will outline the policies, investments, and structural changes needed to deliver meaningful progress for Black mothers, birthing people, and families. Featured speakers: Jamille Fields Allsbrook , Assistant Professor of Law, Howard University School of Law and Senior Fellow, National Partnership for Women & Families Breana Lipscomb , Senior Advisor, U.S. Maternal Health & Rights, Center for Reproductive Rights Toshira Maldonado , Co-Founder & Director of Community Engagement & Programs, Most Beautiful W.O.M.B. Inc. Chanel Porchia-Albert , Founder & Executive Director, Ancient Song Live CART and ASL interpretation will be provided. Presented by The Century Foundation. Speaker Bios Jamille Fields Allsbrook is an Assistant Professor of Law at Howard University School of Law and a Senior Fellow with the National Partnership for Women & Families. Jamille’s research and scholarship centers on advancing health equity for women, people of color, and people with low incomes. She has spent a decade in Washington, D.C. with experiences in the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and in various nonprofit organizations including the Center for American Progress, Planned Parenthood Federation of America, and the National Health Law Program. Breana Lipscomb is the Senior Advisor of Maternal Health & Rights for the Center for Reproductive Rights. She has more than 20 years of public health experience, with deep expertise in state government and nonprofit management. In her current role, she uses the human rights framework to develop advocacy strategies to advance maternal health equity through state and federal policies. Breana is based in Atlanta, GA and serves as the Board of Directors Co-Chair for the Black Mamas Matter Alliance and is a board member of the SisterSong Women of Color Reproductive Justice Collective. Breana has been formally recognized by the Georgia State House of Representatives for her maternal health advocacy work and was named the inaugural Kira Johnson Advocate of the Year by March for Moms in 2020. Toshira Maldonado is the Founder and Director of Community Engagement & Programs at Most Beautiful W.O.M.B. Inc. and the Chief Operating Officer of Melanin and Maternal Wellness and Ubuntu Birth Justice Coalition. She has more than 28 years of experience as a Black maternal health advocate, birthworker, and community leader supporting mothers and families domestically and internationally (Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe), as well as ten years of professional experience in child welfare. She co-chairs Thrive New Jersey’s Maternal Justice Subcommittee and is an active member of the Atlantic County Commission on the Status of Women. Across her work, she promotes maternal mental health, family preservation, and reproductive justice, and connects community knowledge and frontline experiences with policy advocacy to ensure Black mothers and families can thrive. Chanel Porchia-Albert is the founder and executive director of Ancient Song, a global birth justice organization dedicated to eradicating maternal and infant mortality and morbidity among Black and Latinx communities. Chanel’s work has taken her around the world including to Uganda, where she served as a maternal health strategist, and to Ethiopia where she worked with the Ministry of Health to establish a doula program. She also played a vital role in creating the New York City Standards for Respectful Care at Birth and was appointed as a Commissioner by former New York City Mayor Eric Adams to the New York City Commission for Gender Equity.
