title: Angie Nixon keeps hammering on Hope Florida. What happened? What was Ashley Moody’s involvement?
author: Samantha Putterman
content: Florida’s Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, state Rep. Angie Nixon, is accusing Republican Sen. Ashley Moody of stealing from sick children. “Ashley Moody is a lying, cheating, thieving, scamming person who basically took $10 million from sick kids for the Medicaid program,” Nixon said Oct. 14 in an interview on CNN . “And she rerouted that into two political slush funds for Ron DeSantis to defeat two citizen-led ballot initiatives.” Nixon is referring to the 2024 Hope Florida controversy, which involved Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis’ administration diverting $10 million from a Medicaid settlement to the Hope Florida Foundation, a charitable nonprofit connected to his wife, Casey DeSantis. Moody was Florida’s attorney general at the time. Most of the money ended up in political action committees with ties to the governor and was used to campaign against Amendment 3 on the 2024 ballot, which sought to legalize recreational marijuana in Florida but did not pass. Two years later, the story is front and center in Florida’s U.S. Senate and attorney general’s races, with new developments coming as Floridians cast early votes. In the CNN interview , Nixon called for Moody to be jailed. When host Kasie Hunt asked whether there’s enough evidence to warrant that kind of punishment, Nixon said, “What we are seeing is corruption through and through. And so, I would definitely call for an investigation.” A grand jury report about the Hope Florida controversy, which was supposed to remain secret but was leaked to CBS News Miami in August, said the DeSantis administration “misappropriated” $10 million in taxpayer money as part of “a sophisticated scheme to fund political activities.” On Oct. 7, a state appeals court ordered that the grand jury report’s findings be expunged. The court said the grand jury “exceeded its authority” by declaring funds misappropriated and accusing people of criminal conduct without indicting anyone. It also dismissed that the funds were public money. The Republican Party of Florida sued the state Democratic Party and several statewide candidates over TV ads that describe the grand jury report. Moody addressed Hope Florida in a recent interview , saying, “At this point, any insinuations have been totally political. They’re absurd.” Cameron Gambini, Moody’s campaign communications director, told PolitiFact in a statement, “The first District Court of Appeals ruling speaks for itself.” Whether it was “stealing,” as Nixon said, has not been substantiated, and no one involved faces criminal charges. The extent of Moody’s involvement is not clear in available documentation. Like fact-focused Florida coverage? Sign up for our Florida midterms newsletter . Funds stem from a Medicaid drug overcharge settlement Centene Corp., Florida’s largest Medicaid contractor, first contacted Florida officials in 2021 to settle the company’s claims that it overbilled the state’s Medicaid program for prescription drugs. It wasn’t until September 2024 that the state Agency for Health Care Administration finalized and executed a $67 million settlement. The agency negotiated the agreement, which included a provision that $10 million would be donated to the Hope Florida Foundation , the fundraising arm of the Hope Florida welfare initiative launched by Casey DeSantis in 2021. The Agency for Health Care Administration received the settlement payment from Centene in late September 2024 and sent $10 million to the foundation. By October 2024, the foundation sent $5 million apiece to two nonprofits. Within days, the nonprofits wired $8.5 million to the Keep Florida Clean political action committee. Headed by DeSantis’ then-chief of staff, James Uthmeier, the PAC was created to fight the recreational marijuana ballot initiative. Keep Florida Clean later sent millions of dollars to the Republican Party of Florida and the Florida Freedom Fund, another DeSantis-aligned PAC that Uthmeier chaired at the time. Medicaid money is intended for healthcare, primarily for children, pregnant women and disabled, low-income people. Medicaid settlement funds must be placed in a state trust fund to support public health programs, according to Florida law , with a portion owed to the federal government, which co-funds Medicaid. The DeSantis administration has denied any wrongdoing. Democrats say because Centene overcharged the Medicaid program, the full amount should have gone into the state’s healthcare coffers to help low-income families, and that the administration effectively deprived that group of money. The appeals court disagreed, saying in its Oct. 7 order expunging the grand jury report that the $10 million sent to Hope Florida was “never public money.” The money “ neither reimbursed the State for losses from Centene’s overcharges nor ever became the property of the State of Florida, as the transfer of the funds was directly from Centene to Hope Florida,” the court said. This mirrors the DeSantis administration’s position that the $10 million wasn’t part of the settlement, but served as an extra, private donation from Centene. The court’s order didn’t mention that state officials reimbursed the federal government for its share of the $10 million, akin to how it handles public Medicaid money. Emails show that Centene initially offered the state $67 million, with no Hope Florida donation. After a briefing at the governor’s office, the state asked Centene to redirect $5 million of the payment as a donation to Hope Florida and later upped it to $10 million. It’s not unheard of for some settlement money to be diverted to nonprofits that could help the people harmed by the action that led to the settlement, experts previously told PolitiFact. But Hope Florida Foundation’s case was atypical. The organization had no contract with the Agency for Health Care Administration, no record of delivering Medicaid services and wasn’t meeting reporting requirements for its nonprofit status, experts said. If a state agency reaches a settlement and donates some to a nonprofit, the donation is typically considered public funds under Florida law . Moody’s office, other state agencies approved the settlement, didn’t impose limits on the $10 million Moody’s attorney general’s office approved the agreement, though available documents don’t make clear the extent of her involvement. The grand jury said it wasn’t able to bring charges because witnesses couldn’t remember details about who proposed the transfer. Centene’s lawyers insisted during negotiations that Moody’s office or Florida’s Inspector General’s office be listed in the settlement agreement, according to records obtained by the Tampa Bay Times and Miami Herald. John Guard, then-Moody’s chief deputy attorney general, attempted to remove references to the attorney general during the drafting process, records showed. In the end, Guard signed the agreement, saying Moody had approved it. Moody downplayed her office’s role in an Oct. 13 radio interview . She said the settlement included three other agencies that reviewed it for “legal sufficiency.” “So I think any questions regarding that settlement needs to be directed to that agency, AHCA,” she said. Experts previously said that although Moody didn’t sign the agreement, she is responsible for her office’s actions. Centene “insisted the (attorney general) be involved in the settlement because they were concerned about the unusual aspects of the deal and wanted to make sure they were legally protected,” said Aubrey Jewett, a University of Central Florida political science professor. “(Moody) was the chief legal officer for the state of Florida at the time, and if she had raised an objection, the deal would not have happened.” RELATED: Alexander Vindman overstates what is known about Ashley Moody’s role in Hope Florida scandal

title: Fact check: Abdul El-Sayed, Mike Rogers debate NAFTA, Medicare for All, Social Security
author: Caleb McCullough
content: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers met in their second and final debate in the campaign for U.S. Senate in Michigan, casting each other as extreme and offering competing solutions for rising prices. El-Sayed sought to tie Rogers to President Donald Trump’s unpopular decisions like the war in Iran and tariffs. He described Rogers’ responses as “MAGA bingo” and said Rogers wouldn’t stand up to Trump. Rogers painted El-Sayed as dishonest, saying he “lied about being a physician” and his citizenship. (El-Sayed has a doctor of medicine degree , but not a medical license.) Rogers accused him of sympathizing with extremist groups and said El-Sayed’s signature Medicare for All proposal would raise taxes on Michiganders. Still, they focused more on policy this time than in their first meeting . Here’s our fact-checks of the Oct. 21 debate hosted by WXYZ-TV in Detroit. Read our live fact-checking blog of the debate between El-Sayed and Rogers ‘Hot mic’ and ‘he lied’ El-Sayed: “Mike Rogers was just caught on a hot mic talking about how he wanted to make sure that there were retired cops who could intimidate voters in the city of Detroit.” El-Sayed is referring to audio of Rogers speaking to a local Republican group in April. The Detroit News reported the remarks in May, but the recorded audio surfaced the week before the Oct. 21 debate. In the clip , Rogers speculated about a “van full of ballots” showing up in Detroit to swing his 2024 election against him, despite no evidence of fraud affecting the 2024 Michigan Senate race , which he lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. Rogers then suggested using off-duty police officers as his poll watchers in the upcoming election because he said election officials in 2024 had intimidated Republican poll watchers.   View this post on Instagram   A post shared by PolitiFact (@politifact) “Let’s put retired or off-duty police officers as our poll watchers in Detroit,” he said. “Go ahead, try to intimidate them.” Rogers told ABC News in an Oct. 20 interview after the audio surfaced that his point was not about discouraging people from voting. He said he wanted to make it “easy to vote, hard to cheat.” Rogers: El-Sayed “lied about being an Egyptian dual citizen.” El-Sayed previously wrote that he had dual citizenship, but his campaign said that was a mistake. In January, The Washington Free Beacon reported that around 2014 El-Sayed published a resume on an academic networking site and described his citizenship as “USA, Egypt.” After the outlet sent the resume to the campaign for comment, the resume was removed from the site. “Abdul is not a dual citizen by any verifiable metric and never has been,” El-Sayed’s campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told The Washington Free Beacon. She said El-Sayed was “told as a child that his grandfather had pursued Egyptian citizenship on his behalf, for which he was eligible due to his parents being born in Egypt.” Economy: NAFTA, carbon tax El-Sayed: Rogers supported NAFTA, said it would be good for U.S. workers. El-Sayed said Rogers supported the North American Free Trade Agreement, or NAFTA, which Rogers denied. Former President George H. W. Bush signed NAFTA into law in 1992. “By the way, NAFTA was passed about 10 years before I got into Congress,” said Rogers, who entered Congress in 2001. “This is really kind of a ridiculous argument.” El-Sayed then said that Rogers quipped NAFTA “would be good for the American worker” in the long term. Rogers did say that in a 2000 congressional debate, but he has spoken about free trade differently in his Senate campaign. (The Rogers campaign referred us to his debate response.) “I think in the long run NAFTA is going to be good for America, but with any kind of big idea there is sometimes some big problems,” Rogers said in September 2000, when he was running for Michigan’s 8th Congressional District. During his 14 years in the House, Rogers voted in favor of multiple free trade agreements between the U.S. and countries such as Panama, Peru and the Dominican Republic. These agreements between two or more countries reduce barriers to U.S. exports by, for example, reducing tariffs. As a U.S. Senate candidate in 2024 and 2026, Rogers has changed his position on free trade agreements. During an October forum hosted by the Detroit Economic Club, Rogers said “bad trade policy” has affected the car manufacturing industry in Michigan but tariffs were fixing the problem. Rogers has supported most of Trump’s second-term tariffs but recently called for an end to the “tariff war” with Canada. Trump’s 2020 U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement superseded NAFTA. Rogers: El-Sayed “has a carbon tax that he wants to put on that would give you the highest utility rates, over $2,000 in new costs.” The figure is based on a study of policies that partly align with El-Sayed’s platform — though he is not calling for a carbon tax. Rogers released an Oct. 15 ad that made similar claims, citing a webpage from El-Sayed’s unsuccessful 2018 gubernatorial campaign and a Mackinac Center article in April about a different Democrat’s plan. PolitiFact found an archived 2018 campaign page in which El-Sayed proposed a “corporate polluter fee and taxpayer credit” that he said would charge corporations for carbon emissions and give the money back to taxpayers as a stipend. His Senate campaign platform says he will “hold polluters accountable” but does not mention a corporate polluter fee. El-Sayed says he will “fight for a pathway to 100% renewable energy” by investing in solar, wind and battery storage and a modernized smart grid. The Mackinac Center, a free-market focused think tank, studied Democratic Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s “MI Healthy Climate Plan ” that state lawmakers approved in 2023. The center estimated that residential electricity rates could rise by about $2,000 a year by 2035, attributing the potential increase to a transition from Michigan’s electric grid to “almost wholly on wind and solar with battery storage.” El-Sayed’s campaign said he supports temporarily suspending state and federal gas taxes. El-Sayed: Rogers made $14 million advising corporations he was regulating during his time in Congress This needs context. Rogers did paid work for technology and cybersecurity firms after leaving Congress in 2015, with payments exceeding $1 million in 2023. His net worth has increased by millions , according to his financial disclosures, but a full accounting of his post-Congress earnings is not available. Rogers chaired the House Intelligence Committee from 2011 to 2015, and he sat on the Energy and Commerce Committee’s Communications and Technology Subcommittee. Some of the organizations he consulted for, including AT&T, were under his oversight and affected by the decisions those committees made. In 2015, he reported less than $1 million in nonproperty assets on his required financial disclosures. Rogers listed nonproperty assets between $7.2 million and $14.6 million on his 2026 financial disclosure . While his consulting career drove those earnings, it doesn’t mean he was paid $14 million for that work; some of the growth could be attributed to stock market gains over the last decade. Social Security, Medicare for All El-Sayed: Rogers is “on record” saying he wanted to privatize Social Security and “wanted to raise the retirement age to 67.” Rogers’ record on both these issues is not as clear as El-Sayed said. Rogers’ past statements show he was open to raising the retirement age, but his stance was not consistent. And although El-Sayed’s campaign pointed to what they said were votes showing Rogers supported Social Security privatization, the record on that is less definitive. While serving in Congress from 2001 to 2015, Rogers voted against motions in 2011 and 2013 to add amendments that would have prohibited spending funds to privatize Social Security. A vote against something does not necessarily equate to a vote in support of its antithesis. In 2000, Rogers said he supported the idea of allowing people to put some of their Social Security tax in a private investment fund. We found no statements from Rogers during this campaign cycle regarding privatizing Social Security. Rogers did not respond to El-Sayed’s claim on the debate stage; his spokesperson Alyssa Brouillet told PolitiFact afterward that he is “committed to protecting Social Security.” On changing the retirement age, we also found no recent statements from Rogers in support. But in 2023 , when he was exploring a presidential bid, Rogers said he was open to changing the Social Security retirement age. That year, when asked about an effort by former President George W. Bush that would have allowed people to invest their payroll tax funds in the stock market, Rogers said, “I think Americans see Social Security very different than their personal investments, and they don’t want to see them intertwined. And I’m not sure that’s the wrong answer, honestly.” As recently as 2024 , a Rogers spokesperson told PolitiFact Rogers didn’t support raising the retirement age. Rogers: Medicare for All would be “$7 trillion a year in new expenses, about $20,000 per family, in new taxes.” The cost and tax burden of Medicare for All , a national single-payer health insurance program that is core to El-Sayed’s campaign, varies by proposal. El-Sayed hasn’t laid out a funding plan but has acknowledged it will likely increase taxes , while noting the taxes would replace copays and premiums. A Yale study from July estimated that a national healthcare system would lower overall U.S. health spending by $1 trillion annually. In 2018, the Urban Institute estimated Vermont U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders’ Medicare for All proposal would cost $32 trillion over 10 years . John Holahan, a fellow at the Urban Institute, told CNN this year that the price tag could have doubled since then because of inflation and rising healthcare costs. Rogers’ $20,000 in new taxes figure is based on an estimate for the cost if the plan were funded by mandatory public premiums. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget estimated in 2020 that replacing private health insurance premiums with a per-person Medicare premium would average about $7,500 per person, or $20,000 per household. The report said that employers could pay some of that premium, as they do with health insurance costs now, or they could be reduced or waived based on income. But other Medicare for All funding ideas exist, too, including financing it with increased payroll taxes, higher income taxes or a wealth tax. Some proponents have pitched financing the program with increased taxes on corporations and employers rather than individual taxpayers. Rogers: El-Sayed’s Medicare for All plan “takes away your private health insurance. Five million Michiganders will lose their healthcare.” Some versions of Medicare for All call for banning private health insurance that matches Medicare’s coverage, but El-Sayed has said he supports a plan that allows for private health insurance to coexist with a government-operated single-payer plan. Under a Medicare for All plan, every American would be eligible for coverage provided by Medicare. About 5 million Michiganders , and around 49% of Americans, receive employer-provided health insurance. El-Sayed’s campaign website says his plan “does not have to ban additional private insurance through unions or employers, although Medicare for All should make those choices redundant and unnecessary.” In an Oct. 11 interview on “Meet the Press,” El-Sayed said people could keep their employer-provided coverage under his plan, but his website does not explain the mechanisms. That would differ from Sanders’ Medicare for All proposal , which would prohibit private insurers from offering duplicate coverage. title: Fact-checking Roger Marshall, Adam Hamilton on diesel prices, SNAP in Kansas U.S. Senate debate
author: Louis Jacobson
content: In a Senate race that unexpectedly ranks among the nation’s hottest, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall debated his Democratic challenger, pastor Adam Hamilton, with each trying to tie the other to their parties’ most partisan factions. Marshall cited Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., by name 19 times, saying that losing Republican control of the Senate would mean Democrats would use their newfound power to “create open borders,” amounting to “a threat to our republic.” Hamilton argued that President Donald Trump’s policies, including starting the Iran war and imposing tariffs, had raised diesel fuel prices and hampered international trade — key elements for the Kansas economy. The debate was hosted by WDAF-TV in Kansas City, Missouri. Here are fact-checks of some of the candidates’ claims. Marshall: “The real problem with the cost of diesel, in particular, is, No. 1, the Ukraine war, and because of that, diesel production has gone down.” Hamilton, when it was his turn to respond: “Nobody believes that. This happened in response to the war in Iran that didn’t need to happen.” The candidates sparred over the causes of the current high cost of diesel fuel — especially important in a state like Kansas, where agriculture plays a significant role in the economy. Both Marshall and Hamilton have a point. In the U.S., diesel prices soared from $3.81 per gallon on the eve of the Iran war to $6.29 on Oct. 21. What kicked this price rise into high gear in recent months, experts told PolitiFact , is declining Russian production caused by Ukraine’s attacks on oil infrastructure as it tries to fight off the invasion Russia launched in 2022. Ukrainian’s successful attacks have left a hole in the world’s diesel supply. And even though the U.S. implemented an embargo on Russian diesel in 2022, the price for U.S. customers depends on the global price. That means farmers and truckers here feel the pinch from lower diesel output in Russia, too. But Hamilton’s also correct that the Iran war made matters worse. Persian Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia that refine crude oil have been hampered by Iran’s attempt to squeeze the Strait of Hormuz, and also by Iranian counter-attacks on U.S. allies in the region since the war began Feb. 28. Had the Russian oil infrastructure problems occurred on their own — without the added complication of the Iran war — those Persian Gulf nations would have been able to fill some of the gap in diesel production, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for the gasoline price tracker GasBuddy, told PolitiFact this week. Marshall: “Last year, Kansas had in the third quarter the leading GDP in the country of over 6%.” Marshall’s statistic on gross domestic product, which is the sum of a state’s economic activity, is misleading, according to official state-by-state data from the U.S. Commerce Department. In the third quarter of 2025, Kansas saw annualized, year-over-year growth in gross domestic product of 4.7%. That’s a strong showing, but not over 6%, and not first among the 50 states. That quarter, California ranked first with 11.4% growth, followed by Rhode Island, New Hampshire, Nebraska, Idaho, Delaware, New York, Tennessee and Nevada. Kansas came next, at 10th nationally. Generally, state GDP growth figures fluctuate a lot from quarter to quarter, so choosing one amounts to cherry picking. By choosing the quarter he did, Marshall was ignoring three more recent quarterly numbers, each with growth lower than the one he cited. Since the start of 2025, Kansas has experienced some hot quarters (8.3% growth in the second quarter of 2025), some cold ones (6.3% decrease in the first quarter of 2025) and some so-so ones (growth of 1.8% in the fourth quarter of 2025). In the most recent quarter — the second quarter of 2026 — Kansas saw its GDP shrink by 0.6%. Hamilton: “I have never advocated for amnesty.” This needs context. Hamilton was responding to Marshall saying, “My opponent has always supported amnesty and giving illegal immigrants benefits, welfare benefits.” The term “amnesty” has no legal definition in immigration policy. It’s often interpreted as any policy waiving punishments for immigration violations, but it’s also sometimes understood as a widespread granting of citizenship to people in the country illegally. We found no instance in which Hamilton called for across-the-board legalization of immigrants in the country illegally. On the agriculture portion of his campaign agenda , his website references giving a “path to legal status” to farm workers. He calls on Congress to “reform the broken H-2A guest-worker program — permitting year-round visas that reflect modern needs, lowering compliance costs, and giving existing workers a path to legal status.” That temporary visa program is used by farmers . In a questionnaire by the Johnson County Post published earlier this month, Hamilton wrote, “I’m not for open borders, and dangerous criminals don’t belong here.” He also wrote that ICE’s operations caused chaos for families, communities and businesses. During a September debate at the Kansas State Fair, Hamilton called immigration under former President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump a “disaster.” During the Oct. 21 debate, he repeated his talking point about Biden border policies being a “disaster.” Marshall: “We’ve increased the spending on food stamps from $80 billion a year … to $150 billion a year.” That’s exaggerated. In fiscal year 2025, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, sometimes referred to as food stamps, spent $101.7 billion with benefits averaging $187.94 per participant per month, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture . Spending on the program was higher from 2021 to 2023 as the country recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic, but it never reached $150 billion. Marshall is correct that SNAP spending was previously around $80 billion; we found close to that amount in 2019. We asked Marshall’s spokespersons for the source of his figure and did not receive an immediate reply. The Center for Budget and Policy Priorities estimated that SNAP participation nationwide fell in the year after the July 2025 enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which changed work requirements for participants. The total drop came to more than 5 million people, nearly 13% nationally by June 2026, based on USDA data. In Kansas, participation fell by about 25,000, or 13.5%. Hamilton: “More than 36,000 people have lost health insurance in the state of Kansas. We think today, closer to 50,000 people.” Hamilton’s wording is a little hard to follow, but if anything, he understated the numbers. KFF, a healthcare policy think tank, tracks state-by-state data for healthcare coverage losses for both policies purchased on Affordable Care Act marketplaces and Medicaid . Both programs have seen participation decline either because of changes enacted by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’s signature spending and tax bill from 2025, or because of the loss of enhanced subsidies on policies purchased from the ACA marketplace. In 2021, then-President Joe Biden signed legislation that made the subsidies more generous; those enhanced subsidies expired at the end of 2025 after the Republican-controlled Congress did not extend them. Between 2025 and 2026, KFF estimated, marketplace enrollment fell by 36,040 in Kansas, while Medicaid enrollment in the state dropped by 25,736 over a similar period. Combined, those two declines add up to 61,776 — larger than the 50,000 figure Hamilton cited in the debate. PolitiFact researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this article. title: Showers in the Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern and North-western provinces and in Kandy and Nuwara-Eliya districts
author: Priyan
content: WEATHER FORECAST FOR 27 October 2026 Issued at 5.30 a.m. on 27 October 2026 by the Department of Meteorology The Severe Cyclonic Storm “Arnab” over the West central Bay of Bengal intensified into a ‘Very Severe Cyclonic Storm’ and lay centered at 02.30 a.m. today, the 27th October, 2026 over the near latitude 15.9°N and longitude 85.4°E about 890 km to the north-east of Kankasanthurai. It is very likely to continue to move west-northwestwards till 05.30 p.m. of 27th October and thereafter, it is very likely to move northwestwards and cross the Indian land through Andhra Pradesh coast as a very severe cyclonic storm by 11.30 a.m. of 28th October, 2026. Although this system is not expected to have a direct impact on Sri Lanka, the showery condition over the southwestern parts of the island is expected continue today, as the wind flow associated with the system extends across the island. Showers or thundershowers will occur at times in the Western, Sabaragamuwa, Southern and North-western provinces and in Kandy and Nuwara-Eliya districts and, fairly heavy showers above 75 mm are likely at some places in these areas. Showers or thunder showers will occur at a few places after 1.00 p.m. in the Eastern province. Strong winds of about (40-50) kmph can be expected at times over the Western slopes of the Central hills, Northern, North-central and North-western provinces and in Trincomalee and Hambantota Districts. The general public is kindly requested to take adequate precautions to minimize damage caused by temporary localized strong winds and lightning during thundershowers.

title: SL balances humanitarian obligations and mounting geopolitical pressures
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: … ships declare ‘state of emergency’ by Shamindra Ferdinando Forty Iranian sailors from Iranian oil tankers stranded outside Sri Lanka’s territorial waters have been repatriated. Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath confirmed the evacuation of the Iranian sailors by the Navy and their repatriation to Iran on Sunday. Responding to The Island query, Minister Herath said that the government had acted following a request from Iran. Sri Lanka intervened amidst accusations that refusal to provide assistance to vessels was contrary to international laws. About 21 Iranian vessels are believed to be stranded off Sri Lanka’s southern coast for several months due to the ongoing US blockade on Iranian ports. The crew members included Indians and Bangladeshis. The Island learns that humanitarian intervention had been made with the understanding of the US. In March this year, Sri Lanka rescued several dozens of Iranian sailors from a frigate that had been torpedoed by the US Navy, off Galle, within Sri Lanka’s exclusive economic zone. A spokesperson for the Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran, in Colombo, told The Island : “These individuals were brought ashore and taken to hospital for medical treatment due to health issues, following the declaration of a state of emergency by the vessels, in accordance with the obligations arising under the relevant international conventions concerning the rescue of persons aboard ships.”

title: Sajith, Sumanthiran seek diplomatic scrutiny of proposed security laws
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: SJB and Opposition Leader Sajith Premadasa has sought international support to oppose the government’s proposed security laws. Premadasa convened a consultation with representatives of diplomatic missions and international organisations at the Office of the Leader of the Opposition, Colombo 7, on Sunday, to underscore serious concerns relating to proposed security legislation, constitutional safeguards and democratic accountability. The discussion focused on the Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and the Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill. Former MP M. A. Sumanthiran, together with participating serving and former Members of Parliament, also expressed serious concerns about the proposed legislation and its potential implications for fundamental rights and the rule of law. Premadasa underlined the responsibility of the parliamentary Opposition to scrutinise government legislation, protect independent institutions and ensure that executive power remains subject to the Constitution. He reaffirmed that decisive action against terrorism and serious organised crime must be accompanied by effective judicial oversight and respect for civil liberties. Particular attention was drawn to the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka’s (HRCSL) official statement of 21 October, 2026, on the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill. The Commission assessed the proposed Bill as “wholly incompatible” with the fundamental-rights chapter of the Constitution and Sri Lanka’s international human-rights obligations, and described it as potentially more draconian than the Prevention of Terrorism Act of 1979. These are the HRCSL’s assessments, not findings by a court. The Commission identified concerns about the admissibility of confessions made to senior police officers, detention ordered through the executive, the extensive definition of “serious crime”, criteria such as clothing, tattoos or association when assessing alleged criminal-group membership, and provisions that restrict judicial discretion over remand and bail. Crucially, the HRCSL recommended that the Prevention of Organised Crime Bill be withdrawn and substantially revised to comply with constitutional and international human-rights standards. In observations, dated 1 October, 2026, on the Ministry-published draft terrorism Bill, the HRCSL separately urged the Government to narrow the proposed definition of terrorism, subject detention orders to judicial oversight, preserve meaningful judicial authority to grant bail, guarantee prompt access to legal counsel and ensure the independence of the proposed review mechanism. It also reiterated its view that terrorism offences should be addressed under general criminal law. The Bar Association of Sri Lanka (BASL), in its statement of 21 October, called for withdrawal of the organised crime Bill and withdrawal or amendment of the terrorism Bill in its present form. It also sought publication of the expert committee report and recorded dissent relating to the terrorism Bill, raising concerns over departures from the committee-approved draft. Premadasa emphasised the need for a transparent legislative response: publication of relevant expert recommendations; clear and proportionate definitions of offences; meaningful judicial discretion over detention, remand and bail; protection against coerced confessions and arbitrary surveillance; and consultation with the BASL, HRCSL and other relevant stakeholders before legislation with such far-reaching implications proceeds. He stressed that these safeguards are not privileges of politicians or activists. They protect ordinary citizens, young people, families, businesses and all others who may come into contact with the criminal justice system. The Opposition’s position is that national security and the rule of law must reinforce, not undermine, one another. The consultation provided an opportunity to share independently documented concerns with diplomatic and international representatives. Premadasa reaffirmed Sri Lanka’s sovereignty and the primary responsibility of Parliament, the judiciary and national institutions to resolve domestic legal questions, while emphasising constructive dialogue rather than external intervention or partisan endorsement. The Opposition Leader reiterated his commitment to constructive parliamentary engagement on effective security legislation that protects the public from serious crime while upholding constitutional democracy, judicial independence and individual liberty.

title: SC nullifies Ranil’s pardon for man jailed over maintenance arrears
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: The Supreme Court has declared null and void a presidential pardon granted by President Ranil Wickremesinghe to a man sentenced to 29 months in prison for failing to pay Rs. 1.74 million in maintenance arrears. In a judgment delivered last Friday (23), a three-judge bench held that the remission granted to Mohamed Ameen Mohamed Naseem, under a general amnesty in September 2024, violated his former wife’s fundamental right to equality and equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The judgment was delivered by Justice Janak De Silva, with Justices Dr. Sobhitha Rajakaruna and Sampath K.B. Wijeratne agreeing. The case was filed by Naseem’s former wife, Ahamend Jaleel Farmilla Begum, challenging his release after he served less than two months of the 29-month sentence. Naseem had been imprisoned in July 2024 for failing to comply with a maintenance order issued by the Quazi Court. He was released on September 12, 2024, under a general amnesty granted to mark Prisoners’ Day. The Supreme Court found that Naseem had been given preferential treatment after his imprisonment was recorded as being for non-payment of a fine, while another prisoner, imprisoned over similar maintenance arrears, had received only a one-week reduction in his sentence. The Court held that the difference in the wording of the two prisoners’ commitment warrants did not justify the unequal treatment. Accordingly, the Court ruled that former President Wickremesinghe, the Secretary to the Ministry of Justice and the Commissioner General of Prisons, had violated the petitioner’s fundamental rights. The Court declared the remission granted to Naseem null and void, thereby restoring the legal effect of his original sentence. In a significant observation, the Court said Naseem, having been released while his sentence remained legally valid, was now a “fugitive from justice” and should surrender immediately to law enforcement authorities. The Court further held that the original warrant issued by the Negombo Magistrate’s Court remained valid and provided sufficient authority for prison officials to detain Naseem and enforce the sentence. However, it said no further order from the Supreme Court was necessary to enforce the sentence, as the Magistrate’s Court already had the authority to take the necessary steps. The judgment also clarified that the President was not precluded from granting a fresh remission to Naseem, provided it was done in accordance with the law and after considering all relevant circumstances. The ruling was delivered in Fundamental Rights Application No. 319/2024.

title: Gnanasara Thera release campaign suspended
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: The Satyagraha launched at Viharamahadevi Park on 16 October, demanding the release of Ven. Galagodaaththe Gnanasara Thera, has been temporarily suspended. Organisers said the decision had been taken following an assurance from the Mahanayake Theras of the three Nikayas that they would take stepts to resolve the issue through discussions. The government has maintained that Ven. Gnanasara, who was returned to prison in October after the Supreme Court invalidated the presidential pardon granted to him by former President Maithripala Sirisena in May 2019, will not be released through a fresh pardon. The “Justice for the Robe – Freedom March” began in Kandy on 10 October and proceeded to Colombo. The protesters moved to Viharamahadevi Park on 16 October after police obtained a court order preventing identified monks and other individuals from gathering at the Presidential Secretariat. Ven. Gnanasara was sentenced to six years of rigorous imprisonment for contempt of court in 2018. He served about nine months before receiving the presidential pardon in May 2019. The Supreme Court subsequently ruled that the pardon was legally invalid, paving the way for the remainder of his sentence to be enforced.

title: Probe ordered into delay in extradition of ‘Dippitigoda Lahiru’ from Japan
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: A special investigation has been ordered to identify officials allegedly responsible for deliberately delaying the submission of documents required to secure Japanese assistance to arrest and extradite alleged organised crime figure and drug trafficker Pothupitiya Kankanamge Prashith Dinuka, alias ‘Dippitigoda Lahiru’ (31). Lahiru, who operated from Dubai, moved to Japan, while Sri Lankan drug trafficker Pallewatte Gamage Chaminda Dilruk, alias ‘Parevi Suda’, who allegedly provided him protection, remained in Dubai, according to sources. Police said a network involving senior police officers and certain officials attached to the Attorney General’s Department had delayed the submission of documents required to facilitate Lahiru’s extradition. The network is believed to have been maintained through financial inducements allegedly provided by Parevi Suda, the sources claimed. The allegations have prompted authorities to investigate whether officials deliberately withheld or delayed information sought by Japanese authorities. An Interpol Red Notice was issued against Lahiru on June 8, 2023, under reference A-5059/8-2023. According to police records, Lahiru, whose passport number is N7082478, left for Dubai on March 1, 2022. His last known address in Sri Lanka is No. 226/F/11, Dippitigoda, Kelaniya. Despite the Red Notice and a series of serious criminal investigations linked to him, the required documentation had allegedly not been properly transmitted to Japan, sources said. They alleged that some information concerning Lahiru had either not been forwarded or had been forwarded incompletely, hampering efforts to secure his arrest and extradition. Police records reportedly link Lahiru to more than a dozen killings and attempted killings allegedly carried out on his orders while he was abroad. Among the cases under investigation are a series of shootings reported between May and December 2022. According to police records, Lahiru allegedly ordered and financed a series of killings and attempted killings while he was operating from Dubai. The following cases are among those in which he is alleged to have contracted or arranged the killings: On May 30, 2022, Gammana Liyanage Lakshitha Viraj was shot dead with a T-56 firearm at Bastian Mawatha, Pettah, Colombo, while Palle Kumburage Pradeep Sandamal of Alutwatte, Nakiyadeniya, was injured. On June 3, Modara Pelige Gayan Sampath Fernando of Bandarawatte, Beruwala, was shot dead with a revolver at Moragalla, Aluthgama. Two days later, on June 5, Ratnaweera Patabendige Asela Sampath of Nakulugamuwa, Tangalle, was shot dead at Moraketiara Junction, Kudawella, while two others were injured. On June 26, 2022, Hewawasam Aththanayake Aruna Kantha Aththanayake, alias ‘Police Aththanayake,’ of Devalapola, Minuwangoda, was shot dead near Pattiya Junction, Peliyagoda. His two-year-old child was also injured in the shooting. On June 30, 2022, Senanayake Roshan Priyantha of Sri Anandarama Mawatha, Kolonnawa, was shot dead near the clock tower at Kolonnawa Junction. According to police records, the alleged contract killings continued with the shooting of Bombuwala Devage Achira Nethruwan Bombuwala of Kehelbaddara, Udugampola, in front of the Mr Cut salon at Udugampola on August 6, 2022. On August 24, 2022, Basnayake Appuhamilage Anuradha Pushpa Kumara Tissera of Nedagamuwa, Kotugoda, was shot dead outside the Malli Super Hardware shop at Batapotha, Gampaha. On September 14, 2022, Mohamed Arif Mohamed Hussain, alias ‘Arji,’ of Wellawatte, Wellampitiya, was shot dead near Gurukula Vidyalaya at Pattiya Junction, Peliyagoda. On November 15, 2022, Muthukuda Arachchige Dimuthu Subhash of Nedagamuwa, Kotugoda, was shot and injured outside Siyambalapitiya Maha Vidyalaya, Gampaha. On December 23, 2022, Kotagedara Liyanage Gihan Kanchana Perera of Lahuwala, Raddoluwa, was shot dead near Galiganeliya Junction, Seeduwa. Police sources said the latest investigation is aimed at determining whether administrative delays, negligence or deliberate intervention by officials hindered efforts to secure Lahiru’s arrest and extradition from Japan.

title: What Fowzie’s public apology signifies
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: Tuesday 27th October, 2026 Former Minister A. H. M. Fowzie has published an apology in a government-controlled newspaper for having misused a state vehicle while in power. He has done so in compliance with a Supreme Court (SC) order. The case concerned an SUV donated by the Netherlands for disaster-management activities. Fowzie used the vehicle for personal purposes, and state funds were spent on its maintenance while he was Minister of Disaster Management. The SC also ordered him to pay Rs. 6.6 million to the Consolidated Fund. Fowzie’s case raises questions about the wider misuse of state vehicles by politicians. Only a thorough probe will help nab the other culprits who abused power and misused vehicles and state funds to their heart’s content. Presidents, Prime Ministers and Ministers have misused their official vehicles for election campaigns over the years. The Election Commission says it strives to create a level playing field for all parties and candidates contesting elections, but the members of the government in power abuse state resources for the benefit of their parties. When government leaders attend party events, their travel entails huge costs as it involves hundreds of security personnel and a large number of state vehicles. Information obtained from Sri Lanka Air Force Headquarters under the Right to Information Act, in 2024, revealed that former President Mahinda Rajapaksa had made 978 domestic helicopter flights using Air Force aircraft under presidential privilege between 2005 and 2015. Former President Maithripala Sirisena made 557 such flights during his five-year tenure. As an Opposition MP, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake demanded to know why President Rajapaksa used two helicopters at a time, cynically asking whether he could change choppers in mid-air in an emergency. Today, the Opposition accuses President Dissanayake of doing what he once criticised Rajapaksa for. Following the 2024 regime change, state vehicles returned by former government politicians and political appointees were parked at Galle Face Green, where they became a public spectacle and a symbol of alleged misuse of state resources. The JVP-led NPP said those vehicles would be auctioned, and its ministers would use public transport. People obviously bought into such promises because even in some developed countries, people’s representatives travel on public buses and trains. They may have expected the JVP/NPP politicians to emulate the MPs and ministers in Sweden, where ministers and members of parliament travel on ordinary buses and trains rather than having official cars and private drivers as a general entitlement. Only the Prime Minister has access to a state vehicle for security and official duties in Sweden. Ministers and MPs are occasionally seen travelling by bus or train in countries such as Austria, Singapore, Germany and the UK. It may be argued that political leaders need security and their schedules can make public transport impractical, particularly in a country like Sri Lanka. However, the JVP/NPP came to power promising to develop public transport and restore public security by ridding the country of the underworld and drug menace within two months. During the 2024 presidential election campaign, Anura Kumara Dissanayake, as the NPP’s candidate, pledged to dismantle the President’s large security detail and curb politicians’ use of expensive official vehicles. Soon after assuming office, the JVP-NPP administration opened roads near the President’s House and Temple Trees. President Dissanayake has also been seen walking leisurely in Jaffna and Anuradhapura. If public security has improved sufficiently to permit such changes, why can’t at least government MPs travel by bus or train on some of their journeys? One may recall that during the Eelam War, JVP MP Nihal Galappatti, elected on the Sri Lanka Progressive Front ticket in 1994, travelled by bus between Tangalle and Parliament. His example offers a reminder that a parliamentary seat need not automatically entail special privileges. It would not have been possible to make Fowzie and other politicians face the full force of the law if they had been in power. While being ensconced in power, they may not have thought they would ever be held accountable for their transgressions, much less jailed and fined. Hence politicians must not be allowed to remain entrenched in power for long periods. The Opposition has accused the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption and the police of dragging their feet on complaints of corruption against the current rulers. We will have to wait until the next regime change to have the present-day rulers accused of misusing vehicles and indulging in corruption brought to justice.

title: Search for truth and justice in mass graves
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: By Jehan Perera The Chemmani mass grave site has today become a focus of public concern in the North and a challenge to the government’s credibility among the Tamil people. After months of excavation and the recovery of more than 580 human skeletons, a report by Sri Lanka’s leading forensic archaeologist, Prof Raj Somadeva, has concluded that the site bears greater similarities to a formal burial ground than to clandestine burial sites with signs of criminal activity and non-conventional burial. The report acknowledges that the available evidence is insufficient to establish conclusively the nature and circumstances of the burials. Its findings, which are markedly different from two previous interim reports by Prof Somadeva have caused dismay among Tamil political parties, civil society organisations and families of the disappeared. Establishing the scientific truth is essential, but so is ensuring that the investigation is seen to be fair, independent and transparent. The controversy recalls the still inconclusive investigation into the Mannar mass grave, discovered in March 2018 at a construction site in the heart of the town. Radiocarbon dating of some samples at a laboratory in Florida indicated that they were approximately 600 years old. The legal teams representing the families of the disappeared argued that this finding could not establish the age of all the remains, pointing to untested sections of the site and relatively recent objects recovered during excavation. These reportedly included a biscuit wrapper from the 1980s and a skeleton found with its hands chained and manacled. The controversy demonstrated the dangers of drawing conclusions about an entire burial site from limited scientific evidence. The same danger exists at Chemmani. A finding that some remains resemble those in a conventional burial ground cannot establish that all the people buried there died naturally. The mass grave discovered at the Matale District General Hospital in 2013 provides another troubling example of the difficulties Sri Lanka has faced in establishing the truth about suspected mass graves. The recovery of 154 skeletal remains was followed by conflicting forensic interpretations concerning the period of burial, including findings that reportedly pointed to the late 1980s and later radiocarbon results suggesting an earlier historical period. Questions were also raised about the selection and handling of samples and the adequacy of the investigation. These unresolved issues reinforce the need for independent scrutiny of forensic evidence, transparent procedures and a credible explanation of discrepancies between competing findings. The lessons from Matale, Mannar and Chemmani should inform a national framework for investigating all suspected mass graves. No Follow-up More than 15,000 disappearances during the war have been registered with the Office on Missing Persons (OMP) and the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), and many more are believed to have gone unreported. Identifying those responsible remains an even greater challenge. There are many documented cases in which witnesses identified those who took people away before they disappeared, but the authorities have failed to follow up by questioning those who are alleged to have caused the disappearances. One such incident occurred at the refugee camp at Eastern University in September 1990, when people who had sought refuge were taken away. Witness accounts have identified those responsible. Similar incidents occurred in May 2009, when the war ended and many people who surrendered to the military in the presence of others were never seen again. Disappearances also occurred at other times during the conflict, including the period surrounding the military recapture of Jaffna in 1995. Chemmani came to public attention following the rape and murder of schoolgirl Krishanthi Kumaraswamy in September 1996, nine months after the government regained control over Jaffna. Her mother, brother and a family friend who went searching for her were also killed. The soldiers responsible were prosecuted, and six people were sentenced to death in 1998. One of the convicted soldiers, Lance Corporal Somaratne Rajapakse, alleged that hundreds of Tamil civilians who had been arrested and forcibly disappeared during the mid-1990s had been executed and buried in the Chemmani area. Exhumations at that time recovered 15 skeletons. Successive governments, however, failed to pursue these allegations adequately. The convicted soldier’s evidence could now prove important in resolving the present controversy, as is being done successfully today with others in custody in regard to the Easter bombing. His allegations should be investigated alongside the archaeological findings, forensic evidence, witness accounts and historical records. Prof Somadeva’s report points to the positioning of some skeletons, possible coffin fittings and the concentration of children’s remains. It suggests that the burials may be associated with formal burial practices and raises the possibility of an epidemic or natural catastrophe. Yet it identifies no specific epidemic or disaster, neither the Covid epidemic of 2020 nor the Tsunami of 2004, establishes neither the date of death nor the cause of death, and does not rule out unlawful killings. In a court case filed last week, families of the disappeared challenged the report’s conclusions and called for the evidence to be examined more comprehensively. Personal belongings, including school bags and children’s items, have been recovered with some remains. Allegations that certain skeletons were found with their hands bound must also be assessed against excavation records and forensic observations. The objective of investigations must be to establish the truth through rigorous investigation and to pursue accountability wherever the evidence leads. HRCSL Framework The findings of the Human Rights Commission of Sri Lanka (HRCSL) provide an important framework for addressing these questions. In its report, the HRCSL identified weaknesses that threaten both the quality of the investigation and public confidence in its outcome. These included inadequate forensic expertise, limited access to scientific dating and DNA analysis, funding difficulties and the absence of an adopted standard operating procedure for mass grave investigations. These recommendations need to be implemented. Independent international expertise should be obtained where necessary to undertake scientific dating, including carbon-14 testing, and credible DNA analysis. A DNA bank should be established so that relatives can voluntarily provide samples for comparison. Ground-penetrating radar surveys should be extended to determine whether further remains lie beyond the excavated area. A formal procedure for mass grave investigations, developed in consultation with experts, lawyers and civil society, should ensure the preservation of evidence and regular public updates. The Human Rights Commission also recommended an independent institution empowered to investigate and prosecute serious crimes by state officials. This is particularly important where allegations concern institutions whose own conduct may come under scrutiny. Investigations must be sufficiently independent to ensure that evidence is neither overlooked nor suppressed and that responsibility is established wherever the evidence leads. At Chemmani, as at Mannar and Matale, competing explanations must be tested through independent scientific examination. An inquiry into missing persons must be non-partisan, empathetic and attentive to the historical context. Families who have spent decades seeking answers must be kept informed and given meaningful opportunities to participate in the search for truth. People of all communities who lost their loved ones in the past need to trust that the investigation seeks to uncover what happened to their loved ones and not be yet another government cover up as in the past. Their frustration also arises from decades of institutional failure. A credible process must address that history rather than simply ask them to trust a new investigation. For many families, the central question remains not only what happened to those who disappeared, but who was responsible and why those responsible have not been held accountable. Their demand for answers deserves to be treated as a legitimate claim of justice, not merely as a challenge to government credibility. Sri Lanka cannot build lasting reconciliation by asking families to move on while the fate of their loved ones remains unknown.

title: Why Supreme Court needs additional layers of safety
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: by Dr. M. M. Janapriya I first trained as a medical doctor at the university’s medical faculty, and then spent nine more years becoming a Specialist Surgeon. In our training, the senior surgeon, the boss, stands opposite you at the operating table, guiding you through every step. Once he knows you can safely remove an appendix, for example, he lets you do it with a house officer assisting, while he sits in the changing room. This ritual applies to all common operations. You see it all, read it all, do it all and only then face the final hurdle, the FRCS. When you pass, colleagues jokingly call you “007”. Licence to kill? Oh No, a mission to accomplish: Pristine health for the patients. Over the years, our old school dependence on physical diagnostic skills was supplemented and often surpassed by high tech investigations such as CT, MRI, PET, and more. Medicine evolved. Our training evolved. Our safeguards evolved. Lawyers, however, have no such one-to-one apprenticeship. After the law finals and a year’s apprenticeship, you are “good to go”. A few years later, one may be appointed a magistrate, and eventually climb to the Supreme Court. Training is on the job. Support systems are minimal. And yet these individuals or three of them together are entrusted with deciding someone’s fate, or the right and wrong of a 62 year old land dispute that has bounced between courts for decades. Can such a system guarantee justice? Clearly, no. The Problem Like many democracies, Sri Lanka’s legal system is a hierarchy of courts culminating in the Supreme Court. Under Dominion Ceylon, an aggrieved party could appeal beyond our shores to the Privy Council in England, and there are instances where Supreme Court judgments were reversed. This facility was abolished in 1972 when Ceylon became the Republic of Sri Lanka. To preserve the principle that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done , the alternative was introduced, appealing to the Chief Justice for a five- or seven judge bench. This certainly made justice appear more robust. But appearances are not necessarily the reality. Is it fair that a case entering its seventh decade is heard by a panel of three judges of whom only one may be fully awake and leading, while the other two may be slumbering and later sign, “I agree”? Indirectly, the people’s sovereign power appoints judges. The people elect the executive, and the executive appoints the judges. Yet the losing party must accept the verdict, even if the presiding judge does not go through all case notes and concentrates only on “whether the appellant defendants’ case for ownership through prescription has merit”. Cause of the Problem Political influence over Sri Lanka’s judiciary began after Independence (1948) through executive control over appointments, but became structurally entrenched following the introduction of the 1978 Constitution by President J. R. Jayewardene. The first clear instance appears immediately after Independence: Prime Minister D. S. Senanayake bypassed the most senior Supreme Court judge Felix Reginald Dias Bandaranaike, in 1948, instead appointing Arthur Wijewardene, then Attorney General. That was a political appointment. From the 1950s to the 1970s, governments continued appointing judges based on political loyalty. During Sirimavo Bandaranaike’s 1970-77 administration, partisan appointments were made, including individuals with SLFP backgrounds. Barnes Ratwatte, PM Sirimavo’s brother was elevated from a lower court to the Supreme Court by his nephew, Justice Minister Felix Dias Bandaranaike. These were episodic, personality driven interventions. I could list what happened under each and every government since but the story is the same. JRJ openly said he did not want judicial obstruction to deploying what people entrusted him to do. Others followed suit. The public perception is that judges handpicked by ruling party politicians often deliver judgments favourable to the government in power. Justice Neville Samarakoon, appointed by JRJ, was a rare exception. When he delivered a judgment unpalatable to the government, he faced political wrath and retired. Solution In criminal cases, especially murder trials, for example, a jury assists the judge. Why? Because the system recognises its major flaw, a single human being deciding whether a defendant walks free, receives a lesser sentence, or is convicted of premeditated murder. I propose that the Supreme Court, too, have additional layers of safety. Layer 1: Citizens’ Back-up Jury A well-educated, physically and mentally sound group of individuals, selected through a point-based system sits through cases, deliver their own verdict before the judges deliver theirs. Layer 2: Judicial AI Assistant (JAIA) An Artificial Intelligence system trained in Sri Lankan law, relevant precedents, and the Constitution of the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka. JAIA listens to all arguments throughout the proceedings and produces its own judgment. Judges may access JAIA’s output only after they have independently reached their decision. These layers increase transparency, reduce bias, and strengthen public confidence. Analysis This combination minimises the chances of a wrong judgment by a human only court due to: 1. Human Fallibility “To err is human” is not a cliché, it is a reality. Judge fatigue is real, especially in cases that have aged into geriatric status within the court system. 2. Bias and Groupthink In any group, mountaineers, sailors or even cricketers, consensus often emerges before action. This can and may happen in three, five, or seven judge benches. 3. Committee Dynamics Strong voices steer committees. I sat on the Sri Lanka Medical Council for 15 years (1985–2000) as an elected member and was often the lone voice against audaciously insane arguments from senior members. 4. Human Cost A judicial system, shaped by decades of political influence and human limitations, cannot guarantee justice through human judgment alone. Additional layers a Citizens’ Back-up Jury and a Judicial AI Assistant are not luxuries. They are necessities. Justice must not only be done. It must be seen , felt , and trusted . And for that, the system must evolve.

title: Sri Lanka urged to turn strategic location into economic freedom
author: Sahan Weerasooriya
content: By Ifham Nizam Sri Lanka must turn its strategic position in the Indian Ocean into economic freedom, investment opportunities and greater diplomatic influence while safeguarding its sovereignty, Professor Patrick Mendis told The Island Financial Review following a conference in Stockholm. The Sri Lankan-born American scholar-diplomat said the Mahaweli Doctrine offered a framework for navigating intensifying major-power competition while ensuring international partnerships strengthened Sri Lanka’s ability to determine its own economic and political future. ‘Sri Lanka must learn to turn its strategic location in the Indian Ocean into economic freedom and national prosperity. ‘Our relationships with China, India, the United States and other global partners must serve Sri Lanka’s national interests. The Mahaweli Doctrine is about building international connectivity without compromising our sovereignty, because our ultimate responsibility is to the people of Sri Lanka and future generations, he said. ‘For a country seeking economic recovery and national renewal, the challenge is not merely attracting foreign investment or maintaining cordial relations with powerful nations. Sri Lanka must build the institutional strength, policy consistency and diplomatic independence needed to ensure international engagement delivers lasting benefits, he explained. Drawing on his experience in American government, Chinese academia and international organisations, Prof. Mendis argues that Sri Lanka must move beyond viewing geography as an advantage in itself and develop the capacity to convert it into sustainable prosperity. His Mahaweli Doctrine draws inspiration from the river that has shaped Sri Lanka’s agricultural civilisation. Just as the Mahaweli connects communities and sustains livelihoods, foreign policy should connect the country with markets, investment, technology and knowledge while protecting national interests. The principle is that international relationships must serve broad development objectives rather than narrow private or political interests. Sri Lanka’s location along major Indian Ocean shipping routes has long attracted powerful nations. Its ports, maritime infrastructure and potential as a regional commercial hub offer opportunities to expand trade, attract investment and strengthen links with global markets. Yet the Mahaweli Doctrine distinguishes between possessing a strategic advantage and having the institutional capacity to benefit from it. Foreign investment can support infrastructure, employment and technological development, but its value depends on investment terms, governance and the ability to integrate external resources into the domestic economy. Chinese involvement in projects such as Hambantota Port and Colombo Port City illustrates both the opportunities created by international capital and the strategic considerations accompanying large-scale development. The challenge is to maximise their commercial value while protecting economic stability, national security and independent policymaking. For businesses and investors, policy predictability is equally important. A strategic location may attract initial interest, but sustained investment depends on confidence in regulations, institutions, infrastructure and the wider economic environment. Sri Lanka must therefore link foreign policy to a clear domestic economic strategy, ensuring partnerships contribute to exports, employment, local enterprise and technology transfer. Born in Polonnaruwa, Prof. Mendis represented Sri Lanka as its first Youth Ambassador to the United Nations before pursuing a career in diplomacy, public service, international development and academia. He has worked with the United Nations Secretariat and World Bank and served in the US government under six presidents. A former adviser at the US Department of Defense and military professor for NATO and the US Indo-Pacific Command, he has engaged with the security considerations shaping Washington’s approach to Asia. A Harvard alumnus, he is also Distinguished Visiting Professor of Transatlantic Relations at the University of Warsaw.

title: WordPress vs Wix vs Squarespace: Which Wins for Lead Generation?
author: Garry Pickles
content: If your website is simply an online brochure, almost any website builder can get the job done. However, if your website exists to generate leads, enquiries, phone calls, quote requests and sales, choosing the right platform becomes a much more important decision. Three of the most popular website platforms available today are WordPress, Wix and Squarespace. All three allow businesses to create attractive websites without needing advanced technical knowledge. All three provide templates, hosting and tools designed to help businesses establish an online presence. The real question is not which platform looks best. The real question is which platform gives your business the greatest opportunity to generate leads and grow over the long term. When viewed through that lens, WordPress stands apart from the competition. The Open Source Advantage The biggest difference between WordPress and platforms such as Wix or Squarespace is that WordPress is open source software. While that may sound like a technical detail, it is actually one of the main reasons WordPress has become the dominant website platform in the world. Open source means the software is publicly available for anyone to inspect, improve and develop. Rather than relying on a single company to decide which features are available, WordPress benefits from contributions from thousands of developers around the globe. Every day new plugins, integrations, themes and improvements are being created by specialists working across different areas of web development. This has resulted in a platform that evolves at an incredible pace. Whether the latest trend is artificial intelligence, ecommerce automation, advanced analytics, customer relationship management systems or search engine optimisation, WordPress users often gain access to new technology much faster than businesses using closed website builders. For business owners, this creates a major advantage. Instead of being limited by the roadmap of a single software company, WordPress gives you access to a worldwide ecosystem of developers constantly improving the platform. More developers means more innovation, more flexibility and ultimately more opportunities to generate leads. The Power of Numbers There is a simple reason WordPress continues to dominate the market. It has more users, more developers and more resources than any other content management system. When millions of websites are using the same platform, developers naturally focus their attention there. New software integrations are usually developed for WordPress first. New marketing tools often launch WordPress versions before supporting other platforms. Most web development agencies specialise in WordPress because that is where demand exists. This creates a positive cycle. More users attract more developers. More developers create more tools. More tools attract more businesses. Over time, the gap between WordPress and its competitors continues to grow. For businesses investing in lead generation, this matters. The larger the ecosystem, the easier it becomes to find solutions to almost any challenge you encounter online. SEO Flexibility Matters Lead generation starts with visibility. If potential customers cannot find your website, they cannot become enquiries. This is one of the areas where WordPress consistently excels. Search engine optimisation professionals have relied on WordPress for years because it offers a level of control that many other platforms struggle to match. With WordPress, you can optimise every aspect of your website. From page titles and meta descriptions to schema markup, internal linking structures, XML sitemaps and page speed improvements, the platform provides almost unlimited flexibility. Platforms such as Wix and Squarespace have improved significantly in recent years and offer many SEO features. However, users still operate within the limitations of those systems. If a particular feature does not exist or a custom requirement arises, options can quickly become restricted. WordPress allows businesses to implement highly advanced SEO strategies without being constrained by the platform itself. For companies competing in competitive local markets, that flexibility can make a significant difference. More Integrations Mean More Leads Modern lead generation rarely relies on a website alone. Businesses now use CRM systems, email marketing software, booking systems, live chat tools, review platforms, automation software and analytics tools. WordPress integrates with virtually all of them. Because the platform is open source and widely adopted, software companies actively build WordPress integrations. Whether you use HubSpot, Mailchimp, Google Analytics, WooCommerce, WhatsApp, Stripe or hundreds of other business tools, integration is usually straightforward. This flexibility allows businesses to build complete lead generation systems rather than simply operating a website. Visitors can be tracked, nurtured, followed up and converted more efficiently. When lead generation is the objective, these integrations often become just as important as the website itself. Ownership and Control One often overlooked consideration is ownership. When using Wix or Squarespace, your website exists entirely within their ecosystem. You are effectively renting a platform and operating within the rules set by that provider. With WordPress, you own the website. You control the hosting. You control the files. You control the database. You choose the plugins, developers and service providers. This may not seem important on day one. It becomes very important after several years of investment. Businesses frequently spend thousands of pounds on SEO, content creation, advertising and website improvements. Having complete ownership ensures you remain in control of those assets and are not tied to a particular provider. Scalability for Growing Businesses Many businesses begin with a simple website and gradually expand. Perhaps they add ecommerce functionality. Perhaps they introduce online booking systems. Perhaps they launch a customer portal or membership platform. WordPress handles this growth exceptionally well. A small brochure website can evolve into a sophisticated ecommerce platform, learning management system, business directory or lead generation machine without requiring a complete rebuild. This scalability is one of the reasons WordPress powers everything from small local businesses to major global organisations. Businesses rarely regret having too much flexibility. They often regret not having enough. WooCommerce and Ecommerce Growth For businesses selling products online, WooCommerce adds another significant advantage. WooCommerce is built specifically for WordPress and has become one of the most popular ecommerce systems in the world. It provides complete control over products, categories, customer journeys, checkout processes and search engine optimisation. Unlike many hosted ecommerce solutions, WooCommerce gives businesses the freedom to customise virtually every aspect of the online shopping experience. This becomes particularly valuable when integrating with Google Shopping, product feeds, stock management systems and advanced marketing campaigns. Many businesses choose WordPress specifically because WooCommerce allows them to grow without platform restrictions. Easier to Find Help Another practical benefit of WordPress is the availability of expertise. Because WordPress is so widely used, finding developers, designers, SEO consultants and support specialists is relatively straightforward. If you encounter a problem, there are thousands of professionals capable of helping. The same cannot always be said for more niche platforms. The larger WordPress ecosystem creates greater competition among service providers, which often results in better support and more competitive pricing. For businesses investing in long-term growth, having access to a large talent pool provides significant reassurance. The Verdict Wix and Squarespace are both capable website builders. For personal projects, startup websites and businesses requiring a simple online presence, they can be excellent choices. However, when lead generation, search engine visibility and long-term growth become priorities, WordPress continues to stand above the competition. The reason is surprisingly simple. Open source wins. More developers create more innovation. More innovation creates better tools. Better tools create better websites. Better websites generate more leads. WordPress did not become the world’s most popular website platform by accident. It earned that position through flexibility, scalability, ownership and an unrivalled global ecosystem of developers and businesses. If your objective is to build a website that generates enquiries today while remaining capable of supporting your business five years from now, WordPress remains the platform to beat.
