title: 7 Things You Should Unplug Before Leaving for Vacation
author: GBM Staff
content: You’ve packed your bags, locked the doors and double-checked that you have your passport. But what about all the electronics you’re leaving plugged in? Most people don’t think twice about the television, computer, coffee maker or gaming console sitting at home while they’re away. Many electronics continue drawing small amounts of electricity even when they’re turned off. Others can create unnecessary risks if something goes wrong while nobody is home. Unplugging a few devices before vacation can reduce standby electricity use, protect certain electronics from power surges and give you one less thing to worry about. Here are seven things worth unplugging before your next trip, along with a few devices you should leave connected. 1. Televisions and Entertainment Systems Your television might be off, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s using zero electricity. Many modern smart TVs remain partially active in standby mode so they can respond to remote controls, download updates or support connected features. Streaming devices, soundbars and other entertainment equipment can also consume power while idle. If you’re leaving for several days, consider unplugging your entertainment setup. A surge protector with a switch can make this easier, provided everything connected to it is safe to power down. Just remember that unplugging a smart TV or streaming device means it won’t receive updates or respond to remote commands until you reconnect it. 2. Desktop Computers and Monitors If you have a desktop computer, shutting it down before vacation is generally a good idea. Once you’ve saved your work and properly shut down the computer, you can unplug it and its monitor. This eliminates standby power consumption and disconnects the equipment from potential electrical disturbances traveling through the power connection. However, don’t unplug a computer that’s performing an important backup or running services you need while you’re away. If you rely on remote access to your home computer, you’ll need to leave the necessary equipment powered on. For everyone else, a proper shutdown and unplugging the power cord is a reasonable precaution. 3. Gaming Consoles Modern gaming consoles often have standby or rest modes. These allow the system to download games, install updates and charge accessories without being fully powered on. Convenient? Absolutely. Necessary while you’re sitting on a beach for a week? Probably not. Before leaving, shut down your console completely rather than putting it into rest mode. Once it’s fully powered off, unplug it if you won’t need remote downloads or other connected features. This is especially useful for entertainment centers with multiple consoles and accessories connected. 4. Coffee Makers and Small Kitchen Appliances Coffee makers, electric kettles, toasters and similar appliances are worth checking before leaving home. Some have clocks, displays or standby electronics that continue using a small amount of power. Others contain heating elements, making it sensible to disconnect them when they aren’t needed. Unplug countertop appliances you won’t be using during your trip. Pay particular attention to appliances with heating functions. And don’t forget equipment that might be tucked behind other items on the counter. A quick kitchen walkthrough before leaving can catch things you might otherwise overlook. 5. Chargers You’re Not Using Phone chargers, laptop power adapters and other charging equipment can draw small amounts of electricity while plugged into an outlet, even when they aren’t charging anything. The amount varies by charger, and modern efficient chargers generally have very low no-load power consumption. So unplugging one charger isn’t going to produce some miraculous electricity-bill reduction. But if you have several chargers connected around the house, disconnecting unused ones is an easy habit. It also removes unnecessary equipment from powered outlets while you’re away. Check bedrooms, offices and kitchen counters for chargers that can be safely unplugged. 6. Printers and Office Equipment Printers, scanners, shredders and other home-office devices are easy to forget. Some printers remain in standby mode so they can receive wireless print jobs or perform maintenance. If you’re leaving for an extended period, you may want to shut down and unplug equipment you won’t need. However, inkjet printers deserve special consideration. Some models perform maintenance routines that help prevent printheads from drying out. Manufacturers may recommend leaving them connected or following a specific shutdown procedure. Check your printer’s instructions before disconnecting it for a long trip. For equipment that doesn’t require standby power or maintenance, unplugging is usually straightforward. 7. Space Heaters and Portable Heating Devices This is one category where unplugging is particularly important. Portable space heaters and other high-wattage heating appliances should not be left connected unnecessarily when you’re away. Even if a heater is switched off, disconnecting it provides an additional safeguard against accidental activation or equipment problems. The same general precaution applies to portable heating appliances such as electric blankets and heating pads. Turn them off and unplug them before leaving. Never connect a portable space heater to an ordinary power strip or extension cord. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions and use an appropriate wall outlet. What Should You Leave Plugged In? Not everything should be disconnected before vacation. Some devices are important for food safety, security, connectivity or home maintenance. Refrigerator and Freezer Unless you’re intentionally emptying and shutting down the appliance, leave your refrigerator and freezer connected. Unplugging them can lead to spoiled food and water damage as frozen items thaw. Wi-Fi Router and Modem If you use smart security cameras, connected doorbells, smart locks or remote monitoring systems, your internet equipment may need to remain powered on. Unplugging your router could disable those services. Security Cameras and Alarm Systems Leave essential security equipment operating according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Some systems have battery backups, but those batteries aren’t intended to replace normal power indefinitely. Smart Thermostats Your thermostat may need power to maintain appropriate temperatures while you’re away. This can be particularly important during extreme heat or cold. Use your thermostat’s vacation or away settings rather than disconnecting it. Sump Pumps and Other Essential Equipment If your home has a sump pump, water-leak detection system or other equipment that protects against property damage, make sure it remains powered. Unplugging essential equipment can create a much bigger problem than a few dollars of standby electricity use. Should You Turn Off Power Strips Before Vacation? For nonessential electronics, switching off a power strip can be a convenient way to disconnect several devices at once. However, turning off a power strip isn’t necessarily equivalent to physically unplugging it. If your goal is to isolate equipment from the electrical supply during a prolonged absence, unplugging the strip provides a more complete disconnection. Also, don’t assume every appliance belongs on a power strip. High-wattage appliances such as space heaters should be plugged directly into appropriate wall outlets. Does Unplugging Electronics Really Save Money? Yes, but the savings depend on the devices involved. Electronics that continue using electricity while switched off contribute to what’s commonly called standby power consumption. Some devices use very little power. Others, particularly older electronics or equipment designed to remain connected, may use more. Unplugging unused equipment eliminates its standby electricity use. However, the savings from a single vacation may be modest. The bigger benefit is developing habits that reduce unnecessary electricity consumption throughout the year. Will Unplugging Electronics Protect Them From Lightning? Physically disconnecting electronics from power outlets can help isolate them from surges traveling through electrical wiring. But unplugging a power cord doesn’t necessarily disconnect every possible path for a surge. Devices may also have connections through coaxial cables, telephone lines or other wiring. And no simple precaution guarantees protection against every lightning-related event. If you live in an area with frequent electrical storms, consider discussing whole-home surge protection with a qualified electrician. A Quick Electronics Checklist Before Leaving Before heading out, walk through your home and check the following: Turn off and unplug nonessential entertainment equipment. Properly shut down computers you won’t need. Power down gaming consoles. Unplug unused kitchen appliances. Disconnect unnecessary chargers. Check home-office equipment. Unplug portable heaters and heating devices. Confirm refrigerators and freezers remain powered. Make sure security systems and internet equipment stay connected if needed. Verify that essential home equipment is operating normally. This takes only a few minutes and can prevent unnecessary surprises when you return. FAQ Should I Unplug My TV Before Going on Vacation? You can unplug your television if you won’t need its connected features while away. This eliminates standby power consumption and disconnects it from the power outlet. Is It Safe to Leave Chargers Plugged In While Away? Modern chargers from reputable manufacturers are generally designed for continuous connection. However, unplugging unused chargers is a reasonable precaution, especially if they are damaged, unusually hot or of questionable quality. Should I Unplug My Wi-Fi Router Before Vacation? Not if you rely on internet-connected security cameras, smart locks or other devices that require connectivity. Leave your router powered if those services need to remain available. Does Unplugging Appliances Save Electricity? Yes. Devices that consume standby power stop drawing that electricity when disconnected. The amount saved depends on the equipment and how long it remains unplugged. Should I Unplug My Refrigerator Before Vacation? Usually not. Leave it running if it contains food. Only shut it down if you’ve intentionally emptied it and followed the manufacturer’s instructions for extended storage. The Bottom Line You don’t need to unplug every electronic device in your house before going on vacation. But disconnecting unnecessary equipment is a simple way to reduce standby electricity use and avoid leaving certain appliances powered while nobody is home. Focus on entertainment equipment, unused chargers, computers and portable heating appliances. Leave essential systems such as refrigerators, security equipment and necessary networking devices connected. A few minutes of preparation can help you enjoy your trip without wondering what you left running at home.   This article may contain affiliate links. title: Why Your Bluetooth Keeps Disconnecting and How to Fix It
author: GBM Staff
content: You’re listening to music, talking through your car’s speakers or using wireless earbuds when suddenly the sound cuts out. Your Bluetooth connection disappears, reconnects and sometimes drops again a few minutes later. If your Bluetooth keeps disconnecting, the good news is that you probably don’t need to replace your phone, headphones or car stereo. Bluetooth connection problems can happen for several reasons, including wireless interference, outdated software, low batteries and problems with previously paired devices. Here are 10 things worth trying before spending money on new equipment. 1. Turn Bluetooth Off and Back On Start with the simplest fix. Sometimes your phone and Bluetooth accessory just need to establish a fresh connection. On an iPhone: Open Settings. Tap Bluetooth. Turn Bluetooth off. Wait about 10 seconds. Turn Bluetooth back on. On Android: Open Settings. Find Connected devices, Connections or Bluetooth. Turn Bluetooth off. Wait a few seconds. Turn it back on. The exact menu names vary between Android manufacturers. Reconnect your headphones, speaker or car and see whether the connection stays stable. On an iPhone, use Settings rather than the Control Center Bluetooth button if you want to fully turn Bluetooth off. 2. Restart Your Phone It’s not exciting advice, but restarting your phone can clear temporary software problems affecting wireless connections. Turn your phone completely off, wait a few seconds and restart it. Once it’s running again, reconnect your Bluetooth device. If your headphones or speaker have their own power button, restart those too. Sometimes both devices need a fresh start. 3. Check the Battery on Your Bluetooth Device Wireless headphones, earbuds and speakers can behave unpredictably when their batteries are running low. Depending on the accessory, a low battery may cause interruptions, unexpected shutdowns or connection problems. Charge your Bluetooth accessory fully and test it again. If you’re using wireless earbuds, make sure both earbuds are charging properly inside their case. One earbud failing to charge can create problems that initially look like a Bluetooth connection issue. 4. Move Closer to Your Bluetooth Device Bluetooth has a limited wireless range. Walls, furniture, your body and other obstacles can weaken the connection between your phone and accessory. If your Bluetooth keeps disconnecting when you walk into another room, distance may be the problem. Try using your headphones or speaker while standing near your phone. If the connection becomes stable, gradually move farther away. This can help you determine whether you’re dealing with a range problem rather than a software issue. 5. Watch for Wireless Interference Bluetooth shares the crowded 2.4 GHz wireless spectrum with many other devices. Wi-Fi equipment, other Bluetooth accessories and some household electronics can interfere with Bluetooth signals. You might notice problems when you’re near a busy wireless environment or when several devices are operating close together. Try moving away from nearby electronics and testing your Bluetooth connection somewhere else. If the problem happens only in one particular location, interference becomes a more likely explanation. 6. Forget the Device and Pair It Again This is one of the most useful fixes when a Bluetooth accessory repeatedly disconnects. Instead of reconnecting to the existing saved pairing, remove the device and establish a new connection. On an iPhone: Open Settings > Bluetooth. Find the accessory. Tap the information button next to its name. Select Forget This Device. Put the accessory into pairing mode. Pair it with your iPhone again. On Android: Open Settings > Connected devices or Bluetooth. Find the accessory. Open its settings. Choose Forget or Unpair. Put the accessory into pairing mode. Connect it again. If you’re using a car stereo, you may also need to remove your phone from the vehicle’s saved-device list. 7. Check Whether Another Device Is Taking Over Some Bluetooth accessories can connect to multiple devices or automatically switch between them. This is convenient until your headphones decide your laptop is more interesting than your phone. If your earbuds keep disconnecting while you’re working near a computer or tablet, another paired device may be taking over the connection. Temporarily disable Bluetooth on nearby devices and test your headphones again. If the problem disappears, review the accessory’s multipoint or automatic-switching settings. Not every Bluetooth accessory supports these features, but they’re worth checking if yours does. 8. Update Your Phone and Bluetooth Accessory Software updates can fix bugs affecting Bluetooth stability. On an iPhone, check: Settings > General > Software Update On Android, look for Software update or System update in Settings. Also check whether your Bluetooth accessory has a companion app. Some headphones, speakers and car systems receive firmware updates that improve compatibility and connection reliability. Install available updates from the manufacturer, then test the connection again. 9. Reset Your Bluetooth Accessory If your headphones or speaker still won’t maintain a connection, the accessory itself may need to be reset. Many wireless earbuds and speakers have a reset procedure that clears saved connections and restores their pairing settings. The exact steps depend on the manufacturer and model. Check the manufacturer’s instructions before proceeding. After resetting the accessory, pair it with your phone again and see whether the problem continues. Be aware that resetting the accessory may erase its saved pairings and custom settings. 10. Reset Your Phone’s Network Settings If Bluetooth problems affect several different accessories, the issue may be with your phone rather than any individual device. A network settings reset can sometimes resolve persistent wireless connection problems. On an iPhone, go to: Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Reset > Reset Network Settings This resets network-related settings, including saved Wi-Fi networks and passwords, cellular settings, and certain VPN and Bluetooth configurations. On Android, search Settings for Reset options or Reset Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. The available options vary by manufacturer. Only try this after the simpler fixes because you’ll likely need to reconnect to Wi-Fi networks and pair Bluetooth accessories again. Why Does Bluetooth Keep Disconnecting in Your Car? Car Bluetooth problems can be especially frustrating because they often happen during calls or while listening to directions. If Bluetooth disconnects only in your vehicle, start by removing the pairing from both your phone and the car’s infotainment system. Then pair them again. Also check whether your vehicle has a software update available. Some car manufacturers provide infotainment updates that address connectivity problems. If you’re using wireless Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, remember that those systems may also rely on Wi-Fi. A wireless CarPlay or Android Auto disconnection isn’t necessarily caused by Bluetooth alone. Try connecting another phone to the vehicle. If multiple phones experience the same problem, the vehicle’s system becomes a more likely suspect. Why Do Bluetooth Headphones Keep Cutting Out? Wireless headphones can experience brief audio interruptions even when they don’t fully disconnect. This can happen because of interference, distance, connection switching or problems with the headphones themselves. Try keeping your phone close to the headphones and testing them somewhere with fewer nearby wireless devices. If your headphones support connecting to two devices simultaneously, temporarily disable that feature. You can also test the headphones with another phone. If the same interruptions happen on multiple phones, the headphones may be the problem. How to Tell Whether Your Phone or Bluetooth Device Is the Problem The easiest way to narrow down the issue is to test different combinations. Connect your phone to another Bluetooth accessory. Then connect the original accessory to a different phone, if possible. If your phone disconnects from every Bluetooth device, investigate your phone’s software and network settings. If one particular accessory disconnects from multiple phones, focus on that accessory. If the problem happens only when a particular phone and accessory are paired together, you may be dealing with a compatibility or pairing issue. This simple test can save you from replacing perfectly functional hardware. When Is It Time to Replace Your Bluetooth Device? Not every Bluetooth problem can be fixed with settings. If your headphones or speaker continue disconnecting after a reset, firmware update and testing with multiple phones, there may be a hardware problem. Before replacing anything, check whether the device is still covered by its manufacturer’s warranty. And if your phone is having several different problems, not just Bluetooth, our guide to Don’t Buy a New Phone Right Now Without Checking These 7 Things can help you decide whether an upgrade is actually worthwhile. FAQ Why Does My Bluetooth Keep Disconnecting Randomly? Common causes include wireless interference, weak signals, low accessory batteries, outdated software and problems with saved pairings. Testing your device in another location and pairing it again can help identify the cause. Why Does My Bluetooth Disconnect Even When My Phone Is Nearby? Distance isn’t the only cause of Bluetooth problems. Interference, software bugs, multipoint switching and accessory hardware issues can also interrupt a connection. Does Resetting Bluetooth Delete Anything? Forgetting a Bluetooth device removes its saved pairing. Resetting network settings can affect saved Wi-Fi networks, passwords and other network configurations, depending on your phone. Why Does Bluetooth Keep Disconnecting in My Car? Possible causes include outdated infotainment software, pairing problems, competing connections and compatibility issues between the phone and vehicle. Can Wi-Fi Interfere With Bluetooth? Yes. Bluetooth and some Wi-Fi networks use the 2.4 GHz frequency band. Although they’re designed to coexist, crowded wireless environments can sometimes contribute to interference. title: Your Phone Can Identify Almost Anything in a Photo. Here’s How
author: GBM Staff
content: You probably have photos on your phone of plants you couldn’t identify, products you wanted to find later, signs in another language or random objects you couldn’t quite name. You don’t necessarily need to download another app to figure out what you’re looking at. Both iPhones and Android phones have powerful visual-search tools that can identify objects, recognize text, find products, translate signs and tell you more about what’s inside a photo. And there’s a decent chance you’ve barely used them. Here’s how to identify things with your phone and some of the surprisingly useful things these tools can do. Identify Plants and Flowers See a plant you like while walking around the neighborhood? Take a picture. On an iPhone, Apple’s Visual Look Up can recognize plants and flowers in supported photos. Open the picture in Photos and look at the Info button. If Visual Look Up recognizes something, the Info button will display a symbol indicating additional information is available. Apple Support Tap it, then choose the available Look Up option. On Android, open a photo in Google Photos and use Google Lens. You can also open Lens from the Google app and point your camera directly at the plant. Google specifically lists plants and animals among the things Lens can identify. Google Help Just don’t make medical or safety decisions based solely on an automated plant identification. Your phone being confidently wrong about a houseplant is amusing. Being confidently wrong about a mushroom you’re planning to eat is rather less charming. Figure Out What Kind of Dog You Just Saw The same technology works with animals. Apple’s Visual Look Up can recognize pets and provide information about them, while Google Lens can identify animal species and breeds. Apple Support That makes it useful when you see a dog and spend the next ten minutes wondering whether it was a Labradoodle, Goldendoodle or one of the approximately 6,000 other things humanity has apparently decided to combine with a poodle. Take a photo, open it and let your phone take a shot at identifying it. Find a Product You Saw Somewhere This may be one of the most useful tricks. Imagine you’re at a friend’s house and like a lamp, chair, pair of shoes or kitchen gadget. Instead of asking them where they bought it three years ago and receiving the inevitable “I have no idea,” take a picture. Google Lens can search the object and show visually similar products. Google specifically supports product searches for categories including apparel and home goods. Google Help You can also use Lens on an existing image. On Android: Open Google Photos > Choose the photo > Google Lens You can select only the part of the picture you want to search. This also works with screenshots, which is handy when you see something online but don’t know what it’s called. Translate a Menu or Sign Your camera can also function as a translator. Google Lens and Google Translate can recognize text inside an image and translate it. Google says its camera translation works with both live camera views and previously captured images. Google Help That means you can point your phone at things like: Restaurant menus Street signs Product labels Instructions Posters Notices Instead of manually typing everything into a translation app, your phone can work directly from the image. This is especially useful while traveling. Translation won’t always be perfect, particularly with tiny, stylized or unclear text, so use some common sense when the meaning actually matters. Copy Text From Something in the Real World Sometimes you don’t want to know what an object is. You just want the words printed on it. Phones can recognize text inside images, which means you can turn something in the physical world into selectable digital text. Take a picture of a: Business card Receipt Serial number Printed address Flyer Recipe Wi-Fi password Document Then select the text instead of typing it manually. Google Lens lets Android users select and copy recognized text from photos. Google Help iPhone users can use Apple’s Live Text features to interact with text appearing in photos and images. This is one of those tiny phone features that sounds boring until it saves you from manually entering a 22-character serial number. Then suddenly it deserves a parade. Learn About a Landmark Standing in front of a building, monument or statue and have absolutely no idea what you’re looking at? Take a photo. Apple says Visual Look Up can recognize architectural landmarks, popular statues and famous art. Apple Support Google Lens can also identify landmarks and buildings and provide related information. Google Help It’s essentially a visual version of searching Google when you don’t know what words to type into Google. That makes it especially useful while traveling. Identify Artwork The same trick can work in museums, galleries or even when you see artwork online. Apple’s Visual Look Up can identify famous art, while Google says Lens can provide information about paintings, including information about the artist. Apple Support Take a picture or use an existing photo and see what your phone recognizes. Results will obviously depend on the artwork, image quality and whether the service recognizes it. Scan a Barcode Google Lens can recognize barcodes and use them to find information about products, including places where the product may be available. Google Help That’s useful when you have packaging in front of you but don’t know exactly what to search for. Point Lens at the barcode and let it do the tedious part. Find a Book From Its Cover Here’s another useful one for bookstores, libraries and that stack of books sitting at somebody else’s house. Google says Lens can recognize books and provide information such as summaries and reviews. Google Help Instead of typing the entire title into your phone, scan the cover. It can also be useful when the title isn’t clearly visible but you have a picture of the book. Get Information About Food Apple’s Visual Look Up can recognize food in photos and may suggest related recipes. Apple Support Open a food photo in the Photos app and check whether the Info button shows that Visual Look Up information is available. It won’t magically reproduce the secret recipe from the restaurant where you took the picture, unfortunately. Civilization hasn’t advanced quite that far. But it can help identify what you’re looking at and find related information. Search Anything on Your Android Screen Some Android phones have another particularly useful feature called Circle to Search. On supported devices, you can press and hold the Home button or navigation handle and then circle, highlight or tap something on your screen to search for it without leaving the app you’re using. Google Help So if someone sends you a photo of a pair of shoes, you can circle the shoes. See a lamp in a video? Circle it. See an unfamiliar landmark in a social-media post? Search it directly from the screen. Availability varies by Android device, so you may not see Circle to Search on every phone. Newer iPhones Can Use Visual Intelligence Apple has also expanded visual search beyond photos already sitting in your library. On supported Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhones, Visual Intelligence can use the camera to learn about what’s around you. Apple says it can identify plants and animals, translate or summarize text, search for visually similar images and provide information about businesses and other things you’re looking at. Apple Support Visual Intelligence requires a supported Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, so it isn’t available on every model. If your iPhone doesn’t support it, don’t assume you’re completely left out. The older Visual Look Up feature still provides many useful identification tools from compatible photos. How to Try Visual Look Up on an iPhone Open the Photos app and choose a picture. Tap the Info button or swipe up on the photo. If your iPhone recognizes something that supports Visual Look Up, you’ll see an indicator associated with the detected object. Tap Look Up to see the available information. Apple Support If nothing appears, your iPhone may simply not recognize anything in that particular image. Try a clear picture where the subject occupies a significant part of the frame. How to Try Google Lens on Android One easy method is through Google Photos. Open: Google Photos > Select a photo > Google Lens Lens will analyze the image and provide available results and actions. Google Help You can also open the Google app, tap the Lens icon and either take a new picture or choose an existing image from your phone. Google Help If Lens is focusing on the wrong thing, select a smaller portion of the picture. Your Camera Is Becoming a Search Box We’re accustomed to searching the internet by typing words into a box. Visual search removes one rather important requirement: knowing what the thing is called. You can photograph an unknown plant, scan a product, copy text from a document, identify a landmark or translate a sign without first figuring out what search terms to use. It’s not perfect, and you shouldn’t blindly trust every identification it makes. But the next time you catch yourself staring at something and thinking, “What is that?” Take a picture. Your phone might already know. And while you’re exploring features you may have overlooked, 7 iPhone Settings You’ll Wish You Changed Sooner and 7 Android Settings You’ll Be Glad You Changed have several more worth checking. FAQ Can My iPhone Identify Objects in Photos? Yes. Apple’s Visual Look Up can identify supported objects and subjects including plants, pets, landmarks, statues, artwork, books and food. Availability can vary by region and language. Apple Support Can Android Identify Something From a Picture? Yes. Google Lens can analyze existing images or use your phone’s camera to search for objects, plants, animals, products, text and other visual information. Google Help Can My Phone Identify a Plant From a Photo? Both Apple’s Visual Look Up and Google Lens can identify plants from images. Treat the result as a starting point rather than relying on it for health or safety decisions. Apple Support Can I Find a Product by Taking a Picture? Google Lens can find visually similar products from photos, including apparel and home goods. Google Help Can My Phone Translate a Sign From a Picture? Yes. Google offers camera-based image translation, and supported newer iPhones can use Visual Intelligence for text translation. Google Help Your Phone Can Identify Almost Anything in a Photo. title: 7 Things You Should Never Store in Your Phone’s Notes App
author: GBM Staff
content: Your phone’s Notes app is incredibly convenient. Grocery lists, addresses, gift ideas, confirmation numbers and random thoughts you’ll never look at again all make perfect sense there. But convenience can become a problem when Notes turns into the place where you store passwords, PINs and photos of sensitive documents. If you’re wondering what not to store in the Notes app, start with these seven things. 1. Your Passwords If you have a note called “Passwords,” we need to talk. A regular note is not a substitute for a password manager. Password managers are specifically designed to securely store login credentials and make it easier to use different, strong passwords for different accounts. On an iPhone, Apple provides the Passwords app for passwords, passkeys and verification codes. Android users can use Google Password Manager or another reputable password manager. This also solves another problem: you don’t have to open a giant note and hunt through 47 logins every time Netflix decides you’ve forgotten who you are. 2. Your Social Security Number Your Social Security number doesn’t need to live in an ordinary note titled “Important Stuff.” The same goes for Social Security numbers belonging to your children or other family members. Identity information can be extremely valuable if someone gains access to your device or account. If you occasionally need the number, store the original document securely rather than keeping an easily accessible copy in your everyday notes. 3. Credit Card and Bank Account Information Don’t use Notes as your homemade banking vault. Avoid keeping complete: Credit card numbers Debit card numbers Bank account numbers Routing information Card security codes Online banking credentials If someone gets access to that information, you’ve potentially handed them several pieces of the same financial puzzle. Banking and payment apps already provide secure ways to access much of the information you legitimately need. Use them. 4. PINs and Security Codes Your debit-card PIN should not be sitting next to your debit-card information. Neither should the passcode for your home alarm, safe, garage or other security system. The particularly impressive version of this mistake is creating a note containing the name of the account, username, password and PIN. At that point you’ve essentially assembled the burglar’s welcome packet yourself. Keep authentication information separated and use tools designed to protect sensitive credentials. 5. Account Recovery Codes Many services give you backup or recovery codes when you enable two-factor authentication. These codes are important. If you lose access to your normal authentication method, a recovery code may allow you to regain access to the account. That also means someone else may be able to use one. Don’t casually paste recovery codes into an ordinary note alongside information identifying exactly which account they unlock. Store them using the secure options recommended by the service, a reputable password manager or another appropriately protected location. 6. Photos of Sensitive Documents Taking a quick picture of a document can be useful. Leaving copies of every important document sitting around indefinitely is another matter. Think twice before keeping easily accessible images of: Driver’s licenses Passports Social Security cards Tax documents Insurance cards Birth certificates Financial statements If you genuinely need digital copies, think about where they’re stored, how that location is protected and whether you still need the copies once they’ve served their purpose. Also check your Photos app. Taking a picture for a note may leave another copy somewhere you completely forgot about. 7. A Master List of Everything Important Sometimes the biggest security problem isn’t one piece of information. It’s putting everything together. Imagine someone opens a single note and finds: Your email address. Your banking username. Your alarm code. Your kids’ Social Security numbers. Your Wi-Fi password. Your passport number. Your account recovery information. Each item may have a legitimate reason to exist somewhere. Putting them all into one convenient, searchable document creates a much bigger problem if someone gets access to it. Convenience works both ways. But Aren’t Notes on My Phone Protected? This is where things get more nuanced. On an iPhone, Apple lets you lock individual notes using your device passcode or a custom password, and Face ID or Touch ID can also be used with supported configurations. Apple says secured notes are end-to-end encrypted. You can find the relevant Notes options under: Settings > Apps > Notes > Password Apple also lets you control whether Notes can be accessed from the Lock Screen. That’s considerably better than leaving sensitive information sitting in an unlocked note. Google Keep works differently. Google says Keep content is encrypted in transit and at rest and is private unless you choose to share it, but Google Keep currently doesn’t provide a feature for locking an individual note with its own passcode. So don’t assume every notes app protects individual notes in the same way. Be Careful With Shared Notes Too Notes can also be collaborative. That’s wonderful for grocery lists. Less wonderful when somebody accidentally puts sensitive information into one. Apple allows users to collaborate on iCloud notes, although locked notes can’t be shared for collaboration. Google Keep also lets users add collaborators who can access and edit shared notes. Before putting private information into an existing note, check whether that note is shared with anyone else. Where Should You Keep Sensitive Information Instead? It depends on what you’re storing. Passwords, passkeys and authentication credentials belong in a reputable password manager. Original identity documents should be stored securely in the physical world, with carefully protected digital copies only when you actually need them. Financial information should generally stay within the appropriate banking, payment or financial service rather than being copied into random notes. And if you do have a legitimate reason to store sensitive information in Apple Notes, use its locking feature rather than leaving the note openly accessible. The goal isn’t to treat your phone like it’s radioactive. It’s simply to stop using one giant note as a filing cabinet for your entire identity. Give Your Phone a Quick Privacy Check Once you’ve cleaned up your notes, there are a few other settings worth reviewing. iPhone users should go through 7 iPhone Settings You’ll Wish You Changed Sooner to check privacy, tracking, location and security options. Android users can do the same with 7 Android Settings You’ll Be Glad You Changed . And if you’re already thinking about security, 7 Phone Emergency Settings You Should Set Up Before You Need Them covers the safety information that actually does make sense to configure on your phone. FAQ Is It Safe to Store Passwords in Apple Notes? Apple allows individual notes to be locked, which provides additional protection, but a dedicated password manager is the better tool for managing passwords, passkeys and verification codes. Apple’s own Passwords app is designed specifically for those credentials. Can I Lock an Individual Note on an iPhone? Yes. Apple Notes supports locking individual notes with your device passcode or a custom password. Can I Lock an Individual Google Keep Note? Google Keep currently doesn’t provide an individual note-locking feature. Google does state that Keep content is encrypted in transit and at rest. Should I Keep My Social Security Number in My Phone? Avoid keeping highly sensitive identity information unnecessarily in easily accessible apps. If you need a digital record, consider why you need it and choose an appropriately secured storage method. What Should I Use Instead of Notes for Passwords? Use a reputable password manager. iPhone users also have Apple’s built-in Passwords app, which stores passwords, passkeys and verification codes. title: 7 Phone Emergency Settings You Should Set Up Before You Need Them
author: GBM Staff
content: Your phone can do considerably more in an emergency than simply call 911. Modern iPhones and Android phones include emergency contacts, medical information, SOS features and other safety tools that can be useful when you can’t easily unlock or operate your phone. The problem is that some of these features need to be configured before an emergency happens. Take a few minutes today to check these seven phone emergency settings. 1. Add Your Emergency Contacts Start with the people you’d want contacted if something happened to you. On an iPhone, you can add emergency contacts through your Medical ID in the Health app. On Android, the exact location varies by manufacturer, but look for options such as: Settings > Safety & emergency or search Settings for “Emergency contacts.” Choose people who are likely to answer and who know important information about you. Your emergency contact list probably doesn’t need 14 people. This isn’t the group chat. 2. Set Up Your Medical Information Both iPhone and many Android phones allow you to store emergency medical information that may be accessible without fully unlocking the device. Depending on your phone, this can include: Your name Emergency contacts Allergies Medications Blood type Medical conditions Other important notes Only include information you’re comfortable making accessible from the emergency screen. On an iPhone, open the Health app and find Medical ID. On Android, search Settings for “Medical information,” “Emergency information” or “Safety & emergency.” 3. Learn How Emergency SOS Works Don’t wait for an actual emergency to figure out which buttons activate Emergency SOS. On an iPhone, open: Settings > Emergency SOS Review the available activation options on your particular model. Android phones also offer Emergency SOS features, although the settings and behavior can vary between manufacturers and Android versions. Search Settings for: Emergency SOS Then review exactly what happens when it’s activated. Your phone may be able to call emergency services, contact selected people or perform additional safety actions depending on your settings and device. 4. Check Emergency Location Features Location can be extremely important during an emergency. iPhones and Android phones have features designed to help provide location information during emergency calls or SOS events, although availability and behavior vary by device, carrier and region. Review the emergency location options on your phone and make sure you’re comfortable with how they’re configured. This is also a good time to review which everyday apps have access to your location. iPhone users can find additional privacy controls in 7 iPhone Settings You’ll Wish You Changed Sooner . Android users should check 7 Android Settings You’ll Be Glad You Changed for similar settings. 5. Set Up Crash Detection If Your Phone Supports It Some newer smartphones can detect what appears to be a severe car crash and attempt to connect you with emergency services. On supported iPhones, Crash Detection can automatically attempt an emergency call after detecting a severe crash if you don’t respond. Some Android devices also offer crash-detection features. Availability depends heavily on your particular phone, location and software, so don’t assume every device supports it. Search your phone’s Settings for: Crash Detection If it’s available, review how it works and make sure the emergency information associated with your device is current. 6. Check Satellite Emergency Features Satellite connectivity is becoming an increasingly important safety feature on newer smartphones. Supported phones may be able to communicate with emergency services or contacts in certain situations when cellular and Wi-Fi service aren’t available. This can be particularly useful while hiking, camping, traveling through remote areas or driving somewhere without reliable cellular coverage. But satellite emergency features aren’t identical across every phone. Check what your specific device supports, where the service is available and how you’re supposed to use it. If your phone offers a demonstration or practice mode, that’s considerably better than learning how satellite communication works while you’re stranded somewhere with one bar of granola and several questionable life decisions. 7. Make Sure Your Family Knows About These Features Setting everything up is useful. Making sure the people closest to you know about it is even better. Show your spouse, partner, children or other family members where emergency information can be found on your phone without unlocking it. Also make sure they understand how Emergency SOS works on their own phones. If you have children with smartphones, go through their emergency contacts and medical information with them. And don’t just configure everything once and forget about it. Review emergency information when you change phone numbers, medications, addresses or emergency contacts. Don’t Forget Your Lock Screen Emergency information is most useful when someone can actually find it. After configuring everything, lock your phone and see what another person would encounter. Can you reach the Emergency screen? Can you find your Medical ID or emergency information? Are your contacts correct? Checking from the lock screen gives you a much better idea of what someone could actually access if you were unable to explain it yourself. Your Phone Can Help, But It Needs Some Preparation Smartphones have accumulated an enormous number of features over the years. Most of them can wait. Emergency settings are different. Adding emergency contacts, entering important medical information and learning how SOS works takes only a few minutes, and you hopefully won’t need any of it. That’s precisely when you want to set it up. FAQ Can Someone See My Medical Information Without Unlocking My Phone? If you choose to make emergency medical information available from the lock screen, certain information may be accessible without unlocking the phone. The exact behavior depends on your device and settings. Does Emergency SOS Automatically Call 911? Emergency SOS behavior varies depending on the phone, settings and location. Review the SOS settings on your particular device so you know exactly what will happen when you activate it. Do All Phones Have Crash Detection? No. Crash Detection is limited to supported devices and may also depend on software version and region. Can My Phone Contact Someone If I Don’t Have Cell Service? Some newer smartphones support certain satellite-based emergency or messaging features when cellular and Wi-Fi networks aren’t available. Device, location and service restrictions apply. Should Children Have Emergency Contacts on Their Phones? If a child carries a phone, having appropriate emergency contacts and accessible emergency information can be useful. Parents should configure the information based on the child’s needs and the capabilities of the device. This article may contain affiliate links. title: Before You Install iOS 27, Do These 7 Things
author: GBM Staff
content: iOS 27 is officially available, bringing Apple’s latest features and changes to compatible iPhones. But before you tap Download and Install, there are a few things worth doing first. Major iPhone updates don’t always go badly, but when they do, discovering you don’t have a recent backup while staring at an uncooperative phone is a particularly unpleasant way to spend an afternoon. If you’re planning to install the iOS 27 update, do these seven things first. 1. Make Sure Your iPhone Supports iOS 27 Before worrying about anything else, make sure your iPhone is compatible. Apple lists iOS 27 as available for the iPhone 11 and newer compatible models. You can identify your iPhone by opening: Settings > General > About Look for Model Name. If your iPhone isn’t eligible for iOS 27, don’t ignore the Software Update screen. Apple also released iOS 26.7 with security updates for supported devices remaining on iOS 26. 2. Back Up Your iPhone This is the one step I’d consider mandatory before installing a major iOS update. Go to: Settings > [Your Name] > iCloud > iCloud Backup Check the date of your latest successful backup. If it isn’t recent, tap Back Up Now and let the backup finish before starting the update. You can also back up an iPhone using a Mac or PC. Hopefully you’ll never need the backup. That’s rather the point. 3. Check How Much Free Storage You Have Major iOS updates require free storage for the download and installation process. Go to: Settings > General > iPhone Storage Your iPhone will show how much space is currently available and which apps are consuming the most storage. If you’re running low, start with obvious space hogs such as downloaded movies, old podcasts, large videos and apps you no longer use. Don’t start deleting important photos at random just because your phone wants more breathing room. 4. Update Your Apps Open the App Store and make sure your important apps are current. Developers frequently release updates around major iOS launches to improve compatibility with the new operating system. Pay particular attention to apps you rely on every day, including banking, authentication, work, smart-home and password-management apps. If an essential app hasn’t been updated in ages, checking its compatibility before installing iOS 27 isn’t a terrible idea. 5. Know Your Apple Account Password Face ID has made it impressively easy to forget passwords we supposedly know. Before installing a major update, make sure you know your Apple Account credentials and can access any trusted phone numbers or devices associated with your account. You don’t want to discover an account-access problem in the middle of setting your phone back up. This is also a good time to make sure your important passwords are securely stored somewhere you can access if the phone isn’t cooperating. 6. Plug In and Use a Reliable Wi-Fi Connection Don’t start a major iOS update when your battery is nearly dead or when you’re about to leave the house. Plug your iPhone into power and connect it to a reliable network. Give yourself some time when you don’t urgently need the phone. The download, preparation, installation and post-update processes can take a while, particularly when millions of other people have just been handed the same shiny Update button. 7. Decide Whether You Actually Want iOS 27 Today You don’t have to install a major iOS release the moment it appears. Apple released iOS 26.7 alongside iOS 27, giving eligible users another software-update option while still providing security fixes. If your iPhone is critical for work, travel or something important happening in the next few days, waiting a little while before making a major operating-system jump can be reasonable. On the other hand, software updates contain important security improvements. Apple’s security-release information confirms both iOS 27 and iOS 26.7 were released September 14. The important part is not to forget about updates entirely. Don’t Panic If Your Battery Seems Worse After Updating You may notice unusual battery drain, warmth or sluggishness shortly after installing a major update. Your iPhone can perform background tasks following an update, and things may settle after you’ve been using the new software for a while. If your phone continues getting unusually warm, our guide to Why Your iPhone Gets Hot and How to Fix It covers the common causes and what you can do about them. And if charging becomes the problem instead, Phone Won’t Charge? 10 Fixes That Actually Work walks through the things worth checking before assuming the hardware has failed. Check Your Settings After Installing iOS 27 Once the update is complete, spend a few minutes exploring Settings rather than immediately forgetting the Settings app exists for another year. Review privacy permissions, location access, notifications, security features and any new options introduced with the update. Our guide to 7 iPhone Settings You’ll Wish You Changed Sooner is a good place to start. Major software updates are also a good excuse to review settings you may have accepted years ago and never looked at again. Should You Install iOS 27? For most people with a compatible iPhone, iOS 27 will eventually be the natural upgrade path. But there’s nothing wrong with preparing first. Back up your phone, make sure you have enough storage, update important apps and confirm you can access your Apple Account. Ten minutes of preparation is considerably less annoying than troubleshooting an iPhone while wondering whether your photos actually made it to iCloud. FAQ Is iOS 27 Available Now? Yes. Apple released iOS 27 on September 14, 2026. Which iPhones Support iOS 27? Apple’s current security-release information lists iOS 27 for iPhone 11 and later. Do I Need to Back Up Before Installing iOS 27? You should. A backup gives you a recent copy of important information if something goes wrong during or after the update. Do I Have to Install iOS 27 Immediately? No. Apple also released iOS 26.7 on September 14 with security fixes for supported devices remaining on iOS 26. Why Is My iPhone Hot After Installing iOS 27? Some increased activity immediately after a major software update can occur while the device completes background tasks. If excessive heat or battery drain persists, investigate further rather than assuming the update is still responsible. This article may contain affiliate links. title: That Call From Your Family Member Could Be an AI Voice Scam
author: GBM Staff
content: Your phone rings and someone you love is on the other end. They sound scared. There’s been an accident. They’re in trouble. They need money immediately. There’s just one problem. It might not actually be them. AI voice scams are making it easier for criminals to imitate real people and create convincing emergency calls. Modern voice-cloning technology can produce audio that sounds remarkably similar to someone’s actual voice, adding a disturbing new layer to an old scam. The FBI has specifically warned that AI-generated content can be difficult to identify and that criminals are using AI alongside impersonation schemes. Here’s what your family should know before one of these calls happens. What Is an AI Voice Scam? An AI voice scam uses artificial intelligence to imitate someone’s voice. A criminal may pretend to be your child, grandchild, spouse, friend or another person you trust. The story varies, but the objective is usually the same: create panic and convince you to send money or reveal sensitive information before you have time to verify what’s happening. You might hear that your family member: Was arrested Was injured Caused a car accident Lost their phone Is stranded somewhere Needs bail money Needs money for an emergency Can’t talk for very long That last part is convenient for the scammer. The less conversation you have, the less opportunity there is to notice something isn’t right. AI Makes “That Doesn’t Sound Like Them” Less Useful For years, recognizing someone’s voice was a reasonable way to decide whether a phone call was legitimate. That’s becoming less reliable. AI-generated audio has advanced enough that the FBI warns cloned voices can sound nearly identical to a real person’s voice. That means hearing a familiar voice shouldn’t be your only form of verification. Caller ID isn’t enough either. Phone numbers and caller ID information can be spoofed, making a call appear to come from someone or somewhere you recognize. The FTC warns consumers not to rely on caller ID alone to determine whether a call is legitimate. So now we have reached the charming stage of technological progress where both the voice and the phone number can lie to you. Fortunately, there’s an extremely low-tech defense. Create a Family Safe Word Pick a word or short phrase that only close family members know. It shouldn’t be something easily associated with your family or something you’ve posted publicly. If someone calls claiming to be a family member in an emergency, ask for the safe word. Don’t mention the answer. Ask: “What is our family safe word?” Someone genuinely close to you should know it. A scammer relying on information gathered online probably won’t. You can also create a family verification question, but avoid questions whose answers could easily be found through social media. Your dog’s name, high school mascot and mother’s maiden name aren’t particularly secret if you’ve spent the last decade posting your life online. Hang Up and Call Them Yourself This is one of the simplest ways to defeat an emergency impersonation scam. If someone calls claiming to be your daughter, son, spouse or another family member and something feels wrong, hang up. Then call that person using the number already saved in your contacts. Don’t call a number provided by the person who contacted you. If they don’t answer, contact another trusted person who may know where they are. A legitimate emergency can survive an extra minute of verification. A scammer desperately wants to prevent you from taking that minute. Be Suspicious When Someone Creates Extreme Urgency Scammers frequently use fear and urgency because both make people less likely to stop and think. The FBI specifically advises consumers to slow down when a caller creates panic or demands immediate action. Watch for statements such as: “Don’t tell Mom.” “I need the money right now.” “You can’t call anyone.” “The police said I only have an hour.” “My phone is dying.” “I’ll explain everything later.” The details may sound convincing, but urgency itself should be a warning sign. Never Send Money Just Because a Caller Demands It Be particularly suspicious if the supposed emergency suddenly requires payment through: Gift cards Cryptocurrency Wire transfers Cash Payment apps The FTC warns that scammers favor payment methods that make recovering money difficult. If someone claiming to be a government official or law-enforcement officer tells you to move money to “protect” it, that’s another major warning sign. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says legitimate government agencies and financial institutions do not instruct people to send money to protect their funds. Don’t Assume a Video Call Proves Anything Voice isn’t the only thing AI can imitate. The FBI warned in July 2026 that scammers have used AI-generated videos in fraud schemes, including video designed to depict executives, law enforcement officers and other authority figures. A video call therefore shouldn’t automatically override other warning signs. If something seems suspicious, verify the person independently. Talk About This With Parents and Grandparents Older adults are frequent targets of emergency and impersonation scams, but these schemes can fool people of any age. The best time to explain AI voice cloning to your family isn’t while someone is panicking on the phone. Do it beforehand. Agree that nobody in the family will be offended if someone hangs up during an alleged emergency and calls back independently. Set your family safe word. Explain that voices can be cloned and caller ID can be spoofed. Those few minutes of preparation can make an unexpected call much easier to handle. What Should You Do If You Already Sent Money? Act quickly. Contact the bank, credit card company, payment service or other financial institution involved and explain what happened. Depending on how the payment was made and how quickly you respond, there may be options for stopping or recovering it. You can also report internet-enabled fraud to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center and report scams to the Federal Trade Commission. If you gave the scammer passwords or account information, change the affected passwords immediately and secure those accounts. AI Voice Scams Are Another Reason to Verify First AI isn’t creating an entirely new category of crime here. Impersonation scams have existed forever. What’s changing is how convincing they can become. A familiar voice, a recognizable phone number or even convincing video should no longer be enough to make an important financial decision. When a call involves money, sensitive information or an emergency, verify the person through another method before doing anything. And while you’re tightening up your digital defenses, read Stop Scanning Random QR Codes. Here’s What Can Happen for another increasingly common way scammers try to get people from their phones to fraudulent websites. FAQ Can Scammers Really Copy Someone’s Voice With AI? AI technology can generate convincing imitations of real voices. The FBI has warned that AI-generated voice cloning can be difficult to distinguish from a legitimate voice. How Do I Know If a Family Emergency Call Is Real? Hang up and independently call your family member using a phone number you already know. You can also establish a private family safe word ahead of time. Can Scammers Fake Caller ID? Yes. Caller ID can be spoofed, so a familiar name or phone number appearing on your screen doesn’t guarantee the caller is legitimate. What Is a Family Safe Word? It’s a private word or phrase known by trusted family members that can be used to verify someone’s identity during an unexpected or suspicious situation. What Should I Do If I Sent Money to a Scammer? Contact the financial institution or payment provider immediately. You should also report the incident to appropriate authorities, including the FTC or FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center when applicable. This article may contain affiliate links. title: Don’t Buy a New Phone Right Now Without Checking These 7 Things
author: GBM Staff
content: Thinking about buying a new phone? September can be a tempting time to upgrade, with new devices arriving, older models going on sale and carriers suddenly discovering an astonishing number of “limited-time” offers. But before you spend $800, $1,000 or considerably more on a new smartphone, it’s worth figuring out whether you actually need one and whether now is the right time to buy. If you’re wondering, should I buy a new phone now , check these seven things before placing an order. 1. Find Out When Your Current Phone Stops Getting Updates An older phone isn’t automatically obsolete. One of the biggest things to consider is how long your current device will continue receiving operating system and security updates. Check your manufacturer’s support information for your particular model. If your phone still receives security updates, performs well and does everything you need, there may be little reason to replace it simply because something newer exists. On the other hand, a phone that no longer receives important security updates deserves a closer look. 2. Check Your Battery Health A phone that once lasted all day but now desperately searches for a charger by lunchtime can feel ancient. The rest of the device may be perfectly fine. iPhone owners can check battery information under: Settings > Battery > Battery Health Battery information and diagnostics on Android vary by manufacturer. If battery degradation is your biggest complaint, compare the cost of replacing the battery with the cost of replacing the entire phone. A battery replacement could potentially give an otherwise capable phone considerably more life. 3. Look at Your Storage Before Blaming the Phone Constantly running out of storage can make an older phone miserable to use. Open your storage settings and see what’s actually consuming the space. Photos and videos are obvious culprits, but downloaded movies, podcasts, messages and apps you haven’t opened since 2022 can consume surprising amounts of storage. Clean things up before deciding you need a new device. If you’re still constantly running out of space after that, buying a higher-capacity model with your next upgrade may be worthwhile. 4. Decide Which New Features You’d Actually Use New phones arrive with increasingly impressive lists of features. The question isn’t whether those features are cool. It’s whether you’ll use them. Consider what actually bothers you about your current phone: Is the camera not good enough? Is the battery failing? Do you need more storage? Is performance noticeably slow? Is the screen damaged? Are you missing a feature you’d use regularly? Has software support ended? If you can’t identify what a new phone would meaningfully improve, that’s a pretty strong argument for keeping the one you have. 5. Check What’s About to Launch Timing matters. September is traditionally a busy period for smartphone announcements, and 2026 is no exception. A wave of new devices is expected throughout the month, which can change the buying equation even if you don’t want the newest model. When a new generation arrives, previous-generation phones can become more attractive because of discounts, carrier promotions and refurbished inventory. That means buying immediately before a major launch can sometimes leave you paying yesterday’s price for yesterday’s phone. 6. Don’t Judge a Trade-In Offer by the Big Number Carrier and manufacturer advertisements can offer surprisingly large trade-in credits. Read the conditions. The maximum advertised value may require: A specific unlimited plan A qualifying trade-in A new line Monthly bill credits Staying with the carrier for several years A “$1,000 trade-in” isn’t necessarily the same thing as someone handing you $1,000 for your old phone. Compare the total cost of the service plan and device over the entire promotion period. 7. Consider Last Year’s Phone You don’t necessarily need the newest phone to get a major upgrade. Last year’s flagship can offer excellent cameras, fast processors, high-quality displays and years of remaining software support. Once its successor arrives, it may also become substantially cheaper. Compare the previous model with the new one feature by feature. If the improvements don’t matter to you, take the discount. Your phone will somehow continue functioning despite knowing it isn’t the newest one in the room. So, Should You Buy a New Phone Now? Upgrade if your current phone is genuinely interfering with how you use it. A failing battery, broken hardware, inadequate storage, poor performance or the end of software support can all be legitimate reasons to replace a device. But if your phone works well and continues receiving updates, waiting can be the smarter move. New product launches don’t just create new phones. They can also create better deals on the phones that were considered cutting-edge a few weeks earlier. Before You Upgrade, Check Your Settings You may also be able to improve your current phone without replacing it. iPhone owners should check our guide to 7 iPhone Settings You’ll Wish You Changed Sooner for privacy, security and usability settings worth reviewing. If you use Android, 7 Android Settings You’ll Be Glad You Changed covers similar changes for Android devices. FAQ How Often Should You Replace Your Phone? There isn’t a universal replacement schedule. If your phone remains secure, supported and capable of doing what you need, there’s no requirement to replace it after a certain number of years. Is September a Good Time to Buy a Phone? It can be, but timing matters. September is a major smartphone-launch period, so waiting for announcements can give you more options and potentially change pricing on existing models. Is It Better to Replace a Battery or Buy a New Phone? If the battery is the primary problem and the phone otherwise meets your needs, battery replacement may be considerably cheaper than buying a new device. Compare repair cost, remaining software support and the condition of the phone before deciding. Should I Buy Last Year’s Phone? Often, yes. A previous-generation flagship can be an excellent value if it still has years of software support and the newer model doesn’t offer features you need. Should I Trade In My Old Phone? Possibly, but compare the trade-in offer with other options. Pay attention to whether the advertised credit is delivered through monthly bill credits or requires a particular wireless plan. title: Your Smart TV Is Watching More Than You Think. Here’s How to Stop It
author: GBM Staff
content: You probably expect your smart TV to keep track of what you watch on Netflix or YouTube. What you may not realize is that some TVs can also collect information about what appears on the screen, including content coming from other connected devices. One technology behind this is called Automatic Content Recognition, or ACR. Smart TV tracking isn’t necessarily some sinister person sitting in a dark room watching your television habits. It’s generally automated data collection used for things like recommendations, analytics and advertising. Still, if you’d rather your television know a little less about your viewing habits, there are settings worth checking. What Is ACR on a Smart TV? Automatic Content Recognition technology can identify content playing on your television. Depending on the TV and the features you’ve enabled, this can help the manufacturer or its partners understand what programs, movies and advertisements are being watched. ACR can also be used to provide features such as content recommendations. The important part is that this technology can potentially recognize content beyond the streaming apps built directly into your TV. That makes ACR one of the first settings worth investigating if you’re concerned about smart TV tracking. 1. Look for ACR or Viewing Data Settings Unfortunately, TV manufacturers don’t all call their tracking features the same thing, because apparently finding a privacy setting needed an additional difficulty level. Open your television’s Settings menu and look under sections such as: Privacy Terms & Privacy Viewing Information Viewing Data Advertising Smart Features You may see references to Automatic Content Recognition, viewing information or content recognition. Read the description before deciding whether you want the feature enabled. 2. Turn Off Personalized Advertising Your smart TV may have a separate setting for personalized or interest-based advertising. This can be different from ACR. Look through the Privacy or Advertising settings for options related to: Personalized ads Interest-based ads Ad tracking Advertising IDs Disabling personalized advertising doesn’t necessarily eliminate advertisements. It generally limits the use of your activity for tailoring those ads. 3. Review Your TV’s Privacy Choices When you first set up a new television, you’re usually presented with a collection of agreements and privacy choices. And, like nearly every human presented with 4,000 words of legal text while trying to watch television, you probably pressed Accept. Go back and review them. Some smart TVs allow you to change individual privacy permissions without resetting the entire television. Pay particular attention to optional agreements involving viewing data, recommendations, voice features and advertising. 4. Check Voice Assistant Settings Many modern televisions include microphones or work with voice assistants. If you don’t use voice control, check whether you can disable the feature. Also review whether voice recordings or interactions can be stored or used to improve the service. A television having a microphone isn’t automatically a privacy disaster, but there’s little reason to leave features enabled that you never use. 5. Review the Apps Installed on Your TV Smart TVs have effectively become giant smartphones attached to walls. Open your TV’s app section and remove apps you no longer use. You should also review account and privacy settings inside frequently used streaming apps. Remember that disabling tracking by your television manufacturer doesn’t necessarily change the data collected by Netflix, YouTube, Hulu or other individual services. Those services have their own privacy and account settings. 6. Don’t Forget Your Streaming Devices If you use a Roku, Fire TV, Apple TV, Chromecast or another streaming device, your television isn’t the only device involved. The streaming platform may have its own advertising, privacy and data-collection settings. Open the settings on each device and look for sections related to: Privacy Advertising Usage data Personalized recommendations Viewing information If you’ve spent years adding streaming boxes and sticks to your television, you may have several different privacy settings to review. 7. Keep Your Smart TV Updated Privacy isn’t the only reason to dig into your television’s settings. Check for software or firmware updates while you’re there. Manufacturers release updates to fix bugs, improve features and address security issues. Some TVs update automatically, while others require you to manually check. You’ll typically find the option under Settings, Support, System or About. Can You Completely Stop a Smart TV From Collecting Data? Probably not while continuing to use all of its connected features. Streaming services need certain information simply to operate, maintain accounts and deliver content. The more practical goal is to limit optional data collection you don’t want. Turning off ACR or viewing-data features, reviewing advertising preferences and disabling unused smart features can reduce the amount of information being collected for purposes beyond simply delivering the service. What If You Don’t Use the Smart Features? If you use an external streaming box and don’t need your television’s built-in apps, you can take things further. Depending on your setup, you may decide not to keep the television connected to the internet at all. The TV can essentially function as a display while your streaming device handles online content. That approach isn’t practical for everyone, especially if you use built-in streaming apps, but it removes many of the television’s connected features from the equation. Privacy Settings Are Worth Checking Everywhere Your television isn’t the only device in your house collecting information. Phones, streaming devices, smart speakers, apps and websites all have their own privacy settings. If you’re an iPhone user, our guide to 7 iPhone Settings You’ll Wish You Changed Sooner covers several privacy and security settings that are also worth reviewing. Android users can check 7 Android Settings You’ll Be Glad You Changed for similar controls on Android phones. FAQ Is My Smart TV Actually Watching Me? Not in the way the phrase might suggest. Smart TV tracking generally refers to automated technologies that collect information about usage or recognize content being displayed. The exact data collected depends on the television manufacturer, settings and services you use. What Is ACR? ACR stands for Automatic Content Recognition. It is technology that can identify content being displayed on a television and can be used for features including analytics, recommendations and advertising. Will Turning Off ACR Break My TV? Your television should still work, although certain recommendation or smart features that depend on viewing information may be affected. Do Streaming Devices Track Viewing Activity Too? Streaming platforms and devices may collect their own usage information independently of your television. Review the privacy settings for any Roku, Fire TV, Apple TV, Chromecast or other streaming platform you use. Can I Disconnect My Smart TV From the Internet? Yes. If you don’t use its built-in connected features, you can use many televisions primarily as displays for external devices. You will lose internet-dependent features and may need another method for firmware updates. This article may contain affiliate links.
