title: AI, trust and the future of journalism took center stage at ISOJ 2026
author: Knight Center
content: The future of journalism rests on technology and the human relationships that connect news organizations with their audiences. That was the central theme of the 27th International Symposium on Journalism (ISOJ), held Sept. 17-18 at the University of Texas at Austin and broadcast online. The annual conference organized by the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas brought together news executives, journalists, academics and others shaping the future of the news business. This year’s program largely revolved around the topics of artificial intelligence, audience trust and new business models. The first day was headed by keynote speaker Elizabeth Green, CEO of Civic News Company, who urged newsrooms to define their value, build sustainable business models around it and develop revenue streams that protect editorial independence. On the second day, keynote speaker Jonathan Greenberger, editor in chief of Politico, turned to how technology is changing the way news is produced, distributed and consumed. “We made it again!” said Professor Rosental Calmon Alves, founder and director of the Knight Center and ISOJ. “Another great symposium that helped journalists, media executives and scholars from around the world to better understand the challenges and opportunities created by the transformational impact of digital technologies on the news media ecosystem.” The symposium featured 57 speakers and drew more than 800 attendees in person and online from 49 countries and territories. The future hinges on building trust The first day of the conference centered on journalists’ role in democracy and how they can remain relevant with their audiences. Tom Rosenstiel, a veteran journalist and professor at the University of Maryland’s Philip Merrill College of Journalism, said in conversation with Alves that journalism must move from a “journalism of attention” to a “journalism of value” — rethinking both how news organizations make money and what they offer audiences. “What people need is journalism that will help them live their lives and improve their communities,” he said. Community news organizations are taking steps to make audiences participants rather than passive consumers of news, according to speakers at a panel about “live journalism.” The Portugal-based Mensagem de Lisboa hosts events where residents share personal stories, said founder Catarina Carvalho. El Tímpano, which serves Latino and Mayan immigrants in California’s Bay Area, takes its journalism to community spaces, including a Día de los Muertos festival where residents created an altar to remember loved ones. Audiences’ evolving consumption habits are reshaping journalism writ large, said Liz Kelly Nelson, founder of Project C, which supports creator journalists. At a panel on the “new information economy,” she argued that vertical, short-form videos and live events should be considered journalism, even if they’re not produced by traditional news organizations. AI’s threats and opportunities The second day focused on AI’s promise to make journalism faster and cheaper — and its potential to erode the audiences and revenue that sustain it. Consumer chatbots such as Claude and Gemini are reshaping newsrooms. At Politico, journalists use AI to help mine through mountains of documents or to help write code, said Politico Editor in Chief Jonathan Greenberger. At Axios, reporters are using it to develop new products such as summaries of other outlets’ news coverage, said Allison Murphy, chief operating officer. But at a panel on how AI is impacting traffic to news sites, speakers said chatbots are also diverting traffic from websites, raising questions about how publishers will reach audiences if AI becomes a primary gateway to information. “If there’s a mass exodus from news sites to chatbots and AI summaries, journalism is going to get absolutely flattened by products cosplaying as objective omniscient oracles,” unless the industry finds a new approach, said Zach Seward, editorial director of AI initiatives at The New York Times, at a panel on agentic AI. Latin American journalists turn to collaboration Participants at the 19th Ibero-American Journalism Colloquium , held the day after ISOJ ended, took a more practical approach. Rather than asking what journalism will become, its speakers focused on what journalists across Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula are doing now to sustain it. The Colloquium’s 27 speakers from about a dozen countries pointed to collaboration, creativity and independent journalism as ways to confront authoritarianism and the rise of AI. Keynote speaker Carmen Aristegui , an award-winning Mexican investigative reporter, argued journalists should respond to the rise of authoritarianism, the expansion of AI and climate change with a people-first approach. “Everything that encompasses the human condition has to be at the center,” she said. Other speakers highlighted cross-border investigations, local reporting networks and new approaches to sustainability, including solutions journalism. But they also warned that AI is accelerating sophisticated disinformation like deepfakes, while forcing newsrooms to weigh new tools against journalism’s core principles. Conference recordings will be online Recordings of all panels, sessions and workshops are now available to ISOJ 2027 registrants and will soon be available to the public. The 27th ISOJ was sponsored by: Knight Foundation, Google News Initiative, The Lenfest Institute, Moody College of Communication at UT Austin, Chartbeat, John S. Knight Journalism Fellowships at Stanford University, Missouri School of Journalism, Newspack, Wallace House Center for Journalists at the University of Michigan, and the School of Journalism and Media at UT Austin. ISOJ was also made possible with the help of more than 40 volunteers, most of whom are students from UT Austin’s Moody College of Communication. The 28th ISOJ is expected to be held in April 2027. title: Mexican journalist Carmen Aristegui on putting people at the center of journalism
author: Silvia Higuera
content: Talking about the future of journalism makes little sense without addressing the converging crises of the rise of authoritarianism, the expansion of AI and climate change — forces that are driving a civilizational shift for humanity. That was how Mexican journalism pioneer Carmen Aristegui opened her keynote address at the 19th Ibero-American Journalism Colloquium (opens in new tab) , held at the University of Texas at Austin on Sept. 19. These crises are defining for humanity, and journalism should be responding to them, Aristegui said in a conversation with Rosental Calmon Alves, founder and director of the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas, which organized the colloquium. “Journalism needs to broaden its spaces,” she said. “Broaden the spaces for discussion, broaden the spaces for political and social debate around all of these issues so that people can make decisions.” Putting the human at the center Aristegui also said the world order established after World War II is being reshaped. Populist leaders are coming to power through democratic means and, once there, seeking to weaken institutions that serve as checks and balances, from the judicial and legislative branches to the news media. Aristegui described this as a script that is being repeated. “Within this script, within these political patterns that are unfortunately prevailing, a fundamental factor is the critics, the news media, independent journalists, those of us who are dedicated to informing, who are dedicated to making sure society has that fundamental value that is information,” Aristegui said. “The script says they have to be attacked.” And under that script, she added, the news media have been identified as enemies whose reputations must be destroyed. In her home country, she said, those efforts to silence journalists have reached the extreme of murder. Mexico tops the list of the most dangerous countries (opens in new tab) in which to practice journalism. And on top of that, she said, there’s AI, which is driving a global paradigm shift. She pointed to discussions at the International Symposium on Journalism (opens in new tab) — another conference organized by the Knight Center that preceded the colloquium — where AI experts weighed the technology’s benefits against its (opens in new tab) “dark” sides, which could put humanity itself at risk. “All of these things lead us, my dear Rosental, to our own question: What the heck are we doing here?” Aristegui said. “What’s our role? What’s the role of journalists?” For Aristegui, the answer is to center journalism on the human being. Yes, journalists must continue to report on the day-to-day — such as who’s leading Brazil’s elections (opens in new tab) or what the candidates are saying. But they must also, she said, address how social media and the manipulation of technology are affecting democracies. “Everything that encompasses the human condition has to be at the center, as the main point around which everything else revolves,” she said. Aristegui confronts presidential power Aristegui also answered questions about censorship and press freedom, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s controversial morning news conferences and the weakening of institutions in her country. Confrontations with presidents have been a constant throughout her career. Aristegui explained how Aristegui Noticias was born out of efforts to silence her by former presidents Felipe Calderón and Enrique Peña Nieto. In 2011, a public question from Aristegui about an alleged alcohol problem involving Calderón prompted a series of efforts to pressure her into issuing a public apology, which she refused to do (opens in new tab) . But it was the 2014 investigation known as “The White House of Peña Nieto” that set off the conflict that ended with Aristegui’s departure (opens in new tab) and that of her team from her former employer, MVS Radio. Aristegui took the case to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, seeking to shield editorial independence (opens in new tab) from the interests of media owners. More recently, in July 2026, President Claudia Sheinbaum mentioned Aristegui during one of her morning news conferences (opens in new tab) , known as “mañaneras,” and said she would never try to censor her as previous presidents had. Aristegui, in a public response to the president (opens in new tab) , said freedom of expression was a right, not a permission granted by a government official. In her conversation with Alves, Aristegui discussed the role of the mañaneras, a communications tool created by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (opens in new tab) . Aristegui described them as a system for imposing a public narrative. “It’s not that original because it’s part of the same script,” she said. “That mañanera and that way political leaders take the microphone and impose the agenda every day [...] uses the entire communications ecosystem paid for with public money — radio, television, social media. There’s a lot of public money being used to replicate, amplify and endlessly reproduce the message that the media themselves cannot avoid.” Alves asked Aristegui about the closure of Mexico’s National Institute for Transparency, Access to Information and Personal Data Protection (opens in new tab) , an independent body that guaranteed access to public information and for years served as a model for the region. For Aristegui, this is perhaps the clearest example and “sadly, one of Mexico’s greatest losses, but not the only one.” Aristegui also pointed to changes affecting the National Electoral Institute and the judicial system. “We are in a country where, as in others, the script is being carried out,” Aristegui said. “That script says we have to dismantle democratic institutions to create a totalitarian regime, a regime in which our freedoms are shrinking. And that is why the role of critics and journalists has to be stronger than ever, because we need checks and balances when institutions have been dismantled.” The post Mexican journalist Carmen Aristegui on putting people at the center of journalism appeared first on Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas .

title: ISOJ 2026 Day 2: Publishers are facing a new middleman as AI changes the business
author: Knight Center
content: The news business is confronting an existential paradox: AI technology can make journalism faster and cheaper but it also threatens the audience and revenue that sustain it. That tension dominated the second day of the 27th International Symposium on Journalism , where news executives and journalists on Friday debated AI-powered workflows, new products, falling web traffic and the looming rise of AI agents. At Axios, AI is helping local reporters produce regional news roundups in minutes rather than hours. The company is also developing AI-driven products, including a “things to do” guide for local audiences. Politico reporters, meanwhile, are using AI to tackle massive datasets and even write code they don’t know how to write themselves — with help from chatbots and newsroom engineers. But the harder question is what happens when AI becomes the destination rather than the tool. Traffic to news websites has plunged since consumer AI tools took off after 2022. And if AI agents eventually gather and summarize news for consumers, publishers face a new dilemma: How do you make journalism for readers who may never see it? “We’re on the verge of a gigantic transformation of the news media ecosystem,” said Rosental Calmon Alves, founder and director of the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas, which organizes ISOJ , during a panel he moderated on agentic AI. Here are some of the future-looking ideas from the second day of ISOJ: Reporters are using AI to power their investigations Many top news organizations are working to build the news business of the future. That means embracing AI without letting it consume the industry it promises to transform, and serving younger audiences increasingly more via creators rather than traditional news organizations. At Politico,two reporters used AI earlier this year to sort through more than 20,900 court cases involving ICE detention and turn the findings into a format accessible to readers. The reporters manually compiled and categorized the records involving ICE detentions, then used AI to extract basic case information. Their analysis found that most of the rulings involved immigrants eligible for deportation who were detained without basic due-process protections. However, the enthusiasm for the yet-untapped potential of AI comes with caution. Politico editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger, speaking at the “Journalism’s AI moment” panel, said he is also wary of what the technology could mean for the news business. The organization has blocked AI chatbots from scraping its content, he said. All things considered, Greenberger said, “there’s never been a better time to be a journalist, not just because of the incredible story in front of us, but also because AI gives us incredible tools to cover this changing, disruptive world.” New technologies are also changing how people consume news, creating a new challenge for legacy publishers to reach audiences. Among people ages 18 to 24, that increasingly means social media. A Reuters Institute analysis published in March found that 51% of young people pay more attention to individual news creators rather than traditional news brands. Adriana Lacy, chief executive of the Boston-based Field Nine Group, uses her business to connect social media creators with legacy newsrooms to help expand their audience reach. “When we’re looking at creators for newsrooms to work with, we’re looking at who’s the transit advocate in your community that only talks about trains and bikes, and you have a story about how you want to do that,” Lacy said at a panel called “Reaching young audiences.” Lacy added that the worlds of social media creators and newsrooms are increasingly the same. She once met a journalist from a large news organization who described herself as a “secret influencer” but did not want to be identified because she is not creating news content, she said. Ryan Kellett, co-founder of the Independent Journalism Atlas, which tracks models to produce reporting trusted by consumers, described how newsrooms should recognize the potential for newsroom creators and attract new audiences. “If you get to the point where you have an influencer in your newsroom, that is an amazing win for you,” Kellett said. News companies are making money with AI As AI continues to reshape how people find and consume news, executives from Axios and the Sembra Media news incubator discussed how news organizations can use AI to build new revenue streams and create a more sustainable business model. Allison Murphy, chief operating officer of Axios, said the company has incorporated AI into its newsroom and, as a result, strengthened its hyperlocal reporting. Axios — a digital news publication that operates newsletters in 45 communities — is known for its “smart brevity” and usually has two reporters per community. “The economics have to work because the core problem in local journalism is an economic one,” Murphy said. “How do you make the math work to be able to bring great information to communities?” Murphy said AI tools are used to automate some tasks in the newsroom. For example, a news roundup section of their daily newsletter that used to take reporters three hours can be completed in about 10 minutes with AI tools, allowing reporters to spend more time on original reporting. “We're taking anything that isn't a reporter who's talked to a source, who's dug into a story, anything else we want to make as automated as possible,” said Janine Warner, executive director and co-founder of SembraMedia — an organization working to strengthen independent digital media across Latin America. Murphy said the company is also experimenting with AI-generated products that could create new advertising opportunities. Axios is testing a “things to do” newsletter that is about 90% AI-generated. She said that during beta testing, audiences told the company they did not mind the use of AI as long as the content was good. Murphy said, however, human expertise and connection are still at the forefront of their mission. One of the most popular parts of each newsletter is the reporters' sign-off at the end, where reporters share personal details about their lives with readers. “Readers constantly cite that is the thing they love the most: the human connection,” Murphy said. “That is something that the AI can't replicate.” For Warner, the economic question is also central to how news organizations should approach AI. She urges news organizations to begin thinking about how they can monetize it. “If we don't start thinking about how to make money with AI now, we're going to be left behind,” Warner said. Warner highlighted various AI companies and tools that can help newsrooms with monetization. But she also warned newsrooms to be cautious about the risks of generative AI, like intellectual theft and deepfakes. “I still believe that newsletters, events, things that really help us have direct connection, are also very popular right now because people want to connect with people,” Warner said. “If you're going to be using AI, my best advice is let the good bots in, keep the bad ones out.” What AI traffic and agentic AI will mean for news consumption The rise of consumer AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini has sent traffic to news websites off a cliff, as Google puts AI-generated summaries ahead of classic search results and users increasingly turn to chatbots for information. Panelists from outlets including The New York Times, ProPublica and the BBC discussed Friday how news organizations should manage AI-driven traffic and how agentic AI could reshape news consumption. The decline in traffic has sent many publishers asking whether their teams are creating a product that only machines will read. And yet, they are also seeing a growth in traffic coming from readers arriving via “dark social” — in other words, stories that users share through email, private messaging, and text messaging. “This is what the human audience is doing,” said Jill Nicholson, chief marketing officer at Chartbeat, which tracks website data and analytics. Direct traffic is driven by breaking news content and fact-based, in-depth stories that could not be easily replicated by chatbots, according to Dan Petty, former director of audience strategy at ProPublica. “Habits are changing, and changing quickly, and just indicate the importance of brand and the importance of building trust and being very clear about what your value proposition is to your audience”, Petty said. The next frontier seems to be AI agents — systems that can search and act on information with little human prompting — but there is disagreement on whether it should be seen as an opportunity or a threat. Florent Daudens, chief executive of the AI-native distribution platform Mizal, said some organizations are shifting from a business-to-consumer to a business-to-AI-agent model, where the information will be intermediated by an AI agent. “If you treat the agent as a customer, then you start thinking about building a conversion funnel for the agent, the same way we build a conversion funnel for the humans,” Daudens said. However, news organizations seem to be still skeptical about the impacts of Agentic AI. For Zach Seward, editorial director of AI initiatives at The New York Times, consuming news through a personal AI agent remains niche. But he said news organizations urgently need to adapt to other forms of AI, including chatbots. “We need to pretty dramatically change how we publish information in the first place, connected to citations of supporting facts and allow our readers and agents to do their own research along the way,” Seward said. “If there's a mass exodus from news sites to chatbots and AI summaries, journalism is going to get absolutely flattened by products cosplaying as objective omniscient oracles unless we get started working on a different way of doing things.” The post ISOJ 2026 Day 2: Publishers are facing a new middleman as AI changes the business appeared first on Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas .

title: Nonprofit news is betting on unorthodox ways to grow
author: Leonardo Coelho
content: Local public and nonprofit news organizations are getting creative about surviving an industry that keeps getting smaller. They’re buying or launching smaller publications, joining forces with community groups, and looking for ways to grow. At Chicago Public Media, the bet is that public media needs to reclaim its role as a public square—much as it helped create a public forum after broadcasting took off in the 1960s. This October, the company plans to launch a digital platform on Chicago.com where residents of five of the city’s distinctive neighborhoods can gather with neighbors, according to CEO Melissa Bell. “We really believe that today is the day that we can start to set an agenda,” Bell said. “We need to think about the infrastructure that supports people in a way that is truly locally based and locally owned.” Bell spoke on a panel on Thursday about public and nonprofit media at the 27th International Symposium on Journalism, hosted by the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas at the University of Texas at Austin. She was joined by executives from news organizations in Austin, San Antonio and Salt Lake City who are experimenting with new ways to strengthen local journalism and prepare for what comes next. The new platform in Chicago may be best defined by what it isn’t: a news website. Chicago Public Media won’t deploy reporters to cover the five neighborhoods, Bell said. Instead, journalists will participate hopefully alongside local businesses, nonprofits and civic groups, with the goal of connecting residents to the resources already operating in their communities. The initial rollout will include Avondale, Bronzeville, Edgewater, South Shore and the city of Evanston — “vital neighborhoods across Chicago that have very different flavors,” Bell said — with the hope that the project will serve as a pilot for similar public-media platforms around the country. The idea comes as social media has become a primary gateway to news for Americans, even as the major tech platforms aren’t necessarily designed to serve the public interest. The Reuters Institute’s 2026 Digital News Report found that 56% of U.S. respondents had used social media for news in the previous week. Chicago Public Media is developing the project with New Public, a nonprofit research and development studio. “This is a tool for the city of Chicago, and we are merely the stewards of it,” Bell said. Other media outlets are reaching out to smaller but established outlets and forming local media coalitions. The Texas Tribune, which was founded to cover state politics in Austin in 2009, has expanded into regional reporting across the state. In 2025, the company launched the Waco Bridge and acquired the Austin Monitor and relaunched it as the Austin Current. Both publications rely on the Tribune’s statewide coverage and follow its code of ethics and AI policy. “Those are very different communities, with different kinds of experiences and growth trajectories and challenges,” Hartman said. “But they both are really focused on telling stories that are better told because we have both the state newsroom and the local newsroom following that storyline.” In this new environment, even paywalls are coming down. In 2025, The Salt Lake Tribune removed its paywall, giving up $2.6 million in annual digital subscription revenue—about 20% of its total revenue. CEO Lauren Gustus said the decision reflected a belief that the Tribune’s journalism should be accessible to as many people as possible. “As a nonprofit, we didn't think that it was equitable or fair to ask people from Utah who may not be able to afford to pay for news to do so,” Gustus said. “It was really about what do communities need from us and how can we serve them in that need.” The Salt Lake Tribune, which was founded in 1870 and became a non-profit in 2019, spent a year preparing for the transition. And that showed results, Gustus said: more than 90 percent of subscribers stayed on as monthly donors. A newer partnership came less than three months ago. In July, Texas Public Radio and San Antonio Report joined forces to make the largest nonprofit newsroom San Antonio. Ashley Alvarado, president of Texas Public Radio, said that after decades-old calls for the federal government to defund public media, in 2024 those threats became real while both companies were studying to merge. “We looked at how the two newsrooms really complemented each other,” Alvarado said. “And we also were able to – which is a luxury for a smaller nonprofit newsroom – to make the investment to do market research.” Alvarado cited the Future of Public Media Initiative, a joint effort by the Poynter Institute and Boulder-based Public Media Company, which is studying how communities across the country want public media to serve them. The initiative plans to release recommendations in early 2027 on how public media organizations should operate over the next 50 years. The research could be a resource not only for public media outlets but for any journalist, Alvarado said. “People are seeking connectedness. They're seeking moments of awe. They're seeking a way to have information come to them,” Alvarado said. “And so with the public media work that Poynter and Public Media Company are doing together, it’s an opportunity to do a bit of a reset and also to think not just about the services we provide but the models on which we run.” The post Nonprofit news is betting on unorthodox ways to grow appeared first on Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas .

title: Ibero-American journalists respond to AI and democratic crises with collaboration and innovation
author: Knight Center
content: Ibero-American journalists are betting on collaboration, creativity and independent journalism to confront the existential challenges facing the industry and humanity today — from democratic crises around the world to the rise of artificial intelligence. Those were some of the central themes of the 19th Ibero-American Journalism Colloquium , held Sept. 19 at the University of Texas at Austin and organized by the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas. Following the conclusion of the 27th International Symposium on Online Journalism on Sept. 17-18, journalists from Latin America, the Caribbean, Spain and Portugal gathered at the Colloquium to discuss some of the region’s biggest challenges. Renowned Mexican journalist Carmen Aristegui set the tone for the gathering by describing the current moment as a “civilizational shift.” In that context, she said, journalism must not lose sight of the ethical questions that come with that shift or how humans relate to each other. “Humanity has to be at the center,” she said. For many Colloquium participants, partnerships and innovation are essential to pave the way forward. Kevin Hall, editor at the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), a nonprofit organization with a presence across Latin America, explained how his organization fights organized crime through an information network. Investigations such as NarcoFiles have brought together journalists from different countries. OCCRP also provides cybersecurity training and has developed partnerships that go beyond traditional journalistic collaborations — including, Hall said, one to create a video game that brings investigative reporting to new audiences. Daniel Molina, founder and director of Revista Concolón in Panama, spoke about the importance of telling a community’s stories from within and experimenting with different formats. Since its launch, the magazine has created new products, including comics, podcasts and special investigations. Community engagement and collaboration are also central to Puente News Collaborative , its founder, Alfredo Corchado, said. The organization works with a network of 14 independent journalists based in different communities and on both sides of the U.S.-Mexico border. Puente News also seeks to strengthen local newsrooms by offering funding to other journalists and news organizations. Strengthening local journalism was also a key goal for Clavel Rangel Jiménez, co-founder of the Venezuelan Amazon Journalism Network . The organization supports journalists in small communities across Venezuela’s Amazon region, where corruption, organized crime, violence against journalists and illegal economic activities make reporting challenging. To address these challenges, the network offers mentoring and workshops designed to expand journalists’ skills and strengthen trust within their communities. The network currently has 68 journalists and has supported the publication of more than 50 stories, Jiménez said. Tina Rosenberg, co-founder of the Solutions Journalism Network , spoke about her organization’s work training journalists across Latin America in solutions journalism and promoting sustainability models that combine sponsorships for local journalists, audience revenue and philanthropy. Rosenberg said solutions journalism can help rebuild audience trust at a time when many people have chosen to avoid the news altogether. The challenge, she said, is to produce stories that are “more powerful with more hope.” AI challenges and opportunities Journalists across Ibero-America are also experimenting with new tools, formats and products to produce relevant stories that connect with their audiences. In Mexico, Roberto Rock, founder and director of La Silla Rota , one of the country’s leading news sites, spoke about the outlet’s efforts to develop artificial intelligence tools that small and midsize newsrooms can use. One of them, La Morninguera, summarizes Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily news conferences — known as las Mañaneras — to help reporters identify the most relevant topics. In partnership with technology consultancy firm 7Gats, the outlet also developed a tool that identifies the topics trending on social media and makes them available to its journalists. Ramón Zamora, an anthropologist and sociologist with the Central American Independent Media Archive , shared his experience using AI tools to expand the investigative capabilities of journalists working with large amounts of information. Zamora said he used Claude to develop code that enabled an AI agent to review hundreds of pages of public information provided by the Guatemalan government as part of investigations into state corruption. He said the tool allowed him to “go from suspicions to facts” when investigating specific individuals. The use of these tools raised a fundamental question about the future of the profession: How can journalists be prepared to work with artificial intelligence without losing the skills and principles that define journalism? During the panel “Teaching Artificial Intelligence to Journalism Students: Challenges and Opportunities,” Alessandra de Falco, a professor at the Federal Universities of São João del Rei and Mato Grosso do Sul, said AI is already present in virtually every field, including journalism. Students, she added, need to learn how to use these tools, program with them, verify information, protect data and establish clear boundaries for their use in journalism. That need for preparation also extends to newsrooms. During a panel on artificial intelligence and disinformation, participants said AI is making disinformation more sophisticated and allowing it to spread more quickly — from written content to manipulated images and deepfake videos. Colloquium participants shared examples of how some newsrooms are using AI to address some of the same problems the technology is exacerbating. Wendy Selene Pérez, a journalist with Factchequeado , said she uses tools such as Google’s reverse image search to verify the origin of photographs and programs designed to detect deepfakes in text, images and interviews. Participants also emphasized that journalists must help their audiences understand how AI works and what its risks are, particularly as disinformation becomes increasingly widespread. Given the scale of these challenges, Fernanda Camarena, a journalist and professor at the Poynter Institute , highlighted the lack of preparedness in many newsrooms. “What worries me is how unprepared we are as news organizations,” she said. “We have all the good intentions, but we don’t know how to communicate them and we don’t know how to have conversations with our teams.” Correction Sept. 30, 2026, 10:55 a.m.: An earlier version of this story gave an incomplete name for the Venezuelan Amazon Journalism Network and incorrectly stated where it operates from. It works with journalists in Venezuela’s Amazon region. The post Ibero-American journalists respond to AI and democratic crises with collaboration and innovation appeared first on Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas .

title: As exile journalism grows, technology brings opportunities and risks
author: César López Linares
content: Journalists forced into exile around the globe have not only grown in numbers in recent years — the time they live outside their countries of origin has also grown longer. For years, organizations that support journalists in exile used to provide assistance for a few months while the risk decreased. But the conditions of the press in some parts of the world have caused exiled journalists to remain out of their countries for years, sometimes indefinitely. This has led to the emergence of an entirely new form of doing journalism — one in which technology plays a crucial role, speakers said Sept. 18 during the panel “Exiled but not silenced: Technology and the global surge of displaced journalists” during the second day of the 27th International Symposium on Online Journalism (ISOJ) . Carlos Lauría, executive director of the Inter American Press Association (IAPA); Polina Stretter , head of program development at JX Fund — European Fund for Journalism in Exile (Germany); José Zamora, regional director in the Americas of the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ); and Sarah Zaaimi, communication manager of Reporters Without Borders (RSF), discussed how forced relocation is transforming journalism, the challenges media outlets in exile are facing, and how technology helps combat and adds to those challenges. For the panelists, the change in recent years has been evident. Zaaimi said about 1,500 journalists from more than 60 countries were living in exile between 2021 and 2024. Zamora added that the CPJ’s assistance to journalists in exile increased 227% between 2020 and 2023. This form of support now accounts for most of CPJ’s assistance program, he said. For journalists working from another country, digital tools not only allow them to produce and publish news content, they also allow them to communicate with colleagues and sources and generate income, Stretter said. “There are four broader tracks where technology plays a crucial role: it's access to information from exile, it's reaching out to audiences from exile, it's the whole big box of digital security, and it's about efficiency — and therefore cost efficiency — of newsroom operations,” she said. But technology also presents challenges for journalists in exile. Away from their countries of origin, they become highly dependent on digital tools to continue doing journalism, Stretter said. Authoritarian governments use the same digital platforms journalists do to monitor and track them outside their countries’ borders. Stretter said her team found that some repressive governments have shut down digital media outlets run by journalists in exile through copyright claims filed with technology companies. It is difficult for journalists to appeal those decisions, she said, because those processes are often managed by AI. Cyberbullying is another challenge, the panelists said. Zamora mentioned two Ecuadorian journalists in exile in Canada who, after beginning to monetize their digital outlet, received a massive wave of attacks from trolls from their home country. Zaaimi said RSF is publishing a report next week about Chinese Communist Party propaganda targeting Chinese journalists living in the U.S. “Technology can be liberating in terms of offering new economic sources,” Zaaimi said. “But then it can be very isolating technically, but also community-wise.” Other challenges that technology poses for journalists in exile include digital shutdowns in their home countries and audiences who are afraid to consume their news because of possible political repercussions or do not know how to use tools such as VPNs to evade the shutdowns, Stretter said. Mental care and collaboration Many journalists in exile do not know how to use digital tools, and that pressure adds to the personal challenges of rebuilding a life in another country, Zaaimi said. “It is very challenging while you are trying to make a life for yourself and your family abroad, probably in a country where you don't have support networks, you don't speak the language, and then you have to learn new skills to have a livelihood for yourself,” she said. “So it's very hard.” Lauría said IAPA has a partnership with Vita Activa , an organization that supports journalists and activists who face trauma, digital violence or crises. The partnership has helped provide crisis intervention, digital security resources and mental health support to journalists in exile across the American continent, he added. “If people who are forced to flee do not take care of their well-being, of their mental health, at some point, sooner or later, they're going to burn out,” Lauría said. “Some of these media are three-, five-member teams that have to challenge authoritarians, and at the same time be reporters, editors, fundraisers [and] they have to take care of the digital security. It can be overwhelming.” JX Fund has supported media outlets in exile from eight countries and awarded about 200 grants to 119 organizations in about four and a half years. The mission of the organization is to respond to the needs of media outlets in exile, from technology and security to sustainability. Zaaimi said that, in addition to providing relocation support, grants and training, RSF’s assistance program is implementing new and innovative ways to combat censorship. As an example, she mentioned the launch of a shortwave radio frequency in Iran , whose content is produced by journalists in exile in France. Zamora added that CPJ has expanded its work to address the needs of journalists in exile through training, guides and security resources, while also promoting collaboration among support organizations. “Exile journalism is here to stay and it needs to be addressed in a systemic way,” Zamora said. title: ISOJ 2026 Day 1: Journalists look to rebuild trust by creating more value for audiences
author: Knight Center
content: On a day devoted to discussing how news organizations can foster community trust and the role of journalism amid growing democratic challenges around the world, speakers at the 27th International Symposium on Journalism (ISOJ) urged newsrooms to rethink what value they offer their audiences — and how they can work with those audiences to build that value. The question of how to bridge the gap between journalists and audiences was a recurring theme on the first day of the two-day conference, held Sept. 17-18, and emerged during ISOJ ’s opening session with Tom Rosenstiel , a professor at the University of Maryland’s Philip Merrill College of Journalism and author of the recently published book “ The Next Journalism .” During a conversation with Rosental Calmon Alves , founder and director of the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas, which organizes ISOJ , Rosenstiel argued that the future of journalism depends on moving from a “journalism of attention” to a “journalism of value.” For decades, he said, journalism built its business model around capturing audiences’ attention and selling access to those audiences to advertisers. But as the internet fragmented audiences and advertising migrated to technology platforms, that model largely broke down. Tom Rosenstiel at the 27th International Symposium on Journalism, Sept. 17, 2026. Patricia Lim/Knight Center Now, journalism needs to rethink not only how to make money, but what it offers audiences in the first place, Rosenstiel said. He emphasized the importance of making journalism useful to people’s lives, citing products such as The New York Times’ Wirecutter and cooking sections, which he said have become vital to his own day-to-day life. “What people need is journalism that will help them live their lives and improve their communities,” Rosenstiel said. Elizabeth Green , CEO and founder of Civic News Company, echoed those ideas in her keynote speech and offered a three-point plan for journalists to rebuild their business models: Be clear about the value you provide; build an economic model that supports that value; and get the right governance and capital to allow you to work with integrity. “The problem with the wrong kind of governance and capital is that it makes itself God, when the real God here has to be the value we are providing for real, specific people,” Green said. Different ways of serving audiences The idea of bridging the gap between the public and journalists continued during the panel “Rebuilding Trust: Community-Centered Journalism in an Age of Misinformation, Crisis and Uncertainty,” where speakers described ways news organizations are building value by developing lasting relationships with the communities they serve. Jody Chong , executive director of City Bureau, a Chicago-based nonprofit newsroom, described how the organization seeks to fill information gaps through services such as guides to immigration enforcement activity in the city. The outlet also created the Documenters Network , which trains community members to cover public meetings. “They combine the lived experience and personal networks of a community member and a neighbor, paired with the innate curiosity of a journalist and the training to produce accurate information,” Chong said. Martina Guzmán spoke about VERDAD , an AI-powered tool she developed to detect disinformation being spread through Spanish-language radio stations in the United States. She said she hopes the technology can eventually become part of a warning system that alerts journalists to disinformation before it spreads. Nina Weingrill , a journalist and researcher with Democratic Information Governance (D.I.G.) , which seeks to improve the quality of information produced during large-scale events and crises, spoke about her recent research on the 2024 mass flooding in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil. Journalists worked with communities across multiple platforms to communicate information during the disaster. Madeleine Bair at ISOJ on Sept. 17, 2026. Patricia Lim/Knight Center During spotlight talks with founders of community-driven newsrooms in the U.S. and Portugal, media leaders offered other examples of how journalists can rethink their relationships with audiences. Catarina Carvalho , editor and founder of Mensagem de Lisboa , a hyperlocal news outlet in Portugal, said her team hosts live journalism events where community members share their personal stories onstage. One participant was a man who married a Roma woman and had to flee with her after her parents threatened to kill them. Another shared how he became a supermodel after growing up in a slum. “When people see that our stories are true, that we are bringing these people together on stage, they show us that they trust us, and it brings people together,” Carvalho said. Madeleine Bair , founder and co-executive director of El Tímpano , a media organization serving Latino and Indigenous Mayan immigrants in the San Francisco Bay Area, said the outlet regularly brings its journalism into community spaces rather than expecting people to seek out its stories. At the Bay Area’s largest Día de los Muertos festival, for instance, El Tímpano created a community altar where people could share memories of loved ones who had died. “Rather than feeling helpless, afraid or victimized, community members share with us that these programs leave them feeling empowered, connected and part of a larger community,” Bair said. In another panel, Adam Ganucheau , executive editor and chief content officer of Deep South Today , said his outlet builds community trust through accountability reporting. He highlighted a recent story on lead concentrations in playgrounds and the outlet’s efforts to connect with local residents through direct mail and in-person events. The same emphasis on understanding audiences emerged in a discussion about coverage of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. Anna Johnson , Washington bureau chief for The Associated Press, said journalists need to focus on understanding voters’ concerns rather than centering coverage solely on candidates or political figures. “Voters are the center of our coverage, not candidates, not the president,” Johnson said. “And while the presidency is certainly part of that ecosystem, … we're talking to voters to understand better what they care about, what really matters to them.” The shift toward audience-centered journalism also extends beyond traditional newsrooms. Independent and creator journalists at ISOJ emphasized the growing role of the creator economy and the ways it has changed how some people consume news. Liz Kelly Nelson , founder of Project C , an organization that supports independent creator journalists, said many news consumers turned away from traditional media during the COVID-19 pandemic and shifted their focus to independent creators. “It wasn't apathy,” Kelly Nelson said. “It was feeling that institutional journalism was too elite, too complex, biased, depressing, irrelevant; all things that creators are the opposite of.” Through Project C, Kelly Nelson helps independent journalists build sustainable careers. One creator supported by the organization is Becky Bullard, founder of Democrasexy, which aims to demystify Texas politics through Instagram videos, live events and other formats. “Call her whatever you want,” Kelly Nelson said. “Her work is an act of journalism.” The second day of this year’s ISOJ will focus on AI, innovation and the future of news, with panels featuring journalists and industry leaders including Jonathan Greenberger , Global Editor-in-Chief of POLITICO; Allison Murphy , COO of Axios; Sisi Wei , chief impact officer at CalMatters and The Markup; and Zach Seward , editorial director of A.I. initiatives at The New York Times. More than 400 people attended ISOJ in person at the University of Texas at Austin, while almost 400 participated virtually. title: Leading Mexican journalist Carmen Aristegui to headline 2026 Ibero-American Journalism Colloquium
author: Alejandro Martínez-Cabrera
content: Award-winning journalist Carmen Aristegui, one of Mexico’s most influential voices and responsible for some of the country's most explosive investigations in the past 15 years, will deliver the keynote address at the 19th Ibero-American Journalism Colloquium , the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas announced Wednesday. The Colloquium will take place Sept. 19, 2026, one day after the 27th International Symposium on Journalism(ISOJ) . Both conferences are organized by the Knight Center and will be held at The University of Texas at Austin. Registration for ISOJ is required to participate in the Colloquium. Click here to register to attend in person or virtually and then sign up for the Colloquium. Participants registered to attend ISOJ and the Colloquium virtually will be eligible to receive a certificate of participation from the Knight Center. Aristegui has more than three decades of experience in radio, television and digital media. She recently ended her program on CNN en Español after 20 years on the air, a collaboration that expanded her audience across Latin America and the United States. In 2012, she founded Aristegui Noticias , an independent news platform that has gained a reputation for its investigations into politics, corruption and abuses of power. Aristegui launched the news site after publishing an investigation in 2014 into the so-called White House of former Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto (opens in new tab) . Aristegui’s team revealed that the multimillion-dollar mansion where Peña Nieto lived was legally registered to a real estate company owned by a friend of the president and government contractor. Following the investigation, her former broadcaster fired two members of her team (opens in new tab) . The broadcaster also fired Aristegui (opens in new tab) after the journalist demanded that her colleagues be reinstated. Her team has frequently faced criticism and attacks, including attempts at online surveillance and the ransacking of their newsroom . Her work has earned her numerous honors, including the 2008 María Moors Cabot Prize and the El Confidencial International Award for Investigative Journalism, presented by the King and Queen of Spain this year for the investigation Televisa Leaks . In that investigation, Aristegui’s team revealed leaked documents describing how Mexican broadcaster Televisa fabricated news, orchestrated smear campaigns and manipulated information . “It will be a great honor for us to welcome to the Ibero-American Journalism Colloquium one of the most important journalists in Mexico, respected and admired not only in her country but throughout Ibero-America for her courage and professional skill, grounded in ethical values and the best investigative techniques,” said Rosental Calmon Alves, founder and director of the Knight Center. He added: “Carmen Aristegui has been an inspiration to new generations of journalists through her radio and television programs, her news site, her interviewing style and her courage to lead and publish investigations that expose corruption, based on information that is so thoroughly verified that it is indisputable.” Aristegui will open the Colloquium, a Spanish-language conference that since 2008 has brought together journalists and media leaders from Latin America, the Caribbean, Spain and Portugal to discuss their shared challenges. This year’s Colloquium will feature presentations by other leaders in Ibero-American journalism, including Alfredo Corchado , executive director of Puente News Collaborative (U.S.); José Zamora , regional director for the Americas at the Committee to Protect Journalists ; Roberto Rock , founder and director of La Silla Rota (Mexico); Laura Aguirre , co-founder and strategic director of Alharaca (El Salvador/Germany); and Clavel Rangel Jiménez , co-founder of the Amazonian Venezuelan Journalists Network (Venezuela). The conference will focus on topics like sustainability, launching independent news organizations, U.S.-Mexico border coverage, disinformation and fact-checking in the age of artificial intelligence, and solutions journalism, among others. The Colloquium will build on the discussions that start during ISOJ, which this year will take place Sept. 17-18 and focus on two of the most urgent issues facing journalism: strengthening audience trust at a critical moment for democracies around the world and the future of news in the age of artificial intelligence. ISOJ will offer simultaneous English-to-Spanish interpretation for both in-person and virtual attendees. The Colloquium will be held entirely in Spanish, with no interpretation. title: ISOJ’s newly announced 2026 program spotlights audience trust, AI and the future of news
author: Alejandro Martínez-Cabrera
content: The program for the 27th International Symposium on Journalism (ISOJ), which will take place from Sept. 17-18, 2026, will revolve around two of the industry's most pressing issues: strengthening audience trust at a critical moment for democracies around the world and the future of news in the age of artificial intelligence. The newly released program for this year’s ISOJ, happening online and at The University of Texas at Austin, features journalists and industry leaders like Elizabeth Green, CEO and founder of the Civic News Company; Jonathan Greenberger, Global Editor-in-Chief of POLITICO; Allison Murphy, COO of Axios; Sarah Adler Hartman, CEO of The Texas Tribune; Sisi Wei, chief impact officer at CalMatters & The Markup; Zach Seward, editorial director of A.I. initiatives at The New York Times; and Jody Chong, executive director of City Bureau. On day 1, focused on journalism, trust, and democracy, sessions will examine the future of public and nonprofit media, new approaches to community building, and coverage of this year’s U.S. midterm elections. Day 2, organized around the theme of innovation, AI, and the future, includes sessions on reaching young audiences, agentic AI in news consumption, and the role of technology in exile journalism. "This year’s ISOJ program brings together some of the most innovative thinkers and practitioners in journalism to tackle the defining challenges of our time — from rebuilding trust and strengthening democracy to navigating the transformative impact of AI," said Summer Harlow, the Knight Center's associate director. "We’re creating a space for global conversations that are both urgent and deeply practical. Whether community engagement, creator journalism, agentic AI, reaching young audiences, live journalism, or exile journalism, the 27th ISOJ will reflect the biggest conversations happening in the industry right now. The program truly is unmissable!" Early-bird registration is open through July 20 , after which ticket prices will increase. Click here to register today! Since 1999, the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas has organized ISOJ. Each year, the conference attracts journalists, media executives and scholars from around the world, helping lead the conversation on how digital technologies are reshaping the journalism field. With ISOJ’s unique blend of professional practice and academia, participants can engage with the latest research, methods and educational practices. This year’s conference will once again be held at the Shirley Bird Perry Ballroom at the University of Texas. For those unable to attend in-person, ISOJ also offers a Virtual Experience for online participation. Both in-person and online participants will have full access to all sessions and will be able to connect with fellow participants through a dedicated ISOJ 2026 Slack community. The Virtual Experience goes beyond streaming of panels to include ways for remote participants to engage with speakers and fellow attendees. As in recent years, online participants will be able to attend live Q&As with select speakers. The conference will be simultaneously interpreted from English to Spanish for those attending in person and online. Last year’s ISOJ attracted 422 in-person registrants and 455 virtual participants, coming from 58 countries. Traditionally held in April, ISOJ moved to September this year and dropped “Online” from its name, reflecting changes in the conference and the broader journalism landscape. On Sept. 19, the day after ISOJ, the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas will host the 19th Iberoamerican Colloquium on Digital Journalism , a conference conducted in Spanish that brings together journalists, publishers and scholars from Latin America, Spain and Portugal. Follow us on X , Facebook and Instagram for real-time updates, and join the conversation using #ISOJ2026. And if you haven’t already, we encourage you to sign up for the ISOJ2026 newsletter in English or Spanish . title: Podcasting course breaks Knight Center record with more than 7,200 participants
author: Teresa Mioli
content: Podcasting has exploded in Brazil, with the country having the highest number of podcast users globally. Course instructors Flora Thomson-DeVeaux and Paula Scarpin (Photo: Courtesy) A prominent member of that scene, podcasting production company Rádio Novelo, has made a name for itself at home and abroad with its narrative, journalistic storytelling. So, when the Knight Center for Journalism in the Americas teamed up with the audio journalism company for a free online course in Portuguese this May, the response was overwhelming. The four-week course, “Telling stories in audio with Rádio Novelo,” attracted 7,228 students from 58 countries ranging from Brazil to Italy and Mozambique. This is the highest number of participants for any single-language course offered by the Knight Center in the history of its Journalism Courses program. "This course was very special not only because of the record number of participants, not only for the quantity, but also for the quality, on both sides. The instructors were very well organized and efficient, and the students were engaged, enthusiastic and showed a passion for the topic and for Radio Novelo's team that was truly impressive," said professor Rosental Calmon Alves, founder and director of the Knight Center. "The success of this course and the high level of engagement of the participants with Radio Novelo's instructors are a testament to the enormous appetite among journalists to learn how to tell stories in new formats, and proof that the Knight Center's online courses program, which has trained more than 370,000 students since 2012, remains a powerful way to build learning communities of journalists around the world," Alves said. Participants learned how to find a story to tell, investigate and research material, structure stories, and finally, develop script writing. Journalist and course participant Vitor Anastacio said he learned “how to transform reporting into a more engaging narrative that has rhythm, structure and a meticulous attention to sound.” “The course reinforced the idea that podcasting goes beyond mere technique: it is a form of journalism that demands deep listening, clear intention and the crafting of atmosphere right from the very first script," he added. Rádio Novelo President Branca Vianna said the course was a “great experience” for the organization as well. “It allowed us to systematize knowledge that was sort of floating around the newsroom for years and share it with the [Knight Center’s] very engaged and talented audience,” she said. When Rádio Novelo entered the scene in Brazil in 2019, its miniseries were very popular, but they required a lot of time and money to produce, said course instructors Flora Thomson-DeVeaux and Paula Scarpin. So, the production company created a weekly narrative podcast called Rádio Novelo Apresenta to provide a way for contributors who maybe didn’t have expertise in podcasts to collaborate on audio stories. However, the team still didn’t have a way to accommodate the number of interested potential contributors. Thomson-DeVeaux and Scarpin said the free course with the Knight Center was a way to offer that learning opportunity to more people. “Now that the Brazilian public has discovered the power of narrative audio journalism, an ever-growing number of people are eager to tell stories in this format,” the duo said. “We have observed that our thousands of students come from incredibly diverse backgrounds and intend to apply the techniques learned in the course to a myriad of formats—ranging from traditional journalism to science communication.” Journalist and podcast Beatriz Alessi finished the course feeling enriched and ready to tell more stories. "I loved feeling so close to such a professional, dedicated team—one that shares my very own passion for telling stories through audio,” she said. Thomson-DeVeaux and Scarpin said the course was a learning experience for the instructors as well. “We learned a great deal—much of it from one another—and it has been both fun and enlightening to pick up some techniques from the students on how to organize research materials, formulate questions for interviewees and conceptualize the structure of a script,” they said. title: Selling A House On The Cape In This Terrible Market
author: Kris Lippi
content: Selling your house can be a daunting task, especially in a terrible real estate market. When the market is less than favorable, you may find it challenging to attract buyers and secure a best price for your property. However, with a well-planned strategy and proper guidance, you can successfully navigate through these obstacles and sell your home. In such a market, sellers face increased competition and pricing pressures. To stand out among the numerous available properties, you need to be mindful of your home’s presentation, pricing, and marketing tactics. This will help you attract potential buyers and make the most of the current real estate market conditions. Understanding the dynamics of the market is important, as it allows you to make informed decisions and set realistic expectations. By being aware of the market trends, you can better position your property to appeal to buyers and negotiate your way to a successful sale. Stay positive and proactively adapt to the market conditions, and you’ll be well-prepared to sell your house despite the challenges. Understanding the Current Real Estate Market High Interest Rates Makes Monthly Payments High For Buyers In today’s market, high interest rates have caused a significant increase in the monthly payments buyers have to make. As a result, many potential buyers are struggling to secure mortgages that fit their budget. This is a troubling development in the real estate market, as it can put a damper on the overall demand for homes. As a seller in this market, it’s important for you to be aware of these challenges and work closely with your real estate agent to navigate them. Real Estate Prices Are Unaffordable For A lot of Buyers Another issue facing the current real estate market is the rising home prices. Many buyers are finding it difficult to afford homes due to these skyrocketing prices, leading to a contraction in the pool of potential buyers. The high home prices combined with the high interest rates can make it inaccessible for first-time buyers or those with limited budgets. In this buyer’s market, it is crucial for you to understand the impact of these trends on your prospective buyers and make informed decisions when setting your selling price. Real Estate Trends Several trends are impacting the real estate market currently. Some of these include: Low housing supply: A major contributing factor to the high home prices is the low inventory of available properties. The housing supply has not been able to meet the demand, especially when interest rates were lower. Now that interest rates are high, sellers don’t want to let go of their low interest rates and are not selling their home, causing a supply shortage. Strange market: With the imbalance between supply and demand, it created a seller’s market but that is changing. Keep in mind that unaffordable monthly payments due to high interest rates and home prices are now holding back many potential buyers. Economic factors: The broader economy also plays a role in shaping the real estate market. Factors such as job growth, wage increases, and overall consumer confidence can influence both buyer and seller behaviors in the housing market. As you navigate the current real estate market, it’s essential to keep these factors in mind when deciding on the best approach to sell your home. By understanding these trends, you can work alongside your real estate agent to develop strategies for successfully selling your house in a challenging market. Preparing Your House For Sale Make Necessary Home Repairs Before putting your house on the market, it’s crucial to fix any outstanding issues. Buyers are drawn to move-in ready homes, so tackle necessary major repairs first. Look for issues with critical systems, such as plumbing, electrical, and HVAC. Address minor concerns too, like leaky faucets, squeaky doors, and peeling paint. Also, check your flooring and replace carpets that are worn or stained. A well-maintained home will attract more buyers and minimize potential negotiation hurdles. Improving Curb Appeal First impressions matter, and your home’s exterior is the first thing potential buyers will see. Boost your curb appeal by addressing the landscaping. Trim overgrown bushes, mow the lawn, rake the leaves and maybe even add a fresh layer of mulch before winter. Also put out your fall decor, especially on the front porch . Additionally, don’t forget about the facade of the house. Give it a good pressure wash and apply a fresh coat of paint if needed. By improving your home’s curb appeal, you’ll make a lasting impression on buyers, even in a slow market. Staging Your Home When selling your house, you want potential buyers to imagine themselves living there. Staging your home is a vital step in achieving that goal. Start by decluttering and organizing each room. Put away personal items, like family photos, and keep rooms as neutral as possible. A deep clean is essential – ensure all surfaces, including countertops and floors, are spotless. Focus on the main living areas, as well as the bedrooms and bathrooms. Pay special attention to the kitchen, since it’s often a determining factor for potential buyers. Make sure finishes and fixtures are clean and up-to-date. Remove any lingering odors and maintain a pleasant, welcoming atmosphere. Keep your home’s staging looking fresh, even in a tough market. With proper attention to repairs, curb appeal, and staging, you’ll maximize your home’s potential and stand out from the competition. Pricing Your House Right Determining Market Value In a terrible market, it’s essential to price your house right to increase the chances of attracting potential buyers. To determine the market value of your home, you can enlist the help of a real estate agent. They can provide you with comparable sales data and insights into the local market conditions. When setting the price, consider the current home prices in your area, as well as affordability for potential buyers. Keep in mind the return on investment (ROI) you’re aiming for, but be realistic given the market situation. After determining the market value, it’s wise to obtain an appraisal to provide an objective assessment of your home’s worth. In a difficult market, you may receive fewer offers. Don’t dismiss cash offers too quickly, as these often come with a faster closing time and fewer contingencies. Ultimately, listen to your real estate agent, remain flexible, and be prepared for possible price negotiations to successfully sell your house in a terrible market. Home Selling Options Choosing a Real Estate Agent When selling your house in a terrible market, it’s essential to find the right real estate agent . Look for a local agent with experience in listing and promoting hard-to-sell properties. They should understand what it takes to get the best price for houses with certain downsides. A good agent will help you evaluate offers, negotiate terms with the buyer, and ensure the deal goes through. We Buy Houses for Cash Companies Another option is to consider We Buy Houses for Cash companies. These are real estate investors who make cash offers on houses, typically at a discounted price. This could be an attractive option if you need to sell your house quickly and are willing to accept a lower price. Make sure to research the company before making a decision, as not all of them have your best interests in mind. Flat Fee MLS Companies Flat Fee MLS Listing companies are another alternative when trying to sell in a difficult market. These services allow you to list your home on the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) for a flat fee, rather than paying a commission to a traditional real estate agent. This can save you money but means you’ll be responsible for handling showings, negotiations, and other aspects of the sale. Keep in mind, these listings show up on all the same websites that have houses for sale on the Cape . Discount Real Estate Agents Finally, you could explore working with discount real estate agents . These professionals provide similar services as traditional agents but at a reduced commission rate. While this may help you save money on agent fees, keep in mind that their level of service might be less comprehensive than that of a full-service agent. In conclusion, selling your house in a terrible market can be challenging, but choosing the right option for you – be it a traditional real estate agent, a cash buyer, a flat fee MLS listing, or a discount agent – can make all the difference. Closing Thoughts In a terrible real estate market, it’s important for you as a seller to stay level-headed and patient. Keep in mind that many factors can influence the market, and it might take longer than expected to find the right buyer. However, with strategic planning and adaptability, you can make the most of this challenging situation. First and foremost, consider your neighborhood and the specific factors that are impacting the real estate market. This will help you in tailoring your approach for attracting potential buyers. Remember, highlighting the unique aspects of your home and setting a competitive price will be key. Stay in close contact with your real estate agent, as they can provide valuable insights and guidance in navigating the hardships of a terrible market. Collaborate with them to develop a marketing strategy that makes your home stand out among the competition and appeals to the right audience. Lastly, be open to receiving feedback and adjusting your approach accordingly. This may include making small improvements to your home or insuring that the selling process goes as smoothly as possible. With a friendly attitude and a proactive mindset, you can overcome the difficulties of selling your house in a terrible market and eventually find the right buyer for your cherished home. Frequently Asked Questions How can I improve my chances of selling in a bad market? To increase your chances of selling in a bad market, you should: Choose the right real estate agent with experience in listing and promoting hard-to-sell properties. Make necessary repairs and improve your home’s curb appeal. Price your home appropriately, considering the current market conditions. Be ready to negotiate and stay flexible with potential buyers. Remember, patience and persistence are key when selling in a difficult market. What strategies can help sell a house in poor condition? If your house is in poor condition , consider the following strategies: Sell your house “as is” and adjust the price accordingly. Invest in minor repairs that can make a significant difference, such as repainting walls or fixing broken fixtures. Focus on the positive aspects of your property, like location or potential for renovation. Offer incentives to potential buyers, such as closing cost assistance or a home warranty. Is it better to sell now or wait for a better market? Deciding whether to sell now or wait depends on your individual situation. If you’re facing financial difficulties or need to relocate urgently, selling now might make more sense. However, if you have time and can afford to wait for market conditions to improve, you may potentially receive a better price for your property. To make the best decision, consult with a real estate agent and analyze the current market trends in your area. How does a recession impact house selling prospects? During a recession, the demand for houses typically decreases, leading to lower property prices and longer time on the market. Buyers may face increased difficulty securing financing, making it harder for them to purchase a home. To sell your house during a recession: Be prepared to be patient and possibly accept a lower price. Make your property stand out with strategic improvements and competitive pricing. Consider offering incentives to attract buyers. Working closely with a real estate agent who understands the challenges of selling during a recession can help ensure a smoother process.
