title: Judge rejects ex-city councilman’s PTSD diversion bid in SoCal corruption case
author: Quinn Welsch
content: SAN DIEGO (CN) — A San Diego Superior Court judge on Monday had sharp words for a former city councilman from Poway, California , who sought to have his criminal prosecution diverted into mental health treatment after arguing that his military-related post-traumatic stress disorder contributed to his purported misconduct as a public official. Former Poway Councilman Arthur “Tony” Blain, 60, is accused of multiple counts of felony bribery, theft and perjury following his short stint on the city council that began in December 2024. Blain, a former Army colonel and a physician, was recalled in November 2025 . His attorneys filed a motion for mental health diversion, arguing his career in the military resulted in him having a binary view of good versus evil, which led to his misconduct. But Superior Court Judge Polly Shamoon rejected the defense’s arguments in a bench ruling, finding Blain’s actions were the work of sophisticated and strategic political maneuvering that was not obviously connected to his PTSD. The District Attorney’s Office says Blain committed perjury when he submitted a sworn complaint to the Fair Political Practices Commission that claimed he was a current Poway council member in an attack against a political opponent. Blain is also accused of vote trading, which is a felony. “This seems to me nothing more than anger and resentment,” Shamoon said of the former councilman. “Because he is an unsuccessful and unliked politician, he lashes out. Those aren’t behaviors being motivated by mental health. That is not the purpose of mental health diversion.” Defense attorney David Shapiro argued his client’s judgment was clouded by PTSD after serving honorably in the military for decades. “It’s a fight or flight complex,” Shapiro argued. “In his mind, he is fighting against people he thinks are doing the public wrong. Dr. Blain was taking a position that he was righting a wrong. That same interaction is what took place during his time on the council.” But Shamoon questioned this argument. “He thought it was good for the people of Poway to lie?” Shamoon asked Shapiro. “When he realized what he did was wrong, he doesn’t stand down. He doubles down.” Blain is also accused of attempting to destroy evidence of his communications, which is also a felony. He faces a related civil lawsuit from the city of Poway over claims he violated California public records laws . Shamoon found insufficient evidence of a connection between his diagnosis and the crimes he is accused of. “There has to be a substantial connection to the crime, and that’s what I’m having a hard time with now,” she said. The connection did not have to be linear, Shapiro argued. “In this case, in his mind, the PTSD was shadowing his reality,” he continued. “He thought he was the hero. He is a physician. He doesn’t need this. He didn’t have to run for city council.” “If that’s true, why didn’t he back down?” Shamoon asked. “We may think that’s unreasonable, but that’s what the PTSD caused,” Shapiro said. “It goes to show this type of mentality — of the good he thought he was doing.” However, San Diego Deputy District Attorney Chandelle Boyce argued Blain’s PTSD symptoms did not appear to cloud his judgment in other aspects of his life. “We see the defendant was functioning at an exceptionally high level,” she said. “There is no evidence that he was having issues in these other domains of his life.” Blain acted out of defiance, not anxiety, she argued. “Look at the facts of the charged offense,” she said. “They were deliberate, strategic, and happened over a lengthy period of time. It doesn’t fit with him having a cognitive decline.” Poway Mayor Steve Vaus, who was present in the audience, said he was pleased with the judge’s decision to deny Blain’s motion for mental health diversion. “The judge clearly understood that this was systematic,” Vaus told reporters outside the courtroom. “It was calculated. It was for his personal and political gain, and it did not qualify him for mental health diversion.” Blain is said to have harassed city employees and was the first public official to be censured by the city last year . Vaus, who found himself in Blain’s crosshairs at one point, said the saga sowed distrust in the Poway government. “It’s tragic in these days,” Vaus said. “We’re proud of how we run Poway, and it put a stain on it, and we’re still trying to work our way back.”

title: How Lula overcame a first-round defeat to win Brazil’s presidential election
author: Marília Marasciulo
content: RIO DE JANEIRO (CN) — It was shortly before 9 p.m. Sunday when shouts of “Lula! Lula!” began echoing through the streets of Copacabana. Fireworks erupted, residents banged pots and pans from their windows, and others switched on red lights. “É tetra!” (“It’s the fourth!”), some shouted, in a celebration reminiscent of Brazil winning the World Cup. In the background, horns played the familiar tune of “Olê, olê, olê, olá, Lula, Lula,” one of the best-known chants from the president’s election campaigns. After trailing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round , President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a fourth term by winning Sunday’s runoff . Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court officially confirmed the result at 9:10 p.m. With 51.79% of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, Lula became the first presidential candidate since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1985 to win a runoff after finishing second in the first round. “This night does not belong only to the winning tickets. It belongs, above all, to Brazilian voters, the main protagonists of the elections and the beneficiaries of all the work carried out by the Electoral Justice system,” Justice Kassio Nunes Marques , president of the Superior Electoral Court, said. The reversal carried particular significance in Rio de Janeiro, the political birthplace of the Bolsonaro family. In the city, Lula went from 43.91% of the vote in the first round , against Bolsonaro’s 47.88%, to 51.54%, against 48.46%. Rio was one of only two Brazilian state capitals where the president managed to overturn the first-round result. João Feres, a professor at Rio de Janeiro State University’s Institute of Social and Political Studies, said Lula’s win did not follow the traditional logic of electoral campaigns centered on political alliances. He said mobilization both online and in the streets helped bring voters who had stayed home in the first round to the polls. Abstention fell from 21.08% in the first round to 19.22% in the runoff, the lowest rate for a presidential runoff since 2006, according to the Superior Electoral Court. Lula gained 10.38 million additional votes between the two rounds, while Bolsonaro added about 3.7 million. The president finished the race with 64.25 million votes, compared with his rival’s 59.83 million. João Ricardo Matta, a professor of strategy and market intelligence at Fundação Getulio Vargas, attributed Lula’s comeback to higher voter turnout, a decline in rejection of Lula and Bolsonaro’s failure to win over supporters of defeated first-round candidates. According to a Quaest poll released Oct. 21, rejection of Lula fell from 53% to 47%, while Bolsonaro’s edged down from 54% to 52%, within the margin of error. Matta said Lula’s campaign changed strategies after the first round, stepping up digital mobilization, returning to the streets and focusing on voters’ everyday concerns. Congressman André Janones of the Sustainability Network party played a central role in that shift, creating the “Exército do Lula” (“Lula’s Army”) WhatsApp channel, which grew from around 60,000 to nearly 11 million followers in three weeks. “The achievement was turning engagement into action, something most digital campaigns fail to do,” Matta said. Bolsonaro, meanwhile, showed excessive confidence in victory and, according to Matta, damaged his image during the debates. During the final debate, broadcast by TV Globo two days before the runoff, Flávio mocked Lula’s physical disability by referring to his “nine fingers,” a reference to a finger the president lost in a workplace accident. Lula demanded an apology, which Bolsonaro eventually gave. Matta said Flávio’s mocking tone unsettled older voters and hurt his campaign. “Flávio dominated the conversation among his own supporters, while Lula reduced resistance among everyone else. And runoffs are won by doing the latter,” Matta said. Bolsonaro did not immediately acknowledge his defeat. On Sunday night, the senator announced he would seek to annul the election, arguing Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin’s decision to extend voting until 7 p.m. had undermined equal conditions for voters. The extension followed complaints about insufficient public transportation in several cities. Bolsonaro’s campaign had also requested extended voting hours in municipalities affected by heavy rain and flooding. According to electoral court data, only 34,330 votes were recorded after 5 p.m., representing 0.03% of the total. On Monday, Bolsonaro backed away from his plan to seek annulment of the election and instead announced in a social media video that he would seek to disqualify Lula’s winning ticket over claims of abuse of political and economic power. In the same video, he said federal police had ordered him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports under a ruling by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes. He was also barred from leaving Brazil. The restrictions were imposed as part of a money laundering investigation. In his first speech after the victory, Lula gave the floor to Vice President Geraldo Alckmin before thanking voters, particularly young and elderly Brazilians who had participated in the mobilization in the final weeks of the campaign. Lula also thanked Janones for his role in the campaign and announced plans to expand public participation in government decisions and strengthen direct communication with Brazilians through digital platforms. He also called for regulating major technology companies, which he accused of trying to influence the election’s outcome . Rodrigo Stumpf González, a political science professor at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, said he expects a realignment of Brazil’s political forces, with the traditional right regaining some of the influence it had lost to the more confrontational wing represented by the Bolsonaro family. González said Lula will struggle to pass legislation in a Congress dominated by conservative forces . However, with no prospect of seeking a fifth term, the president may focus more on his political legacy and use his electoral support as leverage in negotiations. “Lula is now beginning to think about his legacy, rather than merely managing the present,” González said. Courthouse News reporter Marília Marasciulo is based in Brazil.

title: Relying on circumstantial evidence, prosecutors try to prove man murdered and dismembered his wife
author: Joan Hennessy
content: MANASSAS, Va. (CN) — At the end of July 2024, the household of Naresh Bhatt went through 160 gallons of water during a two-hour period — a way-above-the-norm figure that prosecutors presented as evidence Monday in an attempt to convince a jury that Bhatt murdered his wife, dismembered her body and cleaned up the mess. As the fourth week of the murder trial began, Prince William County, Virginia, prosecutors sought to shore up a circumstantial case against Bhatt, 39, who is accused of murder, defiling a body and concealing a body in connection with the 2024 disappearance of Mamta Bhatt, 28. He has pleaded not guilty.  Wayne Martin, a public works official in Manassas Park, showed the jury a printout of water usage at the Bhatt household, and the line of figures generally ranged from two gallons to 30 gallons per hour. But on July 31, 2024, the household used 48 gallons between 11 a.m. and noon and 111 gallons from noon until 1 p.m. That much water “would be equivalent to having a faucet open all the way or a severe plumbing issue,” Martin said. But he didn’t suspect plumbing issues, because the water usage dropped to normal levels in the next hour. The testimony was an attempt by prosecutors to prove their contention that the missing woman was murdered. Mamta Bhatt was last seen during a video call on July 29, 2024, weeks before her daughter’s first birthday. Police officers were unable to find her body. Prosecutors also displayed a reciprocating saw that Naresh Bhatt purchased at a Home Depot, confirmed by Mark Hernandez of Home Depot’s corporate security. Asked whether the saw could be used to dismember a human being, Hernandez responded that he believed so. After Mamta Bhatt disappeared, Naresh Bhatt gave the saw to a landscaper, who later turned it over to police. “Upon opening the saw on the inside I observed reddish brown stains and what I thought looked to be hairlike strands,” testified Andrea Feldman, a George Mason University professor and former crime scene investigator for Manassas Police. She believed the stains were blood. At one point, jurors stood and leaned forward as Feldman showed them the saw. Another witness examined search engine queries made by Naresh Bhatt, a government contractor, in April 2024, roughly three months before his wife’s disappearance. One of his queries read: “How long does (it) take to get married after spouse dies,” according to Daniel Moore of the White House Military Office, Information Technology, who was asked to examine Naresh Bhatt’s searches. Moore testified that he’d also searched: “How long does (it) take to get married after spouse dead,” and “happy new year message to girlfriend.” Under cross-examination, Moore admitted he was not standing over Naresh Bhatt’s shoulder and thus could not definitively say who wrote those search questions. Prosecutors describe Naresh Bhatt as an abusive husband who offered shifting explanations for his wife’s disappearance. In previous testimony, Feldman described spotting specks of blood on a window in the couple’s bathroom. Officers then used a chemical that detects the presence of blood — even if it is old or has been cleaned up — and discovered a suspected blood stain. Prosecutors also presented footage from an apartment complex security camera showing Naresh Bhatt disposing of trash bags around the time of his wife’s disappearance. Circuit Court Judge Kimberly Irving is presiding over the trial.

title: New Mexico Pueblo tribes sue over eagle-take plan at national preserve
author: Alan Riquelmy
content: (CN) — Two New Mexico Pueblo tribes sued the federal government on Monday over its plan to permit a third Pueblo tribe to “take” eagles within the Valles Caldera National Preserve. The Pueblo of Santa Clara and Pueblo of Zia argue the preserve exists to protect, preserve and restore wildlife. They claim the National Park Service’s decision to grant the Pueblo of Jemez a take permit violates the National Environmental Policy Act because it conflicts with the preserve’s purpose. “Both Pueblos have deep and meaningful connections to the preserve and its wildlife, and the eagle populations of the preserve are considered by the Pueblos to be integral parts of their cultural and religious practices within the preserve, and essential to those practices, and should not be destroyed,” the plaintiffs write. They ask a federal judge to declare a finding of no significant impact, which opens the door to a special use permit, arbitrary and capricious, an abuse of discretion or otherwise unlawful. They also seek to block the Park Service from issuing a permit allowing the eagle take. “Take” means the capturing or killing of an animal. The plaintiffs say the preserve encompasses the crater of a collapsed volcano about 14 miles in diameter and has long been used by Pueblo tribes for religious and cultural practices. This summer, the Pueblo of Jemez applied for a special use permit to conduct eagle take in the preserve this month and next. The Park Service consulted with other tribes, including the plaintiffs, and told them it had proposed a determination of “no adverse effect.” The plaintiffs say the preserve’s superintendent later met with them to discuss their objections to the permit. “Both Pueblos’ representatives expressed their profound religious connections to the landscape of the caldera and the plants and wildlife it contains, and stated that the Valles Caldera should remain a sanctuary for eagles and other non-game wildlife, and maintained their objections to the proposed issuance of the SUP,” they add. The plaintiffs say they continued to object during the environmental assessment’s public comment period, citing what they called misleading or incorrect facts and flawed or incomplete reasoning. On Monday, the day the plaintiffs sued, the Park Service published its finding of no significant impact, clearing the way for a special use permit allowing the Pueblo of Jemez to conduct eagle-take activities. The plaintiffs say the Park Service provided no population studies or other information showing the take would not adversely affect eagles in the area. “Allowing harm to come to eagles in the preserve is strongly against the Pueblos’ cultural and religious values,” they add. “The Pueblos believe that the taking of eagles within the preserve would profoundly and adversely affect their cultural and religious relationship to the preserve.” The Pueblo of Santa Clara and Pueblo of Zia say they consider eagles sacred and that allowing their take would violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. They also say the law requires the Park Service to protect traditional cultural and religious sites within the preserve and does not authorize activity beyond providing access to those sites. The plaintiffs say the Pueblo of Jemez has previously received a special use permit for eagle take and that the Park Service failed to comply with the law. In 2023, the Park Service issued a permit without consulting other tribes — a requirement under the National Historic Preservation Act. The Park Service couldn’t be reached for comment.

title: Federal immigration officials held in contempt for disobeying court orders
author: Megan Butler
content: (CN) — Federal immigration officials failed to obey court orders and arrested a man just two months after his ordered release from immigration detention, a Pennsylvania judge ruled Monday. As a result, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Philadelphia Field Office Director John Rife were held in civil contempt and ordered to pay attorney fees and related costs. U.S. Magistrate Judge J. Maureen Kelly said the officials also failed to comply with an order to produce body camera footage and provided inconsistent explanations and questionable sworn statements about the arrest. Kelly said the June 26, 2026, arrest of Nain Vasquez Gonzalez by Department of Homeland Security agents was “unauthorized and unlawful.” While the circumstances of the arrest are disputed, Kelly said federal immigration officials failed to justify it or explain why they ignored court orders. She said their filings presented in defense contained “baffling inconsistent and changing stories.” Gonzalez claims the agents asked whether his name was Fernando Daniel, did not believe him when he said no and refused to review his identification. Officials told the judge that ICE agents were searching for “intended targets” during a “nationwide surge in enforcement” that day and that Gonzalez resembled one of them, despite reportedly wearing a surgical mask. They claimed agents photographed Gonzalez and analyzed the image using facial recognition software on their cellular devices. Gonzalez was held for 11 hours before being released. The arrest violated a court order granting his release from immigration detention, after the Third Circuit Court of Appeals found Gonzalez’s detention was unconstitutionally prolonged. His more than three years spent in immigration detention was largely attributable to failures by the Board of Immigration Appeals to comply with the Circuit Court’s mandates, Kelly wrote. “The problem – beyond, of course, the issue of petitioner’s underlying arrest in direct violation of the order granting him habeas relief from his immigration detention, is how much effort it has taken to get to this point as the result of respondent’s conduct,” Kelly added. In one of several sworn declarations, ICE Supervisory Detention and Deportation Officer Michael B. Smith said he reviewed two hours of body camera footage from the 20 arrests made that day but found no video of Gonzalez. Smith said ICE policy requires body cameras only under certain circumstances, which he speculated did not apply to Gonzalez’s arrest. The arresting officer told the court his body camera was not operational because the battery had not been charged. Kelly said immigration officials also failed to timely comply with court orders to identify the arresting officer. Assistant Field Office Director John Belluardo said in a declaration that officials could not readily identify the officers involved because they wore masks to obscure their identities for security. He also said none of the officers questioned recalled interacting with Gonzalez. Kelly said the declarations contained seemingly conclusive factual statements from individuals who, upon review, lacked independent knowledge to support what they had attested to under oath. “Such conduct is most disconcerting,” she wrote. “At best, it undercuts the credibility of any future testimony from these individuals, and wastes the resources of the court and the litigants. At worst, it is possible perjury,” Kelly added. Kelly concluded that immigration officials either willfully tried to obfuscate the circumstances of Gonzalez’s arrest and detention and the identities of the agents involved, or were unable to maintain proper records, use their equipment or comply with court orders. The Philadelphia Immigration and Customs Enforcement Field Office has faced other legal challenges. In July, it was sued over a surveillance policy imposing electronic ankle monitoring and intensive supervision requirements on noncitizens without individualized review. The American Civil Liberties Union also sued the office in June for abandoning a policy requiring officers to justify re-arrest and detention through an individualized determination of a material change in circumstances, such as an indication of new danger or flight risk.

title: Ninth Circuit tosses Trump appeal in California election challenge
author: Edvard Pettersson
content: (CN) — The Ninth Circuit on Monday threw out the Trump administration’s emergency appeal to force California to set aside votes by residents who the administration maintains might not be U.S. citizens. The three-judge panel issued a decision the day after it held an unusual Sunday hearing. In a per curium order, the panel said it had no jurisdiction over the case because the federal government gave the trial judge just 15 hours to consider its expedited request for a temporary restraining order before filing its appeal. “The United States’ claimed emergency, at least in part, is a self-constructed one,” the panel wrote. “At least part of the delay here is attributable to the United States’ own delay in filing suit, in realizing that existing California state law governs the issuance and processing of ballots, in recognizing that California has millions of registered voters and processes ballots on a schedule aligned with that scale, and in communicating to the court its desired relief.” The appellate panel granted the request by the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder/county clerk to dismiss the appeal. The Department of Homeland Security claimed in July that there were as many as 190,000 noncitizens included on California’s voter rolls, yet it waited until Oct. 15 to file a lawsuit to prevent the state from counting about 20,000 votes before it could be verified these weren’t from noncitizens. At the same time, the government had initially asked for a decision by Nov. 3 on its bid for a temporary restraining order, and U.S. District Judge David Carter set a hearing Tuesday afternoon in Los Angeles to hear arguments on the request. However, in the evening of Oct. 21, the government asked Carter to issue a decision by noon the next day because, it said, it had just learned LA County had already counted 331,000 mail-in ballots since Oct. 5. Seth Waxman, an attorney for the LA County registrar, argued at Sunday’s hearing that it wasn’t credible that the Justice Department was oblivious that the county had been counting early votes because that’s what it is required to do and the process is well publicized. The Trump administration claims California is violating the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution by knowingly facilitating the votes of noncitizens, thereby frustrating the federal prohibition against noncitizens voting in federal elections. At Sunday’s hearing, an attorney for the U.S. Justice Department failed to give a compelling explanation of the basis for the government’s claims that California permits noncitizens to vote and referred to third-party data bases that Homeland Security had checked against the state’s voter rolls. “Today’s ruling is a positive development and a welcome speed bump to Trump’s disgusting attacks on the Constitution and our country’s democracy,” California Governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement. U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Donald Trump appointee, wrote separately that even if the Ninth Circuit panel had jurisdiction over the government’s appeal, which he didn’t think they did, it was unlikely that the government would prevail on the merits of its appeal. “There is no dispute that it is unlawful under both federal and California law for noncitizens to vote,” Bennett said. “Rather, this dispute is about the procedures used to enforce that prohibition, which plainly implicates the elections clause of the U.S. Constitution.” The federal statute under which voting by noncitizens is criminalized, however, doesn’t preempt California’s comprehensive statutory scheme for conducting elections that has been duly enacted under the elections clause, he said. “There is nothing in the text of § 611 that preempts the states’ primary authority in election administration; California can still (and in fact, it must) craft its own procedures governing congressional elections and ballot challenges in those elections,” Bennett added. U.S. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, also a Trump appointee, disagreed that the appellate panel had no jurisdiction to rule on the government’s appeal and echoed the federal government’s concern that a potentially large number of noncitizens’ ballots would be commingled with legal voters. “With the election only 14 days away and with every passing day bringing the possibility of more illegal votes, the federal government appealed to us,” Bumatay said. “Under Supreme Court precedent, this is enough to confer appellate jurisdiction.” U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Joe Biden appointee, also wrote separately to stress that it would be unfeasible to require that California, which requires a resident to certify they are a citizen when they register to vote, to start sequestering tens of thousands of ballots in the middle of an ongoing election. “At the eleventh hour, the United States seeks to shift the burdens of its priorities onto California and co-opt the state into carrying out the executive branch’s policies on a massive scale,” Sanchez said. Representatives of the U.S. Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: With nation’s oldest science museum on the brink, where is Philly’s mayor?
author: Jackson Healy
content: PHILADELPHIA (CN) — While the Philadelphia City Council sought on Monday to better understand why the oldest natural history museum west of the Atlantic shuttered last month, representatives for the city’s mayor could not be found, announcing they would not appear just minutes before the hearing was set to begin. Founded in 1812 with its museum opening in 1828, the Academy of Natural Sciences is the oldest natural science research institution across the Americas. On Sept. 1, however, Drexel University — which has maintained a close formal affiliation with the academy since 2011 — announced the museum would close its doors by the end of month, ending a nearly 200-year existence. Shortly after the announcement, the William Penn Foundation, a Philadelphia-based grant foundation, proposed a year’s worth of funding as a bridge to finding ongoing support and developing a long-term plan for the museum; Drexel has not accepted the offer. Backlash to the sudden shutdown was swift. Museum advocates accused Drexel of seeking to sell the academy’s building — a lucrative plot on Philadelphia’s Benjamin Franklin Parkway — and have demanded city intervention The City Council obliged, authorizing the council’s Committee on Legislative Oversight to examine the closure and consider possibilities for continuing public access to the museum. Monday’s hearing was set to bring together mayoral representatives, Drexel and academy leadership, and museum advocates to provide clarity as to how the closure was allowed to occur, and how the museum could be revived. The problem? The representative for Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker — Patricia Wellenbach, who serves as deputy mayor for strategic and philanthropic initiatives as well as senior adviser to the Academy of Natural Sciences — informed the City Council at the last minute that she wasn’t showing up. Instead, Wellenbach provided brief written testimony for the hearing and said her testimony would not be appropriate, as she cannot speak on behalf of Drexel or the academy. Councilmember Jeffery Young Jr. disagreed in dramatic fashion, ripping the testimony in half in front of the hearing’s audience to roaring applause before castigating Parker for declining to send any representation. “To tell taxpayers that someone who is on loan to the academy on the taxpayers’ dime is not the right person to come talk to us — I call BS on that,” Young said. “I think that is a disrespect to the Philadelphians as someone who is paid by the taxpayers.” Young continued, announcing plans to subpoena administrative officials in following sessions — plans that committee chair Isaiah Thomas said would be approved. Representing Drexel President Antonio Merlo, the university’s executive director of operations Melissa Richman told the committee Drexel could not find a likely future for the museum at its current location. “These steps, taken jointly by the academy and Drexel’s leadership, to close the museum were neither abrupt nor hasty,” Richman said before facing a rain of boos from audience members. “The reality confronting the academy and Drexel leadership was undeniable: the current operating model was quietly devouring the academy from within.” While Richman expressed the university’s purported plans to find a new home “for the public to engage with the academy and its collection,” Thomas questioned the university’s motives, noting Drexel never contacted the City Council for financial aid regarding the museum despite having done so for other budget shortfalls in recent years. “We love to step up to the plate when our institutions are at a time of need and spend taxpayer dollars in ways that taxpayers want to see their dollars,” Thomas told Richman. “Convince me that it was an accident that you didn’t come to us this time, and that this is not a land grab for business.” In response, Richman stated that Drexel has been discussing the issue with representatives for both Parker and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro — claims that could not be further investigated by the committee, as no representatives for Parker were present. Still, Councilmember Quetcy Lozada continued attacks on the university’s lack of communication with city leaders “When Drexel has been in financial instability, or there has been financial questions, Drexel has never had a problem to come to us and say, ‘This is what is happening, this is how we need help, and we need you to back us up,’” Lozada said. “And now, in a situation like this, that’s what should have occurred.” Speaking to academy board of trustees chair Suzanne Biemiller, the committee sought answers as to how much the academy would need to reopen the museum. Biemiller’s answer — that the museum’s fiscal year 2025 operating costs amounted to about $3.6 million — was so stunningly low that the committee granted her several minutes to verify the math. “If it can cost taxpayers $3.6 million to keep that open — when we as a city have a $7 billion budget, and we contribute millions of dollars to other cultural institutions in the city — I think that’s something that was very, very doable,” Young told Biemiller. “We have the appetite, and we have the capacity to be able to protect and save arts and culture in the city of Philadelphia,” Lozada added, before turning to Drexel’s representatives. “It just needs to be prioritized by those who are leading those causes. And with numbers like the ones you just shared with us, it doesn’t show us that you care about arts and culture.” Further criticizing Drexel, Councilmember Anthony Phillips bashed Merlo for failing to appear before the committee — an absence Richman attributed to academic accreditors visiting the university concurrent to the hearing. “I think he thinks we’re not smart, and if he does think we’re smart, he doesn’t care about how people perceive [him],” Phillips said. “He’s not being perceived very well right now … The fact that he’s not reached out to any Philadelphia City Council member, or even had some meetings with these individuals that are here today, it shows who he is.” In addition to critiques over Drexel’s handling of the academy’s financial needs and its perceived disrespect for the City Council, Councilmember Nina Ahmad suggested Drexel’s use of charitable assets for a now-nonpublic institution may actually run afoul of the law, adding that the City Council would follow up to investigate potential legal concerns. Representing advocates for the museum’s reopening, Paul Steinke, executive director for the Preservation Alliance — a Philadelphia-area nonprofit dedicated to preserving the region’s historic resources — emphasized the importance of maintaining the city’s educational and research establishments. “Paleontologists, biologists, oceanographers, ornithologists — lots of career trajectories that I can’t even pronounce — they come here to Philadelphia to do research because the Academy of Natural Sciences is a world-class institution,” Steinke told the committee. “And if Philadelphia wants to stay a world-class city, it needs to support its world-class institutions.”

title: Texas requests steep penalties against Malcolm Tanner
author: Kirk McDaniel
content: MENTONE, Texas (CN) – Texas attorneys squared off Monday with an Indiana-based social media influencer in a Loving County courthouse, seeking a permanent injunction and stiff penalties over his plans to settle in the county. Arriving at the courthouse Monday afternoon, Malcolm Tanner, an entrepreneur and presidential candidate known on social media as Dr. Malcolm Tanner, offered only a brief comment to Courthouse News: “Come see the show.” The show has been nearly a year in the making. Starting in 2025, Tanner offered free homes and a $5,000 monthly stipend to anyone who moved onto undeveloped land he purchased in Loving County, with the stated goal of uplifting Black Americans. He hoped to register enough followers to outnumber the county’s roughly 60 residents, elect members of his group and gain control of its $60 million budget. The state sued Tanner in October 2025, claiming he violated the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act by falsely advertising nonexistent homes and misrepresenting the property’s condition. The state also claimed he created a public health nuisance by dumping human waste on the property because it lacked sewage, violating the state Health and Safety Code. The court ordered Tanner to stop advertising the land or hosting people there without proper sewage. He was also ordered to pay $220,000 in civil penalties. Before the first case was resolved, however, Tanner moved his followers onto a new parcel uncovered during the lawsuit, prompting the state to file a second case, the subject of Monday’s hearing. Assistant Attorney General Andrew Brown opened the hearing by recalling his words from an earlier proceeding. “A year ago, I stood before you and said Tanner promised homes and provided homelessness,” Brown said. “Today, we are here to determine what to do about that.”  In September, Loving County District Court Judge Alan Nicholas granted the state’s motion for summary judgment, finding Tanner, who is representing himself, liable for violating state law. Monday’s hearing considered the state’s request for a permanent injunction and possible civil penalties. At its peak, about 30 people lived on the property in RVs and tents. Since the state sued, that number has fallen to fewer than six. Brown said Tanner made 100 deceptive online posts seen by his 200,000 followers. At $10,000 per violation, he estimated the state could seek $2 billion in civil penalties. Instead, the state focused on two Facebook posts that received a combined 854 likes, reducing its request to $8.5 million. Assistant Attorney General Lauren McGee also asked the court to award the state $12,350 for Tanner’s Health and Safety Code violations, $2,400.75 for a March 2 deposition he failed to attend and $417,860.50 in attorney fees. The state also asked Nicholas to permanently block Tanner from making false or misleading statements about his property, its dwellings and their quality. Tanner, representing himself, objected to several of the requested awards. When given the opportunity to present evidence and call witnesses, he tried to call followers in the courtroom. McGee objected, saying the state had not been notified that he intended to call witnesses. Nicholas said unless Tanner was able to produce a witness who could speak to the condition of sewage on his property, he would not be permitted to call his witnesses. In her closing statement, McGee told the court that Tanner should be allowed to advertise his land as long as he is honest. “He can buy land in Loving County as long as he follows the law,” McGee said. “But people came from far out of state, giving up their lives for his promises.”  In closing, Tanner blamed the state for making people homeless by blocking him from moving them onto his land. He also invoked the American dream and the freedom to move throughout the country in defending his plan to settle Loving County. “If this is the way Americans are met by moving around the state or the country, then this would put them in fear of having their freedoms stripped away from the state,” Tanner said. Nicholas sympathized with Tanner’s ideals, calling them “as American as it gets.” But he said the issue was not people moving to the county; it was the advertising that brought them there. “We are all taught in school that the idea of manifest destiny pushed people westward until they encompassed the continent,” Nicholas explained. “They came on horseback and in wagons and endured hardships that we could not imagine. They were promised raw land. Not established land.” The state’s attorneys declined to comment on the case. Tanner likewise did not take questions. Nicholas gave Tanner 10 days to file a written objection to the state’s request for attorney fees, meaning a final order will not be entered until next week. While the second lawsuit nears resolution, Tanner’s legal issues in Loving County are far from over. In September, authorities in Crawfordsville, Indiana, arrested him on a Texas warrant. According to the warrant and a probable cause affidavit obtained by Courthouse News Service, Tanner confronted and threatened an oilfield worker who told members of his group not to sell water on property they did not own. He has been charged with terroristic threat, deadly conduct, criminal trespass, unlawful restraint and engaging in organized criminal activity. If convicted, he faces more than 20 years in prison. A formal hearing in the criminal case has yet to be set.

title: FTC accuses Dollar General of overcharging shoppers
author: Christina van Waasbergen
content: (CN) — The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states sued the discount chain Dollar General Monday, claiming it has routinely charged customers higher prices than listed on price tags or in advertisements for years. The chain markets itself as a convenient, low-priced alternative to big-box stores and operates more than 21,000 locations across the U.S., with most located in small towns or rural areas. In a complaint filed in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Tennessee, the FTC and states say it has failed to adopt adequate safeguards to prevent overcharging despite having failed thousands of pricing inspections and receiving tens of thousands of consumer complaints, resulting in millions of dollars in overcharges. “As a direct result of Dollar General’s unlawful conduct, consumers nationwide have paid significantly more than they expected for basic household goods and necessities, enriching Dollar General at the expense of the low-income and rural households it markets itself as serving,” the plaintiffs write in the complaint. “Rather than ensuring its prices at checkout are accurate, for years Dollar General avoided implementing safeguards to prevent continued overcharging, effectively shifting the burden of its own operational shortcomings onto the very communities and consumers who can least afford it.” The plaintiffs claim Dollar General has violated the FTC Act, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and state consumer protection and weights and measures laws. They seek monetary relief, including forfeiture, civil penalties and restitution for affected customers, as well as a permanent injunction to prevent future violations. “Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement . “The FTC’s action underscores the agency’s commitment to lowering costs for consumers by stopping deceptive pricing practices that harm Americans.” Earlier this month, Dollar General reached a settlement with New York’s attorney general in a similar case, agreeing to donate $1.875 million worth of food and personal items to Foodlink, a Rochester-based food bank and public health nonprofit. Dollar General has previously reached overcharge settlements with the attorneys general of Colorado , Pennsylvania and Vermont , as well as a $15 million settlement in a class action on behalf of overcharged consumers. In a statement , Dollar General disputed the allegations in the FTC’s lawsuit and vowed to vigorously defend against it. “Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store. As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur,” the company said. “When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement.”

title: Former FBI Director James Comey faces new criminal case in DC
author: Ryan Knappenberger
content: WASHINGTON (CN) — The Justice Department charged former FBI Director James Comey with two counts of wrongfully transmitting national defense information in 2016, according to a criminal complaint unsealed Monday.  The Justice Department filed the criminal complaint on Oct. 5 , requesting the case to remain under seal to avoid compromising ongoing criminal and grand jury investigations and endangering cooperating witnesses. Comey faces two charges under 18 U.S. Code Section 793, transmission of national defense information and conspiracy to transmit such information, which carry a prison term of 10 years if convicted. According to the criminal complaint, the charges stem from an Oct. 5, 2016, instance where Comey, as FBI director, transmitted a sensitive document related to national defense to New York Times reporter Charlie Savage for an article titled “Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance by Adapting Spam Filter.” In an opposition to Comey’s motion to dismiss the case, Special Assistant U.S. Attorney Dustin Farahnak said the article contained “first-time disclosures of classified information” stemming from an internal government email circulated hours before the article’s publication. “The United States’ investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” Farahnak said. “The investigation has uncovered evidence that Mr. Comey directed staff to speak to Mr. Savage about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.” Comey — represented by Jessica Carmichael of Carmichael Ellis & Brock and Patrick Fitzgerald of Cooley Law — moved to dismiss the charges on Oct. 9 , arguing the statute of limitations for the 2016 conduct had ended in 2021. Specifically, because the government has yet to obtain an indictment from a grand jury, the usual 10-year statute of limitations does not apply in the case. Even if the government had obtained an indictment, the fact the charges were filed on Oct. 9, placed the case still outside the 10-year window by five days. A Justice Department spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the department filed a waiver less criminal information to toll the statute of limitations, pointing to their opposition brief. “Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitation is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple circuit courts of appeals,” the spokesperson said. “This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further.” Under the Trump administration, the Justice Department has increasingly initiated criminal cases without first obtaining a grand jury indictment — despite the lower standard of proof compared to a jury trial, prosecutors have struggled to convince grand juries in Washington to approve felony indictments. On Friday , the Justice Department charged two former FBI officials with lying to Congress via a criminal complaint. The case marks the third federal case against Comey since President Donald Trump returned to the White House and began pushing the Justice Department to prosecute perceived political enemies. Federal prosecutors charged him with lying to Congress in the Eastern District of Virginia in September 2025 — the case was dismissed after a judge ruled interim U.S. Attorney Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed. In April, prosecutors filed charges in the Eastern District of North Carolina against Comey for posting a photo of seashells spelling out “86 47,” a term the government asserts call for violence against Trump. The case remains ongoing. Comey revealed in a Substack video post Monday afternoon, titled “Yet another case in DC,” that he was the subject of a criminal case in the nation’s capital, but did not share any details as to the nature of the case. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the DOJ, one that we cannot become numb to,” Comey said. “Nothing’s changed with me, I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people and I believe in an independent federal judiciary. “I’m still lucky to have an amazing family, an incredible group of lawyers who will stand up in court and fight the latest and whatever comes after this,” Comey added. “The next couple years are going to be hard for all of us, its really important that we stand straight and keep the faith in America.” The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden, a Trump appointee.

title: When funding cuts came — these scientists turned to journalism

content: Amid funding cuts to scientific institutions across the country, Isako Di Tomassi co-founded the McClintock Letters initiative, a science communication project that publishes opinion pieces written by scientists about their work and why it should continue to be funded. title: Andrea Horwath loses mayorship in Hamilton to newcomer Keanin Loomis
author: Meredith Bond
content: Andrea Horwath will no longer be the mayor of Hamilton after she was beat out by Keanin Loomis. Horwath served one term in Hamilton and was seeking reelection in the 2026 mayoral race, however, she is currently in third place with over 60 per cent of polls reporting. Loomism has nearly 42 pre cent of the vote right now with Rob Cooper about nine points behind him. Horwath has spent nearly three decades in politics, starting her career on Hamilton City Council. She was elected as MPP for Hamilton Centre in 2004 and become the Ontario NDP leader in 2009. She spent 13 years as the Ontario NDP leader, including a stint as the Official Opposition Leader, before resigning in 2022 to run for mayor in Hamilton.

title: Seven new councillors to join Toronto City Council after 2026 municipal election
author: Meredith Bond
content: Toronto will welcome seven new councillors for the next term after three incumbents were ousted and four councillors will be taking over in seats left empty. Here are the new and familiar faces who will be joining Toronto City Council for the next term: Beaches-East York Former Beaches-East York MP Nate Erskine-Smith will now be representing the constituency at the municipal level. Erskine-Smith beat out former broadcast journalist Natalie Johnson to win the seat on Toronto City Council. The seat was left empty when Brad Bradford decided to run for mayor. He lost to incumbent Olivia Chow. The former lawyer was first elected to the House of Commons in 2015 and was reelected in the following three elections. Parkdale-High Park Diana Chan McNally will represent Parkdale-High Park for the next council term, succeeding Gord Perks who held the ward for two decades. This is Chan McNally’s first foray into polticis but is a well-known advocate and community and crisis worker in the area. She was up against TDSB trustee Debbie King and community leader Nadia Guerrera. Scarborough North Incumbent Jamaal Myers has failed to capture a second term after being ousted by former MP Shaun Chen who captured over 35 per cent of the vote. Chen stepped down from federal politics earlier this year due to injuries sustained in a car accident that made it harder to travel to Ottawa. He spent a decade in the House of Commons as a part of the Liberal party and was a school board trustee prior to joining federal politics.   Myers came in second followed by former MPP and MP Han Dong. Dong had spent four years as an MPP for Trinity-Spadina before making the jump to federal politics for Don Valley North.  Toronto Centre Chris Moise has been ousted in Toronto Centre in a close race against Curran Stikuts. Stikus has worked at The 519 Community Centre for over a decade, most recently as the Director of Advocacy and receieved the endorsement of NDP MPP and former city councillor Kristyn Wong-Tam. He captured nearly 28 per cent of the vote while Moise was close behind at 23 per cent. Toronto-Danforth Sara Ehrhardt will take over Paula Fletcher’s spot on Toronto council, beating out former city councillor Mary Fragedakis and Dianne Saxe, who was previously the councillor for University-Rosedale. Ehrhardt, a former TDSB trustee, earned the coveted endorsement from Fletcher, pushing her to decisive victory on Monday night. She won with nearly 50 per cent of the vote, followed by Fragedakis. Saxe, who originally was running for reelection in University-Rosedale and jumped over to Toronto-Danforth, only captured eight per cent. University-Rosedale Mike Layton is back in Toronto City Council, winning his old ward University-Rosedale with nearly 50 per cent of the vote. The ward was left wide open after incumbent Dianne Saxe made a last minute decision to withdraw her candidacy for Ward 11 and run in Toronto Danforth. Layton, who is the stepson of Toronto mayor-elect Olivia Chow, originally left municipal politics in 2022 to spend more time with his family. York-South Weston Long-time councillor Francis Nunziata has been ousted in the ward she has held for nearly three decades. Chiara Padovani, who lost by only 94 votes in the last election, beat the incumbent handidly Nunziata had represented York South-Weston since 1997 and was the longest-serving member of council. She finished third in the ward race, capturing just 21 per cent of the vote.

title: Jay-Z will headline the Super Bowl halftime show at SoFi Stadium in Southern California
author: Cole Fortner
content: The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself. The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California. After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his “Jay-Z 30” concerts over the weekend. The run began with three shows at Yankee Stadium in New York, continued in London and ended in Southern California. Jay-Z’s Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league’s entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell, “If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now.” Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all. Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog includes the albums “Reasonable Doubt,” “The Blueprint” and “The Black Album,” and hit songs such as “Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem),” “99 Problems” and “Empire State of Mind,” his collaboration with Alicia Keys. His 1996 debut, “Reasonable Doubt,” was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame last year. Jay-Z’s career has extended into music publishing, artist management and sports. He co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes. Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. Bad Bunny performed at last season’s Super Bowl in February. His songs had sharp gains across streaming charts, playlists and music discovery platforms in the hours following the show.

title: Olivia Chow batters Bradford on way to second term as Toronto mayor
author: Michael Talbot
content: A pesky and persistent Brad Bradford may have been nipping at the heels of Olivia Chow, but in the end, he got the boot. Torontonians voted to give Chow a clear second mandate as mayor on Monday night, emphatically ending Bradford’s improbable comeback story. Chow claimed a resounding double-digit victory, but polls heading into election night were anything but clear. When it mattered most, however, Chow’s supporters assured her re-election. “The people of Toronto have spoken,” Chow said during her victory speech. “I am grateful, I am humble and I am so proud of our city. What an election, it was a hard-fought election.” Chow acknowledged Bradford as a formidable opponent and was gracious in victory. “We had our differences, we fought hard,” she said. “Councillor Bradford brought new energy and introduced new ideas that people cared about and made his case for them and I respect that. “I know we share a love for Toronto and our belief in its future.” Back in September, Bradford trailed by as many as 17 points — a deficit he slowly chipped away at with bold promises, like freezing property taxes for one year, cutting the land transfer tax for homes under $1.1 million, and offering free TTC rides if your vehicle is more than 15 minutes late. His polling numbers gained a boost when Chris Alexander dropped out of the race earlier this month, and at times it seemed to be anyone’s race to win. Bradford conceded defeat and was equally respectful of Chow while speaking to his disappointed supporters. “The people of Toronto have spoken and they have decided that she will be returning to the mayor’s office. She is the mayor of the city. Nobody can doubt that, it’s undisputable and she has my good wishes.” Bradford said he spoke with Chow on the phone shortly after it became clear she would be re-elected. “I said I want her to succeed, and my supporters … they want her to succeed too, they all do, because we all love this city, we know it can be better, and we have to come together to make that happen. “This is not the result that we were hoping for tonight … but I also have this feeling … of immense gratitude for the opportunity to put our ideas forward, our vision of a better Toronto.” &&&&&&&&&&&&&&&& Hard fought campaign During the campaign, Bradford implored Toronto to choose change, while Chow pointed to a track record of progress while painting herself as the more compassionate candidate. “I’m feeling great because at the end of the day, I believe Toronto is a place where people support each other, care for each other, stand up for each other, and they know that we are stronger together and that has always been at the core of the values that I have being the mayor of this city,” Chow said during a stop in Toronto’s Riverdale neighbourhood earlier Monday. Despite her confidence, she still seemed to recognize that her surging opponent was dangerously close to toppling her political ambitions. “The race is close, your vote will decide it,” she said. “The question facing everyone in Toronto is a simple one — who do you trust to make good decisions for our city and who do you trust to stand up for you, to listen when you’re worried about paying the bills, to protect the things that make Toronto special and to make the decisions that will shape the city our children and our grandchildren inherit.” WATCH LIVE: Coverage of CityVote on CityNews 24/7 at 7:30 p.m. ET. You can watch it here . Chow was first elected as the 66 th mayor of Toronto in 2023 following John Tory’s resignation. She became the first woman and first Chinese-Canadian to serve as mayor since amalgamation, edging front-runners Ana Bailão and Mark Saunders. Bradford ran in 2023 too, finishing in eighth place. This time around, the 40-year-old former urban planner and councillor for Beaches-East York promised to make Toronto safer and relieve congestion — issues that clearly resonated with voters, but not enough to award him the city’s top job. “This city is stuck,” Bradford said during a campaign stop in Etobicoke last weekend. “We’re stuck in traffic, we’re stuck waiting for the bus that doesn’t show up, we’re stuck feeling less safe.” To make his lofty goals happen he planned to hire 1,000 new police officers over four years and make the Eglinton East LRT his top transit priority. He’s also vowed to better coordinate construction-related road closures with big events in the city to prevent some of the Big Smoke’s notorious traffic jams. He also vowed to slice Torontonians’ water bills by 25 per cent by making Toronto Water a public agency — a move that irked renowned environmentalist and activist David Suzuki, who called the plan “crazy.” Chow seized the moment to stoke fears that Bradford would “hand control of water to the Ford government,” which would then have the power to bring in private investors. “It’s a scheme that no one is asking for,” Chow said of the plan. “Why is he doing it? Who is talking to him? I don’t understand just putting our water at risk.” Chow and Bradford also clashed on the contentious issue of bike lanes, with Bradford approving of their removal along a stretch of Bloor Street West despite previously voting in favour of them. Chow used that as more evidence that Bradford would do Premier Doug Ford’s bidding, rather than protect the interests of Torontonians. “We had Coun. Bradford inviting (Ford) in to say ‘come and take it (the bike lanes) away,’ ” Chow stressed. “That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of the city.” Bradford accused Chow of inflaming those issues to gain political support. “My opponent has engaged in fear mongering and scare tactics, misinformation, mistruths. I know Torontonians aren’t going to fall for it,” Bradford said on Monday. ‘I’m still that immigrant kid’: Chow Before she became mayor, Chow was previously a school trustee, an NDP MP for Trinity-Spadina, and a Toronto city councillor. Born in Hong Kong, she came to Toronto with her parents at the age of 13. On Monday, she said she’s still that “immigrant kid” who was able to realize a dream that epitomizes the heart of Toronto. “Toronto gave us a home, a place to begin again, a place where an immigrant kid from St. James Town could grow up to become your mayor and I’ve never forgotten that.” “I am still that immigrant kid who was born somewhere else and calls Toronto home. A person who knows how much it means when someone you elect truly cares what happens to you. That’s the kind of mayor I’ve always tried to be.”

title: Tedjo topples political veterans Crombie and Parrish in Mississauga mayoral upset
author: Meredith Bond
content: Alvin Tedjo may have started the Mississauga mayoral election as an underdog, but he has managed to beat out former mayor Bonnie Crombie and incumbent Carolyn Parrish to take over the city’s top job, CityNews projects. He won handidly, leading Parrish in second by over 20,000 votes, despite early polls showing a tight race leading up to election. “Our optimism, our hope, our vision for what this city could be, our positivity and our unstoppable effort to reach every single resident in the city of Mississauga, to put forward practical solutions that would make a difference in their lives and to earn their trust, all of that hard work has led us to this moment,” said Tedjo in his victory speech. “Mississauga has made a clear and historic choice to demand a change at City Hall … it’s the honour of a lifetime to stand here as the next mayor of Mississauga.” Tedjo, who previously served as Ward 2 councillor and finished second in the 2024 mayoral byelection, faced a tough contest from Crombie and Parrish.  He is the first man to be Mississauga’s mayor since 1978. Related: CityVote 2026: Live election results from across the GTA municipal elections Tedjo started the election polling far behind, but made major gains later in the campaign. He was able to secure the Peel police union’s endorsement and has promised a two-year property tax freeze if he was elected.  Crombie vacated her spot as Mississauga’s mayor in 2024 in order to run for the leadership of the Ontario Liberal Party. After failing to win a seat in the last provincial election, she formally resigned as the party leader in January 2026, only to enter the Mississauga mayor’s race in July. Parrish won the byelection triggered by Crombie’s resignation.  &&&&&&&&&&&&&&&& At her election party Monday night, Crombie said she had called Tedjo and congratulated him on his win. “Tonight, a new geneneration takes the reins. I wish you and the incoming council every success. I love Mississauga and I will cheering for our city to succed under your leadership.” In her concession speech, Parrish wished Tedjo good luck and said she was at peace with the result. “I know I did a good job,” Parrish said, adding she could’ve simplified her message. &&&&&&&&&&&&&&&&

title: Suspect wanted for alleged assault on Brampton bus
author: Joseph Ryan
content: Peel Regional Police (PRP) are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying a male suspect connected to an alleged assault that occurred on a Brampton Transit bus in May. Officers were called to Rutherford Road and Steeles Avenue around 5:15 p.m. on May 22. “The suspect and victim were both passengers on a public transit bus when the suspect allegedly attacked the victim without provocation,” police stated in a press release shared Monday. “During the altercation, the suspect struck the victim numerous times.” Officers say the suspect also knocked the victim’s phone out of their hand and their glasses off their face, causing damage to both. The victim sustained serious injuries to their head and face, according to investigators. Photos of the suspect have been shared.  The suspect is described as a male, approximately 5-foot-10. He was last seen wearing a blue baseball cap, a black bandana around his neck, a yellow and navy coloured jacket, blue jeans, dark-coloured shoes. He was also seen with a red, yellow, and blue backpack. Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

title: Trump administration asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 voters it says may be noncitizens
author: News Staff
content: SEATTLE (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges registered to vote without U.S. citizenship, less than two weeks after making a similar demand in California. The announcement is the latest sign of the administration’s attempts to sow doubts about the election or its outcome in states with races that will help determine control of the U.S. Senate and House. In a letter to Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by the more than 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots they might cast in next month’s midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters, and the state issues mail ballots to all of them. One listed voter last cast a ballot in 1994 At a news conference, Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in Seattle, said he believed the 405 voters identified so far represented “the tip of the iceberg.” “Because of limitations the state has placed on our investigation, we’ve only been able to uncover a fraction of the total number,” he said. Hobbs said he was reviewing the DOJ’s request. His office noted that the data shared by the department included the last time each of the 405 people voted. One was in 1994. “The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results,” Hobbs said. Much of the list was built based on “recent contacts” with suspected noncitizens, Floyd said, because federal officers are now routinely checking to see if the people they interact with are registered to vote. Lack of state cooperation a problem, DOJ says Without access to those state records, proving someone illegally voted will be difficult, Floyd said. The Justice Department has demanded information including addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters , even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections. Meanwhile, Washington officials have noted that changes in U.S. Postal Service operations have disenfranchised thousands of legitimate voters. Voting is underway The Washington request marks the third time this month that the Justice Department has brought a direct state challenge as voting is underway. All three states — Washington, California and Alaska — have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation’s Capitol. The race for Washington’s 3rd Congressional District is one of the most competitive in the country in this year’s midterm elections. Democrats are counting on Rep. Maria Gluesenkamp Perez winning reelection as crucial to their strategy of retaking the majority in the U.S. House. She has won twice in a district that also has supported Trump each time he’s been on the ballot. The Justice Department sued in California as part of a similar attempt to require the state to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. Another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. In California, a panel of federal appellate judges heard rare Sunday arguments and questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department’s demand. On Monday, they declined to rule on the expedited timeline the DOJ requested and sent it back to a lower court. The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections. Prior allegations have been overstated Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration’s list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States. The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized. Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump’s administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls but subsequent investigation found zero. In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county’s rolls. The Republican County Attorney determined there were actually eight. ___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho. Gene Johnson And Rebecca Boone, The Associated Press

title: Man accused of shooting pedestrians in Humber River trail with pellet gun
author: Joseph Ryan
content: Toronto police are searching for a man who is accused of firing a pellet gun at pedestrians walking along the Humber River Recreational Trail in Etobicoke. Officers were called to the area southwest of Lambton Park and north of Dundas Street West on Oct. 23 for reports of a man who was spotted riding an electric scooter with an airsoft weapon. Detectives said three individuals were allegedly struck by the pellets. The suspect then fled the trail heading eastbound toward Dundas Street West, according to police. Investigators describe the suspect as a white male, about six-feet in height, with a thin build. He was last seen wearing all black sportswear, and a black medical mask. The suspect vehicle is described as a black stand-up e-scooter with a red design on the rear. Police have not released any images or further description of the alleged suspect.

title: Toronto man sentenced to life with no parole for 16 years in murder of Liberty Village filmmaker, lawyer says
author: Dee Burman
content: A Toronto man has been sentenced to life in prison without a chance of parole for 16 years for killing his neighbour in Liberty Village three years ago, his lawyer confirmed to CityNews. Khoa Tran, 36, was found guilty of second-degree murder in the death of Reeyaz Habib, 56, in June of this year and sentenced in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice on Monday. Second-degree murder carries a sentence of life in prison without a chance of parole for at least 10 years. Related: Couple convicted of murdering neighbour in Liberty Village expected to be sentenced this week Friends of Liberty Village murder victim speak out at sentencing hearing Husband and wife convicted in Liberty Village murder trial Closing arguments in Liberty Village homicide case The body of Habib, a well-loved Toronto filmmaker, was discovered in the garbage compactor of a townhouse complex in Liberty Village in June 2023. Prosecutors alleged the brutal killing was triggered by an escalating dispute that all began over barbecue smoke wafting from Tran’s apartment below Habib’s unit. Tran denied the killing despite being caught on camera throwing Habib’s bike in the garbage shortly before his body was found. He described it as a reaction to a heated argument about the barbecue a few days earlier, calling it a petty move he regrets. Tran’s wife Isabelle Nguyen, 30, who was found guilty of accessory to murder and indignity to a human body, was sentenced to six years in prison. With time served, she will have five years and 4.5 months left to serve in prison.

title: Canada’s longest-serving mayor loses in Milton
author: Denio Lourenco
content: Canada’s longest-serving mayor has lost in his 15th reelection campaign on Monday after more than four decades in office. Gord Krantz has been the mayor of Milton, Ont. since 1980, serving 14 consecutive terms – longer than any other mayor in Canada.  Before he was elected to the town’s top job, Krantz served as a local councillor from 1965 to 1980. He surpassed Hazel McCallion, who was the mayor of Mississauga for 36 years. She was first elected in 1978 and went on to serve 12 consecutive terms before retiring in 2014 at 93 years old. He was ousted Monday by George Minakakis, who previously served as the Ward 1 councillor. Full election coverage is airing now on CityNews 24/7. Watch it here .

title: Girl, 8, seriously injured after being struck in North York collision
author: Joseph Ryan
content: An eight-year-old girl is in life-threatening condition after being struck by a vehicle in North York, police confirm. Investigators say the collision happened at the Willowdale Avenue and Elmwood Avenue intersection just after 3 p.m. According to paramedics, the girl was taken to The Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), with life threatening injuries. She was with an accompanying adult, a 70-year-old woman who was taken to Sunnybrook hospital with non-life threatening injuries. The driver remained at the scene, according to police. There’s no word on possible charges at this point.

title: At least 9 GTA cities elect new mayors
author: Meredith Bond
content: Night GTA cities have elected new mayors as the results of municipal elections are in across Ontario. Mississauga elected Alvin Tedjo , beating out incumbent Carolyn Parrish and Bonnie Crombie while the long-serving mayor was ousted in Milton. Tom Dingwall beat incumbent Adrian Foster in Clarington. Long-time Hamilton politican Andrea Horwath finished a distant third in her bid to be relected as Hamilton’s mayor. She lost to newcomer Keanin Loomis. In Oakville, Rob Burton failed to win his sixth reelection. He was defeated by Jeff Knoll, who has been on city council since 2000. Outgoing mayors in Ajax, Oshawa, Caledon and East Gwillimbury are not seeking re-election on Oct. 26, which meant all four cities are guaranteed to get new mayors Monday. Ajax has elected Marilyn Crawford to be their new mayor after Shaun Collier announced his plans not to seek re-election in May. In April, Caledon Mayor Annette Groves announced her retirement. In a video posted to social media, Groves said it was not an easy decision, but one made with “careful thought and a deep sense of gratitude.” Christina Early is currently in the lead to replace Groves as mayor. In Oshawa, incumbent Dan Carter had sworn off seeking a third term as mayor. Tito-Dante Marimpietri will be the new leader in the Durham Region city. East Gwillimbury Mayor Virginia Hackson has also decided to end her public service career after spending 16 years as mayor. Scott Crone will replace Hackson. title: Police locate vehicle in Scarborough parental abduction investigation
author: Patricia D'Cunha
content: Toronto police say they have located the vehicle in connection with a parental abduction investigation in Scarborough . Investigators received a call about three young children who were allegedly abducted just after 11:30 a.m. on Friday in the Midland Avenue and Eglinton Avenue East area. Police say the children – four-month-old Anastasia, three-year-old Irina, and six-year-old Daniel – were visiting a family member as part of a semi-supervised visit when they were taken by their mother, who does not have custody of the children. “The accused and children are still outstanding. The efforts to locate them remain ongoing,” police said in a update on Monday. Composite photo showing three children who police say were abducted from Scarborough on Oct. 23, 2026. TPS/handout Somerda Miclescu, 22, of Toronto is wanted for abduction by parent. She is described as five-feet seven, around 180 pounds, with long dark black hair. She was last seen wearing a long black skirt and a dark-coloured top. The owner of the vehicle was identified by police on Saturday as 25-year-old Ionut Stroe of Toronto. Stroe is considered a person of interest in the abduction investigation, and is also wanted for four counts of failing to comply with a release order for unrelated matters.
